knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probability-Simplex Representation of a Finite Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(X=[x_1\ \cdots\ x_m]\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), and define \(\Delta_m:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\lambda\geq0,\ \mathbf1^T\lambda=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generator lists in Euclidean space; repetitions and redundant generators are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite convex hull is
\[\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i:\lambda\in\Delta_m\right\}=X\Delta_m.\]
Consequently,
\[x\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\iff\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\ X\lambda=x,\ \mathbf1^T\lambda=1,\ \lambda\geq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) is the linear image \(X\Delta_m\) of the probability simplex. Thus membership is equivalent to feasibility of \(X\lambda=x\), \(\mathbf1^T\lambda=1\), and \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\iff\exists\lambda\in\Delta_m:\ X\lambda=x.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\{X\lambda:\lambda\in\Delta_m\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), \(x=\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\) with \(0\leq\lambda\leq1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite convex hull is a bounded polyhedron, hence a polytope.
boundary_notes: The coefficient vector need not be unique when the generators are affinely dependent.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the generators

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex representation of a finite convex hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(m\geq1\), and let \(M=[x_1\ \cdots\ x_m]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hulls of a prescribed finite list; redundant or repeated generators are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite hull representation of \(X\) is \[\operatorname{conv}X=\left\{M\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m_+,\ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\right\}=M\Delta_m.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{conv}X\) exactly when the linear system \[M\lambda=x,\qquad \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1,\qquad \lambda\geq0\] has a solution. Any feasible \(\lambda\) is a barycentric or convex-coordinate representation of \(x\) relative to the listed generators. Its support \(\{i:\lambda_i>0\}\) records the active generators, but neither the coefficients nor their support need be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many points collected as the columns of M, their convex hull is the image of the standard simplex under the map lambda to M lambda. A point x belongs to the hull exactly when there is a nonnegative coefficient vector lambda summing to one and satisfying M lambda=x. Such a coefficient vector gives convex coordinates; redundant generators can make this representation nonunique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\iff\exists\lambda\geq0:\ M\lambda=x,\ \mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}X=M\Delta_m\).
The finite hull is the affine image of the coefficient simplex under \(\lambda\mapsto M\lambda\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), the coefficient simplex yields the line segment between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).
If \(x_1,,x_m\) are affinely independent, every point of their affine hull has unique affine coordinates and every point of their convex hull has unique convex coordinates.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite convex-hull membership is a linear feasibility problem in the coefficient vector.
The hull of finitely many points is compact because it is the continuous image of the compact simplex \(\Delta_m\).
boundary_notes: Uniqueness fails when the generators are affinely dependent.
This representation does not say that all listed points are necessary; zero coefficients may remove generators.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the hull generators

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull and Closed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\neq\varnothing\) be a subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), equipped with its usual topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean closure; the distinction between algebraic convex hull and closed convex hull is explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The algebraic convex hull is
\[\operatorname{conv}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i:m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\right\}.\]
The closed convex hull is
\[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S:=\bigcap\{C\subseteq\mathbb R^n:C\text{ is closed and convex and }S\subseteq C\}.\]
These regimes are related by
\[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S).\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{conv}S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S,\]
with equality exactly when \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary convex hull of \(S\) consists of its finite convex combinations. The closed convex hull is the intersection of all closed convex sets containing \(S\). In Euclidean space it equals the closure of the ordinary convex hull. Thus the two regimes coincide precisely when the convex hull is already closed; otherwise the closed hull adds limit points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S),\qquad \operatorname{conv}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\iff\operatorname{conv}S\text{ is closed}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{cl}S)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{conv}S).\]
The closed convex hull is the unique smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) is compact in \(\mathbb R^n\), then \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact and hence \(\operatorname{conv}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\).
For a finite set \(S\), its convex hull is a compact polytope and is closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Both hull operations are monotone and idempotent.
Closing first does not change the closed convex hull, although it can change the ordinary convex hull.
boundary_notes: A closed but unbounded set can have a nonclosed convex hull, so closedness of \(S\) alone is insufficient.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the closure depends on the chosen topology; this record uses the Euclidean topology.

The closed convex hull is the intersection of all closed convex sets containing S, equivalently the Euclidean closure of the algebraic convex hull. They coincide precisely when the algebraic hull is closed. Compact generating sets have compact, hence closed, convex hulls, while closed unbounded sets can fail to have closed convex hulls.

equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).

If \(S\) is compact, \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is compact.

Limits of sequences of finite convex combinations belong to \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\), even when they do not belong to \(\operatorname{conv}S\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hull Operator Laws
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex hull is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, and its fixed points are exactly the convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(A,B\) of a real vector space \(X\), \[A\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(A),\qquad A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow\operatorname{conv}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(B),\qquad \operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{conv}(A))=\operatorname{conv}(A).\] Moreover, \(A\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{conv}(A)=A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(A\mapsto\operatorname{conv}(A)\) is a closure operator whose fixed points are precisely the convex subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are the algebraic closure-operator laws for convex generation; no topology is involved.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hulls of Arbitrary Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of an arbitrary set is the intersection of all convex sets containing it, equivalently the smallest convex set containing it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be an arbitrary subset of a real vector space \(X\). The convex hull of \(S\) is defined by \[\operatorname{conv}(S):=\bigcap\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is convex and }S\subseteq C\}.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is the unique smallest convex subset of \(X\) containing \(S\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(S\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex hull is \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\bigcap\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is convex and }S\subseteq C\},\] and is therefore the unique smallest convex subset of \(X\) containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic convex hull in an arbitrary real vector space, without taking a topological closure.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Convex-Hull Operator Laws
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex hull is an extensive, monotone, idempotent operator whose fixed points are the closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(S,T\) of a Hausdorff topological real vector space, \[S\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S),\qquad S\subseteq T\implies\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(T),\] and \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\bigr)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S).\] Moreover, \(S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\) exactly when \(S\) is closed and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(S,T\) are subsets of a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\) is a closure operator with fixed points equal to the closed convex subsets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These are the closure-operator properties of closed convex generation.

knowledge_statements.title: Net Representation of the Closed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the closed convex hull exactly when it is a limit of finite convex combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological real vector space and \(S\subseteq X\). A point \(x\in X\) belongs to \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\) if and only if there exists a net \((x_\alpha)\) in \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) converging to \(x\). Equivalently, every \(x_\alpha\) is a finite convex combination of points of \(S\). If \(X\) is first countable, the net may be replaced by a sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\iff\exists(x_\alpha)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(S):x_\alpha\to x.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequences suffice in first-countable spaces, including normed spaces; general topological vector spaces may require nets.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull is the smallest closed convex set containing the original set, and it equals the closure of the ordinary convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological real vector space and let \(S\subseteq X\). The closed convex hull of \(S\) is defined by \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S):=\bigcap\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is closed and convex and }S\subseteq C\}.\] Since the closure of a convex set in a topological vector space is convex, \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S)).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space and \(S\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed convex hull satisfies \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)=\bigcap\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is closed and convex and }S\subseteq C\}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S)).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness and closure refer to the given topology on the ambient vector space.

knowledge_statements.title: A Closed Planar Set with Nonclosed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed unbounded planar set can have a nonclosed convex hull: adjoining the origin to the epigraph of 1/x yields the open positive quadrant together with the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq x^{-1}\},\qquad S:=C\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \(S\) is closed, while \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(u,v):u>0,\ v>0\}.\] Consequently \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is not closed; for example, \((1,n^{-1})\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) converges to \((1,0)\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is closed but \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(0,0)\}\cup(0,\infty)^2\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite-dimensional example shows that closedness of an unbounded generating set does not ensure closedness of its convex hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Gap in Convex-Hull Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure gap occurs exactly when the ordinary convex hull is not closed and is strictly smaller than its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a subset \(S\) of a topological real vector space, a closure gap in convex-hull generation means \[\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq\overline{\operatorname{conv}(S)},\] equivalently that \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is not closed.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a subset of a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A closure gap occurs iff \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\neq\overline{\operatorname{conv}(S)}\), equivalently iff \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This defines the failure phenomenon owned by this leaf without duplicating the sibling definitions of ordinary and closed convex hulls.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Finite-Dimensional Generators Have No Closure Gap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, compact generating sets, including finite sets, have compact closed convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S\) is a compact subset of a finite-dimensional real topological vector space, then \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is compact and hence closed. Therefore \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(S)}.\] In particular, the convex hull of every finite set is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is compact and equals \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(S)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness eliminates the closure gap in finite-dimensional ambient spaces; the finite-dimensional hypothesis is essential to this formulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: This infinite-dimensional Hilbert-space example shows that finite convex-combination generation need not produce a closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\ell^2\) with its norm topology, let \((e_n)_{n\geq1}\) be its standard orthonormal basis, and set \(S:=\{e_n:n\geq1\}\). For \(N\geq1\), define \[x_N:=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N e_n.\] Then \(x_N\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) and \(\|x_N\|_2=N^{-1/2}\to0\), so \(0\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S))\). Every element of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is a finite nonnegative combination of the \(e_n\) whose coefficients sum to \(1\), so it is nonzero. Thus \[0\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{conv}(S)\neq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences, the convex hull of the standard unit vectors is not closed. Uniform averages of the first N unit vectors lie in the hull and converge to zero, but zero itself is not a finite convex combination of those vectors.

children.top_down_role: Dimension-sensitive finite-witness principles for convex and conic generation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty. Define \(\operatorname{cone}S\) as the set of finite nonnegative combinations of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional convex and conic representation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex Carathéodory witness for \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) is a representation
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i,\qquad 1\leq m\leq n+1,\quad x_i\in S,\quad \lambda_i\geq0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i=1.\]
For nonzero \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\), a conic Carathéodory witness is a representation
\[x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu_i x_i,\qquad 1\leq m\leq n,\quad x_i\in S,\quad \mu_i>0,\]
where the selected vectors may be chosen linearly independent. Carathéodory's theorem asserts that every point in the respective hull possesses such a witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) has a convex representation using at most \(n+1\) points of \(S\). Every nonzero point of \(\operatorname{cone}S\) has a positive representation using at most \(n\) linearly independent vectors of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{conv}S\Rightarrow m\leq n+1,\qquad 0\neq x\in\operatorname{cone}S\Rightarrow m\leq n.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{T\subseteq S\\1\leq |T|\leq n+1}}\operatorname{conv}T.\]
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex-hull and nonzero conic-hull membership in finite dimensions admit exact certificates whose support is bounded by dimension.
boundary_notes: The conic statement treats \(x=0\) separately; the zero vector is represented by the empty sum or by zero coefficients.
These are exact representation results, not approximation bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Carathéodory witness number and its principal regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. For \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\), a convex witness is a finite tuple \((x_i,\lambda_i)_{i=1}^m\) with \(x_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), and \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i x_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex and conic support bounds; the record defines the family of witness regimes rather than supplying a proof.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Carathéodory number of \(S\) is \[c(S):=\min\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}:\text{every }x\in\operatorname{conv}S\text{ has a convex witness using at most }k\text{ points of }S\right\}.\] The classical ambient-dimensional regime asserts \(c(S)\leq n+1\). If \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}S\), the intrinsic affine-dimensional regime asserts \(c(S)\leq d+1\). For conic generation, a conic witness for \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\) is \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i x_i\) with \(\mu_i\geq0\); the corresponding finite-dimensional regime permits at most \(n\) linearly independent active generators for nonzero \(x\). These are the principal convex, intrinsic, and homogeneous members of the Carathéodory family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex witness represents a hull point using finitely many generators and nonnegative coefficients summing to one. The Carathéodory number is the smallest uniform bound on the number of generators needed for all hull points. In n-dimensional space the classical bound is n+1; if the generating set has affine dimension d, the intrinsic bound is d+1. The conic analogue drops normalization and bounds a nonzero conic representation by n linearly independent generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family consists of the bounds \(c(S)\leq n+1\), \(c(S)\leq\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)+1\), and the conic bound of at most \(n\) linearly independent generators.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(c(S)\leq k\) iff every point of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) lies in the convex hull of some subset of \(S\) having at most \(k\) elements.
The intrinsic bound is the ambient theorem applied within the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}S\), whose dimension is \(d\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) lies on an affine line, then \(c(S)\leq2\).
If \(S\) is a singleton, then \(c(S)=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every convex-hull membership assertion in finite dimension has a uniformly sparse finite witness.
The supporting generators may depend on the represented point; the definition does not require one fixed generating subset for the whole hull.
boundary_notes: The coefficients and supporting points need not be unique.
For \(x=0\) in a conic hull, the empty or all-zero representation depends on convention; the stated conic independence form concerns nonzero \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Ambient-Dimension Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior point of a full-dimensional d-simplex needs all d+1 vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(d\geq0\), choose affinely independent \(v_0,\ldots,v_d\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_d\})\). No convex representation of \(x\) using these generators has fewer than \(d+1\) points. Hence the ambient Caratheodory bound \(d+1\) is best possible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{|I|:x\in\operatorname{conv}\{v_i:i\in I\}\}=d+1.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness is uniform over all generating subsets of the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Caratheodory Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the convex hull of a subset of d-dimensional Euclidean space is a convex combination of at most d+1 points from that subset.

If \(x\in \operatorname{conv}(S)\), then there exist an integer \(m\le d+1\), points \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S\), and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\ge 0\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-dimensional Carathéodory regime is the witness condition \[x\in\operatorname{conv}S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists m\leq d+1,\ \exists x_1,\ldots,x_m\in S,\ \exists\lambda_i\geq0:\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\quad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{\substack{F\subseteq S\\1\leq|F|\leq d+1}}\operatorname{conv}F.\] The dimension \(d\) is the dimension of the direction space parallel to \(\operatorname{aff}S\), so this formulation is invariant under affine embeddings and removes unused ambient coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the affine hull of S has dimension d, every point in the convex hull of S is a convex combination of at most d+1 points of S. Equivalently, the hull is the union of the hulls of all subsets of size at most d+1. This intrinsic form can be sharper than the ambient n+1 bound and is unchanged by placing the same affine geometry in a larger surrounding space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) has a convex witness supported on at most \(d+1\) points, where \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}S=\bigcup_{F\subseteq S,\ 1\leq|F|\leq d+1}\operatorname{conv}F\).
The bound is the ambient-dimensional Carathéodory bound computed in the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}S\).
special_cases_latex: For \(d=0\), \(S\) is contained in a singleton affine space and one generator suffices.
For \(d=1\), every hull point lies on a segment joining at most two points of \(S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Embedding \(S\) affinely into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space does not enlarge the intrinsic witness bound.
Any convex representation with more than \(d+1\) active generators can be replaced by a representation with at most \(d+1\) active generators.
boundary_notes: The number \(d+1\) is a universal upper bound and need not be the smallest possible bound for a particular set.
Affine dimension, not topological dimension of a nonconvex generating set, controls this regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Dependence-Elimination Algorithm
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear dependence determines a maximal coefficient step that preserves the represented vector and nonnegativity while deleting at least one generator; repetition produces independent support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\) with \(s_i\in S\) and \(\lambda_i>0\). If the active generators are linearly dependent, choose \(\beta\neq0\) with \(\sum_i\beta_i s_i=0\), changing its sign if necessary so that some \(\beta_i>0\). Set \[t=\min_{\beta_i>0}\frac{\lambda_i}{\beta_i},\qquad \lambda_i'=\lambda_i-t\beta_i.\] Delete generators whose updated coefficient is zero and repeat while the active generators remain dependent. Every update preserves \(x\) and coefficient nonnegativity and removes at least one active generator; the procedure terminates with linearly independent positive support.
assumptions_latex: The active generators \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) are linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each update preserves \(x\), keeps all coefficients nonnegative, removes at least one active generator, and finite repetition yields linearly independent positive support.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the constructive finite-support reduction underlying conic Caratheodory; it specifies the coefficient update without duplicating the theorem statement.

notation.meaning: A nonzero coefficient vector witnessing linear dependence among the active generators.
The maximal dependence step preserving coefficient nonnegativity.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Span-Dimension Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of the coordinate vectors requires all \(r\) coordinate rays, so the span-dimension bound is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r\ge1\), let \(S=\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^r\) and \(x=e_1+\cdots+e_r\). Then \(\dim(\operatorname{span}S)=r\), and every representation \(x=\sum_{s\in S}\mu_s s\) with \(\mu_s\ge0\) has \(\mu_{e_i}=1\) for every \(i\). Thus every such representation has support size exactly \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every conic representation of \(x\) using generators from \(S\) has support size \(r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The coordinate-ray family establishes that the intrinsic generator bound is sharp.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Caratheodory Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic Carathéodory theorem with an ambient-dimension support bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d\in\mathbb N_0\), let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and suppose \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\). If \(x\ne0\), then there exist an integer \(m\) with \(1\le m\le d\), linearly independent points \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S\), and coefficients \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m>0\) such that
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mu_i s_i.
\]
If \(x=0\), the empty conic combination is a representation with support size zero. Thus every element of \(\operatorname{cone}S\) has a conic representation using at most \(d\) linearly independent generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonzero point in a conic hull in Rᵈ can be generated by at most d linearly independent points with positive coefficients; zero has the empty representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) has a conic representation supported on at most \(d\) linearly independent elements of \(S\), with the empty representation used when \(x=0\).

notation.meaning: set of finite nonnegative linear combinations from S, including the empty combination for zero
positive conic coefficients in the nonzero case

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\setminus\{0\}\), where \(\operatorname{cone}S\) consists of finite nonnegative combinations of elements of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonzero conic representations; coefficients are nonnegative and are not normalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic Carathéodory regime is the witness condition \[x\in\operatorname{cone}S\setminus\{0\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists m\leq n,\ \exists s_1,\ldots,s_m\in S,\ \exists\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_m>0:\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m\mu_i s_i,\] where the active generators \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) may be chosen linearly independent. More intrinsically, if \(r=\dim\operatorname{span}S\), then \(m\leq r\). Thus conic normalization removes the additional affine coordinate responsible for the \(n+1\) convex-hull bound: a nonzero conic point needs at most the dimension of the relevant linear span many active rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonzero point in the conic hull of a subset of R^n can be expressed as a positive combination of at most n generators from the set, and the active generators can be chosen linearly independent. If the generators span only an r-dimensional linear subspace, at most r are needed. Unlike a convex combination, the conic coefficients are not required to sum to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonzero \(x\in\operatorname{cone}S\) has a positive representation using at most \(\dim\operatorname{span}S\leq n\) linearly independent generators from \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}S=\bigcup\{\operatorname{cone}F:F\subseteq S,\ F\text{ linearly independent}\}\), with the origin included by convention.
Any conic representation with linearly dependent active generators can be replaced by one with fewer active generators.
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), every nonzero conic-hull point needs at most two linearly independent generators.
If \(S\) lies in a one-dimensional subspace, every nonzero conic-hull point uses one active generator whenever it is representable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonzero conic-hull membership has a certificate supported on at most \(n\) generators.
The selected positive generators determine a simplicial cone containing the represented point.
boundary_notes: The zero vector may be represented by all-zero coefficients; requiring strictly positive coefficients is therefore restricted to nonzero points.
The conic hull need not be closed, even when the generating set is compact.

knowledge_statements.title: Verification Cost of a Sparse Hull Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse convex-combination certificate is verifiable in time linear in dimension times support size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and suppose a certificate lists indices \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and coefficients \((\lambda_i)_{i\in I}\). The conditions \(\lambda_i\geq0\), \(\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i=1\), and \(x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i s_i\) can be verified in \(O(d|I|)\) arithmetic operations. If \(|I|\leq r+1\leq d+1\), the cost is \(O(d(r+1))\), hence at most \(O(d^2)\).
assumptions_latex: The points, target, indices, and coefficients use an exact-arithmetic representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{verify}}=O(d|I|)=O(d(r+1))\subseteq O(d^2).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This counts exact real-arithmetic operations; bit complexity depends additionally on numeric encoding.

notation.meaning: Support of the sparse coefficient vector

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Hull-Membership Witnesses
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite generating set, convex-hull membership is certified by nonnegative coefficients that sum to one, reproduce the point, and have at most r+1 positive entries, where r is the affine dimension of the generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, let \(r=\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)\), and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Then \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for every \(i\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\), \(x=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i s_i\), and \(|\{i:\lambda_i>0\}|\le r+1\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_n\}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, let \(r=\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)\), and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) holds if and only if there is a vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for every \(i\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\), \(x=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i s_i\), and \(|\{i:\lambda_i>0\}|\le r+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The displayed coefficients form a directly checkable convex-hull membership certificate whose support obeys the affine-dimension Caratheodory bound.

notation.meaning: effective affine dimension of the finite generating set

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). A finite family may repeat points, although zero coefficients and repetitions may always be removed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean convex hulls; the bound used here is the ambient-dimension bound \(n+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sparse hull-membership witness for \(x\in\operatorname{conv}X\) is a tuple \(W=((x_i)_{i=1}^m,(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^m)\) such that \[1\le m\le n+1,\qquad x_i\in X,\qquad \lambda_i>0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\qquad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i.\] Its support is \(\operatorname{supp}W=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\), and its support size is \(m\). Thus the witness is an explicitly checkable certificate consisting of at most \(n+1\) generating points and their convex weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a sparse witness certifying that \(x\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}X\) consists of at most \(n+1\) points of \(X\) and positive coefficients summing to one whose weighted sum is \(x\). The number of positive coefficients is the witness support size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[W=((x_i)_{i=1}^m,(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^m),\quad m\le n+1,\quad x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i,\quad \lambda_i>0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: After removing zero coefficients, the certificate is equivalently a finitely supported probability vector \(\lambda:X\to[0,1]\) satisfying \(|\operatorname{supp}\lambda|\le n+1\) and \(x=\sum_{u\in X}\lambda(u)u\).
The lifted vectors \((x_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}\) may be chosen linearly independent; consequently, the selected points are affinely independent.
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), every hull point has a witness supported on at most two points.
If \(x\in X\), the singleton witness \(m=1\), \(x_1=x\), and \(\lambda_1=1\) is valid.
immediate_consequences_latex: Hull membership in \(\mathbb R^n\) always has a certificate whose support cardinality is bounded independently of the cardinality of \(X\).
boundary_notes: The definition is finite-dimensional; no uniform finite support bound follows in a general infinite-dimensional space.
The sharper affine-dimension bound is a neighboring regime and is not asserted as the defining bound in this record.
The representation need not be unique.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topology Relative to the Affine Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, put \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\), and equip \(A\) with the subspace topology inherited from \(\mathbb R^n\). Let \(B(x,r)=\{y:\|y-x\|<r\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative topology in the effective affine ambient space \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative topology of \(C\) is the topology induced on \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\). Its intrinsic topological objects are \[\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\exists r>0,\ B(x,r)\cap A\subseteq C\},\] \[\operatorname{cl}_A C=\{x\in A:\forall r>0,\ B(x,r)\cap C\ne\varnothing\},\qquad \operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}_A C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] A set \(U\subseteq A\) is relatively open when \(U=A\cap O\) for some open \(O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relevant ambient space for a nonempty convex set \(C\) is its affine hull \(A\). Relative interior, closure, and boundary are respectively the interior, closure, and boundary computed in the subspace topology of \(A\). A relative neighborhood of \(x\) is obtained by intersecting an ordinary open ball about \(x\) with \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}_A C,\qquad \operatorname{cl}_A C=\overline C^{\,A},\qquad \operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}_A C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) if and only if \(x\in C\) and some neighborhood of \(x\) in \(A\) is contained in \(C\).
Because \(A\) is closed in finite dimensions and contains \(C\), the relative closure \(\operatorname{cl}_A C\) equals the ordinary Euclidean closure \(\operatorname{cl}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=A\) is affine, then \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\) and \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\varnothing\).
If \(C\) is a nondegenerate line segment, its relative interior is the open segment and its relative boundary consists of its endpoints.
immediate_consequences_latex: Relative topological notions do not become degenerate merely because \(C\) lies in a proper affine subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\).
boundary_notes: Ambient interior and ambient boundary are different objects when \(A\ne\mathbb R^n\).
The finite-dimensional equality between relative and ambient closures can fail in nonclosed affine subspaces of more general topological vector spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set, let \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\), and let \(L=A-A\) be the linear space parallel to \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, including lower-dimensional and nonclosed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative interior of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ x+(B(0,\varepsilon)\cap L)\subseteq C\}.\] Thus \(x\) is a relative interior point precisely when \(C\) contains an open neighborhood of \(x\) in its own affine hull. The relative dimension of \(C\) is \(\dim C=\dim A=\dim L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point \(x\) lies in the relative interior of a nonempty convex set \(C\) when a sufficiently small ball around \(x\), restricted to directions parallel to the affine hull of \(C\), remains inside \(C\). This definition measures interior intrinsically and therefore remains meaningful for lower-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff x\in C\ \text{and}\ \exists\varepsilon>0:\ x+(B(0,\varepsilon)\cap L)\subseteq C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is the ordinary interior of \(C\) in the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
Using any norm on \(\mathbb R^n\) gives the same relative interior because all finite-dimensional norms induce the same topology.
special_cases_latex: For a singleton \(C=\{x\}\), one has \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\).
For an affine set \(C\), one has \(\operatorname{ri}C=C\).
For a nonempty full-dimensional convex set, \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The set \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is nonempty and convex, and \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{aff}C\).
boundary_notes: Convexity is not needed to write the subspace-interior definition, but it is essential for the listed structural consequences.
Relative interior does not require \(C\) to be closed.
Ambient interior may be empty even when relative interior is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic Intrinsic Interior and Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. The definition uses only segments inside \(C\), while the equivalent relative-interior formulation uses the topology of \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine geometry; the stated equivalence is for nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the intrinsic algebraic interior of \(C\) by \[\operatorname{aint}C=\{x\in C:\forall y\in C\ \exists\gamma>0\text{ such that }x+\gamma(x-y)\in C\}.\] A point in \(\operatorname{aint}C\) is therefore an endpoint from which every segment \([y,x]\subseteq C\) can be prolonged a positive distance beyond \(x\) without leaving \(C\). In finite-dimensional convex geometry, \[\operatorname{aint}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic algebraic interior consists of those points \(x\in C\) for which every segment joining another point \(y\in C\) to \(x\) can be extended beyond \(x\) while staying in \(C\). For a nonempty convex subset of finite-dimensional space, this segment-based notion is exactly the relative interior.
assumptions_latex: All quantifiers over directions are restricted to the effective affine space of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{ri}C\iff \forall y\in C\ \exists\gamma>0:\ x+\gamma(x-y)\in C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(z=x+\gamma(x-y)\), the condition says that \(x\) lies in the open segment \((y,z)\) for some \(z\in C\), for every \(y\in C\).
The same points are characterized by the existence of an affine-hull neighborhood \(B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}C\subseteq C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is affine, every point satisfies the prolongation condition.
If \(C=[a,b]\) with \(a\ne b\), exactly the points of \((a,b)\) satisfy it.
immediate_consequences_latex: The intrinsic-interior notion is affine invariant: for an affine bijection \(T\), \(T(\operatorname{aint}C)=\operatorname{aint}(T(C))\).
boundary_notes: The parameter \(\gamma\) may depend on \(y\); no uniform positive prolongation length is required.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, algebraic interior and topological relative interior need not coincide.
Convexity is part of the equivalence.

notation.meaning: intrinsic algebraic interior defined by segment prolongation

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Segment Absorption
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A half-open segment from a relative-interior point toward a closure point remains in the relative interior. Consequently, the relative interior of a convex set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) and \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\), then \[(1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\qquad(0\le t<1).\] In particular, \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\) for every \(0\le t<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The endpoint may lie only in the closure and need not belong to C; no assertion is made at \(t=1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a nonempty set consists of the points having an open neighborhood, measured within the set's affine hull, that is contained in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional normed real vector space \(E\), and set \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\). The relative interior of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B_E(x,\varepsilon)\cap A\subseteq C\}\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional normed real vector space \(E\), and set \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative interior of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B_E(x,\varepsilon)\cap A\subseteq C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition uses the topology induced on the affine hull of the set. In finite dimensions it is independent of the chosen norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Invariance of the Algebraic Core
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine change of coordinates maps the intrinsic algebraic core exactly onto the intrinsic algebraic core of the image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\operatorname{aff}C\to A'\) be an affine bijection. Then \[T\!\left(\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\right)=\operatorname{core}_{A'}T(C).\] Thus intrinsic-core membership is independent of affine coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a real vector space.
\(T:\operatorname{aff}C\to A'\) is an affine bijection onto an affine space \(A'\).
The cores are computed intrinsically in their respective affine hulls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C)=\operatorname{core}_{A'}T(C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bijectivity on the affine hull is essential for the stated equality.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic-Core Segment Absorption
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moving from an intrinsic-core point toward any point of a convex set stays in the core until the possible endpoint; hence the intrinsic core is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\) and \(y\in C\), then \[(1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\qquad(0\le t<1).\] Consequently, the intrinsic algebraic core of a convex set is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
The core is computed relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\) for every \(0\le t<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is purely algebraic and requires no topology or finite-dimensional assumption. The endpoint need not be a core point.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional and Radial Characterizations of the Intrinsic Core
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is in the intrinsic algebraic core exactly when the radial cone there is the full direction space, equivalently when every chord to the point can be extended beyond it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be nonempty and convex, let \(L=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\), and let \(x\in C\). Then \[x\in\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{cone}(C-x)=L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \forall y\in C\ \exists\varepsilon>0:\ x+\varepsilon(x-y)\in C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space.
The core is computed intrinsically in \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=L\Longleftrightarrow\forall y\in C\ \exists\varepsilon>0:\ x+\varepsilon(x-y)\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These equivalences are purely algebraic. Convexity converts the two-sided directional definition into the cone and chord-extension forms.

notation.meaning: direction space parallel to the affine hull of C

assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real vector space and let \(L=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intrinsic algebraic core of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C=\{x\in C:\forall v\in L\ \exists\varepsilon_v>0\ \forall t\in(-\varepsilon_v,\varepsilon_v),\ x+tv\in C\}\).

notation.meaning: direction space parallel to the affine hull of C
algebraic core computed intrinsically in the affine hull of C

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real vector space and let \(L=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\). Its intrinsic algebraic core is \(\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C=\{x\in C:\forall v\in L\ \exists\varepsilon_v>0\ \forall t\in(-\varepsilon_v,\varepsilon_v),\ x+tv\in C\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Failure of Intrinsic Interior Equivalence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A halfspace defined by a discontinuous linear functional has nonempty algebraic core but empty relative interior, so the finite-dimensional equivalence can fail in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an infinite-dimensional normed real vector space admitting a discontinuous linear functional \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and set \(C=\{x\in X:f(x)\le 1\}\). Then \(C\) is convex, \(\operatorname{aff}C=X\), and
\[
\operatorname{core}C=\{x\in X:f(x)<1\}\ne\varnothing,
\qquad
\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an infinite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{core}C=\{x:f(x)<1\}\ne\varnothing\), whereas \(\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The example uses a discontinuous algebraic linear functional. It shows that finite dimensionality is essential in general normed spaces.

notation.meaning: algebraic core of C in X
relative interior of C; here the affine hull is X

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Equivalence Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nonempty convex set in finite dimensions, relative interior equals the algebraic core computed within the affine hull, and this common set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, then \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative interior and the intrinsic algebraic core coincide: \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\). In particular, both sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equivalence is restricted to nonempty convex sets in finite-dimensional spaces and uses the algebraic core relative to the affine hull, not the ambient algebraic core.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Boundary Partition and Degenerate Case
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set's closure is the disjoint union of its relative interior and relative boundary, and the relative boundary is empty exactly for affine sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Then \(\operatorname{rbd}C\) is closed relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\), and \[\operatorname{cl}C=\operatorname{ri}C\,\dot\cup\,\operatorname{rbd}C.\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\varnothing\) if and only if \(C=\operatorname{aff}C\), equivalently, \(C\) is an affine set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}C=\operatorname{ri}C\dot\cup\operatorname{rbd}C\), and \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\varnothing\iff C=\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic intrinsic-topological structure of the relative boundary for a convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative boundary is the relative closure of a set minus its relative interior, with both topological operations performed inside the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional normed real vector space and set \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\). The relative boundary of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}_{A}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\), where \(\operatorname{cl}_{A}C\) denotes closure in the topology induced on \(A\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional normed real vector space and set \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative boundary of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}_{A}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C\), where \(\operatorname{cl}_{A}C\) is closure in the topology induced on \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Both closure and interior are taken in the affine hull. Because affine subspaces are closed in finite dimensions, the relative closure also equals the ambient closure of \(C\).

notation.meaning: closure of C in its affine hull A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial Access from a Relative-Interior Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, choose \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and let \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets; the target may be a missing limit point of a nonclosed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\) is radially accessible from \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) when every point before \(y\) on the segment from \(x\) to \(y\) remains in the relative interior: \[x_t=(1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\qquad(0\le t<1).\] The radial-access set from \(x\) is \[\operatorname{Rad}_C(x)=\{y\in\operatorname{cl}C:\forall t\in[0,1),\ (1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\}.\] For a nonempty convex \(C\), every closure point is accessible, so \(\operatorname{Rad}_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix a relative-interior point \(x\) of a convex set \(C\). A closure point \(y\) is radially accessible from \(x\) if the half-open segment from \(x\) to \(y\) is contained in the relative interior of \(C\). Convexity implies that every point of the closure is accessible in this sense, even when the endpoint itself is absent from \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall t\in[0,1),\quad (1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C,\qquad \operatorname{Rad}_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), the point \(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
The half-open segment \([x,y)\) is contained in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(y\in C\), accessibility holds along an ordinary segment contained in \(C\).
If \(y\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\), every point before the missing endpoint still lies in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every closure point is the limit of a one-dimensional path lying entirely in \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
Consequently, \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C\).
boundary_notes: No assertion is made that the endpoint \(y\) itself belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\) or even to \(C\).
The starting point must lie in the relative interior; an arbitrary boundary starting point need not provide this access.

notation.meaning: point at parameter t on the segment from x to y
closure points radially accessible from x

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Reachability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to any fixed relative-interior point x, a point y of C is itself relatively interior exactly when the ray from x through y can be extended beyond y while remaining in C.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space and fix \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\). For \(y\in C\), one has \(y\in\operatorname{ri}C\) if and only if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(y+\varepsilon(y-x)\in C\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, fix \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and let \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The point \(y\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\) if and only if there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(y+\varepsilon(y-x)\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This characterizes relative-interior points by extendability of the ray from one fixed relative-interior base point beyond the candidate point.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Accessibility Limits
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-boundary point is approached by relative-interior points along every segment from a relative-interior base point, but the ray through that boundary point cannot be extended farther while staying in the convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space. If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) and \(y\in\operatorname{rbd}C\), then \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\) for every \(t\in[0,1)\), and \(\lim_{t\uparrow1}((1-t)x+ty)=y\). Furthermore, \(y+\varepsilon(y-x)\notin C\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
assumptions_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, let \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and let \(y\in\operatorname{rbd}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\in[0,1)\), one has \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and \(\lim_{t\uparrow1}((1-t)x+ty)=y\); moreover, \(y+\varepsilon(y-x)\notin C\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The statement distinguishes approach to a relative-boundary point from radial extension beyond it: the open segment is relatively interior, but the ray cannot remain in the set past the boundary point.

children.title: Ambient-Relative Interior Regimes
children.top_down_role: Comparison between ambient and relative interior.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. Ambient interior is computed in \(\mathbb R^n\), whereas relative interior is computed in \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ambient-relative interior regime of \(C\) is determined by \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)\). It is full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n\), and lower-dimensional when \(\operatorname{aff}C\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\). Precisely, \[\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing\iff\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n,\] and in the full-dimensional regime \[\operatorname{int}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\] In the lower-dimensional regime, \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\), while \(\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set is in the full-dimensional regime when its affine hull is all of the ambient space. Exactly in that regime its ambient interior is nonempty and equals its relative interior. If the affine hull is proper, the ambient interior is empty, but the relative interior remains nonempty because it is measured inside the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n\iff\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb R^n\Rightarrow\operatorname{int}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The full-dimensional regime is equivalently \(\dim C=n\).
The lower-dimensional regime is equivalently \(\dim C<n\), in which case every point of \(C\) is an ambient boundary point.
special_cases_latex: A line segment in \(\mathbb R^2\) has empty ambient interior but a nonempty relative interior.
An affine space \(A\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(\operatorname{ri}A=A\) and \(\operatorname{int}A=\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For lower-dimensional convex sets, statements requiring an interior point must be formulated with \(\operatorname{ri}C\), not \(\operatorname{int}C\).
boundary_notes: Nonemptiness is essential: conventions for the affine hull and relative interior of the empty set vary.
The equivalence uses convexity for the implication from full affine hull to nonempty interior.

notation.meaning: interior relative to the affine hull

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Dimensional Interior Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex subset of Euclidean space is full-dimensional exactly when it has nonempty ambient interior; in that regime its relative interior equals its ordinary interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and convex. Then \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}^d\) if and only if \(\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing\). Under these equivalent conditions, \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The following are equivalent: \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}^d\); \(\operatorname{int}C\ne\varnothing\). Whenever these conditions hold, \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional Euclidean regime in which the affine hull is the entire ambient space, so relative and ambient topology agree on the set.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Essential for Nonempty Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct points in the plane form a nonempty lower-dimensional set with empty relative interior, showing that convexity is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(-1,0),(1,0)\}\subset\mathbb{R}^2\). Then \(C\) is nonempty and \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\), so \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)=1<2\), while \(\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\). Thus convexity cannot be omitted from the lower-dimensional nonempty-relative-interior assertion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)=1<2\), but \(\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite example isolates the necessity of convexity in the assertion that every nonempty lower-dimensional convex set has nonempty relative interior.

notation.meaning: interior relative to the affine hull of C

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Interior Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty lower-dimensional convex set has empty ambient interior but nonempty relative interior in its affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex set. If \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)<n\), then \[\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing.\] Thus the intrinsic interior is taken in \(\operatorname{aff}C\), where it is nonempty, even though no ambient open ball lies in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean regime; nonemptiness is essential for the asserted nonempty relative interior.

notation.meaning: Interior in the ambient Euclidean space

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Essential for the Affine-Hull Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit circle spans the plane affinely but has empty ambient interior, showing that convexity is essential to the affine-hull criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\|x\|_2=1\}\). Then \(C\) is nonempty and \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}^2\), but \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\). Hence the equivalence \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\iff\operatorname{aff}C\ne\mathbb{R}^2\) fails if convexity is omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}^2\) while \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The unit circle shows that full affine hull need not yield nonempty ambient interior for a nonconvex set, so convexity is essential in the seeded equivalence.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Interior Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set has empty ambient interior exactly when its affine hull is a proper affine subspace of the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{aff}C\neq\mathbb{R}^n.\] Equivalently, \(C\) has nonempty ambient interior exactly when it is full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\iff\operatorname{aff}C\neq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This gives the exact finite-dimensional boundary between empty and nonempty ambient interior for a nonempty convex set.

children.title: Relative-Interior Calculus
children.top_down_role: Behavior of intrinsic interiors under basic convex-set constructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be an operation taking one or more nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces to a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-set operations; qualifications are part of compatibility where required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operation \(\Phi\) is relative-interior compatible on inputs \((C_1,\ldots,C_m)\) when \[\operatorname{ri}\Phi(C_1,\ldots,C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{ri}C_1,\ldots,\operatorname{ri}C_m),\] with the right side interpreted using the same set operation. Cartesian products, Minkowski sums, and affine images are compatible without a constraint qualification. Finite intersections are compatible under \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing\); affine preimages are compatible when the preimage meets the target relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior calculus records when taking relative interiors commutes with a convex-set construction. Products, sums, and affine images commute unconditionally. Intersections and affine preimages require a nonempty relative-interior feasibility condition. The qualification is part of the operation's declared domain of compatibility.
assumptions_latex: All participating sets are nonempty and convex in finite-dimensional spaces.
Any intersection or affine-preimage identity is invoked only under its stated relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{ri}\Phi(C_1,\ldots,C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{ri}C_1,\ldots,\operatorname{ri}C_m)\] for each operation on its qualified domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Compatibility means that intrinsic neighborhoods are transported exactly by the set operation, rather than yielding merely one-sided inclusion.
For an affine map \(T\), image compatibility reads \(T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C))\).
special_cases_latex: For products, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1\times C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1\times\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
For sums, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1+\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A compound construction may be evaluated by propagating relative interiors through successive compatible operations while retaining every necessary qualification.
boundary_notes: Closure does not share all of these unconditional commutation properties.
Without a common relative-interior point, the intersection identity can fail.
The definition concerns exact equality, not merely inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without a Common Relative-Interior Point
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposite closed halfplanes have disjoint relative interiors, while their intersection is a line with nonempty relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\ge0\}\) and \(C_2=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\le0\}\). Then \(\operatorname{ri}C_1=\{y>0\}\), \(\operatorname{ri}C_2=\{y<0\}\), and \(C_1\cap C_2=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\). Therefore \[\operatorname{ri}(C_1\cap C_2)=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\ne\varnothing=\operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are the upper and lower closed halfplanes in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1\cap C_2)\ne\operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that the standard compatibility condition cannot simply be omitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interiors of Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a positive finite family of convex sets has a common relative-interior point, the relative interior of its intersection equals the intersection of the sets' relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive, and let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty convex sets satisfying \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\neq\varnothing\). Then \[\operatorname{ri}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersection rule under the standard relative-interior compatibility condition.

notation.meaning: A positive finite number of sets

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.1, The Relative Interior, p. 102

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets, where \(m\ge1\), and put \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections of finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \((C_i)_{i=1}^m\) is relative-interior regular when \[\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing.\] For such a family, the intersection calculus is exact: \[\operatorname{ri}\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{cl}\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{cl}C_i.\] Relative-interior regularity is therefore a geometric constraint qualification for commuting both intrinsic interior and closure with intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family of convex sets is relative-interior regular when all sets share a point that lies in each of their relative interiors. Under this qualification, the relative interior of the intersection is the intersection of the relative interiors, and closure also commutes with the intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{ri}(\bigcap_i C_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\bigcap_i C_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{cl}C_i.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Regularity means that there exists \(\bar x\) and radii \(r_i>0\) such that \(B(\bar x,r_i)\cap\operatorname{aff}C_i\subseteq C_i\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=1\), regularity is automatic because a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set has nonempty relative interior.
For two sets, the qualification is \(\operatorname{ri}C_1\cap\operatorname{ri}C_2\ne\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The qualified intersection is nonempty, and its relative interior contains every common relative-interior point.
boundary_notes: Without the qualification, equality may fail even when the intersection is nonempty; for example, opposite closed half-lines can meet at one point while their relative interiors are disjoint.
For arbitrary infinite families, finite-family induction does not establish the same identities.

children.title: Product-Sum Relative-Interior Calculus
children.top_down_role: Intrinsic-interior behavior under product and additive constructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) be nonempty convex sets. When forming a Minkowski sum, assume all summands lie in a common vector space \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite products and finite Minkowski sums in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Cartesian product and Minkowski sum are \[\prod_{i=1}^m C_i=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m):x_i\in C_i\},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m C_i=\{x_1+\cdots+x_m:x_i\in C_i\}.\] Their relative-interior calculus is \[\operatorname{ri}\left(\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{ri}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i.\] No common-interior qualification is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a finite Cartesian product is the product of the relative interiors. For convex sets in a common vector space, the relative interior of their Minkowski sum is the sum of their relative interiors. Both identities hold without an intersection-type constraint qualification.
assumptions_latex: For the sum identity, \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) for all \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{ri}(\prod_i C_i)=\prod_i\operatorname{ri}C_i,\qquad \operatorname{ri}(\sum_i C_i)=\sum_i\operatorname{ri}C_i.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The sum identity is the affine-image rule applied to the addition map \(A(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_i x_i\) on \(\prod_i C_i\).
special_cases_latex: For two sets, \(\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{ri}C_1+\operatorname{ri}C_2\).
For a scalar \(\alpha>0\), \(\operatorname{ri}(\alpha C)=\alpha\operatorname{ri}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A vector \(z\in\operatorname{ri}(C_1+C_2)\) admits a decomposition \(z=x_1+x_2\) with \(x_i\in\operatorname{ri}C_i\).
boundary_notes: For multiplication by \(\alpha=0\), the image is the singleton \(\{0\}\), whose relative interior is itself.
Analogous closure equality for sums can fail when both summands are unbounded, even if they are closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Product Formula Without Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior commutes with every nonempty finite Cartesian product, even for nonconvex factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) be nonempty for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Then \[\operatorname{aff}\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^m S_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{aff}S_i,\qquad \operatorname{ri}\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^m S_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}S_i.\] No convexity assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(\prod_{i=1}^m S_i)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}S_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite topological-product formulation; convexity is unnecessary for the identity.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interiors of Cartesian Products
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a Cartesian product of nonempty convex sets is the Cartesian product of their relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty convex sets \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), \[\operatorname{ri}(C\times D)=\operatorname{ri}C\times\operatorname{ri}D.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(C\times D)=\operatorname{ri}C\times\operatorname{ri}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The product is regarded as a subset of the product Euclidean space.

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.1, The Relative Interior, p. 102

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Essential for Minkowski-Sum Equality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity, a Minkowski sum can acquire interior even though one summand has empty relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{0,1\}\) and \(D=[0,1]\) in \(\mathbb{R}\). Then \(\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\), whereas \(C+D=[0,2]\). Hence \[\operatorname{ri}(C+D)=(0,2)\ne\varnothing=\operatorname{ri}C+\operatorname{ri}D.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(C+D)\ne\operatorname{ri}C+\operatorname{ri}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional failure when a summand is nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Minkowski-Sum Relative Interiors
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of a finite Minkowski sum of nonempty convex sets is the sum of their relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(m\ge1\) and \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are nonempty convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \[\operatorname{ri}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i)=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the binary sum formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interiors of Minkowski Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of the Minkowski sum of two nonempty convex sets equals the Minkowski sum of their relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty convex sets \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(C+D=\{c+d:c\in C,\ d\in D\}\). Then \[\operatorname{ri}(C+D)=\operatorname{ri}C+\operatorname{ri}D.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(C+D)=\operatorname{ri}C+\operatorname{ri}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Minkowski-sum calculus for nonempty convex sets.

source_witnesses.locator: III.2.1, The Relative Interior, p. 102

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Product or Sum Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With relative interior of the empty set defined as empty, empty factors or summands give empty results, while singleton factors and summands preserve the usual product and translation formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt \(\operatorname{ri}\varnothing=\varnothing\). Products and Minkowski sums involving an empty set are empty. For every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and every \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{ri}(C\times\{d\})=\operatorname{ri}C\times\{d\},\qquad \operatorname{ri}(C+\{a\})=\operatorname{ri}C+\{a\}.\] Hence zero-dimensional factors and summands do not invalidate the relative-interior formulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(C\times\{d\})=\operatorname{ri}C\times\{d\}\) and \(\operatorname{ri}(C+\{a\})=\operatorname{ri}C+\{a\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the empty-set and singleton degeneracies of product and sum calculus.

notation.meaning: Relative interior, with the empty-set convention
