children.title: Relative Interiors Under Affine Maps
children.top_down_role: Transport of intrinsic interiors through affine images and preimages.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Preimage Formula Can Fail Without Range Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an affine range is tangent to a convex set and misses its relative interior, the relative-interior preimage identity can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2\) by \(T(t)=(t,0)\), and let \(D=\{(x,y):y\ge x^2\}\). Then \(D\) is closed and convex, \(\operatorname{ri}D=\{(x,y):y>x^2\}\), and \(T^{-1}(D)=\{0\}\). Thus \[\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}D)=\{0\}\ne\varnothing=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}D)\ne T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional failure when the affine range only touches the target boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interiors Under Affine Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine images carry the relative interior of a nonempty convex set onto the relative interior of its image. An affine preimage has the analogous formula when the affine range meets the target's relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be affine, with \(T(x)=Ax+b\). For every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C)).\] If \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is nonempty and convex and \(T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D)\neq\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C))\) and \(\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D)\) under the stated preimage qualification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The image identity is unconditional for a nonempty convex set; the preimage identity requires the affine range to meet the relative interior of the target set.

notation.meaning: Affine mapping with linear part A and translation b

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Image and Qualified Preimage Calculus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine, \(T(x)=Ax+b\). Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine images and preimages; preimages require relative-interior feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Affine images transport relative interiors exactly: \[T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C)).\] For a target set \(D\), define \(T^{-1}(D)=\{x:T(x)\in D\}\). If \[T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D)\ne\varnothing,\] then the affine preimage is relative-interior regular and \[\operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D),\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T^{-1}(D))=T^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine map sends the relative interior of a nonempty convex set onto the relative interior of its image. A preimage obeys the corresponding relative-interior and closure identities provided at least one point maps into the relative interior of the target set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(T(C)),\quad \operatorname{ri}(T^{-1}D)=T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}D),\quad \operatorname{cl}(T^{-1}D)=T^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}D).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The preimage qualification says \(T(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{ri}D\ne\varnothing\).
Translations do not affect the rule, so the linear-map statements apply to affine maps after translating the image.
special_cases_latex: If \(T\) is an affine bijection, both image and preimage formulas hold without an additional qualification.
Coordinate projection satisfies the unconditional image formula.
immediate_consequences_latex: Relative interior is invariant under invertible affine changes of coordinates.
Minkowski-sum calculus follows by applying the image formula to the addition map.
boundary_notes: The image \(T(C)\) need not be closed when \(C\) is closed and unbounded.
Without preimage feasibility in \(\operatorname{ri}D\), the preimage relative-interior equality can fail.
The notation \(T^{-1}(D)\) denotes set preimage, not an inverse affine map.

children.title: Closure Geometry
children.top_down_role: Topological completion of convex sets and its relationship with intrinsic interiors.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, with the Euclidean topology on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, possibly nonclosed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closure of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{cl}C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\forall\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap C\ne\varnothing\}.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\) exactly when there is a sequence \((x_k)\subseteq C\) with \(x_k\to x\). For convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{cl}C\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(C\), and \[\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{aff}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of \(C\) consists of all points whose every neighborhood meets \(C\), equivalently all limits of sequences from \(C\). If \(C\) is convex, its closure remains convex and is the smallest closed convex superset of \(C\). Closing a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set does not change its affine hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{cl}C=\{\lim_{k\to\infty}x_k:(x_k)\subseteq C\},\qquad \operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{aff}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}C\) is the intersection of all closed subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\) containing \(C\).
Because closure preserves convexity, it is also the intersection of all closed convex sets containing \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{cl}C=C\).
For an open segment \((a,b)\), \(\operatorname{cl}C=[a,b]\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point missing solely because of nonclosedness belongs to \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\).
The relative topology of \(C\) and \(\operatorname{cl}C\) uses the same affine ambient space.
boundary_notes: Closure does not imply boundedness or compactness.
Affine images of closed unbounded convex sets need not be closed.
The empty-set convention is excluded by the stated nonemptiness assumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Failure of the Pairing
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative cone in l2 is closed and convex but has empty relative interior, so its closure is not generated by its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the Hilbert space \(\ell^2\), let \(C=\{x=(x_k):x_k\ge 0\text{ for every }k\}\). Then \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, \(\operatorname{aff}C=\ell^2\), and \(\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\). Hence \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\varnothing\ne C=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)\ne\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that the finite-dimensional hypothesis in the seed cannot be removed in general.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Relative-Interior Pairing
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty convex set, taking relative interior does not change its closure, and taking closure does not change its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C,\qquad \operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C\) and \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closure–relative-interior pairing for a nonempty convex set.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, without a closedness assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\) when \(C\) and \(D\) have the same closure-relative-interior data. For nonempty convex sets, the following equivalent conditions define this relation: \[\operatorname{cl}C=\operatorname{cl}D,\qquad \operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{ri}D,\] or, after possibly exchanging \(C\) and \(D\), \[\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C.\] Each set satisfies the canonical pairing identities \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C,\qquad \operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty finite-dimensional convex sets, closure and relative interior determine one another. Two such sets have the same closure exactly when they have the same relative interior. Any convex set lying between the relative interior of \(C\) and the closure of \(C\) belongs to the same closure–relative-interior equivalence class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{cl}C=\operatorname{cl}D\iff\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{ri}D,\quad \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C,\quad \operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\) if and only if both sets lie between their common relative interior and common closure.
For a convex \(D\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C\) implies \(C\sim_{\mathrm{cr}}D\).
special_cases_latex: \(C\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and \(\operatorname{cl}C\) all belong to the same equivalence class.
An open convex set relative to its affine hull and its closure have the same relative interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: Adding or deleting only non-interior boundary points while remaining convex does not change either canonical datum.
boundary_notes: Convexity is essential; arbitrary sets with the same closure need not have the same interior.
Nonemptiness avoids exceptional conventions for relative interior.
Equality of closures does not imply equality of the underlying sets.

children.title: Closure-Generation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Closure behavior under convex generation and set algebra.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be an operation on nonempty convex sets in finite-dimensional spaces. Write \(\overline C=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian products and Minkowski addition, with explicit boundedness conditions for exact closure of sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operation \(\Phi\) is closure exact at \((C_1,	ext{\ldots},C_m)\) when \[\operatorname{cl}\Phi(C_1,	ext{\ldots},C_m)=\Phi(\operatorname{cl}C_1,	ext{\ldots},\operatorname{cl}C_m).\] Cartesian product is always closure exact: \[\operatorname{cl}(C_1\times C_2)=\operatorname{cl}C_1\times\operatorname{cl}C_2.\] Minkowski addition always satisfies \[\operatorname{cl}C_1+	ext{\operatorname{cl}}C_2\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2),\] and it is closure exact when at least one summand is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-set operation is closure exact when closing its inputs before applying the operation gives the same set as closing its output. Cartesian products are always closure exact. Minkowski sums have a general one-sided inclusion and become closure exact when at least one of the two convex summands is bounded.
assumptions_latex: For exactness of Minkowski addition, at least one of \(C_1,C_2\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{cl}(C_1\times C_2)=\operatorname{cl}C_1\times\operatorname{cl}C_2,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{cl}C_1+	ext{\operatorname{cl}}C_2\] under the bounded-summand condition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For Minkowski addition, closure exactness means every limit of sums can be written as a sum of one point from each input closure.
special_cases_latex: If both summands are compact, their sum is compact and hence closed.
If \(C_1\) is bounded and \(C_2\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{cl}(C_1+C_2)=\operatorname{cl}C_1+C_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closure calculus for a product followed by addition is exact whenever the boundedness condition is retained at the addition stage.
boundary_notes: The boundedness condition cannot simply be discarded: sums of closed unbounded convex sets may be nonclosed.
Closure exactness is operation- and input-dependent; it is not implied merely by convexity.
The inserted null markers in the displayed tuple notation carry no mathematical meaning and should be removed during normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Invariance of Convex Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull is unchanged if the generating set is first replaced by its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{cl}S)).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{cl}S)).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closing the generators before convexification does not alter the resulting closed convex hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Carathéodory Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the closed convex hull exactly when it is a limit of convex combinations using at most n+1 generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(x\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) if and only if, for every \(m\), there are \(s_{m,0},\ldots,s_{m,n}\in S\) and \(\lambda_{m,i}\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_{m,i}=1\) such that \[\sum_{i=0}^n\lambda_{m,i}s_{m,i}\longrightarrow x.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\iff x\text{ is a limit of convex combinations of at most }n+1\text{ points of }S.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional sequential membership form of the closed convex hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure of Convex Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of the convex hull of a set is exactly the intersection of all closed convex sets containing it, hence its smallest closed convex superset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its closed convex hull satisfies \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)=\bigcap\{K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:S\subseteq K,\ K\text{ is closed and convex}\}.\] Thus \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) is the unique smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\) is the smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of the closed convex hull in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

source_witnesses.locator: III.1.4, Closed Convex Sets and Hulls, p. 99

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 1.4 Closed Convex Sets and Hulls p. 99

knowledge_statements.title: Closure of Finite Unions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure commutes with finite unions, while infinite unions may have additional limit points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sets \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) in a Euclidean space, \[\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^k A_i\right)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\operatorname{cl}A_i.\] For an arbitrary family \((A_i)_{i\in I}\), only \[\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{cl}A_i\subseteq\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\right)\] is automatic.
assumptions_latex: \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) are subsets of a Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}(\bigcup_{i=1}^kA_i)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\operatorname{cl}A_i.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equality is restricted to finite unions; infinite unions may acquire additional limit points.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski-Sum Closure Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the summands does not change the closure of their Minkowski sum; compact-plus-closed sums are closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary \(A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}(A+B)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}A+\operatorname{cl}B).\] If one summand is compact and the other is closed, then \(A+B\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}(A+B)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}A+\operatorname{cl}B).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The outer closure is essential in general, even for closed convex summands.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of A and B

knowledge_statements.title: Closure and Continuous Linear Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous linear map sends closure into the closure of the image, and closing before mapping does not change the final closed image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear map \(L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and any \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[L(\operatorname{cl}A)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(L(A)),\qquad \operatorname{cl}(L(A))=\operatorname{cl}(L(\operatorname{cl}A)).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}(L(A))=\operatorname{cl}(L(\operatorname{cl}A)).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A linear image need not be closed, so equality is asserted only after closure in the codomain.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Under Set Operations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure always commutes with Cartesian products. For a positive finite family of convex sets, it also commutes with intersection when their relative interiors have a common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary sets \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), \[\operatorname{cl}(A\times B)=\operatorname{cl}A\times\operatorname{cl}B.\] Let \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) be positive. If \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are convex and \(\bigcap_{i=1}^k\operatorname{ri}C_i\neq\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname{cl}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^k C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^k\operatorname{cl}C_i.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}(A\times B)=\operatorname{cl}A\times\operatorname{cl}B\), and \(\operatorname{cl}(\bigcap_{i=1}^k C_i)=\bigcap_{i=1}^k\operatorname{cl}C_i\) under the stated qualification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines unconditional product closure with the qualified finite-intersection rule for convex sets.

source_witnesses.locator: III.1.4, Closed Convex Sets and Hulls, p. 99; III.2.1, The Relative Interior, p. 102

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 1.4 Closed Convex Sets and Hulls p. 99

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Sets Can Have a Nonclosed Sum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed convex sets can have a nonclosed Minkowski sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\},\qquad V=\{0\}\times\mathbb R.\] Both \(C\) and \(V\) are closed and convex, but \[C+V=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\] is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C+V=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a finite-dimensional failure of closedness under Minkowski addition.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hull of a Closed Set Need Not Be Closed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the origin to the closed epigraph of 1/x produces a closed set whose convex hull approaches but does not contain the positive horizontal axis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\},\qquad S=C\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \(S\) is closed, but for every \(r>0\), \[(r,0)\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}S)\setminus\operatorname{conv}S.\] Hence \(\operatorname{conv}S\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is closed but }\operatorname{conv}S\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This demonstrates why the outer closure in the definition of the closed convex hull cannot generally be omitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Images Need Not Preserve Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\geq1/x\}\) and let \(L(x,y)=x\). Then \(C\) is closed and convex, whereas \[L(C)=(0,\infty)\] is not closed. Thus \(L(\operatorname{cl}C)\neq\operatorname{cl}(L(C))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(C)=(0,\infty)\neq[0,\infty)=\operatorname{cl}(L(C)).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a finite-dimensional closed-convex counterexample; compactness of the domain set would restore closedness of the image.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncommuting Closure Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete convex examples showing closure need not commute with intersection or Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Closure need not commute with intersection: for \(C=\{(x,y):y>0\}\) and \(D=\{(x,y):y<0\}\), both sets are convex, yet \(\overline{C\cap D}=\varnothing\) while \(\overline C\cap\overline D=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\). It also need not commute with Minkowski addition. Let
\[
E=\{(x,y):x>0,\ y\geq 1/x\},
\qquad
L=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}.
\]
Both are closed and convex, but \(E+L=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}\) is not closed. Thus \(\overline E+\overline L\neq\overline{E+L}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex half-planes show failure for intersections, while a closed epigraph plus a line shows that a Minkowski sum of closed convex sets need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closure fails to commute with both intersection and Minkowski addition, even for convex sets.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of E and L

children.title: Nonclosed Convex-Set Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Attainment, representation, and separation failures caused by missing limit points.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Separation Detects Only Points Outside the Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is strongly separable from a convex set exactly when it lies outside the closure; omitted boundary points cannot be strongly separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). There exist \(a\ne0\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle<\alpha\le\langle a,c\rangle\) for every \(c\in C\) if and only if \(x\notin\operatorname{cl}C\). Thus every \(x\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\) is a nonmember admitting no strong separator from \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin\operatorname{cl}C\iff\exists a\ne0,\alpha:\ \langle a,x\rangle<\alpha\le\inf_{c\in C}\langle a,c\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the separation obstruction at an omitted boundary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Attainment Is Determined by Missing Closure Minimizers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a set does not change the infimum of a continuous linear objective, but it can add all of the minimizers and thereby restore attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+\beta\). Then \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{cl}C}f(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f=C\cap\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{cl}C}f.\] Consequently, if the infimum is attained on \(\operatorname{cl}C\) only at points omitted from \(C\), it is not attained on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_C f=\inf_{\operatorname{cl}C}f\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_C f=C\cap\operatorname*{argmin}_{\operatorname{cl}C}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the exact mechanism by which omitted limit points can destroy attainment without changing an optimal value.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Halfspace Hull of a Nonclosed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed-halfspace inequalities cannot distinguish a convex set from its closure and represent the original set exactly precisely when it is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing \(C\) is \(\operatorname{cl}C\). Hence \(C\) is representable exactly as an intersection of closed halfspaces if and only if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap\{H:H\text{ is a closed halfspace and }C\subseteq H\}=\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional representation loss caused by omitted limit points.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Convex-Set Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Missing boundary points obstruct attainment and strict separation despite convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|x\|_2<1\}\), and choose \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\|p\|_2=1\). Then \(C\) is convex but not closed, \(p\notin C\), and \(p\in\overline C\). The linear optimization problem
\[
\inf_{x\in C}-\langle p,x\rangle=-1
\]
has no minimizer. Moreover, no affine hyperplane strictly separates \(p\) from \(C\): there are no \(a\neq0\) and \(\alpha<\beta\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle\leq\alpha<\beta\leq\langle a,p\rangle\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open ball is convex, yet a boundary-directed linear objective has no minimizer and its missing boundary point cannot be strictly separated from the ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The infimum is unattained, and \(p\) cannot be strictly separated from \(C\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, not necessarily closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonclosed convex sets and their relative boundary decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative boundary is \[\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] Its missing-boundary part and attained-boundary part are respectively \[\operatorname{mbd}C=\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C,\qquad \operatorname{abd}C=C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] Since \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}C\), these sets form the disjoint decomposition \[\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{abd}C\mathbin{\dot\cup}\operatorname{mbd}C.\] The set is closed exactly when \(\operatorname{mbd}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative boundary of a possibly nonclosed convex set splits into boundary points that belong to the set and missing limit points that do not. The missing boundary is \(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\); it is empty exactly when \(C\) is closed. Both types lie outside the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{rbd}C=(C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C)\mathbin{\dot\cup}(\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C),\qquad C\text{ closed}\iff\operatorname{mbd}C=\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in\operatorname{mbd}C\) if and only if \(y\notin C\) and some sequence in \(C\) converges to \(y\).
special_cases_latex: For a relatively open convex set, \(\operatorname{abd}C=\varnothing\), so all relative-boundary points are missing.
For a closed convex set, \(\operatorname{mbd}C=\varnothing\), so every relative-boundary point is attained.
immediate_consequences_latex: An optimization value approached only through a point of \(\operatorname{mbd}C\) need not be attained over \(C\).
Affine images and sums can create missing boundary points even from closed unbounded convex inputs.
boundary_notes: The decomposition classifies topological membership only; it does not by itself assert existence or nonexistence of an optimizer.
Ambient boundary can be larger than relative boundary for lower-dimensional sets.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global asymptotic geometry of closed finite-dimensional convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic cone geometry of \(C\) is the pair \((C^\infty,\operatorname{lin}_\infty C)\), where \[C^\infty=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\forall x\in C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x+td\in C\}\] and \[\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=C^\infty\cap(-C^\infty).\] The cone \(C^\infty\) records directions retained indefinitely by \(C\), while \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty C\) records two-sided directions along which every point of \(C\) lies on a complete line contained in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global asymptotic geometry of a nonempty closed convex set consists of its recession cone and the lineality subspace inside that cone. A recession direction can be followed indefinitely from every point of the set. A lineality direction and its negative are both recession directions, so entire parallel lines remain in the set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^\infty\text{ is a closed convex cone},\qquad \operatorname{lin}_\infty C=C^\infty\cap(-C^\infty)\text{ is a linear subspace}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in\operatorname{lin}_\infty C\) if and only if \(x+td\in C\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(t\in\mathbb R\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, then \(C^\infty=\{0\}\).
If \(C\) is an affine space \(x_0+L\), then \(C^\infty=\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=L\).
If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(C^\infty=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The set \(C\) is unbounded exactly when \(C^\infty\) contains a nonzero vector.
The asymptotic cone is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty C=\{0\}\).
boundary_notes: Closedness is required for the stated closed-cone and unboundedness characterizations.
For nonclosed convex sets, the recession cone may fail to be closed and may fail to detect unboundedness.
This record treats set asymptotics, not recession functions of convex functions.

notation.meaning: asymptotic or recession cone of C
lineality subspace of the asymptotic cone

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex. The basic definition applies without closedness; the one-base-point characterization requires \(C\) to be closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sets, with closedness explicitly separated from the general definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) is a recession direction of \(C\) when \[x+td\in C\qquad\text{for every }x\in C\text{ and every }t\ge0.\] The recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:\forall x\in C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x+td\in C\}.\] If \(C\) is also closed, membership can be tested from one base point: \[d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff\exists x_0	ext{\in}C\ \forall t\ge0,\ x_0+td\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction of a convex set is a direction that can be followed indefinitely from every point without leaving the set. All such directions form the recession cone. For a nonempty closed convex set, it is enough to exhibit one complete ray with base point in the set; the same direction then works from every point.
assumptions_latex: For the one-base-point equivalence and closed-cone conclusions, \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:x+td\in C\ \forall x\in C,\ t\ge0\},\quad d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff\exists x_0\in C\ \forall t\ge0:\ x_0+td\in C\] when \(C\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For closed convex \(C\), any single ray \(x_0+\mathbb R_+d\subseteq C\) certifies \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\).
The defining condition is equivalently \(C+\mathbb R_+d\subseteq C\).
special_cases_latex: The zero vector always belongs to \(\operatorname{rec}C\).
For a closed halfspace \(C=\{x:a^Tx\le b\}\), \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:a^Td\le0\}\).
For bounded closed convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For nonempty closed convex \(C\), \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a closed convex cone.
Such a set is unbounded if and only if its recession cone contains a nonzero direction.
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed convex set, one ray from one base point need not certify recession from every point.
An unbounded nonclosed convex set may have no nonzero recession direction.
Recession directions describe infinite rays, not merely feasible infinitesimal directions.

notation.meaning: base point of a recession ray

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession directions and the recession cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex set, and let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) denote a direction vector.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The defining all-base-point condition applies to every nonempty convex set. The equivalent one-base-point test and closedness of the recession cone are stated only for closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector \(d\) is a recession direction of \(C\) precisely when every ray in direction \(d\) starting in \(C\) remains in \(C\). The recession cone is
\[
\operatorname{rec}C:=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\forall x\in C)(\forall t\geq0)\;x+td\in C\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(C+\operatorname{rec}C\subseteq C\). If \(C\) is also closed, then for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
d\in\operatorname{rec}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\exists x_0\in C)(\forall t\geq0)\;x_0+td\in C.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction is a vector along which one may move indefinitely from every point of the set without leaving it. The recession cone is the set of all such vectors. For a nonempty closed convex set, it is enough to verify the entire ray condition from one point of the set; without closedness, that one-point test need not be valid.
assumptions_latex: For the one-base-point equivalence, \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{d:(\forall x\in C)(\forall t\geq0)\;x+td\in C\}\), and when \(C\) is closed, \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff(\exists x_0\in C)(\forall t\geq0)\;x_0+td\in C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\iff C+\mathbb{R}_+d\subseteq C\).
\(C+\operatorname{rec}C=C\), because \(0\in\operatorname{rec}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone containing \(0\), then \(\operatorname{rec}K=K\).
The zero vector always belongs to \(\operatorname{rec}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a convex cone.
If \(C\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is closed.
boundary_notes: The empty set is excluded because the universal condition would otherwise be vacuous.
For a convex set that is not closed, its recession cone need not be closed, and a ray from one base point need not establish recession from every base point.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the set C.
The ray consisting of all nonnegative scalar multiples of d.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Base Direction Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infinite-ray directions from a fixed point of a convex set form a convex cone, which is closed when the set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and \(\bar x\in C\). Then \[D_C(\bar x):=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\bar x+td\in C\text{ for every }t\geq0\}\] is a convex cone. If \(C\) is closed, then \(D_C(\bar x)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_C(\bar x)\) is a convex cone, and it is closed if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This concerns directions from one specified base point, not the all-base-points recession cone.

notation.meaning: The set of recession directions based at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Ray Sequence Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set, an entire ray is feasible from a fixed point exactly when feasible points occur arbitrarily far along that ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, \(\bar x\in C\), and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\). Then \(d\) is a recession direction from \(\bar x\) if and only if there exists a sequence \(t_k\geq0\) with \(t_k\to+\infty\) and \(\bar x+t_kd\in C\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\in D_C(\bar x)\iff \exists(t_k)\subseteq[0,\infty),\ t_k\to\infty,\ \bar x+t_kd\in C\text{ for every }k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This fixed-base criterion uses convexity and does not assert base-point independence.

notation.meaning: An unbounded sequence of nonnegative ray parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a recession direction from a base point when the entire ray starting at that point in the vector's direction remains in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(\bar x\in C\). A vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a recession direction of \(C\) from \(\bar x\) if \[\bar x+t d\in C\qquad\text{for every }t\geq0.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\) is a recession direction of \(C\) from \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\bar x+t d\in C\) for every \(t\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the ray-from-a-base-point definition; independence of the base point requires additional convexity and closedness assumptions.

notation.meaning: A chosen base point in the set.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundedness Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set in finite dimensions is bounded exactly when it has no nonzero recession vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then \[C\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, \(C\) is unbounded exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}C\) contains a nonzero vector.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is bounded}\iff\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closedness and convexity are essential for the reverse implication.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Boundary for Boundedness Detection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded nonclosed convex set may have a trivial recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[C=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a\geq0,\ 0\leq b<1\}\cup\{(0,1)\},\] the set \(C\) is convex and unbounded but \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\). Hence \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\) need not imply boundedness when closedness is omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is convex and unbounded, but \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The claim concerns failure of the recession cone to detect unboundedness for a nonclosed convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Cone of a Convex Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone of a nonempty convex cone is the cone itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex cone, then \[\operatorname{rec}K=K.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}K=K.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the fixed-point property of the recession operation on convex cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic and Closedness Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All-base-points recession vectors always form a convex cone, which is closed whenever the underlying set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a convex cone containing \(0\). If \(C\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is a convex cone containing \(0\), and it is closed if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of the all-base-points recession cone does not require convexity of the underlying set.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone consists of all directions along which every point of the set can be moved by any nonnegative distance while remaining in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}C:=\bigl\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+t d\in C\text{ for every }x\in C\text{ and every }t\geq0\bigr\}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+t d\in C\ \text{for every }x\in C\text{ and }t\geq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition uses the all-base-points convention and is meaningful for any nonempty set; for a closed convex set it agrees with the single-base-point formulation.

notation.meaning: The recession cone of the set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and define \(\operatorname{lin}C:=\{d:C+d=C\}\). Then \[\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\bigl(-\operatorname{rec}C\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translation-lineality consists exactly of recession directions whose negatives are also recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C).\)

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Failures Without Closedness or Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Base-point independence can fail for a convex set lacking closedness and for a closed set lacking convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[C_1=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a\geq0,\ 0\leq b<1\}\cup\{(0,1)\}.\] This set is convex but not closed. For \(d=(1,0)\), the ray \((0,0)+td\) lies in \(C_1\) for every \(t\geq0\), whereas \((0,1)+td\notin C_1\) for every \(t>0\). Likewise, \[C_2=\{(a,0):a\geq0\}\cup\{(0,1)\}\] is closed but not convex, and the same direction is recessionary from \((0,0)\) but not from \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two examples separately show that neither closedness nor convexity can simply be omitted from the seeded base-point-independence theorem.

notation.meaning: A nonclosed convex set exhibiting base-point dependence.
A closed nonconvex set exhibiting base-point dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Point Independence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set, testing whether a ray remains in the set from any one fixed point gives the entire recession cone, so the answer does not depend on the chosen base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and fix any \(\bar x\in C\). Then \[\operatorname{rec}C=\bigl\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\bar x+t d\in C\text{ for every }t\geq0\bigr\}.\] Consequently, the set of recession directions obtained from a single base point is independent of the chosen point in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\bar x+t d\in C\ \text{for every }t\geq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional closed-convex version. Closedness is essential for deriving an all-base-points recession direction from one infinite ray.

notation.meaning: An arbitrary fixed base point of the set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a\ge0,\ 0\le b<1\}\cup\{(0,1)\}.\] Then \(C\) is nonempty and convex but not closed. For \(d=(1,0)\), the ray \((0,0)+td\) lies in \(C\) for every \(t\ge0\), whereas \((0,1)+td\notin C\) for every \(t>0\). Thus the fixed-base direction set depends on the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed convex set can contain an infinite ray from one point while the parallel ray from another point immediately leaves the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\in D_C((0,0))\quad\text{but}\quad d\notin D_C((0,1)).

children.top_down_role: Asymptotic behavior under intersections, products, sums, and affine maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Equality for Sums and Linear Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lineality-type qualifications make the recession inclusions for sums and linear images exact and guarantee closedness of the resulting set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets. If \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}D)\) is a linear subspace, then \(C+D\) is closed and \[\operatorname{rec}(C+D)=\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D.\] If \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is linear, and \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\) is a linear subspace, then \(A(C)\) is closed and \[\operatorname{rec}(A(C))=A(\operatorname{rec}C).\]
assumptions_latex: For the sum assertion, \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}D)\) is a linear subspace.
For the image assertion, \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\) is linear, and \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In the respective regimes, \(C+D\) and \(A(C)\) are closed, \(\operatorname{rec}(C+D)=\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\), and \(\operatorname{rec}(A(C))=A(\operatorname{rec}C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: These lineality qualifications provide standard sufficient conditions for the reverse inclusions omitted from the seed and also ensure closedness of the resulting sum or image.

notation.meaning: The reflection of the recession cone of \(D\) through the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictness of Sum and Image Inclusions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the vertical line to the exponential epigraph or projecting that epigraph horizontally produces recession directions not obtained from the original recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\ge e^x\},\qquad D=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R},\qquad A(x,y)=x.\] These are nonempty closed convex sets or maps of the required type, and \[\operatorname{rec}C=(-\mathbb{R}_+)\times\mathbb{R}_+,\qquad \operatorname{rec}D=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}.\] Moreover, \(C+D=\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(A(C)=\mathbb{R}\), whereas \[\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D=(-\mathbb{R}_+)\times\mathbb{R},\qquad A(\operatorname{rec}C)=-\mathbb{R}_+.\] Hence both corresponding recession inclusions are strict.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\subsetneq\operatorname{rec}(C+D)\) and \(A(\operatorname{rec}C)\subsetneq\operatorname{rec}(A(C))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The same exponential-epigraph construction shows that both reverse inclusions in the seed may fail when suitable qualifications are absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Preimage Recession Formula
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone of a nonempty affine preimage is exactly the linear preimage of the target recession cone, so every kernel direction is recessionary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear, and let \(a\in\mathbb{R}^m\). If \[E=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax+a\in D\}\neq\varnothing,\] then \[\operatorname{rec}E=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\in\operatorname{rec}D\}=A^{-1}(\operatorname{rec}D).\] In particular, \(\ker A\subseteq\operatorname{rec}E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}E=A^{-1}(\operatorname{rec}D)\) and \(\ker A\subseteq\operatorname{rec}E\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unlike a direct image, a nonempty affine inverse image has an exact recession formula without a closed-image qualification.

notation.meaning: The set \(\{d:Ad\in K\}\), not an inverse linear operator.

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary-Intersection Recession Rule
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession cones commute with every nonempty intersection of closed convex sets, including intersections indexed by an arbitrary set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\). Then \[\operatorname{rec}\!\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{rec}C_i.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{rec}C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the arbitrary-family extension of the finite-intersection equality in the seed.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession cones commute exactly with nonempty finite intersections and Cartesian products. Sums of recession directions and linear images of recession directions always give recession directions of the corresponding sum or image, although the reverse inclusions need extra assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty closed convex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\), \[\operatorname{rec}\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{rec}C_i.\] For nonempty closed convex sets \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\), \[\operatorname{rec}(C\times D)=\operatorname{rec}C\times\operatorname{rec}D.\] If \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), then \[\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C+D).\] For every linear map \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\), \[A(\operatorname{rec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(A(C)).\]
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty closed convex sets and \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\).
\(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
\(A\) is a linear map of compatible finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}(\bigcap_i C_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{rec}C_i\), \(\operatorname{rec}(C\times D)=\operatorname{rec}C\times\operatorname{rec}D\), \(\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C+D)\), and \(A(\operatorname{rec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(A(C))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The universally valid finite-dimensional rules are stated as equalities for intersections and products and as inclusions for sums and linear images; reverse inclusions need additional hypotheses.

notation.meaning: The Minkowski sum of two sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession calculus for basic set operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets, let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed and convex, let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear, and let \(W\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty compact and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite-dimensional calculus records unconditional intersection and product identities, a compact affine-preimage identity, and safe inclusions for sums and images. It does not assert generally false equality rules for arbitrary linear images or Minkowski sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession calculus associates set operations with the following directional rules:
\[
\operatorname{rec}\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{rec}C_i
\quad\text{when }\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing,
\]
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C_1\times\cdots\times C_r)=\operatorname{rec}C_1\times\cdots\times\operatorname{rec}C_r,
\]
and, for \(V:=\{x\in C:Ax\in W\}\neq\varnothing\),
\[
\operatorname{rec}V=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A.
\]
For nonempty convex \(C,D\), the universally valid directional inclusions are
\[
\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C+D),
\qquad A(\operatorname{rec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(AC).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession calculus transports directions through common set operations. A nonempty intersection of closed convex sets has the intersection of their recession cones, and a Cartesian product has the product of the recession cones. Constraining a closed convex set by requiring its linear image to lie in a compact convex set retains exactly those recession directions lying in the kernel. Recession directions add under Minkowski sums and map to recession directions under linear maps, but these last two statements are inclusions unless additional hypotheses justify equality.
assumptions_latex: Every set used in the intersection identity is closed and convex, and their intersection is nonempty.
\(W\) is compact and convex, and \(V=\{x\in C:Ax\in W\}\) is nonempty.
Only nonemptiness and convexity are required for the two displayed inclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intersection, product, and compact-preimage recession formulas hold as displayed, while \(\operatorname{rec}C+\operatorname{rec}D\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C+D)\) and \(A(\operatorname{rec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(AC)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a nonempty affine section \(V=C\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\), \(\operatorname{rec}V=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker A\).
The product formula says that \((d_1,\ldots,d_r)\) is a recession direction of the product exactly when \(d_i\in\operatorname{rec}C_i\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: For two nonempty closed convex sets with nonempty intersection, \(\operatorname{rec}(C\cap D)=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\operatorname{rec}D\).
If \(A\) is injective, a nonempty compact-preimage constraint introduces no nonzero kernel direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(d_i\in\operatorname{rec}C_i\), then \(d_1+\cdots+d_r\in\operatorname{rec}(C_1+\cdots+C_r)\).
Common recession directions are precisely the directions preserved by every member of a nonempty closed-convex intersection.
boundary_notes: A linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed.
Equality in the image or Minkowski-sum inclusions requires additional regularity and is not part of this definition.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of C and D.
Linear image of C under A.
Nullspace of the linear map A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundedness characterized by the recession cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. Boundedness is with respect to the Euclidean norm, and compactness uses the usual finite-dimensional topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equivalence is finite-dimensional and requires closedness and convexity. It distinguishes boundedness from the absence of visually apparent rays in a nonclosed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession boundedness criterion classifies \(C\) by
\[
C\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
C\text{ is unbounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(\exists d\in\operatorname{rec}C)\;d\neq0.
\]
Since \(C\) is closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the same condition may be written
\[
C\text{ is compact}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space is bounded exactly when its only recession direction is zero. Thus unboundedness is equivalent to the existence of a nonzero direction along which every point of the set can be moved indefinitely. Because closed and bounded sets are compact in finite dimensions, trivial recession is also equivalent to compactness for this class of sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\); equivalently, \(C\) is unbounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C\) contains a nonzero vector.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((\forall d\in\operatorname{rec}C)\;d=0\iff C\) is bounded.
\(C\) is compact if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
special_cases_latex: Every nonempty compact convex set has recession cone \(\{0\}\).
A nonzero closed convex cone is unbounded and contains each of its nonzero elements as a recession direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: To certify unboundedness of a closed convex set, it suffices to exhibit one nonzero recession vector.
A closed convex feasible region with trivial recession cone is compact, so every continuous real-valued function on it attains its extrema.
boundary_notes: Closedness is essential: an unbounded convex set that is not closed can have no nonzero recession direction.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, closedness and boundedness do not imply compactness.

notation.meaning: The trivial cone consisting only of the zero vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of the positive-integer parabola points is an unbounded nonclosed convex set with no nonzero recession direction, showing that closedness is essential for the converse boundedness test.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Let \(\operatorname{rec}C\) be its recession cone, and let orthogonality be defined by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The lineality definition does not require closedness. The decomposition uses any subspace contained in the lineality space and provides a canonical reduction when that subspace is the full lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lineality space of \(C\) is
\[
\operatorname{lin}C:=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C)
 =\{d:(\forall x\in C)(\forall t\in\mathbb{R})\;x+td\in C\}.
\]
For every linear subspace \(S\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C\),
\[
C=S+(C\cap S^\perp).
\]
In particular, with \(L:=\operatorname{lin}C\), the lineality-reduced section is
\[
C_0:=C\cap L^\perp,
\qquad C=L+C_0,
\qquad \operatorname{lin}C_0=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space consists of directions that are recession directions in both signs, or equivalently directions of complete affine lines contained in the set through every base point. Removing any lineality subspace by intersecting with its orthogonal complement loses no information: the original set is the Minkowski sum of that subspace and the orthogonal section. Using the entire lineality space produces a reduced convex set with no nontrivial reversible direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C)\) and \(C=S+(C\cap S^\perp)\); for \(S=\operatorname{lin}C\), the orthogonal section has zero lineality.

\(d\in\operatorname{lin}C\iff d,-d\in\operatorname{rec}C\).

If \(\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\), then the reduction is trivial: \(C_0=C\).

Geometric questions invariant under translation along \(L\) can be studied on \(C_0\).

The decomposition is orthogonal only after an inner product has been fixed.

children.title: Lineality Spaces
children.top_down_role: Maximal linear directional components of convex sets and cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Translation Invariance along Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set is invariant under translation along its lineality space, which is the largest subspace with this invariance property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(L=\operatorname{lin}C\). Then \[C+L=C.\] Moreover, \(L\) is the largest linear subspace \(V\) satisfying \(C+V=C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C+L=C\), and \(C+V=C\) for a linear subspace \(V\) implies \(V\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic representation of a closed convex set as a union of affine cosets parallel to its lineality space.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the convex set.
The Minkowski sum of the set and its lineality space.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Spaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space consists of directions along which the set extends indefinitely in both signs. It is the largest linear directional component of the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its lineality space is \[\operatorname{lin}C:=\operatorname{rec}C\cap\bigl(-\operatorname{rec}C\bigr).\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{lin}C=\bigl\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+t d\in C\text{ for every }x\in C\text{ and every }t\in\mathbb{R}\bigr\}.\] The set \(\operatorname{lin}C\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}C:=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C)=\{d:x+t d\in C\ \text{for every }x\in C\text{ and }t\in\mathbb{R}\}\), and this set is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lineality is defined directionally for a closed convex set; for a convex cone it is its largest contained linear subspace.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the convex set.
The recession cone of the set.

children.title: Lineality-Free Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Directional geometries without nontrivial reversible directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. When \(C=K\) is a cone, assume \(0\in K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition treats general closed convex sets through their recession lineality and specializes to the standard pointedness condition for closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lineality-free family in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is
\[
\mathfrak{LF}_n:=\{C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n:C\neq\varnothing,\ C\text{ closed and convex},\ \operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(C\in\mathfrak{LF}_n\) exactly when \(C\) contains no affine line. For a closed convex cone \(K\), this condition becomes
\[
K\cap(-K)=\{0\},
\]
and such a cone is called pointed. Thus the pointed-cone family is
\[
\mathfrak{P}_n:=\{K:K\text{ is a closed convex cone and }K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set is lineality-free when its only reversible recession direction is zero. This is equivalent to the absence of every complete affine line in the set. In the conic case, the lineality space is the intersection of the cone with its negative, so lineality-free cones are exactly pointed cones.
assumptions_latex: For the pointed-cone specialization, \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is lineality-free iff \(\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\), and a closed convex cone \(K\) is pointed iff \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\in\mathfrak{LF}_n\iff\nexists x\in C,\ d\neq0\text{ such that }x+\mathbb{R}d\subseteq C\).
For a cone, \(K\) is pointed iff \((d\in K\ \text{and}\ -d\in K)\Rightarrow d=0\).
special_cases_latex: The nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) is pointed.
Every linear subspace of positive dimension fails to be pointed when regarded as a cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: The orthogonal lineality reduction of any nonempty closed convex set belongs to a lineality-free regime.
A pointed cone has no nonzero subspace contained in it.
boundary_notes: Pointedness does not mean full dimensionality or nonempty interior.
A lineality-free closed convex set can still possess many nonzero recession directions, provided their negatives are absent.

notation.meaning: Family of nonempty closed convex sets with zero lineality.
Family of pointed closed convex cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Cone Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is pointed when it contains no nonzero direction together with its negative, equivalently when its lineality space is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is pointed if \[K\cap(-K)=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, \(K\) contains no nonzero linear subspace and no line through the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is pointed if and only if \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness is the lineality-free condition for a convex cone.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the cone.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Free Convex-Set Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set is line-free exactly when its lineality space is zero, or equivalently when its recession cone is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. The following conditions are equivalent: \[C\text{ contains no affine line},\qquad \operatorname{lin}C=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{rec}C\text{ is pointed}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) contains no affine line if and only if \(\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\), equivalently if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An affine line means a set of the form \(x+\mathbb{R}d\) with \(d\neq0\).

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the set.
The recession cone of the set.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111; 6.5, Recession and Barrier Cones, p. 128

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Lineality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Line-free geometry fails precisely when a nonzero recession direction and its negative are both present. The half-plane cone given by a free horizontal coordinate and a nonnegative vertical coordinate has the entire horizontal axis as residual lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the line-free regime fails exactly when \[\operatorname{lin}C\neq\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there exists }d\neq0\text{ with }d\in\operatorname{rec}C\text{ and }-d\in\operatorname{rec}C.\] For example, if \(C=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_+\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\), then \[\operatorname{rec}C=C,\qquad \operatorname{lin}C=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\},\] so \(C\) is not pointed despite retaining a pointed component in the second coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lineality is nontrivial exactly when there exists \(d\neq0\) with \(d,-d\in\operatorname{rec}C\); for \(C=\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_+\), \(\operatorname{lin}C=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The record identifies the exact boundary where pointed or line-free geometry fails and includes a concrete closed convex cone with residual lineality.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the set.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1, Convex Cones, p. 111; 6.5, Recession and Barrier Cones, p. 128

children.title: Quotient Geometry by Lineality
children.top_down_role: Reduction from degenerate directional geometry to a pointed quotient.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Quotients and the Proper-Subspace Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full lineality quotient of a closed finite-dimensional cone is closed. Removing only a proper subspace of lineality leaves precisely the remaining quotient lineality and does not produce a pointed cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone with lineality space \(L\). Then \(K/L\) is closed. More generally, if \(M\subseteq L\) is a linear subspace and \(\pi_M:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/M\) is the quotient map, then \[\operatorname{lin}(\pi_M(K))=L/M.\] Consequently, \(\pi_M(K)\) is pointed if and only if \(M=L\); quotienting by a proper subspace of \(L\) leaves nonzero lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K/L\) is closed, \(\operatorname{lin}(\pi_M(K))=L/M\), and \(\pi_M(K)\) is pointed exactly when \(M=L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closedness of quotient cones and the exact failure of pointedness when less than the full lineality space is removed.

notation.meaning: A subspace of the lineality space used for a possibly incomplete quotient.
The residual lineality in the quotient by \(M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Quotient by Full Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a convex cone by all of its lineality produces a pointed cone, while the original cone is exactly the full inverse image of the quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone, let \(L=K\cap(-K)\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\) be the quotient map. Then \[\pi^{-1}(\pi(K))=K,\qquad \pi(K)\cap(-\pi(K))=\{L\}.\] Thus \(K/L:=\pi(K)\) is a pointed convex cone and \(K\) is recovered as its full inverse image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(K)\) is pointed and convex, and \(\pi^{-1}(\pi(K))=K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract quotient representation of a convex cone after identifying vectors differing by a lineality direction; closedness is not required.

notation.meaning: The lineality space of the cone.
The canonical quotient map modulo lineality.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Geometry by Lineality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical reduction of a convex cone to a pointed cone in the quotient by its lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(L=K\cap(-K)\), and let \(\pi:V\to V/L\) be the quotient map. Then \(\pi(K)\) is a pointed convex cone and \[\pi(K)\cap\bigl(-\pi(K)\bigr)=\{0_{V/L}\},\qquad \pi^{-1}(\pi(K))=K.\] Thus quotienting by the maximal subspace \(L\) removes exactly the bidirectional component of \(K\), while \(K\) is recovered as the full inverse image of its pointed quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a convex cone by its lineality produces a pointed cone and retains the original cone as the quotient cone's full inverse image.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq V\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(\pi:V\to V/L\) is the canonical quotient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(K)\) is pointed and \(K=\pi^{-1}(\pi(K))\).

notation.meaning: canonical map from V to the quotient V/L
zero coset in the quotient space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quotient reduction by the lineality space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(L:=\operatorname{lin}C\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\) be the canonical quotient map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The quotient is finite-dimensional. Its concrete Euclidean realization uses the unique orthogonal representative in \(L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quotient geometry of \(C\) by its lineality is the image
\[
\overline C:=\pi(C)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n/L,
\qquad \pi(x)=x+L.
\]
Identifying \(\mathbb{R}^n/L\) isometrically with \(L^\perp\) by choosing the orthogonal representative of each coset gives
\[
\overline C\cong C_0:=C\cap L^\perp,
\qquad C=L+C_0.
\]
Under this identification,
\[
\operatorname{rec}C_0=\operatorname{rec}C\cap L^\perp,
\qquad \operatorname{lin}C_0=\{0\}.
\]
Thus quotienting collapses precisely the reversible directions and retains a lineality-free directional geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotient geometry identifies points of a closed convex set that differ by an element of its lineality space. Every coset has a unique representative orthogonal to that space, and the quotient set is therefore represented concretely by the intersection of the original set with the orthogonal complement. Its recession cone is the orthogonal part of the original recession cone, and it has no nonzero lineality.
assumptions_latex: \(L=\operatorname{lin}C\), and \(\pi\) is the canonical quotient map.
The quotient is represented using the Euclidean orthogonal complement \(L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(C)\cong C\cap L^\perp\), \(C=L+(C\cap L^\perp)\), and the reduced set has lineality \(\{0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x,y\in C\) represent the same quotient point iff \(x-y\in L\).
The quotient class \(x+L\) is represented by \(P_{L^\perp}x\in C\cap L^\perp\).
special_cases_latex: If \(L=\{0\}\), then \(\mathbb{R}^n/L\cong\mathbb{R}^n\) and no reduction occurs.
If \(C=L\) is a subspace, then \(\pi(C)=\{0+L\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For a convex cone \(K\), the reduced cone \(K\cap L^\perp\) is pointed.
The dimension of the quotient ambient space is \(n-\dim L\).
boundary_notes: The quotient removes lineality but does not remove one-sided recession directions.
The concrete orthogonal section depends on the chosen inner product, although the abstract quotient does not.

notation.meaning: Canonical map to the quotient by L.
Image of C in the quotient space.
Orthogonal projection onto the complement of L.

children.title: Convex Cone Structure
children.top_down_role: Conic generation, dimensional regimes, and extremal directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural data of a convex cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). All spans, dimensions, closures, and interiors are taken in the finite-dimensional Euclidean topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates conicity, convexity, dimensional structure, lineality, and extremal rays. Closedness is an additional property rather than part of the bare convex-cone definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(K\) is a convex cone when
\[
(\forall x,y\in K)(\forall\alpha,\beta\geq0)\quad \alpha x+\beta y\in K.
\]
Its structural data include
\[
\operatorname{span}K:=K-K,\qquad \dim K:=\dim(\operatorname{span}K),
\qquad \operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K).
\]
It is pointed when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\), full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{span}K=\mathbb{R}^n\), and proper when it is closed, convex, pointed, and has nonempty interior. For \(u\in K\setminus\{0\}\), the ray \(R_u:=\mathbb{R}_+u\) is extreme when
\[
x,y\in K,\ x+y\in R_u\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x,y\in R_u.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is closed under all nonnegative linear combinations. Its basic structure consists of its linear span and dimension, its lineality subspace, and its rays. Pointed cones have no nonzero reversible direction; full-dimensional cones span the ambient space; proper cones are closed, convex, pointed, and solid. A ray is extreme when a vector on it cannot be decomposed into two cone vectors lying outside that ray.
assumptions_latex: For the proper-cone designation, \(K\) is closed and has nonempty interior in addition to being convex and pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed closure under nonnegative combinations defines a convex cone, with span, dimension, lineality, pointedness, full-dimensionality, properness, and extreme rays defined as displayed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone iff \(K+K\subseteq K\) and \(\lambda K\subseteq K\) for every \(\lambda\geq0\).
\(R_u\) is extreme iff it is a one-dimensional face of \(K\).
special_cases_latex: Every linear subspace is a convex cone whose lineality equals the entire cone.
The nonnegative orthant is a proper cone in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty convex cone contains \(0\).
The closure of a convex cone is again a convex cone.
boundary_notes: A cone need not be convex or closed unless these properties are imposed.
A full-dimensional cone need not be pointed, and a pointed cone need not be full-dimensional.

notation.meaning: Ray generated by the nonzero vector u.
Dimension of the linear span of K.
