knowledge_statements.title: General Conic Bipolar Formula
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the nonnegative dual twice produces the closed convex conic hull of a nonempty set; exact recovery occurs precisely for closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \[S^*:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in S\}\] and let \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) denote its convex conic hull. Then \[S^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(S)}.\] Consequently, \(S^{**}=S\) holds exactly when \(S\) is a closed convex cone.
assumptions_latex: Duality uses the nonnegative pairing convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(S)}\), and \(S=S^{**}\) if and only if \(S\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This formula gives the exact closure-and-convexification effect of bidualization and characterizes exact bipolar recovery.

notation.meaning: The nonnegative dual cone of S.
The convex conic hull of S.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipolarity Through Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex cone equals its bidual and is exactly the set satisfying every inequality generated by its dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(K^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\) and \(K^{**}=(K^*)^*\). Then \[K^{**}=K=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,z\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }y\in K^*\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bipolar theorem under the nonnegative dual-cone convention.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb R^n\) with its Euclidean pairing. Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional negative-polar convention. The bipolar recovers the closed convex conical hull for arbitrary nonempty input and recovers the original set exactly for closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar cone of \(S\) is \(S^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in S\}\), and its bipolar is \(S^{\circ\circ}=(S^\circ)^\circ\). The bipolar is the intersection of all homogeneous closed halfspaces containing \(S\), and \(S^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}(S))\), where \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) denotes the convex conical hull. Thus a nonempty set equals its bipolar exactly when it is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar consists of all vectors making a nonpositive inner product with every vector in the original set. Polarizing again produces the intersection of every homogeneous closed halfspace containing the set, which is its closed convex conical hull. Consequently, closed convex cones are precisely the bipolar fixed points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}(S)),\qquad K^{\circ\circ}=K\ \text{for every nonempty closed convex cone }K.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), \(x\in K\) if and only if \(\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in K^\circ\).
The polar reverses inclusion: \(S_1\subseteq S_2\Rightarrow S_2^\circ\subseteq S_1^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: If \(L\) is a linear subspace, then \(L^\circ=L^\perp\) and \(L^{\circ\circ}=L\).
For \(S=\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), the polar is \(\bigcap_i\{y:\langle y,a_i\rangle\leq0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar of any nonempty set is always a closed convex cone.
A vector outside a closed convex cone is excluded by a homogeneous inequality supplied by an element of the polar cone.
boundary_notes: Some literature uses the opposite sign and calls \(\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\}\) the dual cone; the convention here is the nonpositive polar.
Without closedness and convexity, the bipolar generally enlarges the original set.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix a finite-dimensional affine space \(L\) of dimension \(d\). A convex-geometric assertion may concern generation of a point, partition of a point configuration, or feasibility of an intersection.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An organizing definition for finite-dimensional witness phenomena. It records the common bounded-witness structure without identifying the distinct Carathéodory, Radon, and Helly constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex-geometric property on \(L\) has a dimension-controlled witness bound if there is an integer \(w(d)\), depending only on \(d\), such that every valid instance has a certificate involving at most \(w(d)\) input objects. In the generation mode, membership \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) has a subset witness \(T\subseteq S\) with \(|T|\leq w(d)\). In the infeasibility mode, \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i=\varnothing\) has a subfamily witness \(J\subseteq I\) with \(|J|\leq w(d)\) in the applicable finite-family regime. In the partition mode, a sufficiently large point set has bounded subconfigurations whose disjoint parts have intersecting convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension-controlled witness principle is one in which a global convex-geometric fact can always be certified by a number of input objects bounded solely by affine dimension. The relevant certificates may be sparse convex generators, small infeasible subfamilies, or small point configurations admitting intersecting convex-hull partitions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{certificate size}\leq w(d),\qquad d=\dim L,\] with \(w\) independent of the total size of the instance.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In contrapositive intersection form, if every subfamily of size at most \(w(d)\) is feasible, then the whole finite family is feasible.
A witness bound is dimension-controlled when it is uniform over all instances embedded in affine spaces of dimension at most \(d\).
special_cases_latex: Carathéodory generation uses \(w(d)=d+1\).
Radon partitioning begins at \(d+2\) points.
Finite-family Helly infeasibility uses witnesses of at most \(d+1\) sets.
immediate_consequences_latex: Data lying in a proper affine subspace may use its affine dimension rather than the larger ambient dimension.
The definition separates witness size from the computational method used to find a witness.
boundary_notes: No single numerical constant applies to all three modes; the certificate type is part of the principle.
Infinite-family intersection statements require an additional compactness or recession hypothesis and are not included automatically.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(L\) be a real affine space and let \(r\geq2\) be an integer. Finite point configurations may be treated as indexed families, so repeated locations remain distinguishable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine convexity. This definition packages the classical two-part Radon phenomenon and its least universal threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine space \(L\) has the Radon property at \(r\) if every indexed family \((x_1,\ldots,x_r)\subseteq L\) admits a partition of its index set into two nonempty disjoint parts \(I_+\dot\cup I_-=[r]\) such that \(\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I_+\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I_-\}\neq\varnothing\). The Radon number \(r(L)\) is the least such \(r\), when it exists. For \(L\cong\mathbb R^d\), the classical value is \(r(L)=d+2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Radon property at a given size says that every point configuration of that size can be divided into two nonempty parts whose convex hulls meet. The Radon number is the smallest size for which this is always possible. A real affine space of dimension d has Radon number d plus two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[r(\mathbb R^d)=d+2.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A Radon partition exists if and only if there are coefficients \(\gamma_i\), not all zero, with \(\sum_i\gamma_i x_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\gamma_i=0\), whose positive and negative index sets are both nonempty.
The convex hull intersection contains a Radon point admitting convex-combination representations over both parts.
special_cases_latex: In dimension \(0\), two indexed points have the same location and give \(r=2\).
In \(\mathbb R\), every three points have a Radon partition and two distinct points need not.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every configuration with at least \(d+2\) points contains a \((d+2)\)-subconfiguration with a Radon partition.
The threshold is invariant under affine isomorphisms.
boundary_notes: The two parts must be nonempty and disjoint as indexed subfamilies.
Tverberg partitions into more than two parts are a distinct generalization and are not included.

children.title: Radon Partition Geometry
children.top_down_role: Partitions whose convex hulls intersect.

knowledge_statements.title: Radon Partition of an Affine Circuit
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimally affinely dependent point configuration has a unique Radon partition, obtained from the positive and negative coefficients of its affine dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be minimally affinely dependent. Then the nonzero solution of \[\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=0\] is unique up to nonzero scaling and has \(\alpha_i\neq0\) for every \(i\). Consequently \[I_+=\{i:\alpha_i>0\},\qquad I_-=\{i:\alpha_i<0\}\] is, up to swapping its parts, the unique partition of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) whose two convex hulls intersect.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign classes of the unique affine dependence give the unique Radon partition, up to interchanging the two classes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the uniqueness form for a minimally affinely dependent finite point configuration; uniqueness is up to interchanging the two parts.

knowledge_statements.title: Radon Partition Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any d+2 points in d-dimensional space can be partitioned into two nonempty groups whose convex hulls intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist two disjoint nonempty index sets \(I,J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d+2\}\) with \(I\cup J=\{1,\ldots,d+2\}\) such that \[\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{x_j:j\in J\}\ne\varnothing.\] Equivalently, there are coefficients \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i\in I\) and \(\mu_j\ge0\) for \(j\in J\), each family summing to \(1\), for which \(\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i x_i=\sum_{j\in J}\mu_j x_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The indices admit a partition \(I\mathbin{\dot\cup}J=\{1,\ldots,d+2\}\) with intersecting convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional Radon theorem in partition form.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.3 Convex Sets p. 101

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=(x_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite indexed family in a real affine space. For \(J\subseteq I\), write \(X_J=\{x_j:j\in J\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of a particular finite configuration; unlike the Radon-number definition, no universal dimension threshold is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Radon partition of \(X\) is an ordered or unordered pair \((I_+,I_-)\) of nonempty disjoint index sets with \(I_+\cup I_-=I\) and \(\operatorname{conv}X_{I_+}\cap\operatorname{conv}X_{I_-}\neq\varnothing\). Any point \(p\) in this intersection is a Radon point. Equivalently, there are coefficients \(\lambda_i\geq0\) for \(i\in I_+\) and \(\mu_j\geq0\) for \(j\in I_-\), each family summing to one, such that \(p=\sum_{i\in I_+}\lambda_i x_i=\sum_{j\in I_-}\mu_j x_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Radon partition divides an indexed point configuration into two nonempty parts whose convex hulls intersect. A point in that intersection is a Radon point and has one convex-combination representation using each side of the partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(I_+,I_-)\text{ is Radon}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists p\in\operatorname{conv}X_{I_+}\cap\operatorname{conv}X_{I_-}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: After subtracting the two convex representations, coefficients \(\gamma_k\) satisfy \(\sum_k\gamma_kx_k=0\), \(\sum_k\gamma_k=0\), with positive support in \(I_+\) and negative support in \(I_-\).
The lifted vectors \((x_i,1)\) admit a nonzero linear dependence having both positive and negative coefficients.
special_cases_latex: If one point lies in the convex hull of all the others, the singleton containing that point and its complement form a Radon partition.
Four vertices of a convex quadrilateral in the plane admit a partition into opposite pairs whose segments meet.
immediate_consequences_latex: Discarding indices with zero coefficients yields a smaller subconfiguration with the same Radon point.
Applying an affine map sends a Radon partition to a Radon partition, though distinct image points may coincide.
boundary_notes: A configuration may have several Radon partitions and several Radon points.
The parts partition indices, not necessarily distinct spatial locations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite point configuration and put \(k=\dim(\operatorname{aff}X)\). Define the Radon threshold of an affine space as the least cardinality forcing a two-part intersecting-hull partition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real affine spaces. The effective affine dimension, rather than the dimension of an arbitrary containing space, controls the sharp threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-dimensional Radon bound assigns threshold \(k+2\) to configurations contained in a \(k\)-dimensional affine space: every configuration of at least \(k+2\) indexed points contains a subconfiguration admitting a Radon partition. The bound is sharp in the universal sense because \(k+1\) affinely independent points form a simplex and admit no partition into two nonempty parts with intersecting convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radon behavior is controlled by effective affine dimension. At least k plus two points in a k-dimensional affine space force an intersecting convex-hull partition, while the k plus one vertices of a simplex show that no smaller universal threshold is possible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[r(L)=\dim(L)+2\quad\text{for every finite-dimensional real affine space }L.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A family of \(m\geq k+2\) lifted vectors \((x_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}\) is linearly dependent, producing a Radon partition after separating coefficient signs.
The absence of a Radon partition for \(k+1\) points is possible exactly at the sharp threshold, as witnessed by affine independence.
special_cases_latex: For points lying on an affine line, the controlling threshold is \(3\), even if the line is embedded in high-dimensional space.
In the plane, \(4\) points always admit a Radon partition, whereas the vertices of a triangle do not.
immediate_consequences_latex: Replacing ambient dimension \(d\) by \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}X)\) can strictly improve the bound.
Any larger configuration contains a Radon witness supported on at most \(k+2\) indices.
boundary_notes: Sharpness concerns a universal guarantee; particular configurations with fewer points may still have intersecting-hull partitions because of repetitions or affine dependence.
The result is specific to real affine convexity and two-part partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Radon-Number Thresholds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Radon number of d-dimensional Euclidean space is exactly d+2; d+2 points always have a Radon partition, while d+1 affinely independent points do not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Radon number \(r(\mathbb{R}^d)\), defined as the least integer \(n\) such that every set of at least \(n\) points admits a partition into two nonempty parts whose convex hulls intersect, equals \(d+2\). Thus every \(d+2\) points have such a partition. Sharpness holds because an affinely independent set of \(d+1\) points admits no such partition.
assumptions_latex: Convexity is the ordinary convexity structure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(\mathbb{R}^d)=d+2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Radon-number threshold for ordinary convexity in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any d+2 points in d-dimensional Euclidean space can be split into two nonempty parts whose convex hulls intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every collection \(x_1,\ldots,x_{d+2}\in\mathbb{R}^d\), there are nonempty disjoint index sets \(I\) and \(J\) satisfying \(I\cup J=\{1,\ldots,d+2\}\) and \[\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{x_j:j\in J\}\ne\varnothing.\] The statement allows repeated points; when the points are distinct, it gives a partition of their underlying set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist nonempty disjoint \(I,J\) with \(I\cup J=\{1,\ldots,d+2\}\) and \(\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{x_j:j\in J\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Radon theorem stated using the ambient Euclidean dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Affine Dimension
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite point set of affine dimension r has a Radon partition whenever it contains at least r+2 points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be finite and let \(r=\dim(\operatorname{aff}A)\). If \(|A|\ge r+2\), then \(A\) has a partition \(A=A_+\mathbin{\dot\cup}A_-\) into two nonempty parts such that \[\operatorname{conv}A_+\cap\operatorname{conv}A_-\ne\varnothing.\] Consequently, the relevant Radon threshold is controlled by the dimension of the smallest affine space containing the points, even when the ambient space has larger dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite nonempty subset of a real affine space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a partition \(A=A_+\mathbin{\dot\cup}A_-\) into nonempty sets with \(\operatorname{conv}A_+\cap\operatorname{conv}A_-\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radon’s bound expressed through the point set’s affine dimension rather than the ambient dimension.

source_witnesses.locator: III. Convex Sets p. 87

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Reduction Route
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine coordinates identify the affine hull with a lower-dimensional Euclidean space and preserve convex hull intersections, transferring Radon’s theorem to the effective dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{aff}A\) have dimension \(r\), and choose an affine isomorphism \(T:L\to\mathbb{R}^r\). For every \(B\subseteq A\), \(T(\operatorname{conv}B)=\operatorname{conv}T(B)\). Hence, for all \(B,C\subseteq A\), \[\operatorname{conv}B\cap\operatorname{conv}C\ne\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{conv}T(B)\cap\operatorname{conv}T(C)\ne\varnothing.\] Applying the ambient Radon theorem to \(T(A)\) therefore yields the effective-dimension form on \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(B,C\subseteq A\), \(\operatorname{conv}B\cap\operatorname{conv}C\ne\varnothing\) iff \(\operatorname{conv}T(B)\cap\operatorname{conv}T(C)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-coordinate reduction used to replace ambient dimension by effective dimension.

children.top_down_role: Passage between affine dependence and sparse hull witnesses.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Dependence Coefficient Elimination
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine dependence permits a maximal coefficient shift that preserves the represented point and total weight while deleting a support point; iteration yields an affinely independent convex representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i\), where \(\lambda_i>0\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), and the active points are affinely dependent. Choose \(\alpha\neq0\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i a_i=0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=0,\] changing its sign if necessary so that some \(\alpha_i>0\). Define \[t=\min_{\alpha_i>0}\frac{\lambda_i}{\alpha_i},\qquad \lambda_i'=\lambda_i-t\alpha_i.\] Delete points whose updated coefficient is zero and repeat while the active points remain affinely dependent. Each update preserves the convex representation and removes at least one active point, so the procedure terminates with affinely independent positive support after at most \(m-1\) updates.
assumptions_latex: The active points \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) are affinely dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update preserves the convex representation of \(x\), removes at least one active point, and finite repetition produces affinely independent positive support.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This formalizes the reduction step and termination behavior implicit in the seed's Radon-to-Caratheodory route.

notation.meaning: A nonzero affine-dependence vector whose coefficients sum to zero.
The maximal feasible elimination step along the dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Radon-Caratheodory Dependency Route
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a finite convex representation by points of A, the Radon–affine-dependence reduction eliminates points until at most d+1 remain, yielding Carathéodory’s sparse witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\in\mathbb{N}_0\), \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), and \(x\in\operatorname{conv}A\). Given a representation \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i\) with \(a_i\in A\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), the affine-dependence reduction associated with Radon partitions can reduce the number of positive coefficients whenever \(m>d+1\). Finite iteration yields a set \(B\subseteq A\) satisfying \[|B|\le d+1\quad\text{and}\quad x\in\operatorname{conv}B.\]
assumptions_latex: A finite convex representation \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i\) is given with \(a_i\in A\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(B\subseteq A\) with \(|B|\le d+1\) and \(x\in\operatorname{conv}B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional route from affine dependence and Radon partitions to Carathéodory sparsity.

notation.meaning: points in the initial convex representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-dependence elimination route to sparse hull witnesses
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and suppose \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\), where \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional algebraic dependency connecting Radon-type signed affine dependence with Carathéodory-type sparse convex representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Radon–Carathéodory dependency step is an affine-dependence elimination applied when \(m>d+1\): choose \(\gamma\neq0\) with \(\sum_i\gamma_i s_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\gamma_i=0\), and choose \(t\) so that \(\lambda_i-t\gamma_i\geq0\) for all \(i\) with equality for at least one index. Then \(x=\sum_i(\lambda_i-t\gamma_i)s_i\), the new coefficients remain convex weights, and the positive support strictly decreases. Iteration yields a representation of \(x\) using at most \(d+1\) points. The positive and negative supports of \(\gamma\) simultaneously define a Radon partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dependency route starts from an overlong convex representation and uses a signed affine dependence to adjust its weights without changing the represented point or the total weight. The adjustment makes at least one coefficient vanish. Repeating this operation gives a Carathéodory representation with at most d plus one generators, while the two signs of the affine dependence encode a Radon partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{conv}S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists T\subseteq S:\ |T|\leq d+1,\ x\in\operatorname{conv}T.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Affine dependence of \(s_1,\ldots,s_m\) is linear dependence of the lifted vectors \((s_i,1)\).
A signed affine dependence can be normalized on its positive and negative supports to give equal convex combinations and hence an intersecting-hull partition.
special_cases_latex: If the active points are already affinely independent, no elimination step is available or needed.
If \(S\) lies in a \(k\)-dimensional affine subspace, the terminal support bound improves to \(k+1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every convex-hull membership assertion in \(\mathbb R^d\) has a witness involving at most \(d+1\) generators.
Radon dependence and Carathéodory sparsification use the same lifted linear-algebraic certificate.
boundary_notes: The step concerns existence of sparse representations, not uniqueness.
For conical rather than convex combinations, the normalization equation and numerical bound change.

children.title: Helly Theorem Family
children.top_down_role: Finite-subfamily principles for intersection feasibility.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be a class of subsets of a common space and let \(h\geq1\). Families are finite unless a separate compactness condition is stated.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract finite-family Helly property specialized to convex subsets of finite-dimensional real affine spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class \(\mathcal C\) has the Helly property of order \(h\) if every finite family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal C\) satisfying \(\bigcap\mathcal G\neq\varnothing\) for every subfamily \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) with \(|\mathcal G|\leq h\) also satisfies \(\bigcap\mathcal F\neq\varnothing\). The Helly number \(h(\mathcal C)\) is the least such \(h\). For all convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\), the Helly number is \(d+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class has Helly order h when feasibility of every subfamily of at most h members guarantees feasibility of the whole finite family. The least valid order is its Helly number. The class of convex subsets of d-dimensional Euclidean space has Helly number d plus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[h(\{C\subseteq\mathbb R^d:C\text{ convex}\})=d+1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Contrapositively, every finite family of convex sets in \(\mathbb R^d\) with empty total intersection has an empty-intersection subfamily of at most \(d+1\) members.
When the family has at least \(d+1\) members, it suffices to test subfamilies of exactly \(d+1\), since smaller subfamilies can be extended.
special_cases_latex: For intervals on a line, pairwise intersection implies common intersection, so the Helly number is \(2\).
For convex sets in the plane, triplewise intersection implies total intersection for finite families.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite convex feasibility has an infeasibility witness whose size is controlled only by dimension.
Affine isomorphisms preserve the Helly number.
boundary_notes: Convexity is essential; arbitrary nonconvex families need not have this dimension-controlled property.
For infinite families, the finite Helly condition alone is insufficient without compactness or another global hypothesis.

children.title: Finite-Family Helly Regime
children.top_down_role: Dimension-controlled intersection testing for finite convex families.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Family Helly Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family of convex sets in R^d intersects globally whenever every d+1 of its members intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a finite family of at least \(d+1\) convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\). If \[\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}C\ne\varnothing\] for every subfamily \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) with \(|\mathcal{G}|=d+1\), then \[\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{F}}C\ne\varnothing.\] Equivalently, if the full intersection is empty, some subfamily containing at most \(d+1\) sets already has empty intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{F}\) is a finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with \(|\mathcal{F}|\ge d+1\).
Every \(d+1\) members of \(\mathcal{F}\) have nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{F}}C\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite Helly theorem for arbitrary convex subsets of Euclidean space.

source_witnesses.locator: III. Convex Sets p. 87

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex sets; they need not be closed or bounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-family regime. No compactness, closedness, boundedness, or recession condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \((C_i)_{i=1}^m\) satisfies the \((d+1)\)-wise Helly condition if \(\bigcap_{i\in J}C_i\neq\varnothing\) for every \(J\subseteq\{1,ldots,m\}\) with \(|J|\leq d+1\). It is Helly-feasible when this local condition certifies \(\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i\neq\varnothing\). Every finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\) is Helly-feasible in this sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex family satisfies the local Helly condition when every subfamily of at most d plus one sets intersects. In the finite-family regime that local condition guarantees a common point of all sets, without requiring the sets to be closed or bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\left(\forall J\subseteq[m],\ |J|\leq d+1:\ \bigcap_{j\in J}C_j\neq\varnothing\right)\Longrightarrow\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(m\geq d+1\), testing all subfamilies of exactly \(d+1\) members is sufficient.
If the total intersection is empty, some subfamily of at most \(d+1\) sets already has empty intersection.
special_cases_latex: When \(m\leq d+1\), the condition includes the whole family and the assertion is immediate.
For \(d=1\), the condition reduces to pairwise intersection of convex subsets of a line.
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite infeasible convex system admits a dimension-bounded subfamily certificate.
The conclusion remains valid for mixtures of open and closed convex sets because finiteness, not topological closure, is decisive here.
boundary_notes: The same assertion for an arbitrary infinite family is false without an additional hypothesis.
The empty set may occur as a member, in which case the singleton subfamily already violates the local condition.

children.title: Compactness-Extended Helly Regime
children.top_down_role: Extension from finite subfamilies using compactness.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without a Compact Member
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed rays [n,infinity) have the finite-intersection property but empty total intersection, demonstrating the need for a compactness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), let \(C_n=[n,\infty)\) for \(n\ge1\). Every finite subfamily has nonempty intersection, but \(\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}C_n=\varnothing\); every \(C_n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and noncompact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{n\in I}C_n\ne\varnothing\) for every finite \(I\subset\mathbb N\), while \(\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}C_n=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness and all finite intersection tests do not suffice for an infinite family without a compact member.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact interval together with shrinking open intervals has the finite-intersection property but empty total intersection, so closedness cannot be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), let \(K=[0,1]\) and \(C_n=(0,1/n)\) for \(n\ge1\). Every finite subfamily of \(\{K,C_1,C_2,\ldots\}\) has nonempty intersection, but \(K\cap\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}C_n=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite subfamily intersects, but \(K\cap\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty}C_n=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One compact member does not suffice when the remaining convex sets need not be closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness-Extended Helly Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed convex sets in R^d, the Helly condition extends to an infinite family if at least one member is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\in\mathbb{N}_0\), and let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a possibly infinite family of nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Suppose some \(K\in\mathcal{F}\) is compact. If every subfamily \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) with \(|\mathcal{G}|\le d+1\) has nonempty intersection, then \[\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{F}}C\ne\varnothing.\]
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{F}\) is a possibly infinite family of nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
At least one member \(K\in\mathcal{F}\) is compact.
Every subfamily of at most \(d+1\) members has nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{F}}C\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-family Helly extension with closedness and one compact member.

notation.meaning: a compact member of the family

source_witnesses.locator: III. Convex Sets p. 87

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be a possibly infinite family of compact convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\), with \(|I|\geq d+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-family extension using compactness of every member. A weaker sufficient formulation only requires one compact member together with the finite-intersection property, but the cited canonical regime assumes compact convex members throughout.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family is a compact Helly family if every \((d+1)\)-member subfamily has nonempty intersection. In this regime, finite-dimensional Helly feasibility extends from finite subfamilies to the entire index set: \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing\). Equivalently, the \((d+1)\)-wise condition gives the finite-intersection property, and compactness converts that property into a common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact Helly family is a possibly infinite family of compact convex sets for which every d plus one members intersect. The finite Helly theorem makes every finite subfamily intersect, and compactness upgrades this finite-intersection property to a common point of the whole family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\left(\forall J\subseteq I,\ |J|=d+1:\ \bigcap_{j\in J}C_j\neq\varnothing\right)\Longrightarrow\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The family of closed subsets \(C_{i_0}\cap C_i\) of any fixed compact member \(C_{i_0}\) has the finite-intersection property.
Every finite subfamily intersects, and the family is anchored in a compact set.
special_cases_latex: For a finite index set, compactness is unnecessary and the definition reduces to the finite-family Helly regime.
The conclusion remains valid when one member is compact and all members are closed and convex, provided the same local intersection condition holds.
immediate_consequences_latex: Infinite compact convex feasibility is determined by subfamilies of size \(d+1\).
Failure of the total intersection forces failure of some finite subfamily and hence of some subfamily of at most \(d+1\) members.
boundary_notes: Compactness cannot simply be omitted: infinite families of closed convex sets may have all small subfamilies intersect but empty total intersection.
The statement is finite-dimensional; infinite-dimensional compact-convex Helly numbers require separate hypotheses.

children.title: Helly Geometry for Linear Inequality Systems
children.top_down_role: Finite intersection witnesses for linear feasibility systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Farkas Certificate from Helly Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every infeasible finite system in d variables has a Farkas multiplier certificate supported on at most d+1 inequalities; any nonnegative multiplier that cancels the variable coefficients and gives a negative right-hand-side value certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). If \(Ax\leq b\) is infeasible, then there exists \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+\) such that \[A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-1,\qquad |\operatorname{supp}(\lambda)|\leq d+1.\] Conversely, any \(\lambda\geq0\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}\lambda<0\) certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The finite system \(Ax\leq b\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists\lambda\geq0:\ A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\ b^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-1,\ |\operatorname{supp}(\lambda)|\leq d+1.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Helly support refinement of the ordinary Farkas certificate for finite non-strict linear inequality systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Helly Geometry for Linear Inequality Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every infeasible finite linear inequality system in d variables contains an infeasible subsystem of at most d+1 inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\in\mathbb{N}_0\), let \(I\) be finite, and let \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\) for every \(i\in I\). If the system \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), \(i\in I\), is infeasible, then there exists \(J\subseteq I\) such that \[|J|\le d+1\] and the subsystem \(a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j\), \(j\in J\), is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: The system \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), \(i\in I\), is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(J\subseteq I\) with \(|J|\le d+1\) such that \(a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le b_j\), \(j\in J\), is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Helly’s theorem interpreted as a sparse infeasibility certificate for finite linear systems.

source_witnesses.locator: III. Convex Sets p. 87

knowledge_statements.source_title: Helly Geometry for Linear Inequality Systems
knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Helly subsystem certificate for linear feasibility
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and write the rows of \(A\) as \(a_i^\top\). Associate the closed halfspace \(H_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:a_i^\top x\leq b_i\}\) with inequality \(i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems of weak affine inequalities in a finite-dimensional variable space. The same intersection formulation applies to strict affine inequalities, but this record uses the canonical weak system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Helly infeasibility certificate for \(Ax\leq b\) is an index set \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \(|J|\leq d+1\) such that \(\bigcap_{j\in J}H_j=\varnothing\). The system has the Helly subsystem property when infeasibility of all \(m\) inequalities is equivalent to existence of such a certificate. Finite affine inequality systems in \(\mathbb R^d\) have this property; equivalently, if every subsystem of at most \(d+1\) inequalities is feasible, then \(Ax\leq b\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Helly certificate for an infeasible linear inequality system is an infeasible subsystem containing at most d plus one inequalities. Every finite weak affine system in d variables has this property, so feasibility of all small subsystems guarantees feasibility of the full system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{x:Ax\leq b\}=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists J\subseteq[m],\ |J|\leq d+1:\ \{x:A_Jx\leq b_J\}=\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The halfspaces \(H_i\) have a common point if every subfamily of at most \(d+1\) of them has a common point.
The implication is an instance of finite Helly applied to the convex feasible regions of individual inequalities.
special_cases_latex: In one variable, an infeasible finite affine system has an infeasible subsystem of at most two inequalities.
Equality constraints may be represented by two opposite weak inequalities, although that representation can affect the counted subsystem size.
immediate_consequences_latex: Large finite linear-feasibility failures always possess dimension-bounded combinatorial witnesses.
The bound depends on the dimension of the variable space, not on the total number of inequalities.
boundary_notes: This is a subsystem certificate, not a nonnegative-multiplier certificate such as Farkas' lemma.
If feasibility is restricted to an additional convex set \(C\), that set must be included as another convex member or absorbed into every feasible region.

children.title: Helly Dimension Bounds
children.top_down_role: Dependence of intersection witnesses on ambient or affine dimension.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(L\) be a real affine space of dimension \(k\), and let \(\mathcal C(L)\) be the class of all convex subsets of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families in an effective affine ambient space. The bound is sharp for the class of all convex subsets and may be smaller for restricted subclasses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Helly dimension bound of \(L\) is the least integer \(h\) such that every finite family \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal C(L)\) with empty intersection contains a subfamily of at most \(h\) members with empty intersection. For a \(k\)-dimensional real affine space, this least integer is \(h=k+1\). Consequently, a family contained in a proper affine subspace is governed by that subspace's dimension rather than by a larger ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Helly dimension bound is the smallest maximum size of an empty-intersection witness for finite convex families. In a k-dimensional real affine space the sharp bound is k plus one, so effective affine dimension controls the certificate size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[h(\mathcal C(L))=\dim(L)+1=k+1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If every \(k+1\) members of a finite convex family in \(L\) intersect, then the entire family intersects.
The contrapositive witness formulation and the local-to-global intersection formulation define the same number.
special_cases_latex: For \(k=0\), every nonempty convex subset of \(L\) is the single point \(L\), and the Helly number is \(1\).
For \(k=1\), intervals have Helly number \(2\).
For \(k=2\), the sharp bound is \(3\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If all sets lie in an affine subspace of dimension \(k<d\), testing \(k+1\) members suffices instead of \(d+1\).
The witness bound is invariant under affine isomorphism.
boundary_notes: The sharp lower bound can be witnessed by \(k+1\) convex sets arranged so that their total intersection is empty while every proper subfamily intersects.
Special classes, such as axis-parallel boxes, can have Helly numbers below the general convex-set bound.

notation.meaning: class of convex subsets of the affine space L
Helly number in the effective affine space

knowledge_statements.title: Helly-Number Thresholds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Helly number of R^d is exactly d+1; every empty intersection has a witness of that size, and smaller universal bounds fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Helly number \(h(\mathbb{R}^d)\), defined as the least integer \(n\) for which every finite family of convex sets with empty intersection has an empty-intersection subfamily of size at most \(n\), equals \(d+1\). The upper bound is Helly’s theorem. Sharpness is witnessed by the halfspaces \(H_i=\{x:x_i\ge0\}\) for \(1\le i\le d\) and \(H_{d+1}=\{x:\sum_{i=1}^d x_i\le-1\}\).
assumptions_latex: Convexity is ordinary Euclidean convexity on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(\mathbb{R}^d)=d+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Helly-number threshold for finite families in Euclidean dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Witness Bounds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty intersection of finitely many convex sets in R^d is witnessed by at most d+1 sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\in\mathbb{N}_0\). If a finite family \(\mathcal{F}\) of convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfies \(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{F}}C=\varnothing\), then there exists a subfamily \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) such that \[|\mathcal{G}|\le d+1\quad\text{and}\quad\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}C=\varnothing.\]
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{F}\) is a finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) with \(|\mathcal{G}|\le d+1\) and \(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrapositive Helly bound formulated as a finite certificate of empty intersection.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Affine-Dimension Bounds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex sets lying in a common r-dimensional affine subspace have empty-intersection witnesses of size at most r+1.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be an affine subspace of dimension \(r\), and let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a finite family of convex subsets of \(L\). If \(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{F}}C=\varnothing\), then some subfamily \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) satisfies \[|\mathcal{G}|\le r+1\quad\text{and}\quad\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}C=\varnothing.\] Thus the Helly witness size depends on the effective affine dimension \(r\), not on the dimension of any larger Euclidean space containing \(L\).
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is an affine subspace with \(r=\dim L<\infty\).
\(\mathcal{F}\) is a finite family of convex subsets of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) with \(|\mathcal{G}|\le r+1\) and \(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Helly witness bound governed by a common affine carrier’s dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Dimensional Family Reduction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine coordinates transfer a finite convex family in an r-dimensional carrier to R^r while preserving intersections, so its Helly witness bound is r+1.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be an affine subspace of dimension \(r<\infty\), let \(T:L\to\mathbb{R}^r\) be an affine isomorphism, and let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a finite family of convex subsets of \(L\). Each \(T(C)\) is convex in \(\mathbb{R}^r\), and for every subfamily \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\), \[T\!\left(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}C\right)=\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}T(C).\] Thus finite-family intersection witnesses transfer between \(L\) and \(\mathbb{R}^r\), with Helly bound \(r+1\).
assumptions_latex: \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is an affine subspace of dimension \(r<\infty\).
\(\mathcal{F}\) is a finite family of convex subsets of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\), \(T(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}C)=\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal{G}}T(C)\), and the finite-family Helly witness bound in \(L\) is \(r+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-coordinate transfer of finite Helly intersection tests to the common lower-dimensional carrier.

children.title: Finite-Witness Dependency Map
children.top_down_role: Navigation among hull, partition, and intersection witnesses.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Witness Dependency Map in Euclidean Dimension
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix an integer \(d\geq 0\). All points and convex sets lie in \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), write \(\operatorname{conv}S\) for its convex hull; for a finite family \(\mathcal F\), write \(\bigcap\mathcal F\) for its intersection.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean convexity; the map records witness types and their standard logical dependency, not computational reductions or infinite-dimensional analogues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-witness dependency map is the labeled directed graph \(\mathfrak D_d=(V_d,E_d)\) with vertices \(V_d=\{\mathsf A_d,\mathsf H_d,\mathsf P_d,\mathsf I_d\}\). Here \(\mathsf A_d\) is affine dependence among more than \(d+1\) points; \(\mathsf H_d(S,x)\) is a hull witness \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i s_i\), where \(r\leq d+1\), \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\); \(\mathsf P_d(X)\) is a partition witness consisting of disjoint nonempty \(I,J\subseteq X\) with \(\operatorname{conv}I\cap\operatorname{conv}J\neq\varnothing\); and \(\mathsf I_d(\mathcal F)\) is an intersection witness consisting of \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\), \(|\mathcal G|\leq d+1\), and \(\bigcap\mathcal G=\varnothing\). Its dependency edges are \(E_d=\{\mathsf A_d\to\mathsf H_d,\mathsf A_d\to\mathsf P_d,\mathsf P_d\to\mathsf I_d\}\). The first two edges encode coefficient elimination and sign partitioning of affine dependences; the last records the Radon-to-Helly witness route.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed Euclidean dimension d, the finite-witness dependency map is a directed graph whose objects are affine-dependence, sparse hull, Radon partition, and small empty-intersection witnesses. A hull witness represents a point using at most d+1 generators. A partition witness divides selected points into two nonempty disjoint parts with intersecting convex hulls. An intersection witness is an empty subfamily of at most d+1 convex sets. The directed dependencies are affine dependence to hull sparsification, affine dependence to partitioning, and partitioning to intersection certification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak D_d=(\{\mathsf A_d,\mathsf H_d,\mathsf P_d,\mathsf I_d\},\{\mathsf A_d\to\mathsf H_d,\mathsf A_d\to\mathsf P_d,\mathsf P_d\to\mathsf I_d\})\), with the witness predicates defined above.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The intersection vertex may equivalently be defined contrapositively: \(\bigcap\mathcal F=\varnothing\Rightarrow\exists\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) with \(|\mathcal G|\leq d+1\) and \(\bigcap\mathcal G=\varnothing\).

A partition witness may be encoded by coefficients \(\gamma_i\), not all zero, satisfying \(\sum_i\gamma_i x_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\gamma_i=0\), with the positive and negative supports forming the two parts.
special_cases_latex: For \(d=1\), hull witnesses use at most two points, Radon witnesses use at most three points, and empty-intersection witnesses use at most two convex sets.
If \(S\) lies in an affine subspace of dimension \(r<d\), the bounds \(d+1\) and \(d+2\) may be replaced by \(r+1\) and \(r+2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The map separates three certificate formats: convex coefficients, signed affine coefficients, and an index subfamily.
The edge \(\mathsf P_d\to\mathsf I_d\) records that the dimension-controlled partition principle supplies the finite obstruction size in Helly-type feasibility.
boundary_notes: The graph is an organizational dependency object; it does not identify the three witness predicates as logically equivalent for the same input data.
No uniform finite bound of this form is asserted for arbitrary infinite-dimensional spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Hull-Witness Route
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in a convex hull is witnessed by a convex combination of at most one more point than the affine dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and let \(r=\dim(\operatorname{aff}S)\). Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) admits a dimension-controlled witness: there exist \(k\le r+1\), points \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\in S\), and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1\) and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i s_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\Longrightarrow x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i s_i\) for some \(k\le r+1\), \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Carathéodory's theorem in intrinsic affine dimension.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\neq\varnothing\) be a subset of \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(x\in\mathbb R^d\). A finite convex combination permits repeated generators and zero coefficients unless a reduced witness is requested.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-hull membership. The route concerns exact convex combinations, not closure of a convex hull or approximate representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hull witness for \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\) is a tuple \(W=(r,(s_i)_{i=1}^r,(\lambda_i)_{i=1}^r)\) satisfying \(1\leq r\leq d+1\), \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i=1\), and \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i s_i\). It is reduced when every \(\lambda_i>0\) and \(s_1,\ldots,s_r\) are affinely independent. The hull-witness route is the passage from the existential condition \(x\in\operatorname{conv}S\), initially allowing an arbitrary finite convex combination, to such a dimension-controlled witness. If \(r\geq2\), affine independence is equivalent to linear independence of \(s_2-s_1,\ldots,s_r-s_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hull witness for a point x in the convex hull of S records at most d+1 points of S and nonnegative coefficients summing to one whose weighted sum is x. A reduced witness has positive coefficients and affinely independent generators. The hull-witness route is the replacement of any finite convex representation by this dimension-controlled certificate. The definition concerns exact membership in the convex hull rather than membership only in its closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\in\mathcal H_d(S,x)\iff 1\leq r\leq d+1,\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\ x=\sum_i\lambda_i s_i\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the lifted points \(\widehat s_i=(s_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}\), the witness equations are \((x,1)=\sum_i\lambda_i\widehat s_i\) with \(\lambda_i\geq0\).
When \(\operatorname{aff}S\) has dimension \(q\), one may require \(r\leq q+1\) instead of \(r\leq d+1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in S\), the one-point witness is \(r=1\), \(s_1=x\), and \(\lambda_1=1\).
For \(d=2\), every convex-hull membership has a witness using at most three generators.
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite hull witness is directly checkable through linear equalities, nonnegativity, and membership of its generators in \(S\).
For finite \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}\), the witness is a vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) with \(\mathbf1^T\lambda=1\), \(\sum_i\lambda_i s_i=x\), and support size at most \(d+1\).
boundary_notes: Replacing \(\operatorname{conv}S\) by \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\) can destroy the existence of an exact finite witness.
The bound depends on affine dimension and is not a dimension-free statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Partition Route
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any d+2 points in d-dimensional space split into two nonempty groups whose convex hulls intersect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(d+2\) points \(p_1,\ldots,p_{d+2}\in\mathbb{R}^d\), their index set has a partition \(\{1,\ldots,d+2\}=I\mathbin{\dot\cup}J\) into two nonempty sets such that \(\operatorname{conv}\{p_i:i\in I\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{p_j:j\in J\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{1,\ldots,d+2\}=I\mathbin{\dot\cup}J\) for nonempty \(I,J\) with \(\operatorname{conv}\{p_i:i\in I\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{p_j:j\in J\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radon's theorem obtained from affine dependence.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subset\mathbb R^d\) consist of distinct points with \(m\geq d+2\). An affine dependence is a nonzero \(\gamma\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \(\sum_i\gamma_i x_i=0\) and \(\sum_i\gamma_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite point configurations in Euclidean space. The witness is a two-part Radon partition obtained from signs of an affine dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An affine-partition witness is a quadruple \((\gamma,I_+,I_-,z)\) such that \(0\neq\gamma\in\mathbb R^m\), \(\sum_i\gamma_i x_i=0\), \(\sum_i\gamma_i=0\), \(I_+=\{i:\gamma_i>0\}\), and \(I_-=\{i:\gamma_i<0\}\). Both sign sets are nonempty. With \(\beta=\sum_{i\in I_+}\gamma_i=-\sum_{j\in I_-}\gamma_j>0\), the common point is \(z=\sum_{i\in I_+}(\gamma_i/\beta)x_i=\sum_{j\in I_-}(-\gamma_j/\beta)x_j\). Thus \(z\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I_+\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{x_j:j\in I_-\}\). The affine-partition route is the conversion of a nontrivial affine dependence into these two disjoint convex-combination supports and their common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine-partition witness starts with nonzero affine-dependence coefficients on a finite point configuration. The positive and negative coefficients define two nonempty, disjoint index sets. After normalizing each sign class by its total positive mass, the two resulting convex combinations are equal. Their common value lies in the convex hull of both parts and is the partition certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_+\cap I_-=\varnothing\) and \(z\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I_+\}\cap\operatorname{conv}\{x_i:i\in I_-\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A Radon partition is a pair of disjoint nonempty subsets \(R,B\subseteq X\) satisfying \(\operatorname{conv}R\cap\operatorname{conv}B\neq\varnothing\).

Given a common point with convex coefficients on \(R\) and \(B\), subtracting the two coefficient vectors produces an affine dependence whose positive and negative supports are contained in \(R\) and \(B\).
special_cases_latex: For \(d=1\), any three distinct points admit a partition in which the middle point lies in the convex hull of the two outer points.
For \(d=2\), any four points admit a partition into two disjoint parts with intersecting convex hulls.
immediate_consequences_latex: Zero coefficients may be discarded; hence the witness uses only the support of \(\gamma\).
The common point comes equipped with two independently checkable convex representations.
boundary_notes: The two parts need not exhaust the original configuration when some affine-dependence coefficients vanish.
The partition and common point need not be unique.

notation.meaning: Positive and negative supports of the affine dependence.
Common total mass used to normalize both sign classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection-Witness Route
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family of convex sets intersects globally whenever every subfamily of at most d+1 sets intersects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F=\{C_1,\ldots,C_n\}\) be a finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\). If \(\bigcap_{C\in\mathcal G}C\ne\varnothing\) for every subfamily \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) with \(|\mathcal G|\le d+1\), then \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}C_i\ne\varnothing\). Thus global intersection feasibility has witnesses controlled solely by ambient dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{F}=\{C_1,\ldots,C_n\}\) is a finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
Every subfamily of cardinality at most \(d+1\) has nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n}C_i\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite-family form of Helly's theorem.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F=\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\) be a finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\). The sets need not be closed or bounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families of convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space; the witness certifies infeasibility of the full intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An intersection witness for \(\mathcal F\) is an index set \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) satisfying \(1\leq |J|\leq d+1\) and \(\bigcap_{j\in J}C_j=\varnothing\). The intersection-witness route is the dimension-controlled implication \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i=\varnothing\Rightarrow\exists J\subseteq\{1,ldots,m\}\) with \(|J|\leq d+1\) and \(\bigcap_{j\in J}C_j=\varnothing\). Equivalently, if every subfamily of at most \(d+1\) members has nonempty intersection, then the whole family has nonempty intersection. A witness is inclusion-minimal when every proper subset \(J'\subsetneq J\) has \(\bigcap_{j\in J'}C_j\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An intersection witness is a subfamily of at most d+1 convex sets whose intersection is empty. The route says that emptiness of a finite family’s total intersection always has such a dimension-controlled subfamily certificate. Equivalently, nonemptiness of every subfamily containing at most d+1 sets guarantees nonemptiness of the full intersection. A minimal witness becomes feasible after removal of any one of its members.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I_d(\mathcal F)=\{J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}:1\leq|J|\leq d+1,\ \bigcap_{j\in J}C_j=\varnothing\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The witness relation is the contrapositive form of finite Helly: \([\forall J,\ |J|\leq d+1\Rightarrow\bigcap_{j\in J}C_j\neq\varnothing]\Rightarrow\bigcap_iC_i\neq\varnothing\).
For convex inequalities \(C_i=\{x:f_i(x)\leq0\}\), a witness is an infeasible subsystem containing at most \(d+1\) inequalities.
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), pairwise intersection of a finite family of intervals implies common intersection.
When \(m\leq d+1\), the full index set itself is already within the allowed witness size.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any inclusion-minimal infeasible finite family of convex sets in \(\mathbb R^d\) has at most \(d+1\) members.
Finite convex feasibility has combinatorial dimension at most \(d+1\) in this witness sense.
boundary_notes: For infinite families, nonempty intersection of every finite subfamily need not imply a nonempty total intersection without compactness or another additional hypothesis.
Convexity is essential; arbitrary nonconvex families need not admit the stated witness bound.

children.title: Linear Alternative Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Mutually exclusive linear feasibility systems and their separating multiplier certificates.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_query: Convex Analysis and Minimization Algorithms I: Fundamentals

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). Vector inequalities are componentwise, and \(A^T\) denotes the transpose.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems of non-strict real linear inequalities. Strict, mixed, and conic variants require modified multiplier conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear alternative certificate system associated with \((A,b)\) is the ordered pair \(\mathfrak A(A,b)=(\mathsf P(A,b),\mathsf C(A,b))\), where \(\mathsf P(A,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b\}\) and \(\mathsf C(A,b)=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:y\geq0,\ A^Ty=0,\ b^Ty<0\}\). A vector \(x\in\mathsf P(A,b)\) is a primal feasibility witness. A vector \(y\in\mathsf C(A,b)\) is a separating multiplier certificate: its nonnegative aggregation eliminates the variable term and produces the contradictory scalar inequality \(0\leq b^Ty<0\). The pair is called an exact alternative when precisely one of its two sets is nonempty. For finite real linear systems this exactness is the standard theorem of the alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given A and b, the linear alternative certificate system consists of the primal feasible set Ax≤b and the multiplier-certificate set of nonnegative y satisfying Aᵀy=0 and bᵀy<0. A primal point directly witnesses feasibility. A multiplier aggregates the inequalities while cancelling all variable coefficients and leaves a strictly negative right-hand side. The system is exact when exactly one witness type exists; finite real linear inequality systems have this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak A(A,b)=(\{x:Ax\leq b\},\{y:y\geq0,\ A^Ty=0,\ b^Ty<0\})\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing the rows of \(A\) as \(a_i^T\), a certificate satisfies \(\sum_i y_i a_i=0\) and \(\sum_i y_i b_i<0\).
Certificate scaling is immaterial: if \(y\) is a certificate, then \(\alpha y\) is a certificate for every \(\alpha>0\); one may normalize \(\mathbf1^Ty=1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(m=0\), the primal system is unconstrained and no multiplier certificate exists.
If some row is \(0^Tx\leq b_i\) with \(b_i<0\), the coordinate vector \(e_i\) is a certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal and certificate sets cannot both be nonempty.
Every certificate has finite support and identifies an infeasible subsystem consisting of its positive-multiplier rows.
boundary_notes: Replacing a weak primal inequality by a strict inequality changes the alternative conditions.
For general cone inequalities, an exact alternative may require closedness or regularity; otherwise certificates characterize failure of approximate feasibility.

children.title: Farkas Lemma Family
children.top_down_role: Linear and conic alternatives organized around multiplier certificates.

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 2.3.1. Polyhedral Cones and Farkas' Lemma p. 102

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_r,c\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(A\) have columns \(a_i\), and let \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}=\{A\lambda:\lambda\geq0\}\). Use the polar convention \(K^\circ=\{z:\langle z,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finitely generated cones and equivalent finite linear systems. The family groups equality, inequality, homogeneous-polar, and qualified conic forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Farkas lemma family is the collection of certificate systems obtained from the canonical cone-membership alternative \(c\in K\), equivalently \(\exists\lambda\geq0\) with \(A\lambda=c\), versus \(\exists z\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(A^Tz\leq0\) and \(c^Tz>0\). Its homogeneous consequence form is \([a_i^Tz\leq0\ \forall i]\Rightarrow c^Tz\leq0\) if and only if \(c\in K\). Equality- and inequality-system forms arise by representing unrestricted variables as differences and equations as paired inequalities. A member of the family is identified by its primal sign restrictions, its multiplier cone, the adjoint cancellation equation, and the strict scalar separation inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Farkas family consists of equivalent linear alternatives organized around membership in a finitely generated cone. The primal asks whether c is a nonnegative combination of the generators. The certificate is a vector whose inner product is nonpositive with every generator but strictly positive with c. The same relation can be written as a consequence theorem for homogeneous inequalities or transformed into equality- and inequality-system feasibility alternatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_i\}\iff [A^Tz\leq0\Rightarrow c^Tz\leq0]\), with infeasibility certificate \(A^Tz\leq0,\ c^Tz>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The polar identity is \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\), because a finitely generated cone is closed.
For \(A\lambda=c,\lambda\geq0\), infeasibility is certified by \(A^Tz\leq0\) and \(c^Tz>0\).
For \(Ax\leq b\), infeasibility is certified by \(y\geq0\), \(A^Ty=0\), and \(b^Ty<0\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(c=0\) yields homogeneous cone and dependence forms, but strict separation must be formulated carefully because \(0\in K\).
Taking \(K=\mathbb R_+^r\) recovers nonnegative multiplier geometry.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any valid homogeneous linear consequence of finitely many homogeneous inequalities has nonnegative multiplier coefficients.
Every infeasible finite equality system with nonnegative variables admits a separating linear functional.
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed cone, bipolarity gives \(K^{\circ\circ}=\overline K\), so exact membership cannot be inferred without closedness.
Sign conventions vary across sources; reversing the polar convention reverses all displayed inequalities simultaneously.

children.title: Equality-System Farkas Forms
children.top_down_role: Alternative formulations centered on linear equations and sign restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Equality-System Infeasibility Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible nonnegative equality system has a Farkas multiplier whose pairing with the right-hand side is normalized to minus one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), is infeasible if and only if there exists \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y=-1.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists x\ge0:Ax=b\iff\exists y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y=-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixing the negative pairing at minus one removes the irrelevant positive scaling of a strict Farkas certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation Is Essential
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-strict certificate condition is invalid because the zero multiplier can coexist with a feasible primal system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) in the equality-form Farkas alternative by \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le0\) destroys exclusivity. For \(A=[1]\) and \(b=1\), the primal system has the feasible solution \(x=1\), while \(y=0\) simultaneously satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x\ge0:Ax=b\) and \(\exists y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y\le0\) both hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This example isolates why a strictly negative pairing, or its normalized equivalent, is required for an exclusive alternative.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Free-and-Nonnegative Equality Alternative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For equations with free and nonnegative variables, infeasibility is certified by a multiplier orthogonal to the free-variable columns, nonnegative on the nonnegative-variable columns, and strictly negative on the right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_F\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}\), \(A_N\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times q}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[A_Fu+A_Nv=b,\qquad u\in\mathbb{R}^p,\quad v\in\mathbb{R}_+^q;\] or \[A_F^{\mathsf T}y=0,\qquad A_N^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists(u,v):A_Fu+A_Nv=b,\ v\ge0\) and \(\exists y:A_F^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ A_N^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the equality-system Farkas variant with free and nonnegative variable blocks; the seed is recovered when the free block is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-System Farkas Forms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either Ax=b has a nonnegative solution, or a linear functional separates b from the cone generated by A's columns, but not both.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \(Ax=b\) with \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n_+\); or \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) with \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) for some \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\). The second system is therefore a verifiable certificate that the equality system has no nonnegative solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x\ge0:Ax=b\) and \(\exists y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas alternative for nonnegative solutions of linear equations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). The primal variable \(x\) is constrained componentwise by \(x\geq0\); the multiplier \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite equality systems with nonnegative primal variables. This is the cone-membership form of Farkas' lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality-system Farkas form associated with \((A,b)\) is the pair \(\mathsf P_{=}(A,b)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\mathsf C_{=}(A,b)=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:A^Ty\leq0,\ b^Ty>0\}\). Thus \(x\) represents \(b\) as a nonnegative combination of the columns of \(A\), while \(y\) separates \(b\) from their generated cone. The defining validity relation is exclusive exactness: precisely one of \(\mathsf P_{=}(A,b)\) and \(\mathsf C_{=}(A,b)\) is nonempty. Under the opposite polar convention one may replace \(y\) by \(-y\), obtaining \(A^Ty\geq0\) and \(b^Ty<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an equality system with nonnegative variables, the primal witness is x≥0 satisfying Ax=b. The alternative certificate is an unrestricted vector y satisfying Aᵀy≤0 and bᵀy>0. Geometrically, the columns of A generate a cone, the primal asserts that b belongs to it, and the certificate strictly separates b from that cone. Exactly one witness type exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathsf P_{=}(A,b)=\{x\geq0:Ax=b\}\), \(\mathsf C_{=}(A,b)=\{y:A^Ty\leq0,\ b^Ty>0\}\), and exactly one is nonempty.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(b\in A\mathbb R_+^n\) versus \(\exists y\) with \(\sup_{k\in A\mathbb R_+^n}y^Tk\leq0<y^Tb\).
Using \(u=-y\), the certificate conditions become \(A^Tu\geq0\) and \(b^Tu<0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A=0\), feasibility holds exactly when \(b=0\); otherwise a separating \(y\) can be chosen parallel to \(b\).
If \(b\) is a column of \(A\), the corresponding coordinate vector is a primal witness.
immediate_consequences_latex: The feasibility question is exactly membership of \(b\) in the polyhedral cone generated by the columns of \(A\).
A certificate remains valid after multiplication by any positive scalar.
boundary_notes: Dropping \(x\geq0\) changes the primal image from a cone to the column space and changes the certificate to \(A^Ty=0\).
The strict inequality \(b^Ty>0\) is essential for separating nonmembership from boundary membership.
