knowledge_statements.title: Singular Codomain Maps Can Destroy Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero codomain map merges an infeasible target with the attainable origin, so transformed feasibility need not imply original feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\), \(A=0\), \(b=1\), and let \(U:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be the zero map. Then \(b\notin A(K)=\{0\}\), but \(Ub=0\in(UA)(K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\notin A(K)\) but \(Ub\in(UA)(K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal counterexample to bidirectional feasibility preservation under a singular codomain transformation.

knowledge_statements.title: Transformation-Compatibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible changes of domain and codomain preserve conic feasibility in both directions and transport strict separators by the inverse adjoint. Singular codomain transformations can merge distinct right-hand sides and need not preserve nonmembership certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in K\), \(Ax=b\) if and only if \(x'=Vx\in K'\) and \((UAV^{-1})x'=Ub\). If \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfies \(\langle y,z\rangle\ge0\) for every \(z\in A(K)\) and \(\langle y,b\rangle<0\), then \(y'=U^{-*}y\) satisfies \(\langle y',z'\rangle\ge0\) for every \(z'\in (UAV^{-1})(K')\) and \(\langle y',Ub\rangle<0\). This bidirectional transport relies on invertibility; for a singular codomain transformation, distinct right-hand sides can have the same image and inverse-adjoint transport is unavailable.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a convex cone, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear, and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
\(U:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(V:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) are invertible linear maps, and \(K'=V(K)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in A(K)\iff Ub\in (UAV^{-1})(K')\), and strict conic separators are transported by \(y\mapsto U^{-*}y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of conic feasibility and certificates with invertible linear transformations, together with the boundary at singular transformations.

notation.meaning: Inverse adjoint of the codomain transformation

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact infeasibility or nonmembership certificates based on strict separation from a closed convex feasible image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A hyperplane certificate that \(z\notin C\) is a pair \((s,\alpha)\in(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}\) such that \[\sup_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle\leq\alpha<\langle s,z\rangle.\] Its separation margin is \[\gamma(s,\alpha;C,z):=\langle s,z\rangle-\alpha>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hyperplane certificate is a nonzero linear functional and a threshold placing the entire closed convex set in one closed halfspace and the excluded target in the opposite open halfspace. The strict scalar gap is the certificate margin. When a feasibility problem is represented as membership of a target in a closed convex image, such a certificate is an exact witness of infeasibility. For finitely generated cones, the functional becomes a Farkas multiplier direction; for affine subspaces, it becomes a vector orthogonal to the range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{SepCert}(C,z):=\{(s,\alpha):s\neq0,\ \sigma_C(s)\leq\alpha<\langle s,z\rangle\},\quad \sigma_C(s)=\sup_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A threshold-free form is \[\langle s,z\rangle>\sigma_C(s).\]
After normalizing \(\|s\|=1\), the largest admissible margin in direction \(s\) is \(\langle s,z\rangle-\sigma_C(s)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a linear subspace, a certificate can be chosen with \(s\in C^{\perp}\) and \(\langle s,z\rangle>0\).
If \(C\) is a cone, finiteness of \(\sigma_C(s)\) forces \(s\in C^{\circ}\) and \(\sigma_C(s)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Existence of a certificate is equivalent to \(z\notin C\) for nonempty closed convex \(C\).
boundary_notes: Closedness is essential for certifying every point outside \(C\) by positive strict separation.
Scaling \((s,\alpha)\) by a positive scalar represents the same oriented separation.

children.title: Affine Feasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Hyperplane witnesses for inconsistent affine systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Construction of an Affine Infeasibility Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The orthogonal least-squares residual detects inconsistency and, after normalization, explicitly supplies an affine infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=(I-AA^{\dagger})b\), where \(A^{\dagger}\) is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. Then \(r\perp\operatorname{range}(A)\), and \(Ax=b\) is infeasible exactly when \(r\ne0\). In that case \(y=r/\|r\|_2^2\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b\text{ is infeasible}\iff r=(I-AA^{\dagger})b\ne0\), and when \(r\ne0\), \(y=r/\|r\|_2^2\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional construction from the least-squares residual of an equality system.

notation.meaning: orthogonal residual of b from the range of A

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Range Failure in Infinite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equation for an operator with dense nonclosed range can be infeasible even though no nonzero orthogonal multiplier certificate exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T:\ell^2\to\ell^2\) by \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\), and let \(b=(1/n)_{n\ge1}\in\ell^2\). Then \(b\notin\operatorname{range}(T)\), but \(\overline{\operatorname{range}(T)}=\ell^2\), so \(\ker T^*=\{0\}\). Consequently no \(y\in\ell^2\) satisfies \(T^*y=0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\notin\operatorname{range}(T)\) and \(\nexists y\in\ell^2\) such that \(T^*y=0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that the finite-dimensional certificate does not extend to operators with nonclosed range without an additional closed-range hypothesis.

notation.meaning: Hilbert space of square-summable scalar sequences

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine equality system is inconsistent exactly when a multiplier annihilates every column of its matrix and has value one on its right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \(Ax=b\) for some \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), or \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\) for some \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Equivalently, the second system supplies a hyperplane certificate that \(b\notin\operatorname{range}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax=b\) is infeasible if and only if \(\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional alternative certificate for an affine equality system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orthogonal Certificate for an Inconsistent Affine System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). The affine system is \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real equality systems; the certificate lives in the equation space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An affine feasibility certificate for the inconsistency of \(Ax=b\) is a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \[A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y\neq0.\] After changing sign and rescaling, it may be normalized by \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine feasibility certificate is a vector orthogonal to every column of \(A\) but not orthogonal to \(b\). Thus the linear functional \(z\mapsto y^{\mathsf T}z\) vanishes on the range of \(A\) and takes a nonzero value at the target \(b\). It separates \(b\) from the attainable right-hand sides and exactly witnesses inconsistency of the equality system. Because the range of a finite-dimensional linear map is a closed subspace, every inconsistent affine system admits such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{AffCert}(A,b):=\{y\in\ker A^{\mathsf T}:b^{\mathsf T}y\neq0\},\qquad Ax=b\text{ is inconsistent}\iff\operatorname{AffCert}(A,b)\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[b\notin\operatorname{range}A\iff\exists y\in(\operatorname{range}A)^{\perp}:\langle b,y\rangle\neq0.\]
A normalized certificate satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A=0\), a certificate exists exactly when \(b\neq0\).
If \(A\) has full row rank, every \(b\) is attainable and the certificate set is empty.
immediate_consequences_latex: For any alleged solution \(x\), the equations would imply \(b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), contradicting certification.
boundary_notes: The condition \(b^{\mathsf T}y\neq0\) excludes the zero vector.
For approximate inconsistency, a quantitative normalization and norm control must be added.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Inequality Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite non-strict linear inequality system is infeasible exactly when a nonnegative multiplier annihilates its variable coefficients and has a strictly negative value on its right-hand side. The negative value can be normalized to minus one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \(Ax\le b\) for some \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), or \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) for some \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\). The strict certificate inequality may equivalently be normalized to \(b^{\mathsf T}y=-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le b\) is infeasible if and only if \(\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m_+\) such that \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas certificate for a finite system of non-strict linear inequalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Farkas Multiplier Certificate for Linear Inequalities
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and consider the componentwise system \(Ax\leq b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonstrict affine inequalities with unrestricted decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear-inequality infeasibility certificate is a multiplier \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \[\lambda\geq0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}\lambda<0.\] The certificate set is \[\operatorname{IneqCert}(A,b):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m_+:A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\ b^{\mathsf T}\lambda<0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-inequality infeasibility certificate is a nonnegative combination of the inequalities whose left-hand sides cancel while whose right-hand sides sum to a negative number. It is an exact finite-dimensional witness: the system \(Ax\leq b\) is infeasible exactly when the certificate set is nonempty. Positive scaling preserves certification, and one may normalize any certificate by \(b^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-1\). The strict negative scalar distinguishes a genuine certificate from a redundant nonnegative dependence with zero pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}=\varnothing\iff\operatorname{IneqCert}(A,b)\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: By setting \(C=-A^{\mathsf T}\) and \(c=b\), the condition is the contrapositive form of linear Farkas: \[C\lambda\geq c\text{ solvable}\iff C^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ y\geq0\Rightarrow c^{\mathsf T}y\leq0.\]
Every certificate has a normalized representative satisfying \(b^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(b\geq0\), then \(x=0\) is feasible, so no certificate exists.
For one inequality, a certificate exists only when its normal is zero and its right-hand side is negative.
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate depends only on a nonnegative dependence among rows of \(A\) and the associated right-hand sides.
boundary_notes: A multiplier with \(b^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\) does not certify infeasibility of a nonstrict system.
The decision variables are unrestricted; sign restrictions require augmentation of the row system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Certificate for Nonmembership in a Generated Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(s_1,\ldots,s_m,b\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(S=[s_1\ \cdots\ s_m]\), and \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}=\{S\lambda:\lambda\geq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finitely generated cones, which are closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone-nonmembership certificate for \(b\notin K\) is a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \[S^{\mathsf T}y\leq0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y>0.\] Equivalently, \(y\in K^{\circ}\) while \(\langle b,y\rangle>0\), where \[K^{\circ}:=\{y:\langle y,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone-membership certificate is a polar vector that is nonpositive on every generator, hence on the entire generated cone, but strictly positive on the target. It separates the target from the cone and certifies that no nonnegative coefficient vector \(\lambda\) can satisfy \(S\lambda=b\). Farkas' lemma states that exactly one of cone membership and existence of such a polar certificate holds. Because a finitely generated cone is closed, no closure qualification is needed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[b\in K\iff\langle b,y\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in K^{\circ};\qquad b\notin K\iff\exists y\in K^{\circ}:\langle b,y\rangle>0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[b=S\lambda,\ \lambda\geq0\quad\text{and}\quad S^{\mathsf T}y\leq0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y>0\] are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
The bipolar form is \(K^{\circ\circ}=K\).
special_cases_latex: For a linear subspace \(K\), the polar is \(K^{\perp}\) and the sign of a nonzero pairing may be reversed.
For \(K=\mathbb{R}^n_+\), nonmembership is certified by some \(y\leq0\) with \(b^{\mathsf T}y>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A certificate may be normalized to \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\).
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed generated cone in an infinite or nonpolyhedral setting, the bipolar describes the closure rather than the original cone.
The polar convention here uses nonpositive, not nonnegative, pairings.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Membership Witnesses
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point belongs to a linear image cone exactly when it has a preimage in the original cone; that preimage is the membership witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=A(K)=\{Au:u\in K\}\), membership \(b\in C\) holds if and only if there exists \(x\in K\) such that \(Ax=b\). Hence the vector \(x\), together with exact verification of cone membership and the linear equality, is a primal certificate of membership. No closedness assumption on \(K\) or \(A(K)\) is required for this existential equivalence, although closedness becomes essential for complete separator certificates of nonmembership.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a convex cone, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear, and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in K\) with \(Ax=b\) certifies \(b\in A(K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal witness for membership in a linear image of a cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Nonmembership Separators
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies outside a closed convex cone exactly when a dual-cone vector is nonnegative on the cone and strictly negative at that point. For a nonclosed cone, the same tests concern its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(C^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:\langle y,c\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }c\in C\}\). Then \(b\notin C\) if and only if there exists \(y\in C^*\) with \(\langle y,b\rangle<0\). If closedness is omitted, these dual tests characterize exclusion from \(\operatorname{cl}C\), rather than exclusion from \(C\) itself.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\notin C\iff\exists y\in C^*\text{ such that }\langle y,b\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong nonmembership certificate for a closed convex cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Certificate Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is dual to a linear image cone exactly when its adjoint pullback is dual to the original cone. When the image cone is closed, such vectors give complete strict nonmembership certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual cone of the image is \((A(K))^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\}\). Consequently, if \(A(K)\) is closed, then for every \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), nonmembership \(b\notin A(K)\) is equivalent to the existence of \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\) and \(\langle y,b\rangle<0\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a convex cone and \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A(K))^*=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\}\).

children.title: Positive-Margin Certificates
children.top_down_role: Robust infeasibility witnesses arising from strict separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Margin Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an exterior point of a nonempty closed convex set, the normalized direction from its projection to the point is a separating certificate. Its positive margin equals the distance from the point to the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=P_C(b)\), let \(d=\|b-p\|=\operatorname{dist}(b,C)\), and set \(y=(b-p)/d\). Then \(d>0\), \(\|y\|=1\), \(\sup_{c\in C}\langle y,c\rangle=\langle y,p\rangle\), and \(\langle y,b\rangle-\sup_{c\in C}\langle y,c\rangle=d\). Thus \(y\) is a positive-margin certificate of nonmembership whose margin equals the point-to-set distance.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\setminus C\).
The inner product and norm are Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) with \(\|y\|=1\) and \(\langle y,b\rangle-\sup_{c\in C}\langle y,c\rangle=\operatorname{dist}(b,C)>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean positive-margin certificate obtained from projection onto a closed convex set.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection of the excluded point

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(z\notin C\). The norm and inner product are Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional robust nonmembership certificates based on strict separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A normalized positive-margin certificate for \(z\notin C\) is a pair \((s,\gamma)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times(0,\infty)\) satisfying \[\|s\|=1,\qquad \sup_{y\in C}\langle s,y\rangle\leq\langle s,z\rangle-\gamma.\] Its maximal directional margin is \[\gamma_C(z;s):=\langle s,z\rangle-\sigma_C(s)>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-margin certificate is a unit separating direction together with an explicit positive gap between the target's functional value and the support value of the closed convex set. Normalization makes the numerical margin independent of arbitrary rescaling. For the projection-generated separator \(s=(z-P_Cz)/\|z-P_Cz\|\), the margin can be chosen as \(\operatorname{dist}(z,C)\). Thus the certificate is both an exact nonmembership witness and a quantitative robustness measure against perturbations of the target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{PMCert}(C,z):=\{(s,\gamma):\|s\|=1,\ \gamma>0,\ \sigma_C(s)+\gamma\leq\langle s,z\rangle\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{PMCert}(C,z)\neq\varnothing\iff z\notin C.\]
With \(p=P_Cz\), one may take \(s=(z-p)/\|z-p\|\) and \(\gamma=\|z-p\|=\operatorname{dist}(z,C)\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed cone \(K\), a positive-margin certificate satisfies \(s\in K^{\circ}\), \(\|s\|=1\), and \(\langle s,z\rangle\geq\gamma>0\).
For an affine subspace, the projection residual supplies the normalized certificate.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\|e\|<\gamma\), then the same unit direction certifies \(z+e\notin C\) with margin at least \(\gamma-\|e\|\).
boundary_notes: A boundary point of \(C\) has zero distance and admits no positive-margin certificate against \(C\).
The exact distance formula uses the Euclidean projection onto a nonempty closed convex set.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection of z onto C

children.top_down_role: Geometric boundaries separating exact strong certificates from weaker closure-based conclusions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Gap and Zero-Margin Certificate Boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone, not necessarily closed, and let \(K^{\circ}=\{y:\langle y,k\rangle\leq0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex cones or convex images for which closure may differ from exact representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strong-certificate failure boundary of \(K\) is \[\mathcal B_{\mathrm{fail}}(K):=\operatorname{cl}K\setminus K.\] For every \(b\in\mathcal B_{\mathrm{fail}}(K)\), exact membership fails, but no strict polar certificate exists: \[b\notin K,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle\leq0\quad\forall y\in K^{\circ}.\] More generally, for a convex set \(C\), the zero-margin boundary is \(\operatorname{bd}C\), where supporting functionals may exist but positive separation from \(C\) does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate failure boundary is the closure gap between exact membership and what all continuous linear inequalities can detect. If a target lies in the closure of a convex cone but not in the cone itself, exact representability fails, yet every polar inequality valid for the cone is also valid at the target. Hence no strict Farkas-style separator can distinguish it. The bipolar relation detects membership in the closed cone \(\operatorname{cl}K\), not necessarily in \(K\). For ordinary closed convex sets, the analogous boundary phenomenon is zero margin: supporting hyperplanes can touch a boundary point, but a positive-margin certificate against the set is impossible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}K,\qquad b\in\operatorname{cl}K\setminus K\Rightarrow\bigl(b\notin K\ \land\ \nexists y\in K^{\circ}:\langle b,y\rangle>0\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\mathcal B_{\mathrm{fail}}(K)=K^{\circ\circ}\setminus K.\]
For nonempty convex \(C\), \[z\in\operatorname{bd}C\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(z,C)=0\] and no unit functional has a positive separation margin from \(C\).
special_cases_latex: For finitely generated cones in finite dimensions, \(K\) is closed and \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{fail}}(K)=\varnothing\).
For a closed convex set, exterior points have positive distance, whereas boundary points have zero distance.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closure is the precise regularity separating exact strong polar certificates from closure-only conclusions.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that nonclosedness occurs for finite polyhedral cones; such cones are closed.
Weak supporting equalities at boundary points are not strict infeasibility certificates.

notation.meaning: closure gap where strict polar certification fails

knowledge_statements.title: Open-System Certificate Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict system requiring a number to be both negative and nonnegative is infeasible, but its closed relaxation meets at zero. Consequently, the usual positive-margin certificate for non-strict inequalities does not capture this open-system infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system \(x<0\), \(-x\le0\) is infeasible. Its closed relaxation \(x\le0\), \(-x\le0\) is feasible at \(x=0\). For nonnegative multipliers \(\lambda,\mu\), cancellation of the variable coefficient requires \(\lambda=\mu\), and the resulting constant is \(0\), so no strictly negative Farkas aggregation exists. This example marks the boundary at which replacing an open halfspace by its closure loses the original infeasibility certificate.
assumptions_latex: The mixed system in \(\mathbb{R}\) consists of \(x<0\) and \(-x\le0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed open system is infeasible, while the closed relaxation \(x\le0\), \(-x\le0\) is feasible and has no positive-margin Farkas contradiction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-inequality certificate boundary exhibited by a touching closed relaxation.

notation.meaning: Closed relaxation of the strict inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary infeasibility of a finite strict linear system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m,n\geq 1\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\beta_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rows \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\). Inequalities between vectors are componentwise. The associated strict and weak systems are denoted by \(O(A,\beta)\) and \(W(A,\beta)\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems of strict affine inequalities in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. The definition isolates infeasibility caused solely by replacing open halfspaces with their closed counterparts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \[O(A, eta):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax< eta\},\qquad W(A, eta):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq eta\}.\] The strict system is at an open-system certificate boundary precisely when \[O(A, eta)=\varnothing\quad	ext{and}\quad W(A, eta)
eq\varnothing.\] Its normalized zero-margin alternative certificates form \[\Lambda_0(A, eta):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m:A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\ \mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1,\  eta^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\}.\] Equivalently, the boundary condition holds exactly when \(W(A, eta)
eq\varnothing\) and \(\Lambda_0(A, eta)
eq\varnothing\). Thus infeasibility of the open system has a nonzero nonnegative alternative multiplier, but every such normalized boundary certificate has zero right-hand-side margin rather than a strictly negative one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many strict affine inequalities, let \(O(A,\beta)\) be the intersection of their open halfspaces and let \(W(A,\beta)\) be the intersection obtained by making every inequality weak. An open-system certificate boundary is the case in which the strict intersection is empty but the weak intersection is nonempty. Equivalently, the weak system is feasible and there is a normalized nonnegative multiplier \(\lambda\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\) and \(\beta^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\). The equality in the last condition is the zero certificate margin distinguishing this boundary case from infeasibility of the weak system, which admits a multiplier with strictly negative right-hand-side value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[O(A, eta)=\varnothing
eq W(A, eta)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad W(A, eta)
eq\varnothing\ 	ext{ and }\ \Lambda_0(A, eta)
eq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\rho(x):=\min_{1\leq i\leq m}(\beta_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x)\), the boundary condition is equivalent to \(\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\rho(x)=0\) with the value \(0\) attained; moreover, \(W(A,\beta)=\{x:\rho(x)=0\}\).
The condition is equivalently that the intersection of the open halfspaces is empty while the intersection of their individual closures is nonempty.
special_cases_latex: For \(a\neq0\), the pair \(a^{\mathsf T}x<\beta\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}x>\beta\) is an open-system boundary: its weak relaxation is the hyperplane \(\{x:a^{\mathsf T}x=\beta\}\), and \((1/2,1/2)\) is a normalized zero-margin multiplier after writing the second inequality as \(-a^{\mathsf T}x<-\beta\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(z\in W(A,\beta)\) activates at least one inequality: \(a_i^{\mathsf T}z=\beta_i\) for some \(i\).

No multiplier \(\lambda\geq0\) can satisfy simultaneously \(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\) and \(\beta^{\mathsf T}\lambda<0\), because the weak system is feasible; the alternative multiplier for strict infeasibility therefore lies exactly at zero margin.
boundary_notes: The set \(W(A,\beta)\) is the intersection of the closures of the defining open halfspaces, not the closure of \(O(A,\beta)\); at a boundary configuration the latter closure is empty.
Mixed systems containing both strict and weak inequalities require the corresponding mixed alternative and are outside this definition.
The normalization \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\) removes positive scaling and is valid because an alternative multiplier is nonzero.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the strict system \(Ax<\beta\).
Feasible set of the weak relaxation \(Ax\leq\beta\).
Set of normalized nonnegative alternative multipliers having zero certificate margin.
Minimum slack among the strict inequalities at \(x\).

children.title: Nonclosed Cone-Image Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of strong conic alternatives when relevant images are not closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Only Certificates for Nonclosed Cone Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual inequalities detect nonmembership in the closure of a cone image. A missing boundary point of a nonclosed image is infeasible but has no strict separator certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and set \(S=A(K)\). With the positive-dual convention, \[S^*=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*\}.\] For \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \[\exists y\in S^*:\langle y,b\rangle<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\notin\operatorname{cl}S.\] Consequently, if \(b\in\operatorname{cl}S\setminus S\), the system \(Ax=b,\ x\in K\) is infeasible but admits no strict dual-cone certificate of this form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists y\ (A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^*,\ \langle y,b\rangle<0)\iff b\notin\operatorname{cl}A(K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General certificate boundary explaining the missing strict separator in the seed example.

notation.meaning: Positive dual cone of the image cone

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Cone-Image Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coordinate image of the two-by-two positive semidefinite cone consists of all pairs with positive first coordinate together with the origin. It is nonclosed, and the missing boundary point with coordinates zero and one is infeasible without a strict image-cone separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the stated cone and map, \(A(K)=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2:a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\). This image cone is not closed, and \((0,1)\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\). Therefore the conic system \(A(X)=(0,1)\), \(X\in K\), is infeasible but has no strict separator from \(A(K)\). This example shows why strong conic alternatives require image closedness or another condition implying it.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\mathbb{S}^2_+\) is the closed cone of positive semidefinite symmetric \(2\times2\) matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(K)=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2:a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\) is not closed, and \((0,1)\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed semidefinite cone with a nonclosed linear image and a missing boundary right-hand side.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed conic image and failure of strict polar certification
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) be linear, and set \(Q:=A(K)\). For a cone \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), use the negative-polar convention \(S^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,s\rangle\leq0\ \forall s\in S\}\). Then \(Q^\circ=\{y:A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^\circ\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic feasibility with an exact linear image. The cone \(K\) is closed, but its image \(A(K)\) is not assumed closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A target \(b\in\mathbb R^n\) lies at a nonclosed cone-image boundary for \((A,K)\) when \[b\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K).\] Equivalently, the conic system \[x\in K,\qquad Ax=b\] is infeasible, while \(b\) satisfies every homogeneous polar inequality valid on \(A(K)\): \[\langle y,b\rangle\leq0\qquad\forall y\in\mathbb R^n\ \text{such that}\ A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^\circ.\] Thus the usual strict polar certificate set \[\mathcal Y_>(b):=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^\circ,\ \langle y,b\rangle>0\}\] is empty even though the exact conic system is infeasible. This is precisely the boundary where polar inequalities characterize \(\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\), rather than the possibly nonclosed image \(A(K)\) itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone and let \(Q=A(K)\) be its image under a linear map. A target \(b\) is at a nonclosed cone-image boundary when it belongs to the closure of \(Q\) but not to \(Q\). The exact system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is then infeasible, but no vector \(y\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^\circ\) strictly separates \(b\) from the image. Equivalently, every such polar vector satisfies \(\langle y,b\rangle\leq0\). Hence homogeneous polar certificates distinguish points outside the closure of the image, but cannot distinguish a missing boundary point from an attainable image point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[b\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b\notin A(K),\ \mathcal Y_>(b)=\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The boundary condition is \(b\in Q^{\circ\circ}\setminus Q\), since \(Q^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}Q\).
It is equivalent to the existence of a sequence \((x_k)\subset K\) such that \(Ax_k\to b\), together with the nonexistence of any \(x\in K\) satisfying \(Ax=b\).
It is equivalent to \(\operatorname{dist}(b,A(K))=0\) and \(b\notin A(K)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A(K)\) is closed, then \(\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)=\varnothing\), so no boundary target exists.
If \(K\) is finitely generated, then \(A(K)\) is also finitely generated and therefore closed; the nonclosed-image boundary is empty in this polyhedral case.
immediate_consequences_latex: An infeasible boundary target cannot possess a strict homogeneous Farkas separator \(y\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y\in K^\circ\) and \(\langle y,b\rangle>0\).
Replacing the exact image \(A(K)\) by its bipolar loses precisely the distinction between attainable points and missing points in \(\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\).
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(K\) alone does not assert closedness of its linear image \(A(K)\).
The definition concerns failure of strict separation at a missing image point; it does not declare the primal system approximately feasible under any metric other than the ambient Euclidean topology.
With the positive-polar convention, all displayed polar inequalities reverse sign.

notation.meaning: The convex cone obtained as the linear image of \(K\).
Negative polar cone \(\{y:\langle y,s\rangle\leq0\ \forall s\in S\}\).
Strict homogeneous polar certificates separating \(b\) from \(A(K)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-distance infeasibility and zero-margin separation certificates
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,C_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty convex sets. Define \(d(C_1,C_2):=\inf\{\|x_1-x_2\|:x_1\in C_1,\ x_2\in C_2\}\). A normalized separating normal is a vector \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(\|u\|=1\) and \(\inf_{x_1\in C_1}\langle u,x_1\rangle\geq\sup_{x_2\in C_2}\langle u,x_2\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Closedness and boundedness are not assumed unless explicitly stated in a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infeasible intersection pair \((C_1,C_2)\) is at a zero-margin certificate boundary when \[C_1\cap C_2=\varnothing\qquad\text{and}\qquad d(C_1,C_2)=0.\] Equivalently, \[0\in\operatorname{cl}(C_1-C_2)\setminus(C_1-C_2).\] For a normalized separating normal \(u\), define its certificate margin by \[\delta(u):=\inf_{x_1\in C_1}\langle u,x_1\rangle-\sup_{x_2\in C_2}\langle u,x_2\rangle.\] At a zero-margin boundary, normalized separating normals exist, but every one satisfies \(\delta(u)=0\); no normal has \(\delta(u)>0\). Consequently the sets admit weak proper separation but admit no strong separation by opposing open halfspaces with a positive buffer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty convex sets form a zero-margin certificate boundary when they are disjoint but their Euclidean distance is zero. Equivalently, the origin is a limit point of their difference set \(C_1-C_2\) without belonging to that difference set. A separating normal can still place the sets in opposing closed halfspaces, but the difference between the lower support value on \(C_1\) and the upper support value on \(C_2\) is necessarily zero. Thus the infeasibility has a separating certificate only at zero margin and cannot be certified by strong separation with a positive gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic definition in a real vector space; closedness, pointedness, and full dimensionality are not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space. A nonempty subset \(C\subseteq X\) is a convex cone if it is closed under nonnegative linear combinations: for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\alpha,\beta\geq 0\), one has \(\alpha x+\beta y\in C\). Equivalently, for every integer \(m\geq 1\), every \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\), and all \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq 0\), the conic combination \(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i x_i\) belongs to \(C\). In particular, \(0\in C\), and \(C\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is a nonempty set closed under every finite linear combination with nonnegative coefficients; consequently it contains zero and is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C\text{ is a convex cone}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\forall x,y\in C)(\forall \alpha,\beta\geq 0)\;\alpha x+\beta y\in C.\]

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(S\subseteq V\), and let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hierarchy records internal generation, topological completion, intrinsic linear geometry, and normalized affine sections in finite dimensions. It is a structured collection of representations, not an assertion that every cone has a finite generator set or compact base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone representation hierarchy associated with \(S\) and \(K=\operatorname{cone}(S)\) is the system \[S\longmapsto K=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i s_i:m\in\mathbb N,\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}\longmapsto\overline K,\] together with the intrinsic spaces \[\operatorname{span}K=K-K,\qquad \operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K),\] and, whenever a linear functional \(u\in V^*\) satisfies \(u(x)>0\) for every \(x\in K\setminus\{0\}\), the transverse section \[B_u=K\cap\{x:u(x)=1\},\qquad K=\{\lambda b:\lambda\geq0,\ b\in B_u\}.\] A finite internal representation occurs when \(S\) may be chosen finite; a closed representation replaces \(K\) by \(\overline K\); and the quotient representation is the image of \(K\) in \(V/\operatorname{lin}K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from directions in a set, the hierarchy first forms all finite nonnegative combinations, then optionally takes the closure. It also records the span, the largest linear subspace contained in the cone, the cone modulo that subspace, and any transverse normalized section supplied by a strictly positive linear functional. Finite generation and compact-section representations are additional regimes, not universal properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak R(K)=\bigl(K,\overline K,\operatorname{span}K,\operatorname{lin}K,K/\operatorname{lin}K,\{B_u\}_u\bigr)\] with each displayed component defined by the stated generation, closure, linear, quotient, or section operation.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{cone}(S)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{s\in S}\{\lambda s:\lambda\geq0\}\right).\]
For a convex cone containing \(0\), \(\operatorname{span}K=K-K=\operatorname{aff}K\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}\), then \(K=\{A\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\}\), where the columns of \(A\) are the generators.
If \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\), the quotient stage leaves \(K\) unchanged up to the canonical identification.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonzero \(x\in K\) intersects a base \(B_u\) at the unique normalized point \(x/u(x)\).
The inclusions \(K\subseteq\overline K\subseteq\operatorname{span}K\) separate topological completion from intrinsic linear dimension.
boundary_notes: A cone can be infinitely generated, nonclosed, nonpointed, or lack a compact base; the hierarchy does not identify these regimes.
The term “cone representation hierarchy” packages several standard constructions and is not a universally standardized single object.

notation.meaning: Conic hull formed from finite nonnegative combinations of elements of the set.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a real vector space and let \(K\subseteq V\). The convention in this record includes \(0\) in every cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is an algebraic definition. Closedness requires a specified topology and is treated as an additional property rather than part of the meaning of convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(K\) is a cone if \[0\in K\quad\text{and}\quad (x\in K,\ \lambda\geq0)\Longrightarrow \lambda x\in K.\] It is a convex cone if, in addition, \[(x,y\in K,\ \alpha,\beta\geq0)\Longrightarrow \alpha x+\beta y\in K.\] Equivalently, a cone is convex precisely when it is closed under addition. A convex cone is pointed when \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\), and it is a linear subspace precisely when \(K=-K\). In a topological vector space, it is a closed convex cone when it is both convex conic and topologically closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone contains the origin and is stable under multiplication by nonnegative scalars. A convex cone is stable under every two-term nonnegative linear combination, equivalently under addition as well as nonnegative scaling. Pointed cones contain no nontrivial line, while a cone symmetric under sign change is a linear subspace. Closedness is a separate topological condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\text{ is a convex cone}\iff \forall x,y\in K\ \forall\alpha,\beta\geq0:\ \alpha x+\beta y\in K.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a cone containing \(0\), \[K\text{ convex}\iff K+K\subseteq K.\]
\[K\text{ is a subspace}\iff K\text{ is a convex cone and }K=-K.\]
special_cases_latex: The ray \(\{\lambda v:\lambda\geq0\}\) is a pointed convex cone when \(v\neq0\).
Every linear subspace is a convex cone, but it is pointed only when it equals \(\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finite nonnegative combination of elements of a convex cone again belongs to the cone.
An arbitrary intersection of convex cones is a convex cone.
boundary_notes: Some authors define a cone using only positive scaling and do not require the origin; this record uses the nonnegative-scaling convention.
A scaling-invariant set need not be convex, and a convex cone need not be closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rays, incidence, and extreme rays of a cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a real vector space, let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone containing \(0\), and let \(v\in K\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definitions are algebraic and scaling invariant. Extreme-ray incidence requires convexity of the ambient cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ray generated by \(v\) is \[R(v)=\mathbb R_+v=\{\lambda v:\lambda\geq0\}.\] A point \(x\in K\setminus\{0\}\) is incident with this ray when \(x\in R(v)\), equivalently when \(R(x)=R(v)\). The ray \(R(v)\) is an extreme ray of \(K\) when \[x,y\in K,\quad x+y\in R(v)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x,y\in R(v).\] Thus the nonzero elements of \(K\) are partitioned by the equivalence relation \(x\sim y\iff x=\lambda y\) for some \(\lambda>0\), and the extreme classes are exactly those whose rays satisfy the displayed decomposition condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each nonzero cone point determines the half-line obtained by nonnegative scaling. Two nonzero points have the same incident ray exactly when one is a positive multiple of the other. Such a ray is extreme when a sum of two cone points can lie on it only if both summands already lie on that same ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal R(K)=(K\setminus\{0\})/\!\sim,\qquad x\sim y\iff \exists\lambda>0:\ x=\lambda y,\] with extreme members characterized by \[x+y\in R,\ x,y\in K\Longrightarrow x,y\in R.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(u\in R(v)\setminus\{0\}\), extremality is equivalently \[u=\tfrac12(x+y),\ x,y\in K\Longrightarrow x,y\in R(v).\]
A ray \(R\subseteq K\) is extreme exactly when it is a one-dimensional face of \(K\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), its extreme rays are \(\mathbb R_+e_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
A one-dimensional pointed cone has exactly one nonzero ray class.
immediate_consequences_latex: The incidence relation is unchanged when a generator is replaced by a positive multiple.
Distinct rays intersect only at \(0\).
boundary_notes: A line \(\mathbb Rv\) contains two opposite rays and is not itself a ray under this convention.
For a nonconvex cone, ray incidence remains defined, but the extreme-ray decomposition criterion is not the standard facial notion.

notation.meaning: Ray generated by a nonzero cone vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set is a convex cone exactly when it is closed under addition and multiplication by nonnegative scalars.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(K\subseteq V\) is a convex cone if and only if it is closed under nonnegative linear combinations: for every \(x,y\in K\) and \(\alpha,\beta\in[0,\infty)\), one has \(\alpha x+\beta y\in K\). Consequently, \(0\in K\), \(K+K\subseteq K\), and \(\lambda K\subseteq K\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\). Conversely, these additive and nonnegative-scaling closure properties imply closure under every nonnegative linear combination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\text{ is a convex cone}\iff (\forall x,y\in K)(\forall \alpha,\beta\ge 0),\ \alpha x+\beta y\in K.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic characterization of convex cones in a real vector space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality as the Largest Subspace of a Convex Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic algebraic structure of an arbitrary convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq V\), its lineality space is \(\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\). It is a vector subspace of \(V\), and every vector subspace contained in \(K\) is contained in \(\operatorname{lin}K\). Consequently, \(K\) is pointed if and only if \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\), while \(K\) is a vector subspace if and only if \(K=\operatorname{lin}K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone's intersection with its negative is its largest contained vector subspace; its triviality is exactly pointedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)\text{ is the largest vector subspace contained in }K.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality as the Largest Subspace of a Convex Cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Span and Difference Representation of a Convex Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic description of the linear hull generated by a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space, then \(K-K:=\{x-y:x,y\in K\}\) is a vector subspace and \[K-K=\operatorname{span}K=\operatorname{aff}K.\] Thus every vector in the linear hull of \(K\) is the difference of two elements of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linear and affine hulls of a convex cone coincide and equal its difference set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K-K=\operatorname{span}K=\operatorname{aff}K.

notation.meaning: set of differences of two cone elements

knowledge_statements.title: Span and Difference Representation of a Convex Cone
Intrinsic Structure of a Ray
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray and its opposite meet only at zero and together form their one-dimensional span; a ray is pointed and has no nontrivial proper face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ne0\), \(R_d\cap R_{-d}=\{0\}\), \(\operatorname{span}R_d=\mathbb{R}d\), and \(\mathbb{R}d=R_d\cup R_{-d}\). Thus \(R_d\) is pointed, and its only faces as a cone in \(\mathbb{R}d\) are \(\{0\}\) and \(R_d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_d\cap R_{-d}=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{span}R_d=\mathbb{R}d=R_d\cup R_{-d}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic geometry of an origin-based ray, independent of incidence with a larger cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Ray Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic ray consists of all nonnegative multiples of one nonzero direction; two directions generate the same ray exactly when they are positive multiples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ray generated by a nonzero vector \(d\in V\) is \(R_d:=\{\lambda d:\lambda\in[0,\infty)\}\). It is a one-dimensional convex cone with endpoint \(0\). For nonzero \(d,e\in V\), the rays coincide precisely when their directions differ by a positive scalar: \(R_d=R_e\) if and only if \(e=\mu d\) for some \(\mu>0\). Thus a ray is determined by a positive-scaling equivalence class of nonzero directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_d=\{\lambda d:\lambda\ge0\}\), and \(R_d=R_e\iff e=\mu d\) for some \(\mu>0\).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Origin-based rays relevant to conic geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional intrinsic topological geometry of a ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\neq0\) in a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(R_d=\{\lambda d:\lambda\ge0\}\). Then \(R_d\) is a closed, pointed, one-dimensional convex cone with \(\operatorname{span}R_d=\mathbb Rd\). Relative to \(\mathbb Rd\), \[\operatorname{ri}R_d=\{\lambda d:\lambda>0\},\qquad \operatorname{relbd}R_d=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray is a closed pointed one-dimensional cone; its nonzero points form its relative interior and the origin its relative boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ri}R_d=R_d\setminus\{0\},\quad \operatorname{relbd}R_d=\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Topology of a Ray
Interior and Boundary Placement of Contained Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All nonzero points of a contained ray have the same relative-interior or relative-boundary status; the origin is relatively boundary unless the cone is a subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda>0\), \(d\in\operatorname{ri}K\) if and only if \(\lambda d\in\operatorname{ri}K\). Consequently, either \(R_d\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\operatorname{ri}K\) or \(R_d\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}K\), according as \(d\) is relatively interior or relatively boundary. Moreover, \(0\in\operatorname{rbd}K\) unless \(K\) is a linear subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\in\operatorname{ri}K\iff \lambda d\in\operatorname{ri}K\quad(\lambda>0).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative placement of a contained ray, using the cone's intrinsic span.

knowledge_statements.title: Rays within Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone contains a generated ray exactly when it contains its direction. The ray is extreme when every conic decomposition along it uses vectors on that ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ne0\), the ray \(R_d:=\{\lambda d:\lambda\ge0\}\) is contained in \(K\) if and only if \(d\in K\). Such a ray is an extreme ray of \(K\) if and only if, whenever \(u,v\in K\) satisfy \(u+v\in R_d\), both \(u\) and \(v\) belong to \(R_d\). Equivalently, \(R_d\) is a one-dimensional face of \(K\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a real vector space \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_d\text{ is extreme in }K\iff [u,v\in K,\ u+v\in R_d\Rightarrow u,v\in R_d].\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Membership and extremality criteria for rays contained in a convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed, relatively closed, and nonclosed cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional normed real vector space and let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone containing \(0\). Put \(L=\operatorname{span}K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness is taken in the norm topology. Relative closedness is measured in the intrinsic space \(L\), not necessarily in the whole ambient presentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) is closed when \[K=\overline K^{\,V},\] equivalently, every convergent sequence \((x_j)\subseteq K\) has its limit in \(K\). It is relatively closed in its span when \[K=\overline K^{\,L}.\] It is nonclosed when \(K\subsetneq\overline K^{\,V}\); the missing-boundary set is \[\partial_{\mathrm{miss}}K=\overline K^{\,V}\setminus K.\] The closed conic hull of a set \(S\subseteq V\) is \[\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(S)=\operatorname{cl}_V\!\left(\operatorname{cone}(S)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is closed when it contains all of its ambient limit points. It is relatively closed when the same requirement is imposed only inside its linear span. A nonclosed cone omits at least one point of its closure, and the omitted points form its missing boundary. Closing a convex cone preserves both convexity and conic scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\text{ closed}\iff K=\operatorname{cl}_V K,\qquad K\text{ nonclosed}\iff \operatorname{cl}_V K\setminus K\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: In finite dimensions, \[K\text{ closed}\iff \bigl(x_j\in K,\ x_j\to x\bigr)\Longrightarrow x\in K.\]
Since \(K\subseteq L\) and \(L\) is closed, relative closedness in \(L\) is equivalent to ambient closedness in \(V\).
special_cases_latex: Every finitely generated convex cone in a finite-dimensional space is closed.

The open positive orthant together with \(0\) is conic but is not convex; the strictly positive orthant without \(0\) illustrates the alternative convention under which a cone need not contain its vertex.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\overline K\) is a closed convex cone containing \(K\).
The closure operation does not change the span: \(\operatorname{span}(\overline K)=\operatorname{span}K\).
boundary_notes: In infinite-dimensional spaces, sequential closedness and topological closedness can differ outside metrizable settings.
Closedness of a cone does not imply pointedness, solidity, finite generation, or polyhedrality.

notation.meaning: Closure of the cone in the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is closed when it contains all of its ambient limit points; in first-countable spaces, it contains every limit of a convergent sequence from the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(K\) in a topological real vector space \(V\) is closed when it contains every limit in \(V\) of a convergent net of its points; equivalently, \(\overline K=K\). If \(V\) is first countable, this is equivalent to: whenever \((x_n)\subseteq K\) and \(x_n\to x\in V\), one has \(x\in K\). Closedness is taken in the ambient topology, not merely in \(\operatorname{span}K\).
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\text{ is closed}\iff \overline K=K.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stability under Intersections, Preimages, and Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic constructions preserving closed convex conicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a topological real vector space. Any intersection of closed convex cones in \(V\) is a closed convex cone. If \(T:U\to V\) is continuous and linear and \(K\subseteq V\) is a closed convex cone, then \(T^{-1}(K)\) is a closed convex cone in \(U\). Finite Cartesian products of closed convex cones are closed convex cones in the product topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex cones remain closed under arbitrary intersections, continuous linear preimages, and finite Cartesian products.
assumptions_latex: Every cone under consideration is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_{i\in I}K_i,\quad T^{-1}(K),\quad K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\text{ are closed convex cones}.

notation.meaning: Set preimage of the cone under a continuous linear map.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability under Intersections, Preimages, and Products
Equivalent Tests for a Nonclosed Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is nonclosed exactly when it omits a point of its closure, equivalently a limit of a net—or, in first-countable spaces, a sequence—of its own points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a topological real vector space \(V\). Then \[K\text{ is nonclosed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K\subsetneq\overline K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \overline K\setminus K\neq\varnothing.\] Equivalently, some net in \(K\) converges in \(V\) to a point outside \(K\). If \(V\) is first countable, the net may be replaced by a sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ nonclosed}\iff K\subsetneq\overline K\iff \overline K\setminus K\neq\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General topological characterization complementing the seed's concrete planar example.

notation.meaning: Ambient topological closure of the cone

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open upper half-plane together with the origin is a convex cone, but it omits nonzero points on its limiting boundary and is therefore nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\). Then \(K\) is a convex cone, \(K\) is not closed, and \(\overline K=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y\ge0\}\). The sequence \((1,1/n)\in K\) converges to the omitted boundary point \((1,0)\notin K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K:=\{(x,y):y>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\text{ is a convex cone but is not closed}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete planar example separating convex conicity from closedness.

notation.meaning: a nonclosed convex cone in the plane

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological characterization of nonclosedness, excluding the separately owned closure construction and geometric boundary-loss mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a topological vector space \(V\). Then \(K\) is nonclosed if and only if \(\overline K\setminus K\neq\varnothing\). Equivalently, some net \((x_i)\subseteq K\) converges to a point \(x\notin K\). If \(V\) is first countable, the net may be replaced by a sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is nonclosed exactly when it omits a limit point; nets detect this generally, while sequences suffice in first-countable spaces.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is nonclosed}\iff \overline K\setminus K\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Characterizations of a Nonclosed Cone
Closure Completion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a convex cone produces the smallest closed convex cone containing it and preserves all conic and convex operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closure \(\overline K\) of a convex cone \(K\) is itself a closed convex cone. Moreover, it is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(K\): 
\[
\overline K=\bigcap\{C\subseteq V:C\text{ is a closed convex cone and }K\subseteq C\}.
\]
Thus closure adds exactly the ambient limit points required for closedness while preserving addition, nonnegative scaling, and convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline K=\bigcap\{C\subseteq V:C\text{ is a closed convex cone and }K\subseteq C\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure as the minimal closed convex-cone completion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure under Products and Linear Coordinate Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functorial properties of closure that do not assume general image closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_i\) be convex cones in topological vector spaces \(V_i\). For every finite family, \[\overline{K_1\times\cdots\times K_r}=\overline{K_1}\times\cdots\times\overline{K_r}.\] If \(T:V\to W\) is a linear homeomorphism, then \[T(\overline K)=\overline{T(K)}.\] For a merely continuous linear map, only \[T(\overline K)\subseteq\overline{T(K)}\] is automatic; equality can fail when the image of a closed cone is nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure commutes with finite products and linear homeomorphisms. Under a general continuous linear map only one inclusion is automatic.
assumptions_latex: All spaces carry their specified vector-space topologies.
\(T\) is a linear homeomorphism for equality, or continuous and linear for the inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{\prod_iK_i}=\prod_i\overline{K_i},\quad T(\overline K)=\overline{T(K)}\text{ for a linear homeomorphism},\quad T(\overline K)\subseteq\overline{T(K)}\text{ for continuous linear }T.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure under Products and Linear Coordinate Changes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure as an Idempotent Monotone Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic laws of the cone-closure transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex cones \(K,L\) in a topological real vector space, \[K\subseteq\overline K,\qquad K\subseteq L\Longrightarrow\overline K\subseteq\overline L,\qquad \overline{\overline K}=\overline K.\] Moreover, \[\overline K=K\iff K\text{ is closed}.\] Thus closure is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, with closed convex cones as its fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone closure is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, and its fixed points are exactly the closed convex cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K,L\) are convex cones in a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\subseteq\overline K,\quad K\subseteq L\Rightarrow\overline K\subseteq\overline L,\quad \overline{\overline K}=\overline K,\quad \overline K=K\iff K\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure as an Idempotent Monotone Completion
Kernel-Saturation Criterion for Image Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image of a closed cone is closed exactly when enlarging the cone along the map's kernel produces a closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone and let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. Then \[T(K)\text{ is closed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K+\ker T\text{ is closed}.\] Thus image boundary loss occurs exactly when saturation of \(K\) along the fibers of \(T\) is nonclosed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(K)\text{ is closed}\iff K+\ker T\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural criterion for boundary loss under a linear map.

knowledge_statements.title: Escaping-Preimage Mechanism
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary point missing from a finite-dimensional linear image is approached by images of preimages that escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. If \(y\in\overline{T(K)}\setminus T(K)\), then there exists a sequence \((x_j)\subseteq K\) such that \[Tx_j\to y\qquad\text{and}\qquad \|x_j\|\to\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists (x_j)\subseteq K:\ Tx_j\to y\text{ and }\|x_j\|\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary sequential mechanism for a missing boundary point of a finite-dimensional linear image.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Loss Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete convex cone made nonclosed by deleting nonzero boundary rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
K:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
Then \(K\) is a convex cone but is not closed. For every \(a\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\), the sequence \((a,1/k)\in K\) converges to \((a,0)\notin K\). Its closure is
\[
\overline K=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\geq0\}.
\]
Thus removing the nonzero boundary rays of a closed half-space cone preserves convex conic operations but destroys closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open upper half-plane together with the origin is a convex cone, but sequences approaching its deleted horizontal boundary show that it is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is a nonclosed convex cone with \(\overline K=\{(x,y):y\geq0\}\).

notation.meaning: upper open half-plane augmented by the origin

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural criterion for boundary loss under a linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone and let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. Then
\[
T(K)\text{ is closed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K+\ker T\text{ is closed}.
\]
Hence boundary loss under \(T\) occurs exactly when saturating \(K\) along fibers of \(T\) produces a nonclosed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image of a closed cone is closed exactly when the cone enlarged along the map's kernel is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(K)\text{ is closed}\iff K+\ker T\text{ is closed}.

notation.meaning: Kernel of the linear map T

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Criterion for Image Closedness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded-Fiber Witness for a Missing Image Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary sequential mechanism for a nonclosed image in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. If \(T(K)\) is not closed, then there exist \(x_j\in K\) and \(y\notin T(K)\) such that
\[
Tx_j\to y\qquad\text{and}\qquad \|x_j\|\to\infty.
\]
Thus a finite-dimensional linear image can lose a boundary point only through an escaping sequence of preimages; bounded preimages would have a convergent subsequence whose limit lies in \(K\) and maps to \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every missing boundary point of a finite-dimensional linear image is approached through preimages escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x_j\in K,\ \exists y\notin T(K):\ Tx_j\to y\text{ and }\|x_j\|\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Fiber Witness for a Missing Image Boundary

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a real vector space and let \(S\subseteq V\) be arbitrary, possibly empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Only finite conic combinations are used. No closure operation is implicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic hull of \(S\) is \[\operatorname{cone}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i s_i:m\in\mathbb N,\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}\cup\{0\}.\] Equivalently, it is the intersection of all convex cones containing \(S\): \[\operatorname{cone}(S)=\bigcap\{K\subseteq V:K\text{ is a convex cone and }S\subseteq K\}.\] Thus \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) is the smallest convex cone containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic hull consists of the origin and all finite linear combinations of points of the set with nonnegative coefficients. It is characterized intrinsically as the smallest convex cone containing the set. Taking a conic hull does not take limits, so it need not produce a closed set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{cone}(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i s_i:m<\infty,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ s_i\in S\right\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{cone}(S)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{s\in S}\mathbb R_+s\right).\]
If \(S\neq\varnothing\), \[\operatorname{cone}(S)=\{\lambda x:\lambda\geq0,\ x\in\operatorname{conv}S\}.\]
special_cases_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(\varnothing)=\{0\}\) under the stated convention.
For \(S=\{v\}\) with \(v\neq0\), \(\operatorname{cone}(S)=\mathbb R_+v\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(S\subseteq T\), then \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\subseteq\operatorname{cone}(T)\).
\(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{cone}(S))=\operatorname{cone}(S)\).
boundary_notes: The closed conic hull is \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}(S)}\) and may strictly contain the conic hull.
The affine hull and convex hull use different coefficient constraints and should not be substituted for the conic hull.

children.title: Finite Conic Hulls
children.top_down_role: Cones generated by finite direction systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Membership as Nonnegative Linear Feasibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership is feasibility of a linear system in nonnegative coefficients and is polynomial-time solvable for rational data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\) and \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_m]\), \(x\in K\) if and only if \(A\lambda=x\) is feasible with \(\lambda\ge0\). For rational binary input, this linear-feasibility problem is solvable in polynomial time by polynomial-time linear-programming algorithms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in K\iff \exists\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m:\ A\lambda=x.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical membership formulation for a cone given by finitely many generators.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Conic Hulls Are Closed Polyhedral Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite conic hull in finite-dimensional space is the linear image of a nonnegative orthant and is a closed polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_m]\), \(\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}=A\mathbb{R}_+^m\). In finite-dimensional space this is a polyhedral convex cone and hence is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}=A\mathbb{R}_+^m\text{ is closed and polyhedral}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural consequence of finite generation.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Conic Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite conic hull of given directions consists of all their nonnegative linear combinations and is the smallest convex cone containing them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For directions \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in V\), their finite conic hull is
\[
\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\in[0,\infty)\right\}.
\]
It is the smallest convex cone containing every \(a_i\): if \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone and \(a_i\in C\) for all \(i\), then \(\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\subseteq C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}=\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\ge0\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite generation by nonnegative linear combinations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}\subseteq V\) be finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: “Finite” refers to the number of available generating directions, not merely to the fact that each individual conic combination has finite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite conic hull generated by \(G\) is \[\operatorname{cone}(G)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i g_i:\lambda_i\geq0\right\}.\] A convex cone \(K\subseteq V\) is finitely generated when there exist \(m<\infty\) and vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\in V\) such that \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}\). Equivalently, after choosing coordinates and the matrix \(A=[g_1\ \cdots\ g_m]\), \[K=A\mathbb R_+^m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite conic hull is formed from a fixed finite list of directions using arbitrary nonnegative coefficients. A cone is finitely generated if it admits such a list. In coordinates it is the linear image of a finite-dimensional nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\text{ finitely generated}\iff \exists m<\infty\ \exists A: \mathbb R^m\to V\text{ linear with }K=A\mathbb R_+^m.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[K=\operatorname{cone}\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}\iff \forall x\in K\ \exists\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m:\ x=A\lambda.\]
In finite dimensions, a convex cone is finitely generated if and only if it is polyhedral.
special_cases_latex: If the generators are linearly independent, each \(x\in K\) has a unique coefficient vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\).
Including a zero generator does not change the conic hull.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finitely generated convex cone in finite dimensions is closed.
Removing a generator \(g_i\) leaves the same cone exactly when \(g_i\in\operatorname{cone}(G\setminus\{g_i\})\).
boundary_notes: Different finite generator lists may define the same cone.
An infinitely generated cone may still have sparse representations of individual points; that does not make the cone finitely generated.

children.title: Infinitely Generated Cones
children.top_down_role: Cones generated by arbitrary families and measures of directions.

knowledge_statements.title: A Closed Cone Requiring Infinitely Many Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-dimensional Lorentz cone is closed but not finitely generated because its circular boundary has uncountably many extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Lorentz cone \(L_3=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^2:t\ge\|u\|_2\}\) is closed, convex, and pointed. Its rays \(\mathbb{R}_+(1,v)\), \(\|v\|_2=1\), are pairwise distinct extreme rays. Hence \(L_3\) has uncountably many extreme rays and is not finitely generated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_3\ne\operatorname{cone}F\quad\text{for every finite }F\subseteq L_3.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional example separating infinite generation from nonclosedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Measure Conic Generation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finitely supported positive measures recover algebraic conic combinations, while general integrable positive measures produce points in the closed conic hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be measurable. If \(\mu\) is a finite positive measure on \(S\) with \(\int_S\|s\|\,d\mu(s)<\infty\), then \(\int_S s\,d\mu(s)\in\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\). Finitely supported positive measures give exactly the finite conic combinations; a general positive-measure barycenter need not belong to \(\operatorname{cone}S\) when that cone is nonclosed.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite positive measure with \(\int_S\|s\|\,d\mu(s)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int_S s\,d\mu(s)\in\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-valued extension of finite conic combinations when the vector integral exists.

notation.meaning: finite positive measure on the generating family

knowledge_statements.title: Infinitely Generated Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinitely generated cone requires no finite subfamily of its directions, although every point in its algebraic conic hull still uses only finitely many directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an arbitrary family \(S\subseteq V\), its algebraic conic hull is
\[
\operatorname{cone}S:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i s_i:n\in\mathbb N,\ s_i\in S,\lambda_i\ge0\right\},
\]
with the empty sum supplying \(0\). The cone is infinitely generated relative to \(S\) when no finite subset \(F\subseteq S\) satisfies \(\operatorname{cone}F=\operatorname{cone}S\). Infinite generation concerns the required family of directions; each individual algebraic conic combination remains finite.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq V\) is not contained in the conic hull of any finite subset of itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}S=\{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i s_i:n\in\mathbb N,\ s_i\in S,\lambda_i\ge0\}\) is not finitely generated by members of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic conic hulls use finite sums even when the generating family is infinite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrary Conic Hulls Need Not Be Closed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological failure motivating the separate closed-conic-hull construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{(1,t):t>0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2\). Then \[\operatorname{cone}(S)=\{0\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\},\] which is not closed; for example, \((1,1/n)\to(1,0)\notin\operatorname{cone}(S)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\text{ is not closed}.\)
