knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact Measure Generation Equals Algebraic Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure representation for compact direction sets in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be compact. Then \[\left\{\int_S s\,d\mu(s):\mu\text{ is a finite nonnegative Borel measure on }S\right\}=\operatorname{cone}(S).\] Thus every such measure integral has a finitely supported atomic representation, while every finite conic combination is obtained from an atomic measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact finite-dimensional direction set, nonnegative measure integrals and finite conic combinations generate the same cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite nonnegative Borel measure on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\int_S s\,d\mu(s):\mu\ge0\text{ finite}\}=\operatorname{cone}(S).\)

notation.meaning: finite nonnegative Borel measure on the direction set

children.title: Closed Conic Hulls
children.top_down_role: Closure-sensitive completion of generated cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Can Add Missing Boundary Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic hull of the strictly positive-slope directions is the open positive quadrant plus zero; closure adds both boundary rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=\{(1,t):t>0\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\operatorname{cone}S=\{0\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\}\), whereas \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S=\mathbb{R}_+^2\). Thus closure adds both coordinate boundary rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cone}S\ne\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S=\mathbb{R}_+^2.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Planar example showing that closure cannot generally be omitted.

notation.meaning: closed nonnegative orthant in the plane

knowledge_statements.title: Limit Representation of the Closed Conic Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the closed conic hull exactly when it is a limit of finite nonnegative combinations of generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(x\) belongs to \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\) if and only if there is a sequence \(x_n=\sum_{i=1}^{m_n}\lambda_{n,i}s_{n,i}\), where each \(m_n\) is finite, \(\lambda_{n,i}\ge0\), and \(s_{n,i}\in S\), such that \(x_n\to x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\iff \exists (x_n)\subseteq\operatorname{cone}S\text{ with }x_n\to x.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Conic Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed conic hull is the closure of the algebraic conic hull, equivalently the smallest closed convex cone containing the generating set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed conic hull of \(S\) is defined by \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S:=\overline{\operatorname{cone}S}\), where closure is taken in \(V\). It admits the intersection representation
\[
\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S=\bigcap\{C\subseteq V:C\text{ is a closed convex cone and }S\subseteq C\}.
\]
Therefore it is the unique smallest closed convex cone containing \(S\). In general, closure is essential because \(\operatorname{cone}S\) need not itself be closed.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S=\overline{\operatorname{cone}S}=\bigcap\{C:C\text{ is a closed convex cone and }S\subseteq C\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological completion of the algebraic conic hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Conic Hull as a Closure Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic laws of closed-conic completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For subsets \(S,T\) of a topological real vector space, write \(\operatorname{ccone}(S):=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\). Then \[S\subseteq\operatorname{ccone}(S),\qquad S\subseteq T\Rightarrow\operatorname{ccone}(S)\subseteq\operatorname{ccone}(T),\qquad \operatorname{ccone}(\operatorname{ccone}(S))=\operatorname{ccone}(S).\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{ccone}(S)=S\) exactly when \(S\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed conic hull is an extensive, monotone, idempotent operation whose fixed points are precisely the closed convex cones.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ccone}\text{ is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, with fixed points equal to the closed convex cones}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intrinsic span and lineality of a convex cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a real vector space and let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The objects depend only on the subset \(K\), not on a chosen generator list or coordinate representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The intrinsic linear hull of \(K\) is the smallest linear subspace containing it, \[\operatorname{span}K=K-K=\{x-y:x,y\in K\}.\] The lineality space of \(K\) is the largest linear subspace contained in it, \[\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)=\{d:d\in K,\ -d\in K\}.\] The intrinsic dimension of \(K\) is \[\dim K:=\dim(\operatorname{span}K).\] The cone is pointed exactly when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\), and it is full-dimensional in \(V\) exactly when \(\operatorname{span}K=V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone carries two canonical subspaces. Its span is the smallest subspace that can contain it, while its lineality is the largest subspace lying inside it. Intrinsic dimension means the dimension of the span. Pointedness means that the lineality space is trivial, and full dimensionality means that the intrinsic span equals the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{lin}K\subseteq K\subseteq\operatorname{span}K,\qquad \operatorname{span}K=K-K,\qquad \operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(0\in K\), \[\operatorname{span}K=\operatorname{aff}K.\]
\[d\in\operatorname{lin}K\iff x+td\in K\quad\forall x\in K,\ \forall t\in\mathbb R.\]
special_cases_latex: For a subspace \(L\), \(\operatorname{span}L=\operatorname{lin}L=L\).
For a nonzero ray \(R\), \(\operatorname{span}R\) is a line and \(\operatorname{lin}R=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Both \(\operatorname{span}K\) and \(\operatorname{lin}K\) are invariant under invertible linear changes of coordinates.
Any intrinsic study of \(K\) may restrict the ambient space from \(V\) to \(\operatorname{span}K\).
boundary_notes: The affine hull of a set not containing \(0\) need not be a linear subspace.
Lineality should not be confused with the span: the former lies inside the cone, whereas the latter generally contains negative directions absent from the cone.

notation.meaning: Smallest linear subspace containing the cone.
Largest linear subspace contained in the cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension of a cone through its linear span
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space \(V\), with \(0\in K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension is intrinsic: redundant ambient coordinates do not affect it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dimension of \(K\) is defined by \[\dim K=\dim(\operatorname{aff}K)=\dim(\operatorname{span}K).\] The equality is valid because a cone containing \(0\) has a linear affine hull. Moreover, \[\operatorname{span}K=K-K.\] Thus \(\dim K=r\) exactly when \(K-K\) is an \(r\)-dimensional subspace, or equivalently when \(K\) contains \(r\) linearly independent vectors but no \(r+1\) linearly independent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension of a cone is the dimension of the smallest subspace containing it. Because the cone contains the origin, its affine hull is already linear and equals both its span and its difference set. Consequently, cone dimension can be read from the maximum number of linearly independent cone vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\dim K=\dim(K-K)=\max\{|F|:F\subseteq K\text{ is linearly independent}\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\dim K=r\iff \exists v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K\text{ linearly independent and }K\subseteq\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\}.\]
\[K\text{ full-dimensional in }V\iff \dim K=\dim V\iff \operatorname{span}K=V.\]
special_cases_latex: Every nonzero ray has dimension \(1\), while a cone generated by linearly independent \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\) has dimension \(m\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(A:V\to W\) is linear, then \(\dim(AK)\leq\dim K\).
Embedding \(K\) into a larger ambient vector space without changing its span leaves \(\dim K\) unchanged.
boundary_notes: The number of generators in a particular representation may exceed \(\dim K\).
Dimension does not measure lineality: a pointed cone and a subspace can have the same dimension.

notation.meaning: Set of all differences of two cone elements.
Dimension of the linear span of the cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Span Functoriality and Generator Spans
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear span commutes with linear images, and a conic hull has the same linear span as its generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every linear map \(A:V\to U\), \[\operatorname{span}(A(C))=A(\operatorname{span}C).\] If \(C=\operatorname{cone}(G)\) for any family \(G\), then \[\operatorname{span}C=\operatorname{span}G.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{span}(A(C))=A(\operatorname{span}C)\), and \(C=\operatorname{cone}(G)\Rightarrow\operatorname{span}C=\operatorname{span}G\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functorial behavior of the cone's intrinsic supporting subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Span of a Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linear span of a convex cone equals all differences of two cone elements and is the cone's smallest containing linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty convex cone \(K\subseteq V\), its linear span satisfies
\[
\operatorname{span}K=K-K:=\{x-y:x,y\in K\}.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{span}K\) is the smallest linear subspace containing \(K\). When it is finite-dimensional, \(\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\) is the intrinsic dimension of the cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty convex cone in a real vector space \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{span}K=K-K=\{x-y:x,y\in K\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic ambient subspace generated by a convex cone.

notation.meaning: Minkowski difference of the cone with itself

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Span Does Not Commute with Intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of span calculus under cone intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex cones \(C,D\subseteq V\), \[\operatorname{span}(C\cap D)\subseteq\operatorname{span}C\cap\operatorname{span}D,\] but equality can fail. In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \[C=\operatorname{cone}(e_1,e_2),\qquad D=\operatorname{cone}(e_1,-e_2).\] Then \(C\cap D=\mathbb R_+e_1\), so \[\operatorname{span}(C\cap D)=\mathbb Re_1\subsetneq\mathbb R^2=\operatorname{span}C\cap\operatorname{span}D.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Span need not commute with intersections: two full-dimensional quadrant cones can intersect in only a ray.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are convex cones in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{span}(C\cap D)\subseteq\operatorname{span}C\cap\operatorname{span}D\), and the inclusion may be strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Span Does Not Commute with Intersections

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Span Calculus for Conic Images and Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic functorial properties of the cone's supporting linear space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\) be convex cones in a real vector space \(V\), and let \(T:V\to U\) be linear. Then \[\operatorname{span}(T(C))=T(\operatorname{span}C),\qquad \operatorname{span}(C+D)=\operatorname{span}C+\operatorname{span}D.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the span of a cone commutes with linear images and converts Minkowski sums of cones into sums of their supporting subspaces.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are convex cones in a real vector space \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{span}(T(C))=T(\operatorname{span}C)\) and \(\operatorname{span}(C+D)=\operatorname{span}C+\operatorname{span}D\).
knowledge_statements.title: Span Calculus for Conic Images and Sums
Intrinsic Dimension Under Linear Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image loses exactly the intrinsic dimensions lying in the map's kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear map \(A:V\to U\), \[\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}(A(C))=\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}(C)-\dim\bigl(\ker A\cap\operatorname{span}C\bigr).\] Hence intrinsic dimension is preserved exactly when \(A\) is injective on \(\operatorname{span}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}(A(C))=\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}(C)-\dim(\ker A\cap\operatorname{span}C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional transformation under linear images.

notation.meaning: Intrinsic directions annihilated by the map.

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Dimension of a Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone's intrinsic dimension is the dimension of its linear span; it equals the ambient dimension exactly when the cone is full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The intrinsic dimension of \(C\) is the dimension of its linear span:
\[
\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}(C):=\dim(\operatorname{span}C),\qquad \operatorname{span}C=C-C.
\]
Thus intrinsic dimension is independent of an embedding of \(C\) into a larger ambient space. The cone is full-dimensional in \(V\) precisely when \(\operatorname{span}C=V\), equivalently when \(\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}(C)=\dim V\).
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}(C)=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)\leq \dim V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition relative to the cone's linear hull.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional characterization using vectors selected from the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space. Then \[\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}C=\max\{k:\text{there exist linearly independent }c_1,\ldots,c_k\in C\}.\] Equivalently, \(C\) contains a basis of \(\operatorname{span}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intrinsic dimension is the largest number of linearly independent vectors selectable from the cone; equivalently, the cone contains a basis of its span.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}C=\max\{k:\exists\text{ linearly independent }c_1,\ldots,c_k\in C\}\).

notation.meaning: Dimension of the linear span of the cone

knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Vector Characterization of Intrinsic Dimension
Ambient and Intrinsic Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-dimensional cone, the entire closure is ambient boundary, whereas the intrinsic boundary excludes the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W=\operatorname{span}C\). Then \[\partial_W C=\operatorname{cl}_V C\setminus\operatorname{ri}_V C.\] If \(W\neq V\), then \[\partial_V C=\operatorname{cl}_V C.\] Thus points in the intrinsic interior of a lower-dimensional cone are nevertheless ambient-boundary points.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_W C=\operatorname{cl}_V C\setminus\operatorname{ri}_V C\), and \(W\neq V\Rightarrow\partial_V C=\operatorname{cl}_V C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary comparison complementary to the seed's interior comparison.

notation.meaning: Boundaries computed in the indicated ambient spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Versus Intrinsic Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty convex cone has nonempty interior within its span, but its ambient interior is nonempty only when the cone spans the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(0\in C\), the affine hull of \(C\) equals \(W=\operatorname{span}C\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{ri}_V C=\operatorname{int}_W C,
\]
and this set is nonempty. By contrast, the ambient interior satisfies
\[
\operatorname{int}_V C\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad W=V.
\]
Hence a lower-dimensional cone has empty ambient interior even though it has nonempty intrinsic, or relative, interior.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subseteq V\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}_V C=\operatorname{int}_W C\), and \(\operatorname{int}_V C\neq\varnothing\) exactly when \(W=V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares ambient topology with topology on the cone's span.

notation.meaning: Relative interior in the affine hull
Interior relative to the indicated space

children.title: Lineality Space
children.top_down_role: Reversible directions contained in a cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Space
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space consists of directions whose positive and negative multiples lie in the cone; it is the cone's largest contained linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lineality space of \(C\) is
\[
\operatorname{lin}(C):=C\cap(-C)=\{d\in V:d\in C\text{ and }-d\in C\}.
\]
It is a linear subspace, is contained in \(C\), and contains every linear subspace contained in \(C\). Its vectors are precisely the reversible conic directions. Moreover, translation along lineality preserves the cone:
\[
C+\operatorname{lin}(C)=C.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(C)=C\cap(-C)\) is the largest linear subspace contained in \(C\), and \(C+\operatorname{lin}(C)=C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic definition valid without closedness or finite dimensionality.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for commuting lineality with closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(C=\{(x,y):y>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\). Then \(C\) is a convex cone with \(\operatorname{lin}(C)=\{0\}\), whereas \(\overline C=\{(x,y):y\ge 0\}\) and \(\operatorname{lin}(\overline C)=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure can create new reversible directions: a pointed nonclosed cone may have a nonpointed closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(C)=\{0\}\subsetneq\operatorname{lin}(\overline C)=\mathbb R\times\{0\}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Can Enlarge Lineality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality as the Smallest Nonempty Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic facial characterization for an arbitrary convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex cone and \(L=\operatorname{lin}(C)\). Then \(L\) is a face of \(C\), and every nonempty face \(F\) of \(C\) contains \(L\). Thus \(L\) is the unique smallest nonempty face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space is the unique smallest nonempty face of a convex cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\unlhd C\quad\text{and}\quad L\subseteq F\text{ for every nonempty face }F\unlhd C.\)

notation.meaning: F is a face of C

children.title: Lineality Quotient Representation
children.top_down_role: Reduction of a cone to its lineality-free geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quotienting a cone by its lineality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone containing \(0\), and put \(L=K\cap(-K)\). Let \(q:V\to V/L\) be the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The quotient removes exactly the directions along which the cone contains complete lines. An orthogonal representative requires an inner product, while the quotient itself does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lineality quotient representation of \(K\) is the cone \[K/L:=q(K)=\{x+L:x\in K\}\subseteq V/L.\] It is lineality-free: \[q(K)\cap(-q(K))=\{L\}.\] If \(V\) is Euclidean and \(P_{L^\perp}\) denotes orthogonal projection, then the quotient is canonically represented after choosing the inner product by \[K_0=K\cap L^\perp=P_{L^\perp}K,\qquad K=L+K_0,\] and the restriction \(q|_{K_0}\) identifies \(K_0\) with \(K/L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quotient cone consists of cosets of the lineality space represented by cone points. Opposite directions that differ only by lineality collapse to the same quotient point, leaving a pointed cone. In a Euclidean realization, the quotient may be represented by intersecting the cone with the orthogonal complement of its lineality, and the original cone is the sum of this pointed part and the lineality space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K=L+(K\cap L^\perp),\qquad K/L\cong K\cap L^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{lin}(K/L)=\{L\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x,y\in K\), \[q(x)=q(y)\iff x-y\in L.\]
The reduced cone can equivalently be realized as the projection \(P_{L^\perp}K\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is pointed, then \(L=\{0\}\) and \(K/L\) is naturally \(K\).
If \(K=L\) is a subspace, then \(K/L\) is the zero cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: \[\dim(K/L)=\dim K-\dim L.\]
Questions invariant under addition of lineality directions may be studied on the pointed quotient.
boundary_notes: The orthogonal-complement model depends on the chosen inner product; the abstract quotient cone does not.
The quotient removes lineality but does not ensure closedness, solidity, finite generation, or polyhedrality.

notation.meaning: Canonical quotient map from the ambient space to the space modulo lineality.
Image cone in the quotient vector space.
Lineality-free orthogonal representative of the quotient.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Property of the Lineality Quotient
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every linear map annihilating lineality factors uniquely through the lineality quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear map \(A:V\to U\) factors through \(\pi:V\to V/L\) exactly when \(L\subseteq\ker A\). In that case there is a unique linear map \(\overline A:V/L\to U\) such that \[A=\overline A\circ\pi,\qquad A(C)=\overline A(\pi(C)).\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with lineality \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\subseteq\ker A\) if and only if there exists a unique linear \(\overline A\) with \(A=\overline A\circ\pi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal linear factorization after annihilating lineality.

notation.meaning: Linear map induced on the quotient.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological and Polyhedral Quotient Invariance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-dimensional lineality quotient preserves closedness and polyhedrality and maps relative interior onto relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In finite dimensions, \[C\text{ is closed}\Longleftrightarrow\pi(C)\text{ is closed},\qquad C\text{ is polyhedral}\Longleftrightarrow\pi(C)\text{ is polyhedral},\] and \[\pi(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(\pi(C)).\] These closedness equivalences use the saturated identity \(C=\pi^{-1}(\pi(C))\); arbitrary linear images of closed cones need not be closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with lineality \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closedness and polyhedrality are equivalent for \(C\) and \(\pi(C)\), and \(\pi(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{ri}(\pi(C))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional preservation for the saturated quotient by full lineality.

notation.meaning: Relative interior in the relevant finite-dimensional space.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotients by Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After quotienting by lineality, cone membership depends only on the resulting coset, and the original cone is the full inverse image of its quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\pi:V\to V/L\) be the canonical quotient map and define \(\overline C:=\pi(C)\). Then \(\overline C\) is a convex cone and
\[
C=\pi^{-1}(\overline C)=\{x\in V:\pi(x)\in\overline C\}.
\]
Equivalently, membership in \(C\) is constant on every coset \(x+L\). Thus quotienting removes exactly the reversible directions while retaining all conic membership information.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a real vector space and \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the quotient map \(\pi:V\to V/L\), \(C=\pi^{-1}(\pi(C))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic quotient representation by the full lineality space.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Cone under the Lineality Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic dual identification; the annihilator becomes an orthogonal complement in finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq V\) be a convex cone, \(L=\operatorname{lin}(C)\), \(\pi:V\to V/L\), and \(\overline C=\pi(C)\). Pullback \[\pi^*:(V/L)^*\to V^*\] is a linear isomorphism onto \[L^\circ=\{f\in V^*:f|_L=0\}.\] For the convention \(C^*=\{f:f(c)\ge0\ \forall c\in C\}\), \[\pi^*(\overline C^*)=C^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of the lineality quotient is the annihilator of lineality, and pullback identifies the quotient cone's dual with the original dual cone.

notation.meaning: Annihilator of lineality in the algebraic dual
Pullback of linear functionals along the quotient map

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Cone under the Lineality Quotient
Residual Lineality Formula
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting by a subspace of lineality leaves exactly the residual lineality L/M.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every linear subspace \(M\subseteq L\), \[\operatorname{lin}(\pi_M(C))=\pi_M(L)=L/M.\] Consequently, \(\pi_M(C)\) is pointed if and only if \(M=L\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with lineality \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(\pi_M(C))=L/M\), so \(\pi_M(C)\) is pointed exactly when \(M=L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact failure boundary when quotienting by less than the full lineality space.

notation.meaning: Lineality remaining in the quotient cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Face Correspondence for the Pointed Quotient
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty faces of a cone correspond order-preservingly to faces of its pointed quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every nonempty face \(F\) of \(C\) contains \(L\). The assignments \[F\longmapsto\pi(F),\qquad \overline F\longmapsto\pi^{-1}(\overline F)\] are mutually inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between the nonempty faces of \(C\) and the faces of \(\overline C=\pi(C)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with lineality \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\mapsto\pi(F)\) is an inclusion-preserving bijection from nonempty faces of \(C\) to faces of \(\overline C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty facial geometry descends unchanged to the quotient by full lineality.

notation.meaning: A nonempty face of the original cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Quotient Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The image of a cone modulo its entire lineality space is pointed; quotienting by a smaller contained subspace leaves nonzero lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quotient cone \(\overline C:=\pi(C)\subseteq V/L\) is pointed:
\[
\overline C\cap(-\overline C)=\{0_{V/L}\}.
\]
More generally, if \(M\) is a linear subspace satisfying \(M\subseteq C\), then the image of \(C\) in \(V/M\) is pointed if and only if \(M=L\). Hence quotienting by the complete lineality space, rather than a proper subspace of it, removes every nonzero reversible direction.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a real vector space and \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone.
\(L=\operatorname{lin}(C)\) and \(\pi:V\to V/L\) is the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness of the algebraic quotient; no closedness assumption.

notation.meaning: Lineality space of the original cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality and Dimension after a Partial Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residual-lineality formula and finite-dimensional dimension consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq V\) be a convex cone with lineality space \(L\), let \(M\subseteq L\) be a linear subspace, and let \(\pi_M:V\to V/M\) be the quotient map. Then \[\operatorname{lin}(\pi_M(C))=L/M.\] If \(V\) is finite-dimensional, then \[\dim\operatorname{span}(\pi_M(C))=\dim\operatorname{span}C-\dim M.\] In particular, \[\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}\pi_L(C)=\dim\operatorname{span}C-\dim L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting by a subspace of lineality leaves exactly the residual lineality L/M; quotienting by all lineality produces a pointed cone whose intrinsic dimension drops by dim L.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with lineality space \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(\pi_M(C))=L/M\); in finite dimensions, \(\dim_{\mathrm{intr}}\pi_L(C)=\dim\operatorname{span}C-\dim L\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality and Dimension after a Partial Quotient
Independence of Complement Choice
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different complementary slices are canonically linearly isomorphic through the quotient, although no slice is intrinsically preferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(V=W_1\oplus L=W_2\oplus L\), then \[T=(\pi|_{W_2})^{-1}\circ(\pi|_{W_1})\] restricts to a linear cone isomorphism \[T:C\cap W_1\longrightarrow C\cap W_2.\] Thus different complementary pointed slices have the same quotient-cone isomorphism type.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with lineality \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=(\pi|_{W_2})^{-1}\circ(\pi|_{W_1})\) maps \(C\cap W_1\) linearly and bijectively onto \(C\cap W_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary representatives are noncanonical but canonically isomorphic through the quotient.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifting from Pointed Quotients
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing a complement to lineality identifies the quotient with a pointed slice of the original cone, and adding lineality reconstructs the cone uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(C_W:=C\cap W\). Then \(C_W\) is a pointed convex cone, the restriction
\[
\pi|_{C_W}:C_W\to\pi(C)
\]
is a linear bijection of cones, and every \(x\in C\) has a unique decomposition \(x=w+\ell\) with \(w\in C_W\) and \(\ell\in L\). Consequently,
\[
C=C_W+L,
\]
so the original cone is recovered by adding its lineality space to any complementary pointed representative.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite-dimensional, \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone, and \(L=\operatorname{lin}(C)\).
\(W\) is a linear complement of \(L\), so \(V=W\oplus L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=(C\cap W)+L\), and \(\pi|_{C\cap W}:C\cap W\to\pi(C)\) is a cone isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lifting after choosing a complement to lineality.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between algebraic lifting and continuous topological splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every vector-space subspace \(L\subseteq V\) admits an algebraic complement, so the algebraic lifting through a chosen complement is always available. If \(V\) is a topological vector space and \(L\) is closed, a continuous linear section \(s:V/L\to V\) of the quotient map exists exactly when \(L\) has a topological complement, equivalently when \(V=L\oplus W\) with the associated projection continuous. Closed subspaces of infinite-dimensional Banach spaces need not be complemented, so continuous complementary lifting can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algebraic complements always permit lifting, but continuous quotient slices require complemented lineality and can fail in infinite-dimensional Banach spaces.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a real vector space for the algebraic assertion.
\(V\) is a topological vector space and \(L\) is closed for the topological quotient assertion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A continuous linear section of \(V\to V/L\) exists if and only if \(L\) is topologically complemented.

notation.meaning: Continuous linear section of the quotient map

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Complement Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transfer of Closure and Relative Interior to a Complement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional transfer of topological cone geometry through a complement of lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite-dimensional, let \(C\subseteq V\) be a convex cone with lineality \(L\), and choose \(V=W\oplus L\). Put \(C_W=C\cap W\). Then \[C\text{ is closed}\iff C_W\text{ is closed},\qquad \operatorname{ri}_V C=\operatorname{ri}_W C_W+L.\] For the quotient map \(\pi:V\to V/L\), \[\pi(\operatorname{ri}_V C)=\operatorname{ri}_{V/L}\pi(C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementary pointed representative preserves closedness and relative-interior geometry, and adding lineality lifts its relative interior to the original cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with lineality space \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed iff \(C_W\) is closed, \(\operatorname{ri}_V C=\operatorname{ri}_W C_W+L\), and \(\pi(\operatorname{ri}_V C)=\operatorname{ri}_{V/L}\pi(C)\).

notation.meaning: Pointed representative cone in the chosen complement

knowledge_statements.title: Transfer of Closure and Relative Interior to a Complement

assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite-dimensional and \(C\subseteq V\) is a convex cone with lineality \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T=(\pi|_{W_2})^{-1}\circ(\pi|_{W_1})\text{ maps }C\cap W_1\text{ linearly and bijectively onto }C\cap W_2.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The concrete slice depends on a complement, but its cone-isomorphism class does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For two complements \(W_1,W_2\) of \(L\), each restriction \(\pi|_{W_i}:W_i\to V/L\) is a linear isomorphism. The transition map \[T=(\pi|_{W_2})^{-1}\circ(\pi|_{W_1})\] restricts to a cone isomorphism \(C\cap W_1\to C\cap W_2\). Hence the embedded pointed representative is noncanonical, but every choice has the same canonical quotient-cone isomorphism type.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different complementary slices of a cone are canonically linearly isomorphic through the quotient, although no slice is intrinsically preferred.
knowledge_statements.title: Independence of the Complement Choice

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transverse affine sections and cone bases
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(K\subseteq V\) be a convex cone, and let \(u\in V^*\) satisfy \(u(x)>0\) for every \(x\in K\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict positivity makes the hyperplane \(u=1\) transverse to every nonzero ray of the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The normalized affine section determined by \(u\) is \[B_u=K\cap H_u,\qquad H_u=\{x\in V:u(x)=1\}.\] It is a base of \(K\): every \(x\in K\setminus\{0\}\) has the unique representation \[x=u(x)b,\qquad b=\frac{x}{u(x)}\in B_u.\] Consequently, \[K=\{\lambda b:\lambda\geq0,\ b\in B_u\}=\operatorname{cone}(B_u).\] Conversely, a convex base meeting every nonzero ray exactly once provides such a section whenever it lies in an affine hyperplane separated from the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly positive linear functional normalizes every nonzero cone point to the hyperplane where the functional equals one. The resulting convex section meets each nonzero ray exactly once, and every cone point is recovered by nonnegative scaling of its unique section point. Such a section is called a base of the cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\setminus\{0\}\longleftrightarrow (0,\infty)\times B_u,\qquad x\longmapsto\left(u(x),\frac{x}{u(x)}\right).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[B_u\text{ meets each nonzero ray of }K\text{ in exactly one point}.\]
\[K=\mathbb R_+B_u\quad\text{and}\quad 0\notin B_u.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(u(x)=\sum_i x_i\), the section is the standard simplex \(\{x\geq0:\sum_i x_i=1\}\).
For the positive-semidefinite cone and \(u(X)=\operatorname{tr}X\), the section consists of positive-semidefinite matrices of trace one.
immediate_consequences_latex: Faces and extreme rays of \(K\) correspond to faces and extreme points of a convex base.
Properties invariant under positive scaling can be studied on \(B_u\).
boundary_notes: A hyperplane through the origin does not normalize rays and is not a base section.
If \(u\) vanishes on a nonzero cone direction, the section \(u=1\) misses that ray and cannot represent the entire cone.

notation.meaning: Affine hyperplane on which the normalizing functional equals one.
Transverse affine section serving as a cone base.

children.title: Bases of Pointed Cones
children.top_down_role: Normalized sections representing ray geometry without lineality.

knowledge_statements.title: Every Convex Base Is a Positive Functional Slice
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex base of a pointed cone is the level-one section of a unique strictly positive linear functional on the cone's span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every convex base \(B\) of \(C\) is the level-one section of a unique linear functional \(f\in W^*\), where \(W=\operatorname{span}C\), satisfying
\[
f(x)>0\quad(x\in C\setminus\{0\}),
\qquad
B=\{x\in C:f(x)=1\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subseteq V\) is a nonzero pointed convex cone.
\(B\subseteq C\) is a convex base of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,f\in W^*:\ f>0\text{ on }C\setminus\{0\}\text{ and }B=\{x\in C:f(x)=1\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse affine-section characterization on the cone's intrinsic span.

notation.meaning: normalizing functional determined by the base

knowledge_statements.title: Bases of Pointed Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone base selects exactly one normalized point from each nonzero ray; a strictly positive linear functional produces such a base by an affine slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A base of \(C\) is a convex set \(B\subseteq C\) such that every \(x\in C\setminus\{0\}\) admits a unique representation
\[
x=\lambda b,\qquad \lambda>0,\quad b\in B.
\]
Equivalently, \(B\) intersects every nonzero ray of \(C\) exactly once. If a linear functional \(f\in V^*\) satisfies \(f(x)>0\) for all \(x\in C\setminus\{0\}\), then
\[
B_f:=\{x\in C:f(x)=1\}
\]
is a base of \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subseteq V\) is a nonzero pointed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A base \(B\) meets every nonzero ray of \(C\) in exactly one point, and \(C=\{\lambda b:\lambda\geq0,\ b\in B\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ray-normalizing bases, including affine slices induced by positive functionals.

source_witnesses.locator: III. Convex Sets p. 87

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointedness Alone Does Not Guarantee a Convex Base
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp obstruction showing that a pointed nonclosed cone need not admit a ray-normalizing convex base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone
\[
C:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\cup\{(x,0):x\geq0\}
\]
is convex and pointed but admits no convex base. Equivalently, it admits no linear functional strictly positive on \(C\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed but nonclosed planar cone can fail to possess a convex base because no linear functional is positive on all its nonzero directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is pointed but admits no convex base.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness Alone Does Not Guarantee a Convex Base

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Functional Characterization of Convex Cone Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse to the seed's affine-section construction, stated in the cone's intrinsic span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\neq\{0\}\) be a convex cone and set \(W=\operatorname{span}C\). A convex set \(B\subseteq C\) is a base of \(C\) if and only if there exists a unique linear functional \(f\in W^*\) such that
\[
f(x)>0\quad(x\in C\setminus\{0\}),
\qquad B=\{x\in C:f(x)=1\}.
\]
For every \(x\in C\setminus\{0\}\),
\[
x=f(x)\frac{x}{f(x)},
\qquad \frac{x}{f(x)}\in B.
\]
Consequently, a cone admitting a convex base is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex cone base is the level-one slice of a unique functional strictly positive on the cone's nonzero elements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is a convex base if and only if \(B=C\cap\{f=1\}\) for a unique \(f\in W^*\) strictly positive on \(C\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Functional Characterization of Convex Cone Bases

children.title: Cone Base Compactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Base geometry distinguished by boundedness and regularity.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a convex cone and let \(B\subseteq K\) be a base: \(0\notin B\), and every \(x\in K\setminus\{0\}\) has a unique expression \(x=\lambda b\) with \(\lambda>0\) and \(b\in B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness is finite-dimensional. The defining uniqueness of a base is separated from boundedness and closedness of the base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The base \(B\) is compact when it is compact as a subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), equivalently when it is closed and bounded. It is a bounded noncompact base when it is bounded but not closed, and an unbounded base when \[\sup_{b\in B}\|b\|=+\infty.\] A cone has a compact-base representation when there exists at least one compact base \(B\) satisfying \[K=\{\lambda b:\lambda\geq0,\ b\in B\}.\] For a hyperplane base \(B_u=K\cap\{u=1\}\), these regimes are determined by the topology and boundedness of that affine section.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact base is a base that is both closed and bounded. Other base regimes include bounded but nonclosed sections and unbounded sections. Saying that a cone has a compact-base representation means that at least one base, not necessarily every arbitrary normalization, is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B\text{ compact}\iff B\text{ closed and bounded},\qquad K=\mathbb R_+B.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For compact \(B\) with \(0\notin B\), \[\min_{b\in B}\|b\|>0.\]
A closed pointed convex cone in finite dimensions admits a compact base, and a cone with a compact base is closed and contains no nontrivial line.
special_cases_latex: The simplex \(\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_i x_i=1\}\) is a compact base of \(\mathbb R_+^n\).
The trace-one positive-semidefinite matrices form a compact base of the positive-semidefinite cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: A convex cone with a compact base is closed.
Extreme points of a compact convex base generate the extreme rays of the cone.
boundary_notes: In infinite-dimensional spaces, closed and bounded need not imply compact.
A cone containing a nontrivial subspace cannot have a base that intersects every nonzero ray exactly once in the stated sense.

notation.meaning: All nonnegative scalar multiples of points in the base.
Base obtained from a normalized affine hyperplane section.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Cone Bases
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a nonzero convex cone admits a compact base exactly when it is both closed and pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone \(C\) possesses a compact base if and only if it is closed and pointed. In that case, working in \(W=\operatorname{span}C\), one may choose a functional \(f\in W^*\) such that \(f(x)>0\) for every \(x\in C\setminus\{0\}\). The normalized section
\[
B_f=\{x\in C:f(x)=1\}
\]
is then nonempty, convex, and compact, and every nonzero element of \(C\) is a unique positive multiple of an element of \(B_f\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a nonzero convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) has a compact base if and only if \(C\) is closed and pointed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization of cones admitting compact bases.

notation.meaning: Affine base normalized by a functional

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Every Strictly Positive Functional Produces a Compact Base
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthens the seed's existence statement from one suitable functional slice to every strictly positive functional slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\neq\{0\}\) be a closed pointed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space. If \(f\in(\operatorname{span}C)^*\) satisfies
\[
f(x)>0\qquad(x\in C\setminus\{0\}),
\]
then
\[
B_f:=\{x\in C:f(x)=1\}
\]
is a compact base of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional closed pointed cone, every strictly positive normalizing functional—not merely one specially selected functional—has a compact level-one base.
assumptions_latex: \(C\neq\{0\}\) is a closed pointed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_f=C\cap\{f=1\}\) is a compact base of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Every Strictly Positive Functional Produces a Compact Base
Bounded Nonclosed Cone Base
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open pointed wedge has a bounded but nonclosed height-one base, so noncompactness need not arise from unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{\lambda(x,1):\lambda>0,\ |x|<1\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
Then \(C\) is a convex pointed cone, \(f(x,y)=y\) is strictly positive on \(C\setminus\{0\}\), and
\[
B_f=\{(x,1):|x|<1\}=(-1,1)\times\{1\}.
\]
This base is bounded but nonclosed and hence noncompact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=\{\lambda(x,1):\lambda>0,\ |x|<1\}\cup\{0\}\text{ has the bounded nonclosed base }B=(-1,1)\times\{1\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary noncompactness mechanism: boundedness without closedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact Cone Bases
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open upper-half-plane cone with the origin is pointed, but its height-one base is an unbounded affine line, showing closedness matters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
C:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
This is a convex pointed cone but is not closed. For the positive functional \(f(x,y)=y\), its normalized base is
\[
B_f=\{(x,y)\in C:f(x,y)=1\}=\mathbb R\times\{1\}.
\]
The set \(B_f\) is closed as an affine line but is unbounded and therefore noncompact. Thus pointedness alone does not ensure that an affine cone base is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointed convex cone \(C=\{(x,y):y>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\) has the noncompact base \(B=\mathbb R\times\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of base compactness when closedness is absent.

notation.meaning: Nonclosed pointed cone in the example

source_witnesses.locator: III. Convex Sets p. 87

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complements the seed's closed but unbounded base by exhibiting the other finite-dimensional mechanism for noncompactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}
\]
and \(f(x,y)=x+y\). Then \(C\) is a pointed nonclosed convex cone and
\[
B_f=C\cap\{f=1\}=\{(t,1-t):0<t<1\}.
\]
Thus \(B_f\) is bounded but not closed, hence noncompact. Its closure adds the normalized representatives of the two boundary rays omitted from \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open positive quadrant with its apex has a bounded open-segment base, so a base can be noncompact through nonclosedness without being unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_f=\{(t,1-t):0<t<1\}\) is bounded but nonclosed and therefore noncompact.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded but Nonclosed Cone Base

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two Mechanisms of Finite-Dimensional Base Noncompactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates missing finite limit points from escape along unbounded normalized directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B_f=C\cap\{f=1\}\) be a nonempty base in a finite-dimensional normed space. Then \(B_f\) is noncompact if and only if it is not closed or it is unbounded. If it is not closed, some bounded sequence in \(B_f\) converges to a point of \(\overline{B_f}\setminus B_f\). If it is unbounded, there are \(b_k\in B_f\) with \(\|b_k\|\to\infty\) and a subsequence for which
\[
\frac{b_k}{\|b_k\|}\to d\in(\overline C\cap\ker f)\setminus\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional base is noncompact through a missing finite limit point or escape to infinity; escape produces a nonzero closure direction annihilated by the normalizing functional.
assumptions_latex: \(B_f=C\cap\{f=1\}\) is a nonempty cone base in a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Noncompactness is equivalent to nonclosedness or unboundedness, with the stated sequential witnesses.

notation.meaning: directions annihilated by the base-normalizing functional

knowledge_statements.title: Two Mechanisms of Finite-Dimensional Base Noncompactness
Boundedness Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized base is bounded exactly when its functional stays uniformly positive on unit cone directions, including limiting directions in the cone's closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(B_f:=\{x\in C:f(x)=1\}\), the following conditions are equivalent:
\[
B_f\text{ is bounded};
\]
\[
\text{there exists }\alpha>0\text{ such that }f(x)\geq\alpha\|x\|\text{ for every }x\in C;
\]
\[
f(x)>0\text{ for every }x\in\overline C\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Thus loss of boundedness occurs precisely when normalized cone directions approach a nonzero direction in \(\overline C\) on which \(f\) vanishes. If \(C\) is closed, strict positivity already yields boundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq V\) is a nonzero convex cone and \(f\in V^*\) is positive on \(C\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_f\) is bounded exactly when \(f(x)\geq\alpha\|x\|\) on \(C\) for some \(\alpha>0\), equivalently when \(f>0\) on \(\overline C\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative boundary separating bounded and unbounded normalized bases.

children.title: Convex-Conic Homogenization Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Passage between convex sets, affine slices, and conic extensions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty convex set and write points of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) as \((t,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record defines the nonclosed homogenization. Its closure may add recession directions at height zero when \(C\) is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conic homogenization of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{hom}(C)=\operatorname{cone}\{(1,x):x\in C\}=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(t,tx):t>0,\ x\in C\}.\] It is a convex cone, and dehomogenization by the affine slice \(t=1\) recovers \(C\): \[C=\{x:(1,x)\in\operatorname{hom}(C)\}.\] Conversely, if a convex cone \(K\subseteq");\mathbb R^{n+1}\) satisfies \(K\cap\{t\leq0\}=\{(0,0)\}\), then its unit slice \(C_K=\{x:(1,x)\in K\}\) determines \(K\) by \[K=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(t,tx):t>0,\ x\in C_K\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenization embeds each point of a convex set at height one and takes the conic hull. Slicing the resulting cone again at height one recovers the original convex set. Conversely, a cone lying strictly on the positive side of the height-zero hyperplane, except at its vertex, is determined by its unit-height slice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C\xmapsto{\operatorname{hom}}K\xmapsto{t=1}C,\qquad \operatorname{hom}(C)\cap\{t=1\}=\{1\}\times C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(t,y)\in\operatorname{hom}(C),\ t>0\iff y/t\in C.\]
\[\operatorname{hom}(C)=\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times C).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a polytope, \(\operatorname{hom}(C)\) is a finitely generated cone.
If \(C\) is a cone containing \(0\), homogenization still records the distinguished affine coordinate and is not identified with \(C\) itself.
immediate_consequences_latex: Affine combinations in \(C\) become conic combinations of the lifted points \((1,x)\).
Affine descriptions of \(C\) can be converted to homogeneous descriptions in one additional dimension.
boundary_notes: For unbounded closed \(C\), \(\operatorname{hom}(C)\) need not be closed; its closure can contain \((0,d)\) for recession directions \(d\).
Cones meeting the height-zero hyperplane nontrivially require recession data in addition to the unit slice.

notation.meaning: Conic homogenization of the convex set.
Unit-height affine slice of a cone.

knowledge_statements.title: When Raw Homogenization Is Closed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raw homogenization is closed exactly for bounded closed convex sets; otherwise closure adds the nonzero recession directions at height zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and define \[R(S):=\{(\lambda x,\lambda):\lambda>0,\ x\in S\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \[\overline{R(S)}=R(S)\cup\bigl(\operatorname{rec}(S)\times\{0\}\bigr).\] Consequently, \[R(S)\text{ is closed}\iff \operatorname{rec}(S)=\{0\}\iff S\text{ is bounded}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{R(S)}=R(S)\cup(\operatorname{rec}(S)\times\{0\}),\qquad R(S)\text{ closed}\iff \operatorname{rec}(S)=\{0\}\iff S\text{ bounded}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional criterion identifying exactly when closure is needed in homogenization.

notation.meaning: Raw, not necessarily closed, homogenization of the set

knowledge_statements.title: Homogenization of Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenization embeds a closed convex set as the height-one slice of a closed cone, whose height-zero slice records the set's recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed homogenization of \(S\) is the convex cone
\[
H(S):=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(S\times\{1\})
=\overline{\{(\lambda x,\lambda):\lambda>0,\ x\in S\}\cup\{(0,0)\}}.
\]
Its positive-height points satisfy
\[
(y,t)\in H(S),\ t>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y/t\in S,
\]
while its zero-height slice is
\[
H(S)\cap(\mathbb R^n\times\{0\})=\operatorname{rec}(S)\times\{0\}.
\]
In particular, the height-one slice recovers \(S\times\{1\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(H(S)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(S\times\{1\})\), \(H(S)\cap\{t=1\}=S\times\{1\}\) and \(H(S)\cap\{t=0\}=\operatorname{rec}(S)\times\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed finite-dimensional homogenization retaining recession directions at height zero.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the convex set

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Convex Sets Attached to a Convex Set p. 102

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional condition for closure to be unnecessary in convex-set homogenization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and define \[H_0(S):=\operatorname{cone}(S\times\{1\})=\{(\lambda x,\lambda):\lambda>0,\ x\in S\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] Then \[H_0(S)\text{ is closed}\iff S\text{ is bounded}.\] If \(S\) is unbounded, its nonzero recession directions occur as missing height-zero limits, so closure is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algebraic homogenization of a nonempty closed convex set is closed exactly when the set is bounded; otherwise closure adds nonzero recession directions at height zero.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cone}(S\times\{1\})\text{ is closed}\iff S\text{ is bounded}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of the Algebraic Homogenization
Dehomogenization through Affine Slices
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed cone with nonempty height-one slice is recovered by closed homogenization of that slice; its zero-height directions are exactly the slice's recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine slice \(B\) is a nonempty closed convex set. Every positive-height point of \(K\) is determined by this slice:
\[
(y,t)\in K,\ t>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y/t\in B.
\]
Moreover,
\[
K=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(B\times\{1\}),
\qquad
K\cap(\mathbb R^n\times\{0\})=\operatorname{rec}(B)\times\{0\}.
\]
Thus dehomogenization by the height-one slice and closed homogenization are inverse constructions for closed convex cones contained in the nonnegative-height half-space and having a nonempty height-one slice.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(B\times\{1\})\), and \((y,t)\in K\) with \(t>0\) exactly when \(y/t\in B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstruction of a closed cone from a nonempty positive affine slice.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: All positive affine slices of a cone carry the same dehomogenized set up to scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+\) be a convex cone and, for \(\alpha>0\), define \(B_\alpha:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:(x,\alpha)\in K\}\). Then \[B_\alpha=\alpha B_1.\] Thus \(x\mapsto x/\alpha\) identifies the height-\(\alpha\) slice with the height-one slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive-height slice is a scaled copy of the height-one slice, so the positive normalization level does not change the dehomogenized geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_\alpha=\alpha B_1.

notation.meaning: Affine slice of the cone at height \(\alpha\).

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Slice Rescaling
Closedness of the Homogeneous Conic Extension
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the representing cone is closed, the homogenized affine conic extension is a closed convex cone whose unit slice is the original affine extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(B:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(c\in\mathbb R^m\). Then \[E:=\{(x,y,t):t\geq0,\ Ax+By+tc\in K\}\] is a closed convex cone, and \[E\cap\{t=1\}=\{(x,y,1):Ax+By+c\in K\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E\text{ is a closed convex cone and }E\cap\{t=1\}=\{(x,y,1):Ax+By+c\in K\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness inherited by the homogeneous extension itself; no closedness of its projection is asserted.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Extension Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine conic lift becomes homogeneous after adding a nonnegative scalar coordinate, and the original represented set is recovered by slicing that cone at scalar value one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ Ax+By+c\in K\}\), and define \(E=\{(x,y,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+p+1}:t\geq0,\ Ax+By+tc\in K\}\). Then \(E\) is a convex cone and the original affine conic representation is recovered from its unit slice: \[C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ (x,y,1)\in E\}=\operatorname{proj}_x(E\cap\{t=1\}).\] Conversely, slicing any cone of this displayed homogeneous form at \(t=1\) yields the corresponding affine conic extension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\operatorname{proj}_x(E\cap\{t=1\})\), where \(E=\{(x,y,t):t\geq0,\ Ax+By+tc\in K\}\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogenization of an affine conic lift by adjoining one scalar coordinate.

notation.meaning: Affine conic extension of the represented set.
Homogeneous conic extension with scalar coordinate.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected Homogeneous Lift and Recession Slice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relation between a homogenized conic extension, its projection, and the closed homogenization of the represented set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a convex cone, let \(C=\{x:\exists y,\ Ax+By+c\in K\}\neq\varnothing\), and set \(E=\{(x,y,t):t\geq0,\ Ax+By+tc\in K\}\) and \(P=\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}E\). Then \[(x,t)\in P,\ t>0\iff x/t\in C.\] Moreover, \[\{d:(d,0)\in P\}=\{d:\exists w,\ Ad+Bw\in K\}\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C),\qquad \overline P=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(C\times\{1\}).\] Thus projection can omit zero-height recession directions, while its closure supplies the closed homogenization of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected homogeneous lift is the conic scaling of the represented set at positive height. Its zero-height points are recession directions, and closing it supplies all missing recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\cap\{t>0\}=\{(tu,t):t>0,\ u\in C\},\quad \operatorname{proj}_x(P\cap\{t=0\})\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(C),\quad \overline P=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(C\times\{1\}).

notation.meaning: Homogeneous conic extension before eliminating the lift variable.
Projection onto the original and scale variables.
Recession cone of the represented set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite internal and external descriptions of cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a convex cone containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition distinguishes finite generator descriptions from finite homogeneous-inequality descriptions. Their equivalence is specific to finite-dimensional polyhedral convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(K\) has a finite internal description when \[K=\operatorname{cone}\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i g_i:\lambda_i\geq0\right\}\] for some finite family of generators. It has a finite external description when \[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\langle a_j,x\rangle\leq0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\] for some finite family of homogeneous linear inequalities. A cone with the second property is polyhedral. In finite dimensions, the Minkowski–Weyl finite-generation principle identifies the two classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite internal description lists finitely many generating directions. A finite external description lists finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities. The latter defines a polyhedral cone. In a finite-dimensional real space, a convex cone admits one type of finite description exactly when it admits the other.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{\text{finitely generated convex cones in }\mathbb R^n\}=\{\text{polyhedral convex cones in }\mathbb R^n\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The internal form is \(K=A\mathbb R_+^m\) for a finite matrix \(A\).
The external form is \(K=\{x:Bx\leq0\}\) for a finite matrix \(B\).
special_cases_latex: A simplicial cone has a finite internal description by linearly independent generators.
A linear subspace has a finite external description by homogeneous equalities, each expressible as two inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finitely generated cone in \(\mathbb R^n\) is closed.
A polyhedral cone has only finitely many faces and only finitely many extreme rays modulo lineality.
boundary_notes: The equivalence can fail in infinite-dimensional spaces.
Neither the finite generator list nor the finite inequality list is generally unique or irredundant.

notation.meaning: Finite generator or V-representation of the cone.
Finite homogeneous inequality or H-representation of the cone.

children.top_down_role: Dimension-sensitive sparsification of conic representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Constructive Dependence-Elimination Procedure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moving coefficients along linear dependencies repeatedly removes generators while preserving the represented vector, ending with independent support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i s_i\) with \(\lambda_i>0\), and let \(r=\dim\operatorname{span}\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}<m\). Choose a nonzero \(c\) with \(\sum_i c_i s_i=0\), change its sign so some \(c_i>0\), set \(\tau=\min_{c_i>0}\lambda_i/c_i\), and replace \(\lambda_i\) by \(\lambda_i-\tau c_i\). Repeating this step preserves \(x\) and nonnegativity and terminates after at most \(m-r\) eliminations with linearly independent active generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{After at most }m-r\text{ eliminations, }x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i's_i\text{ with }\{s_i:i\in I\}\text{ linearly independent}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive conic Carathéodory reduction from a finite representation.

notation.meaning: coefficient vector of an active linear dependence
rank of the initially active generators

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Conic Carathéodory Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic dimension bound is sharp: the all-positive vector in a coordinate orthant needs every basis ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=\{e_1,\ldots,e_q\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) and \(x=e_1+\cdots+e_q\), every conic representation of \(x\) using elements of \(S\) uses all \(q\) generators. Hence the bound \(q=\dim\operatorname{span}S\) cannot be reduced in general.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{|I|:x\in\operatorname{cone}\{e_i:i\in I\}\}=q.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case sharpness of the intrinsic-dimensional support bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Carathéodory Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in a cone generated in dimension d is a nonnegative combination of at most d linearly independent generators, with the sharper bound given by the generators' span dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{cone}(S)\), there are an integer \(r\leq q:=\dim\operatorname{span}(S)\), linearly independent vectors \(s_1,\ldots,s_r\in S\), and coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r>0\) such that \[x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i s_i.\] In particular, although membership in \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\) is defined using arbitrary finite conic combinations, every member has a representation using at most \(q\), hence at most \(d\), generators. For \(x=0\), the empty conic combination may be used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist linearly independent \(s_1,\ldots,s_r\in S\) and \(\lambda_i>0\) with \(x=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i s_i\) and \(r\leq\dim\operatorname{span}(S)\leq d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic Carathéodory theorem with the intrinsic span-dimension bound.

notation.meaning: Set of all finite nonnegative linear combinations of elements of the set.
Dimension of the linear span of the generating set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive support reduction underlying conic Carathéodory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i s_i\) with \(\lambda_i>0\). Whenever the active generators are linearly dependent, choose nonzero \(\alpha\) with \(\sum_i\alpha_i s_i=0\), change its sign so that some \(\alpha_i>0\), and set \[t=\min_{\alpha_i>0}\frac{\lambda_i}{\alpha_i},\qquad \lambda_i'=\lambda_i-t\alpha_i.\] This preserves nonnegativity and the represented vector while eliminating at least one active coefficient. Repetition terminates after at most \(n-1\) eliminations with a linearly independent support of size at most \(q=\dim\operatorname{span}(S)\); if only support size at most \(q\) is required, at most \(\max\{0,n-q\}\) eliminations suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-dependence elimination removes at least one positive coefficient per step and constructs a linearly independent conic representation of size at most the intrinsic span dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After at most \(n-1\) eliminations, \(x\) has a conic representation on a linearly independent support of size at most \(q\).

notation.meaning: coefficient vector of a linear dependence among active generators

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness example for the conic Carathéodory number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=\{e_1,\ldots,e_q\}\subseteq\mathbb R^q\), the vector \(x=e_1+\cdots+e_q\) belongs to \(\operatorname{cone}(S)\), but every conic representation of \(x\) using members of \(S\) uses all \(q\) generators. Hence the bound \(q=\dim\operatorname{span}(S)\) cannot be reduced in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic span-dimension bound is sharp: a positive vector in the cone of a basis requires every basis ray.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\{e_1,\ldots,e_q\}\) is the standard basis of \(\mathbb R^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every representation of \(x\) by generators from \(S\) has support size \(q\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq");\mathbb R^n\), let \(K=\operatorname{cone}(S)\), and put \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The family measures the minimum support size of conic representations. It is dimension-sensitive and does not assume that the generating set itself is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\in\mathbb N\), define the \(k\)-term conic stratum \[\operatorname{cone}_k(S)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i s_i:s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\},\qquad \operatorname{cone}_0(S)=\{0\}.\] For \(x\in K\), its conic Carathéodory number relative to \(S\) is \[c_S(x)=\min\{k:x\in\operatorname{cone}_k(S)\},\] and the global number is \[c(S)=\sup_{x\in K}c_S(x).\] The conic Carathéodory family is the increasing sequence \(\operatorname{cone}_0(S)\subseteq\operatorname{cone}_1(S)\subseteq\cdots\), which stabilizes by dimension: \[K=\operatorname{cone}_d(S),\qquad c(S)\leq d.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The kth conic stratum contains the points representable with at most k generating directions. The pointwise Carathéodory number is the smallest such k, and the global number is the worst pointwise value. In a d-dimensional span, every cone point has a representation using at most d directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x\in\operatorname{cone}(S)\ \exists r\leq d,\ s_1,\ldots,s_r\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0:\ x=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i s_i.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The nonzero generators in the representation may be chosen linearly independent.
\[c(S)=\min\{k:\operatorname{cone}_k(S)=\operatorname{cone}(S)\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) lies on a single ray, then \(c(S)=1\) unless \(S\subseteq\{0\}\).
For \(S=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}\), the vector with every coordinate positive requires all \(n\) generators, so the bound is attained.
immediate_consequences_latex: Each individual point has a sparse conic representation controlled by intrinsic dimension rather than by the cardinality of \(S\).
Redundant or linearly dependent positive terms can be omitted from a minimum-support representation.
boundary_notes: The affine Carathéodory bound is \(d+1\); the conic bound is \(d\).
The bound concerns representation sparsity and does not imply that the entire cone has a finite generator set.

notation.meaning: Points admitting a conic representation with at most k terms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Irredundant, cardinality-minimal, and extreme-ray generator systems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K");\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a finitely generated convex cone and let \(G=\{g_1,\ldots,g_m\}\subseteq K\setminus\{0\}\) satisfy \(K=\operatorname{cone}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimality is relative to finite generator systems. Positive rescalings represent the same ray and are treated as equivalent in ray-based minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generator system \(G\) is inclusion-minimal, or irredundant, when \[\operatorname{cone}(G\setminus\{g_i\})\subsetneq K\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m),\] equivalently when \[g_i\notin\operatorname{cone}(G\setminus\{g_i\})\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] It is cardinality-minimal when \[|G|=\min\{|H|:H\subseteq K,\ |H|<\infty,\ \operatorname{cone}(H)=K\}.\] It is ray-irredundant when distinct elements generate distinct rays and deleting any represented ray changes the cone. For a pointed polyhedral cone, a generator system containing exactly one nonzero vector from each extreme ray is ray-irredundant and cardinality-minimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An irredundant generator list loses part of the cone whenever any generator is removed. A cardinality-minimal list uses the fewest possible generators among all finite lists. Ray-irredundancy additionally identifies positive multiples and retains exactly the indispensable generating rays. For pointed polyhedral cones, these indispensable rays are the extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G\text{ irredundant}\iff\forall g\in G:\ g\notin\operatorname{cone}(G\setminus\{g\}).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Replacing any \(g_i\) by \(\alpha_i g_i\) with \(\alpha_i>0\) preserves all ray-based minimality classes.
For a pointed polyhedral cone, \[G\text{ ray-minimal}\iff\{\mathbb R_+g:g\in G\}=\operatorname{ExtRays}(K).\]
special_cases_latex: A simplicial cone generated by linearly independent vectors has an irredundant generator system.
A list containing two positive multiples of the same nonzero vector is not ray-irredundant.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finite generator system can be reduced to an inclusion-minimal subsystem by deleting redundant elements.
Cardinality-minimal systems are inclusion-minimal, although inclusion-minimal systems need not be unique as vector lists.
boundary_notes: For cones with lineality, extreme rays alone do not generate the linear part; positive and negative generators for a lineality basis may be required.
These minimality notions do not assert uniqueness of generator vectors, because positive rescaling is always possible.

notation.meaning: Collection of extreme rays of the cone.
Generator system after deleting one candidate generator.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence and Irredundancy of Minimum Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-cardinality generator systems exist for finitely generated cones and are irredundant, but need not occur inside every supplied generating family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finitely generated cone has a finite generator system of minimum cardinality. Every such system \(G_*\) is irredundant: \[g\notin\operatorname{cone}(G_*\setminus\{g\})\qquad(g\in G_*).\] A minimum system need not be a subset of an arbitrarily prescribed generating system, and irredundancy alone does not imply minimum cardinality.
assumptions_latex: Generator systems are finite subsets of \(K\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimum-cardinality generator system \(G_*\) exists and every such \(G_*\) is irredundant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and the one-way implication from cardinality minimality to deletion irredundancy.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Generator Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal generator system generates the cone and has the least cardinality among all finite systems that generate the same cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite set \(G\subseteq K\setminus\{0\}\) is a minimal generator system of \(K\) if \(\operatorname{cone}(G)=K\) and its cardinality is smallest among all finite generator systems of \(K\): \[|G|=\min\bigl\{|H|:H\subseteq K\setminus\{0\},\ H\text{ finite},\ \operatorname{cone}(H)=K\bigr\}.\] Thus minimality here compares \(G\) with every finite system generating \(K\), rather than merely requiring that no element can be deleted from \(G\).
assumptions_latex: Generator systems are finite subsets of \(K\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is minimal exactly when \(\operatorname{cone}(G)=K\) and \(|G|\leq|H|\) for every finite \(H\subseteq K\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying \(\operatorname{cone}(H)=K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-minimal finite generator systems; inclusion-minimality is treated separately as irredundancy.

notation.meaning: A finite generator system for the cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R^2\), the system \[G=\{e_1,-e_1,e_2,-e_2\}\] is irredundant and generates \(K\). However \[H=\{e_1,e_2,-e_1-e_2\}\] also generates \(K\), so \(|H|=3<4=|G|\). Thus an irredundant generator system need not have minimum cardinality.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every minimum-cardinality finite generator system is irredundant.
