knowledge_statements.statement_title: Missing Image Points and Strict Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes points outside the image closure from weakly infeasible missing boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(C^*=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in C\}\), \[b\in\operatorname{cl}A(C)\iff \langle y,b\rangle\geq0\quad\text{for every }y\text{ with }A^*y\in C^*.\] Hence \(b\notin\operatorname{cl}A(C)\) admits \(y\) with \(A^*y\in C^*\) and \(\langle y,b\rangle<0\), whereas \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(C)\setminus A(C)\) is infeasible without such a strict separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Points outside the closed image have strict adjoint-dual certificates, while missing boundary points are infeasible but cannot be strictly separated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strict adjoint-dual separator exists exactly when \(b\notin\operatorname{cl}A(C)\), not when \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(C)\setminus A(C)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Image Points and Strict Separation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional characterization of image closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every cone \(C\subseteq V\), \[A^{-1}(A(C))=C+\ker A.\] If \(V,W\) are finite-dimensional, then \[A(C)\text{ is closed in }W\iff C+\ker A\text{ is closed in }V.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone image is closed exactly when its kernel-saturated preimage is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(C)\) is closed if and only if \(C+\ker A\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness via Kernel Saturation

children.title: Inverse Images of Cones
children.top_down_role: Pullback of conic structure through linear mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Pullback Relative-Interior Calculus without Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the map's range misses the relative interior of the target cone, relative interior need not commute with pullback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\) be \(A(t)=(t,0)\) and let \(K=\mathbb R_+^2\). Then
\[
\operatorname{ran}A\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing,
\qquad A^{-1}K=\mathbb R_+,
\]
so
\[
\operatorname{ri}(A^{-1}K)=(0,\infty)
eq A^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}K)=\varnothing.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(A^{-1}K)\neq A^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp planar range-qualification failure for a cone pullback.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality of an Inverse-Image Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lineality pulls back exactly. The pullback is pointed precisely when the map is injective and its range meets the target lineality only at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:V\to W\) be linear and let \(K\subseteq W\) be a convex cone. Then
\[
\operatorname{lin}(A^{-1}K)=A^{-1}(\operatorname{lin}K).
\]
Consequently, \(A^{-1}K\) is pointed if and only if
\[
\ker A=\{0\}\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{ran}A\cap\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(A^{-1}K)=A^{-1}(\operatorname{lin}K)\), with the stated pointedness criterion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic lineality and pointedness rule for a cone pullback.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interior of a Qualified Cone Pullback
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the range of the map meets the relative interior of the target cone, relative interior commutes with pullback.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V,W\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:V\to W\) be linear, and let \(K\subseteq W\) be a nonempty convex cone. If
\[
\operatorname{ran}A\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing,
\]
then
\[
\operatorname{ri}(A^{-1}K)=A^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}K).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq W\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(A^{-1}K)=A^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pullback rule under the standard range qualification.

notation.meaning: Relative interior in the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Images of Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pullback consists of vectors mapped into the cone. It is a convex cone containing the kernel, continuity preserves closedness under pullback, and pullback commutes with arbitrary intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The inverse-image cone is
\[
A^{-1}(K):=\{x\in V:Ax\in K\}.
\]
It is a convex cone in \(V\), and \(\ker A\subseteq A^{-1}(K)\). If \(V\) and \(W\) are topological vector spaces, \(A\) is continuous, and \(K\) is closed, then \(A^{-1}(K)\) is closed. Inverse images also commute with arbitrary intersections:
\[
A^{-1}\!\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i\right)=\bigcap_{i\in I}A^{-1}(K_i).
\]
assumptions_latex: \((K_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of convex cones in \(W\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{-1}(K)\) is a convex cone containing \(\ker A\); closedness is preserved by continuous \(A\), and inverse images commute with arbitrary intersections.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pullback of convex cones through linear maps, including preservation of intersections.

notation.meaning: Inverse image of the cone under the linear map.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Cone of a Closed Linear Pullback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional dual formula; closedness of the target cone prevents loss of information before intersection with the map range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With the positive-dual convention, \[(A^{-1}K)^*=\operatorname{cl}\bigl(A^*(K^*)\bigr).\] If \(A^*(K^*)\) is closed, the closure may be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed target cone, the dual of its pullback is the closure of the adjoint image of the target dual.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq W\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A^{-1}K)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*(K^*))\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Cone of a Closed Linear Pullback

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality and Pointedness of Pullback Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lineality formula and pointedness characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D=A^{-1}(K)\), \[\operatorname{lin}D=A^{-1}(\operatorname{lin}K).\] Moreover, \(D\) is pointed if and only if \(\ker A=\{0\}\) and \(K\cap A(V)\) is pointed in \(A(V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lineality pulls back exactly. A pullback is pointed precisely when the map is injective and the target cone's range section is pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(A^{-1}K)=A^{-1}(\operatorname{lin}K)\), with the stated pointedness criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality and Pointedness of Pullback Cones

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint substitution for finitely represented cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\{y\in W:By\geq0\}\), then \[A^{-1}(K)=\{x\in V:BAx\geq0\}.\] Consequently, finite-dimensional inverse images of polyhedral cones are polyhedral and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pulling back an inequality-described cone composes its constraint map with the linear map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{-1}(K)=\{x:BAx\geq0\}\), hence the pullback is polyhedral and closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Interior of a Qualified Pullback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inverse-image relative-interior rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A(V)\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname{ri}(A^{-1}(K))=A^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}K).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the map range meets the target cone's relative interior, relative interior commutes with pullback.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq W\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(A^{-1}K)=A^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}K)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interior of a Qualified Pullback

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be real vector spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(Q\subseteq Y\) be a cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition is valid algebraically. Statements about closedness additionally assume topological vector spaces and continuity of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse-image, or pullback, cone of \(Q\) through \(A\) is \[A^{-1}Q:=\{x\in X:Ax\in Q\}.\] It is a cone because \(A(\lambda x)=\lambda Ax\). If \(Q\) is convex, then \(A^{-1}Q\) is convex. If \(X,Y\) are topological vector spaces, \(A\) is continuous, and \(Q\) is closed, then \(A^{-1}Q\) is closed. Its lineality contains \(\ker A\), and membership depends only on the coset \(x+\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse image of a cone \(Q\) under a linear map \(A\) consists of all domain vectors whose images lie in \(Q\). It is always a cone and inherits convexity from \(Q\). Under continuity, it also inherits closedness. Every vector in the kernel belongs to the pullback whenever \(0\in Q\), and adding a kernel vector does not change membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{-1}Q=\{x\in X:Ax\in Q\}\) is a cone; it is convex when \(Q\) is convex and closed when \(A\) is continuous and \(Q\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in A^{-1}Q\iff Ax\in Q\).
If \(\pi:X\to X/\ker A\), then \(A^{-1}Q=\pi^{-1}(\widetilde A^{-1}(Q\cap\operatorname{ran}A))\).
special_cases_latex: For a scalar functional \(a^*:X\to\mathbb R\), \((a^*)^{-1}(\mathbb R_+)\) is a homogeneous halfspace.
boundary_notes: Unlike forward images, continuous inverse images always preserve closedness.
Equality in the inverse-image rule for sums need not hold without additional range conditions.

children.title: Quotient Cones
children.top_down_role: Conic structures obtained after collapsing linear subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of a Quotient Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the canonical identification of quotient functionals with functionals annihilating the collapsed subspace, the quotient cone's dual is the intersection of the original dual with that annihilator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(L\subseteq V\) be a linear subspace, and let \(q:V\to V/L\) be the quotient map. Identify \((V/L)^*\) with
\[
L^\circ=\{f\in V^*:f(\ell)=0\ \forall\ell\in L\}
\]
through \(q^*\). For every convex cone \(C\subseteq V\),
\[
q^*((q(C))^*)=C^*\cap L^\circ.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(q:V\to V/L\) is the canonical quotient map.
Dual cones use the nonnegative-pairing convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional quotient duality under the canonical identification of the quotient dual with the annihilator of the collapsed subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient cone comprises cosets represented by cone elements. Its lift is the cone enlarged by the collapsed subspace, whose closedness controls quotient closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone induced by \(C\) in the quotient space is
\[
C/L:=q(C)=\{x+L:x\in C\}=(C+L)/L.
\]
It is a convex cone in \(V/L\). Its saturation in \(V\) is
\[
q^{-1}(C/L)=C+L.
\]
If \(V\) is finite-dimensional, then \(C/L\) is closed in \(V/L\) if and only if \(C+L\) is closed in \(V\). Thus quotienting can destroy closedness even when \(C\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a real vector space and \(L\subseteq V\) is a linear subspace.
\(q:V\to V/L\) is the canonical quotient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quotient cone is \(q(C)=(C+L)/L\), and its full lift is \(q^{-1}(q(C))=C+L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone induced after identifying vectors that differ by an element of a subspace.

notation.meaning: Canonical coset map onto the quotient space.
Cone induced in the quotient space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic criterion for pointedness after collapsing a subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=q(C)\) and \(S=C+L=q^{-1}(D)\). Then \[q^{-1}(D\cap(-D))=S\cap(-S).\] Consequently, \[D\text{ is pointed}\iff (C+L)\cap(-(C+L))=L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient cone is pointed exactly when the lineality of its saturated lift is the collapsed subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a real vector space, \(L\subseteq V\) is a linear subspace, and \(q:V\to V/L\) is the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q(C)\cap(-q(C))=\{L\}\iff(C+L)\cap(-(C+L))=L.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness Criterion for Quotient Cones

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between quotient cones and cones invariant along quotient fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The assignments \(D\mapsto q^{-1}(D)\) and \(S\mapsto q(S)\) are mutually inverse, inclusion-preserving correspondences between convex cones \(D\subseteq V/L\) and convex cones \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \(S+L=S\). In particular, \(q^{-1}(q(C))=C+L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cones in a quotient correspond exactly to cones upstairs that are saturated under addition of the collapsed subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a real vector space, \(L\subseteq V\) is a linear subspace, and \(q:V\to V/L\) is canonical.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{D\subseteq V/L:D\text{ convex cone}\}\longleftrightarrow\{S\subseteq V:S\text{ convex cone and }S+L=S\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Saturated-Cone Correspondence

children.title: Closedness under Cone Operations
children.top_down_role: Closure-preserving regimes and failures for sums and linear images.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_m,Y\) be Hausdorff topological vector spaces, and let \(\mathcal O\) be a set operation defined on tuples of cones \((K_1,\ldots,K_m)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition separates the property of an operation on a specified class from the fact that a particular output happens to be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a class \(\mathfrak C\) of closed cones, the operation \(\mathcal O\) is closedness preserving on \(\mathfrak C\) if \[(K_1,\ldots,K_m)\in\mathfrak C^m\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal O(K_1,\ldots,K_m)\text{ is closed}.\] Intersections and continuous linear inverse images are unconditionally closedness preserving. Minkowski sums and continuous linear forward images are only conditionally closedness preserving: their output may fail to be closed for closed unbounded convex cones. A closedness regime is a specified collection of hypotheses—such as polyhedrality, compactness, or a recession-nullspace condition—under which the implication holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone operation is closedness preserving on a stated class when applying it to closed cones from that class always produces a closed set. Intersections and inverse images under continuous linear maps have this property without further regularity. Sums and forward linear images do not; for them, a closedness regime consists of additional hypotheses that guarantee the output is closed.
assumptions_latex: Every input cone \(K_i\) belongs to the declared class \(\mathfrak C\).
All topological and continuity conditions used by \(\mathcal O\) are included in the declared regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O\) is closedness preserving on \(\mathfrak C\) exactly when closed inputs in \(\mathfrak C\) always yield a closed output.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mathcal O(\mathfrak C^m)\subseteq\{C:C\text{ is closed}\}\).
A failure is witnessed by closed \(K_i\in\mathfrak C\) with \(\operatorname{cl}\mathcal O(K_1,\ldots,K_m)\neq\mathcal O(K_1,\ldots,K_m)\).
special_cases_latex: \(\mathcal O((K_i)_{i\in I})=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i\) preserves closedness.
\(\mathcal O(K)=A^{-1}K\) preserves closedness when \(A\) is continuous.
immediate_consequences_latex: Polyhedral linear-image regimes are closedness preserving in finite dimensions.
A counterexample for projections is also a counterexample for general linear images.
boundary_notes: Convexity preservation and closedness preservation are distinct properties.
The closure \(\operatorname{cl}(K_1+K_2)\) is always closed, but inserting closure changes the original operation.

notation.meaning: declared class of admissible closed cones

knowledge_statements.title: Sufficient Regimes for Closed Cone Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum of closed cones is closed when one summand is polyhedral or when the cones contain no nonzero mutually opposite directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K,L\subseteq V\) be closed convex cones in a finite-dimensional real vector space. The sum \(K+L\) is closed if either one summand is polyhedral or \(K\cap(-L)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\text{ polyhedral or }K\text{ polyhedral or }K\cap(-L)=\{0\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad K+L\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closure guarantees for binary sums of closed convex cones.

notation.meaning: Directions in one cone whose negatives belong to the other cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of Cone Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even two closed convex cones can have a nonclosed sum. Here a sequence in the sum converges to a matrix outside the sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Both \(K\) and \(L\) are closed convex cones, but \(K+L\) is not closed. In particular, the sequence
\[
Z_n=\begin{pmatrix}1/n&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\in K+L
\]
converges to
\[
Z=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\notin K+L.
\]
Thus closedness is not preserved by Minkowski addition of closed convex cones, even in finite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^2\) is the space of real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed convex cones \(K\) and \(L\) have a nonclosed Minkowski sum \(K+L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit finite-dimensional pathology showing that closed cone sums need not be closed.

Dual cones use the nonnegative-pairing convention.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(K_1,\ldots,K_m\subseteq X\) be nonempty closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns ordinary Minkowski addition. The listed recession condition is a standard sufficient regime, not part of the bare definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski sum is \[K_1+\cdots+K_m:=\{x_1+\cdots+x_m:x_i\in K_i\}.\] The family has the closed-sum property when \(K_1+\cdots+K_m\) is closed in \(X\). Equivalently, whenever \(x^k=\sum_i x_i^k\) with \(x_i^k\in K_i\) and \(x^k\to x\), there exist \(x_i\in K_i\) such that \(x=\sum_i x_i\). For cones, the sufficient recession condition from the general closed-sum criterion becomes: \(d_i\in K_i\) and \(\sum_i d_i=0\) imply \(d_i\in K_i\cap(-K_i)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of cones consists of all sums formed by choosing one vector from each cone. A family has the closed-sum property if every limit of such sums is itself representable as a sum of members of the cones. Closedness is not automatic. A standard sufficient condition excludes nonlineal recession directions from cancelling across the cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K_i\subseteq X\) is a nonempty closed convex cone for each \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
The topology on finite-dimensional \(X\) is its usual vector-space topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed-sum property is \(K_1+\cdots+K_m=\operatorname{cl}(K_1+\cdots+K_m)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every convergent sequence \(\sum_i x_i^k\to x\) with \(x_i^k\in K_i\), one has \(x\in\sum_iK_i\).
The addition map \(\Sigma:X^m\to X\), \(\Sigma(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_i x_i\), has closed image on \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\).
special_cases_latex: A finite sum of polyhedral cones is polyhedral and closed.
If every \(K_i\) is pointed and \(d_i\in K_i\), \(\sum_i d_i=0\) implies every \(d_i=0\), then the sufficient cancellation condition holds.
immediate_consequences_latex: For two cones, failure of closedness means \(\operatorname{cl}(K_1+K_2)\setminus(K_1+K_2)\neq\varnothing\).
Closed-sum criteria are instances of closedness criteria for linear images of product cones.
boundary_notes: Closedness of each summand alone is insufficient.
The algebraic sum remains a convex cone even when it is not closed.

children.title: Closedness of Linear Images
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral, facial, and transversality criteria for image closedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Description of the Image Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of a linear cone image is determined by dual vectors whose adjoint images lie in the cone dual; strict negative pairing certifies exclusion from that closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) be a convex cone and \(A:X\to Y\) be linear between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces. Then \[(A(C))^*=\{z\in Y:A^*z\in C^*\}\] and \[\overline{A(C)}=\{y\in Y:\langle z,y\rangle\geq0\text{ whenever }A^*z\in C^*\}.\] Consequently, \(y\notin\overline{A(C)}\) exactly when some \(z\) satisfies \(A^*z\in C^*\) and \(\langle z,y\rangle<0\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is a convex cone and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{A(C)}=\{z\in Y:A^*z\in C^*\}^*.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-dual convention; the formula characterizes the closure even when the image is nonclosed.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality-Adjusted Transversality Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone image is closed when the map's kernel meets the cone only along lineality directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space, let \(L=C\cap(-C)\), and let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear. If \[C\cap\ker A=L,\] then \(A(C)\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(C)\text{ is closed}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of the trivial-kernel criterion allowing kernel directions already contained in the cone's lineality.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Kernel Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the kernel meets the relative interior of a cone, the cone image equals the image of its span and is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(A\) be linear. If \[\ker A\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing,\] then \[A(C)=A(\operatorname{span}C).\] Consequently, \(A(C)\) is a linear subspace and is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(C)=A(\operatorname{span}C)\), hence \(A(C)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A transversality regime in which the cone image becomes a linear subspace.

notation.meaning: Relative interior of C in its span

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel-Saturation Criterion for Image Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear cone image is closed exactly when the cone saturated by the map's kernel is closed, equivalently when its quotient image is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) be a convex cone and \(A:X\to Y\) be linear between finite-dimensional spaces. Then \[A^{-1}(A(C))=C+\ker A,\] and \[A(C)\text{ is closed in }Y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C+\ker A\text{ is closed in }X.\] Equivalently, the image of \(C\) in \(X/\ker A\) is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is a convex cone and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(C)\text{ is closed}\iff C+\ker A\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional reduction to the quotient by the kernel.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of Linear Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image of a closed cone is closed when the cone is polyhedral or meets the map's kernel only at zero; closedness can otherwise fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) be a closed convex cone and let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear. If \(C\) is polyhedral, then \(A(C)\) is a polyhedral cone and hence is closed. Independently, if the transversality condition \(C\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) holds, then \(A(C)\) is closed. Thus polyhedrality and trivial intersection with the kernel are two sufficient mechanisms for closedness; absent such a condition, linear images of closed convex cones need not be closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex cone and a linear map have the closed-image property if the image cone contains all its limit points. Sequentially, every limit of vectors \(Ax_k\), with \(x_k\in K\), must equal \(Ax\) for some \(x\in K\). A standard sufficient condition says that every cone direction annihilated by \(A\) must be a lineality direction. Polyhedral cones satisfy the property for all linear maps.

Closedness of cone sums follows by applying this property to the addition map on a product cone.

\(\mathbb S_+^2\) is the cone of positive semidefinite real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrices.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=U\oplus V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(P_U:X\to U\) be the canonical projection, and let \(K\subseteq X\) be a closed convex cone or closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonclosed projection pathology occurs when \[P_UK\neq\operatorname{cl}(P_UK).\] Equivalently, there exist \(u_k\in P_UK\) and \(\bar u\in U\) such that \(u_k\to\bar u\) but \(\bar u\notin P_UK\). Choosing lifts \(u_k+v_k\in K\), the pathology means that projected coordinates converge while no lift \(\bar u+v\in K\) exists. For a cone, the missing-limit set \(\operatorname{cl}(P_UK)\setminus P_UK\) is conic under positive scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection pathology is the failure of a projected closed convex set or cone to remain closed. It is witnessed by projected points converging to a limit that has no feasible lift in the original set. The eliminated coordinates of chosen lifts may escape without producing a limit in the original space. In the conic case, positive multiples of a missing projected limit are again missing unless they collapse to the origin.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar and Dual Cones in a Hilbert Space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record uses the nonpositive polar convention. The positive dual cone is its negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar cone and dual cone of \(C\) are \[C^{\ominus}:=\{u\in\mathcal H:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,u\rangle\leq0\},\qquad C^{\oplus}:=-C^{\ominus}=\{u:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,u\rangle\geq0\}.\] Both are nonempty closed convex cones and depend only on the closed convex conical hull of \(C\). Polarity reverses inclusion. The bipolar \(C^{\ominus\ominus}\) recovers the closed convex conical hull of \(C\), so polarity converts primal conic geometry into inequalities in the paired space and back.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone contains all vectors having nonpositive inner product with every point of \(C\). The dual cone uses the opposite, nonnegative sign and equals the negative of the polar. These cones are always closed and convex, reverse inclusions, and ignore any difference between \(C\) and its closed convex conical hull. Applying the nonpositive polar twice returns that hull.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(C\subseteq\mathcal H\) is arbitrary for polarity; bipolar recovery assumes \(C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\ominus}=\{u:\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\}\), \(C^{\oplus}=-C^{\ominus}\), and \(C^{\ominus\ominus}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}C\) for nonempty convex \(C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(u\in C^{\ominus}\iff\sigma_C(u)\leq0\), where \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\).
\(C^{\ominus}=(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}\operatorname{conv}C)^{\ominus}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(L\) is a linear subspace, then \(L^{\ominus}=L^{\oplus}=L^{\perp}\).
A closed convex cone \(K\) is self-dual when \(K=K^{\oplus}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(D\subseteq C\Rightarrow C^{\ominus}\subseteq D^{\ominus}\).
\((K_1+K_2)^{\ominus}=K_1^{\ominus}\cap K_2^{\ominus}\) for nonempty cones.
boundary_notes: Some literature writes the nonnegative dual as \(K^*\) and calls it the polar.
For general dual-paired spaces, the polar lies in the paired dual space rather than in the primal space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polarity Relative to a Separating Dual Pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a real separating dual pair: \(X,Y\) are real vector spaces and the bilinear pairing separates points of both spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unlike Hilbert-space polarity, the two polar operations change ambient spaces: subsets of \(X\) polarize into \(Y\), and subsets of \(Y\) polarize into \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C\subseteq X\), its nonpositive polar in \(Y\) is \[C^{\circ}_Y:=\{y\in Y:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,y\rangle\leq0\}.\] For \(D\subseteq Y\), its nonpositive polar in \(X\) is \[D^{\circ}_X:=\{x\in X:(\forall y\in D)\ \langle x,y\rangle\leq0\}.\] The corresponding nonnegative dual cones are \(C^*_Y=-C^{\circ}_Y\) and \(D^*_X=-D^{\circ}_X\). A bipolar is formed by alternating spaces, namely \(C^{\circ\circ}:=(C^{\circ}_Y)^{\circ}_X\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a dual pair, a subset of the primal space has a polar in the paired dual space, defined by nonpositive pairing with every primal element. A subset of the dual space polarizes back into the primal space. Thus a bipolar alternates the two ambient spaces. The positive dual convention is obtained by negating the nonpositive polar.
assumptions_latex: The pairing separates points of \(X\) and \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ}_Y=\{y:(\forall x\in C)\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\}\) and \(C^{\circ\circ}=(C^{\circ}_Y)^{\circ}_X\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in C^{\circ}_Y\iff\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\).
\(C^*_Y=\{y:(\forall x\in C)\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\}=-C^{\circ}_Y\).
special_cases_latex: For a Hilbert space identified with its continuous dual, the two ambient spaces coincide.
For \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=(\mathbb R^n)^*\), the pairing is functional evaluation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Polarity reverses inclusion across the pairing.
Every polar is an intersection of homogeneous closed halfspaces in the weak topology generated by the paired space.
boundary_notes: Writing both polar cones as subsets of one space requires an explicit identification, such as a Hilbert-space Riesz identification.
Changing the paired subspace \(Y\) can change both the polar and the closure recovered by the bipolar.

knowledge_statements.title: Antitonicity and Closed-Conic-Hull Invariance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inner-product dualization reverses inclusion and is unchanged when a set is replaced by its closed convex conic hull.

\[
A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow B^*\subseteq A^*,

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Cones under Inner Products

The set \(K^*\) is always a closed convex cone, whether or not \(K\) itself is convex or closed.

A\subseteq B\Longrightarrow B^*\subseteq A^*,

A^*=\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{cone}(A)}\bigr)^*,

A^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(A)}.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Sign Conventions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonpositive polar cone is the negative of the nonnegative dual cone, so formulas cross conventions by negating every polar object.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the nonpositive convention, define \(K^\circ:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). Under the nonnegative convention, define \(K^*:=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). These conventions translate exactly by \[K^\circ=-K^*,\qquad K^*=-K^\circ.\] Therefore any formula stated with one convention must reverse the sign of each polar cone when translated to the other; omitting this sign change generally reverses the asserted inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^\circ=-K^*\), equivalently \(K^*=-K^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonpositive Polar versus Nonnegative Dual Convention
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition fixes the translation boundary between the two dominant sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonpositive polar convention is \[C^{\ominus}:=\{u\in\mathcal H:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,u\rangle\leq0\}.\] The nonnegative dual convention is \[C^{\oplus}:=\{u\in\mathcal H:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,u\rangle\geq0\}.\] They are related exactly by \(C^{\oplus}=-C^{\ominus}\) and \(C^{\ominus}=-C^{\oplus}\). Consequently, a formula written with one convention is translated to the other by negating every polar cone while retaining the underlying primal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the nonpositive convention, polar vectors pair at most zero with the original set. Under the nonnegative convention, usually called the dual cone convention, they pair at least zero. The two cones differ only by a sign: the dual cone is the negative of the polar cone. Any formula mixing sources must therefore record which convention is being used.
assumptions_latex: \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) is the real Hilbert inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\oplus}=-C^{\ominus}\), where \(C^{\ominus}\) uses \(\leq0\) and \(C^{\oplus}\) uses \(\geq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(u\in C^{\oplus}\iff -u\in C^{\ominus}\).
\(C^{\ominus\ominus}=C^{\oplus\oplus}\) whenever both iterated operations use their respective convention consistently.
special_cases_latex: For a linear subspace \(L\), \(L^{\ominus}=L^{\oplus}=L^{\perp}\).
For \(C=\mathbb R_+^n\), \(C^{\oplus}=\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(C^{\ominus}=-\mathbb R_+^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Self-duality under the positive convention, \(K=K^{\oplus}\), corresponds to \(K^{\ominus}=-K\).
The sum rule has the same form under either consistent convention: \((K_1+K_2)^{\ominus}=K_1^{\ominus}\cap K_2^{\ominus}\).
boundary_notes: The unit-level polar of a general convex body, defined using \(\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\), is not the cone polar defined here.
A superscript \(^*\) is ambiguous unless the source's sign convention is stated.

knowledge_statements.title: Antitone Galois Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive dualization across paired spaces is an inclusion-reversing Galois correspondence; bidualization is extensive and taking three duals returns the first dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For cones \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\),
\[
K\subseteq{}^+L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subseteq K^+.
\]
Consequently \(K\subseteq{}^+(K^+)\), \(L\subseteq({}^+L)^+\), and triple dualization returns the first dual:
\[
({}^+(K^+))^+=K^+,
\qquad
{}^+(({}^+L)^+)={}^+L.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\subseteq{}^+L\iff L\subseteq K^+\), with bidual extensivity and triple-dual identities.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Pair Cone Bipolar Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive bidual of a cone in a separating dual pair is its weakly closed convex conic hull; a convex cone equals its bidual exactly when weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separating real dual pair and let \(K\subseteq X\) be a cone. Then
\[
{}^+(K^+)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}_{\mathrm{cvx}}(K)}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.
\]

knowledge_statements.title: Cones in Dual-Paired Spaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a separating dual pair, a cone is sent to the cone of elements in the opposite space that pair nonnegatively with all its elements; algebraic and continuous duals are special cases when their required structures are present.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separating real dual pair. For cones \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\), define \[K^+:=\{y\in Y:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\] and \[{}^+L:=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }y\in L\}.\] These cones lie in opposite members of the pair. The choice \(Y=X^*\) gives the algebraic-dual construction. If \(X\) is a real topological vector space whose continuous dual \(X'\) separates points, the choice \(Y=X'\) gives the continuous-dual construction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic characterization of mutually nonnegative pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separating real dual pair. For arbitrary subsets \(A\subseteq X\) and \(B\subseteq Y\),
\[
A\subseteq{}^+B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\subseteq A^+.
\]
Consequently, paired dualization reverses inclusion on both sides of the pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paired dualization is an inclusion-reversing Galois connection: all elements of A pair nonnegatively with all elements of B exactly when either set lies in the paired dual of the other.
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a separating real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\subseteq{}^+B\iff B\subseteq A^+\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar Theorem for a Separating Dual Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-topology bipolar closure in either member of a dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separating real dual pair. For every \(A\subseteq X\) and \(B\subseteq Y\),
\[
{}^+(A^+)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(A)}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)},
\qquad
({}^+B)^+=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(B)}^{\,\sigma(Y,X)}.
\]
Consequently, a convex cone is equal to its paired bidual exactly when it is closed in the corresponding weak topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a separating dual pair, the paired bidual is the weakly closed convex conic hull; weakly closed convex cones are precisely the fixed points of paired bidualization.
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a separating real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \({}^+(A^+)=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(A)}^{\sigma(X,Y)}\) and \(({}^+B)^+=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(B)}^{\sigma(Y,X)}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Cone Bipolarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex cone in a Hilbert space is recovered exactly by taking its nonnegative dual cone twice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq H\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and use the nonnegative convention \(K^*=\{y\in H:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). Then the bipolar cone recovers \(K\) exactly: \[K^{**}=K.\] Thus closedness and convexity make the inequalities defining the dual cone sufficient to characterize membership in the original cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq H\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\) be a nonempty convex cone.

Consequently, closed-cone bipolarity is exact recovery of \(K\) from all homogeneous nonpositive inequalities valid on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex cone is bipolar closed when applying the nonpositive polar twice returns the cone exactly. In a Hilbert space, this fixed-point condition is equivalent to the cone being norm closed. Thus a closed convex cone is completely determined by the homogeneous linear inequalities satisfied by all of its points.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\) is a nonempty convex cone.
Closure is taken in the norm topology of \(\mathcal H\).

\(x\in K\iff(\forall u\in K^{\ominus})\ \langle x,u\rangle\leq0\).
special_cases_latex: Every nonempty closed linear subspace \(L\) satisfies \(L=L^{\perp\perp}\).
Every nonempty closed self-dual cone satisfies \(K=K^{\ominus\ominus}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(x\notin K\), some \(u\in K^{\ominus}\) satisfies \(\langle x,u\rangle>0\).
The polar mapping is injective on the class of nonempty closed convex cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Bipolar Completion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double dualization of an arbitrary cone yields its closed convex conic hull, adding convex combinations and missing limit points when necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq H\) be a nonempty cone, without assuming convexity or closedness. Under the nonnegative dual convention, \[K^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(K)}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(K)},\] where closure is taken in the norm topology. Since \(K\) is already closed under nonnegative scaling, its convex hull is a cone. Therefore repeated dualization preserves exactly the closed convex conic hull of \(K\), and it enlarges \(K\) precisely when \(K\) is not already closed and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq H\) is a nonempty cone, not necessarily convex or closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(K)}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(K)}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar Completion of a Nonclosed Convex Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\) be a nonempty convex cone that is not assumed closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition isolates the closure added by repeated polarity; it does not apply an additional convexification because \(K\) is already convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonclosed bipolar completion of \(K\) is \[\widehat K_{\mathrm{bip}}:=K^{\ominus\ominus}=\overline K.\] The completion gap is \[G_{\mathrm{bip}}(K):=K^{\ominus\ominus}\setminus K=\overline K\setminus K.\] Thus \(G_{\mathrm{bip}}(K)=\varnothing\) exactly when \(K\) is closed. Moreover, \(K\) and its completion have the same polar: \(K^{\ominus}=(\overline K)^{\ominus}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex cone that may not be closed, the bipolar completion is its closure. The completion gap consists of the limit directions added by taking the bipolar. This gap is empty precisely for a closed cone. Polarity cannot distinguish the cone from its closure, since both have the same polar.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathcal H\) is a nonempty convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=\overline K\) and \(G_{\mathrm{bip}}(K)=\overline K\setminus K\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\widehat K_{\mathrm{bip}}\) is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(K\).
\(x\in\widehat K_{\mathrm{bip}}\iff(\forall u\in K^{\ominus})\ \langle x,u\rangle\leq0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is closed, then \(\widehat K_{\mathrm{bip}}=K\).
If \(K\) is dense in a closed convex cone \(C\), then \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \((\widehat K_{\mathrm{bip}})^{\ominus}=K^{\ominus}\).
Bipolar completion is idempotent: \((K^{\ominus\ominus})^{\ominus\ominus}=K^{\ominus\ominus}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Changing the Paired Dual Can Change Cone Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A half-space defined by a discontinuous algebraic functional is closed for the algebraic-dual weak topology but dense for the continuous-dual weak topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an infinite-dimensional normed space, let \(f\in X^\#\setminus X^*\), and set \(K=\{x\in X:f(x)\geq0\}\). Then \[\overline K^{\,\sigma(X,X^\#)}=K,\qquad \overline K^{\,\sigma(X,X^*)}=X.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\in X^\#\setminus X^*\) is algebraic-linear and discontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline K^{\,\sigma(X,X^\#)}=K\) and \(\overline K^{\,\sigma(X,X^*)}=X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Is Necessary for Pointwise Bipolar Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the paired space does not separate points, the bipolar of the zero cone is the annihilator rather than the zero cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a bilinear pairing and define its left annihilator \[N:=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle=0\ \forall y\in Y\}.\] Under the nonnegative cone-dual convention, for \(K=\{0\}\) one has \(K^+=Y\) and \[{}^+(K^+)={}^+Y=N.\] Hence, if \(N\ne\{0\}\), even the zero cone is not recovered by bipolarization.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are in bilinear duality, not necessarily separating.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of bipolar recovery when the selected pairing does not separate the original space.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity of Bipolar Completion under Dual Enlargement
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger paired dual yields a smaller or equal bipolar completion because it supplies more separating inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_1\subseteq Y_2\subseteq X^\#\), and suppose both \((X,Y_i)\) are separating dual pairs. For a cone \(K\subseteq X\), let \(B_i={}^+(K^+_{Y_i})\). Then \[B_2\subseteq B_1.\] Thus enlarging the paired dual supplies more separating inequalities and can only shrink the bipolar completion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order relation between bipolar closures formed from two separating paired spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Compatible Topologies Have the Same Closed Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally convex topologies compatible with a fixed dual pair have the same closed convex sets, so bipolar closure changes only when the paired dual space changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y)\) be a separating dual pair. If \(\mathcal T\) is a locally convex topology on \(X\) whose continuous dual is exactly \(Y\), then every convex set \(C\subseteq X\) satisfies \[\overline C^{\,\mathcal T}=\overline C^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.\] In particular, \(\sigma(X,Y)\) and \(\tau(X,Y)\) have the same closed convex cones.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal T\) is locally convex and \((X,\mathcal T)'=Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline C^{\,\mathcal T}=\overline C^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology variation while the separating paired dual space remains fixed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separating dual pairs on the same vector space whose weak closures of one cone differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\ell^1\) and \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1+e_n:n\ge2\}\). Both \((\ell^1,c_0)\) and \((\ell^1,\ell^\infty)\) are separating dual pairs under \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_nx_ny_n\). Since \(e_1+e_n\to e_1\) in \(\sigma(\ell^1,c_0)\), \[e_1\in\overline K^{\sigma(\ell^1,c_0)}.\] In contrast, \(y=(-1,1,1,\ldots)\in\ell^\infty\) is nonnegative on \(K\) but \(\langle e_1,y\rangle=-1\), so \[e_1\notin\overline K^{\sigma(\ell^1,\ell^\infty)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the paired space from all bounded sequences to null sequences weakens the available inequalities and enlarges the weak closure, hence can change the bipolar.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e_1\in\overline K^{\sigma(\ell^1,c_0)}\setminus\overline K^{\sigma(\ell^1,\ell^\infty)}.

For any set \(S\subseteq E\), write \(\operatorname{cone}S\), \(\operatorname{cl}S\), and \(S^\perp\) for its conic hull, closure, and orthogonal complement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry uses the nonnegative dual convention. Rockafellar's polar cone has the opposite sign: \(K^*=-K^\circ\). All closure statements are finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual cone and polar cone of \(K\) are \[K^*:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\},\qquad K^\circ:=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}=-K^*.\] Dualization is antitone and insensitive to conic generation and closure: \[K_1\subseteq K_2\Rightarrow K_2^*\subseteq K_1^*,\qquad S^*=(\operatorname{cone}S)^*=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}S)^*.\] The cone \(K^*\) is always closed and convex, and the bidual relation is \[K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K.\] Consequently, dualization is an order-reversing involution on the class of closed convex cones. The basic terminal cases are \(\{0\}^*=E\), \(E^*=\{0\}\), and \(L^*=L^\perp\) for every linear subspace \(L\subseteq E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a cone K in a finite-dimensional inner-product space, its dual consists of all vectors having nonnegative inner product with every vector of K; its polar uses the opposite inequality. Dualization reverses inclusion, is unchanged by taking conic hull or closure, always produces a closed convex cone, and satisfies K bidual equals the closure of K. Thus it is an order-reversing involution on closed convex cones. The duals of the zero cone, the whole space, and a subspace are respectively the whole space, the zero cone, and the orthogonal complement.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional and carries the displayed inner product.
\(K,K_1,K_2\subseteq E\) are convex cones whenever the corresponding identities are invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=-K^\circ\), dualization is antitone, and \(K^{**}=\operatorname{cl}K\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in K^*\iff \inf_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\).
For closed convex cones, \(K_1=K_2\iff K_1^*=K_2^*\).
special_cases_latex: \(L^*=L^\perp\) for a subspace \(L\).
\((\mathbb R_+^n)^*=\mathbb R_+^n\) under the Euclidean pairing.
immediate_consequences_latex: \((\operatorname{cl}K)^*=K^*\).
The equality \(K=K^{**}\) characterizes closed convex cones among convex cones.
boundary_notes: Changing the pairing changes the representing dual cone.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the bidual formula depends on the chosen dual topology.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Duality rules for sums and intersections of cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Let \(K_1,K_2\subseteq E\) be nonempty convex cones, and define \(K_1+K_2:=\{x_1+x_2:x_i\in K_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formulas use nonnegative dual cones. Closure is retained where it is genuinely needed; it cannot generally be deleted from the dual of an intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sum-intersection duality calculus is the pair of identities \[(K_1+K_2)^*=K_1^*\cap K_2^*,\qquad (K_1\cap K_2)^*=\operatorname{cl}(K_1^*+K_2^*)\] when \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are closed convex cones. More generally, for a family \((K_i)_{i\in I}\), \[\left(\sum_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i^*,\] where the sum denotes the cone of finite sums. If \(K_1^*+K_2^*\) is closed, the closure in the intersection formula is unnecessary. A standard sufficient qualification is \(\operatorname{ri}K_1\cap\operatorname{ri}K_2\neq\varnothing\); polyhedrality of both cones is another sufficient regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a Minkowski sum of convex cones is the intersection of their dual cones. For closed convex cones, the dual of their intersection is the closure of the sum of their duals. The closure may be omitted when that dual sum is already closed, including standard relative-interior-qualified and polyhedral cases. The sum rule extends to arbitrary families when the primal sum means finite sums.
assumptions_latex: For \((K_1\cap K_2)^*=\operatorname{cl}(K_1^*+K_2^*)\), both cones are closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in(K_1+K_2)^*\iff y\in K_1^*\text{ and }y\in K_2^*\).
If \(K_1^*+K_2^*\) is closed, then \(y\in(K_1\cap K_2)^*\iff y=y_1+y_2\) for some \(y_i\in K_i^*\).
special_cases_latex: \((K+L)^*=K^*\cap L^\perp\) for a cone \(K\) and subspace \(L\).
For polyhedral cones, \((K_1\cap K_2)^*=K_1^*+K_2^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite systems of homogeneous inequalities dualize to finitely generated cones.
Finite conic generators dualize to intersections of homogeneous half-spaces.
boundary_notes: The algebraic sum of two closed convex cones need not be closed.
For nonclosed cones, bidualization introduces closure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed Hilbert-space extension of the binary intersection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[
\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i\right)^*=\overline{\operatorname{cone}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}K_i^*\right)},
\]
where the closure is in the norm topology. Equivalently, the right-hand side is the closure of all finite sums of elements drawn from the cones \(K_i^*\). For finite \(I\), this is \((\bigcap_iK_i)^*=\overline{\sum_iK_i^*}\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(E_i\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces and let \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) be convex cones. Equip \(E:=E_1\oplus\cdots\oplus E_m\) with \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: In finite products the Cartesian product and external direct sum have the same underlying set; the terminology records whether the construction is viewed set-theoretically or as a decomposition of the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The product cone is \[\prod_{i=1}^mK_i:=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in E:x_i\in K_i\ \forall i\}.\] Its dual is componentwise: \[\left(\prod_{i=1}^mK_i\right)^*=\prod_{i=1}^mK_i^*.\] Equivalently, if mutually orthogonal subspaces \(E_i\) decompose \(E\) and \(K_i\subseteq E_i\), then for the external conic direct sum \(K_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K_m\), \[(K_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K_m)^*=K_1^*\oplus\cdots\oplus K_m^*,\] with each \(K_i^*\) computed inside \(E_i\). Thus membership, closedness, pointedness, solidity relative to the product space, and self-duality are determined componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an orthogonal direct sum of finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, the dual of a Cartesian product of cones is the Cartesian product of their dual cones. The same formula is written as a direct-sum identity when the ambient space is decomposed into orthogonal components. Consequently, dual membership and the usual regularity or self-duality properties can be checked factor by factor.
assumptions_latex: Each \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left(\prod_iK_i\right)^*=\prod_iK_i^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in(\prod_iK_i)^*\iff y_i\in K_i^*\ \forall i\).
\(\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in\prod_iK_i\iff \langle y_i,x_i\rangle_i\geq0\ \forall x_i\in K_i,\forall i\).
special_cases_latex: A finite product of self-dual cones is self-dual under the product inner product.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(\prod_iK_i)=\prod_i\operatorname{lin}K_i\).
\(\operatorname{int}(\prod_iK_i)=\prod_i\operatorname{int}K_i\).
boundary_notes: For nonorthogonal decompositions, the formula must be transported through the adjoint of the chosen identification.
Infinite products require a specified topology and continuous dual.

Then \[K^*=\prod_{i=1}^m K_i^*.\] Thus a vector \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_m)\) is dual-feasible for the product cone exactly when each component \(y_i\) is dual-feasible for its corresponding factor. No convexity or closedness assumption is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary on extending the finite Cartesian-product formula to infinitely many Hilbert factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For countably many factors \(H_i=\mathbb R\), the Hilbert direct sum is \(H=\ell^2\), not the full Cartesian product \(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\). If \(K_i=\mathbb R_+\), then \[K=\{x\in\ell^2:x_i\ge0\ \forall i\},\qquad K^*=K.\] Thus coordinatewise nonnegativity must be accompanied by \(y\in\ell^2\); the unrestricted product \(\prod_iK_i^*=\mathbb R_+^{\mathbb N}\) is not the Hilbert-space dual cone. In particular, \((1,1,\ldots)\) lies in the unrestricted product but not in \(H\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous-Dual Boundary for Algebraic Direct Sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the seed's algebraic paired dual from the continuous dual induced by an infinite-dimensional norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_{00}=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb N}\mathbb R\) carry the \(\ell^2\)-norm, and let \(K=c_{00,+}\). Under the finite-support pairing, the algebraic paired dual cone is \(\mathbb R_+^{\mathbb N}\). In contrast, every continuous linear functional on \((c_{00},\|\cdot\|_2)\) is represented by a sequence in \(\ell^2\), so the continuous positive dual cone is \(\ell_+^2\). Thus \[K^*_{\mathrm{cont}}=\ell_+^2\subsetneq\mathbb R_+^{\mathbb N}=K^*_{\mathrm{alg}}.\] The sequence \((1,1,\ldots)\) defines a positive algebraic functional on finite-support vectors but is not continuous for the \(\ell^2\)-norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an infinite algebraic direct sum, the full product is the algebraic paired dual, while a chosen topology can reduce the continuous dual to a proper subcone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*_{\mathrm{cont}}=\ell_+^2\subsetneq\mathbb R_+^{\mathbb N}=K^*_{\mathrm{alg}}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Is Necessary in the Pullback-Dual Rule
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite pullback has a dual equal only to the closure of the adjoint image, so closure in the general inverse-image rule is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define \(A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb S^2\) by \[A(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}u&v/2\\v/2&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(A^{-1}C=\mathbb R_+\times\{0\}\), while \[A^*C=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\] is not closed. Consequently, \[\bigl(A^{-1}C\bigr)^*=\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R=\overline{A^*C}\neq A^*C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^2\) carries the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(A^{-1}C\bigr)^*=\overline{A^*C}\neq A^*C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional semidefinite example where the adjoint image of the dual cone is nonclosed.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of a Linear Inverse Image
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of a cone pullback is the closure of the adjoint image of the dual; a relative-interior qualification removes the closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear and let \(C\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone. Then \[\bigl(A^{-1}C\bigr)^*=\overline{A^*C^*}.\] If \(\operatorname{range}A\cap\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing\), then \(A^*C^*\) is closed and \[\bigl(A^{-1}C\bigr)^*=A^*C^*.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(A^{-1}C\bigr)^*=\overline{A^*C^*}\), with closure unnecessary if \(\operatorname{range}A\cap\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pullback rule, including the closure term and a relative-interior qualification that removes it.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of a Cone Section
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual within a subspace of a cone section is the closure of the orthogonal projection of the ambient dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone and let \(L\subseteq E\) be a linear subspace. Forming the dual inside \(L\), \[(K\cap L)^{*_{L}}=\overline{P_L(K^*)}^{\;L}.\] If \(L\cap\operatorname{ri}K\neq\varnothing\), the closure may be omitted.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a cone and let \(L\subseteq E\) be a linear subspace. Then the dual formed inside \(L\) satisfies \[\bigl(P_LK\bigr)^{*_{L}}=K^*\cap L.\] No convexity or closedness of \(K\) or \(P_LK\) is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Duals under Linear Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing a linear image converts the map into an adjoint inverse image of the original dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual cone of the linear image of \(K\) is the adjoint inverse image of its dual: \[(AK)^*=\{y\in Y:A^*y\in K^*\}=(A^*)^{-1}(K^*).\] Equivalently, \(y\in(AK)^*\) if and only if \(\langle A^*y,x\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in K\). This identity requires no closedness of \(K\) or \(AK\).

\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(K\subseteq X\) is a convex cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Cannot Be Dropped from the Pullback Rule

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y=\mathbb S^2\), \(C=\mathbb S_+^2\), and define \(A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb S^2\) by \[A(x_1,x_2)=\begin{pmatrix}x_1&x_2/2\\x_2/2&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Under the trace pairing, \(A^*Z=(z_{11},z_{12})\), and \[A^*C^*=\{(u,v):u>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] which is not closed. Moreover, \[A^{-1}C=\{(x_1,0):x_1\ge0\},\qquad (A^{-1}C)^*=\{(u,v):u\ge0\}=\overline{A^*C^*}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite pullback has a nonclosed adjoint dual image, so the general inverse-image formula genuinely requires closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint calculus for images, inverse images, sections, and projections
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E,F\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:F\to E\), and let \(K\subseteq E\), \(L\subseteq F\) be closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image formulas describe the dual exactly even when the primal image is not closed. The inverse-image and section formulas retain closure unless a standard closedness qualification applies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual-cone rules for a linear map are \[(AK)^*=\{y\in F:A^*y\in K^*\}=(A^*)^{-1}(K^*),\] and \[(A^{-1}L)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*L^*),\qquad A^{-1}L:=\{x\in E:Ax\in L\}.\] If \(M\subseteq E\) is a subspace and \(P_M\) is the orthogonal projection, then, with duals of cones in \(M\) computed using the induced inner product, \[(P_MK)^*=K^*\cap M,\qquad (K\cap M)^{*_{M}}=\operatorname{cl}(P_MK^*).\] Thus projection and section are dual operations, while image and inverse image are related through the adjoint. The closures may be removed whenever the displayed adjoint images are closed, including appropriate polyhedral or relative-interior-qualified cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of the image of a cone under a linear map consists exactly of vectors whose adjoint images lie in the original dual cone. The dual of an inverse image is the closure of the adjoint image of the dual. For an orthogonal projection onto a subspace, the dual of the projected cone is the intersection of the original dual with that subspace, while the dual within the subspace of a section is the closure of the projected dual.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((AK)^*=(A^*)^{-1}(K^*)\) and \((A^{-1}L)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*L^*)\), with the stated projection-section specializations.

\(y\in(P_MK)^*\iff y\in M\cap K^*\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, \((AK)^*=A^{-*}K^*\).
For a coordinate projection, the dual of the projection is the corresponding coordinate section of the dual.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonclosed linear image and its closure have the same dual cone.
Lifted conic formulations turn projection questions into sections of dual cones.

children.top_down_role: Dual relationships among lineality, span, pointedness, solidity, and generation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity dictionary for a cone and its dual
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Define \(\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\) and \(\operatorname{span}K:=K-K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solidity means nonempty interior in the stated ambient space. When intrinsic topology is intended, replace interior and full dimensionality by relative interior and the span of the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The principal regularity properties are: \(K\) is pointed when \(\operatorname{lin}K=\{0\}\); solid when \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\); generating when \(K-K=E\); and proper when it is closed, convex, pointed, and solid. Duality exchanges these properties through \[\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}K)^\perp.\] Hence \[K\text{ pointed}\iff K^*\text{ solid},\qquad K\text{ solid}\iff K^*\text{ pointed},\] and, in finite dimensions, solidity is equivalent to generation. Consequently, \(K\) is proper if and only if \(K^*\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex cone, lineality is the largest reversible subspace and the span is the space generated by differences of cone elements. A cone is pointed when its lineality is zero, solid when it has nonempty ambient interior, generating when its span is the whole space, and proper when it is closed, convex, pointed, and solid. The dual's lineality is the orthogonal complement of the primal span, and the dual span is the orthogonal complement of primal lineality. Therefore pointedness and solidity are exchanged by dualization, while properness is preserved.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp\), \(\operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}K)^\perp\), and pointedness and solidity are dual properties.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is pointed \(\iff \operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\).
\(K\) is generating \(\iff K^*\cap(-K^*)=\{0\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\) is a subspace, \(K^*=K^\perp\), so neither cone is pointed unless its subspace is zero.
A full-dimensional polyhedral cone is pointed exactly when its dual has nonempty interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(K\) and \(K^*\) have complementary lineality and span dimensions.
Dualizing a proper cone remains within the class used for finite-dimensional conic optimization.
boundary_notes: A cone can be pointed without being full-dimensional.
Relative solidity inside \(\operatorname{span}K\) is automatic for nonempty convex cones and is not the ambient solidity used here.

children.title: Pointedness–Solidity Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence between lineality-free and interior-bearing regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity Characterization of Dual Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior of the dual consists exactly of functionals strictly positive on every nonzero primal cone vector; such a functional exists exactly when the closed cone is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(E\). Then
\[
\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle>0\text{ for every }x\in K\setminus\{0\}\}.
\]
Consequently, \(K\) is pointed exactly when some \(y\in E\) is strictly positive on every nonzero element of \(K\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle>0\ \forall x\in K\setminus\{0\}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointwise characterization underlying pointedness–solidity duality.

notation.meaning: Ordinary ambient interior of the dual cone

knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness–Solidity Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed finite-dimensional cones, pointedness of either cone is equivalent to solidity of its dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cone is pointed when \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\), and it is solid when \(\operatorname{int}K
eq\varnothing\). For a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), dualization exchanges these properties: \[K	ext{ is pointed}\iff\operatorname{int}(K^*)
eq\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{int}(K)
eq\varnothing\iff K^*	ext{ is pointed}.\] Thus absence of reversible primal directions is equivalent to full-dimensional dual interior, and conversely.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\text{ is pointed}\iff\operatorname{int}(K^*)\neq\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{int}(K)\neq\varnothing\iff K^*\text{ is pointed}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-cone version using ordinary ambient interior.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the fixed inner product

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise characterization of dual solidity for a closed finite-dimensional convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(E\). Then
\[
\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\{y\in E:\langle y,x\rangle>0\text{ for every }x\in K\setminus\{0\}\}.
\]
Consequently, \(K\) is pointed exactly when there exists a vector strictly positive on every nonzero element of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector lies in the interior of the dual exactly when it pairs strictly positively with every nonzero primal cone vector; existence of such a vector certifies pointedness.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle>0\ \forall x\in K\setminus\{0\}\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity Certificate for Dual Interior

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Is Necessary for Pointedness–Solidity Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed nonconvex conic counterexample in the finite-dimensional ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(K\) be the union of the three rays generated by
\[
(1,0),\qquad\left(-\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),\qquad\left(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right).
\]
Then \(K\) is closed, positively homogeneous, and pointed, but it is not convex and \(K^*=\{0\}\). Thus \(K^*\) has empty interior. Moreover, \(K^*\) is pointed while \(K\) itself has empty interior, so both exchanges can fail without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A union of three rays separated by 120 degrees is a closed pointed nonconvex cone whose dual is only zero; it also has empty interior despite its dual being pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(E=\mathbb R^2\) with its Euclidean inner product.
\(K\) is the union of the three displayed rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\), \(K^*=\{0\}\), and \(\operatorname{int}K=\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Necessary for Pointedness–Solidity Exchange

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness Is Necessary for Pointedness to Imply Dual Solidity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional counterexample at the closedness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb R^2\), let
\[
K=\{(s,t):t>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
Then \(K\) is a convex pointed cone but is not closed, whereas
\[
K^*=\{(0,b):b\geq0\},
\]
which has empty ambient interior. Thus pointedness need not imply solidity of the dual when closedness is dropped.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open upper half-plane together with the origin is a pointed convex cone, but its dual is a ray with empty ambient interior.
assumptions_latex: \(E=\mathbb R^2\) with its Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\text{ is pointed but }\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Is Necessary for Pointedness to Imply Dual Solidity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Dimensionality Is Necessary for Ambient-Interior Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional failure of pointedness-to-solidity under norm interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the Hilbert space \(\ell^2\), let
\[
K=\{x=(x_n):x_n\geq0\text{ for every }n\}.
\]
The cone \(K\) is closed, convex, pointed, and self-dual, but its norm interior is empty. Hence a closed pointed cone in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space need not have a solid dual when solidity means nonempty ambient norm interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative cone in l2 is closed, convex, pointed, and self-dual, yet has empty norm interior, so the finite-dimensional equivalence does not extend using ordinary ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=K^*\), \(K\text{ is pointed}\), and \(\operatorname{int}(K^*)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Square-summable real sequences with nonnegative coordinates

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone with dual \(K^*\).

Pointedness and solidity are defined by \[K	ext{ pointed}\iff K\cap(-K)=\{0\},\qquad K	ext{ solid}\iff\operatorname{int}K
eq\varnothing.\] Their dual correspondence is \[K	ext{ pointed}\iff\operatorname{int}K^*

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is pointed if it contains no nonzero vector together with its negative, and solid if it has nonempty interior. For a nonempty closed convex cone in finite dimensions, pointedness is equivalent to the dual cone having nonempty interior, while solidity is equivalent to the dual being pointed. knowledge_statements.title: Closure Boundary for Span-Lineality Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonclosed convex cone, dual lineality is still orthogonal to the primal span, but dual span is governed by the lineality of the cone's closure; the open upper-halfspace cone shows that using the original lineality can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), without assuming closedness, \[\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}\overline K)^\perp.\] Closedness permits \(\operatorname{lin}\overline K\) to be replaced by \(\operatorname{lin}K\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orthogonal duality between span and lineality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone. Set \(L_K:=K\cap(-K)\) and \(S_K:=\operatorname{span}K=K-K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The span-lineality duality identities are \[\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=(\operatorname{span}K)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{span}(K^*)=(\operatorname{lin}K)^\perp.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{span}K=(\operatorname{lin}K^*)^\perp,\qquad \operatorname{lin}K=(\operatorname{span}K^*)^\perp.\] Hence the directions on which every dual functional vanishes are exactly the primal lineality directions, while dual reversible directions are precisely the vectors orthogonal to the entire primal span. In dimension form, \[\dim\operatorname{span}K+\dim\operatorname{lin}(K^*)=\dim E,\quad \dim\operatorname{lin}K+\dim\operatorname{span}(K^*)=\dim E.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex cone, the lineality of the dual is the orthogonal complement of the primal span, and the span of the dual is the orthogonal complement of primal lineality. \(x\in\operatorname{lin}K\iff\langle y,x\rangle=0\ \forall y\in K^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Properness under Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed finite-dimensional convex cone is proper exactly when its dual is proper, and its second dual is the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), \[K\text{ is proper}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K^*\text{ is proper},\qquad K^{**}=K.\] Thus dualization preserves proper-cone regularity and is involutive on this finite-dimensional closed-cone class.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. A cone \(K\subseteq E\) is called proper here when it is nonempty, closed, convex, pointed, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Some texts use “proper cone” with slightly different conventions. This record fixes the convention explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex cone \(K\subseteq E\), properness is self-dual: \[K\text{ is proper}\iff K^*\text{ is proper}.\] More explicitly, closedness and convexity of \(K^*\) are automatic; primal pointedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\) is equivalent to pointedness of \(K^*\). Since \(K^{**}=K\), the same exchanges apply in both directions. Thus dualization preserves the class of proper cones while interchanging its two nontrivial regularity components, pointedness and solidity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated convention, a proper cone is closed, convex, pointed, and solid. The dual of every proper cone is proper, and conversely. Dual closedness and convexity are automatic, while pointedness of the primal becomes solidity of the dual and solidity of the primal becomes pointedness of the dual. Biduality makes the correspondence symmetric.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is proper if and only if \(K^*\) is proper.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\text{ proper}\iff K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\text{ and }\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\), with closedness and convexity understood.
\(K\text{ proper}\iff \operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\text{ and }\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\).

A nonzero subspace is not proper because it is not pointed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Primal and dual conic programs over proper cones have symmetric cone regularity.
Self-duality is stronger than properness: a proper cone need not equal its dual.
