knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Positivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive map has a positive adjoint; adjoint positivity recovers primal positivity when the target cone equals its bidual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K^*=\{x^*:x^*(k)\ge0\ \forall k\in K\},\qquad L^*=\{y^*:y^*(\ell)\ge0\ \forall\ell\in L\}.
\]
If \(T(K)\subseteq L\), then \(T^*(L^*)\subseteq K^*\). Conversely, if \(T^*(L^*)\subseteq K^*\), then \(T(K)\subseteq L^{**}\); hence the converse gives positivity into \(L\) whenever \(L=L^{**}\) under the chosen dual pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are real vector spaces equipped with separating dual pairings.
\(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\) are convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(K)\subseteq L\Rightarrow T^*(L^*)\subseteq K^*,\qquad T^*(L^*)\subseteq K^*\Rightarrow T(K)\subseteq L^{**}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic-dual formulation; continuous duals and a continuous map are used in topological settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone and Composition Structure of Positive Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive maps form a convex cone, include identity maps, and are closed under compatible composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set
\[
\operatorname{Pos}(K,L)=\{T\in\mathcal L(X,Y):T(K)\subseteq L\}
\]
is a convex cone. The identity map is positive from a cone to itself, and if \(T\in\operatorname{Pos}(K,L)\) and \(S\in\operatorname{Pos}(L,M)\), then \(S\circ T\in\operatorname{Pos}(K,M)\).
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are real vector spaces with convex cones \(K,L,M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Pos}(K,L)\text{ is a convex cone},\qquad S\circ T\in\operatorname{Pos}(K,M).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely algebraic closure properties relative to fixed ordering cones.

notation.meaning: cone of linear maps positive from K to L

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Linear Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear map is positive when it sends every vector in the domain cone into the codomain cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear map \(T:X\to Y\) is positive relative to \((K,L)\) if \[T(K)\subseteq L.\] Equivalently, \(x\ge_K0\) implies \(Tx\ge_L0\) for every \(x\in X\). Positivity therefore depends on the specified pair of ordering cones and is not an intrinsic property of the underlying linear transformation alone.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are real vector spaces ordered by convex cones \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is positive exactly when \(T(K)\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positivity relative to specified domain and codomain cones.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact dual certificate and its nonclosed-target boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq X\) be a convex cone, and let \(L\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone. For a linear map \(T:X\to Y\),
\[
T(K)\subseteq L
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
T^*(L^*)\subseteq K^*.
\]
If \(L\) is not closed, the adjoint inclusion is equivalent only to \(T(K)\subseteq\overline L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A map into a closed cone is positive exactly when its adjoint maps the target dual cone into the source dual cone; for a nonclosed target the test sees only its closure.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(L\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(K)\subseteq L\iff T^*(L^*)\subseteq K^*.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Certificate for Positivity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic structure of positive maps relative to fixed source and target cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For convex cones \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\),
\[
\operatorname{Pos}(K,L)=\{T\in\mathcal L(X,Y):T(K)\subseteq L\}
\]
is a convex cone, with
\[
\operatorname{lin}(\operatorname{Pos}(K,L))=\{T:T(K)\subseteq\operatorname{lin}(L)\}.
\]
Positive maps are closed under compatible composition, and the identity is positive from \((X,K)\) to itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive linear maps form a cone whose lineality consists exactly of maps sending the source cone into target lineality.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\) are convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Pos}(K,L)\text{ is a convex cone and }\operatorname{lin}(\operatorname{Pos}(K,L))=\{T:T(K)\subseteq\operatorname{lin}(L)\}.\)

notation.meaning: cone of linear maps positive relative to K and L

knowledge_statements.title: Cone of Positive Linear Maps
Order-Interval Functoriality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order-preserving maps send intervals into corresponding intervals, while order isomorphisms carry them onto those intervals exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(T:X\to Y\) is order preserving relative to \((K,L)\), then
\[
T([a,b]_K)\subseteq[Ta,Tb]_L
\]
whenever \(a\le_K b\). If \(T\) is bijective and both \(T\) and \(T^{-1}\) are order preserving, then equality holds.
assumptions_latex: \(T:X\to Y\) is linear and order preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T([a,b]_K)\subseteq[Ta,Tb]_L,\quad\text{with equality for an order isomorphism}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion holds for every order-preserving linear map; equality requires an order isomorphism.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Preserving Linear Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a linear map between cone-ordered spaces, preserving the domain cone is equivalent to preserving every cone-induced order comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear map \(T\) is order preserving relative to \((K,L)\) if, for all \(x,y\in X\), \[x\le_K y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Tx\le_L Ty.\] For a linear map, order preservation is equivalent to positivity: \[T(K)\subseteq L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T\text{ is order preserving relative to }(K,L).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are real vector spaces ordered by convex cones \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(K)\subseteq L\iff\bigl(\forall x,y\in X,\ x\le_K y\Rightarrow Tx\le_L Ty\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of positivity and order preservation for linear maps.

notation.meaning: cone-induced orders on the domain and codomain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion for a linear bijection to preserve and reflect cone comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:X\to Y\) be a linear bijection. The following are equivalent:
\[
T(K)=L;
\]
\[
T\text{ and }T^{-1}\text{ are order preserving};
\]
\[
x\le_K y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Tx\le_L Ty\quad\text{for all }x,y\in X.
\]
Such a map is a linear order isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear bijection is an order isomorphism exactly when it carries the source ordering cone onto the target cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\) are convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(K)=L\iff(T,T^{-1}\text{ are order preserving})\iff(x\le_Ky\iff Tx\le_LTy).\)
knowledge_statements.title: Order Isomorphisms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric consequence of preserving cone-induced comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(T:X\to Y\) is linear and order preserving relative to \((K,L)\), then for every \(a\le_K b\),
\[
T([a,b]_K)\subseteq[Ta,Tb]_L.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order-preserving linear map sends every source order interval into the target interval determined by the endpoint images.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\) are convex cones.
\(T:X\to Y\) is linear and order preserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T([a,b]_K)\subseteq[Ta,Tb]_L.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Interval Monotonicity
Kernel Test for Nonannihilating Positivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive map is strictly positive in the nonannihilation sense exactly when its kernel contains no nonzero positive vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a positive linear map \(T:X\to Y\),
\[
T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq L\setminus\{0\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\ker T\cap K=\{0\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\) are convex cones.
\(T:X\to Y\) is linear and satisfies \(T(K)\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq L\setminus\{0\}\iff\ker T\cap K=\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic test for the seed's strict-positivity convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Test for Interior Strong Positivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong positivity into a closed solid finite-dimensional cone is equivalent to strict positivity under every nonzero positive target functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior in a finite-dimensional space. A positive linear map \(T:X\to Y\) satisfies
\[
T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{int}L
\]
if and only if
\[
\langle y^*,Tx\rangle>0
\quad\text{for every }x\in K\setminus\{0\}\text{ and }y^*\in L^*\setminus\{0\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(L\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{int}L\ne\varnothing\) and \(0\notin\operatorname{int}L\).
\(T:X\to Y\) is linear and satisfies \(T(K)\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{int}L\iff\langle y^*,Tx\rangle>0\quad\forall x\in K\setminus\{0\},\ y^*\in L^*\setminus\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed solid target-cone formulation.

notation.meaning: positive dual cone of the target cone

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Interior Obstruction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target cone with empty ordinary interior admits no interior-strongly-positive map from a nontrivial positive cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(K\setminus\{0\}\ne\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{int}L=\varnothing\), then no linear map satisfies
\[
T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{int}L.
\]
Thus ordinary-interior strong positivity is unavailable for such target cones and cannot be replaced silently by quasi-interior or algebraic-interior positivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists T\text{ such that }T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{int}L.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for the ordinary-interior definition of strong positivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Positivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the convention fixed here, strict positivity forbids annihilating nonzero positive vectors, whereas strong positivity sends every such vector into the codomain cone's interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Relative to the terminology fixed in this record, the positive linear map \(T\) is strictly positive in the nonannihilation sense when \[T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq L\setminus\{0\}.\] It is strongly positive in the interior sense when \[T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{int}L.\] Under the assumption \(0\notin\operatorname{int}L\), strong positivity implies strict positivity. These names are source-dependent and the two conditions are not to be identified without an explicit convention.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space, and \(Y\) is a real topological vector space.
\(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\) are pointed convex cones, \(\operatorname{int}L\neq\varnothing\), and \(0\notin\operatorname{int}L\).
\(T:X\to Y\) is linear and satisfies \(T(K)\subseteq L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict positivity means \(T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq L\setminus\{0\}\), while strong positivity means \(T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{int}L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two explicitly distinguished positivity-strength conventions; the chosen terminology is local to this record.

notation.meaning: nonzero positive vectors of the domain
ordinary topological interior of the codomain cone

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Pairing Test for Strong Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional certificate for the ordinary-interior convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\subseteq Y\) be a closed, pointed, full-dimensional convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. A positive linear map \(T:(X,K)\to(Y,L)\) is strongly positive in the ordinary-interior sense exactly when
\[
\langle z,Tx\rangle>0
\quad\text{for every }x\in K\setminus\{0\}\text{ and }z\in L^*\setminus\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong positivity is certified by strict positivity of every nonzero target-dual pairing on every nonzero positive source vector.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{int}L\iff\langle z,Tx\rangle>0\ \forall x\in K\setminus\{0\},\ z\in L^*\setminus\{0\}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Pairing Test for Strong Positivity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic test for the seed's nonannihilation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T:X\to Y\) be positive relative to cones \((K,L)\). Then
\[
T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq L\setminus\{0\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\ker T\cap K=\{0\}.
\]
Moreover, positivity gives \(T(\operatorname{lin}K)\subseteq\operatorname{lin}L\). Hence if \(L\) is pointed and \(T\) is strictly positive, then \(K\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict positivity is equivalent to the absence of nonzero positive vectors in the kernel; a strictly positive map into a pointed cone requires a pointed source cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\) are convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq L\setminus\{0\}\iff\ker T\cap K=\{0\}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Criterion for Strict Positivity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-interior variant for lower-dimensional codomain cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a positive linear map \(T:X\to Y\), relative-interior strong positivity means
\[
T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{ri}L.
\]
When \(\operatorname{span}L=Y\), this agrees with ordinary-interior strong positivity. If \(L\) is lower-dimensional, then \(\operatorname{int}_Y L=\varnothing\), so ordinary-interior strong positivity is impossible for nonzero \(K\), while the relative-interior condition may still hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior strong positivity extends interior positivity to lower-dimensional target cones whose ambient interior is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(K\subseteq X\) and \(L\subseteq Y\) are convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ is relatively strongly positive}\iff T(K\setminus\{0\})\subseteq\operatorname{ri}L.\)

notation.meaning: relative interior of L in its linear span

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Functional Characterization of Cone Comparisons
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex cone, a comparison holds exactly when every continuous positive functional preserves it; without pointedness the relation is a preorder.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(x\preceq_C y\) by \(y-x\in C\), and let \(C^*=\{f\in X':f(c)\ge 0\ \forall c\in C\}\). Every \(f\in C^*\) preserves this preorder. If \(C\) is closed, then
\[
x\preceq_C y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)\le f(y)\quad\text{for every }f\in C^*.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Hausdorff locally convex space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y-x\in C\iff f(y-x)\ge0\quad\forall f\in C^*.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-dual characterization in a Hausdorff locally convex space; the induced relation is a preorder unless the cone is pointed.

notation.meaning: cone of continuous positive linear functionals

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Boundary for Order Separation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonclosed cone, continuous positive functionals detect membership only in its closure, so closure points missing from the cone defeat the comparison equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any convex cone \(C\subseteq X\), continuous positive functionals recover its closure:
\[
\overline C=\{z\in X:f(z)\ge0\ \forall f\in C^*\}.
\]
Consequently, if \(z\in\overline C\setminus C\), then every \(f\in C^*\) satisfies \(f(z)\ge0\), although \(0\not\preceq_C z\). Thus closedness is necessary for positive functionals to characterize comparisons in \(C\) itself.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Hausdorff locally convex space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{z:f(z)\ge0\ \forall f\in C^*\}=\overline C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure boundary when the ordering cone is not closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Dimensional Order Recovery and Its Closure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional recovery of cone-induced comparisons by positive functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(C^*=\{z:\langle z,c\rangle\ge0\ \forall c\in C\}\). Then
\[
\langle z,x\rangle\le\langle z,y\rangle\quad\forall z\in C^*
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in\overline C.
\]
Consequently, the positive functionals recover the preorder induced by \(C\) exactly when \(C\) is closed. For \(C=\{(u,v):v>0\}\cup\{0\}\), they declare \(0\) below \((1,0)\), although \((1,0)\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, positive functionals characterize the preorder induced by the cone closure, and recover the original cone preorder exactly for closed cones.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\forall z\in C^*,\ \langle z,x\rangle\le\langle z,y\rangle\bigr)\iff y-x\in\overline C.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Order Recovery and Its Closure Boundary
Order Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional dual characterization of a closed cone-induced order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex cone and define \(x\preceq_K y\) by \(y-x\in K\). Its dual cone is \[K^*=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,k\rangle\ge 0\ \text{for every }k\in K\}.\] A linear functional \(z\mapsto\langle u,z\rangle\) is order-preserving exactly when \(u\in K^*\). Moreover, bipolarity and separation give \[x\preceq_K y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle u,x\rangle\le \langle u,y\rangle\ \text{for every }u\in K^*.\] Thus the positive functionals in \(K^*\) determine the order completely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone consists exactly of order-preserving linear functionals, and a closed cone-induced order is determined by inequalities against all such functionals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\preceq_K y\iff \langle u,x\rangle\le\langle u,y\rangle\) for every \(u\in K^*\).

notation.meaning: dual cone of nonnegative linear functionals on K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Cone as the Cone of Positive Functionals
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) and \(F\) be real vector spaces in separating duality through a bilinear pairing \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:E\times F\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality of ordered vector spaces under a specified pairing; finite-dimensional Euclidean duality is obtained by identifying \(F\) with \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual cone of \(K\) is \[K^*:=\{f\in F:\langle x,f\rangle\geq0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}.\] Thus \(K^*\) is exactly the set of positive linear functionals on the ordered space \((E,K)\). It induces the dual order \[f\preceq_{K^*}g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g-f\in K^*,\] equivalently \(\langle x,f\rangle\leq\langle x,g\rangle\) for every \(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone consists of all elements of the paired dual space whose pairing with every positive primal element is nonnegative. These are precisely the positive linear functionals. The dual cone itself orders the dual space: one functional lies below another exactly when the second dominates the first on the entire primal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are in separating bilinear duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=\{f:\langle x,f\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\), and \(f\preceq_{K^*}g\iff\langle x,f\rangle\leq\langle x,g\rangle\ \forall x\in K\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\in K^*\iff f\) is order preserving as a map \((E,K)\to(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}_+)\).
In Euclidean space, \(K^*=\{y:y^Tx\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
special_cases_latex: \((\mathbb{R}_+^n)^*=\mathbb{R}_+^n\).
Under the trace pairing, \((\mathbb{S}_+^n)^*=\mathbb{S}_+^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(K^*\) is a convex cone even if \(K\) is not convex.
Every \(f\in K^*\) converts \(x\preceq_Ky\) into the scalar inequality \(\langle x,f\rangle\leq\langle y,f\rangle\).
For a closed convex cone in finite dimensions, \(K^{**}=K\).
boundary_notes: The sign convention here uses nonnegative pairings; polar-cone conventions using nonpositive pairings differ by a minus sign.
The equality \(K^{**}=K\) requires closure and convexity in finite dimensions, or appropriate closedness assumptions in a dual topology.
A nonzero dual cone element need not strictly separate every point outside \(K\).

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the stated nonnegative-pairing convention.
Order on the dual space induced by the dual cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Cone and Its Finite Descriptions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Inequalities between vectors are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real polyhedral cones, including nonpointed and lower-dimensional cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedral cone if there exist \(m\geq0\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) such that \[C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq0\}.\] Equivalently, \(C\) is an intersection of finitely many closed halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes contain the origin. A finite generator description has the form \[C=\operatorname{cone}(R):=\{R\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^q\}\] for some \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\). The pair \((A,R)\) is a compatible polyhedral representation when these two sets coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone in finite-dimensional real space is the solution set of finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities. Equivalently, it is the conic hull of finitely many vectors. An inequality matrix and a generator matrix form a compatible representation when they describe exactly the same cone. The definition allows lineality, empty lists of inequalities or generators under the usual conventions, and cones that are not full-dimensional or pointed.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(R\) are finite real matrices of compatible dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is polyhedral when \(C=\{x:Ax\leq0\}\); in finite dimensions this is equivalent to \(C=\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for a finite matrix \(R\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:(a^i)^Tx\leq0\}\), where \((a^i)^T\) are the rows of \(A\).
\(C=\{\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda_jr^j:\lambda_j\geq0\}\), where \(r^j\) are the columns of \(R\).
special_cases_latex: \(\mathbb{R}_+^n=\{x:-Ix\leq0\}=\operatorname{cone}(e_1,\ldots,e_n)\).
A linear subspace \(L=\ker B\) is the polyhedral cone \(\{x:Bx\leq0,-Bx\leq0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every polyhedral cone is closed and convex.
Finite intersections and linear inverse images of polyhedral cones are polyhedral.
The lineality space is \(\operatorname{lin}C=C\cap(-C)=\ker A\) for an inequality representation \(C=\{x:Ax\leq0\}\).
boundary_notes: This definition is finite-dimensional; finitely generated cones and finite intersections of halfspaces need not coincide in arbitrary infinite-dimensional spaces.
A polyhedral cone need not be pointed, solid, or full-dimensional.
The zero cone and the whole space are permitted polyhedral cones.

notation.meaning: Set of all nonnegative linear combinations of the columns of R.
Lineality space C intersected with its negative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: H- and V-Representation System for a Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedral cone, \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(R=[r^1\ \cdots\ r^q]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite matrix descriptions of real polyhedral cones; representation matrices are not assumed minimal or unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An H-representation of \(C\) is a finite homogeneous inequality system \[C=H(A):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq0\}.\] A V-representation is a finite generator system \[C=V(R):=\operatorname{cone}(r^1,\ldots,r^q)=\{R\lambda:\lambda\geq0\}.\] A double-description or MW-pair is a pair \((A,R)\) satisfying \[H(A)=V(R).\] Two H-representations or two V-representations are representation-equivalent when their represented cones are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone can be stored either by finitely many homogeneous inequalities or by finitely many conic generators. The first is its H-representation and the second its V-representation. A double description pairs an inequality matrix and a generator matrix that define the same cone. Neither representation is canonical: rows may be positively rescaled or repeated, generators may be positively rescaled or repeated, and redundant rows or columns may be present.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(R\) have finitely many rows or columns.

equivalent_formulations_latex: \((A,R)\) is an MW-pair iff \(Ax\leq0\iff x=R\lambda\) for some \(\lambda\geq0\), for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
The inclusion \(V(R)\subseteq H(A)\) is equivalent to \(AR\leq0\) componentwise; equality additionally requires that every point of \(H(A)\) have a nonnegative R-coordinate representation.

For a linear subspace, a V-description must include generators for both directions of each basis vector.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive rescaling or permutation of rows of \(A\), or columns of \(R\), preserves the represented cone.
Deleting a redundant row or generator preserves the represented cone.
Minkowski–Weyl theory guarantees existence of both finite descriptions.

The condition \(AR\leq0\) alone proves only one inclusion, not equality.
Affine polyhedra require nonhomogeneous inequalities and a convex-hull term; they are outside this cone-only definition.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone and let \(r^1,\ldots,r^q\in C\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointed finite-dimensional polyhedral cones, for which one-dimensional faces are extreme rays and admit finite representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A ray generated by \(r\neq0\) is \(\mathbb{R}_+r\). It is an extreme ray of \(C\) when \[u,v\in C,\quad u+v\in\mathbb{R}_+r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u,v\in\mathbb{R}_+r.\] A finite ray-generator representation of \(C\) is \[C=\operatorname{cone}(r^1,\ldots,r^q).\] It is an extreme-ray representation when every \(\mathbb{R}_+r^j\) is an extreme ray of \(C\), and it is ray-complete when every extreme ray of \(C\) equals \(\mathbb{R}_+r^j\) for some \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero vector generates its nonnegative half-line. Such a ray is extreme when a point on it cannot be decomposed into two cone elements lying outside that same ray. A finite generator system represents the cone when every cone point is a nonnegative combination of its columns. For a pointed polyhedral cone, the canonical minimal directions are its finitely many extreme rays; one representative from each extreme ray gives a complete extreme-ray representation.
assumptions_latex: Each proposed ray representative \(r^j\) is nonzero and belongs to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A ray-complete extreme-ray system satisfies \(C=\operatorname{cone}(r^1,\ldots,r^q)\) and \(\{\mathbb{R}_+r^j\}_{j=1}^q\) is exactly the set of extreme rays of \(C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mathbb{R}_+r\) is extreme iff it is a one-dimensional face of the pointed cone \(C\).

For \(C=\{x:Ax\leq0\}\), a ray \(\mathbb{R}_+r\) is extreme iff \(r\) satisfies at equality \(n-1\) linearly independent inequalities after restricting to the span of \(C\) in the full-dimensional pointed case.
special_cases_latex: The coordinate rays \(\mathbb{R}_+e_i\) form the complete extreme-ray system of \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\).
A one-dimensional pointed cone has exactly one extreme ray.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every generator system for a pointed polyhedral cone contains a vector on each extreme ray after redundant generators are removed.
Replacing \(r^j\) by \(\alpha_jr^j\) with \(\alpha_j>0\) leaves the represented rays and cone unchanged.
boundary_notes: For nonpointed cones, lineality must be represented separately or by pairs of opposite generators; the extreme-ray-only description is not sufficient in this form.
A generator can be redundant even when it is nonzero and lies on the boundary.
Extreme-ray representatives are unique only up to positive scaling and ordering.

notation.meaning: Ray generated by the nonzero vector r.
All nonnegative linear combinations of the listed generators.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Ray Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite ray representation expresses a cone as a Minkowski sum of finitely many rays and is invariant under positive rescaling of their representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_i=\operatorname{ray}(v_i)=\{\lambda v_i:\lambda\ge0\}\) with \(v_i\ne0\). The rays \(R_1,\ldots,R_m\) represent a nonzero cone \(C\) when \[C=R_1+\cdots+R_m=\{r_1+\cdots+r_m:r_i\in R_i\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iv_i:\lambda_i\ge0\right\}.\] Replacing \(v_i\) by any positive multiple leaves both \(R_i\) and \(C\) unchanged. The zero cone is represented by the empty ray sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=R_1+\cdots+R_m\) is equivalent to \(C=\{\sum_i\lambda_iv_i:\lambda_i\ge0\}\), independently of positive representative scaling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ray-organized finite conic descriptions; positive rescaling of representatives is immaterial.

notation.meaning: The nonnegative ray generated by a nonzero vector v.
Minkowski sum of the listed rays.

knowledge_statements.title: Ray Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of a pointed polyhedral cone by its finitely many extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone. Then \(C\) has finitely many extreme rays \(R_1,\ldots,R_p\), and \[C=R_1+\cdots+R_p.\] Equivalently, after choosing any nonzero \(r_i\in R_i\), \[C=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i r_i:\lambda_i\ge0\right\}.\] The collection of rays is independent of the scaling used to choose the representatives \(r_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every pointed polyhedral cone is the conic sum of its finitely many extreme rays; choosing one nonzero vector on each ray yields a generator formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=R_1+\cdots+R_p=\{\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i r_i:\lambda_i\ge0\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Generator Representation and Polyhedral Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional cone is polyhedral exactly when it is the conic hull of finitely many vectors, equivalently a linear image of a finite nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_m]\), \[\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_m)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iv_i:\lambda_i\ge0\right\}=V\mathbb R_+^m.\] A convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) admits such a finite generator representation if and only if it is polyhedral. Zero, repeated, or conically redundant generators may occur and can be deleted without changing the represented cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is polyhedral if and only if \(C=V\mathbb R_+^m\) for some finite matrix \(V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-generator side of the finite-dimensional Minkowski–Weyl theorem for cones.

notation.meaning: Matrix whose columns are the selected generators.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal membership and alternative nonmembership certificates for a generator matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=V\mathbb R_+^m\), membership \(x\in C\) is certified by \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfying \(V\lambda=x\). Exactly one of the systems \(V\lambda=x,\ \lambda\ge0\) and \(V^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ \langle y,x\rangle<0\) is feasible; a feasible \(y\) certifies \(x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative generator coordinates certify membership, while a functional nonnegative on every generator and negative on the query point certifies nonmembership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in V\mathbb R_+^m\iff\exists\lambda\ge0:\ V\lambda=x,\quad x\notin V\mathbb R_+^m\iff\exists y:\ V^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ \langle y,x\rangle<0.
knowledge_statements.title: Generator-Coordinate Membership and Separation Certificates
Generator Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite vector-generator representation of a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_p\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \[C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_p\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\ge0\right\}.\] Writing \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_p]\), the same cone has the matrix representation \[C=V\mathbb{R}_+^p=\{V\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\}.\] A cone in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) admits such a finite generator representation if and only if it is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite generator system represents a cone as all nonnegative linear combinations of its vectors, equivalently as the image of a nonnegative orthant; in finite-dimensional space, such a representation exists exactly for polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_p\}=V\mathbb{R}_+^p\), and such a finite representation exists exactly for polyhedral cones.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns are the generators

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the following are equivalent: \[(i)\quad C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\text{ for a finite vector family};\qquad (ii)\quad C\text{ is polyhedral}.\] Consequently every finite generator image \(V\mathbb R_+^m\) is closed, and every finite-dimensional polyhedral cone admits such a generator matrix \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional cone is finitely generated exactly when it is polyhedral; equivalently, it is a linear image of a finite nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is polyhedral if and only if \(C=V\mathbb R_+^m\) for some finite matrix \(V\).

Pointedness Is Essential for Extreme-Ray Minimality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The real line has an irredundant two-vector generator system but no extreme rays, showing that pointedness is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Without pointedness, irredundant finite generators need not correspond to extreme rays. The cone \[\mathbb R=\operatorname{cone}\{1,-1\}\] is irredundantly generated because deleting either generator leaves only a half-line, but \(\mathbb R\) has no extreme ray in the one-dimensional pointed-face sense.
assumptions_latex: Extreme rays mean one-dimensional pointed faces of the original cone, not rays of a quotient by lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extreme-ray characterization of irredundant generators fails for nonpointed cones.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary of the extreme-ray characterization.
Sharp pointedness boundary for the extreme-ray minimality characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonpointed cone \(C=\mathbb R\) has the irredundant representation \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{1,-1\}\), yet it has no extreme rays. Thus an irredundant generator system of a nonpointed cone need not enumerate extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The line is irredundantly generated by two opposite vectors but has no extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ nonpointed}\implies\text{irredundant generators need not correspond to extreme rays}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonpointed Failure of Extreme-Ray Enumeration
Extreme-Ray Minimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimality criterion for generators of a pointed polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone with extreme rays \(R_1,\ldots,R_p\). Every finite set \(G\subseteq C\) satisfying \(C=\operatorname{cone}(G)\) contains at least one nonzero vector on each \(R_i\). Consequently, choosing exactly one nonzero representative from every extreme ray gives an irredundant generating set. Conversely, every irredundant finite generating set consists of exactly one nonzero representative from each extreme ray, up to positive rescaling and permutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed polyhedral cone needs at least one generator on every extreme ray, and its irredundant generator systems select exactly one vector per extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(i\), \(G\cap(R_i\setminus\{0\})\ne\varnothing\); an irredundant finite generating set contains exactly one nonzero representative from each extreme ray.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Inequality Characterization of Polyhedral Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional cone is polyhedral exactly when it is the intersection of finitely many linear halfspaces through the origin; equations can be encoded by opposite inequality pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral if and only if there is a finite matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) such that \[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\}.\] Each halfspace contains the origin. An equation \(u^{\mathsf T}x=0\), as needed for a lower-dimensional cone, is encoded by the opposite pair \(u^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\) and \(-u^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is polyhedral if and only if \(C=\{x:Ax\ge0\}\) for some finite matrix \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional H-representation, including lower-dimensional and nonpointed cones.

notation.meaning: The ith row of the inequality matrix A.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit dense or sparse homogeneous inequality matrices under exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(C=\{x:Ax\geq0\}\), membership of \(x\) is decided by computing \(Ax\) and checking every component for nonnegativity. A direction \(d\) lies in \(\operatorname{lin}C\) exactly when \(Ad=0\). For a dense \(m\times n\) matrix, either test uses \(O(mn)\) arithmetic operations; for a sparse matrix it uses \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership and lineality queries require one matrix-vector product followed by sign or zero tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership and lineality-direction queries use \(O(mn)\) dense or \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) sparse arithmetic operations.

notation.meaning: Number of nonzero entries of A.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite homogeneous systems after zero rows are removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have no zero rows and let \(C=\{x:Ax\geq0\}\). Then \(C\) is full-dimensional if and only if some \(x\) satisfies \(Ax>0\). Exactly one of \[Ax>0\qquad\text{and}\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0,\ \lambda\geq0,\ \lambda\neq0\] is feasible. Thus a strictly feasible point certifies full-dimensionality, whereas a nonzero nonnegative dependence among the rows certifies failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous inequality cone is full-dimensional exactly when all nonzero inequalities can be made strict; otherwise a nonnegative row dependence certifies failure.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has no zero rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim C=n\iff\exists x\ Ax>0\iff\nexists\lambda\geq0,\lambda\neq0:A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\).

notation.meaning: Every component of Ax is strictly positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality and Pointedness from the Inequality Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary finite homogeneous inequality systems, including redundant systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\geq0\}\), \[\operatorname{lin}C=C\cap(-C)=\ker A.\] Consequently, \(C\) is pointed if and only if \(\ker A=\{0\}\), equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}A=n\). Irredundancy is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space is the nullspace of the inequality matrix, so the cone is pointed exactly when the matrix has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}C=\ker A\) and \(C\text{ pointed}\iff\operatorname{rank}A=n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality and Pointedness from the Inequality Matrix
Homogeneous Inequality Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite homogeneous halfspace description of a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), the solution set \[C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge0\}=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:\langle a_i,x\rangle\ge0\}\] is a closed convex polyhedral cone, where \(a_i^\mathsf{T}\) is the \(i\)-th row of \(A\). Conversely, every polyhedral cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) admits such a representation by finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities. Reversing every inequality gives the equivalent convention \((-A)x\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral cones are exactly the intersections of finitely many linear halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes pass through the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is polyhedral exactly when \(C=\{x:Ax\ge0\}\) for some finite matrix \(A\).

notation.meaning: i-th row of the inequality matrix A

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous inequality description is a finite intersection of linear halfspaces through the origin. Its feasible set is automatically a closed convex cone. A row is redundant if removing it does not enlarge that cone, and it is irredundant otherwise. The same cone can have many equivalent descriptions because inequalities may be reordered, positively rescaled, duplicated, or implied by the remaining rows.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Redundancy Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generator and homogeneous-inequality redundancy are conic membership tests certified by nonnegative coefficient vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(C=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_p)\), generator \(v_i\) is redundant exactly when \[v_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\lambda_jv_j\quad\text{for some }\lambda_j\ge0.\] In \(C=\{x:a_j^{\mathsf T}x\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,q\}\), inequality \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\) is implied by the others exactly when \[a_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\mu_ja_j\quad\text{for some }\mu_j\ge0.\] The coefficient vectors are checkable redundancy certificates, and successively deleting certified entries produces an irredundant finite description.
assumptions_latex: The generator and normal families are finite.
The homogeneous inequalities are interpreted over all of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_i\in\operatorname{cone}(v_j:j\ne i)\) and \(a_i\in\operatorname{cone}(a_j:j\ne i)\) are the respective redundancy criteria.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion tests for finite V- and homogeneous H-descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Irredundant Ray and Facet Descriptions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a pointed full-dimensional polyhedral cone, irredundant generators select its extreme rays and irredundant inequalities select its facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be pointed, full-dimensional, and polyhedral. A finite generator description \(C=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_p)\) is irredundant exactly when the rays \(\operatorname{ray}(v_i)\) are distinct and are precisely the extreme rays of \(C\). A homogeneous inequality description \(C=\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\ge0,\ i=1,\ldots,q\}\) is irredundant exactly when its equality sets \(C\cap\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=0\}\) are distinct facets of \(C\). The two irredundant cardinalities are intrinsic, although ordering and positive scaling are not.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is pointed, full-dimensional, and polyhedral.
All listed generators and inequality normals are nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Irredundant V-descriptions correspond to extreme rays, and irredundant homogeneous H-descriptions correspond to facets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness supports the extreme-ray statement, while full dimensionality supports the facet statement without affine-hull qualifications.
Finite deletion procedure for generator and homogeneous-inequality descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a generator list, test each \(v_i\) for membership in \(\operatorname{cone}\{v_j:j\ne i\}\) and delete it when membership holds. For an inequality list, test each \(a_i\) for membership in \(\operatorname{cone}\{a_j:j\ne i\}\) and delete it when membership holds. In either case one pass in any order returns an equivalent irredundant description. For rational data this uses at most one linear-feasibility problem per original generator or row and is polynomial-time in the standard bit model through linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential conic-membership tests delete redundant generators or rows and produce an irredundant description in one pass.
assumptions_latex: The input is a finite generator or homogeneous-inequality description.
For the complexity assertion, the input data are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At most }p+q\text{ linear-feasibility tests suffice for descriptions with }p\text{ generators and }q\text{ rows}.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy-Elimination Procedure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas certificate for redundancy in a finite homogeneous inequality description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a_j^{\mathsf T}x\ge0,\ j=1,\ldots,q\}\). Row \(i\) is redundant if and only if there exist \(\lambda_j\ge0\), \(j\ne i\), such that \(a_i=\sum_{j\ne i}\lambda_j a_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous inequality is redundant exactly when its normal is a nonnegative combination of the other row normals.

Irredundant Polyhedral Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irredundancy criteria for full-dimensional pointed polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be full-dimensional, pointed, and polyhedral. A homogeneous inequality description \(C=\{x:\langle a_i,x\rangle\ge0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) with nonzero normals is irredundant if and only if each set \[F_i=C\cap\{x:\langle a_i,x\rangle=0\}\] is a distinct facet of \(C\). A finite generator description \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_p\}\) with nonzero generators is irredundant if and only if the rays \(\mathbb{R}_+v_j\) are distinct extreme rays of \(C\) and exhaust all its extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional pointed polyhedral cone, irredundant inequalities correspond one-to-one with facets and irredundant generators correspond one-to-one with extreme rays.
assumptions_latex: All displayed normals \(a_i\) and generators \(v_j\) are nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inequality irredundancy is equivalent to distinct facet support, while generator irredundancy is equivalent to selecting every extreme ray exactly once.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Irredundant H- and V-Descriptions of a Pointed Polyhedral Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone with an H-description \(C=\{x:Ax\leq0\}\) and a V-description \(C=\operatorname{cone}(r^1,\ldots,r^q)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointed polyhedral cones; facet statements use the relative dimension of the cone when it is not full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The H-description is irredundant when deleting any row of \(A\) strictly enlarges \(C\). The V-description is irredundant when deleting any generator strictly shrinks \(C\): \[\operatorname{cone}(r^1,\ldots,\widehat{r^j},\ldots,r^q)\subsetneq C\quad\text{for every }j.\] After separating equations defining \(\operatorname{span}C\), an irredundant inequality defines a facet of \(C\). An irredundant generator system contains exactly one positively scaled representative of each extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality description is irredundant if every displayed inequality is necessary, and a generator description is irredundant if every displayed direction is necessary. For a pointed polyhedral cone, minimal V-descriptions are obtained by choosing one nonzero vector from every extreme ray. Once equations defining the cone's span are handled separately, minimal H-descriptions contain one inequality for each facet, up to positive scaling.
assumptions_latex: For the facet correspondence, equations defining \(\operatorname{span}C\) are distinguished from proper inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Irredundancy means that every single row deletion changes \(H(A)\) and every single generator deletion changes \(V(R)\); the remaining rows and rays correspond respectively to facets and extreme rays.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A generator \(r^j\) is redundant iff \(r^j\in\operatorname{cone}(r^i:i\neq j)\).
A row is redundant iff its inequality is valid for the cone defined by all remaining rows.
special_cases_latex: For \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\), the inequalities \(-x_i\leq0\) and generators \(e_i\) are both irredundant.
Repeated positive multiples of the same generator or inequality make a description redundant.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any finite description can be reduced to an irredundant one by deleting redundant members.
Two irredundant extreme-ray descriptions of a pointed cone have the same number of generators and differ only by ordering and positive rescaling.
For a full-dimensional cone, each inequality in an irredundant H-description defines a codimension-one face.
boundary_notes: Minimality is inclusion minimality, not a normalization of coefficients.
For nonpointed cones, lineality requires separate treatment and V-description uniqueness must be stated modulo a lineality basis.
In lower-dimensional cones, equations of the span are not facets.

notation.meaning: Omission of generator r^j from the displayed list.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\) be finite matrices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real cones and the paired H/V representation object underlying the Minkowski–Weyl equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Minkowski–Weyl pair, or MW-pair, is a pair \((A,R)\) satisfying \[\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq0\}=\operatorname{cone}(R)=\{R\lambda:\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^q\}.\] A cone admitting such a pair is simultaneously polyhedral and finitely generated. Minkowski–Weyl theory for cones identifies the two classes: \[\{\text{finite intersections of homogeneous halfspaces}\}=\{\text{finitely generated convex cones}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Minkowski–Weyl pair consists of a finite homogeneous inequality matrix and a finite generator matrix that define exactly the same cone. The associated theory identifies polyhedral cones with finitely generated cones in finite-dimensional real space. The pair is a representation object rather than a unique normal form: either side can contain redundant rows or columns.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(R\) are real matrices of compatible sizes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A,R)\) is an MW-pair iff \(\{x:Ax\leq0\}=\{R\lambda:\lambda\geq0\}\), and every finite-dimensional polyhedral cone admits such a pair.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A subset \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is polyhedral iff it is finitely generated.
\(C=H(A)=V(R)\) for some finite \(A,R\).
special_cases_latex: \((-I,I)\) is an MW-pair for \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\).
A linear subspace has an MW-pair using paired homogeneous inequalities and paired positive generators for a basis.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finitely generated cone is closed in finite-dimensional space.
Conversion between finite H- and V-descriptions is mathematically well-defined, although output size can be large.
Duality exchanges generator and homogeneous-inequality descriptions up to the chosen sign convention.
boundary_notes: The equivalence is a finite-dimensional result.
The theorem asserts existence, not uniqueness or polynomial-size conversion.
For general polyhedra, the V-side additionally contains a convex hull of points.

notation.meaning: Minkowski–Weyl pair of inequality and generator matrices.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real convex cones; this record isolates the class correspondence rather than a particular conversion algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-generation–polyhedrality correspondence is the equivalence \[\bigl(\exists r^1,\ldots,r^q\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ C=\operatorname{cone}(r^1,\ldots,r^q)\bigr)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bigl(\exists A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\ C=\{x:Ax\leq0\}\bigr).\] Accordingly, the class of finitely generated cones in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) equals the class of polyhedral cones in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone in finite-dimensional real space has a finite list of conic generators if and only if it is the intersection of finitely many homogeneous linear halfspaces. Thus finite V-descriptions and finite H-descriptions characterize the same class of cones, even though the numbers and coefficients of generators and inequalities can differ greatly and neither description is unique.
assumptions_latex: The proposed generator list and inequality system are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is finitely generated if and only if \(C\) is polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\exists R\) finite with \(C=V(R)\iff\exists A\) finite with \(C=H(A)\).
Every finite conic hull is a finite homogeneous halfspace intersection, and conversely.
special_cases_latex: A finitely generated linear subspace uses both directions of a finite basis and is polyhedral.
A pointed full-dimensional polyhedral cone is generated by its finitely many extreme rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finitely generated cones are closed and convex in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
Every polyhedral cone has finitely many extreme rays modulo lineality.
Every finite H-description has at least one finite V-description, and conversely.
boundary_notes: This equivalence can fail in infinite-dimensional spaces.
The correspondence does not bound one description's size polynomially in the other description's size.
The generator list need not consist exclusively of extreme rays unless redundancy is removed and lineality is handled.

notation.meaning: Finite conic hull of columns of R.
Finite homogeneous halfspace intersection defined by A.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every element of a finitely generated cone can be represented using at most the dimension of the generators' span, with linearly independent used generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=\dim\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\). Every \(x\in\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) admits a representation \[x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i v_i,\qquad \lambda_i>0,\qquad |I|\le d,\] in which \(\{v_i:i\in I\}\) is linearly independent.
assumptions_latex: \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) are vectors in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) has a conic representation supported on at most \(d\) linearly independent generators.

knowledge_statements.title: Finitely Generated Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone is finitely generated when every element is a nonnegative linear combination of vectors from one finite family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(C\) is finitely generated if there exist vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) such that \[C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\ge0\right\}.\] The family may contain zero, repeated, or redundant vectors. Finite generation is an algebraic property; in finite-dimensional Euclidean space it additionally implies that \(C\) is closed and polyhedral.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex cone in a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is finitely generated if \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) for some finite family.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic definition, without closure or finite-dimensionality assumptions.

notation.meaning: Conical hull of finitely many vectors

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=V\mathbb R_+^m\), the cone \(C\) is nonpointed if and only if there exist \(\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R_+^m\) such that \(V\lambda=-V\mu\ne0\). Such a pair certifies the nonzero line direction \(V\lambda\in C\cap(-C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generated cone is nonpointed exactly when two nonnegative generator combinations produce opposite nonzero vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap(-C)\ne\{0\}\iff\exists\lambda,\mu\ge0:\ V\lambda=-V\mu\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_m]\), then \(\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}=V\mathbb R_+^m\). Hence \(T(\operatorname{cone}\{v_i\})=\operatorname{cone}\{Tv_i\}\) for every linear map \(T\), and \(\operatorname{cone}\{v_i\}+\operatorname{cone}\{w_j\}=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i,w_j\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finitely generated cones are orthant images, and finite generation is preserved by linear images and finite sums.
assumptions_latex: The displayed generating families are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite generation is preserved by linear images and finite Minkowski sums.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic Carathéodory specialization for a prescribed finite generating family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) and \(r=\dim\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\). Every nonzero \(x\in C\) has a representation \(x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i v_i\) with \(\lambda_i>0\), \(\{v_i:i\in I\}\) linearly independent, and \(|I|\le r\); the zero vector uses the empty sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonzero point of a finitely generated cone uses at most the dimension of the generator span many linearly independent generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in C\setminus\{0\}\Rightarrow x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i v_i\) for linearly independent \(\{v_i:i\in I\}\), \(\lambda_i>0\), and \(|I|\le r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) lie in a real vector space and set \(d=\dim\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}<\infty\). Every \(x\in\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) admits a representation \[x=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i v_i,\qquad \lambda_i>0,\qquad |I|\le d,\] in which \(\{v_i:i\in I\}\) is linearly independent. In particular, no more than \(d\) generators are needed for any one cone element.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Carathéodory Sparsity
Finite Homogeneous-Halfspace Definition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone is an intersection of finitely many closed linear halfspaces through the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is polyhedral if there exist \(m<\infty\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) such that \[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}.\] Equivalently, it is an intersection of finitely many closed linear halfspaces through the origin. Such a cone is closed and convex. The inequality representation may contain redundant or zero rows and need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is polyhedral exactly when \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}\) for some matrix with finitely many rows.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous-halfspace definition of a polyhedral cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition by homogeneous linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is polyhedral if it is the intersection of finitely many closed linear halfspaces through the origin. Equivalently, for some integer \(m\ge0\), there are vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle a_i,x\rangle\ge0\}.\] Repeated or implied inequalities are permitted. Zero normals may also be included as vacuous redundant constraints, although they do not define genuine halfspaces; excluding such constraints concerns irredundancy rather than polyhedrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone is the solution set of finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities, equivalently an intersection of finitely many closed linear halfspaces through the origin after vacuous constraints are discarded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is polyhedral exactly when \(C=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:\langle a_i,x\rangle\ge0\}\) for finitely many \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: normal of the i-th homogeneous inequality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lineality from a Homogeneous Inequality Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural information directly readable from any finite homogeneous inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}\), then \(\operatorname{lin}(C)=C\cap(-C)=\ker A\). Consequently, \(C\) is pointed if and only if \(\ker A=\{0\}\), equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}A=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space is the inequality matrix's nullspace, so pointedness is equivalent to full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(C)=\ker A\), and \(C\) is pointed iff \(\operatorname{rank}A=n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality from a Homogeneous Inequality Matrix
Conic Minkowski-Weyl Equivalence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, a cone has a finite homogeneous-inequality description exactly when it has a finite generator description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the following are equivalent: \[C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}\] for a matrix \(A\) with finitely many rows, and \[C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_p\}\] for finitely many vectors. Consequently, a cone satisfying either condition is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated; either representation implies that \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic Minkowski-Weyl theorem in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
Finite-dimensional equivalence of finite generator and finite homogeneous-inequality representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex cone \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), the following are equivalent: \[(i)\quad C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}\text{ for some matrix }A\text{ with finitely many rows},\] \[(ii)\quad C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_p\}\text{ for some finite family }v_1,\ldots,v_p\in\mathbb R^n.\] Consequently, every cone satisfying either condition is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a convex cone is polyhedral exactly when it is finitely generated, and every such cone is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is polyhedral}\iff C\text{ is finitely generated};\qquad C\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Minkowski–Weyl Equivalence
Finite-Dimensional Equivalence Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic Minkowski–Weyl theorem in finite-dimensional real spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a convex cone. The following are equivalent: \(C\) is finitely generated; \(C\) is polyhedral; and there exist finite matrices \(V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) such that \[C=V\mathbb{R}_+^p=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge0\}.\] In particular, either finite description implies that \(C\) is closed. No pointedness or full-dimensionality assumption is required for this equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a cone has finitely many vector generators exactly when it has finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is finitely generated if and only if \(C\) is polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Cone Failure of Finite Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive cone in ell-squared is closed and pointed but has neither finitely many generators nor finitely many continuous homogeneous inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \[H_+=\{x\in\ell^2:x_k\ge0\text{ for every }k\}\] is closed, convex, and pointed. Its coordinate rays \(\operatorname{ray}(e_k)\) are infinitely many distinct extreme rays, so it is not finitely generated. It also cannot equal \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:f_i(x)\ge0\}\) for finitely many continuous linear functionals, because their common kernel contains a nonzero vector and hence a line, whereas \(H_+\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_+\) is a closed pointed convex cone that is neither finitely generated nor representable by finitely many continuous homogeneous inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of finite-dimensional Minkowski-Weyl correspondence.

notation.meaning: Hilbert space of square-summable real sequences

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite-Dimensional Obstructions to Finite Conic Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General algebraic and continuous-halfspace obstructions to transferring Minkowski–Weyl verbatim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be infinite-dimensional. Every finitely generated cone is contained in a finite-dimensional subspace. Moreover, for linear functionals \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\), the cone \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:f_i(x)\ge0\}\) contains \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\ker f_i\), which has finite codimension and is therefore infinite-dimensional. Consequently, a cone with infinite-dimensional span is not finitely generated, and a pointed cone in an infinite-dimensional ambient space cannot be represented by finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite generators have finite-dimensional span, while finitely many homogeneous inequalities leave infinite-dimensional lineality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an infinite-dimensional real vector space.
For a topological halfspace representation, the \(f_i\) are continuous linear functionals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim\operatorname{span}C=\infty\Rightarrow C\) is not finitely generated, while every finite homogeneous-inequality cone in \(X\) is nonpointed.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_+\) is closed and convex but is neither finitely generated nor an intersection of finitely many continuous linear halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of finite-dimensional Minkowski–Weyl equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(H_+=\{x\in\ell^2:x_k\ge0\text{ for every }k\}\) is closed, convex, and pointed. It is not finitely generated because the coordinate rays \(\operatorname{ray}(e_k)\) are infinitely many distinct extreme rays. It also cannot equal \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:f_i(x)\ge0\}\) for finitely many continuous linear functionals: the common kernel \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\ker f_i\) contains a nonzero vector and hence a line, whereas \(H_+\) is pointed. Thus the finite-dimensional equivalence does not extend verbatim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive cone in ℓ² is closed and pointed but has neither finitely many generators nor finitely many continuous homogeneous inequalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The double-description method converts a finite homogeneous inequality description by inserting its halfspaces successively while maintaining both inequalities and generating rays. At each insertion it retains rays satisfying the new inequality and creates boundary rays from adjacent retained/rejected ray pairs, followed by redundancy removal. With exact arithmetic and correct adjacency and redundancy tests, every stage describes the accumulated intersection exactly and the procedure terminates after the finite inequality list. Applying the construction to the dual cone gives the reverse generator-to-inequality conversion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face Lattice and Incidence of a Polyhedral Cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite face organization of polyhedral cones, including improper faces and relative dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subset \(F\subseteq C\) is a face of \(C\) when there exists \(y\in C^*\) such that \[F=C\cap y^\perp=\{x\in C:y^Tx=0\}.\] The face lattice is \[\mathcal{F}(C):=\{F:F\text{ is a face of }C\},\] ordered by inclusion. Two faces are incident when one contains the other. The improper faces are \(C\) and, by convention, \(\varnothing\); the minimal nonempty face is the lineality space. In a pointed cone, one-dimensional faces are extreme rays, and maximal proper faces are facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces of a polyhedral cone are the subsets exposed by dual functionals that are nonnegative on the cone and vanish on the face. Ordered by inclusion, they form the finite face lattice. Incidence means containment. For a pointed cone, the atoms above the zero face are extreme rays and the maximal proper faces are facets. For a cone with lineality, dimensions and minimal faces are measured relative to that lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{F}(C)\) is the finite inclusion-ordered family of sets \(C\cap y^\perp\) with \(y\in C^*\), and its incidence relation is set containment.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(C=\{x:a_i^Tx\leq0,\ i\in M\}\), every nonempty face is obtained by imposing equality on a suitable subset of valid inequalities.
For faces \(F,G\), their meet is \(F\cap G\); the smallest face containing both is their join.
special_cases_latex: For \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\), faces are indexed by subsets of coordinates constrained to zero.
For a pointed two-dimensional polyhedral cone, the proper nonzero faces are its two boundary rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: A polyhedral cone has finitely many faces.
Every proper face is contained in a facet.
Every face of a face of \(C\) is itself a face of \(C\).
boundary_notes: For general closed convex cones, not every face need be exposed; polyhedral faces are exposed.
The empty-face convention varies between sources.
When \(C\) is not pointed, its lineality space replaces \(\{0\}\) as the minimal nonempty face.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty faces of pointed polyhedral cones represented by their incident extreme rays and an exposing polar vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a pointed polyhedral cone, where the \(v_i\) represent the distinct extreme rays of \(C\). For every nonempty face \(F\) of \(C\), there exists \(y\in C^\circ\) such that
\[
F=\{x\in C:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:\langle y,v_i\rangle=0\}.
\]
Conversely, for every \(y\in C^\circ\), the set \(\{x\in C:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}\) is a face of \(C\). Hence every nonempty face is uniquely determined by the extreme rays it contains, although not every subset of extreme rays defines a face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face of a pointed polyhedral cone is generated exactly by its incident extreme rays, namely those lying on an exposing supporting hyperplane; only support-realizable subsets of extreme rays define faces.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a pointed polyhedral cone generated by distinct extreme-ray representatives \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every nonempty face \(F\) of \(C\), \(F=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:v_i\in F\}=\{x\in C:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}\) for some \(y\in C^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone with distinct extreme-ray representatives \(r^1,\ldots,r^q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointed polyhedral cones; nonpointed cones require adding the lineality space to each generator formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a face \(F\in\mathcal{F}(C)\), define its incident-ray index set by \[I(F):=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}:r^j\in F\}.\] The face–generator correspondence assigns \[F\longmapsto I(F),\qquad F=\operatorname{cone}(r^j:j\in I(F)).\] Conversely, a subset \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,q\}\) is facial when there exists \(y\in C^*\) such that \[y^Tr^j=0\ (j\in I),\qquad y^Tr^j>0\ (j\notin I),\] in which case \(F_I=\operatorname{cone}(r^j:j\in I)=C\cap y^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each face of a pointed polyhedral cone is generated by exactly the extreme rays it contains. The face can therefore be encoded by its incident subset of extreme-ray indices. Not every arbitrary subset of extreme rays is facial: a facial subset is precisely one that can be selected as the zero set of a dual cone functional that is strictly positive on all remaining extreme-ray representatives.

For the strict zero-set characterization, duplicate ray representatives are excluded.

For \(F=C\cap y^\perp\), \(I(F)=\{j:y^Tr^j=0\}\).
special_cases_latex: The zero face has \(I(\{0\})=\varnothing\).
The full cone has \(I(C)=\{1,\ldots,q\}\).
A one-dimensional face corresponds to a singleton ray index.

Intersections of faces correspond to intersections of their incident-ray sets.
A face is determined uniquely by the extreme rays it contains.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional polyhedral cone, irredundant facet normals are exactly the extreme rays in a minimal generating system of the dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:a_i^\top x\ge0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) is full-dimensional, then \[C^*=\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}.\] After positive scalar multiples are identified, \(a_i^\top x\ge0\) belongs to an irredundant description and defines a facet of \(C\) if and only if \(\mathbb R_+a_i\) is an extreme ray of \(C^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facet Normals as Extreme Dual Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-dimensional polyhedral cones under the nonnegative dual-cone convention; pointedness is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polyhedral cone and \(C^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in C\}\). For nonzero \(y\in C^*\), \(C\cap y^\perp\) is a facet of \(C\) if and only if \(\mathbb R_+y\) is an extreme ray of \(C^*\). Hence the normals in an irredundant homogeneous inequality description, modulo positive scaling, are precisely the extreme-ray generators of \(C^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facet normals of a full-dimensional polyhedral cone correspond exactly to extreme rays of its dual cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap y^\perp\text{ is a facet}\iff \mathbb R_+y\text{ is an extreme ray of }C^*\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral cones that may be lower-dimensional or described by redundant ambient inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be polyhedral and \(L=\operatorname{span}C\). If \(C=\{x\in L:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) is irredundant after restriction to \(L\), with every restricted functional nonzero, then the relative facets are exactly \(C\cap\{x\in L:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=0\}\). Normals differing by a positive scalar and an element of \(L^\perp\) define the same restricted facet inequality. Equations defining \(L\), zero restrictions, duplicate positive multiples, and other redundant rows do not yield additional facets; without irredundancy the row-to-facet map need not be injective or surjective onto distinct rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-dimensional cone the correspondence is taken inside its span, and redundant or span-defining ambient rows do not correspond bijectively to facets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative facets correspond to the irredundant nonzero restricted inequalities modulo positive scaling and addition of vectors from \(L^\perp\); arbitrary redundant ambient systems need not give a bijection.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\langle a_j,x\rangle\leq0,\ j=1,\ldots,s\}
\]
be full-dimensional, with every \(a_j\neq0\), and suppose this representation is irredundant. Then
\[
F_j=C\cap\{x:\langle a_j,x\rangle=0\}
\]
is a facet of \(C\) for every \(j\). Every facet of \(C\) equals exactly one \(F_j\). Moreover, any valid supporting inequality defining that same facet has a normal that is a positive scalar multiple of \(a_j\).
