knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A facet of \(C\) is a maximal proper face, equivalently a face of dimension \(\dim C-1\). A valid nonzero inequality \(a^Tx\leq0\) is facet defining when \[F_a:=\{x\in C:a^Tx=0\}\] is a facet. In an irredundant homogeneous H-description, each row inequality is facet defining, and every facet is defined by some row. Two nonzero inequalities define the same facet exactly when their normals are positive scalar multiples, under the fixed \(\leq0\) orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facets are the maximal proper faces of a polyhedral cone. A homogeneous valid inequality defines a facet when its equality set inside the cone has codimension one. For a full-dimensional cone, the inequalities in an irredundant H-description correspond one-for-one with facets, up to positive rescaling and reordering of their normal vectors.
assumptions_latex: The H-description contains no redundant rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \((a^i)^Tx\leq0\mapsto F_i=C\cap\{x:(a^i)^Tx=0\}\) gives the irredundant-inequality–facet correspondence, modulo positive row scaling.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\) is a facet iff \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(\dim F=\dim C-1\).
A row is irredundant in a full-dimensional minimal H-description iff its equality set in \(C\) is a facet.
special_cases_latex: The facets of \(\mathbb{R}_+^n\) are \(\{x\geq0:x_i=0\}\), defined by \(-x_i\leq0\).
A full-dimensional pointed cone in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has two facet rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: The number of rows in any irredundant H-description of a full-dimensional cone equals its number of facets.
Positive rescaling of a facet inequality does not change its facet.
A redundant valid inequality cannot represent an additional facet in a minimal description.
boundary_notes: In a lower-dimensional cone, implicit equalities define the span and are not facets.
Opposite rescaling reverses the inequality and generally changes the represented halfspace.
Distinct redundant inequalities may expose the same lower-dimensional face.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone of dimension \(d\), and let \(r^1,\ldots,r^q\) be representatives of its distinct extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointed polyhedral cones classified by linear dependence among their extreme directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(C\) is simplicial when it has exactly \(d\) extreme rays and their representatives are linearly independent, equivalently \[C=\operatorname{cone}(r^1,\ldots,r^d),\qquad \dim\operatorname{span}\{r^1,\ldots,r^d\}=d.\] It is nonsimplicial when its extreme-ray representatives are linearly dependent, necessarily \(q>d\). A proposed finite generator system is redundant when some generator belongs to the cone generated by the others; after all such redundancies are removed, its rays are exactly the extreme rays of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed polyhedral cone is simplicial when its extreme directions form a linear basis of its span. Such a d-dimensional cone has exactly d extreme rays. If the complete extreme-ray family is linearly dependent, the cone is nonsimplicial and has more than d extreme rays. This intrinsic classification is distinct from redundancy in a chosen presentation: an arbitrary generator list may contain removable vectors even when the cone itself is simplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is simplicial iff \(q=d\) and \(r^1,\ldots,r^q\) are linearly independent; otherwise its complete extreme-ray system is dependent.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\) is simplicial iff it is linearly isomorphic, within its span, to \(\mathbb{R}_+^d\).
A generator \(g_j\) is redundant iff \(g_j\in\operatorname{cone}(g_i:i\neq j)\).
special_cases_latex: \(\mathbb{R}_+^d\) is simplicial.
Every pointed cone of dimension one or two is simplicial.
A three-dimensional cone with four distinct extreme rays is nonsimplicial.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every vector of a simplicial cone has unique nonnegative coordinates in its extreme-ray basis.
An irredundant generator system of a pointed polyhedral cone has one representative per extreme ray.
Adding an interior generator creates a redundant presentation without changing the cone's simpliciality class.
boundary_notes: Simpliciality is defined relative to \(\operatorname{span}C\), not necessarily the ambient space.
Nonpointed cones require quotienting or splitting off lineality before applying this classification.
Linear dependence of a nonminimal generator list does not by itself imply that the cone is nonsimplicial.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the linear span of C.
Number of distinct extreme rays of C.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Dual of a Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside its span, the dual of a simplicial cone is generated by the dual basis and is simplicial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}C\) and \(C=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_d)\), where \((v_i)\) is a basis of \(L\). If \((w_i)\) is its inner-product dual basis, \(\langle w_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\), then under the nonnegative-dual convention \[C_L^*=\{y\in L:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in C\}=\operatorname{cone}(w_1,\ldots,w_d).\] Hence the relative dual is again simplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_L^*=\operatorname{cone}(w_1,\ldots,w_d)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality is computed in the cone's span, thereby excluding ambient orthogonal lineality.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative dual cone computed in L.
Basis dual to the generator basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Face Lattice of a Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces of a simplicial cone correspond exactly to subsets of its extreme rays, so its face lattice is Boolean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_d)\) is simplicial, then for every \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\), \(F_I=\operatorname{cone}(v_i:i\in I)\) is a face. Every face is uniquely of this form, \(F_I\subseteq F_J\iff I\subseteq J\), and \(\dim F_I=|I|\). Thus \(C\) has \(\binom{d}{k}\) faces of dimension \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\mapsto F_I\) is an inclusion-preserving bijection from subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\) to the faces of \(C\), with \(\dim F_I=|I|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Class-specific facial-incidence structure of a simplicial cone.

notation.meaning: Face generated by the rays indexed by I.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplicial Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed d-dimensional polyhedral cone is simplicial exactly when its d extreme rays have linearly independent representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pointed polyhedral cone \(C\), of dimension \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)\), is simplicial when it is generated by \(d\) linearly independent vectors: \[C=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_d),\qquad \dim(\operatorname{span}C)=d.\] Equivalently, \(C\) has exactly \(d\) extreme rays. Any choice of one nonzero representative from each extreme ray is then linearly independent and gives the displayed minimal generating system.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a pointed polyhedral cone with \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is simplicial if and only if it has exactly \(d\) extreme rays, equivalently \(C=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_d)\) for linearly independent vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-independence characterization within pointed polyhedral cones.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality within the linear span of a pointed simplicial cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{span}C\) and \(C=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_d)\subseteq L\), where the \(v_i\) form a basis of \(L\). For the dual basis \(w_1,\ldots,w_d\in L\), defined by \(\langle w_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\), the relative dual cone is \[C_L^*=\{y\in L:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in C\}=\operatorname{cone}(w_1,\ldots,w_d).\] Thus the relative dual is simplicial, and \(w_i\) exposes the facet generated by all \(v_j\) with \(j\neq i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative dual of a simplicial cone is generated by the dual basis and is again simplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_L^*=\operatorname{cone}(w_1,\ldots,w_d)\), and \(w_i\) exposes \(\operatorname{cone}\{v_j:j\neq i\}\).

Nonunique Extreme-Ray Coordinates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed polyhedral cone is nonsimplicial exactly when some element has nonunique coordinates over its complete distinct extreme-ray family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With one nonzero representative \(v_i\) from each distinct extreme ray of a pointed polyhedral cone \(C\), the cone is nonsimplicial if and only if there exist distinct \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R_+^r\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^r\alpha_i v_i=\sum_{i=1}^r\beta_i v_i.\] Equivalently, the complete extreme-ray family has a nonzero mixed-sign linear dependence. Pointedness excludes a nontrivial dependence whose coefficients all have the same sign.
assumptions_latex: \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) are nonzero representatives of all distinct extreme rays of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is nonsimplicial}\iff\exists\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R_+^r,\ \alpha\ne\beta:\sum_i\alpha_i v_i=\sum_i\beta_i v_i.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate nonuniqueness relative to one representative of every distinct extreme ray; arbitrary redundant generating lists are excluded.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsimplicial Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed d-dimensional polyhedral cone is nonsimplicial exactly when it has more than d extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pointed polyhedral cone \(C\), of dimension \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)\), is nonsimplicial when it is not simplicial. If \(r\) denotes its number of extreme rays, then pointedness and polyhedrality give \(r\geq d\), and nonsimpliciality is equivalent to \(r>d\). Hence representatives \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) of all extreme rays generate \(C\) but are necessarily linearly dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a pointed polyhedral cone with \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is nonsimplicial if and only if it has more than \(d\) extreme rays; consequently, its complete extreme-ray generating family is linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The complement of the simplicial class among pointed polyhedral cones.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the linear span of the cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square Cone: Dependent but Irredundant Extreme Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical three-dimensional example of nonsimpliciality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^3\), let \(v_1=(1,1,1)\), \(v_2=(-1,1,1)\), \(v_3=(-1,-1,1)\), \(v_4=(1,-1,1)\), and \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\}\). All four displayed rays are extreme, so the three-dimensional cone is nonsimplicial and none of its four generators is redundant. Nevertheless \[v_1+v_3=v_2+v_4=(0,0,2),\] giving distinct nonnegative representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cone over a square has four necessary extreme rays in dimension three and nonunique ray coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is pointed, three-dimensional, and nonsimplicial, with four irredundant extreme rays and \(v_1+v_3=v_2+v_4\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dependence Does Not Imply Generator Redundancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete extreme-ray systems of pointed nonsimplicial polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) contain one representative from every extreme ray of a pointed nonsimplicial polyhedral cone \(C\), then the family is linearly dependent but conically irredundant: \[v_i\notin\operatorname{cone}\{v_j:j\neq i\}\qquad\text{for every }i.\] Thus linear dependence does not imply that a conic generator can be deleted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complete extreme-ray family of a nonsimplicial cone is linearly dependent but every ray remains necessary.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a pointed nonsimplicial polyhedral cone.
One nonzero representative is chosen from every extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The complete extreme-ray family is linearly dependent and conically irredundant.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) represent all extreme rays of a pointed nonsimplicial polyhedral cone \(C\). There exist distinct \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R_+^r\), which may be chosen with disjoint supports, such that \[\sum_{i=1}^r\alpha_i v_i=\sum_{i=1}^r\beta_i v_i\neq0.\] Hence at least one element of \(C\) has two different nonnegative coordinate vectors in the complete extreme-ray system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every pointed nonsimplicial polyhedral cone has an element with two distinct nonnegative extreme-ray representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\alpha\neq\beta\in\mathbb R_+^r\) with \(\sum_i\alpha_i v_i=\sum_i\beta_i v_i\neq0\).

Rank and Circuit Certificate for the Transition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed dimension, the simplicial-to-nonsimplicial transition occurs exactly when the complete extreme-ray matrix acquires a nontrivial kernel, equivalently a linear circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the complete family of distinct extreme-ray representatives of a pointed \(d\)-dimensional polyhedral cone, \[C\text{ is nonsimplicial}\iff r>d\iff\ker V\ne\{0\}.\] Whenever these conditions hold, the family contains a circuit, meaning a minimally linearly dependent subfamily. Thus, at fixed dimension, loss of simpliciality is exactly the onset of rank deficiency in the complete extreme-ray system.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a pointed polyhedral cone with \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)\).
\(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) contain one nonzero representative from every distinct extreme ray of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is nonsimplicial}\iff r>d\iff\ker V\ne\{0\}\iff\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\}\text{ contains a linear circuit}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank and circuit certificate for the boundary between simplicial and nonsimplicial pointed polyhedral cones.

notation.meaning: Dimension and number of distinct extreme rays.

knowledge_statements.title: Generator-Dependence Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank criterion separating simplicial and nonsimplicial pointed polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a pointed polyhedral cone of dimension \(d\), let \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) represent all its distinct extreme rays, and define the linear map \(V:\mathbb{R}^r\to\operatorname{span}C\) by \(V\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i v_i\). Since \(\operatorname{rank}V=d\),
\[
\dim\ker V=r-d.
\]
Thus the generator family is independent, and \(C\) simplicial, exactly when \(r=d\). The transition to nonsimpliciality occurs exactly when \(r>d\), equivalently when \(\ker V\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimal extreme-ray generators, dependence begins precisely when their number exceeds the cone dimension; the dependence-space dimension equals the excess number of rays.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a pointed polyhedral cone of dimension \(d\).
\(v_1,\ldots,v_r\) represent all distinct extreme rays of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim\ker V=r-d\), so \(C\) is simplicial iff \(\ker V=\{0\}\), and nonsimplicial iff \(\ker V\neq\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: linear map whose columns are the extreme-ray generators
space of linear dependencies among the generators

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite systems of real linear inequalities and their nonnegative multiplier certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Farkas alternative pair associated with \((A,b)\) consists of the primal feasibility system \[\mathcal{P}(A,b):\quad Ax\leq b\] and the certificate system \[\mathcal{C}(A,b):\quad u\geq0,\quad u^TA=0,\quad u^Tb<0.\] The alternative principle states that exactly one of \(\mathcal{P}(A,b)\) and \(\mathcal{C}(A,b)\) is feasible. A feasible \(u\) in \(\mathcal{C}(A,b)\) is an infeasibility certificate for \(Ax\leq b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite linear inequality system, the associated alternative compares primal feasibility with existence of a nonnegative multiplier. The multiplier annihilates every variable coefficient while producing a strictly negative combination of the right-hand sides. Exactly one system is feasible: either a primal solution exists, or such a certificate exists, but never both. This is the standard Farkas feasibility-certificate interface rooted in polyhedral cone separation.
assumptions_latex: Primal variables \(x\) are unrestricted in sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\{x:Ax\leq b\}\neq\varnothing\) and \(\{u:u\geq0,\ u^TA=0,\ u^Tb<0\}\neq\varnothing\) holds.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The system \(Ax=b,\ x\geq0\) is feasible iff \(u^Tb\leq0\) for every \(u\) satisfying \(u^TA\leq0\).
For vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), membership \(b\in\operatorname{cone}(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\) is equivalent to \(u^Tb\leq0\) for every \(u\) with \(u^Ta_j\leq0\) for all \(j\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A=0\), primal feasibility is equivalent to \(b\geq0\), while a certificate selects a nonnegative combination of negative components.
For homogeneous \(Ax\leq0\), \(x=0\) is always feasible, so no strict negative certificate exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every infeasible finite linear inequality system has a finite nonnegative multiplier certificate.
A proposed certificate can be checked by verifying linear equalities, inequalities, and one strict scalar inequality.
Farkas alternatives yield validity certificates for linear inequalities over nonempty polyhedra.
boundary_notes: The strict inequality \(u^Tb<0\) is essential for this formulation.
Changing inequality orientation changes the signs in the certificate system.
Infinite systems and strict primal inequalities require separate alternative theorems or closure hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Inequality-Form Farkas Alternative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite nonstrict linear inequality system is infeasible exactly when a nonnegative row multiplier cancels all variables and makes the combined right-hand side negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one of the systems \[Ax\le b\] and \[y\ge0,\qquad A^\top y=0,\qquad b^\top y<0\] is feasible. A certificate in the second system may be positively rescaled so that \(b^\top y=-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Exactly one of }\exists x:Ax\le b\quad\text{and}\quad\exists y\ge0:A^\top y=0,\ b^\top y<0\text{ holds}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonstrict-inequality form of Farkas' alternative.

knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Alternative Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either b is a nonnegative combination of A's columns, or a multiplier strictly separates b from that cone, but never both.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[\text{(i) }Ax=b,\quad x\geq0;\qquad \text{(ii) }A^\top y\geq0,\quad b^\top y<0.\] The inequalities are coordinatewise. A vector \(y\) satisfying the second system is a directly checkable certificate that \(b\) does not belong to the finitely generated cone \(\{Ax:x\geq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x\geq0:Ax=b\) and \(\exists y:A^\top y\geq0,\ b^\top y<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form finite-dimensional Farkas alternative.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional mixed equality and non-strict inequality form; equality multipliers are free.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^q\), exactly one of \(Ax=b,\ Gx\le h\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z=0,\ z\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y+h^{\mathsf T}z<0\) is feasible. A certificate may be positively rescaled so its final scalar equals \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed equality–inequality system is infeasible exactly when free and nonnegative multipliers cancel its variable coefficients and yield a negative constant.
assumptions_latex: All inequalities are coordinatewise and non-strict.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:Ax=b,Gx\le h\}=\varnothing\iff\exists y,z:\ z\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+G^{\mathsf T}z=0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y+h^{\mathsf T}z<0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Inequality Boundary of Ordinary Farkas Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains why systems containing strict inequalities require a Motzkin-type alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system \(x<0\), \(-x<0\) is infeasible. With \(G=(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}\) and \(h=0\), however, no \(z\ge0\) can satisfy both \(G^{\mathsf T}z=0\) and \(h^{\mathsf T}z<0\), since \(h^{\mathsf T}z=0\) always. Thus the ordinary non-strict Farkas certificate does not characterize infeasibility after \(\le\) is replaced by \(<\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two incompatible strict inequalities show that ordinary Farkas certificates do not cover strict systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:x<0,-x<0\}=\varnothing\), but the ordinary non-strict multiplier certificate does not exist.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Inequality Boundary of Ordinary Farkas Certificates

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonemptiness prevents vacuous validity from being mistaken for multiplier representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\). Then \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le d\) for every \(x\in P\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \(A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=c\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}\lambda\le d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every valid inequality for a nonempty polyhedron is dominated by a nonnegative combination of its defining inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq\{x:c^{\mathsf T}x\le d\}\iff\exists\lambda\ge0:\ A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=c,\ b^{\mathsf T}\lambda\le d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Farkas alternatives and linear infeasibility certificates
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and interpret vector inequalities componentwise. Row multipliers belong to \(\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real linear systems; the family includes inequality and nonnegative-variable equality forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Farkas alternative family consists of equivalent primal-feasibility and dual-certificate formulations. In inequality form, exactly one of \[\exists x\in\mathbb R^n:\ Ax\le b,\qquad \exists u\in\mathbb R^m:\ u\ge0,\ u^{\mathsf T}A=0,\ u^{\mathsf T}b<0\] is feasible. In conic-membership form, for \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_n]\), \[b\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\iff \forall y\in\mathbb R^m,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\le0\Rightarrow b^{\mathsf T}y\le0.\] Equivalently, infeasibility of \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\) is certified by some \(y\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite real linear system, the Farkas family pairs feasibility with a nonnegative linear-combination certificate. The system \(Ax\le b\) is infeasible exactly when there is \(u\ge0\) with \(u^{\mathsf T}A=0\) and \(u^{\mathsf T}b<0\); precisely one system in this pair is feasible. For an equality system with nonnegative variables, \(Ax=b, x\ge0\) is feasible exactly when every \(y\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le0\) also satisfies \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le0\). Thus failure of cone membership has a separating linear functional as its certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le b\) is infeasible if and only if \(\exists u\ge0\) such that \(u^{\mathsf T}A=0\) and \(u^{\mathsf T}b<0\); equivalently, \(b\notin A\mathbb R_+^n\) if and only if \(\exists y\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le0<b^{\mathsf T}y\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\) is feasible if and only if \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le0\) for every \(y\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le0\).
After replacing \(A,b\) by \(-A,-b\), the signs may be reversed without changing the alternative's content.
special_cases_latex: For a homogeneous system, \(Ax\le0\) is always feasible, so a strict negative certificate cannot occur.
For one inequality, the certificate reduces to a nonnegative scalar multiplier annihilating its coefficient row while making the right-hand side negative.
immediate_consequences_latex: A vector outside a finitely generated cone admits a linear separator from that cone.
Infeasibility of a rational linear system has a finite multiplier certificate expressible with the same sign convention.
boundary_notes: Strict inequalities and mixed strict/non-strict systems belong to Motzkin-type alternatives unless separately reduced to this form.
This definition is finite-dimensional and does not assert an infinite-dimensional closed-range alternative.

notation.meaning: The cone generated by the columns of \(A\).
Every component of the multiplier vector is nonnegative.

children.title: Gordan–Stiemke Alternative Family
children.top_down_role: Strict-positivity and subspace-intersection variants of polyhedral alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Gordan Strict-Image Alternative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either a linear image contains a strictly positive vector or there is a nonzero nonnegative transpose-kernel dependence, but not both.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), exactly one of \[Ax>0\] and \[y\ge0,\quad y\ne0,\quad A^\top y=0\] is feasible. The second system is a nonzero nonnegative dependence certifying that the range of \(A\) cannot meet the strictly positive orthant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Exactly one of }\exists x:Ax>0\quad\text{and}\quad\exists y\ge0,\ y\ne0:A^\top y=0\text{ holds}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gordan's strict positive-image orientation; simultaneous sign reversal gives the negative-image convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Stiemke Boundary-Kernel Alternative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either the kernel contains a nonzero nonnegative vector or the row space contains a strictly positive vector, exclusively.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), exactly one of \[Ax=0,\quad x\ge0,\quad x\ne0\] and \[A^\top y>0\] is feasible. Thus a strictly positive vector in the row space certifies that the kernel contains no nonzero nonnegative vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Exactly one of }\exists x\ge0,\ x\ne0:Ax=0\quad\text{and}\quad\exists y:A^\top y>0\text{ holds}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-nonnegative kernel orientation complementary to the strict-positive-kernel formulation.
Certificate strengthening of the strict-image form of the Gordan alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). If no \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(Ax<0\), then there exists \(y\in\mathbb R_+^m\setminus\{0\}\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\). It may be normalized by \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y=1\), and one may choose it with at most \(\operatorname{rank}\!\begin{bmatrix}A^{\mathsf T}\\ \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\end{bmatrix}\le n+1\) positive components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of a strictly negative image has a normalized nonnegative null certificate supported on at most n+1 rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists y\ge0:\ A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y=1,\ |\operatorname{supp}y|\le n+1\).
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Sparse Gordan Certificate
Gordan–Stiemke Alternative Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subspace form of Stiemke’s strict-positivity alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) be a linear subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Exactly one of the following assertions holds:
\[
\text{(i)}\quad L\cap\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\neq\varnothing,
\]
\[
\text{(ii)}\quad L^\perp\cap\bigl(\mathbb{R}_+^n\setminus\{0\}\bigr)\neq\varnothing.
\]
Equivalently, either \(L\) contains a vector whose coordinates are all strictly positive, or there exists a nonzero coordinatewise nonnegative vector orthogonal to every vector in \(L\), but never both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subspace either contains a strictly positive vector or has a nonzero nonnegative vector in its orthogonal complement, and the two possibilities are mutually exclusive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(L\cap\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\neq\varnothing\) and \(L^\perp\cap(\mathbb{R}_+^n\setminus\{0\})\neq\varnothing\) holds.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Vector relations \(>0\) and \(\ge0\) are componentwise; \(v\ne0\) excludes the zero vector.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous linear alternatives, emphasizing strict positivity and intersections of a kernel with the orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Gordan–Stiemke family comprises two complementary strict-positivity alternatives. Gordan's form states that exactly one of \[\exists x\in\mathbb R^n:\ Ax>0,\qquad \exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ y\ge0,\ y
e0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y=0\] holds. Equivalently, \(\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\cap(\mathbb R_+^m\setminus\{0\})=\varnothing\) precisely when \(\operatorname{range}(A)\cap\mathbb R_{++}^m
e\varnothing\). Stiemke's form states that exactly one of \[\exists x\in\mathbb R^n:\ Ax\ge0,\ Ax
e0,\qquad \exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ y>0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y=0\] holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gordan's alternative says that the range of \(A\) contains a componentwise strictly positive vector exactly when the kernel of \(A^{\mathsf T}\) contains no nonzero nonnegative vector. Stiemke's alternative exchanges the strictness: the range contains a nonzero nonnegative vector exactly when the transpose kernel contains no strictly positive vector. Each pair is exclusive and exhaustive, and both are homogeneous because no right-hand-side vector occurs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{range}(A)\cap\mathbb R_{++}^m\ne\varnothing\iff\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\cap(\mathbb R_+^m\setminus\{0\})=\varnothing\), while \(\operatorname{range}(A)\cap(\mathbb R_+^m\setminus\{0\})\ne\varnothing\iff\ker(A^{\mathsf T})\cap\mathbb R_{++}^m=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Gordan: \(\exists x\ge0,\ x\ne0,\ Ax=0\) if and only if no \(y\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y>0\), after transposing and renaming the matrix.
Stiemke: \(\exists x>0\) with \(Ax=0\) if and only if \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\Rightarrow A^{\mathsf T}y=0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is square and nonsingular, Gordan's first system is feasible exactly when \(A^{-1}\mathbb R_{++}^m\) is nonempty, which it always is.
If \(A=0\), Gordan's certificate system is feasible and its strict-range system is not.
immediate_consequences_latex: The alternatives characterize whether a linear subspace meets the interior or the nonzero part of the nonnegative orthant.
They provide homogeneous certificates without an affine right-hand side.
boundary_notes: The placement of the transpose varies by source; the two displayed systems fix the convention used here.
Ville and Motzkin alternatives add sign restrictions or mixed strict inequalities and are not included in this slot.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: All spaces are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces. A closed convex cone \(K\) satisfies \(0\in K\), \(x,y\in K\Rightarrow x+y\in K\), and \(\lambda x\in K\) for \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A catalog definition grouping standard primitive cones by their defining geometry; it does not assert that every convex cone belongs to one listed family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical cone families are the following standard classes: polyhedral cones \(K=\{x:Ax\ge0\}=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\}\); norm-epigraph cones \(K_{\|\cdot\|}=\{(x,t):\|x\|\le t\}\); matrix-positivity cones such as \(\mathbb S_+^n=\{X:X=X^{\mathsf T},\ z^{\mathsf T}Xz\ge0\ \forall z\}\); multiplicative and transcendental perspective cones such as power, exponential, and relative-entropy cones; polynomial-positivity cones \(\{p:p(x)\ge0\ \forall x\in S\}\); and hyperbolicity cones \(\Lambda_+(p,e)=\{x:\text{all roots of }t\mapsto p(x-te)\text{ are nonnegative}\}\) for a homogeneous polynomial hyperbolic in direction \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical cone families are standard closed convex cones organized by their defining structure. Polyhedral cones use finitely many linear inequalities or generators. Norm-epigraph cones are epigraphs of positively homogeneous norms. Matrix cones impose spectral, entrywise, or factorization positivity. Power, exponential, and relative-entropy cones encode multiplicative or perspective inequalities. Polynomial cones impose nonnegativity on a specified set or admit structured certificates such as sums of squares. Hyperbolicity cones are root-location regions of homogeneous hyperbolic polynomials. The catalog is structural: a cone may admit more than one representation and therefore belong to several families.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A canonical family is specified by an ambient finite-dimensional space together with one of the displayed defining membership conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a finite generator matrix \(V\), a finitely generated cone is \(V\mathbb R_+^r\).
Every norm-epigraph cone is the epigraph cone of a finite-valued nonnegative sublinear function that is symmetric.
special_cases_latex: \(\mathbb R_+^n\) is polyhedral, simplicial, and a polynomial-inequality cone.
The Euclidean norm-epigraph cone is the second-order cone.
\(\mathbb S_+^n\) is simultaneously a matrix cone and a hyperbolicity cone for the determinant.
immediate_consequences_latex: Direct products of members of these families are convex cones.
Linear images and inverse images may connect distinct representation families.
boundary_notes: This catalog excludes nonconvex positivity sets and nonhomogeneous epigraphs that are not cones.
Closedness must be checked for projected or linearly imaged representations.

notation.meaning: All finite nonnegative linear combinations of the listed vectors.
The hyperbolicity cone determined by \(p\) and direction \(e\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate, finitely generated, and simplicial polyhedral cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_r]\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real polyhedral cones, including coordinate orthants and cones generated by independent rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The elementary polyhedral cone family consists of cones admitting either a finite generator representation \[K=V\mathbb R_+^r=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\ge0\right\}\] or a finite homogeneous inequality representation \[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge0\}.\] Its coordinate members are orthants \(\mathbb R_+^n\) and their images under coordinate sign changes, permutations, and injective linear maps. A generated cone is simplicial in its span when its nonzero generators can be chosen linearly independent; it is full-dimensional simplicial when exactly \(n\) independent generators span \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elementary polyhedral cone is a set of all nonnegative combinations of finitely many vectors, equivalently a cone cut out by finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities. The basic coordinate example is the nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb R_+^n\). If the generators defining the extreme rays are linearly independent, the cone is simplicial in their linear span. An invertible linear image of the nonnegative orthant is therefore a full-dimensional simplicial cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) belongs to the elementary polyhedral family when \(K=V\mathbb R_+^r\), equivalently when \(K=\{x:Ax\ge0\}\) for some finite matrices \(V\) and \(A\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in V\mathbb R_+^r\iff\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^r\) such that \(x=V\lambda\).
If \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular, \(V\mathbb R_+^n=\{x:V^{-1}x\ge0\}\).
special_cases_latex: \(V=I_n\) yields \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\).
A single nonzero generator yields a ray \(\{\lambda v:\lambda\ge0\}\).
A linear subspace is polyhedral but is not pointed unless it is \(\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finitely generated cone is convex and closed in finite dimensions.
Finite intersections and Cartesian products of polyhedral cones are polyhedral.
boundary_notes: Redundant generators need not be extreme-ray generators.
An arbitrary linear image of a pointed cone can fail to remain pointed if the map is not injective.

notation.meaning: The image of the nonnegative orthant under the generator matrix \(V\).

children.title: Nonnegative Orthants
children.top_down_role: Coordinatewise positivity cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Projection and Distance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection clips negative coordinates to zero, the negative part gives the Euclidean distance, and these computations are linear in the dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[P_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x)=x_+:=(\max\{x_1,0\},\ldots,\max\{x_n,0\}),\qquad \operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R_+^n)=\|x_-\|_2,\] where \((x_-)_i=\max\{-x_i,0\}\). Projection, distance evaluation, and membership testing use \(O(n)\) coordinate operations.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\) has its standard Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x)=x_+\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R_+^n)=\|x_-\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection, distance, and membership testing for the coordinate orthant.

knowledge_statements.title: Faces and Extreme Rays of the Nonnegative Orthant
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every orthant face is obtained by fixing selected coordinates to zero; coordinate rays are extreme and coordinate hyperplanes define the facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \[F_I:=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:x_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I\}=\operatorname{cone}\{e_i:i\in I\}.\] These are exactly the faces of \(\mathbb R_+^n\). Its extreme rays are \(\mathbb R_+e_i\), its facets are the sets \(\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:x_i=0\}\), and its face lattice is the Boolean lattice of coordinate subsets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Faces}(\mathbb R_+^n)=\{F_I:I\subseteq\{1,�ldots,n\}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean face structure specific to the coordinate orthant.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Orthants
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative orthant consists of coordinatewise nonnegative vectors; it is polyhedral, simplicial, pointed, full-dimensional, and self-dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a positive integer \(n\), the nonnegative orthant is \[\mathbb{R}_+^n=\{x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_i\geq0\text{ for every }i\}.\] It is a closed, convex, pointed, full-dimensional polyhedral cone generated by the coordinate vectors \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\). Under the Euclidean inner product it is self-dual: \[(\mathbb{R}_+^n)^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n\}=\mathbb{R}_+^n.\]
assumptions_latex: \(n\) is a positive integer and inequalities are interpreted coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{R}_+^n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_i\geq0\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,n\}\), and its Euclidean dual cone equals itself.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise nonnegativity in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean projection, distance, and operation count for the orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\Pi_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x)=x_+:=(\max\{x_i,0\})_{i=1}^n,
\qquad
\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R_+^n)=\|x_-\|_2,
\]
where \(x_-=(\max\{-x_i,0\})_i\). Furthermore, \(x=x_+-x_-\), \(x_+,x_-\in\mathbb R_+^n\), and \(\langle x_+,x_-\rangle=0\). Computing \(x_+\), \(x_-\), and membership requires \(O(n)\) scalar comparisons and arithmetic operations in the standard coordinate model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clipping negative coordinates to zero is the exact orthant projection; the negative part gives the distance, and the computation is linear in the dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R^n\) has its Euclidean inner product.
Arithmetic and coordinate comparisons have unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x)=x_+\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R_+^n)=\|x_-\|_2\), with \(O(n)\) coordinate work.

notation.meaning: Coordinatewise magnitude of the negative part.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Orthant Projection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate certificates supplementing the seed's membership definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
x\in\operatorname{int}\mathbb R_+^n\iff \min_i x_i>0,
\qquad
x\in\partial\mathbb R_+^n\iff x_i\geq0\ \forall i\text{ and }\min_i x_i=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly positive coordinates certify the orthant interior, while nonnegative coordinates with at least one zero certify its boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coordinate signs exactly certify interior and boundary membership.
knowledge_statements.title: Orthant Interior and Boundary Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face Lattice of the Nonnegative Orthant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete facial and extreme-ray structure of coordinatewise positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\),
\[
F_I:=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:x_j=0\text{ for }j\notin I\}
\]
is a face of \(\mathbb R_+^n\), and every face has this form. Its dimension is \(|I|\). In particular, the extreme rays are exactly \(\mathbb R_+e_i\), and the facets are \(\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:x_i=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of the orthant are obtained by fixing selected coordinates to zero; coordinate axes are its extreme rays and coordinate hyperplanes its facets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Faces}(\mathbb R_+^n)=\{F_I:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\}\).

notation.meaning: The coordinate face supported on I.

children.title: Simplicial Cones
children.top_down_role: Cones linearly equivalent to coordinate orthants.

knowledge_statements.title: Membership by Generator Coordinates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership is decided by solving for the unique generator coordinates and checking their signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=V\mathbb R_+^d\) with \(V\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) nonsingular, \[x\in C\iff V^{-1}x\geq0\] coordinatewise. A dense factorization costs \(O(d^3)\), after which each query uses one \(O(d^2)\) linear solve and \(d\) sign tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in C\iff V^{-1}x\in\mathbb R_+^d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Membership testing when a full-dimensional simplicial cone is supplied by a generator basis.

notation.meaning: Unique coordinates in the generator basis

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Generators of a Full-Dimensional Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual generators form the basis dual to the extreme-ray generators, so the dual cone is again simplicial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_d]\) be nonsingular and \(C=V\mathbb R_+^d\). Then \[C^*=V^{-\mathsf T}\mathbb R_+^d=\operatorname{cone}\{w_1,\ldots,w_d\},\qquad w_i=V^{-\mathsf T}e_i,\] with \(\langle w_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\). Thus the Euclidean dual of a full-dimensional simplicial cone is simplicial.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is generated by the columns of a nonsingular matrix \(V\).
Duality uses the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^*=V^{-\mathsf T}\mathbb R_+^d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean dual description in the full-dimensional case.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Coordinates and Boolean Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplicial cone has unique nonnegative generator coordinates and a Boolean face lattice generated by subsets of its rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C=\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\) and the generators are linearly independent, every \(x\in C\) has a unique representation \(x=\sum_{i=1}^d\alpha_i v_i\) with \(\alpha_i\geq0\). Its faces are exactly \[F_I=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:i\in I\},\qquad I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\) are linearly independent in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point has unique nonnegative coordinates and \(\operatorname{Faces}(C)=\{F_I:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic-span structure of a simplicial cone.

notation.meaning: Face generated by rays indexed by I

knowledge_statements.title: Simplicial Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed polyhedral cone is simplicial exactly when it is linearly isomorphic to a nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a pointed polyhedral cone with \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)\). Then \(C\) is simplicial if and only if there exists a linear isomorphism \(T:\operatorname{span}C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) such that \[T(C)=\mathbb{R}_+^d.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a pointed polyhedral cone with \(d=\dim(\operatorname{span}C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is simplicial if and only if some linear isomorphism \(T:\operatorname{span}C\to\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfies \(T(C)=\mathbb{R}_+^d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical realization of simplicial cones as linear images of orthants.

notation.meaning: A linear isomorphism on the span of the cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oblique Simplicial Cones Need Not Be Euclidean Self-Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of self-duality under a fixed Euclidean pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
V=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad C=V\mathbb R_+^2.
\]
Then \(C\) is simplicial, but
\[
C^*=V^{-T}\mathbb R_+^2\neq C.
\]
Thus linear equivalence to an orthant does not preserve self-duality under a fixed Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oblique linear image of an orthant remains simplicial but can fail Euclidean self-duality.
assumptions_latex: Duality uses the fixed Euclidean inner product on \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V\mathbb R_+^2\neq(V\mathbb R_+^2)^*\).

notation.meaning: The displayed nonsingular oblique generator matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boolean Face Lattice of a Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete facial structure inherited from the orthant representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(C=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,\ldots,v_d)\) with linearly independent generators, then every face is uniquely of the form
\[
F_I=\operatorname{cone}\{v_i:i\in I\},
\qquad I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}.
\]
Thus \(\dim F_I=|I|\), the rays \(\mathbb R_+v_i\) are exactly the extreme rays, and the face lattice is isomorphic to the Boolean lattice of subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a simplicial cone is generated by a unique subset of its independent extreme-ray generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Faces}(C)=\{\operatorname{cone}(v_i:i\in I):I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\}\).

notation.meaning: The face generated by the rays indexed by I.

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Face Lattice of a Simplicial Cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and dual coordinate descriptions in the span of a simplicial cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\) be a basis of \(L=\operatorname{span}C\), let \(V:\mathbb R^d\to L\) be defined by \(V\alpha=\sum_i\alpha_iv_i\), and let \(C=V\mathbb R_+^d\). Every \(x\in L\) has unique coordinates \(\alpha=V^{-1}x\), and
\[
x\in C\iff V^{-1}x\geq0.
\]
Relative to the induced Euclidean pairing on \(L\),
\[
C^*=V^{-T}\mathbb R_+^d,
\]
whose generators \(w_i\) satisfy \(\langle w_i,v_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplicial cone has unique nonnegative generator coordinates, and its dual within its span is generated by the biorthogonal basis.
assumptions_latex: \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\) are its linearly independent ray generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in C\iff V^{-1}x\geq0\) and \(C^*=V^{-T}\mathbb R_+^d\) in \(L\).

notation.meaning: The generator isomorphism from coordinate space to the span of C.
The biorthogonal generators of the relative dual cone.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a \(k\)-dimensional linear subspace and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\in L\) be linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointed polyhedral cones, allowing cones that are full-dimensional only in their linear span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone \(K\subseteq L\) is simplicial when there exist linearly independent vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\) such that \[K=\operatorname{cone}(v_1,ldots,v_k)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i v_i:\lambda_i\ge0\right\}.\] Equivalently, if \(V:\mathbb R^k\to L\) is the linear isomorphism satisfying \(Ve_i=v_i\), then \(K=V\mathbb R_+^k\). Every \(x\in K\) has a unique coordinate vector \(\lambda=V^{-1}x\in\mathbb R_+^k\). When \(L=\mathbb R^n\), the cone is full-dimensional simplicial and \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplicial cone of dimension \(k\) is generated by exactly \(k\) linearly independent rays in its span. It is the image of the coordinate orthant \(\mathbb R_+^k\) under a linear isomorphism. Consequently, each point has unique nonnegative coordinates relative to the chosen ray generators. A full-dimensional simplicial cone in \(\mathbb R^n\) is an invertible linear image of \(\mathbb R_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is simplicial if and only if \(K=V\mathbb R_+^k\) for a linear isomorphism \(V:\mathbb R^k\to\operatorname{span}K\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(K\) is a pointed polyhedral cone whose number of extreme rays equals \(\dim K\).
For full-dimensional \(K\), \(K=\{x:V^{-1}x\ge0\}\) for some nonsingular \(V\).
special_cases_latex: For \(k=1\), every nonzero ray is simplicial.
The orthant \(\mathbb R_+^k\) is simplicial with generators \(e_1,\ldots,e_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The conic coordinates of every member are unique.
A simplicial cone is closed, convex, polyhedral, and pointed.
boundary_notes: A cone generated by more than \(\dim K\) extreme rays is not simplicial.
Linearly dependent listed generators do not define a simplicial presentation even if redundant vectors can be deleted.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(\|\cdot\|\) a norm on \(E\). The product space is \(E\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm epigraphs; gauges lacking symmetry are treated as a nearby extension rather than as norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The norm-epigraph cone associated with \(\|\cdot\|\) is \[K_{\|\cdot\|}=\operatorname{epi}\|\cdot\|=\{(x,t)\in E\times\mathbb R:\|x\|\le t\}.\] Its interior is \(\{(x,t):\|x\|<t\}\), and its boundary is \(\{(x,t):\|x\|=t\}\). Because a norm is convex and positively homogeneous, this epigraph is a closed convex pointed cone. Its dual under the product pairing is \[K_{\|\cdot\|}^*=\{(y,s)\in E^*\times\mathbb R:\|y\|_*\le s\},\] where \(\|y\|_*:=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\langle y,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any finite-dimensional normed space, the norm-epigraph cone consists of pairs \((x,t)\) whose scalar coordinate bounds the norm of \(x\). Positive homogeneity makes the epigraph a cone, while convexity and continuity make it closed and convex. The dual cone is the epigraph cone of the dual norm. Thus every norm produces a canonical primal-dual cone pair.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((x,t)\in K_{\|\cdot\|}\iff t\ge0\) and \(x\in tB\), where \(B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}\).
\((x,t)\in K_{\|\cdot\|}\iff \langle y,x\rangle\le t\) for every \(y\) with \(\|y\|_*\le1\).
special_cases_latex: The \(\ell_2\)-norm yields the second-order cone.
The \(\ell_1\)- and \(\ell_\infty\)-norm epigraph cones are polyhedral.
immediate_consequences_latex: A norm inequality \(\|Ax+b\|\le c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) is an affine inverse image of a norm-epigraph cone.
The cone is self-dual exactly when the norm is identified with its dual under the chosen inner product.
boundary_notes: The epigraph of a nonhomogeneous convex function is generally not a cone.
A gauge epigraph may be a closed convex cone without being symmetric in its vector argument.

notation.meaning: The closed unit ball of the norm.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), write a vector as \((x,t)\in\mathbb R^{n-1}\times\mathbb R\), and use the Euclidean norm \(\|x\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The ordinary, unrotated second-order cone in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The \(n\)-dimensional second-order cone, Lorentz cone, or ice-cream cone is \[\mathcal L^n=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^{n-1}\times\mathbb R:\|x\|_2\le t\}.\] Its equivalent quadratic representation is \[\mathcal L^n=\{(x,t):t\ge0,\ t^2-x^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\}.\] Under the standard Euclidean pairing it is self-dual: \((\mathcal L^n)^*=\mathcal L^n\). The representation pair refers to the norm-epigraph and homogeneous quadratic descriptions of the same cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order cone is the epigraph cone of the Euclidean norm. A pair \((x,t)\) belongs to it when \(t\) is nonnegative and at least the Euclidean length of \(x\). Squaring gives the equivalent quadratic inequalities \(t\ge0\) and \(t^2\ge x^{\mathsf T}x\). With the standard inner product, the cone is self-dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L^n=\{(x,t):\|x\|_2\le t\}=\{(x,t):t\ge0,\ t^2\ge x^{\mathsf T}x\}\) and \((\mathcal L^n)^*=\mathcal L^n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((x,t)\in\mathcal L^n\iff \begin{pmatrix}t&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&tI\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\).
\((x,t)\in\mathcal L^n\iff u^{\mathsf T}x+s t\ge0\) for every \((u,s)\in\mathcal L^n\).
special_cases_latex: \(\mathcal L^2=\{(x,t):|x|\le t\}\) is linearly equivalent to \(\mathbb R_+^2\).
\(\mathcal L^3\) is the classical circular ice-cream cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: Constraints \(\|Ax+b\|_2\le c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) are second-order-cone representable.
Cartesian products of Lorentz cones define the standard domain of conic quadratic programming.
boundary_notes: The rotated second-order cone is a linearly isomorphic but differently parameterized cone.
For \(n\ge3\), the Lorentz cone is nonpolyhedral.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Form Projection onto a Second-Order Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection retains points in the cone, sends points in the negative cone to zero, and otherwise projects to the curved boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{m-1}\) and \(r=\|x\|_2\), \[\Pi_{Q_m}(t,x)=\begin{cases}(t,x),&r\leq t,\\(0,0),&r\leq-t,\\\dfrac{t+r}{2}\left(1,\dfrac{x}{r}\right),&|t|<r.\end{cases}\] The formula is noniterative and requires one norm evaluation and \(O(m)\) scalar-vector arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Euclidean projection onto \(Q_m\) has an exact three-case formula and costs \(O(m)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form Euclidean projection onto one standard second-order-cone block.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the second-order cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior, Boundary, and Faces of the Second-Order Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order cone has strict norm inequality in its interior, and its nonzero proper faces are exactly the rays generated by boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\geq2\), \[\operatorname{int}Q_m=\{(t,x):t>\|x\|_2\},\qquad \partial Q_m=\{(t,x):t=\|x\|_2\}.\] Every nonzero boundary point generates an extreme ray. Conversely, every extreme ray has this form, and the faces of \(Q_m\) are \(\{0\}\), \(Q_m\), and these boundary rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}Q_m=\{(t,x):t>\|x\|_2\}\), and the nonzero proper faces are exactly its boundary rays.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial geometry for m>=2; the one-dimensional case is owned by the low-dimensional sibling.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Cone Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order cone is the epigraph cone of the Euclidean norm and is closed, pointed, full-dimensional, and self-dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq1\), the second-order cone of dimension \(n+1\) is the Euclidean norm epigraph \[Q_{n+1}=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n:t\geq\|x\|_2\}.\] Each \(Q_{n+1}\) is a closed, convex, pointed, full-dimensional cone. With the standard Euclidean inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\), it is self-dual: \(Q_{n+1}^*=Q_{n+1}\).
assumptions_latex: \(n\geq1\) and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is the Euclidean norm on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{n+1}=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n:t\geq\|x\|_2\}\) is the \((n+1)\)-dimensional second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean norm-epigraph convention for the second-order cone family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic facial geometry; coordinate-form comparisons and dimensional interpretation remain in sibling leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q_{n+1}=\{(t,x):t\ge\|x\|_2\}\), \[\operatorname{int}Q_{n+1}=\{(t,x):t>\|x\|_2\},\qquad \partial Q_{n+1}=\{(t,x):t=\|x\|_2\}.\] Its extreme rays are exactly \(\mathbb R_+(1,u)\) with \(\|u\|_2=1\), and every nonzero proper face is one of these rays.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior, Boundary, and Proper Faces
Lorentz Cone Realization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order cone is the nonnegative-time sheet of the Lorentz quadratic inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Lorentz quadratic form by \(q(t,x)=t^2-x^\top x\) on \(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n\). The standard second-order cone admits the equivalent realization \[Q_{n+1}=\{(t,x):t\geq\|x\|_2\}=\{(t,x):q(t,x)\geq0,\ t\geq0\}.\] The sign condition \(t\geq0\) selects one of the two sheets of the quadratic set \(q(t,x)\geq0\); the selected sheet is conventionally called the Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{n+1}=\{(t,x):t\geq0,\ t^2-x^\top x\geq0\}\), the future sheet of the quadratic Lorentz cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic, future-sheet realization of the Euclidean norm cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Isomorphism Between Forms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Swapping the scalar and vector coordinate blocks linearly and isometrically identifies the norm-epigraph and Lorentz forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_{n+1}=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\|x\|_2\leq t\}\) denote the norm-epigraph form, and let \(Q_{n+1}=\{(s,u)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n:s\geq\|u\|_2\}\) denote the Lorentz-coordinate form. The coordinate permutation \[P(x,t)=(t,x)\] is a linear isometry with \(P(E_{n+1})=Q_{n+1}\). Hence the two forms have identical facial, duality, and convexity properties under this identification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinate permutation \(P(x,t)=(t,x)\) is a linear isometric isomorphism satisfying \(P(E_{n+1})=Q_{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-order isomorphism between norm-epigraph and Lorentz conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Dimensional Degeneracies
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order cones are polyhedral only in dimensions one and two; genuine curved behavior begins in dimension three.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q_m=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{m-1}:t\geq\|x\|_2\}\), the lowest dimensions degenerate to polyhedral cones. Specifically, \(Q_1=\mathbb{R}_+\), while \[Q_2=\{(t,x):t\geq|x|\}\] is linearly isomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}_+^2\) through \(T(t,x)=(t+x,t-x)\). For every \(m\geq3\), the cone \(Q_m\) is nonpolyhedral; its normalized boundary contains the curved Euclidean sphere rather than finitely many facets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_1=\mathbb{R}_+\), \(Q_2\) is linearly isomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}_+^2\), and \(Q_m\) is nonpolyhedral for every \(m\geq3\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dimensional boundary between polyhedral and genuinely curved second-order cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection onto a Rotated Second-Order Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a rotated second-order cone is obtained by mapping to the standard cone, applying its closed-form projection, and mapping back.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Since \(T^{\mathsf T}T=2I\), Euclidean projection onto the rotated cone is transported by \[\Pi_{\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}}(z)=T^{-1}\!\left(\Pi_{\mathcal Q^{n+2}}(Tz)\right).\] Together with the standard three-case second-order-cone projection, this gives a noniterative \(O(n)\) projection algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{\mathcal Q_r}(z)=T^{-1}\Pi_{\mathcal Q}(Tz)\), computable in \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection transport is valid because T^T T=2I; it is not asserted for an arbitrary nonorthogonal cone isomorphism.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto a cone C.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry and Self-Duality of the Rotated Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rotated second-order cone is proper and self-dual; strict product inequality describes its interior, and its nonzero proper faces are boundary rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone \(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\) is closed, convex, pointed, and full-dimensional, and under the standard Euclidean pairing \((\mathcal Q_r^{n+2})^*=\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\). Its interior is \(\{(u,v,x):u>0,\ v>0,\ 2uv>\|x\|_2^2\}\). Every nonzero boundary point generates an extreme ray, and the only faces are \(\{0\}\), the whole cone, and these rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\) is proper and self-dual; its nonzero proper faces are exactly its boundary rays.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean geometry for the normalization 2uv>=||x||_2^2; T is a scalar multiple of an orthogonal map.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotated Second-Order Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rotated second-order cone imposes nonnegativity and a product bound; an explicit invertible linear map transforms it into the standard second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}=\{(u,v,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n:u\geq0,\ v\geq0,\ 2uv\geq\|x\|_2^2\}.\] This is a closed convex cone. For \(T(u,v,x)=(u+v,u-v,\sqrt2x)\) and \(\mathcal Q^{n+2}=\{(t,y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n+1}:t\geq\|y\|_2\}\), one has \(T(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2})=\mathcal Q^{n+2}\). Hence \(T\) is a linear cone isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(\mathcal Q_{r}^{n+2})=\mathcal Q^{n+2}\), so the rotated cone is linearly isomorphic to the second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention with quadratic constraint \(2uv\geq\|x\|_2^2\).

notation.meaning: Linear isomorphism used in the representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection by Rotation to the Standard Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduces Euclidean projection onto the rotated cone to projection onto the standard second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(u,v,x)=(u+v,u-v,\sqrt2x)=\sqrt2U(u,v,x)\), where \(U\) is orthogonal and \(T(\mathcal Q_r^{n+2})=\mathcal Q^{n+2}\). For every \(z\in\mathbb R^{n+2}\), \[\Pi_{\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}}(z)=T^{-1}\Pi_{\mathcal Q^{n+2}}(Tz)=U^*\Pi_{\mathcal Q^{n+2}}(Uz).\] Using the closed-form standard-cone projection, this reduction requires \(O(n)\) arithmetic and \(O(n)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rotate to the standard second-order cone, project there, and rotate back; the resulting projection is linear-time in the vector dimension.
assumptions_latex: Projection uses the standard Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}}(z)=T^{-1}\Pi_{\mathcal Q^{n+2}}(Tz)\), computable in \(O(n)\) arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection by Rotation to the Standard Cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality for the normalization \(2uv\geq\|x\|_2^2\) under the standard Euclidean pairing.

The isomorphism \(T(u,v,x)=(u+v,u-v,\sqrt2x)\) satisfies \(T^*T=2I\) and is therefore a scaled orthogonal identification with the self-dual standard second-order cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the usual normalization and Euclidean pairing, the rotated second-order cone is self-dual and its standard-cone transformation is scaled orthogonal.
assumptions_latex: Duality uses the standard Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal Q_r^{n+2})^*=\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((u,v,x)\in\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\iff u\ge\|x\|_2^2/(2v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The closed zero-scale face is handled separately by \(v=0\Rightarrow x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v>0\),\[(u,v,x)\in\mathcal Q_r^{n+2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\ge\frac{\|x\|_2^2}{2v}.\] At \(v=0\), membership is equivalent to \(u\ge0\) and \(x=0\). Thus the cone is the closed epigraph of the quadratic-over-linear perspective in these coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Away from the zero-scale face, rotated-cone membership is exactly a quadratic-over-linear epigraph inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-over-Linear Representation

children.title: Nonquadratic Norm-Epigraph Cone Family
children.top_down_role: Epigraph cones associated with norms and gauges beyond the quadratic family.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(1\le p\le\infty\), let \(q\) satisfy \(1/p+1/q=1\), and let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-epigraph cones beyond the Euclidean quadratic case, especially \(\ell_p\) cones with \(p\ne2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p\in[1,\infty]\), the \(\ell_p\)-epigraph cone is \[K_p^{n+1}=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\|x\|_p\le t\}.\] The nonquadratic family consists of these cones for \(p\ne2\), together with epigraph cones of other norms not induced by an inner product. Its dual is \((K_p^{n+1})^*=K_q^{n+1}\), where \(q\) is the Hölder conjugate. For \(1<p<\infty\), membership is equivalently \(t\ge0\) and \(\sum_i|x_i|^p\le t^p\); for \(p=1\) or \(p=\infty\), the cone has a finite linear-inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonquadratic norm-epigraph cone contains the pairs \((x,t)\) for which a non-Euclidean norm of \(x\) does not exceed \(t\). The main examples are the \(\ell_p\) cones with \(p\ne2\). Their dual cones are generated by the Hölder-conjugate norms. The endpoint cones for \(p=1\) and \(p=\infty\) are polyhedral, whereas typical intermediate \(p\)-cones are nonpolyhedral and nonquadratic.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(1<p<\infty\), \((x,t)\in K_p^{n+1}\iff t\ge0\) and \(\sum_i|x_i|^p\le t^p\).
\((x,t)\in K_p^{n+1}\iff y^{\mathsf T}x\le t\) for every \(y\) with \(\|y\|_q\le1\).
special_cases_latex: \(K_1^{n+1}\) is representable using \(-u_i\le x_i\le u_i\), \(u_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_i u_i\le t\).
\(K_\infty^{n+1}=\{(x,t):-t\le x_i\le t\ \forall i\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Rational \(p\)-norm inequalities can often be lifted using power-cone constraints.
The cones \(K_1\) and \(K_\infty\) are dual to one another.
boundary_notes: The case \(p=2\) belongs to the second-order-cone representation pair.
For \(0<p<1\), the corresponding quasi-norm epigraph is not convex and is excluded.

notation.meaning: The Hölder conjugate exponent, with the standard endpoint conventions.
