knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of the Coordinatewise Upper Image
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A componentwise convex map may have a nonconvex exact range, but adding nonnegative coordinatewise slack produces a convex upper image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be convex and let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):C\to\mathbb R^m\) have convex components. Although \(g(C)\) need not be convex, its coordinatewise upper image
\[
\mathcal U=g(C)+\mathbb R_+^m=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:\exists x\in C,\ g_i(x)\leq y_i\text{ for all }i\}
\]
is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(C)+\mathbb R_+^m\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-image geometry generated by a finite vector of convex functions.

notation.meaning: coordinatewise upper image of the attainable range

knowledge_statements.title: Attainable-Range Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Componentwise convexity does not make a vector map's attainable range convex; the map x↦(x,x²) has a parabolic, nonconvex range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\mathbb R\) and \(g(x)=(x,x^2)\), both component functions are convex, while \[g(C)=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v=u^2\}\] is not convex; it contains \((-1,1)\) and \((1,1)\) but not their midpoint \((0,1)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space and \(g:C\to\mathbb R^m\) is a vector-valued mapping with convex component functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The attainable set \(g(C)\) need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A vector mapping can have a curved, nonconvex attainable range even when all component functions are convex.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Certificate Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard coordinatewise rule does not certify h(x²,x²)=x²−x² because the second slot has the wrong curvature, but cancellation makes the composite identically zero and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h\) is nondecreasing in its first coordinate and nonincreasing in its second, while both \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) are convex and \(g_2\) is not concave. Thus the standard coordinatewise certificate does not apply. Nevertheless, \[F(x)=h(g_1(x),g_2(x))=0\] for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), so \(F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite \(h(g_1,g_2)\) is convex although the standard coordinatewise curvature–monotonicity certificate does not apply.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient coordinatewise composition certificate can miss convexity caused by dependence and cancellation between argument slots.

children.title: Variable-Elimination Aggregation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Convexity preservation through variable elimination and aggregation.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Section 3.3: Partial Minimization of Convex Functions

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_query: Bauschke and Combettes, Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), let \(C\subseteq Y\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Also let \((A,\mu)\) be a measure space and \(F_a:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be indexed functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional partial minimization together with deterministic or measure-indexed nonnegative aggregation; closedness and attainment are not built into the basic operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variable-elimination operator sends a jointly convex function \(F\) to its marginal \((\mathcal M_C F)(x)=\inf_{y\in C}F(x,y)\), with effective domain \(\{x:\exists y\in C,\ F(x,y)<+\infty\}\), provided the infimum is never \(-\infty\). The nonnegative aggregation operator sends an indexed family to \((\mathcal A_\mu F)(x)=\int_A F_a(x)\,d\mu(a)\) whenever the extended integral is well defined. Finite sums correspond to atomic \(\mu\). Joint convexity is preserved by \(\mathcal M_C\), and pointwise convexity in \(x\) is preserved by \(\mathcal A_\mu\) for a nonnegative measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable elimination takes the infimum of a jointly convex function over a convex block of variables. Nonnegative aggregation takes a weighted sum or integral of functions convex in the retained variable. The basic calculus consists of these two operations and their compositions. Convexity is preserved when partial infima do not equal minus infinity and integrals are well defined, but closedness and attainment require separate conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\mathcal M_C F)(x)=\inf_{y\in C}F(x,y),\qquad (\mathcal A_\mu F)(x)=\int_A F_a(x)\,d\mu(a).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Variable elimination is projection of the epigraph up to possible missing boundary points caused by nonattainment.
A finite nonnegative weighted sum \(\sum_{j=1}^r w_jF_j(x)\), \(w_j\ge0\), is aggregation with an atomic measure.
special_cases_latex: If \(C=Y\), \(\mathcal M_C\) is unrestricted partial minimization.
An expectation \(\mathbb E[F_\xi(x)]\) is aggregation under a probability measure.
immediate_consequences_latex: Repeated elimination may be represented as a single infimum over a product of convex feasible sets when the constraints separate appropriately.
Positive integration and partial minimization can generate value functions used in stochastic and parametric convex optimization.
boundary_notes: Partial minimization need not preserve closedness, and its infimum need not be attained.
Signed weights or signed measures do not generally preserve convexity.
Undefined expressions such as \(+\infty-\infty\) are excluded.

notation.meaning: Partial minimization over the eliminated variable in C.

children.title: Marginal Value-Function Calculus
children.top_down_role: Variable-elimination constructions and their attainment and closure regimes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal value function and its epigraph projection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \(P:\mathbb R^{n+m+1}\to\mathbb R^{n+1}\) be \(P(x,z,r)=(x,r)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real marginalization; convexity is separated from closedness and attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The marginal value function of \(F\) with respect to \(z\) is \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \(f(x)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^m}F(x,z)\). Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:\inf_zF(x,z)<+\infty\}\). If \(F\) is convex and \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\), then \(f\) is convex. In general its epigraph satisfies \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F)\). The marginal is attained at \(x\) when \(\operatorname{Argmin}_zF(x,z)=\{z:F(x,z)=f(x)\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The marginal value at \(x\) is the infimum of the joint function over the eliminated variable \(z\). For a jointly convex function, the marginal is convex unless it takes minus infinity. Its epigraph lies between the projection of the joint epigraph and the closure of that projection. Attainment means that at least one eliminated-variable value realizes the infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x)=\inf_zF(x,z),\qquad P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite \(f(x)\), attainment at \(x\) is equivalent to \((x,f(x))\in P(\operatorname{epi}F)\).
If the infimum is attained for all finite marginal values, then \(\operatorname{epi}f=P(\operatorname{epi}F)\).
special_cases_latex: Constraining \(z\) to a convex set \(C\) is represented by replacing \(F(x,z)\) with \(F(x,z)+\delta_C(z)\).
An infimal convolution is a marginal after introducing variables constrained by a linear sum relation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closedness of \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) implies both closedness of the marginal and attainment at every \(x\) with finite \(f(x)\).
boundary_notes: A linear projection of a closed convex set need not be closed.
Convexity of \(f\) alone neither guarantees attainment nor lower semicontinuity.

notation.meaning: Projection that eliminates z from epigraph coordinates.
Set of minimizers in the eliminated variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of Attained Minimizer Fibers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each attained fiber-minimizer set of a jointly convex integrand is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(x\in\operatorname{dom}p\) at which the infimum is attained, \[M(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}F(x,y)=\{y:F(x,y)=p(x)\}\] is a nonempty convex subset of \(Y\).
assumptions_latex: The finite value \(p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\) is attained at the fixed \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(x)\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of realized minimizers within a fixed fiber.

notation.meaning: minimizers in the fiber over x

knowledge_statements.title: Attained Marginals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jointly convex function has a convex marginal; attained fiber minima furnish representatives satisfying the marginal convexity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). Then \(p\) is convex. More precisely, for all \(x_0,x_1\in\operatorname{dom}p\), \(y_i\in M(x_i)\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[p((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq F((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1,(1-\lambda)y_0+\lambda y_1)\leq(1-\lambda)p(x_0)+\lambda p(x_1).\]
assumptions_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}p\), the set \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is convex, with its convexity inequality represented by attained fiber minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convex marginalization with attained fiber infima.

children.title: Marginal Attainment-Closure Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Projection-induced attainment and closedness failures.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment and closure defect of a marginal projection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(f(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)\), and let \(P(x,z,r)=(x,r)\). Assume \(f(x)>-\infty\) where considered.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional marginalization; the boundary records projection defects even when the joint function is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The marginal attainment defect set is \(B_{\mathrm{att}}=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:(x,f(x))\notin P(\operatorname{epi}F)\}\). The marginal closure defect set is \(B_{\mathrm{cl}}=\operatorname{epi}f\setminus P(\operatorname{epi}F)\). Thus \(x\in B_{\mathrm{att}}\) exactly when the infimum defining \(f(x)\) is finite but not attained, while \(B_{\mathrm{cl}}\ne\varnothing\) records boundary points added when the projected epigraph is completed. The attainment-closure failure boundary is \(B=B_{\mathrm{cl}}\cap\partial P(\operatorname{epi}F)\), with the boundary taken in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The attainment defect contains parameters whose finite marginal values are approached but never achieved. The closure defect consists of epigraph points missing from the projection of the joint epigraph. Their boundary portion is the marginal attainment-closure failure boundary. It identifies precisely where projection can lose minimizing points or closedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B_{\mathrm{att}}=\{x:(x,f(x))\notin P(\operatorname{epi}F)\},\qquad B_{\mathrm{cl}}=\operatorname{epi}f\setminus P(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(x\notin B_{\mathrm{att}}\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Argmin}_zF(x,z)\ne\varnothing\).
If \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) is closed, then \(B_{\mathrm{cl}}=B_{\mathrm{att}}=\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: When all relevant sublevel sets in the eliminated variable are compact under a standard level-boundedness condition, the marginal is closed and its minima are attained.
A nonclosed projected epigraph can omit exactly the points \((x,f(x))\) while containing every \((x,r)\) with \(r>f(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonemptiness of \(B_{\mathrm{att}}\) certifies failure of exact epigraph projection.
Nonemptiness of \(B_{\mathrm{cl}}\) prevents identifying the marginal epigraph with the unclosed projection.
boundary_notes: The two defects are related but conceptually distinct: a projection may fail to be closed beyond the lower graph.
Closedness of \(F\) alone does not force closedness of its epigraph projection.

notation.meaning: Parameter set where the marginal infimum is not attained.
Epigraph points absent from the projected joint epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Marginal Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the continuous jointly convex function that is exponential in the eliminated variable, every marginal value is zero but no finite fiber point attains it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(F(x,y)=e^y\), and let \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}F(x,y)\). Then \(F\) is continuous and jointly convex, while for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \[p(x)=0\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}}F(x,y)=\varnothing.\] Thus finite convex marginal values need not be attained in their fibers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(x)=0\) for every \(x\), but \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}}F(x,y)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment can fail even for finite continuous convex integrands.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Marginal Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of this closed convex set marginalizes to the indicator of the open interval of positive real numbers, giving a convex but nonclosed marginal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is closed and convex, and \(F=\iota_C\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Its marginal satisfies \[p(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\iota_C(x,y)=\begin{cases}0,&x>0,\\+\infty,&x\leq0.\end{cases}\] Hence \(p=\iota_{(0,\infty)}\) is convex but is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\iota_{(0,\infty)}\) is convex but not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed convex integrand may have a nonclosed convex marginal.

notation.meaning: indicator taking zero on the set and positive infinity outside

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Induced Closure Loss
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginalizing the indicator of a closed convex set gives the indicator of its coordinate projection; a nonclosed projection therefore produces a nonclosed marginal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \[\inf_{y\in Y}\iota_C(x,y)=\iota_{\pi_X(C)}(x).\] Therefore, if the coordinate projection \(\pi_X(C)\) is not closed, the marginal \(\iota_{\pi_X(C)}\) is convex but not lower semicontinuous. Closed convex sets in finite-dimensional product spaces can have nonclosed coordinate projections.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is closed and convex, and \(F=\iota_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)=\iota_{\pi_X(C)}(x)\); if \(\pi_X(C)\) is not closed, the marginal is not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure loss for indicator marginals is identified with nonclosed coordinate projection of a closed convex feasible set.

notation.meaning: coordinate projection onto the retained space

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Closure Recovery by Local Uniform Level-Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, local uniform level-boundedness in the eliminated variable prevents escaping minimizers and makes the marginal proper, closed, convex, and attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). If \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex and is locally uniformly level-bounded in \(y\), then \(p\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Every finite value \(p(x)\) is attained, and \[\operatorname{epi}p=\{(x,r):\exists y\in Y,\ F(x,y)\le r\}\] is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
For every \(\bar x\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and bounded set \(B\subseteq Y\) satisfy \(\{y:F(x,y)\le\alpha\}\subseteq B\) for all \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex; every finite fiber infimum is attained; and the displayed epigraphical projection is closed and equals \(\operatorname{epi}p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional recovery of properness, closedness, and fiber attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Closure Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local level-boundedness recovers attainment and lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and define \(p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\). Suppose \(p\) is proper and, for every compact \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the set
\[\{(x,y):x\in K,\ F(x,y)\leq\alpha\}\]
is bounded. Then every finite fiber infimum is attained, and \(p\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Equivalently, its epigraph is closed and equals the projection of \(\operatorname{epi}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex integrand with locally uniform bounded sublevel fibers has an attained, proper, closed convex marginal.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex
Fiber sublevel sets are locally uniformly bounded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is closed convex and each finite value \(p(x)\) is attained.

notation.meaning: compact subset of the parameter space

children.top_down_role: Variable-splitting construction linking marginalization, conjugacy, and smoothing.

knowledge_statements.title: Order Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing either input pointwise cannot decrease the infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_1\leq f_2\) and \(g_1\leq g_2\) pointwise, then \(f_1\square g_1\leq f_2\square g_2\) pointwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_1\square g_1\leq f_2\square g_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise order preservation in both arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Commutativity and Identity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution is commutative, with the indicator of the origin as its identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For extended-real functions \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f\square g=g\square f\). Moreover, if \(\iota_{\{0\}}(0)=0\) and \(\iota_{\{0\}}(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\ne0\), then \(f\square\iota_{\{0\}}=f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\square g=g\square f\) and \(f\square\iota_{\{0\}}=f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic algebraic laws of binary infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Domain Sum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimal convolution is below positive infinity exactly at sums of points from the two effective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}\), \[\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility of additive decompositions underlying the binary operation.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of two subsets of X

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution assigns to each point the infimum of the total cost over all decompositions into one argument for each function; for convex inputs it is convex when it does not take negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal convolution of \(f\) and \(g\) is the extended-real function \[(f\square g)(x)=\inf\{f(u)+g(v):u,v\in X,\ u+v=x\}=\inf_{y\in X}\bigl(f(y)+g(x-y)\bigr).\] If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex and \((f\square g)(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(f\square g\) is convex. Lower semicontinuity and attainment require additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f\square g)(x)=\inf_{y\in X}(f(y)+g(x-y))\); if \(f\) and \(g\) are convex and \(f\square g\) never takes \(-\infty\), then \(f\square g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary infimal convolution on a common vector space, together with its basic convexity property.

children.title: Convex Integrand Aggregation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Aggregation of convex integrands under deterministic and probabilistic indexing.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((A,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space with \(\mu\ge0\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, and let \(\varphi:C\times A\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be measurable in \(a\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic sums, integrals, and expectations; existence of the integral is imposed separately from pointwise convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex-integrand aggregation generated by \((\varphi,\mu)\) is \(G(x)=\int_A\varphi(x,a)\,d\mu(a)\) on the set of \(x\in C\) for which the extended integral is well defined and does not contain the indeterminate form \(+\infty-\infty\). The integrand is convex for aggregation when \(x\mapsto\varphi(x,a)\) is convex on \(C\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(a\). Under these conditions, \(G\) is convex on its effective domain. An expectation is the case in which \(\mu\) is a probability measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-integrand aggregate is a nonnegative integral of functions that are convex in the decision variable for almost every index. The aggregate is defined wherever the integral exists without an infinity ambiguity. It is convex there. Finite nonnegative weighted sums and probabilistic expectations are special cases of the same operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G(x)=\int_A\varphi(x,a)\,d\mu(a),\qquad \varphi(\cdot,a)\text{ convex for }\mu\text{-a.e. }a.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an atomic measure \(\mu=\sum_{j=1}^r w_j\delta_{a_j}\), the aggregate is \(G(x)=\sum_{j=1}^r w_j\varphi(x,a_j)\) with \(w_j\ge0\).
For a random element \(\xi\), \(G(x)=\mathbb E[\varphi(x,\xi)]\) whenever the expectation exists.
special_cases_latex: A positive scalar multiple of one convex function is aggregation over a one-point index set.
An infinite series of convex functions with nonnegative coefficients is covered when its sum is well defined.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity is inherited when a positive-measure portion of the integrands supplies strict curvature in every nonzero direction, subject to finiteness.
Affine terms may be aggregated with arbitrary nonnegative weights without changing convexity.
boundary_notes: Negative weights can destroy convexity.
Pointwise convexity does not by itself guarantee measurability, integrability, lower semicontinuity, or interchange of integration with minimization.
The effective domain of \(G\) can be smaller than the intersection of the pointwise domains because of integrability.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Under Expectation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expectation of an almost-surely convex integrand is convex under measurable sections and a common integrable lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\). If the random sections are measurable, the decision sections are convex almost surely, and an integrable random lower bound makes the expectations well-defined, then \(F\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space and \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
\(f:C\times\Omega\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and \(\omega\mapsto f(x,\omega)\) is measurable for every \(x\in C\).
Outside one \(\mathbb P\)-null set, \(x\mapsto f(x,\omega)\) is convex.
There exists an integrable random variable \(G\) such that \(f(x,\omega)\geq G(\omega)\) almost surely for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-measure specialization of convex integrand aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation of Strong-Convexity Moduli
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expectation averages nonnegative random strong-convexity moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(\cdot,\omega)\) is \(m(\omega)\)-strongly convex almost surely and every random section \(f(x,\cdot)\) is integrable, then \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\) is \(\mathbb E[m]\)-strongly convex.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space and \(X\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\mathbb E[f(\cdot,\omega)]\) is \(\mathbb E[m]\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-weighted strengthening of convexity preservation.

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space and \(X\) is a real vector space.
For every \(x\in X\), \(\omega\mapsto f(x,\omega)\) is measurable, and for almost every \(\omega\), \(x\mapsto f(x,\omega)\) is convex.
The expectations used below are well-defined and never have the indeterminate form \(+\infty-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\) is convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: expectation preserves pointwise convex inequalities under measurability and well-defined integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity preservation by probability-weighted integration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_0,x_1\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), almost-sure convexity gives \[f((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1,\omega)\leq(1-\lambda)f(x_0,\omega)+\lambda f(x_1,\omega).\] Monotonicity and linearity of expectation, under the stated well-definedness convention, imply \[F((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)F(x_0)+\lambda F(x_1).\] Thus the expectation aggregate \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\) is convex. This conclusion alone does not assert finiteness, lower semicontinuity, or interchange of expectation with minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expectation of an almost-surely convex integrand is convex when its sections are measurable and the relevant extended expectations are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Aggregation

In addition, the integrand's codomain and the precise extended-expectation convention are not fully specified, so the hypotheses supporting linearity and the claimed codomain of the aggregate remain uncertain.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Under Deterministic Integration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating almost-everywhere convex decision sections preserves convexity when the sections are measurable and a common integrable lower bound makes every integral well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(I(x)=\int_T f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\). If the decision sections are convex almost everywhere, the parameter sections are measurable, and \(f\) has a common integrable lower bound, then \(I:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a measure space and \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
\(f:T\times C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is measurable for every \(x\in C\).
Outside one \(\mu\)-null set, \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is convex.
There exists \(g\in L^1(\mu)\) such that \(f(t,x)\geq g(t)\) for almost every \(t\) and every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)=\int_T f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity preservation for a general measure-space aggregate under a well-defined extended-integral regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Semicontinuity Under an Integrable Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-everywhere lower-semicontinuous sections with a common integrable lower bound produce a lower-semicontinuous integral aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated measurability and common-lower-bound assumptions, if \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is lower-semicontinuous for almost every \(t\), then \[I(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}I(x_n)\quad\text{whenever }x_n\to x.\] Hence \(I\) is lower-semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a measure space and \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
For every \(x\in X\), \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is measurable.
For almost every \(t\), \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is lower-semicontinuous.
There exists \(g\in L^1(\mu)\) such that \(f(t,x)\geq g(t)\) for almost every \(t\) and every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)=\int_T f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\) is lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fatou-type closedness regime for deterministic integral aggregation.

assumptions_latex: \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a measure space and \(X\) is a real vector space.
For each \(x\in X\), \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is measurable, and for almost every \(t\), \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is convex.
All displayed integrals are well-defined, with no \(+\infty-\infty\) ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)=\int_T f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\) is convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integration preserves almost-everywhere pointwise convex inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity preservation under deterministic measure integration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary \(x_0,x_1\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), pointwise convexity holds for almost every \(t\): \[f(t,(1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)f(t,x_0)+\lambda f(t,x_1).\] Integrating this inequality and using linearity on the well-defined terms yields \[I((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)I(x_0)+\lambda I(x_1).\] Therefore \(I\) is convex. Additional domination, normal-integrand, or compactness hypotheses are required for conclusions about continuity, differentiation, or interchange with optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating functions that are convex in the decision variable almost everywhere preserves convexity, provided the sections are measurable and all integrals are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Integral Aggregation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits deterministic integral aggregation, but the record has no source, does not explicitly type the integrand, and relies on an underspecified extended-integral well-definedness convention. An authoritative source is needed before fixing the exact hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Everywhere Pointwise Convex Integrands
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-everywhere pointwise convexity means that every decision section is convex outside one common null set; it is independent of parameter measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integrand \(f:T\times X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex in its decision variable almost everywhere if there exists a measurable null set \(N\subseteq T\) such that \(f(t,\cdot)\) is convex for every \(t\notin N\). Equivalently, outside that one common null set, \[f(t,(1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)f(t,x_0)+\lambda f(t,x_1)\] for all \(x_0,x_1\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). This condition alone does not imply measurability of \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\).
assumptions_latex: \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a measure space and \(X\) is a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside one common null set, every section \(f(t,\cdot)\) satisfies the convexity inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-null-set definition of convexity in the decision variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative Pointwise Combinations of Convex Integrands
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative parameter-dependent combinations preserve pointwise convexity of decision sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) and \(g\) have convex decision sections outside a common null set and \(a,b:T\to[0,+\infty)\), then \[h(t,x)=a(t)f(t,x)+b(t)g(t,x)\] also has convex decision sections outside that null set, using the convex-analysis convention \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\).
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:T\times X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have convex decision sections outside a common null set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(t,\cdot)=a(t)f(t,\cdot)+b(t)g(t,\cdot)\) is convex for almost every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of the pointwise-convex integrand class before aggregation.

assumptions_latex: \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a measure space and \(X\) is a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise convexity means that \(f(t,(1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)f(t,x_0)+\lambda f(t,x_1)\) for almost every \(t\), all \(x_0,x_1\), and all \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the defining pointwise convexity predicate for an integrand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-everywhere convexity of decision-variable sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The integrand \(f\) is pointwise convex in its decision variable if there exists a measurable null set \(N\subseteq T\) such that, for every \(t\in T\setminus N\), every \(x_0,x_1\in X\), and every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[f(t,(1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)f(t,x_0)+\lambda f(t,x_1).\] Equivalently, each section \(f_t:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex outside one common null set. This condition concerns convexity only and does not itself ensure measurability of \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrand is pointwise convex when, outside one null set, every section in the decision variable satisfies the convexity inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Convexity Does Not Ensure Measurability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmeasurable coefficient gives affine decision sections but nonmeasurable parameter sections, preventing integral aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\subseteq[0,1]\) be non-Lebesgue-measurable and define \(f(t,x)=\mathbf 1_A(t)x\). Every decision section \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is affine. For every \(x\neq0\), however, \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is nonmeasurable, so its Lebesgue integral is undefined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\neq0\) implies that \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is nonmeasurable and \(\int f(t,x)\,dt\) is undefined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurability failure despite affine decision-variable sections.

notation.meaning: Indicator of the nonmeasurable set A

knowledge_statements.title: Measurability Does Not Ensure Integrability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measurable affine sections need not have a defined integral: over the real line, tx has infinite positive and negative parts for every nonzero x.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \((\mathbb R,\mathcal L,\lambda)\), define \(f(t,x)=tx\). Every decision section is affine and every parameter section is measurable. For each \(x\neq0\), the positive and negative parts of \(t\mapsto tx\) both have infinite integral, so \(\int_{\mathbb R}tx\,dt\) is undefined rather than an extended-real value.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathbb R,\mathcal L,\lambda)\) is Lebesgue measure space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\neq0\) implies \(\int f(t,x)\,dt\) is undefined because \(\int f^+=\int f^-=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent integrability boundary after parameter-section measurability holds.

notation.meaning: Positive and negative parts of a measurable function

assumptions_latex: \(A\subseteq[0,1]\) is not Lebesgue measurable, and \(f(t,x)=\mathbf 1_A(t)x\) for \(x\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every section \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is affine, but for \(x\neq0\) the map \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is nonmeasurable, so \(\int f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\) is undefined.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a nonmeasurable coefficient gives affine decision sections but nonmeasurable parameter sections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise convexity does not supply the measurability required for aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(t\), the function \(x\mapsto f(t,x)=\mathbf 1_A(t)x\) is linear and hence convex. However, for any \(x\neq0\), the parameter section \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is a nonzero scalar multiple of \(\mathbf 1_A\), which is not Lebesgue measurable. Consequently the Lebesgue integral \(\int_{[0,1]}f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\) is not defined. Thus pointwise convexity alone cannot justify deterministic integral or expectation aggregation; measurability is an independent necessary boundary condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonmeasurable coefficient produces affine decision-variable sections but nonmeasurable parameter sections, so the proposed integral aggregate is not defined.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perspective homogenization of an extended-real function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Introduce a scale variable \(t\in\mathbb R\) and a homogeneous spatial variable \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scale perspective and its basic homogeneous geometry; values at zero scale belong to the separate closed-extension regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The positive perspective homogenization of \(f\) is \(\widetilde f:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined by \(\widetilde f(t,x)=t f(x/t)\) for \(t>0\), and \(\widetilde f(t,x)=+\infty\) for \(t\le0\). Its domain is \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=\{(t,x):t>0,\ x/t\in\operatorname{dom}f\}=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{dom}f)\). It is positively one-homogeneous on positive scales: \(\widetilde f(\lambda t,\lambda x)=\lambda\widetilde f(t,x)\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perspective homogenization adds a positive scale variable and assigns \(t f(x/t)\) to the scaled point \((t,x)\). Its domain is the positive cone generated by the unit-scale copy of the original domain, and scaling all homogeneous coordinates by a positive factor scales the function value by the same factor. The raw perspective assigns infinity at nonpositive scales.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widetilde f(t,x)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\+\infty,&t\le0,\end{cases}\qquad \widetilde f(\lambda t,\lambda x)=\lambda\widetilde f(t,x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Its epigraph is \(\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f)\).
The unit-scale slice recovers the original function: \(\widetilde f(1,x)=f(x)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is an indicator \(\delta_C\), then the perspective domain is the positive homogenization of \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then \(\widetilde f\) is convex on its extended domain.
The perspective converts the affine unit-scale slice of an epigraph into positive homogeneous geometry.
boundary_notes: The raw perspective is generally not closed at \(t=0\), even when \(f\) is closed.
Positive homogeneity here initially concerns \(\lambda>0\); inclusion of zero scale requires closure and recession data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric perspective transform of domains and epigraphs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and let \(\widetilde f(t,x)=t f(x/t)\) for \(t>0\), with value \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scale domain and epigraph geometry prior to closed completion at zero scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perspective transform geometry of \(f\) is the pair of positive homogeneous sets \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=\{(t,x):t>0,\ x/t\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\) and \(\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f=\{(t,x,r):t>0,\ f(x/t)\le r/t\}\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{dom}f)\) and \(\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f)\). Thus every positive-scale point is uniquely normalized to the unit-scale slice by \((t,x,r)\mapsto(x/t,r/t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geometric perspective replaces the original domain and epigraph by all their strictly positive homogeneous scalings after embedding them in the unit-scale hyperplane. Dividing by the positive scale returns a point in the original domain or epigraph. Conversely, every original epigraph point generates a positive ray in the perspective epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad \operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{dom}f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((t,x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f\) if and only if \(t>0\) and \((x/t,r/t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\).
The slice \(t=1\) of the perspective epigraph is \(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex, its positive homogenization \(\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times C)\) is convex.
If \(f\) is convex, the perspective epigraph is a convex positive cone, though it omits its zero-scale boundary.
immediate_consequences_latex: Epigraph inequalities for a perspective can be represented by membership of normalized points in \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
Closing the positive cone adds precisely the limiting zero-scale directions governed by recession geometry.
boundary_notes: Because \(t>0\), the raw domain and epigraph do not contain the origin.
The closure may add nonzero points at \(t=0\); these are not determined solely by finite points of the original domain without asymptotic information.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity and Unit-Scale Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-scale perspective is degree-one homogeneous under joint scaling and recovers the source function at scale one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda>0\) and \(t>0\), \[P_f(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda P_f(x,t).\] Moreover, \(P_f(x,1)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_f(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda P_f(x,t)\) for \(\lambda>0\), and \(P_f(x,1)=f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Differential Calculus of a Positive Perspective
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At positive scale, the spatial derivative is the source gradient and the scale derivative is the negative linearization gap; together they satisfy Euler's identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u=x/t\). If \(f\) is differentiable at \(u\), then \[
abla_xP_f(x,t)=
abla f(u),\qquad \partial_tP_f(x,t)=f(u)-\langle
abla f(u),uangle.\] The derivatives satisfy \[\langle
abla_xP_f(x,t),xangle+t\partial_tP_f(x,t)=P_f(x,t).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(
abla P_f(x,t)=(
abla f(u),f(u)-\langle
abla f(u),uangle)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient formula at positive scale for a differentiable source function.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Scale Perspectives
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-scale perspective multiplies a function value by a positive scale after inversely scaling its argument; it preserves convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((x,t)\in X\times(0,\infty)\), the positive-scale perspective of \(f\) is \[P_f(x,t)=t f(x/t).\] Its effective domain is \[\operatorname{dom}P_f=\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in\operatorname{dom}f\}=\{(tu,t):t>0,\ u\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.\] If \(f\) is convex, then \(P_f\) is convex on \(X\times(0,\infty)\). This positive-scale definition does not prescribe the boundary value at \(t=0\); a closed perspective extension requires recession data.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The positive-scale perspective is \(P_f(x,t)=t f(x/t)\); convexity of \(f\) implies convexity of \(P_f\) on \(X\times(0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perspective construction restricted to strictly positive scale.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

children.title: Perspective Epigraph Cones
children.top_down_role: Conic epigraph geometry induced by homogenization.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Epigraph Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the closed perspective is the closed conic hull of the original epigraph embedded at unit scale, using coordinate order value-variable, scale, and epigraph height.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With coordinates ordered as \((x,t,r)\in X\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\), the closed perspective has the epigraph representation \[\operatorname{epi}\bar P_f=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(u,1,\alpha):(u,\alpha)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}=\operatorname{cl}\{(tu,t,t\alpha):t>0,\ f(u)\leq\alpha\}.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}\bar P_f\) is a closed convex cone; its positive-scale slices are scaled copies of \(\operatorname{epi}f\), and its zero-scale slice is determined by \(f^{\infty}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\bar P_f(x,t)=t f(x/t)\) for \(t>0\), \(\bar P_f(x,0)=f^{\infty}(x)\), and \(\bar P_f(x,t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\bar P_f=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(u,1,\alpha):f(u)\leq\alpha\}\), a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed perspective and its homogenized epigraph.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111
10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive and closed perspective epigraph cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex, and embed \(\operatorname{epi}f\) in the hyperplane \(t=1\) of \(\mathbb R^{n+2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic epigraph geometry; the positive cone and its closed completion are distinguished explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The positive perspective epigraph cone of \(f\) is \(K_+(f)=\{\lambda(1,x,r):\lambda>0,\ (x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\). It equals the epigraph of the raw perspective on \(t>0\). The closed perspective epigraph cone is \(K(f)=\operatorname{cl}K_+(f)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f)\), where \(\operatorname{cone}\) includes the zero multiplier. For convex \(f\), \(K_+(f)\) is convex and positively scale invariant, while \(K(f)\) is a closed convex cone containing the origin and any zero-scale recession rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive perspective epigraph cone consists of all strictly positive multiples of the original epigraph placed at unit scale. Its closure is the closed perspective epigraph cone. The raw cone represents the positive-scale perspective, whereas the closed cone also contains the origin and limiting rays at zero scale that encode recession behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K_+(f)=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad K(f)=\operatorname{cl}K_+(f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(t>0\), \((t,x,r)\in K_+(f)\) if and only if \(r\ge t f(x/t)\).
The unit-scale section satisfies \(K_+(f)\cap(\{1\}\times\mathbb R^{n+1})=\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is positively one-homogeneous and closed, its perspective cone reflects the epigraph cone already associated with \(f\).
When \(f\) has bounded domain, nonzero zero-scale spatial points generally do not enter the closed cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity of \(f\) is equivalent to convexity of its epigraph and therefore to convexity of the positive perspective epigraph cone.
The zero-scale slice of \(K(f)\) is determined by the recession cone of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
boundary_notes: Some authors call \(K_+(f)\) a cone despite its omission of the origin; \(K(f)\) is the closed cone in the conventional sense.
Closedness of \(f\) does not make \(K_+(f)\) closed because the scale boundary \(t=0\) is absent.

notation.meaning: Closed conic completion of the perspective epigraph.

children.title: Domain Homogenization
children.top_down_role: Lifted domains, scaling rays, and boundary faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure and Zero-Scale Face of a Homogenized Domain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a positively homogenized convex domain closes every positive slice and adds exactly its recession cone at scale zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty convex \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(H_C=\{(tx,t):t>0,\ x\in C\}\). Then \[\operatorname{cl}H_C=\{(tx,t):t>0,\ x\in\operatorname{cl}C\}\cup\{(d,0):d\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{cl}C)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}H_C=\{(tx,t):t>0,x\in\operatorname{cl}C\}\cup(\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{cl}C)\times\{0\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional closure of the positive homogenization of a convex domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Homogenization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain is lifted along positive scaling rays. The lift is convex, has the original domain as its unit-scale slice, and may gain asymptotic points when closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the positive homogenization of the effective domain by
\[
H_f:=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:t>0,\ x/t\in\operatorname{dom}f\}
     =\{(tu,t):t>0,\ u\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.
\]
For every \(\lambda>0\), \((x,t)\in H_f\) implies \((\lambda x,\lambda t)\in H_f\), and
\[
\{x:(x,1)\in H_f\}=\operatorname{dom}f.
\]
Because \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex, \(H_f\) is convex. Its closure may acquire a face contained in \(\{t=0\}\), representing asymptotic directions of \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_f\) is convex, is invariant under positive scaling, and its section at \(t=1\) is \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scale lift of an effective domain; its zero-scale completion is treated separately.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the source function.
Positive homogenization of the effective domain.

children.title: Perspective Convexity Principle
children.top_down_role: Convexity preservation under perspective lifting across ordinary, extended-value, and concave regimes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) or \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and define \(g(x,t)=t f(x/t)\) on \(\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scale ordinary and extended-value regimes; closed zero-scale completion is not part of this slot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perspective convexity principle is the curvature-preservation rule \(f\text{ convex}\Rightarrow g\text{ convex}\) and, for finite-valued functions, \(f\text{ concave}\Rightarrow g\text{ concave}\), where \(g(x,t)=t f(x/t)\) for \(t>0\). For convex extended-value \(f\), the perspective is assigned \(+\infty\) outside its natural positive-scale domain. The same positive scaling that normalizes \((x,t)\) also scales the function value, so the lifted function is positively one-homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perspective lifting preserves convexity: multiplying a convex function evaluated at the normalized point \(x/t\) by the positive scale \(t\) produces a jointly convex function of \((x,t)\). The sign-dual statement preserves concavity for finite-valued concave functions. Extended-value convex perspectives take infinity outside their natural positive-scale domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow ((x,t)\mapsto t f(x/t))\text{ convex on }t>0;\] likewise with both occurrences of “convex” replaced by “concave” in the finite-valued regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For convex \(f\), \(\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,t,r):t>0,\ (x/t,r/t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\) is convex.
The principle may be viewed as convexity of the positive cone generated by \(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: The quadratic-over-linear function \((x,t)\mapsto\|x\|_2^2/t\) is convex for \(t>0\).
The perspective of a positive concave geometric mean is concave on its natural positive-scale domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: Perspective reformulations provide jointly convex homogeneous representations of many fractional-looking expressions.
The lifted function restricts to \(f\) at \(t=1\).
boundary_notes: The principle requires \(t>0\); extending to \(t=0\) needs the recession-based closed perspective.
It does not assert convexity for negative scales.
Strict convexity need not be preserved along rays because every perspective is one-homogeneous.

children.title: Finite-Valued Perspective Regime
children.top_down_role: Perspective convexity away from extended-value boundary effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Valued Perspective Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex function remains convex after perspective transformation on its positive homogenized domain, and the resulting function is positively homogeneous of degree one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
H_C:=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:t>0,\ x/t\in C\},
\qquad p_f(x,t):=t f(x/t).
\]
Then \(H_C\) is convex and \(p_f\) is convex on \(H_C\). Explicitly, for \((x_i,t_i)\in H_C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
p_f(\theta x_1+(1-\theta)x_2,\theta t_1+(1-\theta)t_2)
\leq \theta p_f(x_1,t_1)+(1-\theta)p_f(x_2,t_2).
\]
Moreover, \(p_f(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda p_f(x,t)\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \((x,t)\mapsto t f(x/t)\) is convex on \(\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical positive-scale perspective theorem without zero-scale or extended-value completion.

notation.meaning: Positive perspective of the finite-valued function.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be finite-valued. Define \(C^{\mathrm p}=\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary real-valued perspective away from zero-scale and extended-value boundary effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-valued perspective regime of \(f\) is the real-valued function \(g:C^{\mathrm p}\to\mathbb R\) given by \(g(x,t)=t f(x/t)\). Its domain is the positive homogenization \(C^{\mathrm p}=\{(ty,t):y\in C,\ t>0\}\). The regime excludes \(t=0\), negative scales, and extended-value points. If \(f\) is convex, then \(g\) is jointly convex; if \(f\) is concave, then \(g\) is jointly concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite real-valued function, the perspective is defined at positive scales by \(g(x,t)=t f(x/t)\). Its domain is obtained by positively scaling the original domain together with a unit scale coordinate. No value is assigned at zero or negative scale in this regime. Convexity and concavity are each preserved by the perspective operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[g(x,t)=t f(x/t),\qquad C^{\mathrm p}=\{(ty,t):y\in C,\ t>0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(x=ty\) gives \(g(ty,t)=t f(y)\) for \(y\in C\) and \(t>0\).
The graph at scale \(t\) is the positive dilation by \(t\) of the graph at unit scale.
special_cases_latex: If \(f(x)=a^Tx+b\), then \(g(x,t)=a^Tx+bt\), an affine function of \((x,t)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The finite-valued regime avoids ambiguity involving \(+\infty\) and does not require an extended-domain convention.
Positive one-homogeneity implies \(g(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda g(x,t)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
boundary_notes: Even if \(f\) is continuous, a finite limit at \(t=0\) need not exist for every direction \(x\).
Strict convexity of \(f\) does not make \(g\) strictly convex along positive rays.

notation.meaning: Positive homogenization of the original domain C.

children.title: Extended-Value Perspective Regime
children.top_down_role: Perspective convexity with explicit domain encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Unclosed Positive Perspective at the Origin
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-scale extended perspective is always nonclosed at the origin under the convention that all nonpositive scales have value infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the positive perspective convention
\[
p_f(x,t)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\+\infty,&t\le0,\end{cases}
\]
the function \(p_f\) is not lower semicontinuous at \((0,0)\). Indeed, for every \(u\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the points \((tu,t)\) approach \((0,0)\) as \(t\downarrow0\) and their values \(t f(u)\) approach \(0\), whereas \(p_f(0,0)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_f\) is not lower semicontinuous at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp closedness boundary for the convention assigning positive infinity at every nonpositive scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Value Perspective Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended-valued perspective equals the usual formula on positive admissible scales and infinity elsewhere. It is convex and homogeneous, but may fail to be closed at zero scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The positive extended-valued perspective of \(f\) is
\[
p_f(x,t):=
\begin{cases}
t f(x/t),&t>0,\\
+\infty,&t\leq 0.
\end{cases}
\]
Here the extended-real convention automatically excludes points with \(x/t\notin\operatorname{dom}f\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{dom}p_f=\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.
\]
The function \(p_f:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, convex, and positively homogeneous: \(p_f(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda p_f(x,t)\) for every \(\lambda>0\). It need not be closed at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extended-valued positive perspective \(p_f\) is convex and has domain \(H_f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value encoding on positive scales; no lower-semicontinuous value is yet assigned at zero scale.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the source function.

children.title: Concave Perspective Counterparts
children.top_down_role: Sign-dual perspective constructions for concave functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Concave Perspective by Sign Reversal
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating the closed perspective of the convex sign dual gives the closed concave perspective and its zero- and negative-scale branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\bar q_g(x,t):=-\bar p_{-g}(x,t).
\]
Then \(\bar q_g\) is proper, upper semicontinuous, concave, and positively homogeneous for positive scalars, with
\[
\bar q_g(x,t)=\begin{cases}t g(x/t),&t>0,\\-(-g)^\infty(x),&t=0,\\-\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}
\]
Its hypograph is a closed convex cone.
assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) is proper, upper semicontinuous, and concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar q_g=-\bar p_{-g}\) is the closed concave homogeneous extension of the positive perspective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-semicontinuous completion of the concave perspective, including zero and negative scales.

notation.meaning: Recession function of the convex sign dual.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave Perspective Counterparts
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive perspective of a concave function is concave. It is exactly the negative of the perspective of the function's convex sign dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\) and \(x/t\in C\), define
\[
q_g(x,t):=t g(x/t).
\]
Then \(q_g\) is concave and positively homogeneous on \(\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in C\}\). Equivalently, with the convex sign-dual \(f:=-g\),
\[
q_g(x,t)=-p_f(x,t).
\]
Consequently, for admissible \((x_i,t_i)\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\),
\[
q_g(\theta x_1+(1-\theta)x_2,\theta t_1+(1-\theta)t_2)
\geq\theta q_g(x_1,t_1)+(1-\theta)q_g(x_2,t_2).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and \(g:C\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) is proper and concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perspective \(q_g(x,t)=t g(x/t)\) is concave on its positive homogenized domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign dual of the positive-scale convex perspective construction.

notation.meaning: Positive perspective of the concave function.
Convex sign-dual of the concave function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave perspective and its sign-dual convex representation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be concave and finite-valued. Let \(C^{\mathrm p}=\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued concave perspective; hypograph geometry is used instead of extended-real convex epigraph conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The concave perspective of \(f\) is \(g:C^{\mathrm p}\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(g(x,t)=t f(x/t)\). It is jointly concave and positively one-homogeneous for positive scales. Its sign-dual representation is \(-g(x,t)=t(-f)(x/t)\), the convex perspective of the convex function \(-f\). Geometrically, \(\operatorname{hypo}g=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{hypo}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The concave counterpart of perspective lifting uses the same formula \(t f(x/t)\) on positive scales. It preserves concavity, and negating it gives exactly the convex perspective of the convex function \(-f\). Its hypograph is the positive homogeneous cone generated by the unit-scale hypograph of the original function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[g(x,t)=t f(x/t),\qquad -g(x,t)=t(-f)(x/t),\qquad \operatorname{hypo}g=\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{hypo}f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Concavity of \(g\) is equivalent to convexity of its negative \(-g\).
\((x,t,r)\in\operatorname{hypo}g\) if and only if \(t>0\) and \((x/t,r/t)\in\operatorname{hypo}f\).
special_cases_latex: For a positive concave geometric mean, the perspective remains concave on the positively homogenized domain.
For affine \(f(x)=a^Tx+b\), the concave and convex perspectives coincide as the affine function \(a^Tx+bt\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Hypograph constraints involving a concave perspective define convex feasible sets after adopting the standard inequality orientation.
Results for finite convex perspectives transfer by applying them to \(-f\) and reversing epigraph/hypograph inequalities.
boundary_notes: The usual extended-real convention for concave functions uses \(-\infty\) outside the domain, not \(+\infty\).
Zero-scale closure requires a concave recession convention or, equivalently, sign-dual convex recession data.

children.title: Closed Perspective Extensions
children.top_down_role: Boundary completion of perspectives through recession and closure geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed perspective extension through the recession function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. Its recession function is \(f^\infty(d)=\sup_{\alpha>0}[f(x_0+\alpha d)-f(x_0)]/\alpha\) for any \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper closed convex functions; the extension completes the positive perspective at zero scale and excludes negative scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed perspective extension of \(f\) is \(\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \((\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f)(x,t)=t f(x/t)\) for \(t>0\), \((\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f)(x,0)=f^\infty(x)\), and \((\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f)(x,t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\). Equivalently, its epigraph is the closure of the positive perspective epigraph: \(\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f)=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,t,r):t>0,\ r\ge t f(x/t)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective agrees with \(t f(x/t)\) at positive scales, assigns the recession value \(f^\infty(x)\) at zero scale, and assigns infinity at negative scales. Its epigraph is exactly the closure of the raw positive perspective epigraph. Thus zero-scale values encode the asymptotic slopes of the original function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f)(x,t)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\f^\infty(x),&t=0,\\+\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f)=\operatorname{cl}\mathbb R_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f)\).
The zero-scale slice satisfies \(\{(x,r):(x,0,r)\in\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f)\}=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty\).
special_cases_latex: At the origin, \((\overline{\operatorname{persp}}f)(0,0)=f^\infty(0)=0\).
If \(f\) is coercive in every nonzero direction, then \(f^\infty(x)=+\infty\) for nonzero \(x\), so only the origin has a finite zero-scale value.
If \(f\) is affine, its recession function is its linear part.
immediate_consequences_latex: The closed perspective is proper, closed, convex, and positively one-homogeneous.
Its zero-scale epigraph is the recession cone of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
boundary_notes: Properness and closed convexity are essential for the stated recession-function completion.
The raw convention \(+\infty\) at \(t=0\) is generally not closed.
No finite negative-scale branch is included.

children.title: Zero-Scale Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary behavior at vanishing homogenizing coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Scale Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex perspective assigns the recession value at zero scale and infinity at negative scales. This completes the positive perspective as a closed homogeneous convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed perspective extension of \(f\) is
\[
\bar p_f(x,t):=
\begin{cases}
t f(x/t),&t>0,\\
f^\infty(x),&t=0,\\
+\infty,&t<0,
\end{cases}
\]
where \(f^\infty\) is the recession function. Then \(\bar p_f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and positively homogeneous. In particular, the finite points on its zero-scale face are exactly
\[
\{(x,0):f^\infty(x)<+\infty\}.
\]
This boundary assignment is the lower-semicontinuous completion of the positive-scale perspective.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed perspective has zero-scale value \(\bar p_f(x,0)=f^\infty(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuous completion of a proper closed convex perspective at the homogenizing boundary.

notation.meaning: Recession function of the source function.

children.title: Perspective–Recession Interface
children.top_down_role: Relationship between closed perspective boundaries and asymptotic function geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective–Recession Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value of the closed perspective at zero scale is the recession slope of the original function, independent of the base point used to compute that slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the zero-scale value of the closed perspective is
\[
\bar p_f(d,0)=f^\infty(d)
=\sup_{s>0}\frac{f(x_0+s d)-f(x_0)}{s}
=\lim_{s\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+s d)-f(x_0)}{s},
\]
with values in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\). The expression is independent of the selected \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Hence the boundary face \(t=0\) records precisely the asymptotic slopes of \(f\), while positive scales record ordinary values through \(\bar p_f(x,t)=t f(x/t)\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar p_f(d,0)=f^\infty(d)=\sup_{s>0}\bigl(f(x_0+s d)-f(x_0)\bigr)/s\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional recession formula identifying every zero-scale perspective value.

notation.meaning: Recession function of the source function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed perspective and its recession boundary
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), meaning that \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Let \(\operatorname{rec}f\) denote its recession function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the closed, extended-real-valued perspective in a Hilbert space. It includes the zero-scale boundary and excludes negative scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\widetilde f(\xi,x):=\begin{cases}\xi f(x/\xi),&\xi>0,\\(\operatorname{rec}f)(x),&\xi=0,\\+\infty,&\xi<0.\end{cases}\] The perspective–recession interface is the equality \(\widetilde f(0,x)=(\operatorname{rec}f)(x)\), which completes the positive-scale perspective at its scale-zero boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function equals the usual scaled function at positive scale, its recession function at zero scale, and positive infinity at negative scale. Thus the entire zero-scale slice records the asymptotic geometry of the source function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widetilde f(\xi,x)=\begin{cases}\xi f(x/\xi),&\xi>0,\\(\operatorname{rec}f)(x),&\xi=0,\\+\infty,&\xi<0.\end{cases}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}\bigl(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f\bigr).\]
For any \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is supercoercive, then \((\operatorname{rec}f)(0)=0\) and \((\operatorname{rec}f)(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\ne0\).
If \(f\) is sublinear and lower semicontinuous, then \(\operatorname{rec}f=f\), so the zero-scale boundary is another copy of \(f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\widetilde f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R\oplus\mathcal H)\) and is positively homogeneous.
The boundary point \((0,x,r)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f\) exactly when \(r\ge(\operatorname{rec}f)(x)\).
boundary_notes: The raw rule \(\xi f(x/\xi)\) for \(\xi>0\), extended by \(+\infty\) at \(\xi\le0\), generally omits limit points at \(\xi=0\).
For a source function that is not proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, this formula need not be its lower-semicontinuous convex closure.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on the Hilbert space.
Recession function of the source function.

children.title: Nonclosed Perspective Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by omitted boundary completion or nonclosed source functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Origin Defect of the Raw Perspective
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitting the entire zero-scale face makes the raw perspective nonclosed at the origin for every proper source function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and define
\[
p(x,t)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\+\infty,&t\leq0.\end{cases}
\]
For any \(u\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t_k\downarrow0\),
\[
(t_k u,t_k)\to(0,0),\qquad p(t_k u,t_k)=t_k f(u)\to0,
\]
whereas \(p(0,0)=+\infty\). Hence the raw perspective is not lower semicontinuous at the origin.
assumptions_latex: The perspective is assigned \(+\infty\) at every nonpositive scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The raw perspective is not lower semicontinuous at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General nonclosedness caused by excluding every zero-scale point.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Sources Remain Nonclosed on the Unit Slice
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-scale completion cannot repair a perspective whose source function is already nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous, and let \(q(x,t)=t f(x/t)\) for \(t>0\). Since \(q(x,1)=f(x)\), any sequence \(u_k\to u\) with
\[
\liminf_k f(u_k)<f(u)
\]
also satisfies
\[
\liminf_k q(u_k,1)<q(u,1).
\]
Thus no assignment confined to the zero-scale face can make \(q\) lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\) is not lower semicontinuous on its unit-scale slice, regardless of its zero-scale assignment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure that cannot be repaired solely by assigning zero-scale values.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Perspective Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even the perspective of the zero function is nonclosed if zero scale is omitted. Closing it adds every zero-scale point with recession value zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(u)=0\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the raw extended perspective is
\[
p(x,t)=
\begin{cases}
0,&t>0,\\
+\infty,&t\leq0.
\end{cases}
\]
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the sequence \((x,1/k)\to(x,0)\) satisfies \(p(x,1/k)=0\), while \(p(x,0)=+\infty\). Thus \(p\) is convex but not lower semicontinuous. Since \(f^\infty(x)=0\) for every \(x\), its lower-semicontinuous closure is
\[
(\operatorname{cl}p)(x,t)=0\ \text{for}\ t\geq0,
\qquad (\operatorname{cl}p)(x,t)=+\infty\ \text{for}\ t<0.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The raw positive perspective is not lower semicontinuous at any \((x,0)\), whereas its closure equals \(0\) for \(t\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure caused solely by omitting the recession boundary.

notation.meaning: Raw perspective with the zero-scale boundary omitted.
Lower-semicontinuous closure of the raw perspective.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex. No lower-semicontinuity assumption is imposed in the general regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition isolates the perspective before boundary completion. Nonclosedness can arise from the missing zero-scale slice, from a nonclosed source function, or from both.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[P_f(\xi,x):=\begin{cases}\xi f(x/\xi),&\xi>0,\\+\infty,&\xi\le0.\end{cases}\] A nonclosed perspective regime is one in which \(P_f\) is used without replacing it by its lower-semicontinuous convex envelope. Its epigraph is \(\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f)\), and the regime is nonclosed whenever this cone is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The raw perspective is defined only at strictly positive scale and is positive infinity elsewhere. Its epigraph is the nonnegative conic hull of the unit-scale epigraph. The nonclosed regime consists of retaining this raw epigraph rather than adjoining its missing limit points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_f(\xi,x)=\begin{cases}\xi f(x/\xi),&\xi>0,\\+\infty,&\xi\le0,\end{cases}\qquad \operatorname{epi}P_f=\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_f\) is closed exactly when \(\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f)\) is closed.
When \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \[\operatorname{cl}P_f(\xi,x)=\begin{cases}\xi f(x/\xi),&\xi>0,\\(\operatorname{rec}f)(x),&\xi=0,\\+\infty,&\xi<0.\end{cases}\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f(x)=\|x\|^2\), then \(P_f(\xi,x)=\|x\|^2/\xi\) for \(\xi>0\); its closure additionally assigns value \(0\) at \((0,0)\).
If the source epigraph is itself nonclosed, closing only the scale-zero boundary does not repair all missing epigraph points.
immediate_consequences_latex: Optimization models using strict inequalities \(\xi>0\) can represent the raw perspective but not its zero-scale limit points.
Replacing \(P_f\) by \(\operatorname{cl}P_f\) may enlarge its effective domain at \(\xi=0\).
boundary_notes: Nonclosed does not mean nonconvex: \(P_f\) is convex whenever \(f\) is convex.
If \(f\notin\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), the recession-boundary formula for a closed source function cannot be applied without first specifying the relevant closure.

notation.meaning: Lower-semicontinuous hull of the raw perspective.
