knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\neq\varnothing\) be a target set, let \(r:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a residual, and let \((x_k)\subseteq U\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract deterministic transfer from a residual estimate to a distance estimate; the definition does not itself supply an algorithmic residual rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An error-bound rate-transfer interface on \(U\) is an inequality \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\omega(r(x))\qquad(x\in U),\] where \(\omega:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\) is nondecreasing, \(\omega(0)=0\), and \(\omega(t)\downarrow0\) as \(t\downarrow0\). For any sequence \(x_k\in U\) with a certified residual estimate \(r(x_k)\leq a_k\), the transferred estimate is \[\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq\omega(a_k).\] A Hölder interface has \(\omega(t)=\kappa t^q\), \(\kappa,q>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An error-bound rate-transfer interface is a modulus that converts any available residual bound into a bound on distance to the solution or feasible set. In the Hölder case, a residual rate is raised to the error-bound exponent.
assumptions_latex: \(\omega\) is nondecreasing, vanishes at zero, and is continuous at zero from the right.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq\omega(a_k)\) for every \(k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\omega(t)=\kappa t^q\) and \(a_k=O(k^{-\alpha})\), the interface records \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)=O(k^{-\alpha q})\).
special_cases_latex: A linear error bound has \(q=1\).
If \(a_k\leq C\rho^k\) with \(0<\rho<1\), then the Hölder interface gives \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\leq\kappa C^q\rho^{qk}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Residual convergence implies convergence in distance to \(S\).
boundary_notes: The interface transfers only while iterates remain in the region where the error bound holds.
It does not imply convergence to a particular point when \(S\) is not a singleton.
review_flags: The construction is mathematically precise, but no inspected source identifies it under this interface name.
knowledge_statements.title: Error-bound rate-transfer interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rate-transfer construction is precise, but no inspectable source supports it as the canonical definition of this node.

knowledge_statements.title: Sublevel-Tube Characterization of a Hölder Error Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder error bound is equivalent to every gap-t sublevel lying, within U, inside the solution-set tube of radius c times t to the theta.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) attain its minimum \(f^*\) on \(S\neq\varnothing\), let \(U\subset X\), and let \(c,\theta>0\). The bound
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq c\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)^\theta
\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f)
\]
holds if and only if, for every \(t\geq0\),
\[
U\cap\{x:f(x)\leq f^*+t\}
\subseteq
\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq ct^\theta\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise Hölder error bound is equivalent to the stated family of sublevel-set tube inclusions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric reformulation through containment of objective sublevels in metric enlargements of the solution set.

notation.meaning: closed metric tube of radius r around S

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric conversion between objective growth and level-set distance bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have minimum value \(F^*\) and nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\). For \(p>0\), the local growth inequality
\[
F(x)-F^*\ge c\operatorname{dist}^p(x,X^*)
\]
is equivalent, on the same neighborhood and for \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), to the Hölder error bound
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le c^{-1/p}\bigl(F(x)-F^*\bigr)^{1/p}.
\]
Thus objective sublevel gaps define nested tubes around \(X^*\); in particular, quadratic growth yields a square-root error-bound geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A power-growth inequality is exactly a Hölder distance bound obtained by inversion; quadratic growth corresponds to a square-root level-gap bound.
assumptions_latex: The inequalities are restricted to a common neighborhood and \(\operatorname{dom}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F-F^*\ge c\operatorname{dist}^p(\cdot,X^*)\) if and only if \(\operatorname{dist}(\cdot,X^*)\le c^{-1/p}(F-F^*)^{1/p}\) locally.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Objective Convergence under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz Inequality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Polyak–Łojasiewicz slope bound converts the smooth descent inequality into linear objective-value convergence of gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex and Fréchet differentiable with nonempty minimizer set and \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Suppose \(\frac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\geq\mu(f(x)-f^*)\) on a set containing every iterate and its gradient step. For \(x^{k+1}=x^k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x^k)\), \[f(x^{k+1})-f^*\leq\left(1-\frac{\mu}{L}\right)(f(x^k)-f^*).\] Thus the objective residual converges Q-linearly while the hypotheses remain applicable.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable with an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and an attained minimum.
\(\frac12\|\nabla f(x)\|^2\geq\mu(f(x)-f^*)\) holds along the iterates and their steps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-value contraction for fixed-step gradient descent under a slope error bound valid along the iterates.

assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and has minimizer set \(S\neq\varnothing\).
\(f(y)-f^*\geq(\mu/2)\operatorname{dist}(y,S)^2\) on a neighborhood containing the proximal iterates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},S)\leq(1+\lambda\mu)^{-1/2}\operatorname{dist}(x^k,S)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: proximal descent inequality combined with set-relative quadratic growth
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance contraction for the exact proximal-point iteration under quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). Suppose \(f(y)-f^*\geq(\mu/2)\operatorname{dist}(y,S)^2\) on a neighborhood containing the iterates. For fixed \(\lambda>0\), define \(x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x^k)\). Then, while the iterates remain in that neighborhood,
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x^{k+1},S)
\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\lambda\mu}}\operatorname{dist}(x^k,S).
\]
Hence the distances converge locally at a Q-linear rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic growth turns exact proximal-point steps into a local linear contraction of distance to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rate Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the linear-rate leaf and the statement is plausible, but the exact contraction factor and locality assumptions require a source with a specific theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Rate-Transfer Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard descent and relative-error conditions, the KL exponent separates finite, linear, and polynomially sublinear convergence regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((x^k)\) converge to \(\bar x\), and suppose that for some \(a,b>0\),
\[
f(x^k)-f(x^{k+1})\geq a\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\leq b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|.
\]
If near \(\bar x\), \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq c(f(x)-f(\bar x))^\theta\), then the induced regimes are: finite termination when \(\theta=0\); local linear convergence when \(0<\theta\leq1/2\); and polynomial sublinear decay when \(1/2<\theta<1\), with objective residual of order \(O(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)})\).
assumptions_latex: A descent sequence converges to \(\bar x\) and satisfies sufficient decrease and a relative-error subgradient bound.
Near \(\bar x\), \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq c(f(x)-f(\bar x))^\theta\) for \(\theta\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regimes are finite termination for \(\theta=0\), linear convergence for \(0<\theta\leq1/2\), and polynomial sublinear convergence for \(1/2<\theta<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative KL rate trichotomy for standard descent sequences.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard KL rate trichotomy under abstract sufficient-decrease and relative-error hypotheses
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative KL trichotomy fits the leaf, but the function, ambient space, subdifferential, residual positivity, and eventual applicability of the inequalities are not fully specified. A source is needed to determine the correct abstract hypotheses and whether each rate concerns values, iterates, or both.

children.title: Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz Exponent Interface
children.top_down_role: Exponent-based bridge between growth geometry and convergence regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz Slope Exponent
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KL exponent specifies the power relating subgradient slope to the positive objective residual near a critical value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\). An exponent \(\theta\in[0,1)\) is admissible at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(c,\eta>0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq c\bigl(f(x)-f(\bar x)\bigr)^\theta\] whenever \(x\in U\) and \(f(\bar x)<f(x)<f(\bar x)+\eta\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq c(f(x)-f(\bar x))^\theta\) locally above the critical value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-form KL inequality for a proper closed convex function at a minimizing critical point.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex KL Inequality Implies Power Growth
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed convex functions, a local KL slope inequality with exponent theta yields local power growth of order one over one minus theta.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\), and let \(\bar x\in S\). Suppose that for some \(c>0\) and \(\theta\in[0,1)\), \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq c(f(x)-f^*)^\theta\] holds for all \(x\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\) whose objective value lies in a sufficiently small interval above \(f^*\). Then there exist \(\alpha,\varepsilon>0\) such that \[f(x)-f^*\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^{1/(1-\theta)}\] whenever \(\|x-\bar x\|<\varepsilon\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The KL slope inequality with exponent \(\theta\in[0,1)\) holds locally and uniformly for sufficiently small positive residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^*\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^{1/(1-\theta)}\) locally for some \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse direction of the local convex growth–KL exponent interface, with existential constants.

assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq\mu^{1/p}(f(x)-f^*)^{1-1/p}\) locally outside \(S\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: convex subgradient inequality transfers power growth to a KL slope inequality
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex power growth implies a KL inequality with the conjugate exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). Suppose that locally around \(S\),
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p
\]
for some \(\mu>0\) and \(p>1\). Then every nearby \(x\notin S\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))
\geq\mu^{1/p}\bigl(f(x)-f^*\bigr)^{1-1/p}.
\]
Thus power growth of order \(p\) yields a Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz slope inequality with exponent \(\theta=1-1/p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex functions, power growth of order p transfers to a KL slope inequality with exponent 1−1/p.
knowledge_statements.title: Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz Exponent Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the exponent-interface leaf and the exponent is plausible, but the exact constant and the meaning of growth locally around the entire solution set require verification from a specifically located source.

children.title: Growth-Certificate Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Flat, degenerate, nonuniform, and locality-limited regimes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure boundary of a prescribed growth certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\), let \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\psi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\) satisfy \(\psi(0)=0\) and \(\psi(t)>0\) for \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-relative definition for a fixed modulus and region; it distinguishes failure of uniform constants from total absence of local growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The \(\psi\)-growth certificate holds on \(U\) with constant \(c>0\) when \[f(x)-\min f\geq c\,\psi(\operatorname{dist}(x,S))\qquad(x\in U).\] Its failure boundary consists of those regimes for which no uniform \(c>0\) is admissible, equivalently \[\inf_{x\in U\setminus S}\frac{f(x)-\min f}{\psi(\operatorname{dist}(x,S))}=0.\] Local failure at \(\bar x\in S\) means this infimum is zero on every neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prescribed growth certificate fails uniformly when the ratio of objective gap to the chosen distance-growth modulus can become arbitrarily small. Local failure means this happens in every neighborhood of a selected minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform failure is characterized by \(\inf_{x\in U\setminus S}(f(x)-\min f)/\psi(\operatorname{dist}(x,S))=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Failure is equivalent to the existence of a sequence \(x_k\in U\setminus S\) such that \((f(x_k)-\min f)/\psi(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S))\to0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\psi(t)=t^2\), this is failure of quadratic growth.
For \(\psi(t)=t\), this is failure of weak sharpness.
immediate_consequences_latex: No positive uniform growth constant can be inferred on the specified region.
boundary_notes: Failure for one modulus does not imply failure for every weaker modulus.
Global failure may coexist with a valid local certificate near each individual minimizer.
review_flags: No inspected source states this named failure-boundary definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure boundary of a prescribed growth certificate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio characterization is a coherent negation of a fixed growth certificate, but the named failure-boundary concept and its exact scope are unsupported.

children.title: Flat Minimum Valleys
children.top_down_role: Weak objective separation from the solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Criterion for Order-p Flatness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform order-p growth fails arbitrarily near the solution set exactly when normalized objective gaps approach zero along nonoptimal points approaching that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) attain its minimum \(f^*\) on \(S\neq\varnothing\), where \(X\) is a metric space, and let \(p>0\). A positive order-\(p\) growth modulus fails on every tubular neighborhood of \(S\) if and only if there exists \((x_k)\subset\operatorname{dom}f\setminus S\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\to0,
\qquad
\frac{f(x_k)-f^*}{\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^p}\to0.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(p>0\), and locality is measured by tubular neighborhoods \(\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<r\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every positive uniform local order-\(p\) modulus fails if and only if such a normalized-gap sequence exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of failure of every uniform order-p growth modulus on tubular neighborhoods of the minimizer set.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). Fix \(p>0\) and \(\bar x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local, set-relative notion of inadequate objective separation; it permits a non-singleton minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimum valley is \(p\)-flat at \(\bar x\) if, for every \(c>0\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(x\in B(\bar x,\varepsilon)\setminus S\) such that \[0<f(x)-\min f<c\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p.\] Equivalently, there is a sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(x_k\notin S\), for which \[(f(x_k)-\min f)/\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^p\to0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum valley is flat of order p at a minimizer when the objective gap can be arbitrarily smaller than every positive multiple of the p-th power of distance to the full solution set, even arbitrarily close to that minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No local positive constant \(c\) yields \(f(x)-\min f\geq c\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p\) near \(\bar x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\liminf_{x\to\bar x,\ x\notin S}(f(x)-\min f)/\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p=0\).
special_cases_latex: \(p=2\) describes failure of local quadratic growth.
\(p=1\) describes failure of local weak sharpness.
immediate_consequences_latex: Objective gaps alone cannot provide a local \(p\)-power distance estimate with a uniform positive constant.
boundary_notes: A non-singleton solution set is not by itself a flat valley because distance is measured to the entire set.
Flatness of order \(p\) does not determine flatness for every other exponent.
review_flags: The formulation is an exact negation of local power growth, but the supplied sources do not establish this terminology.
knowledge_statements.title: Flat minimum valley of order \(p\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement precisely characterizes failure of local \(p\)-power growth, but no source supports the “flat minimum valley” terminology or exact definition.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f(x,y)=\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)^4\), no positive local quadratic-growth modulus exists relative to \(S\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonisolated valley with exact fourth-order, but not quadratic, separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(x,y)=x^4\). This function is convex, its minimum value is \(0\), and its minimizer set is the valley \(S=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\). Moreover,
\[
f(x,y)=\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)^4.
\]
For every \(\mu>0\) and every neighborhood of \(S\), points with sufficiently small nonzero \(|x|\) violate
\[
f(x,y)\geq\frac{\mu}{2}\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)^2.
\]
Hence exact higher-order separation may coexist with failure of every quadratic growth certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The valley function x⁴ has exact fourth-order separation from its minimizers but no quadratic separation, however locally it is examined.
knowledge_statements.title: Flat Minimum Valleys

children.title: Set-Relative Growth Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometries requiring set-relative rather than pointwise growth.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of point-relative growth with valid set-relative growth
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have a nonempty minimizer set \(S\), let \(\bar x\in S\), and let \(\psi:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)\) be positive away from zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry with nonisolated minimizers, where distance to the solution set is the appropriate growth variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set-relative growth regime on \(U\) is specified by a constant \(c>0\) such that \[f(x)-\min f\geq c\psi(\operatorname{dist}(x,S))\qquad(x\in U).\] It is a point-relative growth failure regime at \(\bar x\in S\) if no \(c'>0\) satisfies \[f(x)-f(\bar x)\geq c'\psi(\|x-\bar x\|)\qquad(x\in U).\] In particular, if \(U\cap(S\setminus\{\bar x\})\neq\varnothing\), the point-relative inequality fails automatically while the set-relative inequality may remain valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-relative growth measures displacement normal to the entire minimizer set. A point-relative certificate can fail simply because other minimizers lie near the reference minimizer, even though objective growth away from the solution set is quantitatively strong.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set-relative growth holds on \(U\), but no positive point-relative growth constant at \(\bar x\) is admissible.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Point-relative failure is \(\inf_{x\in U\setminus\{\bar x\}}(f(x)-f(\bar x))/\psi(\|x-\bar x\|)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For a manifold of minimizers, quadratic growth may hold in normal directions through \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\) while pointwise quadratic growth fails.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convergence of objective values can control distance to \(S\) without selecting a unique minimizer.
boundary_notes: When \(S=\{\bar x\}\), set-relative and point-relative distances coincide.
The definition does not impose smoothness or manifold structure on \(S\).
review_flags: No precise source locator for this named failure regime was found.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of point-relative growth with valid set-relative growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between set-relative and point-relative growth is mathematically coherent, but the proposed named regime lacks independent source support.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness Implies Nonisolation for Convex Objectives
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex objective, two minimizers generate an entire minimizing segment; therefore a nonsingleton minimizer set has no isolated points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex on a real normed space and let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). Then \(S\) is convex. If \(x_0,x_1\in S\) are distinct, every point \((1-t)x_0+tx_1\), \(0\leq t\leq1\), belongs to \(S\), and every point of that segment is nonisolated in \(S\). Consequently, \(S\) contains an isolated minimizer if and only if \(S\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|S|>1\), then no point of \(S\) is isolated; equivalently, \(S\) contains an isolated minimizer exactly when it is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity turns any pair of distinct minimizers into a minimizing segment.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Solution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonisolated minimizers preclude growth measured from one fixed minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(f(x,y)=y^2\). Its minimizer set is \(S=\mathbb{R}\times\{0\}\), and \[f(x,y)-\min f=\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)^2.\] For every \(\bar z=(a,0)\in S\), every neighborhood of \(\bar z\) contains a distinct \(z\in S\), for which \(f(z)-f(\bar z)=0\) and \(\|z-\bar z\|>0\). Thus set-relative quadratic growth holds exactly, whereas no positive pointwise growth bound relative to \(\bar z\) holds on a full neighborhood of \(\bar z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective y squared has exact quadratic growth relative to its nonisolated solution set, but no positive growth bound relative to any fixed solution on a full neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: Pointwise growth is required on a full neighborhood of a fixed \(\bar z\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set-relative quadratic growth holds, but every positive pointwise growth bound at \(\bar z\) fails.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Solution Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat solution direction can destroy pointwise growth even when exact quadratic growth relative to the whole solution set holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(x,y)=x^2\). Its solution set is \(S=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\), and
\[
f(x,y)=\operatorname{dist}((x,y),S)^2,
\]
so set-relative quadratic growth holds globally. However, for any fixed \(\bar z=(0,\bar y)\in S\) and any \(\mu>0\), the point \(z=(0,y)\in S\) with \(y\neq\bar y\) satisfies \(f(z)-f(\bar z)=0\) while \(\|z-\bar z\|>0\). Thus pointwise quadratic growth about \(\bar z\) fails because the solution geometry contains an unpenalized tangent direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set-relative quadratic growth holds exactly, while pointwise quadratic growth about any fixed minimizer fails because of the tangent solution direction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular curvature along a nonisolated solution direction.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary example separating pointwise and set-relative growth
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Local Comparison of Set-Relative Growth Orders
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded-distance region, order-p growth implies every higher order q with a rescaled modulus; this need not extend to an unbounded global region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that for some \(p>0\), \(\mu>0\), and set \(U\),
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \mu\,\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p
\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f),
\]
and that \(0<\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq R\) for all \(x\in(U\cap\operatorname{dom}f)\setminus S\), where \(R>0\). Then for every \(q\geq p\),
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \mu R^{p-q}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^q
\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f).
\]
Thus order-\(p\) growth implies every higher-order bound on a bounded-distance region, but this implication is not automatic globally when distances from \(S\) are unbounded.
assumptions_latex: Order-\(p\) set-relative growth holds on U.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(q\geq p\), order-\(q\) growth holds on U with modulus \(\mu R^{p-q}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponent monotonicity on bounded-distance regions and its global limitation.

notation.meaning: growth exponents with q at least p
uniform upper bound on distance to S

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Relative Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power growth measured by distance to the entire minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and let \(S=\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\), with \(f^*=\min f\). For an order \(p>0\), the function has local set-relative growth of order \(p\) if there exist constants \(c,\varepsilon>0\) such that \[f(x)-f^*\geq c\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p\] for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\varepsilon\). It has global set-relative growth when the same inequality holds for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The case \(p=2\) is called quadratic growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set-relative growth lower-bounds objective suboptimality by a power of distance to the full solution set, either locally or globally.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^*\geq c\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^p\) defines set-relative growth of order \(p\).

source_refs.locator: A. Convex Sets and Functions p. 38

source_witnesses.locator: A. Convex Sets and Functions p. 38

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Pointwise Growth Forces Local Isolation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any positive point-centered growth bound makes its center locally unique, so a nonisolated minimizer defeats every such bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) attain its minimum \(f^*\), let \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\), and suppose that for some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(\mu>0\), and \(p>0\),
\[
f(x)-f^*\geq \mu\,d(x,\bar x)^p
\qquad(x\in U\cap\operatorname{dom}f).
\]
Then \(U\cap\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{\bar x\}\). Consequently, if \(\bar x\) is a nonisolated minimizer, no positive-modulus pointwise growth inequality of any order \(p>0\) can hold near \(\bar x\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a metric space and f attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise growth implies \(U\cap\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{\bar x\}\); nonisolation implies failure of every positive pointwise growth modulus.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General obstruction to every positive-order growth inequality centered at one minimizer.

notation.meaning: selected minimizer serving as the pointwise center

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Growth Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An isolated minimizer need not possess quadratic pointwise growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(f(x)=x^4\). The function is convex and has the unique minimizer \(\bar x=0\). Moreover, \[\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{|x-\bar x|^2}=x^2\longrightarrow0\quad\text{as }x\to0.\] Hence there are no constants \(c,\varepsilon>0\) such that \(f(x)-f(0)\geq c|x-\bar x|^2\) for every \(|x-\bar x|<\varepsilon\), although \(f(x)-f(0)=|x-\bar x|^4\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function x to the fourth has a unique minimizer and exact quartic growth there, but it admits no local quadratic pointwise-growth bound.
assumptions_latex: The proposed pointwise certificate has quadratic order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(c,\varepsilon>0\) satisfy \(f(x)-f(0)\geq c|x|^2\) for every \(|x|<\varepsilon\).

children.title: Local–Global Error-Bound Gap
children.top_down_role: Failure of neighborhood regularity to extend over the full domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Local–Global Error-Bound Gap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function can grow quadratically near its minimizer but only linearly at infinity, so its local quadratic error bound has no global extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,&|x|\leq 1,\\2|x|-1,&|x|>1.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is convex and continuously differentiable, with \(f^*=0\) and \(S=\{0\}\). On \([-1,1]\),
\[
f(x)-f^*=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2.
\]
For every \(\mu>0\), there exists \(x>1\) such that
\[
f(x)-f^*=2x-1<\mu x^2=\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2.
\]
Hence the local quadratic error bound has no global extension with a positive constant.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is the stated convex continuously differentiable function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A quadratic error bound valid near \(S\) need not extend globally with any positive constant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex example separating neighborhood quadratic growth from global quadratic growth.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bregman geometry generated by a Legendre function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex with \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\), and suppose \(h\) is differentiable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional non-Euclidean geometry; the second Bregman argument must lie in the differentiability domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Bregman divergence generated by \(h\) is \[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle,\qquad x\in\operatorname{dom}h,\ y\in C.\] If \(h\) is Legendre, then \(h^*\) is Legendre, \(
abla h:C	o C^*=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\) is bijective with inverse \(
abla h^*\), and the associated Bregman–Legendre geometry consists of the primal divergence together with these dual coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bregman–Legendre geometry is generated by the first-order deviation of a convex Legendre function from its supporting affine function. Legendre duality supplies one-to-one gradient coordinates between the interiors of the primal and conjugate domains.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, convex, and Legendre.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x,y)\) is defined as above, and \(\nabla h:C\to C^*\) has inverse \(\nabla h^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x,y\in C\), \(D_h(x,y)=D_{h^*}(\nabla h(y),\nabla h(x))\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity gives \(D_h(x,y)\geq0\).
Strict convexity on \(C\) gives \(D_h(x,y)=0\) only when \(x=y\) for \(x,y\in C\).
boundary_notes: A Bregman divergence is generally asymmetric and need not satisfy the triangle inequality.
Boundary points at which \(h\) is not differentiable cannot serve as the second argument.

children.title: Bregman Generators
children.top_down_role: Reference functions organized by curvature, differentiability, domain, and boundary behavior.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Set \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional generator class suitable for Bregman divergences; strong convexity is included when quantitative distance domination is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Bregman generator on a nonempty convex reference domain \(Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}h\) is a proper, closed, strictly convex function \(h\) that is differentiable on \(C
eq\varnothing\), with \(Q\cap C
eq\varnothing\). It generates \[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle\quad(x\in Q,\ y\in Q\cap C).\] It is a \(\sigma\)-strong distance generator relative to \(\|\cdot\|\) if \[h(x)\geq h(y)+\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle+ rac\sigma2\|x-y\|^2\] for all admissible \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman generator is a proper closed convex reference function, differentiable on the interior of its domain, whose first-order remainder defines a nonnegative divergence. Strong convexity makes that divergence dominate squared norm distance.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, closed, strictly convex, and differentiable on \(C\neq\varnothing\).
\(Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}h\) is nonempty and convex, with \(Q\cap C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h\) is defined on \(Q\times(Q\cap C)\), and strong generation yields \(D_h(x,y)\geq\frac\sigma2\|x-y\|^2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The strong-generator inequality is exactly the lower bound \(D_h(x,y)\geq\frac\sigma2\|x-y\|^2\).
special_cases_latex: The Euclidean generator is \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\).
Negative entropy is a generator on the positive orthant or simplex interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity implies positive definiteness of \(D_h\) on the differentiability domain.
boundary_notes: Differentiability is required at the second argument only.
A generator need not produce a metric because symmetry and the triangle inequality may fail.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Generating Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance-generating function is a differentiable strongly convex reference function whose Bregman divergence controls squared displacement in a chosen norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(h:C\to\mathbb R\) is a distance-generating function with modulus \(\sigma>0\) relative to \(\|\cdot\|\) if it is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, differentiable on \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and
\[
h(y)\geq h(x)+\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2
\]
for all \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) and \(y\in C\). Its associated Bregman divergence is \(D_h(y,x)=h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle\), hence \(D_h(y,x)\geq(\sigma/2)\|y-x\|^2\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Such an \(h\) supplies a non-Euclidean prox geometry through its Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable, strongly convex reference functions.

children.title: Legendre Functions
children.top_down_role: Duality-adapted generators with controlled interior and boundary behavior.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, with \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional Rockafellar definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h\) is essentially smooth if it is differentiable throughout \(C\) and \(\|\nabla h(x_k)\|\to+\infty\) whenever \(x_k\in C\) converges to a boundary point of \(\operatorname{dom}h\). It is essentially strictly convex if it is strictly convex on every convex subset of \(\operatorname{dom}\partial h\). A Legendre function is a proper closed convex function that is both essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Legendre function is a closed proper convex function combining interior differentiability and gradient blow-up at the domain boundary with strict convexity on convex subsets where subgradients exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is Legendre exactly when it is both essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In finite dimensions, essential smoothness gives \(\operatorname{dom}\partial h=C\), while essential strict convexity is dual to essential smoothness of \(h^*\).
special_cases_latex: Every differentiable strictly convex cofinite function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is of Legendre type.
The negative entropy on the strictly positive orthant is a standard boundary-steep Legendre generator.
immediate_consequences_latex: The conjugate \(h^*\) is also Legendre.
The gradient is one-to-one from \(C\) onto \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).
boundary_notes: Strict convexity alone does not imply essential smoothness.
A smooth convex function on all of \(\mathbb R^n\) satisfies the boundary condition vacuously but must still satisfy essential strict convexity to be Legendre.

children.title: Essential Smoothness
children.top_down_role: Interior differentiability and boundary-gradient behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior Differentiability Does Not Suffice
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square function restricted to the nonnegative half-line is interior differentiable but not essentially smooth because its gradient remains bounded at the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[h(x)=\begin{cases}x^2,&x\ge0,\\+\infty,&x<0.\end{cases}\] Then \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex and is differentiable on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)=(0,\infty)\). Nevertheless, for \(x_k\downarrow0\), \(\nabla h(x_k)=2x_k\to0\), so \(h\) is not essentially smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\text{ is differentiable on }(0,\infty)\text{ but is not essentially smooth}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of the boundary-gradient condition.

notation.meaning: an interior sequence approaching the domain boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential-Domain Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an essentially smooth closed convex function, subgradients exist exactly in the domain interior and there equal the unique gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, convex, and essentially smooth. Then \[\operatorname{dom}\partial h=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h),\qquad \partial h(x)=\{\nabla h(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h).\] Thus no finite boundary point of the domain admits a convex subgradient.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and essentially smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}\partial h=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h),\qquad \partial h(x)=\{\nabla h(x)\}\text{ on this set}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequence of essential smoothness for closed proper convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Essential Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition for proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper closed convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is essentially smooth if \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\neq\varnothing\), it is differentiable throughout \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), and, whenever \(x_k\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) converges to a boundary point of \(\operatorname{dom}f\), one has \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential smoothness means differentiability on the nonempty domain interior and unbounded gradient norm along every interior sequence approaching the domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is essentially smooth exactly when the stated interior differentiability and boundary steepness conditions hold.

notation.meaning: The effective domain where f is finite.

children.title: Essential Strict Convexity
children.top_down_role: Strict curvature on subdifferentially active regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Essential Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential strict convexity requires strict convexity on every convex region where the function has at least one subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(h\) is essentially strictly convex if its restriction to every nonempty convex subset \(K\subset\operatorname{dom}\partial h\) is strictly convex. Equivalently, for every such \(K\), all distinct \(x,y\in K\), and every \(t\in(0,1)\),
\[
h((1-t)x+ty)<(1-t)h(x)+t h(y).
\]
The definition does not require strict convexity on portions of \(\operatorname{dom}h\) lying outside \(\operatorname{dom}\partial h\).
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: This strictness on subdifferentially active convex regions defines essential strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict convexity restricted to convex subsets where subgradients exist.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Hessians in Legendre Coordinates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable Legendre generator with positive-definite interior Hessian, conjugate coordinates invert the Hessian metric.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order Legendre duality under positive-definite interior curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Legendre Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Legendre function and its conjugate are Legendre, and their gradients are mutually inverse maps between the interiors of their domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(h\) is Legendre, then \(h^*\) is Legendre and
\[
\nabla h:\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\to\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)
\]
is a bijection with inverse \(\nabla h^*\). For \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) and \(p\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\),
\[
p=\nabla h(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=\nabla h^*(p)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h(x)+h^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is closed, proper, and Legendre.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conjugation preserves the Legendre class and exchanges primal and dual interior gradient coordinates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Legendre conjugacy and inverse-gradient correspondence.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be Legendre, let \(h^*\) be its Fenchel conjugate, and set \(C=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), \(C^*=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Legendre conjugacy on the interiors of the effective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Legendre duality is the bijective coordinate correspondence \[y=
abla h(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=
abla h^*(y),\qquad x\in C,\ y\in C^*,\] together with the Fenchel equality \[h(x)+h^*(y)=\langle x,yangle.\] Thus \(
abla h:C	o C^*\) and \(
abla h^*:C^*	o C\) are mutually inverse continuous maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Legendre duality identifies every interior primal point with a unique interior dual point through the gradient. The conjugate gradient returns the primal point, and the pair satisfies Fenchel equality.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a proper closed Legendre convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla h^*=(\nabla h)^{-1}\) between \(C^*\) and \(C\), and paired points satisfy \(h(x)+h^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y=\nabla h(x)\iff y\in\partial h(x)\iff x\in\partial h^*(y)\iff x=\nabla h^*(y)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\), both gradients are the identity.
For negative entropy, primal positive coordinates correspond to logarithmic dual coordinates up to affine normalization.
immediate_consequences_latex: Both interior domains are open convex sets and are homeomorphic through the gradient maps.
Bregman divergences admit a dual-coordinate representation.
boundary_notes: The bijection is asserted only between domain interiors.
Without essential strict convexity, the gradient need not be one-to-one; without essential smoothness, its range need not fill the dual interior.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Domain Geometries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic, entropy, logarithmic-barrier, and log-determinant generators furnish natural Bregman geometries for Euclidean, simplex, positive-orthant, and positive-definite matrix domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Canonical reference geometries are generated by
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{domain}&h(x)\\ \hline
\mathbb R^n&\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\\
\operatorname{ri}\Delta_n&\sum_i x_i\log x_i\\
\mathbb R_{++}^n&-\sum_i\log x_i\\
\mathbb S_{++}^m&-\log\det X.
\end{array}
\]
Their Bregman divergences are, respectively, squared Euclidean distance divided by two, relative entropy on the simplex, the Burg divergence on the positive orthant, and the log-determinant divergence \(\operatorname{tr}(XY^{-1})-\log\det(XY^{-1})-m\) on \(\mathbb S_{++}^m\).
assumptions_latex: Each generator is considered on the relative interior or interior of its stated convex domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These generators induce geometries adapted respectively to Euclidean, simplex, orthant, and positive-definite matrix domains.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical generators for four commonly used reference domains.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and put \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\). Assume that \(U\neq\varnothing\) and that \(h\) is differentiable on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, differentiable convex-generator formulation. The divergence is directed, with its second argument restricted to the differentiability region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\) and \(y\in U\), the Bregman divergence generated by \(h\) is
\[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle.\]
It is extended by \(D_h(x,y)=+\infty\) when \(x
otin\operatorname{dom}h\) or \(y
otin U\). Thus \(D_h(x,y)\) is the error between \(h(x)\) and the affine first-order model of \(h\) based at \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bregman divergence from the base point y to x is the value of h at x minus the first-order affine model of h at y, namely h(x)−h(y)−〈∇h(y),x−y〉. Its natural finite-valued domain has x in dom h and y in the interior region where h is differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h:(\operatorname{dom}h)\times U\to[0,+\infty]\) is defined by \(D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(D_h(x,y)=h(x)-\bigl(h(y)+\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\bigr)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), then \(D_h(x,y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity gives \(D_h(x,y)\geq0\) for all \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\) and \(y\in U\).
For every \(y\in U\), \(D_h(y,y)=0\).
If \(h\) is strictly convex on \(U\), then \(D_h(x,y)=0\) with \(x,y\in U\) implies \(x=y\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not generally produce a symmetric function or a metric.
A subgradient-based divergence requires choosing \(g_y\in\partial h(y)\) and is not covered by this differentiable formulation.
For infinite-dimensional spaces, interior, differentiability, and dual-pairing hypotheses require separate treatment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and conjugate representations of a Bregman divergence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a Legendre convex function. Write \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), \(U^*=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\), and let \(h^*\) be the Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Legendre setting, so primal and dual gradients are mutually inverse on the interiors of their effective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y\in U\), the primal-dual Bregman representation pair is
\[D_h(x,y)=h(x)+h^*(
abla h(y))-\langle x,
abla h(y)angle
=D_{h^*}(
abla h(y),
abla h(x)).\]
The first expression represents the primal divergence as a Fenchel-Young gap at \((x,
abla h(y))\); the second represents the same value as the conjugate Bregman divergence with reversed gradient-coordinate order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Legendre generator, the divergence from y to x equals the Fenchel–Young gap h(x)+h*(∇h(y))−〈x,∇h(y)〉. The same number is the conjugate divergence from ∇h(x) to ∇h(y), with the argument order reversed in dual coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is Legendre on a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(D_h(x,y)=h(x)+h^*(
abla h(y))-\langle x,
abla h(y)angle=D_{h^*}(
abla h(y),
abla h(x))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(u=\nabla h(x)\) and \(v=\nabla h(y)\), \(D_h(x,y)=D_{h^*}(v,u)\).
Using \(h(y)+h^*(\nabla h(y))=\langle y,\nabla h(y)\rangle\), the gap representation is equivalent to the defining formula for \(D_h(x,y)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), one has \(h^*=h\), \(\nabla h=\operatorname{Id}\), and both representations equal \(\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal divergence is nonnegative as a Fenchel-Young gap.
Primal orientation reversal corresponds to dual orientation reversal: \(D_h(y,x)=D_{h^*}(\nabla h(x),\nabla h(y))\).
boundary_notes: The dual-divergence identity requires gradient coordinates to lie in the differentiability domain of \(h^*\).
For a merely differentiable convex function that is not Legendre, the gradient need not be invertible or cover \(U^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Integrated-Hessian Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth primal Bregman divergence is an averaged Hessian quadratic form along the segment between its arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, let \(h\in C^2(C)\), and take \(x,y\in C\). With \(d=x-y\), \[D_h(x,y)=\int_0^1(1-t)d^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2h(y+td)d\,dt.\] If \(mI\preceq\nabla^2h\preceq LI\) along the segment, then \[\frac m2\|x-y\|^2\le D_h(x,y)\le\frac L2\|x-y\|^2.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h(x,y)=\int_0^1(1-t)(x-y)^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2h(y+t(x-y))(x-y)\,dt.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order representation along a segment in the smooth primal domain.

notation.meaning: displacement from the base point to the evaluation point

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Bregman–Fenchel Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected base-point subgradient defines a generalized Bregman divergence equal to a Fenchel–Young gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(y\in\operatorname{dom}\partial h\), and choose \(g\in\partial h(y)\). For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\), define \[D_h^g(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle g,x-y\rangle.\] Equivalently, \[D_h^g(x,y)=h(x)+h^*(g)-\langle g,x\rangle\ge0.\] Moreover, \(D_h^g(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(g\in\partial h(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h^g(x,y)=h(x)+h^*(g)-\langle g,x\rangle\ge0,\quad D_h^g(x,y)=0\iff g\in\partial h(x).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth primal variant based on a selected base-point subgradient.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Bregman Divergence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual Bregman divergence applies the usual construction to the Fenchel conjugate; under gradient coordinates it equals the primal divergence with reversed arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual Bregman divergence generated by the conjugate \(h^*\) is
\[
D_{h^*}(p,q)=h^*(p)-h^*(q)-\langle\nabla h^*(q),p-q\rangle.
\]
It is nonnegative by convexity of \(h^*\). When \(p=\nabla h(x)\) and \(q=\nabla h(y)\) for \(x,y\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), Legendre duality gives
\[
D_{h^*}(p,q)=D_h(y,x),
\]
so passage to dual coordinates reverses the primal arguments.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a closed proper Legendre function on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Bregman divergence of the conjugate is the dual-coordinate divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bregman divergence formed in conjugate gradient coordinates.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the primal generator

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate-Coordinate Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Legendre gradient map sends primal points to conjugate coordinates and identifies each primal divergence with a dual divergence having reversed arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(p=\nabla h(x)\) and \(q=\nabla h(y)\). Legendre duality yields \(x=\nabla h^*(p)\), \(y=\nabla h^*(q)\), and the Fenchel equalities \(h(x)+h^*(p)=\langle p,x\rangle\) and \(h(y)+h^*(q)=\langle q,y\rangle\). Consequently,
\[
D_h(x,y)=D_{h^*}(q,p).
\]
Thus the gradient bijection identifies the ordered primal pair \((x,y)\) with the reversed ordered dual pair \((q,p)\).
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a closed proper Legendre function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gradient coordinates convert primal Bregman divergence into reversed dual Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual divergence identity under Legendre gradient coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Point Bregman Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-point identity expresses a gradient pairing as the difference of three Bregman divergences and underlies projection and mirror-descent calculations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the convention \(D_h(a,b)=h(a)-h(b)-\langle\nabla h(b),a-b\rangle\), the three-point identity is
\[
D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z)
=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle
=D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z).
\]
The identity requires only differentiability at the base points \(y\) and \(z\); convexity additionally ensures that all displayed divergences are nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex and differentiable on an open convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The difference of two divergences sharing the base point decomposes into a third divergence and a gradient-pairing correction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-point identity using the second argument as the divergence base point.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and let \(D_h\) be its Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional geometry. All three points lie in the differentiability region so every displayed divergence and gradient is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y,z\in U\), define the three-point Bregman defect by
\[\Delta_h(x,y,z)=D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z).\]
The three-point geometry is the identity
\[\Delta_h(x,y,z)=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle,\]
or equivalently
\[D_h(x,z)=D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)+\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-point Bregman defect compares the direct divergence from z to x with the two-stage divergences through y. It equals the pairing of the dual-coordinate displacement ∇h(y)−∇h(z) with the primal displacement x−y.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper and convex and is differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z)=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)-D_h(x,z)=\langle\nabla h(z)-\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\).
\(D_h(x,z)-D_h(y,z)=D_h(x,y)+\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), the identity becomes \(\tfrac12\|x-z\|^2=\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2+\tfrac12\|y-z\|^2+\langle y-z,x-y\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\geq0\), then \(D_h(x,z)\geq D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)\).
If the pairing term vanishes, the three divergences satisfy an exact Pythagorean equality.
boundary_notes: This identity is algebraic and does not itself assert that any point is a projection.
The three-point defect need not have a fixed sign without an additional variational or orthogonality condition.

children.title: Bregman Metric-Axiom Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating Bregman divergences from metric distances.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-axiom profile of a Bregman divergence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h\) be differentiable and convex on a nonempty open convex set \(U\subseteq E\), and let \(D_h:U\times U\to[0,+\infty)\) be its Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records exactly where a Bregman divergence agrees with or departs from the axioms of a metric; it does not classify all generators producing metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the symmetry and triangle defects by
\[S_h(x,y)=D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,x),\qquad T_h(x,y,z)=D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z).\]
The Bregman metric-axiom profile consists of nonnegativity \(D_h(x,y)\geq0\), reflexivity \(D_h(x,x)=0\), separation when \(D_h(x,y)=0\Rightarrow x=y\), symmetry when \(S_h\equiv0\), and the triangle inequality when \(T_h\leq0\) for every ordered triple. A Bregman divergence is metric-valued on \(U\) precisely when separation, symmetry, and the triangle inequality all hold in addition to nonnegativity and reflexivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric boundary is described by two defects. The symmetry defect compares the two orientations, while the triangle defect compares a direct divergence with a two-leg route. Every convex differentiable generator gives nonnegativity and zero diagonal; strict convexity gives point separation, but symmetry and the triangle inequality are additional properties and generally fail.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq E\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h\) has the metric axioms on \(U\) exactly when \(D_h(x,y)=0\Rightarrow x=y\), \(S_h(x,y)=0\), and \(T_h(x,y,z)\leq0\) for all \(x,y,z\in U\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(S_h(x,y)=2(h(x)-h(y))-\langle\nabla h(x)+\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\).
\(T_h(x,y,z)=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For a positive-definite quadratic generator, \(D_h\) is a squared norm: it is symmetric and separating, but \(D_h\) itself generally fails the triangle inequality; \(\sqrt{2D_h}\) is the associated metric.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity supplies separation but does not supply symmetry or a triangle inequality.
The term “divergence” does not imply that \(D_h\) is a distance metric.
boundary_notes: A squared norm is not itself a metric except in degenerate restrictions, despite being symmetric and nonnegative.
This profile concerns \(D_h\), not transformations such as \(\sqrt{D_h}\) or symmetrizations such as \(D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,x)\).

notation.meaning: Symmetry defect of the directed divergence.

review_flags: The supplied source hints did not provide an inspected locator supporting the complete Bregman metric-axiom profile.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetrized Bregman Identity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two orientations of a Bregman divergence sum to the gradient-monotonicity pairing of their endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h\) is convex and differentiable on an open convex set \(C\), then for all \(x,y\in C\), \[D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,x)=\langle\nabla h(x)-\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle.\]
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex and differentiable on an open convex set \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,x)=\langle\nabla h(x)-\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic identity measuring orientation dependence.
A one-dimensional negative-entropy counterexample to symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(t)=t\log t\) on \((0,\infty)\). Its Bregman divergence is \[D_f(x,y)=x\log(x/y)-x+y.\] At \(x=1\) and \(y=2\), one has \[D_f(1,2)=1-\log 2,\qquad D_f(2,1)=2\log 2-1.\] These values are unequal, so a Bregman divergence need not satisfy \(D_f(x,y)=D_f(y,x)\), even when its generator is smooth and strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative-entropy Bregman divergence assigns different values to the ordered pairs (1,2) and (2,1), so symmetry fails.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic characterization proposed under sufficient smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let \(h\in C^3(C)\) be convex. Then \(D_h\) is symmetric on \(C\times C\) if and only if \(h(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+b\) with constant \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under sufficient smoothness, symmetric Bregman divergences are generated by quadratic functions up to affine terms.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h\text{ is symmetric}\iff h(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+b.

knowledge_statements.title: Triangle Inequality Forces Affinity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice-differentiable Bregman divergence satisfies the global triangle inequality only in the trivial affine, zero-divergence case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let \(h\in C^2(C)\) be convex. If \[D_h(x,z)\le D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)\quad\text{for all }x,y,z\in C,\] then \(h\) is affine on \(C\) and \(D_h\equiv0\). Conversely, an affine generator produces the zero divergence, which satisfies the triangle inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h\equiv0\quad\text{and}\quad h\text{ is affine on }C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp smooth boundary for the triangle inequality applied to the divergence itself.
Failure concerns the divergence itself, not its square root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the smooth strictly convex generator \(f(t)=\tfrac12t^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the associated Bregman divergence is \[D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^2.\] Taking \(x=0\), \(y=1\), and \(z=2\) gives \[D_f(0,2)=2>1=D_f(0,1)+D_f(1,2).\] Thus even a symmetric Bregman divergence need not obey the triangle inequality and therefore need not itself be a metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared Euclidean distance is a Bregman divergence, but at 0, 1, and 2 it violates the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Triangle-Inequality Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The squared-Euclidean calculation correctly demonstrates failure of the triangle inequality for the divergence itself, and counterexample fits the leaf. No source reference or inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Quadratics Give a Quotient Metric
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic yields a Mahalanobis pseudometric; it is a genuine metric exactly for positive-definite curvature, and otherwise becomes one on the quotient by the null space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\langle b,x\rangle+c\) with symmetric \(Q\succeq0\), \[D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y),\qquad \sqrt{2D_f(x,y)}=\|Q^{1/2}(x-y)\|_2.\] The square root is a metric on \(\mathbb R^n\) exactly when \(Q\succ0\). If \(Q\) is singular, it is a pseudometric on \(\mathbb R^n\) and induces a metric on \(\mathbb R^n/\ker Q\). The affine part of \(f\) does not affect the divergence.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt{2D_f}\) is a metric on \(\mathbb R^n\iff Q\succ0\); for singular \(Q\), it induces a metric on \(\mathbb R^n/\ker Q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic metric-compatible cases and their exact point-separation boundary.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_f(x,y):=\sqrt{2D_f(x,y)}=\sqrt{(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y)}\) is a metric.

notation.meaning: metric induced by the positive-definite quadratic form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite quadratic generators yield Mahalanobis metric geometry after taking a square root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be symmetric positive definite and let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\langle b,x\rangle+c\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \[D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y).\] Consequently \[d_f(x,y):=\sqrt{2D_f(x,y)}=\|Q^{1/2}(x-y)\|_2\] is a metric. The affine part of \(f\) does not affect \(D_f\). The divergence \(D_f\) remains a squared metric and generally does not itself satisfy the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite quadratic generator produces half the squared Mahalanobis distance; its square root is a genuine metric.
