intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited sections support the three ingredients separately, but no locator supports the synthesized gap predicate or both asserted bridges with the record's exact uniform polynomial-size compilation requirements. Moreover, “every objective and feasibility comparison” and “prescribed epsilon-solution” are not formally defined, so the representability and tractability predicates lack necessary conventions.

assumptions_latex: Representability refers to an available finite exact formulation in a specified standard-form library.
Tractability refers to computational accessibility under a stated input encoding, accuracy criterion, and algorithmic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither \(C(f)\Rightarrow R_{\mathcal L}(f)\) nor \(R_{\mathcal L}(f)\Rightarrow T_{\mathcal M}(f)\) holds without additional assumptions on the library, representation size, data access, and computational model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates semantic convexity, library-relative representation, and model-relative computational tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function \(f\), the predicates \(C(f)\), \(R_{\mathcal L}(f)\), and \(T_{\mathcal M}(f)\) describe distinct properties. Convexity \(C(f)\) is a semantic inequality on the domain of \(f\). Representability \(R_{\mathcal L}(f)\) requires an available finite exact graph formulation using a chosen library \(\mathcal L\). Tractability \(T_{\mathcal M}(f)\) requires an algorithm with a specified resource bound in model \(\mathcal M\). In general, convexity need not yield a formulation in \(\mathcal L\), and possession of a formulation need not yield tractability when its size, conditioning, data encoding, cone oracles, or accuracy requirements are uncontrolled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity, availability of an exact standard-form representation, and computational tractability are distinct; neither transition follows without library and complexity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity–Representability–Tractability Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind is appropriate for this gap container, and the distinctions are conceptually sound. The two non-implication claims are nontrivial and depend on precise definitions of the representation library and computational model, but no supporting citation or sourced counterexample is provided.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core convex subdifferential for proper extended-real-valued convex functions on finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The convex subdifferential of \(f\) at \(x\) is
\[
\partial f(x):=\left\{g\in X: f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in X\right\}.
\]
Each \(g\in\partial f(x)\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\); its affine minorant supports \(f\) globally at \(x\). By convention, \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) when \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential consists of all slopes whose affine functions touch the convex function at the given point and remain global lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\{g\in X: f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\text{ for all }y\in X\}\).

children.title: Convex Subgradient Geometry
children.top_down_role: Foundational supporting geometry, subdifferential-set structure, directional representations, and differentiability interfaces.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and use the Euclidean pairing \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finite-valued convex analysis. In this regime the subdifferential is nonempty, compact, and convex at every point; extended-valued boundary behavior is treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex subdifferential of \(f\) at \(x\) is
\[
\partial f(x):=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n: f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
Each \(g\in\partial f(x)\) is a subgradient. Equivalently, if
\[
f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t},
\]
then
\[
\partial f(x)=\{g:\langle g,d\rangle\le f'(x;d)\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
Thus \(f'(x;\cdot)\) is the support function of \(\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector \(g\) is a convex subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) exactly when the affine function \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) globally minorizes \(f\). The set of every such vector is \(\partial f(x)\). For finite-valued convex \(f\), the same set consists of the linear functionals dominated in every direction by the one-sided directional derivative \(f'(x;d)\), so the directional derivative is precisely the support function of the subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial f(x)=\{g:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\}=\{g:\langle g,d\rangle\le f'(x;d)\ \forall d\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f'(x;d)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle\qquad(d\in\mathbb{R}^n).\]
\[g\in\partial f(x)\iff y\mapsto f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\text{ supports }f\text{ from below at }x.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\).
If \(f\) is affine, \(f(y)=\langle a,y\rangle+b\), then \(\partial f(x)=\{a\}\) for every \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The set \(\partial f(x)\) is closed and convex because it is an intersection of closed half-spaces.
For finite-valued convex \(f\), local Lipschitz continuity makes \(\partial f(x)\) bounded; existence of supporting affine minorants makes it nonempty.
boundary_notes: For a proper extended-valued convex function, the same global inequality defines \(\partial f(x)\), but the value may be empty or unbounded at domain-boundary points.
This is the convex-analytic subdifferential, not a generalized subdifferential for nonconvex functions.

notation.meaning: One-sided directional derivative at \(x\) in direction \(d\).

children.title: Supporting-Model Foundations
children.top_down_role: Equivalent geometric viewpoints underlying convex subgradients.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine supporting model at a convex function value
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and fix \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). An affine function is written \(m(y)=\alpha+\langle g,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex functions. The definition records the global affine-minorant viewpoint rather than merely a local linear approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An affine supporting model of \(f\) at \(x\) is an affine function
\[
m_{x,g}(y):=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle
\]
that satisfies
\[
m_{x,g}(y)\le f(y)\quad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\qquad m_{x,g}(x)=f(x).
\]
Its slope \(g\) is a subgradient, and the set of admissible slopes is
\[
\{g:m_{x,g}\le f\}=\partial f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supporting model at \(x\) is an affine global lower model that touches the convex function at \(x\). It necessarily has the form \(m_{x,g}(y)=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\). The model is supporting exactly when it never exceeds \(f\), and its slope then belongs to \(\partial f(x)\). Conversely, every convex subgradient supplies one such supporting model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[g\in\partial f(x)\iff m_{x,g}(x)=f(x)\ \text{and}\ m_{x,g}(y)\le f(y)\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(m(y)=\alpha+\langle g,y\rangle\), contact at \(x\) forces \(\alpha=f(x)-\langle g,x\rangle\), so every supporting model at \(x\) is uniquely determined by its slope.
The support condition can be written \(f(y)-m_{x,g}(y)\ge0\) for every \(y\), with equality at \(y=x\).
special_cases_latex: For differentiable convex \(f\), the unique supporting slope is \(g=\nabla f(x)\).
For \(f(y)=\max_i\{\langle a_i,y\rangle+b_i\}\), each convex combination of slopes active at \(x\) defines a supporting model at \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The supporting-model error \(e_{x,g}(y):=f(y)-m_{x,g}(y)\) is nonnegative globally and vanishes at \(x\).
The existence of a supporting model is equivalent to subdifferentiability at \(x\).
boundary_notes: A first-order Taylor expression for a nonconvex function need not be a global minorant and therefore is not a supporting model in this sense.
At a boundary point of an extended-valued convex function, a supporting model may fail to exist.

notation.meaning: Affine model touching \(f\) at \(x\) with slope \(g\).

knowledge_statements.title: Global Affine Support
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a subgradient exactly when its affine model globally underestimates the convex function and touches it at the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g\in X\), define \(a_{x,g}(y)=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\). Then \(g\) is a convex subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) exactly when \(a_{x,g}\) is a global affine minorant of \(f\): \[g\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in X.\] In this case the minorant contacts \(f\) at \(x\), since \(a_{x,g}(x)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\in\partial f(x)\iff a_{x,g}(y)\le f(y)\) for every \(y\in X\), with equality at \(y=x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space characterization of a convex subgradient by a globally supporting affine minorant.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-Normal Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients are precisely the horizontal components of epigraph normals normalized to have final coordinate minus one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(g\in X\), \[g\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (g,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x)).\] Thus subgradient information is represented by epigraph normals whose final coordinate is \(-1\), and the corresponding hyperplane supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\in\partial f(x)\iff(g,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone representation using the epigraph normal whose final coordinate is normalized to \(-1\).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to a closed convex set C at z.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.4 Tangent and Normal Cones p. 125

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, let \(z_x:=(x,f(x))\), and define \(\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(y,r):r\ge f(y)\}\). For a convex set \(C\), use \(N_C(z):=\{v:\langle v,w-z\rangle\le0\ \forall w\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex epigraph geometry. The vertical component is normalized to \(-1\) to recover a subgradient rather than an arbitrary conic multiple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The epigraph-normal representation of the convex subdifferential is
\[
g\in\partial f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(g,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x)).
\]
Equivalently, the entire normal cone is
\[
N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))
=
\{(\lambda g,-\lambda):g\in\partial f(x),\ \lambda\ge0\}.
\]
The associated tangent cone is
\[
T_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))
=
\{(d,r):r\ge f'(x;d)\}
=
\operatorname{epi}(f'(x;\cdot)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subgradient is exactly a normal to the epigraph whose vertical coordinate has been normalized to minus one. Allowing nonnegative scaling generates the complete normal cone. Dually, the tangent cone to the epigraph at the graph point is the epigraph of the directional-derivative function. Thus the subdifferential is a horizontal slice of epigraph-normal geometry, while directional behavior is encoded by epigraph tangents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial f(x)\times\{-1\}=N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{-1\}).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(g,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\iff \langle g,y-x\rangle-(r-f(x))\le0\quad\forall (y,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f.\]
It is enough in the preceding inequality to take \(r=f(y)\), yielding the subgradient inequality.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), the nonvertical boundary ray of the normal cone is generated by \((\nabla f(x),-1)\).
The zero vector in the epigraph normal cone corresponds to \(\lambda=0\), not to an additional subgradient.
immediate_consequences_latex: The support hyperplane with normal \((g,-1)\) touches \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\).
The polar relation between epigraph tangent and normal cones reproduces \(f'(x;d)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle\).
boundary_notes: For extended-valued functions the normal cone may contain nonzero horizontal normals \((v,0)\); these encode domain geometry and are not obtained by normalizing the vertical coordinate to \(-1\).
The displayed full-cone formula is stated here in the finite-valued setting supported by the cited source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural profile of a convex subdifferential value
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb{E}\) be a finite-dimensional normed space with dual \(\mathbb{E}^*\), and let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper convex functions, including extended-valued functions. Closedness and convexity hold at every point; nonemptiness and boundedness depend on domain position.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{E}\), define
\[
\partial f(x):=\{g\in\mathbb{E}^*:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in\mathbb{E}\}.
\]
Its structural profile is governed by
\[
\partial f(x)\text{ is always closed and convex},
\]
with the convention \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) when no supporting slope exists. If \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), then \(\partial f(x)\) is nonempty and bounded, hence compact. If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), it is nonempty, but it need not be bounded in the ambient dual space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex subdifferential value is an intersection of closed half-spaces in the dual space and is therefore closed and convex, even when empty. At an interior domain point it is nonempty and bounded, so finite dimensionality makes it compact. Relative-interior points still guarantee existence, but lower-dimensional domains can contribute arbitrary normal directions and hence unbounded subdifferential values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Longrightarrow \varnothing\ne\partial f(x)\text{ is compact and convex},\qquad \operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\partial f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\partial f(x)=\bigcap_{y\in\mathbb{E}}\{g\in\mathbb{E}^*:\langle g,y-x\rangle\le f(y)-f(x)\}.\]
\[\operatorname{dom}(\partial f):=\{x:\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued and convex, then \(\partial f(x)\) is nonempty and compact for every \(x\in\mathbb{E}\).
If \(\dim(\operatorname{dom}f)<\dim(\mathbb{E})\) and \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\), then \(\partial f(x)\) is unbounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: A singleton value is compatible with differentiability, whereas a non-singleton compact value records finite nonsmoothness.
Compact subsets of \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) have uniformly bounded unions of subdifferential values.
boundary_notes: At boundary points, proper convexity alone guarantees neither existence nor boundedness.
Closedness of the function is not required for the elementary closedness and convexity of each subdifferential value.

notation.meaning: Set of points where the convex subdifferential is nonempty.
Relative interior in the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferentiability by Domain Position
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex functions are subdifferentiable throughout their relative domain interior; ambient interior is a special case, while boundary values can fail or become unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every point \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) admits a relative supporting affine minorant and hence satisfies \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\). In particular, \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) implies subdifferentiability in the ambient space. If \(A\ne\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\partial f(x)\) contains the affine family obtained by adding \((A-A)^\perp\) to any one subgradient. At relative-boundary points, the subdifferential may be empty or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Rightarrow\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\), while no such conclusion holds at \(x\in\operatorname{rbd}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative-interior theorem, including lower-dimensional effective domains and boundary limitations.

notation.meaning: Relative interior within the affine hull A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior, relative-interior, and boundary subdifferentiability regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on a finite-dimensional space. Write \(D:=\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(A:=\operatorname{aff}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition classifies points by their position in the effective domain and records the corresponding guaranteed subdifferential behavior in the ambient dual space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The domain-position regime of \(x\in\mathbb{E}\) is defined as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{full interior: }x\in\operatorname{int}D,\\
&\text{relative interior: }x\in\operatorname{ri}D=\{x\in A:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap A\subseteq D\},\\
&\text{relative boundary: }x\in D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D,\\
&\text{outside domain: }x\notin D.
\end{aligned}
\]
The associated guarantees are
\[
x\in\operatorname{int}D\Rightarrow\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\text{ and bounded},
\qquad
x\in\operatorname{ri}D\Rightarrow\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing.
\]
For \(x\notin D\), \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\). No general nonemptiness guarantee holds on \(D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is classified using the ordinary interior, the relative interior inside the affine hull of the domain, the relative boundary, or the exterior of the domain. Ordinary interior points have nonempty bounded subdifferentials. Relative-interior points have nonempty subdifferentials, although ambient normal directions may make them unbounded when the domain is lower dimensional. Relative-boundary points may or may not be subdifferentiable. Outside the effective domain the convex subdifferential is empty by convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{int}D\subseteq\{x:0<|\partial f(x)|<\infty\text{ in the set-theoretic nonemptiness sense and }\partial f(x)\text{ bounded}\},\qquad \operatorname{ri}D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}(\partial f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{ri}D\iff \exists\varepsilon>0:\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}D\subseteq D.\]
When \(A=\mathbb{E}\), one has \(\operatorname{ri}D=\operatorname{int}D\).
special_cases_latex: If \(D=\mathbb{E}\), every point is an interior point and every subdifferential value is nonempty and bounded.
If \(D\) is contained in a proper affine subspace and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}D\), then \(\partial f(x)\) is nonempty and unbounded in \(\mathbb{E}^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty convex domain has a relative-interior point, so every proper convex function is subdifferentiable somewhere.
Domain boundary is the only possible location of subdifferentiability failure for a proper convex function when position is understood relative to \(\operatorname{aff}D\).
boundary_notes: Relative-interior existence does not imply boundedness unless the domain has full ambient dimension.
Boundary membership alone does not decide whether \(\partial f(x)\) is empty, bounded, or unbounded.

notation.meaning: Affine hull of the effective domain.

children.title: Subgradient Boundedness-Lipschitz Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Local regularity organized through bounded and unbounded subgradient behavior.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz regularity characterized by uniformly bounded subgradients
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\mathbb{E},\|\cdot\|)\) be finite dimensional, let \(\|\cdot\|_*\) be the dual norm, let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(X\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two-sided equivalence uses an open set \(X\). On an arbitrary subset, uniform subgradient boundedness still implies the Lipschitz inequality, but the converse need not follow from values restricted to that subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L\ge0\), define uniform \(L\)-boundedness of subgradients on \(X\) by
\[
\sup\{\|g\|_*:x\in X,\ g\in\partial f(x)\}\le L,
\]
and \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity on \(X\) by
\[
|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in X).
\]
Uniform \(L\)-boundedness implies \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity for every such \(X\). If \(X\) is open, the two conditions are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients are uniformly bounded by \(L\) on a set when every subgradient at every point of the set has dual norm at most \(L\). This bound implies that function values vary by at most \(L\) times the distance. When the set is open, the converse also holds: an \(L\)-Lipschitz convex function cannot possess a subgradient of dual norm greater than \(L\) there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bigl(\|g\|_*\le L\ \forall x\in X,\forall g\in\partial f(x)\bigr)\Rightarrow |f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\ \forall x,y\in X,\] with equivalence when \(X\) is open.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For open \(X\), the least Lipschitz constant equals \(\sup_{x\in X}\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\|g\|_*\), allowing the value \(+\infty\).
In Euclidean space, \(\partial f(X):=\bigcup_{x\in X}\partial f(x)\subseteq L B_*\) is equivalent to \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity on open \(X\).
special_cases_latex: If \(X\) is compact and contained in \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), then \(\partial f(X)\) is bounded and \(f\) is Lipschitz on \(X\).
If \(f\) is differentiable on open \(X\), the condition reduces to \(\|\nabla f(x)\|_*\le L\) for every \(x\in X\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Unbounded subgradients on an open region rule out every finite Lipschitz constant there.
Local boundedness of the subdifferential mapping on the domain interior is equivalent to local Lipschitz regularity of the convex function.
boundary_notes: The converse can fail for nonopen \(X\), because the values of \(f\) on \(X\) may not probe directions in which a boundary subgradient is large.
The assumption \(X\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) ensures that the relevant subdifferentials are nonempty.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Subgradient Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients are uniformly bounded near every interior-domain point, and uniformly over compact subsets of the domain interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist \(r>0\) and \(M<+\infty\) such that \(B(x,2r)\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and \[\|g\|\le M\quad\text{for every }y\in B(x,r)\text{ and every }g\in\partial f(y).\] More generally, for every compact set \(K\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), the union \(\bigcup_{y\in K}\partial f(y)\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcup_{y\in B(x,r)}\partial f(y)\) is bounded for some \(r>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Regularity Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open convex domain, a convex function is L-Lipschitz exactly when every subgradient has norm at most L.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following statements are equivalent: \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(U\), meaning \(|f(y)-f(x)|\le L\|y-x\|\) for all \(x,y\in U\); and every subgradient satisfies \(\|g\|\le L\) for all \(x\in U\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\). Consequently, local boundedness of subgradients and local Lipschitz continuity are interchangeable on interior neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(U\) if and only if \(\|g\|\le L\) for all \(x\in U\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Lipschitz–subgradient-bound equivalence on an open convex Euclidean domain.

notation.meaning: Euclidean norm and its induced dual norm.
Convex subdifferential relative to the open domain U.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Breakdown Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a domain boundary, a continuous convex function can lose all subgradients while nearby subgradient norms diverge and Lipschitz regularity fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended-real function \(f(t)=-\sqrt t\) for \(t\ge0\) and \(f(t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For \(t>0\), \(\partial f(t)=\{-1/(2\sqrt t)\}\), so subgradients diverge as \(t\downarrow0\). At the boundary, no \(g\in\mathbb{R}\) can satisfy \(-\sqrt y\ge gy\) for every \(y\\ge0\); hence \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), and \(f\) is not locally Lipschitz at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is finite and continuous at \(0\), but \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\) and its interior subgradients are unbounded near \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary example showing loss of subgradients, boundedness, and local Lipschitz regularity.

notation.meaning: Extended-real convex function on the real line.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The boundary example is mathematically plausible and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but it has no cited source. The expression intended as \(y\ge0\) also contains a duplicated backslash and requires repair once sourced.

children.title: Subdifferential Value Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure and boundary regimes for existence and boundedness.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on a finite-dimensional space, and let \(D:=\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record classifies failure of a convex subdifferential value through emptiness and unboundedness. It does not assert that every domain-boundary point fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the subdifferential failure sets
\[
F_{\varnothing}(f):=\{x\in D:\partial f(x)=\varnothing\},
\qquad
F_{\infty}(f):=\{x\in D:\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\text{ and }\partial f(x)\text{ is unbounded}\}.
\]
For every proper convex \(f\),
\[
F_{\varnothing}(f)\subseteq D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D,
\qquad
F_{\infty}(f)\cap\operatorname{int}D=\varnothing.
\]
If \(\dim D<\dim\mathbb{E}\), then every nonempty value is unbounded:
\[
x\in D,\ \partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\Longrightarrow x\in F_{\infty}(f).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The empty-value failure set consists of domain points having no supporting affine slope. The unbounded-value failure set consists of points where supporting slopes exist but are not bounded in the ambient dual space. Empty values can occur only outside the relative interior of the effective domain. Unbounded values cannot occur at ordinary interior points. If the domain is lower dimensional, every nonempty subdifferential contains an affine line of ambient normal directions and is therefore unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_{\varnothing}(f)\subseteq D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D,\qquad F_{\infty}(f)\subseteq D\setminus\operatorname{int}D.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in F_{\varnothing}(f)\iff x\in D\setminus\operatorname{dom}(\partial f).\]

For \(x\in D\) with \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\), lower-dimensionality gives \(\partial f(x)+\bigl(\operatorname{aff}D-x\bigr)^\perp=\partial f(x)\), hence unboundedness when the orthogonal complement is nonzero.
special_cases_latex: For \(f(t)=-\sqrt{t}\) on \([0,+\infty)\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise, \(0\in F_{\varnothing}(f)\).
For an indicator \(f=\delta_A\) of a proper affine subspace \(A\), \(\partial f(x)=A^\perp\) at every \(x\in A\), so every value is nonempty and unbounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: No empty-value failure occurs on \(\operatorname{ri}D\).
A finite-valued convex function has neither empty nor unbounded subdifferential values.
boundary_notes: The inclusions need not be equalities: some relative-boundary points have nonempty bounded subdifferentials, and some have nonempty unbounded values.
Unboundedness caused by a lower-dimensional domain is an ambient-space phenomenon; quotienting out normal directions changes the profile.

notation.meaning: Domain points with nonempty unbounded subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3, §3.2, Example 3.12 and Theorems 3.14, 3.18, and 3.20

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Subdifferential Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex function minus square root on the nonnegative half-line has no finite subgradient at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), defined by \(f(t)=-\sqrt t\) for \(t\ge0\) and \(f(t)=+\infty\) otherwise, is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. If \(g\in\partial f(0)\), then the subgradient inequality would require \(-\sqrt y\ge gy\) for every \(y>0\), equivalently \(g\le-1/\sqrt y\) for every \(y>0\). No finite \(g\) has this property, so \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed convex function with an empty subdifferential at a finite boundary point.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential at the domain endpoint.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample fits the empty-value leaf, but no source or locator is supplied, and the statement includes a derivation that should be removed in a sourced replacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Subdifferential Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of a half-line has an unbounded normal-cone subdifferential at its endpoint but only the zero subgradient in its interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the indicator \(f=\iota_{[0,+\infty)}\), \[\partial f(0)=N_{[0,+\infty)}(0)=(-\infty,0].\] Thus its subdifferential at the boundary point \(0\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and unbounded, whereas \(\partial f(x)=\{0\}\) for every \(x>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(0)=(-\infty,0]\), an unbounded closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator-function example of an unbounded subdifferential at a domain boundary.

notation.meaning: Zero on C and positive infinity outside C.
Normal cone to C at zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Boundary Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approaching a domain boundary can produce diverging subgradients, an empty limiting subdifferential, or a nonempty but unbounded boundary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Interior or relative-interior subdifferentiability does not extend uniformly to the domain boundary. Along a sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\), subgradients may satisfy \(\|g_k\|\to+\infty\) for every selection \(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\), while \(\partial f(\bar x)\) may be empty, as for \(f(t)=-\sqrt t\). Alternatively, the boundary value may be nonempty but unbounded, as \(\partial\iota_{[0,+\infty)}(0)=(-\infty,0]\). Additional boundary regularity is therefore required for persistence.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither boundedness nor nonemptiness of \(\partial f(x_k)\) necessarily persists at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary transition alternatives for subdifferential nonemptiness and boundedness.

notation.meaning: Relative boundary of the effective domain.
Distance from the origin to a set, with infinity for the empty set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative and its subgradient correspondence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and fix \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued finite-dimensional convex functions, for which every one-sided directional derivative is finite and the subdifferential is nonempty compact convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define
\[
f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}
=\inf_{t>0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.
\]
The map \(d\mapsto f'(x;d)\) is finite and sublinear. Its associated subdifferential correspondence is
\[
\partial f(x)=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle g,d\rangle\le f'(x;d)\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n\},
\]
and reciprocally
\[
f'(x;d)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-sided directional derivative is the decreasing-stepsize limit, equivalently the infimum, of convex difference quotients. As a function of direction it is finite, positively homogeneous, and subadditive. The convex subdifferential is the unique compact convex set whose support function is this directional derivative: subgradients are precisely the linear forms dominated by every directional derivative value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f'(x;\cdot)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)},\qquad \partial f(x)=\{g:\langle g,\cdot\rangle\le f'(x;\cdot)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[g\in\partial f(x)\iff \langle g,d\rangle\le f'(x;d)\quad\forall d.\]
\[f'(x;\lambda d)=\lambda f'(x;d)\quad(\lambda\ge0),\qquad f'(x;d_1+d_2)\le f'(x;d_1)+f'(x;d_2).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(f'(x;d)=\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle\) for every \(d\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every direction \(d\), at least one exposed subgradient \(g_d\in\partial f(x)\) satisfies \(f'(x;d)=\langle g_d,d\rangle\).
Linearity of \(f'(x;\cdot)\) is equivalent to \(\partial f(x)\) being a singleton.
boundary_notes: For extended-valued functions at boundary points, directional derivatives may be infinite and the compact-support representation requires additional qualification or an extended-real formulation.
The derivative is one-sided in the scalar step \(t\downarrow0\); it is not generally odd in \(d\).

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Support-Function Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a relative-interior point, every directional derivative equals the support function of the subdifferential evaluated in that direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the extended one-sided directional derivative exists and satisfies \[f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)=\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle.\] If \(d\) leaves \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), both sides equal \(+\infty\); otherwise the formula describes directional growth inside the affine hull. Thus the closed convex set \(\partial f(x)\) determines all first-order directional behavior through its support function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)=\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle\) for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional directional derivative as the support function of the full subdifferential.

notation.meaning: Support function of a set S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative as the support function of the subdifferential
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on a finite-dimensional space, and take \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-point representation. Here \(\partial f(x)\) is nonempty and compact and all directional derivatives are finite, so the support supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(d\in\mathbb{E}\), the directional support-function representation is
\[
f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)
:=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle.
\]
The maximizing face exposed by \(d\) is
\[
F_x(d):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle
=\{g\in\partial f(x):\langle g,d\rangle=f'(x;d)\}.
\]
Thus \(F_x(d)\) is nonempty for every \(d\), and the complete directional-derivative function uniquely determines the closed convex set \(\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative in a direction \(d\) is the largest pairing of \(d\) with a subgradient at \(x\). The subgradients attaining this maximum form the exposed face selected by that direction. Knowing these support values in all directions uniquely recovers the subdifferential, while a single direction generally reveals only one exposed face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f'(x;d)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle\quad\text{and}\quad F_x(d)\ne\varnothing\qquad\forall d\in\mathbb{E}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\partial f(x)=\bigcap_{d\in\mathbb{E}}\{g:\langle g,d\rangle\le f'(x;d)\}.\]
\[g\in F_x(d)\iff g\in\partial f(x)\text{ and }\langle g,d\rangle=f'(x;d).\]
special_cases_latex: For \(d=0\), every subgradient is maximizing: \(F_x(0)=\partial f(x)\).
If \(\partial f(x)=\{g\}\), then \(F_x(d)=\{g\}\) and \(f'(x;d)=\langle g,d\rangle\) for all \(d\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The width of \(\partial f(x)\) in direction \(d\) is \(f'(x;d)+f'(x;-d)\).
A positive width in some direction certifies that the subdifferential is not a singleton.
boundary_notes: Support values determine the closed convex hull of any candidate slope set; nonclosed or nonconvex generating sets are not distinguished by their support functions.
At noninterior domain points, compactness and finiteness may fail, so a maximum may have to be replaced by an extended-real supremum.

notation.meaning: Face of \(\partial f(x)\) exposed by direction \(d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Descent cone and polar subgradient cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, fix \(x\), and let \(S_x:=\{y:f(y)\le f(x)\}\). For a cone \(K\), set \(K^\circ:=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\le0\ \forall d\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued convex functions at a nonminimal level point satisfying \(0\notin\partial f(x)\). This qualification is essential for the exact sublevel tangent formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed descent cone at \(x\) is
\[
D_f(x):=T_{S_x}(x).
\]
If \(0\notin\partial f(x)\), then
\[
D_f(x)=\{d:f'(x;d)\le0\}
=\{d:\langle g,d\rangle\le0\ \forall g\in\partial f(x)\}
=(\mathbb{R}_+\partial f(x))^\circ.
\]
Its polar, equivalently the normal cone to \(S_x\), is
\[
D_f(x)^\circ=N_{S_x}(x)=\mathbb{R}_+\partial f(x).
\]
Strict descent directions are exactly \(\operatorname{int}D_f(x)=\{d:f'(x;d)<0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The descent cone is the tangent cone to the sublevel set passing through \(x\). Away from the minimizer regime, it consists exactly of directions whose convex directional derivative is nonpositive. It is the polar of the cone generated by the subdifferential, while its own polar is that generated subgradient cone. Directions with strictly negative directional derivative form the interior of the descent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D_f(x)=(\operatorname{cone}\partial f(x))^\circ,\qquad D_f(x)^\circ=\operatorname{cone}\partial f(x),\qquad 0\notin\partial f(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in D_f(x)\iff \sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)=f'(x;d)\le0.\]
\[v\in N_{S_x}(x)\iff \exists\lambda\ge0,\exists g\in\partial f(x):v=\lambda g.\]

Strict descent exists under the qualification: \(\{d:f'(x;d)<0\}\ne\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A direction is certified as nonascending exactly when every subgradient has nonpositive pairing with it.
Normal certificates to the active sublevel set are precisely nonnegative multiples of subgradients.

knowledge_statements.title: Descent-Cone Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The descent cone consists of all nonnegative scalings of displacements from the base point to points with no larger objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The descent cone of \(f\) at \(x\) is \[D_f(x)=\operatorname{cone}\bigl(\{y-x:y\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ f(y)\le f(x)\}\bigr).\] Equivalently, \(d\in D_f(x)\) when \(d=\lambda(y-x)\) for some \(\lambda\ge0\) and some \(y\) with \(f(y)\le f(x)\). Convexity ensures that the segment from \(x\) toward such a point remains in the sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(x)=\operatorname{cone}\{y-x:f(y)\le f(x)\}\), and every \(d\in D_f(x)\) generates a nonincreasing feasible segment from \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Separation Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is strictly descending exactly when it places every subgradient in the same open negative halfspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the directional derivative exists in \(\mathbb{R}\) and satisfies \[f'(x;d)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle.\] Consequently, \(d\) is a strict descent direction, meaning \(f'(x;d)<0\), exactly when the entire compact convex set \(\partial f(x)\) lies in the open halfspace \(\{g:\langle g,d\rangle<0\}\). children.title: Subdifferential Cardinality Profiles
children.top_down_role: Smooth and nonsmooth directional signatures encoded by subdifferential values.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empty, singleton, and multivalued subdifferential profiles
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on a finite-dimensional space, and let \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) unless explicitly stated otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The smooth-versus-nonsmooth equivalence is an interior-point statement. Empty values are included only as a boundary profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the subdifferential cardinality profile at \(x\) by
\[
\kappa_f(x):=
\begin{cases}
0,&\partial f(x)=\varnothing,\\
1,&\partial f(x)\text{ is a singleton},\\
>1,&\partial f(x)\text{ contains at least two points}.
\end{cases}
\]
At an interior domain point, \(\kappa_f(x)\ne0\), and
\[
\kappa_f(x)=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }x,
\]
in which case
\[
\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\},
\qquad
f'(x;d)=\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle\quad\forall d.
\]
Hence \(\kappa_f(x)>1\) is the convex nonsmooth profile at an interior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profile distinguishes an empty subdifferential, a unique subgradient, and multiple subgradients. Interior points cannot have the empty profile. There, having exactly one subgradient is equivalent to differentiability, and that unique vector is the gradient. A multivalued subdifferential therefore records convex nonsmoothness through direction-dependent supporting slopes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Longrightarrow\bigl(\partial f(x)=\{g\}\iff f\text{ is differentiable at }x\text{ and }g=\nabla f(x)\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: At an interior point, \(\kappa_f(x)=1\) if and only if \(d\mapsto f'(x;d)\) is linear.
At an interior point, \(\kappa_f(x)>1\) if and only if the support function \(\sigma_{\partial f(x)}\) is non-linear.
special_cases_latex: For \(f(t)=|t|\), \(\kappa_f(0)>1\) because \(\partial f(0)=[-1,1]\), whereas \(\kappa_f(t)=1\) for \(t\ne0\).
A boundary point can have \(\kappa_f(x)=0\), as for \(f(t)=-\sqrt{t}\) on \([0,+\infty)\) at \(t=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If there exist directions for which different subgradients maximize the directional pairing, then \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x\).
Differentiability at an interior point can be tested entirely from the set-valued size of \(\partial f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Singleton Subdifferential Profiles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior singleton subdifferential produces a linear directional-derivative profile and equals the ordinary gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support representation of the directional derivative reduces to \[f'(x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,d\rangle=\langle g,d\rangle\qquad(d\in\mathbb{R}^n).\] Hence the complete directional-derivative profile is linear. At an interior point of the effective domain, this linearity implies that \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), and its gradient is the unique subgradient: \(\nabla f(x)=g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\langle g,d\rangle\) for every \(d\), and \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) with \(\nabla f(x)=g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-point profile in finite-dimensional convex analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Multivalued Subdifferential Profiles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple subgradients create positive directional width, making the directional-derivative profile nonlinear and ruling out differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d).\] Because \(\partial f(x)\) is not a singleton, its support function is not linear. More concretely, some \(d\) has positive subgradient width, so \[f'(x;d)+f'(x;-d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)+\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(-d)>0.\] Therefore the directional derivatives cannot be represented by one linear functional, and \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\mapsto f'(x;d)\) is not linear, and \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability Transition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point, differentiability, a singleton subdifferential, and a linear directional-derivative profile are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following conditions are equivalent: \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\); the set \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton; and the map \(d\mapsto f'(x;d)\) is linear on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). When they hold, the unique element of \(\partial f(x)\) is \(\nabla f(x)\), and \[f'(x;d)=\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle\qquad(d\in\mathbb{R}^n).\] Thus loss or acquisition of differentiability occurs precisely through a change between multivalued and singleton subdifferential profiles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) if and only if \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate contact interface for convex subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb{E}\) be finite dimensional, let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and define \(f^*:\mathbb{E}^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(f^*(y):=\sup_{z\in\mathbb{E}}\{\langle y,z\rangle-f(z)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equality certificate is valid for proper convex \(f\). The inverse-subdifferential equivalence additionally uses closedness of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\mathbb{E}\) and \(y\in\mathbb{E}^*\), the conjugate–subdifferential contact interface is
\[
y\in\partial f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle.
\]
If \(f\) is also closed, then this is further equivalent to
\[
x\in\partial f^*(y).
\]
Thus, for proper closed convex \(f\),
\[
y\in\partial f(x)
\Longleftrightarrow
(x,y)\text{ is a zero Fenchel--Young-gap pair}
\Longleftrightarrow
x\in\partial f^*(y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate pairs a primal point and a dual point through Fenchel–Young equality. A dual vector is a subgradient at the primal point exactly when the universal Fenchel–Young inequality is tight at that pair. If the function is closed as well as proper and convex, contact is symmetric: the primal point is then a subgradient of the conjugate at the dual point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle,\] and, for closed \(f\), this is equivalent to \(x\in\partial f^*(y)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[y\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in\mathbb{E}}\{\langle y,z\rangle-f(z)\}.\]
For closed \(f\), \[x\in\partial f^*(y)\iff y\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in\mathbb{E}^*}\{\langle x,v\rangle-f^*(v)\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), contact forces \(y=\nabla f(x)\).
If \(f=\delta_C\) for a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), then \(f^*=\sigma_C\), and contact becomes \(x\in C\) together with \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sigma_C(y)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The graph of \(\partial f\) is the zero set of the Fenchel–Young gap.
For closed convex \(f\), \(\operatorname{gra}(\partial f^*)\) is obtained from \(\operatorname{gra}(\partial f)\) by swapping primal and dual coordinates.
boundary_notes: Without closedness, equality still characterizes \(y\in\partial f(x)\), but the reverse membership \(x\in\partial f^*(y)\) naturally pertains to the closed convex hull of \(f\).
The pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle\) is the duality pairing, not necessarily a Euclidean dot product.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel–Young gap as a subgradient certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with conjugate \(f^*\). For \((x,y)\in\mathbb{E}\times\mathbb{E}^*\), allow extended-real gap values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex subgradient certificates. The zero-gap equivalence does not require differentiability; inverse membership additionally requires closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Fenchel–Young gap is
\[
G_f(x,y):=f(x)+f^*(y)-\langle x,y\rangle\in[0,+\infty].
\]
A pair \((x,y)\) is a Fenchel–Young subgradient certificate when
\[
G_f(x,y)=0.
\]
The certificate is valid exactly when
\[
G_f(x,y)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
y\in\partial f(x).
\]
If \(f\) is closed, the same certificate is equivalent to \(x\in\partial f^*(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel–Young gap measures the slack in the conjugacy inequality. It is always nonnegative. A zero gap is an exact certificate that the dual point is a subgradient of the primal function at the primal point. For a closed convex function, the same equality simultaneously certifies the reverse subgradient relation for the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G_f(x,y)=0\iff y\in\partial f(x),\qquad G_f(x,y)\ge0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[G_f(x,y)=0\iff f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle-f(x),\] meaning that \(x\) attains the supremum defining \(f^*(y)\).
For closed \(f\), \[G_f(x,y)=0\iff (x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}(\partial f)\iff (y,x)\in\operatorname{gra}(\partial f^*).\]
special_cases_latex: At a differentiability point, \(G_f(x,y)=0\) holds exactly for \(y=\nabla f(x)\).
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\), one has \(G_f(x,y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2\), so zero gap means \(x=y\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Any positive finite gap rules out exact subgradient membership for that pair.
The set of all exact certificates is precisely \(\operatorname{gra}(\partial f)\).
boundary_notes: An infinite gap is permitted when either point lies outside the effective domain of the corresponding function.
This exact certificate should not be confused with an \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient certificate, where a positive gap up to \(\varepsilon\) is allowed.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Contact Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero Fenchel–Young gap certifies that the primal and dual points are mutual subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fenchel–Young inequality gives \(G_f(x,y)\geq0\). The pair \((x,y)\) is in primal–dual contact exactly when this computable gap vanishes: \[G_f(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle.\] This equality is equivalent both to \(y\in\partial f(x)\) and to \(x\in\partial f^*(y)\). Hence equality of the primal value, dual value, and pairing certifies mutual subgradient compatibility.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\iff y\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\partial f^*(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Young equality as a verifiable primal–dual contact certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–dual contact set of a convex function and its conjugate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(f^*\) be its Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual contact for closed convex functions. Contact means equality in conjugacy, not merely feasibility of the two domain points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The primal–dual contact set of \(f\) is
\[
\mathcal C_f:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{E}\times\mathbb{E}^*:f(x)<+\infty,\ f^*(y)<+\infty,\ f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\}.
\]
It admits the equivalent graph descriptions
\[
\mathcal C_f
=\{(x,y):y\in\partial f(x)\}
=\{(x,y):x\in\partial f^*(y)\}.
\]
Thus a contact pair simultaneously certifies primal support, dual support, and attainment in both conjugate supremum representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal point and a dual point are in contact when both conjugate values are finite and their Fenchel–Young inequality is tight. For a proper closed convex function, the contact set is exactly the graph of its subdifferential and, after swapping the roles of the coordinates, the graph of the conjugate subdifferential. Contact therefore records compatible primal and dual support at once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_f=\operatorname{gra}(\partial f)=\{(x,y):(y,x)\in\operatorname{gra}(\partial f^*)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x,y)\in\mathcal C_f\iff x\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{z}\{\langle y,z\rangle-f(z)\}.\]
\[(x,y)\in\mathcal C_f\iff y\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{v}\{\langle x,v\rangle-f^*(v)\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), the only dual point in contact with \(x\) is \(y=\nabla f(x)\).
If \(f^*\) is differentiable at \(y\), the only primal point in contact with \(y\) is \(x=\nabla f^*(y)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal projection of \(\mathcal C_f\) is \(\operatorname{dom}(\partial f)\), and its dual projection is \(\operatorname{dom}(\partial f^*)\).
Contact is symmetric under conjugation: \((x,y)\in\mathcal C_f\) exactly when \((y,x)\in\mathcal C_{f^*}\), with the natural primal-dual identification.
boundary_notes: A pair with finite \(f(x)\) and \(f^*(y)\) need not be a contact pair; equality is essential.
Closedness ensures \(f^{**}=f\) and therefore the symmetric dual subgradient characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Inverse Relation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate subdifferential is exactly the inverse relation of the original subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), Fenchel–Young equality yields the graph equivalence \[y\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(y).\] Equivalently, reversing the ordered pairs in the graph of \(\partial f\) gives the graph of \(\partial f^*\): \[\operatorname{gra}(\partial f^*)=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}(\partial f)\}.\] Thus, as set-valued relations, \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-graph identity for closed proper convex functions in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: Inverse relation of the set-valued subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse graph identity for conjugate subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. For a set-valued map \(T:\mathbb{E}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{E}^*\), define \(T^{-1}(y):=\{x:y\in T(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex conjugacy. The identity is set-valued and remains meaningful when either subdifferential value has multiple points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The subdifferential of the conjugate is the inverse relation of the original subdifferential:
\[
(\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*.
\]
Explicitly, for every \(x\in\mathbb{E}\) and \(y\in\mathbb{E}^*\),
\[
y\in\partial f(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in\partial f^*(y).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{gra}(\partial f^*)
=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gra}(\partial f)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Viewing the subdifferential as a relation from primal points to dual points, conjugation reverses that relation. A dual point is a subgradient of \(f\) at a primal point exactly when the primal point is a subgradient of \(f^*\) at the dual point. Thus the two graphs are coordinate transposes of one another.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\partial f)^{-1}(y)=\partial f^*(y)\qquad\forall y\in\mathbb{E}^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[y\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\iff x\in\partial f^*(y).\]
\[x\in(\partial f)^{-1}(y)\iff x\in\partial f^*(y).\]
special_cases_latex: If both \(f\) and \(f^*\) are differentiable at corresponding points, \(y=\nabla f(x)\) if and only if \(x=\nabla f^*(y)\).
For a strictly convex but nonsmooth function, \(\partial f\) may still be set-valued; the relation identity does not require single-valuedness.
immediate_consequences_latex: The domain of \(\partial f^*\) equals the range of \(\partial f\).
The range of \(\partial f^*\) equals the domain of \(\partial f\).
boundary_notes: Closedness is essential for identifying the reverse relation with \(\partial f^*\) without replacing \(f\) by its closed convex hull.
The inverse is a set-valued relational inverse, not a matrix inverse or a claim of bijectivity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infimal-convolution interface for conjugates and subgradients
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h_1:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(h_2:\mathbb{E}\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. Define \((u\square v)(y):=\inf_{z\in\mathbb{E}^*}\{u(z)+v(y-z)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact conjugate-of-sum interface under the stated real-valued qualification on \(h_2\). The operation is retained because its exact decompositions encode subgradient splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conjugate operation interface for a sum is the exact infimal convolution
\[
(h_1+h_2)^*(y)
=(h_1^*\square h_2^*)(y)
=
\min_{z\in\mathbb{E}^*}\{h_1^*(z)+h_2^*(y-z)\}.
\]
A minimizing decomposition \(y=y_1+y_2\) is a subgradient-compatible decomposition at \(x\) when
\[
y_1\in\partial h_1(x),
\qquad
y_2\in\partial h_2(x).
\]
For such a decomposition,
\[
x\in\partial h_1^*(y_1)\cap\partial h_2^*(y_2),
\qquad
y=y_1+y_2\in\partial(h_1+h_2)(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated qualification, conjugating a sum produces an attained infimal convolution of the individual conjugates. A dual vector is decomposed as \(y=y_1+y_2\), with the conjugate costs added. When both pieces contact the same primal point, each piece is a subgradient of its corresponding summand, and their sum is a subgradient of the primal sum. The same contact can be read through the inverse subdifferentials of the conjugates.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a compatible contact point \(x\), \[y_i\in\partial h_i(x)\iff h_i(x)+h_i^*(y_i)=\langle x,y_i\rangle\quad(i=1,2).\]
Summing the two contact equalities gives \[(h_1+h_2)(x)+(h_1^*\square h_2^*)(y)=\langle x,y\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(h_2\equiv0\), then \(h_2^*=\delta_{\{0\}}\), so the only decomposition has \(y_2=0\).
When both summands are differentiable at \(x\), the compatible decomposition is \(y_1=\nabla h_1(x)\), \(y_2=\nabla h_2(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact dual decompositions provide componentwise subgradient certificates for a sum.
The infimal convolution is attained at every \(y\) in the effective domain of \((h_1+h_2)^*\) under the cited hypotheses.
boundary_notes: Without an appropriate domain qualification, the infimum may fail to be attained or the infimal convolution may require lower-semicontinuous closure.

The displayed componentwise contact conditions characterize compatible decompositions; an arbitrary minimizing decomposition should not be assigned a common contact point unless the relevant subgradient membership is established.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum–Infimal-Convolution Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under relative-interior qualification, conjugating a sum gives an attained infimal convolution, with dual components supplied by the subgradient sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[(f+g)^*(y)=(f^*\mathbin{\square}g^*)(y)=\min_{u+v=y}\bigl(f^*(u)+g^*(v)\bigr)\] whenever the value is finite. Moreover, for \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[y\in\partial(f+g)(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists u\in\partial f(x),\ v\in\partial g(x)\text{ with }u+v=y.\] Such a decomposition attains the displayed infimal convolution and provides compatible Fenchel–Young contacts for both summands.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f+g)^*=f^*\mathbin{\square}g^*\), with attained decompositions at finite values and compatible subgradients.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional conjugacy under relative-interior qualification.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions. Their Fenchel conjugates are \(f_i^*(u)=\sup_x\{\langle u,x\rangle-f_i(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex analysis; closure and attainment are separated from the unconditional conjugacy identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal convolution is \[(f_1\square\cdots\square f_m)(x)=\inf_{x_1+\cdots+x_m=x}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i).\] The sum–infimal-convolution duality consists of \[(f_1\square\cdots\square f_m)^*=f_1^*+\cdots+f_m^*\] whenever the infimal convolution has no value \(-\infty\), and \[(f_1+\cdots+f_m)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f_1^*\square\cdots\square f_m^*).\] If \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\neq\varnothing\), the closure is unnecessary and the dual infimum is attained at every point where it is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution assigns to \(x\) the least total value obtained by decomposing \(x\) as \(x_1+\cdots+x_m\). Conjugation turns infimal convolution into pointwise addition. Conversely, the conjugate of a sum is the lower-semicontinuous closure of the infimal convolution of the conjugates. A common relative-interior point of the primal domains makes the latter infimal convolution exact and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(f_1\square\cdots\square f_m)^*=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*,\qquad (\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f_1^*\square\cdots\square f_m^*).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\neq\varnothing\), \[(\sum_i f_i)^*(u)=\min_{u_1+\cdots+u_m=u}\sum_i f_i^*(u_i).\]
If \(x=\sum_i x_i\) attains the primal infimal convolution, then \[u\in\partial(f_1\square\cdots\square f_m)(x)\iff u\in\bigcap_i\partial f_i(x_i).\]
special_cases_latex: For two functions, \((f\square g)(x)=\inf_y\{f(x-y)+g(y)\}\).
If one factor is \(\iota_{\{a\}}\), then \((f\square\iota_{\{a\}})(x)=f(x-a)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A minimizing dual decomposition \(u=\sum_i u_i\) is compatible with the sum subgradient rule when \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\).
The domain satisfies \(\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\) when the infimal convolution is proper.

children.title: Affine Linear-Image Duality Family
children.top_down_role: Conjugate representations associated with affine precomposition and linear images.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be linear, with adjoint \(A^*\), and let \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine precomposition and infimal linear images; exact formulas require the stated relative-interior condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), define \(h(x)=g(Ax+b)+\langle c,x\rangle+\alpha\). Its conjugate is the lower-semicontinuous closure of \[u\mapsto\inf_{A^*v=u-c}\bigl(g^*(v)-\langle b,v\rangle-\alpha\bigr).\] If \(A\mathbb{R}^n\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g-b)\neq\varnothing\), the infimum is attained and the closure is unnecessary. The complementary linear-image operation is \[(A\mathbin{\triangleright}f)(y)=\inf_{Ax=y}f(x),\] for which \[(A\mathbin{\triangleright}f)^*(v)=f^*(A^*v)\] whenever the image function has no value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine precomposition pulls a dual vector back through the adjoint. Thus the conjugate at \(u\) is obtained by minimizing the shifted conjugate of \(g\) over all \(v\) satisfying \(A^*v=u-c\). In the reverse construction, the infimal image of \(f\) assigns to \(y\) the infimum of \(f\) on the fiber \(A^{-1}\{y\}\), and its conjugate is simply \(f^*\circ A^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[h^*(u)=\operatorname{cl}\inf_{A^*v=u-c}\{g^*(v)-\langle b,v\rangle-\alpha\},\qquad (A\mathbin{\triangleright}f)^*=f^*\circ A^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(b=c=0\) and \(\alpha=0\), \[(g\circ A)^*(u)=\operatorname{cl}\inf_{A^*v=u}g^*(v).\]
The infimal image has domain \(\operatorname{dom}(A\mathbin{\triangleright}f)=A(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, \((g\circ A)^*(u)=g^*(A^{-*}u)\).
Translation alone gives \((x\mapsto g(x+b))^*(v)=g^*(v)-\langle b,v\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Dual feasibility for affine precomposition is the adjoint equation \(A^*v=u-c\).
Linear images and affine precomposition form a conjugate pair of operations.
boundary_notes: If the adjoint equation has no solution, the corresponding infimum is \(+\infty\).
Without the relative-interior condition, closure or nonattainment can occur.

notation.meaning: infimal postcomposition, or infimal linear image, of the function

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Precomposition Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of an affine precomposition is a constrained minimum over adjoint-compatible dual vectors, with a translation correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=f(Ax+b)\). For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[h^*(u)=\min_{v\in\mathbb{R}^m}\bigl\{f^*(v)-\langle v,b\rangle:A^*v=u\bigr\},\] with the convention that the minimum is \(+\infty\) when the constraint is infeasible. Under the stated qualification, every finite value is attained. Thus dual variables for an affine precomposition must satisfy the adjoint compatibility equation \(A^*v=u\), while translation contributes the linear correction \(-\langle v,b\rangle\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f\circ(A\cdot+b))^*(u)=\min_{A^*v=u}\{f^*(v)-\langle v,b\rangle\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine-precomposition conjugacy with relative-interior qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Image Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating an infimal linear image composes the original conjugate with the adjoint map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(v\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the conjugate of the infimal image satisfies \[g^*(v)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\bigl(\langle v,y\rangle-g(y)\bigr)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(\langle A^*v,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr)=f^*(A^*v).\] This conjugate identity does not require attainment in the definition of \(g\). Lower semicontinuity or exact primal-image formulas, however, can require additional closedness or relative-interior hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g^*(v)=f^*(A^*v)\) for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^m\).

knowledge_statements.title: Range-Qualification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absent a range qualification, affine-precomposition duality may require lower-semicontinuous closure, and the dual infimum may be unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[q(u)=\inf\bigl\{f^*(v)-\langle v,b\rangle:A^*v=u\bigr\}.\] In general the exact identity is \[h^*(u)=(\operatorname{cl}q)(u),\] where closure is taken in the lower-semicontinuous convex sense. Without a condition such as \((b+\operatorname{range}A)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\neq\varnothing\), the value function \(q\) need not be closed at \(u\), and its infimum need not be attained. Therefore replacing \(\operatorname{cl}q\) by an attained minimum is not valid without qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h^*=\operatorname{cl}q\); the unclosed minimum formula can fail without a range qualification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Biconjugate as a Supremum of Affine Minorants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and admit an affine minorant. Define \(f^*(u)=\sup_x\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Moreau representation, including nonclosed or nonconvex input through its closed convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The biconjugate is \[f^{**}(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)\}.\] It is the pointwise supremum of all affine functions \(x\mapsto\langle u,x\rangle-\beta\) majorized by \(f\), and hence equals \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}f\), the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function not exceeding \(f\). Consequently, a proper function is lower semicontinuous and convex exactly when \(f=f^{**}\). At a point of equality, subgradients are recoverable from active affine minorants: \[u\in\partial f^{**}(x)\iff f^{**}(x)+f^*(u)=\langle u,x\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconjugate evaluates the supremum of all affine functions encoded by the conjugate. It is the closed convex envelope of the original function. Therefore closed proper convex functions are precisely the fixed points of biconjugation. A dual vector is a subgradient of the biconjugate exactly when its associated affine minorant is active at the point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}f=\sup\{h:h\text{ affine and }h\leq f\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\), \[f(x)=\sup_u\{\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)\}.\]
The equality \(u\in\partial f^{**}(x)\) is equivalent to \(x\in\partial f^*(u)\) and to \(f^{**}(x)+f^*(u)=\langle u,x\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f=\iota_C\), then \(f^{**}=\iota_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\).
If \(f\) is already closed proper convex, biconjugation changes neither its values nor its subdifferential.
immediate_consequences_latex: Each \(u\) supplies the global affine minorant \(x\mapsto\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)\).
Active affine minorants identify supporting hyperplanes and subgradients.
boundary_notes: If no proper affine minorant exists, the usual proper closed-convex-envelope interpretation requires adjustment.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the closure topology and continuous dual pairing must be specified.

knowledge_statements.title: Supremal Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every closed proper convex function is the pointwise supremum of its affine minorants, equivalently of the conjugate-generated supporting functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{A}_f\) be the set of pairs \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\langle a,z\rangle+\beta\leq f(z)\) for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f(x)=\sup_{(a,\beta)\in\mathcal{A}_f}\bigl(\langle a,x\rangle+\beta\bigr)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\bigr).\] Thus a closed proper convex function is recovered pointwise as the supremum of its continuous affine minorants.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\sup_y\{\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\}\), equivalently the supremum of all affine minorants of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supremal affine-minorant representation of a closed proper convex function.

notation.meaning: Set of continuous affine minorants of f.

knowledge_statements.title: Biconjugate Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugation returns the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope and fixes exactly the proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The biconjugate satisfies \[f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}f,\] where the right-hand side is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\). Equivalently, \(f^{**}\) is the pointwise supremum of all continuous affine minorants of \(f\). In particular, \[f=f^{**}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex}.\] Hence biconjugation closes and convexifies a proper function, while leaving every proper closed convex function unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and admits a continuous affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}f\), and \(f=f^{**}\) exactly when \(f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Recovery Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal subgradient is exactly a dual point attaining Fenchel–Young equality, and conjugation reverses the subdifferential graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f^*(u)=\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,z\rangle-f(z)\}\). Then the Fenchel–Young equality and the two subgradient inclusions are equivalent:
\[
u\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle u,x\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(u).
\]
Thus either subdifferential recovers the inverse graph of the other: \(\partial f^*=(\partial f)^{-1}\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\partial f^*(u)\iff f(x)+f^*(u)=\langle u,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Young recovery of primal and dual subgradients.

children.top_down_role: Perspective and partial-conjugate structures used in marginal and dual subgradient models.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, and let \(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The perspective uses the open positive scale convention; the partial conjugate acts only in the second variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perspective of \(f\) is \[\operatorname{persp}f(t,x)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\+\infty,&t\leq0.\end{cases}\] Its epigraph is the positive conic hull of \(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f\). The partial conjugate of \(F\) in its second variable is \[F^{*_{2}}(x,v)=\sup_{y\in Y}\{\langle v,y\rangle-F(x,y)\}.\] For each fixed \(x\), this is the ordinary Fenchel conjugate of \(F(x,\cdot)\); when that section is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, \[F(x,y)=\sup_{v\in Y}\{\langle v,y\rangle-F^{*_{2}}(x,v)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perspective homogenizes a function by adding a positive scale variable. Partial conjugation keeps the first argument as a parameter and conjugates only the second section. Thus every closed proper convex section can be reconstructed from its partial conjugate, while the perspective converts the original epigraph into a cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{persp}f)=\mathbb{R}_{++}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad F^{*_{2}}(x,v)=\sup_y(\langle v,y\rangle-F(x,y)).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For fixed \(x\), \(F^{*_{2}}(x,\cdot)=(F(x,\cdot))^*\).
For closed proper convex sections, \(F(x,\cdot)=(F^{*_{2}}(x,\cdot))^*\).
special_cases_latex: At scale \(t=1\), \(\operatorname{persp}f(1,x)=f(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The perspective is convex whenever \(f\) is convex.
Partial conjugation provides the saddle-function interface used for parameterized marginal and dual models.
boundary_notes: The lower-semicontinuous closed perspective may assign the recession value at \(t=0\); that convention is not used here.
Partial conjugation does not conjugate the parameter \(x\), and it need not preserve joint convexity in the same form.
