knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), and let \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate global convex optimality measured by objective-value error, not merely by subgradient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential is
\[\partial_\varepsilon F(x):=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:F(y)\geq F(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\]
An approximate stationarity certificate of value tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is
\[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x).\]
It is equivalent to
\[F(y)\geq F(x)-\varepsilon\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n,\]
and hence to
\[F(x)\leq\inf_yF(y)+\varepsilon.\]
For a constrained problem, take \(F=f+\delta_C\); then the certificate includes feasibility because \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-subdifferential relaxes the global supporting-hyperplane inequality by epsilon. Approximate stationarity in the value sense means that zero belongs to this enlarged subdifferential. This happens exactly when the point's objective value is no more than epsilon above the global infimum. Constraints are included by using an indicator-augmented objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\iff F(x)-\inf F\leq\varepsilon.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[F(y)\geq F(x)-\varepsilon\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
\[\varepsilon\geq F(x)-\inf F.\]
special_cases_latex: At \(\varepsilon=0\), the definition reduces to exact stationarity.
For \(F=f+\delta_C\), it is equivalent to \(x\in C\) and \(f(x)\leq\inf_{y\in C}f(y)+\varepsilon\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The sets \(\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\) increase with \(\varepsilon\).
Every exact subgradient is an \(\varepsilon\)-subgradient for every \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
boundary_notes: A certificate \(g\in\partial F(x)\) with small \(\|g\|\) is not equivalent to this value certificate without bounded-domain or growth assumptions.
The epsilon-normal set of an indicator is generally not a cone when \(\varepsilon>0\).

children.title: Separation Certificates
children.top_down_role: Supporting models used to certify improvement, exclusion, or lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient generates an affine global underestimator whose minimum supplies a lower bound and can exclude points from improving the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subgradient inequality gives the verifiable supporting model \[f(y)\geq m_{x,g}(y):=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\qquad(y\in\mathbb{R}^n).\] Hence \(\inf_{y\in C}m_{x,g}(y)\) is a certified lower bound on \(\inf_{y\in C}f(y)\). Moreover, any \(y\in C\) satisfying \(m_{x,g}(y)>f(x)\) is certified not to improve upon \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{y\in C}f(y)\geq\inf_{y\in C}\bigl(f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane lower and exclusion certificates.

notation.meaning: affine supporting model generated at x

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be finite and convex, fix \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(S:=\partial f(x)\), a nonempty compact convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order certificates of nonoptimality and global affine lower support for finite convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A strict separation certificate for nonoptimality of \(x\) is a direction \(d\neq0\) satisfying
\[\sigma_S(d):=\sup_{g\in S}\langle g,d\rangle<0.\]
Because
\[f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d),\]
this condition is exactly \(f'(x;d)<0\), so \(d\) is a descent direction and \(x\) cannot minimize \(f\). Independently, each \(g\in\partial f(x)\) defines the global supporting model
\[m_{x,g}(y):=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\leq f(y)\quad\forall y.\]
Thus separation supplies an improvement certificate, while the supporting model supplies a globally valid affine lower-bound certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the compact convex subdifferential at a point can be strictly separated from the origin, the separating direction has negative pairing with every subgradient. Its directional derivative is negative, so it certifies nonoptimality. Each individual subgradient also defines an affine function supporting the objective globally from below, which can certify lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\partial f(x)\) is evaluated using the fixed Euclidean pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)<0\Rightarrow f'(x;d)<0\Rightarrow x\notin\operatorname*{argmin}f,\]
and \[m_{x,g}\leq f\quad\forall g\in\partial f(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle<0.\]
\[0\notin\partial f(x)\iff\text{there exists a strict separating direction for the compact convex set }\partial f(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable, the separation test is \(\langle\nabla f(x),d\rangle<0\).
Taking \(d=-\operatorname{proj}_{S}(0)\) gives a canonical separating direction when \(0\notin S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strict separation certificate excludes exact stationarity.
The supporting model yields \(\inf_y f(y)\geq\inf_y m_{x,g}(y)\), whenever the latter lower bound is finite over the relevant domain.
boundary_notes: A supporting model alone need not certify that its base point is optimal; zero slope is required for that conclusion in the unconstrained case.
Strict separation may fail for nonclosed or nonconvex generalized subdifferentials.

notation.meaning: Affine supporting model generated at \(x\) by \(g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness of a Subdifferential Calculus Rule
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\) be a convex function constructed from convex data \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) by an operation for which a candidate set-valued expression \(\mathcal R(x)\) is formed from their subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of exactness for convex subdifferential rules, with finite-valued positive sums and affine precomposition as canonical instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A subdifferential calculus rule is exact at \(x\) when its constructed set equals the true subdifferential:
\[\partial f(x)=\mathcal R(x).\]
For finite convex functions \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(t_1,t_2>0\), the positive-sum rule is exact everywhere:
\[\partial(t_1f_1+t_2f_2)(x)=t_1\partial f_1(x)+t_2\partial f_2(x).\]
For an affine map \(A(x)=A_0x+b\) and finite convex \(g\), the affine-chain rule is likewise exact:
\[\partial(g\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial g(Ax).\]
Exactness means that every subgradient of the constructed function is represented by the prescribed component subgradients, not merely that the construction produces valid subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subdifferential calculus is exact at a point when the set assembled from the component subdifferentials equals the entire subdifferential of the resulting function. Positive combinations of finite convex functions and precomposition of a finite convex function by an affine map are canonical globally exact rules. Equality is stronger than a one-sided validity inclusion.
assumptions_latex: All functions in the two displayed canonical rules are finite and convex on their full Euclidean spaces.
\(A(x)=A_0x+b\) is affine and \(A_0^*\) is its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial(t_1f_1+t_2f_2)=t_1\partial f_1+t_2\partial f_2,\qquad \partial(g\circ A)=A_0^*\partial g\circ A.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Exactness at \(x\): \[s\in\partial f(x)\iff s\in\mathcal R(x).\]
For the sum: \[s\in\partial(t_1f_1+t_2f_2)(x)\iff s=t_1s_1+t_2s_2\text{ for some }s_i\in\partial f_i(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If one summand is differentiable, its subdifferential contribution is its gradient singleton.
If \(A\) is linear, then \(b=0\) and the same adjoint rule applies.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact rules permit stationarity of a structured objective to be rewritten as an explicit inclusion involving component subgradients.
Repeated application yields exact formulas for finite positive sums of finite convex functions.
boundary_notes: For extended-valued functions, the same-looking equalities may require relative-interior, continuity, or other qualification conditions.
A universal inclusion is not an exact rule unless the reverse inclusion is also established.

notation.meaning: Candidate subdifferential expression assembled from component data.
Adjoint of the linear part of \(A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of Inclusion, Qualified Equality, and Approximate Recovery
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f_1\cap\operatorname{dom}f_2\), and set \(f=f_1+f_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex sum calculus used as the canonical model of qualification regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The qualification hierarchy for the sum rule consists of the following distinct levels. The universal weak relation is
\[\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\subseteq\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
Under an exactness qualification such as
\[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_1)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2)\neq\varnothing,\]
the inclusion strengthens to equality. At positive tolerance, the approximate rule is
\[\partial_\varepsilon(f_1+f_2)(x)\supseteq\bigcup_{\substack{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\geq0\\\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2\leq\varepsilon}}\bigl(\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f_1(x)+\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f_2(x)\bigr),\]
with equality when the corresponding conjugate infimal convolution is exact, in particular under the displayed relative-interior condition. Qualification-free exact recovery can instead use closures and intersections of enlarged subdifferentials:
\[\partial(f_1+f_2)(x)=\bigcap_{0<\eta\leq\bar\eta}\operatorname{cl}\bigl(\partial_\eta f_1(x)+\partial_\eta f_2(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum-rule hierarchy separates four levels that must not be conflated: an always-valid inclusion, equality under a relative-interior or equivalent exactness qualification, an epsilon-subdifferential formula that allocates approximation error among the summands, and a qualification-free recovery formula using closures and intersections of enlarged subdifferentials.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are proper, closed, and convex.
The equality in the approximate allocation formula requires exactness of the conjugate infimal convolution; the relative-interior condition is a sufficient qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{unqualified inclusion}\ \subseteq\ \text{qualified equality},\qquad \text{and exact recovery without qualification is available through closed approximate sums.}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Qualified exactness: \[s\in\partial(f_1+f_2)(x)\iff s=s_1+s_2\text{ with }s_i\in\partial f_i(x).\]
Approximate allocation: \[s=s_1+s_2,\ s_i\in\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x),\ \varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow s\in\partial_\varepsilon(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If both functions are finite everywhere, the relative-interior condition holds automatically.
At \(\varepsilon=0\), the qualified approximate equality reduces to the exact sum rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: Failure of a qualification does not invalidate the weak inclusion.
Enlarged subdifferentials retain enough information to recover the exact sum subdifferential after closure and intersection.
boundary_notes: The relative-interior condition is sufficient, not necessary.
The closure-intersection formula is materially different from simply closing \(\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\).

notation.meaning: Arbitrary positive upper scale for approximate recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Inclusion Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one subgradient from each summand always yields a subgradient of the sum, but the reverse decomposition requires additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Without any interior or continuity qualification, subgradients can always be added: \[\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\subseteq\partial(f+g)(x).\] The reverse inclusion may fail, so an unqualified calculus rule generally supplies only this weak inclusion rather than an exact decomposition of every subgradient of the sum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\subseteq\partial(f+g)(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification-free direction of the convex sum rule.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the two subdifferentials

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f_1\cap\operatorname{dom}f_2\). Empty subdifferentials are allowed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification-free convex subdifferential calculus; the claim is an inclusion, not an exact formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The weak sum-calculus regime is the universally valid inclusion
\[\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\subseteq\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
Equivalently, for every \(g_1\in\partial f_1(x)\) and \(g_2\in\partial f_2(x)\),
\[g_1+g_2\in\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
Its approximate counterpart is: for \(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\geq0\),
\[\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f_1(x)+\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f_2(x)\subseteq\partial_{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
These relations require no relative-interior or continuity qualification. They assert validity of every constructed sum subgradient but do not assert that every subgradient of the sum admits such a decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without any exactness qualification, component subgradients can always be added to obtain a valid subgradient of the sum. The same is true for approximate subgradients, with their error tolerances added. This is a one-sided construction rule: the full subdifferential of the sum may contain elements that cannot be decomposed using exact component subgradients at the same point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f_1(x)+\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f_2(x)\subseteq\partial_{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}(f_1+f_2)(x),\]
including the exact case \(\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(g_i\in\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\), then \[f_1(y)+f_2(y)\geq f_1(x)+f_2(x)+\langle g_1+g_2,y-x\rangle-(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)\quad\forall y.\]
Exact weak inclusion: \[g_i\in\partial f_i(x)\Rightarrow g_1+g_2\in\partial(f_1+f_2)(x).\]
special_cases_latex: If either component subdifferential is empty, the exact left-hand side is empty and the inclusion remains valid.
When a suitable relative-interior condition holds, the exact inclusion strengthens to equality.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any computable component certificate produces a valid certificate for the summed function.
Approximation errors combine additively.
boundary_notes: The reverse inclusion can fail when domains meet without an exactness qualification.
Calling the weak inclusion an equality would lose the essential distinction encoded by this regime.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum when applied to sets of subgradients.

children.title: Classical Exactness Qualification Pair
children.top_down_role: Finite-dimensional and continuity-point mechanisms supporting exact calculus.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(f,g:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, and write \(D_f=\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(D_g=\operatorname{dom}g\). For a convex function \(h\), \(\partial h(x)=\{u\in E:h(y)\ge h(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in E\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex subdifferential calculus. The definition records two classical sufficient mechanisms for an exact sum rule: overlap of relative interiors and finiteness-continuity of one summand at a point of the other domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
\[Q_{\mathrm{ri}}(f,g):\Longleftrightarrow \operatorname{ri}D_f\cap\operatorname{ri}D_g
e\varnothing,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{cont}}(f,g):\Longleftrightarrow D_f\cap\operatorname{cont}g
e\varnothing.\]
The classical exactness qualification pair is \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{cl}}(f,g)=\{Q_{\mathrm{ri}}(f,g),Q_{\mathrm{cont}}(f,g)\}\). A pair \((f,g)\) is classically qualified when at least one member of \(\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{cl}}(f,g)\) holds. In that case \(f+g\) is proper and, for every \(x\in E\),
\[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper convex functions on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the classical qualification pair consists of either a common point of the relative interiors of their effective domains or a point in the domain of one function at which the other is finite and continuous. A pair is classically qualified if at least one condition holds. Under either condition, the subdifferential of the sum equals the Minkowski sum of the two subdifferentials at every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Q_{\mathrm{ri}}(f,g)\lor Q_{\mathrm{cont}}(f,g)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (\forall x\in E)\;\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite-dimensional \(E\), \(Q_{\mathrm{ri}}(f,g)\) is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(D_f-D_g)\).
If \(g\) is finite on all of \(E\), then \(\operatorname{cont}g=E\), so \(Q_{\mathrm{cont}}(f,g)\) holds whenever \(f\) is proper.
special_cases_latex: If both functions are finite-valued convex functions on \(E\), exactness holds everywhere without any additional domain test.

For indicator functions \(f=\iota_C\) and \(g=\iota_D\), the relative-interior condition becomes \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap\operatorname{ri}D\ne\varnothing\), and the formula becomes \(N_{C\cap D}(x)=N_C(x)+N_D(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: At every \(x\in D_f\cap D_g\), each \(u\in\partial(f+g)(x)\) admits a decomposition \(u=u_f+u_g\) with \(u_f\in\partial f(x)\) and \(u_g\in\partial g(x)\).
For positive weights \(\alpha,\beta>0\), the same qualifications yield \(\partial(\alpha f+\beta g)=\alpha\partial f+\beta\partial g\).
boundary_notes: The conditions are sufficient, not necessary; exactness may hold when both fail.
Relative interior is the finite-dimensional mechanism. Infinite-dimensional replacements such as strong relative interior belong to the generalized-interior regime.
Without qualification, only \(\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\subseteq\partial(f+g)(x)\) is automatic.

notation.meaning: Set of points at which g is finite and continuous.
Minkowski sum of subsets of the dual space.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, intersecting relative interiors of the domains guarantees that every subgradient of a sum decomposes into subgradients of its summands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative-interior qualification is \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing,\] equivalently \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\). Under this condition, the convex subdifferential sum rule is exact at every common-domain point: \[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\]
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative-interior sum-rule qualification.

notation.meaning: relative interior in the affine hull

knowledge_statements.title: Continuity-Point Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact subdifferential addition holds in a Banach space when one summand is continuous at some point where both functions are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuity-point qualification holds when some \(z\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) is a norm-continuity point of at least one summand. Under this hypothesis, every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) satisfies the exact rule \[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\] The continuity is relative to the ambient norm topology, not merely sequential continuity on the common domain.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
There exists \(z\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) at which one summand is norm-continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space continuity-point sum-rule qualification.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential as a subset of the dual

knowledge_statements.title: Dimensional Scope Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In infinite dimensions, even a nonempty closed convex cone can have empty relative interior, making the classical relative-interior qualification unusable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-dimensional relative-interior qualification does not extend as an informative condition to every infinite-dimensional domain. For the closed convex cone \[P=\{x\in\ell^2:x_k\geq0\text{ for every }k\},\] one has \(\operatorname{aff}P=\ell^2\) but \(\operatorname{ri}P=\operatorname{int}P=\varnothing\). Thus a nonempty convex domain may have empty relative interior, requiring continuity, core-type, or generalized-interior alternatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}P=\varnothing\), although \(P\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional failure of relative-interior availability.

notation.meaning: nonnegative cone in the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences

children.title: Generalized-Interior Qualification Family
children.top_down_role: Infinite-dimensional closed-subspace and generalized-interior mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(H)\), where \(\Gamma_0(H)\) denotes the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions \(H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Set \(D=\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The primary generalized-interior mechanism is strong relative interior, whose definition incorporates closedness of the direction subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a convex set \(C\subset H\), define
\[\operatorname{core}C=\{x\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=H\},\]
\[\operatorname{sri}C=\{x\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(C-x)\},\]
\[\operatorname{ri}C=\{x\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=\operatorname{span}(C-x)\},\quad \operatorname{qri}C=\{x\in C:\overline{\operatorname{cone}}(C-x)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(C-x)\}.\]
The generalized-interior qualification for the pair \((f,g)\) is
\[0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g).\]
When it holds,
\[\partial(f+g)=\partial f+\partial g.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized-interior family consists of core, strong relative interior, relative interior, and quasirelative interior. For exact Hilbert-space sum calculus, the canonical qualification requires zero to belong to the strong relative interior of the difference of the effective domains. Strong relative interior means that the cone generated by the translated set equals the closed linear span of that set. Under this condition, the subdifferential of the sum is exactly the pointwise sum of the subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial(f+g)=\partial f+\partial g.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(0\in D\), the condition \(0\in\operatorname{sri}D\) means that \(\operatorname{cone}D\) is a closed linear subspace of \(H\).
In finite dimensions, \(\operatorname{sri}C=\operatorname{ri}C\), so the qualification reduces to \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{dom}g=H\), then the exact sum rule holds.
If \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\), the strong-relative-interior condition is satisfied.
For a closed linear subspace \(V\subset H\), \(\operatorname{sri}V=V\), even when \(\operatorname{int}V=\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The condition accommodates lower-dimensional closed subspace geometry that ordinary interior cannot detect.
Under the qualification, every \(u\in\partial(f+g)(x)\) splits as \(u_f+u_g\) with \(u_f\in\partial f(x)\) and \(u_g\in\partial g(x)\).
boundary_notes: Quasirelative interior is weaker than strong relative interior and does not by itself give the stated exact sum rule.
The closure in \(\overline{\operatorname{span}}(C-x)\) is essential in infinite dimensions.
The family is stated for Hilbert spaces; extensions to broader locally convex spaces require topology-specific duality hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.title: Attouch–Brézis Closed-Subspace Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed linear positive hull of the domain difference is an infinite-dimensional qualification yielding exact subdifferential addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Attouch–Brézis qualification requires the positive hull \[L=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda\bigl(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr)\] to be a closed linear subspace of \(X\). Under this qualification, the subdifferential sum rule is exact: \[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\qquad\bigl(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\bigr).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(L=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\) is a closed linear subspace of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-subspace qualification for Banach-space exact calculus.

notation.meaning: positive hull of the difference of effective domains

knowledge_statements.title: Core-Type Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The core qualification requires the domain difference to contain a short two-sided segment from zero in every algebraic direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The core-type domain qualification is \[0\in\operatorname{core}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr).\] Explicitly, for every direction \(d\in X\), there exists \(\epsilon>0\) such that \(td\in\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\) whenever \(|t|<\epsilon\). This predicate is algebraic and does not require the domain difference to contain a neighborhood in a specified topology.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(D=\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\operatorname{core}D\iff\forall d\in X\ \exists\epsilon>0\ \forall |t|<\epsilon:\ td\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic-interior qualification predicate; theorem scope requires sourcing.

notation.meaning: algebraic interior of a convex set

review_flags: exact-calculus consequences depend on the ambient locally convex setting

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic core predicate is internally correct and appropriately classified as a condition, but no authoritative definition locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Relative-Interior Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the quasi-relative interior when the closed cone of feasible displacements from it is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quasi-relative interior of \(D\) is \[\operatorname{qri}D=\{x\in D:\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(D-x)\text{ is a linear subspace of }X\}.\] A quasi-relative-interior domain qualification is commonly expressed as \(0\in\operatorname{qri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\). The exact calculus consequence depends on the accompanying topology, closure, and separation hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a locally convex space and \(D\subset X\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{qri}D\iff\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(D-x)\) is a linear subspace of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition underlying quasi-relative-interior qualification regimes.

notation.meaning: closed conic hull of D translated by x

children.title: Qualification-Free Recovery Family
children.top_down_role: Qualification-free recovery through nearby-point, closure, and approximate-subgradient constructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper closed convex. For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define \(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)=\{s:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle s,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^n\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex functions. Recovery is qualification-free but approximate: an epsilon-subgradient is represented through an exact subgradient at a nearby point with a controlled dual error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The qualification-free nearby-point recovery family is the collection of inclusions, indexed by \(\eta>0\),
\[\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\subseteq igcup_{\|y-x\|\le\eta}\left(\partial f(y)+ rac{\varepsilon}{\eta}Bight),\]
where \(B=\{u\in\mathbb R^n:\|u\|\le1\}\). Equivalently, for every \(s\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\) and every \(\eta>0\), there exist \(x_\eta\) and \(s_\eta\) such that
\[\|x_\eta-x\|\le\eta,\qquad s_\eta\in\partial f(x_\eta),\qquad\|s_\eta-s\|\le\varepsilon/\eta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient can always be recovered, without a domain qualification, from an exact subgradient evaluated at a nearby point. For every chosen radius eta, the nearby point lies within eta of the base point and the exact subgradient lies within epsilon divided by eta of the target epsilon-subgradient. The family trades primal displacement against dual error and includes the exact case when epsilon is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\forall s\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x))(\forall\eta>0)(\exists x_\eta,s_\eta)\quad \|x_\eta-x\|\le\eta,\ s_\eta\in\partial f(x_\eta),\ \|s_\eta-s\|\le\varepsilon/\eta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\subseteq\bigcap_{\eta>0}\bigcup_{\|y-x\|\le\eta}\left(\partial f(y)+(\varepsilon/\eta)B\right).\]
Choosing \(\eta=\sqrt\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon>0\) gives simultaneous bounds \(\|x_\eta-x\|\le\sqrt\varepsilon\) and \(\|s_\eta-s\|\le\sqrt\varepsilon\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\varepsilon=0\), one may choose \(x_\eta=x\) and \(s_\eta=s\).
Every \(s\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\) lies in \(\overline{\partial f(\mathbb R^n)}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Approximate first-order information can be reconstructed from exact subgradients sampled away from the reference point.
The parameter \(\eta\) explicitly controls the primal-distance versus dual-error tradeoff.
boundary_notes: The recovery statement is an inclusion, not an assertion that every nearby perturbed exact subgradient is an epsilon-subgradient.
For fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), demanding a small dual error may require a large displacement.
Closedness and finite dimensionality are part of the cited formulation.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball in the primal-dual Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a qualification, exact subgradients of a sum are recovered as limits of sums of arbitrarily accurate approximate subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even without an exactness qualification, the subdifferential of a sum can be recovered from approximate decompositions: \[\partial(f+g)(x)=\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\operatorname{cl}\bigl(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)+\partial_\varepsilon g(x)\bigr).\] Thus \(u\in\partial(f+g)(x)\) precisely when, for every positive tolerance, \(u\) is a limit of sums of epsilon-subgradients of the two summands at \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\operatorname{cl}\bigl(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)+\partial_\varepsilon g(x)\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional qualification-free recovery by approximate subgradients.
review_flags: verify the precise allocation of approximation tolerances between summands

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Subgradient Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every epsilon-subgradient is close to an exact subgradient at a nearby point, with position error at most lambda and subgradient error at most epsilon divided by lambda.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\lambda>0\), there exist \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\) satisfying
\[
\|\bar x-x\|\le \lambda
\quad\text{and}\quad
\|\bar v-v\|\le \frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}.
\]
Thus every approximate subgradient can be recovered, with an explicit position-versus-subgradient error tradeoff, as an exact subgradient at a nearby point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\lambda>0\;\exists(\bar x,\bar v)\) such that \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\), \(\|\bar x-x\|\le\lambda\), and \(\|\bar v-v\|\le\varepsilon/\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Brøndsted–Rockafellar recovery from an approximate subgradient.

notation.meaning: The epsilon-subdifferential of f at x.

source_witnesses.locator: 1 The Approximate Subdifferential p. 92

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Based Replacement
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without qualification, the exact subdifferential of a finite sum is the intersection of closures of sums of approximate subdifferentials with arbitrarily small total error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Without a relative-interior or continuity qualification, the exact subdifferential is recovered by
\[
\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x)
=
\bigcap_{\eta>0}\operatorname{cl}
\bigcup_{\substack{\varepsilon_i\ge0\\\sum_{i=1}^m\varepsilon_i=\eta}}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\right).
\]
The closure and arbitrarily small distributed errors replace the qualification needed for an exact Minkowski-sum formula.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\sum_i f_i)(x)=\bigcap_{\eta>0}\operatorname{cl}\bigcup_{\varepsilon_i\ge0,\,\sum_i\varepsilon_i=\eta}\sum_i\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification-free finite-sum formula using approximate subgradients and closure.

notation.meaning: The epsilon-subdifferential of the ith summand.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic calculus generated by positive combinations and separable products
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex functions and let \(\alpha_i>0\). Subdifferential sums and scalar multiples are Minkowski operations on subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finite-valued convex functions. In this regime the elementary algebraic rules are exact without an additional qualification because every function is continuous everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The algebraic subdifferential calculus is the operation-preserving assignment \(f\mapsto\partial f\) specified by
\[\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f_iight)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i\partial f_i(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n),\]
and, for finite convex \(p:\mathbb R^r	o\mathbb R\) and \(q:\mathbb R^s	o\mathbb R\), by
\[F(x,y)=p(x)+q(y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial F(x,y)=\partial p(x)	imes\partial q(y).\]
Constants contribute \(\{0\}\), and multiplication by a positive scalar acts by the same scalar on the subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algebraic subdifferential calculus assigns exact set operations to positive linear combinations and separable sums. The subdifferential of a positive finite combination is the corresponding Minkowski combination of the component subdifferentials. For a function on a product space that separates as a sum of two component functions, its subdifferential is the Cartesian product of the two component subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial\!\left(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i\right)=\sum_i\alpha_i\partial f_i,\qquad \partial(p\oplus q)=\partial p\times\partial q.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A vector \(u\) belongs to \(\partial(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i)(x)\) exactly when \(u=\sum_i\alpha_i u_i\) for some \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\).
For \(F=p\oplus q\), \((u,v)\in\partial F(x,y)\) exactly when \(u\in\partial p(x)\) and \(v\in\partial q(y)\).
special_cases_latex: \(\partial(\alpha f)(x)=\alpha\partial f(x)\) for \(\alpha>0\).
\(\partial(f+c)(x)=\partial f(x)\) for every constant \(c\in\mathbb R\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If every component is differentiable at \(x\), the rule reduces to \(\nabla(\sum_i\alpha_i f_i)(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i\nabla f_i(x)\).
A separable convex minimization problem has \(0\in\partial F(x,y)\) exactly when \(0\in\partial p(x)\) and \(0\in\partial q(y)\).
boundary_notes: Negative coefficients are excluded because they need not preserve convexity and the displayed subdifferential identity can fail.
For extended-valued summands, an exact sum formula requires a qualification; only the easy inclusion is unconditional.

notation.meaning: Separable sum on the product space, (p⊕q)(x,y)=p(x)+q(y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact rules for affine value and argument perturbations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex, let \(a,b\in\mathbb R^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R\), and \(\lambda>0\). Identify linear functionals with vectors under the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional and finite-valued. These transformations inherit the subgradient structure directly and require no constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Elementary affine perturbation calculus is defined by the transformed functions
\[g(x)=\lambda f(x)+\langle a,xangle+c,\qquad h(x)=f(x+b).\]
Their subdifferentials are, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[\partial g(x)=\lambda\partial f(x)+\{a\},\qquad \partial h(x)=\partial f(x+b).\]
Combining the two operations, if \(k(x)=\lambda f(x+b)+\langle a,xangle+c\), then
\[\partial k(x)=\lambda\partial f(x+b)+\{a\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling of a convex function rescales its subdifferential, addition of an affine functional translates the subdifferential by the functional's coefficient, addition of a constant has no effect, and translation of the argument evaluates the original subdifferential at the translated point. These operations may be combined in one exact formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial\bigl(\lambda f(\cdot+b)+\langle a,\cdot\rangle+c\bigr)(x)=\lambda\partial f(x+b)+a.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(u\in\partial k(x)\) if and only if \((u-a)/\lambda\in\partial f(x+b)\).
The graph transformation is \(\operatorname{gra}\partial k=\{(x,\lambda v+a):(x+b,v)\in\operatorname{gra}\partial f\}\).
special_cases_latex: With \(a=b=0\), \(\partial(\lambda f+c)=\lambda\partial f\).
With \(\lambda=1\) and \(b=0\), \(\partial(f+\langle a,\cdot\rangle+c)=\partial f+a\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(0\in\partial k(x)\) exactly when \(-a/\lambda\in\partial f(x+b)\).
If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x+b\), then \(k\) is differentiable at \(x\) with \(\nabla k(x)=\lambda\nabla f(x+b)+a\).
boundary_notes: The scalar \(\lambda\) must be positive for the stated convex subdifferential rule.
A nontrivial linear precomposition \(f(Ax+b)\) is governed by the affine chain rule, not merely by this perturbation rule.

notation.meaning: Translation of a set A by the singleton {a}.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Scaling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying a proper convex function by a strictly positive scalar multiplies every subgradient by the same scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
v\in\partial(\alpha f)(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{v}{\alpha}\in\partial f(x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\partial(\alpha f)(x)=\alpha\,\partial f(x).
\]
Strict positivity of \(\alpha\) preserves the direction of the defining subgradient inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\alpha f)(x)=\alpha\,\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex-subdifferential rule for strictly positive objective scaling.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Subdifferentials of Extended-Valued Functions p. 47

knowledge_statements.title: Argument Translation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translating the argument shifts the point where the original subdifferential is evaluated but does not change its vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the translated function \(g(x)=f(x-a)\), a vector \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies
\[
v\in\partial g(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v\in\partial f(x-a).
\]
Hence
\[
\partial g(x)=\partial f(x-a).
\]
Translation changes the evaluation point but leaves the subgradient vectors themselves unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial g(x)=\partial f(x-a)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient covariance under translation of the function argument.

source_witnesses.locator: 1 The Elementary Mechanism p. 2

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Perturbation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding an affine functional translates the subdifferential by its slope; the constant term has no effect.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
v\in\partial g(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
v-a\in\partial f(x).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\partial g(x)=\partial f(x)+a.
\]
The constant \(b\) has no effect on the subdifferential, while the linear term translates every subgradient by its slope \(a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial g(x)=\partial f(x)+a\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact subdifferential rule for adding a finite affine functional.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated zero-scaling convention, the scaled function is the domain indicator and its subdifferential is the domain normal cone, which need not equal the zero-scaled original subdifferential. Negative scaling of a nonaffine real-valued convex function destroys convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated convention, \(0f=\delta_{\operatorname{dom}f}\). Hence, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\),
\[
\partial(0f)(x)=N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x).
\]
This set need not equal \(0\,\partial f(x)\); in particular, \(0\,\partial f(x)\) is empty when \(\partial f(x)\) is empty and is \(\{0\}\) otherwise. If \(\alpha<0\) and \(f\) is nonaffine and real-valued on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\alpha f\) is concave and not convex. Thus the positive-scaling identity has no general extension to nonpositive scalars.
assumptions_latex: For zero scaling, \((0f)(x)=0\) on \(\operatorname{dom}f\) and \((0f)(x)=+\infty\) otherwise.
For the negative-scaling clause, \(\alpha<0\) and \(f\) is nonaffine and real-valued on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(\partial(0f)(x)=N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)\), which need not equal \(0\,\partial f(x)\); under the negative-scaling assumptions, \(\alpha f\) is concave and not convex, so convex subdifferential calculus does not apply to it as a convex function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the positive-scaling rule under the stated extended-real zero-scaling convention and under negative scaling of a nonaffine real-valued convex function.

A strictly negative scaling factor in the negative-scaling clause.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak, exact, and approximate convex sum-rule regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions with nonempty common effective domain, and set \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\). For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), use the epsilon-subdifferential \(\partial_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The family separates what holds for every proper convex sum from exact formulas requiring domain regularity and from epsilon-level decompositions requiring exact conjugate infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Moreau–Rockafellar sum-rule family consists of the following nested relations at \(x\in igcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial F(x),\]
\[\partial F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\quad	ext{under an exactness qualification},\]
and, when the conjugate infimal convolution is exact,
\[\partial_\varepsilon F(x)= igcup_{\substack{\varepsilon_i\ge0\\sum_i\varepsilon_i\le\varepsilon}}\sum_{i=1}^m\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x).\]
In finite dimensions, \( igcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)
e\varnothing\) is a standard qualification for both exact formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Moreau–Rockafellar family organizes sum calculus into three regimes. The sum of exact component subdifferentials is always contained in the subdifferential of the sum. Under a domain qualification this inclusion becomes equality. At the approximate level, exactness of the conjugate infimal convolution yields a union over all nonnegative allocations of the total epsilon among the summands.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial\!\left(\sum_i f_i\right)(x),\quad\text{with equality under qualification, and an epsilon-allocation formula under conjugate exactness}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Exactness at \(x\) means every \(u\in\partial F(x)\) can be decomposed as \(u=\sum_i u_i\) with \(u_i\in\partial f_i(x)\).
For two summands, conjugate exactness means \((f_1+f_2)^*(u)=\min_{u_1+u_2=u}(f_1^*(u_1)+f_2^*(u_2))\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\varepsilon=0\), the epsilon-allocation formula reduces to the exact subdifferential sum rule.
For finite-valued convex summands on \(\mathbb R^n\), exactness holds everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: Qualified first-order optimality can be written \(0\in\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\).
The epsilon formula assigns a separate error budget \(\varepsilon_i\) to each summand.
boundary_notes: The weak inclusion has the direction \(\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial F(x)\).
The approximate equality is not qualification-free; it depends on exactness of the relevant conjugate infimal convolution.
Empty subdifferentials are permitted, so an inclusion may be strict or uninformative.

knowledge_statements.title: Unqualified Sum Inclusions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a common domain point, every sum of individual subgradients is a subgradient of the function sum, without any qualification condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary choices \(v_i\in\partial f_i(x)\), their sum satisfies
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\in\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)
\subseteq
\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x).
\]
This inclusion requires no continuity or relative-interior qualification; only the reverse inclusion can fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The universally valid direction of the finite convex sum rule.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of the subdifferential sets.
Pointwise extended-real sum of the functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Qualification-free exact and epsilon sum inclusions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, let \(x\in\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\), and put \(F=\sum_i f_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No relative-interior, continuity, or closed-subspace qualification is imposed. The statement records only relations valid directly from the defining subgradient inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unqualified sum inclusions are
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\subseteq\partial F(x)\]
and, for every \(\varepsilon\ge0\),
\[ igcup_{\substack{\varepsilon_i\ge0\\sum_i\varepsilon_i\le\varepsilon}}\sum_{i=1}^m\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\subseteq\partial_\varepsilon F(x).\]
Thus any selection \(u_i\in\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\) with total error at most \(\varepsilon\) produces \(\sum_i u_i\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without any qualification, component subgradients may always be added to obtain a subgradient of the sum. The same statement holds for approximate subgradients: if nonnegative component error budgets add to at most the target error, then the sum of the selected component epsilon-subgradients is a target epsilon-subgradient of the sum. No converse decomposition is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\forall\varepsilon_i\ge0)\quad \sum_i\varepsilon_i\le\varepsilon\ \Longrightarrow\ \sum_i\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\subseteq\partial_\varepsilon\!\left(\sum_i f_i\right)(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(u_i\in\partial_{\varepsilon_i}f_i(x)\), then \(F(y)\ge F(x)+\langle\sum_i u_i,y-x\rangle-\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) for every \(y\in E\).
The exact inclusion is the case \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_1=\cdots=\varepsilon_m=0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=2\), \(\partial f_1(x)+\partial f_2(x)\subseteq\partial(f_1+f_2)(x)\).
If a component subdifferential is empty, the corresponding Minkowski sum is empty and the inclusion remains valid.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any computable decomposition of a dual vector into component subgradients certifies membership in the subdifferential of the total objective.
Approximate component certificates combine additively in both slope and error.
boundary_notes: The reverse inclusion can fail when the domains meet only at their boundaries.
Closure of the right-hand Minkowski sum does not automatically supply the missing converse.
This definition does not assert properness of \(F\) outside the stipulated common-domain point.

notation.meaning: Pointwise sum of the component functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Exact Sum Rules
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common relative-interior domain point makes the finite convex sum rule exact, so every subgradient of the sum decomposes into individual subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the domains have a common relative-interior point, then at every \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i\),
\[
\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x)
=
\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x).
\]
Thus every subgradient of the sum admits an exact decomposition \(v=\sum_{i=1}^m v_i\) with \(v_i\in\partial f_i(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Moreau–Rockafellar rule under a common relative-interior qualification.

notation.meaning: Relative interior of a convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact finite-sum rule under domain regularity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\Gamma_0(H)\). Set \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\) and assume the common effective domain is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex finite-sum calculus. The primary Hilbert-space condition is stated sequentially with strong relative interiors; its finite-dimensional specialization is common relative-interior intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The qualified exact finite-sum regime is defined by
\[0\in igcap_{i=2}^m\operatorname{sri}\!\left(\operatorname{dom}f_i- igcap_{j=1}^{i-1}\operatorname{dom}f_jight).\]
Under this qualification,
\[\partial F=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i.\]
In finite-dimensional \(H\), the symmetric condition
\[ igcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)
e\varnothing\]
is a standard sufficient qualification for the same identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family is in the qualified exact sum regime when each new effective domain meets the preceding common domain with strong-relative-interior regularity. Under this condition, the subdifferential of the total sum is exactly the pointwise Minkowski sum of all component subdifferentials. In finite dimensions, it is enough that all relative interiors have a common point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\forall x\in H)\qquad\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(m=2\), the Hilbert-space condition is \(0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2-\operatorname{dom}f_1)\).

In finite dimensions, \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2-\operatorname{dom}f_1)\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_1)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2)\ne\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: If one summand has full domain, the two-function exact rule holds.
If all summands are finite-valued on \(\mathbb R^n\), the relative-interior qualification is automatic.
For indicator functions, the rule specializes to an exact normal-cone intersection formula.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every total subgradient has a componentwise decomposition.
The optimality condition \(0\in\partial F(x)\) becomes \(0\in\sum_i\partial f_i(x)\).
boundary_notes: The displayed sequential condition depends on the ordering but is only a sufficient criterion; exactness itself is order-independent.
The rule is not valid merely from nonempty intersection of the effective domains.
In infinite dimensions, ordinary relative-interior intersection is not an adequate substitute for strong relative interior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential calculus for affine and monotone convex compositions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), where each \(f_i\) is finite convex, and let \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex and nondecreasing in each coordinate. Separately, let \(A(x)=A_0x+b\) be affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite-valued composition calculus. It combines affine precomposition and componentwise-monotone postcomposition, the two basic mapping transformations covered by the cited source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convex composition mapping calculus assigns to \(h=g\circ F\) the exact set
\[\partial h(x)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^mho_i s_i:ho=(ho_1,\ldots,ho_m)\in\partial g(F(x)),\ s_i\in\partial f_i(x)ight\}.\]
Every \(ho\in\partial g(F(x))\) satisfies \(ho_i\ge0\). For affine precomposition of a finite convex \(q:\mathbb R^m	o\mathbb R\),
\[\partial(q\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial q(Ax).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex composition mapping calculus covers two exact transformations. For a componentwise nondecreasing convex outer function applied to a vector of finite convex inner functions, subgradients are nonnegative weighted sums of inner subgradients, with weights taken from the outer subdifferential. For a finite convex function precomposed with an affine map, the outer subdifferential is pulled back by the adjoint of the linear part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial(g\circ F)(x)=\bigcup_{\rho\in\partial g(F(x))}\sum_i\rho_i\partial f_i(x),\qquad \partial(q\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial q(Ax).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The first formula is the union of Minkowski sums \(\sum_i\rho_i\partial f_i(x)\) over \(\rho\in\partial g(F(x))\).
When every function is differentiable, it becomes \(\nabla(g\circ F)(x)=\sum_i(\partial_i g)(F(x))\nabla f_i(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(m=1\), the first formula gives monotone scalar composition.
For \(g(y)=\max_i y_i\), it gives the active-index finite-maximum rule.
For linear \(A\), the affine formula has \(b=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Coordinatewise monotonicity forces the outer subgradient weights to be nonnegative, preserving convex combinations of inner subgradient inequalities.
Affine and monotone postcomposition rules can be nested when their respective hypotheses hold.
boundary_notes: If the outer function is not monotone on the relevant range, convexity of \(g\circ F\) and the displayed rule can fail.
Extended-valued outer functions require domain qualifications absent from this finite-valued formulation.
A general cone order requires a cone-dual formulation beyond the componentwise specialization stated here.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex, let \(A_0:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and define \(A(x)=A_0x+b\) and \(f=h\circ A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued convex outer functions. The family distinguishes the unconditional pullback inclusion from exactness under range-domain regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine chain-rule family is
\[A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\subseteq\partial(h\circ A)(x)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n),\]
with exactness whenever
\[(b+\operatorname{ran}A_0)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)
e\varnothing.\]
Under this qualification,
\[\partial(h\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an affine precomposition, pulling an outer subgradient back through the adjoint always produces a subgradient of the composite. The reverse representation is guaranteed when the affine range meets the relative interior of the outer effective domain. The exact chain rule then identifies every composite subgradient with the adjoint image of an outer subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(b+\operatorname{ran}A_0)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial(h\circ A)=A_0^*\circ(\partial h)\circ A.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h-b-\operatorname{ran}A_0)\).
Exactness means \(u\in\partial(h\circ A)(x)\) if and only if there exists \(v\in\partial h(Ax)\) with \(u=A_0^*v\).
special_cases_latex: If \(h\) is finite-valued on \(\mathbb R^m\), exactness is automatic.
If \(A_0\) is surjective, its affine range is \(\mathbb R^m\), so exactness holds whenever \(h\) is proper.
If \(h\) is polyhedral, meeting \(\operatorname{dom}h\) is sufficient in the cited finite-dimensional rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(h\) is differentiable at \(Ax\), then \(h\circ A\) is differentiable at \(x\) with gradient \(A_0^*\nabla h(Ax)\).
The kernel of \(A_0\) is automatically annihilated by every subgradient represented through the exact chain rule.
boundary_notes: Injectivity of \(A_0\) alone does not ensure that its range meets the relative interior of \(\operatorname{dom}h\).
If \(Ax\notin\operatorname{dom}h\), both sides are interpreted at a point where the composite is infinite and its subdifferential is empty.
Outside the qualification, the displayed inclusion can be strict.

knowledge_statements.title: Elementary Affine-Mapping Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Surjective affine maps give the usual adjoint chain rule. Injective maps give the same rule after restricting the outer function to the mapped affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(A:X\to Y\) is surjective, then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}(f\circ T)\),
\[
\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial f(Ax+b).
\]
If \(A\) is injective, set \(S=b+\operatorname{ran}A\) and regard \(f|_S\) as a convex function on \(S\). Since \(T:X\to S\) is an affine bijection,
\[
\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial_S(f|_S)(Ax+b).
\]
For bijective \(A\), both formulas coincide with the ordinary ambient-space chain rule.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(f:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(T(x)=Ax+b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(A\) is surjective, then \(\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial f(Tx)\); if \(A\) is injective, then \(\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial_S(f|_S)(Tx)\), where \(S=b+\operatorname{ran}A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct finite-dimensional formulas for surjective maps and injective parametrizations of affine subspaces.

notation.meaning: Affine mapping from X to Y.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A(x)=A_0x+b\) map \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R^m\), and let \(h:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine precomposition. The definition collects elementary structural cases in which the exact adjoint chain rule is immediate from full domain, surjectivity, or polyhedral feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The elementary exact affine-mapping regimes are the following alternatives:
\[(\mathrm F)\quad\operatorname{dom}h=\mathbb R^m;\qquad (\mathrm S)\quad\operatorname{ran}A_0=\mathbb R^m;\qquad (\mathrm P)\quad h	ext{ is polyhedral and }A(\mathbb R^n)\cap\operatorname{dom}h
e\varnothing.\]
Under \((\mathrm F)\), or under \((\mathrm S)\) with \(h\) proper, or under \((\mathrm P)\), the composite is proper and
\[\partial(h\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\qquad(x\in\mathbb R^n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three elementary mapping structures give an exact affine chain rule. The outer function may have full domain; the linear part may be surjective; or the outer function may be polyhedral while the affine range meets its domain. In each regime every subgradient of the composite is the adjoint pullback of an outer subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\mathrm F)\lor(\mathrm S)\lor(\mathrm P)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial(h\circ A)=A_0^*\circ(\partial h)\circ A.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Regime \((\mathrm F)\) makes the range-relative-interior test automatic because \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)=\mathbb R^m\).
Regime \((\mathrm S)\) makes \(A(\mathbb R^n)=\mathbb R^m\), which necessarily meets the nonempty relative interior of the domain of a proper finite-dimensional convex function.
special_cases_latex: If \(A_0\) is invertible, it is surjective and \(\partial(h\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\).
For a coordinate projection with full-row rank, the surjective regime applies.
Every finite convex outer function belongs to regime \((\mathrm F)\), regardless of whether \(A_0\) is injective or surjective.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under surjectivity, \(A_0^*\) is injective, so the representing outer subgradient is unique whenever a composite subgradient is fixed.
For a differentiable outer function, all three regimes reduce to the classical adjoint gradient formula.
boundary_notes: Injectivity without surjectivity is not listed as an exactness mechanism for an extended-valued outer function.
The polyhedral regime still requires feasibility of the composite.
These are sufficient structural regimes, not an exhaustive characterization of exactness.

children.title: Affine Chain-Rule Exactness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Exactness boundaries governed by mapping range and effective-domain geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex and let \(A(x)=A_0x+b\). Put \(R=b+\operatorname{ran}A_0\) and \(D=\operatorname{dom}h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued affine composition. The boundary is geometric: it compares the affine range with the relative interior and boundary of the outer effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The affine chain-rule exactness boundary is the trichotomy
\[R\cap\operatorname{ri}D
e\varnothing\quad	ext{(qualified exact region)},\]
\[R\cap D
e\varnothing\ 	ext{ and }\ R\cap\operatorname{ri}D=\varnothing\quad	ext{(boundary-only feasible region)},\]
\[R\cap D=\varnothing\quad	ext{(infeasible region)}.\]
In the qualified exact region,
\[\partial(h\circ A)(x)=A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\quad orall x.\]
In every region the forward inclusion \(A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\subseteq\partial(h\circ A)(x)\) remains valid wherever the composite is finite, but the cited general rule does not guarantee the reverse inclusion in the boundary-only region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exactness boundary is determined by how the affine range meets the effective domain of the outer function. Meeting its relative interior is the qualified region and guarantees the exact adjoint chain rule. Meeting only the relative boundary leaves the composite feasible but does not guarantee that every composite subgradient has an outer multiplier representation. Missing the domain makes the composite improper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R\cap\operatorname{ri}D\ne\varnothing\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial(h\circ A)=A_0^*\circ(\partial h)\circ A.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The qualified region is equivalently \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(D-R)\).
At a finite point \(x\), exactness is the multiplier-surjectivity statement \(\partial(h\circ A)(x)\subseteq A_0^*\partial h(Ax)\), since the reverse inclusion is automatic.
special_cases_latex: If \(D=\mathbb R^m\), every affine range lies in the qualified region.
If \(h\) is polyhedral, boundary-only feasibility is still sufficient for exactness by the polyhedral alternative.
If \(R\cap D=\varnothing\), then \(h(Ax)=+\infty\) for all \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The obstruction to exactness is not nonlinearity of the inner map but failure of transversal contact between its range and the outer domain.
The boundary identifies when multiplier representations require a separate closedness or polyhedral argument.
boundary_notes: The boundary-only regime does not assert failure of exactness; it states that relative-interior exactness is unavailable.
Range geometry concerns the entire affine range, not only the value \(Ax\) at one point.
Infinite-dimensional analogues replace relative interior by stronger generalized-interior or closedness conditions.

review_flags: The boundary trichotomy is an organizational definition built directly from the sufficient exactness and feasibility conditions in the cited theorem; boundary-only feasibility is not claimed to characterize failure.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Range Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a support-function composition, the subdifferential at zero is the closure of the adjoint image. The ordinary chain rule is exact precisely when that image is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support-function composition satisfies
\[
\sigma_K(Ax)=\sigma_{A^*K}(x)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\partial(\sigma_K\circ A)(0)=\operatorname{cl}(A^*K).
\]
Since \(\partial\sigma_K(0)=K\), the ordinary chain-rule expression is \(A^*\partial\sigma_K(0)=A^*K\). Therefore the chain rule is exact at \(0\) whenever \(A^*K\) is closed, and in this model closedness is also necessary for exactness.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(K\subset Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\sigma_K\circ A)(0)=A^*\partial\sigma_K(0)=A^*K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-image exactness criterion for the support-function model of affine chain rules.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Compatibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine chain rule is exact when the affine image meets the relative interior of the outer function's domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the affine space reached by \(T\) meets the relative interior of the effective domain,
\[
(b+\operatorname{ran}A)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\ne\varnothing,
\]
then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}(f\circ T)\),
\[
\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial f(Ax+b).
\]
Thus domain compatibility eliminates the possible closure or approximation defect in the reverse chain-rule inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(f:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(T(x)=Ax+b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f\circ T)(x)=A^*\partial f(Ax+b)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Image Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite-cone support function and a two-dimensional linear map produce a nonclosed adjoint image, making the ordinary affine chain-rule inclusion strict at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\), one has \(A^*M=(a,b)\), and hence
\[
A^*K=\bigl\{(a,b):a>0,\ b\in\mathbb{R}\bigr\}\cup\{(0,0)\},
\]
which is not closed. Since \(\partial\sigma_K(0)=K\),
\[
A^*\partial f(0)=A^*K
\subsetneq
\operatorname{cl}(A^*K)=\{(a,b):a\ge0,\ b\in\mathbb{R}\}
=
\partial(f\circ A)(0).
\]
Thus the unclosed chain-rule image can be strictly smaller than the true subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(Y=\mathbb{S}^2\) has the Frobenius inner product, \(K=\mathbb{S}_+^2\), and \(X=\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^*\partial f(0)=A^*K\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}(A^*K)=\partial(f\circ A)(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete strict chain-rule failure caused by a nonclosed adjoint image of a semidefinite cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Scalar Composition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of an increasing convex scalar composition consists exactly of nonnegative outer subgradients multiplying inner subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) and \(\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) satisfy the assumptions above. Monotonicity implies \(\partial\phi(g(\bar x))\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+\). The exact convex-composition rule is
\[
\partial(\phi\circ g)(\bar x)=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\partial\phi(g(\bar x))}\alpha\,\partial g(\bar x)
=\{\alpha u:\alpha\in\partial\phi(g(\bar x)),\ u\in\partial g(\bar x)\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper convex and finite and continuous near \(\bar x\).
\(\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper convex, nondecreasing, and continuous at \(g(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\phi\circ g)(\bar x)=\{\alpha u:\alpha\in\partial\phi(g(\bar x)),\ u\in\partial g(\bar x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact chain rule under continuity qualifications.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact subdifferential of an increasing convex scalar composition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex and let \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be finite convex and nondecreasing. Define \(h=g\circ f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional and finite-valued. Monotonicity of the scalar outer function preserves convexity and forces its subgradients to be nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A monotone scalar composition is a function
\[h(x)=g(f(x))\]
with \(f\) convex and \(g\) convex nondecreasing. Its exact subdifferential is
\[\partial h(x)= igcup_{ho\in\partial g(f(x))}ho\,\partial f(x)=\{ho s:ho\in\partial g(f(x)),\ s\in\partial f(x)\}.\]
Since \(g\) is nondecreasing, \(\partial g(f(x))\subseteq\mathbb R_+\). The convention \(0\,\partial f(x)=\{0\}\) applies in the finite-valued regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone scalar composition applies a finite convex nondecreasing scalar function to a finite convex inner function. Its subdifferential consists of all products of an outer scalar subgradient and an inner vector subgradient. Every outer scalar subgradient is nonnegative, which is the order property needed to preserve the inner convex subgradient inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial(g\circ f)(x)=\{\rho s:\rho\in\partial g(f(x)),\ s\in\partial f(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\partial(g\circ f)(x)=\bigcup_{\rho\in\partial g(f(x))}\rho\partial f(x).\]
If \(g\) is differentiable at \(f(x)\), then \(\partial(g\circ f)(x)=g'(f(x))\partial f(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(g(t)=t_+=\max\{t,0\}\), the rule gives \(\partial(f_+)(x)=\partial f(x)\) when \(f(x)>0\), \(\{0\}\) when \(f(x)<0\), and \([0,1]\partial f(x)\) when \(f(x)=0\).
For differentiable \(f\), \(\partial(g\circ f)(x)=\{\rho\nabla f(x):\rho\in\partial g(f(x))\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If both functions are differentiable at the relevant points, \(\nabla(g\circ f)(x)=g'(f(x))\nabla f(x)\).
If \(0\in\partial g(f(x))\), then \(0\in\partial(g\circ f)(x)\).
boundary_notes: If \(g\) is convex but decreasing on part of the range of \(f\), the composite need not be convex.
Extended-valued functions require additional domain qualifications.
The union over \(\rho\) need not reduce to one scaled set unless the outer subdifferential is a singleton.

=\{\alpha u:\alpha\in\partial\phi(g(\bar x)),\ u\in\partial g(\bar x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of an increasing convex scalar composition consists exactly of nonnegative outer subgradients multiplying inner subgradients.
