knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Convex Function and Its Finite Active-Generator Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral convex set, and let \((a_i,b_i)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper extended-valued polyhedral convex functions represented by finitely many affine pieces over a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper polyhedral convex function is equivalently a function of the form \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}+\delta_P(x),\] where \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set. Its epigraph is polyhedral, and every proper polyhedral convex function admits such a representation. For \(x\in P\), define the active affine set \[I(x):=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i=f(x)\}.\] The finite active-generator representation of its subdifferential is \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x).\] If \(P=\{x:Cx\le d\}\) and \(J(x):=\{j:(Cx)_j=d_j\}\), then \[N_P(x)=\operatorname{cone}\{C_j^*:j\in J(x)\},\] and consequently \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+\operatorname{cone}\{C_j^*:j\in J(x)\}.\] For \(x\notin P\), \(f(x)=+\infty\) and \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\). Thus every subdifferential value is a polyhedral convex set described by finitely many active point generators and active recession generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper polyhedral convex function is a finite maximum of affine functions restricted to a polyhedral domain. At a point in the domain, its subdifferential is the convex hull of the slopes of active affine pieces plus the normal cone of the domain. When the domain is given by finitely many inequalities, that normal cone is generated conically by the active constraint normals. Hence the entire subdifferential has a finite point-and-ray representation.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set.
The maximum contains finitely many affine functions.
The normal-cone formula using \(C_j^*\) uses the displayed inequality representation of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x)\quad(x\in P).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a polyhedral convex set.
A proper convex function is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated.
special_cases_latex: If \(P=\mathbb R^n\), then \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).
For an affine function, the subdifferential is the singleton containing its slope.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(\partial f(x)\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set for \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
Directional derivatives of \(f\) are polyhedral support functions of these subdifferentials.
boundary_notes: A general piecewise-linear formula that is not convex need not be representable as a maximum of affine pieces.
Redundant affine pieces or constraints do not change the represented subdifferential.

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to P at x

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is polyhedral exactly when it is a finite maximum of affine functions on a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is polyhedral when its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a nonempty polyhedron. Equivalently, there exist a nonempty polyhedron \(D\subset E\), vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in E\), and scalars \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb R\) such that \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}+\delta_D(x).\] In this representation, \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(f\) is finite and piecewise affine on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a nonempty polyhedron, equivalently when it has a finite affine maximum on a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued representation of proper convex polyhedral functions.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex piecewise-linear function is a maximum of finitely many affine pieces; its subdifferential is the convex hull of active slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\) be given by \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}.\] Then \(f\) is convex and piecewise linear-affine, and for every \(x\in E\), \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\},\qquad I(x)=\{i:f(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}.\] Conversely, every finite-valued convex piecewise-linear function on \(E\) admits such a finite maximum representation.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i\in E\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(1\le i\le m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex piecewise-linear functions represented by affine pieces.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Face Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polytope, the active face exposed by a direction is the convex hull of maximizing vertices and equals the support-function subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\), then for every \(x\in E\), \[\sigma_P(x)=\max_{1\le j\le m}\langle x,v_j\rangle\] and \[\partial\sigma_P(x)=F_P(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{v_j:j\in J(x)\},\qquad J(x)=\{j:\langle x,v_j\rangle=\sigma_P(x)\}.\] Thus the active generators determine precisely the exposed face, including nonvertex points obtained by their convex combinations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\sigma_P(x)=F_P(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{v_j:j\in J(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-face formula for support functions of finitely generated polytopes.

notation.meaning: Face of P exposed by x

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Support Functions p. 135

knowledge_statements.title: Generator Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral subdifferential is generated by convex combinations of active affine slopes plus conic combinations of active domain normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in D\), define \(I(x)=\{i:f(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}\). Then \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_D(x).\] If \(D=\{x:\langle c_j,x\rangle\le d_j,\ 1\le j\le q\}\) and \(K(x)=\{j:\langle c_j,x\rangle=d_j\}\), then \[N_D(x)=\operatorname{cone}\{c_j:j\in K(x)\}.\] Hence active slope generators and active constraint normals generate the entire subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_D(x)\) for \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slope-generator and domain-normal representation of polyhedral subdifferentials.

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to D at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block-Separable Convex Function and Product Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=E_1\times\cdots\times E_m\) be a finite product of Euclidean spaces, let \(f_i:E_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, and write \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian block decompositions with independent block functions; coupled linear compositions require the separate chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is block-separable when \[f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i).\] Its domain and subdifferential decompose as \[\operatorname{dom}f=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i,\qquad \partial f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x_i).\] Equivalently, a vector \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\in E\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) exactly when \[g_i\in\partial f_i(x_i)\quad\text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m.\] A coordinate-separable function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is the special case \(E_i=\mathbb R\), so \[f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi_i(x_i),\qquad \partial f(x)=\partial\phi_1(x_1)\times":["\cdots"]\times\partial\phi_n(x_n).\] More generally, if \(A_i:\mathbb R^p\to E_i\) are linear and \(F(z)=\sum_i f_i(A_i z)\), an exact qualified chain-and-sum construction gives \[\partial F(z)=\sum_i A_i^*\partial f_i(A_i z).\] The product identity is the defining uncoupled block model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-separable convex function is a sum in which each term depends on its own block of variables. Its effective domain is the Cartesian product of the block domains, and its subdifferential is the Cartesian product of the block subdifferentials. Thus a full subgradient is obtained by independently choosing one subgradient per block. Linear maps that mix blocks form a related composite model and use adjoint pullbacks rather than the defining product formula.
assumptions_latex: The number of blocks \(m\) is finite.
Each \(f_i\) is proper and convex on \(E_i\).
For the composite extension, the usual qualification for the extended-valued sum and chain rules holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\partial f_1(x_1)\times\cdots\times\partial f_m(x_m).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[g\in\partial f(x)\iff g_i\in\partial f_i(x_i)\ \forall i.\]
special_cases_latex:
For differentiable blocks, \(
abla f(x)=(
abla f_1(x_1),\ldots,
abla f_m(x_m))\).
For coordinatewise absolute values, each zero coordinate contributes an interval \([-1,1]\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Subgradient selection decomposes independently across blocks.
The subdifferential is a singleton exactly when every block subdifferential is a singleton.
boundary_notes: A sum \(\sum_i f_i(x)\) sharing the same variable is not block-separable in this sense; its subdifferential uses a Minkowski sum.
Infinite products require topological and dual-space qualifications absent here.

notation.meaning: adjoint of the block linear map

knowledge_statements.title: Separable Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a separable convex sum is the Cartesian product of the component subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(E=E_1\times\cdots\times E_m\), define \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\). Then \(f\) is proper and convex, and its subdifferential separates exactly by components: \[\partial f(x)=\partial f_1(x_1)\times\cdots\times\partial f_m(x_m).\] Equivalently, \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\) belongs to \(\partial f(x)\) if and only if \(g_i\in\partial f_i(x_i)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact subdifferential decomposition for finite separable convex sums.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Subdifferentials of Extended-Valued Functions p. 47

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Structured Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite sum of convex functions composed with linear block maps, the relative-interior qualification makes the subdifferential equal to the sum of the adjoint-transformed component subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be defined by \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(A_i x)\). Under the stated relative-interior qualification, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), \[\partial F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m A_i^*\partial f_i(A_i x)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m A_i^*g_i:g_i\in\partial f_i(A_i x)\text{ for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\right\}.\] Thus component subgradients are transported to \(E\) by the adjoint maps and added there.
assumptions_latex: For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(A_i:E\to E_i\) is linear and \(f_i:E_i\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\), \(\partial F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m A_i^*\partial f_i(A_i x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Assembly
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate vector is a subgradient of a coordinate-separable sum exactly when each entry is a subgradient of the corresponding scalar function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \(f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)\), a vector \(g\in\mathbb R^n\) is a subgradient at \(x\) precisely when each coordinate is a scalar subgradient: \[g\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_i\in\partial f_i(x_i)\ \text{for every }i.\] Consequently, any independent choices \(g_i\in\partial f_i(x_i)\) assemble into a subgradient of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\in\partial f(x)\iff g_i\in\partial f_i(x_i)\) for every \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Assembly

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Identify \(E\times E\) with \(\prod_{i=1}^m(E_i\times E_i)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Spectral and Unitarily Invariant Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb S^n\) carry the trace inner product, let \(\lambda(X)\in\mathbb R^n\) list eigenvalues of \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), and let \(\sigma(X)\in\mathbb R^r\), \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), list singular values of \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real symmetric and rectangular matrix spaces; the definition covers eigenvalue-symmetric and singular-value-symmetric convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric spectral function on \(\mathbb S^n\) is a function \[F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X)),\] where \(\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and invariant under coordinate permutations. A unitarily invariant spectral function on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is \[G(X)=\psi(\sigma(X)),\] where \(\psi:\mathbb R^r\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and invariant under signed coordinate permutations. Equivalently, \(F(QXQ^T)=F(X)\) for every orthogonal \(Q\), and \(G(UXV^T)=G(X)\) for all orthogonal \(U,V\). Closedness and convexity of \(F\) or \(G\) are equivalent to closedness and convexity of their associated symmetric scalar functions. The subgradient structure is spectral: if \(X=Q\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda(X))Q^T\), then commuting subgradients have the form \[Z=Q\operatorname{Diag}(z)Q^T,\qquad z\in\partial\varphi(\lambda(X)),\] with freedom inside repeated-eigenvalue eigenspaces. In particular, \[\partial\lambda_{\max}(X)=\operatorname{co}\{uu^T:\|u\|=1,\ Xu=\lambda_{\max}(X)u\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric spectral function on symmetric matrices depends only on the eigenvalues through a permutation-invariant scalar function. A unitarily invariant rectangular-matrix function depends only on singular values through an absolutely symmetric scalar function. Orthogonal changes of eigenvectors or singular vectors therefore leave the value unchanged. Convexity and closedness transfer exactly between the matrix function and its scalar representative. Subgradients align with the relevant spectral subspaces; the maximum-eigenvalue function is generated by rank-one projectors onto its top eigenspace.
assumptions_latex: The matrix spaces use the trace or Frobenius inner product.
\(\varphi\) is permutation invariant; \(\psi\) is invariant under permutations and sign changes.
For the convex subgradient representation, the associated scalar function is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F=\varphi\circ\lambda,\qquad G=\psi\circ\sigma,\] with orthogonal invariance and scalar-to-matrix transfer of convexity; for the canonical maximum-eigenvalue instance, \[\partial\lambda_{\max}(X)=\operatorname{co}\{uu^T:Xu=\lambda_{\max}(X)u,\ \|u\|=1\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F(QXQ^T)=F(X)\) for every orthogonal \(Q\).
\(G(UXV^T)=G(X)\) for every compatible orthogonal \(U,V\).
special_cases_latex: The spectral radius on \(\mathbb S^n\), nuclear norm, spectral norm, and Schatten norms are spectral functions with suitable symmetric scalar representatives.
If \(\lambda_{\max}(X)\) is simple, its subdifferential is \(\{uu^T\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Repeated eigenvalues or singular values create subgradient freedom within invariant subspaces.
Matrix subgradient computations reduce to scalar symmetric subgradient data plus a spectral decomposition.
boundary_notes: For nonsymmetric square matrices, eigenvalues may be complex; the eigenvalue-spectral definition here is restricted to \(\mathbb S^n\).
The displayed general diagonal form must respect multiplicity-induced rotations; it is not a claim that an arbitrary fixed eigenbasis works independently of the scalar subgradient.

notation.meaning: ordered eigenvalue vector of a symmetric matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient of a convex eigenvalue spectral function shares an eigenbasis with the matrix and has eigenvalues from the underlying vector subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:\mathbb S^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(F(X)=\varphi(\lambda(X))\). Then \(Y\in\partial F(X)\) if and only if there exist an orthogonal matrix \(U\) and a vector \(z\in\partial\varphi(\lambda(X))\) such that \[X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda(X))U^{\mathsf T},\qquad Y=U\operatorname{Diag}(z)U^{\mathsf T}.\] Thus a spectral subgradient shares an eigenbasis with \(X\), while its eigenvalue vector is a subgradient of the underlying symmetric function.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and permutation invariant.
\(X\in\mathbb S^n\), with eigenvalues arranged in nonincreasing order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y\in\partial(\varphi\circ\lambda)(X)\) exactly when \(X\) and \(Y\) admit a common ordered eigenbasis with \(\lambda(Y)\in\partial\varphi(\lambda(X))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex subdifferential representation for symmetric eigenvalue spectral functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue-Based Structures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient of a convex eigenvalue function shares a compatible eigenbasis with the matrix, and its eigenvalue vector subgradates the underlying symmetric function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(X)=\phi(\lambda(X))\) on \(\mathbb{H}^n\). Then
\[
\partial F(X)=\left\{U\operatorname{Diag}(z)U^*:X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda(X))U^*,\ z\in\partial\phi(\lambda(X))\right\}.
\]
Thus every subgradient is obtained by diagonalizing it in an eigenbasis compatible with \(X\), with its diagonal vector belonging to the ordinary convex subdifferential of \(\phi\). The union over compatible diagonalizations accounts for eigenvalue multiplicities.
assumptions_latex: \phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and permutation invariant}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial F(X)=\bigcup_{X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda(X))U^*}U\operatorname{Diag}(\partial\phi(\lambda(X)))U^*
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Hermitian spectral functions, including repeated eigenvalues through the union over compatible eigenbases.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value-Based Structures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subgradients of a convex singular-value function arise from compatible singular vectors and vector subgradients of its absolutely symmetric generating function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(X)=\phi(\sigma(X))\). Then
\[
\partial F(X)=\left\{U\operatorname{Diag}_{m,n}(z)V^\top:X=U\operatorname{Diag}_{m,n}(\sigma(X))V^\top,\ z\in\partial\phi(\sigma(X))\right\}.
\]
Here \(U\) and \(V\) range over orthogonal factors of full singular-value decompositions compatible with \(X\). This union incorporates freedom in singular subspaces associated with repeated or zero singular values.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial F(X)=\bigcup_{X=U\operatorname{Diag}_{m,n}(\sigma(X))V^\top}U\operatorname{Diag}_{m,n}(\partial\phi(\sigma(X)))V^\top
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real rectangular matrices; complex matrices use unitary factors and conjugate transpose.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection and Active-Set Subdifferential Templates for Distance-Max Models
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(P_C\) be the Euclidean projection, and let \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be finitely many convex functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean distance functions and finite convex maxima, including sums or positive combinations formed under the standard calculus rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The distance-max representation family consists of convex functions assembled from the primitives \[d_C(x):=\min_{y\in C}\|x-y\|\] and \[m(x):=\max_{1\le i\le q}f_i(x).\] Their canonical subdifferential templates are \[\partial d_C(x)=\begin{cases}N_C(x)\cap\mathbb B,&x\in C,\\ \left\{\dfrac{x-P_C(x)}{\|x-P_C(x)\|}\right\},&x\notin C,\end{cases}\] and, with \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=m(x)\}\), \[\partial m(x)=\operatorname{co}\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x).\] A represented model may combine these primitives by positive sums, affine precomposition, or another qualified convex operation. For example, if \[F(x)=\alpha d_C(Ax-b)+\max_i f_i(x),\qquad \alpha>0,\] and the stated calculus qualifications hold, then \[\partial F(x)=\alpha A^*\partial d_C(Ax-b)+\operatorname{co}\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x).\] Projection residuals therefore govern exterior distance subgradients, normal directions govern points on the set, and active pieces govern maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family uses two canonical nonsmooth primitives. The distance to a closed convex set is represented through projection: outside the set its unique subgradient is the normalized projection residual, while on the set its subdifferential is the unit-truncated normal cone. A finite maximum is represented by the convex hull of the subdifferentials of its active pieces. Positive sums and affine maps combine these templates under the usual convex calculus conditions.
assumptions_latex: The distance uses the Euclidean norm and projection.
Composite members satisfy the qualifications needed by their sum and chain rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap\mathbb B\text{ on }C,\quad \partial d_C(x)=\left\{\frac{x-P_C(x)}{d_C(x)}\right\}\text{ off }C,\quad \partial\max_i f_i(x)=\operatorname{co}\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x\notin C\), \(\nabla d_C(x)=(x-P_C(x))/d_C(x)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is an affine subspace, \(x-P_C(x)\) is its orthogonal residual.
The pointwise maximum of affine functions yields the active-slope polytope.
immediate_consequences_latex: The kink set of \(d_C\) is contained in the boundary of \(C\).
One projection or one active piece supplies a valid subgradient in the corresponding regime.
boundary_notes: For a non-Euclidean norm, projections may be nonunique and the displayed exterior singleton formula changes.
Distance to a nonconvex set is generally nonconvex and is outside this family.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside a closed convex set, distance has the normalized projection residual as its unique subgradient; on the set, subgradients are unit-bounded normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The distance function \(d_C\) is finite, convex, and continuous. Its subdifferential is
\[
\partial d_C(x)=
\begin{cases}
\left\{\dfrac{x-P_Cx}{\|x-P_Cx\|}\right\},&x\notin C,\\
N_C(x)\cap\{u\in H:\|u\|\le 1\},&x\in C.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently, outside \(C\) the distance has a unique subgradient directed from the projection toward \(x\); on \(C\), its subgradients are precisely the normal vectors of norm at most one.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
C\subset H\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial d_C(x)=\{(x-P_Cx)/d_C(x)\}\text{ off }C,\quad \partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap\overline{B}\text{ on }C
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex subdifferential of distance to a nonempty closed convex set in a Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Type Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite convex maximum is the convex hull of subgradients belonging to functions active at the evaluation point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\) and \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). Then \(f\) is convex and
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).
\]
Equivalently, every subgradient of \(f\) is a convex combination \(\sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i g_i\), where \(g_i\in\partial f_i(x)\), \(\alpha_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\!\left(\max_i f_i\right)(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite pointwise maxima of finite-valued convex functions on a common open domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Based Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection residual represents distance, is the gradient of half the squared distance, and normalizes to the distance gradient outside the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in H\), the projection \(P_Cx\) is uniquely defined and
\[
d_C(x)=\|x-P_Cx\|,
\qquad
\nabla\left(\frac12d_C^2\right)(x)=x-P_Cx.
\]
If \(x\notin C\), then \(d_C\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\) and
\[
\nabla d_C(x)=\frac{x-P_Cx}{\|x-P_Cx\|}.
\]
Thus the projection residual supplies exact first-order information for the squared distance everywhere and for the distance outside \(C\).
assumptions_latex: H\text{ is a real Hilbert space}
C\subset H\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_C(x)=\|x-P_Cx\|,\quad \nabla\!\left(\tfrac12d_C^2\right)(x)=x-P_Cx
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection formulas for distance and squared distance in a Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Index Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact max-function subgradient is a convex combination of component subgradients indexed only by functions attaining the maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\max_i f_i(x)\). With \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\),
\[
\partial f(x)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i g_i:\ g_i\in\partial f_i(x),\ \alpha_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i=1\right\}.
\]
Inactive indices receive zero weight. Hence an exact subgradient can be constructed from one subgradient of each selected active component and simplex coefficients supported entirely on \(I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\left\{\sum_{i\in I(x)}\alpha_i g_i:\alpha\in\Delta_{I(x)},\ g_i\in\partial f_i(x)\right\}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient form of the active-index subdifferential representation for a finite maximum.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Based Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior domain point, the directional derivative of a convex function is exactly the support function of its subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the one-sided directional derivative exists and satisfies
\[
f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)=\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle.
\]
Thus the closed convex subdifferential \(\partial f(x)\) is represented through its support function by the complete directional-derivative map. In particular, every subgradient supplies a linear lower estimate, while the support value gives the sharp directional slope.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)=\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle\quad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support-function representation of the directional derivative at an interior domain point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact, Approximate, and Separation Subgradient Information
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic information objects supplied at a query point to an external optimization method; no iterative method or complexity statement is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subgradient information interface at \(x\) returns one of the following certified objects. An exact response is \[(f(x),g),\qquad g\in\partial f(x),\] meaning \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\quad\forall y\in\mathbb R^n.\] An approximate response is \[(f(x),g,\varepsilon),\qquad g\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x),\] meaning \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\quad\forall y\in\mathbb R^n.\] A separation-cut response for the epigraph is the affine inequality \[r\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon,\] valid for every \((y,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\). The response is deterministic if repeated queries at the same input return the same certified tuple, although \(\partial f(x)\) or \(\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\) may contain many elements. The information interface is the graph of the admissible response relation, not a rule for choosing query points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient information interface supplies certified first-order data at a query point. Exact information gives a function value and an exact supporting slope. Approximate information permits a stated vertical error in the global affine minorant. Either response induces a valid affine cut for the epigraph. Determinism means that repeated calls at the same point select the same admissible response; it does not imply that the mathematical subdifferential is single-valued. Query generation and convergence analysis belong to external methods.
assumptions_latex: Every returned tuple satisfies its global support inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[g\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\quad\forall y.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\varepsilon=0\), the approximate interface reduces to the exact interface.
The approximate condition is equivalent to \(f(x)+f^*(g)-\langle g,x\rangle\le\varepsilon\) when conjugacy is available.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), the exact slope is uniquely \(\nabla f(x)\).
A value-only interface is not a subgradient information interface unless it also certifies a supporting slope.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every response supplies a globally valid affine lower model of \(f\).
The associated epigraph inequality can be passed directly to a cutting-plane or bundle model.
boundary_notes: A noisy vector without a certified error bound is not an approximate subgradient in this sense.
Stochastic unbiasedness is distinct from the deterministic global support inequality.

children.title: Exact Subgradient Information
children.top_down_role: Exact supporting information exposed to optimization methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Subgradient Information
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact subgradient and function value define a globally valid affine lower bound that agrees with the convex function at the query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Exact subgradient information at \(x\) consists of \(f(x)\) and a vector \(g\in\partial f(x)\), equivalently a vector satisfying
\[
f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
The affine function \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) is therefore a globally valid lower model of \(f\), exact at \(x\). The pair \((f(x),g)\) is directly usable as exact supporting information by first-order methods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\in\partial f(x)\iff f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order oracle information for an extended-real-valued convex function.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of f at x

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Subdifferentials of Extended-Valued Functions p. 47

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact deterministic supporting information for a convex function at a finite-valued query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact subgradient information response for \(f\) at \(x\) is a pair \[\mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),g_x)\] with \(g_x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \[g_x\in\partial f(x):=\{g\in\mathbb R^n:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^n\}.\] Equivalently, the affine function \[\ell_x(y):=f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\] is a global minorant of \(f\) that is exact at \(x\), namely \(\ell_x(x)=f(x)\). The response also determines the supporting half-space \[H_x:=\{(y,r)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:r\ge\ell_x(y)\},\] and \(\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq H_x\), with \((x,f(x))\) on the boundary hyperplane. A single-valued exact oracle is a selection \(x\mapsto g_x\in\partial f(x)\) on a specified query domain \(D\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\partial f\). Exactness concerns membership in \(\partial f(x)\); it does not require returning every subgradient or imply that \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact subgradient information at a query point consists of the exact function value and one vector satisfying the global subgradient inequality. The associated affine function touches the objective at the query point and lies below it everywhere, thereby defining a supporting half-space containing the epigraph. A deterministic exact oracle may select one subgradient whenever several exist. Returning only one does not mean that the function is differentiable or that the full subdifferential has been computed.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), so at least one exact subgradient exists.
The returned value equals \(f(x)\) and the returned vector satisfies the inequality for every \(y\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),g_x)\text{ is exact}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\quad\forall y\in\mathbb R^n.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[g_x\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(g_x)=\langle g_x,x\rangle\] for proper closed convex \(f\).
\[(g_x,-1)\] is normal to \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\), up to the chosen normal-cone sign convention.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(g_x=\nabla f(x)\).
For affine \(f(y)=a+\langle c,y\rangle\), every exact response returns \(g_x=c\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The returned affine minorant is a valid exact cutting plane.
For every minimizer \(x^*\), \(f(x^*)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,x^*-x\rangle\).
boundary_notes: At points outside \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), no exact response of this form exists.
Finite numerical precision or an inexact function value requires a separately quantified approximate interface.

notation.meaning: exact value–subgradient response relation or a selected oracle
supporting affine minorant returned at x

children.title: Approximate Subgradient Information
children.top_down_role: Controlled inexact supporting information and tolerance-indexed certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Subgradient Information
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient defines an affine global lower model allowed to fall below exact supporting contact by at most epsilon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential of \(f\) at \(x\) is
\[
\partial_\varepsilon f(x)=\left\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
Thus \((f(x),g,\varepsilon)\) supplies a globally valid affine lower model with additive deficit at most \(\varepsilon\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), this interface reduces to exact subgradient information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\iff f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error approximate subgradient information for proper convex functions.

children.title: Separation-Cut Information Interface
children.top_down_role: Subgradient-generated separating models passed to external cutting-plane and bundle methods.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Write \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(z,r):r\ge f(z)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact first-order information for a convex function; the interface supplies valid global affine cuts, not merely local linearizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A separation-cut information interface for \(f\) is an oracle \(\mathcal O_f\) whose successful response at every query \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is a pair \((f(x),g_x)\) with \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\), equivalently
\[f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,z-x\rangle\quad(\forall z\in E).\]
The response induces the affine minorant \(\ell_x(z)=f(x)+\langle g_x,z-x\rangle\) and the epigraph cut
\[H_x^+=\{(z,r)\in E\times\mathbb R:r\ge \ell_x(z)\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f\subseteq H_x^+.\]
For a convex inequality \(f(z)\le0\), if \(f(x)>0\), the same response induces the separating feasibility cut
\[H_x^-:=\{z\in E:f(x)+\langle g_x,z-x\rangle\le0\},\qquad \{z:f(z)\le0\}\subseteq H_x^-,\quad x\notin H_x^-.\]
For finitely many responses \((y_i,f(y_i),g_i)\), the transmitted cutting-plane model is \(m_I(z)=\max_{i\in I}\{f(y_i)+\langle g_i,z-y_i\rangle\}\le f(z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every point \(x\) in the effective domain, the interface returns the value \(f(x)\) and an exact subgradient \(g_x\). Their affine linearization is a global minorant of \(f\), hence defines a half-space containing the epigraph. If the query violates \(f\le0\), the corresponding linear inequality contains every feasible point but excludes the query. A finite collection of responses is represented by the maximum of their affine minorants, which remains below \(f\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
A successful query satisfies \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and returns \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_f(x)=(f(x),g_x)\) provides a globally valid supporting cut, and finite collections provide the model \(m_I\le f\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\iff \operatorname{epi}f\subseteq H_x^+\) with equality at \((x,f(x))\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), a returned subgradient is a normal to \(C\), and the cut is a supporting half-space of \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every cutting-plane or bundle model assembled solely from successful responses is a convex piecewise-affine lower model of \(f\).
boundary_notes: If \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\), this exact interface has no successful subgradient response at \(x\).
Approximate subgradients produce relaxed cuts and belong to the separate approximate-information interface.

notation.meaning: Affine supporting minorant generated at the query point.
Maximum of finitely many transmitted affine cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Information
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient strictly separates any point below the function value from the function's epigraph, with margin at least the vertical deficit before normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every point \((x,t)\) with \(t<f(x)\), the vector \((g,-1)\) defines a strict separator from the epigraph:
\[
\langle(g,-1),(y,s)-(x,t)\rangle<0
\qquad\text{for every }(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f.
\]
The corresponding separation margin is at least \(f(x)-t\) before normalization of the separating normal.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle(g,-1),(y,s)-(x,t)\rangle<0\quad\forall (y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation of a point below a closed convex epigraph using exact subgradient information.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Separation p. 64

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Information
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of finitely many subgradient cuts is a convex polyhedral global lower model of the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Each oracle pair \((f(x_i),g_i)\) defines the cut \(\ell_i(x)=f(x_i)+\langle g_i,x-x_i\rangle\). The accumulated model
\[
m_k(x)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\ell_i(x)
\]
is convex and polyhedral, and satisfies
\[
m_k(x)\le f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Moreover, \(m_k(x_i)=f(x_i)\) whenever the cut generated at \(x_i\) remains among the maximizers there, which it necessarily does against all valid cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m_k(x)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\{f(x_i)+\langle g_i,x-x_i\rangle\}\le f(x)\quad\forall x
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite cutting-plane model assembled from exact function values and subgradients.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2 The Cutting-Plane Algorithm p. 174
3.2.8 Cutting Plane Schemes p. 217

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Hyperplane Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is an exact subgradient precisely when its affine graph supports the epigraph at the queried function value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vector \(g\) belongs to \(\partial f(x)\) if and only if
\[
\langle(g,-1),(y,s)-(x,f(x))\rangle\le0
\qquad\text{for every }(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f.
\]
Equivalently, the hyperplane
\[
s=f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle
\]
supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\), with the epigraph lying in the upper closed halfspace. This supporting relation is a verifiable geometric certificate of exact subgradient membership.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\in\partial f(x)\iff \langle(g,-1),(y,s)-(x,f(x))\rangle\le0\quad\forall(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph supporting-hyperplane certificate equivalent to exact convex subgradient membership.

3.4 Separation p. 64

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Cut Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient gives a globally valid affine lower cut, but its intercept may lie epsilon below the function value and need not support the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inexact subdifferential is \[\partial_\varepsilon f(x)=\{g\in X\mid f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }y\in X\}.\] Thus every \(g\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\) yields the affine minorant \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}f\) lies in the halfspace \[\{(y,r)\in X\times\mathbb R\mid r\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\varepsilon\}.\] When \(\varepsilon=0\), this is an exact supporting cut; for \(\varepsilon>0\), the hyperplane need not touch the epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex on a real Hilbert space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\) defines a valid cut with vertical error at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error boundary for affine minorants and epigraph cuts.

children.title: Subdifferential Failure Boundary Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Canonical boundaries where subdifferentiability, exact calculus, attainment, closure, topology-independent reasoning, or convex-specific interpretations fail.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_query: Convex Analysis and Monotone Operator Theory in Hilbert Spaces

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real locally convex space, let \(X^*\) be its continuous dual, and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). For convex \(f\), set \(\partial f(x)=\{x^*\in X^*:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle x^*,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in X\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal classification object for boundaries of applicability; it does not assert that the listed classes are mutually exclusive or exhaustive in every topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The subdifferential failure-boundary profile of \((X,f,x)\) is the set
\[\mathfrak F(X,f,x)\subseteq\{\mathrm D,\mathrm S,\mathrm Q,\mathrm A,\mathrm T,\mathrm C\}\]
defined by: \(\mathrm D\in\mathfrak F\) when properness, lower semicontinuity, or effective-domain geometry needed by the proposed result fails; \(\mathrm S\in\mathfrak F\) when \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\); \(\mathrm Q\in\mathfrak F\) when an asserted exact calculus equality has only its unconditional inclusion or otherwise fails; \(\mathrm A\in\mathfrak F\) when a representation requires an optimizer or measurable selector that does not exist; \(\mathrm T\in\mathfrak F\) when the claimed closure, compactness, or convergence statement changes with the norm, weak, or weak-star topology; and \(\mathrm C\in\mathfrak F\) when \(f\) is nonconvex and the global convex-support inequality is no longer the intended generalized derivative. A failure boundary is therefore a tuple together with at least one witnessed membership in \(\mathfrak F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The taxonomy assigns labels to a function, point, and ambient space. The labels record domain or closedness failure, absence of a supporting subgradient, failure of an exact calculus equality, nonattainment or missing selection, topology-sensitive failure, and departure from convexity. Several labels may apply simultaneously; the taxonomy classifies the obstruction rather than prescribing a replacement derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak F(X,f,x)\) is the set of witnessed obstruction classes attached to \((X,f,x)\).
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb R^n\), the topology label omits distinctions among compatible finite-dimensional Hausdorff vector topologies, while domain, qualification, attainment, and convexity failures remain possible.
boundary_notes: The six-way profile is a sidecar taxonomy synthesized for this node; no inspected source establishes it as a standard named definition.
A failed sufficient qualification condition does not by itself establish that the corresponding calculus equality is false.

notation.meaning: Set of failure-class labels witnessed at the specified function and point.

review_flags: No authoritative source was found that defines this exact six-class taxonomy.
The classification should be checked for intended exhaustiveness and terminology.
knowledge_statements.title: Taxonomy of convex-subdifferential failure boundaries

children.title: Domain-Closedness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by improperness, missing lower semicontinuity, and adverse effective-domain geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex. Its effective domain is \(D=\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}\), and its epigraph is \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r):r\ge f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex analysis, where relative interiors are available and lower semicontinuity is equivalent to epigraph closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The domain-closedness failure profile of \(f\) at \(x\) is
\[\mathfrak D_f(x)=\big(I_f,C_f,R_f(x)\big),\]
where \(I_f=1\) iff \(f\) is improper, meaning \(D=\varnothing\) or \(f\) takes the value \(-\infty\); \(C_f=1\) iff \(f\) is not closed, equivalently \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is not closed or \(f\ne\operatorname{cl}f\); and \(R_f(x)=1\) iff \(x\in D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D\). The tuple is a domain-closedness failure boundary at \(x\) when at least one component equals one. The components distinguish logically different obstructions: improperness invalidates the standard proper-convex framework, nonclosedness permits a gap between \(f\) and its lower-semicontinuous hull, and relative-boundary membership removes the general finite-dimensional guarantee \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This boundary is encoded by three indicators. The first records that the convex function is not proper. The second records failure of lower semicontinuity, equivalently nonclosedness of the epigraph. The third records that the point lies in the effective domain but outside its relative interior. Any positive indicator places the tuple on the domain-closedness boundary, while keeping the three mechanisms distinct.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and extended-real-valued on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak D_f(x)\ne(0,0,0)\) precisely denotes the defined domain-closedness boundary.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper convex \(f\), \(C_f=1\iff \operatorname{epi}f\text{ is not closed}\iff f\ne\operatorname{cl}f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is proper and closed and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}D\), then \(\mathfrak D_f(x)=(0,0,0)\) and the standard subgradient-existence result applies.
immediate_consequences_latex: The condition \(R_f(x)=1\) identifies loss of a general guarantee, not automatic emptiness of \(\partial f(x)\).
boundary_notes: A relative-boundary point may still possess subgradients.
Closedness of \(D\) is not equivalent to closedness of \(f\); the latter concerns the epigraph.

notation.meaning: Indicators of improperness, nonclosedness, and relative-domain-boundary membership.

source_refs.locator: §7, lower-semicontinuous hull and closure, extraction lines 2223-2265 and 2453; §23, Theorem 23.4, extraction lines 8551-8567

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absence of a supporting subgradient at a point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex subgradients in finite dimensions; the condition concerns nonvertical affine support at \((x,f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Supporting subgradients are absent for \(f\) at \(x\) when
\[\partial f(x)=\varnothing,\qquad \partial f(x):=\{g\in\mathbb R^n:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in\mathbb R^n\}.\]
Equivalently, there is no continuous affine function \(a(z)=f(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle\) that coincides with \(f\) at \(x\) and globally minorizes \(f\). Geometrically, \(\operatorname{epi}f\) has no nonvertical supporting hyperplane through \((x,f(x))\). For finite convex \(f\), this condition cannot occur at a relative-interior point of its effective domain; it is a possible boundary phenomenon at points of \(\operatorname{dom}f\setminus\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Supporting subgradients are absent exactly when the convex subdifferential at the point is empty. This means that no affine function touching the graph at the point lies below the function everywhere. In epigraph language, no nonvertical supporting hyperplane passes through the corresponding boundary point. Finite-dimensional proper convex functions always have a subgradient on the relative interior of their domain, so absence can only arise outside that guaranteed region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) is the defining condition for absence of exact supporting-subgradient information at \(x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\iff\nexists g\in\mathbb R^n\;\forall z,\ f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle\).
\(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) iff no nonvertical hyperplane supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and \(f\) is proper convex, then supporting subgradients are not absent.
immediate_consequences_latex: An exact subgradient oracle cannot return a valid response at such an \(x\).
boundary_notes: A vertical supporting hyperplane of the epigraph does not define a finite subgradient.
Emptiness is pointwise; it need not hold at neighboring relative-interior points.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of the extended-real-valued function at the point.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A downward jump immediately beside a domain endpoint produces a convex but nonclosed function, an empty endpoint subdifferential, and a strict biconjugate gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is proper and convex but is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\). Its biconjugate is \[f^{**}(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\geq0,\\+\infty,&t<0,\end{cases}\] and \[\partial f(0)=\varnothing,\qquad f^{**}(0)=0<f(0)=1.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex but nonclosed, with \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\) and \(f^{**}(0)=0<f(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional example linking nonclosedness, biconjugate regularization, and subgradient loss.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed proper convex function and its closure gap
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Define \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r):r\ge f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex functions; closed means lower semicontinuous on the whole ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is nonclosed when its epigraph is not closed:
\[\operatorname{epi}f\ne\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
Equivalently, \(f\) is not lower semicontinuous, so there exist \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and a sequence \(x_k\to x\) such that
\[f(x)>\liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k).\]
Its lower-semicontinuous hull, or closure, is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function majorized by \(f\), characterized by
\[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad \operatorname{cl}f\le f.\]
The nonclosedness gap set is \(G_f=\{x:(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)<f(x)\}\); for a proper convex function it can occur only on the relative boundary of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is nonclosed when its epigraph is not a closed subset of the product space. This is equivalent to failure of lower semicontinuity. Closing the epigraph defines the lower-semicontinuous hull \(\operatorname{cl}f\), which lies below \(f\). The points where the inequality is strict form the closure-gap set. In finite dimensions, a proper convex function agrees with its closure on the relative interior of its effective domain, so any gap is confined to the relative boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is nonclosed iff \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is nonclosed iff \(f\ne\operatorname{cl}f\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\text{ nonclosed}\iff\exists x_k\to x:\ f(x)>\liminf_k f(x_k)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb R^n\), then a proper convex \(f\) is continuous and hence closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), one has \((\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=f(x)\).
boundary_notes: A nonclosed effective domain does not by itself make \(f\) nonclosed; epigraph closedness is decisive.
The definition excludes improper convex functions, whose closure convention requires separate treatment.

notation.meaning: Set where the function strictly exceeds its lower-semicontinuous hull.

children.title: Ambient-Affine-Hull Representation Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Lower-dimensional domain effects on subgradient and normal-cone descriptions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(M=\operatorname{aff}D=x_0+L\), and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex with \(\operatorname{dom}f=D\). Identify \(L^*\) with \(L\) by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional functions whose effective domain lies in a proper affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in D\), define the relative subdifferential
\[\partial_M f(x)=\{u\in L:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle u,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in D\}\]
and the ambient subdifferential
\[\partial_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)=\{g\in\mathbb R^n:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in\mathbb R^n\}.\]
An ambient-affine-hull representation mismatch occurs when \(L\ne\mathbb R^n\) and an ambient vector is treated as a unique relative slope. Since every displacement \(z-x\) lies in \(L\), only \(P_Lg\) affects the supporting inequality, and
\[\partial_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)=\partial_M f(x)+L^\perp\]
whenever either side is nonempty. Thus one relative subgradient corresponds to an entire affine family of ambient representatives. The ambient normal cone to \(D\) likewise contains \(L^\perp\), and ambient subdifferentials are generally unbounded even when their relative representatives are bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the domain lies in a proper affine hull, subgradient inequalities only test displacements parallel to that hull. The projection of an ambient subgradient onto the parallel subspace is the relative subgradient, while every orthogonal component is invisible. Consequently, one relative slope has all vectors obtained by adding the orthogonal complement as ambient representatives. Treating an ambient representative as unique is the representation mismatch.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex with \(\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq M=x_0+L\).
The relative and ambient subdifferentials use the same Euclidean pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)=\partial_M f(x)+L^\perp\), so ambient representatives are nonunique when \(L\ne\mathbb R^n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) induce the same affine support on \(M\) iff \(g_1-g_2\in L^\perp\).
special_cases_latex: If \(M=\mathbb R^n\), then \(L^\perp=\{0\}\) and the mismatch disappears.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a relative-interior point, an ambient subdifferential may be nonempty but unbounded solely because of \(L^\perp\).
boundary_notes: The relative subdifferential must be defined on the affine hull, not by assigning arbitrary finite values outside \(D\).
In Banach spaces, annihilators replace Euclidean orthogonal complements.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal complement of the subspace parallel to the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Space Descriptions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function confined to an affine subspace, every ambient subgradient consists of a relative subgradient plus an arbitrary normal component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \[\partial_A h(x)=\{u\in L\mid h(y)\geq h(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in A\},\] the ambient subdifferential has the representation \[\partial_H f(x)=\partial_A h(x)+L^\perp.\] Equivalently, \(g\in\partial_Hf(x)\) exactly when \(P_Lg\in\partial_Ah(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A=a+L\) is a nonempty closed affine subspace, and \(L\) is its direction space.
\(h:A\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex, and \(f=h+\iota_A\) on \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_H f(x)=\partial_A h(x)+L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient Hilbert-space representation for a function whose effective domain lies in a closed affine subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Hull Descriptions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine-hull subdifferential tests the subgradient inequality along feasible affine directions and represents subgradients in the direction space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subdifferential of \(h\) relative to \(A\), represented in its direction space \(L=A-A\), is \[\partial_A h(x)=\{u\in L\mid h(y)\geq h(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in A\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(A=a+L\) is a nonempty closed affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine-hull subdifferential is determined solely by displacements in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic subgradient definition on the affine hull, represented in its direction space.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relative-interior point of the domain of a proper finite-dimensional convex function has a subgradient; boundary points need not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), \[\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing.\] This finite-dimensional nonemptiness statement does not assert nonemptiness at relative-boundary points of \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional subgradient nonemptiness on the relative interior of the effective domain.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Hull Orthogonal Components
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding any vector orthogonal to the affine hull preserves an ambient subgradient; only its tangential projection carries intrinsic information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(g\in\partial_Hf(x)\) and \(n\in L^\perp\), \[g+n\in\partial_Hf(x).\] More precisely, \[\partial_Hf(x)=\{u+n\mid u\in\partial_Ah(x),\ n\in L^\perp\}.\] The tangential component \(P_Lg\) is intrinsic, whereas the component in \(L^\perp\) is unrestricted.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space, \(A=a+L\) is a closed affine subspace, and \(f=h+\iota_A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g+n\in\partial_Hf(x)\), and all ambient subgradients with the same tangential component differ by an element of \(L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of ambient representatives caused by directions normal to the affine hull.

children.title: Calculus-Attainment Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of exact sum, chain, supremum, marginal, integral, and intersection rules.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal profile for detecting failed equalities or missing optimizers in standard finite-dimensional convex constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A calculus-attainment failure is a specified construction together with failure of its target exact representation. Its profile may contain: a sum gap at \(x\) when
\[\partial(\textstyle\sum_i f_i)(x)\supsetneq\sum_i\partial f_i(x);\]
a chain gap when \(\partial(h\circ A)(x)\supsetneq A^*\partial h(Ax)\); an intersection gap when
\[N_{\cap_i C_i}(x)\supsetneq\sum_iN_{C_i}(x);\]
a marginal nonattainment at \(x\) when \(p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\in\mathbb R\) but \(\operatorname{Argmin}_yF(x,y)=\varnothing\); or a representation nonattainment when a dual infimum or supremum appearing in a conjugate or subgradient formula has the correct value but no optimizing representative. The profile records actual strict inequality or emptiness, not merely failure to verify a sufficient qualification condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This taxonomy classifies an actual breakdown of an exact convex-calculus representation. It includes strict gaps in sum, composition, and normal-cone intersection formulas, as well as empty optimizer sets for marginal functions or dual representations. Merely lacking a standard regularity condition is not itself a failure: the relevant equality must be false or the required optimizer must genuinely be absent.
assumptions_latex: All displayed subdifferentials and normal cones are the convex-analytic ones.
Each compared expression is well-defined at the stated point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A construction belongs to the failure taxonomy exactly when its stated exact representation has a strict gap or requires an unattained optimizer.
special_cases_latex: Under a common-relative-interior condition, the finite sum and intersection gaps displayed above do not occur.
boundary_notes: Failure of a standard constraint qualification is only a warning and is not equivalent to failure of exact calculus.
Closure-only formulas are classified separately as closure-gap phenomena.

notation.meaning: Set of minimizers in the eliminated variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a relative-interior qualification, the subdifferential sum rule can be strict; tangent convex sets provide an explicit two-dimensional example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For these sets, \(C\cap D=\{z\}\) and \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap\operatorname{ri}D=\varnothing\). At \(z\), \[\partial f(z)=\{(0,\beta)\mid\beta\leq0\},\qquad \partial g(z)=\{(0,\beta)\mid\beta\geq0\},\] while \[\partial(f+g)(z)=\mathbb R^2.\] Consequently, \[\partial f(z)+\partial g(z)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\subsetneq\partial(f+g)(z).\]
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\mid v\geq u^2\}\) and \(D=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\mid v\leq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(z)+\partial g(z)\subsetneq\partial(f+g)(z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete strict sum-rule inclusion when the relative-interior qualification fails.

normal cone to C at z

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) be linear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative-interior qualifications for exact sum, intersection, and linear-composition rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sum-rule relative-interior qualification fails when
\[\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)=\varnothing.\]
For convex sets \(C_i\), the corresponding intersection qualification fails when \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}C_i=\varnothing\). For the composition \(h\circ A\), the range qualification fails when
\[\operatorname{ran}A\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}h)=\varnothing.\]
More generally, qualification failure means that the explicitly selected regularity condition required by a stated exact rule is false. It identifies loss of the theorem's guarantee; it does not define an exact-calculus gap. Thus qualification failure and calculus failure are distinct predicates: the former is failure of a hypothesis, whereas the latter is strict failure of the claimed equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A qualification failure occurs when the regularity hypothesis selected for a convex-calculus rule is false. For sums it is emptiness of the common relative interior of the effective domains. For intersections it is emptiness of the common relative interior of the sets. For a linear composition it is failure of the operator range to meet the relative interior of the outer function's domain. This removes a sufficient guarantee but does not imply that the formula itself fails in a particular instance.
assumptions_latex: The relevant functions are proper and convex.
The qualification being tested is identified before declaring failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Qualification failure is the negation of the selected regularity hypothesis, not the negation of the resulting calculus equality.
special_cases_latex: If some summands or sets are polyhedral, their relative interiors may be replaced by their domains in the weakened qualification stated by the finite-dimensional polyhedral rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: After qualification failure, only unconditional inclusions remain automatically available from the cited sum and chain rules.
boundary_notes: Exact equality may still hold accidentally or for structural reasons after the displayed qualification fails.
Infinite-dimensional rules generally require continuity-point, core, strong-relative-interior, or other topology-sensitive conditions.

notation.meaning: Range of the linear mapping used in the composition rule.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Gap Phenomena
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a sum is the closed infimal convolution of the conjugates; without qualification, the unclosed or unattained formula may have a gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[(f^*\square g^*)(u)=\inf_{v\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(f^*(v)+g^*(u-v)\bigr).\] In finite dimensions, \[(f+g)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f^*\square g^*).\] Without an additional qualification, the unclosed infimal convolution can differ from \((f+g)^*\), and its defining infimum need not be attained.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f+g)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f^*\square g^*)\), while the unclosed infimal convolution may differ from \((f+g)^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conjugate-sum formula showing where closure or limiting dual decompositions enter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure gap in a convex representation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Y\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, and let \(S\subseteq Y\) or \(q:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) arise from a convex-calculus construction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional set or function representations where closing the candidate object changes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set-valued closure gap occurs when a convex representation produces \(S\) but the valid target is its closure and
\[S\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}S.\]
A functional closure gap occurs when a convex candidate \(q\) must be replaced by its lower-semicontinuous hull and
\[\operatorname{cl}q<q\quad\text{at some point},\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}q)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}q).\]
For a proposed subdifferential representation \(R(x)\), a pointwise closure gap is
\[R(x)\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}R(x)=\partial f(x).\]
The term also covers formulas represented only by limits of nearby points when the unclosed direct union or sum omits limiting subgradients. A closure gap is therefore an actual strict difference between a raw convex construction and its prescribed closed or lower-semicontinuous completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure gap is present when a raw convex construction is not already closed. For sets, the raw set is strictly smaller than its closure. For functions, the function strictly exceeds its lower-semicontinuous hull somewhere. For a subdifferential formula, the directly generated candidates omit points that appear after closure. The definition requires a strict gap, not merely the appearance of a closure symbol in a formula.
assumptions_latex: The ambient topology used by \(\operatorname{cl}\) is fixed.
The raw and completed objects belong to the same ambient set or function space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A closure-gap phenomenon is characterized by strict inequality \(S\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}S\), \(\operatorname{cl}q<q\) somewhere, or \(R(x)\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}R(x)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper convex \(q\), \(q\ne\operatorname{cl}q\iff\operatorname{epi}q\text{ is not closed}\).
special_cases_latex: If the raw representation is polyhedral in finite dimensions, it is often already closed, but this must be checked for the particular operation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Dropping the closure from a strict-gap formula loses valid limiting points or changes the represented function.
boundary_notes: Closure depends on topology in infinite-dimensional dual spaces.
Nonattainment and closure gaps may coexist but are distinct: an infimum can be unattained even when the value function is closed.

notation.meaning: Raw candidate set in a subdifferential representation.

children.title: Marginal-Infimal Nonattainment Family
children.top_down_role: Failure of optimizer-based calculus when infima or suprema are not attained.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonattainment of a finite marginal infimum
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^p\), and let \(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Define \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex marginal functions; the definition isolates optimizer nonexistence from value-function closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The marginal problem is infimally nonattained at \(x\in X\) when
\[p(x)\in\mathbb R\quad\text{and}\quad M(x):=\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in Y}F(x,y)=\{y:F(x,y)=p(x)\}=\varnothing.\]
Equivalently, there exists a minimizing sequence \((y_k)\) with \(F(x,y_k)\downarrow p(x)\), but no \(y\in Y\) realizes the value. The marginal-infimal nonattainment family is
\[\mathcal N_F:=\{x\in X:p(x)\in\mathbb R,\ M(x)=\varnothing\}.\]
Any calculus formula whose right-hand side is indexed by \(M(x)\), such as a union of partial subgradients over active minimizers, is optimizer-based and is not directly evaluable at points of \(\mathcal N_F\); a valid replacement, if available, must use approximate minimizers, limiting constructions, or an independently justified closed representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function of two variables, the marginal value at \(x\) is the infimum over the eliminated variable. Nonattainment means that this value is finite but no eliminated-variable point realizes it. The set of all such \(x\) is the nonattainment family. Formulas indexed by exact minimizers have an empty index set there and require a separately justified limiting or approximate formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper and convex on \(X\times Y\).
The marginal value \(p(x)\) is finite at the point under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\mathcal N_F\iff p(x)\in\mathbb R\) and \(\operatorname{Argmin}_yF(x,y)=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\mathcal N_F\) iff finite-valued minimizing sequences exist but every \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(F(x,y)>p(x)\).
special_cases_latex: If a lower level set \(\{y:F(x,y)\le\alpha\}\) is nonempty and compact for some \(\alpha>p(x)\), then nonattainment at \(x\) is excluded.
immediate_consequences_latex: An exact-minimizer union cannot by itself represent a nonempty subdifferential at a point in \(\mathcal N_F\).
boundary_notes: The definition excludes the cases \(p(x)=\pm\infty\).
Nonattainment does not alone imply that \(p\) is nonclosed.

notation.meaning: Exact minimizer set of the marginal problem.
Set of points with finite but unattained marginal infimum.
