knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex marginal can be perfectly regular even though no fiber optimizer exists, making optimizer-based subgradient formulas unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(\Phi\) is finite, continuous, and jointly convex. For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[p(x)=0,\qquad \partial p(x)=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb R}\Phi(x,y)=\varnothing.\] Thus optimizer-based marginal-subgradient formulas are unavailable although the marginal is finite, closed, convex, and subdifferentiable everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(\Phi(x,y)=e^y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(x)=0\) for every \(x\), but \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y}\Phi(x,y)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary convex marginal whose fiber infimum is finite but nowhere attained.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential function is closed, smooth, and strictly convex, yet its finite infimum is unattained and no point satisfies the zero-subgradient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is finite, smooth, strictly convex, and lower semicontinuous, with \[\inf_{t\in\mathbb R}f(t)=0,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}f=\\varnothing.\] For every \(t\in\mathbb R\), \[\partial f(t)=\{e^t\},\] so \(0\notin\partial f(t)\) at every finite point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{t\in\mathbb R}f(t)=0\) is not attained, and \(0\notin\partial f(t)\) for every \(t\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth closed convex example separating a finite infimum from minimizer existence.

source_witnesses.locator: 11.5 Minimizing Sequences p. 195

knowledge_statements.title: Escaping Minimizing Sequences
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every minimizing sequence for the exponential function diverges to minus infinity, so compactness cannot produce a minimizer or a zero-subgradient certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every minimizing sequence \((t_k)\) for \(f(t)=e^t\) satisfies \[t_k\to-\infty.\] Hence it eventually leaves every bounded subset of \(\mathbb R\) and has no convergent subsequence in \(\mathbb R\).
assumptions_latex: \((t_k)\) is a minimizing sequence, meaning \(f(t_k)\to\inf f=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t_k\to-\infty\), so every minimizing sequence escapes every bounded subset of \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit escape mechanism accompanying nonattainment of the exponential infimum.

source_witnesses.locator: 11.5 Minimizing Sequences p. 195

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer-Free Fallbacks
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A near-minimizer whose joint approximate subgradient has zero auxiliary component yields an approximate subgradient of the marginal value, without requiring an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\operatorname{dom}v\). If a pair \((y_\delta,x^*)\in Y\times X^*\) satisfies \(F(x,y_\delta)\leq v(x)+\delta\) and \((x^*,0)\in\partial_{\varepsilon-\delta}F(x,y_\delta)\), then \(x^*\in\partial_\varepsilon v(x)\). Thus a near-minimizer and an approximate subgradient of the joint function provide a verifiable marginal-subgradient certificate even when \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y}F(x,y)=\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real locally convex spaces.
\(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper convex and \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\partial_\varepsilon v(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate-subgradient certificate requiring only a near-minimizer, not attainment of the marginal infimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure boundary for subdifferentiation under an integral
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)\) be a measure space, let \(X\) be a Banach space with dual \(X^*\), and let \(\varphi:\Omega\times X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be measurable in \(\omega\) and convex in \(x\). Set \(I(x)=\int_\Omega\varphi(\omega,x)\,d\mu\) when well-defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal boundary predicate for exact integral-subdifferential interchange; no universal interchange theorem is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}I\), define the set of integrable pointwise selections
\[\mathcal S(x)=\{s:\Omega\to X^*:s\text{ is measurable and integrable, }s(\omega)\in\partial_x\varphi(\omega,x)\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}\]
and their integrals \(A(x)=\{\int__Omega s\,d\mu:s\in\mathcal S(x)\}\), with the integral interpreted in a fixed stated sense. The integral-expectation interchange boundary is reached at \(x\) when the intended exact identity
\[\partial I(x)=A(x)\]
is not meaningful or is false because \(I\) is not proper, \(\mathcal S(x)=\varnothing\), the selections are not integrable, the integral does not belong to the intended dual space, or \(A(x)\subsetneq\partial I(x)\) and closure or singular dual terms are required. For a probability measure, the same definition applies with \(I(x)=\mathbb E[\varphi(\omega,x)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise subdifferentials form a multifunction. Its measurable integrable selections can be integrated to produce candidate subgradients of the integral functional. The interchange boundary consists of points where equality between these candidates and the subdifferential of the integral is undefined or fails, including missing selections, nonintegrability, dual-space mismatch, or omitted closure or singular terms.
assumptions_latex: The measurability and integral notions used for \(X^*\)-valued selections are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interchange failure is the failure or ill-posedness of \(\partial I(x)=\{\int s\,d\mu:s(\omega)\in\partial_x\varphi(\omega,x)\text{ a.e.}\}\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\mu\) is a probability measure, \(\int s\,d\mu\) is written \(\mathbb E[s]\).
boundary_notes: Bochner, Pettis, and weak-star integrals yield different admissible regimes.
Pointwise nonemptiness of the subdifferentials does not ensure a measurable integrable selection.
No inspected local source supports the exact scope of this definition.

notation.meaning: Measurable integrable selections of the pointwise subdifferential.
Set of integrals of admissible pointwise selections.

review_flags: A source is required for the measurable-selection hypotheses, integration topology, and possible singular terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure boundary for subdifferentiation under an integral
Integral Interchange Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integration and subdifferentiation can fail to commute when measurable integrable pointwise subgradients or an interchange qualification are absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_x\) be the set of strongly measurable selections \(s\) satisfying \(s(\omega)\in\partial f(\omega,x)\) almost everywhere and \(\int_\Omega\lVert s(\omega)\rVert\,d\mu<\infty\). The expression \(\int_\Omega^{A}\partial f(\omega,x)\,d\mu\) equals \(\{\int_\Omega s\,d\mu:s\in S_x\}\). If this set is empty or differs from \(\partial I(x)\), subdifferentiation and integration do not interchange. Normal-integrand measurability, a qualification condition, and an integrable local bound are standard hypotheses preventing these failures.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\Omega\times X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is an extended-real convex integrand.
\(I(x)=\int_\Omega f(\omega,x)\,d\mu(\omega)\) is proper at the point considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The identity \(\partial I(x)=\int_\Omega^{A}\partial f(\omega,x)\,d\mu(\omega)\) is not valid without additional interchange hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the convex subdifferential rule for parameterized integrals.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon fits the container, but no source is supplied for the asserted integral-subdifferential boundary or the listed sufficient hypotheses. The record also does not specify the Banach-space structure needed for strong measurability and Bochner integration in the dual.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Interchange Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise convexity and finite expected value alone do not justify exchanging expectation with the subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S_x^1=\{s\in L^1(\Omega;X^*):s(\omega)\in\partial f(\omega,x)\text{ almost surely}\}\). The Aumann expectation is \(\mathbb E^{A}[\partial f(\omega,x)]=\{\mathbb E[s]:s\in S_x^1\}\). Consequently, if \(S_x^1=\varnothing\) while \(\partial F(x)\neq\varnothing\), or if the two displayed sets differ, expectation and subdifferentiation fail to interchange. Pointwise convexity and finiteness of \(F(x)\) alone do not establish the interchange identity.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(\omega,x)]\) is proper at the point considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without measurable integrable selections and an interchange qualification, \(\partial F(x)=\mathbb E^{A}[\partial f(\omega,x)]\) need not hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-space specialization of subgradient–integral interchange failure.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The expectation-interchange failure is appropriately classified, but the exact claim has no citation. The space X and the integration convention for X*-valued selections are not specified, so the meaning of L^1, the expectation, and the claimed identity is not yet reliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Measurable-Selection Obstructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty pointwise subdifferentials are insufficient: without a measurable selection their Aumann integral is empty, invalidating a nonempty integral-subgradient formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A measurable selection of \(M\) is a measurable map \(s:\Omega\to X^*\) such that \(s(\omega)\in M(\omega)\) almost everywhere. If no such selection exists, the Aumann integral \(\int__\Omega^{A}M(\omega)\,d\mu\) is empty. Hence, whenever \(\partial I(x)\neq\varnothing\), the formula \(\partial I(x)=\int__\Omega^{A}\partial f(\omega,x)\,d\mu\) fails. Nonempty pointwise values alone do not remove this obstruction; measurability of the multifunction or an applicable selection theorem is essential.
assumptions_latex: \(M(\omega)=\partial f(\omega,x)\subseteq X^*\) is the pointwise subgradient multifunction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(M\) has no measurable selection, then \(\int__\Omega^{A}M\,d\mu=\varnothing\), so it cannot equal any nonempty \(\partial I(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurability obstruction in Aumann-integral subgradient formulas.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The measurable-selection obstruction fits the terminal container, but it is uncited and uses malformed expressions such as \(\int__\Omega\). The Aumann integral also requires an integration convention and integrable selections, not merely a definition of measurable selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable subgradient selection is usable precisely when its norm is integrable; an integrable pointwise bound guarantees this property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(S_x^1=\{s:s(\omega)\in\partial f(\omega,x)\text{ almost everywhere},\ s\text{ strongly measurable},\ \int__\Omega\lVert s(\omega)\rVert\,d\mu<\infty\}\). Only members of \(S_x^1\) possess a Bochner integral usable in the Aumann subgradient formula. If every measurable selection has infinite norm integral, then \(S_x^1=\varnothing\). Conversely, if \(\lVert u\rVert\leq m(\omega)\) for all \(u\in\partial f(\omega,x)\), almost everywhere, with \(m\in L^1(\mu)\), every measurable selection is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selection contributes to the integral formula exactly when \(\lVert s(\cdot)\rVert\in L^1(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bochner-integrability threshold for pointwise subgradient selections.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The Bochner-integrability condition is standard and the selected content kind fits, but no source supports its use in the asserted subgradient-integral context. The statement also contains malformed \(\int__\Omega\) notation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of ambient regimes for subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, where \(X\) is respectively \(\mathbb R^n\), a real Hilbert space \(H\), or a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A regime index specifying the ambient pairing and topologies before a subdifferential statement is interpreted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dimension-topology regime descriptor is
\[\mathfrak R(X)=(\mathcal P,\tau_p,\tau_d,\mathcal K),\]
where \(\mathcal P\) is the primal-dual pairing used in the subgradient inequality, \(\tau_p\) and \(\tau_d\) are the declared primal and dual topologies, and \(\mathcal K\) records the compactness principle available to the statement. In the finite-dimensional regime, \(X=X^*=\mathbb R^n\), \(\mathcal P=\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), compatible vector topologies coincide, and bounded closed sets are compact. In the Hilbert regime, the Riesz map identifies \(H^*\) with \(H\), but norm and weak topologies differ in infinite dimension; bounded closed convex sets are weakly compact. In the Banach regime, subgradients lie in \(X^*\), pairing is \(\langle x^*,x\rangle\), and norm, weak, and weak-star closure or convergence must be distinguished. A subdifferential claim is regime-complete only after these components are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hierarchy records four pieces of ambient information: the primal-dual pairing, the primal topology, the dual topology, and the compactness mechanism. Euclidean spaces identify primal and dual and have ordinary compactness of bounded closed sets. Hilbert spaces retain a vector identification through the Riesz map but distinguish weak and norm behavior. General Banach spaces use a separate dual and require explicit weak-star choices. Statements should not be transferred between these regimes without checking those components.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is one of the three stated classes of real spaces.
All duals are continuous duals for the declared norm topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak R(X)\) fixes the pairing and topology needed to interpret \(\partial f\), closure, compactness, and convergence.
special_cases_latex: Every finite-dimensional Hilbert space belongs simultaneously to the Euclidean and Hilbert descriptions, with weak and norm topologies coinciding.
immediate_consequences_latex: A sequential closure statement in a dual space is incomplete unless the dual topology is specified.
boundary_notes: Asplundness is an additional Banach-space property, not a consequence of being Banach.
The descriptor is a local organizational definition rather than a standard named hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, intersecting relative interiors of the domains guarantee the exact convex-subdifferential sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In finite dimension, the relative-interior qualification \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing\) yields the exact sum rule \[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\] for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\). Here the sum on the right is the Minkowski sum in \((\mathbb R^n)^*\), canonically identified with \(\mathbb R^n\).
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\), \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative-interior qualification for exact subdifferential calculus.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with the Euclidean pairing \(\langle g,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex analysis, including lower-dimensional effective domains handled by relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite-dimensional subdifferential regime consists of statements interpreted with
\[\partial f(x)=\{g\in\mathbb R^n:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in\mathbb R^n\},\]
Euclidean closure, and relative interior taken in \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Its characteristic existence guarantee is
\[x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Longrightarrow\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing.\]
If \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), then \(\partial f(x)\) is nonempty, closed, and bounded, hence compact. For a finite convex function on all of \(\mathbb R^n\), these properties hold at every point, and the directional derivative satisfies
\[f'(x;d)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle.\]
The regime also uses common-relative-interior qualifications for exact finite sums and normal-cone intersections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, subgradients are vectors in the same Euclidean space. Relative interior handles domains contained in lower-dimensional affine sets and guarantees subgradient existence there. At ordinary interior points the subdifferential is bounded as well as closed, so finite-dimensional compactness applies. A finite convex function on the whole space therefore has a nonempty compact subdifferential everywhere, and its directional derivative is the support function of that set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative-interior points have nonempty subdifferentials; interior points have nonempty compact subdifferentials.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite convex \(f\), \(f'(x;\cdot)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}\) at every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
special_cases_latex: For polyhedral convex \(f\), every point of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is subdifferentiable and \(\partial f(x)\) is polyhedral.
immediate_consequences_latex: Euclidean bounded sequences admit convergent subsequences, a fact not available in the strong topology of infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
boundary_notes: At a relative-boundary point, subgradient existence is not guaranteed.
Ambient subdifferentials can be unbounded when the effective domain has a proper affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert-Space Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Hilbert space, the resolvent of a convex subdifferential is the everywhere-defined, firmly nonexpansive proximity operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), the strongly convex problem \[\operatorname*{minimize}_{y\in H}\;f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\] has a unique solution \(p\). Its optimality condition is \(x-p\in\lambda\partial f(p)\), and therefore \[p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=(\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}(x).\] The resolvent is defined on all of \(H\), is single-valued, and is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{Id}+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\), an everywhere-defined single-valued firmly nonexpansive map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space resolvent representation of the convex subdifferential.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically standard and well matched to the Hilbert-space regime, but the record supplies no citation for the resolvent-proximity identity, global single-valuedness, or firm nonexpansiveness. A specific theorem or proposition locator is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; dual vectors are identified with primal vectors using Riesz representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Hilbert-space convex subdifferential is the set-valued operator
\[\partial f:H\rightrightarrows H,\qquad \partial f(x)=\{u\in H:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\ \forall y\in H\}.\]
The Hilbert regime uses the Riesz identification \(H^*\simeq H\), so \(\partial f\) can be added to the identity operator. For \(\gamma>0\), its resolvent is
\[J_{\gamma\partial f}=(\operatorname{Id}+\gamma\partial f)^{-1}=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f},\]
and
\[p=J_{\gamma\partial f}(x)\iff \gamma^{-1}(x-p)\in\partial f(p).\]
Topology remains explicit: norm convergence and weak convergence differ in infinite dimension, although bounded closed convex subsets are weakly compact. Thus weak-strong graph limits, weak compactness, and strong resolvent evaluations are not interchangeable without a stated topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Hilbert space, Riesz representation identifies continuous linear functionals with vectors, so subgradients belong to the same space as primal points. This permits the identity-plus-subdifferential resolvent. For a closed proper convex function the resolvent is its proximity operator, and its defining inclusion links a proximal point to a subgradient. Infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces still distinguish norm and weak convergence, even though bounded closed convex sets are weakly compact.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f:H\rightrightarrows H\) and \(J_{\gamma\partial f}=\operatorname{Prox}_{\gamma f}\) are the canonical Hilbert-space interfaces.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(u\in\partial f(x)\iff f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\ \forall y\in H\).
\(p=J_{\gamma\partial f}(x)\iff x-p\in\gamma\partial f(p)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\iota_C\) with \(C\) nonempty closed and convex, \(J_{\gamma\partial f}=P_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The Riesz identification is what makes \(\operatorname{Id}+\partial f\) an operator sum on one space.
boundary_notes: Weak and strong convergence coincide only in finite dimensions.
The Riesz identification is unavailable in a general Banach space without an additional duality map.

children.title: Banach-Asplund Topological Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dual-pairing, weak-star, approximation, and differentiability boundaries in Banach spaces.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\), canonical pairing \(\langle x^*,x\rangle\), and weak-star topology \(\sigma(X^*,X)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Banach spaces and the Asplund subclass; primal and dual spaces are not identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the Banach-space convex subdifferential is
\[\partial f(x)=\{x^*\in X^*:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle x^*,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in X\}.\]
A Banach topological regime is specified by declaring norm, weak, or weak-star topology for every closure and limit involving \(X\) or \(X^*\). The regime is Asplund when every continuous convex real-valued function on every nonempty open convex subset of \(X\) is Fréchet differentiable on a dense \(G_\delta\) subset. In this subclass, dense differentiability and approximation by Fréchet subgradients support limiting constructions unavailable in arbitrary Banach spaces. The descriptor therefore consists of \((X,X^*,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle,\tau_X,\tau_{X^*},a_X)\), where \(a_X\) records whether \(X\) is Asplund.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Banach space, convex subgradients are continuous linear functionals in the separate dual space. Every closure and convergence assertion must state whether it uses norm, weak, or weak-star topology. An Asplund space is distinguished by generic Fréchet differentiability of continuous convex functions on open convex sets. This property enables stronger approximation-based nonsmooth analysis than is available in a completely general Banach space.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space and \(X^*\) is its continuous dual.
The topology of each closure or limit is explicitly declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Banach-Asplund regime is determined by the dual pairing, chosen topologies, and the Asplund differentiability property.
special_cases_latex: Every Hilbert space is Asplund, but its Riesz identification provides additional structure not included in the general Banach descriptor.
immediate_consequences_latex: An unqualified symbol \(\operatorname{cl}\) is ambiguous for subsets of \(X^*\) when norm and weak-star closures can differ.
boundary_notes: The Asplund characterization and approximation consequences require an authoritative Banach-space source.
A general Banach space need not have the stated generic Fréchet differentiability property.

knowledge_statements.title: Banach dual-pair and Asplund regimes
Banach-Space Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Banach space has a dual-valued, maximally monotone convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Banach-space convex subdifferential is \[\partial f(x)=\{x^*\in X^*: f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle x^*,y-x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in X\}.\] If \(x_i^*\in\partial f(x_i)\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\), then \(\langle x_1^*-x_2^*,x_1-x_2\rangle\geq0\). Moreover, no proper monotone extension of its graph in \(X\times X^*\) exists: \(\partial f\) is maximally monotone.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f:X\rightrightarrows X^*\) is monotone and maximally monotone under the dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space convex subdifferentials as dual-valued maximal monotone operators.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The Banach-space maximal-monotonicity claim is correct in the stated proper lower-semicontinuous convex setting, and the property kind fits. However, the supplied locators are generic dual-space and subdifferential sections and do not establish support for the exact Banach-space maximal-monotonicity theorem; an authoritative theorem locator is needed.

knowledge_statements.title: Asplund-Space Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asplund spaces are precisely Banach spaces where continuous convex functions are generically Fréchet differentiable on open convex domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Banach space \(X\) is Asplund if every separable closed subspace \(Y\subseteq X\) has separable dual \(Y^*\). Equivalently, for every nonempty open convex set \(U\subseteq X\) and every continuous convex function \(f:U\to\mathbb R\), the set of points at which \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable contains a dense \(G_\delta\) subset of \(U\). This generic differentiability property distinguishes the Asplund regime in nonsmooth subdifferential calculus.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\) is Asplund exactly when every continuous convex function on an open convex subset is Fréchet differentiable on a dense \(G_\delta\) subset.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability characterization defining the favorable Asplund regime.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The stated generic Fréchet-differentiability characterization is appropriate for the Asplund-space regime, but it is a nontrivial equivalence and has no source. A specific authoritative characterization theorem is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Star Topology Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subdifferentials are weak-star closed; bounded slices are weak-star compact, but an unbounded subdifferential need not be compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the set \[\partial f(x)=\bigcap_{y\in X}\{x^*\in X^*: \langle x^*,y-x\rangle\leq f(y)-f(x)\}\] is convex and closed for the weak-star topology \(\sigma(X^*,X)\). For every \(r>0\), its bounded slice \(\partial f(x)\cap rB_{X^*}\) is weak-star compact. The entire subdifferential is weak-star compact only when it is norm bounded; weak-star closedness alone does not imply compactness.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(X^*\) carries \(\sigma(X^*,X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)\) is weak-star closed and convex; each bounded slice \(\partial f(x)\cap rB_{X^*}\) is weak-star compact.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-star closure and compactness boundary for dual-valued subdifferentials.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The weak-star closure and bounded-slice compactness claims are mathematically sound, but the cited generic dual-space section does not adequately support the infinite-dimensional weak-star and Banach-Alaoglu assertions. A precise topology or compactness theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Pairing Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel–Young equality is equivalent to reciprocal primal and dual subgradient relations under the Banach-space dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(f^*(x^*)=\sup_{y\in X}(\langle x^*,y\rangle-f(y))\), Fenchel–Young inequality gives \(f(x)+f^*(x^*)\geq\langle x^*,x\rangle\). Equality holds precisely when \[x^*\in\partial f(x).\] Because \(f=f^{**}\) under the canonical embedding of \(X\) into \(X^{**}\), the same equality is equivalent to \(x\in\partial f^*(x^*)\). Thus the duality pairing, rather than an inner product identification, governs Banach-space subgradient inversion.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(x^*)=\langle x^*,x\rangle\iff x\in\partial f^*(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Young equality expressed through the primal–dual pairing.

notation.meaning: duality pairing between the dual and primal spaces

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singleton convex subdifferential characterizes Gâteaux differentiability, but in infinite dimensions it need not imply Fréchet differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(x\) if and only if \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton; then its unique member is the Gâteaux derivative. If \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(x\), necessarily \(\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}\) and \[f(x+h)=f(x)+\langle Df(x),h\rangle+o(\lVert h\rVert).\] In an infinite-dimensional Banach space, singleton-valuedness alone does not ensure this norm-uniform remainder, so it does not generally imply Fréchet differentiability.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is an open convex subset of a Banach space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fréchet differentiability implies \(\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}\), while a singleton subdifferential characterizes only Gâteaux differentiability in general.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between singleton subdifferentials, Gâteaux differentiability, and Fréchet differentiability.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary between convex subgradients and nonconvex generalized derivatives
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real normed space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition distinguishes the global convex-support subdifferential from local generalized derivatives used without convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function lies in the convex regime when
\[f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\quad(\forall x,y\in X,\ \forall t\in[0,1]).\]
In this regime the convex subdifferential is
\[\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(x)=\{x^*\in X^*:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle x^*,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in X\}.\]
The convexity boundary is crossed when the displayed Jensen inequality fails for some \((x,y,t)\). Beyond that boundary, \(\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(x)\) still denotes global affine minorants if retained, but it is not a general local derivative: it may be empty at points of local interest and does not encode arbitrary local first-order behavior. A nonconvex statement must therefore name its replacement construction—such as a regular, limiting, or Clarke-type subdifferential—and its topology and regularity assumptions rather than silently reusing convex calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity means that every chord lies above the function. In that regime, a convex subgradient is a continuous affine global support. Crossing the boundary means that the convexity inequality fails somewhere. The same global-support set can still be written for a nonconvex function, but it is no longer a general local derivative and may be empty. Any extension must explicitly choose a generalized subdifferential and its assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper on a real normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of the Jensen inequality marks departure from the regime in which global supporting-affine subgradients furnish the canonical nonsmooth derivative.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper \(f\), convexity is equivalent to convexity of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable and convex at \(x\), then \(\partial_{\mathrm{cvx}}f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\) in a finite-dimensional or Hilbert identification.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convex sum and chain rules cannot be transferred unchanged to an unspecified nonconvex generalized subdifferential.
boundary_notes: Different nonconvex subdifferentials are not interchangeable.
The inspected sources define convex subgradients but do not support a canonical choice among nonconvex generalized derivatives.

notation.meaning: Global convex-support subdifferential, explicitly distinguished from nonconvex constructions.

review_flags: A variational-analysis source is required for the named nonconvex generalized-subdifferential boundary.
No canonical nonconvex replacement was selected, preventing fabricated equivalences.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Global Supporting Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the finite continuous nonconvex function −|t|, no affine function touching the graph at zero lies globally below it, so its convex-analytic global subdifferential at zero is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(t)=-|t|\), let \[\partial f(x)=\{g\in\mathbb{R}: f(y)\geq f(x)+g(y-x)\ \text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}\}.\] Then \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), although \(f\) is finite and continuous at \(0\). Hence the global affine-support interpretation can fail outside convexity.
assumptions_latex: The convex-analytic subdifferential is defined through global affine support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\); thus a finite continuous nonconvex function need not possess a global affine support at a point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional boundary showing that nonconvexity can destroy every global affine support.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic global subdifferential of f at x.

review_flags: The cited textbook section provisionally supports the global subdifferential definition; the elementary counterexample remains candidate-review knowledge.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of a Global Affine Supporting Model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and fix \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). For \(v\in E\), identify \(v\) with the linear functional \(y\mapsto\langle v,y\rangle\), and define the affine model \(m_{\bar x,v}(y)=f(\bar x)+\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns exact global affine minorants touching the function at one point. It applies to arbitrary proper extended-real-valued functions in finite dimensions; convexity is not assumed, although convexity is the regime in which this construction becomes the standard convex subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in E\;\middle|\;f(y)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle\ \text{for every }y\in E\right\}.\] The function \(f\) has a global affine supporting model at \(\bar x\) precisely when \(\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\). It exhibits loss of global supporting models at \(\bar x\) precisely when \[\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)=\varnothing,\] equivalently, when for every \(v\in E\) there exists \(y\in E\) such that \(f(y)<f(\bar x)+\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle\). Function-level loss occurs when this condition holds at at least one point of \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper extended-real-valued function \(f\) and a finite point \(\bar x\), the global affine-support subdifferential consists of all slopes \(v\) whose affine model through \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) lies below \(f\) at every point. Global supporting models are lost at \(\bar x\) when this set is empty. Equivalently, every proposed slope is defeated somewhere by a point at which its affine model exceeds the function. The definition is pointwise: a nonconvex function may lose global support at some points while retaining it at others.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{loss at }\bar x\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\forall v\in E)(\exists y\in E)\;f(y)<f(\bar x)+\langle v,y-\bar x\rangle.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[v\in\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m_{\bar x,v}\le f\ \text{on }E\ \text{and }m_{\bar x,v}(\bar x)=f(\bar x).\]
\[v\in\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in E}\bigl(f(y)-\langle v,y\rangle\bigr).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then \(\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\) is the usual convex subdifferential \(\partial f(\bar x)\).
For convex \(f\), \(v\in\partial f(\bar x)\) is equivalently characterized by \(\langle v,d\rangle\le f'(\bar x;d)\) for every direction \(d\in E\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \[0\in\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(y)\ge f(\bar x)\ \text{for all }y\in E,\] so a zero global subgradient characterizes a global minimizer even without convexity.
Whenever \(\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)\ne\varnothing\), the epigraph of \(m_{\bar x,v}\) supplies a global one-sided affine model touching \(f\) at \(\bar x\).
boundary_notes: Nonconvexity alone does not imply \(\partial_{\mathrm{glob}}f(\bar x)=\varnothing\) at every point; the loss condition must be checked at the specified point.
A local affine lower estimate with an error term is not a global supporting model. Such local objects belong to regular or limiting generalized-subdifferential theory.
The definition excludes \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\), where no finite touching affine model can be formed.

notation.meaning: Set of slopes of exact global affine minorants of the function that touch at the base point.
Affine model through the graph point \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) with slope \(v\).

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Monotone Potential Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative mapping of the smooth nonconvex function −x² is not monotone and consequently is not cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(f(x)=-x^2\), and define \(T:\mathbb{R}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}\) by \(T(x)=\{f'(x)\}=\{-2x\}\). Then \(T\) is not monotone and therefore is not cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph of \(T\) is neither monotone nor cyclically monotone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth concave quadratic destroys the monotone and cyclically monotone graph structure characteristic of convex subdifferentials.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Monotone and Cyclically Monotone Potential Structure
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) be a set-valued mapping with graph \(\operatorname{gph}T=\{(x,v)\mid v\in T(x)\}\). For a finite cycle, write \(x_{m+1}=x_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition isolates the graph property that distinguishes subdifferentials generated by proper closed convex potentials. Ordinary monotonicity is a two-point condition, while cyclic monotonicity tests cycles of arbitrary finite length and is the exact convex-potential condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(T\) is monotone when \[\langle x_1-x_0,v_1-v_0\rangle\ge0\qquad\text{for all }(x_0,v_0),(x_1,v_1)\in\operatorname{gph}T.\] It is cyclically monotone when, for every integer \(m\ge1\) and every \((x_i,v_i)\in\operatorname{gph}T\), \[\sum_{i=0}^{m}\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,v_i\rangle\le0,\qquad x_{m+1}=x_0.\] The graph loses monotonicity if the two-point inequality is violated. It loses convex-potential structure if cyclic monotonicity is violated, namely if some finite cycle satisfies \[\sum_{i=0}^{m}\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,v_i\rangle>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping is monotone when every two graph points have a nonnegative displacement pairing. It is cyclically monotone when the sum of slope-displacement pairings around every finite closed cycle is nonpositive. Loss of monotonicity means that some pair violates the first condition. Loss of convex-potential structure means that some finite cycle violates the second condition. Cyclic monotonicity is the precise property permitting the graph to be contained in the subdifferential of a proper closed convex function; maximal cyclic monotonicity identifies graphs that are themselves such subdifferentials.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is a set-valued mapping.
For cyclic tests, \(m\ge1\) is arbitrary and \(x_{m+1}=x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{loss of convex-potential structure}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(\exists m\ge1)(\exists(x_i,v_i)\in\operatorname{gph}T)\;\sum_{i=0}^{m}\langle x_{i+1}-x_i,v_i\rangle>0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[T\text{ is cyclically monotone}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists\text{ proper closed convex }f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ such that }T(x)\subseteq\partial f(x)\ \forall x.\]
\[T=\partial f\text{ for some proper closed convex }f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T\text{ is maximal cyclically monotone}.\]
The monotonicity inequality is the \(m=1\) instance of cyclic monotonicity.
special_cases_latex: For a proper convex function \(f\), its convex subdifferential \(\partial f\) is cyclically monotone and therefore monotone.
When \(n=1\), monotonicity and cyclic monotonicity coincide for these mappings; in dimensions \(n>1\), a mapping can be monotone without being cyclically monotone.

For a linear mapping \(T(x)=Qx\), cyclic monotonicity requires \(Q\) to be symmetric positive semidefinite, whereas monotonicity only requires the symmetric part \((Q+Q^*)/2\) to be positive semidefinite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Failure of ordinary monotonicity automatically implies failure of cyclic monotonicity.
If cyclic monotonicity fails, no proper closed convex function \(f\) can satisfy \(T(x)\subseteq\partial f(x)\) for every \(x\).
A graph may retain ordinary monotonicity yet lose its interpretation as a convex-potential subdifferential.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that every generalized subdifferential of every nonconvex function violates monotonicity; the graph inequalities must be tested for the chosen construction.
Ordinary monotonicity is weaker than convex-potential representability in dimensions greater than one.
Maximal monotonicity and maximal cyclic monotonicity are different notions; convex subdifferential representation is characterized by the cyclic version.

notation.meaning: Closure convention for a finite cycle.
Convex subdifferential of a proper convex potential.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Subdifferential Handoff
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After global convex support fails, regular, limiting, and Clarke subdifferentials can differ: for −|x| at zero they are empty, two-point, and interval-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|\), the regular subgradient condition at \(0\) is \[\liminf_{x\to 0,\,x\ne 0}\frac{f(x)-f(0)-vx}{|x|}\geq 0.\] The one-sided limits make this impossible for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}\), so \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\). At each \(x\ne 0\), \(f\) is differentiable, with derivative \(-1\) for \(x>0\) and \(1\) for \(x<0\). Consequently, limits of nearby regular subgradients give \(\partial_L f(0)=\{-1,1\}\). Since \(f\) is locally Lipschitz, convexification gives the Clarke subdifferential \(\partial_C f(0)=\operatorname{co}\{-1,1\}=[-1,1]\).
assumptions_latex: Regular, limiting, and Clarke subdifferentials are understood in their standard finite-dimensional senses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(0\), \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), \(\partial_L f(0)=\{-1,1\}\), and \(\partial_C f(0)=[-1,1]\); the generalized constructions are not interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The example marks the handoff from global convex supports to distinct local and limiting generalized derivatives.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the regular, limiting, and Clarke subdifferential comparison.
standard_field_rationale: the one-dimensional values follow from the standard definitions, but authoritative nonconvex-analysis sourcing is required.

The attentive condition \(f(x^\nu)\to f(\bar x)\) is essential and cannot in general be replaced by location convergence alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Legendre conjugacy for functions taking values in the full extended real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) with the Euclidean pairing \(\langle y,x\rangle\), and let \(\overline{\mathbb{R}}=[-\infty,+\infty]\). For a function \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), its Fenchel–Legendre conjugate is the function \(f^*:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) defined by
\[
f^*(y):=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\}.
\]
The biconjugate is \(f^{**}:=(f^*)^*\). Two functions \(f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) form a conjugate pair when \(g=f^*\) and \(f=g^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let X be Euclidean n-space and let f take values in the full extended real line. The Fenchel–Legendre conjugate of f at y is the supremum, over x in X, of the Euclidean pairing of y and x minus f(x). Applying conjugation twice gives the biconjugate. Two functions f and g form a conjugate pair exactly when each is the conjugate of the other.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\}.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel conjugacy as a dual-geometric interface
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in the Euclidean dual pair \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and \(X^*=\mathbb R^n\), with pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle\). Let \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real Fenchel conjugacy; no smoothness or convexity of the input is required for the transform itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel conjugate of \(f\) is \[f^*(y):=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)\},\qquad y\in X^*.\] Its epigraph is the parameter set of all affine minorants of \(f\): \[\operatorname{epi}f^*=\{(y,\beta)\in X^*\times\mathbb R:\langle x,y\rangle-\beta\le f(x)\ \forall x\in X\}.\] Thus each \((y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\) represents the affine function \(x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle-\beta\) lying below \(f\). The associated biconjugate is \[f^{**}(x):=\sup_{y\in X^*}\{\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\}.\] For every \(x,y\), \(\langle x,y\rangle\le f(x)+f^*(y)\), and \(f^{**}\le f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real function on Euclidean space, its Fenchel conjugate at a dual vector is the supremum of the dual pairing minus the function. The epigraph of the conjugate consists exactly of the slope-offset pairs whose affine functions minorize the original function. Conjugating again takes the supremum of this complete family of encoded affine minorants. Fenchel's inequality holds for every primal-dual pair, and the biconjugate never exceeds the original function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*(y)=\sup_x(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x))\), with \((y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\iff \langle x,y\rangle-\beta\le f(x)\) for every \(x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^*(y)=-\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)-\langle x,y\rangle\}.\]
\[f^{**}(x)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle-\beta:(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is closed, proper, and convex, then \(f^{**}=f\).
If \(f=\delta_C\), then \(f^*\) is the support function of \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The transform converts a function into a closed convex function whenever the conjugate is proper.
The inequality \(f_1\le f_2\) implies \(f_1^*\ge f_2^*\).
boundary_notes: The values \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) require the usual extended-real conventions; expressions of the indeterminate form \(+\infty-\infty\) are excluded.
Infinite-dimensional dual pairs require a specified topology and continuous dual; that regime is not asserted here.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the extended-real function \(f\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and identify its algebraic and continuous dual with \(X^*=\mathbb R^n\) through the bilinear pairing \((x,y)\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real dual-pair viewpoint. The notation distinguishes primal and dual copies even though both are coordinatized by \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), its dual-pair conjugate is the function \(f^*:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \[f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in X}\bigl(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)\bigr).\] Conversely, for \(g:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \[g^*(x)=\sup_{y\in X^*}\bigl(\langle x,y\rangle-g(y)\bigr).\] A pair \((f,g)\) is a mutually conjugate dual pair precisely when \(g=f^*\) and \(f=g^*\). Equivalently, it is a minimal pair, under pointwise order, among those satisfying \[\langle x,y\rangle\le f(x)+g(y)\qquad\forall(x,y)\in X\times X^*.\] Mutual conjugacy therefore requires both members to be closed proper convex functions, apart from the two constant improper functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and dual spaces are treated as distinct copies of Euclidean space linked by their bilinear pairing. Conjugating a primal function takes a supremum over primal points and produces a dual function; the same formula with the variables reversed returns a primal function. Two functions form a mutually conjugate pair when each is the conjugate of the other. Equivalently, they give a pointwise-minimal valid decomposition of the pairing into a primal term plus a dual term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f,g)\) is mutually conjugate exactly when \(g(y)=\sup_x(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f(x)=\sup_y(\langle x,y\rangle-g(y))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For closed proper convex \(f\), the pair is \((f,f^*)\) and \(f^{**}=f\).
The valid inequality \(\langle x,y\rangle\le f(x)+g(y)\) is tight as a function pair exactly when \(g=f^*\) and \(f=g^*\).
special_cases_latex: Under the Euclidean identification \(X=X^*\), the self-conjugate quadratic \(x\mapsto\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\) is its own dual partner.
For a linear subspace \(L\), \(\delta_L^*=\delta_{L^\perp}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Fenchel's inequality is the universal pairing inequality associated with \((f,f^*)\).
The effective domain of \(f^*\) records the dual vectors for which \(f-\langle\cdot,y\rangle\) is bounded below.
boundary_notes: The Euclidean identification does not eliminate the directional distinction between primal and dual variables.
No locally convex infinite-dimensional topology or restricted continuous dual is specified.

notation.meaning: Dual copy of the primal Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Minorant Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex function is the pointwise supremum of all its affine minorants; equivalently, its conjugate supplies every affine lower bound needed to recover it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)\}=\sup_{(u,\alpha)\in M_f}\{\langle u,x\rangle-\alpha\}.
\]
Equivalently, the epigraph of \(f\) is the intersection of the closed half-spaces lying above its continuous affine minorants. Thus every value of \(f\) is recovered from the family of affine lower bounds encoded by its conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) equals the pointwise supremum of all continuous affine functions minorizing it.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Moreau representation by continuous affine minorants.

notation.meaning: Set of slope-intercept pairs defining affine minorants of f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Epigraph Parameterization of Affine Minorants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact slope-intercept parameterization of all finite continuous affine lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and set \(a_{u,\alpha}(x)=\langle u,x\rangle-\alpha\). Then \[a_{u,\alpha}\le f\iff \alpha\ge f^*(u).\] Consequently, \[M_f=\{(u,\alpha):\alpha\ge f^*(u)\}=\operatorname{epi}f^*.\] If \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous and convex, the pointwise supremum of the affine functions parameterized by this set equals \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the conjugate is precisely the parameter set of all finite affine minorants of the original function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_f=\operatorname{epi}f^*\), and for closed convex f the associated affine minorants have supremum f.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation by all continuous affine minorants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Write \(\mathcal A(f)\) for the family of finite affine functions majorized by \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointwise representation. Exact recovery applies to closed convex functions; arbitrary inputs are replaced by their lower-semicontinuous convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the affine-minorant family \[\mathcal A(f):=\{a_{y,\beta}:a_{y,\beta}(x)=\langle x,y\rangle-\beta,\ (y,\beta)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R,\ a_{y,\beta}\le f\}.\] Its pointwise envelope is \[M_f(x):=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A(f)}a(x),\] with the supremum of the empty family interpreted as \(-\infty\). Then \[M_f=f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f),\] where the right side denotes the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\). Hence a function \(f\) is closed and convex exactly when \[f(x)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle-\beta:(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\}\qquad\forall x.\] For proper convex \(f\), at least one finite affine minorant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine-minorant family contains every finite affine function lying pointwise below the given extended-real function. Its pointwise supremum is the biconjugate, equivalently the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant of the input. Therefore a closed convex function is recovered exactly as the supremum of all its affine minorants. Each such minorant is parametrized by a point in the epigraph of the conjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{a\in\mathcal A(f)}a=f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\), and this envelope equals \(f\) when \(f\) is closed and convex.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[a_{y,\beta}\in\mathcal A(f)\iff \beta\ge f^*(y).\]
\[\operatorname{epi}M_f=\bigcap_{a\in\mathcal A(f)}\operatorname{epi}a.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is finite affine, its representation includes \(f\) itself and the envelope is \(f\).
If \(f=\delta_C\), the representation reduces to the intersection of all closed half-spaces containing \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Two functions have the same affine minorants exactly when their closed convex envelopes coincide.
The conjugate depends only on \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\).
boundary_notes: If no finite affine minorant exists, the envelope is identically \(-\infty\).
Closedness means lower semicontinuity in the Euclidean topology.

notation.meaning: Family of all finite affine minorants of \(f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph half-space correspondence induced by conjugacy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and let \(F=\operatorname{epi}f\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional geometric encoding of conjugacy through epigraphs and upper half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \((y,\beta)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\), define the upper half-space \[H_{y,\beta}:=\{(x,r)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:r\ge\langle x,y\rangle-\beta\}.\] The support-epigraph correspondence is \[(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\subset H_{y,\beta}.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}f^*\) is precisely the set of parameters of all nonvertical upper closed half-spaces containing \(F\). If \(f\) is closed and convex, then \[F=\bigcap_{(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*}H_{y,\beta}.\] Equivalently, the lower boundary of this intersection is the affine-minorant envelope \(f^{**}=f\). Vertical supporting half-spaces are redundant in this intersection because their exclusion can be replicated by suitable upper half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slope and offset belong to the epigraph of the conjugate exactly when the upper half-space above the corresponding affine graph contains the epigraph of the original function. Thus the conjugate epigraph parametrizes all upper half-spaces supporting or containing the primal epigraph. For a closed convex function, intersecting all these half-spaces recovers the primal epigraph exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*\iff\operatorname{epi}f\subset H_{y,\beta}\), and for closed convex \(f\), \(\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*}H_{y,\beta}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^*(y)=\inf\{\beta:\operatorname{epi}f\subset H_{y,\beta}\}.\]
\[f(x)=\sup_{(y,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f^*}(\langle x,y\rangle-\beta)\] for closed convex \(f\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), the construction encodes the closed half-spaces containing \(C\) through the support values \(\sigma_C(y)\).
For finite affine \(f(x)=\langle x,y_0\rangle-\beta_0\), \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{y_0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed convex functions are uniquely determined by their conjugate epigraphs.
Epigraph inclusion reverses under conjugacy through the order reversal of functions.
boundary_notes: The asserted exact intersection requires closed convexity; otherwise it recovers the epigraph of the biconjugate.
This record concerns upper half-spaces, not arbitrary support functions of unbounded epigraphs.

notation.meaning: Upper closed half-space whose lower boundary is an affine graph.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is convex exactly when its epigraph is convex, and lower semicontinuous exactly when its epigraph is closed; every epigraph is vertically upward closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). It is lower semicontinuous if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed. Consequently, \(f\) is closed convex precisely when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a closed convex set. Vertical upward closure also holds: if \((x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(s\ge r\), then \((x,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity and lower semicontinuity of \(f\) are equivalent to convexity and closedness, respectively, of its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraph characterization of convexity and lower semicontinuity.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Lower Semi-Continuity: Closed Convex Functions p. 17

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 3.2 Lower Semi-Continuity: Closed Convex Functions p. 17

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of an extended-real function from its epigraph and the induced order relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \[f(x)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb R:(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\},\] where the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). Hence the epigraph uniquely determines \(f\). For any such functions \(f,g\), \[f\le g\iff\operatorname{epi}f\supseteq\operatorname{epi}g.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is recovered as the lower boundary of its epigraph, and pointwise function order corresponds to reverse epigraph inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The epigraph determines the function, and \(f\le g\iff\operatorname{epi}f\supseteq\operatorname{epi}g\).
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Recovery and Reversed Inclusion
Vertical Supporting Hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertical epigraph supports encode supporting normals of the effective domain, not finite subgradients; only supports with a negative vertical normal component yield finite affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and define
\[
N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)=\{a:\langle a,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }y\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.
\]
For every nonzero \(a\in N_{\operatorname{dom}f}(x)\), the vertical hyperplane
\[
\{(y,r):\langle a,y-x\rangle=0\}
\]
supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\). Its normal \((a,0)\) cannot be normalized to \((u,-1)\), so this support records a supporting normal of the effective domain rather than a finite affine minorant or a subgradient through the usual epigraph formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normal \((a,0)\) defines a vertical support of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) but cannot represent a finite subgradient affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes domain supports from the nonvertical epigraph supports representing finite subgradients.

notation.meaning: normal cone to the effective domain at x

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Hyperplane Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a subgradient precisely when its affine subgradient inequality defines a hyperplane supporting the function's epigraph at the corresponding graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following are equivalent: \(u\in\partial f(x)\); the epigraph satisfies
\[
\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\{(y,r)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:r\ge f(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\};
\]
and \(H_{x,u}\) supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\). The supporting half-space has normal \((u,-1)\), and its boundary is the graph of the affine minorant \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle u,y-x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) is a subgradient at \(x\) exactly when the corresponding nonvertical hyperplane supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradients as nonvertical supporting hyperplanes of an epigraph.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of f at x

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Properties of Closed Convex Functions p. 19

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 3.3 Properties of Closed Convex Functions p. 19

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary distinction between arbitrary epigraph support and support arising from a finite affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A supporting hyperplane to \(\operatorname{epi}f\) with normal \((v,0)\) is vertical and constrains only \(\operatorname{dom}f\); it does not correspond to a finite subgradient. For example, \[f(t)=\begin{cases}-\sqrt t,&t\ge0,\\+\infty,&t<0,\end{cases}\] is proper, closed, and convex, but \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), while the vertical line \(t=0\) supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a domain boundary, epigraph support may be purely vertical and need not yield a subgradient; minus square root at zero is an explicit example.
assumptions_latex: Supporting hyperplanes are considered at finite graph points of a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of some epigraph support does not imply \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\); nonvertical support is essential.

notation.meaning: normal of a vertical epigraph-supporting hyperplane

knowledge_statements.title: Vertical-Support Boundary and Empty Subdifferentials

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonvertical Epigraph Support on the Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of subgradient-defined supporting hyperplanes at relative-interior graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. For every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), \[\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing.\] Consequently, at every graph point \((x,f(x))\) over \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), the epigraph admits a nonvertical supporting hyperplane with normal proportional to \((u,-1)\) for some \(u\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every relative-interior domain point has a subgradient and therefore a nonvertical supporting hyperplane to the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\), yielding a nonvertical epigraph support at \((x,f(x))\).

notation.meaning: relative interior of the effective domain

knowledge_statements.title: Nonvertical Epigraph Support on the Relative Interior
All Epigraph Support Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every epigraph support direction is classified by its vertical component: negative directions rescale conjugate values, zero directions support the domain, and positive directions have infinite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and set \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\). For \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
\sigma_E(u,\beta)=
\begin{cases}
(-\beta)f^*\!\left(u/(-\beta)\right),&\beta<0,\\
\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}(u),&\beta=0,\\
+\infty,&\beta>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus negative vertical coefficients are homogeneous rescalings of conjugate values, zero vertical coefficient records only effective-domain support, and positive vertical coefficient gives infinite support because epigraphs are upward closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_E(u,\beta)\) obeys the stated three-regime formula.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous extension of the normalized support identity to every vertical coefficient.

notation.meaning: vertical component of the support direction

knowledge_statements.title: Support–Epigraph Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each conjugate value is an epigraph support value in direction (u,-1), and for every real alpha its upper bounds correspond exactly to affine minorants of the original function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}=\sup_{(x,r)\in E}\{\langle u,x\rangle-r\}=\sigma_E(u,-1).
\]
For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the inequality \(f^*(u)\le\alpha\) holds exactly when \(E\subseteq\{(x,r)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:\langle u,x\rangle-r\le\alpha\}\), or equivalently when \(x\mapsto\langle u,x\rangle-\alpha\) is an affine minorant of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate is the support function of the epigraph restricted to covectors whose last coordinate is \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugacy represented through support values of the epigraph.

notation.meaning: Support function of a set C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Directional Support Formula for an Epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends the seed's normalized direction to every vertical component without importing contact-point geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\). Then
\[
\sigma_E(u,s)=\begin{cases}
(-s)f^*\!\left(u/(-s)\right),&s<0,\\
\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}(u),&s=0,\\
+\infty,&s>0.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative-vertical epigraph supports are scaled conjugate values, horizontal supports are domain supports, and positive-vertical supports are infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_E(u,s)=(-s)f^*(u/(-s))\) for \(s<0\), \(\sigma_E(u,0)=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}(u)\), and \(\sigma_E(u,s)=+\infty\) for \(s>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Full Directional Support Formula for an Epigraph
Conjugation as an Order Anti-Isomorphism
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On proper closed convex functions, conjugation is an involutive order anti-isomorphism: primal order is exactly reversed in the dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\) denote the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. For \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\),
\[
f\le g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g^*\le f^*.
\]
Moreover, \(f^*\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\) and \(f^{**}=f\). Hence Fenchel conjugation is an order-reversing bijection of \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb{R}^n)\) onto itself, with conjugation as its inverse.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Reversing Dual Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing a function decreases its conjugate. Conjugation reverses pointwise inequalities, while biconjugation preserves them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the pointwise inequality \(f\le g\) gives
\[
g^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-g(x)\}\le\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}=f^*(u).
\]
Thus conjugation is antitone. Applying it twice restores the original order, so \(f^{**}\le g^{**}\). In particular, equality \(f=g\) implies equality of their conjugates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fenchel conjugation reverses pointwise order: \(g^*\le f^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal F(f)=f^*\) by Fenchel conjugation. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation reverses pointwise inequalities: a smaller primal function has a larger conjugate. Every function dominates its biconjugate, and taking three conjugates returns the first conjugate. On proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, conjugation is an order-reversing involution, so the primal inequality and the reversed dual inequality are equivalent.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\overline{\mathbb R}=[-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). Define \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended-real Fenchel transform is \[f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)).\] The input is called proper when \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\); otherwise it is improper. Three regimes are distinguished: \[(i)\ f\in\Gamma_0:\ f\text{ is proper, convex, and lower semicontinuous};\] \[(ii)\ f\text{ is proper but is nonconvex or not lower semicontinuous};\] \[(iii)\ f\text{ is improper}.\] In regime \((i)\), \(f^*\in\Gamma_0\) and \(f^{**}=f\). In regime \((ii)\), \(f^*=(f^{**})^*\), while \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\) whenever a proper lower-semicontinuous convex minorant exists. Regime \((iii)\) includes constant and pointwise degeneracies and need not produce a proper conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same supremum formula defines conjugacy for every extended-real function. Inputs are separated into proper closed convex functions, proper functions lacking convexity or lower semicontinuity, and improper functions. Conjugacy is involutive in the first regime. In the second, it discards precisely the information lost upon passage to the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope. In the third, the transform can collapse to an infinite constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The extended-real conjugate is defined in all three regimes, with exact involution on \(\Gamma_0\) and envelope recovery through \(f^{**}\) for proper nonclosed or nonconvex inputs.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Properness is \(\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing\) together with \(f^{-1}(-\infty)=\varnothing\).
For a proper convex function, lower semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
special_cases_latex: The constants \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) are conjugate to one another.
A finite-valued function is automatically proper but need not be convex or closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every proper conjugate is lower semicontinuous and convex.
Nonconvex features above the closed convex envelope cannot be recovered from \(f^*\).
boundary_notes: The notation \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\) denotes the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant, not pointwise closure of values.
Extended-real arithmetic must avoid indeterminate sums.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Closed Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function, the conjugate remains proper closed convex and the biconjugate equals the original function everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conjugate \(f^*:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Moreover, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),

f^{**}(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f^*(u)\}=f(x).
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proper closed convex regime is the class \[\Gamma_0(X):=\{f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]:\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing,\ f\text{ is convex, and }\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}\}.\] Equivalently, its members are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. Fenchel conjugation maps this class onto itself and is involutive: \[f\in\Gamma_0(X)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^*\in\Gamma_0(X^*),\qquad f^{**}=f.\] Consequently, \(f\mapsto f^*\) is a symmetric one-to-one correspondence between \(\Gamma_0(X)\) and \(\Gamma_0(X^*)\), and every member satisfies \[f(x)=\sup_{y\in X^*}\{\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proper closed convex regime consists of extended-real convex functions with nonempty effective domain, no value minus infinity, and closed epigraph. These are exactly the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. Their conjugates remain in the same class, and conjugating twice returns the original function. Thus Fenchel conjugacy is a bijective, symmetric, order-reversing correspondence on this class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in\Gamma_0(X)\Rightarrow f^*\in\Gamma_0(X^*)\) and \(f^{**}=f\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f\in\Gamma_0(X)\iff f=f^{**}\text{ and }f\not\equiv\pm\infty.\]
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{y\in X^*}\{(x,r):r\ge\langle x,y\rangle-f^*(y)\}.\]
special_cases_latex: Indicators of nonempty closed convex sets belong to \(\Gamma_0\).
Finite continuous convex functions, norms, and positive-semidefinite finite quadratics belong to \(\Gamma_0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy of proper nonclosed or nonconvex inputs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, without assuming convexity or lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact description of what conjugacy retains from a proper arbitrary input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonclosed/nonconvex input regime consists of proper functions \(f\notin\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\). Their conjugates are still defined by \[f^*(y)=\sup_x\{\langle x,y\rangle-f(x)\}\] and are pointwise suprema of affine functions of \(y\), hence closed and convex whenever proper. Define the closed convex envelope by \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f:=\sup\{h:h\le f,\ h\text{ is lower-semicontinuous and convex}\}.\] When this envelope is proper, \[f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f,\qquad f^*=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f)^*.\] Thus two proper inputs have the same conjugate whenever they have the same closed convex envelope; exact recovery of the original input occurs only if it already belongs to \(\Gamma_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function may be conjugated even if it is nonconvex or lacks lower semicontinuity. Its conjugate is a supremum of affine functions and therefore has closed convex structure. Conjugating twice returns the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function below the input, provided that envelope is proper. Consequently, conjugacy retains the closed convex envelope and discards nonconvex elevations and nonclosed boundary values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a proper input with proper closed convex envelope, \(f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\) and \(f^*=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f)^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{epi}f)\] under the proper-envelope convention.
\[f^*(y)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle-r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For convex but nonclosed \(f\), \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\).
For finite nonconvex \(f\), \(f^{**}\) is its lower-semicontinuous convex envelope.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing \(f\) without changing its affine minorants does not change \(f^*\).
The strict inequality \(f^{**}<f\) somewhere certifies failure of closed convexity.
boundary_notes: The envelope may be identically \(-\infty\) if no proper closed convex minorant exists.
The biconjugate is a minorant, not a convex majorant.
