knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex but nonclosed function, biconjugation returns its lower-semicontinuous closure, not the original function, while conjugation already ignores the missing closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The biconjugate is the lower-semicontinuous hull of \(f\):
\[
f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f,
\qquad
\operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}.
\]
Hence \(f^{**}\le f\) everywhere, and because \(f\) is not lower semicontinuous, equality fails at at least one point. Nevertheless, conjugation cannot distinguish \(f\) from its closure: \(f^*=(\operatorname{cl}f)^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Biconjugation closes \(f\): \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\), with strict inequality wherever closure lowers its value.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper nonconvex input with an affine lower bound, biconjugation returns the greatest closed convex minorant and therefore cannot reproduce the input everywhere.

The biconjugate satisfies

f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f
=\sup\{a:a\text{ is continuous affine and }a\le f\}.
\]
It is lower semicontinuous and convex, obeys \(f^{**}\le f\), and dominates every lower-semicontinuous convex function lying below \(f\). Since \(f\) is not convex, \(f^{**}\) cannot equal \(f\) everywhere.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The improper-degenerate regimes are characterized as follows. knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constant positive- and negative-infinity inputs conjugate to the opposite infinite constants, so no finite support or affine-minorant information survives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the usual extended-real conventions, the constant extreme inputs satisfy
\[
(+\infty)^*\equiv-\infty,
\qquad
(-\infty)^*\equiv+\infty.
\]
Consequently, their conjugates contain no finite support values, and a second conjugation merely exchanges the two extremes again. These cases are degenerate because conjugation no longer produces a proper closed convex function or meaningful finite affine-minorant data.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is an extended-real input to Fenchel conjugation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extreme constant inputs yield constant infinite conjugates and destroy informative dual geometry.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy interpreted as the two constant infinite-valued extreme inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Improperness–Degeneracy Overlap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two constant infinite-valued degeneracies are both improper, and Fenchel conjugation swaps positive infinity with negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Both constant extreme functions are improper: \(+\infty\) has empty effective domain, while \(-\infty\) assumes the forbidden negative-infinite value everywhere. Fenchel conjugation interchanges them:
\[
f\equiv+\infty\Longleftrightarrow f^*\equiv-\infty,
\qquad
f\equiv-\infty\Longleftrightarrow f^*\equiv+\infty.
\]
Thus the constant degenerate regime lies inside the improper regime and forms a two-element cycle under conjugation.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is one of the constant functions \(+\infty\) or \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These degenerate inputs are improper, and conjugation swaps them.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection of improperness with constant infinite-valued degeneracy.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Conjugation does swap the two constant infinite functions, but the displayed reverse implication from an identically positive-infinite conjugate to an identically negative-infinite primal is false without the record's restrictive two-function assumption; other functions can have conjugate identically positive infinity. More importantly, the cited source has not been shown to define the degenerate regime as exactly these constants. A source fixing that scope and convention is needed before a mathematically reliable revision can be chosen.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Embedding convex sets into functional conjugacy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty. Define its indicator \(\delta_C\), support function \(\sigma_C\), polar \(C^\circ\), and gauge \(\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional correspondences for nonempty convex sets; closure and origin assumptions are stated where required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set–function embedding is \[\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\qquad \sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle.\] Fenchel conjugacy gives \[\delta_C^*=\sigma_C,\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}.\] If \(C\) is closed and convex, indicator and support functions are mutually conjugate. If additionally \(0\in C\), define \[C^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\},\qquad \gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\}.\] Then \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C,\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C.\] These identities embed indicator-support, gauge-polar, and norm-dual-norm correspondences into conjugate geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is represented analytically by its extended-real indicator, whose conjugate is the set's support function. Conjugating the support function returns the indicator of the closed convex hull, and returns the original indicator for a closed convex set. When a closed convex set contains the origin, its gauge equals the support function of its polar, and polarity is involutive. Norm duality is the symmetric bounded-body specialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^*=\sigma_C\), \(\sigma_C^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\), and for closed convex \(C\ni0\), \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\) with \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C\iff \langle x,y\rangle\le\sigma_C(y)\ \forall y.\]
\[C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), its polar is also a closed convex cone and \(\delta_K^*=\delta_{K^\circ}\) under the cone-polar sign convention of the source.
For a centrally symmetric convex body, its gauge is a norm and the polar gauge is the dual norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed convex sets are uniquely determined by their support functions.
Set inclusion becomes pointwise support-function order and reverses under polarity.
boundary_notes: For nonclosed or nonconvex \(C\), the support function cannot distinguish \(C\) from its closed convex hull.
The polar-set inequality uses level \(1\); cone polarity may use level \(0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator and support functions as a conjugate pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact conjugate pair for a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\qquad \sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle.\] The indicator-support conjugacy pair is \[\delta_C^*=\sigma_C,\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_C.\] Equivalently, \(\sigma_C\) is the unique closed proper positively homogeneous convex function whose conjugate is \(\delta_C\). The support function encodes every containing half-space through \[C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\le\beta\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sigma_C(y)\le\beta.\] Accordingly, \[C=\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\le\sigma_C(y)\ \forall y\in\mathbb R^n\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended-real indicator of a nonempty closed convex set and its support function are Fenchel conjugates of one another. The support value in each direction is the least offset of a closed half-space with that normal containing the set. Collecting these inequalities reconstructs the set exactly. Support functions are precisely the closed proper positively homogeneous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For nonempty closed convex \(C\), \(\delta_C^*=\sigma_C\) and \(\sigma_C^*=\delta_C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\sigma_C(y)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle:x\in C\}.\]
\[x\in C\iff\langle x,y\rangle\le\sigma_C(y)\quad\forall y.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\{a\}\), then \(\sigma_C(y)=\langle a,y\rangle\).
If \(C\) is a linear subspace \(L\), then \(\sigma_L=\delta_{L^\perp}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\sigma_C\) is closed, convex, proper, and positively homogeneous.
If \(C_1,C_2\) are closed convex, then \(C_1\subseteq C_2\iff\sigma_{C_1}\le\sigma_{C_2}\).
boundary_notes: For arbitrary nonempty \(C\), \(\sigma_C^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\), so exact recovery requires closed convexity.
The support function may take \(+\infty\) when \(C\) is unbounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Calculus for Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding indicators imposes both set constraints, and positive scaling leaves an indicator unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary sets \(C,D\subseteq X\),
\[
\delta_C+\delta_D=\delta_{C\cap D}.
\]
The common function is proper exactly when \(C\cap D\neq\varnothing\). For every scalar \(\lambda>0\), \(\lambda\delta_C=\delta_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C+\delta_D=\delta_{C\cap D}\) and \(\lambda\delta_C=\delta_C\) for \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary extended-real calculus intrinsic to set indicators.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator is zero on the set and positive infinity outside it; its convexity and lower semicontinuity correspond respectively to convexity and closedness of the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The indicator function of \(C\) is the extended-real-valued function \(\delta_C:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined by
\[
\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}
\]
It is proper because \(C\neq\varnothing\). It is convex exactly when \(C\) is convex, and it is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\), and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convex-analysis indicator, not a Boolean-valued characteristic function.

knowledge_statements.title: Finiteness and Lipschitz Boundaries for Support Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support function is finite and globally Lipschitz exactly when its generating set is bounded; the least Lipschitz constant is the set's maximal radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R=\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|\). The support function \(\sigma_C\) is finite everywhere if and only if \(C\) is bounded. In that case
\[
|\sigma_C(u)-\sigma_C(v)|\leq R\|u-v\|,
\]
and \(R\) is the least global Lipschitz constant. Hence \(\sigma_C\) is globally Lipschitz exactly when \(C\) is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ bounded}\iff\sigma_C\text{ finite everywhere}\iff\sigma_C\text{ globally Lipschitz}\), and the least Lipschitz constant is \(\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundedness characterization intrinsic to support functions.

notation.meaning: supremal norm of points in C

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Support-Function Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support functions turn Minkowski addition into addition, scaling into scaling, translation into an affine term, and linear images into adjoint composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty sets \(C,D\subseteq X\), \(\lambda\geq0\), \(a\in X\), and a linear map \(A:X\to Y\),
\[
\sigma_{C+D}=\sigma_C+\sigma_D,\quad \sigma_{\lambda C}=\lambda\sigma_C,\quad \sigma_{C+a}(u)=\sigma_C(u)+\langle u,a\rangle,
\]
and
\[
\sigma_{AC}(v)=\sigma_C(A^*v).
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{C+D}=\sigma_C+\sigma_D\), \(\sigma_{\lambda C}=\lambda\sigma_C\), \(\sigma_{C+a}(u)=\sigma_C(u)+\langle u,a\rangle\), and \(\sigma_{AC}=\sigma_C\circ A^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary transformations within the support-function representation family.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of C and D

knowledge_statements.title: Support Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function gives the supremum of each linear functional over the set and depends only on the set's closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support function of \(C\) is \(\sigma_C:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) given by
\[
\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle.
\]
It is convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively homogeneous. Moreover, it depends only on the closed convex hull: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued support function on a real Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness criterion and exact continuity modulus for Hilbert-space support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, and set \(R=\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|\). Then \(\sigma_C\) is finite everywhere if and only if \(C\) is bounded. When \(R<+\infty\),
\[
|\sigma_C(u)-\sigma_C(v)|\le R\|u-v\|\qquad(u,v\in X),
\]
and the least global Lipschitz constant of \(\sigma_C\) is \(R=\sup_{x\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\|x\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hilbert-space support function is finite everywhere exactly when its set is bounded, and its least global Lipschitz constant is the set's radius about the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C\text{ is finite everywhere}\iff C\text{ is bounded}\), and, when bounded, \(\operatorname{Lip}(\sigma_C)=\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|\).

notation.meaning: radius supremum of C about the origin

Indicator–Support Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a set indicator is its support function; conjugating again yields the indicator of the closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in X\), Fenchel conjugation gives
\[
\delta_C^*(u)=\sup_{x\in X}\bigl(\langle u,x\rangle-\delta_C(x)\bigr)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u).
\]
Consequently, the biconjugate of the indicator is \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\), and equivalently
\[
\sigma_C^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}.
\]
If \(C\) is closed and convex, this reduces to \(\sigma_C^*=\delta_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^*=\sigma_C\) and \(\sigma_C^*=\delta_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy for an arbitrary nonempty set and its closed convex hull.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets containing the origin; gauges may be infinite or vanish away from the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Minkowski gauge and polar set by \[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad C^\circ:=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}.\] The gauge-polar correspondence is \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C,\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C.\] In particular, \(\gamma_C\) is a closed nonnegative positively homogeneous convex function with \(\gamma_C(0)=0\), and its Fenchel conjugate is \[(\gamma_C)^*=\delta_{C^\circ}.\] The polar gauge may equivalently be written \[\gamma_C^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle:\gamma_C(x)\le1\}=\gamma_{C^\circ}(y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a closed convex set containing the origin measures the least nonnegative dilation needed to contain a point. The polar set consists of dual vectors pairing to at most one with every point of the set. The gauge equals the support function of the polar, and the gauge of the polar equals the original support function. Taking the polar twice returns the set. The Fenchel conjugate of the gauge is the indicator of the polar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\), \((\gamma_C)^*=\delta_{C^\circ}\), and \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, its gauge reduces to its indicator and set polarity reduces to cone polarity.
If \(C\) is bounded with \(0\) in its interior and is centrally symmetric, \(\gamma_C\) is a norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The generalized Hölder inequality \(\langle x,y\rangle\le\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)\) holds whenever the gauge values are finite.
Polarity reverses inclusion: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\Rightarrow C_1^\circ\supseteq C_2^\circ\).
boundary_notes: Without closed convexity, the bipolar is the closed convex hull augmented by the origin.
A gauge need not be symmetric, finite everywhere, or positive away from zero.

notation.meaning: Polar set at pairing level one.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Gauge Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set's gauge vanishes precisely along its recession cone, so definiteness is equivalent to boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\), then \[\{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C.\] Thus \(\gamma_C\) is definite exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\), equivalently, in finite dimensions, when \(C\) is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C;\quad \gamma_C\text{ is definite}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\Longleftrightarrow C\text{ is bounded}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary between a definite gauge and collapse along recession directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Domain and Finiteness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is finite on the cone generated by its set and is finite everywhere exactly when the set is absorbing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(C\) containing \(0\), \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C=\operatorname{cone}C.\] Consequently, \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere exactly when \(C\) is absorbing.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\operatorname{cone}C,\qquad \gamma_C\text{ is finite on }X\Longleftrightarrow C\text{ is absorbing}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic domain characterization for the extended-valued gauge generated by a convex set containing the origin.

notation.meaning: Set of points where the gauge is finite

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge is the least positive dilation factor needed to place a point in the set; convex sets produce convex, positively homogeneous gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge of \(C\) is the function \(\gamma_C:X\to[0,+\infty]\) defined by
\[
\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\},
\]
where \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). If \(C\) is convex, then \(\gamma_C\) is convex and positively homogeneous. If \(C\) is also closed, then its unit sublevel set satisfies \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}=C\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued Minkowski gauge of a set containing the origin.

notation.meaning: gauge or Minkowski functional of C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic characterization of extended-valued gauges through unit sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be convex and positively homogeneous, and set \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\). Then \[ \kappa=\gamma_{B_\kappa}. \] Conversely, if \(C\) is convex and contains \(0\), then \(\gamma_C\) is nonnegative and sublinear. If \(C\) is also closed, then \(\gamma_C\) is lower semicontinuous and \(C=B_{\gamma_C}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative sublinear function is the gauge of its unit sublevel set, and every closed convex set containing zero is recovered from its gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa=\gamma_{B_\kappa}\); for closed convex \(C\ni0\), \(C=B_{\gamma_C}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary between a definite gauge and collapse along recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero sublevel set of the gauge is exactly the recession cone of \(C\): \[\{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C.\] Consequently \(\gamma_C(x)>0\) for every \(x\ne0\) if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\); in finite dimensions this is equivalent to boundedness of the nonempty closed convex set \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set's gauge vanishes precisely along its recession cone, so definiteness is equivalent to having no nonzero recession direction.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C;\quad \gamma_C\text{ is definite}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\Longleftrightarrow C\text{ is bounded}.

Finiteness Boundary for Polar Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polar function is finite everywhere exactly when the original gauge unit ball is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\leq1\}\). Then \(\kappa^\circ=\sigma_{B_\kappa}\) is finite on all of \(X\) if and only if \(B_\kappa\) is bounded. If \(B_\kappa\) is unbounded, then \(\kappa^\circ(y)=+\infty\) for at least one \(y\in X\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\kappa^\circ=X\iff B_\kappa\text{ is bounded}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional criterion for the polar function to be real-valued everywhere.

notation.meaning: unit sublevel set of the gauge
effective domain of the polar function

knowledge_statements.title: Domination Characterization of the Polar Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar value is the least positive factor by which the gauge must be multiplied to dominate the pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y\in X\),
\[
\kappa^\circ(y)=\inf\{\lambda>0:\langle y,x\rangle\leq\lambda\kappa(x)\ \text{for every }x\in X\},
\]
where \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa^\circ(y)=\inf\{\lambda>0:\langle y,x\rangle\leq\lambda\kappa(x)\ \forall x\in X\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic domination characterization of a gauge's polar value.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a gauge is the support function of its unit sublevel set, equivalently the largest pairing over gauge-unit points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B_\kappa=\{x\in X:\kappa(x)\leq1\}\). The polar function of \(\kappa\) is the extended-valued gauge \(\kappa^\circ:X\to[0,+\infty]\) defined by
\[
\kappa^\circ(y)=\sup_{x\in B_\kappa}\langle y,x\rangle.
\]
Thus \(\kappa^\circ=\sigma_{B_\kappa}\); in particular, it is convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively homogeneous.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:\kappa(x)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar transform of a nonnegative, positively homogeneous convex function.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finiteness and Attainment of the Polar Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp geometric conditions for global finiteness and a standard sufficient condition for attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\). Then \(\kappa^\circ=\sigma_{B_\kappa}\) is finite everywhere if and only if \(B_\kappa\) is bounded. If \(B_\kappa\) is compact, then for every \(y\) there exists \(x_y\in B_\kappa\) such that \[ \kappa^\circ(y)=\langle y,x_y\rangle. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polar function is finite everywhere exactly when the primal gauge unit ball is bounded; compactness guarantees attainment of every polar evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa^\circ\) is finite everywhere iff \(B_\kappa\) is bounded; compact \(B_\kappa\) implies attainment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Unit Ball and Normalized-Pairing Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent set and homogeneous descriptions of a polar function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\). Then \[ B_{\kappa^\circ}=B_\kappa^\circ =\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le\kappa(x)\ \forall x\in X\}. \] Moreover, if no \(d\) satisfies \(\kappa(d)=0\) and \(\langle y,d\rangle>0\), then \[ \kappa^\circ(y)=\max\!\left\{0,\sup_{0<\kappa(x)<+\infty}\frac{\langle y,x\rangle}{\kappa(x)}\right\}, \] where the supremum of the empty set is \(-\infty\); if such a zero-gauge direction exists, \(\kappa^\circ(y)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar unit ball is the set polar of the primal unit ball; polar values are normalized pairings, with positively paired zero-gauge directions causing infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge on a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\kappa^\circ}=B_\kappa^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le\kappa(x)\ \forall x\}\), with the stated normalized-pairing formula.

notation.meaning: set polar of the primal gauge unit ball

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domination and Unit-Ball Characterizations of the Polar Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent intrinsic descriptions of a gauge's polar function, without asserting bipolar recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge and \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\leq1\}\). Then
\[
\kappa^\circ(y)=\inf\{\lambda\geq0:\langle y,x\rangle\leq\lambda\kappa(x)\ \text{for every }x\in X\},
\]
where \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Consequently,
\[
\{y:\kappa^\circ(y)\leq1\}=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq\kappa(x)\ \text{for every }x\in X\}=B_\kappa^\circ.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar value is the least factor by which the gauge must be multiplied to dominate the pairing; its unit ball is the polar of the original gauge unit ball.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa^\circ(y)=\inf\{\lambda\geq0:\langle y,x\rangle\leq\lambda\kappa(x)\ \forall x\}\) and \(B_{\kappa^\circ}=B_\kappa^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.title: Domination and Unit-Ball Characterizations of the Polar Function
Fenchel Conjugates of Gauges and Supports
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex gauge is the support function of the polar set and conjugates to that polar set's indicator; the original support function conjugates to the original set's indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\) containing \(0\), \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad (\gamma_C)^*=\delta_{C^\circ},\qquad \sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ},\qquad (\sigma_C)^*=\delta_C.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\quad (\gamma_C)^*=\delta_{C^\circ},\quad \sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ},\quad (\sigma_C)^*=\delta_C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-conjugacy form of the gauge–polar correspondence, distinct from functional gauge polarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Functional Bipolar Closure Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double gauge polarity closes a nonclosed gauge and recovers it exactly precisely in the lower-semicontinuous regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a proper convex positively homogeneous function with \(\kappa(0)=0\). Its double polar is its lower-semicontinuous hull: \[\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\kappa.\] Hence \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\kappa\) exactly when \(\kappa\) is lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is proper, convex, positively homogeneous, and satisfies \(\kappa(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\kappa,\qquad \kappa^{\circ\circ}=\kappa\Longleftrightarrow\kappa\text{ is lower semicontinuous}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp functional boundary for double gauge polarity outside the closed-gauge class.

notation.meaning: Polar transform of the gauge κ

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Gauge Inequality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and polar gauges bound the pairing as a norm and dual norm do, without requiring symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x,y\in X\) with \(\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\) and \(\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)<+\infty\), \[\langle y,x\rangle\leq\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y).\] Equivalently, \(\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)\leq1\) implies \(\langle y,x\rangle\leq\gamma_C(x)\) for every \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle y,x\rangle\leq\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)\quad\text{whenever both gauge values are finite}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauge analogue of the dual-norm inequality, including asymmetric and extended-valued gauges when both values are finite.

notation.meaning: Gauge generated by the polar set

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge–Polar Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set's polar gauge equals its support function and the gauge of its polar set; applying polarity twice recovers the original gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the polar set by \(C^\circ=\{y\in X:\langle y,x\rangle\leq1\text{ for every }x\in C\}\). Then
\[
(\gamma_C)^\circ=\sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ}.
\]
Since \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), the bipolar identity \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\) implies
\[
(\gamma_C)^{\circ\circ}=\gamma_C.
\]
Hence passage from a gauge to its polar reverses the corresponding unit balls and is involutive on this class.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\gamma_C)^\circ=\sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ}\) and \((\gamma_C)^{\circ\circ}=\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional gauge polarity for closed convex sets containing the origin.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery boundary for a proper gauge not assumed lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a proper gauge, then \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}\) is its lower-semicontinuous hull. Equivalently, if \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\), then \[ B_{\kappa^{\circ\circ}}=B_\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\overline{B_\kappa}. \] Hence \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\kappa\) exactly for lower-semicontinuous gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double polarity closes a proper gauge; exact recovery holds precisely when the gauge is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\kappa\), with equality to \(\kappa\) iff \(\kappa\) is lower semicontinuous.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic pairing inequality and antitonicity induced by gauge polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\kappa(x)<+\infty\) and \(\kappa^\circ(y)<+\infty\), with their product defined, then \[ \langle y,x\rangle\le \kappa(x)\kappa^\circ(y). \] Moreover, if \(\kappa_1\le\kappa_2\) pointwise, then \[ \kappa_2^\circ\le\kappa_1^\circ. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and polar gauges bound the pairing, and polarity reverses pointwise gauge order.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa,\kappa_1,\kappa_2\) are gauges on a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle y,x\rangle\le\kappa(x)\kappa^\circ(y)\) when defined, and \(\kappa_1\le\kappa_2\Rightarrow\kappa_2^\circ\le\kappa_1^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp set-side boundary for involutive gauge polarity when the generating set lacks closedness, convexity, or the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an arbitrary nonempty set \(A\subseteq X\), polarity ignores precisely the defects repaired by the bipolar hull: \[A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(A\cup\{0\}),\qquad A^\circ=\bigl(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(A\cup\{0\})\bigr)^\circ.\] Therefore exact recovery of the generating set by two polarizations holds exactly when \(A\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without closedness, convexity, and inclusion of zero, double polarity recovers the closed convex hull with zero adjoined rather than the original set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(A\cup\{0\}),\quad A^{\circ\circ}=A\Longleftrightarrow A\text{ is closed, convex, and }0\in A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual norm as polar gauge and Fenchel conjugate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(\mathbb R^n\), with closed unit ball \(B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm duality under the canonical Euclidean pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual norm is \[\|y\|_*:=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\langle x,y\rangle=\sigma_B(y).\] Its unit ball is the polar body \[B^\circ=\{y:\|y\|_*\le1\}.\] Since \(\|\cdot\|=\gamma_B=\sigma_{B^\circ}\), norm polarity is involutive: \[(\|\cdot\|_*)_* =\|\cdot\|.\] The associated Fenchel conjugacy identities are \[(\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{B^\circ},\qquad \left(\tfrac12\|\cdot\|^2\right)^*=\tfrac12\|\cdot\|_*^2.\] Equivalently, \[\langle x,y\rangle\le\|x\|\,\|y\|_*\qquad\forall x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\] with the dual norm being the least function of \(y\) making this inequality valid for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual norm is the support function of the primal unit ball. Its unit ball is the polar of the primal unit ball, while the primal norm is the support function of that polar ball. Hence dualizing twice returns the original norm. As Fenchel identities, the conjugate of a norm is the indicator of the dual unit ball, and the conjugate of one half the squared norm is one half the squared dual norm.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\|x\|=\sup_{\|y\|_*\le1}\langle x,y\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: The Euclidean norm is self-dual.
The \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) norms are dual to one another; for \(1<p<\infty\), \(\ell_p\) is dual to \(\ell_q\) where \(1/p+1/q=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The dual norm is a finite continuous norm.
The primal and dual unit balls determine one another by polarity.
boundary_notes: Central symmetry and boundedness distinguish norms from general gauges.
The pairing used to define the dual norm must be fixed; changing the pairing changes the coordinate formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Norms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm is positive definite, absolutely homogeneous, and subadditive; it is the gauge of its compact, convex, symmetric unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A primal norm is a function \(\|\cdot\|:X\to[0,+\infty)\) satisfying, for all \(x,z\in X\) and scalars \(\alpha\),
\[
\|x\|=0\iff x=0,\qquad \|\alpha x\|=|\alpha|\|x\|,\qquad \|x+z\|\leq\|x\|+\|z\|.
\]
Its unit ball \(B=\{x:\|x\|\leq1\}\) is compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and contains \(0\) in its interior, while \(\|\cdot\|=\gamma_B\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm viewed as the gauge of its unit ball.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite-Dimensional Norms Need Not Be Equivalent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of universal norm equivalence outside finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(X=C([0,1])\), both
\[
\|f\|_\infty=\max_{t\in[0,1]}|f(t)|,
\qquad
\|f\|_1=\int_0^1|f(t)|\,dt
\]
are norms, but they are not equivalent. For example, the triangular functions
\[
f_n(t)=\max\{1-n|t-\tfrac12|,0\}
\]
satisfy \(\|f_n\|_\infty=1\) and \(\|f_n\|_1=1/n\) for \(n\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sup norm and integral norm on continuous functions are inequivalent, demonstrating the necessity of finite dimensionality in the equivalence theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) and \(\|\cdot\|_1\) are not equivalent norms on \(C([0,1])\).

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Norms Need Not Be Equivalent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological equivalence of arbitrary norms on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\|\cdot\|_a\) and \(\|\cdot\|_b\) are norms on a finite-dimensional real vector space \(X\), then there exist \(m,M>0\) such that
\[
m\|x\|_a\le \|x\|_b\le M\|x\|_a
\qquad(x\in X).
\]
Consequently all norms on \(X\) induce the same topology, and each norm is continuous and coercive relative to every other norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two norms on a finite-dimensional space bound each other by positive constants and therefore induce the same topology.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists m,M>0\ \forall x\in X:\ m\|x\|_a\le\|x\|_b\le M\|x\|_a\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Equivalence of Norms

knowledge_statements.title: Duals of Finite-Dimensional Coordinate Norms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of an ell-p norm is the ell-q norm for the conjugate exponent, including the one/infinity endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R^n\), if \(1\leq p\leq\infty\) and \(1/p+1/q=1\), then
\[
\|y\|_{p,*}=\|y\|_q.
\]
In particular, the duals of \(\ell_1\), \(\ell_2\), and \(\ell_\infty\) are respectively \(\ell_\infty\), \(\ell_2\), and \(\ell_1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical coordinate-space examples of the dual-norm construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Norms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual norm is the largest absolute value attained by a linear functional on the primal unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual norm of \(y\in X^*\) is
\[
\|y\|_* = \sup_{\|x\|\leq1}|\langle y,x\rangle|.
\]
Because the primal unit ball is centrally symmetric, the absolute value may equivalently be omitted. The supremum is finite and attained in finite dimensions, and \(\|\cdot\|_*\) is a norm on \(X^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
\(X^*\) is its algebraic dual with pairing \(\langle y,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|y\|_*=\sup_{\|x\|\leq1}|\langle y,x\rangle|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator norm of a linear functional relative to the primal norm.

notation.meaning: dual norm on the dual space

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-Norm Supremum Need Not Be Attained in Infinite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the seed's finite-dimensional attainment assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=c_0\) with \(\|x\|_\infty=\sup_n|x_n|\), and let \(y=(2^{-n})_{n\ge1}\in X^*=\ell_1\). Then
\[
\|y\|_*=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-n}=1,
\]
but no \(x\in c_0\) with \(\|x\|_\infty\le1\) satisfies \(\langle y,x\rangle=1\). Hence the defining supremum of a continuous dual norm need not be attained outside finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On c-zero, a positive ell-one functional has dual norm one but does not attain it on the sup-norm unit ball, showing why finite dimensionality matters for attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\|x\|_\infty\le1}\langle y,x\rangle=1\) but the supremum is not attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Norm Supremum Need Not Be Attained in Infinite Dimensions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional coordinate examples, including endpoint norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(1\le p\le\infty\), let \(q\) satisfy \(1/p+1/q=1\), with \(1/\infty=0\). On \(\mathbb R^n\) with its standard pairing,
\[
\sup_{\|x\|_p\le1}|y^\top x|=\|y\|_q.
\]
Thus \(\ell_1^n\) and \(\ell_\infty^n\) are mutually dual, while \(\ell_2^n\) is self-dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual of the finite-dimensional ell-p norm is the ell-q norm for conjugate exponents, including the ell-one/ell-infinity endpoints and Euclidean self-duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Norming-Functional and Subgradient Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vector is a norm subgradient exactly when it saturates the primal-dual norm inequality; at zero the subdifferential is the dual unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\),
\[
\partial\|\cdot\|(x)=\{y\in X^*:\|y\|_*\leq1,\ \langle y,x\rangle=\|x\|\}.
\]
If \(x\neq0\), this is equivalent to \(\|y\|_*=1\) and \(\langle y,x\rangle=\|x\|\); at \(x=0\), \(\partial\|\cdot\|(0)=B_*\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\|\cdot\|(x)=\{y:\|y\|_*\leq1,\ \langle y,x\rangle=\|x\|\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality certificate linking primal and dual norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Norm Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a positively scaled norm is the indicator of the correspondingly scaled dual ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\lambda>0\),
\[
(\lambda\|\cdot\|)^*(y)=\delta_{\lambda B_*}(y).
\]
Equivalently, \(\delta_{\lambda B_*}^*(x)=\lambda\|x\|\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\lambda\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{\lambda B_*}\) and \(\delta_{\lambda B_*}^*=\lambda\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scaling variant of norm-indicator conjugacy.

notation.meaning: dual norm ball of radius lambda

knowledge_statements.title: Norm–Dual-Norm Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and dual norms satisfy Hölder's inequality, determine each other by support over their unit balls, and form a norm-indicator conjugate pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in X^*\),
\[
|\langle y,x\rangle|\leq\|x\|\,\|y\|_*.
\]
Moreover, polarity is exact:
\[
\|x\|=\sup_{\|y\|_*\leq1}\langle y,x\rangle,
\]
so the bidual norm equals the primal norm under the canonical identification of \(X\) with \(X^{**}\). In Fenchel-conjugate form,
\[
(\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{B_*},\qquad \delta_{B_*}^*=\|\cdot\|.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|x\|=\sup_{y\in B_*}\langle y,x\rangle\) and \((\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{B_*}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm polarity and Fenchel conjugacy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal–dual pairing certificate for a norm subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in X\) and \(y\in X^*\),
\[
y\in\partial\|\cdot\|(x)
\iff
\|y\|_*\le1\ \text{ and }\ \langle y,x\rangle=\|x\|.
\]
If \(x\ne0\), then necessarily \(\|y\|_*=1\); at \(x=0\), \(\partial\|\cdot\|(0)=B_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vector is a norm subgradient exactly when it lies in the dual unit ball and saturates the primal–dual support inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in\partial\|\cdot\|(x)\iff \|y\|_*\le1\text{ and }\langle y,x\rangle=\|x\|\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the norm at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled primal- and dual-norm Fenchel conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}\), \(B_*=\{y:\|y\|_*\le1\}\), and let \(\lambda,\mu>0\). Then
\[
(\lambda\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{\lambda B_*},
\qquad
(\mu\|\cdot\|_*)^*=\delta_{\mu B},
\]
where the second conjugate uses the pairing between \(X^*\) and \(X\). Equivalently, \(\lambda\|x\|=\sigma_{\lambda B_*}(x)\) and \(\mu\|y\|_*=\sigma_{\mu B}(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling either a primal or dual norm scales the opposite unit ball appearing in its indicator conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\lambda\|\cdot\|)^*=\delta_{\lambda B_*}\) and \((\mu\|\cdot\|_*)^*=\delta_{\mu B}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Scaled-Norm Conjugacy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy of norm powers for Hölder-conjugate exponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(1<p<\infty\) and \(q=p/(p-1)\). Then
\[
\left(\frac1p\|\cdot\|^p\right)^*(y)=\frac1q\|y\|_*^q.
\]
In particular,
\[
\left(\frac12\|\cdot\|^2\right)^*=\frac12\|\cdot\|_*^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugation exchanges a normalized p-th power of a norm with the normalized q-th power of the dual norm.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left(\frac1p\|\cdot\|^p\right)^*=\frac1q\|\cdot\|_*^q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Power-Norm Conjugacy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy-stable classes of closed convex functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\), on which \(f\mapsto f^*\) is an involution.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional named structural classes preserved by Fenchel conjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subclass \(\mathcal C\subseteq\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\) is called conjugacy-stable when \[f\in\mathcal C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^*\in\mathcal C.\] Canonical conjugacy-stable classes include: \[(a)\ \text{partial affine functions }f(x)=\delta_{L+a}(x)+\langle x,a^*\rangle+\alpha;\] \[(b)\ \text{partial quadratic convex functions }f(x)=q(x)+\delta_M(x),\] where \(L\) is a linear subspace, \(M\) is affine, and \(q\) is a finite convex quadratic; and \[(c)\ \text{polyhedral convex functions, equivalently functions with polyhedral epigraphs}.\] The full class \(\Gamma_0\) is itself conjugacy-stable. Each member belongs to a conjugacy orbit \([f]_*:=\{f,f^*\}\), which is a singleton exactly when \(f=f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical conjugate class is a structural family of proper closed convex functions preserved in both directions by Fenchel conjugation. Important examples are partial affine functions, partial quadratic convex functions, polyhedral convex functions, and the entire Fenchel–Moreau class. Each function and its conjugate form a two-element orbit unless the function is self-conjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A class is conjugacy-stable when \(f\in\mathcal C\iff f^*\in\mathcal C\); partial affine, partial quadratic convex, polyhedral convex, and all proper closed convex functions have this property.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(f^{**}=f\) on \(\Gamma_0\), one-sided closure \(f\in\mathcal C\Rightarrow f^*\in\mathcal C\) already implies conjugacy stability.
\([f]_*\) has cardinality one or two.
special_cases_latex: The function \(x\mapsto\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\) is a singleton self-conjugate orbit.
Indicators and support functions of closed convex sets form conjugate pairs but do not individually remain within the indicator subclass.
immediate_consequences_latex: Structural formulas for one class member can be transferred to its conjugate within the same class.
Polyhedral and partial-quadratic subclasses permit finite-dimensional representations on both sides.
boundary_notes: A collection of familiar examples is not conjugacy-stable unless membership is preserved in both directions.
Finite-valued affine functions alone are not stable because their conjugates are generally partial affine.

notation.meaning: A subclass of proper closed convex functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of affine and polyhedral convex functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex piecewise-affine and polyhedral functions; extended values encode polyhedral domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite affine function has the form \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\). A finite convex piecewise-linear-affine function has a representation \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i).\] A polyhedral convex function is one whose epigraph is a polyhedral convex set. Equivalently, every proper polyhedral convex function can be written \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)+\delta_P(x),\] where \(P=\{x:Ax\le c\}\) is a nonempty polyhedral convex set. Thus finite affine functions form a subclass of finite convex piecewise-linear-affine functions, which form the full-domain subclass of proper polyhedral convex functions. Partial affine functions arise when the domain \(P\) is affine and the maximum has one term. Fenchel conjugation preserves the polyhedral class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite affine functions have one affine formula. Finite convex piecewise-linear-affine functions are finite maxima of affine formulas. Proper polyhedral convex functions allow the same maximum together with an extended-real indicator imposing a polyhedral domain. This yields a strict hierarchy from affine to finite piecewise linear to general polyhedral functions, with partial affine functions occupying the affine-domain branch. Conjugacy preserves polyhedrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proper polyhedral convex functions are exactly the functions \(\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)+\delta_P(x)\) with polyhedral \(P\), and their conjugates are polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is an intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces.
A convex function is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated in the epigraph sense.
special_cases_latex: The absolute value and \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) norms are finite polyhedral convex functions.
Indicators of nonempty polyhedral convex sets are polyhedral convex functions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every proper polyhedral convex function is closed.
A finite convex piecewise-linear-affine function has a polyhedral epigraph and full effective domain.
boundary_notes: Some terminology uses “piecewise linear” for affine pieces; constants \(b_i\) are included here.
A nonconvex piecewise-affine function is not part of this hierarchy.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant Subdifferential and Optimization Dichotomy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function has its slope as its unique subgradient everywhere and is bounded below exactly when that slope is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\),
\[
\partial f(x)=\{a\}\qquad(x\in X).
\]
If \(a=0\), then \(\operatorname*{argmin}f=X\) and \(\inf f=b\). If \(a\ne0\), then \(\inf f=-\infty\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}f=\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonzero finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\{a\}\), with the stated minimization dichotomy.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order and minimization structure of an everywhere-finite affine function.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine function is a linear functional plus a constant; its conjugate is finite only at its slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An affine function is an everywhere-finite function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) of the form
\[
f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b
\]
for fixed \(a\in X^*\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\). It is both convex and concave. Its Fenchel conjugate is concentrated at its slope:
\[
f^*(y)=\delta_{\{a\}}(y)-b.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\) for some \(a\in X^*\) and \(b\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Everywhere-finite affine functions and their Fenchel conjugates.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral First-Order Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point minimizes a polyhedral convex function exactly when a convex combination of active slopes is canceled by a domain normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in P\),
\[
x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0\in\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x).
\]
Equivalently, there are \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i\in I(x)\), with \(\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i=1\), and \(n\in N_P(x)\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in I(x)}\lambda_i a_i+n=0.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has the accepted domain-restricted max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\iff0\in\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact minimizer test obtained from the local subdifferential representation.

notation.meaning: normal vector to P at x

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential of a Domain-Restricted Max-Affine Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral function's subdifferential is the active-slope convex hull plus the normal cone to its polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}+\delta_P(x),
\]
and for \(x\in P\) let
\[
I(x):=\{i:f(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}.
\]
Then
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x)
\qquad(x\in P),
\]
while \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\notin P\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has the accepted domain-restricted max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x)\) on \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order representation for the accepted polyhedral-function normal form.

notation.meaning: normal cone of P at x

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is polyhedral when its epigraph is a polyhedron, equivalently when it is a finite affine maximum over a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is polyhedral when its epigraph
\[
\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\leq t\}
\]
is a nonempty polyhedron. Equivalently, there are a polyhedron \(P\subseteq X\), finitely many \(a_i\in X^*\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
f(x)=\max_i\bigl(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\bigr)\quad\text{for }x\in P,
\]
and \(f(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin P\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper extended-valued convex polyhedral functions in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order geometry of the domain-restricted max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)+\delta_P(x)
\]
for a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), then for \(x\in P\),
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x).
\]
Consequently, \(x\) minimizes \(f\) exactly when \(0\in\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral function's subdifferential is the active-slope hull plus the domain normal cone.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has the displayed proper domain-restricted max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}+N_P(x)\) for \(x\in P\).

notation.meaning: normal cone to P at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession and Attainment for Polyhedral Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic representation and bounded-minimization dichotomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f=\max_i(\langle a_i,\cdot\rangle+b_i)+\delta_P\),
\[
f^\infty(d)=
\begin{cases}
\max_i\langle a_i,d\rangle,&d\in\operatorname{rec}P,\\
+\infty,&d\notin\operatorname{rec}P.
\end{cases}
\]
Furthermore, \(\inf f>-infty\) exactly when \(f^\infty(d)\ge0\) for every \(d\), and every finite infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function is the maximum of recession slopes on the domain recession cone, and a polyhedral objective has no finite unattained infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a proper polyhedral convex function with the displayed representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf f> -\infty\iff f^\infty\ge0\), and finite infimum implies \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: recession cone of the effective domain

knowledge_statements.title: Recession and Attainment for Polyhedral Functions
Active-Slope Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite max-affine function is the convex hull of its active slopes, giving its differentiability test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
I(x):=\{i:f(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}.
\]
Then
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}.
\]
Consequently, \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) exactly when the active slopes have singleton convex hull; its gradient is then that unique slope.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has the accepted finite max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\), with differentiability exactly when this set is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order geometry of a finite max-affine representation.

notation.meaning: indices of affine pieces active at x

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex piecewise-linear function is the pointwise maximum of finitely many affine functions and is affine on each cell of a polyhedral subdivision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is convex piecewise-linear when there exist \(m\geq1\), slopes \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in X^*\), and offsets \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\bigl(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\bigr)
\]
for every \(x\in X\). Such a function is continuous and polyhedral, with a polyhedral subdivision of \(X\) on each cell of which \(f\) agrees with an affine function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is convex and finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)\) for finitely many affine functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Everywhere-finite convex piecewise-linear functions, also called finite polyhedral convex functions.

notation.meaning: slopes and offsets of the affine pieces

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Class Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation preserves polyhedral convexity, transforms a finite maximum of affine functions through a simplex linear program, and sends an affine function to a shifted singleton indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Polyhedrality is preserved by Fenchel conjugation: \(f\) is polyhedral if and only if \(f^*\) is polyhedral. In particular, if \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}\), then
\[
f^*(y)=\min\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i b_i:\lambda\in\Delta_m,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i=y\right\},
\]
where an infeasible minimum equals \(+\infty\). Thus a finite piecewise-affine convex function transforms into a polyhedral function whose effective domain is \(\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\). An affine function \(x\mapsto\langle a,x\rangle+b\) is the limiting case, with conjugate \(\delta_{\{a\}}-b\).
assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\) is polyhedral; for finite piecewise-affine \(f\), its conjugate is given by the displayed finite-dimensional linear program with objective \(-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i b_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional transitions among affine, piecewise-affine, and polyhedral convex functions.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate of a Domain-Restricted Max-Affine Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General extended-valued polyhedral transition formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Cx\le d\}\ne\varnothing\) and \(f(x)=\max_i(a_i^Tx+b_i)+\delta_P(x)\). Then
\[
f^*(y)=\min_{\substack{\lambda\ge0,\ \mathbf1^T\lambda=1,\ \mu\ge0\\C^T\mu=y-\sum_i\lambda_i a_i}}
\left(d^T\mu-\sum_i\lambda_i b_i\right),
\]
with value \(+\infty\) when infeasible. Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{dom}f^*=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i\}+C^T\mathbb R_+^p.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a domain-restricted max-affine function is an LP over piece weights and domain multipliers.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is the displayed finite affine maximum on \(P\), extended by positive infinity outside.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\) has the displayed multiplier-LP representation and \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i\}+C^T\mathbb R_+^p\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of a Domain-Restricted Max-Affine Function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subclass correspondence within proper closed polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper closed polyhedral convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\),
\[
\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb R^n
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{dom}f^*\text{ is a nonempty bounded polyhedron}.
\]
Consequently, conjugation exchanges finite convex piecewise-linear functions with proper closed polyhedral convex functions having bounded effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full primal domain is equivalent to bounded dual domain within the polyhedral class.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, and polyhedral on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb R^n\iff\operatorname{dom}f^*\) is nonempty and bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Full-Domain–Bounded-Domain Conjugacy Transition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite, singular, and partial convex quadratic classes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work on \(\mathbb R^n\). Let \(Q\) be symmetric, \(M\) an affine set, and \(\delta_M\) its indicator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex quadratic taxonomy, including singular Hessians and affine domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite quadratic convex function is \[q(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+\alpha,\qquad Q\succeq0.\] It is strictly convex when \(Q\succ0\), and degenerate when \(Q\succeq0\) is singular. A partial quadratic convex function is any proper function \[f(x)=q(x)+\delta_M(x),\] with \(q\) finite convex quadratic and \(M\) affine. After an invertible affine change of coordinates and addition of an affine function, every such function has an elementary diagonal form \[h(z)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i z_i^2,\qquad 0\le\lambda_i\le+\infty,\] where \(\lambda_i=+\infty\) imposes \(z_i=0\). Its conjugate has the same form with \(\lambda_i^*=1/\lambda_i\), using \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\). Hence partial quadratic convex functions form a conjugacy-stable class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex quadratic has a symmetric positive-semidefinite quadratic matrix; positive definiteness gives the nondegenerate strictly convex subclass, while a singular matrix gives flat directions. A partial quadratic adds an indicator of an affine set, allowing restricted domains. Up to invertible affine coordinates and affine terms, these functions are diagonal with coefficients ranging from zero to positive infinity. Conjugation reciprocates the coefficients, exchanging zero curvature with a domain constraint, and preserves the partial-quadratic class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Partial quadratic convex functions are exactly affine-coordinate transforms of elementary diagonal quadratics with \(0\le\lambda_i\le+\infty\), and conjugacy replaces each \(\lambda_i\) by \(1/\lambda_i\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle\) with \(Q\succeq0\), \[h^*(y)=\tfrac12\langle y,Q^\dagger y\rangle+\delta_{\operatorname{range}Q}(y).\]
When \(Q\succ0\), \[h^*(y)=\tfrac12\langle y,Q^{-1}y\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=I\), \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|_2^2\) is self-conjugate.
For \(Q=0\), the conjugate of the zero function is \(\delta_{\{0\}}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Singular primal curvature becomes a restricted dual effective domain.
Adding affine shifts preserves the partial-quadratic class and transforms the conjugate by the corresponding adjoint inverse and affine correction.
boundary_notes: Indefinite quadratic forms are not convex and are excluded.
The reciprocal-coefficient convention encodes both flat and constrained directions; it is not ordinary finite scalar arithmetic.

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose inverse of the positive-semidefinite matrix \(Q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite convex quadratic conjugates to another quadratic: the curvature matrix is inverted, the dual variable is shifted by the linear coefficient, and the constant changes sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}\), let
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle+c.
\]
Then \(f\) is proper, closed, and strictly convex, and its Fenchel conjugate is
\[
f^*(y)=\tfrac12\langle y-b,Q^{-1}(y-b)\rangle-c.
\]
Consequently, conjugation maps the positive-definite quadratic class onto itself, reverses the linear translation through \(y-b\), negates the additive constant, and replaces the curvature operator \(Q\) by \(Q^{-1}\).
assumptions_latex: The matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate is a quadratic with Hessian \(Q^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Everywhere-finite strictly convex quadratic functions in Euclidean space.

Let \(f(x)=	frac12\langle x,Qxangle+\langle b,xangle+c\), where \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n	imes n}\) is symmetric positive definite. Then \(
abla f(x)=Qx+b\) is bijective and \[
abla f^*(y)=Q^{-1}(y-b)=(
abla f)^{-1}(y).\] Consequently, \[y=
abla f(x)\iff x=
abla f^*(y)\iff f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,yangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite quadratic, the primal and conjugate gradients are mutually inverse affine maps, and corresponding points satisfy Fenchel equality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f^*=(\nabla f)^{-1}\), with Fenchel equality at corresponding primal–dual points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal Curvature Bounds Under Quadratic Conjugation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp spectral smoothness and strong-convexity constants for positive-definite quadratic conjugate pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=\lambda_{\min}(Q)\) and \(L=\lambda_{\max}(Q)\). Then \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, while \(f^*\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex with \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz gradient. These constants are sharp because \[\nabla^2f=Q,\qquad \nabla^2f^*=Q^{-1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic conjugation reciprocates the extreme curvature eigenvalues, exchanging the sharp smoothness and strong-convexity constants.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sharp curvature interval \([\mu,L]\) becomes \([1/L,1/\mu]\) under conjugation.

knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Curvature Bounds Under Quadratic Conjugation
Affine-Shifted Partially Quadratic Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centering and affinely shifting a partially quadratic function shifts both conjugate blocks; its subgradient relation separates into the general block and a linear quadratic-block equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb R^n=U\oplus V\) orthogonally, let \(g\in\Gamma_0(U)\), let \(Q:V\to V\) be self-adjoint positive definite, and write \(b=b_U+b_V\). If
\[
f(x)=g(P_Ux)+\frac12\langle P_Vx-v_0,Q(P_Vx-v_0)\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle+c,
\]
then
\[
f^*(y)=g^*(P_Uy-b_U)+\langle P_Vy-b_V,v_0\rangle+ rac12\langle P_Vy-b_V,Q^{-1}(P_Vy-b_V)\rangle-c.
\]
Moreover,
\[
y\in\partial f(x)
\iff
P_Uy-b_U\in\partial g(P_Ux),\quad P_Vy-b_V=Q(P_Vx-v_0).
\]
assumptions_latex: Q:V\to V\text{ is self-adjoint and positive definite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*(y)=g^*(P_Uy-b_U)+\langle P_Vy-b_V,v_0\rangle+\frac12\langle P_Vy-b_V,Q^{-1}(P_Vy-b_V)\rangle-c
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonally separable partially quadratic functions with a quadratic center, affine term, and constant.

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Quadratic Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partially quadratic function separates across orthogonal subspaces into a general convex term and a positive-definite quadratic. Its conjugate separates similarly and inverts only the quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A convex function belongs to the orthogonally separable partially quadratic class when it has the form
\[
f(x)=g(P_Ux)+\tfrac12\langle P_Vx,Q P_Vx\rangle.
\]
For \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), its conjugate separates as
\[
f^*(y)=g^*(P_Uy)+\tfrac12\langle P_Vy,Q^{-1}P_Vy\rangle.
\]
Thus conjugation preserves this class: the unrestricted convex component is conjugated within \(U\), while the quadratic curvature on \(V\) is inverted.
assumptions_latex: There is an orthogonal decomposition \(\mathbb{R}^n=U\oplus V\).
The function \(g:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
The operator \(Q:V\to V\) is self-adjoint and positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate separates into \(g^*\) on \(U\) and an inverse quadratic on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonally separable functions having one general convex block and one quadratic block.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Degeneracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular convex quadratic conjugates to a pseudoinverse quadratic restricted to the affine range of its Hessian; dual components along null directions make the conjugate infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conjugate of the possibly degenerate quadratic is
\[
f^*(y)=\tfrac12\langle y-b,Q^{\dagger}(y-b)\rangle-c+\delta_{b+\operatorname{ran}Q}(y).
\]
Hence loss of positive definiteness changes the conjugate from an everywhere-finite quadratic to an extended-valued quadratic supported on the affine subspace \(b+\operatorname{ran}Q\). Equivalently, if \(y-b\) has a nonzero component in \(\ker Q\), the supremum defining \(f^*(y)\) is \(+\infty\). The positive-definite regime is recovered precisely when \(\operatorname{ran}Q=\mathbb{R}^n\).
assumptions_latex: The matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conjugate is finite exactly on \(b+\operatorname{ran}Q\) and uses the Moore–Penrose inverse there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular positive-semidefinite quadratics and the domain restriction created by null directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-curvature direction makes the Fenchel supremum unbounded for every dual vector.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is symmetric and has at least one negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\equiv+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar entropy, exponential, and logarithmic conjugate pairs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work on \(\mathbb R\) with pairing \(\langle x,u\rangle=xu\). For an extended-real function \(f\), set \(f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}(ux-f(x))\), and use \(0\log 0=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records canonical scalar closed convex pairs. Finite-dimensional separable versions are obtained by summing the scalar functions coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the negative Boltzmann–Shannon entropy \(h:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(h(x)=x\log x-x\) for \(x>0\), \(h(0)=0\), and \(h(x)=+\infty\) for \(x<0\). Then \(h^*(u)=e^u\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R\), equivalently \((\exp)^*=h\). Define the negative Burg entropy \(b(x)=-\log x\) for \(x>0\) and \(b(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Its conjugate is \(b^*(u)=-\log(-u)-1\) for \(u<0\) and \(b^*(u)=+\infty\) for \(u\geq0\). These functions and identities constitute the scalar entropy–exponential–logarithmic conjugacy family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family consists of two standard scalar conjugate pairs. The extended negative Boltzmann–Shannon entropy, equal to x log x minus x on the positive half-line and zero at the origin, is conjugate to the exponential function. The negative logarithm on the positive half-line is conjugate to the function minus log of minus u minus one on the negative half-line, extended by positive infinity elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[h^*=\exp,\qquad (\exp)^*=h,\qquad b^*(u)=\begin{cases}-\log(-u)-1,&u<0,\\+\infty,&u\geq0.\end{cases}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[e^u=\sup_{x\geq0}\{ux-x\log x+x\}.\]
\[h(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\{xu-e^u\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(H(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N h(x_i)\) on \(\mathbb R^N\), separability gives \(H^*(u)=\sum_{i=1}^N e^{u_i}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domains are \(\operatorname{dom}h=[0,+\infty)\), \(\operatorname{dom}h^*=\mathbb R\), \(\operatorname{dom}b=(0,+\infty)\), and \(\operatorname{dom}b^*=(-\infty,0)\).
boundary_notes: Changing the normalization from \(x\log x-x\) to \(x\log x\) translates the exponential conjugate by a constant in its argument.
The logarithmic pair here is the negative Burg entropy, not the concave logarithm regarded without a sign change.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Boundary Subgradient
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized entropy has logarithmic derivative in the positive interior but no finite subgradient at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(h_a(x)=a(x\log x-x)+\delta_{[0,+\infty)}(x)\) with \(a>0\),
\[
\partial h_a(x)=\{a\log x\}\quad(x>0),
\qquad
\partial h_a(0)=\varnothing.
\]
Thus \(h_a\) is strictly convex and differentiable on \((0,+\infty)\), but it has no finite supporting slope at its finite boundary point \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial h_a(x)=\{a\log x\}\ (x>0),\qquad \partial h_a(0)=\varnothing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential behavior of scalar normalized entropy at the boundary of its nonnegative domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled normalized entropy on the nonnegative half-line conjugates to a scaled exponential that is finite and smooth on the entire dual line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the scaled normalized entropy by
\[
h_a(x)=
\begin{cases}
a(x\log x-x),&x\geq0,\\
+\infty,&x<0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(h_a\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and strictly convex on its effective domain, and
\[
h_a^*(y)=a\exp(y/a),\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Thus the entropy class is an extended-valued class enforcing nonnegativity, while its conjugate is finite and smooth on the entire dual line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized entropy function has conjugate \(h_a^*(y)=a\exp(y/a)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar normalized entropy extended to the nonnegative half-line.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Conjugate Boundary Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential conjugate is finite at zero, but its defining supremum is attained only for positive dual arguments, not at the boundary zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(e_a(y)=a\exp(y/a)\) with \(a>0\), the conjugate value at \(x=0\) is
\[
e_a^*(0)=0,
\]
but the supremum \(\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}\{-e_a(y)\}\) is not attained at any finite \(y\). For \(x>0\), the unique maximizer is \(y=a\log x\); for \(x<0\), the conjugate is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e_a^*(0)=0\text{ is unattained},\qquad \operatorname*{argmax}_{y}\{xy-e_a(y)\}=\{a\log x\}\text{ for }x>0
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment boundary for the conjugate of a scaled scalar exponential.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled exponential conjugates to normalized entropy with a nonnegative-domain constraint; their interior gradients are inverse through the exponential and logarithm maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e_a(y)=a\exp(y/a)\) for \(y\in\mathbb{R}\). Its Fenchel conjugate is
\[
e_a^*(x)=
\begin{cases}
a(x\log x-x),&x\geq0,\\
+\infty,&x<0,
\end{cases}
\]
with \(0\log0=0\). Hence every member of this scaled exponential class is proper, closed, strictly convex, and everywhere finite, whereas its conjugate imposes the nonnegative-domain constraint. The gradient relation \(x=\exp(y/a)\) identifies the mutually inverse interior gradient coordinates \(y=a\log x\) for \(x>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled exponential \(e_a(y)=a\exp(y/a)\) has conjugate equal to normalized entropy on \([0,+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled scalar exponentials and their extended-valued conjugates.
