knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scaled negative logarithm on the positive half-line conjugates to a shifted negative logarithm on the negative half-line, with primal and dual variables related reciprocally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
\ell_a(x)=
\begin{cases}
-a\log x,&x>0,\\
+\infty,&x\leq0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then its Fenchel conjugate is
\[
\ell_a^*(y)=
\begin{cases}
a\bigl(\log a-1-\log(-y)\bigr),&y<0,\\
+\infty,&y\geq0.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus conjugation maps the positive-domain negative-logarithm class to a logarithmic class on the negative dual half-line. On the interiors of their domains, the primal and dual variables satisfy \(y=-a/x\), expressing the reciprocal gradient correspondence characteristic of logarithmic barriers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The negative-logarithm barrier conjugates to a shifted negative logarithm supported on the negative dual half-line.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar negative-logarithm barriers on the positive half-line.

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy–Exponential Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized entropy and scaled exponential are mutual Fenchel conjugates. Their gradient maps, logarithm and exponential, are inverse and characterize equality in the Fenchel–Young inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
h_a(x)=a(x\log x-x)+\delta_{[0,+\infty)}(x)
\quad\text{and}\quad
e_a(y)=a\exp(y/a),
\]
one has the reciprocal conjugacy relations
\[
h_a^*=e_a\qquad\text{and}\qquad e_a^*=h_a.
\]
For \(x>0\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}\), Fenchel–Young equality is equivalent to
\[
y=a\log x\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad x=\exp(y/a),
\]
and then \(h_a(x)+e_a(y)=xy\). Coordinatewise summation gives the corresponding separable entropy–exponential duality on finite-dimensional product spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The entropy and exponential functions form a Fenchel-conjugate pair, and their interior gradients are inverse.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar Fenchel duality between normalized entropy and scaled exponential.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space with norm \(\|\cdot\|\), let \(q(x)=\|x\|^2/2\), and define \(d_C(u)=\inf_{x\in C}\|u-x\|\) for each nonempty \(C\subset\mathcal H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The radial formula uses Hilbert self-duality and an even scalar profile. The distance formula permits a nonconvex set \(C\), since the conjugate is defined for arbitrary proper extended-real functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The distance–radial conjugacy family consists of the following templates. First, for an even proper function \(\phi:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the radial lifting \(R_\phi(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\) has conjugate \(R_\phi^*(u)=\phi^*(\|u\|)\). Second, for a nonempty set \(C\subset\mathcal H\), define \(F_C=\iota_C+q\), where \(\iota_C\) is zero on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) off \(C\). Its conjugate is the distance-generated function \(F_C^*(u)=(\|u\|^2-d_C(u)^2)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An even scalar profile can be lifted to a radial function by composing it with the Hilbert norm, and conjugation acts by conjugating the scalar profile. A second canonical class starts from the squared norm restricted to a nonempty set; its conjugate is one half of the squared norm minus the squared distance to that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bigl(\phi\circ\|\cdot\|\bigr)^*=\phi^*\circ\|\cdot\|,\qquad \left(\iota_C+\frac12\|\cdot\|^2\right)^*=\frac12\left(\|\cdot\|^2-d_C^2\right).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\phi^*(\|u\|)=\sup_{\rho\geq0}\{\rho\|u\|-\phi(\rho)\}\quad\text{when \(\phi\) is even}.\]
\[F_C^*(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\left\{\langle x,u\rangle-\frac12\|x\|^2\right\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathcal H\), then \(d_C=0\) and \(q^*=q\).
If \(\phi(t)=|t|\), then \(R_\phi(x)=\|x\|\) and \(R_\phi^*=\iota_{B(0,1)}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The function \(u\mapsto\|u\|^2-d_C(u)^2\) is convex even when \(C\) is not convex.
boundary_notes: For a general Banach norm, the radial conjugate is naturally expressed using the dual norm rather than the same norm.
The distance-generated identity concerns \(\iota_C+q\), not the conjugate of \(d_C\) itself.

knowledge_statements.title: Hölder-Power Distance Conjugates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder power of distance conjugates to the support function of the set plus the corresponding dual Hölder power.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(1<p<\infty\), and set \(q=p/(p-1)\). For \(F_p(x)=d_C(x)^p/p\),
\[
F_p=\delta_C\square \frac1p\|\cdot\|^p,
\qquad
F_p^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)+\frac1q\|y\|^q.
\]
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\frac1p d_C^p\right)^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)+\frac1q\|y\|^q
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive powers greater than one of Euclidean distance to a nonempty closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a closed convex set conjugates to its support function with a unit-ball constraint; half squared distance replaces that constraint by a quadratic penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d_C(x)=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|\), the conjugacy formulas are
\[
d_C^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)+\delta_B(y)
\]
and
\[
\left(\tfrac12 d_C^2\right)^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)+\tfrac12\|y\|^2.
\]
Thus the unsquared distance class produces a hard dual-norm constraint, while the half squared-distance class produces a quadratic dual penalty. Both formulas retain the geometry of \(C\) solely through its support function. In particular, translations of \(C\) contribute the corresponding linear term to each conjugate.
assumptions_latex: The set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Distance and support are computed using the Euclidean norm and pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The distance and squared-distance conjugates equal the support function plus, respectively, a unit-ball indicator or a dual quadratic.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean distance and half squared distance to a closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection and Differential Structure of Convex Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric and differential properties for distance to a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Each \(x\) has a unique projection \(P_Cx\), characterized by
\[
\langle x-P_Cx,z-P_Cx\rangle\le0\quad(z\in C).
\]
The function \(d_C\) is convex and \(1\)-Lipschitz, with
\[
\partial d_C(x)=
\begin{cases}
\{(x-P_Cx)/d_C(x)\},&x\notin C,\\
N_C(x)\cap B,&x\in C.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover, \(\tfrac12d_C^2\) is continuously differentiable and
\[
\nabla(\tfrac12d_C^2)(x)=x-P_Cx,
\]
with a \(1\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection is unique; distance is convex and Lipschitz, while half squared distance is smooth with projection-residual gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection characterization, distance-subdifferential formulas, and \(\nabla(\tfrac12d_C^2)=I-P_C\) hold.

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection of x onto C

knowledge_statements.title: Projection and Differential Structure of Convex Distance
Convex Radial Profile Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean radial function is closed proper convex exactly when its unique radius profile is closed proper convex and nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge1\), a radial function \(f(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex if and only if \(\phi:[0,+\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and nondecreasing. Its profile is unique and satisfies \(\phi(r)=f(re)\) for every unit vector \(e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\iff \phi\in\Gamma_0([0,+\infty))\text{ and }\phi\text{ is nondecreasing}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of proper lower-semicontinuous convex Euclidean radial functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugation preserves Euclidean radial convexity: conjugating a function of the norm reduces exactly to taking the one-sided scalar conjugate of its radial profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f(x)=\phi(\|x\|)\) and the one-sided scalar conjugate
\[
\phi_+^*(s)=\sup_{r\geq0}\{rs-\phi(r)\},\qquad s\geq0.
\]
Then \(f\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and radial, and its Fenchel conjugate satisfies
\[
f^*(y)=\phi_+^*(\|y\|).
\]
Hence Euclidean Fenchel conjugation preserves the radial class and reduces the multidimensional transform to a scalar transform of the radius profile. knowledge_statements.title: Radial Distance Profiles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a centered ball is a radial hinge profile. In the conjugate, the ball radius becomes a norm coefficient and squaring replaces the dual ball constraint by a quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Distance to the centered ball has the radial profile
\[

\[
d_{RB}^*(y)=R\|y\|+\delta_B(y),
\qquad
\left(\tfrac12d_{RB}^2\right)^*(y)=R\|y\|+\tfrac12\|y\|^2.
\]
These formulas exhibit the radial distance transition explicitly: the primal threshold radius becomes a dual norm coefficient, while the unsquared or squared outer profile becomes, respectively, a unit-ball constraint or a quadratic penalty.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The biconjugation–convexification correspondence identifies \(f^{**}\) with the closed lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(f\): \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}f\). Equivalently, \(f^{**}\) is the pointwise greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function \(g\) satisfying \(g\leq f\), and its epigraph is the closed convex hull of the original epigraph, \(\operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper finite-dimensional function admitting an affine lower bound, taking two Fenchel conjugates is exactly closed convexification. The biconjugate is the largest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant of the original function, and its epigraph is the closed convex hull of the original epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ is lower-semicontinuous and convex}\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^{**}(x)=\sup\{\langle u,x\rangle-\beta:\langle u,y\rangle-\beta\leq f(y)\ \forall y\}.\]
\[f=f^{**}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\text{ is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex but not lower-semicontinuous, then \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\).
If \(f\) is already proper, closed, and convex, biconjugation leaves it unchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: The universal inequality \(f^{**}\leq f\) holds pointwise.
Conjugation cannot distinguish \(f\) from its closed convex envelope because \(f^*=(f^{**})^*\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space. Extended-real functions take values in \((-\infty,+\infty]\), and proper means nowhere \(-\infty\), not identically \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry defines the Hilbert-space Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation operator and the class of its proper fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), its Fenchel conjugate and biconjugate are \(f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal H}(\langle x,u\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f^{**}(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathcal H}(\langle x,u\rangle-f^*(u))\). Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation is the operation \(f\mapsto f^{**}\). Its proper fixed-point class is exactly \(\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions: for proper \(f\), \(f=f^{**}\) if and only if \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation applies the Fenchel conjugate twice. On a real Hilbert space, the proper functions fixed by this operation are exactly the lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^{**}(x)=\sup_{u\in\mathcal H}\left\{\langle x,u\rangle-\sup_{y\in\mathcal H}(\langle y,u\rangle-f(y))\right\},\qquad f=f^{**}\iff f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper \(f\), \(f=f^{**}\) is equivalent to \(\operatorname{epi}f\) being a nonempty closed convex subset of \(\mathcal H\times\mathbb R\).
special_cases_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), \(\iota_C^{**}=\iota_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every proper \(f\), \(f^{**}\leq f\).
If \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), then \(f^*\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\).
boundary_notes: On a nonreflexive Banach space, the second conjugate naturally lives on the bidual unless it is explicitly restricted back to the canonical image of the primal space.
The fixed-point characterization requires properness; identically infinite functions require separate conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Biconjugation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a proper function equals its biconjugate exactly when it is lower-semicontinuous and convex; otherwise the proper biconjugate is its closed convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\},
\qquad
f^{**}(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f^*(y)\}.
\]
The finite-dimensional Fenchel–Moreau theorem states that
\[
f=f^{**}
\]
if and only if \(f\) is lower-semicontinuous and convex. More generally, whenever the closed convex envelope is proper,
\[
f^{**}=\operatorname{clconv}f,
\]
meaning that \(f^{**}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\). Thus biconjugation is precisely the finite-dimensional closed-convexification operation.
assumptions_latex: The space is finite-dimensional, identified with \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and its usual dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \(f=f^{**}\) exactly when \(f\) is lower-semicontinuous and convex; generally \(f^{**}\) is its closed convex envelope when proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Moreau biconjugation on finite-dimensional real vector spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Then \(f^{**}\) is proper if and only if \(f\) admits an affine minorant, equivalently if and only if \(f^*(y)<+\infty\) for some \(y\in\mathbb R^n\). If no affine minorant exists, then \(f^*\equiv+\infty\) and \(f^{**}\equiv-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper finite-dimensional function has a proper biconjugate exactly when it has an affine lower bound; otherwise its biconjugate is identically minus infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Biconjugation relative to a separating dual pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a real separating dual pair, so each nonzero element of either space is detected by an element of the other. Equip \(X\) with a Hausdorff locally convex topology \(\tau\) whose continuous dual is \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition distinguishes biconjugates by the chosen dual pair and topology. It does not identify \(X\) with \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define the dual-pair conjugates by \(f^Y(y)=\sup_{x\in X}(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f^{YY}(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}(\langle x,y\rangle-f^Y(y))\). The \((X,Y)\)-biconjugation regime is the operator \(f\mapsto f^{YY}\) together with the closure topology \(\sigma(X,Y)\), or more generally any compatible locally convex topology \(\tau\). For a proper function, its fixed-point condition is \(f=f^{YY}\), equivalently that \(f\) is convex and lower-semicontinuous for the compatible topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally convex biconjugate depends on a chosen separating dual pair. The first conjugate is defined on the paired dual space and the second returns to the primal space. Proper fixed points are the convex functions closed for the topology compatible with that dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^{YY}(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}\left\{\langle x,y\rangle-\sup_{z\in X}(\langle z,y\rangle-f(z))\right\},\qquad f=f^{YY}\iff f\text{ is proper, convex, and \(\tau\)-lower-semicontinuous}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The fixed-point condition is equivalent to \(\operatorname{epi}f\) being convex and closed in \((X,\tau)\times\mathbb R\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb R^n\) recovers Euclidean biconjugation.
For a Banach space \(X\), the canonical dual pair is \((X,X^*)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing the selected dual space can change both the weak topology and the resulting biconjugate.
boundary_notes: Separation of points is essential; otherwise all biconjugates are constant on cosets of the common annihilator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every pairing-based biconjugate is constant on cosets of the annihilator: for all \(x\in X\) and \(n\in N\), \[f^{**}(x+n)=f^{**}(x).\] Consequently, if \(N\ne\{0\}\), the proper convex function \(\delta_{\{0\}}\) cannot equal its biconjugate, since its values at \(0\) and a nonzero \(n\in N\) differ whereas the biconjugate cannot distinguish those points. knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without a Separating Pairing
Mackey–Arens Compatibility Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally convex topology is compatible with a separated dual pair exactly when it lies between the weak and Mackey topologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Hausdorff locally convex topology \(\tau\) on \(X\) is compatible with the separated dual pair \((X,Y)\) precisely when its continuous dual is \(Y\). The Mackey–Arens theorem gives the equivalent characterization \[(X,\tau)'=Y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\sigma(X,Y)\subseteq\tau\subseteq\tau(X,Y),\] where \(\tau(X,Y)\) is the topology of uniform convergence on absolutely convex \(\sigma(Y,X)\)-compact subsets of \(Y\). Thus \(\sigma(X,Y)\) and \(\tau(X,Y)\) are respectively the coarsest and finest compatible locally convex topologies.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Banach dual and Hilbert self-dual biconjugation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Banach space with continuous dual \(X^*\), bidual \(X^{**}\), and canonical embedding \(J:X\to X^{**}\). A Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\) is identified with its continuous dual through the Riesz map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition explicitly separates the Banach-space bidual transform from the Hilbert-space self-dual specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \(f^*:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in X}(\langle x^*,x\rangle-f(x))\). Its full Banach biconjugate is \(f^{**}:X^{**}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f^{**}(x^{**})=\sup_{x^*\in X^*}(\langle x^{**},x^*\rangle-f^*(x^*))\); the primal biconjugate is \(f^{**}\circ J\). In a Hilbert space, the Riesz identification turns both conjugates into functions on \(\mathcal H\), yielding \(f^{**}(x)=\sup_u(\langle x,u\rangle-f^*(u))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Banach space the first conjugate lives on the continuous dual and the full second conjugate lives on the bidual; evaluation on the canonical image returns a primal function. In a Hilbert space, Riesz self-duality lets all three functions be represented on the same space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^*(x^*)=\sup_{x\in X}(\langle x^*,x\rangle-f(x)),\qquad f^{**}(x^{**})=\sup_{x^*\in X^*}(\langle x^{**},x^*\rangle-f^*(x^*)),\qquad f^{**}_{X}=f^{**}\circ J.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(X\) is reflexive, \(J(X)=X^{**}\), so the full and primal biconjugation regimes can be identified.
For Hilbert \(\mathcal H\), the Riesz map replaces \(X^*\) and \(X^{**}\) by copies of \(\mathcal H\).
special_cases_latex: Every finite-dimensional Banach space is reflexive, although the coordinate formula still depends on the chosen primal-dual pairing.
immediate_consequences_latex: For proper norm-lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\), the primal restriction satisfies \(f=f^{**}\circ J\).
boundary_notes: In a nonreflexive Banach space, values of the full biconjugate outside \(J(X)\) are not values of the original primal function.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real Banach space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Then \(f^{**}\) is proper if and only if \(f\) admits a norm-continuous affine minorant, equivalently if and only if \(f^*(x^*)<+\infty\) for some \(x^*\in X^*\). If no such minorant exists, then \(f^*\equiv+\infty\) and \(f^{**}\equiv-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper Banach-space function has a proper biconjugate exactly when it has a continuous affine lower bound; otherwise its biconjugate is identically minus infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex envelope of \(f\) is \(\operatorname{co}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ convex}\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope is the greatest convex minorant, while the closed convex envelope is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant. The latter equals the biconjugate and can lie strictly below the convex envelope when the convex envelope is not closed.

immediate_consequences_latex: The two possible defects are the nonconvexity gap \(f-\operatorname{co}f\) and the nonclosedness gap \(\operatorname{co}f-\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Envelopes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope is the greatest convex minorant of a function, equivalently the infimum of its values averaged over finite convex decompositions of each point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex envelope of \(f\) is the pointwise greatest convex function below \(f\). knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Convexification Operator Laws
Pointwise Lower-Limit Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous closure is the neighborhood lower limit; equivalently it is obtained from convergent nets, or from sequences in first-countable spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in X\),
\[
(\operatorname{cl}g)(x)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\inf_{z\in U}g(z)
=\inf_{z_\alpha\to x}\liminf_\alpha g(z_\alpha),
\]
where the second infimum ranges over all convergent nets. If \(X\) is first countable, nets may be replaced by sequences:
\[
(\operatorname{cl}g)(x)=\inf_{z_n\to x}\liminf_{n\to\infty}g(z_n).
\]
assumptions_latex: The displayed lower-semicontinuous regularization is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{cl}g)(x)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\inf_{z\in U}g(z)=\inf_{z_\alpha\to x}\liminf_\alpha g(z_\alpha)\).

Moreover, \(\operatorname{cl}g=g\) exactly when \(g\) is lower semicontinuous.

\(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex, and its lower-semicontinuous minorant is proper.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraphical convexification of \(f\) is the lower-bound function \(\ell_{\operatorname{co}E}\); equivalently it is \(\operatorname{co}f\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphical convexification forms a convex hull of the epigraph and reads off its lower boundary. knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{co}f=\ell_{\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{co}}f=\ell_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f)},\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\ell_C(x)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb R:(x,r)\in C\}.\]
The epigraphical hull of \(C\) is the smallest epigraph containing \(C\), namely \(\operatorname{epi}\ell_C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) already has closed vertical bottoms, it equals \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Epigraphical convexification converts a geometric hull operation in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) into a pointwise envelope operation on functions.
boundary_notes: In general \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\neq\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)\); bottom closure is the missing operation.
Topological closure and vertical-bottom closure are conceptually distinct.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Attainment Criterion for Epigraph-Hull Equality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph hull equals the convex-envelope epigraph exactly when every finite envelope value has an attaining finite mixture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:V\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have nonempty domain. Then \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\) if and only if, for every \(x\) with \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)<+\infty\), the finite-mixture infimum defining \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)\) is attained. Equivalently, every lower-boundary point \((x,(\operatorname{co}f)(x))\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\) if and only if every finite convex-envelope value is attained by a finite mixture.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion distinguishing the algebraic epigraph hull from the full convex-envelope epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Missing Lower-Boundary Point Under Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this function, the convex-envelope value at the origin is zero but no finite mixture attains it, so the epigraph hull omits the lower-boundary point while containing every point strictly above it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(f(-1)=0\), \(f(x)=x\) for \(x>0\), and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then \((\operatorname{co}f)(0)=0\), but no finite convex decomposition of \(0\) attains weighted value \(0\). Consequently \((0,0)\in\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\setminus\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), whereas \((0,r)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) for every \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\notin\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) although \((0,0)\in\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional example witnessing strict inclusion between the algebraic epigraph hull and the convex-envelope epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Hulls of Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of an epigraph consists of finite mixtures of epigraph points; it matches the convex-envelope epigraph above the boundary, while unattained boundary points may be missing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \((x,r)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) exactly when there are finitely many \(x_i\in V\), \(r_i\geq f(x_i)\), and \(\lambda_i\geq0\) such that \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), \(x=\sum_i\lambda_i x_i\), and \(r=\sum_i\lambda_i r_i\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\), while every \((x,r)\) with \(r>(\operatorname{co}f)(x)\) lies in \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\). Boundary equality may fail when the defining infimum is unattained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\) and the two sets have identical strict upper sections.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic epigraph convexification, including possible nonattainment at the lower boundary.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of equality between the algebraic convex hull of an epigraph and the epigraph of its convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be given by \(f(1/n)=f(-1/n)=1/n\) for \(n\in\mathbb N\), and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Then \((\operatorname{co}f)(0)=0\), every \((0,1/n)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), but \((0,0)\notin\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\). Hence \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subsetneq\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{co}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete symmetric function attains convex-envelope value zero at the origin only as a limiting mixture, so its epigraph hull omits the lower boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{co}f)(0)=0\) and \((0,0)\notin\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Function generated by the convex hull of an epigraph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and bounded below by an affine function, and let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry concerns the nonclosed convex hull \(\operatorname{co}E\) and the lower boundary it induces, rather than its topological closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex-hull-of-epigraph function is \(h(x)=\inf\{r:(x,r)\in\operatorname{co}E\}\). It is convex and equals the convex envelope \(\operatorname{co}f\). Its epigraph is the epigraphical hull of \(\operatorname{co}E\), obtained by adding the omitted vertical bottom points when the infimum is not attained. Equivalently, \(h\) is the greatest convex function satisfying \(h\leq f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take all finite convex combinations of points in the epigraph and then read the lowest attainable height over each base point. The resulting lower-bound function is the convex envelope. Its epigraph can be slightly larger than the raw convex hull because an unattained lowest height must be inserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[h=\ell_{\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\operatorname{co}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ convex}\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[h(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(x_i):k\geq1,\ \lambda\in\Delta_k,\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x\right\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If the infimum defining \(h(x)\) is attained for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\), then \(\operatorname{co}E\) has its vertical bottoms and equals \(\operatorname{epi}h\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The projection of \(\operatorname{co}E\) onto \(\mathbb R^n\) is \(\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), which is the effective-domain hull of \(h\).
boundary_notes: The raw set \(\operatorname{co}E\) need not be closed and need not itself be an epigraph.
Replacing \(\operatorname{co}E\) by its closed convex hull produces the closed convex envelope instead.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without a Continuous Affine Minorant
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minus x squared, the conjugate is everywhere infinite, the biconjugate is minus infinity, and the closed convex hull of the epigraph is the whole plane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x)=-x^2\). Then \(f\) is proper but has no affine minorant, \(f^*(u)=+\infty\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R\), and hence \(f^{**}\equiv-\infty\). Moreover, \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\mathbb R^2\). Thus, without an affine minorant, the closed convex hull need not be the epigraph of a proper extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\equiv+\infty\), \(f^{**}\equiv-\infty\), and \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of proper epigraphical biconjugation when the affine-minorant hypothesis is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Epigraph Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the convex hull of a function's epigraph produces the epigraph of its closed convex envelope, equivalently its continuous-dual biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Taking closure in \(X\times\mathbb R\) removes finite-mixture nonattainment and yields an epigraph: \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f).\] Since the closed convex envelope equals the continuous-dual biconjugate, this is equivalently \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\operatorname{epi}(f^{**}).\] Thus closed epigraphical convexification and Fenchel biconjugation describe the same function under the stated properness and affine-minorant assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and has a continuous affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(f^{**})=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-topology closure supplies both convexification and lower-semicontinuous boundary completion.

notation.meaning: Closure in the product topology on X times the reals
Fenchel biconjugate against the continuous dual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed convex epigraph hull and its lower-bound function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and admit an affine minorant. Set \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(K=\overline{\operatorname{co}}E\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure is Euclidean closure in the product space. The affine-minorant condition prevents vertical lines extending to \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed epigraph hull of \(f\) is \(K=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f)\). It is an upward-closed closed convex set and therefore the epigraph of the function \(h(x)=\inf\{r:(x,r)\in K\}\). This function is closed and convex, equals \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\), and equals \(f^{**}\). Thus \(K=\operatorname{epi}h=\operatorname{epi}f^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull of an epigraph remains upward closed and has closed vertical bottoms, so it is itself an epigraph. Its lower-bound function is the closed convex envelope and the Fenchel biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K=\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{co}}f)=\operatorname{epi}f^{**},\qquad f^{**}(x)=\inf\{r:(x,r)\in K\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^{**}=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ closed and convex}\}.\]
\[f^{**}(x)=\sup\{\langle u,x\rangle-\beta:\langle u,\cdot\rangle-\beta\leq f\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is already closed and convex, then \(K=\operatorname{epi}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The hull operation is idempotent: \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}K=K\), corresponding to \((f^{**})^{**}=f^{**}\).
boundary_notes: For functions without an affine lower bound, the closed convex hull can contain downward vertical lines and may fail to encode a proper extended-real function.
The closure is taken after convexification; the result nevertheless equals the closure of the convex envelope under the stated hypotheses.

notation.meaning: closed convex hull of the original epigraph

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and admit an affine minorant. Let \(\Delta_k=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^k:\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Carathéodory is applied to the epigraph in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), giving the direct bound \(n+2\) on mixture size. A sharper \(n+1\) bound for the function-value formula requires an additional refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Carathéodory finite-mixture convexification of \(f\) is \(M_f(x)=\inf\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(x_i):1\leq k\leq n+2,\ \lambda\in\Delta_k,\ x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x\}\). It equals \(\operatorname{co}f(x)\). Geometrically, every point of \(\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) is a convex combination of at most \(n+2\) epigraph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-dimensional convexification can be computed using only finite mixtures. Applying Carathéodory’s theorem in the epigraph space shows that no more than n plus two epigraph points are needed, and the resulting infimum is the convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{co}f(x)=M_f(x)=\inf_{\substack{1\leq k\leq n+2,\ \lambda\in\Delta_k,\ x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f\\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x}}\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(x_i).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For each \((x,r)\in\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), there exist \(k\leq n+2\), \((x_i,r_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f\), and \(\lambda\in\Delta_k\) such that \((x,r)=\sum_i\lambda_i(x_i,r_i)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the direct epigraph bound is three mixture points.
When the infimum is attained at an exposed lower-boundary point, redundant mixture points may often be removed.
immediate_consequences_latex: The algebraic convex envelope in finite dimensions requires no infinite probability measure or infinite convex combination.
boundary_notes: The formula defines \(+\infty\) when \(x\notin\operatorname{co}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
Carathéodory alone yields \(n+2\) in the \((n+1)\)-dimensional epigraph; the cited source notes a refinement to \(n+1\) for the envelope formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Mixture Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex-envelope value at a point is the infimum of weighted function values over all finite convex decompositions of that point; attainment is not automatic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), the convex envelope satisfies \[(\operatorname{co}f)(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i):m\in\mathbb N,\ x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i=x\right\}.\] Outside \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), its value is \(+\infty\). The infimum ranges over finite mixtures but need not be attained; dimension-dependent support reduction requires additional finite-dimensional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i):m<\infty,\ \sum_i\lambda_i x_i=x,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-mixture formula without a dimension-dependent support bound or attainment claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Mixture Infimum Need Not Be Attained
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional example showing that the algebraic finite-mixture formula can have a finite unattained infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[f(-1)=1,\qquad f(t)=0\ \text{for }t>0,\qquad f(t)=+\infty\ \text{otherwise}.\] Then \((\operatorname{co}f)(0)=0\), but no finite feasible mixture at zero has value zero: every such mixture assigns positive weight to \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper one-dimensional function can have convex-envelope value zero at a point even though every finite mixture representing that point has strictly positive value.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is defined by the displayed formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{co}f)(0)=0\), but the finite-mixture infimum at \(0\) is not attained.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Mixture Infimum Need Not Be Attained
Intrinsic-Dimension Carathéodory Bounds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support bounds sharpen to one plus the relevant affine dimension: d+1 epigraph points and q+1 locations for an attained envelope value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\), and put \(d=\dim\operatorname{aff}(E)\). Every point of \(\operatorname{conv}E\) is a convex combination of at most \(d+1\) points of \(E\). If \(q=\dim\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and a finite value \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)\) is attained by a finite mixture, then an attaining mixture exists with at most \(q+1\) positive weights.
assumptions_latex: Attainment by a finite mixture is assumed for the convex-envelope assertion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \((x,t)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) has support at most \(d+1\), and every attained finite envelope value has location support at most \(q+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-dimension refinement of the epigraph and attained-value support bounds.

notation.meaning: Affine dimension of the effective domain

knowledge_statements.title: Carathéodory Support Bounds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point in the convex hull of the epigraph uses at most n+2 epigraph points, while an attained finite convex-envelope value has an optimal mixture supported on at most n+1 locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \((x,t)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), there exist an integer \(m\le n+2\), weights \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\), and points \((x_i,t_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) such that \((x,t)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i(x_i,t_i)\). Moreover, let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and suppose there exist an integer \(k\ge1\), weights \(\mu_j\ge0\), and points \(z_j\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(\sum_{j=1}^k\mu_j=1\), \(\sum_{j=1}^k\mu_jz_j=x\), and \((\operatorname{co}f)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^k\mu_jf(z_j)\). Then there is such an optimal representation with at most \(n+1\) positive weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point of \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) has a representation using at most \(n+2\) epigraph points, and every attained finite convex-envelope value has an optimal mixture using at most \(n+1\) locations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Carathéodory bounds for epigraphs and attained convex-envelope mixtures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharpness of the Intrinsic Epigraph Support Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex family showing that the epigraph-specific bound \(r+1\) cannot generally be reduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_0,\ldots,v_r\) be affinely independent and define \(f(v_i)=0\) and \(f(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. If \(x\) lies in the relative interior of \(\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,\ldots,v_r\}\), then \((x,0)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\), and every epigraph mixture representing \((x,0)\) uses all \(r+1\) locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex-domain indicator requires r+1 epigraph locations at every relative-interior point, so the intrinsic bound is sharp.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Every representation of }(x,0)\text{ uses at least }r+1\text{ epigraph points}.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Intrinsic Epigraph Support Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp support bound exploiting vertical upward closure of an epigraph, rather than applying ordinary Carathéodory in one higher dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=\dim\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Every \((x,t)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) admits a representation \[(x,t)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i(x_i,t_i),\qquad (x_i,t_i)\in\operatorname{epi}f,\] with \(m\le r+1\). In particular, when \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), at most \(n+1\) epigraph points suffice. The seed's general ambient Carathéodory bound \(n+2\) remains valid but is not sharp for upward-closed epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertical upward closure sharpens the epigraph-hull support bound to one plus the affine dimension of the effective domain, hence at most n+1 in R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,t)\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f)\Longrightarrow (x,t)\text{ has an epigraph mixture with }m\le r+1\le n+1.\)

notation.meaning: Affine dimension of the effective domain of f

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-Specific Carathéodory Refinement
Minimal Mixture Supports
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support-minimal mixture attaining the convex envelope uses affinely independent locations, so it has no more than n+1 positive weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider an optimal mixture
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i,\qquad (\operatorname{co}f)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i),\qquad \lambda_i>0,
\]
whose number of positive weights is minimal among all optimal mixtures at \(x\). Then \(\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\) is affinely independent. Consequently \(m\le n+1\). Equivalently, if the active locations are affinely dependent, the mixture is not support-minimal: an optimal feasible perturbation of its weights can eliminate at least one active index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every support-minimal optimal mixture has affinely independent locations and therefore at most \(n+1\) positive weights.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support minimality among mixtures attaining one convex-envelope value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Independence Is Necessary but Not Sufficient for Support Minimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits the affine-independence test to a necessary condition for global support minimality among all optimal mixtures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Affine independence of an optimal mixture's active locations does not by itself imply support minimality. For example, let \(f(-1)=f(0)=f(1)=0\) and \(f=+\infty\) elsewhere. At \(x=0\), the mixture \(0=\tfrac12(-1)+\tfrac12(1)\) is optimal and has affinely independent active locations, but the one-point mixture supported at \(0\) is also optimal. Hence the two-point mixture is not support-minimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine independence prevents reduction within a fixed active set but does not exclude a different optimal mixture with smaller support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{-1,1\}\text{ is affinely independent, but its optimal two-point mixture is not support-minimal}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure set for exact recovery by biconjugation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and admit an affine minorant, so \(f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\leq f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary is defined pointwise in finite dimensions and separates failure caused by nonconvexity from failure caused solely by lack of lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The biconjugation failure boundary of \(f\) is \(\mathcal B(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f^{**}(x)<f(x)\}\), where the extended-real order is used. With \(c=\operatorname{co}f\), it decomposes into the nonconvexity boundary \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cvx}}(f)=\{x:c(x)<f(x)\}\) and the closure boundary \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)=\{x:f^{**}(x)<c(x)\}\). Hence \(\mathcal B(f)=\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cvx}}(f)\cup\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)\), and exact biconjugate recovery is equivalent to \(\mathcal B(f)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The failure boundary is the set where the biconjugate lies strictly below the original function. It is the union of points lost during convexification and points lost during lower-semicontinuous closure. It is empty exactly for proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal B(f)=\{f^{**}<f\}=\{\operatorname{co}f<f\}\cup\{f^{**}<\operatorname{co}f\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\mathcal B(f)=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=f^{**}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\text{ is closed and convex}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cvx}}(f)=\varnothing\).
If \(f\) is lower-semicontinuous but nonconvex, failure may remain entirely in \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{cvx}}(f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A point outside \(\mathcal B(f)\) is a contact point between \(f\) and its greatest closed convex minorant.
boundary_notes: This definition concerns strict pointwise loss, not numerical instability or dual nonattainment.
If the affine-minorant condition fails, the biconjugate may be improper and the decomposition needs extended-value conventions beyond this scope.

notation.meaning: pointwise failure set of exact biconjugate recovery

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Biconjugate Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function equal to zero at minus one and one, and one elsewhere, has zero biconjugate everywhere and a strict gap at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(-1)=f(1)=0\) and \(f(x)=1\) for \(x\notin\{-1,1\}\). Every convex minorant of \(f\) that is finite on \(\mathbb{R}\) and bounded above by \(1\) is constant, and the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant is the zero function. Hence \(f^{**}(x)=0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), while \(f(0)=1\). In particular, \(f^{**}(0)<f(0)\), exhibiting the loss incurred by biconjugate convexification.
assumptions_latex: Conjugacy uses the standard pairing on \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proper nonconvex function can satisfy \(f^{**}(x)<f(x)\), with the biconjugate equal to its lower-semicontinuous convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional gap caused solely by nonconvexity.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.6 A Glimpse of Biconjugate Calculus p. 71

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, admit an affine minorant, and let \(f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}f\). Define the finite comparison domain \(D_f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty,\ f^{**}(x)>-\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The gap is defined numerically only where extended-real subtraction is unambiguous; its positivity set remains meaningful using strict extended-real order everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonconvex biconjugate gap is \(G_f:D_f\to[0,+\infty]\), \(G_f(x)=f(x)-f^{**}(x)\). Its contact set is \(\mathcal C_f=\{x:f(x)=f^{**}(x)\}\), and its strict-gap set is \(\mathcal G_f=\{x:f^{**}(x)<f(x)\}\). Since \(f^{**}\) is the greatest closed convex minorant of \(f\), \(G_f\geq0\), and \(G_f\equiv0\) exactly when \(f\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconjugate gap measures the vertical distance from a function to its greatest closed convex minorant wherever subtraction is defined. Zero-gap points are contact points, while positive-gap points are precisely those not recovered by biconjugation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G_f(x)=f(x)-f^{**}(x)\geq0\quad(x\in D_f),\qquad \mathcal G_f=\{x:f^{**}(x)<f(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[G_f(x)=f(x)-\sup\{a(x):a\text{ is continuous affine and }a\leq f\}.\]
\[G_f\equiv0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=f^{**}.\]
special_cases_latex: For an indicator \(f=\iota_S\), the biconjugate is \(\iota_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}S}\); the gap is infinite on \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}S\setminus S\) under the extended-value convention.
If \(f\) is convex but nonclosed, the gap is purely a closure defect.
immediate_consequences_latex: The minimizers of \(f\) that also minimize \(f^{**}\) must lie in the contact set whenever their optimal values agree.
boundary_notes: The gap is not a metric distance and need not be continuous.
Expressions such as \(+\infty-(+\infty)\) are excluded by restricting the numerical definition to \(D_f\).

notation.meaning: contact set of f and its biconjugate

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Convex Inputs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconjugate of a nonclosed convex set's indicator is the indicator of its closure, producing a strict boundary gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise. Since \(C\) is convex, \(\delta_C\) is convex; since \(C\) is not closed, it is not lower semicontinuous. Its Fenchel biconjugate is
\[
\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\overline C}.
\]
Thus every \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\) satisfies \(\delta_C^{**}(x)=0<+\infty=\delta_C(x)\). Closedness, equivalently lower semicontinuity of the indicator, is therefore necessary for exact recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, convex, and not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The indicator satisfies \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\overline C}\), so biconjugation changes its values on \(\overline C\setminus C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional failure of exact biconjugation without closedness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conjugacy of indicators before and after closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\), \[\delta_C^*(y)=\sigma_C(y)=\sigma_{\overline C}(y)=\delta_{\overline C}^*(y)\quad(y\in\mathbb R^n).\] Thus the first conjugate cannot distinguish \(C\) from its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set and its closure have the same support function and conjugate indicator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^*=\delta_{\overline C}^*=\sigma_C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure defect of a proper convex function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and convex. Its lower-semicontinuous hull is \((\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional convex-but-not-closed regime. Convexification is already complete, so biconjugation performs only lower-semicontinuous closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonclosed convex input is a proper convex function \(f\) for which \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is not closed, equivalently \(f\neq\operatorname{cl}f\). Its biconjugate satisfies \(f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f\), and \(\operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}\). The closure-defect set is \(D_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)=\{x:(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)<f(x)\}\); it is nonempty exactly when the convex input is nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed convex input is convex but fails lower semicontinuity. Biconjugation does not further convexify it; it replaces the function by its lower-semicontinuous hull, whose epigraph is the closure of the original epigraph. The closure-defect set records where values drop.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^{**}=\operatorname{cl}f,\qquad \operatorname{epi}f^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f},\qquad D_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)=\{x:f^{**}(x)<f(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f\text{ is closed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_{\mathrm{cl}}(f)=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=f^{**}.\]
\[(\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is finite on an open set, convexity implies continuity there, so closure defects can occur only at the boundary of its effective domain.
For an indicator of a nonclosed convex set \(C\), \(\iota_C^{**}=\iota_{\overline C}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The conjugates agree: \(f^*=(\operatorname{cl}f)^*\).
boundary_notes: Nonclosedness refers to the epigraph in the ambient topology, not merely to whether the effective domain is closed.
A convex function can have a nonclosed domain while still being lower-semicontinuous; domain nonclosedness alone is not the defining defect.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Annihilator boundary for nonseparating conjugate duality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces with a bilinear pairing \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\), not assumed to separate points. Define \(N_X=\{n\in X:\langle n,y\rangle=0\ \forall y\in Y\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition isolates failure caused by an insufficient dual space, independently of nonconvexity or lower-semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The topological dual-separation failure boundary is the regime \(N_X\neq\{0\}\). For \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define \(f^Y(y)=\sup_x(\langle x,y\rangle-f(x))\) and \(f^{YY}(x)=\sup_y(\langle x,y\rangle-f^Y(y))\). Every such biconjugate is invariant along annihilator cosets: \(f^{YY}(x+n)=f^{YY}(x)\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(n\in N_X\). Consequently, exact recovery \(f=f^{YY}\) is possible only if \(f(x+n)=f(x)\) for all annihilator directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the chosen dual space does not distinguish all primal points, its common annihilator is nonzero. Every biconjugate is then constant on the corresponding affine cosets. Therefore, a function that varies along an invisible direction cannot be recovered by that conjugacy, even if it is convex and closed in some stronger topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_X\neq\{0\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^{YY}(x+n)=f^{YY}(x)\ \ \forall x\in X,\ \forall n\in N_X,\] \[f=f^{YY}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x+n)=f(x)\ \ \forall x\in X,\ \forall n\in N_X.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The pairing separates points of \(X\) exactly when \(N_X=\{0\}\).
The weak topology \(\sigma(X,Y)\) is Hausdorff exactly when \(Y\) separates points of \(X\).
special_cases_latex: If \(Y=\{0\}\), then \(N_X=X\), and every biconjugate is constant on \(X\).
For the canonical pairing \((X,X^*)\) of a normed space, Hahn–Banach separation gives \(N_X=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Dual separation is a structural prerequisite for a pointwise Fenchel–Moreau recovery theorem on the original primal space.
boundary_notes: This failure is distinct from a topology being too weak to make a particular epigraph closed; here the topology is non-Hausdorff because the dual does not separate points.
No supplied or inspected source gives this exact annihilator-boundary formulation, so independent sourcing is required.

notation.meaning: primal annihilator of the chosen paired dual space
biconjugate formed using the pairing with Y

review_flags: Needs an authoritative dual-pair source for the equivalence between separation, Hausdorff weak topology, and annihilator-coset invariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Annihilator boundary for nonseparating conjugate duality
Sequentially Closed Dense Convex Subspace
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an uncountable product space, the countable-support subspace is sequentially closed but dense, so its indicator is sequentially lower semicontinuous yet continuous-dual biconjugation fills the entire space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be uncountable, let \(X=\mathbb R^I\) have the product topology, and set
\[
\Sigma(I)=\{x\in X:\operatorname{supp}x\text{ is countable}\}.
\]
The linear subspace \(\Sigma(I)\) is sequentially closed: the support of the limit of any convergent sequence in \(\Sigma(I)\) is contained in a countable union of countable sets. It is nevertheless dense and proper in \(X\). Hence \(\delta_{\Sigma(I)}\) is sequentially lower semicontinuous but not lower semicontinuous. The continuous dual of \(X\) consists of finitely supported coordinate functionals, and
\[
\delta_{\Sigma(I)}^{**}=\delta_X\equiv0\ne\delta_{\Sigma(I)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Sigma(I)\) is sequentially closed but not closed, and \(\delta_{\Sigma(I)}^{**}\equiv0\ne\delta_{\Sigma(I)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit nonmetrizable example where sequential lower semicontinuity does not imply topological lower semicontinuity or exact continuous-dual biconjugation.

notation.meaning: subspace of vectors having countable support

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit nonmetrizable example separating sequential lower semicontinuity from topological lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be uncountable, let \(X=\mathbb R^I\) have the product topology, and let \[C=\{x\in X:\operatorname{supp}x\text{ is countable}\}.\] The linear subspace \(C\) is sequentially closed because the support of the limit of a sequence in \(C\) is contained in a countable union of countable sets. It is dense and not closed because the finitely supported vectors lie in \(C\) and are dense in \(X\). Every continuous linear functional on \(X\) depends on finitely many coordinates; hence every nonzero such functional is unbounded above on \(C\). Therefore \[\delta_C^{**}=0=\delta_X\ne\delta_C.\] Thus \(\delta_C\) is sequentially lower semicontinuous but is not recovered by continuous-dual biconjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an uncountable product space, the countable-support subspace is sequentially closed but dense, so its sequentially lower-semicontinuous indicator has zero biconjugate everywhere.
assumptions_latex: Conjugation uses the continuous dual of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is sequentially closed but not closed, and \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_X\ne\delta_C\).

notation.meaning: set of coordinates at which x is nonzero

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Closedness Does Not Suffice
Topological Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Biconjugation closes epigraphs in the weak topology induced by the chosen continuous dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological vector space with continuous dual \(X'\), and define conjugates using the pairing \(\langle X',X\rangle\). For any proper extended-real function \(f\), the biconjugate \(f^{**}\) is lower semicontinuous for \(\sigma(X,X')\). Therefore biconjugation can recover a proper convex \(\tau\)-lower-semicontinuous function only if its epigraph is also closed in \(\sigma(X,X')\). If \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is \(\tau\)-closed but not \(\sigma(X,X')\)-closed, then \(f^{**}\ne f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugation uses weak closure generated by the continuous dual; closure in another topology alone does not guarantee recovery.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f\) not \(\sigma(X,X')\)-closed implies \(f^{**}\ne f\).

notation.meaning: weak topology induced by the continuous dual

knowledge_statements.title: Trivial-Dual Separation Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only the zero functional available, biconjugation cannot distinguish any exterior point from the singleton set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Take \(X=\mathbb R\), \(Y=\{0\}\), and \(C=\{0\}\). Then \(H_Y(C)=\mathbb R\), so
\[
\delta_C^{**}\equiv0,
\]
even though \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\mathbb R}\ne\delta_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal algebraic example showing that an inadequate functional family can make every point indistinguishable under biconjugation.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairing-Invisible Exterior Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator biconjugate is the indicator of the intersection of all halfspaces detected by the selected functional family; an exterior point is incorrectly recovered precisely when that family cannot separate it from the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces in duality through a bilinear pairing, and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty. Define
\[
H_Y(C)=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq \sigma_C(y)\text{ for every }y\in Y\}.
\]
Then
\[
\delta_C^*(y)=\sigma_C(y),\qquad \delta_C^{**}=\delta_{H_Y(C)}.
\]
Consequently, for \(x_0\notin C\), one has \(\delta_C^{**}(x_0)=0<+\infty=\delta_C(x_0)\) exactly when every pairing-defined affine inequality valid on \(C\) is also valid at \(x_0\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are paired real vector spaces; separation of points is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{H_Y(C)}\), and \(x_0\in H_Y(C)\setminus C\) is exactly a pairing-invisible exterior point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact indicator-recovery boundary for a chosen linear-functional family, without assuming that the pairing separates points.

notation.meaning: intersection of all pairing-defined closed affine halfspaces containing C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical example in which the chosen functional family detects no nonmembership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonzero real vector space, let \(Y=\{0\}\), and let \(C=\{0\}\). Then \(H_Y(C)=X\), so \[\delta_C^{**}=0=\delta_X,\] although \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only the zero functional available, biconjugation cannot distinguish the origin from any other point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_X\ne\delta_C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Trivial-Dual Nonseparation Example
Dual-Separation Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A trivial continuous dual makes biconjugation unable to distinguish points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\ne\{0\}\) be a topological vector space whose continuous dual is \(X'=\{0\}\), and let \(f:X\to[0,+\infty)\) satisfy \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)>0\) for \(x\ne0\). Conjugacy with respect to \(X'\) gives \(f^*(0)=0\), hence \(f^{**}(x)=0\) for every \(x\in X\). Thus \(f^{**}(x)<f(x)\) at every nonzero point: a dual that does not separate points cannot recover such a function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the continuous dual contains only zero, every biconjugate is blind to point distinctions; a positive function with minimum zero collapses to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{**}\equiv0\), with \(f^{**}(x)<f(x)\) for all \(x\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hull Generated by the Selected Dual Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator biconjugation for an arbitrary bilinear pairing, including a nonseparating family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real vector spaces in bilinear pairing and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty. Define \[H_Y(C)=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\le \sigma_C(y)\text{ for every }y\in Y\}.\] Then \[\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{H_Y(C)}.\] Consequently, \(x_0\notin C\) is incorrectly admitted by biconjugation exactly when no \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(\langle x_0,y\rangle>\sigma_C(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The biconjugate of an indicator is the indicator of the intersection of all halfspaces generated by the selected dual family.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces with a bilinear pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{H_Y(C)}\), and \(x_0\in H_Y(C)\) exactly when the family \(Y\) supplies no strict separating inequality.

notation.meaning: support function of C relative to the pairing
intersection of all Y-generated closed affine halfspaces containing C

knowledge_statements.title: Hull Generated by the Selected Dual Family
Ambient–Pairing Closure Agreement Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugation using a selected separating dual subspace performs weak closure for that pairing; it agrees with ambient closed convexification exactly when the two topologies close every convex set identically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((X,\tau)\) be a Hausdorff locally convex space and let \(Y\subset X'\) separate points. For every nonempty convex set \(C\subset X\), conjugation with the pairing \((X,Y)\) gives
\[
\delta_C^{**}=\delta_{\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}C}.
\]
The pairing-induced and \(\tau\)-closed convexifications agree for every function having a proper pairing-closed convex minorant if and only if
\[
\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}C=\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C
\]
for every convex \(C\subset X\). Thus one convex set with unequal closures is an exact mismatch witness.
assumptions_latex: \((X,\tau)\) is a Hausdorff locally convex space.
For the function-level formulation, the relevant closed convex minorant is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairing and ambient convexification agree exactly when \(\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}C=\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C\) for every convex \(C\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact set-level criterion for agreement between ambient closed convexification and biconjugation using a selected separating subspace of the ambient continuous dual.

notation.meaning: weak topology induced by the selected functional space Y
continuous dual of the ambient topology τ

knowledge_statements.title: Norm–Coordinatewise Closure Mismatch
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero-sum hyperplane in ℓ¹ is norm closed but dense for the coordinatewise topology induced by c₀₀, so c₀₀-biconjugation loses the norm-closed constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\ell^1\) with its norm topology and pair it only with \(Y=c_{00}\subset\ell^\infty=X'\). The space \(Y\) separates points and \(\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})\) is coordinatewise convergence. For
\[
C=\left\{x\in\ell^1:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n=0\right\},
\]
\(C\) is a norm-closed hyperplane, but it is \(\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})\)-dense in \(\ell^1\): any finite collection of prescribed coordinates can be matched while one unused coordinate corrects the total sum. Therefore
\[
\operatorname{cl}_{\|\cdot\|_1}C=C,
\qquad
\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})}C=\ell^1,
\qquad
\delta_C^{**}\equiv0
\]
for conjugation against \(c_{00}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})}C=\ell^1\ne C=\operatorname{cl}_{\|\cdot\|_1}C\), and \(\delta_C^{**}\equiv0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit mismatch between norm closure and closure induced by a separating proper subspace of the norm-continuous dual.
Exact criterion for equality of pairing-induced and ambient closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y)\) be a separated dual pair and let \(\tau\) be a Hausdorff locally convex topology on \(X\). Pairing biconjugation agrees with \(\tau\)-closed convexification for all functions admitting a proper closed convex minorant if and only if \[\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(X,Y)}C=\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}C\] for every convex set \(C\subset X\). A strict inequality for one convex set yields different convexifications of its indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairing biconjugation matches ambient closed convexification exactly when the weak pairing topology and ambient topology give every convex set the same closure.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau\) is a Hausdorff locally convex topology on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pairing and \(\tau\)-closed convexifications agree exactly when all convex \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closures and \(\tau\)-closures agree.

notation.meaning: weak topology induced on X by Y

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Compatibility Criterion
Topology–Separation Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery criterion when ambient and dual-induced topologies need not agree on convex epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\tau)\) be a topological vector space, let \(Y\subseteq X^\#\) be a separating linear subspace of the algebraic dual, and define conjugates using the pairing \(\langle Y,X\rangle\). For a proper convex function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), equality \(f=f^{**}\) holds if and only if \(f\) is lower semicontinuous for \(\sigma(X,Y)\), equivalently if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed in \(\sigma(X,Y)\times\mathbb{R}\). Consequently, \(\tau\)-lower semicontinuity of a particular \(f\) yields recovery only when its epigraph is also \(\sigma(X,Y)\times\mathbb{R}\)-closed; a uniform implication for all proper convex functions requires the corresponding closure property for all such convex epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Biconjugate recovery of a proper convex function is equivalent to closure of its epigraph in the topology induced by the selected separating dual. Lower semicontinuity in the ambient topology alone is insufficient unless that epigraph also has the required weak closure.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq X^\#\) is a separating linear subspace
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=f^{**}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed in }\sigma(X,Y)\times\mathbb{R}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\ell^1\) with its norm topology and pair it with \(Y=c_{00}\) by \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_n x_ny_n\). The pairing separates points. The affine hyperplane \[C=\left\{x\in\ell^1:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n=1\right\}\] is norm closed, but it is dense for \(\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})\): any finite set of prescribed coordinates can be completed in an unused coordinate so that the total sum is one. Hence \[\delta_C^{**}=0=\delta_X\] for conjugation against \(c_{00}\), whereas the norm-lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(\delta_C\) is \(\delta_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-closed hyperplane in ℓ1 is dense for the coordinate pairing with finitely supported sequences, so pairing biconjugation and norm-closed convexification disagree.
assumptions_latex: \(Y=c_{00}\) is used for conjugation under the standard coordinate pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}_{\sigma(\ell^1,c_{00})}C=\ell^1\ne C=\operatorname{cl}_{\|\cdot\|_1}C\), and \(\delta_C^{**}=\delta_X\ne\delta_C\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\) with its Euclidean pairing, and let \(\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). For every proper function \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), its Fenchel conjugate is \(f^*(s)=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex analysis; the calculus records how standard primal constructions are transformed by Fenchel conjugation, including any closure or qualification required for an exact identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conjugate calculus on a class \(\mathcal F\) of proper functions is the transformation system \(\mathfrak C=\{\mathfrak C_{\mathcal O}\}_{\mathcal O}\) indexed by admissible primal operations \(\mathcal O\), where \(\mathfrak C_{\mathcal O}(f_1^*,\ldots,f_m^*)=(\mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m))^*\). Its canonical operations include affine changes of variables, linear images, sums, infimal convolutions, pointwise extrema, marginals, and monotone convex postcomposition. A rule is exact when it gives pointwise equality without an additional lower-semicontinuous closure and, when an infimum occurs in the dual representation, that infimum is attained. Thus each rule comprises its primal construction, the dual expression, and the domain or relative-interior qualification under which closure and nonattainment disappear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel-conjugate calculus is the indexed family of rules that assigns to each admissible construction \(\mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m)\) an expression for its conjugate \((\mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m))^*\) in terms of \(f_1^*,\ldots,f_m^*\). The family covers affine transformations, linear images, sums, infimal convolutions, extrema, marginalization, and increasing convex postcomposition. A calculus rule is called exact only when its displayed equality needs no lower-semicontinuous closure and every dual infimum appearing in it is attained; consequently, qualifications are part of the rule rather than optional annotations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak C_{\mathcal O}(f_1^*,\ldots,f_m^*)=(\mathcal O(f_1,\ldots,f_m))^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The calculus may equivalently be viewed as a collection of dual pairs of operations: addition versus infimal convolution, linear image versus linear precomposition, and supremum versus closed convexification of an infimum.
special_cases_latex: For the identity operation, \(\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{Id}}(f^*)=f^*\).
For an invertible linear map \(A\), the corresponding elementary rule is \((f\circ A)^*=f^*\circ(A^{-1})^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every rule specifies whether closure, exactness, or a relative-interior qualification is necessary.
The system reduces computation of a structured function's conjugate to conjugates of its constituent functions.
boundary_notes: This definition does not assert that every formal dual expression is closed or proper.
Infinite-dimensional variants may require topological duals and weak or weak-star lower-semicontinuous closures.

notation.meaning: Conjugate-calculus rule associated with the primal operation \(\mathcal O\).
