knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[f\text{ is of Legendre type}\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\ne\varnothing,\ f|_C\text{ is differentiable and strictly convex, and }\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to\infty\] \[\text{for every sequence }x_k\in C\text{ converging to a boundary point of }C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed proper convex function is of Legendre type when the restriction to the nonempty interior of its effective domain is both strictly convex and essentially smooth. Essential smoothness means differentiability throughout that interior together with blow-up of the gradient norm along every interior sequence approaching the boundary. Equivalently, \(f\) is both essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex. This class is stable under Fenchel conjugation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is Legendre type exactly when it satisfies strict convexity on \(C\), differentiability on \(C\), and the displayed boundary-gradient condition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f\text{ is essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex}.\]
\[\partial f\text{ is one-to-one, and on }C\text{ it equals }\nabla f.\]
special_cases_latex: A finite differentiable strictly convex cofinite function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is Legendre type.
A differentiable convex function can fail to be Legendre type if its gradient does not diverge at a finite boundary point.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(f^*\) is also of Legendre type.
The gradient mapping is injective on \(C\).
boundary_notes: Strict convexity merely on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) is not by itself the full essential-strict-convexity condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Characterization of Essential Smoothness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential smoothness is equivalent to having exactly one subgradient at every interior-domain point and no subgradient at any finite boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is essentially smooth if and only if
\[
\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)
\]
and \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton for every \(x\) in this set. In that case,
\[
\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\quad\text{for }x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f),
\]
and
\[
\partial f(x)=\varnothing\quad\text{for }x\in\operatorname{bdry}(\operatorname{dom}f).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is essentially smooth if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional subdifferential characterization equivalent to the boundary-gradient definition.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the convex subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Essential Smoothness Without Essential Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates essential smoothness from the sibling strict-convexity regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq1\), the constant function \(f(x)=0\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) is proper, closed, convex, differentiable on its full domain, and has empty domain boundary. It is therefore essentially smooth. Since \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\mathbb R^n\) and \(f\) is affine on every segment, it is not essentially strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant full-domain function is essentially smooth because the boundary condition is vacuous, but it is not essentially strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is essentially smooth but not essentially strictly convex.

Essential Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is essentially smooth when \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\neq\varnothing\), the restriction of \(f\) to \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) is differentiable, and every sequence \((x_k)\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) converging to a point of \(\operatorname{bdry}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) satisfies \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to+\infty\). The boundary condition is vacuous when \(\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Domain of an Essentially Smooth Function
Essential Strict Convexity Does Not Ensure Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential strict convexity gives uniqueness conditional on attainment but does not make every conjugate supremum attain its value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), \(f(x)=e^x\), is proper, closed, differentiable, and strictly convex, hence essentially strictly convex. At \(u=0\),
\[
f^*(0)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}(-e^x)=0,
\]
but the supremum is not attained, and
\[
\partial f^*(0)=\varnothing.
\]
Thus essential strict convexity guarantees at most one conjugate maximizer, not its existence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is essentially strictly convex while \(\partial f^*(0)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates uniqueness of an attained conjugate maximizer from existence of such a maximizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness of Conjugate Maximizers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential strict convexity makes every attained conjugate maximization problem have a unique primal maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(u\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\underset{x\in\mathbb R^n}{\operatorname{argmax}}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}
=\partial f^*(u)
\]
contains at most one point. Thus whenever the supremum defining \(f^*(u)\) is attained, its maximizer is unique.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and essentially strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\partial f^*(u)\rvert\leq1\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness, conditional on existence, of maximizers defining the conjugate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Essential Strict Convexity Without Essential Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates essential strict convexity from the sibling boundary-steepness regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[f(x)=x^2+\delta_{[0,+\infty)}(x).\] This function is proper, closed, convex, and strictly convex on its effective domain, hence essentially strictly convex. Nevertheless, \(f'(x)=2x\) for \(x>0\), so \[\lim_{x\downarrow0}f'(x)=0.\] Its gradient therefore does not diverge as interior points approach the boundary point \(0\), and \(f\) is not essentially smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared function restricted to the nonnegative half-line is essentially strictly convex but lacks the boundary-gradient blow-up required for essential smoothness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is essentially strictly convex but not essentially smooth.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator of the nonnegative half-line.

knowledge_statements.title: Essential Strict Convexity Without Essential Smoothness
Essential Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar-type finite-dimensional definition using the subdifferential domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is essentially strictly convex when its restriction to every nonempty convex subset \(C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\partial f\) is strictly convex. Thus, for distinct \(x,z\in C\) and every \(t\in(0,1)\), one has \(f((1-t)x+tz)<(1-t)f(x)+tf(z)\). The definition imposes strict convexity only where subgradients exist, rather than necessarily on the entire effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Essential strict convexity requires strict convexity on every convex subset of the points where the function has a subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is essentially strictly convex if and only if it satisfies the displayed strict inequality on every convex \(C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\partial f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and essentially strictly convex, then for every \(u\in\mathbb R^n\), \[u\in\partial f(x)\cap\partial f(y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y.\] Equivalently, every value of \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\) contains at most one point.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mutually inverse Legendre gradient maps are continuous in both directions and identify the primal and dual domain interiors topologically.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The map
\[
\nabla f:\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)
\]
is a homeomorphism, and its inverse homeomorphism is \(\nabla f^*\). Consequently, for any sequence \((x_k)\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and any \(x\) in that interior,

\]

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Blow-Up Does Not Imply Value Blow-Up
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Legendre function may have an unbounded gradient while remaining finite and continuous at a boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}x\log x-x,&x>0,\\0,&x=0,\\+\infty,&x<0.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(f\) is Legendre, \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=(0,\infty)\), and
\[
f'(x)=\log x\longrightarrow-\infty\quad\text{as }x\downarrow0,
\]
whereas
\[
f(x)\longrightarrow0=f(0).
\]
Thus Legendre boundary-gradient blow-up does not imply boundary value blow-up.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is the extended normalized-entropy function stated in the record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert f'(x)\rvert\to+\infty\) but \(f(x)\to f(0)<+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Legendre Boundary Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient exclusion and gradient blow-up at a Legendre function's effective-domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a Legendre function. Then \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), and \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\) for every \(x\) in this interior. If \((x_k)\) is an interior sequence converging to any \(\bar x\in\operatorname{bdry}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), then \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to+\infty\). Consequently, no finite subgradient extends to such a boundary point, while the conjugate gradients map the escaping dual sequence back to \((x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Legendre function has singleton subgradients exactly on its domain interior, and gradient norms diverge along every interior approach to a finite boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sequential boundary behavior defining essential smoothness and hence the boundary component of Legendre type.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathsf{LB}(f):\quad \forall \bar x\in\operatorname{bdry}C\ \forall (x_k)\subset C,\quad x_k\to\bar x\Longrightarrow\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to+\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Legendre boundary behavior of \(f\) is the steepness condition that the norm of the gradient diverges along every sequence in the interior of the effective domain that converges to a boundary point of that interior. Together with nonempty interior and differentiability throughout the interior, this condition defines essential smoothness. It prevents the convex subdifferential from acquiring a finite value at a finite boundary point.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathsf{LB}(f)\Longleftrightarrow \|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to+\infty\text{ for every interior sequence approaching every point of }\operatorname{bdry}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under the stated interior hypotheses, \(\mathsf{LB}(f)\) is the boundary condition in the definition of essential smoothness.
For closed proper convex \(f\), \[\mathsf{LB}(f)\Longleftrightarrow\partial f(x)=\varnothing\quad(\forall x\notin C).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb R^n\), the boundary condition is vacuous.
For a barrier-type function on an open convex domain, gradient blow-up at every finite boundary point is the characteristic steepness requirement.
immediate_consequences_latex: For closed proper convex \(f\), \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\) on \(C\) and is empty outside \(C\).
A Legendre-type function satisfies \(\mathsf{LB}(f)\), as does its conjugate on its own interior domain.
boundary_notes: Divergence must hold for every approaching sequence, not merely for radial approaches.
The condition concerns finite boundary points; behavior as \(\|x\|\to\infty\) is a separate coercivity or recession issue.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Its Fenchel conjugate is \(f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle u,x\rangle-f(x)\}\). For a nonempty set \(C\), write \(\sigma_C(d)=\sup_{z\in C}\langle d,z\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex analysis; the identities concern effective domains and recession functions, not differentiability or attainment of conjugate suprema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The domain-growth-recession duality associated with \(f\) is the pair of identities \[\operatorname{rec}f(d)=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}(d)\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{rec}f^*(u)=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}(u),\] where, for any \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[\operatorname{rec}f(d)=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.\] Thus the asymptotic growth of either member of a conjugate pair is the support function of the effective domain of the other member.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function \(f\), define its recession function by the asymptotic difference quotient along each direction. Domain-growth-recession duality is the exact correspondence \(\operatorname{rec}f=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}\) and \(\operatorname{rec}f^*=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}\). Hence finiteness, linearity, or infinite growth of the recession function records the support geometry of the opposite effective domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}f=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}\) and \(\operatorname{rec}f^*=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every direction \(d\), \(\operatorname{rec}f(d)=\sup\{\langle d,u\rangle:u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}\).
For every \(u\), \(\operatorname{rec}f^*(u)=\sup\{\langle u,x\rangle:x\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq \alpha B\), then \(\operatorname{rec}f(d)\leq\alpha\lVert d\rVert\) for every \(d\).
If \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is bounded, then \(\operatorname{rec}f^*(u)<+\infty\) for every \(u\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The recession function determines the closed convex hull of the opposite effective domain through its support function.
A direction \(d\) has \(\operatorname{rec}f(d)=+infty\) precisely when the linear functional \(u\mapsto\langle d,u\rangle\) is unbounded above on \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
boundary_notes: The second identity uses closedness through \(f^{**}=f\).
In infinite-dimensional spaces, analogous statements require attention to the chosen dual pairing and topology.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\). Define \(f^*(u)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal H}(\langle x,u\rangle-f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space convex analysis. Coercivity is norm coercivity; the condition is interiority in the norm topology of the dual domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The coercivity-dual-domain correspondence is the equivalence \[f(x)\to+infty\ \text{as}\ \lVert x\rVert\to+infty \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*.\] Equivalently, it holds exactly when there exist \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \[f(x)\geq \alpha\lVert x\rVert+\beta\qquad(\forall x\in\mathcal H).\] The same condition is equivalent to boundedness of every lower level set \(\{x:f(x)\leq\xi\}\) and to \(f^*\) being bounded above on some neighborhood of the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f\) is coercive when \(f(x)\) tends to \(+infty\) whenever \(\lVert x\rVert\) tends to infinity. The conjugate-domain correspondence identifies this property with \(0\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*\). It is also equivalent to a global positive linear lower bound, bounded lower level sets, and local boundedness above of \(f^*\) around zero.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((\forall\xi\in\mathbb R)\;\{x:f(x)\leq\xi\}\) is bounded.
\(\liminf_{\lVert x\rVert\to+infty}f(x)/\lVert x\rVert>0\).
\((\exists\alpha>0)(\exists\beta\in\mathbb R)(\forall x)\;f(x)\geq\alpha\lVert x\rVert+\beta\).
\(f^*\) is bounded above on a neighborhood of \(0\).
special_cases_latex: For any \(u\in\mathcal H\), the tilted function \(f-\langle\cdot,u\rangle\) is coercive exactly when \(u\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(f\) is coercive, every minimizing sequence of \(f\) is bounded.
The correspondence is stable under adding a bounded linear functional after translating the distinguished interior point from \(0\) to \(u\).
boundary_notes: Supercoercivity, defined by \(f(x)/\lVert x\rVert\to+infty\), is stronger than coercivity.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=\mathcal H\) alone need not imply supercoercivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior conjugate-domain points are exactly coercive linear tilts; ordinary coercivity corresponds to zero being interior, while supercoercivity corresponds to a full conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The tilted function \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle u,x\rangle\) is coercive, meaning that its value tends to \(+\infty\) as \(\|x\|\to\infty\), if and only if \[u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*).\] In particular, \(f\) is coercive if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\). Moreover, \(f\) is supercoercive, meaning that \(f(x)/\|x\|\to+\infty\) as \(\|x\|\to\infty\), if and only if \[\operatorname{dom}f^*=\mathbb{R}^n.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f-\langle u,\cdot\rangle\) is coercive if and only if \(u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\), and \(f\) is supercoercive if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coercive and supercoercive regimes, including linear tilts.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Tests for Coercive and Supercoercive Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional tests for the growth regimes related to conjugate-domain geometry by the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then \[f\text{ is coercive}\iff f^\infty(d)>0\quad\text{for every }d\neq0.\] Moreover, \[f\text{ is supercoercive}\iff f^\infty(d)=+\infty\quad\text{for every }d\neq0,\] equivalently \(f^\infty=\delta_{\{0\}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coercivity is strict positive recession growth in every nonzero direction; supercoercivity is infinite recession growth in every such direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive iff \(f^\infty(d)>0\) for all \(d\ne0\), and supercoercive iff \(f^\infty=\delta_{\{0\}}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional level-boundedness formulation and its attainment consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \[f\text{ is coercive}\iff \{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\text{ is compact for every }\alpha\in\mathbb R.\] In this regime \(f\) attains its finite minimum, and \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, coercivity is equivalent to compactness of all sublevel sets and guarantees a nonempty compact minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive iff every sublevel set is compact; then \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is nonempty and compact.

Dual-Domain Interior Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior of the conjugate domain consists exactly of slopes whose linear tilts make the primal function coercive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The interior geometry of the conjugate domain admits the representation \[\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)=\left\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lim_{\|x\|\to\infty}\bigl(f(x)-\langle u,x\rangle\bigr)=+\infty\right\}.\] Thus \(u\) belongs to this interior exactly when the tilt \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle u,x\rangle\) is coercive. Equivalently, some \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \(u+\varepsilon\mathbb{B}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:f-\langle u,\cdot\rangle\text{ is coercive}\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative directional representation of depth inside the effective conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{dom}f^*\) and \(u\in C\). The supremal radius of a closed Euclidean ball centered at \(u\) and contained in \(C\) satisfies \[r_C(u):=\sup\{r\geq0:u+r\mathbb B\subseteq C\}=\inf_{\|d\|=1}\bigl(f^\infty(d)-\langle u,d\rangle\bigr).\] Consequently, \[u\in\operatorname{int}C\iff \langle u,d\rangle<f^\infty(d)\quad\text{for every }d\neq0.\] The defining supremum need not itself be attained when \(C\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior depth equals the smallest directional gap between recession growth and the candidate slope; strict directional gaps characterize interior membership.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\mathbb B\) is the closed Euclidean unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_C(u)=\inf_{\|d\|=1}(f^\infty(d)-\langle u,d\rangle)\), and \(u\in\operatorname{int}C\) iff \(\langle u,d\rangle<f^\infty(d)\) for every \(d\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Interior Radius from Recession Growth
Coercivity Correspondence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slope in the conjugate domain but outside its interior gives a bounded-below noncoercive tilt; outside the conjugate domain, the tilted infimum is negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\setminus\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\), then \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(f(x)-\langle u,x\rangle\bigr)=-f^*(u)>-\infty,\] but the tilted function is not coercive. If \(u\notin\operatorname{dom}f^*\), then \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(f(x)-\langle u,x\rangle\bigr)=-\infty.\] Thus finiteness of the conjugate gives boundedness below, whereas interior membership is the stronger condition furnishing coercive growth.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\setminus\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\), the tilt is bounded below but noncoercive; if \(u\notin\operatorname{dom}f^*\), its infimum is \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction among interior-domain, noninterior-domain, and exterior conjugate slopes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Slopes Need Not Produce Coercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp example separating finite conjugate value from interior-domain membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max\{0,x\}\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \[f^*=\delta_{[0,1]}.\] For \(u\in\{0,1\}\), the tilt \(f-u\,\mathrm{id}\) is bounded below but not coercive. For every \(u\notin[0,1]\), \(\inf_x(f(x)-ux)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hinge function realizes boundary slopes as bounded-below noncoercive tilts and exterior slopes as unbounded-below tilts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\delta_{[0,1]}\); endpoint tilts are bounded below and noncoercive, while exterior tilts are unbounded below.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation of ordinary coercive and supercoercive growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\|x\|\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), \(f\) is coercive but not supercoercive, and \[f^*=\delta_{\mathbb B_*},\] where \(\mathbb B_*\) is the closed dual-unit ball. Thus \(0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\), but \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\neq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm is coercive but not supercoercive, so interior containment of zero is strictly weaker than a full conjugate domain.

\(\mathbb B_*\) is the corresponding closed dual-unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive but not supercoercive and \(f^*=\delta_{\mathbb B_*}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Lipschitz continuity and bounded conjugate domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(f^*\) be its Fenchel conjugate, and let \(B=\{u:\lVert u\rVert\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional global Lipschitz continuity with respect to the Euclidean norm; local Lipschitz properties on the relative interior are not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\geq0\), the Lipschitz-bounded-dual-domain correspondence is \[|f(x)-f(z)|\leq\alpha\lVert x-z\rVert\quad(\forall x,z\in\mathbb R^n) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq\alpha B.\] In particular, \(f\) is finite everywhere and globally Lipschitz if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\) is bounded. When these conditions hold, the least global Lipschitz constant is \[\operatorname{Lip}(f)=\sup\{\lVert u\rVert:u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The correspondence pairs global Lipschitz regularity of a proper convex function with boundedness of its conjugate domain. More precisely, \(f\) has Lipschitz constant \(\alpha\) exactly when every \(u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\) satisfies \(\lVert u\rVert\leq\alpha\). The optimal Lipschitz constant is the supremum of the norms of points in the conjugate domain.
assumptions_latex: The norm and dual pairing are Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is globally \(\alpha\)-Lipschitz if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq\alpha B\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f(x+d)\leq f(x)+\alpha\lVert d\rVert\) for all \(x,d\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(\operatorname{rec}f(d)\leq\alpha\lVert d\rVert\) for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}(d)\leq\alpha\lVert d\rVert\) for every \(d\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\alpha=0\), \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq\{0\}\), and a finite convex \(f\) is constant.
If \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\) lies in a dual-norm ball in a finite-dimensional normed space, the analogous statement holds with the primal and dual norms.
immediate_consequences_latex: Boundedness of \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\) forces \(\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb R^n\).
The exact global Lipschitz modulus is encoded by the radius of the smallest centered ball containing \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
boundary_notes: Bounded subgradients only on a restricted subset yield local or relative Lipschitz continuity, not this global correspondence.
The closure of \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\) may be used without changing its support function or its supremal radius.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Lipschitz Behavior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed proper convex function is globally L-Lipschitz exactly when its conjugate domain lies in the radius-L ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is finite-valued and globally \(L\)-Lipschitz, namely \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n),\] if and only if \[\operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq L\mathbb{B}.\] Consequently, when the conjugate domain is bounded, the least global Lipschitz constant is \[L_{\min}=\sup\{\|u\|:u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is globally \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) iff \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq L\mathbb{B}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional global Lipschitz–conjugate-domain correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Dual Domains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded conjugate domain supplies uniformly bounded slopes, and its maximal radius is the least global Lipschitz constant of the primal function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{dom}f^*\) and \[R:=\sup_{u\in C}\|u\|<+\infty.\] Then \(f\) is finite-valued on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq R\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] The least global Lipschitz constant of \(f\) equals \(R\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\sup_{u\in C}\|u\|\,\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation geometry of a bounded effective conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{dom}f^*\) be bounded. For every \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), the least global Lipschitz constant of \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle a,x\rangle\) is \[R(a)=\sup_{u\in C}\|u-a\|.\] Consequently, \(\inf_aR(a)\) is the circumradius of \(C\), and its minimizers are the centers of minimum enclosing balls of \(\overline C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After subtracting the best affine slope, the smallest attainable Lipschitz modulus is the circumradius of the dual domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic characterization of bounded effective conjugate domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(C=\operatorname{dom}f^*\). Since \(f^\infty=\sigma_C\), \[C\text{ is bounded}\iff f^\infty(d)<+\infty\quad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb R^n.\] In that case \(\overline C\) is compact and \[f^\infty(d)=\max_{u\in\overline C}\langle u,d\rangle\quad\text{for every }d.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Boundedness via Finite Recession Support
Local Lipschitz Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper convex function is Lipschitz on compact subsets of its domain interior, even when no global Lipschitz constant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every compact set \(K\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), there exists a finite constant \(L_K\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L_K\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in K.\] More locally, every point \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) has a neighborhood on which \(f\) is Lipschitz. Convex subgradients are locally bounded on the domain interior, although they need not be bounded uniformly over the entire domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(L_K<+\infty\) such that \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L_K\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in K\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every compact set \(K\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), there exists a finite constant \(L_K\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L_K\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in K.\] More locally, every point \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) has a neighborhood on which \(f\) is Lipschitz. Convex subgradients are locally bounded on the domain interior, although they need not be bounded uniformly over the entire domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper convex function is Lipschitz on compact subsets of its domain interior, even when no global Lipschitz constant exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz–Domain Correspondence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local interior Lipschitz continuity does not imply global Lipschitz continuity: an indicator of a half-line has an unbounded conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Local interior Lipschitz continuity alone gives no boundedness of the conjugate domain. For example, let \(f=\iota_{[0,+\infty)}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). Then \(f\) is constant, hence locally Lipschitz, on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=(0,+\infty)\), while \[f^*(u)=\iota_{(-\infty,0]}(u)\] and \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=(-\infty,0]\) is unbounded. Thus global Lipschitz behavior requires bounded dual-domain geometry, not merely local regularity inside the primal domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local Lipschitz continuity on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) does not imply boundedness of \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\) or global Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates automatic interior regularity from the global bounded-dual-domain criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession geometry of a closed convex function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For \(\xi\in\mathbb R\), let \(L_\xi=\{x:f(x)\leq\xi\}\), and let \(0^+C=\{d:C+\mathbb R_+d\subseteq C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional asymptotic geometry of epigraphs and nonempty lower level sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic geometry interface of \(f\) consists of the recession function and its induced cones: \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}f)=0^+(\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad 0^+L_\xi=\{d:\operatorname{rec}f(d)\leq0\}\] for every nonempty lower level set \(L_\xi\). Under conjugacy, \[\operatorname{rec}f=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}.\] Hence the common recession cone of all nonempty lower level sets is \[\{d:\langle d,u\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every}\ u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\},\] the polar cone of the cone generated by \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymptotic geometry interface attaches to \(f\) the recession function whose epigraph is the recession cone of \(\operatorname{epi}f\). Its nonpositive directions form the common recession cone of every nonempty lower level set. Conjugacy identifies this function with the support function of \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\), so level-set recession directions are precisely the directions polar to the cone generated by the dual domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(L_\xi\neq\varnothing\) whenever its recession cone is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0^+\operatorname{epi}f=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}f)\) and \(0^+L_\xi=\{d:\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}(d)\leq0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in0^+L_\xi\) if and only if \(f(x+td)\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in L_\xi\) and \(t\geq0\).
\(d\in0^+L_\xi\) if and only if \(\langle d,u\rangle\leq0\) for all \(u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\).
special_cases_latex: All nonempty lower level sets are bounded exactly when \(\{d:\operatorname{rec}f(d)\leq0\}=\{0\}\).
If \(0\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*\), then every nonempty lower level set is bounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: The asymptotic behavior of every lower level set is determined by a single function \(\operatorname{rec}f\).
Dual-domain interiority eliminates nonzero recession directions of lower level sets.
boundary_notes: Boundedness of one nonempty level set implies boundedness of all lower levels in finite dimensions under the stated closed-convex assumptions.
The recession cone records directions, not the rate of growth when \(\operatorname{rec}f(d)>0\).

notation.meaning: Lower level set of f at height ξ.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function records asymptotic directional growth and equals the support function of the conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The recession function of \(f\) is defined by \[f^\infty(d):=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x+d)-f(x)\bigr).\] For every \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), it also satisfies \[f^\infty(d)=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}.\] It is independent of \(x_0\), lower semicontinuous, convex, and positively homogeneous, and it has the conjugate-domain representation \[f^\infty(d)=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}(d)=\sup_{u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*}\langle u,d\rangle.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\infty(d)=\lim_{t\to+\infty}(f(x_0+td)-f(x_0))/t=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}(d)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the closed convex recession function and its conjugate-domain representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elementary calculus for recession functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex with \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\). For \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), \(c\in\mathbb R\), and \(\lambda>0\), \[(f+g)^\infty=f^\infty+g^\infty,\qquad (f+\langle a,\cdot\rangle+c)^\infty=f^\infty+\langle a,\cdot\rangle,\qquad (\lambda f)^\infty=\lambda f^\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession functions commute with compatible sums and positive scaling, while affine perturbation adds its linear slope.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f+g)^\infty=f^\infty+g^\infty\), \((f+\langle a,\cdot\rangle+c)^\infty=f^\infty+\langle a,\cdot\rangle\), and \((\lambda f)^\infty=\lambda f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.title: Basic Recession-Function Calculus

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Cones of Convex Sublevel Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional characterization shared by all nonempty sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) with \(L_\alpha:=\{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\neq\varnothing\), \[\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:f^\infty(d)\leq0\}.\] Consequently, all nonempty sublevel sets of \(f\) have the same recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction recedes in a nonempty sublevel set exactly when its recession cost is nonpositive.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha=\{d:f^\infty(d)\leq0\}\).

notation.meaning: recession cone of the sublevel set

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Cones of Convex Sublevel Sets
Barrier Cones Need Not Be Closed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the scalar quadratic has a nonclosed barrier cone, making closure essential in the recession-polar identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\operatorname{epi}(x\mapsto x^2)\), \[\sigma_C(u,v)=\begin{cases}-u^2/(4v),&v<0,\\0,&(u,v)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Thus its barrier cone is not closed, while its closure equals \((\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{bar}C=\{(u,v):v<0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\qquad\overline{\operatorname{bar}C}=\{(u,v):v\leq0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete closed convex set with a nonclosed barrier cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Full Barrier Cone Characterizes Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set is bounded exactly when its barrier cone is the whole dual space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty closed convex set is bounded if and only if every linear functional is bounded above on it, equivalently \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\mathbb R^n\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{bar}C=\mathbb R^n.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundedness characterized by finite support in every direction.

notation.meaning: Barrier cone, equivalently the support-function domain

knowledge_statements.title: Barrier Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The barrier cone consists of linear functionals bounded above on a closed convex set; its closure is the negative polar of the recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The barrier cone of \(C\) is the effective domain of its support function: \[\operatorname{bar}C:=\left\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle<+\infty\right\}=\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C.\] If \(\operatorname{rec}C\) denotes the recession cone and the negative polar convention is \[K^\circ:=\left\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,d\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }d\in K\right\},\] then \[\overline{\operatorname{bar}C}=(\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ.\] Thus the barrier cone comprises directions of finite support, while its closure is determined solely by recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bar}C=\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) and \(\overline{\operatorname{bar}C}=(\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional barrier cone with recession-polar closure relation.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Recession and Barrier Cones p. 128

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic cone structure and consequences of the accepted recession-polar closure identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\operatorname{bar}C=\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) is a convex cone containing the origin, \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{bar}C)=\operatorname{ri}\bigl((\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ\bigr),\] and \[\operatorname{bar}C=\mathbb R^n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\text{ is bounded}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The barrier cone is convex, has the same relative interior as the polar of the recession cone, and fills the dual space exactly when the set is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{bar}C\) is a convex cone, \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{bar}C)=\operatorname{ri}((\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ)\), and \(\operatorname{bar}C=\mathbb R^n\iff C\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity, Relative Interior, and Boundedness
Epigraph–Horizon Recession Identity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizon function is the closed sublinear function whose epigraph is the recession cone of the original epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph of the horizon function is the recession cone of the original epigraph. Equivalently, \[(d,\alpha)\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^\infty(d)\leq\alpha.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical representation of the closed-convex horizon function.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of a nonempty closed convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizon function records the asymptotic slope of a closed proper convex function along each direction, independently of the selected base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the horizon function of \(f\) is defined by \[f^{\infty}(d)=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t},\qquad d\in X.\] The value is independent of the chosen \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\infty}\) is positively homogeneous, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-convex horizon function, equal here to the recession function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-convex-set specialization of the horizon function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then \[(\delta_C)^\infty=\delta_{\operatorname{rec}C}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizon function of a closed convex set's indicator is the indicator of its recession cone.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\delta_C)^\infty=\delta_{\operatorname{rec}C}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraphical Representation of the Horizon Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph geometry of finite-dimensional proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then \[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=\{(d,\beta):f^\infty(d)\leq\beta\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the horizon function is the recession cone of the original epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty\).

notation.meaning: recession cone of the epigraph of f

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Representation of the Horizon Function
Supercoercivity–Full Conjugate Domain Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Growth faster than every linear rate is equivalent to the conjugate having full effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper closed convex function is supercoercive exactly when its Fenchel conjugate is finite at every dual vector.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lim_{\|x\|\to\infty}\frac{f(x)}{\|x\|}=+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{dom}f^*=X^*.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional supercoercivity characterized by an everywhere-finite conjugate.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the Fenchel conjugate

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz–Bounded Conjugate Domain Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global Lipschitz continuity of a finite convex function is equivalent to boundedness of its conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An everywhere-finite closed convex function is globally \(L\)-Lipschitz if and only if its conjugate domain is contained in the closed dual ball of radius \(L\). Consequently, it is globally Lipschitz for some finite constant exactly when \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\) is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\).
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is lower semicontinuous and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is globally }L\text{-Lipschitz}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq L\mathbb B_*.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global finite-valued Lipschitz regularity characterized by a bounded conjugate domain.

notation.meaning: Closed dual ball of radius L

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Interface Correspondences
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function's horizon is the support function of its conjugate domain, while the conjugate's horizon supports the primal domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic behavior of \(f\) and \(f^*\) is determined by the opposite effective domain: \[f^{\infty}(d)=\sup_{x^*\in\operatorname{dom}f^*}\langle x^*,d\rangle=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}(d),\] and \[(f^*)^{\infty}(d^*)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\langle d^*,x\rangle=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}(d^*).\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\infty}=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}\) and \((f^*)^{\infty}=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-domain characterization of primal and conjugate asymptotic growth.

notation.meaning: support function of a set C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-sensitive equivalence between global Lipschitz continuity and bounded conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex, let \(L\ge0\), and let \(\|\cdot\|_*\) be dual to \(\|\cdot\|\). Then \[|f(x)-f(z)|\le L\|x-z\|\quad(\forall x,z)\] if and only if \[\operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq\{u:\|u\|_*\le L\}.\] The least global Lipschitz constant is \(\sup_{u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*}\|u\|_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex function is globally L-Lipschitz exactly when its conjugate domain lies in the dual ball of radius L.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is finite and convex on all of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is globally }L\text{-Lipschitz}\iff\operatorname{dom}f^*\subseteq L B_*\).

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball of the dual norm

knowledge_statements.title: Global Lipschitz–Bounded Conjugate-Domain Correspondence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between level-bounded linear tilts and the interior of the conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\). For every \(u\in\mathbb R^n\), \[u\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\] if and only if \[x\mapsto f(x)-\langle u,x\rangle\] is level-bounded, equivalently coercive in the extended-valued sense. In particular, \(f\) is coercive if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear tilt of a closed proper convex function is level-bounded exactly when the tilt vector lies in the interior of the conjugate domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f^*\iff f-\langle u,\cdot\rangle\) is level-bounded.

notation.meaning: Proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on Euclidean space

knowledge_statements.title: Tilted Coercivity–Conjugate-Domain Correspondence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between faster-than-linear growth and an everywhere-finite conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathbb R^n)\), \[\lim_{\|x\|\to\infty}\frac{f(x)}{\|x\|}=+\infty\] in the extended-valued sense if and only if \[\operatorname{dom}f^*=\mathbb R^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed proper convex function is supercoercive exactly when its conjugate is finite at every dual vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is supercoercive}\iff\operatorname{dom}f^*=\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the Fenchel conjugate

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H,\mathcal K\) be real Hilbert spaces, \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathcal K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the linear-composite Fenchel–Rockafellar pair, including weak-duality sign conventions; no qualification or attainment is built into the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel–Rockafellar dual pair generated by \((f,g,L)\) is \[\text{(P)}\quad \inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\bigl(f(x)+g(Lx)\bigr),\qquad \text{(D)}\quad \inf_{v\in\mathcal K}\bigl(f^*(-L^*v)+g^*(v)\bigr).\] Writing \(p^*\) and \(d^*\) for these two infimal values, respectively, the maximization-form dual value is \(-d^*\), weak duality is \(p^*\geq-d^*\), and the duality gap is \(p^*+d^*\) when this extended-real sum is defined. Strong duality means \(p^*=-d^*\); dual attainment means that the infimum in (D) is achieved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fenchel–Rockafellar pair consists of the primal minimization of \(f+g\circ L\) and the dual minimization of \(v\mapsto f^*(-L^*v)+g^*(v)\). With this minimization convention, the dual objective enters the value comparison with a minus sign. Weak duality gives \(p^*\geq-d^*\), while strong duality is equality. Attainment is a separate property and is not part of merely forming the pair.
assumptions_latex: \(L:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K\) is bounded and linear, with adjoint \(L^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical pair is \((\inf_x f(x)+g(Lx),\;\inf_v f^*(-L^*v)+g^*(v))\), with weak-duality relation \(p^*\geq-d^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The maximization-form dual is \(\sup_{v\in\mathcal K}\{-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\}\).
After substituting \(w=-v\), the dual can be written \(\inf_w f^*(L^*w)+g^*(-w)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(L=\operatorname{Id}\) and both functions on \(\mathcal H\), the pair reduces to sum-form Fenchel duality.
Taking \(g=\iota_C\) yields a dual involving the support function \(\sigma_C=g^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \(x\in\mathcal H\) and \(v\in\mathcal K\) satisfy \(f(x)+g(Lx)+f^*(-L^*v)+g^*(v)\geq0\).
Zero gap, primal attainment, and dual attainment are logically distinct outcomes unless additional hypotheses are imposed.
boundary_notes: Properness alone does not guarantee feasibility, finite values, zero gap, or attainment.
Alternative sign conventions produce an equivalent dual after replacing \(v\) by \(-v\).

notation.meaning: Primal and minimization-form dual infimal values.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H,\mathcal K\) be real Hilbert spaces and let all displayed functions be proper extended-real-valued functions on their stated spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A structural definition of the two standard Fenchel architectures; qualification conditions and optimality certificates are separate layers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical Fenchel primal–dual architectures are the following templates. The sum architecture uses \[\inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\bigl(f(x)+h(x)\bigr)\quad\leftrightarrow\quad \inf_{u\in\mathcal H}\bigl(f^*(-u)+h^*(u)\bigr).\] The linear-composite architecture uses \[\inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\bigl(f(x)+g(Lx)\bigr)\quad\leftrightarrow\quad \inf_{v\in\mathcal K}\bigl(f^*(-L^*v)+g^*(v)\bigr).\] The sum architecture is the specialization of the linear-composite architecture obtained by taking \(\mathcal K=\mathcal H\), \(L=\operatorname{Id}\), and \(g=h\). A perturbation representation \(F(x,y)=f(x)+g(Lx+y)\) generates the composite pair by evaluating the perturbation at \(y=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel primal–dual architectures are reusable templates rather than assertions of strong duality. The sum template pairs minimization of \(f+h\) with minimization of \(f^*(-u)+h^*(u)\). The linear-composite template replaces \(h\) by \(g\circ L\) and inserts the adjoint \(L^*\) into the dual. The former is the identity-map specialization of the latter, and both arise from a bivariate perturbation model.
assumptions_latex: The functions in each template are proper.
The composite template uses a bounded linear map \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sum, linear-composite, and perturbation representations form compatible canonical Fenchel architectures, with the sum form obtained by setting \(L=\operatorname{Id}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The composite dual may be written as \(\sup_v[-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)]\).
For \(F(x,y)=f(x)+g(Lx+y)\), the primal objective is \(F(x,0)\).
special_cases_latex: Indicator functions turn either template into constrained convex optimization.
When \(L=0\), the primal separates into minimization of \(f\) plus the constant \(g(0)\), while the dual retains the feasibility condition encoded by \(g^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Sign changes in the dual variable give equivalent presentations of the same architecture.
Qualification, equality of values, and attainment must be appended to the architecture rather than inferred from it.
boundary_notes: A nonlinear inner map is not covered by the linear-composite template.
The displayed perturbation is one canonical realization; other perturbations may yield different but valid dual architectures.

notation.meaning: Pairing of primal and dual problem forms, not automatic equality of their values.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Splitting Representation of Sum Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating the primal variable and imposing equality gives a saddle representation whose lower value is the sum-form Fenchel dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sum problem has the equivalent constrained form \[\inf_{x,z\in X}\{f(x)+g(z):x=z\}.\] For \(u\in X^*\), define \[\mathcal L(x,z,u)=f(x)+g(z)-\langle u,x-z\rangle.\] Its lower value in \((x,z)\) is \[\inf_{x,z}\mathcal L(x,z,u)=-f^*(u)-g^*(-u),\] so the associated dual is \(\sup_u\{-f^*(u)-g^*(-u)\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{u\in X^*}\inf_{x,z\in X}\mathcal L(x,z,u)=\sup_{u\in X^*}\{-f^*(u)-g^*(-u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent split-variable saddle representation of the sum-form Fenchel pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum-Form Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-interior qualification makes the infimum of a convex sum equal to its attained Fenchel dual maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal problem \(p=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(x)\}\), the Fenchel dual is \[d=\sup_{u\in X^*}\{-f^*(u)-g^*(-u)\}.\] Weak duality gives \(d\le p\). Under the stated relative-interior qualification, \(p=d\); moreover, if \(p\) is finite, the dual supremum is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel duality for a sum under relative-interior qualification.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise primal-dual optimality certificate for the two-summand architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(u\), \[f(x)+g(x)+f^*(u)+g^*(-u)=[f(x)+f^*(u)-\langle u,x\rangle]+[g(x)+g^*(-u)+\langle u,x\rangle]\ge 0.\] Equality holds exactly when \(u\in\partial f(x)\) and \(-u\in\partial g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum-form primal-dual gap is the sum of two Fenchel–Young residuals and vanishes exactly at the coupled subgradient conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)+g(x)+f^*(u)+g^*(-u)=0\iff u\in\partial f(x)\ \text{and}\ -u\in\partial g(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel-Gap Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-splitting representation specific to the two-summand primal-dual architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem \(\inf_x\{f(x)+g(x)\}\) is equivalent to \(\inf_{x,z}\{f(x)+g(z):x=z\}\). For \(L(x,z,u)=f(x)+g(z)-\langle u,x-z\rangle\), \[\inf_{x,z}L(x,z,u)=-f^*(u)-g^*(-u),\] so its Lagrange dual is \(\sup_u\{-f^*(u)-g^*(-u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting the common argument and dualizing the equality constraint produces the sum-form Fenchel dual.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Constrained Split Representation

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f,g:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the sum-form primal, dual, values, and gap. Closed convex hypotheses are required only for standard strong-duality results, not to form the pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sum-form Fenchel primal problem associated with the ordered pair \((f,g)\) is \[\text{(P)}\quad\inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\{f(x)+g(x)\}.\] Its Fenchel dual in minimization form is \[\text{(D)}\quad\inf_{u\in\mathcal H}\{f^*(-u)+g^*(u)\}.\] If \(p^*=\inf(f+g)\) and \(d^*=\inf(f^{*\vee}+g^*)\), where \(f^{*\vee}(u)=f^*(-u)\), then weak duality is \(p^*\geq-d^*\). The pair has zero duality gap when \(p^*=-d^*\); dual attainment means \(d^*=f^*(-\bar u)+g^*(\bar u)\) for some \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sum-form duality pairs the primal minimization of \(f(x)+g(x)\) with the dual minimization of \(f^*(-u)+g^*(u)\). The construction depends on the ordered pair because the sign is attached to the first conjugate. Weak duality always compares the primal value with the negative dual value. Zero gap and attainment are additional outcomes, not defining assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper functions on the same Hilbert space.
Their Fenchel conjugates are taken with respect to the Hilbert-space pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sum-form dual pair is \(\inf_x(f+g)(x)\) and \(\inf_u(f^*(-u)+g^*(u))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The maximization-form dual is \(\sup_u\{-f^*(-u)-g^*(u)\}\).
Replacing \(u\) by \(-u\) yields \(\inf_u(f^*(u)+g^*(-u))\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=\iota_C\), the primal is minimization of \(f\) over \(C\), and the dual contains \(\sigma_C=g^*\).
If \(g=0\), then \(g^*=\iota_{\{0\}}\), so the dual variable is forced to zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: For every \(x,u\), \(f(x)+g(x)+f^*(-u)+g^*(u)\geq0\).
The dual depends on the decomposition of the primal objective into the ordered summands \(f\) and \(g\).
boundary_notes: The equality \(p^*=-d^*\) can fail without a constraint qualification.
The definition allows extended optimal values; care is required when forming their arithmetic gap.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of the sum-form Fenchel dual by duplicating the primal variable and dualizing equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sum problem admits the equivalent split form \[\inf_{x,z}\{f(x)+g(z):x=z\}.\] With multiplier \(u\in X^*\), its Lagrangian is \[\mathcal L(x,z,u)=f(x)+g(z)-\langle u,x-z\rangle.\] Therefore its dual function is \[q(u)=\inf_{x,z}\mathcal L(x,z,u)=-f^*(u)-g^*(-u),\] and maximizing \(q\) gives the sum-form Fenchel dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating the primal variable and dualizing the equality constraint yields the conjugate objective minus f-star at u minus g-star at minus u.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{u\in X^*}\inf_{x,z}\mathcal L(x,z,u)=\sup_{u\in X^*}\{-f^*(u)-g^*(-u)\}.

Linear-Composite Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A qualified linear-composite problem has the same value as its Fenchel–Rockafellar dual, whose dual variable acts through the adjoint map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\), the Fenchel–Rockafellar dual problem is \[d=\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}.\] Weak duality gives \(d\le p\). Under the stated qualification, \(p=d\); if the common value is finite, the dual supremum is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Rockafellar duality for a linear composite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel duality for a linear composite
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H,\mathcal K\) be real Hilbert spaces, \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(g:\mathcal K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-composite convex architecture with a bounded linear map and Hilbert adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear-composite Fenchel pair generated by \((f,g,L)\) is \[\text{(P)}\quad\inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\{f(x)+g(Lx)\},\qquad \text{(D)}\quad\inf_{v\in\mathcal K}\{f^*(-L^*v)+g^*(v)\}.\] Its primal feasibility domain is \[\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:Lx\in\operatorname{dom}g\},\] and its dual feasibility domain is \[\{v\in\operatorname{dom}g^*:-L^*v\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}.\] The coupling of primal and dual variables is mediated by \(L\) in the primal and by \(-L^*\) in the dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-composite duality is the Fenchel architecture for minimizing \(f(x)+g(Lx)\). Its dual variable belongs to the codomain of \(L\), and the adjoint transports it back to the domain through \(-L^*v\). The effective-domain conditions shown in the definition specify primal and dual feasibility independently of any strong-duality qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite primal–dual objectives are \(f+g\circ L\) and \(v\mapsto f^*(-L^*v)+g^*(v)\), with the stated feasibility domains.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The dual maximizes \(-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\).
Using \(w=-v\), the dual minimizes \(f^*(L^*w)+g^*(-w)\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(L=\operatorname{Id}\) recovers sum-form duality.
Taking \(f=\iota_C\) or \(g=\iota_D\) produces constrained composite problems involving support functions in the dual.
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal is proper only if \(L(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\).
Dual certificates naturally live in \(\mathcal K\), even when primal variables live in \(\mathcal H\).
boundary_notes: Unbounded or nonlinear operators require a different functional-analytic setup.
Feasibility of both problems does not alone imply equality or attainment.

notation.meaning: Adjoint map from K to H.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbation value function and conjugate dual
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(U=\mathbb R^m\), and let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex function. The unperturbed parameter is \(0\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex perturbation framework; the value function may fail to be closed at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The value function of the perturbation \(F\) is \[p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u),\qquad u\in U.\] The associated primal value is \(p(0)=\inf_xF(x,0)\). With the conjugate \[F^*(x^*,u^*)=\sup_{x,u}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle+\langle u^*,u\rangle-F(x,u)\},\] the perturbation dual is \[\sup_{u^*\in U}\{-F^*(0,u^*)\}=-\inf_{u^*\in U}F^*(0,u^*).\] A vector \(\bar u^*\) is a supporting multiplier at the origin when \(-\bar u^*\in\partial p(0)\), equivalently \[p(u)\geq p(0)-\langle\bar u^*,u\rangle\qquad(\forall u\in U).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex perturbation function \(F(x,u)\) generates the value function \(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\). The original problem is the slice at \(u=0\). Conjugating jointly in the decision and perturbation variables yields the dual objective \(-F^*(0,u^*)\). Supporting subgradients of \(p\) at zero are precisely the perturbation multipliers, with the displayed sign convention.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a proper convex function on \(X\times U\).
The primal slice is indexed by the distinguished parameter \(u=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\), the primal value is \(p(0)\), and the conjugate dual value is \(\sup_{u^*}-F^*(0,u^*)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The dual minimization form is \(\inf_{u^*}F^*(0,u^*)\).
\(-\bar u^*\in\partial p(0)\) is equivalent to \(p(u)+\langle\bar u^*,u\rangle\geq p(0)\) for every \(u\).
special_cases_latex: For \(F(x,y)=f(x)+g(Lx+y)\), this construction yields the linear-composite Fenchel dual.
If \(F\) is polyhedral, then its value function is polyhedral whenever it is proper.
immediate_consequences_latex: The lower-semicontinuous closure of \(p\) at zero governs the possible duality gap.
Sensitivity multipliers are encoded by the subdifferential \(\partial p(0)\).
boundary_notes: The infimum defining \(p(u)\) need not be attained.
Convexity of \(F\) makes \(p\) convex, but it does not automatically make \(p\) closed at \(0\).

notation.meaning: Dual variable paired with the perturbation parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perturbation function embeds one convex problem into a parameterized family, with parameter zero representing the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A perturbation function for a convex optimization problem is a proper convex mapping \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that the reference primal problem is \[\inf_{x\in X}F(x,0).\] For each \(u\in U\), the function \(x\mapsto F(x,u)\) specifies the problem obtained by applying perturbation \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) represents a parameterized primal family with reference problem \(\inf_x F(x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex perturbation model with reference parameter zero.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Improper Marginals from Proper Joint Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex joint function can have a marginal identically equal to negative infinity, so marginal properness must be assumed or verified separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Properness of \(F\) does not ensure properness of its marginal. For example, on \(X=U=\mathbb R\), the proper closed convex function \(F(x,u)=x\) has \[p(u)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}x=-\infty\qquad\text{for every }u.\] Consequently a general marginal must be allowed to take the value \(-\infty\); statements treating \(p\) as a proper convex function require that properness as an additional assumption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is proper closed convex but \(p\equiv-\infty\), so \(p\) is not proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value failure boundary for partial minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Projection and Attainment Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected epigraph contains every strict marginal epigraph point, while a finite boundary point is present exactly when the corresponding fiber infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\). Then \[\operatorname{proj}_{U\times\mathbb R}(\operatorname{epi}F)=\{(u,t):\exists x\in X,\ F(x,u)\le t\}\subseteq\operatorname{epi}p.\] Whenever \(p(u)<t\), the point \((u,t)\) belongs to this projection. If \(p(u)\in\mathbb R\), the boundary point \((u,p(u))\) belongs to the projection exactly when \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x}F(x,u)\neq\varnothing\). Thus equality with \(\operatorname{epi}p\) at finite boundary values is an attainment property, not a consequence of joint convexity alone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite boundary membership in the projected epigraph is equivalent to attainment of the marginal infimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph relation for partial minimization, including the boundary distinction caused by nonattainment.

notation.meaning: epigraph of the joint perturbation function
minimizers in the decision fiber at parameter u

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Value Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The marginal value function assigns each perturbation parameter the infimum of the corresponding primal problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The marginal value function induced by \(F\) is \[p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u),\qquad u\in U,\] where the infimum may take an extended-real value. Because partial minimization preserves convexity, \(p\) is convex whenever it is proper. Its reference value \(p(0)\) is the primal optimal value.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex perturbation function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(0)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,0)\) is the reference primal value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value function obtained by partial minimization over primal variables.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact subgradient transfer at a parameter whose fiber minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_xF(x,\bar u)\), so \(F(\bar x,\bar u)=p(\bar u)\in\mathbb R\). Then, for every \(u^*\in U^*\), \[u^*\in\partial p(\bar u)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(0,u^*)\in\partial F(\bar x,\bar u).\] Each such \(u^*\) supplies the global sensitivity bound \(p(u)\ge p(\bar u)+\langle u^*,u-\bar u\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an attained fiber minimum, marginal subgradients are exactly joint subgradients with zero eliminated-variable component and give global affine sensitivity bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) attains the finite marginal value at \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u^*\in\partial p(\bar u)\iff(0,u^*)\in\partial F(\bar x,\bar u)\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the marginal value function
joint dual vector with zero eliminated-coordinate component

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Subgradients as Sensitivity Prices
Conjugate Dual Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of the marginal value function is the joint conjugate of the perturbation function at zero primal dual coordinate; maximizing its negative gives the conjugate dual value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u^*\in U^*\), the conjugate of the marginal value function satisfies \[p^*(u^*)=\sup_{u\in U}\{\langle u^*,u\rangle-p(u)\}=F^*(0,u^*).\] Hence the conjugate dual of the reference problem has value \[\sup_{u^*\in U^*}\{-p^*(u^*)\}=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}\{-F^*(0,u^*)\}=p^{**}(0),\] and weak duality gives \(p^{**}(0)\le p(0)\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(U\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces with duals \(X^*\) and \(U^*\).
\(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex perturbation function.
The marginal value function \(p:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), defined by \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\), is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*(u^*)=F^*(0,u^*)\) for every \(u^*\in U^*\), and the conjugate dual value is \(\sup_{u^*\in U^*}-F^*(0,u^*)=p^{**}(0)\le p(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate dual obtained from the marginal value function in finite-dimensional perturbation duality.

notation.meaning: joint Fenchel conjugate of F on the dual product space
zero element of the primal dual space

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Parameter Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, closedness of the marginal value function at zero is equivalent to equality between the reference primal value and the conjugate dual value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Reference-parameter closedness means that \(p\) is lower semicontinuous at \(0\), namely \[p(0)\le\liminf_{u\to0}p(u).\] For a proper convex function on finite-dimensional \(U\) with finite \(p(0)\), this is equivalent to \[p(0)=p^{**}(0).\] Since the conjugate dual value is \(p^{**}(0)\), reference-parameter closedness is equivalent to zero conjugate-duality gap at the reference parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(p:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex marginal value function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is lower semicontinuous at \(0\) if and only if \(p(0)=p^{**}(0)\), equivalently if and only if the reference primal and conjugate dual values coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointwise closedness criterion at the reference perturbation.

notation.meaning: Fenchel biconjugate, equal to the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Attainment at the Reference Parameter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between zero gap and attainment of the reference conjugate-dual supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be finite-dimensional and let \(p:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex with \(p(0)\in\mathbb R\). A vector \(u^*\in U^*\) attains the conjugate-dual value \(p(0)\) in \[\sup_{v^*\in U^*}\{-p^*(v^*)\}\] if and only if \[u^*\in\partial p(0),\] equivalently \(p(0)+p^*(u^*)=0\). Thus reference closedness gives equality of values, while \(\partial p(0)\ne\varnothing\) is additionally required for dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-gap reference dual optimizer exists exactly when the value function has a subgradient at zero; reference closedness alone only ensures equality of values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u^*\) attains the conjugate-dual value \(p(0)\) if and only if \(u^*\in\partial p(0)\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the marginal value function
convex subdifferential at the reference parameter

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Attainment at the Reference Parameter

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Sufficient Condition for Reference Closedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional parameter-space condition ensuring reference closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on a finite-dimensional space. If \[0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}p),\] then \(p\) is continuous relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}p)\) at \(0\), hence is lower semicontinuous there and satisfies \[p(0)=p^{**}(0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reference parameter in the relative interior of the value-function domain guarantees reference closedness and zero gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is lower semicontinuous at \(0\) and \(p(0)=p^{**}(0)\).

notation.meaning: relative interior of the effective domain of p
