knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be nonempty sets and \(\Phi:X\times Z\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). The first variable is minimized and the second is maximized.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract minimax definition; convexity, concavity, compactness, and semicontinuity are sufficient-condition regimes rather than parts of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((\bar x,\bar z)\in X\times Z\) is a saddle point of \(\Phi\) when \[\Phi(\bar x,z)\leq\Phi(\bar x,\bar z)\leq\Phi(x,\bar z)\qquad(\forall x\in X)(\forall z\in Z).\] Equivalently, \[\sup_{z\in Z}\Phi(\bar x,z)=\Phi(\bar x,\bar z)=\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x,\bar z).\] The lower and upper minimax values are \[\underline v=\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x,z),\qquad \overline v=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\Phi(x,z),\] and always satisfy \(\underline v\leq\overline v\). The saddle-minimax interface is exact when a saddle point exists, in which case \(\underline v=\overline v=\Phi(\bar x,\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle point simultaneously minimizes the function in its first variable and maximizes it in its second. Its defining two-sided inequality is equivalent to equality between the corresponding row supremum, saddle value, and column infimum. The general minimax inequality places the supremum-infimum below the infimum-supremum; a saddle point forces equality and attainment at the chosen pair.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is an extended-real bifunction for which the displayed extrema are interpreted in the extended-real order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar z)\) is a saddle point exactly when \(\Phi(\bar x,z)\leq\Phi(\bar x,\bar z)\leq\Phi(x,\bar z)\) for all \(x,z\); its existence yields minimax equality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}_x\Phi(x,\bar z)\) and \(\bar z\in\operatorname{argmax}_z\Phi(\bar x,z)\).
\(\sup_z\Phi(\bar x,z)=\Phi(\bar x,\bar z)=\inf_x\Phi(x,\bar z)\).
special_cases_latex: For a Fenchel Lagrangian \(\mathcal L(x,v)=f(x)+\langle Lx,v\rangle-g^*(v)\), saddle points encode simultaneous primal and dual optimality when the values are finite and equal.
immediate_consequences_latex: If minimax equality fails, no saddle point exists.
When equality holds and both outer extrema are attained, any primal minimizer and dual maximizer combine into a saddle point.
boundary_notes: Minimax equality without attainment does not produce a saddle point.
The inequality orientation reverses if the first variable is maximized and the second minimized.

knowledge_statements.title: Sectionwise Subgradient Certificate for Saddle Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is a saddle point exactly when it minimizes the constrained section in the minimizing variable and the negative constrained section in the maximizing variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((\bar x,\bar y)\in X\times Y\), set \[F_{\bar y}(x)=L(x,\bar y)+\delta_X(x),\qquad G_{\bar x}(y)=-L(\bar x,y)+\delta_Y(y).\] If both are proper convex and finite at \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y\), respectively, then \[(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is a saddle point}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial F_{\bar y}(\bar x)\ \text{and}\ 0\in\partial G_{\bar x}(\bar y).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F_{\bar y}\) and \(G_{\bar x}\) are proper convex and finite at their candidate minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is a saddle point}\iff 0\in\partial F_{\bar y}(\bar x)\text{ and }0\in\partial G_{\bar x}(\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order characterization using constrained convex sections.

notation.meaning: constrained section in the minimizing variable
negative constrained section in the maximizing variable

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Concave Saddle Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-concave function is convex in its minimizing variable and concave in its maximizing variable; a saddle point satisfies both unilateral optimality inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty convex sets. A function \(L:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex-concave when \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex for every \(y\in Y\) and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave for every \(x\in X\). A point \((\bar x,\bar y)\in X\times Y\) with \(L(\bar x,\bar y)\in\mathbb R\) is a saddle point when \[L(\bar x,y)\le L(\bar x,\bar y)\le L(x,\bar y)\quad\text{for all }x\in X,\ y\in Y.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of real vector spaces.
The extended-real sections of \(L\) are well-defined.
\(L(\bar x,\bar y)\) is finite at a candidate saddle point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a saddle point exactly when \(L(\bar x,y)\le L(\bar x,\bar y)\le L(x,\bar y)\) for every \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of convex-concave sections and saddle points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential Certificate for a Convex-Concave Saddle Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order saddle certificate for finite-dimensional convex-concave sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and suppose the sections \(x\mapsto L(x,\bar y)\) and \(y\mapsto-L(\bar x,y)\) are proper convex functions with \(L(\bar x,\bar y)\in\mathbb R\). Then \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a saddle point if and only if \[0\in\partial_xL(\bar x,\bar y),\qquad 0\in\partial_y[-L](\bar x,\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex-concave pair is a saddle point exactly when zero belongs to the two appropriate section subdifferentials.
assumptions_latex: \(x\mapsto L(x,\bar y)\) and \(y\mapsto-L(\bar x,y)\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a saddle point if and only if \(0\in\partial_xL(\bar x,\bar y)\) and \(0\in\partial_y[-L](\bar x,\bar y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Certificate for a Convex-Concave Saddle Point
Saddle-Function Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex–concave saddle functions and saddle points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional real vector spaces. A real-valued function \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is a convex–concave saddle function when \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), and \(y\mapsto L(x,y)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). A pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point when
\[L(\bar x,y)\le L(\bar x,\bar y)\le L(x,\bar y)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X,\ y\in Y.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle function is convex in its minimizing variable and concave in its maximizing variable. A saddle point simultaneously satisfies both one-sided optimality inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a saddle point exactly when \(L(\bar x,y)\le L(\bar x,\bar y)\le L(x,\bar y)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic characterization through unilateral optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be nonempty sets and let \(L(\bar x,\bar y)\in\mathbb R\). A pair \((\bar x,\bar y)\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point if and only if \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,\bar y),\qquad \bar y\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}L(\bar x,y).\] Every such pair satisfies \[\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=L(\bar x,\bar y)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite saddle point is exactly a simultaneous section minimizer and maximizer, and its value equals both minimax values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a saddle point exactly when it is a simultaneous section minimizer and maximizer; then both minimax values equal \(L(\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer Characterization of Saddle Points

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order geometric characterization of a saddle point using constrained convex sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional real vector spaces, and let \(L:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\). For \((\bar x,\bar y)\in X\times Y\), define \(F_{\bar y}(x)=L(x,\bar y)+\delta_X(x)\) and \(G_{\bar x}(y)=-L(\bar x,y)+\delta_Y(y)\), and assume these functions are proper convex. Then \[(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is a saddle point}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\partial F_{\bar y}(\bar x)\ \text{ and }\ 0\in\partial G_{\bar x}(\bar y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is a saddle point exactly when it minimizes the constrained convex section in the minimizing variable and minimizes the negative constrained concave section in the maximizing variable; equivalently, both sectionwise convex subdifferentials contain zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex for each \(y\), and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave for each \(x\).
\(F_{\bar y}=L(\cdot,\bar y)+\delta_X\) and \(G_{\bar x}=-L(\bar x,\cdot)+\delta_Y\) are proper convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\text{ is a saddle point}\iff 0\in\partial F_{\bar y}(\bar x)\text{ and }0\in\partial G_{\bar x}(\bar y).

knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Characterization of Saddle Points
Weak Minimax Ordering and Sion Equality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower minimax value never exceeds the upper value; Sion's compact convex-concave regime makes them equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\), define \[\underline v=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y),\qquad \overline v=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y).\] Always \(\underline v\le\overline v\). If \(X\) and \(Y\) are convex subsets of Hausdorff topological vector spaces, \(X\) is compact, every \(L(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous and convex on \(X\), and every \(L(x,\cdot)\) is upper semicontinuous and concave on \(Y\), then \(\underline v=\overline v\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex subsets of Hausdorff topological vector spaces.
\(L(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous and convex for every \(y\in Y\).
\(L(x,\cdot)\) is upper semicontinuous and concave for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-level minimax relation and its standard convex-concave compactness regime.
Universal ordering of lower and upper minimax values without convexity or topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(X,Y\) and every function \(L:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), \[\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\le \inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower minimax value never exceeds the upper minimax value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_y\inf_xL(x,y)\le\inf_x\sup_yL(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Minimax Inequality
Minimax Value Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak minimax inequality and the value equality induced by a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any function \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) on nonempty sets, define
\[\underline v=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y),\qquad \overline v=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y).\]
Then the weak minimax inequality \(\underline v\le\overline v\) always holds. If \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is a finite-valued saddle point, then
\[\underline v=L(\bar x,\bar y)=\overline v,\]
and \(\bar x\) minimizes \(x\mapsto\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\), while \(\bar y\) maximizes \(y\mapsto\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The max–min value never exceeds the min–max value. A finite saddle point makes both values equal to its saddle value.
assumptions_latex: \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has well-defined iterated extrema.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\underline v\le\overline v\); if a finite-valued saddle point \((\bar x,\bar y)\) exists, then \(\underline v=L(\bar x,\bar y)=\overline v\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Dual Embeddings
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions, a linear-composite Fenchel primal and its dual are respectively the upper and lower values of one convex-concave saddle function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Fenchel saddle function \[L(x,y^*)=f(x)+\langle Ax,y^*\rangle-g^*(y^*),\qquad (x,y^*)\in X\times Y^*.\] Fenchel biconjugacy for \(g\) gives \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}L(x,y^*)=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}.\] Minimizing first gives \[\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y^*)=\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces with duals \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\), and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}L(x,y^*)\) is the linear-composite primal value, while \(\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y^*)\) is its Fenchel dual value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle representation of finite-dimensional linear-composite Fenchel primal and dual problems.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saddle Certificate for the Fenchel Embedding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality certificate intrinsic to the linear-composite Fenchel saddle representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[L(x,y^*)=f(x)+\langle Ax,y^*\rangle-g^*(y^*),\] a pair \((\bar x,\bar y^*)\) is a saddle point if and only if \[-A^*\bar y^*\in\partial f(\bar x),\qquad \bar y^*\in\partial g(A\bar x).\] Equivalently, the two associated Fenchel--Young residuals vanish. Such a pair solves the embedded primal and dual problems and has equal primal and dual objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pair solves the embedded Fenchel primal and dual with zero gap exactly when the two associated subgradient inclusions hold.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y^*)\) is a saddle point if and only if \(-A^*\bar y^*\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(\bar y^*\in\partial g(A\bar x)\).

Noncompact Bilinear Minimax Gap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On two noncompact positive rays, the bilinear payoff has lower minimax value zero and upper minimax value infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=(0,+\infty)\) and \(L(x,y)=xy\). Then \[\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=0,\qquad \inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=+\infty.\] Thus separate affinity, and hence convex-concavity, does not imply minimax interchange without an additional compactness, coercivity, or comparable qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_y\inf_xL(x,y)=0<+\infty=\inf_x\sup_yL(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of minimax interchange for an affine payoff on noncompact convex domains.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness Alone Does Not Permit Minimax Interchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite compact strategy sets lacking convex-concave structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\{0,1\}\) and let \(L(x,y)=1\) when \(x=y\), with \(L(x,y)=0\) otherwise. Then \[\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=0<1=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y).\] Thus compactness of both strategy sets alone does not imply minimax interchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-action matching payoff has lower value zero and upper value one despite both strategy sets being compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_y\inf_xL(x,y)=0<1=\inf_x\sup_yL(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Alone Does Not Permit Minimax Interchange

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A continuous convex–affine example separating structural shape assumptions from compactness or coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R\), \(Y=(0,+\infty)\), and \(L(x,y)=e^x y\). For every \(y>0\), \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex and continuous, and for every \(x\), \(L(x,\cdot)\) is affine. Nevertheless, \[\sup_{y>0}\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}e^xy=0,\qquad \inf_{x\in\mathbb R}\sup_{y>0}e^xy=+\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity–concavity and continuity do not prevent a strict minimax gap on noncompact domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_y\inf_xL(x,y)=0<+\infty=\inf_x\sup_yL(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact Convex–Concave Interchange Failure
Minimax Interchange Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict minimax gap caused by loss of compactness and coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Convexity–concavity alone does not justify interchanging infimum and supremum. Take \(X=Y=(0,+\infty)\) and \(L(x,y)=xy\). The function is affine, hence both convex and concave, in each variable. Nevertheless,
\[\sup_{y>0}\inf_{x>0}xy=\sup_{y>0}0=0,\]
whereas
\[\inf_{x>0}\sup_{y>0}xy=\inf_{x>0}(+\infty)=+\infty.\]
Thus the minimax equality fails when compactness, coercivity, or another hypothesis controlling escape to the boundary or infinity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On positive open half-lines, the bilinear payoff has max–min value zero and min–max value infinity. Convexity–concavity alone therefore does not permit interchange.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be convex sets, with \(X\) compact. Suppose that for every \(y\in Y\), \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\) is lower semicontinuous and quasiconvex on \(X\), and for every \(x\in X\), \(y\mapsto L(x,y)\) is upper semicontinuous and quasiconcave on \(Y\). Then \[\min_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\sup_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactness of the minimizing strategy set, together with appropriate semicontinuity and quasiconvex–quasiconcave structure, permits minimax interchange.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are convex subsets of real topological vector spaces.
\(L(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous and quasiconvex for every \(y\), while \(L(x,\cdot)\) is upper semicontinuous and quasiconcave for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)=\sup_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singleton indicators violate the ambient continuity-point condition but still exhibit attained strong Fenchel duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=I\), and \(f=g=\delta_{\{0\}}\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuity-point qualification fails, but \(p^\star=d^\star=0\) and both optima are attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The outer-function continuity-point qualification for \(f+g\circ L\) is \[(\exists x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f)\quad Lx_0\in\operatorname{cont}g.\] In finite dimensions, when \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\), this is equivalent to \[(\exists x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f)\quad Lx_0\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}g.\] Consequently \(L(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\), which implies \[0\in\operatorname{int}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr)\subseteq\operatorname{sri}igl(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr).\] For the sum form, one may symmetrically require one summand to be continuous at a point of the other summand's domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuity-point qualification requires a feasible point \(x_0\) for \(f\) whose image \(Lx_0\) is a continuity point of \(g\). In Euclidean spaces this is the familiar requirement that \(Lx_0\) lie in the ordinary interior of \(\operatorname{dom}g\). It is stronger than the relative-interior qualification when the outer domain is lower-dimensional, but it directly yields interiority of the domain difference.
assumptions_latex: For the interior formulation, \(g\) is continuous on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
A continuity point \(Lx_0\in
i\operatorname{cont}g\) with \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) supplies \(0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f))\).

For \(L=\operatorname{Id}\), it becomes \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{cont}g\neq\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g\) is finite and continuous everywhere, every point of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is a qualifying point.
The roles of the two summands in sum-form duality may be exchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: The composite Fenchel dual has zero gap and attains its minimum under the standard closed-convex hypotheses.
The condition ensures primal feasibility because \(Lx_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\).

In infinite dimensions, domain interior may be empty even for important convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Qualification Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of the relative-interior condition does not by itself imply a duality gap or nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=I\), \(f=\delta_{[0,\infty)}\), and \(g=\delta_{\{0\}}\). Then \(0\notin\operatorname{ri}(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g)\), while \[\min_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}=\max_{y^*}\{-f^*(-y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}=0,\] and both extrema are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\notin\operatorname{ri}(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g),\qquad \min_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}=\max_{y^*}\{-f^*(-y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}=0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional Fenchel problem having exact attained duality although the relative-interior qualification fails.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Qualifications
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-interior intersection of the two effective-domain images guarantees zero Fenchel duality gap and dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative-interior qualification is \[0\in\operatorname{ri}\bigl(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr).\] Equivalently, \(A(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f))\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing\). When it holds, the Fenchel primal and dual values agree and the dual supremum is attained: \[p=\max_{y^*\in Y^*}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\bigr).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Qualification Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-dimensional polyhedral Fenchel problems with finite primal value attain equal primal and dual optima without another interior condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) and \(g\) are polyhedral convex and the primal value is finite, no separate relative-interior condition is required. Both optimization problems attain their finite optimal values, and \[\min_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+g(Ax)\bigr)=\max_{y^*\in Y^*}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\bigr).\] Thus polyhedrality supplies the closedness needed for exact Fenchel duality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous polyhedral convex functions.
The composite primal value \(p=\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedral Fenchel duality without an additional relative-interior qualification.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Primal-Dual Optimality Characterizations p. 154

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral closedness underlying the full-polyhedral qualification regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For proper lower-semicontinuous polyhedral convex \(f\) and \(g\), define \[v(u)=\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax-u)\}.\] Its epigraph has the polyhedral projection representation \[\operatorname{epi}v=\operatorname{proj}_{(u,r)}\{(u,r,x,\alpha,\beta):(x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{epi}f,\ (Ax-u,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}g,\ \alpha+\beta\le r\}.\] Thus \(v\) is a closed polyhedral convex value function whenever it is proper; if \(v(0)\in\mathbb R\), the infimum defining \(v(0)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polyhedral perturbation value has a closed polyhedral epigraph, and a finite reference value is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}v\ \text{is a closed polyhedron and }v(0)\text{ is attained}.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\), with \(\mathcal K\) finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral outer functions in finite-dimensional image spaces, plus the fully polyhedral finite-dimensional specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(g\) is polyhedral when \(\operatorname{epi}g\) is an intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces. The polyhedral qualification regime for \(f+g\circ L\) consists of either \[(i)\quad g\ \text{polyhedral and}\quad \operatorname{dom}g\cap\operatorname{ri}L(\operatorname{dom}f)\neq\varnothing,\] or, when both spaces are finite-dimensional, \[(ii)\quad f\ \text{and}\ g\ \text{polyhedral and}\quad \operatorname{dom}g\cap L(\operatorname{dom}f)\neq\varnothing.\] Thus full polyhedrality reduces the qualification to ordinary primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral convex function has a polyhedral epigraph. If the outer function is polyhedral, Fenchel duality requires only that its domain meet the relative interior of the image of the other domain. If both functions are polyhedral in finite dimensions, even this relative-interior requirement drops away: nonempty intersection of the two relevant domains, equivalently primal feasibility, is sufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
For the pure-feasibility regime, \(\mathcal H\) is finite-dimensional and both functions are polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polyhedrality permits the relative-interior qualifications to be weakened as in conditions \((i)\) and \((ii)\), with condition \((ii)\) requiring only feasibility.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Condition \((ii)\) is \((\exists x\in\operatorname{dom}f)\;Lx\in\operatorname{dom}g\).
For \(L=\operatorname{Id}\) and polyhedral \(f,g\), condition \((ii)\) is \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: Piecewise-affine convex functions and indicators of polyhedral convex sets are polyhedral functions.
Linear programming is contained in the fully polyhedral feasibility regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under either regime, the Fenchel–Rockafellar primal and dual values agree with the conventional sign change and the dual minimum is attained.
The relaxation reflects closedness properties of polyhedral projections and sums.
boundary_notes: If only one function is polyhedral, arbitrary feasibility is generally weaker than the cited sufficient condition.
Finite-dimensionality is part of the stated polyhedral projection regime.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H,\mathcal K\) be real Hilbert spaces, \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\). Set \(Q=\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces with norm closure in the strong-relative-interior definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathcal K\), its strong relative interior is \[\operatorname{sri}C=\{z\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-z)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(C-z)\}.\] The canonical infinite-dimensional Fenchel–Rockafellar qualification is \[0\in\operatorname{sri}Q,\qquad Q=\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f),\] equivalently \[\operatorname{cone}Q=\overline{\operatorname{span}}Q.\] A standard sufficient Attouch–Brézis form is that \(\operatorname{cone}Q\) itself be a closed linear subspace. For sum-form duality, this becomes \(0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, the canonical domain qualification uses strong relative interior. Zero qualifies when the cone generated by the domain difference equals the closed linear span of that difference. This explicitly incorporates the closed-span requirement absent from finite-dimensional relative-interior rules. The Attouch–Brézis condition states the same geometry by requiring the generated cone to be a closed linear subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
Closures are taken in the norm topology of \(\mathcal K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f))\), equivalently equality of its generated cone and closed span.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f))=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f))\).
For sum form, \(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\) is a closed linear subspace.
special_cases_latex: If the domain difference is a closed linear subspace, the qualification holds.
If the domain difference has nonempty norm interior containing zero, the qualification holds.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Fenchel–Rockafellar dual value equals the primal value with the standard sign convention, and the dual minimum is attained.
The condition also yields exact conjugation formulas for sums and linear composites.
boundary_notes: Replacing \(\operatorname{sri}\) by \(\operatorname{ri}\) can fail when the relevant linear span is not closed.
Nonempty quasi-relative interior alone is not the qualification asserted here.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal K\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\), and let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) and \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\). Set \(C=\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\subseteq\mathcal K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the algebraic-core qualification in a Hilbert-space Fenchel–Rockafellar composite problem. It distinguishes core membership from strong-relative-interior, relative-interior, and ordinary-interior conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{core}C:=\{y\in C\mid \operatorname{cone}(C-y)=\mathcal K\}.\] The core qualification holds precisely when \[0\in\operatorname{core}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr),\] equivalently, when \(0\in C\) and, for every \(d\in\mathcal K\), there exist \(t>0\), \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(z\in\operatorname{dom}g\) such that \(d=t(z-Lx)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the displacement set \(C=\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\), the core consists of those \(y\in C\) for which every direction of \(\mathcal K\) is a positive multiple of an element of \(C-y\). The core qualification requires the origin to have this property. Thus every \(d\in\mathcal K\) must admit \(d=t(z-Lx)\) for some \(t>0\), \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(z\in\operatorname{dom}g\).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal K\) are real Hilbert spaces.
\(L:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K\) is bounded and linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathrm{CQ}_{\mathrm{core}}(f,g,L)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\operatorname{core}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{cone}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr)=\mathcal K.\]
\[\forall d\in\mathcal K\;\exists t>0,\ x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ z\in\operatorname{dom}g:\ d=t(z-Lx).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then the core qualification holds.
If \(L=\operatorname{Id}\) and \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), the condition becomes \(0\in\operatorname{core}(\operatorname{dom}g-\operatorname{dom}f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The inclusions \(\operatorname{int}C\subseteq\operatorname{core}C\subseteq\operatorname{sri}C\subseteq\operatorname{ri}C\) place the core condition strictly between ordinary-interior and strong-relative-interior qualifications in general.
Because \(\operatorname{cone}C=\mathcal K\), the core condition also implies \(0\in\operatorname{sri}C\).
boundary_notes: The core is taken in the whole ambient space \(\mathcal K\), not merely in \(\operatorname{aff}C\); hence it may be empty for a lower-dimensional displacement set.
The condition is sufficient in standard Fenchel–Rockafellar results but is not necessary for zero duality gap or dual attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic-Core Qualifications
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algebraic-core qualification requires the origin to admit a small feasible displacement in every ambient direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(D\subseteq Y\), its algebraic core is \[\operatorname{core}D=\left\{z\in D:\forall d\in Y\;\exists\varepsilon>0\;\forall t\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon),\ z+td\in D\right\}.\] The algebraic-core Fenchel qualification is the predicate \(0\in\operatorname{core}(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g)\). It is an algebraic condition and, without additional topology-dependent hypotheses, does not itself specify a continuous-dual strong-duality theorem.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(f,g\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algebraic-core qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{core}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient algebraic-core condition for a Fenchel domain-difference set.

notation.meaning: Algebraic interior relative to all ambient directions.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The ambient algebraic-core definition and qualification predicate are plausible and carefully avoid an unsupported topological strong-duality consequence, but no inspectable source is supplied for the convention or its use as a Fenchel qualification.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp geometric limitation of the ambient algebraic-core qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space \(Y\). If \(\operatorname{core}D\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{aff}D=Y\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{aff}D\neq Y\) implies \(\operatorname{core}D=\varnothing\), even when \(D\) has nonempty algebraic core relative to its affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set contained in a proper affine subspace has empty ambient algebraic core.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{core}\) is computed using all ambient directions in \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{core}D\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{aff}D=Y\).

notation.meaning: Algebraic core computed in the ambient vector space.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient Full-Dimensionality Boundary
Intrinsic-Core Qualifications
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic-core qualification requires the origin to be algebraically interior relative to the directions generated by the domain difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(D\subseteq Y\), define \[\operatorname{icr}D=\{z\in D:\operatorname{cone}(D-z)\text{ is a linear subspace of }Y\}.\] The intrinsic-core Fenchel qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{icr}(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g)\). Unlike the ambient algebraic core, it tests only directions generated by the affine hull of the domain-difference set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(f,g\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intrinsic-core qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{icr}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic-core qualification using the affine directions generated by the domain difference.

notation.meaning: Intrinsic core of a convex set.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The cone-based intrinsic-core convention is standard in parts of convex analysis, but terminology varies across sources. An authoritative locator is required before fixing this convention as candidate-review knowledge.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent relative-algebraic formulation of intrinsic core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(C\) in a real vector space \(Y\), let \(L=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\). Then \[\operatorname{icr}C=\left\{x\in C:\forall d\in L\;\exists\varepsilon>0\;\forall t\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon),\ x+td\in C\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{icr}C\) is the algebraic core of \(C\) computed in \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intrinsic core is the algebraic core relative to the affine hull of the convex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{icr}C=\operatorname{core}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\).

notation.meaning: Algebraic core using directions parallel to the affine hull of \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Hull Algebraic-Core Representation
Core-Notion Comparisons
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong relative interior lies inside intrinsic core; in finite dimensions both equal relative interior, while ambient core may vanish on lower-dimensional sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cone definitions imply \(\operatorname{sri}C\subseteq\operatorname{icr}C\), because a closed linear cone is linear, and \(\operatorname{core}C\subseteq\operatorname{icr}C\). In finite dimensions, \[\operatorname{sri}C=\operatorname{icr}C=\operatorname{ri}C.\] If \(\operatorname{aff}C=Y\), these sets also equal \(\operatorname{core}C=\operatorname{int}C\); for a proper affine hull, the ambient core and interior are empty although the relative notions may be nonempty.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real normed space \(Y\).
The intrinsic and strong relative interiors use the cone characterizations stated here.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sri}C\subseteq\operatorname{icr}C\), with equality in finite dimensions; \(\operatorname{core}C\subseteq\operatorname{icr}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under ambient-core and cone-based intrinsic-interior conventions.

notation.meaning: Algebraic core, intrinsic core, and strong relative interior.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The stated inclusions are plausible under the declared cone conventions, but the assertion equating all notions when the affine hull is the ambient space must be explicitly confined to the preceding finite-dimensional setting. The statement also contains proof-style justification and has no source supporting the conventions or comparison claims.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact comparison of intrinsic core and strong relative interior under the cone-based conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a normed space \(Y\), and set \(L=\operatorname{span}(C-C)\). Under the conventions \[\operatorname{icr}C=\{x\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=L\},\qquad \operatorname{sri}C=\{x\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=L\text{ and }L\text{ is closed}\},\] one has \[\operatorname{sri}C=\begin{cases}\operatorname{icr}C,&L\text{ is closed},\\ \varnothing,&L\text{ is not closed}.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong relative interior equals intrinsic core when the affine direction space is closed and is empty otherwise.
assumptions_latex: Intrinsic core and strong relative interior use the displayed cone conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\text{ closed}\Rightarrow\operatorname{sri}C=\operatorname{icr}C\), and \(L\text{ nonclosed}\Rightarrow\operatorname{sri}C=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Direction space parallel to the affine hull of \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Direction-Space Dichotomy
Infinite-Dimensional Core Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finitely supported sequences have full intrinsic core but empty strong relative interior inside the Hilbert space of square-summable sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=c_{00}\subset\ell^2\). For every \(x\in C\), \(\operatorname{cone}(C-x)=C\), which is a linear subspace; hence \(\operatorname{icr}C=C\). However, \(C\) is dense and not closed in \(\ell^2\), so this cone is never a closed linear subspace and \(\operatorname{sri}C=\varnothing\). Thus nonempty intrinsic core does not imply a strong-relative-interior qualification in infinite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: \(C=c_{00}\), the linear subspace of finitely supported sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{icr}C=C\) but \(\operatorname{sri}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense nonclosed subspace separating intrinsic core from strong relative interior.

notation.meaning: Intrinsic core and strong relative interior.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The dense nonclosed subspace example correctly separates intrinsic core from strong relative interior under the stated cone definitions, and counterexample is the right content kind for this failure leaf. It nevertheless lacks an authoritative source and includes derivational proof text.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional closed convex cone for which all three core-based qualification predicates fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a nonatomic finite measure space, let \(1\le p<\infty\), and set \(C=L^p_+(\Omega)\subset L^p(\Omega)\). Then \[\operatorname{core}C=\operatorname{icr}C=\operatorname{sri}C=\varnothing.\] Thus even a closed generating convex cone in an infinite-dimensional Banach space can fail all three core-based interior qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative cone in a nonatomic Lp space has empty ambient core, intrinsic core, and strong relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a nonatomic finite measure space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{core}C=\operatorname{icr}C=\operatorname{sri}C=\varnothing\).

Strong-Relative-Interior Qualifications
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The origin satisfies the strong-relative-interior qualification when its domain-difference cone is a closed linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strong relative interior of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{sri}C=\{z\in C:\operatorname{cone}(C-z)\text{ is a closed linear subspace of }Y\}.\] Accordingly, the strong-relative-interior Fenchel qualification is \[0\in\operatorname{sri}\bigl(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr).\] It strengthens the intrinsic-core condition by requiring the generated direction space to be topologically closed.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a real Banach space and \(C\subseteq Y\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strong-relative-interior qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{sri}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone-closedness definition of strong relative interior in Banach spaces.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The cone-closedness definition and resulting qualification fit the leaf, but no source is supplied. Because strong-relative-interior terminology and ambient-space assumptions can vary, an authoritative locator is required.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H,\mathcal K\) be real Hilbert spaces, \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\), \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), and \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\). Define \(C=\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition is for possibly infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, where strong relative interior can be strictly smaller than relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathcal K\), \[\operatorname{sri}C:=\{y\in C\mid \operatorname{cone}(C-y)=\overline{\operatorname{span}}(C-y)\}.\] The strong-relative-interior qualification for the composite Fenchel problem is \[0\in\operatorname{sri}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point \(y\) lies in the strong relative interior of a convex set \(C\) when the cone generated by \(C-y\) is exactly the closed linear subspace generated by \(C-y\). The strong-relative-interior qualification requires this equality at the origin for \(C=\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C=\operatorname{dom}g-L(\operatorname{dom}f)\) is viewed with the norm topology of \(\mathcal K\).
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, and \(L\) is bounded linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathrm{CQ}_{\mathrm{sri}}(f,g,L)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{cone}C=\overline{\operatorname{span}}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Since \(0\in\operatorname{sri}C\) entails \(0\in C\), the condition is equivalent to \(0\in C\) together with \(\operatorname{cone}C\) being a closed linear subspace of \(\mathcal K\).
special_cases_latex: In finite dimensions, \(\operatorname{sri}C=\operatorname{ri}C\), so the condition reduces to \(0\in\operatorname{ri}C\).
If \(C\) is a closed linear subspace, then \(\operatorname{sri}C=C\), even when \(C\neq\mathcal K\).
If \(0\in\operatorname{core}C\), then \(0\in\operatorname{sri}C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Under this qualification, the Attouch–Brézis exact-conjugacy and Fenchel dual-attainment conclusions apply to the corresponding sum formulation.
The condition permits displacement sets confined to a proper closed subspace, unlike the ambient-space core condition.
boundary_notes: In infinite-dimensional spaces, \(0\in\operatorname{ri}C\) does not by itself imply \(0\in\operatorname{sri}C\); closedness of the generated linear subspace is essential.
The closure occurs on \(\operatorname{span}(C-y)\), whereas \(\operatorname{cone}(C-y)\) itself is not closed by definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Attouch–Brézis Closedness Qualifications
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness of the linear cone generated by the domain difference guarantees exact Fenchel duality and dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Attouch–Brézis qualification requires \[\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda\bigl(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr)\] to be a closed linear subspace of \(Y\). Under this closedness condition, the composite Fenchel dual is exact and attained: \[\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+g(Ax)\bigr)=\max_{y^*\in Y^*}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\bigr).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is bounded linear, and \(f,g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda D\) is a closed linear subspace, then \(p=\max_{y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attouch–Brézis closed-subspace qualification for composite Fenchel duality.

notation.meaning: Continuous dual of the Banach space.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The closed-linear-subspace condition is recognizable as an Attouch–Brézis-type qualification, but the exact composite formulation, hypotheses, and dual-attainment conclusion require a direct authoritative source. Reversing the domain-difference sign is harmless once the generated cone is a linear subspace, but the cited theorem variant is presently unsupported.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate-level form of the Attouch–Brézis closed-subspace theorem for a composite convex sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) bounded linear, and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. If \[L=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda\bigl(A(\operatorname{dom}f)-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr)\] is a closed linear subspace of \(Y\), then for every \(x^*\in X^*\) with \((f+g\circ A)^*(x^*)<+\infty\), \[(f+g\circ A)^*(x^*)=\min_{y^*\in Y^*}\left[f^*(x^*-A^*y^*)+g^*(y^*)\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Attouch–Brézis closed-subspace condition gives an exact and attained conjugate formula for a composite convex sum.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces and \(A:X\to Y\) is bounded linear.
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\). Put \(D=\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition isolates the closedness-and-linearity form of the Attouch–Brézis qualification for a sum of two closed convex functions on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Attouch–Brézis closedness qualification holds when \[\operatorname{cone}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr)\] is a closed linear subspace of \(\mathcal H\). Equivalently, \[0\in\operatorname{sri}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\bigr).\] Under this terminology, the qualification concerns the geometry of the domain difference; exactness of conjugate infimal convolution is its associated duality outcome, not part of the defining condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Attouch–Brézis qualification requires the cone generated by the domain difference \(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g\) to be both closed and a linear subspace. This is exactly the statement that the origin lies in the strong relative interior of that domain difference.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathrm{CQ}_{\mathrm{AB}}(f,g)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\text{ is a closed linear subspace}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\mathrm{CQ}_{\mathrm{AB}}(f,g)\Longleftrightarrow 0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{cone}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)=\mathcal H\), the condition reduces to the ambient-space core-type regime.
In finite dimensions the condition is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every \(w\in\mathcal H\), the associated exact infimal convolution relation is \[(f+g)^*(w)=\min_{u+v=w}\bigl(f^*(u)+g^*(v)\bigr).\]
The function \((f+g)^*=f^*\mathbin{\square}g^*\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex under the qualification.
boundary_notes: Merely requiring the cone to be a linear subspace is insufficient in infinite dimensions if that subspace is not closed.
The record defines the qualification; it does not assert that the condition is necessary for exact conjugacy or strong duality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value-and-Attainment Outcome of a Fenchel Pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\), define \(F(x)=f(x)+g(Lx)\) and \(Q(v)=-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\). Let \(p=\inf_xF(x)\) and \(d=\sup_vQ(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The taxonomy records value equality separately from primal and dual attainment. It applies to extended-real optimal values, with finite proper cases singled out when a numerical gap is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The duality outcome-attainment type of the Fenchel pair is the tuple \[\mathfrak O=(p,d,A_P,A_D),\qquad A_P=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal H}F(x),\quad A_D=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in\mathcal K}Q(v).\] Its value component is classified as zero-gap when \(p=d\), positive finite-gap when \(-\infty<d<p<+\infty\), and extended-value failure otherwise. Its attainment component is the ordered pair \[(\mathbf 1_{A_P\ne\varnothing},\mathbf 1_{A_D\ne\varnothing})\in\{0,1\}^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A duality outcome is determined by four objects: the primal value \(p\), dual value \(d\), primal solution set \(A_P\), and dual solution set \(A_D\). Value equality and attainment are independent coordinates. Thus zero gap does not by itself mean that either optimum is achieved, and attainment of one side does not imply attainment of the other.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
Primal and dual values use the extended-real conventions for infima and suprema.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak O(f,g,L)=\bigl(p,d,\operatorname*{argmin}F,\operatorname*{argmax}Q\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite \(p,d\), the value coordinate may be encoded by \(\Delta=p-d\in[0,+\infty)\), while the attainment coordinate remains a separate element of \(\{0,1\}^2\).
special_cases_latex: Strong duality with dual attainment means \(p=d\in\mathbb R\) and \(A_D\ne\varnothing\), without requiring \(A_P\ne\varnothing\).
Full primal–dual solvability means \(p=d\in\mathbb R\) and both \(A_P\) and \(A_D\) are nonempty.
immediate_consequences_latex: There are four attainment patterns: both attained, primal only, dual only, and neither attained.
Weak duality orders the value coordinates as \(d\le p\) whenever the pair is well-defined.
boundary_notes: Equality \(p=d=+\infty\) or \(p=d=-\infty\) is an extended-value equality and should not be conflated with finite strong duality.
The taxonomy records outcomes; it does not impose a constraint qualification guaranteeing any particular cell.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p\in[-\infty,+\infty]\) be a primal infimum and \(d\in[-\infty,+\infty]\) the corresponding dual supremum, with weak duality \(d\le p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The numerical gap is defined without ambiguous extended-real subtraction. Finite-valued and extended-valued regimes are separated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The value-gap type of \((p,d)\) is defined as follows: \[\begin{array}{ll}\text{finite zero gap:}&p=d\in\mathbb R,\\ \text{finite positive gap:}&-\infty<d<p<+\infty,\\ \text{primal-infinite separation:}&d< p=+\infty,\\ \text{dual-minus-infinite separation:}&d=-\infty<p,\\ \text{degenerate extended equality:}&p=d\in\{-\infty,+\infty\}.\end{array}\] In the finite regime the duality gap is the real number \(\Delta=p-d\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under weak duality, the dual value cannot exceed the primal value. When both values are finite, the gap is \(\Delta=p-d\): it is zero for finite strong duality and strictly positive for a positive duality gap. Cases involving infinite values are classified separately so that expressions such as \(+\infty-(+\infty)\) are never used.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual values are defined in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p,d\in\mathbb R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta:=p-d\in[0,+\infty),\qquad \Delta=0\Longleftrightarrow p=d.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite values, \(\Delta>0\Longleftrightarrow d<p\).
Finite zero gap is equivalent to equality of the primal infimum and dual supremum; it is independent of whether either extremum is attained.
special_cases_latex: If a regularity condition yields \(p=d\in\mathbb R\), the pair lies in the finite zero-gap class.
If \(p\in\mathbb R\) and the dual objective is identically \(-\infty\), then \(d=-\infty<p\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A positive finite gap precludes a zero-gap optimality certificate.
Gap classification alone contains no information about \(\operatorname*{argmin}\) or \(\operatorname*{argmax}\).
boundary_notes: The convention does not assign a numerical value to \(+\infty-(+\infty)\) or \((-\infty)-(-\infty)\).
Some texts reserve the phrase strong duality for finite equality plus an attainment assertion; here finite value equality is called finite zero gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Gap as Two Fenchel–Young Residuals
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\). For \(x\in\mathcal H\) and \(v\in\mathcal K\), set \(F(x)=f(x)+g(Lx)\) and \(Q(v)=-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is pointwise weak-duality geometry for the unconstrained composite Fenchel pair. Extended values are allowed, but a finite certificate requires all four function values to be finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pointwise primal–dual gap is \[G(x,v):=F(x)-Q(v)=f(x)+g(Lx)+f^*(-L^*v)+g^*(v).\] It decomposes as \[G(x,v)=\underbrace{f(x)+f^*(-L^*v)+\langle Lx,v\rangle}_{R_f(x,v)}+\underbrace{g(Lx)+g^*(v)-\langle Lx,v\rangle}_{R_g(x,v)},\] where \(R_f(x,v)\ge0\) and \(R_g(x,v)\ge0\) by Fenchel–Young inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a primal point \(x\) and dual point \(v\), the weak-duality gap is the primal objective minus the dual objective. It is the sum of two nonnegative Fenchel–Young residuals: one pairs \(x\) with \(-L^*v\), and the other pairs \(Lx\) with \(v\). This decomposition is the local geometry behind weak duality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
The displayed residual equality is interpreted in the extended-real sense whenever no indeterminate sum occurs.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite terms, \(G(x,v)=0\) if and only if \(R_f(x,v)=R_g(x,v)=0\).
\[G(x,v)=0\Longleftrightarrow -L^*v\in\partial f(x)\ \text{and}\ v\in\partial g(Lx).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(L=\operatorname{Id}\), then \(G(x,v)=f(x)+g(x)+f^*(-v)+g^*(v)\).
If \(g=\iota_C\), the second residual becomes \(\iota_C(Lx)+\sigma_C(v)-\langle Lx,v\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finite pair satisfies \(Q(v)\le F(x)\).
A zero pointwise gap simultaneously certifies primal optimality, dual optimality, finite value equality, and both Fenchel–Young equalities.
boundary_notes: The infimum-level gap \(p-d\) and the pointwise gap \(G(x,v)\) are different objects unless \(x\) and \(v\) attain their respective optima.
If any term is infinite, \(G(x,v)=0\) cannot serve as a finite certificate.

notation.meaning: The two Fenchel–Young residuals comprising the gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise primal–dual gap is the sum of the nonnegative Fenchel–Young residuals for the two convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(P(x)=f(x)+g(Ax)\), \(D(y^*)=-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\), and \(G(x,y^*)=P(x)-D(y^*)\). The gap has the representation \[G(x,y^*)=\bigl(f(x)+f^*(-A^*y^*)+\langle A^*y^*,x\rangle\bigr)+\bigl(g(Ax)+g^*(y^*)-\langle y^*,Ax\rangle\bigr)\ge 0.\] Both bracketed terms are nonnegative Fenchel–Young residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(A^*:Y^*\to X^*\) is its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y^*)=f(x)+f^*(-A^*y^*)+g(Ax)+g^*(y^*)\ge 0\), with the stated decomposition into two nonnegative Fenchel–Young residuals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-Part Decomposition of the Primal–Dual Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition into primal objective error, optimal-value duality gap, and dual objective error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=\inf_x P(x)\) and \(d=\sup_{y^*}D(y^*)\). Whenever \(p,d,P(x),D(y^*)\in\mathbb R\), \[G(x,y^*)=P(x)-D(y^*)=\bigl(P(x)-p\bigr)+\bigl(p-d\bigr)+\bigl(d-D(y^*)\bigr).\] All three terms are nonnegative. Consequently, \(P(x)-p\le G(x,y^*)\) and \(d-D(y^*)\le G(x,y^*)\). If \(p=d=q\), this reduces to \(G=(P-q)+(q-D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite pointwise gap splits into primal error, the optimal-value gap, and dual error; under exact value duality only the two objective errors remain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(x,y^*)=(P(x)-p)+(p-d)+(d-D(y^*)),\qquad P(x)-p\le G(x,y^*),\quad d-D(y^*)\le G(x,y^*).

notation.meaning: Finite primal and dual optimal values.

knowledge_statements.title: Three-Part Decomposition of the Primal–Dual Gap
Zero-Gap Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero pointwise gap is equivalent to the two coupled subgradient conditions and certifies primal and dual optimality with equal attained values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[G(x,y^*)=f(x)+f^*(-A^*y^*)+g(Ax)+g^*(y^*).\] The zero-gap boundary is characterized by \[G(x,y^*)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -A^*y^*\in\partial f(x)\ \text{ and }\ y^*\in\partial g(Ax).\] Every pair satisfying these conditions is primal optimal and dual optimal and certifies equality of the attained objective values.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(A^*:Y^*\to X^*\) is its adjoint.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y^*)=0\iff -A^*y^*\in\partial f(x)\ \text{and}\ y^*\in\partial g(Ax)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero pointwise gap as a Fenchel–Young primal–dual optimality certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value Equality Without a Pointwise Zero-Gap Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment separates equality of optimal values from existence of a pair on the pointwise zero-gap boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=0\), \(f(x)=e^x\), and \(g\equiv0\), the primal value is \(p=0\) and is not attained, while the dual value is \(d=0\) and is attained only at the finite-valued dual point \(y^*=0\). Nevertheless, \[G(x,0)=e^x>0\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).\] Thus \(p=d\) does not imply existence of a pointwise zero-gap pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal primal and dual values need not yield a zero-gap pair when an optimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p=d=0,\qquad G(x,0)>0\ \text{for every }x\in\mathbb R.
knowledge_statements.title: Value Equality Without a Pointwise Zero-Gap Pair
Positive-Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-gap regime occurs when weak duality holds strictly: the dual value is below the primal value, possibly by an infinite extended-real gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be locally convex spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be continuous linear, and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper convex functions. For the Fenchel primal and dual values \(p^\star\) and \(d^\star\), a positive-gap regime is one in which both values are ordered by weak duality and are not equal. When their extended-real difference is defined, this is precisely \[0<p^\star-d^\star\le+\infty.\] If both values are finite, the condition reduces to \(d^\star<p^\star\). This classification concerns optimal values and does not assert attainment on either side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<p^\star-d^\star\le+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real classification within weak Fenchel–Rockafellar duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Duality Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the finite-valued regime, strong duality means equality of the primal and dual optimal values; attainment on either side is separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Fenchel primal value \(p^\star:=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\) and dual value \(d^\star:=\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}\), strong value duality in the finite-valued regime means \[p^\star=d^\star\in\mathbb R.\] This equality concerns optimal values only. It neither requires nor implies, by definition alone, attainment of the primal infimum or dual supremum.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are locally convex spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is continuous linear, and \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper convex functions.
The primal and dual values \(p^\star\) and \(d^\star\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong value duality is \(p^\star=d^\star\in\mathbb R\), independently of attainment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite equality of primal and dual values, separated from attainment outcomes.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be the Fenchel primal objective and \(Q:\mathcal K\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) its concave dual objective. Set \(p=\inf F\), \(d=\sup Q\), \(A_P=\{x:F(x)=p\}\), and \(A_D=\{v:Q(v)=d\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment is classified independently on the primal and dual sides and independently of whether the two values coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The attainment outcome is \[\operatorname{att}(F,Q):=(\mathbf1_{A_P\ne\varnothing},\mathbf1_{A_D\ne\varnothing})\in\{0,1\}^2.\] The four classes are \((1,1)\) bilateral attainment, \((1,0)\) primal-only attainment, \((0,1)\) dual-only attainment, and \((0,0)\) bilateral nonattainment. A finite value is unattained when it lies in \(\mathbb R\) while its optimizer set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal attainment means that some \(x\) satisfies \(F(x)=p\); dual attainment means that some \(v\) satisfies \(Q(v)=d\). Recording the two truth values gives four possible outcomes. These outcomes do not encode the size of the duality gap.
assumptions_latex: The infimum \(p\) and supremum \(d\) are defined in the extended real line.
Attainment means equality with the optimal value at a point in the stated ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A_P\ne\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow p=\min_{x\in\mathcal H}F(x),\qquad A_D\ne\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow d=\max_{v\in\mathcal K}Q(v).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Primal nonattainment with finite value is \(p\in\mathbb R\) and \(F(x)>p\) for every \(x\in\mathcal H\).
Dual nonattainment with finite value is \(d\in\mathbb R\) and \(Q(v)<d\) for every \(v\in\mathcal K\).
special_cases_latex: A constraint qualification may yield \((0,1)\) or \((1,1)\) by guaranteeing dual attainment without guaranteeing existence of a primal minimizer.
Coercivity or compact level sets can provide primal attainment independently of dual attainment.
immediate_consequences_latex: A primal–dual zero-gap certificate exists only in the bilateral-attainment class.
Finite zero gap can occur in any attainment class, including \((0,0)\).
boundary_notes: An infeasible problem is not described merely as an unattained finite value; feasibility and extended-value status must be recorded separately.
Attainment of an infinite value is convention-dependent and is excluded from the phrase finite attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Duality without Dual Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-dimensional closed convex Fenchel pair has equal finite values and a primal optimizer, but no dual optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=I\), \(f=\delta_{\{0\}}\), and \(g=(\exp)^*\). The resulting primal and dual satisfy \[p^\star=d^\star=0,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}(f+g)=\{0\},\qquad \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in\mathbb R}(-e^y)=\varnothing.\] Thus finite strong duality and primal attainment can coexist with failure of dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=d^\star=0\), \(\operatorname*{argmin}(f+g)=\{0\}\), and \(\operatorname*{argmax}D=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite zero-gap example separating dual attainment from value equality and primal attainment.

notation.meaning: indicator function of the singleton zero
Fenchel conjugate of the exponential function

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Attainment Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual is attained exactly when some dual feasible point realizes the supremum; this is distinct from equality with the primal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel dual value is attained when there exists \(\bar y^*\in Y^*\) such that \[D(\bar y^*)=d^\star=\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}D(y^*),\qquad D(y^*):=-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*).\] Equivalently, the dual solution set \(S_D\) is nonempty. Dual attainment is logically independent of value equality: an attained dual value may lie strictly below the primal value, while under strong duality it supplies a dual optimizer at the common value. If the supremum is finite but \(S_D=\varnothing\), the dual value is unattained.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are locally convex spaces and \(A:X\to Y\) is continuous linear.
\(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual attainment is equivalent to nonemptiness of \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{y^*\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment of the Fenchel dual supremum, distinct from zero gap.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Primal-Dual Optimality Characterizations p. 154

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-method attainment and optimizer-set geometry for finite-dimensional concave dual objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D:\mathbb R^m\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) be proper, concave, and upper semicontinuous, with finite supremum \(d^\star\). If, for some \(\alpha<d^\star\), the upper level set
\[
L_\alpha:=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:D(y)\ge\alpha\}
\]
is nonempty and compact, then \(D\) attains \(d^\star\), and \(S_D:=\operatorname*{argmax}D\) is nonempty, compact, and convex. More generally, every nonempty maximizer set of a concave function is convex; if \(D\) is strictly concave on its effective domain, it contains at most one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper semicontinuity and a compact upper level set ensure dual attainment; the optimizer set is convex and is unique under strict concavity.
assumptions_latex: \(D:\mathbb R^m\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) is proper, concave, and upper semicontinuous.
For some \(\alpha<d^\star\), the set \(L_\alpha=\{y:D(y)\ge\alpha\}\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varnothing\ne S_D:=\operatorname*{argmax}D\text{ is compact and convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Level Compactness and Dual-Solution Geometry
Strong Duality without Primal Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential objective has finite unattained infimum zero while its Fenchel dual attains the same value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=0\), \(f(x)=e^x\), and \(g\equiv0\). The resulting pair satisfies \[p^\star=d^\star=0,\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname*{argmax}D=\{0\}.\] Thus finite strong duality and dual attainment can coexist with failure of primal attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=d^\star=0\), \(\operatorname*{argmin}F=\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname*{argmax}D=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite zero-gap example separating primal attainment from value equality and dual attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Attainment Interfaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal is attained when a point realizes its infimum; lower semicontinuity plus a compact nonempty sublevel set is a standard sufficient interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal value is attained when there exists \(\bar x\in X\) satisfying \[F(\bar x)=p^\star=\inf_{x\in X}F(x).\] Equivalently, \(S_P\ne\varnothing\). In a Hausdorff topological vector space, a standard existence interface is lower semicontinuity of \(F\) together with nonemptiness and compactness of some sublevel set \(\{x:F(x)\le\alpha\}\) for a finite \(\alpha>p^\star\); under these conditions a minimizing net has a cluster point in \(S_P\). Primal attainment alone makes no assertion about the dual value or dual attainment.
assumptions_latex: The primal value \(p^\star:=\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal attainment is equivalent to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value attainment and its standard sublevel-compactness interface.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and Uniqueness of Primal Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity, closedness, compactness, and uniqueness properties of an attained primal solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Whenever \(S_P:=\operatorname*{argmin}F\) is nonempty, it is convex. If \(X\) is Hausdorff and \(F\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(S_P\) is closed. If, in addition, \(S_P\) is contained in a compact sublevel set of \(F\), then \(S_P\) is compact. If \(F\) is strictly convex on its effective domain, then \(S_P\) contains at most one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal optimizer set is convex, is closed under lower semicontinuity, is compact under the compact-sublevel interface, and is unique under strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_P\text{ is convex; under the respective additional hypotheses it is closed, compact, or a singleton}.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry and Uniqueness of Primal Minimizers

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\). The primal and dual objectives are \(F(x)=f(x)+g(Lx)\) and \(Q(v)=-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The certificate is exact and deterministic. It is a property of a candidate pair \((x,v)\), not a constraint qualification ensuring that such a pair exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((\bar x,\bar v)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal K\) is a Fenchel optimality certificate when all four objective terms are finite and \[F(\bar x)=Q(\bar v),\] equivalently, \[f(\bar x)+g(L\bar x)+f^*(-L^*\bar v)+g^*(\bar v)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fenchel certificate is a primal–dual pair with finite objective terms whose pointwise duality gap is zero. It certifies the primal and dual optimality of the two components and equality of their objective values.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, and \(L\) is bounded linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\bar x,\bar v)\text{ is a certificate}\Longleftrightarrow F(\bar x)-Q(\bar v)=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[-L^*\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x),\qquad \bar v\in\partial g(L\bar x).\]
\[f(\bar x)+f^*(-L^*\bar v)=-\langle L\bar x,\bar v\rangle,\qquad g(L\bar x)+g^*(\bar v)=\langle L\bar x,\bar v\rangle.\]
\[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}F,\quad \bar v\in\operatorname*{argmax}Q,\quad \inf F=\sup Q\in\mathbb R.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(L=\operatorname{Id}\), the system is \(-\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(\bar v\in\partial g(\bar x)\).

For differentiable \(f\) and \(g\), it becomes \(

No separate constraint qualification is needed to validate a displayed certificate; qualifications concern existence.
boundary_notes: A small positive gap is an approximate certificate, not an exact certificate under this definition.
Zero equality involving indeterminate extended-real expressions is excluded by the finiteness requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Subdifferential Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two conjugate subgradient inclusions exactly certify finite-valued joint primal-dual optimality and zero gap; the explicit continuity qualification supplies the corresponding chain-and-sum rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\) and \(\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}\), the coupled inclusions \[-A^*\bar y^*\in\partial f(\bar x),\qquad \bar y^*\in\partial g(A\bar x)\] hold exactly when \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y^*\) are respectively primal and dual optimal and their finite objective values coincide. Under the stated continuity qualification, the subdifferential calculus identity \[\partial(f+g\circ A)(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)+A^*\partial g(A\bar x)\] also makes this system equivalent to primal stationarity together with a compatible multiplier \(\bar y^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are locally convex spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is continuous linear, and \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper convex lower-semicontinuous functions.
\((\bar x,\bar y^*)\in X\times Y^*\), and all displayed primal and dual objective values are finite.
For the chain-and-sum-rule formulation, there exists \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that \(g\) is continuous at \(Ax_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inclusions \(-A^*\bar y^*\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(\bar y^*\in\partial g(A\bar x)\) are equivalent to joint primal-dual optimality with zero gap.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel primal-dual optimality certificate with an explicit qualification for subdifferential calculus.
