knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns exact convex subdifferentials in Hilbert spaces. It characterizes certificate pairs but does not assert existence or a subdifferential chain rule without qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal–dual subdifferential system is the coupled inclusion problem of finding \((x,v)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal K\) such that \[0\in\partial f(x)+L^*v,\qquad 0\in\partial g^*(v)-Lx.\] Equivalently, \[-L^*v\in\partial f(x),\qquad Lx\in\partial g^*(v).\] Since \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), the second inclusion is also equivalent to \(v\in\partial g(Lx)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual subdifferential solution is a pair \((x,v)\) satisfying two coupled inclusions. The dual variable balances a subgradient of \(f\) through \(-L^*v\), while the image \(Lx\) is a subgradient of \(g^*\) at \(v\). Conjugate-subgradient inversion gives the equivalent relation \(v\in\partial g(Lx)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(x,v)\in\operatorname{Sol}_{\partial}(f,g,L)\Longleftrightarrow -L^*v\in\partial f(x)\ \text{and}\ v\in\partial g(Lx).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[0\in\partial f(x)+L^*v,\qquad 0\in\partial g^*(v)-Lx.\]
\[x\in(\partial f)^{-1}(-L^*v),\qquad v\in\partial g(Lx).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(L=\operatorname{Id}\), then \(-v\in\partial f(x)\) and \(v\in\partial g(x)\).
If \(g=\iota_C\), then \(v\in N_C(Lx)\) and \(-L^*v\in\partial f(x)\).
If both functions are differentiable at the relevant points, the inclusions reduce to gradient equalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every solution makes both associated Fenchel–Young residuals zero.
Every solution is an exact primal–dual certificate for \(\inf_x f(x)+g(Lx)\) and its Fenchel dual.
boundary_notes: The formal stationarity inclusion \(0\in\partial(f+g\circ L)(x)\) need not decompose into this system without an appropriate subdifferential-calculus condition.
For nonclosed or nonconvex functions, conjugate-subgradient inversion requires a different formulation.

notation.meaning: Solution set of the coupled subdifferential inclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Young Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonnegative Fenchel–Young residuals sum to the primal-dual gap; a zero sum certifies the coupled subgradient conditions and joint optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Fenchel–Young residuals \[r_f(x,y^*):=f(x)+f^*(-A^*y^*)+\langle A^*y^*,x\rangle,\qquad r_g(x,y^*):=g(Ax)+g^*(y^*)-\langle y^*,Ax\rangle.\] Each residual is nonnegative, and cancellation of the pairings gives \[r_f(x,y^*)+r_g(x,y^*)=f(x)+g(Ax)+f^*(-A^*y^*)+g^*(y^*).\] Thus their sum is the primal objective minus the dual objective. It vanishes exactly when \(-A^*y^*\in\partial f(x)\) and \(y^*\in\partial g(Ax)\), thereby certifying joint optimality and zero gap.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper convex functions.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \((x,y^*)\) makes all displayed values finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonnegative residual sum equals the primal-dual objective gap and vanishes exactly at the two Fenchel equalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise certificate for the standard Fenchel composite pair.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-error bounds furnished by the finite pointwise Fenchel–Young gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(x)=f(x)+g(Ax)\), \(D(y^*)=-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\), \(p^*=\inf P\), and \(d^*=\sup D\). For every pair with finite \(P(x)\) and \(D(y^*)\), weak duality yields \[0\le P(x)-p^*\le P(x)-D(y^*),\qquad 0\le d^*-D(y^*)\le P(x)-D(y^*).\] Hence a Fenchel–Young residual sum at most \(\varepsilon\) certifies primal and dual objective errors at most \(\varepsilon\). If \(p^*=d^*\in\mathbb R\), then \[P(x)-D(y^*)=(P(x)-p^*)+(d^*-D(y^*)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite Fenchel–Young gap bounds both primal and dual objective errors; under equality of optimal values, it is their sum.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper convex functions and \(A\) is linear.
\(P(x),D(y^*),p^*,d^*\) are finite for the displayed error bounds.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, with conjugate \(h^*\). For \((x,u)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal H\), suppose \(h(x)\) and \(h^*(u)\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The record defines both a single-function Fenchel–Young residual and its paired use in composite primal–dual certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel–Young residual of \(h\) at \((x,u)\) is \[\operatorname{FY}_h(x,u):=h(x)+h^*(u)-\langle x,u\rangle\ge0.\] A zero Fenchel–Young certificate is a pair satisfying \(\operatorname{FY}_h(x,u)=0\). For the composite pair \(f(x)+g(Lx)\), a Fenchel–Young gap certificate \((x,v)\) satisfies \[\operatorname{FY}_f(x,-L^*v)=0,\qquad \operatorname{FY}_g(Lx,v)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel–Young residual measures the slack in the Fenchel–Young inequality. It is always nonnegative when finite. Residual zero is an exact certificate that the two arguments are conjugate subgradients. In the composite primal–dual problem, two such residuals—one for \(f\) and one for \(g\)—form the complete certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper and convex; the inverse-subgradient equivalence additionally uses lower semicontinuity.
The function and conjugate values entering each residual are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{FY}_h(x,u)=0\Longleftrightarrow u\in\partial h(x),\] and, for \(h\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), also \[\operatorname{FY}_h(x,u)=0\Longleftrightarrow x\in\partial h^*(u).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[h(x)+h^*(u)=\langle x,u\rangle.\]
\[u\in\partial h(x).\]
If \(h\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), then \(x\in\partial h^*(u)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h=\iota_C\), \(\operatorname{FY}_h(x,u)=\iota_C(x)+\sigma_C(u)-\langle x,u\rangle\), and zero means \(x\in C\) and \(u\in N_C(x)\).
For differentiable \(h\), residual zero implies \(u=\nabla h(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The composite pointwise gap equals \(\operatorname{FY}_f(x,-L^*v)+\operatorname{FY}_g(Lx,v)\).
Because both terms are nonnegative, a zero composite gap forces each residual to vanish separately.
boundary_notes: A finite positive residual is a quantitative violation measure, not an exact optimality certificate.
If \(h\) is not lower-semicontinuous, the implication involving \(\partial h^*\) naturally refers to the closed convex hull through biconjugacy.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Point Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued Fenchel Lagrangian saddle point is equivalent to the coupled subgradient conditions and certifies both optimizers and zero gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(L(x,y^*):=f(x)+\langle y^*,Ax\rangle-g^*(y^*)\). A pair \((\bar x,\bar y^*)\) is a saddle point when \[L(\bar x,y^*)\le L(\bar x,\bar y^*)\le L(x,\bar y^*)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X\text{ and }y^*\in Y^*.\] This saddle condition is equivalent to \[-A^*\bar y^*\in\partial f(\bar x),\qquad \bar y^*\in\partial g(A\bar x).\] Consequently, \(\bar x\) is primal optimal, \(\bar y^*\) is dual optimal, and \[f(\bar x)+g(A\bar x)=-f^*(-A^*\bar y^*)-g^*(\bar y^*).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are locally convex spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is continuous linear, and \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper convex lower-semicontinuous functions.
\((\bar x,\bar y^*)\in X\times Y^*\), and all displayed objective values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A saddle point of \(L\) is equivalent to the coupled subgradient system and certifies both optima and zero gap.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued saddle-point certificate for the standard composite Fenchel pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saddle-Point Certificate for the Fenchel Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\). Define the convex–concave Fenchel Lagrangian \(\mathcal L(x,v)=f(x)+\langle Lx,v\rangle-g^*(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The saddle inequalities are global over \(\mathcal H\times\mathcal K\). The definition does not assume differentiability, strict convexity, compactness, or prior strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((\bar x,\bar v)\in\mathcal H\times\mathcal K\) is a saddle-point certificate when \[\mathcal L(\bar x,v)\le\mathcal L(\bar x,\bar v)\le\mathcal L(x,\bar v)\qquad(\forall x\in\mathcal H)(\forall v\in\mathcal K).\] Equivalently, \(\bar x\) minimizes \(x\mapsto\mathcal L(x,\bar v)\) and \(\bar v\) maximizes \(v\mapsto\mathcal L(\bar x,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle-point certificate is a pair at which the Fenchel Lagrangian cannot be increased by changing the dual variable alone and cannot be decreased by changing the primal variable alone. The inequalities are required against every primal and dual competitor.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\bar x,\bar v)\text{ is a saddle point}\Longleftrightarrow \sup_v\mathcal L(\bar x,v)=\mathcal L(\bar x,\bar v)=\inf_x\mathcal L(x,\bar v).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[-L^*\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x),\qquad L\bar x\in\partial g^*(\bar v).\]
\[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\sup_v\mathcal L(x,v),\qquad \bar v\in\operatorname*{argmax}_v\inf_x\mathcal L(x,v),\] together with equality of the minimax values.
special_cases_latex: For \(g=\iota_C\), the Lagrangian is \(f(x)+\langle Lx,v\rangle-\sigma_C(v)\).
For a standard inequality-constrained convex program, the same definition specializes to the usual Lagrangian saddle inequalities with dual feasibility encoded in the dual domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: A saddle pair is a Fenchel optimality certificate and yields a common finite primal–dual value.
If the minimax equality fails, no saddle-point certificate exists.
boundary_notes: Separate primal and dual optimizers do not form a saddle pair unless their optimal values agree.
Local stationarity for a nonconvex–nonconcave Lagrangian is not the global saddle condition defined here.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F\) and \(Q\) be a weakly dual primal minimization and dual maximization pair, with \(p=\inf F\), \(d=\sup Q\), optimizer sets \(A_P\) and \(A_D\), and a convex perturbation value function \(\varphi\) satisfying \(\varphi(0)=p\) and \(\varphi^{**}(0)=d\) when the standard conjugate representation is proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The taxonomy separates failures of value equality, attainment, perturbation closedness, and proper feasibility/boundedness. These labels may overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A duality failure regime is present when at least one of the following holds: \[\begin{aligned}&\text{value failure: }d<p,\\&\text{primal nonattainment: }p\in\mathbb R\text{ and }A_P=\varnothing,\\&\text{dual nonattainment: }d\in\mathbb R\text{ and }A_D=\varnothing,\\&\text{perturbation-closedness failure: }\varphi(0)>\varphi^{**}(0),\\&\text{status failure: }p\in\{-\infty,+\infty\}\text{ or }d\in\{-\infty,+\infty\}.\end{aligned}\] The failure signature is the set of all applicable labels, rather than a mutually exclusive single label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duality can fail in several logically distinct ways. The primal and dual values can differ; either finite optimum can be unattained; the perturbation value function can fail to be closed at the reference perturbation; or feasibility and boundedness can produce infinite values. A problem may exhibit several of these failures simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: The perturbation label is used only when \(\varphi^{**}(0)\) represents the dual value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Fail}(F,Q,\varphi)=\{\text{all failure predicates above that are true}\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: In the finite proper perturbation setting, value failure is \(\varphi(0)>\varphi^{**}(0)\).
Absence of every listed failure means \(p=d\in\mathbb R\) and both optimizer sets are nonempty.
special_cases_latex: Zero gap with \(A_D=\varnothing\) is a pure dual-attainment failure.
A finite positive gap with both optima attained is a pure value-equality failure, possibly accompanied by perturbation nonclosedness.
Primal infeasibility or unboundedness is a status failure rather than merely an attainment failure.
immediate_consequences_latex: Failure labels should be reported independently because repairing one condition need not repair the others.
A zero-gap certificate excludes every listed finite value and attainment failure.
boundary_notes: Constraint-qualification failure is not itself included: a sufficient qualification may fail even when duality outcomes are perfect.
The taxonomy is descriptive and does not assert causal equivalence between nonclosedness and every form of nonattainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Duality Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive duality gap is strict separation between ordered dual and primal values; it is a value failure, not merely nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a weakly dual pair with primal value \(p^\star\) and dual value \(d^\star\), a positive duality gap occurs precisely when \[d^\star<p^\star.\] If both values are finite, its magnitude is the finite number \(\Delta=p^\star-d^\star>0\). An infinite positive gap occurs when the ordered extended-real values make \(\Delta=+\infty\), excluding indeterminate expressions such as \((+\infty)-(+\infty)\). A positive gap is a failure of strong duality; it is not merely failure of primal or dual attainment, since unattained problems may still have equal values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive duality gap is the strict inequality \(d^\star<p^\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of value equality despite weak-duality ordering.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p=\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\) and \(d=\sup_{v\in V}Q(v)\) be the values of a weakly dual minimization–maximization pair, so \(d\le p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition uses finite optimal values. Infinite separations are classified separately as feasibility or boundedness pathologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair has a positive duality gap when \[-\infty<d<p<+\infty.\] Its gap magnitude is the strictly positive real number \[\Delta:=p-d>0.\] For the composite Fenchel pair, \[p=\inf_x\bigl(f(x)+g(Lx)\bigr),\qquad d=\sup_v\bigl(-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive duality gap occurs when both primal and dual values are finite but the dual supremum is strictly smaller than the primal infimum. The positive number \(p-d\) is the gap magnitude. Whether either side attains its value is a separate question.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual optimal values are real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Delta>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d<p\quad\text{for }p,d\in\mathbb R.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a proper convex perturbation function \(\varphi\) with \(p=\varphi(0)\) and \(d=\varphi^{**}(0)\), \[\Delta>0\Longleftrightarrow \varphi(0)>\varphi^{**}(0).\]
No sequence of dual feasible points can have objective values converging to \(p\), since every such value is bounded above by \(d<p\).
special_cases_latex: A positive gap may occur even when both the primal minimum and dual maximum are attained.
If either value is infinite, the case is not a finite positive gap under this definition.
immediate_consequences_latex: No exact zero-gap primal–dual certificate exists.
Strong duality fails at the level of values regardless of attainment.
boundary_notes: A failure of a chosen constraint qualification does not imply a positive gap.
The difference between a primal objective value at a nonoptimal point and a dual objective value is a pointwise gap, not necessarily the optimal-value gap \(\Delta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Elementary Finite Unattained Supremum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear objective on an open interval has a finite supremum approached by a sequence but no maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D=(0,1)\) and \(\Phi(y)=y\), one has \(\sup_{y\in D}\Phi(y)=1\), but \(\Phi(y)<1\) for every \(y\in D\). Thus the finite supremum is unattained, although the sequence \(y_k=1-1/k\) has objective values converging to it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{y\in D}\Phi(y)=1\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in D}\Phi(y)=\varnothing.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example separating a finite supremum from existence of a maximizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness–Upper-Semicontinuity Attainment Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact feasible upper level sets together with upper semicontinuity exclude finite dual nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a nonempty compact topological space and let \(\Phi:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) be upper semicontinuous and not identically \(-\infty\). Then \(\Phi\) attains its finite supremum on \(D\). Consequently, a finite unattained dual value requires failure of compactness of the relevant feasible upper level set or failure of upper semicontinuity of the dual objective.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a nonempty compact topological space.
\(\Phi:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) is upper semicontinuous and not identically \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{y^*\in D}\Phi(y^*)\ne\varnothing.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic sufficient condition excluding finite dual nonattainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Dual Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual value is unattained when feasible points approach its finite supremum arbitrarily closely but no feasible point realizes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite dual value \(d^\star\) is unattained when \[d^\star=\sup_{y^*\in D}\Phi(y^*)\quad\text{and}\quad \Phi(y^*)<d^\star\ 
\text{for every }y^*\in D.\] Equivalently, the dual maximizing set \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{y^*\in D}\Phi(y^*)\) is empty, although for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(y^*_{\varepsilon}\in D\) with \(\Phi(y^*_{\varepsilon})>d^\star-\varepsilon\). Unattainment can coexist with zero duality gap; hence it records failure of existence of a dual optimizer, not necessarily failure of value equality.
assumptions_latex: The dual feasible set \(D\) is nonempty.
The dual objective \(\Phi:D\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has finite supremum \(d^\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual value is unattained exactly when \(\Phi(y^*)<d^\star\) for every \(y^*\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite dual supremum approached but not achieved.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Gap with an Unattained Dual Supremum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel example separating value equality from dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\{0\}\), \(Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=0\), and \(f(0)=0\). Define the proper closed convex function
\[
g(t)=\begin{cases}t\log t-t,&t>0,\\0,&t=0,\\+\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(g^*(y)=e^y\). The primal value is \(p^\star=f(0)+g(0)=0\), while the dual objective is \(D(y)=-e^y\). Thus
\[
d^\star=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}(-e^y)=0=p^\star,
\]
but \(D(y)<0\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R\), so the dual supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed finite-dimensional Fenchel pair can have zero duality gap while its dual supremum is approached only as the dual variable tends to negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^\star=d^\star=0\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in\mathbb R}(-e^y)=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Gap with an Unattained Dual Supremum

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Escape of Maximizing Sequences under Unattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness boundary for an upper-semicontinuous dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D:\mathbb R^m\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) be upper semicontinuous with finite supremum \(d^\star\). If a maximizing sequence \((y_k)\), satisfying \(D(y_k)\to d^\star\), has a bounded subsequence, then \(D\) attains \(d^\star\). Consequently, if \(d^\star\) is unattained, every maximizing sequence satisfies \(\|y_k\|\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an upper-semicontinuous finite-dimensional dual objective, unattainment forces every maximizing sequence to escape every bounded set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}D=\varnothing\Longrightarrow \bigl(D(y_k)\to d^\star\Rightarrow\|y_k\|\to+\infty\bigr).
knowledge_statements.title: Escape of Maximizing Sequences under Unattainment

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q:V\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) be a concave dual objective on a real vector or Hilbert space \(V\), and let \(d=\sup_{v\in V}Q(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns finite nonattainment of a dual maximization problem. It is independent of the primal value and hence independent of whether the duality gap vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual value is finite and unattained when \[d\in\mathbb R\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in V}Q(v)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, \[Q(v)<d\quad(\forall v\in V),\qquad \exists(v_n)_{n\ge1}\subset V:\ Q(v_n)\to d.\] For the Fenchel dual, \(Q(v)=-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual value is unattained when the dual supremum is a real number but no dual point realizes it. Every feasible dual point then has value strictly below the supremum, although a maximizing sequence exists whose objective values converge to it.
assumptions_latex: The dual feasible domain \(\{v:Q(v)>-\infty\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[d\text{ is unattained}\Longleftrightarrow d\in\mathbb R\ \text{and}\ (\forall v\in V)\ Q(v)<d.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in\mathbb R,\qquad \operatorname*{argmax}Q=\varnothing.\]
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(v_\varepsilon\in V\) such that \(d-\varepsilon<Q(v_\varepsilon)<d\).
special_cases_latex: It is possible to have \(d=p\in\mathbb R\) and an unattained dual value; this is zero gap without dual attainment.
It is also possible to have \(d<p\) with the dual supremum unattained.
immediate_consequences_latex: No primal–dual certificate can contain a dual maximizer.
Approximate dual certificates may be formed from maximizing sequences, but they are not exact attainment certificates.
boundary_notes: If the dual objective is identically \(-\infty\), the problem is dual-infeasible rather than a finite unattained-value case.
Nonuniqueness is not nonattainment: a nonempty optimizer set of any cardinality means the value is attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Form of the Closure Gap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perturbation closure gap occurs geometrically when the closed epigraph reaches a lower height over the reference parameter than the original epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be a proper convex perturbation value function and suppose that \(\operatorname{epi}p^{**}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}p}\) in the topology under consideration. Then \[p^{**}(0)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb R:(0,r)\in\overline{\operatorname{epi}p}\}.\] Consequently, \(p(0)>p^{**}(0)\) exactly when the closed epigraph contains a point \((0,r)\) strictly below the original epigraph height \(p(0)\).
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a proper convex perturbation value function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(0)>p^{**}(0)\iff\exists r<p(0)\text{ such that }(0,r)\in\overline{\operatorname{epi}p}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric equivalent of the seed's perturbation closure-gap inequality.

notation.meaning: epigraph of the perturbation value function

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Perturbation Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the perturbation value lies strictly above its lower-semicontinuous convex envelope at zero, their difference is a positive primal-dual gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the perturbation value function \[p(u):=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax-u)\},\] the unperturbed primal value is \(p(0)\), while the conjugate dual value is \(p^{**}(0)\) under the stated representation. Since \(p^{**}\le p\), weak duality follows. Failure of lower semicontinuity of \(p\) at the origin can produce \[p(0)>p^{**}(0),\] in which case the primal-dual gap is exactly \(p(0)-p^{**}(0)>0\). Thus closedness of the perturbation value at the reference point is the boundary excluding this gap mechanism.
assumptions_latex: \(p(u):=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax-u)\}\) is a proper convex perturbation value function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonclosedness at the origin is \(p(0)>p^{**}(0)\), and this difference is the duality gap.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation-function mechanism for a Fenchel duality gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Convex Perturbation Value with a Closure Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal one-dimensional example isolating nonclosedness of the value function at the reference perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(p:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[p(u)=\begin{cases}+\infty,&u<0,\\1,&u=0,\\0,&u>0.\end{cases}\] This function is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous at \(0\). Its conjugate is \(p^*(y)=0\) for \(y\le0\) and \(+\infty\) for \(y>0\), while \[p^{**}(u)=\begin{cases}+\infty,&u<0,\\0,&u\ge0.\end{cases}\] Thus \(p(0)=1>0=p^{**}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-dimensional proper convex value function can jump upward at the reference point; biconjugation fills the jump and produces a closure gap of one.
assumptions_latex: Conjugates use the standard pairing on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: A Convex Perturbation Value with a Closure Gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Perturbation Value at the Reference Parameter
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and \(L\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H,\mathcal K)\). Define the perturbation value function \(\varphi:\mathcal K\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(\varphi(u)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\{f(x)+g(Lx-u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns lower-semicontinuity at the reference perturbation \(u=0\). It assumes the perturbation function is proper convex when identifying its closure with its biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal perturbation value is nonclosed at the origin when \[\varphi(0)>(\operatorname{cl}\varphi)(0),\] equivalently, for proper convex \(\varphi\), when \[\varphi(0)>\varphi^{**}(0).\] In sequential form on the Hilbert space \(\mathcal K\), this is \[\varphi(0)>\liminf_{u\to0}\varphi(u).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perturbation value is nonclosed at the reference parameter when the value at zero lies strictly above the lower-semicontinuous envelope approached by nearby perturbations. For a proper convex value function, this envelope is the biconjugate \(\varphi^{**}\).
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\) is proper and convex for the biconjugate equivalence.
\(\varphi(0)\in\mathbb R\) when interpreting the strict difference as a finite duality gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\varphi\text{ is nonclosed at }0\Longleftrightarrow \varphi(0)>\varphi^{**}(0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exist \(u_n\to0\) and values approaching a level strictly below \(\varphi(0)\), equivalently \(\liminf_n\varphi(u_n)<\varphi(0)\).
With \(d=\varphi^{**}(0)\) in the standard perturbation duality representation, nonclosedness at zero is equivalent to \(d<p=\varphi(0)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), then \(\varphi=\varphi^{**}\), so this failure cannot occur.
Closedness of the entire epigraph is stronger than the local requirement \(\varphi(0)=\varphi^{**}(0)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: When \(p=\varphi(0)\) and \(d=\varphi^{**}(0)\) are finite, nonclosedness produces the positive gap \(p-d>0\).
Nearby perturbations can have limiting values strictly better than the unperturbed primal value.
boundary_notes: A nonclosed epigraph away from \(u=0\) need not create a gap for the unperturbed problem.
Dual nonattainment may occur even when \(\varphi(0)=\varphi^{**}(0)\); value closedness and attainment are distinct.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The primal status is: infeasible if \(D_P=\varnothing\) (hence \(p=+\infty\)); feasible and unbounded below if \(D_P
e\varnothing\) and \(p=-\infty\); finite unattained if \(p\in\mathbb R\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}F=\varnothing\); and finite solvable if \(p\in\mathbb R\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}F
e\varnothing\). The dual status is: infeasible if \(D_D=\varnothing\) (hence \(d=-\infty\)); feasible and unbounded above if \(D_D
e\varnothing\) and \(d=+\infty\); finite unattained if \(d\in\mathbb R\) and \(\operatorname*{argmax}Q=\varnothing\); and finite solvable if \(d\in\mathbb R\) and \(\operatorname*{argmax}Q
e\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each side of a dual pair first receives its own status. A minimization problem can be infeasible, feasible but unbounded below, finite but unattained, or finite and solved. A maximization problem has the sign-reversed analogues: infeasible, unbounded above, finite but unattained, or finite and solved.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) never takes \(-\infty\) and \(Q\) never takes \(+\infty\) pointwise, although their optimal values may be infinite.
Infima and suprema use extended-real conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{status}(F,Q)=\bigl(\operatorname{status}_P(F),\operatorname{status}_D(Q)\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Primal feasibility is \(\operatorname{dom}F\ne\varnothing\); dual feasibility is \(\operatorname{dom}(-Q)\ne\varnothing\).
Finite solvability is feasibility plus a real optimal value attained by at least one point.
special_cases_latex: For \(F(x)=f(x)+g(Lx)\), primal feasibility is \(L(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\).
For \(Q(v)=-f^*(-L^*v)-g^*(v)\), dual feasibility is the existence of \(v\) with \(-L^*v\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\) and \(v\in\operatorname{dom}g^*\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If the primal is feasible, weak duality rules out a dual value \(d=+\infty\) whenever a finite primal feasible value exists.
If the dual is feasible, weak duality rules out \(p=-\infty\) whenever a finite dual feasible value exists.
Only after assigning these statuses is a finite numerical duality gap well-defined.
boundary_notes: The equality \(D_P=\varnothing\Rightarrow p=+\infty\) does not imply the converse for arbitrary extended-real models unless pointwise values and conventions are fixed as above.
Feasibility does not imply boundedness, and finite boundedness does not imply attainment.
A problem with finite unattained value is feasible and bounded but not solvable.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Infeasibility Status
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal infeasibility means that no primal feasible point exists; under the standard minimization convention, the primal value is positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal minimization problem is infeasible exactly when its feasible set is empty: \[F_P=\varnothing.\] Under the standard convention \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), its value is then \[p^\star:=\inf_{x\in F_P}F(x)=+\infty.\] This differs from unboundedness below, which requires \(F_P\ne\varnothing\) and \(p^\star=-\infty\). Primal infeasibility alone does not determine the dual feasibility, boundedness, or attainment status.
assumptions_latex: The primal problem minimizes an extended-real objective \(F\) over its feasible set \(F_P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal infeasibility means \(F_P=\varnothing\), with \(p^\star=+\infty\) under the convention \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Feasibility Test for the Fenchel–Rockafellar Pair
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stated Fenchel dual is infeasible exactly when no dual vector lies in the domain of g-star and maps into the domain of f-star under the negative adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}
\]
and the dual
\[
\sup_{y\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\},
\]
the dual feasible set is
\[
F_D=\{y\in Y^*:y\in\operatorname{dom}g^*,\ -A^*y\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}.
\]
Thus the dual is infeasible exactly when this set is empty.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces in duality with \(X^*,Y^*\).
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_D=\varnothing\iff\operatorname{dom}g^*\cap(-A^*)^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)=\varnothing.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain test for dual infeasibility in the stated composite Fenchel formulation.

notation.meaning: adjoint map from the dual of Y to the dual of X
effective domain of the Fenchel conjugate of f

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Infeasibility Is Distinct from Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty dual feasible set, feasible nonattainment, and feasible unboundedness above are distinct statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dual infeasibility is \(F_D=\varnothing\). If \(F_D\neq\varnothing\), the dual is feasible regardless of attainment. A feasible problem with finite value and no maximizer has dual nonattainment, while a feasible problem with value \(+\infty\) is dual unbounded; neither is dual infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The dual is a maximization problem over a feasible set \(F_D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_D=\varnothing\) is disjoint from both feasible nonattainment and feasible unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp separation of empty feasibility from failure to attain a supremum.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Infeasibility Status
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual infeasibility means that no dual feasible point exists; under the standard maximization convention, the dual value is negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dual maximization problem is infeasible exactly when its feasible set is empty: \[F_D=\varnothing.\] Under the standard convention \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\), its value is then \[d^\star:=\sup_{y^*\in F_D}D(y^*)=-\infty.\] This differs from unboundedness above, which requires \(F_D\ne\varnothing\) and \(d^\star=+\infty\). Dual infeasibility alone does not determine the primal feasibility, boundedness, or attainment status.
assumptions_latex: The dual problem maximizes an extended-real objective \(D\) over its feasible set \(F_D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual infeasibility means \(F_D=\varnothing\), with \(d^\star=-\infty\) under the convention \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of dual infeasibility under the standard extended-real maximization convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of empty feasibility from failure to attain a finite supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The absence of a dual optimizer does not imply dual infeasibility. Dual infeasibility is \(F_D=\varnothing\), whereas dual nonattainment can occur with \(F_D\ne\varnothing\) and a finite value \(d^\star\in\mathbb R\) for which no \(y\in F_D\) satisfies \(D(y)=d^\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure to produce a dual optimizer is not an infeasibility certificate because a feasible dual problem may have a finite but unattained supremum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in F_D}D(y)=\varnothing\not\Rightarrow F_D=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Is Not Dual Infeasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Value Alone Need Not Certify Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between empty feasibility and a negative-infinite extended value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a dual maximization problem, \(F_D=\varnothing\) implies \(d^\star=-\infty\) under \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\). The converse follows from the value alone if every feasible point satisfies \(D(y)>-\infty\). Without that condition, a nonempty feasible set on which \(D\equiv-\infty\) also has \(d^\star=-\infty\). Thus infeasibility is fundamentally the emptiness of \(F_D\), not merely a value label.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative-infinity dual value implies infeasibility only when feasible objective values cannot themselves equal negative infinity.
assumptions_latex: The dual problem maximizes an extended-real objective \(D\) over \(F_D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_D=\varnothing\Rightarrow d^\star=-\infty\), while \(d^\star=-\infty\Rightarrow F_D=\varnothing\) requires \(D(y)>-\infty\) for every \(y\in F_D\).
review_flags: feasibility conventions that define feasible points through finite objective values make the converse automatic
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Value Alone Need Not Certify Infeasibility
Primal Unboundedness Status
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal is unbounded below when feasible objective values fall below every real threshold, so its extended-real optimal value is minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal problem \(p:=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\), primal unboundedness means that the feasible domain \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap A^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}g)\) is nonempty and the objective has no finite lower bound. Equivalently, for every \(M\in\mathbb{R}\), there exists \(x_M\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap A^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}g)\) such that \(f(x_M)+g(Ax_M)<M\), and hence \(p=-\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real locally convex spaces in separating duality with \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\).
\(A:X\to Y\) is continuous linear, and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-based status for the standard Fenchel–Rockafellar primal minimization problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Unboundedness Status
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual is unbounded above when feasible dual objective values exceed every real threshold, giving dual value plus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the dual problem \(d:=\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}\), dual unboundedness means that the dual feasible set \(\{y^*\in Y^*:f^*(-A^*y^*)<+\infty,\ g^*(y^*)<+\infty\}\) is nonempty and the dual objective has no finite upper bound. Equivalently, for every \(M\in\mathbb{R}\), some dual-feasible \(y_M^*\in Y^*\) satisfies \(-f^*(-A^*y_M^*)-g^*(y_M^*)>M\), so \(d=+\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real separated locally convex spaces with continuous duals \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\).
\(A:X\to Y\) is continuous linear, \(A^*:Y^*\to X^*\) is its adjoint, and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
The conjugates \(f^*\) and \(g^*\) are taken with respect to the specified dual pairings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-based status for the standard Fenchel–Rockafellar dual maximization problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Status-Pair Compatibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak duality forbids a feasible dual when the primal is unbounded below, and forbids a feasible primal when the dual is unbounded above.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every primal-feasible \(x\in X\) and dual-feasible \(y^*\in Y^*\) satisfy \(-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\le f(x)+g(Ax)\). Consequently, primal unboundedness \(p=-\infty\) is incompatible with dual feasibility, while dual unboundedness \(d=+\infty\) is incompatible with primal feasibility. If both sides are feasible, then \(-\infty<p\) and \(d<+\infty\), although either value may be unattained and a positive duality gap may remain.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real separated locally convex spaces with continuous duals \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\).
\(A:X\to Y\) is continuous linear, \(A^*:Y^*\to X^*\) is its adjoint, and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions.
The primal and dual values are \(p:=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\) and \(d:=\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}\), and weak duality \(d\le p\) is interpreted in the extended-real order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=-\infty\Rightarrow\) dual infeasibility, and \(d=+\infty\Rightarrow\) primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility consequences of extended-real weak duality; no constraint qualification is imposed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Infeasibility Need Not Make the Dual Unbounded
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness of the one-way compatibility implication for proper convex, nonclosed data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=I\), \(f=\delta_{(0,\infty)}\), and \(g=\delta_{\{0\}}\). The primal feasible domain is empty. Moreover, \(f^*(s)=0\) for \(s\le 0\) and \(+\infty\) for \(s>0\), while \(g^*(y)=0\) for every \(y\). Hence the dual is feasible exactly for \(y\ge 0\), its objective equals \(0\) there, and its finite value \(d=0\) is attained. Thus primal infeasibility does not imply dual unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex nonclosed example has an infeasible primal but a feasible, bounded, attained dual, disproving the converse of the dual-unboundedness implication.
assumptions_latex: \(\delta_C\) denotes the extended-real indicator of a convex set \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=+\infty\) through primal infeasibility, while \(d=0\) is attained; therefore primal infeasibility \(\nRightarrow\) dual unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Infeasibility Need Not Make the Dual Unbounded
Nonclosed Range of a Bounded Linear Operator
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal compact operator on ell-squared has dense nonclosed range, exhibiting closure loss that can underlie infinite-dimensional perturbation pathologies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\ell^2\to\ell^2\) be defined by \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\). Then \(T\) is bounded, injective, and compact, but \(\operatorname{ran}T\) is not closed. Every finitely supported sequence lies in \(\operatorname{ran}T\), whereas \(y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}\) belongs to \(\ell^2\) and to \(\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}\) but not to \(\operatorname{ran}T\). Thus a continuous linear image of a closed convex set in an infinite-dimensional Banach space need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ran}T\) is a nonclosed convex linear subspace of \(\ell^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit infinite-dimensional closure-loss mechanism; it does not by itself assert a duality gap without a specified perturbation model.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Gap with an Unattained Hilbert-Space Dual
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagonal compact operator gives a finite Hilbert-space primal whose dual has the same value but no maximizing multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(H=\ell^2\), define \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\), let \(b=(1/n^2)_{n\ge1}\), and consider \[\min\left\{\tfrac12\|x\|^2:Tx=b\right\}.\] Its unique feasible point is \(\bar x=(1/n)_{n\ge1}\). The Lagrange dual is \[\sup_{y\in\ell^2}\left\{\langle b,y\rangle-\tfrac12\|T^*y\|^2\right\}.\] Its supremum equals \(\tfrac12\|\bar x\|^2\), but it is not attained: attainment would require \(T^*y=\bar x\), hence \(y_n=1\) for every \(n\), which is not in \(\ell^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min(P)=\sup(D)=\tfrac12\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-2}\), while \(\operatorname*{argmax}(D)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit conjugate-duality realization of dual nonattainment caused by nonclosed operator range.

notation.meaning: Hilbert-space adjoint of T; here T is self-adjoint

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Positive Gap from a Discontinuous Algebraic Functional
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discontinuous algebraic functional produces a proper convex perturbation value with a finite unit gap when conjugation uses only continuous functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be an infinite-dimensional normed space, choose \(f\in Y^\#\setminus Y^*\), and define \[v(0)=1,\qquad v(y)=1-f(y)\ \text{if }0<f(y)\leq1,\qquad v(y)=+\infty\ \text{otherwise}.\] Then \(v\) is proper and convex. With conjugation over the continuous dual, \[v^*(y^*)=\begin{cases}0,&y^*=0,\\+\infty,&y^*\ne0.\end{cases}\] Hence the primal perturbation value is \(v(0)=1\), whereas its conjugate-dual value is \(\sup_{y^*\in Y^*}-v^*(y^*)=0\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\in Y^\#\setminus Y^*\) is algebraic-linear and discontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit infinite-dimensional perturbation-duality pair with finite primal and dual values and a strictly positive gap.

notation.meaning: Conjugate formed using the continuous dual pairing

knowledge_statements.title: James Attainment Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: James's theorem shows that a nonreflexive Banach space admits a finite continuous-linear optimization problem over its closed bounded unit ball whose supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: James's theorem states that a Banach space \(X\) is reflexive if and only if every \(x^*\in X^*\) attains its supremum on the closed unit ball \(B_X\). Consequently, if \(X\) is nonreflexive, some \(x^*\in X^*\) satisfies \(\sup_{x\in B_X}x^*(x)=\|x^*\|<+\infty\) while no \(x\in B_X\) realizes this supremum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\text{ nonreflexive}\Rightarrow\exists x^*\in X^*:\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in B_X}x^*(x)=\varnothing.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional compactness boundary for finite but unattained continuous-linear objectives.

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of the Banach space

knowledge_statements.title: Attouch–Brézis Closed-Subspace Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Attouch–Brézis closed-subspace condition guarantees equality of the Fenchel primal and dual values and attainment of the dual maximum in Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be continuous linear, and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. If \[\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda\bigl(\operatorname{dom}g-A(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr)\] is a closed linear subspace of \(Y\), then, whenever the primal infimum is finite, \[\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}=\max_{y^*\in Y^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces and \(A:X\to Y\) is continuous linear.
\(f\) and \(g\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional Fenchel strong-duality qualification based on effective-domain geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Range Boundary for Quadratic Multiplier Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible minimum-norm Hilbert-space problem has zero duality gap, while multiplier attainment is exactly an adjoint-range condition and is automatic under closed range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\to G\) be bounded linear between real Hilbert spaces and let \(b\in\operatorname{ran}A\). The problem \[\min\{\tfrac12\|x\|^2:Ax=b\}\] has a unique minimum-norm feasible point \(\bar x\). Its dual is \[\sup_{y\in G}\{\langle b,y\rangle-\tfrac12\|A^*y\|^2\}.\] The dual supremum equals \(\tfrac12\|\bar x\|^2\), and it is attained if and only if \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ran}A^*\), equivalently \(b\in\operatorname{ran}(AA^*)\). If \(\operatorname{ran}A\) is closed, attainment holds for every \(b\in\operatorname{ran}A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf(P)=\sup(D)=\tfrac12\|\bar x\|^2\) and \(\operatorname*{argmax}(D)\ne\varnothing\iff \bar x\in\operatorname{ran}A^*\iff b\in\operatorname{ran}(AA^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space characterization of equality-constraint multiplier attainment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convex Projections Need Not Be Closed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical infinite-dimensional closure-loss mechanism, without duplicating sibling classifications of resulting gaps or nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\ell^2\) and let \(T:H\to H\) be the bounded injective operator \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\). Its range is not closed: \(y^{(k)}=(1,1/2,\ldots,1/k,0,\ldots)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ran}T\) and converges in \(H\) to \(y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}\notin\operatorname{ran}T\). The graph \(G(T)\subset H\times H\) is a closed convex subspace, whereas its second-coordinate projection is the nonclosed set \(\operatorname{ran}T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded diagonal operator on l2 has nonclosed range, so a continuous projection of a closed convex subspace can be nonclosed in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(T)\) is closed and convex, but \(\pi_2(G(T))=\operatorname{ran}T\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Projections Need Not Be Closed

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dependence on the Chosen Continuous Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological dependence specific to infinite-dimensional conjugate duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) carry separated locally convex topologies \(\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2\), with \(\tau_2\) finer. Then \(E'_{\tau_1}\subseteq E'_{\tau_2}\). Conjugates and dual problems formed with these continuous duals therefore range over different sets of linear functionals, and biconjugation gives the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope for the corresponding dual pairing. Consequently, conjugate-dual values, closedness assertions, and attainment claims must specify the topology and continuous dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In infinite dimensions the chosen topology determines the continuous dual and thus the conjugates, closed convex envelope, and potentially the dual value or attainment status.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a real vector space with separated locally convex topologies \(\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2\).
Conjugates are taken with respect to the indicated continuous dual pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E'_{\tau_1}\subseteq E'_{\tau_2}\), so conjugate-duality conclusions must specify the topology and continuous dual.

notation.meaning: Continuous dual of E under topology tau_i

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence on the Chosen Continuous Dual

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be separated locally convex spaces with continuous duals \(X^*\) and \(U^*\). Let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and define the perturbation value function \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\). The primal value is \(p=v(0)\), while the associated perturbation dual value is \(d=\sup_{u^*\in U^*}-F^*(0,u^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This candidate formalizes the standard perturbation-value meaning of infinite-dimensional duality pathology. It does not claim that every pathology is uniquely attributable to infinite dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathcal P(F)=\{\text{positive gap}:d<p\}\cup\{\text{dual nonattainment}:d=p\in\mathbb R,\ \operatorname{argmax}_{u^*\in U^*}[-F^*(0,u^*)]=\varnothing\}\cup\{\text{nonclosed value}:v(0)<v^{**}(0)\text{ or }v\text{ is not lower semicontinuous at }0\}.\] An infinite-dimensional duality pathology is the occurrence of at least one member of \(\mathcal P(F)\) for a convex perturbation problem on an infinite-dimensional locally convex space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex perturbation function \(F\) on locally convex spaces, define the primal value by \(p=\inf_x F(x,0)\) and the dual value by \(d=\sup_{u^*}-F^*(0,u^*)\). An infinite-dimensional duality pathology occurs when at least one of the following holds: there is a positive duality gap \(d<p\); the values agree finitely but the dual supremum has no maximizer; or the perturbation value function \(v(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\) is not lower semicontinuous at the origin, equivalently in the stated convex setting its biconjugate can satisfy \(v^{**}(0)<v(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[d<p\quad\text{or}\quad\bigl(d=p\in\mathbb R\text{ and the dual supremum is unattained}\bigr)\quad\text{or}\quad v^{**}(0)<v(0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(v\) is proper convex, failure of lower semicontinuity at \(0\) is recorded pointwise by \(v^{**}(0)<v(0)\).
Under the perturbation-duality convention above, \(d=v^{**}(0)\); hence a positive gap is the strict inequality between the value and its lower-semicontinuous convex envelope at the origin.
special_cases_latex: In finite-dimensional convex programming, standard relative-interior qualification conditions commonly exclude the listed gap and nonattainment phenomena; this definition concerns the regime where such closure mechanisms are unavailable or fail.
immediate_consequences_latex: The three labels distinguish value failure, attainment failure, and closure failure; they should not be conflated even when they occur in the same problem.
boundary_notes: No inspected source in the supplied corpus supported this exact three-part taxonomy in the stated infinite-dimensional locally convex scope.
The equality \(d=v^{**}(0)\) depends on the specified perturbation pairing and dual convention.
Primal nonattainment is not included unless it is separately imposed as part of the pathology taxonomy.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the perturbation function on the paired dual product.
Biconjugate, hence the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope when the standard hypotheses apply.

review_flags: Exact authoritative support is missing for the proposed combined taxonomy and its infinite-dimensional scope.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), where \(\Gamma_0\) denotes the proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. Write \(\operatorname{rec}\varphi\) for the recession function and \(C=\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space formulation for proper closed convex functions; the correspondence concerns epigraph homogenization and includes the zero-scale closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
\[\widetilde\varphi(\xi,x)=\begin{cases}\xi\varphi(x/\xi),&\xi>0,\\(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(x),&\xi=0,\\+\infty,&\xi<0.
\end{cases}\] The perspective-homogenization correspondence is \[\operatorname{epi}\widetilde\varphi=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}\varphi)}.\] Thus positive scaling homogenizes the original epigraph, and recession directions supply precisely its closed zero-scale face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective of \(\varphi\) assigns \(\xi\varphi(x/\xi)\) at positive scale, the recession value \((\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(x)\) at zero scale, and \(+\infty\) at negative scale. Its epigraph is the closure of the cone generated by \(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}\varphi\). This equality is the perspective-homogenization correspondence: the slice at scale one recovers the original epigraph, positive slices are scaled copies, and the scale-zero slice records recession geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}\widetilde\varphi=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}\varphi)}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\xi>0\), \((\xi,x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}\widetilde\varphi\) if and only if \((x/\xi,r/\xi)\in\operatorname{epi}\varphi\).
The unit-scale slice satisfies \(\widetilde\varphi(1,x)=\varphi(x)\), while the zero-scale slice is \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\varphi\) is supercoercive, then \(\operatorname{rec}\varphi=\iota_{\{0\}}\), so the only finite point at zero scale is \((0,0)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The closed perspective is positively homogeneous: \(\widetilde\varphi(\lambda\xi,\lambda x)=\lambda\widetilde\varphi(\xi,x)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
The function \(\widetilde\varphi\) belongs to \(\Gamma_0(\mathbb R\oplus\mathcal H)\).
boundary_notes: The unclosed positive-scale perspective that assigns \(+\infty\) at \(\xi\le 0\) has epigraph \(\operatorname{cone}C\), which need not contain the recession face.
Negative scales are excluded by assigning \(+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry of the Closed Perspective Epigraph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) on a real Hilbert space and let \(P_\varphi:\mathbb R\times\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) denote its closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex Hilbert-space geometry, including positive, zero, and negative scale regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
\[P_\varphi(\xi,x)=\begin{cases}\xi\varphi(x/\xi),&\xi>0,\\(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(x),&\xi=0,\\+\infty,&\xi<0.
\end{cases}\] Its closed perspective geometry is the closed convex cone \[K_\varphi:=\operatorname{epi}P_\varphi=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}\varphi)}\subset\mathbb R\times\mathcal H\times\mathbb R.\] The section \(K_\varphi\cap(\{1\}\times\mathcal H\times\mathbb R)\) is \(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}\varphi\), and its zero-scale section is \(\{0\}\times\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed perspective geometry is the closed convex cone obtained by homogenizing the epigraph of a proper closed convex function. At positive scale \(\xi\), the epigraph condition rescales to the epigraph of \(\varphi\); the unit slice recovers \(\operatorname{epi}\varphi\). At scale zero, the finite boundary is the epigraph of the recession function. No negative-scale point is in the effective domain. This cone, rather than only the formula at \(\xi>0\), is the geometric object defined by the closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K_\varphi=\overline{\operatorname{cone}(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}\varphi)},\qquad K_\varphi\cap(\{0\}\times\mathcal H\times\mathbb R)=\{0\}\times\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((\xi,x,r)\in K_\varphi\) with \(\xi>0\) if and only if \(r\ge\xi\varphi(x/\xi)\).
\((0,x,r)\in K_\varphi\) if and only if \(r\ge(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\varphi(x)=\|x\|^p\) with \(p>1\), \(P_\varphi(\xi,x)=\|x\|^p/\xi^{p-1}\) for \(\xi>0\), and the zero-scale domain is only \(x=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every sublevel epigraph inequality \(P_\varphi(\xi,x)\le r\) is convex and positively homogeneous in \((\xi,x,r)\).
Closure may add nontrivial points at \(\xi=0\), even though the original positive-scale perspective is undefined there.
boundary_notes: Closed perspective geometry does not assert continuity relative to its effective domain at the origin.
If \(\varphi\) is not lower semicontinuous, this construction corresponds to an appropriate closed convex envelope rather than preserving every original boundary value.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Scale Perspectives
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At positive scale, the perspective evaluates the original convex function at the normalized point and multiplies the value by the scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \((x,t)\in X\times(0,+\infty)\), the positive-scale perspective of \(f\) is defined by \(\widetilde f(x,t):=t f(x/t)\). Its effective domain on positive scales is \(\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\). The transformation is positively homogeneous there: for every \(\lambda>0\), \(\widetilde f(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda\widetilde f(x,t)\). It is convex because its epigraph is obtained by positive homogenization of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real locally convex space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde f(x,t)=t f(x/t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scale branch of the closed perspective construction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph geometry at each strictly positive scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(t>0\), \[\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f\cap(X\times\{t\}\times\mathbb R)=\{(ty,t,ts):(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\] Consequently, \((x,t,r)\in\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f\) if and only if \((x/t,r/t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\), and the unit-scale slice recovers \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive-scale epigraph slice is a scaled copy of the original epigraph and dehomogenizes by division by the scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f\cap(X\times\{t\}\times\mathbb R)=\{(ty,t,ts):(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\) for \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Epigraph Slices and Dehomogenization
Radial Limit Formula for the Zero-Scale Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approaching a zero-scale point along a ray based at any finite point of the original function yields exactly the recession value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). For every direction \(d\), the extended-real difference quotients \[q_s(d)=\frac{f(x_0+s d)-f(x_0)}{s},\qquad s>0,\] are nondecreasing in \(s\) and satisfy \[f^{\infty}(d)=\lim_{s\to+\infty}q_s(d).\] Moreover, \[\widetilde f(d+t x_0,t)=t f(x_0+d/t)=q_{1/t}(d)+t f(x_0),\] and therefore \[f^{\infty}(d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\widetilde f(d+t x_0,t).\] Thus the recession value is the radial lower-semicontinuous limit of the positive-scale perspective approaching \((d,0)\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\infty}(d)=\lim_{s\to+\infty}(f(x_0+sd)-f(x_0))/s=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\widetilde f(d+t x_0,t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent limiting formulation of recession closure at zero perspective scale.

notation.meaning: recession difference quotient at base point x_0

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Scale Recession Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the perspective at zero scale assigns each direction its recession cost, preserving convexity, lower semicontinuity, and positive homogeneity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower-semicontinuous closure of the positive-scale perspective at scale zero is the recession function: \(\widetilde f(d,0):=f^{\infty}(d)\). Together with \(\widetilde f(x,t)=t f(x/t)\) for \(t>0\) and \(\widetilde f(x,t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\), this defines a proper lower-semicontinuous convex positively homogeneous function on \(X\times\mathbb{R}\). In particular, zero-scale points record precisely the finite-cost recession directions of \(f\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The recession function is defined by \(f^{\infty}(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\,s>0}(f(x+sd)-f(x))/s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde f(d,0)=f^{\infty}(d)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuous closure of the perspective at scale zero.

notation.meaning: Recession function of the convex function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization of the zero-scale value as the lower-semicontinuous envelope of positive perspective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is finite-dimensional, then for every \(d\in X\), \[\widetilde f(d,0)=f^{\infty}(d)=\liminf_{\substack{(x,t)\to(d,0)\\t>0}}t f(x/t).\] Thus the recession assignment is exactly the lower-semicontinuous closure of the strictly positive perspective at scale zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession value is the joint lower limit of positive-scale perspective values approaching the zero-scale point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde f(d,0)=\liminf_{(x,t)\to(d,0),\,t>0}t f(x/t)=f^{\infty}(d)\).

notation.meaning: Joint lower limit over positive scales

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Scale Value of a Closed Perspective
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), choose any \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\), and define \((\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(d)=\sup_{\alpha>0}[\varphi(x_0+\alpha d)-\varphi(x_0)]/\alpha\). This definition is independent of the chosen \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns the lower-semicontinuous closure of the positive-scale perspective at scale zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero-scale recession closure of the perspective of \(\varphi\) is the assignment \[P_\varphi(0,d):=(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(d).\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{epi}P_\varphi\cap(\{0\}\times\mathcal H\times\mathbb R)=\{0\}\times\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi).\] Together with \(P_\varphi(\xi,x)=\xi\varphi(x/\xi)\) for \(\xi>0\), this is the unique lower-semicontinuous convex closure specified by Proposition 9.42.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero scale, the closed perspective is defined by the recession function: \(P_\varphi(0,d)=(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(d)\). Therefore a direction \(d\) has a finite zero-scale value exactly when it is a finite-cost recession direction of \(\varphi\). Geometrically, closing the cone generated by the positive-scale epigraph adds the scale-zero epigraph \(\{0\}\times\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)\). Assigning zero only at the origin is valid only in special coercive cases, not for a general closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_\varphi(0,d)=(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(d),\qquad \operatorname{epi}P_\varphi\big|_{\xi=0}=\{0\}\times\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(d\in\mathcal H\), \(P_\varphi(0,d)<+\infty\) if and only if \((\operatorname{rec}\varphi)(d)<+\infty\).
The zero-scale points are precisely the recession cone of \(\{1\}\times\operatorname{epi}\varphi\) embedded at scale zero.
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{rec}\varphi=\iota_{\{0\}}\), then \(P_\varphi(0,0)=0\) and \(P_\varphi(0,d)=+\infty\) for \(d\ne0\).
If \(\varphi\) is sublinear and closed, then \(\operatorname{rec}\varphi=\varphi\), so its entire epigraph appears at zero scale.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero finite recession direction produces a nontrivial finite point on the zero-scale face.
Replacing the zero-scale recession value by an arbitrary constant can destroy lower semicontinuity or convexity.
boundary_notes: The formula is for proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(\varphi\); a nonclosed function requires prior closure.
No value is assigned at negative scale other than \(+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective-Domain Homogenization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perspective domain is the positive homogenization of the original domain together with its finite-cost recession directions at zero scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The effective domain of the closed perspective decomposes as \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:t>0,\ x\in t\operatorname{dom}f\}\cup\{(d,0):d\in\operatorname{dom}f^{\infty}\}\). Equivalently, its positive-scale portion is the homogenization of \(\operatorname{dom}f\times\{1\}\), and its zero-scale portion consists of the recession directions having finite recession cost. No point with negative scale belongs to \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde f\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=\{(x,t):t>0,\ x\in t\operatorname{dom}f\}\cup\{(d,0):d\in\operatorname{dom}f^{\infty}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain decomposition of the closed perspective into positive and zero scales.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogenized Effective Domain of a Perspective
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), let \(D=\operatorname{dom}\varphi\), and let \(P_\varphi\) be its closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective-domain geometry of closed perspectives on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perspective-domain homogenization of \(D\) is \[\operatorname{dom}P_\varphi=\{(\xi,x):\xi>0,\ x\in\xi D\}\cup\bigl(\{0\}\times\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)\bigr).\] Equivalently, its positive-scale portion is \(\{(\xi,\xi y):\xi>0,\ y\in D\}\), and its closed zero-scale boundary is determined by the finite recession directions of \(\varphi\). No point with \(\xi<0\) belongs to the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of the closed perspective is the homogenization of the original effective domain together with its recession boundary. For positive scale \(\xi\), a pair \((\xi,x)\) is feasible exactly when \(x/\xi\) belongs to \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\), or equivalently \(x\in\xi\operatorname{dom}\varphi\). At scale zero, feasibility means that the recession function is finite. Negative scales are outside the effective domain. Thus domain homogenization includes both scaled copies of the original domain and the scale-zero directions required by closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}P_\varphi=\{(\xi,\xi y):\xi>0,\ y\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\}\cup\bigl(\{0\}\times\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\xi>0\), \((\xi,x)\in\operatorname{dom}P_\varphi\iff x/\xi\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\).
The domain is the projection onto \((\xi,x)\) of the closed perspective epigraph cone.
special_cases_latex: If \(\varphi\) is supercoercive, then \(\operatorname{dom}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)=\{0\}\).
If \(\varphi=\iota_C\) for a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), then the domain is \(\{(\xi,x):\xi>0,\ x\in\xi C\}\cup(\{0\}\times\operatorname{rec}C)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The homogenized domain is convex because it is the effective domain of a convex function.
Unbounded directions of \(\operatorname{dom}\varphi\) can create nonzero feasible points at zero scale.
boundary_notes: The effective domain need not itself be closed even though the epigraph is closed.
Domain homogenization alone does not determine perspective values; the epigraph heights are also required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate of a Perspective as an Indicator
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), pair \(\mathbb R\oplus\mathcal H\) with itself by \(\langle(\xi,x),(\mu,u)\rangle=\xi\mu+\langle x,u\rangle\), and let \(P_\varphi\) be the closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy for closed perspectives on real Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closed convex set \[C_\varphi:=\{(\mu,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathcal H:\mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\}.\] The perspective conjugacy interface is \[P_\varphi^*=\iota_{C_\varphi}.\] Consequently, \(P_\varphi=\sigma_{C_\varphi}\), where \(\sigma_C\) is the support function of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of the closed perspective is the indicator of the hypograph-like set \(C_\varphi=\{(\mu,u):\mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\}\). It is zero on that set and \(+\infty\) outside. Since the closed perspective is proper, closed, and convex, biconjugation also identifies it with the support function of \(C_\varphi\). This gives the precise interface between perspective geometry and the conjugate of the original function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_\varphi^*=\iota_{\{(\mu,u):\mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\}},\qquad P_\varphi=\sigma_{\{(\mu,u):\mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\}}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_\varphi^*(\mu,u)=0\) if \(\mu\le-\varphi^*(u)\), and \(P_\varphi^*(\mu,u)=+\infty\) otherwise.
\(P_\varphi(\xi,x)=\sup\{\xi\mu+\langle x,u\rangle:\mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\}\).
special_cases_latex: At unit scale, \(\varphi(x)=\sup_u\{\langle x,u\rangle-\varphi^*(u)\}\) is recovered by choosing the largest admissible \(\mu=-\varphi^*(u)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The perspective is sublinear because it is a support function.
The dual feasible set is closed and convex whenever \(\varphi^*\) is lower semicontinuous and convex.
boundary_notes: The pairing and ordering of scalar and Hilbert-space coordinates must be preserved.
For the unclosed positive-scale perspective, the same conjugate formula holds, but recovering the primal by biconjugation returns its closed perspective.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator: zero on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) outside.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Epigraph Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perspective conjugate is the indicator of a reflected epigraph of the original conjugate; equivalently, the perspective is that set's support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(C_f:=\{(u,\eta)\in X^*\times\mathbb{R}:f^*(u)+\eta\le0\}\). The conjugate of the closed perspective is \(\widetilde f^*(u,\eta)=\delta_{C_f}(u,\eta)\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}f^*=\{(u,r):(u,-r)\in C_f\}\), so the dual feasible set of the perspective is a reflected epigraph of \(f^*\). By biconjugacy, \(\widetilde f=\sigma_{C_f}\), the support function of \(C_f\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a separated locally convex space.
\(\widetilde f\) is the closed perspective and conjugacy uses the product pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde f^*=\delta_{C_f}\), where \(C_f=\{(u,\eta):f^*(u)+\eta\le0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate representation of the closed perspective as an indicator function.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and \(f\equiv0\). Then \(C_f=\{(0,\eta):\eta\le0\}\), \(K_f=X\times\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R_+\), and \(K_f^{\circ}=\{0\}\times\mathbb R_-\times\mathbb R_-\). The nonclosed cone \(\operatorname{cone}(C_f\times\{-1\})\) omits every \((0,\eta,0)\) with \(\eta<0\); hence closure in the polar formula is essential.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polar-cone form of perspective epigraph duality, including the necessary closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_f:=\operatorname{epi}\widetilde f\subseteq X\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\), and use the negative polar \(K_f^{\circ}:=\{w:\langle w,z\rangle\le0\ \forall z\in K_f\}\). Then \[K_f^{\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(u,\eta,-1):(u,\eta)\in C_f\},\qquad C_f=\{(u,\eta):f^*(u)+\eta\le0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative polar of the perspective epigraph cone is the closed conic hull of the reflected-conjugate feasible set placed at last coordinate minus one.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The stated negative-polar convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_f^{\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C_f\times\{-1\})\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Halfspace Description of the Perspective Epigraph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\varphi\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), let \(P_\varphi\) be its closed perspective, and define \(C_\varphi=\{(\mu,u):\mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph-dual description induced by the conjugate of a closed perspective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Perspective epigraph duality is the representation \[\operatorname{epi}P_\varphi=\bigcap_{(\mu,u)\in C_\varphi}\{(\xi,x,r):\xi\mu+\langle x,u\rangle\le r\}.\] Equivalently, \[P_\varphi(\xi,x)=\sup_{(\mu,u)\in C_\varphi}\bigl(\xi\mu+\langle x,u\rangle\bigr).\] Thus the homogenized primal epigraph is the intersection of the closed halfspaces indexed by the conjugate inequality \(\mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a closed perspective is described dually by all affine homogeneous inequalities generated by pairs \((\mu,u)\) satisfying \(\mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\). A triple \((\xi,x,r)\) belongs to the epigraph exactly when \(r\) dominates \(\xi\mu+\langle x,u\rangle\) for every such dual pair. Equivalently, the perspective value is the support function of the dual feasible set. The definition links the conic epigraph directly to the conjugate geometry of \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}P_\varphi=\{(\xi,x,r):\forall(\mu,u),\ \mu+\varphi^*(u)\le0\Rightarrow\xi\mu+\langle x,u\rangle\le r\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The defining halfspaces are exactly the epigraph inequalities of the support function \(\sigma_{C_\varphi}\).
At \(\xi=1\), the representation reduces to the Fenchel biconjugate formula for \(\varphi\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\xi=0\), the intersection describes \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}\varphi)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every \((\mu,u)\in C_\varphi\) supplies a valid homogeneous lower bound \(P_\varphi(\xi,x)\ge\xi\mu+\langle x,u\rangle\).
The epigraph is a closed convex cone as an intersection of closed homogeneous halfspaces.
boundary_notes: This is an exact representation for the closed perspective; using only a strict subset of \(C_\varphi\) generally yields an outer approximation.
The result is not an assertion that \(C_\varphi\) is the polar cone of the epigraph without an additional coordinate/sign convention.

notation.meaning: Dual index set defined by the conjugate inequality.
