knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a cone-family-dependent size vector; scalar size conventions require an explicit aggregation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal K\) be a specified family of closed convex cones. An exact \(K\)-lift of \(C\) is data \((K,A,b,\pi)\), with \(K\in\mathcal K\), satisfying \[C=\pi\bigl(K\cap\{z\in\mathbb{R}^m:Az=b\}\bigr).\] Its size vector is \((m,q,\sigma(K))\), where \(q\) is the number of scalar rows of \(A\) and \(\sigma\) is fixed for the cone family. The lift-size measure \(\operatorname{size}_{\mathcal K}(C)\) is the componentwise infimum of these vectors over all exact \(\mathcal K\)-lifts of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift size records lifted dimension, affine-equation count, and a cone-specific parameter, minimized over all exact lifts from the prescribed cone family.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Representation Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact representation complexity is the infimum size of an exact description in a fixed language, is infinite for an unrepresentable target, and need not be attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a representation language \(\mathfrak R\), an interpretation map \(R\mapsto\llbracket R\rrbracket\), and a scalar size map \(s\). The exact representation complexity of a target \(C\) is \[\operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C):=\inf\{s(R):R\in\mathfrak R,\ \llbracket R\rrbracket=C\}.\] The value is \(+\infty\) when no exact representation exists. Because the definition uses an infimum, a finite value need not be realized by any representation unless attainment is separately established.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak R\) is a fixed representation language with an interpretation map.
\(s:\mathfrak R\to[0,+\infty]\) is a fixed scalar size map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C)=\inf\{s(R):\llbracket R\rrbracket=C\},\text{ with }\inf\varnothing=+\infty.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension complexity as the minimum inequality size of an exact polyhedral lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its linear extension complexity under the convention that affine equations are free is \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\Bigl\{r:\exists k,q\in\mathbb N_0,\ A\in\mathbb R^{r\times n},\ B\in\mathbb R^{r\times k},\ b\in\mathbb R^r,\ E\in\mathbb R^{q\times n},\ F\in\mathbb R^{q\times k},\ d\in\mathbb R^q,\ P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^k,\ Ax+By\leq b,\ Ex+Fy=d\}\Bigr\}.\] The minimum ranges over all auxiliary dimensions and all exact finite polyhedral lifts, while only the \(r\) inequality rows are charged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope's extension complexity is the smallest number of inequalities in any exact polyhedral lift, with auxiliary dimensions unrestricted and affine equations uncharged.
assumptions_latex: Only inequality rows are charged; affine equality rows are free under the stated convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\) is the minimum inequality count among all exact finite polyhedral extended formulations of \(P\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of exact representation complexities under a denotation-preserving translation between fixed representation languages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathfrak R_i,\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket_i,s_i)\), \(i=1,2\), be representation languages. If \(T:\mathfrak R_1\to\mathfrak R_2\) satisfies \(\llbracket T(R)\rrbracket_2=\llbracket R\rrbracket_1\) and \(s_2(T(R))\le a s_1(R)+b\) for all \(R\in\mathfrak R_1\), where \(a>0\) and \(b\ge0\), then \[\operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R_2}(C)\le a\operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R_1}(C)+b\] for every represented set \(C\). Mutually size-controlled translations yield the corresponding two-sided complexity comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A denotation-preserving translation with affine size overhead transfers that overhead to exact representation complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity Comparison under Size-Controlled Translation
Budget–Expressiveness Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger size budgets weakly increase exact representational power. Complexity below a budget guarantees membership, membership bounds complexity by the budget, and equality requires attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed representation language \(\mathfrak R\) and size map \(s\), define \[\mathfrak B_b:=\{C:\exists R\in\mathfrak R,\ \llbracket R\rrbracket=C,\ s(R)\le b\}.\] If \(b\le c\), then \(\mathfrak B_b\subseteq\mathfrak B_c\). Moreover, \[\operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C)<b\Longrightarrow C\in\mathfrak B_b\Longrightarrow\operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C)\le b.\] At equality, \(\operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C)=b\) implies \(C\in\mathfrak B_b\) exactly when the infimum is attained by a representation of size \(b\). Strict inclusion between budget classes requires a language-specific separating target.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak R\), its interpretation map, and its scalar size map \(s\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathfrak B_b\subseteq\mathfrak B_c,\qquad \operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C)<b\Rightarrow C\in\mathfrak B_b\Rightarrow\operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C)\le b.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity of exact-representation classes and the sharp infimum-attainment boundary.

notation.meaning: targets with an exact representation of size at most b

knowledge_statements.title: Size–Expressiveness Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral lift size is measured by the number of inequalities in an exact extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), define \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\) as the minimum number of inequalities in any polyhedron \(Q=\{(x,y):Ax+By\leq b\}\) satisfying \(P=\operatorname{proj}_x Q\). If \(\mathcal{E}_s\) denotes the polytopes admitting such a lift with at most \(s\) inequalities, then \(\mathcal{E}_s\subseteq\mathcal{E}_t\) whenever \(s\leq t\), and \(P\in\mathcal{E}_s\) holds exactly when \(s\geq\operatorname{xc}(P)\). Thus increasing the lift-size budget weakly enlarges the exactly representable class, while extension-complexity lower bounds identify sets excluded from every smaller budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact representability is monotone in the allowed number of lifted inequalities, and a polytope enters the representable class precisely when the budget reaches its extension complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polytope in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
Lift size counts inequalities; equations and auxiliary-variable dimension are not counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{E}_s\subseteq\mathcal{E}_t\) for \(s\leq t\), and \(P\in\mathcal{E}_s\iff s\geq\operatorname{xc}(P)\).

notation.meaning: linear extension complexity of the polytope P
class of polytopes having an exact lift with at most s inequalities

knowledge_statements.title: Invariant Lower-Bound Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any invariant proved never to exceed representation size lower-bounds exact representation complexity and can exclude all exact lifts within a stated budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a representation language \(\mathfrak R\) with interpretation \(R\mapsto\llbracket R\rrbracket\) and scalar size \(s(R)\). If an invariant \(L\) satisfies \[L(\llbracket R\rrbracket)\le s(R)\qquad(R\in\mathfrak R),\] then every exactly representable target \(C\) satisfies \[L(C)\le \operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C).\] Consequently, \(L(C)>b\) certifies that no exact representation of \(C\) has size at most \(b\).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak R\) is a fixed representation language with interpretation map and scalar size map \(s\).
\(L(\llbracket R\rrbracket)\le s(R)\) for every admissible representation \(R\in\mathfrak R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(C)\le\operatorname{rc}_{\mathfrak R}(C),\quad L(C)>b\Longrightarrow C\notin\mathfrak B_b.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Language-relative certificate converting a sound invariant into an exact-representation lower bound.

notation.meaning: exact representation complexity in the fixed language
targets having an exact representation of size at most b

knowledge_statements.title: Lift Lower-Bound Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical polytope families demonstrate exponential barriers to exact linear lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{CUT}(K_n)\) be the cut polytope and let \(\operatorname{MATCH}(K_n)\) be the matching polytope of the complete graph on \(n\) vertices. There are absolute constants \(c_{m cut}>0\) and \(c_{m match}>0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(n\), \[\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{CUT}(K_n))\geq 2^{c_{m cut}n},\qquad \operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{MATCH}(K_n))\geq 2^{c_{m match}n}.\] Consequently, every exact linear extended formulation of either family requires exponentially many inequalities, irrespective of the number of auxiliary variables or equations allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut and matching polytopes require exponentially many inequalities in every exact linear extended formulation, even when arbitrarily many auxiliary variables and equations are permitted.
assumptions_latex: Lift size is the number of inequalities in an exact linear extended formulation.
The underlying graph is the complete graph \(K_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{CUT}(K_n))=2^{\Omega(n)}\) and \(\operatorname{xc}(\operatorname{MATCH}(K_n))=2^{\Omega(n)}\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of incidence vectors of cuts of the complete graph
convex hull of incidence vectors of matchings of the complete graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lower-bound interface between polyhedral extension size and nonnegative factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polytope of positive dimension, and let \(S_P\) be a facet-versus-vertex slack matrix of \(P\). If \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\) is the minimum number of inequalities in a polyhedral extended formulation, with affine equations not counted, then \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S_P),\] where \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S_P)\) is the least inner dimension \(r\) in a factorization \(S_P=UV\) with \(U,V\) entrywise nonnegative. Therefore \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S_P)>r\) certifies that no exact polyhedral lift with at most \(r\) inequalities exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope's linear extension complexity equals the nonnegative rank of its slack matrix, converting factorization lower bounds into lift lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polytope of positive dimension.
\(S_P\) is a facet-versus-vertex slack matrix of \(P\).
Extension size counts inequalities and does not count affine equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S_P).\)

notation.meaning: facet-versus-vertex slack matrix of the polytope
nonnegative rank of the slack matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Yannakakis Factorization Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lower-bound interface between semidefinite lift size and PSD rank for polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polytope and let \(S_P\) be a slack matrix. The least integer \(r\) for which \(P\) has an exact lift through an affine slice of \(\mathbb S_+^r\) equals the PSD rank of \(S_P\), namely the least \(r\) for which there exist \(A_i,B_j\in\mathbb S_+^r\) satisfying \[(S_P)_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(A_iB_j)\quad\text{for every }i,j.\] Thus \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{psd}}(S_P)>r\) excludes every exact \(\mathbb S_+^r\)-lift of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidefinite lift size equals the PSD rank of a polytope's slack matrix, so PSD-rank bounds certify semidefinite lift lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: Lift size is the matrix order \(r\) of a single cone \(\mathbb S_+^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sxc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{psd}}(S_P).\)

notation.meaning: cone of real positive-semidefinite matrices of order r
least order of a PSD factorization of the slack matrix
semidefinite extension complexity under the stated convention

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interface Boundary for an External Reformulation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let the original minimization model be \(\inf\{f(x):x\in X\}\). Let an external reformulation use variables \((x,u)\in Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\) and objective \(F(x,u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This navigational interface records what must agree across a reformulation boundary. It deliberately excludes the construction theory of particular conic, bilinear, or global relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The external reformulation interface associated with \((X,f)\\) and \((Q,F)\) consists of the projected feasible set and reduced objective \[Y:=\pi_x(Q),\qquad \widehat f(x):=\inf\{F(x,u):(x,u)\in Q\}.\] The reformulation is feasible-set exact when \(Y=X\), objective exact when \(\widehat f(x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), and fully exact when both conditions hold and every finite \(\widehat f(x)\) is attained by an auxiliary witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An external reformulation crosses an interface through two induced objects: the projection of its feasible set and the objective obtained after minimizing over auxiliary variables. Feasible-set exactness requires the projection to equal the original feasible set. Objective exactness requires the reduced objective to equal the original objective on that set. Full exactness additionally requires an auxiliary witness to attain each finite reduced value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Y=\pi_x(Q),\quad\widehat f(x)=\inf_{u:(x,u)\in Q}F(x,u),\quad\text{full exactness}:\ Y=X,\ \widehat f|_X=f,\ \operatorname{argmin}_{u:(x,u)\in Q}F(x,u)\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Feasible-set exactness is \(x\in X\iff\exists u\ (x,u)\in Q\).
Objective exactness is the marginal identity \(f(x)=\inf_u(F(x,u)+\iota_Q(x,u))\) for every \(x\in X\).
special_cases_latex: A pure feasibility reformulation takes \(f=F=0\), leaving only projected-set exactness.
An epigraph reformulation is fully set-exact when the projection of its lifted epigraph equals \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Full exactness implies equality of optimal values whenever either side has a finite infimum.
Equality of optimal values alone does not imply feasible-set or objective exactness.
boundary_notes: The definition does not describe cone-specific reformulation machinery.
It excludes approximate, stochastic, and global-relaxation quality guarantees.
No inspected source states this exact three-part interface under the supplied node title.

notation.meaning: objective induced by eliminating auxiliary variables

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Lift Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic lift represents a convex set exactly as the linear image of an affine slice of a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact conic lift of \(C\) consists of a closed convex cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\), a linear map \(A:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^q\), a vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^q\), and a linear projection \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[C=\pi\bigl(K\cap\{z\in\mathbb{R}^m:Az=b\}\bigr).\] Membership in \(C\) is therefore equivalent to the existence of a lifted variable \(z\in K\) satisfying \(Az=b\) and \(\pi z=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data form an exact conic lift precisely when \(C=\pi(K\cap\{z:Az=b\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records only the abstract convex-analytic interface; cone catalogs, certificates, and solver behavior remain external.

notation.meaning: Closed convex cone used in the lifted formulation.
Linear projection onto the original variable space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Conic Lift of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) be a convex cone, let \(A\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{q\times m}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry defines only the representability interface. Cone-specific catalogs, dual certificates, constraint qualifications, and solver implications belong to conic-optimization chapters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(K\)-conic lift of a set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is affine data \((A,B,b)\) such that \[X=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists u\in\mathbb R^m,\ Ax+Bu-b\in K\}.\] Equivalently, with \[Q_K:=\{(x,u):Ax+Bu-b\in K\},\] one has \(X=\pi_x(Q_K)\). An extended-real convex function \(f\) has a \(K\)-conic lift when its epigraph admits such a representation in variables \((x,t,u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic lift represents a target set as the projection of an affine conic system in original and auxiliary variables. A point belongs to the target exactly when it can be completed by auxiliary variables so that the affine residual lies in the chosen cone. A function is conically lifted when this construction represents its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in X\iff\exists u\in\mathbb R^m:\ Ax+Bu-b\in K,\qquad X=\pi_x\{(x,u):Ax+Bu-b\in K\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(L(x,u)=Ax+Bu-b\), the lifted feasible set is \(Q_K=L^{-1}(K)\).
For a function, \(f\) is \(K\)-representable iff \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):\exists u,\ A_xx+A_tt+Bu-b\in K\}.\]
special_cases_latex: Taking \(K=\mathbb R_+^q\) yields a polyhedral lift.
A product of second-order cones yields a conic-quadratic representation.
Taking \(K=\mathbb S_+^k\) with a symmetric affine map yields a semidefinite representation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity of \(K\) implies convexity of the lifted set and its projection.
A known conic lift converts membership in \(X\) into feasibility of an affine conic system with auxiliary variables.
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(K\) does not guarantee closedness of its projected affine slice.
The definition does not impose strict feasibility or guarantee dual attainment.
Lift size, cone choice, and numerical performance are not part of this interface.

knowledge_statements.title: McCormick Envelope Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over a bounded rectangle, four affine McCormick inequalities describe exactly the convex hull of a single bilinear graph; broader substitutions generally provide only relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:=\{(x,y,w):l_x\le x\le u_x,\ l_y\le y\le u_y,\ w=xy\}\). Its convex hull consists exactly of the bound-feasible points satisfying \[w\ge l_xy+l_yx-l_xl_y,\qquad w\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y,\] \[w\le u_xy+l_yx-u_xl_y,\qquad w\le l_xy+u_yx-l_xu_y.\] Consequently, these four inequalities give the exact convex envelope interface for one bilinear equality on a rectangle. Replacing \(w=xy\) by them outside this bounded single-term setting generally yields only a relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four McCormick inequalities describe \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,w):w=xy\}\) over the rectangle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the single-bilinear-term hull; recursive relaxations, tightening, and branching remain external.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The four displayed affine inequalities are the classical exact convex hull of a bilinear graph over a rectangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: McCormick Envelope Interface for a Bounded Bilinear Product
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x,y,w\in\mathbb R\), let \(\ell_x<u_x\) and \(\ell_y<u_y\) be finite, and set \(B=[\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\). The auxiliary variable \(w\) represents the bilinear expression \(xy\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns one continuous bilinear term over a finite rectangular domain. It specifies the exact polyhedral convexification used as an interface when the nonlinear equality is lifted into an auxiliary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The McCormick envelope interface for \(w=xy\) on \(B\) is the polyhedron
\[
\mathcal M(B):=\left\{(x,y,w)\in\mathbb R^3:\begin{array}{l}
\ell_x\le x\le u_x,\quad \ell_y\le y\le u_y,\\
w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\\
w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y,\\
w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\\
w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y
\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Thus the interface replaces the graph equation \(w=xy\) by two affine underestimators and two affine overestimators, while retaining the factor bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded real factors \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), introduce \(w\) for their product. The McCormick envelope interface is the set of all bounded triples \((x,y,w)\) satisfying the two lower inequalities \(w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y\) and \(w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y\), together with the two upper inequalities \(w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y\) and \(w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal M(B):=\{(x,y,w)\in\mathbb R^3:(x,y)\in B,\ w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\ w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y,\ w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\ w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The lower boundary is the convex envelope of the product: \[\operatorname{vex}_{B}(xy)=\max\{\ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\ u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y\}.\]
The upper boundary is the concave envelope of the product: \[\operatorname{cav}_{B}(xy)=\min\{u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\ \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y\}.\]
Equivalently, the interface is the convex hull of the bounded bilinear graph: \[\mathcal M(B)=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,xy):(x,y)\in B\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\{0,1\}\) and \(0\le y\le u_y\), taking \(\ell_x=0\), \(u_x=1\), and \(\ell_y=0\) yields \[0\le w,\qquad w\le y,\qquad w\le u_yx,\qquad w\ge y-u_y(1-x),\] which gives the exact convex hull of the binary-continuous product graph.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point satisfying \(w=xy\) with \((x,y)\in B\) belongs to \(\mathcal M(B)\), so replacing the graph equation by this interface is a valid convex relaxation.
All four defining inequalities are affine; consequently, the interface can be inserted directly into a linear-programming relaxation.
At each of the four corners of \(B\), the permitted value of \(w\) is exactly \(xy\).
boundary_notes: Finite lower and upper bounds are material: the stated four-facet interface is not the corresponding bounded polytope when a factor has an infinite bound.
The definition covers a single scalar bilinear product. Multilinear terms require additional constructions, often recursive bilinear lifting, whose strength may depend on the chosen factorization.

For continuous factors on a box, the four inequalities describe the convex hull of the isolated product graph; after coupling the variables to other constraints, they need not describe the convex hull of the entire optimization model.

knowledge_statements.title: Polarity-Gauge Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polarity and the extended-valued gauge–support correspondence for closed convex sets containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\). Define
\[
C^\circ=\{y\in X:\langle y,c\rangle\leq 1\ \text{for every }c\in C\},\qquad
\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\geq 0:x\in tC\},
\]
with the infimum of the empty set equal to \(+\infty\). Then, for every \(x\in X\),
\[
\gamma_C(x)=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)=\sup_{y\in C^\circ}\langle x,y\rangle,
\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C.
\]
Thus the gauge of \(C\) is represented by the support function of its polar, while polarity recovers \(C\) under the stated closure and convexity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set containing zero equals its bipolar, and its possibly infinite gauge equals the support function of its polar set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and satisfies \(0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\) on \(X\), and \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).

notation.meaning: The polar set of C with unit upper bound under the inner product.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Function of a Nonempty Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\) be equipped with an inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and let \(S\subset E\) be nonempty. The codomain is the extended real line \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional support function of an arbitrary nonempty set. Convexity, closedness, boundedness, and attainment are not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support function of \(S\) is the map
\[
\sigma_S:E\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\},\qquad \sigma_S(d):=\sup_{s\in S}\langle s,d\rangle .
\]
Its effective domain is
\[
\operatorname{dom}\sigma_S:=\{d\in E:\sigma_S(d)<+\infty\}.
\]
Thus \(d\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_S\) exactly when \(S\) is contained in a halfspace \(\{s:\langle s,d\rangle\le r\}\) for some \(r\in\mathbb{R}\). The function is positively homogeneous and subadditive:
\[
\sigma_S(td)=t\sigma_S(d)\quad(t\ge0),\qquad
\sigma_S(d_1+d_2)\le\sigma_S(d_1)+\sigma_S(d_2).
\]
It is a closed convex function, satisfies \(\sigma_S(0)=0\), and depends only on the closed convex hull:
\[
\sigma_S=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}S}=\sigma_{\operatorname{co}S}=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}S}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each direction, the support function is the supremum over the set of the corresponding linear functional. Its finite-value domain consists precisely of directions in which the set has a finite upper supporting level. It is closed, convex, positively homogeneous, and subadditive, and replacing the set by its closure, convex hull, or closed convex hull does not change it.
assumptions_latex: \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\) has the fixed inner product used to identify directions with linear functionals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_S(d)=\sup_{s\in S}\langle s,d\rangle\), with \(\sigma_S\) closed and sublinear and \(\sigma_S=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}S}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\sigma_S=\{(d,r):\langle s,d\rangle\le r\ \forall s\in S\}\).
\(d\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_S\iff \exists r\in\mathbb{R}\text{ such that }S\subseteq\{s:\langle s,d\rangle\le r\}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(S=\{s_0\}\), \(\sigma_S(d)=\langle s_0,d\rangle\).
For the Euclidean unit ball \(B\), \(\sigma_B(d)=\|d\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(S\subseteq T\Rightarrow\sigma_S\le\sigma_T\).
Support data cannot distinguish a nonconvex or nonclosed set from its closed convex hull.
boundary_notes: The supremum may equal \(+\infty\).
A finite supremum need not be attained unless additional compactness or coercivity is available.
The definition depends on the chosen dual pairing.

notation.meaning: support function of the nonempty set S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Levels, Hyperplanes, and Contact Sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and write \(\sigma_C(d)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,d\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition covers arbitrary nonempty sets and distinguishes finite support, supporting hyperplanes, and actual contact. No convexity or compactness is needed to define these objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A direction \(d\) is a finite support direction for \(C\) when \(\sigma_C(d)<+\infty\). For such \(d\), define the supporting halfspace, supporting level hyperplane, and support-point set by
\[
H_C^-(d):=\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\},
\]
\[
H_C(d):=\{x:\langle x,d\rangle=\sigma_C(d)\},
\qquad
M_C(d):=C\cap H_C(d)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle x,d\rangle.
\]
Then \(C\subseteq H_C^-(d)\), and \(\sigma_C(d)\) is the least real number \(r\) such that \(C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le r\}\). The hyperplane supports \(C\) in direction \(d\) precisely when \(M_C(d)\neq\varnothing\). For \(t>0\),
\[
H_C(td)=H_C(d),\qquad M_C(td)=M_C(d),
\]
so the geometry depends on the oriented ray generated by \(d\), not its positive normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite support direction is one in which the set has a finite maximal linear value. That value is the smallest upper halfspace threshold containing the set. The boundary hyperplane at that threshold is supporting only when it meets the set, and its contact set is exactly the set of maximizers. Positive rescaling of a nonzero direction leaves the hyperplane and contact set unchanged.
assumptions_latex: For the displayed hyperplane and contact-set definitions, \(d\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_C(d)=C\cap\{x:\langle x,d\rangle=\sigma_C(d)\}\), and \(\sigma_C(d)=\min\{r:C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le r\}\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in M_C(d)\iff x\in C\text{ and }\langle x,d\rangle\ge\langle y,d\rangle\ \forall y\in C\).
\(M_C(d)\neq\varnothing\iff \sup_{x\in C}\langle x,d\rangle\text{ is attained}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, then \(M_C(d)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(d\).
With the convention \(M_C(0)=C\), the zero direction exposes the whole set.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(C\) is convex, then every nonempty \(M_C(d)\) is convex.
If \(C\) is closed and \(\sigma_C(d)<+\infty\), the contact set is closed, although it may still be empty.
boundary_notes: Finite support does not imply attainment for an unbounded closed convex set.
If \(\sigma_C(d)=+\infty\), there is no finite supporting level orthogonal to \(d\).
Directions \(d\) and \(-d\) represent opposite orientations and generally produce different support levels.

notation.meaning: minimal closed halfspace with outward normal d containing C
support-point or contact set in direction d

children.title: Support-Point Sets
children.top_down_role: Directional maximizers and their attainment regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Direction-Ray Invariance of Support-Point Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling does not change a support-point set, while the zero direction selects the entire set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(S_C(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\). For every \(\alpha>0\), \[S_C(\alpha u)=S_C(u),\] including simultaneous emptiness when the supremum is not attained. Moreover, \[S_C(0)=C.\] Thus, for \(u\ne0\), the support-point set depends only on the positive ray generated by \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_C(\alpha u)=S_C(u)\quad\text{and}\quad S_C(0)=C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive rescaling and the zero-direction regime for support-point sets.

notation.meaning: Support-point set of C in direction u.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Point Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support points maximize a linear functional over the set. Compactness guarantees attainment; closedness alone does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support-point set of \(C\) in direction \(u\) is \[S_C(u):=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=h_C(u)\}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle.\] Thus \(S_C(u)\) is nonempty exactly when the defining supremum is attained. If \(C\) is compact, then \(S_C(u)\) is nonempty and compact for every \(u\); if \(C\) is also convex, it is a face of \(C\). For a general closed convex set, a finite value \(h_C(u)\) need not imply attainment, so \(S_C(u)\) may be empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_C(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\), with \(S_C(u)\neq\varnothing\) exactly when the support supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support-point definition, including compact and nonattainment regimes.

notation.meaning: Support function of the set C.
Support-point set of C in direction u.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence Between Exposed Faces and Normal Directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. For \(x\in C\), define \(N_C(x):=\{d:\langle y-x,d\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is finite-dimensional closed convex geometry. Empty exposed faces are allowed when a finite support value is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define the face exposed by \(d\) as
\[
F_C(d):=\{x\in C:\langle x,d\rangle=\sigma_C(d)\}.
\]
For \(d\neq0\), every nonempty \(F_C(d)\) is an exposed face of \(C\); set \(F_C(0):=C\). The face-direction incidence relation is
\[
\mathcal I_C:=\{(x,d)\in C\times\mathbb{R}^n:x\in F_C(d)\}.
\]
It has the equivalent normal-cone description
\[
(x,d)\in\mathcal I_C
\iff \langle y-x,d\rangle\le0\quad\forall y\in C
\iff d\in N_C(x).
\]
For a nonempty exposed face \(F\) of \(C\), its exposing-direction cone is
\[
D_C(F):=\{d:F_C(d)=F\}.
\]
Thus \(F_C(d)\) records all points incident to the supporting direction \(d\), while \(N_C(x)\) records all supporting directions incident to the point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point and a direction are incident when the point maximizes the direction's linear functional over the set. Equivalently, the direction belongs to the normal cone at the point. Fixing the direction gives an exposed face; fixing the point gives its cone of supporting directions. Directions exposing exactly a prescribed face form that face's exposing-direction set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in F_C(d)\iff d\in N_C(x)\), where \(F_C(d)=\{x\in C:\langle x,d\rangle=\sigma_C(d)\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in F_C(d)\iff \langle x,d\rangle=\sup_{y\in C}\langle y,d\rangle\).
\(x\in F_C(d)\iff C\subseteq\{y:\langle y,d\rangle\le\langle x,d\rangle\}\).
special_cases_latex: \(F_C(0)=C\) and \(N_C(x)\) always contains \(0\).
If \(F_C(d)=\{x\}\), then \(x\) is an exposed point.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty \(F_C(d)\) is a face of \(C\).
If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(N_C(x)=\{0\}\).
boundary_notes: A face need not be exposed.
For an unbounded set, a direction may have finite support but no incident point.
The set \(D_C(F)\) uses equality of exposed faces, whereas \(\bigcap_{x\in F}N_C(x)\) also contains directions exposing a larger face.

notation.meaning: face of C exposed by d
convex-analytic normal cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Need Not Mean Exposed
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tangency point where a disk joins an exterior apex is extreme but not exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\|x\|_2\leq1\}\), \(a=(2,0)\), and \(C=\operatorname{conv}(B\cup\{a\})\). For \(p=(1/2,\sqrt3/2)\), the singleton \(\{p\}\) is an extreme face of \(C\), but it is not exposed: the supporting line of \(B\) at \(p\) also contains \(a\), and its contact set with \(C\) is \([p,a]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{p\}\) is an extreme face of \(C\) but is not exposed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Planar compact convex example separating extreme and exposed points.

knowledge_statements.title: Straszewicz Density Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of a compact convex set is a limit of exposed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, then \[\operatorname{ext}C\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{exp}C}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext}C\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{exp}C}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density of exposed points among extreme points in finite-dimensional compact convex sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed face is the set of maximizers of one nonzero linear functional over a convex set, and every exposed face is a face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty subset \(F\subseteq C\) is an exposed face of \(C\) if there exists \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[F=F_C(u):=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=h_C(u)\}.\] Equivalently, \(F\) is the intersection of \(C\) with a supporting hyperplane having outward normal \(u\). Every exposed face is a face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is exposed exactly when \(F=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=h_C(u)\}\) for some \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for nonempty exposed faces generated by nonzero supporting directions.

notation.meaning: Face of C exposed by direction u.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Support Points p. 133

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Normal-Cone Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directions exposing a proper face are exactly the relative-interior directions of the normal cone along that face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, let \(F\) be a nonempty proper exposed face, and choose \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\). Then \[E_C(F)=\operatorname{ri}N_C(x).\] Thus the exposing directions form a relatively open convex cone and do not depend on the chosen \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\).
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a nonempty proper exposed face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_C(F)=\operatorname{ri}N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All directions exposing a nonempty proper exposed face of a compact convex set.

notation.meaning: Normal cone to C at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposing Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposing direction is a nonzero normal whose maximizing set is exactly the given exposed face; positive rescaling preserves it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonzero vector \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) exposes \(F\) when \[F=F_C(u):=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=h_C(u)\}.\] The exposing-direction set is \[E_C(F):=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}:F_C(u)=F\}.\] It is positively homogeneous: if \(u\in E_C(F)\) and \(\lambda>0\), then \(\lambda u\in E_C(F)\). Hence an exposing direction represents a ray of equivalent supporting normals rather than a distinguished normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq C\) is a nonempty exposed face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_C(F)=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}:F_C(u)=F\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directions are identified up to positive scaling, not normalization.

notation.meaning: Face of C exposed by u.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Support Points p. 133

knowledge_statements.title: Setwise Face–Normal Incidence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is normal at every point of a subset exactly when its support face contains that subset; inclusion reverses common-normal inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty subset \(F\subseteq C\), define \(N_C(F):=\bigcap_{x\in F}N_C(x)\). Then, for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[u\in N_C(F)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\subseteq F_C(u).\] Consequently, if \(F\subseteq G\subseteq C\), then \(N_C(G)\subseteq N_C(F)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in N_C(F)\iff F\subseteq F_C(u)\), and \(F\subseteq G\Rightarrow N_C(G)\subseteq N_C(F)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-normal extension of point incidence and its order reversal.

knowledge_statements.title: Face–Direction Incidence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point lies in the support face selected by a direction exactly when that direction belongs to the point's normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[F_C(u):=\{z\in C:\langle u,z\rangle=\sup_{y\in C}\langle u,y\rangle\}\] and \[N_C(x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }y\in C\}.\] Then the point-direction incidence relation is \[x\in F_C(u)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in N_C(x).\] Thus a direction belongs to the normal cone at every point of its support face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in F_C(u)\iff u\in N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point-normal incidence for finite-dimensional closed convex sets.

notation.meaning: Support face of C in direction u.
Normal cone to C at x.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty subset \(F\subseteq C\), define \(N_C(F):=\bigcap_{x\in F}N_C(x)\). Then, for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[u\in N_C(F)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\subseteq F_C(u).\] Consequently, if \(F\subseteq G\subseteq C\), then \(N_C(G)\subseteq N_C(F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is normal along every point of a set exactly when its support face contains that set; face inclusion therefore reverses common-normal inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\in N_C(F)\iff F\subseteq F_C(u)\), and \(F\subseteq G\Rightarrow N_C(G)\subseteq N_C(F)\).

children.title: Support Smoothness-Uniqueness Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Smoothness and strict-convexity correspondences expressed through support geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiability as Uniqueness of the Supporting Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex. Then \(\sigma_C\) is finite and convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(F_C(d)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle x,d\rangle\) is nonempty for every \(d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The correspondence is pointwise in direction and uses ordinary finite-dimensional Fréchet differentiability. The global strict-convexity equivalence is stated for compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support smoothness-uniqueness correspondence is the identity
\[
\partial\sigma_C(d)=F_C(d)
=\{x\in C:\langle x,d\rangle=\sigma_C(d)\},
\qquad d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sigma_C\text{ is differentiable at }d
\iff F_C(d)\text{ is a singleton}.
\]
When \(F_C(d)=\{x_d\}\),
\[
\nabla\sigma_C(d)=x_d.
\]
Equivalently, the support value has a unique maximizing point exactly when the support function has a unique subgradient at that direction. Globally, \(C\) is strictly convex exactly when every nonzero supporting direction has a unique contact point, equivalently when \(\sigma_C\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of the support function at a direction is exactly the face exposed by that direction. Hence the support function is differentiable there precisely when the exposed face consists of one point, and its gradient is that unique support point. For a compact convex set, strict convexity is equivalent to this uniqueness, and therefore differentiability, in every nonzero direction.
assumptions_latex: Differentiability is considered at \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\); the strict-convexity equivalence uses \(d\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\sigma_C(d)=F_C(d)\), so \(\sigma_C\) is differentiable at \(d\) iff \(F_C(d)=\{x_d\}\), in which case \(\nabla\sigma_C(d)=x_d\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F_C(d)=\{x_d\}\iff \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle x,d\rangle=\{x_d\}\).

\(C\text{ strictly convex}\iff \forall d\neq0,\ |F_C(d)|=1\iff \sigma_C\in C^1\text{ pointwise on }\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), where the last notation asserts differentiability, not continuity of the gradient.
special_cases_latex: At \(d=0\), \(F_C(0)=C\); hence \(\sigma_C\) is differentiable at \(0\) iff \(C\) is a singleton.
If \(C\) is a polytope, differentiability fails in directions exposing a positive-dimensional face.
immediate_consequences_latex: A unique exposed support point can be recovered as \(\nabla\sigma_C(d)\).
Nondifferentiability of \(\sigma_C\) records multiplicity of supporting points.
boundary_notes: Strict convexity of \(C\) concerns uniqueness of support points; it does not assert smoothness of the boundary of \(C\).
Uniqueness may fail at some directions even though exposed points are dense among extreme points.
For noncompact sets, finiteness or attainment may fail, so the stated global correspondence requires modification.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the support function at d
unique support point in direction d when it exists

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiability at the Origin
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact convex set's support function is differentiable at the origin exactly when the set is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty compact convex set \(C\), \(F_C(0)=C\). Hence \[h_C\text{ is differentiable at }0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C=\{c\}\text{ for some }c.\] In that case \(h_C(u)=\langle u,c\rangle\) and \(\nabla h_C(0)=c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_C\text{ is differentiable at }0\iff C\text{ is a singleton}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp exceptional behavior at the zero direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Constancy on Positive Rays
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Where a support function is differentiable, its gradient is constant along the corresponding positive ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(h_C\) is differentiable at \(u
eq0\), then it is differentiable at every \(\lambda u\) with \(\lambda>0\), and \[
abla h_C(\lambda u)=
abla h_C(u).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla h_C(\lambda u)=\nabla h_C(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-homogeneity consequence at differentiability points.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Differentiability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact convex set's support function is differentiable in a direction exactly when that direction has one support point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the support function is finite and its convex subdifferential is \[\partial h_C(u)=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=h_C(u)\}=F_C(u).\] Therefore \(h_C\) is differentiable at \(u\) if and only if the support face is a singleton, say \(F_C(u)=\{x_u\}\). In that case its gradient is the unique support point: \[\nabla h_C(u)=x_u.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_C\) is differentiable at \(u\) iff \(F_C(u)=\{x_u\}\), and then \(\nabla h_C(u)=x_u\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiability criterion for compact convex sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Support Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction has a unique support point precisely when its support face, equivalently the support function's subdifferential, is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(u\) has a unique support point on \(C\) when there is exactly one \(x_u\in C\) satisfying \[\langle u,x_u\rangle=h_C(u).\] Equivalently, \[F_C(u)=\{x_u\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\partial h_C(u)=\{x_u\}.\] For \(u=0\), one has \(F_C(0)=C\), so uniqueness at the origin occurs only when \(C\) itself is a singleton. For nonzero \(u\), uniqueness means the supporting hyperplane normal to \(u\) touches \(C\) at exactly one point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) has a unique support point iff \(F_C(u)=\{x_u\}\), equivalently \(\partial h_C(u)=\{x_u\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness characterized through support faces and subgradients.

notation.meaning: Support face of C in direction u.
Convex subdifferential of the support function.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Support Points p. 133

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Support Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nondifferentiability occurs exactly at directions exposing multiple points, and directional derivatives are the support function of that exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support function is nondifferentiable at \(u\) exactly when its support face \(F_C(u)=\partial h_C(u)\) contains more than one point. Its one-sided directional derivative in any direction \(v\) exists and is represented by \[h_C'(u;v):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{h_C(u+tv)-h_C(u)}{t}=\max_{x\in F_C(u)}\langle v,x\rangle.\] Thus the local first-order nonsmoothness of \(h_C\) records the full geometry of the face exposed by \(u\), rather than a single supporting point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_C\) is nondifferentiable at \(u\) iff \(F_C(u)\) is not a singleton, and \(h_C'(u;v)=\max_{x\in F_C(u)}\langle v,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional-derivative description of nonsmooth support geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Segment Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-dimensional closed convex set is strictly convex exactly when its boundary contains no nontrivial segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex with \(\operatorname{int}C\neq\varnothing\). Then \(C\) is strictly convex if and only if \(\partial C\) contains no nontrivial line segment; equivalently, for distinct \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in(0,1)\), \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is strictly convex}\iff\partial C\text{ contains no nontrivial line segment}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent geometric formulation for full-dimensional closed convex sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Convexity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-dimensional compact convex set is strictly convex exactly when every nonzero direction has one support point, equivalently when its support function is differentiable away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\operatorname{int}C\neq\varnothing\). The following conditions are equivalent: \(C\) is strictly convex; for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), the support face \(F_C(u)\) is a singleton; and \(h_C\) is differentiable at every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\). Here \(C\) is strictly convex when \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{int}C\) for all distinct \(x,y\in C\) and all \(t\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is strictly convex iff \(F_C(u)\) is a singleton for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\), equivalently iff \(h_C\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional full-dimensional compact-set correspondence, excluding the zero direction.

children.top_down_role: Reconstruction and comparison of convex sets and sublinear functions through support data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mutually Inverse Set and Support Representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be the class of nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\mathcal S\) be the class of proper closed sublinear functions \(p:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The representation is finite-dimensional and extended-valued. Properness excludes the identically infinite function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the support transform and supporting-set transform by
\[
\mathfrak S(C):=\sigma_C,
\qquad
\mathfrak C(p):=C_p:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,d\rangle\le p(d)\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
Support-function representation is the correspondence
\[
\mathfrak C(\mathfrak S(C))=C\quad(C\in\mathcal C),
\qquad
\mathfrak S(\mathfrak C(p))=p\quad(p\in\mathcal S).
\]
Thus \(C\mapsto\sigma_C\) is a bijection from \(\mathcal C\) onto \(\mathcal S\), with inverse \(p\mapsto C_p\). For an arbitrary nonempty set \(A\),
\[
\mathfrak C(\sigma_A)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}A,
\]
so complete support data represents exactly the closed convex hull of the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support transform sends a nonempty closed convex set to its closed sublinear support function. The inverse transform takes all points whose linear values lie below the prescribed sublinear function in every direction. These transforms are mutually inverse on nonempty closed convex sets and proper closed sublinear functions. Applied to an arbitrary set, the inverse recovers its closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(C\in\mathcal C\) or \(p\in\mathcal S\), according to the transform being used.
The fixed Euclidean pairing identifies points with continuous linear functionals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\sigma_C}=C\), \(\sigma_{C_p}=p\), and \(C_{\sigma_A}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}A\) for every nonempty \(A\subset\mathbb{R}^n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in C\iff \langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(p(d)=\sup\{\langle x,d\rangle:x\in C_p\}\).
special_cases_latex: A linear function \(p(d)=\langle x_0,d\rangle\) represents the singleton \(\{x_0\}\).
An everywhere-finite support function represents a bounded, hence compact, closed convex set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two nonempty closed convex sets are equal iff their support functions agree in every direction.
Every proper closed sublinear function has at least one linear minorant.
boundary_notes: Without closedness and convexity, support data reconstructs only the closed convex hull.
A sublinear function that is not lower semicontinuous is not itself the support function of a set under this correspondence.
The representation permits \(+\infty\) values.

supporting-set transform from functions to sets

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Set Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set equals the intersection of all halfspaces prescribed by its support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The complete directional support data determine \(C\) through \[C=\bigcap_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,x\rangle\leq h_C(u)\}.\] Equivalently, a point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) belongs to \(C\) if and only if \(\langle u,x\rangle\leq h_C(u)\) for every direction \(u\). Values \(h_C(u)=+\infty\) impose no restriction in their directions. Closedness and convexity are essential because the same intersection reconstructs the closed convex hull of an arbitrary nonempty set.
assumptions_latex: \(h_C(u):=\sup_{x\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\) may take the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\bigcap_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle u,x\rangle\leq h_C(u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued finite-dimensional reconstruction by all supporting halfspaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reconstruction from Complete Directional Support Data
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, with support function \(\sigma_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The reconstruction uses all directions, although positive homogeneity permits restriction to a unit ball, unit sphere, or effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The reconstruction determined by a function \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is
\[
R(h):=\bigcap_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,d\rangle\le h(d)\}.
\]
For the support data of a nonempty closed convex set,
\[
R(\sigma_C)=C.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
x\in C
\iff \langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
The quantifier may instead range over the Euclidean unit ball, the unit sphere, or \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\). If \(A\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is merely nonempty, then
\[
R(\sigma_A)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}A.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reconstruction intersects, over all directions, the halfspaces whose thresholds are the supplied support values. For a nonempty closed convex set this returns exactly the original set. Membership is therefore equivalent to satisfying every support inequality. For arbitrary input sets, the same construction returns the closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: Complete directional values \(\sigma_C(d)\) are available on a positively generating direction set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\bigcap_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C=\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\ \forall d\in B(0,1)\}\).
\(C=\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\ \forall d\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, it suffices to know \(\sigma_C\) on the unit sphere.
For \(C=\{x_0\}\), the inequalities reconstruct the unique point \(x_0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_D\Rightarrow C=D\) for nonempty closed convex \(C,D\).
Any point outside \(C\) violates at least one support inequality.
boundary_notes: A proper subset of directions reconstructs an outer approximation unless it is sufficient by positive homogeneity or other structure.
Closure and convexity are essential for exact recovery of the original set.
Numerically approximate support values generally produce an approximate outer description, not the exact equality stated here.

notation.meaning: intersection reconstruction induced by directional upper bounds h

children.title: Support Order-Embedding Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Order correspondence between closed convex sets and support functions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal C\) be the partially ordered class of nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), ordered by inclusion. Closed sublinear functions are ordered pointwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is an exact finite-dimensional order correspondence. Both directions require closed convex sets for the reverse implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support map is an order embedding:
\[
C_1\subseteq C_2
\iff \sigma_{C_1}(d)\le\sigma_{C_2}(d)
\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\qquad C_1,C_2\in\mathcal C.
\]
Accordingly, define
\[
C_1\preceq_{\sigma} C_2
\quad:\!\iff\quad
\sigma_{C_1}\le\sigma_{C_2}\text{ pointwise}.
\]
On \(\mathcal C\), this support order is exactly set inclusion. In particular,
\[
C_1=C_2\iff \sigma_{C_1}=\sigma_{C_2}.
\]
Because support functions are positively homogeneous, pointwise comparison may equivalently be checked on the unit sphere or unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One nonempty closed convex set is contained in another exactly when its support value is no larger in every direction. Thus the support-function map preserves and reflects order, and equality of support functions is equivalent to equality of the represented sets.
assumptions_latex: Function inequalities are interpreted pointwise in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\iff \forall d,\ \sigma_{C_1}(d)\le\sigma_{C_2}(d)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\iff \sigma_{C_1}|_{\mathbb S^{n-1}}\le\sigma_{C_2}|_{\mathbb S^{n-1}}\).
\(C_1=C_2\iff \sigma_{C_1}(d)=\sigma_{C_2}(d)\ \forall d\).
special_cases_latex: For singletons, \(\{x_1\}\subseteq\{x_2\}\iff\langle x_1,d\rangle\le\langle x_2,d\rangle\ \forall d\), which forces \(x_1=x_2\).
If \(C_2=C_1+rB\), then \(\sigma_{C_2}(d)=\sigma_{C_1}(d)+r\|d\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Support inequalities provide certificates for set inclusion.
A strict support inequality in one direction implies that the two represented sets are unequal.
boundary_notes: For arbitrary nonclosed or nonconvex sets, pointwise support order compares their closed convex hulls, not necessarily the original sets.
Pointwise strict inequality in every nonzero direction is stronger than strict set inclusion and is not equivalent to it.
Extended values must be retained for unbounded sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Inclusion Order
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty closed convex sets are partially ordered by ordinary set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathcal{C}_n\), define the set-inclusion order by \[C\preceq_{\mathrm{set}}D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\subseteq D.\] This is a partial order: it is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Its comparison is geometric and pointwise in membership: \(C\preceq_{\mathrm{set}}D\) means that every \(x\in C\) also belongs to \(D\). No boundedness assumption is imposed, so the associated support functions may be extended-real-valued.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{C}_n\) is the family of nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\preceq_{\mathrm{set}}D\iff C\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion order on nonempty closed convex sets.

notation.meaning: Family of nonempty closed convex subsets of Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Support Order
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support functions are compared pointwise: one precedes another when its value is no larger in every direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pointwise order on extended-real-valued functions is defined by \[f\preceq_{\mathrm{pt}}g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(u)\leq g(u)\ \text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] For support functions this becomes \[h_C\preceq_{\mathrm{pt}}h_D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_C(u)\leq h_D(u)\ \text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^n,\] with inequalities interpreted in the usual order on \(( -\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\preceq_{\mathrm{pt}}g\iff f(u)\leq g(u)\) for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise order specialized to extended-valued support functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Embedding Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set inclusion is equivalent to pointwise support-function order; consequently, equal support functions determine equal nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support-function assignment is an order embedding: \[C\subseteq D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_C(u)\leq h_D(u)\ \text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Equivalently, \[C\preceq_{\mathrm{set}}D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_C\preceq_{\mathrm{pt}}h_D.\] In particular, \(h_C=h_D\) implies \(C=D\), so the support-function assignment is injective on nonempty closed convex sets.
assumptions_latex: \(h_C\) and \(h_D\) are their extended-real-valued support functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\subseteq D\iff h_C(u)\leq h_D(u)\) for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-embedding theorem for nonempty closed convex sets using extended support functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Exterior-Point Separation Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is outside a nonempty closed convex set exactly when it violates one support-function halfspace inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(z\in E\). Then \[z\notin C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists u\in E^*:\ \langle u,z\rangle>\sigma_C(u).\]
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subset E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\notin C\iff\exists u\in E^*:\langle u,z\rangle>\sigma_C(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-direction certificate for failure of the support-halfspace inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure–Convexification Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support halfspaces reconstruct an arbitrary set's closed convex hull, so exact recovery characterizes closed convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty \(A\subset E\), \[\bigcap_{u\in E^*}\{x\in E:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_A(u)\}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}A.\] Consequently this intersection equals \(A\) exactly when \(A\) is closed and convex.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{u\in E^*}\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_A(u)\}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact result of applying the support-halfspace construction to an arbitrary nonempty set.

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Halfspace Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set equals the intersection of all halfspaces whose bounds are supplied by its support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\sigma_C:E^*\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) by \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle\). Then every point of \(C\) satisfies every inequality \(\langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\), and separation of points outside the closed convex set gives the exact outer description \[C=\bigcap_{u\in E^*}\{x\in E:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}.\] Directions for which \(\sigma_C(u)=+\infty\) contribute no effective restriction.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
\(C\subset E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\bigcap_{u\in E^*}\{x\in E:\langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-convex reconstruction by all dual supporting halfspaces.

notation.meaning: Support function of the set C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Outer Description by Supporting Halfspaces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(H_C^-(d)=\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The representation is an exact, generally infinite outer description indexed by dual directions. Directions with infinite support impose no restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The supporting-halfspace representation of \(C\) is the family
\[
\mathcal H(C):=\{H_C^-(d):d\in\mathbb{R}^n\},
\qquad
H_C^-(d):=\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\}.
\]
It satisfies
\[
C=\bigcap_{d\in\mathbb{R}^n}H_C^-(d).
\]
For each fixed \(d\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\), the threshold \(\sigma_C(d)\) is minimal:
\[
\sigma_C(d)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb{R}:C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le r\}\}.
\]
More generally, the halfspace \(H_{d,r}^-:=\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le r\}\) contains \(C\) exactly when \(r\ge\sigma_C(d)\). Hence the canonical family keeps, for each normal direction, the tightest containing halfspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty closed convex set equals the intersection of its direction-indexed supporting halfspaces. In a fixed finite-support direction, the support value is the smallest halfspace threshold that still contains the set. Any larger threshold gives a redundant containing halfspace, while a smaller threshold cuts off part of the set.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\); minimal finite thresholds are considered only for \(d\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\bigcap_d\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le\sigma_C(d)\}\), and \(C\subseteq H_{d,r}^-\iff r\ge\sigma_C(d)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\notin C\iff \exists d\text{ such that }\langle x,d\rangle>\sigma_C(d)\).
\(C=\bigcap_{(d,r)\in\operatorname{epi}\sigma_C}H_{d,r}^-\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed convex polyhedron, a finite subfamily may suffice, although the canonical family contains all valid directions.
If \(\sigma_C(d)=+\infty\), then the corresponding inequality is vacuous.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every exterior point is separated from \(C\) by at least one canonical support inequality.
Support data is an outer-description language for closed convex sets.
boundary_notes: The hyperplane boundary need not meet an unbounded set even when the support value is finite.
A finite sampled family generally yields only an outer approximation.
Exact equality may fail for a nonclosed or nonconvex original set; the intersection then gives its closed convex hull.

notation.meaning: closed halfspace with normal d and upper threshold r
canonical family of tight direction-indexed halfspaces

children.title: Closed Sublinear Function Representation
children.top_down_role: Representation of closed sublinear functions by supporting sets in the dual space.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuity Is the Exact Representation Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without lower semicontinuity, dominated linear functionals represent only the closed hull of a sublinear function; the indicator of a nonclosed convex cone gives strict failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p:E\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper and sublinear, and set
\[
C_p=\{u\in E^*: \langle u,x\rangle\leq p(x)\ \forall x\in E\}.
\]
Then \(\sigma_{C_p}=p^{**}=\operatorname{cl}p\leq p\); hence \(p=\sigma_{C_p}\) holds exactly when \(p\) is lower semicontinuous. Strict inequality can occur: for
\[
K=\{0\}\cup\{(s,t)\in\mathbb{R}^2:t>0\},\qquad p=\delta_K,
\]
\(p\) is proper sublinear but not lower semicontinuous, and \(\sigma_{C_p}=\delta_{\overline K}\neq p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{C_p}=p^{**}=\operatorname{cl}p\), so \(p=\sigma_{C_p}\iff p\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for representing a proper sublinear function by its dominated linear functionals.

notation.meaning: Set of linear functionals dominated by p

knowledge_statements.title: Converse Support-Function Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of every nonempty closed convex dual set is a proper closed sublinear function, and its dominated-linear-functional set recovers the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset E^*\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Its support function \(\sigma_C:E\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and sublinear, and
\[
C=\{u\in E^*: \langle u,x\rangle\leq\sigma_C(x)\ \text{for every }x\in E\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subset E^*\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C\) is proper lower-semicontinuous sublinear and \(C=\{u:\langle u,\cdot\rangle\leq\sigma_C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse completing the finite-dimensional correspondence between closed sublinear functions and nonempty closed convex dual sets.

notation.meaning: Support function of the dual set

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Sublinear Function Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper lower-semicontinuous sublinear function is the support function of its closed convex set of dominated linear functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C:=\{u\in E^*: \langle u,x\rangle\leq p(x)\text{ for every }x\in E\}.\] Then \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of \(E^*\), equals \(\partial p(0)\), and represents \(p\) pointwise through \[p(x)=\sigma_C(x):=\sup_{u\in C}\langle u,x\rangle\qquad(x\in E).\] Equivalently, the convex conjugate satisfies \(p^*=\delta_C\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(p:E\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\sigma_C\) for \(C=\partial p(0)=\{u\in E^*: \langle u,x\rangle\leq p(x)\ \forall x\in E\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional representation of proper closed sublinear functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supporting Set of a Closed Sublinear Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, positively homogeneous, and subadditive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The function may be extended-valued. Lower semicontinuity is essential for exact equality with a support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The supporting set represented by \(p\) is
\[
C_p:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,d\rangle\le p(d)\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
It is a nonempty closed convex set, and \(p\) is its support function:
\[
p(d)=\sigma_{C_p}(d)=\sup_{x\in C_p}\langle x,d\rangle
\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Equivalently, \(p\) is the pointwise supremum of all linear functions that minorize it:
\[
p(d)=\sup\{\langle x,d\rangle:\langle x,u\rangle\le p(u)\ \forall u\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
The set \(C_p\) is uniquely determined among nonempty closed convex sets by this identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed sublinear function determines the set of all vectors whose associated linear functionals lie below it in every direction. This supporting set is nonempty, closed, and convex, and taking its support function recovers the original function. Thus every closed sublinear function is the supremum of its linear minorants and has a unique closed convex representing set.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is lower semicontinuous and sublinear on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_p\neq\varnothing\) and \(p=\sigma_{C_p}\), where \(C_p=\{x:\langle x,d\rangle\le p(d)\ \forall d\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C_p\) is the set of coefficients of all linear minorants of \(p\).
\(p=\sup_{x\in C_p}\langle x,\cdot\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: If \(p(d)=\langle x_0,d\rangle\), then \(C_p=\{x_0\}\).
If \(p\) is finite everywhere, then \(C_p\) is bounded and therefore compact.
immediate_consequences_latex: A proper closed sublinear function has at least one linear minorant.
The representing set is unique because closed convex sets are reconstructed from their support functions.
boundary_notes: If \(p\) is sublinear but not lower semicontinuous, the support of \(C_p\) represents its lower-semicontinuous hull rather than necessarily \(p\).
The representation is extended-valued and does not require boundedness of \(C_p\).
The identically infinite function is excluded because it is not proper.

notation.meaning: closed convex supporting set represented by p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Calculus for Standard Set Operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\{C_i\}_{i\in I}\) be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, and let all support functions use the corresponding dual pairings.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The calculus is extended-valued. Closure and closed convex hull may appear because support functions retain only closed convex information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Support-function calculus is the collection of operation identities obtained by transporting set operations to support functions. Its canonical rules include
\[
\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}(\alpha C+\beta D)}=
\alpha\sigma_C+eta\sigma_D\qquad(\alpha,\beta>0),
\]
\[
\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i)}
=\sup_{i\in I}\sigma_{C_i},
\]
\[
\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}A(C)}(y)=\sigma_C(A^*y)
\]
for a linear map \(A\), and
\[
\sigma_{C\times D}(u,v)=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v).
\]
For nonempty intersections of closed convex sets, the corresponding rule is
\[
\sigma_{\bigcap_i C_i}=\overline{\operatorname{co}}\left(\inf_i\sigma_{C_i}\right),
\]
with pointwise infimum followed by the closed-convex hull as a function. These identities define the support calculus as an operation-preserving correspondence, with the stated closures accounting for possible nonclosed images or sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support calculus translates weighted Minkowski sums into sums of support functions, closed convex hulls of unions into pointwise suprema, linear images into composition with the adjoint, and Cartesian products into separable sums. Intersections correspond to the closed convex hull of the pointwise infimum. Closure terms are retained whenever the underlying set operation need not preserve closedness.
assumptions_latex: Every set whose support is taken is nonempty.
For the intersection rule, the sets are closed and convex and their intersection is nonempty.
\(A^*\) denotes the adjoint relative to the chosen inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Standard convex-set operations are transported to the displayed algebraic operations on support functions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\sigma_{\alpha C+\beta D}(d)=\alpha\sigma_C(d)+\beta\sigma_D(d)\) whenever the unclosed sum is used, since support is unchanged by closure.
\(\sigma_{\bigcup_i C_i}=\sup_i\sigma_{C_i}=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\bigcup_i C_i)}\).
special_cases_latex: \(\sigma_{C+x_0}(d)=\sigma_C(d)+\langle x_0,d\rangle\).
\(\sigma_{-C}(d)=\sigma_C(-d)\).
\(\sigma_{rB}(d)=r\|d\|\) for \(r\ge0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Complicated set constructions can be compared through pointwise functional identities.
Closure of a set never changes its support function.
boundary_notes: The pointwise infimum of support functions need not itself be closed or convex, so the intersection rule requires regularization.
A linear image or Minkowski sum of closed convex sets need not be closed in every unbounded case.
The formulas do not encode nonconvex features lost under closed convexification.
