children.title: Additive-Homogeneous Support Calculus
children.top_down_role: Support calculus for additive and homogeneous set operations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C,D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(a,b\ge0\), and define \(aC+bD:=\{ax+by:x\in C,\ y\in D\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The identities hold for arbitrary nonempty sets. A closure may be inserted on the set side without changing the support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The additive-homogeneous support calculus is
\[
\sigma_{aC+bD}(d)=a\sigma_C(d)+b\sigma_D(d)
\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\]
with the conventions \(0C:=\{0\}\) and \(0\cdot(+\infty):=0\). In particular,
\[
\sigma_{C+D}=\sigma_C+\sigma_D,
\qquad
\sigma_{aC}=a\sigma_C\quad(a\ge0).
\]
For any scalar \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), including negative values,
\[
\sigma_{tC}(d)=\sigma_C(td).
\]
Translations satisfy
\[
\sigma_{C+x_0}(d)=\sigma_C(d)+\langle x_0,d\rangle.
\]
If \(C,D\) are closed and convex, the function \(a\sigma_C+b\sigma_D\) represents \(\operatorname{cl}(aC+bD)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted Minkowski addition becomes pointwise weighted addition of support functions. Nonnegative set scaling becomes function scaling, arbitrary scalar multiplication can be transferred to the direction argument, and translation adds the corresponding linear functional. If a weighted sum of closed convex sets is not closed, its support function represents its closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{aC+bD}=a\sigma_C+b\sigma_D\), \(\sigma_{tC}(d)=\sigma_C(td)\), and \(\sigma_{C+x_0}=\sigma_C+\langle x_0,\cdot\rangle\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}(aC+bD)}=a\sigma_C+b\sigma_D\).
\(\sigma_{-C}(d)=\sigma_C(-d)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(D=\{x_0\}\), Minkowski addition is translation.
For \(C=rB\), \(\sigma_C(d)=r\|d\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Minkowski sums can be reconstructed from sums of support functions after closed convexification.
Repeated Minkowski addition gives \(\sigma_{C_1+\cdots+C_m}=\sum_i\sigma_{C_i}\).
boundary_notes: When \(a=0\), defining \(0C=\{0\}\) avoids ambiguity for unbounded \(C\).
A sum of closed unbounded convex sets need not be closed.
Negative scaling is not represented by multiplying an extended-valued support function by a negative number; it acts on the direction instead.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski-Sum Support Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a Minkowski sum is the pointwise sum of the two support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(u\in E^*\), the support function converts Minkowski addition into extended-real addition: \[\sigma_{C+D}(u)=\sup_{c\in C,\,d\in D}\langle u,c+d\rangle=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(u).\] Because both sets are nonempty, their support values lie in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), so the sum is unambiguous.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subset E\) are nonempty subsets of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{C+D}(u)=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(u)\) for every \(u\in E^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real support calculus for two nonempty sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Scaling Support Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplying a nonempty set by a positive scalar multiplies every support value by that scalar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u\in E^*\), positive scaling of the set scales its support value by the same factor: \[\sigma_{\lambda C}(u)=\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,\lambda c\rangle=\lambda\sup_{c\in C}\langle u,c\rangle=\lambda\sigma_C(u).\] The identity holds in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\lambda C}(u)=\lambda\sigma_C(u)\) for every \(u\in E^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive scalar homogeneity in the set argument.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Minkowski Combinations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a finite nonnegative weighted Minkowski combination is the correspondingly weighted sum of support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt the set-scaling convention \(0C_i=\{0\}\) and the extended-real convention \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\). Then, for every \(u\in E^*\), \[\sigma_{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iC_i}(u)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\sigma_{C_i}(u).\] Thus finite Minkowski addition and nonnegative weighting become pointwise addition and weighting of support functions.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iC_i}(u)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\sigma_{C_i}(u)\), with \(0\cdot(+\infty):=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Set Exception at Zero Scaling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero image of the empty set remains empty, so its support is minus infinity rather than zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Adopt \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\) and define \(\lambda C=\{\lambda c:c\in C\}\). Then
\[
0\varnothing=\varnothing,
\qquad
\sigma_{0\varnothing}(u)=-\infty
\quad(u\in E^*).
\]
Thus \(0C=\{0\}\) and \(\sigma_{0C}=0\) require \(C\neq\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\varnothing=\varnothing\) and \(\sigma_{0\varnothing}(u)=-\infty\) for every \(u\in E^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the nonempty-set zero-scaling rule under image-based scalar multiplication.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative Scaling Reverses the Support Direction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative set scaling multiplies support by the absolute scale and reverses the queried direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(C\subset E\) is nonempty and \(\lambda<0\), then for every \(u\in E^*\),
\[
\sigma_{\lambda C}(u)=(-\lambda)\sigma_C(-u).
\]
Consequently, \(\sigma_{\lambda C}=\lambda\sigma_C\) does not extend verbatim from positive to negative scalars.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\lambda C}(u)=(-\lambda)\sigma_C(-u)\) for every \(u\in E^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-sensitive extension of set-scaling support calculus to strictly negative scalars.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Scaling Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero scaling always produces the singleton zero and support value zero, requiring a convention when the original support value is infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), one has \(\sigma_{\lambda C}=\lambda\sigma_C\). At \(\lambda=0\), set scaling gives \(0C=\{0\}\), hence \[\sigma_{0C}(u)=0\qquad(u\in E^*).\] Consequently the formula at zero is valid only with the convention \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\); ordinary extended-real multiplication leaves that expression undefined when \(\sigma_C(u)=+\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
Set multiplication is defined by \(\lambda C=\{\lambda c:c\in C\}\) for \(\lambda\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0C=\{0\}\) and \(\sigma_{0C}(u)=0\), whereas \(\lambda>0\) gives \(\sigma_{\lambda C}(u)=\lambda\sigma_C(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at zero scaling for nonempty sets and extended-real supports.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative Set Scaling Reverses the Support Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-sensitive extension of set-scaling support calculus to strictly negative scalars.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(C\subset E\) be nonempty, and define \(\lambda C=\{\lambda c:c\in C\}\). For every \(\lambda<0\) and \(u\in E^*\),
\[
\sigma_{\lambda C}(u)=(-\lambda)\sigma_C(-u).
\]
Thus the positive-scaling identity \(\sigma_{\lambda C}=\lambda\sigma_C\) does not extend verbatim across a change of sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative set scale multiplies the support value by its absolute value and reverses the queried direction.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\lambda C}(u)=(-\lambda)\sigma_C(-u)\) for every \(u\in E^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support of a Union and Its Closed Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\{C_i\}_{i\in I}\) be a nonempty family of nonempty subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and set \(U:=\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The index set may be infinite, and support values may be infinite. The result explicitly records the information loss caused by closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The union-hull support correspondence is
\[
\sigma_U(d)=\sup_{i\in I}\sigma_{C_i}(d)
\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\]
and, because support is invariant under closure and convexification,
\[
\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}U}(d)
=\sigma_U(d)
=\sup_{i	ext{ in }I}\sigma_{C_i}(d).
\]
Hence the pointwise supremum of the family of support functions is the support function of the closed convex hull of the union:
\[
\sup_{i\in I}\sigma_{C_i}
=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i)}.
\]
For two sets this becomes
\[
\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}(C\cup D)}=\max\{\sigma_C,\sigma_D\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support value of a union is the supremum of the support values of its members. The union and its closed convex hull have identical support functions, so the pointwise supremum represents the closed convex hull of the union. For two sets, the operation is the pointwise maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}(\bigcup_i C_i)}=\sup_i\sigma_{C_i}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\sigma_{\bigcup_iC_i}=\sup_i\sigma_{C_i}\).
For finite \(I\), \(\sigma_{\operatorname{co}(\bigcup_iC_i)}=\max_i\sigma_{C_i}\), with closure harmless on the support side.
special_cases_latex: For points \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), the support of their convex hull is \(d\mapsto\max_j\langle x_j,d\rangle\).
For two closed convex sets, the support of their closed convex hull is the pointwise maximum of their supports.
immediate_consequences_latex: Pointwise suprema of support functions are closed and sublinear when not identically infinite.
Convex-hull generation can be performed entirely in support-function coordinates.
boundary_notes: Support data cannot distinguish the union from its closed convex hull.
For an infinite family, the unclosed convex hull need not be closed.
The pointwise supremum may take \(+\infty\) even when every individual support value is finite at some directions.

notation.meaning: union of the indexed family of sets

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Member Formula for Union Maximizers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A union maximizer is exactly a maximizer from a member having maximal support among the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\), \(M(u)=\sup_{j\in I}\sigma_{C_j}(u)\), and \(I(u)=\{i:\sigma_{C_i}(u)=M(u)\}\). Then \[F_U(u)=\bigcup_{i\in I(u)}F_{C_i}(u).\] Thus union support is attained exactly when some member attains both the outer family supremum and its own support value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_U(u)=\bigcup_{i:\,\sigma_{C_i}(u)=\sup_j\sigma_{C_j}(u)}F_{C_i}(u)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact attainment structure behind the supremum of member support values.

notation.meaning: Points of S attaining support in direction u.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Union Support Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support value of a union is the supremum of the support values of its member sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u\in E^*\), taking the supremum over a union is equivalent to taking the supremum of the member support values: \[\sigma_{\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i}(u)=\sup_{c\in\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i}\langle u,c\rangle=\sup_{i\in I}\sigma_{C_i}(u).\] The equality is interpreted in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
\(I\) is a nonempty index set, and \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of nonempty subsets of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i}(u)=\sup_{i\in I}\sigma_{C_i}(u)\) for every \(u\in E^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary nonempty families of nonempty sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support maximizers of a convex hull are exactly the convex hull of the original support maximizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F_S(u)=\{s\in S:\langle u,s\rangle=\sigma_S(u)\}\), \[F_{\operatorname{conv}S}(u)=\operatorname{conv}F_S(u).\] Thus ordinary convexification creates no support maximizer when none exists in \(S\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\operatorname{conv}S}(u)=\operatorname{conv}F_S(u)\).

assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\operatorname{conv}S}(u)=\sigma_S(u)\) for every \(u\in E^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Union–Hull Indistinguishability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A union and its convex hull have the same support function, so support data cannot distinguish them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\). For every \(u\in E^*\), \[\sigma_U(u)=\sup_{i\in I}\sigma_{C_i}(u)=\sigma_{\operatorname{conv}U}(u).\] Hence the union and its convex hull have identical support functions, even when the union is nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space with dual \(E^*\).
\(I\) is a nonempty index set, and \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of nonempty subsets of \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i}=\sigma_{\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support functions cannot distinguish a union from its convex hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Restores an Unattained Infinite-Family Support Value
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A countable family has support value one, but its union and ordinary convex hull do not attain it; closing the hull adds the maximizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq1\), let \(C_n=\{1-1/n\}\subset\mathbb R\) and \(U=\bigcup_{n\geq1}C_n\). Then \(\operatorname{conv}U=[0,1)\), \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}U=[0,1]\), and in direction \(1\), \[\sup_n\sigma_{C_n}(1)=\sigma_U(1)=\sigma_{\operatorname{conv}U}(1)=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}U}(1)=1.\] Only the closed convex hull attains the value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All four support values equal \(1\), but only \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}U\) attains it.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical distinction between an infinite union’s algebraic and closed convex hulls.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Family Hull Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any family, the closed convex hull of its union has support equal to the pointwise supremum of member supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an arbitrary nonempty index set \(I\), put \(U=\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\). Continuity of each linear functional and invariance under convexification yield, for every \(u\in E^*\), \[\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}U}(u)=\sigma_U(u)=\sup_{i\in I}\sigma_{C_i}(u).\] No compactness, boundedness, or finiteness of the family is required; the common value may be \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i)}(u)=\sup_{i\in I}\sigma_{C_i}(u)\) for all \(u\in E^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary families with closed convexification in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: Support function of the ith set

children.title: Linear-Adjoint Support Transport
children.top_down_role: Support transformations induced by linear mappings.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transport of Support Through a Linear Image
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear with adjoint \(A^*:F\to E\), and let \(C\subset E\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No convexity or boundedness is needed. Closure may be placed on the image because support functions are closure-invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The linear-adjoint support transport of \(C\) through \(A\) is the identity
\[
\sigma_{A(C)}(y)=\sigma_C(A^*y)
\quad\forall y\in F.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}A(C)}=\sigma_C\circ A^*.
\]
Thus a direction \(y\) in the image space is pulled back to the direction \(A^*y\) in the source space. The effective domain transforms as
\[
\operatorname{dom}\sigma_{A(C)}
=\{y\in F:A^*y\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\}
=(A^*)^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C).
\]
For an affine image \(A(C)+b\),
\[
\sigma_{A(C)+b}(y)=\sigma_C(A^*y)+\langle b,y\rangle_F.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support of a linear image in an image-space direction equals the original support in the adjoint-pulled-back direction. Consequently, the finite-support domain is the inverse image under the adjoint of the original finite-support domain. Adding a translation contributes the corresponding linear functional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{A(C)}(y)=\sigma_C(A^*y)\) and \(\sigma_{A(C)+b}(y)=\sigma_C(A^*y)+\langle b,y\rangle_F\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}A(C)}=\sigma_C\circ A^*\).
\(y\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_{A(C)}\iff A^*y\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\).
special_cases_latex: For \(A=tI\), \(\sigma_{tC}(d)=\sigma_C(td)\).
For an orthogonal map \(Q\), \(\sigma_{Q C}(y)=\sigma_C(Q^{-1}y)\).
For a coordinate projection, support is obtained by evaluating the original support on directions with zero discarded component.
immediate_consequences_latex: Linear-image support computations require no explicit image-set construction.
If \(C\) is compact, then \(A(C)\) is compact and its support is finite everywhere.
boundary_notes: A linear image of a closed convex unbounded set need not be closed, hence the explicit closure in the representation form.
The formula uses the adjoint determined by the selected inner products.
This rule concerns direct images; inverse images require different qualification conditions.

notation.meaning: adjoint of A under the chosen inner products

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Image Support Transport
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support of a linear image at a dual direction equals the original support evaluated at the adjoint direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A^*:F^*\to E^*\) be determined by \(\langle A^*v,x\rangle=\langle v,Ax\rangle\). Then every \(v\in F^*\) satisfies \[\sigma_{A(C)}(v)=\sup_{c\in C}\langle v,Ac\rangle=\sup_{c\in C}\langle A^*v,c\rangle=\sigma_C(A^*v).\] Thus a dual direction is transported backward through the adjoint before evaluating the original support function.
assumptions_latex: \(A:E\to F\) is linear between finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{A(C)}(v)=\sigma_C(A^*v)\) for every \(v\in F^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact support transport through a finite-dimensional linear image.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Preimage Support Transport
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a relative-interior qualification, preimage support is the minimum support of the target set over all adjoint lifts of the direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the relative-interior qualification, the preimage is nonempty and its support is obtained by minimizing over dual lifts. For every \(u\in E^*\), \[\sigma_{A^{-1}(C)}(u)=\min\{\sigma_C(v):v\in F^*,\ A^*v=u\},\] where the minimum over an empty feasible set is \(+\infty\). When a lift exists, the minimum is attained; directions outside \(\operatorname{range}A^*\) therefore have support value \(+\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(A:E\to F\) is linear between finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(C\subset F\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{A^{-1}(C)}(u)=\min\{\sigma_C(v):v\in F^*,\ A^*v=u\}\) for every \(u\in E^*\), with \(\min\varnothing:=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional preimage formula under a relative-interior qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Transport of Support Points and Exposed Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support maximizers of a linear image are precisely the images of support maximizers in the adjoint-transformed direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in X\), define
\[
F_C(u):=\{x\in C:\langle u,x\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\},
\]
with this set empty when the support supremum is not attained. Then every \(y\in Y\) satisfies
\[
F_{L(C)}(y)=L\bigl(F_C(L^*y)\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, \(Lx\) is a support point of \(L(C)\) in direction \(y\) exactly when \(x\) is a support point of \(C\) in direction \(L^*y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{L(C)}(y)=L(F_C(L^*y))\) for every \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise realization of adjoint direction transport for support maximizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Direction Transport
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support of a linear image in direction y equals the original set's support in the adjoint direction L*y.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y\in Y\), linear-image support is transported to the adjoint direction: \[\sigma_{L(C)}(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,Lx\rangle=\sup_{x\in C}\langle L^*y,x\rangle=\sigma_C(L^*y).\] This identity remains valid with values in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\); neither convexity nor closedness of \(C\) is required.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty and \(L:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{L(C)}=\sigma_C\circ L^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact support transport for a linear image in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.

notation.meaning: Support function of a nonempty set S.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Support Functions p. 135

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Invariance of a Linear Preimage
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear preimage is invariant under kernel translations; for a convex target, the kernel is contained in its lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=L^{-1}(D)\neq\varnothing\). Then \(C+k=C\) for every \(k\in\ker L\). If \(D\) is convex, then \(C\) is convex and \(\ker L\subseteq\operatorname{lin}C\).
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(L:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L^{-1}(D)+\ker L=L^{-1}(D)\), and if \(D\) is convex then \(\ker L\subseteq\operatorname{lin}(L^{-1}(D))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric source of the rank-deficient support boundary.

notation.meaning: Lineality space of the convex set C.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Mapping Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty linear preimage has infinite support in every direction outside the range of the adjoint; belonging to that range is necessary but not sufficient for finite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u\in X\), if \(u\notin\operatorname{ran}L^*=(\ker L)^\perp\), then \[\sigma_{L^{-1}(D)}(u)=+\infty.\] Thus membership in \(\operatorname{ran}L^*\) is necessary, but not sufficient by itself, for finite support of the nonempty preimage.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and \(L:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(u\in X\), \(u\notin\operatorname{ran}L^*\Longrightarrow \sigma_{L^{-1}(D)}(u)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel directions delimit finite support of a nonempty linear preimage.

notation.meaning: Inverse image of D under L.
Adjoint of L and its range.
Support function of a nonempty subset S of X.

children.title: Product-Space Support Calculus
children.top_down_role: Support calculus in product and projected spaces.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E,F\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces. Equip \(E\times F\) with \(\langle(x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle_E+\langle y,v\rangle_F\). Let \(C\subset E\) and \(D\subset F\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The product rule is extended-valued and requires no convexity. The projection rule applies to any nonempty subset of a product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support function of a Cartesian product separates by coordinates:
\[
\sigma_{C\times D}(u,v)=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v)
\quad\forall(u,v)\in E\times F.
\]
If \(S\subset E\times F\) is nonempty and \(P_E(x,y)=x\), then
\[
\sigma_{P_E(S)}(u)=\sigma_S(u,0)
\quad\forall u\in E.
\]
More generally, for an orthogonal projection \(P_V:E\to V\) onto a subspace \(V\),
\[
\sigma_{P_V(C)}(v)=\sigma_C(v)
\quad\forall v\in V.
\]
Closures may be added to the projected sets without changing these functions. These identities define product-space support calculus by separating independent product coordinates and embedding projected directions with zeros in the eliminated coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support of a Cartesian product is the sum of the component support functions. The support of a projection is obtained by evaluating the original support function at a direction whose discarded coordinates are zero. For an orthogonal projection onto a subspace, the projected support is simply the restriction of the original support to that subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D,S\) are nonempty in their stated spaces.
Product pairings are the sums of the component inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{C\times D}(u,v)=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v)\) and \(\sigma_{P_E(S)}(u)=\sigma_S(u,0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}P_E(S)}(u)=\sigma_S(u,0)\).
\(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_{C\times D}=\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\times\operatorname{dom}\sigma_D\).
special_cases_latex: For \(D=\{0\}\), \(\sigma_{C\times\{0\}}(u,v)=\sigma_C(u)\).
For \(S=C\times D\), projection onto \(E\) recovers \(C\) and restriction at \((u,0)\) recovers \(\sigma_C(u)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Support computations for rectangular uncertainty sets decompose componentwise.
Projection can be analyzed without explicitly eliminating the discarded variables.
boundary_notes: Projection must not be confused with the slice \(\{x:(x,0)\in S\}\); the latter has a different support rule.
A projection of a closed convex set need not be closed in an unbounded setting.
The sum uses extended-real arithmetic, so it may equal \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: coordinate projection from E times F onto E
dual direction u embedded with zero discarded component

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Faces of a Cartesian Product
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support maximizers of a Cartesian product are exactly the products of the factor maximizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F_S(w)=\{s\in S:\langle w,s\rangle=\sigma_S(w)\}\). Then \[F_{A\times B}(u,v)=F_A(u)\times F_B(v).\] Thus product support is attained exactly when both factor support values are attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{A\times B}(u,v)=F_A(u)\times F_B(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimizer structure accompanying separable product support.

notation.meaning: Points of S attaining its support value in direction w.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Set Support Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a Cartesian product is the sum of the support functions of its factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \((u,v)\in X\times Y\), the independent suprema separate: \[\sigma_{A\times B}(u,v)=\sup_{x\in A,\,y\in B}\bigl(\langle u,x\rangle+\langle v,y\rangle\bigr)=\sigma_A(u)+\sigma_B(v).\] The equality is interpreted in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), where the sum is always well-defined because support functions of nonempty sets never take the value \(-\infty\). Convexity and closedness are unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{A\times B}(u,v)=\sigma_A(u)+\sigma_B(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable support calculus for Cartesian products.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Support Functions p. 135

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Geometry of a Coordinate Slice
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession directions of a closed convex slice are exactly the horizontal recession directions of the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is closed and convex and \(C_{y_0}\neq\varnothing\), then \(C_{y_0}\) is closed and convex and \[\operatorname{rec}C_{y_0}=\{d\in X:(d,0_Y)\in\operatorname{rec}C\}.\] Consequently, \(C_{y_0}\) is bounded exactly when this set equals \(\{0_X\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}C_{y_0}=\{d:(d,0_Y)\in\operatorname{rec}C\}\), and \(C_{y_0}\) is bounded iff this cone is \(\{0_X\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-convex slice geometry and its boundedness boundary.

notation.meaning: Coordinate slice of C at y0.

knowledge_statements.title: Slice Support Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slice's support is the supremum of the first-coordinate linear functional over points of the original set having the prescribed second coordinate; the value may be infinite or unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u\in X\), fixing the second coordinate gives \[\sigma_{C_{y_0}}(u)=\sup\{\langle u,x\rangle:(x,y_0)\in C\}.\] The value lies in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and need not be attained when the slice is noncompact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(u\in X\), \(\sigma_{C_{y_0}}(u)=\sup\{\langle u,x\rangle:(x,y_0)\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support of a nonempty fiber obtained by fixing one product coordinate.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Support Functions p. 135

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Exposed-Face Transport
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected support maximizers are precisely the projections of maximizers in the zero-extended direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u\in X\), \[F_{P_X(C)}(u)=P_X\bigl(F_C(u,0_Y)\bigr).\] Hence projected support is attained exactly when support over \(C\) in direction \((u,0_Y)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimizer transport through coordinate projection.

notation.meaning: Points of S attaining support in direction w.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Set Support Calculus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Supporting the projection of a set onto X in direction u is the same as supporting the original product-space set in direction (u,0).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u\in X\), coordinate projection transports support through the adjoint embedding \(u\mapsto(u,0_Y)\): \[\sigma_{P_X(C)}(u)=\sigma_C(u,0_Y).\] This extended-real identity requires neither convexity nor closedness of \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(P_X:X\times Y\to X\) is the coordinate projection defined by \(P_X(x,y)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(u\in X\), \(\sigma_{P_X(C)}(u)=\sigma_C(u,0_Y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-projection support as restriction to the zero dual direction.

notation.meaning: Support function of a nonempty set S in a Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Fiber Dual Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the zero-height slice of the squared epigraph, marginal duality has the correct value but no minimizing multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y\geq x^2\}\), \(y_0=0\), and \(u\neq0\). Then \(C_0=\{0\}\), \(\sigma_{C_0}(u)=0\), and \[\sigma_C(u,v)=\begin{cases}-u^2/(4v),&v<0,\\+\infty,&v\geq0.\end{cases}\] Consequently \(\inf_v\sigma_C(u,v)=0\), but the infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{C_0}(u)=\inf_v\sigma_C(u,v)=0\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_v\sigma_C(u,v)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary feasibility can preserve the dual value without producing a finite multiplier.

notation.meaning: Boundary slice of C at height zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Marginal Duality for Slice Support
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginal dualization always upper-bounds slice support, and relative-interior feasibility makes the multiplier formula exact and attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(u\in X\), weak duality gives \[\sigma_{C_{y_0}}(u)\leq\inf_{v\in Y}\{\sigma_C(u,v)-\langle v,y_0\rangle\}.\] If \(y_0\in\operatorname{ri}P_Y(C)\), then the infimum is attained and \[\sigma_{C_{y_0}}(u)=\min_{v\in Y}\{\sigma_C(u,v)-\langle v,y_0\rangle\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak duality always holds; if \(y_0\in\operatorname{ri}P_Y(C)\), equality holds with a minimizing multiplier.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact multiplier representation under relative-interior feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Form of Unqualified Marginal Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without qualification, slice support is the lower-semicontinuous closure of the multiplier infimum; value exactness and multiplier attainment are distinct questions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(q(u)=\inf_{v\in Y}\{\sigma_C(u,v)-\langle v,y_0\rangle\}\). Without a qualification, \[\sigma_{C_{y_0}}=\operatorname{cl}q,\] where \(\operatorname{cl}q\) is the lower-semicontinuous convex hull of \(q\). Hence equality at \(u\) requires no closure correction there; attainment of the infimum is a separate issue.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{C_{y_0}}=\operatorname{cl}q\), with \(q(u)=\inf_v\{\sigma_C(u,v)-\langle v,y_0\rangle\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact description of a possible unqualified value gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginalization Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection preserves support values but may destroy closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\ge 1/x\}\). This set is nonempty, closed, and convex, but its projection onto the first coordinate is \(P_X(C)=(0,\infty)\), which is not closed. Nevertheless, \(\sigma_{P_X(C)}=\sigma_{\overline{P_X(C)}}\). Hence support marginalization through projection determines only the closed convex hull of the projected set and cannot certify that the projection itself is closed or that boundary points are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set can have a nonclosed projection; support values recover the projection’s closure but cannot reveal missing boundary points or attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_X(C)=(0,\infty)\neq[0,\infty)=\overline{P_X(C)}\) while \(\sigma_{P_X(C)}=\sigma_{\overline{P_X(C)}}\).

children.title: Support-Function Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Finiteness, continuity, attainment, and information-loss regimes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed convex. Define its recession cone by \(C^\infty:=\{v:x+tv\in C\ \forall x\in C,\ t\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates three logically distinct questions: whether support is finite, whether a finite supremum is attained, and what set information support data retains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The support-regularity profile of \(C\) is the pair
\[
D_C:=\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C
=\{d:\sigma_C(d)<+\infty\},
\qquad
A_C:=\{d:F_C(d)\neq\varnothing\},
\]
where \(F_C(d)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle x,d\rangle\). It partitions directions into
\[
A_C\subseteq D_C,
\quad D_C\setminus A_C,
\quad \mathbb{R}^n\setminus D_C,
\]
corresponding respectively to finite attained support, finite unattained support, and infinite support. The finiteness cone is recession-controlled through
\[
\overline{D_C}=(C^\infty)^\circ
:=\{d:\langle v,d\rangle\le0\ \forall v\in C^\infty\}.
\]
The support function is convex and lower semicontinuous everywhere and continuous relative to \(\operatorname{ri}D_C\). Finally, for any nonempty set \(S\),
\[
\sigma_S=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}S},
\]
which defines the associated information-loss regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularity profile records directions of finite support and directions where that finite value is attained. These distinguish finite attained, finite unattained, and infinite-support regimes. The closure of the finite-support domain is the polar of the recession cone, and the support function is continuous on the relative interior of its domain. Independently, support data loses all distinctions between a set and its closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The polar convention is \(K^\circ=\{d:\langle v,d\rangle\le0\ \forall v\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_C\subseteq D_C\), \(\overline{D_C}=(C^\infty)^\circ\), and \(\sigma_S=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}S}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d\in D_C\iff C\) has a finite upper bound in direction \(d\).
\(d\in A_C\iff \exists x\in C\text{ with }\langle x,d\rangle=\sigma_C(d)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is bounded, then \(D_C=\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(C\) is compact, then \(A_C=D_C=\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(C=K\) is a closed convex cone, then \(\sigma_K\) is the indicator of \(K^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonzero recession directions determine where support must become infinite.
Finiteness alone does not guarantee existence of a support point on the boundary of \(D_C\).
boundary_notes: The domain \(D_C\) need not be closed.
The inclusion \(A_C\subseteq D_C\) can be strict even for closed convex sets.
Support functions erase nonconvexity and nonclosedness of the represented set.

children.title: Compact-Set Support Regime
children.top_down_role: Finite-valued and attained support behavior for compact sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Set Support Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every direction has a finite, attained support value on a nonempty compact set, and the support function is globally Lipschitz with constant at most the maximum norm of points in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=\max_{x\in K}\|x\|\). For every \(u\in X\), there exists \(x_u\in K\) such that \[\sigma_K(u)=\max_{x\in K}\langle u,x\rangle=\langle u,x_u\rangle\in\mathbb{R}.\] Moreover, \[|\sigma_K(u)-\sigma_K(v)|\leq R\|u-v\|\quad\text{for all }u,v\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(u\in X\), \(\sigma_K(u)=\max_{x\in K}\langle u,x\rangle\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\sigma_K\) is globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued, attained, and Lipschitz support behavior for compact sets.

notation.meaning: Maximum norm of points in K.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Support Points p. 133
7.2 Support Functions p. 135

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite, Lipschitz, and Attained Support for Compact Sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subsetaR^n\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(R_K:=\max_{x\in K}\|x\|<+\infty\). Convexity is not required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional compact regime. The support function represents the compact convex set \(\operatorname{co}K\), while maximizers may be taken in the original compact set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty compact set \(K\) is in the compact-set support regime when its support function is everywhere a maximum:
\[
\sigma_K(d)=\max_{x\in K}\langle x,d\rangle\in\mathbb{R}
\quad\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Its support-point set
\[
F_K(d):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in K}\langle x,d\rangle
\]
is nonempty and compact for every \(d\). Moreover,
\[
|\sigma_K(d)|\le R_K\|d\|,
\qquad
|\sigma_K(d_1)-\sigma_K(d_2)|\le R_K\|d_1-d_2\|.
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_K=\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\sigma_K\) is finite, continuous, and globally Lipschitz. It remains closed, convex, and positively homogeneous, and
\[
\sigma_K=\sigma_{\operatorname{co}K}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty compact set, every directional support value is finite and attained. The maximizer set is nonempty and compact. The maximal norm of points in the set is a global Lipschitz constant for the support function, so the function is finite and continuous everywhere. The same support function represents the compact convex hull of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\sigma_K(d)=\max_{x\in K}\langle x,d\rangle\), \(F_K(d)
eq\varnothing\), and \(|\sigma_K(d_1)-\sigma_K(d_2)|\le R_K\|d_1-d_2\|\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_K=\mathbb{R}^n\) and every direction belongs to the attainment set.
\(\sigma_K|_{\mathbb S^{n-1}}\) is bounded and determines \(\sigma_K\) everywhere by positive homogeneity.
special_cases_latex: If \(K=\{x_0\}\), then \(F_K(d)=\{x_0\}\) for every \(d\).

If \(K\) is compact and strictly convex, then \(F_K(d)\) is a singleton for every \(d
eq0\).
If \(K=rB\), then \(\sigma_K(d)=r\|d\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonzero direction defines a supporting hyperplane that meets \(K\).
Uniform convergence of compact-set support functions on the unit ball is the natural metric counterpart of Hausdorff convergence for compact convex sets.
boundary_notes: Compactness, not merely closedness, guarantees attainment in every direction.
The support-point set relative to a nonconvex \(K\) need not be convex, although the exposed face of \(\operatorname{co}K\) is convex.
Differentiability still requires uniqueness of the maximizing point and does not follow from compactness alone.

notation.meaning: maximum Euclidean norm of a point of K
set of support maximizers in K for direction d

children.title: Recession-Controlled Support Regimes
children.top_down_role: Finite and infinite support directions governed by recession geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-controlled finiteness domain of a support function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set. Its support function is \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\), and its recession cone is \(C_\infty=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+td\in C\ \forall x\in C,\ \forall t\geq0\}\). For a cone \(K\), use the nonpositive polar \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle d,u\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean regime for nonempty closed convex, possibly unbounded sets; boundary directions of the support-function domain are retained explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C:=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C}=(C_\infty)^\circ.\] Thus a support direction \(u\) is finite precisely when \(u\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\); every such direction satisfies \(\langle d,u\rangle\leq0\) for all \(d\in C_\infty\), whereas \(u\notin(C_\infty)^\circ\) forces \(\sigma_C(u)=+\infty\). The recession-controlled support regime is the partition of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) into the finite domain \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\), its possibly nonattained boundary inside \((C_\infty)^\circ\), and the infinite-valued complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), the finite support directions form \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\), whose closure is the nonpositive polar of the recession cone. Consequently, a direction pairing positively with some recession direction has infinite support value. Recession geometry determines the closure of the finite regime, but it need not determine whether individual boundary directions belong to the domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C}=(C_\infty)^\circ,\qquad u\notin(C_\infty)^\circ\Longrightarrow\sigma_C(u)=+\infty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\iff \exists\beta\in\mathbb{R}\ \text{such that}\ C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\beta\}.\]
\[(C_\infty)^\circ=\overline{\{u:\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle<+\infty\}}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is bounded, then \(C_\infty=\{0\}\) and \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(C=K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, then \(\sigma_K=\iota_{K^\circ}\), so \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_K=K^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every \(u\in\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) and \(d\in C_\infty\), one has \(\langle d,u\rangle\leq0\).
The recession cone determines the closure, but not necessarily the exact boundary, of \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\).
boundary_notes: Membership of \(u\in\partial(C_\infty)^\circ\) in \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) is not guaranteed by recession data alone.
This statement concerns finiteness of the supremum, not attainment by a point of \(C\).

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the closed convex set.
Directions where the support value is finite.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Support Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the square is unbounded yet has finite support for downward directions; its recession-polar boundary contains both finite and infinite directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and unbounded, with \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{(0,s):s\geq0\}\). Direct maximization gives \[\sigma_C(a,b)=\begin{cases}-a^2/(4b),&b<0,\\0,&(a,b)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&b>0\text{ or }(b=0,\ a\neq0).\end{cases}\] Thus support is finite in the open half-space \(b<0\), but on the boundary \(b=0\) finiteness depends on the tangential component \(a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C(a,b)=-a^2/(4b)\) for \(b<0\), while boundary directions can have finite or infinite support.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed convex epigraph exhibiting finite interior support and mixed boundary behavior.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Recession and Barrier Cones p. 128

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Support Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite support holds throughout the relative interior of the recession cone's polar and nowhere outside that polar, while boundary behavior can vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-support directions satisfy \[\operatorname{ri}\bigl((\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ\bigr)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\subseteq(\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ.\] Thus every direction in the relative interior of the polar recession cone has finite support, while no direction outside that polar has finite support. Boundary directions may have finite or infinite support.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}((\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\subseteq(\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite support directions relative to the polar recession cone.

notation.meaning: Relative interior of a convex set.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Recession and Barrier Cones p. 128

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Support Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive pairing with a recession direction forces infinite support, but the converse fails: curved escape can produce infinite support even when every recession direction has zero pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If there exists \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\) such that \(\langle u,d\rangle>0\), then \[\sigma_C(u)=+\infty.\] The converse fails: for \(C_0=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^2:t\geq x^2\}\) and \(u_0=(1,0)\), one has \(\sigma_{C_0}(u_0)=+\infty\), although \(\langle u_0,d\rangle=0\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C_0=\{(0,s):s\geq0\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\langle u,d\rangle>0\) for some \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\), then \(\sigma_C(u)=+\infty\); the converse implication fails in general.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive recession pairing is sufficient, but not necessary, for infinite support.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Recession and Barrier Cones p. 128

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Cone Control
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of the recession cone is precisely the closure of the directions having finite support; the closure cannot generally be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The recession cone determines the closure of the finite-support directions through polar duality: \[\overline{\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C}=(\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ.\] Equivalently, \(u\) belongs to this closure exactly when \(\langle u,d\rangle\leq0\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{rec}C\). Closure is essential: the effective domain of \(\sigma_C\) need not itself be closed, and boundary directions of the polar recession cone may have either finite or infinite support.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C}=(\operatorname{rec}C)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure-level duality between finite support directions and recession geometry.

notation.meaning: Effective domain of the support function.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Values without Support Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the exponential has finite downward support equal to zero, but no point of the set attains that value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and noncompact. In direction \(u=(0,-1)\), \[\sigma_C(u)=0,\] but \(\langle u,z\rangle<0\) for every \(z\in C\). Hence the finite support value is not attained by any support point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C(u)=0\), but no \(z\in C\) satisfies \(\langle u,z\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite support without a support point for a closed noncompact convex set.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Support Points p. 133

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and let \(u\in H\setminus\{0\}\). Define \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\) and the exposed support face \(F_C(u)=\{x\in C:\langle x,u\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition applies to noncompact finite-dimensional sets and to infinite-dimensional sets. It separates finiteness of a support value from attainment of the defining supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direction \(u\neq0\) has a support value without a support point when \[\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\quad\text{and}\quad F_C(u)=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, \(C\) is contained in the closed half-space \(\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}\), this half-space is minimal among those with outward normal \(u\), and its boundary hyperplane \(\{x:\langle x,u\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\}\) does not meet \(C\). Thus the support function records a finite optimal value even though no element of the represented set realizes that value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite support value without a support point occurs when \(\sigma_C(u)\) is finite but no \(x\in C\) satisfies \(\langle x,u\rangle=\sigma_C(u)\). The corresponding limiting supporting hyperplane contains no point of \(C\), despite being the boundary of the smallest closed half-space with normal \(u\) that contains \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[u\text{ is a finite nonattaining support direction}\iff \sigma_C(u)\in\mathbb{R}\ \text{and}\ F_C(u)=\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[F_C(u)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle,\qquad F_C(u)=\varnothing\ \text{although}\ \sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle<+\infty.\]
There exists a sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) with \(\langle x_k,u\rangle\to\sigma_C(u)\), but no constant or convergent-to-a-point-of-\(C\) maximizing representative is required.
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is compact, every continuous linear functional attains its supremum, so this regime is empty.
For \(C=\{(\rho,\tau)\in\mathbb{R}^2:\rho>0,\ \tau\geq1/\rho\}\), finite support values on certain boundary directions of \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) are not attained.
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite value \(\sigma_C(u)\) alone does not imply \(F_C(u)\neq\varnothing\).
Support-value data cannot by itself certify existence of a maximizing support point.
boundary_notes: The zero direction is excluded because every point trivially realizes \(\sigma_C(0)=0\) when \(C\neq\varnothing\).
Nonattainment may result from nonclosedness, noncompactness, or failure of compactness in the relevant topology; the definition does not prescribe the cause.

children.title: Support-Representation Information Loss
children.top_down_role: Set information discarded by support-function representation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S,T\) be nonempty subsets of a real Hilbert space \(H\). Their support functions are \(\sigma_S(u)=\sup_{x\in S}\langle x,u\rangle\) and \(\sigma_T(u)=\sup_{x\in T}\langle x,u\rangle\), with values in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space support representation of arbitrary nonempty sets; closure and convexification are taken in the norm topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define support-equivalence by \[S\sim_\sigma T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma_S(u)=\sigma_T(u)\ \ \forall u\in H.\] The information discarded by support representation is exactly the distinction among sets having the same closed convex hull: \[\sigma_S=\sigma_{\operatorname{conv}S}=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S},\qquad S\sim_\sigma T\iff \overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}T.\] Hence the canonical set represented by \(\sigma_S\) is \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\), recoverable as the intersection of its support half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty sets are support-equivalent when their support functions agree in every direction. This happens exactly when their closed convex hulls agree. Accordingly, a support function forgets nonconvex arrangement, omitted convex combinations, and nonclosed boundary distinctions, while retaining the unique closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S\sim_\sigma T\iff\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}T.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S=\bigcap_{u\in H}\{x\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_S(u)\}.\]
\[\sigma_S=\sigma_T\iff \{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_S(u)\ \forall u\}=\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_T(u)\ \forall u\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(S\) is already closed and convex, then it is uniquely determined by \(\sigma_S\).
A finite set and its polytope hull have identical support functions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Support functions cannot distinguish \(S\) from \(\operatorname{conv}S\), its closure, or any intermediate set with the same closed convex hull.
The support representation becomes injective after restricting its domain to nonempty closed convex sets.
boundary_notes: The statement does not claim that exposed points, extreme points, or topology of the original nonconvex set can be recovered.
The empty set is excluded because conventions for its support function vary.

notation.meaning: Equality of support functions in all directions.
Closed convex hull of the set.

knowledge_statements.title: Open and Closed Balls Are Support-Indistinguishable
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open and closed unit balls have the same support function, although only the closed ball contains maximizing boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\neq\{0\}\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(B^\circ=\{x:\|x\|<1\}\), and \(B=\{x:\|x\|\leq1\}\). Then \(B^\circ\neq B\), but
\[
\sigma_{B^\circ}(y)=\sigma_B(y)=\|y\|\qquad(y\in X).
\]
For every \(y\neq0\), the supremum is attained on \(B\) but not on \(B^\circ\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\{0\}\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(B^\circ\) and \(B\) are its open and closed unit balls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B^\circ\neq B\) while \(\sigma_{B^\circ}=\sigma_B=\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional witness that support data do not record boundary inclusion or support attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Information Loss
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the closure of a nonempty set does not change its support function, so support data cannot detect missing boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y\in X\),
\[
\sigma_{\operatorname{cl} C}(y)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{cl} C}\langle x,y\rangle=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle=\sigma_C(y).
\]
Thus the support function cannot distinguish \(C\) from its closure; information carried solely by omitted boundary points is lost.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\operatorname{cl} C}=\sigma_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support functions, allowing the value \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Support function of a nonempty set

knowledge_statements.title: Sphere and Ball Are Support-Indistinguishable
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit sphere and unit ball have identical support functions, so support data cannot distinguish a closed nonconvex set from its convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\neq\{0\}\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(S=\{x:\|x\|=1\}\), and \(B=\{x:\|x\|\leq1\}\). Then \(S\neq B\), \(\operatorname{conv}S=B\), and
\[
\sigma_S(y)=\sigma_B(y)=\|y\|\qquad(y\in X).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\{0\}\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(S\) and \(B\) are its unit sphere and closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\neq B=\operatorname{conv}S\) and \(\sigma_S=\sigma_B=\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete witness that support data discard nonconvex structure even when both sets are closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Information Loss
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying a nonempty set leaves its support function unchanged, so support data cannot recover nonconvex structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y\in X\),
\[
\sigma_{\operatorname{conv} C}(y)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{conv} C}\langle x,y\rangle=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle=\sigma_C(y).
\]
Consequently, support-function data discard the nonconvex structure of \(C\), retaining only information determined by its convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\operatorname{conv} C}=\sigma_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support functions, allowing unbounded sets and the value \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Support function of a nonempty set

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Convex Representative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set's support function uniquely determines its closed convex hull, represented as the intersection of all support halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed convex hull \(D=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} C)\) is the unique closed convex set having support function \(\sigma_C\). Explicitly,
\[
\sigma_D=\sigma_C,
\qquad
D=\bigcap_{y\in X}\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq\sigma_C(y)\}.
\]
The inequalities with \(\sigma_C(y)=+\infty\) impose no restriction. Hence the support function determines exactly the canonical closed-convex representative \(D\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} C)}\), and \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} C)=\bigcap_{y\in X}\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\leq\sigma_C(y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical representative of a support function in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: Closed convex hull of the set

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Equivalent Set Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty sets have identical support functions exactly when their closed convex hulls coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(C\) and \(D\) are support-equivalent precisely when
\[
\sigma_C(y)=\sigma_D(y)\quad\text{for every }y\in X.
\]
In finite dimensions this condition is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} C)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} D).
\]
Therefore each support-equivalence class consists exactly of all nonempty sets sharing one closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty subsets of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_D\iff\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} C)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv} D)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence classes induced by equality of extended-real support functions.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\). The pairing is the inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Origin-anchored polarity for arbitrary subsets of a Hilbert space, with the normalization level fixed at one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar set of \(C\) is \[C^\circ:=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}=\{u\in H:\sigma_C(u)\leq1\}.\] The polar is always closed, convex, and contains \(0\). Polarity is order reversing, and the associated bipolar is \[C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Consequently, the natural objects fixed by bipolarization are precisely the closed convex subsets containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Origin-anchored polarity sends a set \(C\) to all dual vectors whose pairing with every point of \(C\) is at most one. The output is closed, convex, and origin-containing. Applying the operation twice replaces the original set by the closed convex hull of the set together with the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^\circ=\operatorname{lev}_{\leq1}\sigma_C,\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in C^\circ\iff C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\}.\]
For subsets \(C,D\subseteq H\), \(C\subseteq D^\circ\iff D\subseteq C^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a cone, the level-one polar reduces to \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in C\}\).
If \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), then \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(C\subseteq D\), then \(D^\circ\subseteq C^\circ\).
The polar depends only on \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})\).
boundary_notes: The threshold-one polar is origin anchored and is not translation invariant.
The symbol \(C^\circ\) may denote a sign-normalized cone polar in other texts; the normalization is explicit here.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold, conic, and dual-cone polarity regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\), and let \(K\subseteq H\) be a cone. All constructions use the pairing \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space taxonomy distinguishing general origin-anchored set polarity from its homogeneous conic specialization and the opposite-sign dual-cone convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The principal set-polarity regimes are defined by \[C^\odot:=\{u:\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\},\qquad K^\ominus:=\{u:\sup_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\},\qquad K^\oplus:=-K^\ominus.\] Here \(C^\odot\) is the threshold-one polar set, \(K^\ominus\) is the nonpositive polar cone, and \(K^\oplus=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\) is the dual cone. For every cone \(K\), positive homogeneity makes the thresholds one and zero equivalent, so \(K^\odot=K^\ominus\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General sets use the threshold-one polar. Cones use a homogeneous nonpositive polar because scaling a cone forces every admissible pairing to be nonpositive. The dual cone uses the opposite sign and equals the negative of the polar cone. These conventions coincide only after the sign and conic assumptions are made explicit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K^\odot=K^\ominus,\qquad K^\oplus=-K^\ominus.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in K^\ominus\iff\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K.\]
\[u\in K^\oplus\iff\langle x,u\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K.\]
special_cases_latex: For a linear subspace \(V\), \(V^\ominus=V^\oplus=V^\perp\).
For the nonnegative orthant \(K=\mathbb{R}^n_+\), \(K^\oplus=K\) and \(K^\ominus=-K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Each of \(C^\odot\), \(K^\ominus\), and \(K^\oplus\) is closed and convex; the conic outputs are cones.
Changing between polar-cone and dual-cone conventions changes a sign, not the underlying orthogonality structure.
boundary_notes: The threshold-one construction is not homogeneous for arbitrary sets.
Self-duality refers to \(K=K^\oplus\), not to equality with the nonpositive polar \(K^\ominus\).

children.title: Origin-Anchored Polar Sets
children.top_down_role: The standard polarity regime for arbitrary subsets of a dual pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Origin-Anchored Polar Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The origin-anchored polar consists of dual vectors pairing by at most one with every point of the set; it is weakly closed, convex, and contains zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separated real dual pair and \(C\subseteq X\). Its origin-anchored polar is \[C^\circ=\{y\in Y:\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\le1\}=\{y\in Y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}.\] It is \(\sigma(Y,X)\)-closed and convex and contains \(0\). With \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\), one has \(\varnothing^\circ=Y\).
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a separated real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=\{y\in Y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}\) is \(\sigma(Y,X)\)-closed, convex, contains \(0\), and \(\varnothing^\circ=Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided unit polar for arbitrary subsets of a separated real dual pair.

notation.meaning: origin-anchored unit polar in the opposite member of the dual pair

children.title: Centrally Symmetric Body Polars
children.top_down_role: The balanced convex-body regime underlying norm duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Centrally Symmetric Body Polars
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity sends a centrally symmetric convex body containing the origin internally to another such body and exchanges its gauge with its support function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar \(B^\circ\) is again compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and contains \(0\) in its interior. Moreover,
\[
(B^\circ)^\circ=B,
\qquad
p_{B^\circ}(y)=\sigma_B(y),
\qquad
p_B(x)=\sigma_{B^\circ}(x).
\]
Thus \(p_B\) and \(p_{B^\circ}\) are mutually dual norms, with respective closed unit balls \(B\) and \(B^\circ\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(B\subseteq X\) is compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and has \(0\in\operatorname{int}B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B^\circ\) is a centrally symmetric convex body and \(p_{B^\circ}(y)=\sigma_B(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric convex-body polarity and its norm-duality identities.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar of an origin-symmetric convex body
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb{R}^n\). Let \(B\subset H\) be a compact convex set with \(0\in\operatorname{int}B\) and \(B=-B\). Define its gauge by \(\gamma_B(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tB\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional centrally symmetric convex-body regime underlying norm and dual-norm unit balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar body of the centrally symmetric convex body \(B\) is \[B^\circ=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in B\}=\{u:\sup_{x\in B}|\langle x,u\rangle|\leq1\}.\] It is again a compact centrally symmetric convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}B^\circ\), and \(B^{\circ\circ}=B\). The gauge \(\gamma_B\) is a norm with unit ball \(B\), while \(\gamma_{B^\circ}\) is its dual norm and satisfies \[\gamma_{B^\circ}(u)=\sigma_B(u)=\sup_{\gamma_B(x)\leq1}\langle x,u\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact convex body symmetric about the origin and containing the origin in its interior, the polar consists of vectors pairing with the body by absolute value at most one. The polar is another body of the same type. The gauge of the original body is a norm, and the gauge of the polar is the corresponding dual norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B^\circ=\{u:\sup_{x\in B}|\langle x,u\rangle|\leq1\},\quad B^{\circ\circ}=B,\quad \gamma_{B^\circ}=\sigma_B.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[B=\{x:\gamma_B(x)\leq1\},\qquad B^\circ=\{u:\gamma_B^*(u)\leq1\},\] where \(\gamma_B^*=\sigma_B\) denotes the dual norm.
\[\langle x,u\rangle\leq\gamma_B(x)\gamma_{B^\circ}(u)\quad\forall x,u\in H.\]
special_cases_latex: For the Euclidean unit ball \(B_2\), one has \(B_2^\circ=B_2\).
For \(1\leq p\leq\infty\) and Hölder conjugate \(q\), the \(\ell_p\)-unit ball has polar equal to the \(\ell_q\)-unit ball.
immediate_consequences_latex: Central symmetry of \(B\) implies central symmetry of \(B^\circ\).
Boundedness and nonempty interior are exchanged by polarity and, for a convex body containing \(0\) in its interior, both properties hold on each side.
boundary_notes: Without central symmetry, \(\gamma_B\) need not be even and therefore need not be a norm.
If \(0\) is not an interior point, the polar can be unbounded.

source_refs.locator: §14, Theorem 14.5 and Corollary 14.5.1, “Polars of Convex Sets,” p. 121 onward

children.title: Nonsymmetric Convex-Body Polars
children.top_down_role: Convex-body polarity beyond balanced unit balls.

knowledge_statements.title: A Nonsymmetric Polar-Body Example
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interval from minus one to two has a noneven gauge although polar involution still holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=[-1,2]\subset\mathbb R\), \[K^\circ=[-1,\tfrac12],\qquad p_K(x)=\begin{cases}x/2,&x\ge0,\\-x,&x<0.\end{cases}\] Hence \(p_K(1)=1/2\ne1=p_K(-1)\), while \((K^\circ)^\circ=K\).
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R\) with its usual inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional body showing loss of gauge evenness without loss of polar involution.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsymmetric Convex-Body Polars
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsymmetric convex body containing the origin internally has a polar body; polarity is involutive and exchanges gauges with support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar \(K^\circ\) is a compact convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K^\circ\), and
\[
(K^\circ)^\circ=K,
\qquad
p_K(x)=\sigma_{K^\circ}(x),
\qquad
p_{K^\circ}(y)=\sigma_K(y).
\]
Without central symmetry, \(p_K\) need not satisfy \(p_K(x)=p_K(-x)\); it is a sublinear gauge rather than necessarily a norm.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subseteq X\) is compact and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\), without any symmetry assumption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((K^\circ)^\circ=K\) and \(p_K=\sigma_{K^\circ}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex bodies containing the origin, without central symmetry.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar of a nonsymmetric convex body
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be compact and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), without assuming \(C=-C\). Let \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-body polarity beyond balanced or centrally symmetric unit balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar body is \[C^\circ:=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}=\{u:\sigma_C(u)\leq1\}.\] It is a compact convex body containing \(0\) in its interior and satisfies \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\). Its gauge-support correspondence is \[\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C.\] In general \(\gamma_C(x)\neq\gamma_C(-x)\), so the gauge is a positively homogeneous convex asymmetry rather than a norm; polarity nevertheless remains involutive on this class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsymmetric convex body containing the origin in its interior has the usual threshold-one polar. The polar is again a convex body and the bipolar recovers the original set. The gauges of the two bodies equal the opposite support functions, but the original gauge need not be even and therefore need not define a norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^{\circ\circ}=C,\qquad \gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ},\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in C^\circ\iff\sigma_C(u)\leq1.\]
\[C=\bigcap_{u\in C^\circ}\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If additionally \(C=-C\), the gauge is a norm and this reduces to centrally symmetric norm duality.
For a simplex containing \(0\) in its interior, the polar is a generally nonsymmetric polytope determined by the simplex's facet inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Compactness of \(C\) implies \(0\in\operatorname{int}C^\circ\), while \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\) implies boundedness of \(C^\circ\).
The inequality \(\langle x,u\rangle\leq\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(u)\) holds without symmetry.
boundary_notes: No absolute value may be inserted into the defining inequality unless the body is centrally symmetric.
If \(0\) lies only on the boundary of \(C\), the polar remains closed and convex but may be unbounded.

notation.meaning: Polar of the nonsymmetric convex body.

children.title: Polar-Dual Cone Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Conic specialization and sign-convention correspondence.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign correspondence between polar and dual cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(K\subseteq H\) be a nonempty cone. Define the nonpositive polar and nonnegative dual using the same inner-product pairing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic specialization with explicit sign conventions; no closedness or convexity of the input cone is required for the definitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar cone and dual cone of \(K\) are \[K^\ominus:=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\},\qquad K^*:=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}.\] They correspond by \[K^*=-K^\ominus.\] Moreover, if \(K\) is viewed as an ordinary set and \(K^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in K\}\), then conicity gives \(K^\circ=K^\ominus\). Thus the threshold-one set polar specializes exactly to the nonpositive polar cone, while the conventional dual cone differs only by reflection through the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a cone, the nonpositive polar consists of vectors having nonpositive pairing with every cone element, and the dual cone uses nonnegative pairing. The two are negatives of one another. Because cone elements can be scaled arbitrarily, the ordinary threshold-one polar of the underlying set is the same as its nonpositive polar cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K^*=-K^\ominus,\qquad K^\circ=K^\ominus.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in K^*\iff -u\in K^\ominus.\]
\[\sup_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\iff\sup_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle\leq0.\]
special_cases_latex: For a subspace \(V\), both signs yield \(V^*=V^\ominus=V^\perp\).
For a self-dual cone, \(K=K^*\) and hence \(K^\ominus=-K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Both \(K^\ominus\) and \(K^*\) are closed convex cones even when \(K\) is not closed or convex.
If \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, then \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
boundary_notes: Some authors write \(K^\circ\) for the nonnegative dual rather than the nonpositive polar; formulas must be adjusted by a sign.
The equality between threshold-one and threshold-zero polars relies essentially on conicity.

notation.meaning: Threshold-one polar of the underlying set.
