knowledge_statements.title: Polar Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone consists of vectors making a nonpositive inner product with every vector of the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The negative polar cone of \(K\) is
\[
K^\ominus=\{y\in X:\sup_{x\in K}\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\}
          =\{y\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.
\]
The set \(K^\ominus\) is always a closed convex cone, even when \(K\) is neither closed nor convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^\ominus=\{y\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative-sign convention for cone polarity in a real Hilbert space.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Polar and Dual Cones p. 122

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual cone consists of vectors making a nonnegative inner product with every vector of the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dual cone of \(K\), under the positive-sign convention, is
\[
K^*=\{y\in X:\inf_{x\in K}\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\}
   =\{y\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.
\]
It is a closed convex cone regardless of whether \(K\) itself is closed or convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*=\{y\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-sign dual cone in a real Hilbert space.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Polar and Dual Cones p. 122

knowledge_statements.title: Cone Sign Conventions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative polar cones and positive dual cones differ by a minus sign, so formulas must state which convention they use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The two standard cone conventions differ only by reflection:
\[
K^\ominus=-K^*,
\qquad
K^*=(-K)^\ominus.
\]
Accordingly, any formula written with \(K^\ominus\) and inequalities \(\leq0\) converts to the dual-cone convention by replacing the polar cone with \(-K^*\). The sign convention must therefore be fixed before interpreting cone-polarity identities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^\ominus=-K^*\) and \(K^*=(-K)^\ominus\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation between the negative-polar and positive-dual conventions.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Polar and Dual Cones p. 122

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Polarity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone polarity reverses inclusion, and applying it twice returns the closed convex hull of the original cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cone polarity reverses inclusion: if \(K_1\subseteq K_2\), then \(K_2^\ominus\subseteq K_1^\ominus\). Its bipolar satisfies
\[
K^{\ominus\ominus}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}K),
\]
where the right-hand side is the smallest closed convex cone containing \(K\). In particular, polarity is an inclusion-reversing involution on closed convex cones: for such \(K\), \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}K)\), and if \(K\) is closed and convex then \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cone bipolarity under the negative-polar convention.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.3 Polar and Dual Cones p. 122

children.title: Polarity Calculus for Sets
children.top_down_role: Transformation rules organized by convex-set operations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polarity as an antitone Galois transform
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. For \(C\subseteq H\), define \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract set-level calculus generated by the threshold-one polar operation; individual algebraic and transport rules are specializations of this structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polarity calculus is the antitone correspondence \(\mathcal{P}(H)\to\mathcal{P}(H)\), \(C\mapsto C^\circ\), characterized by \[C\subseteq D^\circ\iff D\subseteq C^\circ.\] It satisfies \[C\subseteq C^{\circ\circ},\qquad C^{\circ\circ\circ}=C^\circ,\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Hence polar calculations may first replace an input by its closed convex origin-containing canonicalization, after which polarity is an order-reversing involution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set polarity is an antitone Galois correspondence: one set lies in the polar of another exactly when the reverse inclusion holds after exchanging the sets. Every set lies in its bipolar, triple polarity equals single polarity, and bipolarization is closed convex origin-containing canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C\subseteq D^\circ\iff D\subseteq C^\circ,\qquad C^{\circ\circ\circ}=C^\circ.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[C\subseteq D\Longrightarrow D^\circ\subseteq C^\circ.\]

The map \(C\mapsto C^{\circ\circ}\) is extensive, monotone, and idempotent: \(C\subseteq C^{\circ\circ}\), \(C\subseteq D\Rightarrow C^{\circ\circ}\subseteq D^{\circ\circ}\), and \(C^{\circ\circ\circ\circ}=C^{\circ\circ}\).
special_cases_latex: On closed convex sets containing \(0\), polarity is an antitone involution.
On cones, the same calculus uses the homogeneous nonpositive polar.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any identity between canonical closed convex origin-containing sets can be dualized by reversing inclusions and applying the polar.
The polar of an arbitrary set is unchanged by closure, convexification, or adjoining the origin.
boundary_notes: The transform is not a Boolean complement and does not exchange arbitrary intersections and unions without convex closure operations.
Translations are not intrinsic operations of origin-anchored polarity.

notation.meaning: Power set of the Hilbert space.

children.title: Polar-Invariant Set Canonicalization
children.top_down_role: Polarity under convexification and closure constructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-convex origin hull as polar-invariant canonicalization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\). Define \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-closed Hilbert-space canonicalization associated with threshold-one set polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar-invariant canonicalization of \(C\) is \[\operatorname{can}_\circ(C):=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})=C^{\circ\circ}.\] It is the smallest closed convex set containing both \(C\) and the origin, and it is polar invariant in the sense that \[\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)^\circ=C^\circ.\] Two sets therefore have the same polar exactly when their polar canonicalizations coincide: \[C^\circ=D^\circ\iff\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)=\operatorname{can}_\circ(D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: To canonicalize a set without changing its polar, adjoin the origin, take the convex hull, and close it. This set equals the bipolar and is the smallest closed convex origin-containing superset. Equality of polars is equivalent to equality of these canonicalized sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)=C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}),\qquad \operatorname{can}_\circ(C)^\circ=C^\circ.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[C^\circ=(C\cup\{0\})^\circ=(\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}))^\circ=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}))^\circ.\]
\[C^\circ=D^\circ\iff C^{\circ\circ}=D^{\circ\circ}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(0\in C\), then \(\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C\).
If \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), then \(\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Canonicalization is idempotent: \(\operatorname{can}_\circ(\operatorname{can}_\circ(C))=\operatorname{can}_\circ(C)\).
Any polar formula may replace each input set by its canonicalization without changing the result.
boundary_notes: Ordinary closed convex hull without adjoining \(0\) is insufficient when \(0\notin\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C\).
Closure is taken in the ambient Hilbert-space norm topology.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Hull Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set and its convex hull have exactly the same origin-anchored polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Convexification does not alter the origin-anchored polar:
\[
(\operatorname{conv}C)^\circ=C^\circ.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(y\in Y\), the inequalities \(\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\) for all \(x\in C\) hold if and only if they hold for every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}C\). Thus polarity discards the nonconvex arrangement of points in \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) is a separated real dual pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{conv}C)^\circ=C^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar invariance under convexification for arbitrary subsets of a dual pair.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The identity is mathematically standard, but the cited Hilbert-space source does not inspectably support the record's separated-dual-pair formulation. A source covering polarity in dual pairs with a precise locator is required.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Closure Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak closure, like norm closure, leaves the unit polar unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(C\subseteq H\). If \(\overline C^{\,w}\) denotes the weak closure of \(C\), then \[(\overline C^{\,w})^\circ=C^\circ.\] Consequently the norm closure and weak closure of an arbitrary set have the same unit polar, although the closures themselves need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\overline C^{\,w})^\circ=C^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-closure invariance of the unit polar in a real Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set and its norm closure have exactly the same unit polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Taking the norm closure of \(C\) does not change its unit polar: \[(\overline C)^\circ=C^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\overline C)^\circ=C^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-polar convention in a real Hilbert space.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.title: Origin-Adjoining Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjoining the origin to any set does not change its unit polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adjoining the origin to \(C\) does not change its unit polar: \[(C\cup\{0\})^\circ=C^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((C\cup\{0\})^\circ=C^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjoining the origin under the unit-polar convention.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-of-Polars Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sets have the same unit polar exactly when their closed convex origin-containing canonicalizations coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary \(C,D\subseteq H\), \[C^\circ=D^\circ\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C^{\circ\circ}=D^{\circ\circ}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(D\cup\{0\}).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C^\circ=D^\circ\iff C^{\circ\circ}=D^{\circ\circ}\iff \overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(D\cup\{0\}).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of unit-polar equivalence classes for arbitrary subsets of a real Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Points of Polar Canonicalization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed points of bipolar canonicalization are exactly the closed convex sets containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C\subseteq H\), \[C=C^{\circ\circ}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\text{ is norm closed, convex, and }0\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=C^{\circ\circ}\iff C\text{ is norm closed and convex and }0\in C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point class of the bipolar closure operator.

notation.meaning: bipolar of C under unit polarity

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Invariant Canonicalization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar is the unique canonical closed convex, origin-containing representative with the same polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical closed convex set containing the origin and having the same polar as \(C\) is its bipolar: \[C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}).\] It satisfies \[(C^{\circ\circ})^\circ=C^\circ.\] Thus the map \(C\mapsto C^{\circ\circ}\) is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, and it preserves the polar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})\) and \((C^{\circ\circ})^\circ=C^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipolar canonicalization for arbitrary subsets of a Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Union, intersection, and scaling rules for polar sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be subsets of a real Hilbert space \(H\), and define \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic set-algebra rules for threshold-one polarity; intersection formulas require closed convex origin-containing inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set-algebra polarity is governed by \[\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\right)^\circ=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i^\circ,\qquad (\lambda C)^\circ=\lambda^{-1}C^\circ\quad(\lambda>0).\] Since a polar is insensitive to closed convex origin-containing hulls, also \[\left(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\cup\{0\}\right)\right)^\circ=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i^\circ.\] For two closed convex sets \(C,D\) containing \(0\), the dual intersection rule is \[(C\cap D)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C^\circ\cup D^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a union is the intersection of the individual polars, positive scaling is inverted, and convexifying or closing a union does not change its polar. Conversely, for closed convex origin-containing sets, the polar of an intersection is the closed convex hull of the union of their polars.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\left(\bigcup_i C_i\right)^\circ=\bigcap_iC_i^\circ,\qquad (C\cap D)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C^\circ\cup D^\circ)\ \text{for closed convex }C,D\ni0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[u\in\left(\bigcup_iC_i\right)^\circ\iff u\in C_i^\circ\ \forall i.\]
For closed convex \(C,D\ni0\), \(C\cap D=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C^\circ\cup D^\circ))^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: For cones under the nonpositive convention, \((K_1+K_2)^\circ=K_1^\circ\cap K_2^\circ\).
For a finite family of closed convex origin-containing sets, the intersection rule iterates with a final closed convex hull.
immediate_consequences_latex: Polarity reverses inclusion and converts generated hulls into intersections.
The closure in the intersection rule cannot generally be omitted in infinite-dimensional spaces.
boundary_notes: There is no unconditional formula \((C\cap D)^\circ=C^\circ\cup D^\circ\); convexification and usually closure are essential.
The scaling rule stated here assumes \(\lambda>0\); negative scaling introduces reflection.

notation.meaning: Set obtained by scaling the polar by the reciprocal positive scalar.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of an intersection is the closed convex hull of the union of the individual polars.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty index set \(I\), the polar of an intersection is \[\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\right)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i^\circ\right).\] The closure is taken in the norm topology of \(H\); in finite dimensions it is the ordinary Euclidean closure.
assumptions_latex: \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) is a nonempty family of closed convex subsets of \(H\) containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i^\circ)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary nonempty intersections of closed convex origin-containing sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski-Sum Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a Minkowski sum is the unit sublevel set of the sum of the two support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar of the Minkowski sum has the representation \[(A+B)^\circ=\{y\in H:\sigma_A(y)+\sigma_B(y)\le 1\},\] where the support functions take values in the extended reals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A+B)^\circ=\{y\in H:\sigma_A(y)+\sigma_B(y)\le 1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact support-function formula; no convexity or closedness is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Weighted-Combination Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a finite nonnegative weighted Minkowski combination is the unit sublevel set of the weighted sum of the factor support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_i\subseteq H\) be nonempty and let \(\lambda_i\ge0\). Then \[\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_iA_i\right)^\circ=\left\{y\in H:\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\sigma_{A_i}(y)\le1\right\},\] where a zero coefficient contributes zero even if the corresponding support value is \(+\infty\). In particular, this applies when \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\sum_i\lambda_iA_i\right)^\circ=\left\{y:\sum_i\lambda_i\sigma_{A_i}(y)\le1\right\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonnegative weighted Minkowski combinations, including zero weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Combination Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a weighted Minkowski combination is the unit sublevel set of the correspondingly weighted support functions, with the endpoint convention that a zero coefficient contributes zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), the polar of the weighted Minkowski combination is \[(\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B)^\circ=\{y\in H:\lambda\sigma_A(y)+(1-\lambda)\sigma_B(y)\le 1\}.\] At an endpoint, a zero coefficient multiplying \(+\infty\) is interpreted as \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\lambda A+(1-\lambda)B)^\circ=\{y\in H:\lambda\sigma_A(y)+(1-\lambda)\sigma_B(y)\le 1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted Minkowski combination, including both endpoint weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Indispensable Closure in Intersection Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed subspaces with a nonclosed sum yield closed convex origin-containing sets for which intersection polarity strictly requires closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\ell^2\), let \(T:E\to E\) be \(T(x_n)=(x_n/n)\), and in \(H=E\oplus E\) set \[M=E\oplus\{0\},\qquad N=\operatorname{gra}T.\] Then \(M,N\) are closed subspaces but \(M+N=E\oplus\operatorname{ran}T\) is not closed. With \(C_1=M^\perp\) and \(C_2=N^\perp\), \[C_1^\circ=M,\qquad C_2^\circ=N,\] and \[(C_1\cap C_2)^\circ=\overline{M+N}\supsetneq M+N=\operatorname{conv}(C_1^\circ\cup C_2^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (C_1\cap C_2)^\circ\supsetneq\operatorname{conv}(C_1^\circ\cup C_2^\circ).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional subspace example showing that closed convexification cannot generally be replaced by algebraic convexification.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Sensitive Set Algebra
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Union polarity is exact, whereas intersection polarity generally needs both convexification and closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polarity converts arbitrary unions exactly into intersections: \[\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\right)^\circ=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i^\circ.\] By contrast, if every \(C_i\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), then \[\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\right)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i^\circ\right),\] and omission of the closure can fail in infinite-dimensional spaces.
assumptions_latex: \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) is a nonempty family of subsets of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bigcup_i C_i)^\circ=\bigcap_i C_i^\circ\), while intersection polarity generally requires closed convexification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact union laws from closure-sensitive intersection laws.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar transport through a linear map and its adjoint
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\) be Euclidean spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(A^*:Y\to X\) satisfy \(\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_X\). Let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear-image transport for threshold-one polar sets; the image need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Linear-adjoint polarity transport is the identity \[(A C)^\circ=(A^*)^{-1}(C^\circ)=\{y\in Y:A^*y\in C^\circ\}.\] Equivalently, support functions transform by \[\sigma_{A C}(y)=\sigma_C(A^*y)\quad\forall y\in Y.\] Since support functions and polars are unchanged by closure, the same formulas hold with \(AC\) replaced by \(\overline{AC}\). Thus a primal linear image is tested in the dual space by pulling the test vector back through the adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a linear image consists exactly of dual vectors whose adjoint pullback lies in the original polar. Equivalently, the support function of the image at \(y\) equals the support function of the original set at \(A^*y\). Closing the image does not alter either identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(AC)^\circ=(A^*)^{-1}(C^\circ),\qquad \sigma_{AC}=\sigma_C\circ A^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[y\in(AC)^\circ\iff\langle Ax,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\iff A^*y\in C^\circ.\]
\[(\overline{AC})^\circ=(AC)^\circ.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is orthogonal, then \((AC)^\circ=A(C^\circ)\).
If \(A\) is invertible, then \((AC)^\circ=A^{-*}C^\circ\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The kernel of \(A^*\) is always contained in \((AC)^\circ\).
Linear image support calculations can be performed without explicitly constructing \(AC\).
boundary_notes: A formula for the polar of an inverse image generally involves image closure and additional structure; it is not asserted here.
Closedness of \(AC\) is not automatic, even when \(C\) is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: Inverse of the adjoint when \(A\) is invertible.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Image Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a linear image is the inverse image of the original polar under the adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar of the linear image \(T(C)\subseteq Y\) is the adjoint inverse image of the polar of \(C\subseteq X\): \[(T(C))^\circ=\{y\in Y:T^*y\in C^\circ\}=(T^*)^{-1}(C^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded linear images under Hilbert-space unit polarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint-Image Closure Cannot Be Omitted
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite example makes the adjoint image of the target polar nonclosed, so only its closure equals the inverse-image polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y=\mathbb S^2\) have the Frobenius inner product, let \(X=\mathbb R^2\), and define \(T(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}u&v/2\\v/2&0\end{pmatrix}\). For \(D=-\mathbb S_+^2\), one has \(D^\circ=\mathbb S_+^2\), \[T^*(D^\circ)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] whereas \[(T^{-1}D)^\circ=\{(a,b):a\geq0\}=\overline{T^*(D^\circ)}.\] Hence the closure in the inverse-image polarity formula cannot generally be deleted, even in finite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R^2\) and \(Y=\mathbb S^2\) carry their standard Hilbert structures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*(D^\circ)\subsetneq (T^{-1}D)^\circ=\overline{T^*(D^\circ)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inverse-image polarity example in which the adjoint image of the target polar is nonclosed.

notation.meaning: cone of two-by-two positive-semidefinite symmetric matrices

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Image Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a closed convex inverse image is the closure of the adjoint image of the polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar of the inverse image satisfies \[(T^{-1}D)^\circ=\overline{T^*(D^\circ)},\] where closure is in the norm topology of \(X\). Thus every element of \(T^*(D^\circ)\) is a polar certificate for \(T^{-1}D\), and all polar elements arise as limits of such adjoint images.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq Y\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((T^{-1}D)^\circ=\overline{T^*(D^\circ)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space inverse-image formula with the necessary closure retained.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Polar Transport
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is polar to a linear image exactly when its adjoint image is polar to the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y\in Y\), polar membership transports through the adjoint according to \[y\in(TC)^\circ\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T^*y\in C^\circ.\] Equivalently, the support functions obey \[\sigma_{TC}(y)=\sigma_C(T^*y).\] This transport identity requires neither injectivity nor surjectivity of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in(TC)^\circ\iff T^*y\in C^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise adjoint transport of polar membership.

notation.meaning: unit polar in the ambient space

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Nonclosed Adjoint Range
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact diagonal injection has a proper dense adjoint range, so the closure in the kernel-polar formula is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\ell^2\), define \((Tx)_n=x_n/n\). Then \(T=T^*\), \(\ker T=\{0\}\), and \(\operatorname{ran}T\) is dense but not closed. Consequently \[(\ker T)^\circ=\ell^2=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T^*}\neq\operatorname{ran}T^*.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\ker T)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T^*}=\ell^2\) while \(\operatorname{ran}T^*\neq\ell^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal Hilbert-space operator showing that the closure in the kernel-polar identity can be strict.

notation.meaning: Hilbert space of square-summable real sequences

knowledge_statements.title: Injectivity and Dense-Range Polar Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Injectivity is dual to density of the adjoint range, and dense range is dual to injectivity of the adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bounded linear operator \(T:X\to Y\) between real Hilbert spaces, \[\ker T=\{0\}\iff \overline{\operatorname{ran}T^*}=X,\qquad \overline{\operatorname{ran}T}=Y\iff \ker T^*=\{0\}.\] Thus injectivity corresponds to density, not necessarily surjectivity, of the adjoint range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker T=\{0\}\iff\overline{\operatorname{ran}T^*}=X\) and \(\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}=Y\iff\ker T^*=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp density consequences of the kernel and range polar identities.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel–Range Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of the kernel is the closed adjoint range, while the polar of the range is the adjoint kernel; the closure on the adjoint range can be dropped exactly under the closed-range condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The kernel and range satisfy \[(\ker T)^\circ=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T^*},\qquad (\operatorname{ran}T)^\circ=(\operatorname{ran}T)^\perp=\ker T^*.\] The equality \((\ker T)^\circ=\operatorname{ran}T^*\) holds exactly when \(\operatorname{ran}T^*\) is closed, equivalently when \(\operatorname{ran}T\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\ker T)^\circ=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T^*}\) and \((\operatorname{ran}T)^\circ=\ker T^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-range boundary for replacing adjoint-range closure by equality.

children.title: Product-Space Polarity Calculus
children.top_down_role: Polarity in product-space and marginal constructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar and marginal rules in a product space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\), paired componentwise by \(\langle(x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle\). Let \(C\subseteq X\), \(D\subseteq Y\), and \(S\subseteq X\times Y\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional threshold-one polarity for Cartesian products and coordinate projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Cartesian-product support function separates as \[\sigma_{C\times D}(u,v)=\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v),\] and hence \[(C\times D)^\circ=\{(u,v):\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v)\leq1\}.\] If \(P_X(x,y)=x\) is the coordinate projection, then the polar of the marginal projection is the zero-slice of the product-space polar: \[(P_XS)^\circ=\{u\in X:(u,0)\in S^\circ\}.\] Thus products produce additive support constraints, while projection in the primal space becomes restriction to a coordinate slice in the polar space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a product space, the support value of a Cartesian product is the sum of the two component support values. Its polar is therefore a coupled sublevel set, not generally the product of the component polars. Projecting a set onto one coordinate corresponds to intersecting its polar with the complementary dual coordinate set to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(C\times D)^\circ=\{(u,v):\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v)\leq1\},\qquad (P_XS)^\circ=\{u:(u,0)\in S^\circ\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(u,v)\in(C\times D)^\circ\iff \sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle+\sup_{y\in D}\langle y,v\rangle\leq1.\]
\[u\in(P_XS)^\circ\iff\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall(x,y)\in S.\]
special_cases_latex: For nonempty cones \(K,L\), \((K\times L)^\ominus=K^\ominus\times L^\ominus\), because each support term must be nonpositive.
If \(D=\{0\}\), then \((C\times\{0\})^\circ=C^\circ\times Y\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The general identity \((C\times D)^\circ=C^\circ\times D^\circ\) is false for threshold-one polarity.
Marginal polar constraints can be read directly from the zero-coordinate slice of \(S^\circ\).
boundary_notes: The additive formula uses the componentwise product pairing.
For infinite products, topological-dual and summability choices require separate specification.

notation.meaning: Threshold-one polar in the product pairing.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Factor Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empty factor makes the product empty and its polar the whole product space, so the ordinary support-sum formula is stated for nonempty factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_j=\varnothing\) for some \(j\), then \[\prod_{i=1}^n C_i=\varnothing,\qquad \left(\prod_{i=1}^n C_i\right)^\circ=\prod_{i=1}^n H_i.\] Thus the ordinary support-sum formula is stated for nonempty factors, avoiding extended-real indeterminacies involving \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\prod_i C_i\right)^\circ=\prod_i H_i.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp nonemptiness boundary for the support-sum product formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Product-Set Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a finite Cartesian product is the unit sublevel set of the sum of the factor support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty sets \(C_i\subseteq H_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), \[\left(\prod_{i=1}^n C_i\right)^\circ=\left\{(u_i)_{i=1}^n:\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_{C_i}(u_i)\le1\right\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(H_1,\ldots,H_n\) are real Hilbert spaces with the standard product inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\prod_{i=1}^n C_i\right)^\circ=\left\{(u_i):\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_{C_i}(u_i)\le1\right\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products under the standard product Hilbert structure.

notation.meaning: support function of the ith factor

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Set Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a Cartesian product is the unit sublevel set of the sum of the factor support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar of the Cartesian product is \[(C\times D)^\circ=\{(u,v)\in H_1\times H_2:\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v)\le 1\}.\] The support functions are understood as extended-real-valued functions.
assumptions_latex: \(H_1,H_2\) are real Hilbert spaces with the product inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((C\times D)^\circ=\{(u,v)\in H_1\times H_2:\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_D(v)\le 1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cartesian products under the standard product Hilbert structure.

notation.meaning: unit polar in the product space

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Polar Projection Counterexample
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated second-order cone has a nonclosed coordinate projection, producing a central slice whose polar strictly exceeds the unclosed projection of the original polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[K=\{(a,b,c)\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R:a\ge0,\ c\ge0,\ 2ac\ge b^2\}\] and let \(C=K^\ominus\), where \(K^\ominus=\{z:\langle z,k\rangle\le0\ \forall k\in K\}\). Then \(C^\circ=K\), while \[\pi_{\mathbb R^2}(K)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\] is not closed. Hence, for \(S=\{x:(x,0)\in C\}\), \[S^\circ=\overline{\pi_{\mathbb R^2}(C^\circ)}\supsetneq\pi_{\mathbb R^2}(C^\circ).\]
assumptions_latex: The spaces are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K\) and \(C\) are the displayed closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^\circ=\overline{\pi_{\mathbb R^2}(C^\circ)}\supsetneq\pi_{\mathbb R^2}(C^\circ).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit finite-dimensional example showing that closure in central-slice polarity is indispensable.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Origin Closure Removal
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the origin is interior to the product-space set, its polar is compact and the closure in the central-slice formula may be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(C^\circ\) is compact and therefore \(\pi_X(C^\circ)\) is closed. Consequently, for \(S=\{x:(x,0)\in C\}\), \[S^\circ=\pi_X(C^\circ).\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:(x,0)\in C\}^\circ=\pi_X(C^\circ).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient exactness regime for central-slice polarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Affine-Slice Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the relative-interior qualification, the polar of an affine coordinate slice is a projection of a support-function sublevel set incorporating the slice offset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[S_{y_0}=\{x\in X:(x,y_0)\in C\}.\] If \(y_0\in\operatorname{ri}(\pi_YC)\), then \[S_{y_0}^\circ=\left\{u\in X:\exists v\in Y,\ \sigma_C(u,v)-\langle v,y_0\rangle\le1\right\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{y_0}^\circ=\{u:\exists v,\ \sigma_C(u,v)-\langle v,y_0\rangle\le1\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar representation for a noncentral coordinate fiber under a relative-interior qualification.

notation.meaning: fiber of C at coordinate value y0
support function of C in the product space

knowledge_statements.title: Slice Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar of a coordinate slice embedded in a finite-dimensional product space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces and let \(C\subseteq X\times Y\). Define the zero slice \(C_0:=\{x\in X:(x,0)\in C\}\) and its embedding \(S:=C_0\times\{0\}\). With polar convention \(D^\circ:=\{z:\langle z,d\rangle\leq 1\text{ for every }d\in D\}\), one has \[S^\circ=C_0^\circ\times Y.\] Thus the product-space polar imposes precisely the polar inequalities generated by the sliced coordinates and leaves the complementary dual coordinate unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a zero-coordinate slice equals the polar of its nonzero-coordinate section times the unrestricted complementary dual space.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((C_0\times\{0\})^\circ=C_0^\circ\times Y\).

notation.meaning: Zero-coordinate slice of C in X.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity converts a coordinate projection into the corresponding zero-coordinate slice of the product-space polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(C^\circ=\{(u,v):\langle u,x\rangle+\langle v,y\rangle\le1\text{ for every }(x,y)\in C\}\). A vector \(u\in X\) belongs to the polar of \(\pi_XC\) exactly when its zero extension \((u,0)\) belongs to \(C^\circ\). Thus
\[
(\pi_X C)^\circ=\{u\in X:(u,0)\in C^\circ\}.
\]
No convexity or closedness assumption on \(C\) is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\pi_X C)^\circ=\{u\in X:(u,0)\in C^\circ\}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate projections under the unit-polar convention.

notation.meaning: unit polar in the relevant Euclidean space

knowledge_statements.title: Slice–Projection Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection becomes a central slice after polarity, while a central slice becomes the closure of a projection of the polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With the unit-polar convention, coordinate projection and zero-coordinate slicing exchange roles under polarity. Explicitly,
\[
(\pi_XC)^\circ=\iota_X^{-1}(C^\circ),
\qquad
\{x:(x,0)\in C\}^\circ_X=\operatorname{cl}(\pi_XC^\circ).
\]
The first identity holds for arbitrary \(C\subseteq X\times Y\); the stated closedness, convexity, and origin assumptions ensure the second identity. The analogous pair follows after interchanging \(X\) and \(Y\).
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq X\times Y\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\pi_XC)^\circ=\iota_X^{-1}(C^\circ),\qquad (C\cap\iota_X(X))^\circ_X=\operatorname{cl}(\pi_XC^\circ)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired projection and central-slice identities for Euclidean product spaces.

notation.meaning: canonical embedding of X into the product

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subseteq H\). Define \(C^\circ=\{u\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space threshold-one bipolar family, including the fixed-point representation class and its conic specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bipolar operator is \[\mathfrak{b}(C):=C^{\circ\circ}=\{x\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall u\in C^\circ\}.\] Its canonical value is \[\mathfrak{b}(C)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Therefore \(C\) admits exact polar representation, meaning \(C=C^{\circ\circ}\), precisely when \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\). For a cone \(K\), threshold-one polarity becomes homogeneous nonpositive polarity and \(K^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}K\); hence a cone is bipolar exactly when it is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar of a set consists of all points satisfying every unit-threshold inequality indexed by the polar. It equals the closed convex hull after adjoining the origin. The fixed points are exactly closed convex origin-containing sets. In the conic regime, the bipolar is the closed convex conical hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\}),\qquad C=C^{\circ\circ}\iff C\text{ is closed, convex, and }0\in C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in C^{\circ\circ}\iff\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall u\text{ satisfying }\langle c,u\rangle\leq1\ \forall c\in C.\]
For a nonempty cone \(K\), \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}K\).
special_cases_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\ni0\), one has \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
For a nonempty closed convex cone \(K\), one has \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Bipolarization is a closure operator on subsets of \(H\).
Every closed convex origin-containing set is the intersection of the half-spaces \(\{x:\langle x,u\rangle\leq1\}\) indexed by its polar.
boundary_notes: For a general set not containing the origin, the bipolar does not equal merely \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C\); the origin must be adjoined.
The topology governing closure changes in general dual-pair formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Set Bipolarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Euclidean set’s bipolar is its closed convex hull after adjoining the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(A^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,a\rangle\le1\text{ for every }a\in A\}\). Then
\[
A^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\}).
\]
Consequently, \(A=A^{\circ\circ}\) if and only if \(A\) is closed, convex, and contains the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Euclidean bipolar theorem using the one-sided unit polar.

notation.meaning: unit polar of a subset of Euclidean space

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), with the standard Euclidean pairing. Define \(C^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean bipolarity; closure is ordinary Euclidean closure and no weak-topology distinction arises.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Euclidean bipolar of \(C\) is \[C^{\circ\circ}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall y\in C^\circ\},\] and satisfies \[C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Equivalently, a set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is representable exactly by its polar inequalities, \[D=\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall y\in D^\circ\},\] if and only if \(D\) is closed, convex, and contains the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In Euclidean space, applying threshold-one polarity twice produces the ordinary closed convex hull of the original set together with the origin. Thus exact recovery from all polar inequalities holds precisely for closed convex sets containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\notin\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})\iff\exists y\in C^\circ\text{ with }\langle x,y\rangle>1.\]
\[D=D^{\circ\circ}\iff D\text{ is Euclidean closed, convex, and }0\in D.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is finite, \(C^{\circ\circ}\) is the polytope \(\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})\), which is already closed.
If \(C\) is a closed convex body containing \(0\), then \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite-dimensional polar inequalities give a complete representation of closed convex origin-containing sets.
For a cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the conic bipolar is its closed convex conical hull.
boundary_notes: The closure cannot be discarded for arbitrary nonclosed sets, although convex hulls of finite sets are closed.
This record uses the threshold-one polar; cone-polar sign conventions must be normalized separately.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolarity in a separating dual pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,Y,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a separating real dual pair. Equip \(X\) with \(\sigma(X,Y)\) and \(Y\) with \(\sigma(Y,X)\). For \(C\subseteq X\), define \(C^\circ=\{y\in Y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\); for \(D\subseteq Y\), define \(D^\circ=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall y\in D\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General separating dual-pair regime; the closure in the bipolar formula is weak closure induced by the designated pairing, not an unspecified norm closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The weak dual-pair bipolar of \(C\subseteq X\) is \[C^{\circ\circ}=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall y\in C^\circ\}.\] Its canonical representation is \[C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.\] Consequently, \(C=C^{\circ\circ}\) exactly when \(C\) is convex, contains \(0\), and is closed for the weak topology \(\sigma(X,Y)\). The symmetric statement holds for subsets of \(Y\) with \(\sigma(Y,X)\)-closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a separating dual pair, polar sets live in the opposite member of the pair. Applying polarity twice returns the weakly closed convex hull after adjoining the origin. Exact bipolar representation therefore uses closure in the weak topology generated by the chosen pairing, and the corresponding statement holds on both sides of the pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in C^{\circ\circ}\iff\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall y\in Y\text{ such that }\langle c,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall c\in C.\]
\[C=C^{\circ\circ}\iff C\text{ is }\sigma(X,Y)\text{-closed, convex, and contains }0.\]
special_cases_latex: For a finite-dimensional Euclidean dual pair, \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closure agrees with ordinary Euclidean closure.
For a Banach space paired with its continuous dual, the relevant primal closure is weak closure \(\sigma(X,X^*)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The bipolar depends on the designated separating duality, because that pairing determines both the polar and weak topology.
Weakly closed convex origin-containing subsets are precisely the fixed points of dual-pair bipolarization.
boundary_notes: No inspected local source supplied an exact weak-dual-pair statement and locator for this slot; independent source verification is required.
If the pairing is not separating, the asserted topology and point-separation characterization require modification.
Norm closure must not replace weak closure without an additional closed-convex closure equivalence appropriate to the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm Closedness Does Not Imply Weak-Star Bipolar Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The norm-closed subspace c0 is weak-star dense in l-infinity, so its bipolar is all of l-infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\ell^\infty=(\ell^1)^*\) with \(\sigma(\ell^\infty,\ell^1)\). Consequently, \[\overline{c_0}^{\,\sigma(\ell^\infty,\ell^1)}=c_0^{\circ\circ}=\ell^\infty\ne c_0.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Repeated polarity selects closure in the weak topology generated by the pairing:
\[
A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.
\]
Moreover, polar inequalities are unchanged by this operation:
\[
A^\circ=\left(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}\right)^\circ.
\]
Thus weak closedness, rather than closedness in an unspecified stronger topology, is the intrinsic regularity condition for bipolar reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipolarization performs convexification, adjoins the origin, and closes the result in the pairing-induced weak topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Topology Closure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly identifies weak-topology closure as the closure intrinsic to the dual pairing and states the polar-invariance property consistently. Property is an appropriate knowledge kind here, but no source reference is provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipolar Recovery on the Separated Quotient
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonseparating pairing, bipolarization is separated bipolarization in the quotient, pulled back to the original space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=Y_\perp\), \(M=X_\perp\), \(\bar X=X/N\), and \(\bar Y=Y/M\). The pairing descends to a separating pairing between \(\bar X\) and \(\bar Y\). If \(q:X\to\bar X\) is the quotient map, then for every \(A\subseteq X\), \[A^{\circ\circ}=q^{-1}\!\left(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(q(A)\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(\bar X,\bar Y)}\right).\] Consequently every bipolar subset of \(X\) is saturated by cosets of \(N\).
assumptions_latex: X,Y\text{ are real vector spaces with a bilinear pairing}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\circ\circ}=q^{-1}\!\left(\overline{\operatorname{conv}(q(A)\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X/N,Y/M)}\right)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact quotient representation for a bilinear pairing that may fail to separate either space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(Y\) does not separate points of \(X\), let \(N=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in Y\}\). Then \(N\ne\{0\}\), while
\[
\{0\}^\circ=Y,
\qquad
\{0\}^{\circ\circ}=N.
\]
Hence even the closed convex origin set \(\{0\}\) is not recovered. More generally, all polar data are constant on cosets of \(N\), so reconstruction is possible only modulo \(N\), equivalently in the separated quotient \(X/N\).

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Bipolarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone’s double negative polar is its closed convex conic hull, and closed convex cones are exactly the fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cone \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define its negative polar cone by \(K^\ominus=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). Then
\[
K^{\ominus\ominus}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(K).
\]
Because \(K\) is a cone, \(\operatorname{conv}(K)\) is its convex conic hull. Consequently, \(K=K^{\ominus\ominus}\) if and only if \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K^{\ominus\ominus}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(K)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bipolar theorem specialized to the negative-polar convention for cones.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Cone and Conic Bipolar Closure
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\), and let \(S\subseteq H\) be nonempty. Write \(\operatorname{cone}S\) for its conic hull and \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\) for the norm closure of that hull.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space negative-polar convention; the finite-dimensional Euclidean statement is obtained by taking \(H=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[S^{\ominus}:=\{u\in H:\sup_{x\in S}\langle x,u\rangle\le 0\}=\{u\in H:(\forall x\in S)\ \langle x,u\rangle\le0\}.\] The conic bipolar of \(S\) is \(S^{\ominus\ominus}:=(S^{\ominus})^{\ominus}\), and conic bipolarity is the identity \[S^{\ominus\ominus}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S.\] Consequently, a nonempty cone \(K\) satisfies \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\) exactly when it is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar cone of a nonempty set \(S\) consists of all vectors making a nonpositive inner product with every point of \(S\). Applying this operation twice produces the closed convex cone generated by \(S\). Thus repeated conic polarity is a closure-and-convexification operation, and it fixes precisely the nonempty closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S^{\ominus\ominus}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S,\qquad K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\ \Longleftrightarrow\ K\text{ is a nonempty closed convex cone}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: With the dual-cone convention \(S^{\oplus}:=-S^{\ominus}\), one has \(S^{\oplus\oplus}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\).
For \(x\in H\), \(x\in\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S\) if and only if every \(u\in H\) satisfying \(\langle s,u\rangle\le0\) for all \(s\in S\) also satisfies \(\langle x,u\rangle\le0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K\subseteq H\) is already a nonempty closed convex cone, then \(K^{\ominus\ominus}=K\).
If \(V\subseteq H\) is a closed linear subspace, then \(V^{\ominus}=V^\perp\) and \(V^{\ominus\ominus}=V\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar is invariant under conic convex closure: \(S^{\ominus}=(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S)^{\ominus}\).
Polarity reverses inclusion: \(S_1\subseteq S_2\Rightarrow S_2^{\ominus}\subseteq S_1^{\ominus}\).
boundary_notes: Without closedness or convexity, a cone need not equal its bipolar; the bipolar supplies both missing regularizations.
The sign convention differs from the nonnegative dual cone used in some conic-optimization texts.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Representation Consequences
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set containing the origin is exactly the intersection of all unit halfspaces indexed by its polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bipolar theorem gives the exact outer representation
\[
C=C^{\circ\circ}=\bigcap_{y\in C^\circ}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(x\notin C\), then some \(y\in C^\circ\) satisfies \(\langle y,x\rangle>1\). Thus every excluded point violates a valid polar halfspace, and the intersection of all such valid halfspaces reconstructs \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=C^{\circ\circ}=\bigcap_{y\in C^\circ}\{x:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-halfspace reconstruction for closed convex origin-containing Euclidean sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb R^n\) with its Euclidean pairing. Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex set containing \(0\), and define \(C^\circ:=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\text{ for every }x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets anchored at the origin; the representation uses normalized supporting halfspaces whose offsets equal one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar representation family of \(C\) is \[\mathcal H(C):=\{H_y:y\in C^\circ\},\qquad H_y:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\}.\] Its represented set is \[R(C):=\bigcap_{y\in C^\circ}H_y=C^{\circ\circ}.\] Since \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), bipolarity gives \[C=R(C)=\bigcap_{y\in C^\circ}\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set containing the origin is represented by all normalized closed halfspaces indexed by its polar. A point belongs to the set exactly when it satisfies every inequality \(\langle x,y\rangle\le1\) with \(y\in C^\circ\). The intersection of these halfspaces is the bipolar and hence recovers \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\forall y\in C^\circ)\ \langle x,y\rangle\le1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The representation may be written as the support-function test \(x\in C\Longleftrightarrow\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)\le1\).
Equivalently, \(C\) is the unit sublevel set of the support function of its polar: \(C=\{x:\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)\le1\}\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), normalization collapses to homogeneous inequalities and \(K=K^{\ominus\ominus}\).
If \(C\) is bounded with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(C^\circ\) is also a convex body containing \(0\) in its interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point outside \(C\) violates at least one polar inequality: \(x\notin C\Rightarrow(\exists y\in C^\circ)\ \langle x,y\rangle>1\).
The gauge-support identity is \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\).
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is not closed, convex, or origin-containing, the same intersection represents \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})\), not necessarily \(C\).
Not every indexed halfspace must define a facet or an irredundant constraint.

notation.meaning: Normalized closed halfspace associated with \(y\in C^\circ\).
Intersection of all polar-indexed normalized halfspaces.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipolar Regularization and Its Fixed Points
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be arbitrary and define \(C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:(\forall x\in C)\ \langle x,y\rangle\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean polarity; this entry isolates exactly which regularity properties are imposed by taking the bipolar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bipolar regularization of \(C\) is \[\mathcal B(C):=C^{\circ\circ}.\] It has the explicit form \[\mathcal B(C)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}).\] Accordingly, \(C\) is a fixed point of bipolar regularization, meaning \(\mathcal B(C)=C\), if and only if \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bipolar of an arbitrary finite-dimensional set is its closed convex hull after adjoining the origin. This formula records the three regularity boundaries of ordinary set polarity: convexification repairs missing convexity, closure repairs missing closedness, and adjoining zero repairs failure of origin inclusion. Equality with the original set occurs exactly when none of those repairs changes it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}),\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C\Longleftrightarrow C\text{ is closed, convex, and }0\in C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C^\circ\) depends only on the regularization: \(C^\circ=\mathcal B(C)^\circ\).
\(\mathcal B\) is an extensive, monotone, idempotent closure operator on subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is convex and contains \(0\) but is not closed, then \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}C\).
If \(C\) is closed and convex but \(0\notin C\), then \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\})\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Different sets with the same closed origin-containing convex hull have the same polar.
The polar \(C^\circ\) is always closed, convex, and origin-containing, regardless of the regularity of \(C\).
boundary_notes: In an infinite-dimensional dual pair, closure must be taken in the topology determined by the chosen duality, commonly the appropriate weak topology.
For conic polarity with threshold zero, the corresponding regularization is the closed convex conic hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipolar Closure Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipolarization successively accounts for the missing origin, missing convexity, and missing weak closedness; exact recovery occurs when all three already hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})\). Bipolarization always yields
\[
A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{B}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.
\]
Hence, if \(A\) is convex and contains \(0\), then \(A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{A}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}\). If \(A\) is additionally \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closed, then \(A^{\circ\circ}=A\). These are the convexification, origin-adjunction, and closure regimes of the same operation, not distinct bipolar conventions.
assumptions_latex: (X,Y)\text{ is a separating real dual pair}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact effects of bipolarization under progressively stronger regularity assumptions.

notation.meaning: convex hull after adjoining the origin

knowledge_statements.title: Incompatible Topologies Can Change Convex Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On l1, the kernel of the summation functional is closed for the weak topology induced by l-infinity but dense for the weaker topology induced by c0, so convex closures need not agree without dual compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\ell^1\), pair it with \(Y=\ell^\infty\), and let \(\tau=\sigma(\ell^1,c_0)\). Define
\[
C=\left\{x\in\ell^1:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x_n=0\right\}.
\]
The functional \(\mathbf 1=(1,1,\ldots)\) belongs to \(Y\setminus c_0\). The subspace \(C=\ker\mathbf1\) is \(\sigma(\ell^1,\ell^\infty)\)-closed, whereas it is \(\tau\)-dense in \(\ell^1\). Consequently,
\[
\overline C^{\,\sigma(\ell^1,\ell^\infty)}=C,
\qquad
\overline C^{\,\tau}=\ell^1.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline C^{\,\sigma(\ell^1,Y)}=C\neq\ell^1=\overline C^{\,\tau}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An infinite-dimensional failure of replacing dual-pair weak closure by closure in a topology having a smaller continuous dual.

notation.meaning: weak topology induced on E by the separating space F
space of scalar sequences converging to zero

assumptions_latex: (X,Y)\text{ is a separating real dual pair}
\tau\text{ is a locally convex topology on }X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\tau}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}

notation.meaning: continuous dual of the locally convex space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology compatibility required to replace weak closure by another locally convex closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A locally convex topology \(\tau\) is compatible with the dual pair when its continuous dual is exactly \(Y\), namely \((X,\tau)'=Y\). Under this condition, every convex subset of \(X\) has the same \(\tau\)-closure as its \(\sigma(X,Y)\)-closure. Therefore, for every \(A\subseteq X\),
\[
A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\tau}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}(A\cup\{0\})}^{\,\sigma(X,Y)}.
\]
Without compatibility, substituting \(\tau\)-closure is not generally valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any compatible locally convex topology gives the same closure of convex sets as the weak topology, so either closure computes the bipolar.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Topology Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility condition and equality of closures for convex sets are stated with the necessary locally convex and continuous-dual hypotheses. knowledge_statements.title: Missing-Convexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without convexity, taking two polars returns the closed convex hull after adjoining the origin, not necessarily the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^2\), the bipolar theorem gives \(C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})\). Hence convexity cannot be omitted from the fixed-point characterization. Concretely, for \(C=\{e_1,e_2\}\), one has \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,e_2\}\supsetneq C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})\), which can strictly contain \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real bipolar theorem; convexity is omitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Missing-Origin Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a closed convex set may differ from its bipolar when it omits the origin; the bipolar adjoins and convexifies with zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(C\subset\mathbb{R}\), one has \(C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})\). Thus origin containment is necessary for a closed convex set to equal its bipolar. For example, if \(C=\{1\}\), then \(C^\circ=(-\infty,1]\) and \(C^{\circ\circ}=[0,1]\neq C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C\cup\{0\})\), so omission of the origin can enlarge \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real bipolar theorem; origin containment is omitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Set Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set containing zero, the bipolar is its closure; the open unit ball therefore becomes the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and contains \(0\), then the bipolar theorem reduces to \(C^{\circ\circ}=\overline C\). Consequently, closedness is necessary for bipolar equality. In particular, for the open Euclidean unit ball \(C=\{x:\|x\|_2<1\}\), one has \(C^{\circ\circ}=\{x:\|x\|_2\leq1\}\supsetneq C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=\overline C\), which may strictly contain \(C\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), where \(\mathbb R^n\) is identified with its dual by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional, one-sided polarity with normalization level one; no convexity or closedness is needed to form the polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Euclidean polar of \(C\) is \[C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \text{for every }x\in C\}=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\}.\] The operation is inclusion reversing: \[C_1\subseteq C_2\Longrightarrow C_2^\circ\subseteq C_1^\circ.\] Every polar is a closed convex set containing \(0\), and repeated polarity satisfies \[C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a set in Euclidean space is the collection of vectors whose inner product with every point of the set is at most one. It is equivalently the unit sublevel set of the support function. Polarity reverses containment, always produces a closed convex origin-containing set, and its second application produces the closed convex hull of the original set together with the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\},\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup\{0\}).\]

For the Euclidean unit ball \(B_2\), \(B_2^\circ=B_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \((\lambda C)^\circ=\lambda^{-1}C^\circ\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
If \(C\) is closed and convex with \(0\in C\), then \(C\mapsto C^\circ\) is an involution on that class.

children.title: Polar-Polytope Face Duality
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial duality between the facial structures of polar polytopes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(Q=P^\circ\). Include \(\varnothing\) and the whole polytope among the faces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-dimensional finite polytopes whose polar is taken about an interior origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every face \(F\) of \(P\), define its polar-dual face by \[F^\diamond:=\{y\in Q:\langle x,y\rangle=1\ \text{for every }x\in F\},\] with \(\varnothing^\diamond=Q\) and \(P^\diamond=\varnothing\). Then \(F^\diamond\) is a face of \(Q\), the map \(F\mapsto F^\diamond\) is a bijection between the face lattices of \(P\) and \(Q\), and it reverses inclusion. For every proper nonempty face, \[\dim F+\dim F^\diamond=d-1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face of a polytope containing the origin in its interior determines the face of the polar on which all points of the original face pair to one. This assignment is an inclusion-reversing bijection of face lattices. It interchanges the empty and whole faces and sends a \(k\)-dimensional proper face to a \((d-1-k)\)-dimensional face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F\subseteq G\Longrightarrow G^\diamond\subseteq F^\diamond,\qquad (F^\diamond)^\diamond=F,\qquad \dim F+\dim F^\diamond=d-1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a face \(G\) of \(Q\), its inverse image is \(G^\diamond=\{x\in P:\langle x,y\rangle=1\text{ for every }y\in G\}\).
The face lattices \(\mathcal F(P)\) and \(\mathcal F(P^\circ)\) are anti-isomorphic.
special_cases_latex: Vertices of \(P\) correspond to facets of \(P^\circ\), and facets of \(P\) correspond to vertices of \(P^\circ\).
In dimension three, edges correspond to edges, while vertices and facets are interchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: The face numbers satisfy \(f_k(P)=f_{d-1-k}(P^\circ)\).
Combinatorial simplicity of \(P\) corresponds to simpliciality of \(P^\circ\).
boundary_notes: The hypothesis \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\) ensures that \(P^\circ\) is a full-dimensional polytope and that the level-one face correspondence is well defined.
For lower-dimensional or unbounded polyhedra, the stated face-lattice duality requires modification.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Polytope Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity converts a polytope’s vertex representation into normalized halfspaces and its normalized halfspace representation into a convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(P^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in P\}\). If \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\), then \(P^\circ=\{y:\langle v_i,y\rangle\leq1,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Conversely, if \(P=\{x:\langle a_j,x\rangle\leq1,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\), then \(P^\circ=\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_r\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_i\}\Rightarrow P^\circ=\bigcap_i\{y:\langle v_i,y\rangle\leq1\}\), and \(P=\bigcap_j\{x:\langle a_j,x\rangle\leq1\}\Rightarrow P^\circ=\operatorname{conv}\{a_j\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Meet–Join Exchange for Polar Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polar face duality exchanges intersections of faces with their lattice joins, including the empty and whole faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). In the extended face lattices, let \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\), and let \(F\vee G\) be the smallest face containing \(F\cup G\). Polar face duality exchanges these operations:
\[
(F\wedge G)^*=F^*\vee G^*,\qquad
(F\vee G)^*=F^*\wedge G^*.
\]
These formulas include improper faces under \(\varnothing^*=P^\circ\) and \(P^*=\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: The extended face lattices include the empty and whole faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((F\wedge G)^*=F^*\vee G^*\) and \((F\vee G)^*=F^*\wedge G^*\) for all faces \(F,G\) of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lattice-operation form of face-poset reversal for polar polytopes.

notation.meaning: meet in the extended face lattice
join in the extended face lattice
face of the polar paired with F

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Lattice Anti-Isomorphism for Polar Polytopes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polar dualization is an involutive order-reversing bijection between the extended face lattices of a full-dimensional polytope containing zero internally and its polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). For every nonempty proper face \(F\) of \(P\), set
\[
F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\text{ for every }x\in F\},
\]
and extend the assignment by \(\varnothing^*=P^\circ\) and \(P^*=\varnothing\). Then \(F\mapsto F^*\) is a bijection from the extended face lattice of \(P\) onto that of \(P^\circ\), satisfies
\[
F\subseteq G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G^*\subseteq F^*,
\]
and is involutive under \(P^{\circ\circ}=P\): \((F^*)^*=F\).
assumptions_latex: The extended face lattices include the empty and whole faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\mapsto F^*\) is an involutive inclusion-reversing bijection between the extended face lattices of \(P\) and \(P^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctly qualified extended-face-lattice duality, including improper faces and involution.

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Lattice Reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-reversing correspondence between faces of mutually polar polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be full-dimensional with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). For every nonempty proper face \(F\) of \(P\), define
\[
F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\ \text{for every }x\in F\}.
\]
Then \(F^*\) is a nonempty proper face of \(P^\circ\), the map \(F\mapsto F^*\) is a bijection, and \((F^*)^*=F\). With the conventions \(\varnothing^*=P^\circ\) and \(P^*=\varnothing\), this extends to an anti-isomorphism of the complete face lattices. In particular, \(F\subseteq G\) holds exactly when \(G^*\subseteq F^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity bijects the faces of an origin-interior polytope with those of its polar and reverses every face inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \(F\mapsto F^*\) is an inclusion-reversing involutive bijection between the face lattices of \(P\) and \(P^\circ\).

notation.meaning: The face of the polar dual to F.

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Number Reversal under Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity reverses the face-number sequence: k-faces of a polytope are counted by complementary-dimensional faces of its polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(f_k(P)\) denote the number of \(k\)-dimensional faces of \(P\). Then
\[
f_k(P)=f_{d-1-k}(P^\circ),\qquad k=0,\ldots,d-1.
\]
In particular, vertices of either polytope correspond in number to facets of its polar partner.
assumptions_latex: \(f_k(P)\) counts the k-dimensional faces of P.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_k(P)=f_{d-1-k}(P^\circ)\) for \(k=0,\ldots,d-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumerative consequence of complementary dimensions for proper faces of polar polytopes.

notation.meaning: number of k-dimensional faces of P

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Dimensions of Polar-Polytope Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paired proper faces of a full-dimensional polytope containing zero internally and its polar have dimensions adding to d−1.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). For every nonempty proper face \(F\) of \(P\), define
\[
F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\text{ for every }x\in F\}.
\]
Then \(F^*\) is a nonempty proper face of \(P^\circ\) and
\[
\dim F+\dim F^*=d-1.
\]
Consequently, \(k\)-faces correspond to \((d-1-k)\)-faces.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a nonempty proper face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim F+\dim F^*=d-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctly qualified dimension-complementarity formula for paired proper faces of polar polytopes.

notation.meaning: face of the polar paired with F

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Dimension Reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank complementarity for proper faces under polar duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be full-dimensional with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(F\) be a nonempty proper face of \(P\). For its dual face
\[
F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\ \text{for every }x\in F\},
\]
one has
\[
\dim F+\dim F^*=d-1.
\]
Consequently, a \(k\)-dimensional face of \(P\) corresponds to a \((d-1-k)\)-dimensional face of \(P^\circ\). In particular, vertices correspond to facets, facets correspond to vertices, and edges correspond to faces of codimension two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual proper faces have complementary dimensions summing to one less than the ambient dimension; vertices and facets are exchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a nonempty proper face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim F+\dim F^*=d-1\).

notation.meaning: Affine dimension of the face F.
The polar-dual face corresponding to F.

knowledge_statements.title: Incidence and Chain Reversal under Polytope Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional polytope containing the origin in its interior, polar duality preserves face incidence while reversing containment, and therefore reverses every strict face chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(P^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le 1\ \forall x\in P\}\). For every face \(F\) of \(P\), set \(F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:\langle x,y\rangle=1\ \forall x\in F\}\), with \(\varnothing^*=P^\circ\) and \(P^*=\varnothing\). Then, for all faces \(F,G\) of \(P\), \[F\subseteq G\iff G^*\subseteq F^*.\] Consequently, every strict face chain \(F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_k\) corresponds to the strict reversed chain \(F_k^*\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_0^*\) in \(P^\circ\).
assumptions_latex: \(F,G\) are faces in the augmented face lattice of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq G\iff G^*\subseteq F^*\), and strict face chains correspond in reverse order.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise incidence and chain correspondence for the augmented face lattices of polar polytopes.

notation.meaning: Face of the polar dual to F, including the stated improper-face conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Incidence Preservation under Reversal
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence correspondence induced by the anti-isomorphism of face lattices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be full-dimensional with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). For nonempty proper faces \(F,G\) of \(P\), polar duality satisfies
\[
F\subseteq G\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G^*\subseteq F^*.
\]
Hence a chain \(F_0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_r\) corresponds to the reversed chain \(F_r^*\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_1^*\subsetneq F_0^*\). In particular, two faces are incident by inclusion precisely when their dual faces are incident in the opposite order, and cover relations in the face lattice of \(P\) correspond to reversed cover relations in the face lattice of \(P^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Face incidence is retained by polar duality after reversing inclusion, so flags and cover relations correspond in reverse order.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(G\) are nonempty proper faces of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq G\) if and only if \(G^*\subseteq F^*\).

notation.meaning: The faces of the polar corresponding to F and G.
