knowledge_statements.title: Origin-Placement Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior placement of zero is exactly what makes the polar bounded; boundary or exterior placement breaks the usual polar-polytope duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar \(P^\circ\) is a bounded full-dimensional polytope exactly when \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\). If \(0\in\partial P\), a supporting normal gives a nonzero direction in \(\operatorname{rec}(P^\circ)\), so the polar is unbounded. If \(0\notin P\), then \(P^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{conv}(P\cup\{0\})\neq P\), preventing involutive face duality for \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^\circ\) is bounded if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\); moreover, \(P^{\circ\circ}=P\) requires \(0\in P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of bounded polar-polytope duality outside interior origin placement.

However, no citation is supplied for the exact origin-placement assertions, so source support is required before acceptance.

children.title: Ellipsoidal Polarity
children.top_down_role: Polarity for quadratic convex-body representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Origin-Containment Boundary for Ellipsoid Polars
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-dimensional ellipsoid has a bounded polar exactly when it contains the origin in its interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(E=\{x:(x-c)^{\mathsf T}A(x-c)\leq1\}\) with \(A\succ0\), \[E^\circ\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\operatorname{int}E\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c^{\mathsf T}Ac<1.\] If \(c^{\mathsf T}Ac\geq1\), then \(E^\circ\) is unbounded and is not a convex body.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\text{ is symmetric positive definite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E^\circ\text{ is bounded}\iff c^{\mathsf T}Ac<1
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness boundary for the polar of a full-dimensional translated ellipsoid.

knowledge_statements.title: Polarity of a Translated Ellipsoid
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of an origin-containing translated ellipsoid is another explicitly computable translated ellipsoid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{x:(x-c)^{\mathsf T}A(x-c)\leq1\}\), where \(A\succ0\) and \(\delta=c^{\mathsf T}Ac<1\). Then \[E^\circ=\{y:c^{\mathsf T}y+\sqrt{y^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}y}\leq1\}.\] Equivalently, with \(B=A^{-1}-cc^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), \[E^\circ=\left\{y:(y+B^{-1}c)^{\mathsf T}B(y+B^{-1}c)\leq\frac1{1-\delta}\right\}.\]
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\text{ is symmetric positive definite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E^\circ=\{y:c^{\mathsf T}y+\sqrt{y^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}y}\leq1\}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-dimensional ellipsoids containing the origin internally, without a centering assumption.

notation.meaning: positive-definite matrix A inverse minus c c-transpose

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoidal Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a centered ellipsoid is obtained by inverting its quadratic-form matrix, equivalently by applying the inverse transpose to the unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_A=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:x^{\mathsf T}Ax\leq1\}\). Its polar is \(E_A^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:y^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}y\leq1\}\). Equivalently, if \(E=T B_2\) for an invertible linear map \(T\) and the Euclidean unit ball \(B_2\), then \(E^\circ=T^{-\mathsf T}B_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:x^{\mathsf T}Ax\leq1\}^\circ=\{y:y^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}y\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Centered full-dimensional ellipsoids in Euclidean space.

notation.meaning: Centered ellipsoid defined by a positive-definite quadratic form

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S_{++}^d\) be a real symmetric positive-definite matrix and use the standard Euclidean inner product on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Origin-centered, full-dimensional ellipsoids; translated ellipsoids do not obey the same inverse-matrix formula without changing the polarity model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quadratic ellipsoid generated by \(Q\) is \[E_Q:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:x^\top Qx\le1\}.\] Its Euclidean polar is the inverse-quadratic ellipsoid \[E_Q^\circ=E_{Q^{-1}}:=\{y\in\mathbb R^d:y^\top Q^{-1}y\le1\}.\] Equivalently, if \(E=T B_2\) for an invertible linear map \(T\), then \[E^\circ=T^{-\top}B_2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An origin-centered ellipsoid described by the positive-definite quadratic form \(Q\) has as its polar the ellipsoid described by the inverse quadratic form \(Q^{-1}\). In linear-image form, polarity replaces the invertible map \(T\) by its inverse transpose. Thus principal directions are preserved while squared semiaxis lengths are reciprocated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{x:x^\top Qx\le1\}^\circ=\{y:y^\top Q^{-1}y\le1\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Q=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)U^\top\), then the semiaxes of \(E_Q\) have lengths \(\lambda_i^{-1/2}\), while those of \(E_Q^\circ\) have lengths \(\lambda_i^{1/2}\).
The associated gauge is \(\gamma_{E_Q}(x)=\sqrt{x^\top Qx}\), and its polar gauge is \(\gamma_{E_Q}^\circ(y)=\sqrt{y^\top Q^{-1}y}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=I\), the Euclidean unit ball is self-polar.
For a diagonal \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(a_1^{-2},\ldots,a_d^{-2})\), the polar semiaxes are \(a_1^{-1},\ldots,a_d^{-1}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \((E_Q^\circ)^\circ=E_Q\).
The volume product is \(\operatorname{vol}(E_Q)\operatorname{vol}(E_Q^\circ)=\operatorname{vol}(B_2)^2\).
boundary_notes: Positive definiteness is essential for a bounded full-dimensional ellipsoid; singular positive-semidefinite forms produce unbounded cylinders.
A nonzero center introduces affine terms and is outside this centered formula.

children.title: Minkowski Gauge Theory
children.top_down_role: Positively homogeneous convex functionals generated by origin-anchored convex sets and their functional polars.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex with \(0\in C\). Adopt \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly asymmetric and extended-valued gauges generated by origin-containing convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski gauge of \(C\) is \[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^n.\] A gauge is equivalently a function \(k:\mathbb R^n\to[0,+\infty]\) that is convex, positively homogeneous, and satisfies \(k(0)=0\). Its functional polar is \[k^\circ(y):=\inf\{\mu\ge0:(\forall x)\ \langle x,y\rangle\le\mu k(x)\}.\] When \(k=\gamma_C\), one has \(k^\circ=\gamma_{C^\circ}\) and \(k^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski gauge measures the smallest nonnegative dilation of an origin-containing convex set needed to contain a point, with value infinity if no dilation contains it. Gauges are exactly nonnegative convex positively homogeneous functions vanishing at zero. Functional polarity assigns the smallest multiplier controlling the pairing by the gauge; for set-generated gauges it coincides with taking the gauge of the polar set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[k=\gamma_C\Longrightarrow k^\circ=\gamma_{C^\circ},\qquad k^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}k.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Positive homogeneity and convexity are equivalent to positive homogeneity and subadditivity: \(k(x+z)\le k(x)+k(z)\).
For finite definite \(k\), \(k^\circ(y)=\sup_{x\ne0}\langle x,y\rangle/k(x)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a cone, \(\gamma_C\) is the indicator of \(C\) with values \(0\) and \(+\infty\).
If \(C\) is a symmetric convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(\gamma_C\) is a norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar-gauge inequality is \(\langle x,y\rangle\le k(x)k^\circ(y)\) on the effective domains.
If \(C\) is closed, then \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\).
boundary_notes: A gauge need not be symmetric or definite and may take the value \(+\infty\).
Closure in \(k^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}k\) is epigraphical lower-semicontinuous closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Correspondence Between Closed Gauges and Unit Sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in \(\mathbb R^n\). Let \(\mathcal C_0\) be the class of nonempty closed convex sets containing \(0\), and let \(\mathcal G_{\mathrm{cl}}\) be the class of closed gauges.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed correspondence; without closedness, generating sets are not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the two maps \[C\in\mathcal C_0\longmapsto\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\},\] and \[k\in\mathcal G_{\mathrm{cl}}\longmapsto U_k:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:k(x)\le1\}.\] These maps are mutually inverse: \[U_{\gamma_C}=C\quad(C\in\mathcal C_0),\qquad \gamma_{U_k}=k\quad(k\in\mathcal G_{\mathrm{cl}}).\] Hence closed origin-containing convex sets and closed gauges encode the same objects in set and functional form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set containing the origin determines its gauge, and a closed gauge determines its unit sublevel set. These operations undo each other. The set therefore records all radial unit bounds of the function, while positive homogeneity reconstructs every other sublevel set by scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\le1\},\qquad k=\gamma_{\{x:k(x)\le1\}}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\alpha>0\), \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)\le\alpha\}=\alpha C\).
The epigraph is determined by the unit set: \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_C=\{(x,t):t\ge0,\ x\in tC\}\).
special_cases_latex: Symmetric closed bounded \(C\) with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\) correspond exactly to norms.
Closed convex cones correspond to indicator gauges taking only \(0\) and \(+\infty\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Set inclusion reverses pointwise gauge order: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\Rightarrow\gamma_{C_2}\le\gamma_{C_1}\).
The effective domain satisfies \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\operatorname{cone}C\).
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed generator \(C\), the unit sublevel set of \(\gamma_C\) can exceed \(C\); closedness restores exact recovery.
The correspondence allows asymmetric and unbounded generators, so it is broader than norm-unit-ball duality.

notation.meaning: Nonempty closed convex origin-containing subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Recovery from Its Unit Sublevel Set
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-valued positively homogeneous function is the Minkowski functional of its unit sublevel set, and every positive sublevel is the corresponding dilation of that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be positively homogeneous with \(p(0)=0\), and set
\[
B=\{x\in X:p(x)\le1\}.
\]
Then
\[
p=\gamma_B,
\qquad
\{x:p(x)\le r\}=rB\quad(r>0).
\]
If \(p\) is sublinear, then \(B\) is convex and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\gamma_{\{p\le1\}}\) and \(\{p\le r\}=r\{p\le1\}\) for every \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional reconstruction and positive-sublevel dilation for an extended-valued positively homogeneous function.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit Sublevel-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex absorbing set containing zero is recovered exactly as the unit sublevel set of its Minkowski gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\). Then \(C\) is exactly the unit sublevel set of its gauge: \(C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}\). More generally, without closedness one always has \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)<1\}\subseteq C\subseteq\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real topological vector space
\(C\subset X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery for closed convex absorbing gauge generators.

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge of the generating set

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge Unit Set and Homothetic Sublevels
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(k:\mathbb R^n\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge and define its unit set \(U:=\operatorname{lev}_{\le1}k=\{x:k(x)\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued gauges; exact closed-set recovery is asserted when \(k\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The unit sublevel-set geometry of \(k\) is the set \[U_k:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:k(x)\le1\}.\] It is convex and contains \(0\), and the gauge is recovered by \[k(x)=\gamma_{U_k}(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda U_k\}.\] For every \(\alpha>0\), positive homogeneity gives \[\{x:k(x)\le\alpha\}=\alpha U_k.\] If \(k\) is closed, then \(U_k\) is closed and is the unique closed convex origin-containing generator of \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit sublevel set contains the complete geometry of a gauge. Every positive sublevel set is a homothetic copy of it, and the gauge value of a point is the least scale at which the point enters that unit set. For a closed gauge, the unit set is the unique closed convex set containing the origin that generates the gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[k=\gamma_{U_k},\qquad \operatorname{lev}_{\le\alpha}k=\alpha U_k\quad(\alpha>0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(k(x)\le\alpha\Longleftrightarrow x\in\alpha U_k\) for \(\alpha>0\).
\(\operatorname{epi}k=\{(x,t):t\ge0,\ x\in tU_k\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(k\) is a norm, \(U_k\) is its symmetric closed unit ball.
If \(k=\delta_K\) for a convex cone \(K\), then \(U_k=K\) and every positive sublevel set equals \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Pointwise order becomes reverse unit-set inclusion: \(k_1\le k_2\Rightarrow U_{k_2}\subseteq U_{k_1}\).
Closedness of \(k\) is equivalent to closedness of its epigraph and entails closedness of every sublevel set.
boundary_notes: The zero sublevel set need not equal \(\{0\}\); it records degenerate zero directions.
Negative sublevel levels are empty because a gauge is nonnegative.

children.title: Radial Absorption Geometry
children.top_down_role: Raywise geometry determining gauge finiteness and domain.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex with \(0\in C\), and let \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda\ge0:x\in\lambda C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional raywise absorption for possibly nonabsorbing generators and extended-valued gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is absorbed by \(C\) when \[(\exists\lambda>0)\quad x\in\lambda C.\] The absorbed-direction set is therefore \[\operatorname{Abs}(C):=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C=\operatorname{cone}C.\] It is exactly the effective domain of the gauge: \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C:=\{x:\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\}=\operatorname{Abs}(C).\] The set \(C\) is absorbing in \(\mathbb R^n\) precisely when \(\operatorname{Abs}(C)=\mathbb R^n\), equivalently when \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is absorbed by an origin-containing convex set if some positive dilation of the set contains the direction. All absorbed directions form the conic hull of the set, and this cone is exactly the finite-valued domain of the Minkowski gauge. Thus failure of radial absorption is represented functionally by infinite gauge values outside the absorbed cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C=\operatorname{cone}C,\qquad C\text{ absorbing}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\mathbb R^n.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\Longleftrightarrow(\exists\lambda>0)\ \lambda^{-1}x\in C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Scaling Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Minkowski functional scales linearly along every positive ray, with infinity retained on directions never absorbed by the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), define \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\). For every \(x\in X\) and \(\lambda>0\), the equivalence \(\lambda x\in tC\iff x\in(t/\lambda)C\) yields \(\gamma_C(\lambda x)=\lambda\gamma_C(x)\). Thus each positive ray is parameterized linearly by the gauge, including infinite-valued directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(\lambda x)=\lambda\gamma_C(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(\lambda>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Absorbing-Set Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set absorbs every vector exactly when its Minkowski functional is finite everywhere; otherwise the gauge is infinite in at least one direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is absorbing precisely when \(\forall x\in X\ \exists t>0\) such that \(x\in tC\). For \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\) with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), this is equivalent to \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=X\), or explicitly \(\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is absorbing}\iff\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\ \forall x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic absorption characterized by gauge finiteness.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Absorption
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is absorbed when some positive dilation of the set contains it. Absorbed directions form the generated cone and exactly equal the gauge's finite domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The direction \(u\in X\) is absorbed by \(C\) if there exists \(t>0\) such that \(u\in tC\). The directional absorption set is
\[
D_C:=\bigcup_{t>0}tC.
\]
Because \(C\) is convex and contains \(0\), this union is the convex cone generated by \(C\). Moreover,
\[
u\in D_C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma_C(u)<+\infty,
\]
so \(D_C=\operatorname{cone}(C)=\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_C=\operatorname{cone}(C)=\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional absorption is identified with the effective domain of an extended-valued gauge.

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge of C, with the infimum of the empty set equal to positive infinity.
Set of directions absorbed by positive dilations of C.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Membership Does Not Determine Gauge Finiteness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same planar boundary direction has zero gauge for a closed absorption cone and infinite gauge for an open-sided absorption cone, so boundary membership alone is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1=\mathbb R_+^2\) and \(C_2=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\cup\{0\}\). Both are convex cones and hence \(D_{C_i}=C_i\). For \(u=(1,0)\),
\[
u\in\partial D_{C_1}\cap D_{C_1},\qquad \gamma_{C_1}(u)=0,
\]
whereas
\[
u\in\partial D_{C_2}\setminus D_{C_2},\qquad \gamma_{C_2}(u)=+\infty.
\]
Thus membership in \(\partial D_C\) alone determines neither finiteness nor infiniteness of \(\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\in\partial D_{C_1}\cap D_{C_1},\ \gamma_{C_1}(u)=0,\qquad u\in\partial D_{C_2}\setminus D_{C_2},\ \gamma_{C_2}(u)=+\infty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired planar convex cones realize both possible gauge behaviors at a boundary direction.

notation.meaning: Boundary direction used in both examples.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonabsorbing Direction Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued behavior outside the absorbed-direction cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) contain \(0\) and let \(D_C=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C\). If \(u\notin D_C\), then no positive multiple of \(u\) is absorbed: for every \(t>0\), \[\gamma_C(tu)=+\infty.\] Equivalently, the radial reach \(\rho_C(u)=\sup\{r\ge0:ru\in C\}\) equals \(0\). Hence the complement of \(D_C\) is the exact directional failure region for finite gauge values; when \(D_C\ne X\), the gauge cannot be finite-valued on all of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside the cone of absorbed directions, every positive point on the ray has infinite gauge and zero radial reach.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(0\in C\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(tu)=+\infty\) for every \(t>0\), and \(\rho_C(u)=0\).

notation.meaning: Cone-like region reached by positive dilations of C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocity of Radial Size and Gauge Value
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex with \(0\in C\). For \(u\ne0\), define the radial size \(\rho_C(u):=\sup\{t\ge0:tu\in C\}\), allowing values in \([0,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raywise extended-value reciprocity; the most direct formula applies when the intersection of \(C\) with the ray is radially closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a direction \(u\ne0\), radial-gauge reciprocity is the extended-real relation \[\gamma_C(u)=\rho_C(u)^{-1},\] with conventions \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\), whenever the ray section \(\{t\ge0:tu\in C\}\) is closed at its supremum. More generally, for every \(t>0\), \[\gamma_C(tu)=t\gamma_C(u)=\frac{t}{\rho_C(u)}.\] Equivalently, \(tu\in C\) exactly when \(t\le\rho_C(u)\), while \(tu\in\lambda C\) exactly when \(t\le\lambda\rho_C(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial function measures how far the generating set extends along a ray, while the gauge measures the dilation needed to reach a point on that ray. These quantities are reciprocal: an absent ray gives radial size zero and infinite gauge, an unbounded ray gives infinite radial size and zero gauge, and a finite positive radial size gives its ordinary reciprocal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\rho_C(u)=\frac{1}{\gamma_C(u)},\qquad \gamma_C(tu)=\frac{t}{\rho_C(u)}\quad(t>0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\rho_C(u)=\sup\{t\ge0:\gamma_C(tu)\le1\}\).
For \(\gamma_C(u)\in(0,+\infty)\), the normalized point \(u/\gamma_C(u)\) lies on the radial boundary of a raywise closed \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a convex body with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(0<\rho_C(u)<+\infty\) and \(0<\gamma_C(u)<+\infty\) for every \(u\ne0\).
If the entire ray \(\mathbb R_+u\) lies in \(C\), then \(\rho_C(u)=+\infty\) and \(\gamma_C(u)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Gauge sublevel geometry and radial boundary data determine each other ray by ray.
Positive homogeneity reduces evaluation on a ray to one directional value.
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is not closed along a ray, the supremal radial endpoint need not belong to \(C\); closure qualifications are then necessary for endpoint membership.
The radial function here is direction-dependent and is not the recession function of a convex function.

notation.meaning: Maximum extended radial scale of \(C\) in direction \(u\).

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Supremum Does Not Recover a Non-Star-Shaped Ray Section
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the two-point set {0,2u}, radial reach equals 2 although all intermediate positive points are missing, so star-shapedness is necessary for interval recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(u\neq0\) and let \(C=\{0,2u\}\). Then \(0\in C\) and \(\rho_C(u)=2\), but
\[
S_C(u)=\{0,2\}\neq[0,2]\quad\text{and}\quad[0,2)\nsubseteq S_C(u).
\]
Thus the radial supremum alone does not recover ray membership unless an interval-producing assumption such as star-shapedness is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_C(u)=2\quad\text{but}\quad S_C(u)=\{0,2\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of interval recovery when star-shapedness is absent.

notation.meaning: Radial parameter set in direction u.
Supremum of the radial parameter set.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Sections and Inverse Homogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a set star-shaped about zero, each ray section is an interval determined by its radial value, possibly excluding its finite endpoint; rescaling the direction inversely rescales radial reach.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in X\), define \(S_C(u):=\{r\geq0:ru\in C\}\). If \(C\) is star-shaped with respect to \(0\), then \(S_C(u)\) is an interval containing \(0\), and
\[
[0,\rho_C(u))\subseteq S_C(u)\subseteq[0,\rho_C(u)].
\]
When \(\rho_C(u)<+\infty\), the right endpoint belongs to \(S_C(u)\) exactly when \(\rho_C(u)u\in C\). Moreover, for every \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\rho_C(\lambda u)=\lambda^{-1}\rho_C(u),
\]
and \(\rho_C(0)=+\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is star-shaped with respect to \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [0,\rho_C(u))\subseteq S_C(u)\subseteq[0,\rho_C(u)],\qquad \rho_C(\lambda u)=\lambda^{-1}\rho_C(u)\quad(\lambda>0).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ray-section structure for sets star-shaped with respect to the origin, including the endpoint-attainment distinction.

notation.meaning: Radial section of C in direction u.
Radial reach of C in direction u.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended radial reach of a set from the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) contain \(0\), where \(X\) is a real vector space. The radial function of \(C\) is the extended-valued map \(\rho_C:X\to[0,+\infty]\) defined by \[\rho_C(u)=\sup\{r\ge0:ru\in C\}.\] The conventions are \(\sup\{0\}=0\) and \(\sup[0,+\infty)=+\infty\). If \(C\) is star-shaped about \(0\), its intersection with the ray generated by \(u\) is determined, up to possible endpoint inclusion, by \(0\le r<\rho_C(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial function assigns to each vector u the supremum of the nonnegative scalars r for which ru belongs to the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_C(u)=\sup\{r\ge0:ru\in C\}\).

notation.meaning: A direction vector, not necessarily normalized.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial Sections and Directional Homogeneity
Gauge Ray Profiles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along each ray, the gauge scales linearly with positive radius; a nonabsorbed direction has an identically infinite positive-radius profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a fixed \(u\in X\), define \(g_u(r):=\gamma_C(ru)\) for \(r>0\). Positive homogeneity gives
\[
g_u(r)=r\gamma_C(u),\qquad r>0.
\]
This equality is interpreted in \([0,+\infty]\), with \(r(+\infty)=+\infty\) for \(r>0\). Thus the profile is linear when \(\gamma_C(u)<+\infty\) and identically infinite on positive radii when \(\gamma_C(u)=+\infty\). Moreover, \(\gamma_C(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(ru)=r\gamma_C(u)\) for every \(u\in X\) and \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive homogeneity determines every gauge profile along a fixed ray.

notation.meaning: Gauge profile along the ray generated by u.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity-Free Radial–Minkowski Reciprocity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radial reach and the Minkowski functional are extended reciprocals for any set containing zero; convexity, closedness, and star-shapedness are unnecessary for this identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq X\) contain \(0\), and define
\[
\gamma_C(u):=\inf\{t>0:u\in tC\},\qquad
\rho_C(u):=\sup\{r\geq0:ru\in C\}.
\]
Then for every \(u\in X\),
\[
\rho_C(u)=\frac1{\gamma_C(u)},
\]
with \(1/0:=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty):=0\). No convexity, closedness, or star-shapedness assumption on \(C\) is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_C(u)=1/\gamma_C(u)\quad\text{for all }u\in X.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp-assumption variant: reciprocal conversion is set-theoretic and does not require convexity or star-shapedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Radial–Gauge Reciprocity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise reciprocal relation with extended-value conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) contain \(0\). Define \(\gamma_C(u)=\inf\{\lambda>0:u\in\lambda C\}\) and \(\rho_C(u)=\sup\{r\ge0:ru\in C\}\). Then for every nonzero \(u\in X\), \[\gamma_C(u)=\frac{1}{\rho_C(u)},\qquad \rho_C(u)=\frac{1}{\gamma_C(u)},\] using the extended conventions \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\). The identity follows from the reciprocal correspondence between feasible scales \(u\in\lambda C\) and feasible radii \(\lambda^{-1}u\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In every nonzero direction, radial reach and the Minkowski gauge are reciprocals, including the zero and infinity cases.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(0\in C\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(u)=1/\rho_C(u)\) and \(\rho_C(u)=1/\gamma_C(u)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Is Essential for the Recession-Cone Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of the nonnegative horizontal ray and the point e2 has zero gauge and infinite radial reach in direction e1, but e1 is not a recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_+e_1\cup\{e_2\}\bigr)\subset\mathbb{R}^2.
\]
Then \(C\) is convex, contains \(0\), and is not closed. Since \(te_1\in C\) for every \(t\ge0\),
\[
\rho_C(e_1)=+\infty,\qquad \gamma_C(e_1)=0.
\]
Nevertheless \(e_1\notin\operatorname{rec}C\): one has \(e_2\in C\), but \(e_2+e_1\notin C\).
assumptions_latex: \(e_1,e_2\) are the standard basis vectors of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(e_1)=0\), \(\rho_C(e_1)=+\infty\), and \(e_1\notin\operatorname{rec}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonclosed convex generator can have an unbounded radial direction that is not a recession direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero–Infinite Reciprocity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate endpoints of radial–gauge reciprocity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under radial–gauge reciprocity, the two degenerate directional regimes are exact opposites. For every nonzero \(u\in X\), \[\rho_C(u)=0\iff\gamma_C(u)=+\infty,\qquad \rho_C(u)=+\infty\iff\gamma_C(u)=0.\] The first regime means that no positive point on the ray belongs to \(C\); the second means that points of \(C\) occur arbitrarily far along the ray. These equivalences use \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero radial reach corresponds to infinite gauge, while unbounded radial reach corresponds to zero gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(0\in C\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_C(u)=0\iff\gamma_C(u)=+\infty\) and \(\rho_C(u)=+\infty\iff\gamma_C(u)=0\).

children.title: Gauge-Generator Closedness Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Closedness correspondence between gauges and their generating unit sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex with \(0\in C\), and let \(\gamma_C\) be its Minkowski gauge. Let \(k\) be an arbitrary gauge with unit set \(U_k=\{x:k(x)\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-semicontinuous closedness and closed convex generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge-generator closedness correspondence consists of the implications \[C\text{ closed}\Longrightarrow\gamma_C\text{ closed and }\{x:\gamma_C(x)\le1\}=C,\] and \[k\text{ closed}\Longrightarrow U_k\text{ closed},\quad k=\gamma_{U_k}.\] Consequently, the mutually inverse assignments \(C\mapsto\gamma_C\) and \(k\mapsto U_k\) restrict to a bijection between nonempty closed convex sets containing \(0\) and closed gauges. For every \(\alpha>0\), \[\operatorname{lev}_{\le\alpha}\gamma_C=\alpha C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness is preserved across the set–gauge correspondence. A closed convex origin-containing generator has a closed gauge whose unit sublevel set is exactly the generator. Conversely, a closed gauge has a closed unit set and is precisely the gauge generated by that set. All positive sublevel sets are closed dilations of the unit generator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C\text{ closed}\Longleftrightarrow\gamma_C\text{ is closed when }C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{lev}_{\le\alpha}\gamma_C=\alpha C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Closedness of a gauge means lower semicontinuity, equivalently that \(\operatorname{epi}k\) is closed.
For a gauge \(k\), \(\operatorname{cl}k=\gamma_{\operatorname{cl}U_k}\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed convex cone \(K\), its indicator gauge \(\delta_K\) is closed.
For a norm, closedness is automatic because every finite convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is continuous.
immediate_consequences_latex: A closed gauge has a unique closed convex origin-containing generator.
If two closed generators have the same gauge, then the generators are equal.
boundary_notes: A nonclosed generating set need not be recovered exactly from the unit sublevel set of its gauge.
The correspondence is stated in finite dimensions; in general topological vector spaces the relevant lower-semicontinuity topology must be specified.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Gauge Functionals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is closed when its epigraph is closed, equivalently when it is lower semicontinuous or all its sublevel sets are closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge functional \(p\) is closed if its epigraph
\[
\operatorname{epi}p:=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:p(x)\leq r\}
\]
is closed in \(X\times\mathbb R\). Equivalently, \(p\) is lower semicontinuous, or every sublevel set
\[
\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\alpha}p:=\{x\in X:p(x)\leq\alpha\}
\]
is closed for \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). For a gauge, positive homogeneity reduces the nonnegative sublevels to scaled copies of its unit sublevel.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is closed exactly when it is lower semicontinuous, equivalently when every set \(\{x:p(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness is taken in the epigraphical, equivalently lower-semicontinuous, sense.

notation.meaning: Sublevel set of p at height alpha.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Generators
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex generator is a closed convex set containing the origin, viewed as the unit set that generates its Minkowski gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed convex generator is a set \(C\subseteq X\) that is closed, convex, and contains \(0\). It generates the extended Minkowski gauge
\[
\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\},
\]
where \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\). Convexity and origin containment make \(\gamma_C\) sublinear. Closedness makes \(C\) recoverable as the unit sublevel of \(\gamma_C\) and makes \(\gamma_C\) lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A closed convex generator is a closed convex set \(C\subseteq X\) satisfying \(0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator means the unit set from which an extended Minkowski gauge is formed.

notation.meaning: Closed convex generator containing the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Sublevel Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex generator equals its gauge's unit sublevel; conversely, a lower-semicontinuous sublinear functional is recovered as the gauge of its unit sublevel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The generator is exactly the unit sublevel of its Minkowski gauge:
\[
C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}.
\]
Conversely, if \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a lower-semicontinuous sublinear functional and \(C_p:=\{x\in X:p(x)\leq1\}\), then \(C_p\) is closed, convex, contains \(0\), and
\[
\gamma_{C_p}=p.
\]
Thus closed convex generators and closed extended-valued gauges are mutually recoverable through gauge formation and the unit-sublevel operation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff topological real vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery for closed convex generators, including nonabsorbing directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Closure Can Change an Extended Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonabsorbing convex generator, topological closure can change the gauge: closing the upper open half-plane together with the origin changes missing horizontal directions from infinite gauge to zero gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v>0\}\). Then \(C\) is convex, contains the origin, and \(\overline C=\{(u,v):v\geq0\}\). Moreover, \[\gamma_C(u,v)=\begin{cases}0,&v>0\text{ or }(u,v)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&v<0\text{ or }(v=0,\ u\ne0),\end{cases}\] whereas \[\gamma_{\overline C}(u,v)=\begin{cases}0,&v\geq0,\\+\infty,&v<0.\end{cases}\] Hence \(\gamma_C\ne\gamma_{\overline C}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u\ne0\), \(\gamma_C(u,0)=+\infty\) but \(\gamma_{\overline C}(u,0)=0\), so \(\gamma_C\ne\gamma_{\overline C}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonabsorbing two-dimensional example showing that replacing a convex generator by its topological closure need not preserve its gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Generator Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of exact unit-sublevel recovery when generator closedness is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closedness cannot be omitted from exact generator recovery. Take \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(C=(-1,1)\). The set \(C\) is convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\), but is not closed. Its Minkowski gauge is \(\gamma_C(x)=|x|\), so \[\{x\in\mathbb R:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}=[-1,1]\neq C.\] Hence the gauge does not distinguish this open generator from its closure; boundary points lost from \(C\) reappear in the unit sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open convex generator and its closure can induce the same gauge, so the gauge's unit sublevel need not recover a nonclosed generator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C=|\cdot|\quad\text{and}\quad\{\gamma_C\leq1\}=[-1,1]\neq C.\)

children.title: Gauge Geometry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Gauge classes distinguished by symmetry, definiteness, domain, and representational structure.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(k:\mathbb R^n\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge, let \(U_k=\{x:k(x)\le1\}\), let \(D_k=\operatorname{dom}k\), and let \(Z_k=\{x:k(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional classification by domain, symmetry, definiteness, and generator structure; the regimes may overlap unless explicitly incompatible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The principal gauge geometry regimes are defined by the following predicates: \[\begin{aligned} &\text{finite: }D_k=\mathbb R^n;\qquad \text{definite: }Z_k=\{0\};\\ &\text{symmetric: }k(-x)=k(x)\ (\forall x);\qquad \text{closed: }\operatorname{epi}k\text{ is closed};\\ &\text{polyhedral: }U_k\text{ is polyhedral}.\end{aligned}\] A finite, definite, symmetric gauge is a norm. An asymmetric gauge fails symmetry; a lineality-degenerate gauge has \(Z_k\ne\{0\}\); and a nonabsorbing gauge has \(D_k\ne\mathbb R^n\) and therefore takes \(+\infty\) outside its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge regimes are distinguished by four independent geometric questions: whether every direction is absorbed, whether nonzero zero-cost directions exist, whether opposite directions have equal cost, and whether the gauge is closed. Additional representational structure, such as polyhedrality, is read from the unit set. The norm regime occurs when the gauge is finite, symmetric, and definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[k\text{ is a norm}\Longleftrightarrow D_k=\mathbb R^n,\ Z_k=\{0\},\ k(-x)=k(x)\ (\forall x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Finiteness is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{int}U_k\) for a closed gauge.
Definiteness is equivalent to the unit generator containing no nonzero ray when the generator is closed and convex.
special_cases_latex: A norm belongs simultaneously to the finite, definite, symmetric, and closed regimes.
An indicator of a proper closed convex cone is closed but generally nonfinite and highly degenerate on its domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: Symmetry of \(k\) is equivalent to central symmetry of \(U_k\).
Polyhedrality of \(U_k\) yields a polyhedral gauge.
boundary_notes: Asymmetry does not imply degeneracy or nonfiniteness.
A regime label does not by itself assert differentiability, strict convexity, or smoothness.

children.title: Norm-Generating Gauge Regime
children.top_down_role: The balanced, absorbing, and definite regime.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\), and let \(\gamma_C\) be its gauge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm regime characterized simultaneously in functional and generating-set language.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generator \(C\) is in the norm-generating regime when it is centrally symmetric, bounded, and absorbing, equivalently \[C=-C,\qquad C\text{ bounded},\qquad 0\in\operatorname{int}C.\] In that case \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere, symmetric, and positive away from the origin, hence is a norm. Conversely, every norm \(\|\cdot\|\) has the unique unit ball \[C=\{x:\|x\|\le1\},\] which is closed, bounded, convex, centrally symmetric, contains \(0\) in its interior, and satisfies \(\gamma_C=\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set generates a norm exactly when it is a centrally symmetric convex body centered at the origin. Interior inclusion supplies finiteness in every direction, boundedness excludes nonzero zero-cost rays, and central symmetry supplies absolute homogeneity. Every norm is recovered from its closed unit ball in this way.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\gamma_C\text{ is a norm}\Longleftrightarrow C=-C,\ C\text{ is bounded},\ 0\in\operatorname{int}C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Functionally, \(\gamma_C(x)>0\) for \(x\ne0\), \(\gamma_C(x+z)\le\gamma_C(x)+\gamma_C(z)\), and \(\gamma_C(\lambda x)=|\lambda|\gamma_C(x)\).
Geometrically, \(C\) is a centrally symmetric convex body whose center is the origin.
special_cases_latex: For \(C=B_2\), \(\gamma_C\) is the Euclidean norm.
For \(C=[-1,1]^n\), \(\gamma_C=\|\cdot\|_\infty\); for the cross-polytope, \(\gamma_C=\|\cdot\|_1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar \(C^\circ\) is also norm-generating and its gauge is the dual norm.
The norm topology agrees with the Euclidean topology in finite dimensions.
boundary_notes: Dropping symmetry yields an asymmetric gauge, not a norm.
Dropping boundedness permits nonzero directions with zero gauge; dropping interior inclusion permits infinite values.

notation.meaning: Central symmetry of the generator about the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Generating Unit-Set Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Finite Gauges Are Seminorms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite symmetric gauge is a seminorm. Its zero set is a linear subspace, and the induced functional on the quotient by that subspace is a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(p:X\to[0,\infty)\) be a finite gauge. If \(p(-x)=p(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(p(\alpha x)=|\alpha|p(x)\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), so \(p\) is a seminorm. Its null set \(N=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}\) is a linear subspace, and \(\bar p(x+N):=p(x)\) is a norm on \(X/N\).
assumptions_latex: \(p:X\to[0,\infty)\) is finite, subadditive, and positively homogeneous for nonnegative scalars.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is a seminorm, \(N=\{p=0\}\) is a linear subspace, and \(\bar p\) is a norm on \(X/N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic functional consequences of evenness for finite real gauges; definiteness is not assumed.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is symmetric when it is even. This is equivalent to central symmetry of its unit sublevel or generating set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge \(p\) is symmetric if
\[
p(-x)=p(x)
\]
for every \(x\in X\). Its unit sublevel \(C_p:=\{x\in X:p(x)\leq1\}\) is then centrally symmetric, meaning \(C_p=-C_p\). Conversely, if \(C\subseteq X\) contains \(0\) and satisfies \(C=-C\), then its Minkowski gauge satisfies \(\gamma_C(-x)=\gamma_C(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is symmetric exactly when \(p(-x)=p(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evenness of a gauge and central symmetry of its unit generator.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Generator Characterization of Definiteness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex generator in finite dimensions, its gauge is definite exactly when the generator is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\). Then \[\gamma_C\text{ is definite}\iff\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\iff C\text{ is bounded}.\] No absorption or central-symmetry assumption is required.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C\text{ is definite}\iff C\text{ is bounded}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional gauges generated by nonempty closed convex sets containing the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Definiteness–Polar Finiteness Equivalence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed finite-dimensional gauge is definite exactly when its polar gauge is finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a proper lower-semicontinuous gauge on a finite-dimensional space, and let \(p^\circ\) be its polar gauge. Then \[p\text{ is definite}\iff p^\circ(y)<+\infty\quad\text{for every }y\in X^*.\] Equivalently, definiteness of \(p\) is dual to global finiteness of its polar gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:p(x)=0\}=\{0\}\iff\operatorname{dom}p^\circ=X^*.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper lower-semicontinuous gauges and their polar gauges.

knowledge_statements.title: Definite Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is definite when only the zero vector has gauge zero. For a closed convex generator this means that its recession cone is trivial, but definiteness alone does not ensure a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge \(p\) is definite if
\[
Z(p):=\{x\in X:p(x)=0\}=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(p(x)>0\) for every nonzero \(x\in X\), where \(+\infty>0\). If \(p=\gamma_C\) for a closed convex generator \(C\), definiteness is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.
\]
Definiteness alone does not make \(p\) a norm: finiteness on all of \(X\) and symmetry are also required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is definite exactly when \(p(x)=0\Rightarrow x=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definiteness excludes nonzero directions having zero gauge.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.title: Norm Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed, bounded, symmetric convex body containing zero in its interior generates a norm, and the body is exactly that norm's unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(C\subset X\) be closed, convex, bounded, centrally symmetric, with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Define \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\). Then \(\gamma_C\) is finite, subadditive, absolutely homogeneous, and positive definite; hence it is a norm on \(X\). Moreover, \(C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)\leq 1\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subset X\) is closed, convex, bounded, centrally symmetric, and satisfies \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C\) is a norm on \(X\), and its closed unit ball is \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization of convex bodies whose Minkowski gauges are norms.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical norm-unit-ball characterization for Minkowski gauges

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically precise and correctly classified, but no inspectable source supports the norm and unit-ball characterization.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry–Definiteness Interaction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evenness upgrades positive homogeneity to absolute homogeneity; definiteness then turns a finite sublinear gauge into a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(q:X\to[0,\infty)\) be subadditive and positively homogeneous for nonnegative scalars. If \(q(-x)=q(x)\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(q(\alpha x)=|\alpha|q(x)\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). If additionally \(q(x)=0\) implies \(x=0\), the resulting absolutely homogeneous sublinear functional satisfies all norm axioms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\) is a norm; symmetry supplies absolute homogeneity, while definiteness separates points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical decomposition of the extra properties turning a finite sublinear gauge into a norm.

notation.meaning: scalar field of the real vector space

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Regime Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Asymmetry breaks evenness, recession directions break definiteness, and nonabsorption forces infinite gauge values; each failure already occurs on the real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C_1=[-1,2]\subset\mathbb R\), the gauge is finite and positive definite but satisfies \(\gamma_{C_1}(1)=1/2\neq1=\gamma_{C_1}(-1)\). For \(C_2=\mathbb R\), one has \(\gamma_{C_2}(x)=0\) for every \(x\), so definiteness fails. For \(C_3=[0,1]\), one has \(\gamma_{C_3}(x)=x\) when \(x\geq0\) and \(\gamma_{C_3}(x)=+\infty\) when \(x<0\), so finiteness fails.
assumptions_latex: Each displayed generator is convex and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dropping symmetry, boundedness, or absorption can respectively destroy evenness, definiteness, or finiteness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional failures at the boundary of the norm-generating hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge of C, with empty infimum equal to infinity

children.title: Asymmetric Gauges
children.top_down_role: Directional size models without central symmetry.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Genuine Asymmetry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different positive slopes on the two half-lines produce a finite definite gauge that is not symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,b>0\) with \(a\neq b\), \[q(t)=a\max\{t,0\}+b\max\{-t,0\}\] is a finite positive-definite gauge. Since \(q(1)=a\neq b=q(-1)\), it is not a norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\) is a finite definite asymmetric gauge but not a norm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example separating finite definite asymmetric gauges from norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward and Reverse Symmetrizations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum and sum of the forward and reverse gauges are equivalent symmetric norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite, subadditive, positively homogeneous, positive-definite \(q\), define \[q_{\max}(x)=\max\{q(x),q(-x)\},\qquad q_{\Sigma}(x)=q(x)+q(-x).\] Both are norms and satisfy \(q_{\max}\leq q_{\Sigma}\leq2q_{\max}\).
assumptions_latex: \(q:X\to[0,\infty)\) is finite, subadditive, positively homogeneous, and positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_{\max}\) and \(q_{\Sigma}\) are norms satisfying \(q_{\max}\leq q_{\Sigma}\leq2q_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical norm-valued symmetrizations of a finite definite asymmetric gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Gauges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional gauge functionals lacking central symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An asymmetric gauge on a real vector space \(X\) is a gauge \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) for which there exists \(x\in X\) such that \(p(-x)\neq p(x)\). Equivalently, its unit sublevel set \(B_p=\{x\in X:p(x)\leq1\}\) is not centrally symmetric. Such a gauge retains positive homogeneity and subadditivity but generally measures the two directions \(x\) and \(-x\) differently; even when finite and definite, it is not a norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymmetric gauge assigns different sizes to some pair of opposite directions, equivalently having a non-centrally-symmetric unit set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\text{ is asymmetric}\iff\exists x\in X:\ p(-x)\neq p(x)\iff B_p\neq-B_p.\)

children.title: Lineality-Degenerate Gauge Regimes
children.top_down_role: Gauges with nontrivial zero directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(0\in C\), and let \(k=\gamma_C\). Denote the recession cone of \(C\) by \(0^+C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed finite-dimensional gauges; zero directions may form a cone that is not a linear subspace unless symmetry is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero cone of \(k\) is \[Z(k):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:k(x)=0\}.\] For a closed generator, \[Z(k)=0^+C.\] The gauge is lineality-degenerate when \(Z(k)\ne\{0\}\), equivalently when \(C\) contains a nonzero recession direction. Its two-sided lineality subspace is \[L(k):=Z(k)\cap(-Z(k))=(0^+C)\cap(-0^+C).\] Along every \(z\in L(k)\), one has \(k(x+z)=k(x)\) whenever both sides are interpreted on the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed gauge is degenerate when it assigns zero to a nonzero direction. The complete cone of such directions is the recession cone of its unit generator. Directions that occur together with their negatives form the lineality subspace; translation along this subspace leaves the gauge unchanged. For asymmetric gauges, the zero cone may be one-sided and therefore need not itself be a subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Z(\gamma_C)=\{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=0^+C,\qquad L(\gamma_C)=0^+C\cap(-0^+C).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(z\in Z(k)\Longleftrightarrow k(tz)=0\) for every \(t\ge0\).
For a symmetric gauge, \(Z(k)=L(k)\) is a linear subspace.
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is bounded, then \(0^+C=\{0\}\), so the gauge is definite.
If \(C=K\) is a closed convex cone, then \(k=\delta_K\) and \(Z(k)=K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A norm has no nonzero zero directions.
Quotienting a symmetric finite gauge by its zero subspace yields a definite gauge on the quotient space.
boundary_notes: The term lineality-degenerate should not obscure one-sided degeneracy: \(Z(k)\) may strictly contain \(L(k)\).
Zero directions concern unboundedness of the generator, whereas infinite values concern failure of absorption.

notation.meaning: Two-sided lineality subspace of the zero cone.

source_refs.locator: Corollary 9.7.1; §8, definition of recession cone and Theorem 8.4

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Cone Degeneracy of a Gauge

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Representation and Kernel Annihilation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional seminorm is the support function of a polar unit ball whose functionals annihilate the kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[B_p^\circ=\{u\in X^*:\langle u,x\rangle\leq1\text{ whenever }p(x)\leq1\}.\] Then \[p(x)=\sup_{u\in B_p^\circ}\langle u,x\rangle,\qquad B_p^\circ\subseteq(\ker p)^\perp.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\sigma_{B_p^\circ}\) and \(B_p^\circ\subseteq(\ker p)^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional dual representation of a seminorm and its kernel relation.

notation.meaning: polar of the seminorm unit ball

knowledge_statements.title: Seminorms as Gauges of Balanced Unit Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite seminorms are exactly gauges of convex absorbing balanced sets, with exact unit-set recovery under radial closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a seminorm \(p\), its unit set \(B_p=\{x:p(x)\leq1\}\) is convex, absorbing, and balanced, and \(p=\gamma_{B_p}\). Conversely, the gauge of a convex absorbing balanced set containing \(0\) is a finite seminorm. If the generator is radially closed, it equals \(\{x:\gamma_B(x)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\gamma_{B_p}\), and convex absorbing balanced generators yield finite seminorms.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact generator correspondence for finite seminorm gauges.

notation.meaning: unit sublevel set of the seminorm

knowledge_statements.title: Seminorm Gauges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of seminorms as gauges of closed, convex, balanced, absorbing sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be closed, convex, balanced, absorbing, and contain \(0\). Its Minkowski gauge is \[\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}.\] Then \(\gamma_C\) is a finite-valued seminorm and \(C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq 1\}\). Conversely, for every seminorm \(p:X\to[0,\infty)\), its closed unit ball \(C_p:=\{x:p(x)\leq1\}\) has these properties and \(p=\gamma_{C_p}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convex balanced absorbing sets are precisely seminorm unit balls, and their Minkowski gauges recover the corresponding seminorms.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\) is closed, convex, balanced, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C\) is a seminorm with unit ball \(C\), and every seminorm arises this way.

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of the seminorm p

source_refs.locator: 1. Polarity in Euclidean Space p. 143

source_witnesses.locator: 1. Polarity in Euclidean Space p. 143

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Sided Kernel of a General Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge lineality is the two-sided zero kernel and the maximal translation-invariance subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite sublinear gauge \(q\), define \[L_q=\{\ell:q(\ell)=q(-\ell)=0\}.\] Then \(L_q\) is a vector subspace, \(q(x+\ell)=q(x)\) for all \(x\) and \(\ell\in L_q\), and every translation-invariance subspace is contained in \(L_q\). If \(q\) is even, then \(L_q=\ker q\).
assumptions_latex: \(q:X\to[0,\infty)\) is finite, subadditive, and positively homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_q\) is the maximal subspace satisfying \(q(x+\ell)=q(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation lineality for a possibly asymmetric finite gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Lineality Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the null space of a seminorm gauge with the generator's lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be closed, convex, balanced, absorbing, and contain \(0\), and let \(\gamma_C\) be its Minkowski gauge. Define \(L:=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)=0\}\). Then \(L\) is a linear subspace, \(C+L=C\), and \(\gamma_C(x+\ell)=\gamma_C(x)\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(\ell\in L\). Moreover, \[L=\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{d\in X:C+td\subseteq C\text{ for every }t\geq0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed, convex, balanced, absorbing generator in a finite-dimensional real vector space, the zero directions of its gauge equal its recession, hence lineality, space; translations along those directions preserve both the generator and the gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is closed, convex, balanced, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker\gamma_C=\operatorname{rec}(C)=L\), \(C+L=C\), and \(\gamma_C(x+\ell)=\gamma_C(x)\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(\ell\in L\).

notation.meaning: gauge null space and lineality space of C

source_refs.locator: 3.6 Lineality Space and Recession Cone p. 97

source_witnesses.locator: 3.6 Lineality Space and Recession Cone p. 97

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient-Space Norm Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring a seminormed space by the seminorm's kernel produces a well-defined norm on the quotient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) be a seminorm on a real vector space \(X\), let \(L=\ker p\), and write elements of the quotient as \(x+L\). The formula \(\bar p(x+L)=p(x)\) is independent of the representative because \(p(x+\ell)=p(x)\) for \(\ell\in L\). The function \(\bar p:X/L\to[0,\infty)\) is subadditive, absolutely homogeneous, and satisfies \(\bar p(x+L)=0\) only when \(x+L=L\); hence \(\bar p\) is a norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formula \(\bar p(x+L)=p(x)\) defines a norm on \(X/L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic quotient construction; no completeness assertion is included.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical descent of a seminorm to its kernel quotient
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The quotient construction is correct, makes no unwarranted completeness claim, and reasonably fits representation, but it lacks a cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: A Zero Cone Need Not Be a Lineality Space
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymmetric gauge can vanish on a one-sided ray rather than a lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite sublinear gauge \(q(t)=\max\{t,0\}\) satisfies \[\{t:q(t)=0\}=(-\infty,0].\] It is nondefinite, but its zero set is a proper convex cone rather than a vector subspace.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Valued Gauge of a Nonabsorbing Generator
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex with \(0\in C\), and define \(k=\gamma_C\) using \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional generators that do not absorb the entire ambient space; gauges are allowed to be proper extended-real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generator \(C\) is nonabsorbing when \[\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C\ne\mathbb R^n.\] Its gauge is then extended-valued with effective domain \[\operatorname{dom}k=\{x:k(x)<+\infty\}=\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda C=\operatorname{cone}C\subsetneq\mathbb R^n,\] and \[k(x)=+\infty\qquad(x\notin\operatorname{cone}C).\] Conversely, \(k\) is finite everywhere if and only if \(C\) is absorbing; for convex \(C\) in finite dimensions this is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonabsorbing generator misses at least one ambient direction under every finite positive dilation. Its Minkowski gauge therefore takes the value infinity in each missed direction. The finite-valued domain is exactly the conic hull of the generator, so nonabsorption is equivalent to that domain being a proper convex cone rather than the whole space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C\text{ nonabsorbing}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\operatorname{cone}C\subsetneq\mathbb R^n\Longleftrightarrow(\exists x)\ \gamma_C(x)=+\infty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C\Longleftrightarrow(\forall\lambda>0)\ x\notin\lambda C\).
For closed convex \(C\), nonabsorption is equivalent to \(0\notin\operatorname{int}C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is contained in a proper subspace \(L\), then \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x\notin L\).
If \(C=K\) is a proper convex cone, then \(\gamma_C=0\) on \(K\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The effective domain of every gauge is a convex cone.
Extended values encode unreachable directions independently of zero-valued recession directions.
boundary_notes: Nonabsorption does not imply that the gauge is improper: it remains proper because \(k(0)=0\) and never takes \(-\infty\).
A generator may be absorbing yet unbounded, producing a finite but degenerate gauge.

notation.meaning: Set on which the extended-valued gauge is finite.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Valued Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set containing zero generates an extended-valued sublinear gauge; unreachable directions receive value positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty convex set \(C\subset X\) with \(0\in C\), its extended-valued Minkowski gauge is \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). It takes values in \([0,+\infty]\), satisfies \(\gamma_C(0)=0\), \(\gamma_C(sx)=s\gamma_C(x)\) for \(s>0\), and \(\gamma_C(x+y)\leq\gamma_C(x)+\gamma_C(y)\) under extended-real arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is an extended-valued sublinear gauge.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness Criterion for an Extended-Valued Gauge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-semicontinuity of an extended-valued gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and let \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge. Then \(p\) is lower semicontinuous if and only if its unit sublevel \(C_p=\{x:p(x)\leq1\}\) is closed. In this case \(p\) is a closed proper convex positively homogeneous function whenever it is not identically \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional extended-valued gauge is lower semicontinuous exactly when its unit set is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is lower semicontinuous if and only if \(C_p\) is closed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary extended-valued gauge functionals on a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge and set \(C_p=\{x\in X:p(x)\leq1\}\). Then \(C_p\) is convex and contains \(0\), and \[p(x)=\gamma_{C_p}(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC_p\}\] for every \(x\in X\), including points where \(p(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extended-valued gauge is exactly the Minkowski functional of its unit sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\gamma_{C_p}\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge generated by the unit sublevel

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Sublevel Representation of Extended-Valued Gauges
Separating Certificate of Nonabsorption
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonabsorption is certified by a nonzero functional supporting the generator at the origin; every strictly separated direction has infinite gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and let \(C\subset X\) be convex with \(0\in C\). The set \(C\) is nonabsorbing if and only if there exists a nonzero linear functional \(y\in X^*\) such that \[\langle y,c\rangle\leq0\quad\text{for every }c\in C.\] Every \(x\) with \(\langle y,x\rangle>0\) then lies outside \(tC\) for every \(t>0\), so \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is nonabsorbing}\iff\exists y\in X^*\setminus\{0\}:\sup_{c\in C}\langle y,c\rangle\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex generators; certificate expressed by a supporting functional at the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior Characterization of Absorption
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-dimensional convex generator, absorption is equivalent to the origin being an interior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and let \(C\subset X\) be convex with \(0\in C\). Then \(C\) is absorbing if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Equivalently, \(C\) is nonabsorbing exactly when the origin is not an interior point of the generator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is absorbing}\iff0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex generators containing the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonabsorbing Generators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for a gauge generator to produce infinite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\subseteq X\) containing \(0\), absorption means \[X=\bigcup_{t>0}tC.\] Therefore \(C\) is nonabsorbing if and only if there exists \(x\in X\) such that \(x\notin tC\) for every \(t>0\). For every such witness \(x\), the defining feasible set of the Minkowski gauge is empty and \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generator is nonabsorbing exactly when some vector belongs to no positive dilation of it; that vector receives infinite gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is nonabsorbing if and only if \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\) for some \(x\in X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Realizability of Gauge Effective Domains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex cone is realizable as a gauge effective domain, although the domain does not determine the gauge's finite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every convex cone \(D\subset X\) containing \(0\) occurs as the effective domain of an extended-valued gauge. Treating \(D\) itself as a convex generator gives \[\gamma_D(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D,\end{cases}\qquad \operatorname{dom}\gamma_D=D.\] Thus convex-cone structure is the only algebraic restriction on a gauge effective domain; the domain alone does not determine the positive finite values of a gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset X\) is a convex cone containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_D=D\), with \(\gamma_D=0\) on \(D\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic realization of arbitrary convex cones as gauge domains.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is nonempty, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\bigcup_{t>0}tC=\operatorname{cone}C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset X\) be nonempty, convex, and contain \(0\). The effective domain of its gauge satisfies \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\}=\bigcup_{t>0}tC=\operatorname{cone}C\). This set is a convex cone. Thus the gauge is a finite sublinear functional on \(\operatorname{cone}C\) and equals \(+\infty\) on \(X\setminus\operatorname{cone}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite-valued region of a gauge is exactly the positive hull of its generator, which is a convex cone.

knowledge_statements.title: A Nonclosed Finite-Value Region
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge can be finite on a nonclosed cone and infinite at nonzero limit points of that cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^2\), let \[C=\{0\}\cup\{(u,v):v>0,\ u^2+v^2<1\}.\] Then \(C\) is convex, contains \(0\), and \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\{0\}\cup\{(u,v):v>0\}\). Thus \(\gamma_C\) is finite throughout the open upper half-plane but equals \(+\infty\) at every nonzero point of the horizontal axis, although those points lie in the closure of its effective domain. In particular, \(\gamma_C\) is not lower semicontinuous at those axis points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\{0\}\cup\{(u,v):v>0\}\), and \(\gamma_C(u,0)=+\infty\) for every \(u\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional example showing that a gauge's finite-value region need not be closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite–Infinite Value Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp membership boundary between finite and infinite gauge values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be convex with \(0\in C\), and put \(K:=\operatorname{cone}(C)=\bigcup_{t>0}tC\). Then \[x\in K\iff\gamma_C(x)<+\infty,\qquad x\notin K\iff\gamma_C(x)=+\infty.\] Thus the finite–infinite transition is governed by membership in \(K\), not merely by membership in its closure: if \(K\) is not closed, every \(x\in\overline K\setminus K\) has \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional real vector space, membership in the generated cone is the exact finite-value test; a limit point outside a nonclosed generated cone still has infinite gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C\) is finite exactly on \(K\) and equals \(+\infty\) on \(X\setminus K\), including on \(\overline K\setminus K\).

notation.meaning: topological closure of K in the finite-dimensional vector-space topology
