knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Form Primal–Dual Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching feasible primal and dual solutions certify a finite vertex-form gauge value, while a Farkas separator certifies that the gauge is infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(V=[v_1\ \cdots\ v_n]\), the dual of the vertex-form gauge program is \[\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:V^Ty\leq\mathbf1\}.\] If \(V\lambda=x\), \(\lambda\geq0\), \(V^Ty\leq\mathbf1\), and \(\mathbf1^T\lambda=\langle y,x\rangle\), then \(\lambda\) and \(y\) certify \(\gamma_C(x)\). If the primal is infeasible, equivalently \(x\notin\operatorname{cone}\{v_j\}\), there exists \(y\) with \(V^Ty\leq0\) and \(\langle y,x\rangle>0\), certifying \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal-dual equality certifies a finite value, and \(V^Ty\leq0<\langle y,x\rangle\) certifies \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality and domain certificates for the vertex-form gauge linear program.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Piece Subdifferential Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential of a finite-maximum polyhedral gauge is the convex hull of its active linear pieces, and any maximizing piece certifies the value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(a_0=0\) and suppose \(\gamma_C(x)=\max_{0\leq i\leq m}\langle a_i,x\rangle\). For \(I(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle=\gamma_C(x)\}\), \[\partial\gamma_C(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}.\] Thus an index \(i\in I(x)\), together with the inequalities \(\langle a_k,x\rangle\leq\langle a_i,x\rangle\) for every \(k\), certifies the evaluated gauge value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\gamma_C(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local first-order geometry for a polyhedral gauge in finite-maximum form.

notation.meaning: indices of the active linear pieces at x
convex subdifferential of the gauge at x

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Halfspace-Form Evaluation Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicitly stored halfspace-form polyhedral gauge and one active-piece certificate can be evaluated in O(md) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(\gamma_C(x)=\max\{0,\langle a_1,x\rangle,\ldots,\langle a_m,x\rangle\}\), a streaming scan of the inner products computes \(\gamma_C(x)\) and one active-piece certificate using \(O(md)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(1)\) auxiliary storage beyond the input and output.
assumptions_latex: The \(m\) inequality normals are explicitly represented in \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(x)\) and one active index can be computed in \(O(md)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic evaluation cost when normalized inequality normals are explicitly stored.

knowledge_statements.title: Halfspace–Polar Representation of a Polyhedral Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of an absorbing polyhedron in normalized halfspace form is the convex hull of zero and its facet normals, and its gauge is the corresponding finite maximum. Boundedness makes the zero term redundant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\langle a_i,x\rangle\leq1,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) and suppose \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Then \[C^\circ=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\{0,a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\bigr),\qquad \gamma_C(x)=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)=\max\{0,\langle a_1,x\rangle,\ldots,\langle a_m,x\rangle\}.\] If \(C\) is bounded, then \(0\in\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\), so the zero term is redundant and the seed's facet-maximum formula is recovered.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is described by finitely many normalized inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^\circ=\operatorname{conv}(\{0,a_1,\ldots,a_m\})\) and \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}=\max\{0,\langle a_i,\cdot\rangle:i=1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral polarity for an absorbing polyhedron; unlike the bounded case, the zero vector may be an essential polar vertex.

notation.meaning: support function of the polar polytope

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Form Linear Programming Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polytope given by vertices, gauge evaluation is a linear program minimizing total nonnegative coefficient mass. Infeasibility is exactly infinite gauge value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{conv}\{0,v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\subset\mathbb R^d\). Then \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_j:\sum_{j=1}^n\lambda_jv_j=x,\ \lambda_j\geq0\right\}.\] The value is \(+\infty\) exactly when \(x\notin\operatorname{cone}\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}\); whenever it is finite, the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(x)=\min\{\mathbf1^T\lambda:V\lambda=x,\lambda\geq0\}\) when feasible, and \(+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polyhedral generator described by vertices, including lower-dimensional and nonabsorbing cases.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of an absorbing polytope is the maximum of its normalized facet functionals, hence is finite, convex, positively homogeneous, and piecewise linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(C=\{x\in X:\langle a_i,x\rangle\leq 1,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Its Minkowski gauge has the finite maximum representation \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\langle a_i,x\rangle.\] Consequently, \(\gamma_C\) is convex, positively homogeneous, finite-valued, and piecewise linear. On every region where one fixed index attains the maximum, the gauge agrees with the corresponding linear functional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C\) is a finite polyhedral gauge and is linear on each cone of a finite polyhedral subdivision of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, absorbing polyhedral unit balls.

notation.meaning: facet normals normalized to right-hand side one

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\). A gauge is an extended-real-valued, nonnegative, convex, positively homogeneous function \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) with \(\gamma(0)=0\). Its unit set is \(C_\gamma=\{x\in E:\gamma(x)\le 1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued gauges are covered; symmetry, definiteness, and finiteness are not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gauge \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) is polyhedral when its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma=\{(x,t)\in E\times\mathbb{R}:\gamma(x)\le t\}\) is a polyhedral convex cone. Equivalently, \(\gamma\) is closed and its unit set \(C_\gamma\) is a polyhedral convex set containing \(0\). Equivalently, there exist finitely many vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_p\in E\) and a polyhedral cone \(K\subseteq E\) such that \[\gamma(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}\langle a_i,x\rangle+\delta_K(x),\] with the maximum nonnegative on \(K\). If \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, convex, polyhedral, and contains \(0\), then its Minkowski functional \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC\}\] is a polyhedral gauge, with value \(+\infty\) when no such \(t\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral gauge on a finite-dimensional space is a nonnegative positively homogeneous convex function whose epigraph is a polyhedral cone. For a closed gauge this is equivalent to its unit sublevel set being a polyhedral convex set containing the origin. It can be represented on a polyhedral conic domain as the maximum of finitely many linear functionals. Conversely, the Minkowski functional of any closed polyhedral convex set containing the origin is a polyhedral gauge, possibly taking infinity outside the cone generated by that set.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge, or \(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, convex, polyhedral, and \(0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma\text{ is polyhedral}\iff\operatorname{epi}\gamma\text{ is a polyhedral cone}\iff C_\gamma\text{ is polyhedral}\), and \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\gamma(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}\langle a_i,x\rangle+\delta_K(x)\) for finite \(\{a_i\}\) and a polyhedral cone \(K=\operatorname{dom}\gamma\).
\(C_\gamma=\{x:\gamma(x)\le1\}\) is polyhedral and \(\gamma=\gamma_{C_\gamma}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(K=E\), then \(\gamma\) is finite and piecewise linear: \(\gamma(x)=\max_i\langle a_i,x\rangle\).
The norms \(\|x\|_1\) and \(\|x\|_\infty\) are symmetric, definite polyhedral gauges.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every sublevel set \(\{x:\gamma(x)\le r\}=rC_\gamma\) for \(r>0\) is polyhedral.
The polar unit set \(C_\gamma^\circ\) is polyhedral.
boundary_notes: A gauge of a nonpolyhedral unit set need not be piecewise linear.
Extended values occur when \(C_\gamma\) is not absorbing; this does not prevent polyhedrality.

notation.meaning: Indicator taking value zero on K and positive infinity outside K.
Closed unit sublevel set of the gauge.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb{S}^n\) be the real symmetric matrices with trace pairing \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\), let \(\mathbb{O}^n\) be the orthogonal group, and let \(\lambda(X)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) list the eigenvalues of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns real symmetric matrices and invariance under orthogonal similarity. Rectangular unitarily invariant gauges require a singular-value formulation not asserted here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix gauge \(\Gamma:\mathbb{S}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) is orthogonally invariant when \[\Gamma(U^{\mathsf T}XU)=\Gamma(X)\qquad(\forall X\in\mathbb{S}^n)(\forall U\in\mathbb{O}^n).\] Such a gauge is spectral: there is a permutation-invariant gauge \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfying \(g(Px)=g(x)\) for every permutation matrix \(P\), such that \[\Gamma(X)=g(\lambda(X)).\] Conversely, every permutation-invariant gauge \(g\) defines an orthogonally invariant matrix gauge by this formula. Its unit set is invariant under orthogonal similarity and equals \(\{X:g(\lambda(X))\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonally invariant matrix gauge on real symmetric matrices is a gauge whose value is unchanged by orthogonal similarity transformations. It is equivalently a spectral gauge obtained by applying a permutation-invariant vector gauge to the eigenvalue vector. Conversely, a permutation-invariant vector gauge induces an orthogonally invariant gauge. Thus the family is classified by symmetric vector gauges, while its unit sets are precisely the convex gauge unit sets stable under orthogonal similarity.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma:\mathbb{S}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) is convex, nonnegative, positively homogeneous, and \(\Gamma(0)=0\).
\(\lambda(X)\) is ordered by a fixed convention, while \(g\) is invariant under coordinate permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma(U^{\mathsf T}XU)=\Gamma(X)\) for all \(X,U\), equivalently \(\Gamma=g\circ\lambda\) for a permutation-invariant gauge \(g\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The unit set \(C_\Gamma=\{X:\Gamma(X)\le1\}\) satisfies \(U^{\mathsf T}C_\Gamma U=C_\Gamma\) for every \(U\in\mathbb{O}^n\).
\(g(x)=\Gamma(\operatorname{Diag}x)\) is permutation invariant and recovers \(\Gamma\) through eigenvalues.
special_cases_latex: If \(g(x)=\|x\|_\infty\), then \(\Gamma(X)=\max_i|\lambda_i(X)|\), the spectral norm on \(\mathbb{S}^n\).
If \(g(x)=\|x\|_1\), then \(\Gamma(X)=\sum_i|\lambda_i(X)|\), the nuclear norm on \(\mathbb{S}^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Closedness and convexity of \(\Gamma\) are equivalent to closedness and convexity of its diagonal restriction \(g\).
The polar of a closed invariant gauge is again invariant under the same orthogonal group.
boundary_notes: Permutation invariance alone does not impose sign invariance, so the resulting gauge need not be a norm.
For general rectangular matrices, left-right orthogonal invariance is represented through singular values rather than eigenvalues.

notation.meaning: Eigenvalue vector of a real symmetric matrix.
Group of real orthogonal n-by-n matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathbb R^n\to[0,+\infty]\) be a closed permutation-invariant gauge and define \(\Gamma_\phi(X)=\phi(\lambda(X))\) on \(\mathbb S^n\). Under the trace pairing, \[\Gamma_\phi^\circ(Y)=\phi^\circ(\lambda(Y)),\qquad Y\in\mathbb S^n.\] No sign invariance is required, so neither \(\phi\) nor \(\Gamma_\phi\) need be even.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma_\phi^\circ(Y)=\phi^\circ(\lambda(Y))\) for all \(Y\in\mathbb S^n\).

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{S}^n\) is the space of real symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The spectral gauge generated by \(\phi\) is the function \[\Gamma_\phi(X)=\phi(\lambda(X)),\qquad X\in\mathbb{S}^n.\] Permutation invariance makes this definition independent of eigenvalue ordering. The resulting function is convex and positively homogeneous, and it satisfies \(\Gamma_\phi(QXQ^{\mathsf T})=\Gamma_\phi(X)\) for every orthogonal matrix \(Q\). If \(\phi\) vanishes only at the origin, then \(\Gamma_\phi\) also vanishes only at the zero matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral gauge applies a permutation-invariant vector gauge to a symmetric matrix's eigenvalues, producing an orthogonally invariant matrix gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Space Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix-space gauge is a nonnegative, subadditive, positively homogeneous matrix functional; orthogonal invariance is optional rather than definitional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix-space gauge is a function \(\Gamma:\mathbb{M}_{m,n}\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfying \(\Gamma(tX)=t\Gamma(X)\) for all \(t\geq0\) and \(\Gamma(X+Y)\leq\Gamma(X)+\Gamma(Y)\). Its unit set \(C_\Gamma=\{X:\Gamma(X)\leq1\}\) is convex, contains the zero matrix, and recovers the gauge through \[\Gamma(X)=\inf\{t>0:X\in tC_\Gamma\}.\] Left-right orthogonal invariance is an additional property, not part of the general definition.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{M}_{m,n}\) is a finite-dimensional real matrix space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A matrix-space gauge is precisely a nonnegative convex positively homogeneous functional on \(\mathbb{M}_{m,n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real matrix spaces, without an invariance assumption.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar of a Singular-Value Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a singular-value gauge applies the polar vector gauge to the singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Gamma(X)=\phi(\sigma(X))\), where \(\phi\) is a closed signed-permutation-invariant gauge on \(\mathbb R^r\). With polar gauges defined using the Frobenius pairing on matrices and the Euclidean pairing on vectors, \[\Gamma^\circ(Y)=\phi^\circ(\sigma(Y)).\] Thus polarity preserves the singular-value representation and replaces the generating vector gauge by its polar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma^\circ(Y)=\phi^\circ(\sigma(Y))\) for every \(Y\in\mathbb M_{m,n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar gauges under the Frobenius and Euclidean pairings.

knowledge_statements.title: Transfer of Finiteness and Definiteness Through Singular Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finiteness, definiteness, and the norm property transfer exactly between a signed-permutation-invariant vector gauge and its singular-value matrix gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), let \(\phi:\mathbb R^r\to[0,+\infty]\) be invariant under signed permutations, and set \(\Gamma(X)=\phi(\sigma(X))\). Then \(\Gamma\) is finite on all of \(\mathbb M_{m,n}\) if and only if \(\phi\) is finite on all of \(\mathbb R^r\), and \(\Gamma(X)=0\Rightarrow X=0\) if and only if \(\phi(s)=0\Rightarrow s=0\). Consequently, \(\Gamma\) is a norm exactly when \(\phi\) is a norm.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is a signed-permutation-invariant gauge on \(\mathbb R^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma\) is finite, definite, or a norm exactly when \(\phi\) has the corresponding property.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real rectangular matrices and signed-permutation-invariant generating gauges.

notation.meaning: singular-value matrix gauge generated by phi

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value Gauge Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangular biunitarily invariant gauges represented by symmetric gauges of ordered singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\), let \(m,n\geq1\), and set \(r=\min\{m,n\}\). For \(X\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}\), let \(\sigma(X)=(\sigma_1(X),\ldots,\sigma_r(X))\) list its singular values in nonincreasing order. A finite gauge \(\Gamma:\mathbb F^{m\times n}\to[0,+\infty)\) satisfies \(\Gamma(UXV^*)=\Gamma(X)\) for every orthogonal or unitary \(U\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}\) and \(V\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}\) if and only if there exists a gauge \(\phi:\mathbb R^r\to[0,+\infty)\), invariant under coordinate permutations and sign changes, such that \[\Gamma(X)=\phi(\sigma(X)).\] The representing gauge is unique and satisfies \(\phi(z)=\Gamma(\operatorname{Diag}_r(z))\), where \(\operatorname{Diag}_r(z)\) is the rectangular matrix with \(z\) on its principal diagonal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over the real or complex field, a rectangular matrix gauge is invariant under all compatible left and right orthogonal or unitary transformations exactly when it is a unique signed-permutation-invariant gauge of the singular-value vector.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma:\mathbb F^{m\times n}\to[0,+\infty)\) is a finite gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma(X)=\phi(\sigma(X))\) for a unique signed-permutation-invariant gauge \(\phi\).

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue Gauge Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unitary-conjugation-invariant gauges on Hermitian matrices represented by permutation-invariant eigenvalue gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}\), let \(n\geq1\), and let \(\mathbb H_{\mathbb F}^n\) be the real vector space of symmetric matrices when \(\mathbb F=\mathbb R\) and Hermitian matrices when \(\mathbb F=\mathbb C\). knowledge_statements.title: Orbit-Constancy Test for Spectral Representability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two matrices with identical complete invariant data but unequal gauge values certify failure of spectral representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) act on a matrix space and let \(s\) classify its orbits. A function \(\Gamma\) admits a factorization \(\Gamma(X)=\phi(s(X))\) if and only if it is constant on every \(G\)-orbit. Thus \(s(X)=s(Y)\) and \(\Gamma(X)\neq\Gamma(Y)\) certify that no such representation exists.
assumptions_latex: \(s\) is a complete invariant for the orbits of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma=\phi\circ s\) for some \(\phi\) if and only if \(\Gamma\) is constant on \(G\)-orbits.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact diagnostic for failure of representation by complete invariant data.

notation.meaning: complete orbit invariant such as singular values or unordered eigenvalues

knowledge_statements.title: Broken-Invariance Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete entry-weighted gauge showing failure of singular-value representation without two-sided invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R^{2\times2}\), choose positive weights \(w_{11}\neq w_{12}\) and define \[\Gamma(X)=\sum_{i,j=1}^2 w_{ij}|X_{ij}|.\] This is a norm and hence a gauge. The rank-one matrices \(E_{11}\) and \(E_{12}\) have the same singular-value vector \((1,0)\), while \(\Gamma(E_{11})=w_{11}\neq w_{12}=\Gamma(E_{12})\). Moreover, a right permutation matrix sends \(E_{11}\) to \(E_{12}\), so \(\Gamma\) is not two-sided orthogonally invariant. Consequently no function \(\phi\) depending only on singular values can satisfy \(\Gamma(X)=\phi(\sigma(X))\) for all \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal entry weights define a valid matrix norm but distinguish matrices with identical singular values, so the norm has no singular-value-only representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(E_{11})=\sigma(E_{12})\) but \(\Gamma(E_{11})\neq\Gamma(E_{12})\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E_i\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces. A gauge is a function into \([0,+\infty]\) that is nonnegative, convex, positively homogeneous, and zero at the origin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The entry defines the standard finite-dimensional calculus generated by positive combinations, maxima, linear pullbacks, and linear infimal images. Closedness of an infimal image requires separate qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Gauge calculus is the family of operations that sends gauges to gauges. For gauges \(\gamma_i:E\to[0,+\infty]\), coefficients \(\alpha_i\ge0\), and a linear map \(A:E\to F\), the basic constructions are \[\gamma_\Sigma(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i\gamma_i(x),\qquad \gamma_\vee(x)=\max_i\gamma_i(x),\qquad (\eta\circ A)(x)=\eta(Ax),\] and the quotient or infimal image \[(A\gamma)(y)=\inf\{\gamma(x):Ax=y\},\qquad\inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] The first three are gauges whenever their inputs are gauges. The infimal image is a gauge provided it never takes \(-\infty\), which is automatic for nonnegative gauges; it may require lower-semicontinuous closure to be a closed gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge calculus consists of operations preserving nonnegative convex positive homogeneity. Nonnegative weighted sums and pointwise maxima of gauges are gauges. Pulling a gauge back through a linear map also produces a gauge. Pushing a gauge forward through a linear map is defined by minimizing over each fiber; because gauges are nonnegative, the result is an extended-valued gauge, although it may fail to be closed without an additional closed-image condition. These constructions include restrictions, quotients, products, intersections of unit sets, and infimal decompositions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_\Sigma,\gamma_\vee,\eta\circ A\), and \(A\gamma\) are extended-valued gauges, with closure applied to \(A\gamma\) when a closed gauge is required.
equivalent_formulations_latex: At the epigraph level, nonnegative scaling, intersection, inverse linear image, and linear projection are the corresponding convex-cone operations.
For \(C_i=\{x:\gamma_i(x)\le1\}\), \(\{x:\gamma_\vee(x)\le1\}=\bigcap_i C_i\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(A\) to be an inclusion gives restriction of a gauge to a subspace.
Taking \(A\) to be a coordinate projection gives a quotient gauge.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every construction remains positively homogeneous of degree one.
Extended values are retained when the relevant unit set is nonabsorbing.
boundary_notes: Pointwise minima of gauges are generally not convex and hence are not basic gauge-preserving operations.
A linear infimal image of a closed gauge need not be closed unless an image-closedness condition holds.

notation.meaning: Infimal image of gamma through the linear map A.
Pointwise maximum of finitely many gauges.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be finite dimensional, let \(\gamma_i:E\to[0,+\infty]\) be gauges, and put \(C_i=\{x:\gamma_i(x)\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite combinations on a common space are covered. Closure is stated explicitly where infimal convolution may not be lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical finite gauge combinations are the maximum, the nonnegative weighted sum, and the infimal convolution: \[\gamma_\vee(x)=\max_i\gamma_i(x),\qquad \gamma_\Sigma(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i\gamma_i(x)\quad(\alpha_i\ge0),\] \[\gamma_\square(x)=\inf\Big\{\sum_i\gamma_i(x_i):\sum_i x_i=x\Big\}.\] Each is an extended-valued gauge. Their unit-set interpretations include \[C_{\gamma_\vee}=\bigcap_i C_i,\qquad C_{\gamma_\square}=\operatorname{conv}\Big(\bigcup_i C_i\Big)\] whenever the displayed convex hull is closed; otherwise \(C_{\operatorname{cl}\gamma_\square}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iC_i)\). Thus maximum corresponds to intersection, while infimal convolution corresponds to convex-hull aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauge combination calculus combines gauges on one space without losing convexity or positive homogeneity. The pointwise maximum has the intersection of the unit sets as its unit set. A nonnegative weighted sum is again a gauge. Infimal convolution minimizes the sum of component gauges over all decompositions of a vector and corresponds, after closure when necessary, to the convex hull of the component unit sets. These constructions are distinct: maximum enforces all component bounds, weighted sum penalizes them jointly, and infimal convolution permits allocation among components.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_i:E\to[0,+\infty]\) are gauges and the index set is finite.
For the unclosed unit-set identity of \(\gamma_\square\), \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iC_i)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_\vee,\gamma_\Sigma,\gamma_\square\) are gauges, with \(C_{\gamma_\vee}=\bigcap_iC_i\) and \(C_{\operatorname{cl}\gamma_\square}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iC_i)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\gamma_\square\) is the greatest gauge majorized by every \(\gamma_i\), up to lower-semicontinuous closure.
\(\gamma_\vee=\gamma_{\cap_iC_i}\) for closed gauge unit sets.
special_cases_latex: For two gauges, \((\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)(x)=\inf_{u+v=x}\{\gamma_1(u)+\gamma_2(v)\}\).
If all \(\gamma_i\) are finite, \(\gamma_\Sigma\) and \(\gamma_\vee\) are finite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Combination unit sets remain convex and contain the origin.
If the inputs are polyhedral, these finite combinations are polyhedral.
boundary_notes: The pointwise minimum \(\min_i\gamma_i\) is generally not convex.
The weighted-sum unit set does not generally equal a Minkowski sum or intersection of the individual unit sets.

notation.meaning: Unit sublevel set of a gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Weighted Gauge Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite positive weighted sum of gauges is a gauge; its domain is the intersection of the component domains, while closedness and definiteness inherit under the stated conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m\) be gauges and let \(w_i>0\). Then \[\Gamma(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\gamma_i(x)\] is a gauge with unit set \[C_\Gamma=\left\{x:\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\gamma_i(x)\leq1\right\}.\] Its effective domain is \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}\gamma_i\). If every \(\gamma_i\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(\Gamma\) is lower semicontinuous. If at least one component gauge is definite, then \(\Gamma(x)=0\) implies \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Gamma=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\gamma_i\text{ is a gauge},\qquad \operatorname{dom}\Gamma=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}\gamma_i.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite positive-weight extension of the binary gauge-sum operation.

notation.meaning: unit set of the weighted sum gauge

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise sum of two gauges is a gauge, with unit set defined by the corresponding sum inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\gamma_\Sigma(x)=\gamma_1(x)+\gamma_2(x)\). Then \(\gamma_\Sigma\) is nonnegative, convex, and positively homogeneous, hence is a gauge. Its unit set is exactly \[C_\Sigma=\{x\in X:\gamma_1(x)+\gamma_2(x)\leq1\}.\] If both gauges are lower semicontinuous on a finite-dimensional space, then their sum is lower semicontinuous. If both vanish only at zero, their sum also vanishes only at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_1+\gamma_2\) is a gauge with unit set \(\{x:\gamma_1(x)+\gamma_2(x)\leq1\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Gauge Suprema
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The supremum of a nonempty family of gauges is a gauge whose unit set and effective domain are the intersections of the corresponding component sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\gamma_i)_{i\in I}\) be a nonempty family of gauges and set \[\gamma_\vee(x)=\sup_{i\in I}\gamma_i(x).\] Then \(\gamma_\vee\) is an extended-valued gauge and, for \(C_i=\{x:\gamma_i(x)\leq1\}\), \[\{x:\gamma_\vee(x)\leq1\}=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i,\qquad \gamma_\vee=\gamma_{\cap_{i\in I}C_i}.\] If every \(\gamma_i\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(\gamma_\vee\) is lower semicontinuous. Its effective domain is \(\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{dom}\gamma_i\), which may reduce to \(\{0\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_i:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{i\in I}\gamma_i=\gamma_{\bigcap_{i\in I}\{\gamma_i\leq1\}},\qquad \operatorname{dom}\left(\sup_{i\in I}\gamma_i\right)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{dom}\gamma_i.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty-family extension of the binary gauge-maximum construction.

notation.meaning: pointwise supremum of the gauge family

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Maxima
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise maximum of two gauges is a gauge whose unit set is the intersection of the two component unit sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma_\vee(x)=\max\{\gamma_1(x),\gamma_2(x)\}\) for \(x\in X\). Then \(\gamma_\vee\) is a gauge and \[\{x\in X:\gamma_\vee(x)\leq 1\}=C_1\cap C_2.\] Consequently, \(\gamma_\vee=\gamma_{C_1\cap C_2}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2\}=\gamma_{C_1\cap C_2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise maximum of two gauges and intersection of their unit sets.

notation.meaning: unit sets of the component gauges

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Gauge Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution combines two gauges by optimally decomposing the argument; geometrically it is the gauge of the convex hull of their unit sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal convolution of the gauges is \[(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)(x)=\inf_{x_1+x_2=x}\bigl(\gamma_1(x_1)+\gamma_2(x_2)\bigr).\] It is a gauge and admits the unit-set representation \[\gamma_1\square\gamma_2=\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)}.\] The infimum need not be attained, and without additional topological assumptions this gauge need not be lower semicontinuous even when the component gauges are lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2=\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-gauge infimal convolution; attainment is not asserted.

source_witnesses.locator: 12 Infimal Convolution p. 203

knowledge_statements.title: Functional Polar Form of Gauge Combinations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarization converts primal infimal convolution into a maximum of polar gauges, while the polar of a primal maximum is the closed infimal convolution of the polar gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1,C_2\) be closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional space containing \(0\), let \(\gamma_i=\gamma_{C_i}\), and define \(\gamma_i^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:\gamma_i(x)\leq1\}\). Then
\[
(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)^\circ=\max\{\gamma_1^\circ,\gamma_2^\circ\},
\qquad
(\max\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2\})^\circ=\operatorname{cl}(\gamma_1^\circ\square\gamma_2^\circ),
\]
where \(\operatorname{cl}\) denotes the lower-semicontinuous hull. The closure in the second identity cannot be omitted without an additional exactness condition.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2\) are closed convex sets containing \(0\) in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(\gamma_i=\gamma_{C_i}\), and functional polarity is defined by support over the gauge unit set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)^\circ=\max\{\gamma_1^\circ,\gamma_2^\circ\}\) and \((\max\{\gamma_1,\gamma_2\})^\circ=\operatorname{cl}(\gamma_1^\circ\square\gamma_2^\circ)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional polar-gauge counterparts of the two accepted unit-set polarity identities.

notation.meaning: lower-semicontinuous hull of a convex function

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Polar Combination Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity exchanges convex hull of a union with intersection, while intersection polarizes to the closed convex hull of the polar sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polarization reverses the two basic unit-set combinations: \[(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2))^\circ=C_1^\circ\cap C_2^\circ,\qquad (C_1\cap C_2)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C_1^\circ\cup C_2^\circ).\] Hence infimal convolution of primal gauges, whose unit set is \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\), corresponds to intersection on the polar side, while pointwise maximum of primal gauges corresponds to closed convex-hull combination on the polar side.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2\subset X\) are closed convex sets containing \(0\), and \(C^\circ=\{u:\langle u,x\rangle\leq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2))^\circ=C_1^\circ\cap C_2^\circ\) and \((C_1\cap C_2)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C_1^\circ\cup C_2^\circ)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polar identities for gauge unit-set combinations.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.3 Polar Sets p. 136

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-Sum Closedness Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph sum is closed exactly when the infimal gauge is lower semicontinuous and every finite infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h=\gamma_1\square\gamma_2\), where \[h(x)=\inf_{u+v=x}\bigl(\gamma_1(u)+\gamma_2(v)\bigr).\] Then \[\operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2\subseteq\operatorname{epi}h,\qquad \overline{\operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2}=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}h).\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2\) is closed if and only if \(h\) is lower semicontinuous and its defining infimum is attained at every \(x\) where \(h(x)<+\infty\). In that case, \[\operatorname{epi}h=\operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}\gamma_1+\operatorname{epi}\gamma_2\text{ is closed}\iff h\text{ is lower semicontinuous and every finite defining infimum is attained}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional criterion separating lower semicontinuity and attainment for an infimal convolution of closed gauges.

notation.meaning: infimal convolution of the two gauges

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Gauges with Nonclosed Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indicators of the positive-semidefinite cone and a one-dimensional matrix subspace are closed gauges whose infimal convolution is the indicator of a nonclosed cone sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb S^2\), let \(K=\mathbb S^2_+\), and let \(L=\operatorname{span}\{E_{22}\}\). The indicator gauges \(\gamma_1=\delta_K\) and \(\gamma_2=\delta_L\) are proper and lower semicontinuous, but \[\gamma_1\square\gamma_2=\delta_{K+L}.\] Writing matrices as \(\begin{psmallmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{psmallmatrix}\), one has \[K+L=\left\{a>0\right\}\cup\left\{a=0,\ b=0\right\},\] with the entry \(c\) unrestricted. Hence \(K+L\) is not closed: \(\begin{psmallmatrix}1/n&1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}\in K+L\) converges to \(\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}\notin K+L\). Thus the infimal convolution of two closed gauges need not be lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb S^2\) with its usual finite-dimensional topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_K\square\delta_L=\delta_{K+L}\quad\text{and}\quad K+L\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional cone example showing that separate closedness of the input gauges does not ensure closedness of their infimal convolution.

notation.meaning: matrix having one in entry \((2,2)\) and zero elsewhere

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Repair by Closing the Generated Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing an infimal gauge construction amounts to replacing the convex hull of its unit sets by its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_i=\{x:\gamma_i(x)\leq1\}\) and \(D=\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\). Then \[\gamma_1\square\gamma_2=\gamma_D,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)=\gamma_{\overline D}.\] Consequently, the infimal construction is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(\gamma_D=\gamma_{\overline D}\). Closedness of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) separately does not guarantee this equality because their convex hull need not be closed.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\) are proper lower-semicontinuous gauges with unit sets \(C_1,C_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2)=\gamma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)}}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric lower-semicontinuous closure of a possibly nonclosed infimal gauge construction.

notation.meaning: convex hull of the two unit sets
lower-semicontinuous hull of an extended-real convex function

review_flags: The equality concerns gauges and their lower-semicontinuous hulls; a nonclosed generator need not equal the unit sublevel set of its gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of Infimal Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, lower semicontinuity and coercivity make the unit sets compact, ensuring that the infimal gauge is closed and its infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Coercivity means that every sublevel set of each \(\gamma_i\) is bounded; together with lower semicontinuity, this makes the unit sets \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) compact. Consequently, \(\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)\) is compact, and \[h(x)=\inf_{x_1+x_2=x}\bigl(\gamma_1(x_1)+\gamma_2(x_2)\bigr)=\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(C_1\cup C_2)}(x)\] is a finite lower-semicontinuous gauge. For every \(x\in X\), the displayed infimum is attained by at least one decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_1\square\gamma_2\) is finite and lower semicontinuous, and every defining infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient compactness condition, not a necessary characterization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pullback and quotient transport of a gauge
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:E\to F\) be linear between finite-dimensional real vector spaces. Let \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) and \(\eta:F\to[0,+\infty]\) be gauges.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Both contravariant pullback and covariant infimal transport are included. The quotient formula is extended-valued outside the range of the map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pullback of \(\eta\) through \(A\) is \[A^*\eta:E\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (A^*\eta)(x)=\eta(Ax).\] The quotient or infimal image of \(\gamma\) through \(A\) is \[A_\#\gamma:F\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (A_\#\gamma)(y)=\inf\{\gamma(x):Ax=y\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Both are gauges. If \(C_\gamma=\{x:\gamma(x)\le1\}\) and \(C_\eta=\{y:\eta(y)\le1\}\), then \[C_{A^*\eta}=A^{-1}C_\eta,\qquad C_{A_\#\gamma}=A(C_\gamma)\] when the fiber infimum is attained; in general the closed quotient gauge has unit set \(\operatorname{cl}A(C_\gamma)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge can be transported through a linear map in two directions. Pullback evaluates the target gauge after applying the map and has the inverse image of the target unit set as its unit set. Quotient transport minimizes the source gauge over the affine fiber mapping to a target point; it is infinite outside the range and has the image of the source unit set as its unit set when the minimum is attained. Closure may be needed because a linear image of a closed convex set need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A^*\eta)(x)=\eta(Ax)\) and \((A_\#\gamma)(y)=\inf_{Ax=y}\gamma(x)\) define gauges transported through \(A\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(A^*\eta)\) is the inverse image of \(\operatorname{epi}\eta\) under \((x,t)\mapsto(Ax,t)\).
\(\operatorname{epi}(A_\#\gamma)\) is the lower boundary generated by the image of \(\operatorname{epi}\gamma\) under \((x,t)\mapsto(Ax,t)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is injective, pullback restricts a gauge to an embedded subspace.
If \(A\) is surjective, \(A_\#\gamma\) is the quotient gauge on \(F\cong E/\ker A\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\ker A\subseteq\{x:(A^*\eta)(x)=0\}\).
A polyhedral source gauge has a polyhedral quotient gauge, and its fiber infimum is attained whenever finite.
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(A_\#\gamma\) is not automatic for arbitrary closed nonpolyhedral gauges.
The notation \(A^*\eta\) here denotes functional pullback, not the adjoint-map action on dual vectors.

notation.meaning: Infimal or quotient image of gamma through A.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Image Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a linear image is obtained by minimizing the original gauge over each linear fiber; compactness ensures attainment and closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge transported through the linear image is the marginal function \[\gamma_{A(C)}(y)=\inf\{\gamma_C(x):x\in X,\ Ax=y\},\qquad y\in Y,\] where the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). Thus its effective domain is \(A(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C)\), and its unit set is \(A(C)\) up to possible nonattainment at the unit boundary. If \(C\) is compact, then \(A(C)\) is compact, the infimum is attained whenever finite, and the image gauge is lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is linear between finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(C\subset X\) is convex, contains \(0\), and has gauge \(\gamma_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{A(C)}(y)=\inf\{\gamma_C(x):Ax=y\}\), with value \(+\infty\) when the fiber is empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued image gauge; closedness of the image is not assumed.

notation.meaning: linear image of the unit set

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Preimage Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a linear preimage is the original gauge evaluated after the linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the Minkowski gauge by \(\gamma_D(y)=\inf\{t>0:y\in tD\}\), with infimum \(+\infty\) when the set is empty. For the linear preimage \(C=A^{-1}D=\{x\in X:Ax\in D\}\), one has, for every \(x\in X\), \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:Ax\in tD\}=\gamma_D(Ax).\] Thus linear precomposition preserves positive homogeneity and convexity, while any directions mapped into the zero set of \(\gamma_D\) become zero-gauge directions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces, and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{A^{-1}D}=\gamma_D\circ A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pullback formula for extended-valued Minkowski gauges under a linear map.

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge of a set containing the origin

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Linear Operators and Functionals p. 31

knowledge_statements.title: Polar of a Quotient Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a quotient gauge is the original polar gauge restricted to functionals annihilating the quotient subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional, \(N\subseteq X\) a subspace, \(q:X\to X/N\) the quotient map, and \(p=\gamma_C\) a gauge. Identify \((X/N)^*\) with \(N^\perp\subseteq X^*\). If \(\bar p(q(x))=\inf_{n\in N}p(x+n)\), then \[\bar p^\circ(u)=p^\circ(u),\qquad u\in N^\perp.\] Equivalently, under this identification, \((q(C))^\circ=C^\circ\cap N^\perp\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(N\subseteq X\) is a linear subspace.
\(p=\gamma_C\) is a gauge and \(q:X\to X/N\) is the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar p^\circ=p^\circ|_{N^\perp},\qquad (q(C))^\circ=C^\circ\cap N^\perp.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of quotient duals with the annihilator of the quotient subspace.

notation.meaning: annihilator of N in the dual space

knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Unit Quotient Attainment and Definiteness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge with compact unit set induces a finite definite quotient gauge, and every quotient value has a minimizing representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(X\) is finite-dimensional and the unit set \(C=\{x:p(x)\leq1\}\) of a finite gauge \(p\) is compact. For every subspace \(N\subseteq X\), the quotient unit set \(q(C)\) is compact, \[\bar p(q(x))=\min_{n\in N}p(x+n),\] and \(\bar p\) is a finite definite gauge on \(X/N\).
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a finite gauge whose unit set is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar p(q(x))=\min_{n\in N}p(x+n),\quad \bar p\text{ is finite and definite on }X/N.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A standard sufficient regime in which coset minimization is attained and the quotient gauge remains definite.

notation.meaning: canonical quotient map from X to X/N

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient gauge is the infimum of the original gauge over all representatives of the quotient class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(q(C)\subseteq X/N\) with its Minkowski gauge. For every representative \(x\in X\), the quotient value is independent of that representative and satisfies \[\gamma_{q(C)}(q(x))=\inf_{n\in N}\gamma_C(x+n).\] Equivalently, the quotient gauge is the marginal of \(\gamma_C\) over the affine coset \(x+N\). The infimum need not be attained unless additional compactness, coercivity, or finite-dimensional closedness conditions are imposed.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space, \(N\subseteq X\) is a linear subspace, and \(q:X\to X/N\) is the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{q(C)}(q(x))=\inf_{n\in N}\gamma_C(x+n)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued quotient gauge represented by minimization along kernel cosets.

notation.meaning: image of C in the quotient space

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of quotient duals with the annihilator of the quotient subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional, let \(N\subseteq X\) be a subspace, and let \(p=\gamma_C\) be a closed gauge. Identify \((X/N)^*\) with \(N^\perp\subseteq X^*\). If \(\bar p(q(x))=\inf_{n\in N}p(x+n)\), then its polar gauge satisfies \[\bar p^\circ(u)=p^\circ(u),\qquad u\in N^\perp.\] Equivalently, \((q(C))^\circ=C^\circ\cap N^\perp\) under this identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a quotient gauge is the original polar gauge restricted to functionals that annihilate the quotient subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(N\subseteq X\) is a linear subspace.
\(p=\gamma_C\) is a closed gauge and \(q:X\to X/N\) is the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar p^\circ=p^\circ|_{N^\perp},\qquad (q(C))^\circ=C^\circ\cap N^\perp.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual of a Quotient Gauge
Definiteness Criterion for a Pullback Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pullback gauge is definite exactly when the map is injective and the target gauge has no nonzero zero direction in the map's range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear and let \(p:Y\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge with zero set \(Z_p\). Then \(p\circ A\) is definite if and only if \(\ker A=\{0\}\) and \(Z_p\cap\operatorname{ran}A=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\circ A\text{ is definite}\iff \ker A=\{0\}\text{ and }Z_p\cap\operatorname{ran}A=\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion separating degeneracy introduced by the map from degeneracy already present in the target gauge.

notation.meaning: zero set of the target gauge

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Invariance of Pullback Sublevels
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every pullback sublevel is invariant along the kernel, so a nontrivial kernel makes every nonempty sublevel unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S_t=\{x:p(Ax)\leq t\}\) and every \(t\geq0\), \[S_t+\ker A=S_t.\] Consequently, if \(\ker A\neq\{0\}\), every nonempty \(S_t\) contains an affine line and is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_t+\ker A=S_t;\quad \ker A\neq\{0\},\ S_t\neq\varnothing\Longrightarrow S_t\text{ is unbounded}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric manifestation of kernel-induced degeneracy in every nonempty pullback sublevel.

notation.meaning: level-t sublevel of the pullback gauge

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel-Induced Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pulling back a definite gauge makes every kernel direction, and only those directions, have zero gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the pullback gauge \(r=p\circ A\), its zero set is exactly \[\{x\in X:r(x)=0\}=A^{-1}(Z_p).\] Since \(A x=0\) for every \(x\in\ker A\) and every gauge satisfies \(p(0)=0\), one always has \(\ker A\subseteq A^{-1}(Z_p)\). If \(p\) is definite, meaning \(Z_p=\{0\}\), then \(r(x)=0\) holds exactly when \(x\in\ker A\). Hence the pullback descends to a definite gauge on \(X/\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z_{p\circ A}=A^{-1}(Z_p)\supseteq\ker A\), with equality to \(\ker A\) when \(Z_p=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of degeneracy created by a noninjective linear transport.

notation.meaning: zero set of the gauge p

knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Lines in Pullback Sublevels
Gauge Invariance Under Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex origin-containing set and its closure have the same gauge, whose closed unit sublevel is the closure of the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\) is a convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(0\in D\), then \[\gamma_D=\gamma_{\overline D}\qquad\text{and}\qquad \{y:\gamma_D(y)\leq1\}=\overline D.\] Hence for a nonclosed linear image \(A(C)\), its gauge unit sublevel recovers \(\overline{A(C)}\), not \(A(C)\).
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is convex in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma_D=\gamma_{\overline D},\qquad \{y:\gamma_D(y)\leq1\}=\overline D.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General mechanism by which a gauge loses missing boundary information from a convex origin-containing image.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Image Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set may have a nonclosed projection, whose gauge unit sublevel recovers the closure rather than the image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains the origin, but its projection is \(A(C)=[0,1)\), which is not closed. Its gauge is \[\gamma_{A(C)}(z)=\begin{cases}z,&z\geq0,\\+\infty,&z<0.\end{cases}\] Consequently \(\gamma_{A(C)}(1)=1\) although \(1\notin A(C)\), and \(\{z:\gamma_{A(C)}(z)\leq1\}=[0,1]=\overline{A(C)}\). Thus recovering an image set from the closed unit sublevel of its gauge silently closes a nonclosed radial boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(C)=[0,1)\) is not closed and \(\{z:\gamma_{A(C)}(z)\leq1\}=[0,1]\neq A(C)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional example showing that a closed convex set can have a nonclosed linear image.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sum and maximum gauges on a product space
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=E_1\times\cdots\times E_m\), and let \(\gamma_i:E_i\to[0,+\infty]\) be gauges with unit sets \(C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The canonical separable sum and Cartesian-product maximum constructions are covered for finitely many factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The product-space sum gauge and maximum gauge induced by \(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_m\) are \[\Gamma_1(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m\gamma_i(x_i),\qquad \Gamma_\infty(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\gamma_i(x_i).\] Both map \(E\) into \([0,+\infty]\) and are gauges. Their unit sets are \[C_{\Gamma_1}=\Big\{(x_i):\sum_i\gamma_i(x_i)\le1\Big\},\qquad C_{\Gamma_\infty}=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m.\] More generally, nonnegative weights \(w_i\) give \(\sum_iw_i\gamma_i(x_i)\), while positive weights give \(\max_i\gamma_i(x_i)/w_i\) with unit set \(\prod_i w_iC_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Product-space gauge calculus constructs a gauge on a Cartesian product from gauges on its factors. The sum construction measures the total component gauge, whereas the maximum construction measures the largest component gauge. The maximum gauge has exactly the Cartesian product of the component unit sets as its unit set. Weighted variants rescale the factors. The constructions remain meaningful for asymmetric, degenerate, or extended-valued component gauges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma_1=\sum_i\gamma_i\circ\pi_i\) and \(\Gamma_\infty=\max_i\gamma_i\circ\pi_i\) are gauges on \(\prod_iE_i\), with \(C_{\Gamma_\infty}=\prod_iC_i\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\Gamma_\infty=\gamma_{C_1\times\cdots\times C_m}\).
Each construction is a finite combination of the pullbacks \(\gamma_i\circ\pi_i\) through coordinate projections.
special_cases_latex: If every \(\gamma_i\) is a norm, both \(\Gamma_1\) and \(\Gamma_\infty\) are product-space norms.
For two factors, \(\Gamma_\infty(x_1,x_2)=\max\{\gamma_1(x_1),\gamma_2(x_2)\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The product gauge is finite exactly when all component gauges are finite at their respective coordinates.
The zero set of \(\Gamma_1\) or \(\Gamma_\infty\) is the product of the component zero sets.
boundary_notes: The sum-gauge unit set is generally not the Cartesian product of the component unit sets.
Infinite products require additional topological and summability choices and are excluded.

notation.meaning: Coordinate projection from the product space to its i-th factor.

source_refs.locator: §5, convexity-preserving sums, suprema, and composition with linear transformations, especially Theorem 5.7, extracted lines 1583–1630 and 1803–1825; §15, gauge definition, extracted lines 5159–5171

knowledge_statements.title: Polar of a Cartesian-Product Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity transforms the maximum gauge of a Cartesian product into the sum of the component polar gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\). Then \[\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)=\sigma_C(y)=\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_{C_i}(y_i)=\sum_{i=1}^m\gamma_{C_i^\circ}(y_i),\] and therefore \[C^\circ=\left\{y:\sum_{i=1}^m\gamma_{C_i^\circ}(y_i)\leq1\right\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subseteq X_i\) are nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)=\sum_{i=1}^m\gamma_{C_i^\circ}(y_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual formula for the Cartesian-product construction.

notation.meaning: unit polar of the Cartesian product
support function of the product set

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a Cartesian product is the maximum of the gauges of its component sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in X\), membership \(x\in tC\) is equivalent to \(x_i\in tC_i\) for every block \(i\). Therefore the product-set gauge satisfies \[\gamma_C(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\gamma_{C_i}(x_i),\] with the maximum interpreted in \([0,+\infty]\). In particular, the product gauge is finite exactly at points whose component gauges are all finite, and its unit sublevel is the Cartesian product of the component unit sublevels.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\) are real vector spaces and \(C_i\subseteq X_i\) are convex sets containing \(0\), for \(1\leq i\leq m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\gamma_{C_i}(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauge formula for a Cartesian product of convex origin-containing sets.

source_witnesses.locator: 9.5 Construction of Functions in \( {\Gamma }_{0}\left( \mathcal{H}\right) \) p. 166

knowledge_statements.title: Domain, Zero Set, and Definiteness of an Additive Block Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain and zero set of a positive additive block gauge decompose as products, so finiteness and definiteness hold exactly blockwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p_\Sigma(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i p_i(x_i)\) with \(\alpha_i>0\), \[\operatorname{dom}p_\Sigma=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}p_i,\qquad Z_{p_\Sigma}=\prod_{i=1}^m Z_{p_i}.\] Consequently, \(p_\Sigma\) is finite if and only if every \(p_i\) is finite, and it is definite if and only if every \(p_i\) is definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}p_\Sigma=\prod_i\operatorname{dom}p_i,\quad Z_{p_\Sigma}=\prod_iZ_{p_i}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural decomposition inherited from positive additive block separation.

notation.meaning: zero set of the ith component gauge
positive weighted sum of component gauges

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Separable Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive weighted sum of component gauges is the gauge of the corresponding shared-budget unit set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\), define \(p_{\Sigma}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i p_i(x_i)\). This function is convex, positively homogeneous, and vanishes at the origin, hence is an extended-valued gauge. For its unit set \[B_1=\left\{x\in X:\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i p_i(x_i)\leq1\right\},\] one has \(\gamma_{B_1}=p_{\Sigma}\). Thus additive block separation corresponds to a single scalar budget shared among the component gauges.
assumptions_latex: \(p_i:X_i\to[0,+\infty]\) are gauges on real vector spaces \(X_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{B_1}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i p_i(x_i)\), where \(B_1=\{x:\sum_i\alpha_ip_i(x_i)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted additive aggregation of independent block gauges.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Sum of Two Functions p. 61

knowledge_statements.title: Polar of Weighted Ell-r Block Aggregation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of weighted ell-r block aggregation is the ell-s aggregation of component polar gauges with reciprocal weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_i\) be gauges on finite-dimensional spaces with compact unit sets, let \(\alpha_i>0\), and define \[p_r(x)=\left(\sum_i(\alpha_i p_i(x_i))^r\right)^{1/r}\] for \(1\leq r<\infty\), with \(p_\infty(x)=\max_i\alpha_i p_i(x_i)\). If \(s\) is conjugate to \(r\), then \[p_r^\circ(y)=\left(\sum_i\left(\frac{p_i^\circ(y_i)}{\alpha_i}\right)^s\right)^{1/s},\] using the usual maximum interpretation when \(s=\infty\).
assumptions_latex: Each \(p_i\) is a finite-dimensional gauge with compact unit set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_r^\circ(y)=\left\|\left(p_i^\circ(y_i)/\alpha_i\right)_{i=1}^m\right\|_s.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-exponent formula for component gauges with compact unit sets.

notation.meaning: polar gauge of the ith component gauge

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Outer-Gauge Aggregation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex, homogeneous, coordinatewise monotone outer functional aggregates independent block gauges into a product-space gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_i:X_i\to[0,+\infty)\) be finite gauges and let \(\Phi:\mathbb R_+^m\to[0,+\infty)\) be convex, positively homogeneous, coordinatewise nondecreasing, and satisfy \(\Phi(0)=0\). Then \[p_\Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\Phi(p_1(x_1),\ldots,p_m(x_m))\] is a gauge on \(\prod_iX_i\).
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is convex, positively homogeneous, coordinatewise nondecreasing on \(\mathbb R_+^m\), and \(\Phi(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_\Phi=\Phi\circ(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\text{ is a gauge}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General construction encompassing finite block ell-r aggregation without imposing additive separability.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Aggregation Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block gauges aggregated with different ell-r rules are equivalent, with constants determined by the number of blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(1\leq r<\infty\), define \[p_r(x)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i(x_i)^r\right)^{1/r},\] and define \(p_\infty(x)=\max_i p_i(x_i)\). Each \(p_r\) is a gauge on \(X\). For \(1\leq r\leq s\leq\infty\), the standard finite-dimensional norm comparison applied to the nonnegative vector \((p_i(x_i))_{i=1}^m\) yields \[p_s(x)\leq p_r(x)\leq m^{1/r-1/s}p_s(x).\] The endpoints are respectively additive aggregation when \(r=1\) and maximum aggregation when \(r=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_s(x)\leq p_r(x)\leq m^{1/r-1/s}p_s(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of finite-block \(\ell_r\) gauge aggregation regimes.

notation.meaning: ell-r aggregation of component gauge values

source_witnesses.locator: 9.5 Construction of Functions in \( {\Gamma }_{0}\left( \mathcal{H}\right) \) p. 166

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Block-Symmetry Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge depends only on separate Euclidean block radii exactly when it is invariant under independent orthogonal transformations within each block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb R^{d_i}\) and let \(p:X\to[0,+\infty)\) be a finite gauge. There exists \(\Phi:\mathbb R_+^m\to[0,+\infty)\) such that \[p(x)=\Phi(\|x_1\|_2,\ldots,\|x_m\|_2)\] if and only if \(p(Q_1x_1,\ldots,Q_mx_m)=p(x)\) for every \(Q_i\in O(d_i)\). When this holds, \(\Phi\) is uniquely determined and is convex, positively homogeneous, and coordinatewise nondecreasing on \(\mathbb R_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p=\Phi(\|\cdot\|_2,\ldots,\|\cdot\|_2)\iff p(Q_1x_1,\ldots,Q_mx_m)=p(x)\ \forall Q_i\in O(d_i).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional criterion for dependence only on Euclidean block radii.

notation.meaning: orthogonal group acting on block i
induced outer functional on block radii

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-Block Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero cross term creates a gauge that no aggregation depending only on separate block magnitudes can represent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The positive-definite quadratic form defining \(p_\rho\) makes it a norm and hence a gauge. Nevertheless, \[p_\rho(1,1)=\sqrt{2+2\rho}\neq\sqrt{2-2\rho}=p_\rho(1,-1).\] Any expression \(\Phi(|x_1|,|x_2|)\) takes equal values at \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\). Therefore this coupled gauge cannot be recovered by applying a scalar aggregation rule solely to the separate block radii \(|x_1|\) and \(|x_2|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_\rho\) cannot be expressed as \(\Phi(|x_1|,|x_2|)\) for any \(\Phi:[0,+\infty)^2\to[0,+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross terms mark the boundary of aggregation based only on separate block radii.

children.top_down_role: Passage between asymmetric and balanced gauge models.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersection and convex-hull balancing of a gauge
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be finite dimensional, let \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge, and let \(C=\{x:\gamma(x)\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two canonical symmetrizations are defined. They produce symmetric gauges but need not be definite or finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The intersection-balanced gauge and hull-balanced gauge associated with \(\gamma\) are \[\gamma_{\cap}(x)=\max\{\gamma(x),\gamma(-x)\}=\gamma_{C\cap(-C)}(x),\] and \[\gamma_{\mathrm{h}}(x)=\inf_{u-v=x}\big(\gamma(u)+\gamma(v)\big).\] After lower-semicontinuous closure when necessary, \[\operatorname{cl}\gamma_{\mathrm{h}}=\gamma_{\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup(-C))}.\] Both balanced gauges satisfy \(\gamma_{\cap}(-x)=\gamma_{\cap}(x)\) and \((\operatorname{cl}\gamma_{\mathrm{h}})(-x)=(\operatorname{cl}\gamma_{\mathrm{h}})(x)\). The intersection balance is the larger symmetric gauge, while the hull balance is the smaller symmetric closed gauge generated by \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balancing converts an asymmetric gauge into a symmetric one. Intersection balancing takes the maximum of the forward and reverse gauges; its unit set is the intersection of the original unit set with its reflection. Hull balancing uses an infimal decomposition into a forward and a reverse component; after closure, its unit set is the closed convex hull of the original unit set and its reflection. The first construction tightens the unit set, while the second enlarges it.
assumptions_latex: Lower-semicontinuous closure is taken for the hull balance if the convex hull is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\cap}=\gamma_{C\cap(-C)}\) and \(\operatorname{cl}\gamma_{\mathrm h}=\gamma_{\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(C\cup(-C))}\) are symmetric gauges.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\gamma_{\mathrm h}=\gamma\square(\gamma\circ(-I))\).
Balancing is reflection followed respectively by intersection or closed convex-hull aggregation of unit sets.
special_cases_latex: If \(\gamma(-x)=\gamma(x)\), both balancing operations return \(\gamma\) when \(\gamma\) is closed.
If the balanced unit set is bounded and contains \(0\) in its interior, the balanced gauge is a norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\gamma_{\mathrm h}(x)\le\gamma(x)\le\gamma_{\cap}(x)\).
Both constructions remove directional asymmetry but may preserve nontrivial zero directions.
boundary_notes: Symmetry alone does not guarantee definiteness or finiteness.
Closure is essential when \(\operatorname{conv}(C\cup(-C))\) is not closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Symmetrization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combining a gauge and its reverse through a symmetric monotone homogeneous convex aggregator produces an even gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the reverse gauge by \(p^\vee(x)=p(-x)\). Given \(\Phi\) as assumed, set \[s_\Phi(x)=\Phi\bigl(p(x),p^\vee(x)\bigr).\] Convexity, positive homogeneity, and coordinatewise monotonicity of \(\Phi\), together with the gauge properties of \(p\) and \(p^\vee\), make \(s_\Phi\) a gauge. Swap invariance gives \(s_\Phi(-x)=s_\Phi(x)\). Thus \(s_\Phi\) is a symmetric gauge; choosing \(\Phi(a,b)=\max\{a,b\}\) or \(\Phi(a,b)=a+b\) gives the two canonical constructions.
assumptions_latex: \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge on a real vector space.
\(\Phi:[0,+\infty]^2\to[0,+\infty]\) is convex, positively homogeneous, coordinatewise nondecreasing, and invariant under swapping its arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_\Phi(x)=\Phi(p(x),p(-x))\) is an even gauge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general scalar-aggregation framework containing maximum and sum symmetrizations.

source_witnesses.locator: 9.5 Construction of Functions in \( {\Gamma }_{0}\left( \mathcal{H}\right) \) p. 166

knowledge_statements.title: Balanced-Hull Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balancing a convex set means adjoining its negative and convexifying; the new gauge is an infimal decomposition of the old gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The balanced convex hull of \(C\) is \[C_{\mathrm{bal}}=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(C\cup(-C)\bigr).\] It is the smallest convex centrally symmetric set containing \(C\). Its gauge admits the decomposition formula \[\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{bal}}}(x)=\inf\{p(u)+p(v):u-v=x\}.\] The infimum is taken over \(u,v\in X\) and may be unattained. Moreover, \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{bal}}}\) is the greatest even gauge \(q\) satisfying \(q(x)\leq p(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(C\subseteq X\) is convex with \(0\in C\).
\(p=\gamma_C\) is the extended-valued Minkowski gauge of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\operatorname{conv}(C\cup(-C))}(x)=\inf_{u-v=x}\bigl(p(u)+p(v)\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-space balanced hull and its infimal-decomposition gauge formula.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Based Symmetrization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the maximum of a gauge and its reverse yields the gauge of the unit set intersected with its reflection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[p_{\max}(x)=\max\{p(x),p(-x)\}.\] Then \(p_{\max}\) is an even gauge. Because closedness and absorption give \(C=\{x:p(x)\leq1\}\), its unit set is \[\{x:p_{\max}(x)\leq1\}=C\cap(-C).\] Consequently \(p_{\max}=\gamma_{C\cap(-C)}\). It is also the least even gauge \(q\) satisfying \(q(x)\geq p(x)\) for every \(x\), since evenness forces \(q(x)\geq p(-x)\) as well.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(C\subseteq X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_{\max}(x)=\max\{p(x),p(-x)\}=\gamma_{C\cap(-C)}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical symmetrization by maximum, corresponding to intersection with the reflected unit set.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5 Maximum of Functions p. 123

knowledge_statements.title: Sum-Based Symmetrization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a gauge to its reverse produces an even gauge lying between the maximum symmetrization and twice that maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the additive symmetrization by \[p_\Sigma(x)=p(x)+p(-x).\] The function \(p_\Sigma\) is convex, positively homogeneous, and even, so it is a symmetric gauge. With \(B_\Sigma=\{x:p_\Sigma(x)\leq1\}\), positive homogeneity gives \(p_\Sigma=\gamma_{B_\Sigma}\). If \(p_{\max}(x)=\max\{p(x),p(-x)\}\), then for every \(x\in X\), \[p_{\max}(x)\leq p_\Sigma(x)\leq2p_{\max}(x).\] Thus the sum and maximum symmetrizations are equivalent with universal constants.
assumptions_latex: \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge on a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_\Sigma(x)=p(x)+p(-x)=\gamma_{B_\Sigma}(x)\), and \(p_{\max}\leq p_\Sigma\leq2p_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical additive symmetrization and its comparison with maximum symmetrization.

notation.meaning: unit set of the sum symmetrization

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1 Sum of Functions p. 113

knowledge_statements.title: Reflection-Orbit Nonidentifiability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every swap-invariant symmetrization identifies a gauge with its reflection, so directional orientation is unrecoverable unless the gauge is already even.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^\vee(x)=p(-x)\), and let \(\Phi:[0,+\infty]^2\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfy \(\Phi(a,b)=\Phi(b,a)\). If \(S_\Phi p(x)=\Phi(p(x),p^\vee(x))\), then \[S_\Phi(p^\vee)=S_\Phi(p).\] Thus whenever \(p\ne p^\vee\), symmetrization cannot distinguish the two reflected gauges.
assumptions_latex: \(p:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge on a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_\Phi(p^\vee)=S_\Phi(p),\qquad p\ne p^\vee\Longrightarrow S_\Phi\text{ is noninjective on }\{p,p^\vee\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-loss boundary for any swap-invariant scalar symmetrization of a gauge and its reverse.

notation.meaning: symmetrization induced by the swap-invariant aggregator \(\Phi\)

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetry Information Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional family showing that gauge symmetrization is noninjective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,b>0\), define the asymmetric gauge on \(\mathbb R\) by \[g_{a,b}(x):=\begin{cases}x/a,&x\ge0,\\-x/b,&x<0.\end{cases}\] If \(a\ne b\), then \(g_{a,b}\ne g_{b,a}\), but both gauges have identical symmetrizations: \[\max\{g_{a,b}(x),g_{a,b}(-x)\}=\frac{|x|}{\min\{a,b\}},\qquad g_{a,b}(x)+g_{a,b}(-x)=|x|\left(\frac1a+\frac1b\right).\] Consequently neither maximum-based nor sum-based symmetrization determines the orientation of the original gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Swapping the two directional scales changes an asymmetric gauge but leaves both its maximum and sum symmetrizations unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_{a,b}\ne g_{b,a}\), while their maximum-based and sum-based symmetrizations coincide.

notation.meaning: gauge with positive and negative directional scales a and b

children.title: Functional Gauge Polarity
children.top_down_role: Functional polarity connecting gauges, support functions, polar unit sets, and dual norms.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\) with dual \(E^*\) and pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle\). Let \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-valued gauges are covered, including asymmetric and degenerate gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar gauge of \(\gamma\) is the function \(\gamma^\circ:E^*\to[0,+\infty]\) defined by \[\gamma^\circ(y)=\inf\{\mu\ge0:\langle x,y\rangle\le\mu\gamma(x)\ \text{for every }x\in E\}.\] Equivalently, with \(C_\gamma=\{x:\gamma(x)\le1\}\), \[\gamma^\circ(y)=\sup_{x\in C_\gamma}\langle x,y\rangle=\sigma_{C_\gamma}(y)=\gamma_{C_\gamma^\circ}(y),\] where \(C_\gamma^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C_\gamma\}\). The polar gauge is always closed, even when \(\gamma\) is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of a gauge is the smallest nonnegative factor that makes the pairing bounded by that factor times the original gauge for every primal vector. It is equivalently the support function of the primal unit set and the Minkowski functional of that unit set's polar. This definition accommodates infinite values and zero directions; no symmetry or norm assumptions are required. Functional polarity therefore matches set polarity at the level of unit sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma^\circ(y)=\inf\{\mu\ge0:\langle x,y\rangle\le\mu\gamma(x)\ \forall x\}=\sigma_{C_\gamma}(y)=\gamma_{C_\gamma^\circ}(y)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(0<\gamma(x)<+\infty\) for every \(x\ne0\), then \(\gamma^\circ(y)=\sup_{x\ne0}\langle x,y\rangle/\gamma(x)\).
\(C_{\gamma^\circ}=C_\gamma^\circ\).
special_cases_latex: For a norm, \(\gamma^\circ\) is its dual norm.
For \(\gamma=\gamma_C\) with closed convex \(C\ni0\), \(\gamma^\circ=\gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\gamma^\circ\) is a closed gauge.
Functional polarity reverses pointwise order: \(\gamma_1\le\gamma_2\) implies \(\gamma_1^\circ\ge\gamma_2^\circ\).
boundary_notes: The ratio formula is unsuitable when the primal gauge has nonzero zero directions or infinite values; the quantified definition remains valid.
The polar gauge is not the Fenchel conjugate of a gauge.

children.top_down_role: Reciprocal representation of support and Minkowski functionals through polar sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Support–Minkowski Reciprocity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a closed convex set is its polar's support function, while its support function is its polar's gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\) and \(y\in X^*\), polarity and the bipolar theorem give the reciprocal representations \[\gamma_C(x)=\sup_{y\in C^\circ}\langle y,x\rangle=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x),\qquad \sigma_C(y)=\inf\{t>0:y\in tC^\circ\}=\gamma_{C^\circ}(y).\] Both equalities are interpreted in \([0,+\infty]\); consequently they remain valid when \(C\) is nonabsorbing or unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\) and \(\sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ}\), with extended-real values allowed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real reciprocity, including nonabsorbing and unbounded sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocity between support functions and Minkowski functionals
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex with \(0\in C\). Define \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets containing the origin are covered; boundedness, symmetry, and absorption are unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Support–Minkowski reciprocity is the pair of identities \[\gamma_C(x)=\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)=\sup_{y\in C^\circ}\langle x,y\rangle,\] \[\sigma_C(y)=\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)=\inf\{t\ge0:y\in tC^\circ\}.\] Hence the Minkowski functional of a closed convex set containing the origin is the support function of its polar, while its support function is the Minkowski functional of its polar. Both identities are extended-real identities and remain valid for unbounded or nonabsorbing sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set containing the origin, the Minkowski functional equals the support function of the polar set, and the support function equals the Minkowski functional of the polar set. The equalities use extended values, so neither compactness nor an interior-point assumption is needed. This reciprocity identifies set polarity with the exchange between unit-set and supported-set representations of closed gauges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\) and \(\sigma_C=\gamma_{C^\circ}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C=\{x:\sigma_{C^\circ}(x)\le1\}\).
\(C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is a norm unit ball, the two identities become the usual primal-dual norm formulas.
If \(C\) is unbounded, \(\sigma_C\) and \(\gamma_{C^\circ}\) may both take \(+\infty\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\).
Every closed gauge is the support function of the polar of its unit set.
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed or nonconvex set, bipolar closure replaces the original set.
If \(0\notin C\), the stated Minkowski-polar reciprocity does not apply in this form.
