children.title: Polar-Gauge Inequality Family
children.top_down_role: The generalized dual-pair inequality associated with a gauge and its polar.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality and Subgradient Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality in the polar-gauge inequality is equivalent to the normalized dual vector being a subgradient of the primal gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma\) be a proper lower-semicontinuous convex gauge and let \(\gamma^\circ\) be its polar. If \(0<\gamma(x)<+\infty\) and \(0<\gamma^\circ(y)<+\infty\), then \[\langle y,x\rangle=\gamma(x)\gamma^\circ(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{y}{\gamma^\circ(y)}\in\partial\gamma(x).\] Equivalently, \(z\in\partial\gamma(x)\) exactly when \(\gamma^\circ(z)\leq1\) and \(\langle z,x\rangle=\gamma(x)\).
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle y,x\rangle=\gamma(x)\gamma^\circ(y)\iff y/\gamma^\circ(y)\in\partial\gamma(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact saturation condition for the polar-gauge inequality at finite positive values.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the gauge at x

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetry Obstructs an Absolute-Value Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymmetric interval gives a concrete failure of the absolute-value polar-gauge inequality while preserving the one-sided inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[-1,2]\subset\mathbb{R}\). Then \(C^\circ=[-1,1/2]\). For \(x=2\) and \(y=-1\), \[\gamma_C(x)=1,\qquad \gamma_{C^\circ}(y)=1,\qquad |yx|=2>1=\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y),\] although the valid one-sided inequality \(yx\leq\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\langle y,x\rangle|\leq\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)\) fails in general for asymmetric gauges.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional counterexample showing that the generalized inequality cannot generally contain an absolute value.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Gauge Inequality Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual pairing is bounded above by the product of a gauge and its polar gauge; asymmetry prevents an absolute-value bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar-gauge inequality is \[\langle y,x\rangle\leq\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y).\] More generally, whenever \(x\in aC\) and \(y\in bC^\circ\) for \(a,b\geq0\), one has \(\langle y,x\rangle\leq ab\). Taking infima over admissible positive \(a\) and \(b\) yields the displayed inequality. Because the gauges need not be symmetric, no corresponding bound for \(|\langle y,x\rangle|\) follows without additional balance assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
\(x\in X\) and \(y\in X^*\) have finite polar-gauge values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle y,x\rangle\leq\gamma_C(x)\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided generalized Hölder inequality for possibly asymmetric gauges.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(E^*\) be its dual, and let \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge with polar \(\gamma^\circ:E^*\to[0,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The inequality is stated for asymmetric, degenerate, and extended-valued gauges. Its informative finite form applies on the effective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar-gauge inequality associated with \(\gamma\) is \[\langle x,y\rangle\le\gamma(x)\gamma^\circ(y)\qquad\bigl(x\in\operatorname{dom}\gamma,\ y\in\operatorname{dom}\gamma^\circ\bigr).\] Equivalently, \[\gamma^\circ(y)=\inf\{\mu\ge0:\langle x,y\rangle\le\mu\gamma(x)\ \forall x\in E\}.\] When \(0<\gamma(x)<+\infty\) for every nonzero \(x\), this becomes \[\gamma^\circ(y)=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{\gamma(x)}=\sup_{\gamma(x)\le1}\langle x,y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every gauge and its polar determine a generalized dual-pair inequality: the pairing of a primal vector and a dual vector is at most the product of their gauge values. The polar gauge is the smallest function making all such inequalities valid. In the finite definite regime it is the supremum of the pairing-to-gauge ratio, or equivalently the support over the primal unit set. No absolute value appears unless symmetry is separately imposed.
assumptions_latex: For the ratio formula, \(0<\gamma(x)<+\infty\) for all \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x,y\rangle\le\gamma(x)\gamma^\circ(y)\) on \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma\times\operatorname{dom}\gamma^\circ\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\gamma^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle:\gamma(x)\le1\}\).
\(y\in tC_\gamma^\circ\iff\langle x,y\rangle\le t\gamma(x)\) for every \(x\).
special_cases_latex: For a norm, applying the inequality to \(y\) and \(-y\) gives \(|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|_*\).
For the Euclidean gauge, it is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\gamma(x)=0\), then \(\langle x,y\rangle\le0\) for every \(y\in\operatorname{dom}\gamma^\circ\).
The unit sets satisfy \(C_{\gamma^\circ}=C_\gamma^\circ\).
boundary_notes: For asymmetric gauges, replacing the left side by its absolute value is generally false.
Products involving \(+\infty\) are avoided by restricting the displayed inequality to effective domains.

notation.meaning: Set on which the gauge is finite.

children.title: Dual Norms as Polar Gauges
children.top_down_role: Norm duality as the symmetric definite specialization of gauge polarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Bidual Norm Recovery and Norming Functionals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal norm is the attained support function of the dual unit ball, and finite-dimensional bidualization recovers it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \[\|x\|=\max_{\|y\|_*\leq1}\langle y,x\rangle.\] If \(x\neq0\), some \(y\in X^*\) satisfies \(\|y\|_*=1\) and \(\langle y,x\rangle=\|x\|\). Under the canonical embedding \(X\hookrightarrow X^{**}\), the bidual norm therefore equals the original norm.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-specialized recovery from the polar unit ball, including finite-dimensional attainment.

notation.meaning: bidual norm under the canonical embedding
norming functional when equality is attained

knowledge_statements.title: Polar Gauges of Finite-Dimensional Ell-p Balls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of an ell-p unit ball is the conjugate-exponent ell-q ball, including the ell-one/ell-infinity endpoints and Euclidean self-duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(1\leq p\leq\infty\) and choose \(q\) with \(1/p+1/q=1\), using \(1/\infty=0\). Then \[B_p^\circ=B_q,\qquad \gamma_{B_p}(x)=\|x\|_p,\qquad \gamma_{B_p^\circ}(y)=\|y\|_q.\] In particular, \(B_1^\circ=B_\infty\), \(B_\infty^\circ=B_1\), and \(B_2\) is self-polar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_p^\circ=B_q\) and \(\gamma_{B_p^\circ}=\|\cdot\|_q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical coordinate-norm specialization of polar-gauge norm duality.

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of the ell-p norm

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Norms as Polar Gauges
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm and its dual are exactly the Minkowski gauges of a symmetric unit ball and its polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski functional of \(B\) is the original norm, \(\gamma_B(x)=\|x\|\). Its polar is \[B^\circ=\{y\in X^*: \langle y,x\rangle\leq1\ \text{for every }x\in B\}=\{y\in X^*: \|y\|_*\leq1\}.\] Consequently \(\gamma_{B^\circ}(y)=\|y\|_*\), where \(\|y\|_* =\sup_{\|x\|\leq1}\langle y,x\rangle\), and the polar-gauge inequality becomes the usual dual-norm Hölder inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real normed space with dual \(X^*\).
\(B=\{x\in X:\|x\|\leq1\}\) is the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_B=\|\cdot\|\) and \(\gamma_{B^\circ}=\|\cdot\|_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric, absorbing, and definite specialization of gauge polarity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual norm as the polar of a norm gauge
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\) with norm \(\|\cdot\|\), dual space \(E^*\), and primal unit ball \(B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm duality is treated as the symmetric, finite, definite specialization of gauge polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual norm is the polar gauge of the primal norm: \[\|y\|_*:=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\langle x,y\rangle=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{|\langle x,y\rangle|}{\|x\|}=\gamma_{B^\circ}(y)=\sigma_B(y),\] where \[B^\circ=\{y\in E^*:|\langle x,y\rangle|\le1\ \forall x\in B\}.\] Because \(B=-B\), the one-sided support supremum equals the absolute-value supremum. The dual unit ball is \(B_*=B^\circ\), and the polar of \(\|\cdot\|_*\) recovers \(\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual norm is precisely the polar gauge of the original norm. It is the largest pairing with a vector in the primal unit ball, the Minkowski functional of the polar unit ball, and the support function of the primal unit ball. Symmetry permits the equivalent absolute-value formula. The dual unit ball is the set polar of the primal unit ball, and applying norm polarity twice recovers the original norm.
assumptions_latex: The pairing identifies dual vectors with linear functionals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\cdot\|_*=(\|\cdot\|)^\circ=\sigma_B=\gamma_{B^\circ}\), and \(B_*=B^\circ\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\|y\|_*=\inf\{t\ge0:y\in tB^\circ\}\).
\(\|y\|_*=\sup_{x\ne0}|\langle x,y\rangle|/\|x\|\).
special_cases_latex: The dual of \(\|\cdot\|_1\) is \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\), and conversely.
The Euclidean norm is self-polar under the Euclidean pairing.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|_*\).
\(\|x\|=\sup_{\|y\|_*\le1}\langle x,y\rangle\).
boundary_notes: The absolute-value formula relies on symmetry and does not define the polar of a general asymmetric gauge.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the bidual identification and compactness issues require additional care.

notation.meaning: Polar of the primal unit ball.

children.title: Polar-Gauge Bipolarity
children.top_down_role: Recovery of closed gauges under repeated functional polarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipolar Recovery as Lower-Semicontinuous Envelope
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without lower semicontinuity, double functional polarity returns the closed gauge envelope rather than the original gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a proper convex positively homogeneous function with \(\gamma(0)=0\), not necessarily lower semicontinuous. Then \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex gauge majorized by \(\gamma\): \[\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\gamma\leq\gamma.\] Consequently \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\gamma\) if and only if \(\gamma\) is lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is proper, convex, positively homogeneous, and satisfies \(\gamma(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\gamma\), with exact recovery if and only if \(\gamma\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp recovery statement when the original convex gauge is not lower semicontinuous.

notation.meaning: lower-semicontinuous convex closure of the gauge

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Gauge Bipolarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying functional gauge polarity twice recovers every proper lower-semicontinuous convex gauge exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\gamma^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:\gamma(x)\leq1\}\) and apply the same construction to \(\gamma^\circ\). Then \[\gamma^{\circ\circ}(x)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:\gamma^\circ(y)\leq1\}=\gamma(x)\qquad(x\in X).\] Equivalently, if \(C=\{x:\gamma(x)\leq1\}\), then \(C\) is closed, convex, contains \(0\), and \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\). Lower semicontinuity is essential for exact rather than closed-envelope recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(\gamma:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, positively homogeneous, and satisfies \(\gamma(0)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}(x)=\gamma(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bipolar recovery for closed extended-real gauges.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\gamma:\mathbb{R}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge, and define \(\gamma^\circ\) by functional polarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional gauges are covered without assuming initial lower semicontinuity. Closure is epigraphical lower-semicontinuous closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bipolar gauge is \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=(\gamma^\circ)^\circ\). Gauge bipolarity states that \[\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\gamma,\] where \(\operatorname{cl}\gamma\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by no larger closed epigraphical extension, equivalently the function whose epigraph is \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}\gamma)\). Consequently, \[\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\gamma\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma\text{ is closed}.\] If \(C=\{x:\gamma(x)\le1\}\), then \(\gamma^\circ=\gamma_{C^\circ}\) and the unit set of \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}\) is \(C^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}C\) for convex \(C\ni0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying functional gauge polarity twice returns the lower-semicontinuous closure of the original gauge. Thus closed gauges are exactly the fixed points of bipolarization. At the unit-set level, the operation corresponds to taking the set polar twice, which closes the convex unit set containing the origin. The statement includes extended-valued and degenerate gauges and does not require norm properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\gamma\), hence \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\gamma\) exactly for closed gauges.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\gamma^{\circ\circ})=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}\gamma)\).
For \(C=\{x:\gamma(x)\le1\}\), \(C_{\gamma^{\circ\circ}}=C^{\circ\circ}\).
special_cases_latex: Every norm is closed, so its double polar is itself.
If \(\gamma=\gamma_C\) for closed convex \(C\ni0\), then \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\gamma_C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar \(\gamma^\circ\) is always closed.
Functional polarity is an involution on the class of closed gauges.
boundary_notes: A nonclosed gauge is not generally recovered pointwise before closure.
This bipolar operation is functional gauge polarity, not Fenchel biconjugation, although both encode closure phenomena.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain and zero-set boundaries of a degenerate gauge pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and contain \(0\). Put \(\gamma=\gamma_C\) and \(\gamma^\circ=\gamma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records the degeneracies caused by nonabsorption, recession directions, and nonclosed gauges; it does not impose norm-like regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The degeneracy data of the polar-gauge pair are the effective domains and zero cones \[D=\operatorname{dom}\gamma=\operatorname{cone}C,\qquad Z=\{x:\gamma(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C,\] \[D^\circ=\operatorname{dom}\gamma^\circ=\operatorname{cone}(C^\circ),\qquad Z^\circ=\{y:\gamma^\circ(y)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}(C^\circ).\] Thus \(C\) is absorbing exactly when \(D=\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\gamma\) is definite exactly when \(Z=\{0\}\). If an initial gauge is not closed, polarity discards the nonclosed boundary data because \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge can fail to behave like a norm in three independent ways. It can be infinite outside the cone generated by its unit set, vanish on nonzero recession directions of that set, or fail to be lower semicontinuous. The polar gauge has analogous domain and zero-set data determined by the polar unit set. Double polarity retains only the closed gauge. These domain, zero-cone, and closure features define the degenerate boundary regime.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and \(0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma=\operatorname{cone}C\), \(\{\gamma=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C\), and the analogous identities hold for \(\gamma^\circ\) and \(C^\circ\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\gamma\) is finite everywhere iff \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
\(\gamma\) is a norm iff \(C\) is symmetric, bounded, and contains \(0\) in its interior.
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) contains a line, then \(\gamma\) vanishes along that line.
If \(C\) is nonabsorbing, \(\gamma(x)=+\infty\) for some \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonzero elements of \(Z\) pair nonpositively with every element of \(D^\circ\).
Nonclosed gauge boundary values cannot be reconstructed from the polar without taking closure.
boundary_notes: The equality \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma=\operatorname{cone}C\) uses the union of positive dilates; this cone need not be closed.
Degeneracy does not prevent the polar from being a closed gauge.

notation.meaning: Effective domain and zero cone of the primal gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: A Gauge with Nonclosed Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the square generates a gauge whose domain is the open upper half-plane together with the origin, so a gauge domain need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v\ge u^2\}\). Then \(C\) is closed and convex and contains \(0\), while \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\operatorname{cone}C=\{(u,v):v>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] and \[\gamma_C(u,v)=\begin{cases}u^2/v,&v>0,\\0,&(u,v)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Thus the effective domain is a nonclosed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\{(u,v):v>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional example showing that a closed convex generator may have a nonclosed gauge domain.

notation.meaning: Closed convex epigraph generating the gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Gauge Domains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is finite exactly on the positive cone generated by its defining set; nonabsorbed directions receive value infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \(\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\) holds exactly when \(x\in tC\) for some \(t>0\). Therefore \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\bigcup_{t>0}tC=\operatorname{cone}C,\qquad x\notin\operatorname{cone}C\Longrightarrow\gamma_C(x)=+\infty.\] Thus failure of absorption appears precisely as a proper effective domain; convexity makes this domain a convex cone, though it need not be closed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\operatorname{cone}C\), and \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\) outside this cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective-domain characterization for a possibly nonabsorbing gauge set.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Test and Barrier-Cone Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive pairing with a recession direction certifies an infinite polar value, while the recession-polar condition only characterizes the closure of the finite-value domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq X\) be nonempty, closed, and convex and let \(\gamma^\circ=\sigma_U\). Then \[\overline{\operatorname{dom}\gamma^\circ}=(\operatorname{rec}U)^-=\{y\in X^*: \langle y,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in\operatorname{rec}U\}.\] Hence \(\langle y,d\rangle>0\) for some \(d\in\operatorname{rec}U\) implies \(\gamma^\circ(y)=+\infty\). Membership in \((\operatorname{rec}U)^-\) need not imply finiteness; exact finiteness is membership in \(\operatorname{bar}U\).
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{dom}\sigma_U}=(\operatorname{rec}U)^-\), and positive pairing with a recession direction implies \(\sigma_U(y)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-direction certificate for an infinite polar value and the sharp limitation of that certificate.

notation.meaning: negative polar cone of the recession cone
barrier cone, equal to the effective domain of the support function

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Polar Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polar gauge is infinite precisely outside the barrier cone of the original gauge's unit sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Since \(\gamma^\circ=\sigma_U\), its effective domain is the barrier cone of \(U\): \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma^\circ=\operatorname{bar}U=\{y\in X^*: \sup_{x\in U}\langle y,x\rangle<+\infty\}.\] Consequently \(\gamma^\circ(y)=+\infty\) if and only if \(U\) is unbounded in directions on which \(y\) has arbitrarily large positive pairing. Unboundedness alone does not force infinity for every dual vector.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge with unit sublevel set \(U=\{x:\gamma(x)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma^\circ(y)=+\infty\) exactly when \(y\notin\operatorname{bar}U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain boundary for an extended-valued polar gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonabsorption Produces Polar Nondefiniteness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal set is nonabsorbing exactly when its polar gauge has a nonzero zero direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq X\) containing \(0\), \[C\text{ is nonabsorbing}\iff C^\circ\text{ is unbounded}\iff\operatorname{rec}(C^\circ)\neq\{0\}\iff\{y:\gamma_{C^\circ}(y)=0\}\neq\{0\}.\] Thus failure of primal absorption is equivalent, in finite dimensions, to failure of definiteness of the polar gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is nonabsorbing if and only if \(\gamma_{C^\circ}\) is nondefinite.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonabsorption-Induced Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonabsorption is exactly the failure of everywhere-finite gauging and, in finite dimensions, exactly the emergence of an unbounded polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following are equivalent: \(C\) is absorbing; \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\); \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=X\); and \(C^\circ\) is bounded. Hence if \(C\) is not absorbing, some \(x\in X\) satisfies \(\gamma_C(x)=+\infty\), and the polar set possesses an unbounded sequence. This identifies nonabsorption as the exact boundary at which a finite gauge and bounded polar cease to be available.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is absorbing if and only if \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere, if and only if \(C^\circ\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between absorption, gauge finiteness, and polar boundedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonabsorption Produces Dual Nondefiniteness
Definiteness–Boundedness–Polar Absorption Equivalence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-set gauge is definite exactly when its unit set is bounded, equivalently when its polar is absorbing and has an everywhere-finite gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subseteq X\) containing \(0\), the following are equivalent: \[\gamma_C(x)=0\Rightarrow x=0;\qquad \operatorname{rec}C=\{0\};\qquad C\text{ is bounded};\qquad C^\circ\text{ is absorbing};\qquad \operatorname{dom}\gamma_{C^\circ}=X.\] Hence nondefiniteness of the primal gauge is exactly failure of absorption, and therefore failure of everywhere-finite gauging, on the polar side.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C\) is definite if and only if \(C\) is bounded, if and only if \(C^\circ\) is absorbing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional criterion for definiteness of a closed-set gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Nondefiniteness-Induced Polarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge vanishes on exactly the recession cone, which polarity describes through nonpositive pairing with every polar vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge's zero cone is exactly the recession cone: \[Z_C=\{x\in X:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C.\] Support–Minkowski reciprocity also gives \[Z_C=\{x\in X:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }y\in C^\circ\}.\] Thus \(\gamma_C\) is definite precisely when \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\); any nonzero zero direction forces the entire polar into its associated nonpositive halfspace.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C=\{x:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in C^\circ\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polarity description of directions where a gauge fails definiteness.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Polarity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity ignores missing boundary points: the double polar returns the closed convex hull, not a nonclosed original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ordinary polarity cannot distinguish \(A\) from its closed convex hull: \[A^\circ=(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}A)^\circ,\qquad A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}A.\] Therefore repeated polarity recovers \(A\) exactly if and only if \(A\) is closed and convex, given \(0\in A\). If \(A\) is convex but nonclosed, the second polar fills precisely its missing closure boundary; the original boundary inclusion data are lost after the first polarity operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{\circ\circ}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}A\); hence exact recovery holds exactly when \(A\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-level bipolar boundary caused by nonclosedness or nonconvexity.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb{R}^n\) with dual \(E^*\), and let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The standard finite-dimensional antipolar operation is stated. No inspected local source in the supplied evidence set supported the exact antipolar terminology and reconstruction calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The antipolar, or reverse polar, of \(C\) is \[C':=\{y\in E^*:\langle x,y\rangle\ge1\ \text{for every }x\in C\}.\] It is the intersection of the closed halfspaces \(\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\ge1\}\), hence is closed and convex whenever nonempty. It is order reversing: \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) implies \(C_2'\subseteq C_1'\). It is also ray-like in the outward direction: \(y\in C'\) and \(\lambda\ge1\) imply \(\lambda y\in C'\). The operation encodes strict separation of \(C\) from the origin with normalization level one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipolar of a nonempty set consists of all dual vectors whose pairing with every point of the set is at least one. It reverses containment, produces a closed convex set when nonempty, and is stable under scaling away from the origin. Unlike ordinary polarity, which imposes an upper bound of one and always contains the origin, antipolarity imposes a lower bound of one and excludes the origin. It therefore expresses normalized reverse separation and supplies feasible regions for gauge-dual models.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C'=\{y:\inf_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\ge1\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in C'\iff\langle x,y\rangle\ge1\) for every \(x\in C\).
\(C'=\bigcap_{x\in C}\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\ge1\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(0\in C\), then \(C'=\varnothing\).
For \(C=\{x_0\}\) with \(x_0\ne0\), \(C'=\{y:\langle x_0,y\rangle\ge1\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(0\notin C'\) whenever \(C'\ne\varnothing\).
\(C'=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C)'\).

Nonemptiness requires a separation condition; arbitrary origin-excluding nonclosed sets may require closure-sensitive treatment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Admissible and ray-like antipolar set regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and define \(C'=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\ge1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This entry classifies finite-dimensional sets by origin exclusion, convex closure, and radial stability. Exact source support was not located in the supplied corpus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An antipolar-admissible set is a nonempty set \(C\) with \(C'\ne\varnothing\). For closed convex \(C\), this regime is equivalent to \(0\notin C\). A set is ray-like when \[x\in C,\ \lambda\ge1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda x\in C.\] The principal regimes are: closed convex origin-excluding sets; closed convex ray-like sets; non-ray-like origin-excluding sets; and the origin-contact boundary \(0\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C\), where \(C'=\varnothing\). Every nonempty antipolar \(C'\) is itself closed, convex, origin-excluding, and ray-like.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Antipolar set regimes distinguish whether normalized reverse separators exist and whether the set is stable under outward radial scaling. For a nonempty closed convex set, excluding the origin is exactly the separation condition needed for a nonempty antipolar. Ray-like sets remain feasible when points are scaled away from the origin and form the stable class for double-antipolar reconstruction. Non-ray-like sets lose radial information under repeated antipolarization. If the origin belongs to the closed convex hull, the antipolar is empty.
assumptions_latex: For the equivalence \(C'\ne\varnothing\iff0\notin C\), \(C\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is ray-like iff \((\forall x\in C)(\forall\lambda\ge1)\ \lambda x\in C\); every nonempty \(C'\) is closed, convex, and ray-like.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Ray-likeness is equivalent to \([1,+\infty)C\subseteq C\).
Antipolar admissibility is \(\inf_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle>0\) for some \(y\), after positive rescaling to level one.
special_cases_latex: A closed halfspace \(\{x:\langle a,x\rangle\ge1\}\) is ray-like.
A bounded origin-excluding convex body is generally not ray-like.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(0\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C\), then \(C'=\varnothing\).
If \(C'\ne\varnothing\), then \(0\notin C\).
boundary_notes: Origin exclusion alone is insufficient for nonclosed nonconvex sets unless the closed convex hull also excludes the origin.
Ray-like is weaker than being a convex cone because scaling factors below one are not required.

notation.meaning: Union of outward dilates of C by factors at least one.

knowledge_statements.title: Ray-Like Closed Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex set stable under outward radial scaling is recovered exactly by applying antipolarity twice, provided its antipolar is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated hypotheses, the antipolar operation is exact under repetition: \[C^{\prime\prime}=\{x\in X:\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\ \text{for every }y\in C'\}=C.\] The condition \(\lambda C\subseteq C\) for \(\lambda\geq1\) makes \(C\) outward ray-like, while closedness and convexity supply the separation needed for the reverse inclusion. Nonemptiness of \(C'\) excludes sets that cannot be strictly separated from the origin at level one.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, satisfies \(0\notin C\), and has nonempty antipolar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\prime\prime}=C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact antipolar reconstruction for closed convex outward ray-like sets.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, and let \(C'=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\ge1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The stable finite-dimensional class used by antipolar reconstruction is defined. No exact authoritative antipolar source was found among the inspected local materials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A ray-like closed convex set is a set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying: \(C\ne\varnothing\); \(C\) is closed and convex; \(0\notin C\); and \[x\in C,\ \lambda\ge1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda x\in C.\] Equivalently, \([1,+\infty)C=C\). For such a set the antipolar is nonempty, and the defining stable-class relation is \[C''=(C')'=C.\] More generally, double antipolarization replaces an admissible set by its closed convex ray-like hull, so ray-like closed convex sets are precisely the fixed points of the antipolar operation applied twice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray-like closed convex set is nonempty, closed, convex, excludes the origin, and contains every outward dilation of each of its points. It need not contain inward dilations and therefore need not be a cone. This is the stable class for antipolarity: its antipolar is nonempty and applying antipolarity twice returns the same set. For a more general admissible set, double antipolarization retains only its closed convex outward-radial hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is ray-like closed convex and satisfies \(C''=C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every ray \(\{\lambda x:\lambda>0\}\) meets \(C\), when it meets it at all, in a closed outward interval.
special_cases_latex: Every nonempty antipolar set \(D'\) is ray-like, closed, and convex.
A halfspace \(\{x:\langle a,x\rangle\ge1\}\) is ray-like closed convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(C'\ne\varnothing\).
Repeated antipolarization is idempotent on this class: \(C'''=C'\).
boundary_notes: A closed convex set excluding the origin need not be ray-like.
A ray-like set is not required to contain the origin or to be stable under addition, so it is not generally a cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Ray-Like Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Double antipolarity replaces a non-ray-like set by its closed convex outward radial completion; a singleton at one becomes the ray from one onward.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The second antipolar is the smallest closed, convex, outward ray-like set containing \(C\): \[C^{\prime\prime}=\mathcal R(C)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left(\bigcup_{\lambda\geq1}\lambda C\right).\] Consequently, if \(C\neq\mathcal R(C)\), repeated antipolarity strictly enlarges \(C\). For example, in \(X=\mathbb R\), the set \(C=\{1\}\) has \(C'=[1,+\infty)\) and \(C^{\prime\prime}=[1,+\infty)\), exhibiting the added outward ray.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty and has nonempty antipolar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C^{\prime\prime}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\bigl(\bigcup_{\lambda\geq1}\lambda C\bigr)\), so non-ray-like sets are not recovered exactly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Double antipolarity as closed convex outward radial completion.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty. Define its outward radial hull by \(\operatorname{rad}C:=\bigcup_{\lambda\geq 1}\lambda C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns arbitrary nonempty feasible sets; convexity, closedness, and separation from the origin are not presumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is ray-like when \(x\in C\) and \(\lambda\geq1\) imply \(\lambda x\in C\), equivalently \(\operatorname{rad}C=C\). It is non-ray-like precisely when \[\exists x\in C\;\exists\lambda\geq1:\quad \lambda x\notin C,\] equivalently \(C\subsetneq\operatorname{rad}C\). Its closed radial-convex completion is \[\mathcal R(C):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{rad}C).\] Thus non-ray-likeness records failure of outward radial stability, while \(\mathcal R(C)\) additionally repairs convexity and closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set is non-ray-like if at least one of its points leaves the set when multiplied by some scalar at least one. Equivalently, the set is strictly smaller than the union of all of its outward dilations. The closed convex hull of those dilations is its radial-convex completion.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is non-ray-like}\iff\exists x\in C,\ \exists\lambda\geq1\text{ with }\lambda x\notin C\iff C\subsetneq\operatorname{rad}C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C\text{ is ray-like}\iff C=\operatorname{rad}C\).
\(C\text{ is non-ray-like}\iff\mathcal R(C)\neq C\) whenever \(C\) is closed and convex.
special_cases_latex: Every cone \(K\) is ray-like because \(\lambda K\subseteq K\) for every \(\lambda\geq1\).
A bounded nonempty set containing a nonzero point is non-ray-like.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\mathcal R(C)\) is closed, convex, ray-like, and contains \(C\).
Any closed convex ray-like set containing \(C\) also contains \(\mathcal R(C)\).
boundary_notes: A set containing only the origin is ray-like, despite having no nonzero ray.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, and define \(C':=\{y\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary is formulated for arbitrary nonempty sets through their closed convex hull, which is the part visible to linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) has origin contact when \[0\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C.\] This condition is the failure boundary for normalized reverse separation: it is equivalent to \(C'=\varnothing\). Strict origin separation means \(0\notin\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C\); in finite dimension it is equivalent to the existence of \(y\in X\) and \(\alpha>0\) such that \(\inf_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\geq\alpha\), after which rescaling \(y/\alpha\) produces an antipolar point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set has origin contact when the origin belongs to its closed convex hull. At this boundary no vector can have inner product at least one with every point of the set, so the antipolar is empty. Away from the boundary, strict separation from the origin can be normalized to produce an antipolar vector.
assumptions_latex: The antipolar threshold is normalized to \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C\iff C'=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C'\neq\varnothing\iff0\notin\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. For \(C\subseteq X\), define \(C':=\{y\in X:\inf_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the threshold-one antipolar used for reverse separation, not the ordinary polar defined by upper inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Antipolar calculus is the collection of set transformations generated by \(C\mapsto C'\). The operator is inclusion reversing: \[C\subseteq D\quad\Longrightarrow\quad D'\subseteq C'.\] It ignores convexification and closure, \[C'=(\operatorname{conv}C)'=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C)',\] and every antipolar \(C'\) is closed, convex, and ray-like. Repetition gives the antibipolar \(C'':=(C')'\), which contains \(C\) whenever \(C'\neq\varnothing\) and selects the smallest closed convex ray-like superset of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipolar of a set consists of vectors whose inner product with every point of the set is at least one. The transformation reverses inclusion, is unchanged by taking the convex or closed convex hull of its input, and always produces a closed convex ray-like set. Applying it twice yields the antibipolar completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C'=(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C)'\), \(C\subseteq D\Rightarrow D'\subseteq C'\), and \(C'\) is closed, convex, and ray-like.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in C'\iff\inf_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\).
\(C'=\bigcap_{x\in C}\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\}\).
special_cases_latex: \(\varnothing'=X\).
If \(0\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C\), then \(C'=\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \((\bigcup_i C_i)'=\bigcap_i C_i'\).
If \(C'\neq\varnothing\), then \(C'''=C'\).
boundary_notes: Ordinary polarity uses \(\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\) and has different behavior at the origin.
The threshold-zero reverse polar would be conic and is not the operator defined here.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \((C_i)_{i\in I}\) be a nonempty family of subsets of \(X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The union–hull antipolar equivalence is the identity \[\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\right)'=\left(\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\right)'=\left(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\bigcup_{i\in I}C_i\right)'=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i'.\] Thus aggregating primal alternatives by union, convex hull, or closed convex hull produces exactly the same antipolar feasible region: a dual vector must satisfy the normalized reverse-separation inequality on every component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipolar of a union equals the intersection of the component antipolars. Taking the convex hull or closed convex hull of the union does not change this antipolar. Consequently, all three primal aggregations encode the same collection of reverse-separating dual vectors.

If one component has empty antipolar, then the aggregated antipolar is empty.
immediate_consequences_latex: Adding a component to the union can only shrink the antipolar.
Convexifying a disjunctive feasible set introduces no new antipolar inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failures for the Intersection Formula
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hull formula can fail when the common intersection is empty or when a constituent contains the origin, even though the intersection itself is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Common feasibility is necessary: for \(C_1=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x_1\ge1\}\) and \(C_2=\{x:x_1\le-1\}\), \[(C_1\cap C_2)'=\mathbb R^2\neq\mathbb R\times\{0\}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C_1'\cup C_2').\] Origin avoidance of each constituent is also necessary: for \(E_1=\{x:x_1\ge0\}\) and \(E_2=\{x:x_2\ge1\}\), \[E_1'=\varnothing,\quad E_2'=\{(0,b):b\ge1\},\] while \[(E_1\cap E_2)'=\{(a,b):a\ge0,\ b\ge1\}.\]
assumptions_latex: All displayed sets are closed, convex, and outward ray-like.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(C_1\cap C_2)'\ne\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C_1'\cup C_2'),\qquad (E_1\cap E_2)'\ne\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(E_1'\cup E_2').\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why common feasibility and canonical origin avoidance cannot be omitted from the intersection rule.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualified Intersection Antipolar Formula
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many canonical ray-like sets having a common point, the intersection antipolar is the closed convex hull of their antipolars.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be nonempty closed convex sets such that \(0\notin C_i\), \(\lambda C_i\subseteq C_i\) for every \(\lambda\ge1\), and \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\neq\varnothing\). Then \[\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)'=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i'\right).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
Each \(C_i\) is nonempty, closed, convex, avoids the origin, and satisfies \(\lambda C_i\subseteq C_i\) for \(\lambda\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\right)'=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i'\right).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family intersection rule for canonical antibipolar sets with nonempty common intersection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empty-Intersection Failure of the Hull Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that individual nonemptiness of closed convex ray-like sets is insufficient for the proposed intersection-antipolar equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[C_1=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x_1\ge1\},\qquad C_2=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x_1\le-1\}.\]
Then \(C_1\cap C_2=\varnothing\), so \((C_1\cap C_2)'=\mathbb R^2\). However,
\[C_1'=\{(a,0):a\ge1\},\qquad C_2'=\{(a,0):a\le-1\},\]
and hence
\[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C_1'\cup C_2')=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\ne\mathbb R^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two incompatible ray-like halfspaces have empty intersection, whose antipolar is the whole plane, while the closed convex hull of their antipolars is only a line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\left(C_1\cap C_2\right)'=\mathbb R^2\ne\mathbb R\times\{0\}=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(C_1'\cup C_2').\]

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, let \(Q\subseteq Y\), and set \(C:=A^{-1}(Q)\neq\varnothing\) and \(E:=Q\cap\operatorname{ran}A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formula accounts explicitly for a nonsurjective map by antipolarizing the reachable portion of the target set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the ambient lift of the antipolar of \(E\) by \[E'_{Y}:=\{z\in Y:\langle w,z\rangle\geq1\ \forall w\in E\}.\] The preimage–adjoint correspondence is \[\bigl(A^{-1}Q\bigr)'=A^*E'_{Y}=\{A^*z:z\in Y,\ \inf_{w\in Q\cap\operatorname{ran}A}\langle w,z\rangle\geq1\}.\] If \(A\) is surjective, then \(E=Q\) and the formula reduces to \((A^{-1}Q)'=A^*Q'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipolar of a nonempty linear preimage is obtained by taking vectors that reverse-separate the reachable part of the target set and mapping them back with the adjoint. If the map is surjective, the reachable part is the whole target set and the formula becomes the adjoint image of the target antipolar.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(A^{-1}Q\bigr)'=A^*\{z\in Y:\inf_{w\in Q\cap\operatorname{ran}A}\langle w,z\rangle\geq1\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every \(u\in(A^{-1}Q)'\) annihilates \(\ker A\) and therefore lies in \(\operatorname{ran}A^*\).
When \(A\) is surjective, \((A^{-1}Q)'=A^*Q'\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, \((A^{-1}Q)'=A^*Q'\) and the representing target vector is unique.
If \(A\) is the identity, the correspondence reduces to \(Q'=Q'\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Only \(Q\cap\operatorname{ran}A\) affects the preimage or its antipolar.
Different lifts \(z\) differing by an element of \(\ker A^*\) produce the same antipolar vector.
boundary_notes: The simpler expression \(A^*Q'\) can fail when \(A\) is not surjective.
In infinite dimensions, \((\ker A)^\perp\) may equal only the closure of \(\operatorname{ran}A^*\), so additional range assumptions are required.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Failure Under Tangential Range Contact
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex target can meet a deficient range tangentially so that a certificate valid on the reachable section has no representative valid on the whole target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2\) be \(Ax=(x,0)\), and let
\[
D=\{(u,v):v\ge0,\ u\ge1-\sqrt v\}.
\]
Then \(D\) is closed and convex,
\[
A^{-1}D=[1,\infty),\qquad 1\in(A^{-1}D)',
\]
but \(1\notin A^*(D')\). Indeed, every representative of the scalar functional \(1\) has the form \((1,\beta)\), and
\[
\inf_{(u,v)\in D}(u+\beta v)<1
\]
for every \(\beta\in\mathbb R\). Consequently,
\[
A^*(D')\subsetneq(A^{-1}D)'.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(Y=\mathbb R^2\) have their Euclidean pairings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^*(D')\subsetneq(A^{-1}D)'\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional rank-deficient example showing that the full-target adjoint image can be strictly smaller than the preimage antipolar.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(D\subseteq Y\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(A^{-1}D)'=\{A^*z:z\in Y,\ \inf_{u\in D\cap\operatorname{ran}A}\langle z,u\rangle\ge 1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boundary for replacing an adjoint image by an unqualified antipolar formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every functional bounded below on \(A^{-1}D\) must lie in \(\operatorname{ran}A^*\). More precisely,
\[(A^{-1}D)'=\{A^*z:z\in Y,\ \inf_{u\in D\cap\operatorname{ran}A}\langle z,u\rangle\ge1\}.\]
Consequently, \((A^{-1}D)'=A^*D'\) is generally invalid when \(A\) is not surjective: the preimage tests only \(D\cap\operatorname{ran}A\), and different representatives of a functional in \(\operatorname{ran}A^*\) may differ by an element of \(\ker A^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deficient range restricts antipolar tests to the portion of the target set lying in the range, so the usual adjoint-image formula can fail.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Antipolar of a Surjective Linear Residual Region
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be surjective, let \(b\in Y\), let \(\rho:Y\to[0,+\infty]\) be a closed gauge, and let \(\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surjectivity is imposed so every residual in the gauge ball is attainable; nonsurjective maps require intersecting that ball with the affine reachable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the residual-feasible set \[C:=\{x\in X:\rho(b-Ax)\leq\sigma\},\] define the polar gauge \(\rho^\circ(y):=\sup\{\langle r,y\rangle:\rho(r)\leq1\}\). Its antipolar has the representation \[C'=A^*\{y\in Y:\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\geq1\}.\] Thus a residual constraint becomes a reverse-separation inequality consisting of a data pairing minus the support value of the residual ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a surjective linear forward map, the antipolar of a gauge-bounded residual set is the adjoint image of vectors whose pairing with the data exceeds one plus the polar-gauge support penalty. This is the residual-set formula underlying the familiar linear-residual gauge dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C'=A^*\{y:\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\geq1\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\) satisfies the residual reverse-separation condition iff \(\inf_{\rho(r)\leq\sigma}\langle b-r,y\rangle\geq1\).
\(\inf_{\rho(r)\leq\sigma}\langle b-r,y\rangle=\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\rho=\|\cdot\|\), then the inequality is \(\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\|y\|_*\geq1\).
If \(A\) is invertible, every element of \(C'\) has the form \(A^*y\) with a unique \(y\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The represented target set is closed, convex, and ray-like.
The data vector \(b\) enters only through the linear functional \(y\mapsto\langle b,y\rangle\).
boundary_notes: Without surjectivity, the exact support term must be restricted to residuals compatible with \(b-\operatorname{ran}A\).
The case \(\sigma=0\) requires care when \(\rho\) has a nontrivial zero cone.

notation.meaning: Polar gauge of the residual gauge rho.

Geometry and Recession of Gauge Residual Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge residual set is closed and convex, and its recession directions are exactly those whose negative image lies in the gauge zero cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{x\in X:\gamma(b-Ax)\le\sigma\},\qquad \sigma\ge0.
\]
Then \(C\) is closed and convex. If \(C\neq\varnothing\), then
\[
\operatorname{rec}C=\{d\in X:\gamma(-Ad)=0\}.
\]
Thus gauge-zero image directions, not only directions in \(\ker A\), can generate recession.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma:Y\to[0,+\infty]\) is a closed convex gauge and \(C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is closed and convex},\quad \operatorname{rec}C=\{d:\gamma(-Ad)=0\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional geometry of a nonempty residual sublevel for a closed convex gauge.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Residual Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge residual set is the inverse image of a translated gauge sublevel set. Positive tolerances yield dilations of the unit set, while zero tolerance uses the gauge's entire zero cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gauge residual set with center \(b\), linear model \(A\), and tolerance \(\sigma\) is
\[C_{\gamma}(A,b,\sigma):=\{x\in X:\gamma(b-Ax)\le\sigma\}.\]
If
\[R_\sigma:=\{r\in Y:\gamma(r)\le\sigma\},\]
then
\[C_{\gamma}(A,b,\sigma)=A^{-1}\bigl(b-R_\sigma\bigr).\]
Writing \(B_\gamma:=\{r\in Y:\gamma(r)\le1\}\), positive homogeneity gives \(R_\sigma=\sigma B_\gamma\) when \(\sigma>0\). At \(\sigma=0\), however,
\[R_0=Z_\gamma:=\{r\in Y:\gamma(r)=0\},\]
which need not equal the scalar dilation \(0B_\gamma=\{0\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces in separating duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_{\gamma}(A,b,\sigma)=A^{-1}\bigl(b-R_\sigma\bigr),\qquad R_\sigma:=\{r\in Y:\gamma(r)\le\sigma\},\]\[R_\sigma=\sigma B_\gamma\ \text{if }\sigma>0,\qquad R_0=Z_\gamma:=\{r\in Y:\gamma(r)=0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual feasibility for a possibly asymmetric extended-valued gauge, including the nontrivial zero-cone case at zero tolerance.

notation.meaning: Closed unit set of the gauge
Gauge sublevel set at tolerance sigma

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility and Recession of Norm Residual Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm residual set is feasible exactly when the tolerance reaches the distance to the operator range; if feasible, its recession cone is the operator kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
C=\{x\in X:\|b-Ax\|\le\sigma\},\qquad \sigma\ge0,
\]
one has
\[
C\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{dist}(b,\operatorname{ran}A)\le\sigma.
\]
Whenever \(C\neq\varnothing\),
\[
\operatorname{rec}C=\ker A.
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\neq\varnothing\iff\operatorname{dist}(b,\operatorname{ran}A)\le\sigma;\quad C\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{rec}C=\ker A.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasibility threshold and recession characterization for a norm residual region.

notation.meaning: Distance from the data vector to the operator range.
Recession cone of the residual feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm Residual Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm residual set is the inverse image of a translated norm ball and is unchanged when the residual sign is reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The norm residual set determined by \(A\), \(b\), and \(\sigma\) is
\[C_{\|\cdot\|}(A,b,\sigma):=\{x\in X:\|b-Ax\|\le\sigma\}.\]
If \(B:=\{r\in Y:\|r\|\le1\}\), then
\[C_{\|\cdot\|}(A,b,\sigma)=\{x\in X:b-Ax\in\sigma B\}=A^{-1}(b-\sigma B).\]
Because every norm is even, the equivalent convention \(\|Ax-b\|\le\sigma\) defines the same set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_{\|\cdot\|}(A,b,\sigma)=\{x\in X:\|b-Ax\|\le\sigma\}=A^{-1}(b-\sigma B).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard norm-ball specialization of a gauge residual set.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball of the norm

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Residual Antipolar Specialization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipolar of a surjective norm-residual region is described by an adjoint vector satisfying a dual-norm margin inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\gamma(r)=\|r\|\), then \(R_\sigma=\sigma B\) for every \(\sigma\ge0\), and for surjective \(A\),
\[
\{x:\|b-Ax\|\le\sigma\}'
=
\{A^*z:\langle b,z\rangle-\sigma\|z\|_*\ge1\}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces and \(Y\) carries a norm \(\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C'=\{A^*z:\langle b,z\rangle-\sigma\|z\|_*\ge1\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surjective norm-residual specialization of the support-function representation.

notation.meaning: Dual norm on the paired target space.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Representation of Residual-Set Antipolars
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a surjective residual map, the antipolar is an adjoint image subject to a support-function margin. Positive tolerance gives the polar-gauge formula, while zero tolerance requires the support of the gauge zero cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
R_\sigma=\{r\in Y:\gamma(r)\le\sigma\},\qquad
C=\{x\in X:b-Ax\in R_\sigma\},
\]
and suppose \(A:X\to Y\) is surjective and \(C\neq\varnothing\). Then
\[
C'=\{A^*z:\langle b,z\rangle-\sigma_{R_\sigma}(z)\ge1\},
\]
where \(\sigma_{R_\sigma}\) is the support function of \(R_\sigma\). For \(\sigma>0\),
\[
\sigma_{R_\sigma}(z)=\sigma\gamma^\circ(z),
\qquad
C'=\{A^*z:\langle b,z\rangle-\sigma\gamma^\circ(z)\ge1\}.
\]
At \(\sigma=0\), the support term is \(\sigma_{Z_\gamma}(z)\), not an unqualified product \(0\gamma^\circ(z)\).
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is linear and surjective, \(b\in Y\), and \(\sigma\ge0\).
\(\gamma\) is a closed convex gauge and \(C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C'=\{A^*z:\langle b,z\rangle-\sigma_{R_\sigma}(z)\ge1\}\), with \(\sigma_{R_\sigma}=\sigma\gamma^\circ\) when \(\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surjective finite-dimensional formula valid at every nonnegative tolerance, including gauges with a nontrivial zero cone.

notation.meaning: Support function of the residual sublevel.
Polar gauge, equal to the support function of the gauge unit set.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Set Antipolars
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact multiplier representation for surjective affine gauge residual systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:E\to F\) be surjective, let \(\kappa\) be a closed finite gauge on \(F\), let \(b\in F\), and let \(\sigma>0\). Define \(C=\{x\in E:\kappa(b-Ax)\leq\sigma\}\) and \(\kappa^{\circ}(z)=\sup\{\langle z,r\rangle:\kappa(r)\leq1\}\). Then
\[
C'=\{A^*z:z\in F,\ \langle b,z\rangle-\sigma\kappa^{\circ}(z)\geq1\}.
\]
For a norm gauge, \(\kappa^{\circ}\) is the dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under surjectivity, a residual-set antipolar consists of adjoint multipliers whose pairing with the data is at least one plus the tolerance times the polar gauge.
assumptions_latex: \(A:E\to F\) is linear and surjective between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
\(\kappa\) is a closed finite gauge and \(\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C'=\{A^*z:z\in F,\ \langle b,z\rangle-\sigma\kappa^{\circ}(z)\geq1\}\).

notation.meaning: Polar gauge, the support function of the κ-unit ball.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Gauge Sign-Reversal Witness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple asymmetric one-dimensional gauge produces different feasible intervals under the two residual-sign conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), let
\[
\gamma(r)=\begin{cases}r,&r\ge0,\\-2r,&r<0.\end{cases}
\]
With \(A=I\), \(b=1\), and \(\sigma=1\),
\[
\{x:\gamma(1-x)\le1\}=[0,3/2],
\qquad
\{x:\gamma(x-1)\le1\}=[1/2,2].
\]
Thus the two residual-sign conventions are genuinely different for an asymmetric gauge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\gamma(1-x)\le1\}\neq\{x:\gamma(x-1)\le1\}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional example in which residual reversal changes the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Reflection Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing the residual replaces the gauge by its reflection and reflects the polar-gauge argument. The two conventions agree universally exactly in the even-gauge regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the reversed gauge \(\gamma^{\leftarrow}(r)=\gamma(-r)\). For every linear \(A:X\to Y\), \(b\in Y\), and \(\sigma\ge0\),
\[
\{x:\gamma(Ax-b)\le\sigma\}
=
\{x:\gamma^{\leftarrow}(b-Ax)\le\sigma\}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
(\gamma^{\leftarrow})^\circ(z)=\gamma^\circ(-z).
\]
Hence an even gauge makes the two residual-sign conventions identical. Conversely, if they agree for every \(b\) and \(\sigma\) when \(X=Y\) and \(A=I_Y\), then \(\gamma\) is even.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces in separating duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_-(\gamma)=C_+(\gamma^{\leftarrow})\), \((\gamma^{\leftarrow})^\circ(z)=\gamma^\circ(-z)\), and universal sign invariance is equivalent to evenness of \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relationship between the two residual-sign conventions and their polar-gauge terms.

assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space in separating duality with its dual.
\(A:X\to Y\), \(b\in Y\), and \(\sigma\ge0\) define residual sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_+=C_-\ \text{for all }A,b,\sigma\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma(r)=\gamma(-r)\ \text{for all }r\in Y.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes symmetric norm residuals from genuinely asymmetric gauge residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(C_+:=\{x:\gamma(b-Ax)\le\sigma\}\) and \(C_-:=\{x:\gamma(Ax-b)\le\sigma\}\). These conventions agree for every choice of \(A\), \(b\), and \(\sigma\) exactly when \(\gamma\) is even:
\[C_+=C_-\ \text{for all }A,b,\sigma\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma(r)=\gamma(-r)\ \text{for all }r\in Y.\]
Equivalently, the polar gauge is even. Without symmetry, reversing the residual replaces the antipolar margin term \(\gamma^\circ(z)\) by \(\gamma^\circ(-z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual sign is immaterial for norms and even gauges, but an asymmetric gauge produces a reflected polar-gauge term.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Dependent Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the equivalence or reflected polar-gauge claim, and the quantified maps use a space X that is not introduced or quantified.

children.title: Antibipolar Principle
children.top_down_role: Repeated antipolarity and the radial closed convex completion it selects.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(C\subseteq X\) satisfy \(C'\neq\varnothing\), where \(C':=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The nonempty-antipolar hypothesis excludes origin contact and makes repeated antipolarity a meaningful completion operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The antibipolar of \(C\) is \[C'':=\{x\in X:\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\ \forall y\in C'\}.\] The antibipolar principle identifies it as \[C''=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{\lambda\geq1}\lambda C\right).\] Equivalently, \(C''\) is the intersection of all closed convex ray-like sets containing \(C\), hence the smallest set with those three properties that contains the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying antipolarity twice produces the closed convex outward-radial completion of a set, provided the first antipolar is nonempty. The resulting antibipolar is exactly the smallest closed convex ray-like superset of the original set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C''=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{\lambda\geq1}\lambda C)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C''=\bigcap\{D:C\subseteq D,\ D\text{ closed, convex, and ray-like}\}\).
\(x\in C''\iff\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\) for every \(y\) that reverse-separates \(C\) at threshold one.
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is already closed, convex, and ray-like, then \(C''=C\).
For a singleton \(C=\{c\}\) with \(c\neq0\), \(C''=\{\lambda c:\lambda\geq1\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The completion is extensive: \(C\subseteq C''\).
Repeated completion is idempotent: \(C''''=C''\).
The first antipolar is stable under three applications: \(C'''=C'\).
boundary_notes: If \(C'=\varnothing\), the literal double antipolar is \(X'=\varnothing\), so the stated completion formula is not applicable.
The completion uses outward scalings \(\lambda\geq1\), not the conic hull generated with all \(\lambda\geq0\).

notation.meaning: Antibipolar or double antipolar of C.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Characterization of Proper Antibipolar Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty proper set is fixed by double antipolarization exactly when it is closed, convex, avoids the origin, and is stable under outward dilation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subsetneq X\) be nonempty. Then \[C=C''\] if and only if \(C\) is closed and convex, \(0\notin C\), and \[\lambda C\subseteq C\qquad(\lambda\ge1).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C=C''\iff C\text{ is closed and convex},\ 0\notin C,\ \lambda C\subseteq C\ (\lambda\ge1).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic characterization of nonempty proper fixed points of double antipolarization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Antibipolarity in the Ray-Like Regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This fixed-point characterization is the canonical exact-recovery regime for threshold-one antipolarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is antibipolar-exact when \(C'=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\ \forall x\in C\}\) is nonempty and \(C''=C\). In finite dimensions, this is equivalent to the geometric conditions \[C\text{ is closed and convex},\qquad x\in C,\ \lambda\geq1\Rightarrow\lambda x\in C,\qquad0\notin C.\] Hence nonempty closed convex ray-like sets excluding the origin are precisely the fixed points of double antipolarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set is exactly recovered by applying the antipolar twice precisely when it is closed, convex, outward ray-like, and does not contain the origin. These are the fixed points of the antibipolar completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C''=C\iff C\text{ is closed, convex, ray-like, and }0\notin C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C=C''\iff C\) is a fixed point of the radial-convex completion \(\mathcal R\).
Under the stated geometric conditions, \(C=\bigcap_{y\in C'}\{x:\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\}\).
special_cases_latex: Every nonempty closed convex cone translated away from the origin need not be ray-like; outward stability must be checked after translation.
A closed halfspace \(\{x:\langle a,x\rangle\geq1\}\) is antibipolar-exact.
immediate_consequences_latex: For such \(C\), antipolarity is an involution between \(C\) and \(C'\).
Both \(C\) and \(C'\) are nonempty closed convex ray-like sets excluding the origin.
boundary_notes: Dropping closedness recovers the closure; dropping convexity recovers a convex hull; dropping ray-likeness recovers an outward radial completion.
A set containing the origin has empty antipolar and cannot be an exact fixed point.
review_flags: No inspected source supports the exact fixed-point characterization for threshold-one antipolarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Antibipolarity in the Ray-Like Regime

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and \(0\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional antibipolar theorem for closed convex ray-like sets avoiding the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[C':=\{y\in X:\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\ \text{for every }x\in C\}.\]
Under the stated hypotheses, strict separation of \(0\) from \(C\) ensures \(C'\neq\varnothing\). The second antipolar
\[C'':=\{x\in X:\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\ \text{for every }y\in C'\}\]
recovers the original set exactly:
\[C''=C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set that avoids the origin and contains every outward dilation of its points equals its second antipolar.

children.title: Radial-Convex Completion Calculus
children.top_down_role: The geometric completion induced outside the canonical regime.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(C\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a purely geometric completion; its identification with the antibipolar additionally requires nonempty antipolarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The radial-convex completion operator is \[\mathcal R(C):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{\lambda\geq1}\lambda C\right).\] It is extensive, monotone, and idempotent: \[C\subseteq\mathcal R(C),\qquad C\subseteq D\Rightarrow\mathcal R(C)\subseteq\mathcal R(D),\qquad\mathcal R(\mathcal R(C))=\mathcal R(C).\] Its values are closed, convex, and ray-like, and its fixed points are exactly the closed convex ray-like sets. If \(C'\neq\varnothing\), then \(\mathcal R(C)=C''\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial-convex completion of a set is the closed convex hull of all outward dilations of that set. It is an extensive, monotone, idempotent operator whose fixed points are exactly the closed convex ray-like sets. Away from origin contact it coincides with double antipolarity.
assumptions_latex: The identity \(\mathcal R(C)=C''\) is asserted only when \(C'\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R(C)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{\lambda\geq1}\lambda C)\) is a closure operator onto the family of closed convex ray-like sets.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mathcal R(C)=\bigcap\{D:C\subseteq D,\ D\text{ closed, convex, and ray-like}\}\).
\(C=\mathcal R(C)\iff C\) is closed, convex, and ray-like.
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is convex, then \(\bigcup_{\lambda\geq1}\lambda C\) is convex, so only closure may remain.
If \(C=\{c\}\), then \(\mathcal R(C)=\{\lambda c:\lambda\geq1\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\mathcal R(C\cup D)=\mathcal R(\mathcal R(C)\cup\mathcal R(D))\).
Any closed convex ray-like constraint valid on \(C\) is valid on \(\mathcal R(C)\).
boundary_notes: This completion differs from \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}C\), which also introduces inward scalings and the origin.
For \(C=\varnothing\), the value depends only on the usual conventions \(\operatorname{conv}\varnothing=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{cl}\varnothing=\varnothing\).
review_flags: The supplied sources were not verified to define this radial completion operator or connect it to antibipolarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Radial-Convex Completion Operator
Antipolar Invariance under Outward Radial Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking all outward dilations and then closing them leaves the unit-threshold antipolar unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty \(S\subseteq X\), \[S'=(\operatorname{rad}S)'=(\operatorname{rcl}S)',\] where \(\operatorname{rad}S=\{\lambda x:x\in S,\lambda\ge1\}\) and \(\operatorname{rcl}S=\overline{\operatorname{rad}S}\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S'=(\operatorname{rad}S)'=(\operatorname{rcl}S)'.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The antipolar cannot distinguish a set from its outward radial hull or its closure.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{rcl}S=\overline{\{\lambda x:x\in S,\ \lambda\ge1\}}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outward radial completion used by the antipolar operation, not star-shaped closure toward the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The outward radial hull and its radial closure are defined by
\[\operatorname{rad}S:=\{\lambda x:x\in S,\ \lambda\ge1\},\qquad \operatorname{rcl}S:=\overline{\operatorname{rad}S}.\]
Thus \(\operatorname{rcl}S\) is the smallest closed subset of \(X\) containing \(S\) that is stable under every dilation factor \(\lambda\ge1\). This convention expands away from the origin and should not be confused with star-shaped completion by factors in \([0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Radial closure is the closure of all outward dilations of a set, using factors at least one.
knowledge_statements.title: Radial Closure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and distinguishes outward completion from star-shaped closure, but the specialized term and minimality assertion lack a source.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexification forms every finite convex combination; closing the resulting hull gives the smallest closed convex superset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The convexification of \(S\) is its convex hull
\[\operatorname{conv}S:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i x_i:m\ge1,\ x_i\in S,\ \theta_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1\right\}.\]
It is the smallest convex set containing \(S\). In a finite-dimensional topological vector space, the closed convexification is \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S:=\overline{\operatorname{conv}S}\), the smallest closed convex set containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}S=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i x_i:m\ge1,\ x_i\in S,\ \theta_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\theta_i=1\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex-combination definition and its closed completion.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Convexification and Subdifferentiability p. 49

knowledge_statements.title: Completion Order Effects
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexification and outward radialization commute algebraically, and either order gives the same completed set after final closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Convexification and outward radialization commute:
\[\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{rad}S)=\operatorname{rad}(\operatorname{conv}S).\]
Consequently, both orders generate the same convex ray-like hull. In finite dimensions their topologically completed versions also agree after a final closure:
\[\overline{\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{rad}S)}=\overline{\operatorname{rad}(\operatorname{conv}S)}.\]
This statement concerns the combined completion; inserting intermediate closures may change whether boundary points appear before the final closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{rad}S)=\operatorname{rad}(\operatorname{conv}S).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic commutation of convex and outward-radial completion before topological closure.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The commutation identity is mathematically plausible and correctly classified as a property, but the cited convexification section does not specifically evidence the outward-radial identity.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Convexification and Subdifferentiability p. 49

knowledge_statements.title: Second Antipolar as Radial-Convex Completion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever the antipolar is nonempty, double antipolarization closes, convexifies, and adds every outward dilation of the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S'\neq\varnothing\), then \[S''=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\{\lambda x:x\in S,\ \lambda\ge1\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S''=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\bigl(\{\lambda x:x\in S,\ \lambda\ge1\}\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General nondegenerate completion selected by repeated antipolarization outside the fixed-point regime.

notation.meaning: Antipolar operation on subsets of the real line

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-dilation convention illustrating why nonclosed completions are not canonical for antibipolar recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replace the canonical dilation condition \(\lambda\ge1\) by the strict condition \(\lambda>1\). For \(S=\{1\}\),
\[R_{>}(S)=(1,\infty).\]
Its antipolar and second antipolar are
\[R_{>}(S)'=[1,\infty),\qquad R_{>}(S)''=[1,\infty).\]
Thus \(R_{>}(S)''\neq R_{>}(S)\): antipolarization cannot retain the omitted boundary point. A strict, nonclosed radial completion is therefore noncanonical whenever exact recovery, rather than recovery of a closed completion, is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using strict outward dilations omits a boundary point that double antipolarization restores, so the strict completion is not exactly recoverable.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncanonical Completion Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Origin-Contact Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set has empty antipolar exactly when the origin lies in its closed convex hull; its second antipolar is then the whole space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty \(S\subseteq X\), \[S'=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 0\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S.\] Consequently, under the vacuous-quantifier convention, \(S'=\varnothing\) implies \(S''=X\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar gauge is \[\kappa^\circ(y):=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle:\kappa(x)\leq1\}.\] Gauge optimization duality associates to the datum \((\kappa,C)\) the primal value \[p^*:=\inf_{x\in C}\kappa(x)\] and the antipolar dual value \[d^*:=\inf_{y\in C'}\kappa^\circ(y),\qquad C':=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\geq1\ \forall x\in C\}.\] A primal–dual pair \((x,y)\in C\times C'\) carries the multiplicative certificate \(1\leq\langle x,y\rangle\leq\kappa(x)\kappa^\circ(y)\).

Feasible primal and dual points obey a multiplicative gauge certificate that underlies reciprocal value relations.

\(C'\) is the normalized reverse-separation feasible region associated with \(C\).
