knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Value Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value function assigns each additive residual perturbation the least achievable objective gauge, using positive infinity when the perturbed problem is infeasible; it is convex but need not be lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge value function associated with the residual perturbation is \[v(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\left\{\kappa(x):\rho(b+u-Ax)\leq\sigma\right\},\] with the convention \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Equivalently, if \(C=\{r\in Y:\rho(r)\leq\sigma\}\), then \[v(u)=\inf_{x\in X}\{\kappa(x)+\delta_C(b+u-Ax)\}.\] This partial infimum of a jointly convex extended-real function is convex, although it need not be lower semicontinuous or have a closed epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, \(b\in Y\), and \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are gauges on \(X\) and \(Y\), respectively.
The perturbation \(u\in Y\) enters additively in the residual, and \(\sigma\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(u)=\inf\{\kappa(x):\rho(b+u-Ax)\leq\sigma\}\) is an extended-real convex gauge-optimization value function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive residual perturbations with extended-real values; convexity does not imply lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbation value function of a gauge program
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,U\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces and let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex perturbation function. The nominal gauge program is \(\inf_{x\in X}F(x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex perturbation representation encompassing right-hand-side, residual-radius, and affine-data perturbations of gauge programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge value function associated with \(F\) is the marginal function \[V:U\to[-\infty,+\infty],\qquad V(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u).\] Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}V=\{u:V(u)<+\infty\}\), its nominal value is \(V(0)\), and its solution mapping is \[S(u)=\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in X}F(x,u).\] For the residual perturbation \(F(x,u)=\kappa(x)+\delta_{\{z:\rho(z)\leq\sigma\}}(b+u-Ax)\), \(V(u)=\inf\{\kappa(x):\rho(b+u-Ax)\leq\sigma\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a convex perturbation function F, its gauge value function maps each perturbation parameter u to the infimum of F(x,u) over the decision variable. The nominal value is V(0), and the associated solution mapping collects minimizers. Right-hand-side perturbations of a residual gauge constraint arise by replacing b with b+u.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[V(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u),\qquad S(u)=\{x:F(x,u)=V(u)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The epigraph is \(\operatorname{epi}V=\{(u,\alpha):\exists x\text{ with }F(x,u)\leq\alpha\}\), subject to projection closure when necessary.
The conjugate satisfies \(V^*(y)=F^*(0,y)\) in the standard product-space convention.
special_cases_latex: A scalar radius perturbation is \(V(\tau)=\inf\{\kappa(x):\rho(b-Ax)\leq\sigma+\tau\}\).
An affine right-hand-side perturbation uses \(u\in Y\) and \(b+u\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity of \(F\) makes \(V\) convex, though it need not be closed.
Subgradients of \(V\) at zero encode global first-order sensitivity bounds.
boundary_notes: The infimum may equal \(-\infty\) for a general perturbation function, although nonnegative gauge objectives exclude this in the residual model.
Projection of a closed convex epigraph need not be closed without additional regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable Sensitivity Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a differentiability point every normalized optimal multiplier equals the value gradient; distinct optimal multipliers certify nondifferentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every normalized optimal gauge multiplier \(z^\star\) belongs to \(\partial v(0)\). If the proper convex value function \(v\) is differentiable at \(0\), then \[z^\star=\nabla v(0),\qquad v'(0;h)=\langle z^\star,h\rangle\quad\text{for every }h.\] Consequently, the existence of two distinct normalized optimal multipliers implies that \(v\) is not differentiable at \(0\).
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is a proper convex gauge-optimization value function.
Strong duality and dual attainment place every normalized optimal multiplier in \(\partial v(0)\).
For the gradient conclusion, \(v\) is differentiable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^\star=\nabla v(0)\) and \(v'(0;h)=\langle z^\star,h\rangle\) for every \(h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier sensitivity when the gauge value function is differentiable at the reference perturbation.

notation.meaning: Directional derivative of the value function at zero in direction \(h\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Multipliers as Sensitivity Objects
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized optimal dual multiplier is a subgradient of the perturbation value function and therefore gives a first-order sensitivity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dual feasibility gives, for every perturbation \(u\), \[v(u)\geq\langle b+u,z^\star\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(z^\star)=v(0)+\langle u,z^\star\rangle.\] Thus \(z^\star\in\partial v(0)\). In particular, \(z^\star\) is a sensitivity object: its pairing with a small residual perturbation supplies the supporting affine first-order lower model of the optimal value.
assumptions_latex: The value function \(v\) is proper and strong Fenchel duality holds at \(u=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^\star\in\partial v(0)\), hence \(v(u)\geq v(0)+\langle u,z^\star\rangle\) for every \(u\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subgradient sensitivity for the normalized Fenchel form of a gauge multiplier.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: dual maximizers are subgradients of convex value functions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge multiplier as a value-function subgradient
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V:U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex gauge-program value function with \(V(0)\in\mathbb R\). Let the perturbation convention be fixed so that a multiplier \(y\in U\) has the same sign as a subgradient of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global convex sensitivity definition at the nominal parameter. An opposite perturbation convention changes the multiplier sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gauge multiplier at the nominal problem is a vector \(y\in\partial V(0)\); equivalently, \[V(u)\geq V(0)+\langle y,u\rangle\qquad\forall u\in U.\] The multiplier set is \(M=\partial V(0)\). Under parametric strong duality and dual attainment, \(M\) coincides with the gauge-dual solution set in the matching sign convention. If \(V\) is differentiable at zero, the unique sensitivity multiplier is \(\nabla V(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge multiplier is a subgradient of the gauge-program value function at the nominal perturbation. It supplies a global affine lower bound on every perturbed optimal value. Under strong parametric duality and dual attainment, these sensitivity slopes coincide with gauge-dual solutions, subject to the sign convention used for perturbations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[M=\partial V(0)=\{y:V(u)\geq V(0)+\langle y,u\rangle\ \forall u\in U\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The directional sensitivity bound is \(V'(0;h)\geq\langle y,h\rangle\) for every direction \(h\).
With perturbations entering as \(-u\), the associated dual multiplier is \(-y\).
special_cases_latex: If \(V\) is differentiable at zero, \(M=\{\nabla V(0)\}\).
For scalar radius perturbations, each multiplier is a scalar supporting slope of the optimal-value curve.
immediate_consequences_latex: A non-singleton multiplier set records nonsmooth first-order sensitivity.
Every multiplier gives a simultaneous lower estimate for all finite perturbations.
boundary_notes: A subgradient may fail to exist if \(V\) is not closed at zero or zero lies outside the appropriate relative interior.
The definition gives first-order convex sensitivity, not differentiability or a two-sided Taylor expansion.

children.title: Gauge-Fenchel Dual Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural relationship between gauge and Fenchel–Rockafellar dual constructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, let \(b\in Y\), and let \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) and \(\rho:Y\to[0,+\infty]\) be closed gauges. Their polar gauges are denoted by \(\kappa^\circ\) and \(\rho^\circ\). Fix \(\sigma\ge 0\) and set \(C=\{z\in Y:\rho(b-z)\le\sigma\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, closed, possibly asymmetric and extended-valued gauges; this record defines the algebraic normalization linking a Fenchel dual and a gauge dual, not a strong-duality theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge–Fenchel dual correspondence for \(P=\inf_x\{\kappa(x):Ax\in C\}\) is the identification of its Fenchel dual in the sign convention \[F=\sup_{y\in Y^*}\{\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y):\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\le1\}\] with the homogeneous gauge-dual problem \[D=\inf_{y\in Y^*}\{\kappa^\circ(A^*y):\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\ge1\}.\] Specifically, every \(y\) feasible for \(F\) with positive value \(q(y)=\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)>0\) maps to \(y/q(y)\), which is feasible for \(D\) and has objective \(\kappa^\circ(A^*y)/q(y)\). Conversely, every \(y\) feasible for \(D\) with \(\kappa^\circ(A^*y)>0\) maps to \(y/\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\), which is feasible for \(F\). This reciprocal normalization is the correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a gauge minimization problem with residual region \(C\), the Fenchel dual maximizes the homogeneous margin \(q(y)=\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\) over the polar-gauge unit ball. The gauge dual instead minimizes the polar gauge while requiring that margin to be at least one. Positive feasible points pass between the two formulations by radial rescaling, so their nonzero objective values are reciprocal normalizations of the same dual ray.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces with the canonical dual pairings.
\(A:X\to Y\) is linear and \(A^*:Y^*\to X^*\) is its adjoint.
\(\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are proper closed gauges, and \(\sigma\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) and \(D\) select the same positive dual rays, normalized respectively by \(\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\le1\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\ge1\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: On every ray with both terms positive, \[\frac{\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)}{\kappa^\circ(A^*y)}\] is scale invariant; \(F\) maximizes its numerator after denominator normalization, whereas \(D\) minimizes its denominator after numerator normalization.
special_cases_latex: When \(\sigma=0\), the margin is \(\langle b,y\rangle\), and \(D=\inf\{\kappa^\circ(A^*y):\langle b,y\rangle\ge1\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If finite positive optima are attained on corresponding rays, their values satisfy \(\operatorname{val}(F)\operatorname{val}(D)=1\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert feasibility, attainment, equality between the primal and either dual value, or validity when the relevant normalization denominator is zero.
A source supporting this exact gauge–Fenchel normalization, including the residual term and sign convention, was not located among the supplied sources.
review_flags: Exact source support is missing for the stated gauge–Fenchel radial-normalization correspondence.
knowledge_statements.title: Gauge–Fenchel Normalization Correspondence
Homogeneous Ratio Form of the Gauge Dual
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized gauge dual is equivalently minimization of a scale-invariant polar-gauge-to-surplus ratio over finite positive-surplus directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(\phi(y)=\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\), positive homogeneity gives \[\inf_{\phi(y)\geq1}\kappa^\circ(A^*y)=\inf_{\substack{0<\phi(y)<+\infty\\ \kappa^\circ(A^*y)<+\infty}}\frac{\kappa^\circ(A^*y)}{\phi(y)}.\] Every direction on the right has the normalized representative \(y/\phi(y)\), for which \(\phi=1\).
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa^\circ\) and \(\rho^\circ\) are positively homogeneous polar gauges.
At least one direction has finite positive \(\phi(y)\) and finite \(\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized and homogeneous-ratio gauge-dual values coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent unnormalized representation over finite positive-surplus directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge-Dual Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarizing both gauges and normalizing a positive residual-support surplus yields the gauge-dual minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal problem \[\inf_{x\in X}\{\kappa(x):\rho(b-Ax)\leq\sigma\},\] polarizing the objective gauge and the residual ball produces the normalized gauge dual \[\inf_{y\in Y}\left\{\kappa^\circ(A^*y):\phi(y)=\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\geq1\right\}.\] Positive homogeneity permits every \(y\) with \(\phi(y)>0\) to be scaled onto \(\phi(y)=1\); consequently, the construction compares the primal value with the reciprocal of the gauge-dual objective.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, \(b\in Y\), and \(\sigma\geq0\).
\(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) and \(\rho:Y\to[0,+\infty]\) are closed gauges, the primal value is finite and positive, and some \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized gauge dual is \(\inf\{\kappa^\circ(A^*y):\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\geq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized polar-gauge dual for a residual gauge constraint with positive primal value.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Rockafellar Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating the objective gauge and a positive-radius residual-ball indicator produces a maximization dual constrained by the polar objective gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the primal objective as \(\kappa(x)+\delta_C(b-Ax)\). Fenchel–Rockafellar conjugation gives \[\sup_{z\in Y}\{\langle b,z\rangle-\kappa^*(A^*z)-\delta_C^*(z)\}.\] For a closed gauge, \[\kappa^*(w)=\delta_{\{w:\kappa^\circ(w)\leq1\}}(w),\] while the positive-radius gauge ball satisfies \(\delta_C^*(z)=\sigma\rho^\circ(z)\). Hence the dual is \[\sup_{z\in Y}\left\{\langle b,z\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(z):\kappa^\circ(A^*z)\leq1\right\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(b\in Y\).
\(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) and \(\rho:Y\to[0,+\infty]\) are proper closed gauges, \(\sigma>0\), and \(C=\{r\in Y:\rho(r)\leq\sigma\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Fenchel dual is \(\sup\{\langle b,z\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(z):\kappa^\circ(A^*z)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel–Rockafellar dual of the extended-real residual formulation for a positive residual radius.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conjugates of gauges and support functions of positive-radius gauge balls

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Feasible-Boundary Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive homogeneity gives a bijection between the active normalization boundaries of the gauge and Fenchel dual feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(w)=\langle b,w\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(w)\). The maps \[y\mapsto z=\frac{y}{\kappa^\circ(A^*y)},\qquad z\mapsto y=\frac{z}{\phi(z)}\] are mutually inverse between \(\{y:\phi(y)=1,\ 0<\kappa^\circ(A^*y)<+\infty\}\) and \(\{z:\kappa^\circ(A^*z)=1,\ 0<\phi(z)<+\infty\}\). For corresponding points, \(\phi(z)=1/\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\).
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is linear, and \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are gauges with polar gauges \(\kappa^\circ\) and \(\rho^\circ\).
The displayed normalizing quantities are finite and strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The radial normalizations are mutually inverse and exchange their objective quantities reciprocally.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive boundary points of the normalized gauge and Fenchel dual feasible sets, without requiring optimality or attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Variable Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attained positive optima of the Fenchel and gauge duals correspond through reciprocal positive-homogeneous normalizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(y^\star\) solves the gauge dual and \(d^\star=\kappa^\circ(A^*y^\star)>0\), optimality and homogeneity give \(\phi(y^\star)=1\), and \[z^\star=\frac{y^\star}{d^\star}\] satisfies \(\kappa^\circ(A^*z^\star)=1\) and maximizes the Fenchel dual with value \(1/d^\star\). Conversely, if \(z^\star\) maximizes the Fenchel dual and \(q^\star=\phi(z^\star)>0\), then \(\kappa^\circ(A^*z^\star)=1\), and \[y^\star=\frac{z^\star}{q^\star}\] is gauge-dual feasible with active normalization and objective \(1/q^\star\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, \(b\in Y\), \(\sigma\geq0\), and \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are closed gauges on \(X\) and \(Y\).
The gauge dual and Fenchel dual attain finite positive optimal values \(d^\star\) and \(q^\star\), respectively, and \(q^\star=1/d^\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimal variables correspond by \(z^\star=y^\star/\kappa^\circ(A^*y^\star)\) and \(y^\star=z^\star/\phi(z^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling correspondence restricted to attained dual optima with finite positive values and reciprocal optimal values.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Primal-Dual Optimality Characterizations p. 154

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Value Normalization Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded Fenchel dual can coexist with a zero-valued normalized gauge dual, so finite reciprocal-value and optimizer correspondences fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=0\), \(b=1\), \(\sigma=0\), and \(\kappa=\rho=|\cdot|\). The Fenchel dual feasible set is all of \(\mathbb R\) and its objective is \(\phi(z)=z\), so its supremum is \(+\infty\) and it has no optimizer. The normalized gauge dual is \[\inf_y\{\kappa^\circ(A^*y):y\ge1\}=0.\] Thus no finite reciprocal optimal values or optimizer-to-optimizer normalization exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Fenchel dual value is \(+\infty\), the normalized gauge-dual value is \(0\), and reciprocal optimizer normalization is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of reciprocal optimizer correspondence when the Fenchel dual value is unbounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Obstructs Optimizer Normalization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive but unattained Fenchel dual value supplies no optimizer for the gauge–Fenchel normalization map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[\phi(z)=\langle b,z\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(z),\qquad D=\{z:\kappa^\circ(A^*z)\le1\}.\] If \(0<\sup_{z\in D}\phi(z)<+\infty\) but the supremum is not attained, there is no optimal Fenchel dual vector to normalize. Normalizable maximizing sequences do not establish an optimizer-to-optimizer gauge–Fenchel correspondence.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is linear and \(\kappa,\rho\) are gauges with polar gauges \(\kappa^\circ,\rho^\circ\).
\(0<\sup_{z\in D}\phi(z)<+\infty\), and the supremum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No optimizer-level correspondence follows because there is no attained Fenchel optimizer to normalize.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of optimizer-level gauge–Fenchel correspondence when a positive Fenchel dual value is not attained.

assumptions_latex: Gauge and Fenchel dual variables are related through positive homogeneous normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the relevant optimal value or normalization surplus is zero, the dual-variable scaling correspondence need not exist.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero optimal values obstruct normalization even when the primal is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The positive-value hypothesis is essential. Consider \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(A=1\), \(b=0\), \(\sigma=0\), and \(\kappa(x)=\rho(x)=|x|\). The primal constraint forces \(x=0\), so \(p^\star=0\). Its Fenchel dual has objective identically zero on \(\{|z|\leq1\}\), hence every optimizer satisfies \(\phi(z)=0\). The gauge-dual constraint is \(0\geq1\), so the gauge dual is infeasible. Division by \(\phi(z)\) is impossible, and no dual-variable correspondence exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero primal value can leave the Fenchel dual solvable while making the normalized gauge dual infeasible, so scaling correspondence fails.

children.title: Bidual Primal-Recovery Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Recovery correspondence obtained by dualizing the gauge-dual problem.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y,A,b,\sigma,\kappa,\rho\) be as in a finite-dimensional gauge optimization model, and write \(\operatorname{cl}\kappa=\kappa^{\circ\circ}\) and \(\operatorname{cl}\rho=\rho^{\circ\circ}\) for the bipolar closures. Consider the gauge dual \(D=\inf_y\{\kappa^\circ(A^*y):\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma\rho^\circ(y)\ge1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bidualization at the level of closed gauge data; recovery here means identification of the primal model represented by the bidual, not an algorithm for extracting a primal optimizer from an arbitrary dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bidual primal-recovery correspondence assigns to \(D\) the gauge primal \[D^\diamond=\inf_{x\in X}\{\kappa^{\circ\circ}(x):\rho^{\circ\circ}(b-Ax)\le\sigma\}.\] The original primal \(P=\inf\{\kappa(x):\rho(b-Ax)\le\sigma\}\) is called bidually recoverable when its objective and residual gauges are closed on the relevant finite-dimensional spaces, so that \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\kappa\) and \(\rho^{\circ\circ}=\rho\), and hence \(D^\diamond=P\) as an optimization problem. If the original gauges are not closed, the recovered object is the lower-semicontinuous gauge relaxation obtained by replacing each gauge with its bipolar closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing the gauge-dual data a second time replaces each polar gauge by its bipolar. The recovered primal therefore minimizes \(\kappa^{\circ\circ}\) subject to the residual constraint measured by \(\rho^{\circ\circ}\). Closed gauges equal their bipolars, so in that regime the bidual has exactly the original primal objective and feasible region. For nonclosed gauges, bidualization recovers the closed gauge relaxation rather than the unclosed model.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are proper gauges; their polar and bipolar gauges are formed with the relevant dual pairings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^\diamond=\inf_x\{\kappa^{\circ\circ}(x):\rho^{\circ\circ}(b-Ax)\le\sigma\}\), and \(D^\diamond=P\) whenever \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using unit sets \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\) and \(B_\rho=\{z:\rho(z)\le1\}\), bidual recovery replaces them by \(B_\kappa^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}B_\kappa\) and \(B_\rho^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}B_\rho\).
special_cases_latex: For norms in finite dimensions, the gauges are closed and finite, so the bidual model has the same norm objective and norm residual constraint as the primal.
immediate_consequences_latex: Bidualization cannot retain nonclosed boundary exclusions encoded only by an unclosed unit set.
boundary_notes: Problem equality under bidualization is distinct from equality of optimal values, attainment, or a pointwise primal-recovery formula from a dual optimizer.
No inspected source gave this exact bidualization of the stated gauge-dual problem.

notation.meaning: The primal-form problem assigned by gauge bidualization of \(D\).
The bipolar gauge, equal to the closed hull of \(\kappa\) in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge-Bidual Primal-Recovery Correspondence
Second Dual Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying gauge polarity twice returns the lower-semicontinuous closure of the gauge, and therefore returns the original gauge when it is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\gamma^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle:x\in E,\ \gamma(x)\leq1\},\qquad \gamma^{\circ\circ}(x)=\sup\{\langle x,y\rangle:y\in E,\ \gamma^\circ(y)\leq1\}.\] The second-dual construction applies gauge polarity a second time and replaces \(\gamma\) by its bipolar. The finite-dimensional bipolar theorem yields \[\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\gamma.\] Thus a closed gauge is recovered exactly, whereas a nonclosed gauge is recovered through its lower-semicontinuous closure.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and \(\gamma:E\to[0,+\infty]\) is a proper gauge.
Polarity is taken with respect to the given inner product, and \(\operatorname{cl}\gamma\) denotes the lower-semicontinuous closure of \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The second polar satisfies \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\operatorname{cl}\gamma\); in particular, \(\gamma^{\circ\circ}=\gamma\) when \(\gamma\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipolar construction for a proper gauge in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Recovery Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal solutions are exactly feasible points paired with dual-feasible points that saturate both the polar-gauge and residual-support inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p=\inf\{\kappa(x):b-Ax\in C\}\) and \(d=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle-\sigma_C(y):y\in Y^*,\ \kappa^\circ(A^*y)\le 1\}\). Under the stated qualification, \(p=d\), and a feasible point \(x\in X\) is primal optimal if and only if there exists a dual-feasible \(y\in Y^*\) such that \[\langle A^*y,x\rangle=\kappa(x),\qquad \langle y,b-Ax\rangle=\sigma_C(y).\] These equalities respectively expose \(x\) through the polar-gauge constraint and expose its residual through the support function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, \(b\in Y\), and \(C\subseteq Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a closed convex gauge, and there exists \(x_0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\kappa)\) with \(b-Ax_0\in\operatorname{ri}C\).
The primal value is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible \(x\in X\) is primal optimal exactly when it satisfies the displayed correspondence with some dual-feasible \(y\in Y^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel recovery for a gauge objective with a convex residual set.

notation.meaning: Polar gauge of the primal gauge, defined on the dual space
Support function of the residual set, defined on \(Y^*\)

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Dependent Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bidual recovers the closed value function and agrees with the original primal value exactly where no closure gap occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The biconjugate is the lower-semicontinuous convex closure of the proper convex value function: \[v^{**}=\operatorname{cl}v,\qquad \operatorname{epi}v^{**}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}v).\] Consequently, exact value recovery at \(b\in Y\) holds if and only if \(v(b)=v^{**}(b)\). When this equality fails, the closed epigraph describes limiting value pairs rather than the original value at \(b\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, \(C\subseteq Y\) is convex, and \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a proper convex gauge.
The value function \(v:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), defined by \(v(b)=\inf\{\kappa(x):b-Ax\in C\}\), is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(b\in Y\), \(v^{**}(b)=v(b)\) exactly when the primal value function agrees with its lower-semicontinuous closure at \(b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery is expressed through closure of the finite-dimensional primal value function; no minimizer recovery is asserted.

knowledge_statements.title: Value Recovery Does Not Ensure Minimizer Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact bidual recovery of the value cannot produce a primal solution when the primal infimum is unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[v(b)=\inf\{\kappa(x):b-Ax\in C\}.\] Even when \(v(b)=v^{**}(b)<+\infty\), bidual equality recovers only the value. If \[\operatorname*{argmin}\{\kappa(x):b-Ax\in C\}=\varnothing,\] no primal minimizer is recovered. Thus value-function closedness does not replace primal attainment in point recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, \(C\subseteq Y\) is convex, and \(\kappa\) is a proper convex gauge.
The infimum defining \(v(b)\) is not attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bidual value equality at \(b\) does not yield a primal minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates equality of primal and bidual values from existence of a primal optimizer.

notation.meaning: Fenchel biconjugate of the value function.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(b=(0,1)\), \(v(b)=+\infty\) while \(v^{**}(b)=0\), so bidual closure does not recover the primal problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(K\) is a closed convex cone, so \(\delta_K\) is a closed gauge. Its image is \[A(K)=\{(s,t):s>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] which is not closed. Hence \(v=\delta_{A(K)}\). For \(b=(0,1)\), no \(z\in K\) satisfies \(Az=b\), and therefore \(v(b)=+\infty\). Nevertheless, \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\), so \(v^{**}(b)=\delta_{\operatorname{cl}A(K)}(b)=0\). Closedness of the relevant projected epigraph or image is therefore essential for exact recovery.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge Modeling Tuple and Its Size–Fidelity Regions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces. Let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, \(b\in Y\), and let \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) and \(\rho:Y\to[0,+\infty]\) be gauges with unit sets \(B_\kappa\) and \(B_\rho\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex modeling with extended-valued, possibly asymmetric gauges; the definition covers constrained size and fidelity templates but not nonconvex penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gauge modeling relationship is a tuple \(\mathcal M=(X,Y,A,b,\kappa,\rho)\) in which structural size is represented by the homothetic regions \(tB_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le t\}\), while data fidelity is represented by \(b-sB_\rho=\{Ax:\rho(b-Ax)\le s\}\). Its canonical minimum-size model at tolerance \(\sigma\ge0\) and budget-feasibility model at budget \(\tau\ge0\) are respectively \[v(\sigma)=\inf\{\kappa(x):\rho(b-Ax)\le\sigma\},\qquad w(\tau)=\inf\{\rho(b-Ax):\kappa(x)\le\tau\}.\] Thus \(v(\sigma)\le\tau\) exactly when the structural region \(\tau B_\kappa\) intersects the inverse image \(A^{-1}(b-\sigma B_\rho)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tuple records how a gauge on the decision space measures model size and a gauge on the observation space measures residual size. Scaling their unit sets produces structural budgets and fidelity regions. The minimum-size and minimum-residual formulations exchange which gauge supplies the objective and which supplies the constraint. Their common geometric content is intersection between a structural gauge ball and the inverse image of a residual gauge ball.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are proper gauges with \(0\) in their unit sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(\sigma)\le\tau\iff \tau B_\kappa\cap A^{-1}(b-\sigma B_\rho)\ne\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v(\sigma)=\inf\{t\ge0:A(tB_\kappa)\cap(b-\sigma B_\rho)\ne\varnothing\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are norms, the structural and fidelity regions are centrally symmetric norm balls.
If \(\rho=\delta_{\{0\}}\), the minimum-size model reduces to \(\inf\{\kappa(x):Ax=b\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The value function \(v\) is nonincreasing in \(\sigma\), and \(w\) is nonincreasing in \(\tau\).
boundary_notes: Extended-valued gauges may encode conic restrictions through their domains.
The definition does not claim that either infimum is attained.

notation.meaning: Minimum structural size and minimum residual size value functions.

children.title: Minimum-Size Gauge Templates
children.top_down_role: Canonical models built from symmetric or asymmetric size functionals and convex fidelity regions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, let \(b\in Y\), let \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) be a gauge, and let \(F\subseteq Y\) be a nonempty convex fidelity region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex constrained models with a gauge objective and an arbitrary convex fidelity region; symmetry of the gauge is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimum-size gauge template generated by \((\kappa,A,F)\) is \[\operatorname{minsize}(\kappa,A,F):=\inf_{x\in X}\{\kappa(x):Ax\in F\}.\] If \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\), its value is equivalently \[\inf\{t\ge0:A(tB_\kappa)\cap F\ne\varnothing\}.\] A residual-gauge instance takes \(F=b-\sigma B_\rho\), where \(\rho\) is a gauge on \(Y\), \(B_\rho=\{r:\rho(r)\le1\}\), and \(\sigma\ge0\), yielding \(\inf\{\kappa(x):\rho(b-Ax)\le\sigma\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-size gauge model seeks a feasible decision having the smallest gauge value. Geometrically, it asks for the least dilation of the gauge unit set whose image under \(A\) meets the prescribed fidelity region. A common specialization defines fidelity by requiring the residual \(b-Ax\) to lie in a scaled residual-gauge ball.
assumptions_latex: For the residual specialization, \(\rho\) is a proper gauge and \(\sigma\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{minsize}(\kappa,A,F)=\inf\{t\ge0:A(tB_\kappa)\cap F\ne\varnothing\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the indicator \(\delta_F\), the template is \(\inf_x\{\kappa(x)+\delta_F(Ax)\}\).
special_cases_latex: Exact fitting uses \(F=\{b\}\), giving \(\inf\{\kappa(x):Ax=b\}\).
Norm-bounded residual fitting uses \(F=\{z:\|b-z\|\le\sigma\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F_1\subseteq F_2\), then \(\operatorname{minsize}(\kappa,A,F_1)\ge\operatorname{minsize}(\kappa,A,F_2)\).
boundary_notes: The optimal value may be \(+\infty\) when \(A^{-1}(F)\cap\operatorname{dom}\kappa\) is empty.
Closedness or coercivity is needed separately for attainment.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator, equal to \(0\) on \(F\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(F\).

children.title: Least-Norm Gauge Model Family
children.top_down_role: Minimum-size models over convex feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|_X)\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(Y\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(F\subseteq Y\) be a nonempty convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric-gauge specialization of minimum-size modeling; the objective is a norm and therefore finite, positive definite, and centrally symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The least-norm model associated with \((\|\cdot\|_X,A,F)\) is \[\inf_{x\in X}\{\|x\|_X:Ax\in F\}.\] Its solution set is \[S_F=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in A^{-1}(F)}\|x\|_X,\] and its value is the least \(t\ge0\) for which \(A(tB_X)\cap F\ne\varnothing\), where \(B_X=\{x:\|x\|_X\le1\}\). The family includes exact least-norm interpolation with \(F=\{b\}\) and tolerance models with \(F=b-\sigma B_Y\) for a residual norm ball \(B_Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A least-norm model selects, among all decisions whose image lies in a convex fidelity region, one with minimum norm. It is the symmetric, everywhere-finite case of a minimum-size gauge model. Its geometric value is the first radius at which the image of the norm ball intersects the fidelity region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf\{\|x\|_X:Ax\in F\}=\inf\{t\ge0:A(tB_X)\cap F\ne\varnothing\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The epigraph form is \(\inf\{t:(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R,\ Ax\in F,\ x\in tB_X,\ t\ge0\}\).
special_cases_latex: With \(F=\{b\}\) and the Euclidean norm, this is the minimum-Euclidean-norm solution of \(Ax=b\).
With \(\|\cdot\|_X=\|\cdot\|_1\) and \(F=\{b\}\), this is basis pursuit.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F\) is closed and feasible, finite dimensionality and norm coercivity imply that \(S_F\) is nonempty and compact.
boundary_notes: Replacing the norm by a nonsymmetric or extended-valued gauge leaves the least-norm family and enters the broader minimum-size gauge template.
Uniqueness is not part of the definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Norm Dual and Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The least-norm value is the maximum datum pairing over dual vectors whose adjoint image has dual norm at most one; equality gives an exact certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[p(b)=\min\{\|x\|_X:Ax=b\},\] the dual problem is \[\max_{y\in Y^*}\ \langle b,y\rangle\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|A^*y\|_{X,*}\le1.\] If \(Ax=b\), \(\|A^*y\|_{X,*}\le1\), and \(\langle b,y\rangle=\|x\|_X\), then \(x\) and \(y\) are optimal. When \(Ax=b\) is consistent, the primal and dual values agree and the dual maximum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(b)=\max\{\langle b,y\rangle:\|A^*y\|_{X,*}\le1\}\), and primal-dual objective equality certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual program and exact certificate for the finite-dimensional equality-constrained least-norm model.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Convexity Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly convex norm gives a unique least-norm point on every nonempty affine fiber, whereas a flat-sided norm can admit a face of minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\|\cdot\|_X\) is strictly convex and \(Ax=b\) is consistent, then the least-norm solution is unique. Without strict convexity uniqueness can fail: minimizing \(\|x\|_\infty\) subject to \(x_1=1\) has solution set \(\{(1,t):|t|\le1\}\).
assumptions_latex: The norm is strictly convex for the uniqueness assertion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict convexity makes \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b}\|x\|_X\) a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient uniqueness condition and its flat-unit-ball failure boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Norm Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A least-norm model selects, among all solutions of a linear equation, those with minimum norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The least-norm model associated with \(A\), \(b\), and \(\|\cdot\|_X\) is \[p(b)=\min_{x\in X}\{\|x\|_X:Ax=b\},\qquad S(b)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=b}\|x\|_X.\] It is the minimum-gauge model whose gauge is the symmetric gauge \(\kappa(x)=\|x\|_X\). In finite dimensions, consistency of \(Ax=b\) ensures that \(S(b)\) is nonempty because norm sublevel sets are compact.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(b\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The least-norm model returns the points in \(A^{-1}(b)\) having smallest \(X\)-norm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained finite-dimensional least-norm formulation.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.3 Constrained Minimization p. 50

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Gauge Primal-Dual Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal feasibility, polar dual feasibility, and equality of objective values exactly certify a minimum-gauge solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Ax=b\), \(\kappa(x)<+\infty\), and \(\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\le1\). Then \(x\) and \(y\) have equal optimal values if and only if \[\langle b,y\rangle=\kappa(x).\] When \(\kappa(x)>0\), this equality is equivalent to \(A^*y\in\partial\kappa(x)\), or equivalently to \(A^*y\) exposing \(x/\kappa(x)\) on the gauge unit set.
assumptions_latex: The displayed primal and dual feasibility conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle b,y\rangle=\kappa(x)\) is an exact primal-dual optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimality certificate for feasible primal and dual points.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Strong-Duality Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-interior condition on attainable finite-gauge right-hand sides ensures exact polar-gauge dual recovery; failure of the condition removes that guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(b\in\operatorname{ri}(A(\operatorname{dom}\kappa))\) and \(p(b)<+\infty\), then \[p(b)=\max\{\langle b,y\rangle:\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\le1\}.\] If this relative-interior condition fails, weak duality remains valid, but this qualification alone no longer guarantees equality or dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal value equals an attained dual maximum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional qualification for exact dual recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Gauge Weak Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar-gauge dual maximizes the right-hand-side pairing subject to a polar bound on the adjoint image and always provides lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[p(b)=\inf\{\kappa(x):Ax=b\},\] define \[d(b)=\sup_{y\in Y^*}\{\langle b,y\rangle:\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\le1\}.\] Every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\) satisfy \[\langle b,y\rangle=\langle A^*y,x\rangle\le\kappa(x),\] so \(d(b)\le p(b)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(b)\le p(b)\) for the displayed primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical polar-gauge dual and weak-duality bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Gauge Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-gauge model finds the smallest scale of a gauge unit set that intersects the linear feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimum-gauge model is \[p(b)=\inf_{x\in X}\{\kappa(x):Ax=b\}.\] Equivalently, with \(B_\kappa=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\), its value is the least scale \(t\ge0\) for which the affine fiber meets the scaled unit set: \[p(b)=\inf\{t\ge0:\{x:Ax=b\}\cap tB_\kappa\ne\varnothing\}.\] Extended values permit the gauge domain itself to encode structural restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(b\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model minimizes the gauge-defined size over the affine feasible set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General equality-constrained minimum-size template using an extended-valued gauge.

notation.meaning: Minimum gauge value at the right-hand side

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.3 Constrained Minimization p. 50

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-to-Gauge Specialization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norms are precisely gauges of closed, bounded, centrally symmetric convex neighborhoods of zero; polar gauges then become dual norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge \(\gamma_B\) is finite, definite, and symmetric, hence is a norm with closed unit ball \(B\). Conversely, if \(\|\cdot\|\) is any norm and \(B=\{x:\|x\|\le1\}\), then \(\gamma_B(x)=\|x\|\). Moreover, the polar gauge specializes to the dual norm: \[\gamma_B^\circ(y)=\sup_{x\in B}\langle y,x\rangle=\|y\|_*,\] and its unit ball is \(B^\circ\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(B\subset X\) is closed, convex, bounded, centrally symmetric, and has \(0\in\operatorname{int}B\).
\(\gamma_B(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tB\}\) is the Minkowski gauge of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_B\) is a norm, and every finite-dimensional norm arises as the gauge of its closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of norms as symmetric, finite, definite gauges.

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge of the unit set
Polar set of the unit set
Dual norm induced by the polar unit ball

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetry-Driven Distinctions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymmetric gauge prices opposite directions differently; symmetrizing it can change both the optimal value and the selected solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gauge need not satisfy \(\kappa(-x)=\kappa(x)\). Thus the models \(\inf\{\kappa(x):Ax=b\}\) and \(\inf\{\kappa(-x):Ax=b\}\) can have different values and minimizers. Replacing \(\kappa\) by \[\kappa_{\mathrm{sym}}(x)=\max\{\kappa(x),\kappa(-x)\}\] produces a symmetric gauge but changes the unit set from \(B_\kappa\) to \(B_\kappa\cap(-B_\kappa)\). Hence norm-based interpretations apply only after symmetry is imposed, and symmetrization is a genuine model modification.
assumptions_latex: \(\kappa:X\to[0,+\infty]\) is a gauge on a real vector space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Directional reversal changes gauge costs and generally changes minimum-gauge models, unlike the norm case.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of dropping central symmetry from least-size models.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: gauge symmetry is exactly the additional condition distinguishing norms from general gauges

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Residual Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility plus equality of primal and dual objectives certifies optimality; a nonzero dual vector exposes the active residual-ball boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) satisfy \(\|Ax-b\|_Y\le\varepsilon\) and let \(y\) satisfy \(\kappa^\circ(A^*y)\le1\). If \[\kappa(x)=\langle b,y\rangle-\varepsilon\|y\|_{Y,*},\] then \(x\) and \(y\) are primal and dual optimal. Under these feasibility conditions, objective equality is equivalent to \[\langle A^*y,x\rangle=\kappa(x),\qquad \langle y,b-Ax\rangle=\varepsilon\|y\|_{Y,*}.\] If \(y\ne0\), the residual constraint is active and \(y/\|y\|_{Y,*}\) is norming for \(b-Ax\).
assumptions_latex: The stated primal and dual feasibility conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed objective equality is an exact optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual certificate and active-residual complementarity for the norm-residual model.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Constrained Residual Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model minimizes a structural gauge while requiring the residual to lie in a prescribed norm ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A norm-constrained residual model has the form \[\min_{x\in X}\ \kappa(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \|Ax-b\|_Y\le\varepsilon.\] Its feasible set is \(A^{-1}(b+\varepsilon B_Y)\), where \(B_Y=\{r:\|r\|_Y\le1\}\). At \(\varepsilon=0\) it reduces to an equality-constrained minimum-gauge problem; increasing \(\varepsilon\) enlarges the feasible set and therefore cannot increase the optimal gauge value.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional, \(A:X\to Y\) is linear, and \(b\in Y\).
\(\kappa\) is a closed gauge on \(X\), \(\|\cdot\|_Y\) is a norm on \(Y\), and \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model minimizes structural gauge size over the inverse image of the norm ball centered at \(b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural gauge minimization with norm-bounded data misfit.

notation.meaning: Structural gauge on the decision variable
Closed unit ball of the residual norm

children.title: Asymmetric Cost-Budget Gauges
children.top_down_role: Directional penalties, costs, and budgets modeled by nonsymmetric gauges.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be a closed convex set containing \(0\). The Minkowski gauge of \(C\) is \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional directional cost models; the gauge may be nonsymmetric or extended-valued, so positive and negative directions can have different or infinite costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An asymmetric cost-budget gauge is a closed gauge \(\kappa=\gamma_C\) for which central symmetry is not imposed, and hence there may exist \(x\in X\) with \(\kappa(x)\ne\kappa(-x)\). For a budget \(\tau\ge0\), the admissible budget region is \[B_\kappa(\tau)=\{x:\kappa(x)\le\tau\}=\tau C.\] Given a convex loss \(\ell:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the associated budget model is \[\inf\{\ell(x):\kappa(x)\le\tau\},\] while the penalized directional-cost model is \(\inf_x\{\ell(x)+\lambda\kappa(x)\}\) for \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsymmetric convex unit set defines a gauge that charges different amounts for opposite directions. Scaling that unit set gives the feasible region for a cost budget. The same directional cost can appear either as a hard budget constraint or as a positively weighted penalty.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is closed, convex, nonempty, and contains \(0\).
\(\ell\) is a proper convex loss for the optimization specializations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_\kappa(\tau)=\tau C\), with no requirement that \(B_\kappa(\tau)=-B_\kappa(\tau)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The directional unit cost is encoded by \(C=\{x:\kappa(x)\le1\}\).
The polar cost is \(\kappa^\circ(y)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:x\in C\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=-C\), is absorbing, and contains no line, then \(\gamma_C\) is a norm and the asymmetric regime collapses to a symmetric budget.
If \(C\) lies in a proper cone, directions outside \(\operatorname{cone}C\) have cost \(+\infty\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A feasible step \(x\) need not imply feasibility of \(-x\) at the same budget.
boundary_notes: A gauge is positively homogeneous only for nonnegative scalars; nonsymmetry prevents replacing this by absolute homogeneity.
The constrained and penalized models are not asserted to have identical solution sets for every \(\tau\) and \(\lambda\).

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Soft-Thresholding Proximal Map
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal map is asymmetric soft-thresholding with separate positive and negative thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\tau>0\) and
\[
\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\alpha_i(r_i)_++\beta_i(-r_i)_+\bigr),
\qquad \alpha_i,\beta_i>0.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{prox}_{\tau\ell_{\alpha,\beta}}\) acts coordinatewise, with
\[
[\operatorname{prox}_{\tau\ell_{\alpha,\beta}}(z)]_i=
\begin{cases}
z_i-\tau\alpha_i,&z_i>\tau\alpha_i,\\
0,&-\tau\beta_i\leq z_i\leq\tau\alpha_i,\\
z_i+\tau\beta_i,&z_i<-\tau\beta_i.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proximal operator is the displayed coordinatewise asymmetric soft-thresholding map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-form proximal operator of the separable weighted positive/negative-part loss.

notation.meaning: Euclidean proximal map of the scaled asymmetric loss

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Certificate for Asymmetric Loss
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient is the positive price on positive residuals, the negative price on negative residuals, and an intervening value at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(r\in\mathbb R^m\), \[\partial\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)=\prod_{i=1}^mD_i(r_i),\qquad D_i(t)=\begin{cases}\{\alpha_i\},&t>0,\\[-\beta_i,\alpha_i],&t=0,\\\{-\beta_i\},&t<0.\end{cases}\] Equivalently, \(y\in\partial\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)\) exactly when \(-\beta_i\leq y_i\leq\alpha_i\) and \(y_ir_i=\alpha_i(r_i)_++\beta_i(-r_i)_+\) for every coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)=\prod_iD_i(r_i).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise subdifferential of weighted two-sided linear loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar of a Weighted Asymmetric Loss Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of the separable asymmetric loss is a weighted one-sided maximum gauge whose unit ball is a coordinate box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\alpha_i(r_i)_++\beta_i(-r_i)_+\bigr),\qquad\alpha_i,\beta_i>0,\] the polar gauge is \[\ell_{\alpha,\beta}^\circ(y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\left\{\frac{(y_i)_+}{\alpha_i},\frac{(-y_i)_+}{\beta_i}\right\}.\] Hence \(\ell_{\alpha,\beta}^\circ(y)\leq1\) exactly when \(-\beta_i\leq y_i\leq\alpha_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell_{\alpha,\beta}^\circ(y)=\max_i\left\{(y_i)_+/\alpha_i,(-y_i)_+/\beta_i\right\}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit polar gauge for unequal positive and negative loss prices.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel Conjugate of Asymmetric Linear Loss
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel conjugate of asymmetric linear loss is the indicator of the box bounded by its negative and positive prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)=\sum_{i=1}^m(\alpha_i(r_i)_++\beta_i(-r_i)_+)\), where \(\alpha_i,\beta_i>0\), and set \(Q_{\alpha,\beta}=\prod_{i=1}^m[-\beta_i,\alpha_i]\). Then
\[
\ell_{\alpha,\beta}^*(y)=\delta_{Q_{\alpha,\beta}}(y).
\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\alpha,\beta}^*=\delta_{\prod_i[-\beta_i,\alpha_i]}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator representation of the conjugate of coordinatewise weighted positive/negative-part loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Cross-Polytope Unit Ball
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymmetric weighted l1 unit ball is the convex hull of differently scaled positive and negative coordinate vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\alpha_i,\beta_i>0\) and \(\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\alpha_i(r_i)_++\beta_i(-r_i)_+\bigr)\). If \(e_i\) denotes the \(i\)-th coordinate vector, then
\[
\{r:\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)\leq1\}=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\frac{e_i}{\alpha_i},-\frac{e_i}{\beta_i}:i=1,\ldots,m\right\}.
\]
Thus \(\ell_{\alpha,\beta}\) is the Minkowski functional of a generally nonsymmetric cross-polytope containing the origin in its interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{r:\ell_{\alpha,\beta}(r)\leq1\}=\operatorname{conv}\{e_i/\alpha_i,-e_i/\beta_i:i=1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex representation of the unit ball of coordinatewise weighted positive/negative-part loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Loss Gauges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a coordinatewise gauge assigning different costs to positive and negative residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For weights \(a_i>0\) and \(b_i>0\), define \(r_i^+=\max\{r_i,0\}\) and \(r_i^-=\max\{-r_i,0\}\). The asymmetric loss gauge on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) is \[L_{a,b}(r)=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(a_i r_i^+ + b_i r_i^-\bigr).\] It is finite, convex, positively homogeneous, and vanishes only at \(0\). Its unit ball is generally not centrally symmetric; specifically, \(L_{a,b}(r)=L_{a,b}(-r)\) for every \(r\) if and only if \(a_i=b_i\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymmetric loss gauge charges positive and negative components at different rates. It becomes symmetric exactly when both rates agree in every coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{a,b}\) is a gauge, and \(L_{a,b}(r)=L_{a,b}(-r)\) for all \(r\) if and only if \(a=b\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coefficient Boundary for Asymmetric Linear Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact gauge and definiteness boundaries when zero or negative directional prices are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For real coefficients \(\alpha_i,\beta_i\), define
\[
L(r)=\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(\alpha_i(r_i)_++\beta_i(-r_i)_+\bigr).
\]
If \(\alpha_i,\beta_i\geq0\) for every \(i\), then \(L\) is a finite convex positively homogeneous gauge. It is definite, meaning \(L(r)=0\Rightarrow r=0\), if and only if \(\alpha_i>0\) and \(\beta_i>0\) for every \(i\). If some \(\alpha_i<0\) or some \(\beta_i<0\), then \(L\) is negative on the corresponding positive or negative coordinate ray and is not a gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative directional prices produce a gauge, strictly positive prices are exactly what make it definite, and any negative price destroys the gauge property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) is a finite gauge when all prices are nonnegative, is definite exactly when all prices are positive, and is not a gauge if any price is negative.
knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Boundary for Asymmetric Linear Loss
Polar Resource Price Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of the capacity-normalized resource gauge is the capacity-weighted sum of positive resource prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B_c=\{x:0\le x_i\le c_i\}\), \[\gamma_{B_c}^{\circ}(y)=\sup_{x\in B_c}\langle y,x\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i(y_i)_+.\] Consequently, whenever \(\gamma_{B_c}(x)<+\infty\), \[\langle y,x\rangle\le\gamma_{B_c}(x)\sum_i c_i(y_i)_+.\] Negative resource prices do not contribute because admissible consumptions are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{B_c}^{\circ}(y)=\sum_i c_i(y_i)_+\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar gauge and price interpretation for the nonnegative capacity box.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Gauges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines minimum nonnegative resource cost for synthesizing a vector from directed activities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=[d_1,\ldots,d_p]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\) be a finite activity dictionary and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^p\) contain unit resource costs. The resource gauge is the extended-valued function \[\rho_{D,c}(x)=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}\lambda:D\lambda=x,\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^p\},\] with infimum \(+\infty\) when no such \(\lambda\) exists. Equivalently, \(\rho_{D,c}\) is the gauge of \(C=\operatorname{conv}(\{0,d_1/c_1,\ldots,d_p/c_p\})\). Thus its effective domain is \(\operatorname{cone}\{d_1,
\ldots,d_p\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource gauge is the least positive activity cost needed to synthesize a target, and is infinite outside the generated activity cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_{D,c}=\gamma_C\) and \(\operatorname{dom}\rho_{D,c}=\operatorname{cone}\{d_1,\ldots,d_p\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Soft-Thresholding
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal step has different positive and negative thresholds and becomes ordinary soft-thresholding when the two directional prices agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), the Euclidean proximal map of \(\lambda\ell\) is coordinatewise and satisfies \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\ell}(z)_i=\begin{cases}z_i-\lambda\alpha_i,&z_i>\lambda\alpha_i,\\0,&-\lambda\beta_i\le z_i\le\lambda\alpha_i,\\z_i+\lambda\beta_i,&z_i<-\lambda\beta_i.\end{cases}\]
assumptions_latex: The proximal map uses the Euclidean squared-distance term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed asymmetric soft-threshold formula equals \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\ell}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise proximal operator for the separable directional penalty.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Price-Box Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional penalty is the support function of its box of admissible prices, and its conjugate is the indicator of that box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\ell(r)=\sum_{i=1}^m[\alpha_i(r_i)_++\beta_i(-r_i)_+]\), let \(Q=\prod_{i=1}^m[-\beta_i,\alpha_i]\). Then \[\ell(r)=\sigma_Q(r)=\sup_{g\in Q}\langle g,r\rangle,\qquad \ell^*(g)=\delta_Q(g).\] Thus the admissible price in coordinate \(i\) ranges from \(-\beta_i\) to \(\alpha_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell=\sigma_Q\) and \(\ell^*=\delta_Q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-price representation of the separable two-sided linear penalty.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Penalty Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the raywise scaling law and the independent penalties permitted on opposite directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma\) be a gauge on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). For every direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and scalar \(t\geq0\), positive homogeneity gives \(\gamma(td)=t\gamma(d)\), whereas the opposite ray satisfies \(\gamma(-td)=t\gamma(-d)\). Hence the two rays may have distinct marginal penalties. If both values are finite and positive, their directional asymmetry ratio is \(q(d)=\gamma(d)/\gamma(-d)\), with \(q(-d)=q(d)^{-1}\). The regime is symmetric along \(d\) exactly when \(q(d)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge scales linearly on each positive ray, but opposite rays can have different rates. Their rate ratio quantifies directional asymmetry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma(td)=t\gamma(d)\), \(\gamma(-td)=t\gamma(-d)\), and \(q(-d)=q(d)^{-1}\) for \(t\geq0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of the separable two-sided linear directional penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\ell(r)=\sum_{i=1}^m[\alpha_i(r_i)_++\beta_i(-r_i)_+]\), define \(Q=\prod_{i=1}^m[-\beta_i,\alpha_i]\). Then \[\ell(r)=\sigma_Q(r)=\sup_{g\in Q}\langle g,r\rangle,\qquad \ell^*(g)=\delta_Q(g).\] Thus the admissible dual price in coordinate \(i\) lies between \(-\beta_i\) and \(\alpha_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymmetric piecewise-linear penalty is the support function of the box of admissible directional prices, and its conjugate is that box's indicator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell=\sigma_Q\) and \(\ell^*=\delta_Q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Box-Support Representation of Directional Prices
Unattained Limiting Budget
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed semidefinite image can approach the datum without containing it, making the limiting residual budget infeasible although every positive budget is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb S^2\), \(\kappa=\delta_{\mathbb S_+^2}\), and \(A\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&c\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)=(a,c)\). Then \[A(\operatorname{dom}\kappa)=\{(a,c):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] For \(b=(0,1)\) and the Euclidean residual gauge, \[\inf_{X\succeq0}\|b-A(X)\|_2=0,\] but no \(X\succeq0\) satisfies \(A(X)=b\). Hence \(F_0=\varnothing\), while \(F_\sigma\ne\varnothing\) for every \(\sigma>0\).
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S_+^2\) is the cone of positive-semidefinite real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_{\min}=0\), \(F_0=\varnothing\), and \(F_\sigma\ne\varnothing\) for every \(\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional residual-budget instance whose threshold is not feasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the smallest gauge budget compatible with a norm-bounded residual constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the residual-feasible set \(F_\varepsilon=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|Ax-b\|\leq\varepsilon\}\), define \(v(\varepsilon)=\inf_{x\in F_\varepsilon}\gamma_C(x)\), with \(v(\varepsilon)=+\infty\) when \(F_\varepsilon=\varnothing\). A budget \(\tau\geq0\) is feasible precisely when there exists \(x\) satisfying \(\gamma_C(x)\leq\tau\) and \(\|Ax-b\|\leq\varepsilon\). Consequently, feasibility implies \(\tau\geq v(\varepsilon)\), and the converse holds for every \(\tau>v(\varepsilon)\). It also holds at \(\tau=v(\varepsilon)\) whenever the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum achievable gauge value is the budget boundary: larger budgets are feasible, while the boundary itself is feasible when a minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau>v(\varepsilon)\Rightarrow\exists x\in F_\varepsilon:\gamma_C(x)\leq\tau\), while feasibility implies \(\tau\geq v(\varepsilon)\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(\mathcal A\subseteq X\) be a set of elementary structured objects called atoms. Set \(C_{\mathcal A}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A\cup\{0\})\) and \(\kappa_{\mathcal A}=\gamma_{C_{\mathcal A}}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex models generated by finite or infinite atom sets; symmetry is optional, and asymmetric atom sets produce gauges rather than norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structured atomic-gauge model is an optimization problem of the form \[\inf_{x\in X}\{\kappa_{\mathcal A}(x):x\in F\}\quad\text{or}\quad\inf_{x\in X}\{L(x)+\lambda\kappa_{\mathcal A}(x)\},\] where \(F\subseteq X\) is a convex fidelity region, \(L\) is a proper convex loss, and \(\lambda\ge0\). The atomic gauge is \[\kappa_{\mathcal A}(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC_{\mathcal A}\},\] so its sublevel sets are precisely dilations of the closed convex hull of the prescribed elementary structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set of elementary objects determines a convex structural size by taking their closed convex hull with the origin and then its Minkowski gauge. Constrained and penalized recovery models use this gauge to favor decisions representable with small total atomic weight. Sparse vectors and low-rank matrices arise by choosing coordinate atoms and rank-one atoms, respectively.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is convex, or \(L\) is proper convex with \(\lambda\ge0\), according to the selected formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\kappa_{\mathcal A}(x)\le t\}=tC_{\mathcal A}\) for every \(t\ge0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(\mathcal A=-\mathcal A\), \(\kappa_{\mathcal A}(x)=\inf\{\sum_i|\alpha_i|:x=\sum_i\alpha_i a_i,\ a_i\in\mathcal A\}\), with the infimum interpreted over finite decompositions.
special_cases_latex: For \(\mathcal A=\{\pm e_i\}_{i=1}^n\), \(\kappa_{\mathcal A}=\|\cdot\|_1\).
For unit-norm rank-one matrix atoms and their negatives, \(\kappa_{\mathcal A}\) is the nuclear norm.
immediate_consequences_latex: The modeling geometry is determined by \(C_{\mathcal A}\); distinct atom lists with the same closed convex hull generate the same gauge.
boundary_notes: If \(\mathcal A\) is not centrally symmetric, the atomic functional need not be a norm.
Computational tractability of the gauge is not part of the definition.

notation.meaning: Gauge generated by the atomic unit set.

children.title: Atomic Gauge Construction
children.top_down_role: Convex-hull generation, decomposition, and polar-support representations for atomic sets.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(\mathcal A\subseteq X\) be nonempty. Assume that \(C=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A\cup\{0\})\) is absorbing in its linear span \(L=\operatorname{span}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional construction on the span of the atoms; it allows nonsymmetric atomic sets and therefore uses nonnegative atomic coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The atomic gauge generated by \(\mathcal A\) is \[\gamma_{\mathcal A}(x)=\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC\},\qquad x\in L.\] Equivalently, before lower-semicontinuous closure it is the infimum of total nonnegative atomic weight, \[\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m c_i:m\in\mathbb N,\ c_i\ge0,\ a_i\in\mathcal A,\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m c_i a_i\right\}.\] Its polar gauge is the support function of the atomic set, \[\gamma_{\mathcal A}^\circ(y)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle y,a\rangle,\qquad y\in L^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: To construct an atomic gauge, take the closed convex hull of the atoms and the origin and use it as the unit set of a Minkowski functional. The primal value is the smallest total nonnegative weight of an atomic decomposition, with closure when limiting decompositions are needed. The polar value is obtained by maximizing a linear functional over the atoms.
assumptions_latex: The construction is evaluated on \(L=\operatorname{span}C\), where \(C\) is absorbing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}=\gamma_C\) and \(\gamma_{\mathcal A}^\circ=\sigma_C=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle\cdot,a\rangle\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in tC\iff x\) is a limit of finite sums \(\sum_i c_i a_i\) with \(c_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i c_i\le t\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\mathcal A=-\mathcal A\), signed coefficients may be used and their cost is \(\sum_i|\alpha_i|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Replacing \(\mathcal A\) by its closed convex hull with \(0\) does not change the gauge or polar oracle.
boundary_notes: Without absorption, the gauge is \(+\infty\) outside the conic hull of the atomic unit set.
Closed convex hull is essential when the atom set is not closed or finite.

children.title: Finite-Dictionary Polyhedral Gauges
children.top_down_role: Atomic gauges generated by finite dictionaries.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_m]:\mathbb R^m\to X\) be a finite dictionary in a finite-dimensional real vector space \(X\), and set \(C_D=\operatorname{conv}(\{0,a_1,\ldots,a_m\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finitely generated, potentially asymmetric gauges; the domain is the cone generated by the dictionary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-dictionary polyhedral gauge is \[\gamma_D(x)=\inf\left\{\mathbf1^Tc:c\in\mathbb R_+^m,\ Dc=x\right\},\] with value \(+\infty\) when no nonnegative coefficient vector represents \(x\). Equivalently, \(\gamma_D=\gamma_{C_D}\), and its unit sublevel set is the polytope \(C_D\). Its polar is \[\gamma_D^\circ(y)=\max\{0,\langle y,a_1\rangle,\ldots,\langle y,a_m\rangle\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite dictionary generates a polyhedral gauge by charging the sum of nonnegative representation coefficients. Its unit set is the convex hull of the origin and the dictionary atoms. Gauge evaluation is a linear program, and polar evaluation is the largest pairing with one of the finitely many atoms or the origin.
assumptions_latex: Coefficients in the asymmetric representation satisfy \(c_i\ge0\).
The gauge is extended by \(+\infty\) outside \(\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_D=\gamma_{C_D}\) and \(\gamma_D^\circ(y)=\max_{0\le i\le m}\langle y,a_i\rangle\), where \(a_0=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\gamma_D(x)\le t\iff \exists c\ge0:\ Dc=x,\ \mathbf1^Tc\le t\).
special_cases_latex: If the dictionary contains \(\pm d_j\) for every generator, then \(\gamma_D(x)=\inf\{\|\alpha\|_1:\sum_j\alpha_jd_j=x\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Both primal gauge evaluation and polar evaluation reduce to finite-dimensional polyhedral optimization.
boundary_notes: Redundant atoms do not change the gauge if they lie in the convex hull of the remaining atoms and the origin.
The gauge is a norm only under additional spanning, boundedness, and central-symmetry conditions.

notation.meaning: Linear synthesis map whose columns are the dictionary atoms.
