knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Membership Access Cannot Give Exact Real-Valued Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-information boundary for unrestricted real gauge values, distinct from approximate binary-search evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\ne0\) and suppose only finitely many exact membership queries of the form \(x/t\in C\) are permitted. Over a family for which \(\gamma_C(x)\) may be any value in a nondegenerate real interval, no deterministic finite-query procedure can recover \(\gamma_C(x)\) exactly: each query supplies only the comparison \(\gamma_C(x)\le t\), and finitely many binary answers cannot distinguish all values in the interval. Thus exact membership access yields arbitrarily accurate evaluation by threshold search, but not exact evaluation in finitely many queries without additional discreteness or algebraic structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite membership queries provide only finitely many threshold comparisons, so they cannot exactly identify an unrestricted real gauge value; the general reduction is necessarily approximate.
assumptions_latex: The admissible gauge family allows \(\gamma_C(x)\) to range over a nondegenerate real interval.
The algorithm makes finitely many exact membership queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact evaluation of an unrestricted real value \(\gamma_C(x)\) is impossible from finitely many membership comparisons, although approximation to any prescribed positive tolerance is possible.

notation.meaning: Positive threshold queried through membership of \(x/t\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Membership Access Cannot Give Exact Real-Valued Evaluation
Relative-Error Boundary Band
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relative-error gauge value decides unit-ball membership only outside its multiplicative uncertainty band around level one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be closed, convex, absorbing, and contain \(0\), let \(0\leq\varepsilon<1\), and suppose \(\gamma_K(x)<+\infty\) and \(|\widetilde\gamma(x)-\gamma_K(x)|\leq\varepsilon\gamma_K(x)\). Then \[\frac{\widetilde\gamma(x)}{1+\varepsilon}\leq\gamma_K(x)\leq\frac{\widetilde\gamma(x)}{1-\varepsilon}.\] Consequently, \(\widetilde\gamma(x)\leq1-\varepsilon\) certifies \(x\in K\), whereas \(\widetilde\gamma(x)>1+\varepsilon\) certifies \(x\notin K\). The intervening band does not determine exact membership from this guarantee alone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde\gamma(x)\leq1-\varepsilon\Rightarrow x\in K\) and \(\widetilde\gamma(x)>1+\varepsilon\Rightarrow x\notin K\), while \(1-\varepsilon<\widetilde\gamma(x)\leq1+\varepsilon\) is inconclusive from the error guarantee alone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership decisions obtainable from a multiplicative gauge-value guarantee.

notation.meaning: Relative-error approximation to the gauge value.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Precision Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive-error gauge oracle certifies membership or nonmembership away from level one, but its guarantee alone is inconclusive when the reported value lies strictly above one minus the tolerance and at most one plus the tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every query \(x\), closedness gives \(K=\{x:\gamma_K(x)\leq1\}\), and the error bound implies certified acceptance when \(\widetilde\gamma(x)+\varepsilon\leq1\) and certified rejection when \(\widetilde\gamma(x)-\varepsilon>1\). If \(1-\varepsilon<\widetilde\gamma(x)\leq1+\varepsilon\), both a value satisfying \(\gamma_K(x)\leq1\) and a value satisfying \(\gamma_K(x)>1\) are compatible with the error guarantee, so that guarantee alone does not determine exact membership.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde\gamma(x)\leq1-\varepsilon\Rightarrow x\in K\), and \(\widetilde\gamma(x)>1+\varepsilon\Rightarrow x\notin K\); the error guarantee alone does not force a membership decision when \(1-\varepsilon<\widetilde\gamma(x)\leq1+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-error evaluation determines membership only outside the correctly delimited boundary band around the unit level set.

notation.meaning: Minkowski gauge of the closed unit ball K.

children.top_down_role: Dual evaluation through support optimization.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex with \(0\in C\). Let \(\kappa_C=\gamma_C\), and define \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional value-oracle equivalence; an optimizer-returning support oracle is stronger than a value-only polar-gauge oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polar gauge of \(\kappa_C\) is the support function of its unit ball: \(\kappa_C^\circ(y)=\sigma_C(y)=\sup\{\langle y,x\rangle:x\in C\}\). Hence a value support oracle for \(C\) and a value evaluation oracle for \(\kappa_C^\circ\) are the same map. An optimizing support oracle additionally returns \(x_y\in C\) with \(\langle y,x_y\rangle=\kappa_C^\circ(y)\) when the supremum is finite and attained. Polar membership satisfies \(y\in sC^\circ\iff\kappa_C^\circ(y)\le s\) for \(s\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar gauge evaluated at a dual vector equals the support value of the primal gauge unit ball in that direction. Therefore a support-value oracle for the unit ball is exactly a polar-gauge value oracle. An oracle that also returns a maximizing point contains additional information and requires attainment. Membership in a scaled polar ball is equivalent to comparing the support value with the scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_C^\circ(y)=\sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle,\qquad y\in sC^\circ\iff\kappa_C^\circ(y)\le s.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\le1\}=\{y:\kappa_C^\circ(y)\le1\}.\)
special_cases_latex: For a balanced norm ball, the identity is the usual dual-norm support formula.
immediate_consequences_latex: A returned support maximizer is an exposed point or belongs to the exposed face selected by \(y\).
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is unbounded, the support value may be \(+\infty\).
A finite supremum need not be attained when compactness is absent.
Approximate support and approximate polar evaluation require matched additive or relative error conventions.

notation.meaning: Support function of the primal unit set.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Gauge Evaluation as Support Optimization
Polar-Gauge Value Oracles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polar-gauge value oracle returns the gauge of the polar, which equals the original set's possibly infinite support value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polar-gauge value oracle accepts \(y\) and returns the extended-real value \(\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)=\inf\{t>0:y\in tK^\circ\}\). Since \(0\in K\), this value is nonnegative and satisfies \[\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)=\inf\{t>0:\langle y,x\rangle\leq t\text{ for every }x\in K\}=\sup_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle=\sigma_K(y).\] The value may be \(+\infty\) when \(K\) is unbounded in a direction exposed by \(y\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space with \(0\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns \(\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)=\sigma_K(y)\in[0,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued exact value oracle for the gauge of a polar set.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive Approximate Support Oracle
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite support value admits positive-tolerance approximate support points; a certified upper bound paired with the achieved value certifies the additive gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\ne\varnothing\), \(\sigma_K(y)<+\infty\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). An additive \(\varepsilon\)-support oracle returns \(x_\varepsilon\in K\) satisfying \[\langle y,x_\varepsilon\rangle\ge\sigma_K(y)-\varepsilon.\] Such an output exists for every positive tolerance even when the supremum is not attained. If the oracle also returns a certified bound \(u\ge\sigma_K(y)\) with \(u-\langle y,x_\varepsilon\rangle\le\varepsilon\), the pair is a certificate of additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle y,x_\varepsilon\rangle\ge\sigma_K(y)-\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate linear-optimization output for directions with finite support value.

notation.meaning: Approximately supporting point returned by the oracle.
Optional certified upper bound on the support value.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Oracles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle returns the supremum of a linear functional over the set; a support point may be returned only when the supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a query direction \(y\), a support-function value oracle computes \(v=\sup_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle\) and returns \(v\). A strong support oracle additionally returns \(x_y\in K\) satisfying \(\langle y,x_y\rangle=v\), but only when the supremum is attained. If the supremum is unbounded, the value output is \(+\infty\); if it is finite but unattained, a value oracle remains defined while an exact support-point output does not exist.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty subset of a real inner-product space.
The requested support value is well-defined in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On input \(y\), the oracle outputs \(v=\sigma_K(y)=\sup_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle\), optionally with an attaining \(x_y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value oracle, with an optional optimizer output when support is attained.

notation.meaning: Optional support point returned by the oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Oracle Equivalence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact support evaluation on a set and exact gauge evaluation on its polar are identical value-oracle problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every query \(y\), polar membership gives \[y\in tK^\circ\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle y,x\rangle\leq t\text{ for every }x\in K.\] Taking the infimum over \(t>0\) yields \(\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)=\sigma_K(y)\). Consequently, an exact support-value oracle for \(K\) and an exact gauge-value oracle for \(K^\circ\) simulate one another with one query and no numerical transformation. This equivalence concerns values and does not itself produce a maximizing support point.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and contains \(0\) in a real Hilbert space.
Both oracles use exact extended-real arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)=\sigma_K(y)\) for every \(y\), so either value oracle implements the other query-for-query.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-oracle equivalence; optimizer-returning support oracles require an additional attainment hypothesis.

knowledge_statements.title: James Weak-Compactness Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: James's theorem characterizes weak compactness of a closed bounded convex set by attainment of every continuous linear functional; finite-dimensional compactness is the standard specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a Banach space \(X\). Then \(K\) is weakly compact if and only if every \(y\in X^*\) attains its support value on \(K\): \[\forall y\in X^*\;\exists x_y\in K:\quad \langle y,x_y\rangle=\sigma_K(y).\] In particular, compact sets in finite-dimensional spaces admit exact support points in every direction.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset X\) is nonempty, closed, bounded, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is weakly compact}\iff\forall y\in X^*,\;\sigma_K(y)\text{ is attained on }K.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp Banach-space characterization of universal support attainment for closed bounded convex sets.

notation.meaning: Continuous dual of the Banach space.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Attainment Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite support value may lack a maximizing point: the unit ball of ℓ¹ and coefficients approaching one provide a concrete example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a_n=1-1/n\), one has \(\sup_n a_n=1\), hence \(\sigma_K(a)=1\). Nevertheless, every \(x\in K\) satisfies \[\langle a,x\rangle\leq\sum_{n\geq1}a_n|x_n|<\sum_{n\geq1}|x_n|\leq1\] whenever \(x\neq0\), because every coefficient \(a_n\) is strictly below \(1\). Thus the finite support value is not attained. Compact feasible sets avoid this failure, while closed bounded sets in a general Banach space need not.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_K(a)=1\), but no \(x\in K\) satisfies \(\langle a,x\rangle=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support values need not be attained without compactness or an appropriate weak-compactness condition.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball of the sequence space.
Continuous linear functional represented by a bounded sequence.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.1 Support Points p. 133; 7.2 Support Functions p. 135

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient condition for exact support-point output in locally convex spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty weakly compact subset of a Banach space \(X\). For every \(y\in X^*\), the map \(x\mapsto\langle y,x\rangle\) is weakly continuous and therefore attains its maximum on \(K\): \[\sigma_K(y)=\max_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle.\] Consequently, compactness in finite dimensions, and weak compactness in infinite dimensions, suffice for an exact support-point oracle in every direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every continuous linear functional attains its support value on a nonempty weakly compact set; finite-dimensional compactness is the usual special case.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset X\) is nonempty and weakly compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_K(y)=\max_{x\in K}\langle y,x\rangle\).

notation.meaning: Continuous dual of the Banach space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Oracle for an Antipolar Region
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed with \(0\notin C\). Define its antipolar by \(C'=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\ \forall x\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional feasibility access for reverse-separation regions used in gauge duality; approximate variants require a declared margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An antipolar feasibility oracle for \(C\) is a predicate \(\mathrm{Feas}_{C'}(y)\) satisfying \(\mathrm{Feas}_{C'}(y)=1\iff y\in C'\iff\inf_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\ge1\). A certifying oracle may, upon rejection, return \(x_y\in C\) with \(\langle y,x_y\rangle<1\); upon acceptance it certifies the universal lower bound. For a scaled threshold \(\alpha>0\), the region \(C'_\alpha=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge\alpha\ \forall x\in C\}\) obeys \(C'_\alpha=\alpha C'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipolar of a set not containing the origin consists of dual vectors whose pairing with every primal feasible point is at least one. An exact feasibility oracle accepts precisely those vectors. Equivalently, it checks whether the infimum of the linear functional over the primal set is at least one. A certifying rejection oracle supplies a primal point violating that inequality. Positive threshold changes correspond to scaling the antipolar region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{Feas}_{C'}(y)=1\iff y\in C'\iff\inf_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\ge1.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: Rejection has a finite witness when there exists \(x_y\in C\) satisfying \(\langle y,x_y\rangle<1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\{x:Ax=b\}\) intersects an appropriate gauge domain, the oracle tests the reverse-separation constraints appearing in gauge-dual feasible regions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every accepted vector strictly separates the origin from \(C\) at normalized margin one.
boundary_notes: If \(0\in C\), then \(C'\) is empty.
For nonclosed or unbounded sets, the infimum may be unattained, so rejection need not have an optimizing witness.
An approximate oracle must distinguish acceptance, rejection, and an uncertainty band around level one.

notation.meaning: Antipolar or reverse-polar set of the primal region.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Oracle for an Antipolar Region
Primal-Witness Antipolar Separator
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A violated primal point is an exact antipolar nonmembership witness and directly supplies a separating halfspace with threshold one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be nonempty and let \(C'=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\ \forall x\in C\}\). For every query \(z\), \[z\notin C'\iff \exists x_z\in C:\langle z,x_z\rangle<1.\] Such a witness yields \(C'\subseteq H_{x_z}:=\{y:\langle y,x_z\rangle\geq1\}\) while \(z\notin H_{x_z}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_z\in C\) such that \(C'\subseteq\{y:\langle y,x_z\rangle\geq1\}\) and \(\langle z,x_z\rangle<1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Antipolar-specific separator obtained from a violated defining inequality.

notation.meaning: Primal point witnessing violation by the query.
Separating halfspace generated by the witness.

knowledge_statements.title: Antipolar Separation Oracles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle recognizes antipolar membership or supplies a valid halfspace containing the antipolar and strictly excluding the query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On input \(z\), an antipolar separation oracle first tests whether \(\inf_{x\in C}\langle z,x\rangle\geq1\). If so, it returns feasible. Otherwise it returns \(a\neq0\) and \(\beta\) such that \[\langle a,z\rangle<\beta\leq\langle a,y\rangle\quad\text{for every }y\in C'.\] Thus the reported closed halfspace contains the entire antipolar while excluding the query. The definition requires a strong separating pair, not merely a declaration of infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space and \(0\notin C\).
\(C'=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\text{ for all }x\in C\}\) is its antipolar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each query \(z\), the oracle either confirms \(z\in C'\) or returns a halfspace containing \(C'\) and excluding \(z\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation oracle for the closed convex antipolar feasible region.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical antipolar-specific separation response obtained from a violated defining inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C'=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\ \forall x\in C\}\). For a query \(z\), \[z\notin C'\iff \exists x_z\in C:\ \langle z,x_z\rangle<1.\] Any such witness defines the separating halfspace \[H_{x_z}=\{y:\langle y,x_z\rangle\geq1\},\] which contains \(C'\) and strictly excludes \(z\).

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Witness Separator for Antipolar Nonmembership
Firm Nonexpansiveness of Antipolar Projection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact projection onto a nonempty closed convex antipolar is firmly nonexpansive and therefore 1-Lipschitz in the query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C'\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space. For all \(z,w\), \[\|P_{C'}z-P_{C'}w\|^2\leq\langle P_{C'}z-P_{C'}w,z-w\rangle.\] Consequently, \(\|P_{C'}z-P_{C'}w\|\leq\|z-w\|\).
assumptions_latex: \(C'\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|P_{C'}z-P_{C'}w\|^2\leq\langle P_{C'}z-P_{C'}w,z-w\rangle\), hence \(\|P_{C'}z-P_{C'}w\|\leq\|z-w\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query stability of the exact metric-projection oracle.

notation.meaning: Metric projection onto the antipolar set.

knowledge_statements.title: Antipolar Projection Oracles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection oracle returns the nearest antipolar point; its variational inequality also yields membership or separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(z\), the oracle returns \[p=P_{C'}z=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{y\in C'}\tfrac12\|y-z\|^2.\] Closedness and convexity make \(p\) unique. Its optimality condition is \(\langle z-p,y-p\rangle\leq0\) for all \(y\in C'\). If \(z\notin C'\), then \(p\neq z\), and this inequality defines a separating halfspace containing \(C'\); if \(p=z\), the oracle certifies membership.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns the unique \(p=P_{C'}z\) and the inequality \(\langle z-p,y-p\rangle\leq0\) for every \(y\in C'\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C'\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space. knowledge_statements.title: Empty-Antipolar Projection Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The antipolar projection oracle is globally well-defined exactly when the closed convex primal set excludes zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space and \(C'=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq1\ \forall x\in C\}\). The projection \(P_{C'}z\) exists uniquely for every \(z\) if and only if \(C'\neq\varnothing\), equivalently if and only if \(0\notin C\). If \(0\in C\), then \(C'=\varnothing\) and the projection oracle is undefined.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall z,\ P_{C'}z\text{ exists uniquely})\iff C'\neq\varnothing\iff0\notin C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Reliability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even an arbitrarily accurate approximate projection can lie outside the antipolar, so norm error alone is not an exact certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Here \(P_{C'}z=1\), but the point \(\widetilde p=1-\delta\) satisfies \(|\widetilde p-P_{C'}z|=\delta\) while violating \(\widetilde p\in C'\). Therefore a bound \(\|\widetilde p-P_{C'}z\|\leq\delta\) alone neither certifies exact antipolar feasibility nor validates the exact projection variational inequality. Reliable oracle certificates require an independently verified feasibility residual, a relaxed halfspace with quantified error, or a positive promise gap exceeding the projection error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(|(1-\delta)-P_{C'}z|=\delta\), the approximation \(1-\delta\notin C'\); distance accuracy alone does not certify feasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-accurate approximate projection does not by itself provide exact feasibility or separation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Computational Tractability Boundary for Gauge Models
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\{C_I\}\) be a family of finite-dimensional gauge unit sets indexed by finite encodings \(I\), with gauges \(\kappa_I\) and polars \(C_I^\circ\). Fix a computational model, query domain, norm, and accuracy convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity classification of represented or oracle-accessed gauge families; the definition is relative rather than an intrinsic property of an abstract convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tractability boundary for \(\{C_I\}\) is a stated partition of access tasks and parameter regimes into those admitting algorithms polynomial in \(|I|\) and the declared accuracy size, and those for which such access is unavailable or complexity-hard under a specified reduction. Relevant tasks include exact or weak membership in \(C_I\), evaluation of \(\kappa_I\), separation, support optimization, evaluation of \(\kappa_I^\circ\), and construction of certificates. A boundary statement is well-formed only when it specifies the representation, task, approximation metric, conditioning or radius promises, and complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge tractability boundary identifies where a family of gauge computations changes from efficiently accessible to unavailable or complexity-hard. The classification is always tied to an input representation, a particular task, an approximation convention, geometric promises, and a computational model. Evaluation, membership, separation, support optimization, polar evaluation, and certificate construction are distinct tasks and can lie on different sides of the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T=\{(I,\mathrm{task},\varepsilon,\mathrm{promises}):\mathrm{task}(C_I)\text{ is solvable within the declared polynomial resource bound}\}\) defines the tractable side only relative to the declared access model.
special_cases_latex: A gauge may have easy evaluation but a difficult proximal map.
An atomic hull may have an easy atom-membership test but a hard support-optimization problem.
immediate_consequences_latex: A complexity claim about one representation cannot automatically be transferred to a more succinct representation of the same abstract set.
boundary_notes: Exact and approximate tractability are different classifications.
Poor conditioning can prevent polynomial oracle reductions even when formal convex-analytic identities hold.
Hardness must name its reduction and complexity assumption; lack of a known algorithm is not hardness.

notation.meaning: Encoded input length of the gauge instance.
Declared tractable region of instances and access tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Intractable Atomic Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atomic hull is not automatically tractable: hard linear optimization over its atoms makes exact support and polar-gauge evaluation hard as well.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every query \(y\), linearity and closure give \[\sigma_K(y)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A\cup\{0\}}\langle y,a\rangle=\max\left\{0,\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle y,a\rangle\right\}.\] Polarity then yields \(\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)=\sigma_K(y)\). Thus an atomic description is not by itself a tractable representation: whenever exact linear optimization over the represented atom family lacks a practical oracle, exact support and polar-gauge evaluation inherit that obstruction. A family-specific complexity classification requires an explicit encoding and computational model.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an atomic family and \(K=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A\cup\{0\})\).
Exact linear optimization \(\sup_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle y,a\rangle\) is computationally intractable for the represented family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact evaluation of \(\sigma_K(y)\), and hence of \(\gamma_{K^\circ}(y)\), inherits the same optimization obstruction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional tractability boundary linking atomic linear optimization, support evaluation, and polar-gauge evaluation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The support and polar-gauge identities are correct, but the cited convex-analysis sections do not establish a computational intractability result. An explicit atom family, input encoding, computational model, reduction, and complexity source are required before the terminal claim about intractable atomic hulls is adequately supported.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For every finite encoding \(I\), let \(\mathcal A_I\subset\mathbb{Q}^{n(I)}\) be a succinctly represented atomic family, let \(C_I=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A_I\cup\{0\})\), and let \(\gamma_I=\gamma_{C_I}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity of families of rationally encoded atomic hulls; intractability is task- and approximation-specific rather than a property of one unencoded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \(\{C_I\}\) is an intractable atomic-hull family for a declared task if that task is hard under a specified polynomial-time reduction and complexity assumption. Canonical tasks are weak membership in \(C_I\), evaluation or approximation of \(\gamma_I(x)\), and support optimization \(\sigma_{C_I}(y)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A_I}\langle y,a\rangle\). For approximate hardness, the encoding must specify a rational tolerance \(\varepsilon\), bounded query data, and a promised gap between accepted and rejected cases. Intractability of support immediately concerns polar-gauge evaluation because \(\gamma_I^\circ=\sigma_{C_I}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An intractable atomic hull is defined as a family, not merely as a complicated-looking convex set. Each instance has a succinct atomic description, and the hull is the closed convex hull of the atoms and the origin. The family is intractable only for a named computational task, approximation gap, reduction, and complexity assumption. Typical tasks are weak membership, atomic-gauge evaluation, and support optimization. Support hardness is also polar-gauge evaluation hardness because those values coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_I=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A_I\cup\{0\}),\quad \gamma_I(x)=\inf\{t\ge0:x\in tC_I\},\quad \gamma_I^\circ(y)=\sup_{a\in\mathcal A_I}\langle y,a\rangle,\) with intractability attached to a precisely declared one of these computational tasks.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Support optimization over \(C_I\) and over \(\mathcal A_I\) have the same optimal value.
special_cases_latex: If linear optimization over \(\mathcal A_I\) encodes a known hard combinatorial optimization problem, exact polar-gauge evaluation inherits that declared hardness under the corresponding reduction.
immediate_consequences_latex: A polynomial-size listing of all atoms can remove succinct-representation hardness even when the same abstract construction has exponentially many atoms under another encoding.
boundary_notes: A hard exact task may admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme or relaxation.
Atom-membership hardness, hull-membership hardness, and support hardness are distinct claims.
No hardness conclusion is valid without a specified reduction, encoding, and complexity assumption.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inner-Outer Gauge Approximation Pair and Its Distortion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. A convex body used as a gauge unit set is a closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb E\) with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Its gauge is \(\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\). Its polar is \(C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb E:\langle y,x\rangle\leq 1\text{ for every }x\in C\}\), and its support function is \(\sigma_C(y):=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns finite-dimensional, exact set inclusions and multiplicative representation quality. The sets need not be symmetric, so their gauges need not be norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inner-outer gauge approximation pair for \(C\) is an ordered pair \((C_{\mathrm{in}},C_{\mathrm{out}})\) of closed convex sets satisfying \(0\in\operatorname{int}C_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \[C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\subseteq C_{\mathrm{out}}.\] The pair has multiplicative distortion at most \(\eta\geq1\) when, in addition, \[C_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq \eta C_{\mathrm{in}}.\] Its associated lower and upper gauge models are respectively \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}\) and \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}\); for every \(x\in\mathbb E\), they satisfy \[\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq\gamma_C(x)\leq\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\leq\eta\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x).\] Equivalently, the polar bodies obey \[(C_{\mathrm{out}})^\circ\subseteq C^\circ\subseteq(C_{\mathrm{in}})^\circ\subseteq\eta(C_{\mathrm{out}})^\circ.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex gauge unit set \(C\) containing the origin in its interior, an inner-outer approximation pair consists of closed convex sets \(C_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{out}}\) with \(C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\subseteq C_{\mathrm{out}}\). It has distortion at most \(\eta\) if \(C_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq\eta C_{\mathrm{in}}\). The outer set supplies a lower bound on the true gauge, the inner set supplies an upper bound, and their ratio is bounded by \(\eta\). Polarity reverses the three inclusions and gives the equivalent polar approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E\) is finite-dimensional and carries a fixed inner product.
\(0\in\operatorname{int}C_{\mathrm{in}}\), hence all three gauges are finite on \(\mathbb E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(C_{\mathrm{in}},C_{\mathrm{out}})\text{ is an }\eta\text{-inner-outer gauge approximation pair}\iff C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\subseteq C_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq\eta C_{\mathrm{in}}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The set inclusions are equivalent to \[\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}\leq\gamma_C\leq\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}\leq\eta\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}\quad\text{pointwise on }\mathbb E.\]

Using \(\gamma_D=\sigma_{D^\circ}\), the same approximation is represented by \[\sigma_{(C_{\mathrm{out}})^\circ}\leq\sigma_{C^\circ}\leq\sigma_{(C_{\mathrm{in}})^\circ}\leq\eta\sigma_{(C_{\mathrm{out}})^\circ}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(\eta=1\), then \(C_{\mathrm{in}}=C=C_{\mathrm{out}}\), so both models equal the exact gauge.
If all three sets are centrally symmetric, their gauges are norms and the definition becomes a multiplicative norm approximation.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\leq1\), then \(x\in C_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq C\). If \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)>1\), then \(x\notin C_{\mathrm{out}}\), hence \(x\notin C\).
For every nonzero \(x\), \[1\leq\frac{\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)}{\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)}\leq\eta.\]
boundary_notes: If the origin is not interior to the inner set, the gauges may take the value \(+\infty\), and a finite global distortion factor need not exist.
The term “inner-outer” here denotes simultaneous set containment, not Painlevé-Kuratowski inner and outer limits.
Membership is not decided when \(\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq1<\gamma_{C_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\); this is the approximation band.

notation.meaning: Inner and outer convex gauge unit sets.
Polar set with respect to the fixed inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Ordering
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner-outer set sandwich gives reverse gauge bounds, reverse polar inclusions, and forward support-function bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq K\subseteq K_{\mathrm{out}}\), then inclusion reverses the corresponding gauges: \[\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq\gamma_K(x)\leq\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\qquad(x\in X).\] Polarity reverses inclusion, whereas support functions preserve it: \[K_{\mathrm{out}}^{\circ}\subseteq K^{\circ}\subseteq K_{\mathrm{in}}^{\circ},\qquad \sigma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(y)\leq\sigma_K(y)\leq\sigma_{K_{\mathrm{out}}}(y)\qquad(y\in X).\] These conclusions remain valid with extended-valued gauges when the sets are not absorbing.

\(K_{\mathrm{in}},K,K_{\mathrm{out}}\subset X\) are closed convex sets containing \(0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Quality Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the outer model lies within an alpha-scaling of the inner model, their computable gauges approximate the true gauge within the same factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a computationally tractable pair satisfies \(K_{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq K\subseteq K_{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq\alpha K_{\mathrm{in}}\). Positive homogeneity and inclusion monotonicity give \[\alpha^{-1}\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\leq\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{out}}}(x)\leq\gamma_K(x)\leq\gamma_{K_{\mathrm{in}}}(x)\qquad(x\in X).\] Equivalently, the polar sandwich is \[\alpha^{-1}K_{\mathrm{in}}^{\circ}\subseteq K_{\mathrm{out}}^{\circ}\subseteq K^{\circ}\subseteq K_{\mathrm{in}}^{\circ}.\] Thus the representation factor \(\alpha\) directly bounds the worst-case multiplicative loss in gauge value.

children.top_down_role: Sensitivity and numerical instability associated with narrow or nearly degenerate polar regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Thin-Body Degeneration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Thin rectangles attain the inverse-inner-radius sensitivity scale, while the degenerate limit has an infinite gauge outside its span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<r\le1\), let \(K_r=[-r,r]\times[-1,1]\subset\mathbb R^2\). Then \[\gamma_{K_r}(x)=\max\{|x_1|/r,|x_2|\},\qquad K_r^\circ=\{y:r|y_1|+|y_2|\le1\}.\] The Euclidean Lipschitz modulus of \(\gamma_{K_r}\) is \(1/r\), and the polar reaches distance \(1/r\) along the first coordinate. At \(r=0\), \(K_0=\{0\}\times[-1,1]\) and \(\gamma_{K_0}(x)=+\infty\) whenever \(x_1\ne0\).
assumptions_latex: \(0<r\le1\) for the nondegenerate family; \(r=0\) for its limiting set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sensitivity and polar radius grow as \(1/r\), and global gauge finiteness fails at \(r=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rectangular family showing sharp gauge sensitivity and loss of finiteness at degeneration.

notation.meaning: polar of the rectangular gauge ball

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Polar Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small inner radius produces a large polar radius and unstable gauge evaluation; when the inner radius vanishes, global finiteness and Lipschitz control may fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polarity transforms the radial sandwich into \[R^{-1}B\subseteq K^{\circ}\subseteq r^{-1}B.\] Moreover, for all \(x,z\in X\), \[\left|\gamma_K(x)-\gamma_K(z)\right|\leq r^{-1}\lVert x-z\rVert.\] Hence the ratio \(\kappa=R/r\) measures radial ill-conditioning, while the absolute sensitivity of gauge evaluation is controlled by \(r^{-1}\). As \(r\downarrow0\), these uniform bounds diverge; at \(r=0\), the gauge may cease to be finite or locally Lipschitz on all of \(X\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Euclidean with closed unit ball \(B\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar Asphericity and Geometric Condition Number
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb E\) be a finite-dimensional normed space with unit ball \(B:=\{x:\|x\|\leq1\}\), dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\), and dual unit ball \(B_*\). Let \(C\subset\mathbb E\) be closed and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), and put \(P:=C^\circ\). When \(C\) is also bounded, \(P\) is a compact convex body containing the origin in its interior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The condition number is relative to a specified reference norm. It measures finite-dimensional global radial asphericity of the polar body, not local boundary curvature or floating-point conditioning of a particular algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the polar inradius and outradius relative to \(B_*\) by \[r_*(P):=\sup\{r>0:rB_*\subseteq P\},\qquad R_*(P):=\inf\{R>0:P\subseteq RB_*\}.\] The polar geometric condition number and asphericity coefficient are \[\kappa_*(P):=\frac{R_*(P)}{r_*(P)},\qquad \alpha_*(P):=\frac{r_*(P)}{R_*(P)}=\kappa_*(P)^{-1}.\] For a prescribed level \(K>1\), the polar geometry is called \(K\)-ill-conditioned when \(\kappa_*(P)\geq K\), equivalently \(\alpha_*(P)\leq K^{-1}\). It is degenerate when \(r_*(P)=0\) or \(R_*(P)=+\infty\), in which case \(\kappa_*(P):=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conditioning of a polar body \(P=C^\circ\) is measured by comparing its largest contained dual-norm ball with its smallest containing dual-norm ball. Their radii are \(r_*(P)\) and \(R_*(P)\), and the ratio \(R_*(P)/r_*(P)\) is the polar geometric condition number. Geometry is ill-conditioned at level \(K\) when this ratio is at least \(K\). A vanishing inradius or infinite outradius is declared degenerate and has infinite condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb E\) is finite-dimensional and \(\|\cdot\|\) is a fixed reference norm.
\(C\subset\mathbb E\) is closed and convex with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), and \(P=C^\circ\).
For finite conditioning, \(C\) is bounded, equivalently \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), so \(0<r_*(P)\leq R_*(P)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P\text{ is }K\text{-ill-conditioned}\iff\frac{R_*(P)}{r_*(P)}\geq K\iff\frac{r_*(P)}{R_*(P)}\leq\frac1K.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}=\sigma_P\), \[r_*(P)=\min_{\|x\|=1}\gamma_C(x),\qquad R_*(P)=\max_{\|x\|=1}\gamma_C(x),\] and therefore \[\kappa_*(P)=\frac{\max_{\|x\|=1}\gamma_C(x)}{\min_{\|x\|=1}\gamma_C(x)}.\]
The radius sandwich \(r_*B_*\subseteq P\subseteq R_*B_*\) is equivalent by polarity to \[R_*^{-1}B\subseteq C\subseteq r_*^{-1}B.\]
special_cases_latex: For an ellipsoid \(P=\{y:\langle Hy,y\rangle\leq1\}\) measured in the Euclidean norm, \(\kappa_*(P)=\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(H)/\lambda_{\min}(H)}\).
If \(P\) is a positive scalar multiple of \(B_*\), then \(r_*(P)=R_*(P)\) and \(\kappa_*(P)=1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb E\), \[r_*(P)\|x\|\leq\gamma_C(x)\leq R_*(P)\|x\|.\]
After normalizing \(R_*(P)=1\), increasing ill-conditioning is exactly the narrowing regime \(r_*(P)\downarrow0\).
The number \(\kappa_*(P)\) is invariant under positive rescaling of \(P\).
boundary_notes: The numerical value depends on the reference norm; a coordinate change must transform both the body and the norm to preserve it.
A large condition number records global anisotropy but does not by itself identify a nonsmooth point, a small curvature radius, or a particular unstable algorithm.
If \(C\) is unbounded, its polar may have empty interior and the finite-radius definition enters the degenerate case.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reliability Boundary for an Interval-Certified Inexact Oracle
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q\in\mathbb R\) be an exact scalar gauge value, support value, polar residual, or other scalar certificate quantity, and let the exact decision predicate be \(q\leq\tau\) for a fixed threshold \(\tau\in\mathbb R\). An inexact oracle reports \(\widehat q\in\mathbb R\) together with certified one-sided errors \(\varepsilon_-,\varepsilon_+\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition treats deterministic, certified scalar error bounds. It does not cover merely heuristic error estimates, stochastic confidence intervals, vector-valued separation errors, or unbounded oracle outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The oracle enclosure is \[I(\widehat q):=[L,U]:=[\widehat q-\varepsilon_-,\widehat q+\varepsilon_+],\qquad L\leq q\leq U.\] The report is a reliable positive certificate for \(q\leq\tau\) when \(U\leq\tau\), and a reliable negative certificate when \(L>\tau\). Its reliability boundary, or unresolved band, is \[\mathcal B_\tau:=\{(\widehat q,\varepsilon_-,\varepsilon_+):\widehat q-\varepsilon_-\leq\tau<\widehat q+\varepsilon_+\}.\] Thus a report belongs to \(\mathcal B_\tau\) exactly when its certified interval contains values on both sides of the decision boundary, with equality assigned to the predicate \(q\leq\tau\). No truth value for that predicate is certified by such a report.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact oracle is reliable only through its certified interval from \(L=\widehat q-\varepsilon_-\) to \(U=\widehat q+\varepsilon_+\). It certifies \(q\leq\tau\) if the entire interval lies at or below \(\tau\), and certifies the opposite if the entire interval lies strictly above \(\tau\). The reliability boundary consists of all reports whose interval straddles \(\tau\); those reports do not determine which exact decision is true.
assumptions_latex: The error bounds are valid: \(\widehat q-\varepsilon_-\leq q\leq\widehat q+\varepsilon_+\).
The certificate predicate and its equality convention are fixed as \(q\leq\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[U\leq\tau\Rightarrow q\leq\tau,\qquad L>\tau\Rightarrow q>\tau,\qquad L\leq\tau<U\Rightarrow\text{the oracle report is unresolved}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The report is reliable precisely when \(I(\widehat q)\subseteq(-\infty,\tau]\) or \(I(\widehat q)\subseteq(\tau,+\infty)\); otherwise it lies in \(\mathcal B_\tau\).
For symmetric error \(\varepsilon_- =\varepsilon_+=\varepsilon\), the unresolved condition is \[|\widehat q-\tau|\leq\varepsilon\] with the upper endpoint convention inherited from \(q\leq\tau\).
special_cases_latex: For gauge membership, take \(q=\gamma_C(x)\) and \(\tau=1\). Then \(U\leq1\) certifies \(x\in C\), whereas \(L>1\) certifies \(x\notin C\).
For a support inequality, take \(q=\sigma_C(y)\). Then \(U\leq\tau\) certifies \(\langle y,x\rangle\leq\tau\) for every \(x\in C\).
For an exact oracle, \(\varepsilon_- =\varepsilon_+=0\), so the unresolved band collapses to the threshold itself.
immediate_consequences_latex: A smaller error interval can convert an unresolved report into a certificate, but enlarging the interval cannot convert an unresolved report into a reliable one without changing its center.

If the exact margin is \(m:=|q-\tau|>0\) and a symmetric oracle satisfies \(|\widehat q-q|\leq\varepsilon<m/2\), then its certified interval of radius \(\varepsilon\) lies wholly on the correct side of \(\tau\).
An approximate numerical value without a valid enclosure supplies no certificate under this definition.
boundary_notes: The supplied sources support exact gauge membership and exact gap certificates but do not directly name or formalize this interval-based “reliability boundary.”
For a strict predicate such as \(q<\tau\), endpoint assignments and hence \(\mathcal B_\tau\) must be changed.
Multiplicative errors require positivity assumptions and should first be converted into a valid interval enclosure.
Antipolar conventions differ across formulations; the scalar quantity and comparison direction must be fixed before applying this definition.

notation.meaning: Exact certificate quantity and its reported approximation.
Certified lower and upper bounds on \(q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Reliability Boundary for an Interval-Certified Inexact Oracle
Inexact Gauge Oracles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact gauge oracle returns a certified interval containing the gauge value, with width no greater than its declared tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An absolute-error \(\varepsilon\)-inexact gauge oracle for \(K\) maps each query \(x\in X\) to numbers \(\underline g(x),\overline g(x)\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\underline g(x)\leq\gamma_K(x)\leq\overline g(x),\qquad 0\leq\overline g(x)-\underline g(x)\leq\varepsilon.\] A one-sided implementation may return only a lower or upper bound, but then it cannot support certification requiring the missing inequality. The exact gauge oracle is recovered when \(\varepsilon=0\) and the two outputs coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle encloses \(\gamma_K(x)\) in an interval of width at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-error interval model for finite gauge evaluation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The interval model is a coherent conventional definition, but the cited approximate-subdifferential section does not directly support this particular inexact gauge-oracle model. knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Support Oracles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact support oracle brackets the maximum linear value and may return a feasible point attaining that value within the declared tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An absolute-error \(\varepsilon\)-inexact support oracle for \(C\) maps every direction \(y\in X\) to numbers \(\underline s(y),\overline s(y)\in\mathbb R\) such that \[\underline s(y)\leq\sigma_C(y):=\max_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\leq\overline s(y),\qquad \overline s(y)-\underline s(y)\leq\varepsilon.\] If the oracle also returns \(x_{\varepsilon}\in C\) with \(\langle y,x_{\varepsilon}\rangle\geq\sigma_C(y)-\varepsilon\), then \(\langle y,x_{\varepsilon}\rangle\) is a valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle encloses \(\sigma_C(y)\) in an interval of width at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-error interval model for support-function maximization.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Antipolar Oracles
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact antipolar oracle brackets the minimum pairing; only intervals lying wholly above or below one decide antipolar membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(m_C(y):=\min_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\), so that \(y\in C'\) exactly when \(m_C(y)\geq1\). An absolute-error \(\varepsilon\)-inexact antipolar oracle returns \(\underline m(y),\overline m(y)\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\underline m(y)\leq m_C(y)\leq\overline m(y),\qquad \overline m(y)-\underline m(y)\leq\varepsilon.\] Consequently, \(\underline m(y)\geq1\) certifies antipolar membership, while \(\overline m(y)<1\) certifies nonmembership; neither conclusion follows when the interval crosses \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle encloses \(m_C(y)\), whose threshold at \(1\) determines membership in \(C'\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval oracle for the minimum-pairing characterization of antipolar membership.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The minimum-pairing threshold logic is correct, but the cited polar and cone sections do not directly support either the antipolar definition used here or the selected inexact interval-oracle model. The ambient space X is also not introduced.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Reliability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rigorous interval certifies gauge or polar membership when its upper endpoint is at most one and antipolar membership when its lower endpoint is at least one. The inconclusive crossing condition includes equality on different endpoints for the two threshold directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \([L_g,U_g]\), \([L_s,U_s]\), and \([L_m,U_m]\) contain, respectively, \(\gamma_K(x)\), \(\sigma_K(y)\), and \(m_C(y):=\min_{z\in C}\langle y,z\rangle\). For gauge feasibility \(\gamma_K(x)\leq1\), the condition \(U_g\leq1\) certifies membership and \(L_g>1\) certifies nonmembership. For polar membership \(y\in K^{\circ}\), equivalently \(\sigma_K(y)\leq1\), the condition \(U_s\leq1\) certifies membership and \(L_s>1\) certifies nonmembership. For antipolar membership \(y\in C'\), equivalently \(m_C(y)\geq1\), the condition \(L_m\geq1\) certifies membership and \(U_m<1\) certifies nonmembership. Using only the interval information, the respective inconclusive cases are \(L_g\leq1<U_g\), \(L_s\leq1<U_s\), and \(L_m<1\leq U_m\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(K\subset X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\); \(C\subset X\) is nonempty and compact.
Every oracle interval is rigorous: it contains the corresponding exact scalar value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gauge or polar membership is inconclusive from an interval alone exactly in the crossing case \(L\leq 1<U\), whereas antipolar membership is inconclusive from an interval alone exactly in the crossing case \(L<1\leq U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp threshold rules for certificates derived solely from rigorous inexact-oracle intervals.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^n\). For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), let \(\operatorname{aff}P\) be its affine hull, \(\operatorname{rec}P:=\{d\mid x+td\in P\ \forall x\in P,\ \forall t\geq0\}\), and \(\operatorname{lin}P:=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition classifies nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedra by intrinsic dimension, boundedness, and lineality. Empty-set conventions are treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral geometry regime is the data \(\mathcal R(P):=(k,\operatorname{rec}P,\operatorname{lin}P)\) associated with a nonempty set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) admitting a finite halfspace representation \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n\mid Ax\leq b\}\), where \(k:=\dim(\operatorname{aff}P)\). The regime is full-dimensional when \(k=n\) and lower-dimensional when \(k<n\); bounded when \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}\); pointed when \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{0\}\); pointed unbounded when \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{0\}\neq\operatorname{rec}P\); and nonpointed when \(\operatorname{lin}P\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is classified by its intrinsic dimension \(k=\dim(\operatorname{aff}P)\), recession cone, and lineality space. It is full-dimensional if \(k=n\), lower-dimensional if \(k<n\), bounded if its recession cone is \(\{0\}\), pointed if its lineality space is \(\{0\}\), pointed unbounded if it has a nonzero recession direction but no lineality, and nonpointed if it has nonzero lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R(P)=\bigl(\dim(\operatorname{aff}P),\operatorname{rec}P,\operatorname{lin}P\bigr)\) determines the stated dimension, boundedness, pointedness, and lineality regimes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(P=\{x\mid Ax\leq b\}\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{d\mid Ad\leq0\}\) and \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{d\mid Ad=0\}\).
For nonempty closed convex \(P\), boundedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}\), and containing no affine line is equivalent to \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{0\}\).
special_cases_latex: A polytope has regime \((k,\{0\},\{0\})\).
An affine subspace \(a+L\) has \(\operatorname{rec}(a+L)=\operatorname{lin}(a+L)=L\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty polyhedron belongs to exactly one of the bounded, pointed-unbounded, or nonpointed regimes.
The classifications by dimension and by recession behavior are independent: a lower-dimensional polyhedron may be bounded, pointed unbounded, or nonpointed.
boundary_notes: The recession cone is restricted here to nonempty sets, avoiding vacuous-quantifier conventions for the empty set.
Pointedness for a general polyhedron means absence of affine lines; for a cone \(K\), this is equivalent to \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).

children.title: Principal Polyhedral Classes
children.top_down_role: The affine, bounded, unbounded, and homogeneous objects of polyhedral analysis.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: All sets lie in \(\mathbb R^n\). A closed halfspace is a set \(\{x\mid a^Tx\leq\beta\}\), and a homogeneous halfspace has \(\beta=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a finite-dimensional taxonomy of affine sets, polyhedra, polytopes, and polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The principal polyhedral classes are: (i) affine polyhedra \(M=\{x\mid Fx=g\}\); (ii) polyhedra \(P=\{x\mid Ax\leq b,\ Fx=g\}\), equivalently finite intersections of closed halfspaces and hyperplanes; (iii) polytopes \(Q=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_p\}\), equivalently bounded nonempty polyhedra; and (iv) polyhedral cones \(K=\{x\mid Ax\leq0,\ Fx=0\}\), equivalently finitely generated cones \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\}\). The empty set and \(\mathbb R^n\) are also polyhedral under the finite-intersection convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine polyhedron is the solution set of finitely many affine equations. A polyhedron is the solution set of finitely many weak linear inequalities and affine equations. A polytope is the convex hull of finitely many points, equivalently a nonempty bounded polyhedron. A polyhedral cone is a homogeneous polyhedron, equivalently the conic hull of finitely many vectors. The empty set and the whole space are included as polyhedral boundary cases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=\{Fx=g\}\), \(P=\{Ax\leq b,Fx=g\}\), \(Q=\operatorname{conv}\{v_i\}_{i=1}^p\), and \(K=\{Ax\leq0,Fx=0\}=\operatorname{cone}\{r_j\}_{j=1}^q\) define the principal classes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every equality \(f^Tx=\gamma\) may be represented by the pair \(f^Tx\leq\gamma\) and \(-f^Tx\leq-\gamma\).
By Minkowski–Weyl, finite halfspace representability and finite point-and-ray generation define the same class of nonempty polyhedra.
special_cases_latex: A singleton is simultaneously an affine set and a polytope.
A linear subspace is an affine polyhedron and a polyhedral cone.
A simplex is the convex hull of a finite affinely independent set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every polytope is closed and convex.
Every polyhedral cone contains the origin and is closed under nonnegative linear combinations.
boundary_notes: Some authors reverse the words “polyhedron” and “polytope”; this record uses “polytope” only for bounded polyhedra.
A general cone need not be convex or closed; a polyhedral cone has both properties.

notation.meaning: Convex hull of a finite point set.
Set of all nonnegative linear combinations of the listed generators.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces; it may be empty, equal the whole space, or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a set representable as \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\] for some finite \(m\), matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), with inequalities interpreted componentwise. Equivalently, a polyhedron is the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces. The definition permits \(P=\varnothing\), \(P=\mathbb{R}^n\), and unbounded sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a closed convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), possibly empty or unbounded.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite point-and-direction representation of arbitrary nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonempty set \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron if and only if there exist finite nonempty \(V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and finite \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) such that
\[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R).\]
The empty family \(R=\varnothing\) is allowed, with \(\operatorname{cone}(\varnothing)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set is a polyhedron exactly when it is the sum of the convex hull of finitely many points and the cone generated by finitely many directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron if and only if \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for finite \(V\neq\varnothing\) and finite \(R\).

notation.meaning: Convex hull of the finite point set V.

knowledge_statements.title: Polytopes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope is a bounded polyhedron, equivalently the convex hull of finitely many points; every nonempty polytope is generated by its finitely many vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polytope is a bounded polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). Equivalently, there exist finitely many points \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}.\] When \(P\ne\varnothing\), it is the convex hull of its finite set of extreme points. Under the convention that the convex hull of the empty family is empty, \(\varnothing\) is also a bounded polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a polytope exactly when it is bounded, equivalently when it is the convex hull of finitely many points.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone is an intersection of finitely many homogeneous halfspaces, equivalently the conical hull of finitely many generating directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral cone is a set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) representable as \[K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le 0\}\] for a finite matrix \(A\). Equivalently, there are finitely many vectors \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i r_i:\lambda_i\ge 0\right\}.\] Thus polyhedral cones are precisely finitely generated convex cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone containing the origin and has both a finite homogeneous inequality description and a finite generator description.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous polyhedra and their finite conical generators.

notation.meaning: A polyhedral cone in homogeneous inequality form.
Conical hull of finitely many vectors.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). For vectors \(r_1,\ldots,r_q\), write \(\operatorname{cone}\{r_j\}:=\{\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_jr_j\mid\mu_j\geq0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedral cone if there exist finitely many vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n\mid a_i^Tx\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Equivalently, there exist finitely many generators \(r_1,\ldots,r_q\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\}\). Its lineality space is \(\operatorname{lin}K:=K\cap(-K)\); it is pointed exactly when \(K\cap(-K)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral cone is an intersection of finitely many closed halfspaces whose boundary hyperplanes pass through the origin. By the conic Minkowski–Weyl theorem, this is equivalent to being generated by finitely many conic directions. Its lineality space consists of directions whose positives and negatives both belong to the cone, and the cone is pointed when this space is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\{x\mid Ax\leq0\}=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\}\), with \(\operatorname{lin}K=K\cap(-K)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(K=\{x\mid Ax\leq0\}\), then \(\operatorname{lin}K=\ker A\).
A cone is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated.
special_cases_latex: The nonnegative orthant is \(\mathbb R_+^n=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}\) and is pointed.
Every linear subspace is a nonpointed polyhedral cone unless it is \(\{0\}\).
The zero cone \(\{0\}\) is pointed and polyhedral.
immediate_consequences_latex: A polyhedral cone is closed and convex.
A pointed polyhedral cone has finitely many extreme rays and is generated by representatives of them.
boundary_notes: The displayed finite generating set need not be minimal and may contain redundant or zero generators.
For a nonpointed cone, lineality may be encoded by pairs \(\ell,-\ell\) in a conic generating list.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). An affine combination has the form \(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_ix_i\) with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition applies to arbitrary finite-dimensional sets and specializes to polyhedra; the empty set uses the conventional dimension \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine hull of \(S\) is \(\operatorname{aff}S:=\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_ix_i\mid m\geq1,\ x_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\in\mathbb R,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\), equivalently the smallest affine set containing \(S\). If \(S\neq\varnothing\) and \(x_0\in S\), then \(\operatorname{aff}S=x_0+\operatorname{span}(S-x_0)\), and its intrinsic dimension is \(\dim S:=\dim\operatorname{span}(S-x_0)\). By convention, \(\dim\varnothing=-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull of a set is the set of all finite affine combinations of its points, or equivalently the smallest affine set containing it. For any base point \(x_0\) in a nonempty set, its affine hull is the translate of the span of all differences \(x-x_0\). The dimension of the set is the dimension of this parallel subspace, independently of the chosen base point; the empty set has dimension \(-1\) by convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(S\neq\varnothing\) and \(x_0\in S\), \(\operatorname{aff}S=x_0+\operatorname{span}(S-x_0)\) and \(\dim S=\dim\operatorname{span}(S-x_0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\dim S\) is the largest integer \(k\) for which \(S\) contains \(k+1\) affinely independent points when \(S\) is convex.
If \(\operatorname{aff}S=\{x\mid Fx=g\}\) with \(F\) having independent rows, then \(\dim S=n-\operatorname{rank}F\).
special_cases_latex: \(S\) is full-dimensional exactly when \(\operatorname{aff}S=\mathbb R^n\).
A singleton has dimension \(0\); a nondegenerate line segment has dimension \(1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Intrinsic dimension is invariant under injective affine transformations.
A polyhedron can have empty Euclidean interior while having nonempty relative interior in its affine hull.
boundary_notes: Ambient dimension \(n\) and intrinsic dimension \(\dim S\) need not agree.
The rank formula requires that the equations describe the affine hull, not merely a larger affine set containing \(S\).

notation.meaning: Set of displacement vectors \(\{x-x_0\mid x\in S\}\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(M:=\operatorname{aff}P=x_0+L\), and put \(k:=\dim L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition distinguishes dimension relative to the affine hull from dimension in the ambient coordinate space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedron \(P\) is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^n\) when \(k=n\), equivalently \(M=\mathbb R^n\), equivalently \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}P\neq\varnothing\). It is lower-dimensional when \(k<n\), in which case \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}P=\varnothing\) but \(\operatorname{ri}P\neq\varnothing\). An intrinsic-coordinate realization is obtained from any affine isomorphism \(T:\mathbb R^k\to M\); then \(\widehat P:=T^{-1}(P)\subseteq\mathbb R^k\) is a full-dimensional polyhedron and \(P=T(\widehat P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is full-dimensional when its affine hull is the whole ambient space, and lower-dimensional otherwise. A lower-dimensional polyhedron has empty ordinary interior but nonempty relative interior. Choosing affine coordinates on its affine hull produces a full-dimensional polyhedron in \(\mathbb R^k\), where \(k\) is its intrinsic dimension, and the original polyhedron is recovered by the affine coordinate map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k=n\iff\operatorname{aff}P=\mathbb R^n\iff\operatorname{int}P\neq\varnothing\), while \(k<n\) implies \(\operatorname{int}P=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{ri}P\neq\varnothing\); moreover \(P=T(T^{-1}P)\) in intrinsic coordinates.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(M=\{x\mid Fx=g\}\) and the rows of \(F\) independently describe \(M\), then \(k=n-\operatorname{rank}F\).
For an affine isomorphism \(T:\mathbb R^k\to M\), \(T^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}P)=\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^k}(T^{-1}P)\).
special_cases_latex: A facet of a full-dimensional polyhedron in \(\mathbb R^n\) is intrinsically \((n-1)\)-dimensional.
A singleton is full-dimensional in its intrinsic space \(\mathbb R^0\), although lower-dimensional in every \(\mathbb R^n\) with \(n>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Statements requiring nonempty interior should be applied to a lower-dimensional polyhedron after restriction to its affine hull.
Redundant ambient coordinates do not alter intrinsic facial or recession geometry.
boundary_notes: An arbitrary parametrization of \(M\) must be injective to give intrinsic coordinates.
Ordinary interior and relative interior coincide only in the full-dimensional regime.

notation.meaning: Affine hull and its parallel linear subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Hull Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull is the smallest affine set containing a nonempty set; translating it by any point of the set yields its intrinsic direction space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its affine hull is \[\operatorname{aff}(C)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i:k\in\mathbb{N},\ k\ge 1,\ x_i\in C,\ \lambda_i\in\mathbb{R}\ (1\le i\le k),\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.\] It is the intersection of all affine sets containing \(C\). For every \(x_0\in C\), the associated direction space is \[\operatorname{par}(C)=\operatorname{aff}(C)-x_0=\operatorname{span}(C-x_0),\] and this linear space is independent of the choice of \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\) is the unique smallest affine set containing \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine hull and its translation-invariant direction space for a nonempty set.

notation.meaning: Direction space parallel to the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Behavior of affine hulls and their parallel spaces under arbitrary affine maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(T(x)=Mx+c\) be an affine map into \(\mathbb{R}^p\). Then \[\operatorname{aff}(T(C))=T(\operatorname{aff}(C)),\qquad \operatorname{par}(T(C))=M\operatorname{par}(C).\] No injectivity or surjectivity assumption on \(M\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine hulls commute with affine maps, and the parallel space of the image is the linear image of the original parallel space.
assumptions_latex: \(T(x)=Mx+c\) is an affine map from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}(T(C))=T(\operatorname{aff}(C))\) and \(\operatorname{par}(T(C))=M\operatorname{par}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Map Covariance of Affine Hulls
Intrinsic Dimension
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic dimension of a nonempty set is the dimension of the direction space parallel to its affine hull. It is unchanged by translations and invertible affine coordinate changes and equals the largest dimension of a simplex with vertices in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), its intrinsic dimension is the linear dimension of the direction space parallel to its affine hull: \[\dim(C)=\dim\bigl(\operatorname{aff}(C)-x_0\bigr)=\dim\bigl(\operatorname{span}(C-x_0)\bigr),\qquad x_0\in C.\] This integer is independent of \(x_0\) and satisfies \(0\le\dim(C)\le n\). If \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) has the form \(T(x)=Mx+c\), where \(M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is invertible and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\dim(T(C))=\dim(C)\). Moreover, \(\dim(C)\) equals the maximum dimension of a simplex with affinely independent vertices in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le\dim(C)\le n\), and \(\dim(C)\) is invariant under translations and invertible affine coordinate changes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine dimension of a nonempty subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

notation.meaning: Intrinsic or affine dimension of the set.
Direction space of the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dimension-loss formula for arbitrary affine images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(T(x)=Mx+c\) map into \(\mathbb{R}^p\), and set \(L=\operatorname{par}(C)\). Then \[\dim(T(C))=\dim(M L)=\dim(C)-\dim(L\cap\ker M).\] Consequently \(\dim(T(C))\le\dim(C)\), with equality exactly when \(M\) is injective on \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine map reduces intrinsic dimension by the dimension of the affine carrier's directions annihilated by its linear part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(T(C))=\dim(C)-\dim(\operatorname{par}(C)\cap\ker M)\).

notation.meaning: Direction space parallel to the affine hull of \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension under Affine Maps
Full-Dimensional Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set is full-dimensional precisely when its affine hull is the ambient space, or equivalently when it has nonempty Euclidean interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is in the full-dimensional regime when its affine hull is the ambient space. The following conditions are equivalent: \[\operatorname{aff}(C)=\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad \dim(C)=n,\qquad \operatorname{int}(C)\ne\varnothing.\] In this regime, relative interior and Euclidean interior agree: \(\operatorname{ri}(C)=\operatorname{int}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is full-dimensional exactly when \(\operatorname{aff}(C)=\mathbb{R}^n\), equivalently \(\dim(C)=n\), equivalently \(\operatorname{int}(C)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient full dimensionality for nonempty convex sets in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean interior in the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inequality-description criterion with zero-normal rows handled explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\ne\varnothing\). Then \(P\) is full-dimensional if and only if there exists \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[a_i^{\mathsf T}\bar x<b_i\qquad\text{for every }i\text{ with }a_i\ne0.\] Equivalently, no displayed inequality with a nonzero normal is an implicit equality. Zero-normal rows must be treated separately because a tautological row \(0^{\mathsf T}x\le0\) cannot be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty inequality-defined polyhedron is full-dimensional exactly when all inequalities with nonzero normals can be satisfied strictly at one common point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(P)=n\iff\exists\bar x:\ a_i^{\mathsf T}\bar x<b_i\text{ for every }i\text{ with }a_i\ne0\).

notation.meaning: Common strict-feasibility point for all nonzero-normal rows.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Feasibility Test for Full Dimension
Lower-Dimensional Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex set is lower-dimensional when its affine hull is proper; its ambient interior is empty, while its relative interior is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is in the lower-dimensional regime when its affine hull is a proper affine subspace of the ambient space. Equivalently, \[\dim(C)<n,\qquad \operatorname{aff}(C)\ne\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad \operatorname{int}(C)=\varnothing.\] Although its Euclidean interior is empty, its relative interior within \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is lower-dimensional exactly when \(\dim(C)<n\), equivalently \(\operatorname{aff}(C)\ne\mathbb{R}^n\), equivalently \(\operatorname{int}(C)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper-affine-subspace regime for nonempty convex sets in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Relative interior within the affine hull.
Euclidean interior in the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron of dimension \(r<n\). Choose \(x_0\in P\) and a matrix \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) whose columns form a basis of \(\operatorname{par}(P)\). Then \[Q=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^r:x_0+Uz\in P\}\] is a full-dimensional polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^r\), \[P=x_0+UQ,\] and \(z\mapsto x_0+Uz\) is an affine bijection from \(Q\) onto \(P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Equalities
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inequalities that are tight at every feasible point form an equality system describing the affine hull of a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), and write the rows of \(A\) as \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\). An inequality indexed by \(i\) is an implicit equality when \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\) for every \(x\in P\). If \[I=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\text{ for every }x\in P\},\] then the affine hull is represented by \[\operatorname{aff}(P)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_Ix=b_I\}.\] Redundant rows may make this equality system linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}(P)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_Ix=b_I\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-hull equalities recoverable from a nonempty inequality description.

notation.meaning: Indices of inequalities tight at every feasible point.
Submatrix and subvector indexed by the implicit equalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Detection and Certification of Implicit Equalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rowwise linear-programming test, rational-input complexity, and Farkas certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each row \(i\), let \[s_i^*=\sup\{b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b\}.\] Row \(i\) is an implicit equality exactly when \(s_i^*=0\). Equivalently, it is implicit exactly when there exists \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfying \[A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-a_i,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}\lambda\le-b_i.\] Thus all implicit rows can be detected using at most \(m\) linear programs; for rational input this is polynomial-time in the standard bit model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A row is implicit exactly when its maximum feasible slack is zero, equivalently when Farkas multipliers certify its reverse inequality; all rows can be tested with at most one LP each.
assumptions_latex: For the complexity assertion, \(A\) and \(b\) are rational and linear programs are solved in the standard bit model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i\in I\iff s_i^*=0\iff\exists\lambda\ge0:\ A^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-a_i,\ b^{\mathsf T}\lambda\le-b_i\).

notation.meaning: Farkas multiplier certifying validity of the reverse inequality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank formula for a nonempty inequality-defined polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), and let \(I\) index all rows tight throughout \(P\). Then \[\dim(P)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A_I).\] Linearly dependent or repeated implicit rows do not change the value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine dimension of a nonempty inequality-defined polyhedron is the ambient dimension minus the rank of its implicit-equality rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(P)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A_I)\).

notation.meaning: Submatrix formed from all implicit-equality rows.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relative-interior description induced by implicit and nonimplicit rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), let \(I\) be the indices of inequalities tight everywhere on \(P\). Then \[\operatorname{ri}(P)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_Ix=b_I,\ a_j^{\mathsf T}x<b_j\ \text{for every }j\notin I\}.\] In particular, all nonimplicit inequalities can be made strict simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior consists exactly of points satisfying every implicit equality and strictly satisfying every remaining inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(P)=\{x:A_Ix=b_I,\ A_{I^c}x<b_{I^c}\}\).
