knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Face Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty one-dimensional polyhedral face is a segment, ray, or affine line, distinguished by its recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a nonempty one-dimensional face of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). Exactly one regime holds: \(F=[u,v]\) for distinct \(u,v\), with \(\operatorname{rec}F=\{0\}\); \(F=u+\mathbb{R}_+d\) for \(d\ne0\), with \(\operatorname{rec}F=\mathbb{R}_+d\); or \(F=u+\mathbb{R}d\), with \(\operatorname{rec}F=\mathbb{R}d\). Thus bounded edges, unbounded rays, and lines exhaust the one-dimensional regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is exactly one of a bounded segment, a ray, or an affine line.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremality Modulo Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After quotienting lineality, extreme points correspond exactly to minimal nonempty faces, each of which is a translate of the lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, let \(L=\operatorname{lin}P\), and let \(\pi\) be the quotient map. Then \(\pi(P)\) is pointed. For \(x\in P\), the point \(\pi(x)\) is an extreme point of \(\pi(P)\) if and only if \(x+L\) is a minimal nonempty face of \(P\). Consequently, quotient extreme points are in bijection with the minimal nonempty faces of \(P\), independently of the representative \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extreme points of \(\pi(P)\) correspond bijectively to the minimal nonempty faces \(x+L\) of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the quotient by the full lineality space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme Classes in the Lineality Quotient
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, \(L=\operatorname{lin}P\), and \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\) the quotient map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonpointed finite-dimensional polyhedra and their intrinsic pointed quotient geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The quotient polyhedron is \(\bar P:=\pi(P)\). It is pointed because \[\operatorname{lin}\bar P=\pi(\operatorname{lin}P)=\{0\}.\] An extreme point class of \(P\) modulo lineality is a coset \(v+L\subseteq P\) such that \(\pi(v)\) is an extreme point of \(\bar P\). Equivalently, \(v+L\) is a minimal face of \(P\). An extreme direction class modulo lineality is a nonzero ray \(\operatorname{cone}\{\pi(r)\}\) that is an extreme ray of \(\operatorname{rec}\bar P=\pi(\operatorname{rec}P)\). Equivalently, its inverse image in \(\operatorname{rec}P\) is a face \(L+\operatorname{cone}\{r\}\) of dimension \(\dim L+1\). These classes are independent of the representatives \(v\) and \(r+\ell\), \(\ell\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a polyhedron by its lineality space produces a pointed polyhedron. A point-like extreme object of the original polyhedron is therefore a coset whose image is a vertex of the quotient; this coset is exactly a minimal face. A direction-like extreme object is an extreme ray of the quotient recession cone, represented upstairs by a face consisting of the lineality space plus one additional ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extreme points and rays modulo \(L\) are the vertices of \(\pi(P)\) and the extreme rays of \(\pi(\operatorname{rec}P)\), respectively.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v+L\) is point-extreme modulo \(L\) if and only if it contains no proper nonempty face of \(P\).
\(L+\operatorname{cone}\{r\}\) is direction-extreme modulo \(L\) if and only if its quotient is a one-dimensional face.
special_cases_latex: When \(L=\{0\}\), quotient extremality reduces to ordinary vertices and extreme rays.
When \(P\) is an affine space, \(P/L\) is a singleton and there are no nonzero quotient recession rays.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every minimal face of \(P\) is a translate of \(L\).
Representative choices made by an orthogonal complement produce the same quotient extreme classes.
boundary_notes: Ordinary extreme points do not exist when \(L\ne\{0\}\).
A complement-based pointed section depends on the chosen complement, whereas the quotient classes are canonical.
review_flags: The source states the equivalent orthogonal-section decomposition explicitly; the quotient notation is the coordinate-free formulation of the same reduction.

children.title: Face-Incidence Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial organization of faces and local adjacency.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) denote all its faces, including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite face systems of finite-dimensional polyhedra; incidence is ordered by containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The face-incidence hierarchy of \(P\) is the ranked partially ordered set \[(\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq),\qquad \rho(F):=\dim F+1,\] with the convention \(\dim\varnothing=-1\). Two faces \(F,G\) are incident when \(F\subseteq G\) or \(G\subseteq F\). A cover relation \(F\prec G\) means \(F\subsetneq G\) and no face \(H\) satisfies \(F\subsetneq H\subsetneq G\); for polyhedra this implies \(\dim G=\dim F+1\). The meet and join are \[F\wedge G=F\cap G,
\qquad F\vee G=\text{the unique minimal face of }P\text{ containing }F\cup G.\] Hence \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) is a finite graded lattice, commonly called the face lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces of a polyhedron, ordered by inclusion, form its incidence hierarchy. Comparable faces are incident. A cover is an incidence with no intermediate face and increases dimension by one. Intersections give meets, while the unique smallest face containing two faces gives their join. Including the empty face and the whole polyhedron yields a finite graded lattice ranked by dimension plus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal{F}(P),\subseteq)\) is a finite graded lattice with meet \(F\cap G\) and join equal to the minimal face containing \(F\cup G\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Hasse diagram of \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) records precisely the cover incidences between consecutive face dimensions.
For \(P=\{x:a_i^Tx\le b_i\}\), nonempty faces correspond to feasible active-index closures ordered oppositely by inclusion of their closed active sets.
special_cases_latex: The rank-one elements are vertices, rank-two elements are edges, and coatoms are facets.
For a polytope, the interval \([\varnothing,P]\) is the entire face lattice.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonmaximal face is contained in a facet.
Every face interval \([F,G]\) inherits a finite graded incidence structure.
boundary_notes: Two intersecting faces need not be incident unless one contains the other.
Distinct active-index subsets can define the same face in a redundant inequality representation.

notation.meaning: Set of all faces of P.
Cover relation in the face poset.

source_refs.locator: §3.8, Theorem 3.24 and Proposition 3.25, pp. 101–104; §3.10, Theorem 3.33(ii), p. 108

knowledge_statements.title: Face Lattices
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inclusion-ordered faces of a polyhedron form a finite lattice: intersection is meet, and facial closure of the union is join.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}(P)\) contain every face of \(P\), including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\), ordered by inclusion. This poset is finite and is a lattice. For \(F,G\in\mathcal{F}(P)\), the meet is \(F\wedge G=F\cap G\), while the join \(F\vee G\) is the unique smallest face of \(P\) containing \(F\cup G\). Hence every pair of faces has a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The faces of \(P\), ordered by inclusion, form a finite lattice.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes both the empty face and the whole polyhedron.

notation.meaning: Set of all faces of P, including the empty face and P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates the lattice property from distributivity using a square.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{a,b,c,d\}\) be a square with cyclically ordered vertices. In \(\mathcal F(P)\), \(b\vee d=P\), while \(a\wedge b=a\wedge d=\varnothing\). Hence \(a\wedge(b\vee d)=a\neq\varnothing=(a\wedge b)\vee(a\wedge d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The face lattice of a square is not distributive.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a square with cyclically ordered vertices \(a,b,c,d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F(P)\) is not distributive.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polytope. Write \(V(P)\), \(E(P)\), and \(\Phi(P)\) for its vertices, edges, and facets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The primal skeleton is defined for polytopes; the facet-adjacency graph is the dual codimension-one analogue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The one-skeleton of \(P\) is the undirected graph \[G_1(P):=(V(P),
\mathcal{E}_1),\] where \(\{v,w\}\in\mathcal{E}_1\) if and only if \(v\ne w\) and the segment \([v,w]\) is an edge of \(P\). The facet-adjacency graph is \[G_{d-1}(P):=(\Phi(P),
\mathcal{E}_{d-1}),
\qquad d:=\dim P,\] where \(\{F,G\}\in\mathcal{E}_{d-1}\) if and only if \(F\ne G\) and \(F\cap G\) is a face of dimension \(d-2\). These graphs are the rank-one and corank-one adjacency projections of the face lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The one-skeleton has the vertices of the polytope as graph nodes and joins two nodes exactly when their segment is a polyhedral edge. The facet-adjacency graph has facets as nodes and joins two facets exactly when their intersection is a ridge, a face two dimensions below the polytope. Both graphs are obtained by retaining selected consecutive levels of the face-incidence hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vertex adjacency is incidence through an edge, while facet adjacency is incidence through a ridge.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v\) and \(w\) are adjacent if and only if some one-dimensional face has exactly \(v\) and \(w\) as its vertices.
Facets \(F,G\) are adjacent if and only if they both cover the same \((d-2)\)-face.
special_cases_latex: For a polygon, the one-skeleton is its boundary cycle, and the facet-adjacency graph is the same cycle.
For a simplex, both graphs are complete graphs on \(d+1\) nodes.
immediate_consequences_latex: The degree of a vertex counts incident bounded edges.
In a simple \(d\)-polytope every vertex has degree \(d\).
boundary_notes: Unbounded polyhedra may have one-dimensional half-line faces that are not represented by a pair of vertices in the ordinary skeleton.
Facet intersections of dimension below \(d-2\) do not create facet-adjacency edges.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Skeleta
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The k-skeleton is the union of all faces of dimension at most k; the zero-skeleton is the vertex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron \(P\) and an integer \(-1\le k\le d\), the \(k\)-skeleton is \[\operatorname{Skel}_k(P):=\bigcup_{\substack{F\in\mathcal{F}(P)\\ \dim F\le k}}F.\] In particular, \(\operatorname{Skel}_0(P)\) is the set of vertices, \(\operatorname{Skel}_1(P)\) is the union of all vertices and one-dimensional faces, and \(\operatorname{Skel}_d(P)=P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Skel}_k(P)=\bigcup\{F:F\text{ is a face of }P,\ \dim F\le k\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines skeleta through intrinsic face dimensions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the face collection from its underlying union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron \(P\), let \(\mathcal F_{\le k}(P)=\{F\in\mathcal F(P):\dim F\le k\}\). This collection is closed under taking faces, and intersections of its members are common faces. Hence it is a polyhedral complex with support \(\operatorname{Skel}_k(P)\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{Skel}_{-1}(P)\subseteq\operatorname{Skel}_0(P)\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\operatorname{Skel}_d(P)=P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces of dimension at most k form a polyhedral subcomplex, and the skeleta are nested.

Vertex–Edge Adjacency
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct vertices are adjacent precisely when the segment joining them is a one-dimensional face of the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Distinct vertices \(u,v\in P\) are vertex-adjacent if and only if their segment \([u,v]=\operatorname{conv}\{u,v\}\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\). Equivalently, there exists an edge of \(P\) whose vertex set is exactly \(\{u,v\}\). The vertex-edge incidence graph therefore has the vertices of \(P\) as nodes and one edge for every such adjacent pair.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) are distinct vertices of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent exactly when \([u,v]\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacency is defined through bounded one-dimensional faces.

notation.meaning: Closed segment joining u and v

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\neq v\) be vertices of a polyhedron \(P\). They are adjacent if and only if there exists \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(c^Tx\) is bounded above on \(P\) and \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}c^Tx=[u,v]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two vertices are adjacent exactly when some linear objective has their joining segment as its entire optimal face.
assumptions_latex: \(u\neq v\) are vertices of a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\text{ and }v\text{ are adjacent}\iff\exists c:\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}c^Tx=[u,v].

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid for redundant finite inequality descriptions of full-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\) be full-dimensional and let \(u\neq v\) be vertices. Put \(I(u,v)=\{i:a_i^Tu=b_i=a_i^Tv\}\). The least face containing \(u,v\) is \(F(u,v)=\{x\in P:a_i^Tx=b_i\ \forall i\in I(u,v)\}\), and \(\dim F(u,v)=d-\operatorname{rank}A_{I(u,v)}\). Thus \(u,v\) are adjacent exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}A_{I(u,v)}=d-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two vertices of a full-dimensional H-polyhedron are adjacent exactly when their common active normals have rank d minus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\sim v\iff\operatorname{rank}A_{I(u,v)}=d-1.

Facet Adjacency
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct facets are adjacent when their intersection is a codimension-two face, called a ridge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) have dimension \(d\ge2\). Its facets are the faces of dimension \(d-1\), and its ridges are the faces of dimension \(d-2\). Two distinct facets \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) are facet-adjacent if and only if \(F_1\cap F_2\) is a ridge of \(P\), equivalently \(\dim(F_1\cap F_2)=d-2\). Their common ridge records the incidence witnessing adjacency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) are facet-adjacent exactly when \(F_1\cap F_2\) is a \((d-2)\)-dimensional face.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:0\le y\le1\}\), the facets \(F_0=\{y=0\}\) and \(F_1=\{y=1\}\) are disjoint and share no zero-dimensional ridge. Thus the facet-adjacency graph consists of two isolated vertices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The facet-adjacency graph of \(P\) is disconnected.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\{F:F\text{ is a facet of }P,\ R\subseteq F\}|=2\).

children.title: Face-Flag Incidence Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Nested face chains and local incidence patterns.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron of dimension \(d\), with face lattice \(\mathcal{F}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite chains in the face lattice of a finite-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A face flag of length \(k\) is a strictly increasing chain \[\mathscr{C}=(F_0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_k),
\qquad F_i\in\mathcal{F}(P).\] Its rank set is \(\{\dim F_i+1:0\le i\le k\}\). The flag is saturated when every inclusion is a cover relation, equivalently \(\dim F_{i+1}=\dim F_i+1\). A complete flag is a saturated maximal chain \[\varnothing=F_{-1}\prec F_0\prec F_1\prec\cdots\prec F_d=P,
\qquad \dim F_j=j.\] Two flags have the same local incidence pattern when their rank sets agree and the corresponding containment relations occur inside isomorphic intervals of \(\mathcal{F}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face flag is a nested sequence of distinct faces. It is saturated when no intermediate face can be inserted, so consecutive dimensions differ by one. A complete flag runs from the empty face through one face of every dimension to the whole polyhedron. Rank sets record which dimensions occur and face-lattice intervals encode the local incidence pattern around a partial flag.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flags are chains in \(\mathcal{F}(P)\); complete flags contain exactly one face of every dimension from \(-1\) through \(d\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A saturated flag is a path moving upward along cover edges in the Hasse diagram of the face lattice.
A complete flag is a maximal chain in the finite graded lattice \(\mathcal{F}(P)\).
special_cases_latex: In a polygon, a complete flag has the form \(\varnothing\prec\{v\}\prec e\prec P\).
In a \(d\)-simplex, complete flags correspond to orderings of its \(d+1\) vertices.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every partial flag can be extended to a complete flag.
A complete flag in a \(d\)-polyhedron has \(d+2\) members when \(\varnothing\) and \(P\) are counted.
boundary_notes: A collection of pairwise intersecting faces need not be a flag because comparability by inclusion is required.
The source establishes the graded face hierarchy; the term “flag” is conventional terminology for chains in that hierarchy.

notation.meaning: A chain of faces constituting a flag.

review_flags: Locator supports finiteness, containment, and consecutive face dimensions but does not introduce the word “flag” explicitly.
knowledge_statements.title: Flags and Maximal Face Chains
Face Flags
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face flag is a strictly nested finite sequence of faces; it is saturated when consecutive faces admit no intermediate face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A face flag of \(P\) is a finite sequence \(\Phi=(F_0,\ldots,F_r)\) of faces satisfying \(F_0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_r\). Its length is \(r\). The flag is saturated when no face of \(P\) lies strictly between any consecutive \(F_i\) and \(F_{i+1}\). Thus face flags are precisely finite chains in the inclusion-ordered face lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A face flag is a finite strictly inclusion-increasing sequence of faces of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flags need not contain the empty or maximal face.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard order-theoretic definition of a face flag

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses flags of proper nonempty faces of a polytope; maximal flags remain the responsibility of the maximal-chain sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polytope. The vertices of \(\operatorname{sd}(\partial P)\) are the proper nonempty faces of \(P\), and \(\{F_0,\ldots,F_r\}\) spans an \(r\)-simplex exactly when its members can be ordered as \(F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flags of proper nonempty faces are exactly the simplices in the barycentric subdivision of a polytope's boundary complex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proper nonempty face flags of \(P\) correspond bijectively to simplices of \(\operatorname{sd}(\partial P)\).

notation.meaning: Barycentric subdivision of the boundary face complex of P

knowledge_statements.title: Flags as Barycentric-Subdivision Simplices
Maximal Face Chains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a pointed d-dimensional polyhedron, every maximal face chain contains the empty face and exactly one face of each dimension from zero through d.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be pointed and \(d\)-dimensional. A maximal face chain is a chain \[\varnothing=F_{-1}\subsetneq F_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_d=P\] that cannot be enlarged by inserting another face. Every such chain is saturated and satisfies \(\dim F_i=i\) for \(i=0,\ldots,d\). Conversely, any chain containing exactly one face of each dimension from \(0\) through \(d\), together with \(\varnothing\), is maximal.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a pointed polyhedron of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every maximal face chain has one face of each dimension \(-1,0,\ldots,d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness ensures that maximal chains begin with a vertex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graded face lattice of a pointed polyhedron
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends the pointed seed to nonempty polyhedra with positive-dimensional lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a nonempty \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron with lineality space \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) of dimension \(\ell\). Every maximal chain has the form \(\varnothing\subsetneq F_\ell\subsetneq F_{\ell+1}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_d=P\), where \(\dim F_i=i\). Conversely, every such dimension-complete chain is maximal. Thus it has \(d-\ell+1\) strict inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximal chain contains the empty face and one nonempty face of every dimension from the lineality dimension through the dimension of the polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron of dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every maximal chain has face dimensions \(-1,\ell,\ell+1,\ldots,d\) and \(d-\ell+1\) strict inclusions.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Chains with Lineality
Local Incidence Patterns
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonempty faces lying between two fixed faces form a graded interval; saturated incidence chains have length equal to the dimension difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty faces \(F\subseteq G\) of \(P\), define \([F,G]_{\mathcal F(P)}=\{H\in\mathcal F(P):F\subseteq H\subseteq G\}\). This interval records the local incidence pattern between \(F\) and \(G\). It is graded by \(H\mapsto\dim H-\dim F\): whenever \(H_1\) is covered by \(H_2\) in the interval, \(\dim H_2=\dim H_1+1\). Hence every saturated chain from \(F\) to \(G\) has \(\dim G-\dim F\) inclusions.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq G\) are nonempty faces of a polyhedron \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interval \([F,G]_{\mathcal F(P)}\) is graded, and every saturated chain from \(F\) to \(G\) has \(\dim G-\dim F\) inclusions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes incidence locally inside a fixed face interval.

notation.meaning: Face-lattice interval between F and G

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graded intervals in polyhedral face lattices
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A full-dimensional formulation avoiding quotient notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be full-dimensional and let \(F\neq\varnothing\) be a face. For every \(H\) with \(F\subseteq H\subseteq P\), let \(N_P(H)\) be the normal cone along \(\operatorname{relint}H\). Then \(H\mapsto N_P(H)\) is an inclusion-reversing bijection from \([F,P]_{\mathcal F(P)}\) onto \(\mathcal F(N_P(F))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Faces containing a fixed face are anti-isomorphic to the faces of its normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([F,P]_{\mathcal F(P)}\cong\mathcal F(N_P(F))^{\mathrm{op}}\).

notation.meaning: Normal cone of P along the relative interior of H

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Cone and Lineality Space of a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex sets, specialized in consequences to polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession cone and lineality space of \(C\) are \[\operatorname{rec}C:=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+\lambda r\in C\ \forall x\in C,
\forall\lambda\ge0\},\] \[\operatorname{lin}C:=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:x+\lambda r\in C\ \forall x\in C,
\forall\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\}.\] They satisfy \[\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C),\] so \(\operatorname{lin}C\) is the largest linear subspace contained in \(\operatorname{rec}C\). The set \(C\) is pointed when \(\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\), equivalently when it contains no affine line. For closed convex \(C\), boundedness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction can be added with every nonnegative multiplier to every point of the set without leaving it. A lineality direction permits every real multiplier. The lineality space is exactly the symmetric part of the recession cone and is its largest subspace. A set is pointed when this space is trivial, while a nonempty closed convex set is bounded exactly when it has no nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}C=\operatorname{rec}C\cap(-\operatorname{rec}C)\), with pointedness determined by \(\operatorname{lin}C\) and boundedness by \(\operatorname{rec}C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(r\in\operatorname{rec}C\) if and only if \(C+r\subseteq C\).
\(r\in\operatorname{lin}C\) if and only if \(C+r=C\).
special_cases_latex: For an affine set \(a+L\), both its recession cone and lineality space equal \(L\).
For a polytope, \(\operatorname{rec}C=\operatorname{lin}C=\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty face of a polyhedron has the same lineality space as the polyhedron.
A pointed unbounded polyhedron has nonzero recession directions but no two-sided lineality directions.
boundary_notes: Closedness is material to the stated boundedness characterization for arbitrary convex sets.
Pointedness does not imply boundedness.

source_refs.locator: §8, definition preceding Theorem 8.1 and discussion of lineality following Theorem 8.4, pp. 61–65
§3.6, “Lineality Space and Recession Cone,” pp. 97–99

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Cones of Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron's recession cone consists of inequality-homogeneous feasible directions and equals the cone generated by any valid finite ray representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\), its recession cone is \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{d:x+td\in P\text{ for every }x\in P,t\ge0\}\). If \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), then \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{d:Ad\le0\}\). If also \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for finite sets \(V\) and \(R\), then \(\operatorname{rec}P=\operatorname{cone}(R)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{d:Ad\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}(R)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives both inequality-side and finite-generator descriptions.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The recession formulas are standard and the representation kind fits, but the cited general recession-cone section has not been inspected for the inequality and finite-generator equalities. A source specifically supporting both formulas is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constraint and Generator Descriptions of Polyhedral Recession
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) be nonempty, and suppose also that \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{v^1,
\ldots,
 v^p\}+\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,
\ldots,
 r^q\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedra with both half-space and Minkowski–Weyl representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession cone of \(P\) is \[\operatorname{rec}P=\{r:x+\lambda r\in P\ \forall x\in P,
\forall\lambda\ge0\}.\] For the two displayed representations it has the equivalent descriptions \[\operatorname{rec}P=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ar\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,
\ldots,
 r^q\}.\] Its lineality space is \[\operatorname{lin}P=\{r:Ar=0\}=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P).\] Thus recession removes the offsets \(b\) from an \(H\)-representation and removes the bounded convex-hull component from a \(V\)-plus-ray representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone collects all directions along which the polyhedron can be translated indefinitely. In an inequality description it is obtained by homogenizing the inequalities, replacing b by zero. In a Minkowski–Weyl description it is the cone generated by the recession generators. The lineality space is obtained by turning the homogeneous inequalities into equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\operatorname{rec}P=\{r:Ar\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,
\ldots,
 r^q\}\) and \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{r:Ar=0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(r\in\operatorname{rec}P\) if and only if \(P+r\subseteq P\).
If \(x_0\in P\), then \(r\in\operatorname{rec}P\) if and only if \(x_0+\lambda r\in P\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(P\) is a polytope, then \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}\).
If \(P\) is a polyhedral cone, then \(\operatorname{rec}P=P\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The recession cone of a polyhedron is itself a polyhedral cone.
\(P\) is bounded if and only if the homogeneous system \(Ar\le0\) has only the solution \(r=0\).
boundary_notes: The generator family need not be minimal; nonextreme or repeated rays may be present.
The equality \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{r:Ar\le0\}\) assumes \(P\) is nonempty.

notation.meaning: All nonnegative linear combinations of the listed vectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Spaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lineality space is the largest translation-invariant subspace of a polyhedron and equals the bidirectional part of its recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lineality space of a nonempty polyhedron \(P\) is \[\operatorname{lin}P:=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P).\] It is the largest vector subspace \(L\) satisfying \(P+L=P\). For an inequality representation \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), one has \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{d:Ad=0\}=\ker A\). Thus its elements are exactly the directions along which every point of \(P\) can be translated in both senses indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}P=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P)=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies bidirectional recession directions and translation invariance.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The lineality identities are mathematically standard and fit the representation container, but full-text support for the polyhedral formula \(\operatorname{lin}P=\ker A\) is not established by the supplied locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank and Orthogonal Representation of Polyhedral Lineality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional consequences of the inequality-side lineality formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\neq\varnothing\), and let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\). Then
\[L^\perp=\operatorname{range}(A^{\mathsf T})=\operatorname{span}\{a_i:i\text{ is a row index of }A\},\qquad \dim L=n-\operatorname{rank}A.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The orthogonal complement of a polyhedron's lineality space is the row space of its inequality matrix, and its dimension is the matrix nullity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L^\perp=\operatorname{range}(A^{\mathsf T})\) and \(\dim L=n-\operatorname{rank}A\).

notation.meaning: Rows of the inequality matrix, viewed as vectors.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointed Representative and Quotient by Lineality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\), and let \(M\) be any linear complement of \(L\), so \(\mathbb{R}^n=L\oplus M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonpointed polyhedra; both quotient and complementary-section realizations are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The pointed-quotient reduction of \(P\) is the quotient polyhedron \[\bar P:=\pi(P)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n/L,
\qquad \pi(x)=x+L.\] It satisfies \(\operatorname{lin}\bar P=\{0\}\). A complementary pointed representative is \[Q:=P\cap M,\] after translating coordinates if necessary so that the chosen complement meets \(P\). Under the canonical identification \(M\cong\mathbb{R}^n/L\), \(Q\) represents \(\bar P\), and \[P=Q+L,
\qquad \operatorname{rec}P=\operatorname{rec}Q+L.\] For the orthogonal choice \(M=L^\perp\), the representative is \(Q=P\cap L^\perp\), and every \(x\in P\) has a unique decomposition \(x=q+
\ell\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(\ell\in L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lineality can be removed canonically by passing to the quotient space. The quotient polyhedron is pointed. Choosing a complementary subspace realizes that quotient as a pointed section Q, and the original polyhedron is recovered by adding the lineality space. An orthogonal complement gives a convenient unique representative of each coset, although the quotient itself does not depend on this choice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P/L\) is pointed and any complementary representative \(Q\) gives \(P=Q+L\) and \(\operatorname{rec}P=\operatorname{rec}Q+L\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The fibers of \(\pi|_P\) are precisely the affine sets \(x+L\subseteq P\).
For \(M=L^\perp\), orthogonal projection onto \(L^\perp\) maps \(P\) onto \(Q\) and identifies \(Q\) with \(P/L\).
special_cases_latex: If \(P\) is pointed, then \(L=\{0\}\) and \(Q=P\).
If \(P=a+L\) is affine, then \(P/L\) is a singleton.
immediate_consequences_latex: Minimal faces of \(P\) correspond to vertices of \(Q\).
Faces of \(\operatorname{rec}P\) immediately above \(L\) correspond to extreme rays of \(\operatorname{rec}Q\).
boundary_notes: A section by an arbitrary complement must be positioned to meet \(P\); the quotient construction has no such choice issue.
Different complements yield affinely isomorphic pointed representatives, not identical subsets.

source_refs.locator: §8, direct-sum decomposition following the definition of lineality, pp. 65–66
§3.12, nonpointed case in Theorem 3.37, pp. 111–112

knowledge_statements.title: Pointed Reduction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting a polyhedron with the orthogonal complement of its lineality produces a pointed representative, from which the original polyhedron is reconstructed uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\operatorname{lin}P\) and set \(Q=P\cap L^\perp\). Then \(Q\) is a nonempty pointed polyhedron in \(L^\perp\), and every \(x\in P\) has a unique decomposition \(x=q+\ell\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(\ell\in L\). Consequently, \(P=Q+L\), the sum is direct relative to \(L^\perp\oplus L\), and the quotient polyhedron \(P/L\) is affinely isomorphic to \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(Q=P\cap L^\perp\), \(Q\) is pointed and \(P=Q\oplus L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the Euclidean orthogonal complement as a canonical representative space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Euclidean implementation of reduction by the full lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\), and let \(\Pi_{L^\perp}\) be orthogonal projection onto \(L^\perp\). Then
\[\Pi_{L^\perp}(P)=P\cap L^\perp.\]
The restriction \(\Pi_{L^\perp}|_P\) is constant on every coset modulo \(L\), its image is a pointed polyhedron, and it induces a bijective affine identification of \(P/L\) with \(P\cap L^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonally projecting a polyhedron away from its full lineality produces its pointed orthogonal section and realizes the lineality quotient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pi_{L^\perp}(P)=P\cap L^\perp\), a pointed polyhedron affinely identified with \(P/L\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projection onto the complement of the lineality space.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal-Projection Pointed Reduction
Lineality Quotients
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting a polyhedron by its lineality space preserves polyhedrality and recession directions while eliminating every line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(L=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap(-\operatorname{rec}(P))\). For the canonical map \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n/L\), the image \(\pi(P)\) is a polyhedron and
\[\operatorname{rec}(\pi(P))=\pi(\operatorname{rec}(P)).\]
Moreover,
\[\operatorname{lin}(\pi(P))=\pi(L)=\{0\},\]
so quotienting by the complete lineality space produces a pointed polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(P)\) is a pointed polyhedron, \(\operatorname{rec}(\pi(P))=\pi(\operatorname{rec}(P))\), and \(\operatorname{lin}(\pi(P))=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional quotient by the full lineality space.

notation.meaning: Canonical quotient map onto the vector-space quotient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Lineality Criterion for a Pointed Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for quotienting by a subspace of the lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron with \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\), let \(S\subseteq L\) be a linear subspace, and let \(\pi_S:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n/S\) be the quotient map. Then
\[\operatorname{lin}(\pi_S(P))=\pi_S(L)\cong L/S.\]
Consequently, \(\pi_S(P)\) is pointed if and only if \(S=L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient removes every line exactly when it factors out the entire lineality space; any smaller lineality subspace leaves residual lineality.
assumptions_latex: \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) and \(S\subseteq L\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(\pi_S(P))\cong L/S\), so \(\pi_S(P)\) is pointed exactly when \(S=L\).
knowledge_statements.title: Full-Lineality Criterion for a Pointed Quotient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face-Lattice Correspondence under the Lineality Quotient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial structure of a polyhedron modulo its complete lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\), and let \(\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n/L\). Every nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\) satisfies \(F+L=F\). The assignments
\[F\mapsto\pi(F),\qquad G\mapsto P\cap\pi^{-1}(G)\]
are mutually inverse inclusion-preserving bijections between the nonempty faces of \(P\) and \(\pi(P)\), and
\[\dim F=\dim\pi(F)+\dim L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotienting by lineality preserves the nonempty face lattice and subtracts the lineality dimension from every face dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) and \(\pi\) is the quotient map modulo L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonempty face lattices of \(P\) and \(\pi(P)\) are isomorphic, with \(\dim F=\dim\pi(F)+\dim L\).

notation.meaning: A nonempty face of the original polyhedron.
A nonempty face of the quotient polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Lattice Correspondence under the Lineality Quotient
Pointed Representative Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After choosing a complement to lineality, each quotient class has a unique representative forming a pointed polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\), choose \(x_0\in P\), and select a linear complement \(M\) with \(\mathbb{R}^n=M\oplus L\). Then
\[Q=(P-x_0)\cap M\]
is a polyhedron with \(\operatorname{lin}(Q)=\{0\}\). The restriction of the quotient map is a linear bijection
\[\pi|_M:Q\longrightarrow\pi(P-x_0),\]
whose inverse assigns to each quotient class its unique representative in \(M\). Thus \(Q\) gives a concrete pointed realization of the lineality quotient.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\).
\(M\) is a linear complement satisfying \(\mathbb{R}^n=M\oplus L\), and \(x_0\in P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=(P-x_0)\cap M\) is pointed, and \(\pi|_M:Q\to\pi(P-x_0)\) is a linear isomorphism of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A complement realizes the abstract quotient as a concrete pointed polyhedron.

notation.meaning: A complementary subspace to the lineality space.
Pointed representative in the chosen complement.

knowledge_statements.title: Reconstruction from Quotient Space
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The original polyhedron is uniquely reconstructed by translating the pointed representative and adding its lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated choices, \[P=x_0+Q+L.\] Every \(p\in P\) has a unique pair \((q,\ell)\in Q\times L\) satisfying \[p=x_0+q+\ell.\] Thus the original polyhedron is reconstructed from its pointed representative by restoring the lineality space and translating by \(x_0\).
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=x_0+Q+L\), and every \(p\in P\) has a unique decomposition \(p=x_0+q+\ell\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(\ell\in L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstruction relative to a chosen base point and complementary subspace.

notation.meaning: Lineality space of the original polyhedron.
Pointed representative polyhedron in the complement.

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Convex Sets p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generator-Side Reconstruction from a Pointed Representative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifting a finite point-ray representation through the lineality decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\), choose \(x_0\in P\) and a complement \(\mathbb R^n=M\oplus L\), and put \(Q=(P-x_0)\cap M\). If
\[Q=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\]
for finite \(V,R\subseteq M\), then
\[P=x_0+\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L,
\qquad \operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{cone}(R)+L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite point-ray representation of the pointed representative lifts by translation and addition of lineality, as do its recession generators.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=x_0+\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L\) and \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{cone}(R)+L\).

notation.meaning: Finite point generators of the pointed representative.
Finite recession generators of the pointed representative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Classification of Polyhedral Boundedness and Vertex Existence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, \(K=\operatorname{rec}P\), and \(L=K\cap(-K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedra; empty feasible sets are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The boundedness–vertex regime of \(P\) is classified by the pair \((K,L)\): \[P\text{ is bounded}\iff K=\{0\},\] \[P\text{ has a vertex}\iff P\text{ is pointed}\iff L=\{0\}.\] Accordingly, \(P\) lies in exactly one of three regimes: (i) bounded, where \(K=L=\{0\}\) and \(P\) is a polytope with vertices; (ii) unbounded pointed, where \(K\ne\{0\}\) and \(L=\{0\}\), so vertices and extreme recession rays may coexist; or (iii) nonpointed, where \(L\ne\{0\}\), so \(P\) contains lines and has no ordinary vertices, although its quotient \(P/L\) is pointed and has quotient vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is bounded exactly when its recession cone is trivial. It has an ordinary vertex exactly when its lineality space is trivial. This gives three mutually exclusive regimes: bounded polytopes; unbounded but pointed polyhedra, which may have both vertices and recession rays; and nonpointed polyhedra, which contain lines and have no ordinary vertices but retain vertex classes after quotienting by lineality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\{0\}\) characterizes boundedness, while \(L=\{0\}\) characterizes pointedness and vertex existence.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), boundedness means \(Ar\le0\Rightarrow r=0\).
Pointedness means \(Ar=0\Rightarrow r=0\), equivalently \(A\) has trivial null space after affine-hull reduction.
special_cases_latex: A singleton is bounded and pointed and has one vertex.
An affine line is nonpointed, unbounded, and has no vertex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty polytope has at least one vertex.
Unboundedness alone does not preclude vertices; nontrivial lineality does.
boundary_notes: The equivalence between pointedness and vertex existence is special to nonempty polyhedra and does not hold for all closed convex sets.
An unbounded pointed polyhedron need not have a bounded objective value in every linear direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is bounded exactly when its recession cone is trivial; then it is the convex hull of finitely many vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[P\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}.\]
When these equivalent conditions hold, \(P\) is a polytope: its vertex set \(V=\operatorname{vert}(P)\) is finite and nonempty, and
\[P=\operatorname{conv}(V).\]
Thus bounded polyhedra have neither nonzero recession directions nor nonzero lineality directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\); in that case \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\) for a finite nonempty vertex set \(V\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonempty polyhedra.

notation.meaning: Set of vertices of the polyhedron.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Recession and Barrier Cones p. 128

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Pointed Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbounded pointed polyhedron still has vertices and equals a bounded vertex hull plus a nontrivial pointed recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be nonempty, pointed, and unbounded. Then its vertex set contains a finite nonempty subset \(V\), and there is a finite set \(R\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(P)\setminus\{0\}\) such that
\[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R),\qquad \operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{cone}(R).\]
Conversely, any nonempty polyhedron satisfying \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\) and \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\neq\{0\}\) is pointed and unbounded, while still possessing at least one vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) has a nonempty finite vertex set and admits \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\) with at least one nonzero recession generator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minkowski-Weyl form for nonempty, pointed, unbounded polyhedra.

notation.meaning: Finite set of generators of the recession cone.

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Convex Sets p. 49
6.5 Recession and Barrier Cones p. 128

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpointed Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron with nonzero lineality has no extreme points, while quotienting by its full lineality space produces a pointed polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron with \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\neq\{0\}\). Then \[\operatorname{ext}(P)=\varnothing.\] The quotient polyhedron \(P/L\) has zero lineality and is pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) has no extreme points, while \(P/L\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The obstruction caused by nonzero lineality.

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Convex Sets p. 49

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial obstruction produced by nonzero lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\). Every nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\) satisfies \[F+L=F\] and therefore \(L\subseteq\operatorname{lin}(F)\). If \(L\ne\{0\}\), every nonempty face has dimension at least \(\dim L\), so \(P\) has no zero-dimensional faces or vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face contains all lineality directions; nonzero lineality therefore rules out zero-dimensional faces and vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonempty face \(F\) obeys \(F+L=F\); if \(L\ne\{0\}\), no face is zero-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.title: Faces Inherit Full Lineality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical decomposition after choosing the orthogonal complement of the full lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron with lineality space \(L\), and set \(Q=P\cap L^\perp\). Then \(Q\) is a nonempty pointed polyhedron and \[P=Q+L.\] Every \(x\in P\) has a unique decomposition \(x=q+\ell\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(\ell\in L\), and the quotient polyhedron \(P/L\) is linearly isomorphic to \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonpointed polyhedron decomposes uniquely into a pointed orthogonal cross-section plus its lineality space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(Q=P\cap L^\perp\), \(Q\) is pointed, \(P=Q+L\), and \(P/L\cong Q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Lineality Decomposition and Pointed Cross-Section
Vertex-Existence Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron has a vertex exactly when it is pointed, equivalently when it contains no affine line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the following conditions are equivalent:
\[\operatorname{ext}(P)\neq\varnothing,\qquad P\text{ contains no affine line},\qquad \operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}.\]
Thus pointedness is exactly the boundary for vertex existence among nonempty polyhedra: unboundedness alone does not preclude vertices, whereas any nonzero lineality direction precludes all vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext}(P)\neq\varnothing\) if and only if \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp vertex-existence criterion for nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedra.

notation.meaning: Set of extreme points, which are the vertices for a polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence Excess of a Polyhedral Face
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\) be a \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron and let \(F\) be a nonempty face. Let \(\Phi_F\) be the set of distinct facets of \(P\) containing \(F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial facial degeneracy measured using intrinsic facets, so it is independent of redundant copies in a chosen inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The facial incidence excess of \(F\) is \[\delta_P(F):=|\Phi_F|-\operatorname{codim}_P F.\] The face is incidence-nondegenerate when \(\delta_P(F)=0\), and incidence-degenerate when \(\delta_P(F)>0\). Since a codimension-\(k\) face requires at least \(k\) independent supporting normals, \(\delta_P(F)\ge0\). In an irredundant relative \(H\)-representation, \(|\Phi_F|\) equals the number of facet inequalities active everywhere on \(F\). Degeneracy therefore records excess facet incidence beyond the codimension forced by dimension, rather than mere duplication or scaling of constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a face F, count the distinct facets containing it and subtract its codimension. The result is the facial incidence excess. Zero excess is the nondegenerate incidence pattern; positive excess means more facets meet at the face than dimension alone requires. Using distinct intrinsic facets prevents duplicated or redundant inequalities from creating artificial facial degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is facially degenerate exactly when \(|\Phi_F|>\operatorname{codim}_P F\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In a minimal inequality representation, \(\delta_P(F)=|I(F)|-\operatorname{rank}_{\operatorname{lin}(P-P)}\{a_i:i\in I(F)\}\).
For a vertex \(v\) of a \(d\)-polytope, \(\delta_P(v)=|\Phi_v|-d\).
special_cases_latex: A simple polytope has \(\delta_P(v)=0\) at every vertex.
A vertex incident with more than \(d\) facets has positive incidence excess.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive excess permits several different active-facet subsets to span the same normal space.
Facial degeneracy can complicate enumeration because active descriptions of the same face need not be minimal or unique.
boundary_notes: Representation degeneracy caused solely by repeated inequalities is excluded by counting distinct facets.
Incidence excess is not a condition number and does not quantify metric near-dependence of normals.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\) be a \(d\)-dimensional polytope and let \(v\) be a vertex of \(P\). Denote by \(\Phi(v)\) the facets containing \(v\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic simplicity for vertices of finite-dimensional polytopes, with an active-constraint formulation for irredundant descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The vertex \(v\) is simple when it belongs to exactly \(d\) facets: \[|\Phi(v)|=d.\] It is nonsimple when \(|\Phi(v)|>d\). The polytope \(P\) is simple when every vertex is simple. If \[P=\{x\in\operatorname{aff}P:a_i^Tx\le b_i,
\ i=1,
\ldots,
 m\}\] is irredundant, then \(v\) is simple exactly when precisely \(d\) facet inequalities are active at \(v\). Equivalently, the tangent cone at \(v\), translated to the origin and viewed in \(\operatorname{lin}(P-P)\), has exactly \(d\) extreme rays, and the vertex has exactly \(d\) adjacent vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex of a d-dimensional polytope is simple if exactly d facets contain it, and nonsimple if more than d do. A polytope is simple when all its vertices are simple. In an irredundant description, this is the same as having exactly d active facet inequalities. Locally, a simple vertex has an orthant-like tangent cone, exactly d incident edges, and exactly d neighboring vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is simple if and only if \(|\Phi(v)|=d\), equivalently its local edge degree is \(d\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The normal cone \(N_P(v)\) of a simple vertex is generated by exactly \(d\) linearly independent facet normals.
A vertex is simple if its local face interval is combinatorially equivalent to that of the origin in \(\mathbb{R}_+^d\).
special_cases_latex: Every vertex of a simplex is simple.
Every vertex of a hypercube is simple; the vertices of a cross-polytope are nonsimple when \(d>2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every vertex of a simple \(d\)-polytope has precisely \(d\) neighbors.
Intersections of \(k\le d\) facets incident to a simple vertex give faces of dimension \(d-k\).
boundary_notes: Counting active rows without first removing redundant inequalities can falsely suggest nonsimplicity.
Simplicity is dual to simpliciality under polar duality for full-dimensional polytopes containing the origin in their interior.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Vertices
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex of a full-dimensional d-polyhedron is simple exactly when d facets meet there, equivalently when its tangent cone has d extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be full-dimensional, and let \(v\) be a vertex. The vertex \(v\) is simple when \[|\mathcal{F}(v)|=d.\] Equivalently, the outward normals of the incident facets are linearly independent and generate \(N_P(v)\), or the tangent cone at \(v\) has exactly \(d\) extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is simple if and only if exactly \(d\) facets contain \(v\); equivalently, their outward normals are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facet-incidence definition for vertices of full-dimensional polyhedra.

notation.meaning: Set of facets of the polyhedron containing the vertex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge and Vertex-Figure Structure at a Simple Vertex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local combinatorial structure for a simple vertex of a full-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be full-dimensional and let \(v\) be a simple vertex. Extreme rays of \(T_P(v)\) correspond bijectively to edges of \(P\) incident to \(v\). Consequently exactly \(d\) edges contain \(v\), their directions are linearly independent, and every sufficiently small vertex figure at \(v\) is a \((d-1)\)-simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly d linearly independent edge directions meet at a simple vertex, and its local vertex figure is a simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly \(d\) edges contain \(v\), their directions are linearly independent, and a vertex figure at \(v\) is a \((d-1)\)-simplex.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge and Vertex-Figure Structure at a Simple Vertex
Nonsimple Vertices
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex of a full-dimensional d-polyhedron is nonsimple exactly when more than d facets meet there, equivalently when its local normal and tangent cones are nonsimplicial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be full-dimensional, and let \(v\) be a vertex. The vertex \(v\) is nonsimple if and only if \[|\mathcal{F}(v)|>d.\] Equivalently, the normal cone \(N_P(v)\) and the tangent cone at \(v\) are nonsimplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is nonsimple if and only if more than \(d\) facets contain \(v\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement of simplicity for vertices of full-dimensional polyhedra.

notation.meaning: Set of facets incident to the vertex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Excess Incident Edges at a Nonsimple Vertex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local edge structure for vertices of full-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be full-dimensional and let \(v\) be a nonsimple vertex. Extreme rays of \(T_P(v)\) correspond bijectively to edges of \(P\) incident to \(v\). Since \(T_P(v)\) is nonsimplicial, more than \(d\) edges are incident to \(v\). Equivalently, every sufficiently small vertex figure at \(v\) is a non-simplex \((d-1)\)-polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsimple vertex has more than d incident edges, and its local vertex figure is not a simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: More than \(d\) edges contain \(v\), and a vertex figure at \(v\) is not a simplex.
knowledge_statements.title: Excess Incident Edges at a Nonsimple Vertex
Facet-Incidence Threshold
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every vertex of a full-dimensional d-polyhedron lies on at least d facets; equality characterizes simple vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every vertex \(v\) of a full-dimensional polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\), \[|\mathcal{F}(v)|\ge d.\] Equality holds exactly when \(v\) is simple, and strict inequality holds exactly when \(v\) is nonsimple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal{F}(v)|\ge d\), with equality exactly for simple vertices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum number of facets incident to a vertex of a full-dimensional polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron of affine dimension \(k\), and let \(v\) be a vertex. At least \(k\) relative facets of \(P\) contain \(v\). Equality holds exactly when the tangent cone at \(v\), viewed in \(\operatorname{lin}(P-P)\), is simplicial; equivalently, \(v\) is simple relative to \(\operatorname{aff}P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex of a k-dimensional polyhedron lies on at least k relative facets, with equality exactly in the intrinsically simple case.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone of dimension \(d\), considered in its linear span.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointed finite-dimensional polyhedral cones; lower-dimensional cones are treated relative to their span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cone \(K\) is simplicial when there exist linearly independent vectors \(r^1,
\ldots,
 r^d\) such that \[K=\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,
\ldots,
 r^d\}.\] Equivalently, \(K\) has exactly \(d\) extreme rays, and any choice of one nonzero generator from each extreme ray is linearly independent. The cone is nonsimplicial when it has more than \(d\) extreme rays. If \(R=[r^1\ \cdots\ r^d]\) is expressed in coordinates on \(\operatorname{span}K\), simpliciality is equivalent to \(R\) being nonsingular and \[K=R\mathbb{R}_+^d.\] Thus each \(x\in K\) has a unique coefficient vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^d\) with \(x=R\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A d-dimensional pointed polyhedral cone is simplicial if it is generated by d linearly independent rays. Equivalently, it has exactly d extreme rays. In coordinates on its span, it is an invertible linear image of the nonnegative orthant, and every cone vector has unique nonnegative coordinates in the extreme-ray generators. A pointed cone with more than d extreme rays is nonsimplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is simplicial if and only if it has \(d=\dim K\) linearly independent extreme-ray generators.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists a linear isomorphism \(T:\operatorname{span}K\to\mathbb{R}^d\) such that \(T(K)=\mathbb{R}_+^d\).
A full-dimensional cone \(K=\operatorname{pos}R\) is simplicial when \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is nonsingular.
special_cases_latex: Every one-dimensional pointed cone is simplicial.
The nonnegative orthant \(\mathbb{R}_+^d\) is simplicial.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every face of a simplicial cone is generated by a subset of its extreme rays.
The face lattice of a simplicial \(d\)-cone is Boolean on its \(d\) extreme rays.
boundary_notes: A cone containing a nonzero line is not simplicial under this pointed-cone definition.
A redundant generating list may be linearly dependent even when the cone itself is simplicial; minimal extreme-ray generators must be used.

notation.meaning: Cone of nonnegative linear combinations of the columns of R.

knowledge_statements.title: Simplicial Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A k-dimensional pointed polyhedral cone is simplicial when its k extreme rays have linearly independent generators, yielding unique nonnegative coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a pointed polyhedral cone and let \(k=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\). The cone \(K\) is simplicial if there exist linearly independent vectors \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\) such that
\[K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}.\]
Equivalently, \(K\) has exactly \(k\) extreme rays. In this case every \(x\in K\) has a unique conic-coordinate representation \(x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i r_i\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is simplicial if and only if it has exactly \(k\) extreme rays, generated by linearly independent vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-dimensional definition for pointed polyhedral cones.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the linear span of the cone.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Convex Cones p. 111

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality is taken intrinsically in the linear span of the cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{span}K\) and \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}\), where \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\) form a basis of \(S\). If \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\in S\) is the dual basis, \(\langle u_i,r_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\), then \[K_S^*=\{y\in S:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}=\operatorname{cone}\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}.\] Thus the intrinsic dual of a simplicial cone is simplicial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within its span, the dual of a simplicial cone is generated by the dual basis and is again simplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_S^*=\operatorname{cone}\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}\) is simplicial.

notation.meaning: Dual cone computed in the span \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boolean Face Structure of a Simplicial Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face representation relative to fixed extreme-ray generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_k\}\) with \(r_1,\ldots,r_k\) linearly independent, then its nonempty faces are exactly \[F_I=\operatorname{cone}\{r_i:i\in I\},\qquad I\subseteq\{1,�\ldots,k\}.\] Moreover, \(F_I\subseteq F_J\) if and only if \(I\subseteq J\). Hence the nonempty face lattice is Boolean and has \(2^k\) faces, counting \(\{0\}\) and \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty face of a simplicial cone is generated by a unique subset of its extreme rays, so its face lattice is Boolean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment \(I\mapsto F_I\) is an inclusion-preserving bijection from subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\) to nonempty faces of \(K\).

notation.meaning: Face generated by rays indexed by \(I\).

Nonsimplicial Cones
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed k-dimensional polyhedral cone is nonsimplicial exactly when it has more than k extreme rays; generators chosen from all those rays are then linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone, let \(k=\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\), and let \(m\) be the number of its extreme rays. Then \(K\) is nonsimplicial if and only if \[m>k.\] In this case, every family containing one nonzero generator from each extreme ray is linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is nonsimplicial if and only if it has more than \(k\) extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of simpliciality within pointed polyhedral cones.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the cone's linear span.
Number of extreme rays of the cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{span}K\) and let \(K\subseteq S\) be a pointed polyhedral cone with full dimension in \(S\). Then \[K\text{ is nonsimplicial}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K_S^*=\{y\in S:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\text{ is nonsimplicial}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed polyhedral cone is nonsimplicial exactly when its intrinsic dual cone is nonsimplicial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is nonsimplicial if and only if \(K_S^*\) is nonsimplicial.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate nonuniqueness caused by excess extreme rays; points on simplicial boundary faces may still have unique coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_m\}\) be a pointed \(k\)-dimensional polyhedral cone, with one nonzero generator from each extreme ray and \(m>k\). The map \(R:\mathbb R_+^m\to K\), \(R\lambda=\sum_i\lambda_i r_i\), is not injective. Moreover, every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}K\) has distinct \(\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R_+^m\) with \(R\lambda=R\mu=x\). Boundary points contained in simplicial faces need not have this nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extreme-ray coordinates are nonunique throughout the relative interior of a nonsimplicial cone, although boundary points in simplicial faces may have unique coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a pointed polyhedral cone of dimension \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is noninjective, and every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}K\) has at least two nonnegative extreme-ray coordinate vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness of Extreme-Ray Coordinates
Generator-Dependence Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed cone is simplicial precisely when its number of extreme rays equals its dimension; additional extreme rays force generator dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_m\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be pointed, where the listed vectors represent all distinct extreme rays, and let \(d=\dim K\). Every spanning set of \(K\) contains at least \(d\) rays. The cone is simplicial if and only if \(m=d\), equivalently, its extreme-ray generators are linearly independent in \(\operatorname{span}K\). Consequently, the first nonsimplicial case occurs at \(m>d\), when the irredundant extreme-ray generators are necessarily linearly dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(d=\dim K\), and \(r_1,\ldots,r_m\) generate its distinct extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is simplicial exactly when \(m=d\); generator dependence begins when \(m>d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointed cones; the boundary concerns irredundant extreme-ray generators.

notation.meaning: Dimension of the linear span of the cone

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality representation is degenerate at a feasible point when its active constraint normals are linearly dependent, a property that redundant constraints can create.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a represented polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) and a point \(\bar x\in P\), define the active set by \(I(\bar x)=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}\bar x=b_i\}\). The representation is degenerate at \(\bar x\) when the active normals \(\{a_i:i\in I(\bar x)\}\) are linearly dependent. This property depends on the displayed system: adding a redundant inequality can create representation degeneracy without changing \(P\), its minimal face containing \(\bar x\), or its intrinsic local geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is a fixed inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation is degenerate at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(\{a_i:i\in I(\bar x)\}\) is linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy is relative to a chosen inequality representation, not solely to the underlying polyhedron.

notation.meaning: Active inequality indices at the point
Row normal of the indexed inequality

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches representation-dependent degeneracy, but terminology varies across polyhedral and optimization sources. An authoritative locator is required to support this exact active-normal definition at an arbitrary feasible point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Redundant Constraints Can Create Active-Normal Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A representation-dependent example that does not resolve the leaf's canonical terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedron \(P=[0,\infty)\subseteq\mathbb R\) has the representation \(-x\le0\), whose active-normal family at \(0\) is \(\{-1\}\). The equivalent representation \[-x\le0,\qquad -2x\le0\] has two active, linearly dependent normals at \(0\). Thus active-normal dependence can be introduced without changing the polyhedron or its local face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a positively rescaled duplicate inequality creates dependent active normals without changing the represented half-line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent inequality systems can differ in active-normal dependence at the same feasible point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal Cones and the Normal Fan of a Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. For a nonempty face \(F\), choose any \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedra; normal cones encode dual objective directions and are constant on relative interiors of faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The normal cone of \(P\) along \(F\) is \[N_P(F):=N_P(x):=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^T(y-x)\le0\ \forall y\in P\},
\qquad x\in\operatorname{ri}F.\] Equivalently, \[c\in N_P(F)\iff F\subseteq\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in P}c^Ty.\] Its relative interior consists of objective vectors whose maximizing face is exactly \(F\): \[c\in\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\iff \operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in P}c^Ty=F.\] The collection \[\mathcal{N}(P):=\{N_P(F):F\text{ a nonempty face of }P\}\] is the normal-cone complex, or normal fan when these cones cover the relevant dual space. Face inclusion reverses: \(F\subseteq G\) implies \(N_P(G)\subseteq N_P(F)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cone of a face consists of linear objective vectors maximized throughout that face. Vectors in its relative interior select exactly that face as the optimizer set. Collecting the normal cones over all faces yields the normal-cone complex, which organizes objective space into polyhedral regions. Larger primal faces correspond to smaller dual cones, so the correspondence reverses face inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_P(F)=\{c:F\subseteq\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in P}c^Ty\}\), and the family \(\mathcal{N}(P)\) reverses the face-incidence order.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(N_P(x)=\partial\delta_P(x)\), where \(\delta_P\) is the convex indicator of \(P\).
For \(P=\{y:a_i^Ty\le b_i\}\) and \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F\), \(N_P(F)=\operatorname{cone}\{a_i:i\in I(F)\}\), modulo normals to \(\operatorname{aff}P\) in the lower-dimensional case.
special_cases_latex: At an interior point of a full-dimensional polyhedron, the normal cone is \(\{0\}\).
At a vertex of a full-dimensional polytope, the normal cone is full-dimensional.
immediate_consequences_latex: Linear objectives with coefficients in the same relative-open normal cone have the same optimal face.
Facet normals, active-constraint representations, primal faces, and linear-objective optimality regions are linked by the normal-cone correspondence.
boundary_notes: For an unbounded polyhedron, normal cones need not cover all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\); objectives outside their union may be unbounded above.
For a lower-dimensional polyhedron, every normal cone contains \(\operatorname{lin}(P-P)^\perp\).

notation.meaning: Normal cone of P along the relative interior of F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar of a Polyhedral Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Work in the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\). Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedral convex set containing \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional set polarity with the unit-level convention; conic polarity is recorded as the homogeneous special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polar of \(C\) is
\[
C^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle x,y\rangle\leq 1\ \text{for every }x\in C\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\leq1\}\), where \(\sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,y\rangle\). Polarity reverses inclusion: for sets \(C_1,C_2\) containing the origin, \(C_1\subseteq C_2\) implies \(C_2^\circ\subseteq C_1^\circ\). Since a polyhedral convex set is closed, the bipolar identity is \(C^{\circ\circ}=C\). If \(C=K\) is a convex cone, positive scaling makes the unit bound equivalent to the homogeneous condition, so
\[
K^\circ=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty polyhedral convex set C in Euclidean space that contains the origin, its polar consists of all vectors y whose inner product with every point of C is at most one. It is the unit sublevel set of the support function. Polarity reverses containment, and applying it twice returns C because C is closed and convex and contains zero. For a cone, the defining upper bound becomes zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C^\circ=\{y:\sigma_C(y)\leq1\},\qquad C^{\circ\circ}=C,\qquad C_1\subseteq C_2\Rightarrow C_2^\circ\subseteq C_1^\circ.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[C^\circ=\bigcap_{x\in C}\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq1\}.\]
For a cone \(K\), \[K^\circ=\{y:\sigma_K(y)=0\}=\{y:\langle x,y\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\), then \[C^\circ=\{y:\langle v_i,y\rangle\leq1,5 i\leq m\}.\]
If \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r_1,\ldots,r_q\}\), then \[K^\circ=\{y:\langle r_j,y\rangle\leq0,5 j\leq q\}.\]
immediate_consequences_latex: The polar of a polyhedral convex set is polyhedral.
If \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(C^\circ\) is bounded; if in addition \(C\) is bounded, both members of the polar pair are polytopes.
boundary_notes: If a convex set does not contain the origin, the bipolar is the closed convex hull of the set together with the origin, not necessarily the original set.
Some authors define a dual cone using nonnegative inner products; under that convention the dual cone is \(-K^\circ\).

notation.meaning: Unit-level polar of the set C.
