knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Refinement Normal Fan of a Minkowski Sum
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P,Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty polytopes, and let \(P+Q=\{p+q:p\in P,q\in Q\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded polyhedral Minkowski sums; the normal fans are complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every objective \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the selected face of the Minkowski sum is
\[
F_{P+Q}(u)=F_P(u)+F_Q(u),
\]
and its normal cone is
\[
N_{P+Q}(F_P(u)+F_Q(u))=N_P(F_P(u))\cap N_Q(F_Q(u)).
\]
Consequently the normal fan of \(P+Q\) is the common refinement
\[
\mathcal{N}(P+Q)=\mathcal{N}(P)\wedge\mathcal{N}(Q),
\]
whose cones are the nonempty intersections \(C\cap D\) with \(C\in\mathcal{N}(P)\) and \(D\in\mathcal{N}(Q)\), together with all their faces. Thus \(\mathcal{N}(P+Q)\) refines each summand fan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For polytopes P and Q, an objective selects on their Minkowski sum the sum of the faces it selects on the two summands. The corresponding normal cone is the intersection of the two normal cones. Therefore the normal fan of the sum is precisely the common refinement of the summand fans.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F_{P+Q}(u)=F_P(u)+F_Q(u),\qquad \mathcal{N}(P+Q)=\mathcal{N}(P)\wedge\mathcal{N}(Q).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\sigma_{P+Q}=\sigma_P+\sigma_Q.\]
Two objectives lie in the same relatively open cone of \(\mathcal{N}(P+Q)\) exactly when they select the same face in both \(P\) and \(Q\).
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=\{q\}\), translation does not change the normal fan: \(\mathcal{N}(P+q)=\mathcal{N}(P)\).
For \(Q=\lambda P\) with \(\lambda>0\), \(\mathcal{N}(P+Q)=\mathcal{N}(P)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every cone of \(\mathcal{N}(P+Q)\) is contained in a cone of each summand fan.
Repeated Minkowski addition produces the common refinement of all participating normal fans.
boundary_notes: For unbounded polyhedra the same formulas require restriction to the common finite-support domain.
The inspected support-function source gives additivity but not an explicit locator for the normal-fan common-refinement statement.

notation.meaning: Common refinement of the two fans.

review_flags: A source explicitly supporting the normal-fan refinement identity is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Refinement Normal Fan of a Minkowski Sum
Support Convention for Common Refinements
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection construction has support equal to the intersection of the input supports; unequal supports must therefore be restricted before it is a common refinement under the equal-support convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) be finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb R^n\), and form \[\mathcal F:=\left\{\bigcap_{i=1}^m\sigma_i:\sigma_i\in\mathcal F_i\right\}\] with duplicates removed. Then \[|\mathcal F|=\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal F_i|,\qquad |\mathcal G|:=\bigcup_{\sigma\in\mathcal G}\sigma.\] Thus \(\mathcal F\) is complete exactly when every input fan is complete. Under the convention that refinement requires equal support, \(\mathcal F\) is a common refinement of all inputs only when their supports coincide; otherwise it is the common refinement of their restrictions to the common support.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) are finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal F|=\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal F_i|\), with equal input supports required for an equal-support common refinement.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support identity and the refinement-order boundary for finite fans that need not have equal support.

notation.meaning: Support, or union of cones, of a fan.
Fan formed by all intersections of one cone from each input fan.

knowledge_statements.title: Common Fan Refinements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the canonical simultaneous refinement of finitely many polyhedral fans, including its support condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{F}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{F}_m\) be finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Their common refinement is
\[\mathcal{F}_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\mathcal{F}_m:=\{C_1\cap\cdots\cap C_m:C_i\in\mathcal{F}_i\},\]
with repeated cones identified. This collection is a polyhedral fan whose support is
\[|\mathcal{F}_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\mathcal{F}_m|=\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal{F}_i|.\]
Every cone of the common refinement is contained in a cone of each \(\mathcal{F}_i\). Among polyhedral fans with support \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal{F}_i|\) and this simultaneous-refinement property, it is the coarsest. In particular, the common refinement of complete fans is complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The common refinement consists of all intersections of one cone from each fan. Its support is the intersection of the fan supports, and it is the coarsest fan on that support refining every original fan.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{F}_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\mathcal{F}_m\) is a fan supported on \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal{F}_i|\) and is the coarsest simultaneous refinement having that support.

notation.meaning: Union of all cones in the fan.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support of a Common Fan Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support identity and completeness boundary for finite fans in one ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) be finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\mathcal F=\bigwedge_{i=1}^m\mathcal F_i\) be their intersection refinement. Then \[|\mathcal F|=\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal F_i|,\qquad |\mathcal G|:=\bigcup_{\sigma\in\mathcal G}\sigma.\] Hence \(\mathcal F\) is complete if and only if every \(\mathcal F_i\) is complete. For incomplete fans the construction refines only their common support; it does not fill directions absent from an input fan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support of a common refinement is the intersection of the input supports, so completeness is preserved exactly when all input fans are complete.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_m\) are finite polyhedral fans in \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(\mathcal F\) is their common intersection refinement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal F|=\bigcap_{i=1}^m|\mathcal F_i|\).

notation.meaning: Support, or union of the cones, of a fan.
Common intersection refinement of the fans.

knowledge_statements.title: Support of a Common Fan Refinement
Normal Fans of Minkowski Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exposed face of a Minkowski sum is the sum of exposed faces, and its normal fan is the common refinement of the summand fans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the face of the Minkowski sum exposed by \(c\) satisfies \[F_{P+Q}(c)=F_P(c)+F_Q(c).\] If \(F=F_P(c)\) and \(G=F_Q(c)\), then the associated normal cone is \[N_{P+Q}(F+G)=N_P(F)\cap N_Q(G).\] Consequently the normal fan of the sum is exactly the common refinement of the summand normal fans: \[\mathcal N(P+Q)=\mathcal N(P)\wedge\mathcal N(Q).\]
assumptions_latex: Normal cones use the maximization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N(P+Q)=\mathcal N(P)\wedge\mathcal N(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-fan identity for Minkowski sums of polytopes.

notation.meaning: Face of P exposed by objective c.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically standard and fits the Minkowski-sum normal-fan leaf, but the exposed-face, normal-cone, and common-refinement identities have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Summand Fan Comparisons
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Minkowski sum's normal fan refines both summand fans; it equals one summand fan exactly when that fan already refines the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(\mathcal F\preceq\mathcal G\) when every cone of \(\mathcal F\) is contained in a cone of \(\mathcal G\). Then \[\mathcal N(P+Q)\preceq\mathcal N(P)\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal N(P+Q)\preceq\mathcal N(Q).\] Equality with a summand fan is characterized by comparability: \[\mathcal N(P+Q)=\mathcal N(P)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal N(P)\preceq\mathcal N(Q),\] and symmetrically after exchanging \(P\) and \(Q\). Thus adding a summand can subdivide, but cannot coarsen, the original normal regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N(P+Q)\preceq\mathcal N(P)\) and \(\mathcal N(P+Q)\preceq\mathcal N(Q)\); moreover, \(\mathcal N(P+Q)=\mathcal N(P)\iff\mathcal N(P)\preceq\mathcal N(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Refinement order among normal fans of two summands and their sum.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The property and refinement direction are consistent with the stated convention and fit the leaf, but no supporting citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Normal Regions for Unbounded Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an unbounded polyhedron, exact optimal-face regions remain the relative interiors of normal cones, but they partition only the recession-polar finite-support domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=\operatorname{rec}(P)\). For every nonempty face \(F\) define \[\mathcal R_F:=\{c:\operatorname{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle=F\}.\] Then \[\mathcal R_F=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F),\qquad \overline{\mathcal R_F}=N_P(F),\] and the nonempty regions \(\mathcal R_F\) partition \(R^\circ\). If \(c\notin R^\circ\), the objective is unbounded above and belongs to no optimal-face region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\operatorname{ri}N_P(F):F\ne\varnothing\}\) partitions \(R^\circ\), and objectives outside \(R^\circ\) are unbounded above.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends objective-region stratification from polytopes to the finite-support domain of an arbitrary polyhedron.

notation.meaning: Objectives selecting exactly the face F.
Nonpositive polar of the recession cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Normal Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective regions for linear maximization over a nonempty polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polytope and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(P\). Define \[N_P(F)=\{c\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle c,y-x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }x\in F\text{ and }y\in P\}.\] The objective vectors having exactly \(F\) as their optimal face satisfy \[\{c:\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle=F\}=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).\] Thus the relative interiors of the normal cones are disjoint parametric regions on each of which the optimal face is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objectives selecting exactly a face F form the relative interior of its normal cone, so optimal faces remain constant within these objective-space regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{c:\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}\langle c,x\rangle=F\}=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F)\).

notation.meaning: normal cone of P along the face F under the maximization convention

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-Parameter Region of a Fixed Optimal Face
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and consider the parametric linear optimization problem \(\max_{x\in P}\langle u,x\rangle\), with parameter \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-parametric linear optimization over a fixed polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each nonempty face \(F\unlhd P\), its closed parametric normal region and exact-face region are
\[
\mathcal{R}_{\supseteq F}:=\{u:F\subseteq F_P(u)\}=N_P(F),
\]
\[
\mathcal{R}_{=F}:=\{u:F_P(u)=F\}=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F).
\]
Thus the closed region permits enlargement of the optimal face on its boundary, while the relatively open region has a stable exact optimal face. The regions \(\mathcal{R}_{=F}\) are pairwise disjoint and partition \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=(\operatorname{rec}P)^\circ\). Their closures are the cones of the normal-fan complex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an objective-parametric linear program, the closed normal region of a face contains all objective vectors for which that face remains optimal, possibly as part of a larger optimizer face. Its relative interior contains exactly the objectives whose full optimizer set equals that face. These exact-face regions partition the domain of finite objectives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal{R}_{=F}=\operatorname{ri}N_P(F),\qquad \operatorname{dom}\sigma_P=\bigsqcup_{F\neq\varnothing}\mathcal{R}_{=F}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x_F\in\operatorname{ri}F\), \[\mathcal{R}_{\supseteq F}=\{u:\langle u,y-x_F\rangle\leq0\ \forall y\in P\}.\]
If \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\), a normal region is generated by the normals of constraints active on the corresponding face.
special_cases_latex: For a polytope, the exact-face regions partition all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
A generic objective belongs to the relative interior of a maximal normal cone and selects a vertex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Crossing a common boundary between regions can enlarge or change the optimal face.
Within one exact-face region, the support value is given by the same linear form \(u\mapsto\langle u,x_F\rangle\).
boundary_notes: This record parametrizes the objective only; right-hand-side or matrix perturbations produce different critical-region constructions.
No supplied source explicitly names these sets as parametric normal regions.

notation.meaning: Objectives whose exact optimizer face is F.
Objectives for which F is contained in the optimizer face.

review_flags: A source on objective-parametric polyhedral optimization or normal-fan regions is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Parameter Region of a Fixed Optimal Face
Finite Polyhedral Complexes and Their Support
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite polyhedral complex is face-closed and its cells meet, if at all, in a common face; its support is their union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite collection \(\mathcal C\) of polyhedra in \(\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedral complex when every face of every \(C\in\mathcal C\) belongs to \(\mathcal C\), and for all \(C,D\in\mathcal C\), \(C\cap D\) is empty or a face of both. Its support is \[|\mathcal C|:=\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal C}C.\] Members are cells, and inclusion-maximal members are maximal cells.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a finite collection of polyhedra in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a polyhedral complex exactly when it is face-closed and every nonempty pairwise intersection is a face of both cells.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite polyhedral complexes; conical specialization is owned by the conical-complex sibling.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Partition of a Polyhedral Complex
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interiors of the cells form a disjoint partition of the support, so every support point has a unique carrier cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite polyhedral complex \(\mathcal C\), the relative interiors of its nonempty cells are pairwise disjoint and satisfy \[|\mathcal C|=\bigsqcup_{C\in\mathcal C,\,C\ne\varnothing}\operatorname{ri}C.\] Equivalently, every point of the support lies in the relative interior of a unique cell, namely the inclusion-minimal cell containing it.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a finite polyhedral complex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(x\in|\mathcal C|\) belongs to \(\operatorname{ri}C\) for exactly one cell \(C\in\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic stratification property of a finite polyhedral complex.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Complex Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complex structure of the normal cones of a polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polytope, and associate with every nonempty face \(F\) its normal cone \(N_P(F)\). The collection \(\mathcal N(P)=\{N_P(F):F\text{ is a nonempty face of }P\}\) is a finite polyhedral complex: every face of a cone in \(\mathcal N(P)\) also belongs to \(\mathcal N(P)\), and the intersection of any two cones is a face of each. More precisely, \(N_P(F)\cap N_P(G)=N_P(H)\), where \(H\) is the smallest face of \(P\) containing \(F\cup G\). Its union is \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cones of all nonempty faces of a polytope form a finite complete polyhedral complex, with intersections corresponding contravariantly to common containing faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal N(P)\) is a finite polyhedral complex and \(\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal N(P)}C=\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: normal cone of P along F
collection of normal cones of all nonempty faces of P

knowledge_statements.title: Conical Complex Compatibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite cone collection is a conical complex precisely when it contains all cone faces and every pair intersects in a common face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The collection \(\mathcal C\) is a polyhedral conical complex if and only if both conditions hold: every face of every \(C\in\mathcal C\) belongs to \(\mathcal C\), and for all \(C,D\in\mathcal C\), the intersection \(C\cap D\) is a face of both \(C\) and \(D\). If additionally \[\bigcup_{C\in\mathcal C}C=\mathbb{R}^n,\] the complex is complete. These conditions ensure face-compatible gluing of its cones.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a finite collection of polyhedral cones in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\) is a conical complex exactly when it is face-closed and \(C\cap D\) is a face of both \(C\) and \(D\) for all \(C,D\in\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate defining a finite polyhedral conical complex.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The stated condition is the standard compatibility definition for a finite conical complex and fits the leaf, but it has no supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper convex function, and define \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):t\geq f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper extended-real convex functions; polyhedrality includes domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is polyhedral convex when its epigraph is a nonempty polyhedral convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). Equivalently, there exist vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\), scalars \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k\), and a nonempty polyhedron
\[
D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:B x\leq d\}
\]
such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}+\delta_D(x),
\]
where \(\delta_D(x)=0\) for \(x\in D\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Hence \(f\) is closed and is piecewise affine on its polyhedral effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is polyhedral when its epigraph is a polyhedron. Equivalently, on a polyhedral domain it is the maximum of finitely many affine functions, and it is positive infinity outside that domain. Such a function is closed and piecewise affine on its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\ \text{is polyhedral}\Longleftrightarrow f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq k}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_D(x)\ \text{for a polyhedron }D.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):Bx\leq d,\ t\geq\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i,5 i\leq k\}.\]
A proper convex function is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated in the epigraphical point-and-direction sense.
special_cases_latex: If \(D=\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(f\) is a finite maximum of affine functions and is finite everywhere.
If \(k=1\) with affine term zero, \(f=\delta_D\) is the indicator of a nonempty polyhedron.
The support function of a nonempty polyhedron is a polyhedral convex function.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Fenchel conjugate of a polyhedral convex function is polyhedral.
Every sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\leq\beta\}\) is polyhedral.
Finite maxima of polyhedral convex functions and finite intersections of their epigraphical constraints remain polyhedral.
boundary_notes: A merely piecewise-affine function need not be convex; the maximum representation enforces convexity.
Allowing the improper constant functions requires separate conventions and is excluded by properness.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, epigraph polyhedrality requires a different finite-codimensional formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Epigraphical and Max-Affine Representations of a Polyhedral Convex Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper convex function. A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, extended-real-valued convex functions; properness excludes the identically \(+\infty\) function and all values \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is polyhedral convex precisely when \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):f(x)\le t\}\) is a polyhedron in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\). Equivalently, there exist finite families \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb R\), \(c_j\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(d_j\in\mathbb R\) such that \[C:=\{x:\langle c_j,x\rangle\le d_j\ \text{for every }j\}\ne\varnothing\] and \[f(x)=\max_i\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}+\delta_C(x).\] Thus \(\operatorname{dom}f=C\), and its epigraph has the inequality representation \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):\langle c_j,x\rangle\le d_j\ \forall j,\ t\ge\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\ \forall i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space is polyhedral when its epigraph is a polyhedron. This is equivalent to representing it on a nonempty polyhedral domain as the maximum of finitely many affine functions and assigning value plus infinity outside that domain. The domain inequalities give the vertical half-spaces of the epigraph, while the affine pieces give its nonvertical lower supporting half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is polyhedral convex}\iff \operatorname{epi}f\text{ is polyhedral}\iff f=\max_i(\langle a_i,\cdot\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C\text{ for a polyhedron }C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A convex function is polyhedral if and only if it is finitely generated: its epigraph is the convex hull of finitely many points and recession directions, including the upward direction \((0,1)\).
For proper \(f\), the finite max-affine representation implies that \(f\) is closed and that every finite value is attained by the lower boundary of its epigraph.
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb R^n\), then \(f(x)=\max_i\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}\) is finite everywhere.
If there is a single affine piece, then \(f\) is an affine function restricted to the polyhedron \(C\).
Taking every affine piece equal to zero yields the indicator \(\delta_C\) of a polyhedron.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every sublevel set \(\{x:f(x)\le r\}\) is a polyhedron.
The effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is a polyhedron, and a proper polyhedral convex function is lower semicontinuous.
boundary_notes: An arbitrary piecewise-affine function need not be convex and therefore need not admit a maximum-of-affine-pieces representation.
This definition is finite-dimensional; infinite-dimensional notions of polyhedrality require separate conventions.

notation.meaning: The convex indicator, equal to \(0\) on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph–Domain Data for an Extended-Valued Polyhedral Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be a finite maximum of affine functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper polyhedral convex functions represented by separate domain and lower-epigraph data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An epigraph–domain representation pair consists of finite data \[(C,h),\qquad C=\{x:\langle c_j,x\rangle\le d_j\ \forall j\},\qquad h(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i),\] with \(C\ne\varnothing\). The represented extended-valued function is \[f(x)=h(x)+\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}h(x),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Its domain and epigraph are recovered exactly as \[\operatorname{dom}f=C,\qquad \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):x\in C,\ t\ge h(x)\}.\] Equivalently, the epigraph is cut out jointly by the domain inequalities and the inequalities \(t\ge\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The representation pair separates an extended-valued polyhedral function into a nonempty polyhedral domain and a finite max-affine function. On the domain the represented function equals the max-affine part, and outside it the value is plus infinity. The epigraph is obtained by imposing both the domain inequalities and all lower bounds on the height variable supplied by the affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(C,h)\longmapsto f=h+\delta_C,\qquad \operatorname{dom}f=C,\qquad \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):x\in C,\ t\ge h(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(h(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)\), then \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):\langle c_j,x\rangle\le d_j\ \forall j,\ \langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\le t\ \forall i\}.\]
Conversely, any proper polyhedral convex function admits such a pair by separating the vertical and nonvertical inequalities in an epigraph representation.
special_cases_latex: For \(h\equiv0\), the pair represents the indicator function \(\delta_C\).
For \(C=\mathbb R^n\), the pair represents a globally finite max-affine function.
For a single affine piece, it represents a partial affine function on \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The domain can be manipulated as a polyhedral set independently of the affine lower-envelope data.
Redundant domain inequalities or affine pieces may be removed without changing the represented function.
boundary_notes: The pair is generally not unique because either inequality system may contain redundant members.
Nonemptiness of \(C\) is required for properness.
The maximum must contain finitely many affine pieces in this polyhedral representation.

notation.meaning: The domain polyhedron and finite max-affine part of the representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real function is polyhedral convex exactly when its epigraph is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph of \(f\) is \[\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:t\geq f(x)\}.\] The function \(f\) is called polyhedral convex when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a nonempty polyhedron. Properness excludes \(f\equiv+\infty\) and finite values equal to \(-\infty\); consequently the epigraph has a nonempty projection onto \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and contains no complete vertical line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a nonempty polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph definition of a proper extended-real polyhedral convex function.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Domains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of a proper polyhedral convex function is the epigraph's coordinate projection and is therefore a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The effective domain is \[\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)<+\infty\}.\] It equals the coordinate projection of the epigraph: \[\operatorname{dom}f=\pi_x(\operatorname{epi}f).\] Because a linear image of a polyhedron is polyhedral, \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is a nonempty polyhedron. It need not equal all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\); points outside it are precisely those where \(f\) takes the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective domains of proper polyhedral convex functions in finite dimensions.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph–Domain Projection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point belongs to the effective domain exactly when some finite-height epigraph point projects onto it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi_x:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be defined by \(\pi_x(x,t)=x\). Then \[\pi_x(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{dom}f.\] Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) if and only if there exists \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \((x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\). For a polyhedral convex function, this identity realizes its polyhedral effective domain as a linear projection of its polyhedral epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact set-theoretic relation between an extended-real function's epigraph and domain.

notation.meaning: Projection onto the first n coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Value Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function agrees with its finite restriction on the effective domain and equals positive infinity outside it, where its epigraph has empty vertical fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=f|_D:D\to\mathbb{R}\). The extended-value boundary convention is \[f(x)=\begin{cases}g(x),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}\] Consequently, for every \(x\in D\), \[\{t\in\mathbb{R}:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}=[f(x),+\infty),\] whereas this vertical epigraph fiber is empty for every \(x\notin D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin D\), while \(\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}=[f(x),+\infty)\) for \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value convention encoding a polyhedral domain restriction.

notation.meaning: Finite-valued restriction of f to D.

children.title: Finite Max-Affine Functions
children.top_down_role: Globally finite piecewise-linear convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant and Essential Affine Pieces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine piece is removable exactly when it never strictly exceeds all the other pieces; every piece of an irredundant representation is uniquely active somewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell_i(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\) and \(f=\max_i\ell_i\). Then \(\ell_i\) is redundant if and only if \[\ell_i(x)\leq\max_{j\ne i}\ell_j(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n.\] Equivalently, \(\ell_i\) is essential if and only if there exists \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(\ell_i(x)>\ell_j(x)\) for every \(j\ne i\).
assumptions_latex: Duplicate affine functions have been identified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_i\text{ is essential}\iff\exists x\;\forall j\ne i:\ell_i(x)>\ell_j(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimality criterion for a finite global max-affine representation, after duplicate affine functions are identified.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Lipschitz Bound and Exact Irredundant Constant
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite max-affine function is globally Lipschitz, and the largest slope norm in an irredundant representation is its least global Euclidean Lipschitz constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}\), then \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|_2\quad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n),\qquad L=\max_i\|a_i\|_2.\] After redundant pieces are deleted, the least global Euclidean Lipschitz constant is exactly \(\max_i\|a_i\|_2\) over the remaining pieces.
assumptions_latex: Sharpness refers to an irredundant representation and the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Lip}(f)\leq\max_i\|a_i\|_2\), with equality after redundant pieces are removed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean Lipschitz behavior intrinsic to globally finite max-affine functions.

notation.meaning: Least global Euclidean Lipschitz constant of f.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Max-Affine Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An everywhere-finite function is polyhedral convex exactly when it is the maximum of finitely many affine functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is finite and polyhedral convex if and only if there exist \(m\geq1\), vectors \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and scalars \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \[f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Its epigraph is consequently \[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{(x,t):t\geq\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}.\] Conversely, every such finite maximum is an everywhere-finite polyhedral convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral convex if and only if \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)\) for finitely many affine functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global finite-dimensional representation without a domain restriction.

notation.meaning: Slope and intercept of the i-th affine component.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix a positive integer \(p\), vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_p\in\mathbb R^n\), and scalars \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_p\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Globally finite, continuous, piecewise-affine convex functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite max-affine function is a function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) of the form \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}.\] Its epigraph is the polyhedron \[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{i=1}^p\{(x,t):t\ge\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}.\] For each \(x\), its active index set is \[I(x)=\{i:f(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}.\] This set is nonempty, and \(f\) agrees with every active affine piece at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite max-affine function is the pointwise maximum of a nonempty finite collection of real affine functions on Euclidean space. It is finite everywhere, convex, continuous, and polyhedral because its epigraph is the intersection of the finitely many half-spaces lying above its affine pieces. The active indices at a point are precisely the pieces attaining the maximum there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i),\qquad \operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb R^n,\qquad \operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_i\{(x,t):t\ge\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A convex function is finite max-affine if and only if it is a polyhedral convex function with full domain \(\mathbb R^n\).
The regions \(P_i=\{x:\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\ge\langle a_j,x\rangle+\alpha_j\ \forall j\}\) are polyhedra whose union is \(\mathbb R^n\), and \(f\) is affine on each nonempty \(P_i\).
special_cases_latex: With \(p=1\), \(f\) is affine.
Choosing the pieces \(x\mapsto x_k\) gives \(f(x)=\max_k x_k\).
The absolute value satisfies \(|x|=\max\{x,-x\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every sublevel set has the finite inequality description \(\{x:f(x)\le r\}=\bigcap_i\{x:\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\le r\}\).
At every \(x\), the subdifferential is the polytope \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).
boundary_notes: A minimum of finitely many affine functions is generally concave rather than convex.
Allowing infinitely many pieces can produce nonpolyhedral convex functions.
Adding a polyhedral domain restriction produces an extended-valued polyhedral function rather than a globally finite max-affine function.

notation.meaning: Indices of affine pieces attaining the maximum at \(x\).
The dominance region of the \(i\)-th affine piece.

children.title: Domain-Restricted Max-Affine Functions
children.top_down_role: Affine-piece models combined with polyhedral domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Affine Representation Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper polyhedral convex function, and only such a function, is a finite affine maximum restricted to a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper polyhedral convex if and only if there exist a nonempty polyhedron \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), an integer \(m\ge1\), and affine functions \(x\mapsto\langle a_i,x\rangle+\beta_i\) such that \[f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\beta_i\}+\iota_D(x).\] One may take \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is polyhedral convex}\iff f=\max_{1\le i\le m}(\langle a_i,\cdot\rangle+\beta_i)+\iota_D\) for some nonempty polyhedron \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse to the seed construction for proper finite-dimensional polyhedral convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Restricted Max-Affine Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A domain-restricted max-affine function is the finite maximum of specified affine functions on a nonempty polyhedron D, extended by positive infinity outside D. Its domain is D, and its epigraph consists of the pairs (x,t) with x in D and t at least every affine-piece value. It is a proper lower-semicontinuous polyhedral convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A domain-restricted max-affine function is an extended-real function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) of the form \[f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+\beta_i\}+\iota_D(x),\qquad \iota_D(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}\] Equivalently, \(f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\beta_i)\) on \(D\) and \(f(x)=+\infty\) outside \(D\). Its epigraph is the polyhedron \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):x\in D,\ t\geq\langle a_i,x\rangle+\beta_i\text{ for every }i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous polyhedral convex function with \(\operatorname{dom}f=D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real max-affine representation on a nonempty polyhedral effective domain.

children.title: Piecewise-Affine Cell Complexes
children.top_down_role: Primal-space cells sharing common affine behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Cell Complexes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite inequality description of D together with all pairwise affine-piece comparisons partitions D into a finite polyhedral cell complex. The ordering and active set of the affine pieces are constant on each cell interior, and the function is affine on every cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell_i(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+\beta_i\). Partition \(D\) according to all realizable sign patterns of the finitely many affine functions defining \(Cx-d\) and \(\ell_i-\ell_j\) for \(1\leq i<j\leq m\), and include all faces of the resulting closed polyhedral cells. These cells form a finite polyhedral cell complex with union \(D\). On the relative interior of each cell, the ordering of the functions \(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m\) and the active set \(I(x)\) are constant, and \(f\) agrees with an active affine function. Thus \(f\) is affine on each cell.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\beta_i)+\iota_D(x)\), where \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
\(D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Cx\leq d\}\) for some finite system \(Cx\leq d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign cells induced on \(D\) by the defining inequalities of \(D\) and the affine-piece comparisons form a finite polyhedral cell complex covering \(D\), and \(f\) is affine on every cell.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal cell decomposition induced by affine-piece comparisons and a finite inequality description of the polyhedral domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Cell Complex Induced by Affine Pieces
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron and let \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}\ell_i(x)\) on \(C\), where every \(\ell_i(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-space decomposition associated with a finite convex max-affine representation on a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonempty index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\), define the active-set cell \[P_I:=\{x\in C:\ell_i(x)=f(x)\ \forall i\in I,\ \ell_j(x)\le f(x)\ \forall j\}.\] Equivalently, after fixing any \(i_0\in I\), \[P_I=\{x\in C:\ell_i(x)=\ell_{i_0}(x)\ \forall i\in I,\ \ell_j(x)\le\ell_{i_0}(x)\ \forall j\}.\] The piecewise-affine cell complex generated by the representation is the finite collection of all nonempty faces of the polyhedra \(P_{\{i\}}\). Its cells cover \(C\), the intersection of any two cells is empty or a common face, every face of a cell is included, and \(f\) restricts to an affine function on every cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite max-affine representation partitions its polyhedral domain into polyhedral regions on which specified affine pieces are active. Taking all nonempty faces of the single-piece dominance regions produces a finite polyhedral complex: its cells cover the domain, meet along common faces, and inherit all of their faces. On each cell the function agrees with one affine formula, while lower-dimensional cells record ties among several formulas.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal P}P,\qquad f|_P\text{ is affine for every }P\in\mathcal P,\] where \(\mathcal P\) is finite, face-closed, and any two cells meet in a common face or not at all.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The relative interiors of the cells may be indexed by the exact active sets \(I(x)=\{i:\ell_i(x)=f(x)\}\).
The graph pieces \(\{(x,f(x)):x\in P\}\) are faces or unions of faces of the lower boundary of the polyhedral epigraph.
special_cases_latex: If one affine piece dominates throughout \(C\), the complex consists of \(C\) and its faces.
For \(f(x)=\max\{x,-x\}\) on \(\mathbb R\), the maximal cells are the two half-lines and their common face is \(\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Only finitely many distinct active sets occur.
The function is differentiable on the relative interior of a full-dimensional cell whenever all active pieces there have the same slope.
boundary_notes: The exact-active-set regions themselves are relatively open in their affine hulls; the closed cells are obtained by retaining the weak inequalities and including faces.
Different redundant max-affine representations can induce different nonminimal complexes while representing the same function.
For a nonconvex piecewise-affine function, cells need not arise as dominance regions of a maximum.

notation.meaning: A polyhedron on which all indices in \(I\) are active.
The induced finite polyhedral cell complex.

children.title: Polyhedral Function Calculus
children.top_down_role: Operations preserving polyhedral function structure.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_n\) denote the proper polyhedral convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact operations whose epigraphs are obtained through finite intersections, linear inverse images, linear images, or Minkowski sums of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedral function calculus is the collection of operations whose outputs remain polyhedral under their stated properness conditions. It includes finite pointwise maxima, nonnegative scaling, proper finite sums, affine precomposition, infimal images, marginalization, and proper infimal convolution. In formulas, representative operations are \[\max_{i\le p}f_i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i f_i\ (\lambda_i\ge0),\qquad g(Ax+b),\] \[(Ag)(y):=\inf\{g(x):Ax=y\},\qquad p(x):=\inf_yF(x,y),\] and \[(f\square g)(x):=\inf_z\{f(z)+g(x-z)\}.\] An operation belongs to this calculus when the relevant output epigraph is a polyhedron and the output is proper whenever properness is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral function calculus means the standard finite-dimensional operations that preserve polyhedral convex structure. These operations are read geometrically through epigraphs: maxima and sums impose finite systems of inequalities, affine precomposition takes an inverse image, marginalization and infimal images take linear projections, and infimal convolution corresponds to adding epigraphs. Properness qualifications are retained because some value operations can otherwise produce an improper function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{The listed operations map appropriate finite families of polyhedral convex functions to polyhedral convex functions.}\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The calculus may be characterized epigraphically by closure of finite-dimensional polyhedra under finite intersection, linear inverse image, linear image, and Minkowski addition.
Using max-affine-plus-indicator representations, the operations reduce to finite linear inequality manipulations and elimination of auxiliary variables.
special_cases_latex: The maximum of finitely many affine functions is a globally finite polyhedral convex function.
Partial minimization of a jointly polyhedral convex function is a polyhedral marginal whenever the resulting value function is proper.
The indicator-function cases reduce the calculus to intersections, affine inverse images, projections, and sums of polyhedral sets.
immediate_consequences_latex: Finite compositions of compatible operations in the calculus remain polyhedral, subject to properness at value-function steps.
The resulting functions admit finite epigraph or max-affine-domain representations.
boundary_notes: Negative scalar multiplication does not generally preserve convexity.
A pointwise minimum of convex polyhedral functions need not be convex.
Infinite sums or suprema need not be polyhedral.
Properness is not automatic for infimal convolution or unrestricted marginalization.

notation.meaning: Proper polyhedral convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\).
Infimal image of \(g\) under the linear map \(A\).

children.top_down_role: Direct combinations of polyhedral functions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f_1,ldots,f_p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct finite pointwise combinations on a common finite-dimensional variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite combination calculus consists of the pointwise maximum \[f_{\max}(x):=\max_{1\le i\le p}f_i(x)\] and the nonnegative weighted sum \[f_{\Sigma}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i f_i(x),\qquad \lambda_i\ge0.\] The maximum is proper when \(\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\ne\varnothing\), and then \[\operatorname{epi}f_{\max}=\bigcap_i\operatorname{epi}f_i.\] The sum is proper when \(\bigcap_{i:\lambda_i>0}\operatorname{dom}f_i\ne\varnothing\), and it is polyhedral. Zero coefficients are interpreted by omitting the corresponding summands, avoiding an undefined product \(0\cdot(+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite combination calculus comprises finite pointwise maxima and finite nonnegative weighted sums of polyhedral convex functions. A common point in the relevant domains guarantees properness. The maximum has an epigraph equal to the intersection of the input epigraphs. The weighted sum remains polyhedral because finite max-affine-domain representations can be combined into another finite representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f_{\max}\text{ and }f_{\Sigma}\text{ are polyhedral convex whenever their stated common-domain conditions make them proper}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For two represented functions \(f_i=h_i+\delta_{C_i}\), the sum satisfies \[f_1+f_2=(h_1+h_2)+\delta_{C_1\cap C_2}.\]
If \(h_1=\max_i\ell_i\) and \(h_2=\max_jm_j\), then \[h_1+h_2=\max_{i,j}(\ell_i+m_j).\]
special_cases_latex: Finite maxima of affine functions produce finite max-affine functions.
Finite intersections of polyhedra follow by applying the maximum operation to their indicator functions.
A positive scalar multiple \(\lambda f\), with \(\lambda>0\), is a one-term weighted sum.
immediate_consequences_latex: Both operations preserve finite representability.
Domains satisfy \(\operatorname{dom}f_{\max}=\bigcap_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f_{\Sigma}=\bigcap_{i:\lambda_i>0}\operatorname{dom}f_i\).
boundary_notes: Pointwise minima are excluded because they generally fail to preserve convexity.
Negative weights are excluded because they generally destroy convexity.
Without a common domain point, the resulting extended-valued function may be identically \(+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Piece Representation of a Finite Maximum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum pools all affine pieces from its inputs and restricts them to the intersection of the input domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f_i(x)=\max_{k\in K_i}\ell_{ik}(x)+\iota_{D_i}(x)\), where every \(K_i\) is finite and every \(D_i\) is polyhedral. If \(D=\bigcap_iD_i\neq\varnothing\), then \[\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)=\max_{(i,k):k\in K_i}\ell_{ik}(x)+\iota_D(x).\]
assumptions_latex: \(f_i=\max_{k\in K_i}\ell_{ik}+\iota_{D_i}\) are proper polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i f_i=\max_{(i,k)}\ell_{ik}+\iota_{\cap_iD_i}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit polyhedral representation obtained by pooling component affine pieces.

notation.meaning: Finite affine-piece index set for the ith function

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Maxima
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain of a finite pointwise maximum is the intersection of the input domains, and its epigraph is the intersection of the input epigraphs. The maximum is proper polyhedral convex exactly when the input domains have a common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x)\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}f=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}f_i,\qquad \operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{epi}f_i.\] Hence \(f\) is a proper polyhedral convex function if and only if the participating effective domains have a common point.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper polyhedral convex functions, where \(m\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i\) is proper polyhedral convex and \(\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{epi}f_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of extended-real polyhedral convex functions under finite pointwise maxima.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Sums
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum of proper polyhedral convex functions is proper polyhedral convex when their domains intersect; its affine pieces are all sums of selected input pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(j\), write \(f_j(x)=\max_{k\in K_j}\ell_{jk}(x)+\iota_{D_j}(x)\), where \(K_j\) is finite, each \(\ell_{jk}\) is affine, and \(D_j=\operatorname{dom}f_j\) is polyhedral. Then \[s(x)=\max_{(k_1,\ldots,k_m)\in K_1\times\cdots\times K_m}\sum_{j=1}^m\ell_{jk_j}(x)+\iota_{\cap_jD_j}(x).\] Hence \(s\) has a domain-restricted finite max-affine representation. The nonempty common domain makes this representation proper, so \(s\) is polyhedral convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s=\sum_{j=1}^m f_j\) is a proper polyhedral convex function with \(\operatorname{dom}s=\bigcap_j\operatorname{dom}f_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum closure with explicit interaction of effective domains.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Polyhedral Functions p. 76

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Direct-Combination Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any finite separable sum on a Cartesian product is proper polyhedral convex, with product domain and tuple-indexed affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(f_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper polyhedral convex and define \[F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i).\] Then \(F\) is proper polyhedral convex and \(\operatorname{dom}F=\prod_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\). If \(f_i=\max_{k\in K_i}\ell_{ik}+\iota_{D_i}\), then \[F=\max_{(k_1,\ldots,k_m)\in\prod_iK_i}\sum_{i=1}^m\ell_{ik_i}+\iota_{\prod_iD_i}.\]
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper polyhedral convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigoplus_{i=1}^m f_i\) is proper polyhedral convex with domain \(\prod_i\operatorname{dom}f_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-arity extension of the binary separable direct combination.

notation.meaning: Finite direct combination on the product space

knowledge_statements.title: Direct-Combination Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The separable sum of two proper polyhedral convex functions on a product space is proper polyhedral convex, with product domain and pairwise-combined affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(F(x,y)=f(x)+g(y)\). Its domain is \[\operatorname{dom}F=\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g.\] If \(f(x)=\max_i\ell_i(x)+\iota_D(x)\) and \(g(y)=\max_j r_j(y)+\iota_E(y)\), then \[F(x,y)=\max_{i,j}\{\ell_i(x)+r_j(y)\}+\iota_{D\times E}(x,y).\] Since \(D\times E\) is a nonempty polyhedron and the displayed maximum is finite, \(F\) is proper polyhedral convex.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathbb{R}^p\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The direct combination \(F(x,y)=f(x)+g(y)\) is proper polyhedral convex on \(\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable direct combination on a Cartesian product of finite-dimensional spaces.

notation.meaning: Direct combination on the product space

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Interaction Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum and finite extended-real sum have the common domain given by the intersection of all input domains. Both are proper polyhedral convex exactly when that intersection is nonempty; otherwise both are identically positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the pointwise maximum \(M=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i\) and the extended-real sum \(S=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\), one has \[\operatorname{dom}M=\operatorname{dom}S=D.\] Thus \(M\) and \(S\) are proper polyhedral convex functions if and only if \(D\neq\varnothing\). If \(D=\varnothing\), then \(M\equiv+\infty\) and \(S\equiv+\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper polyhedral convex functions, where \(m\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both \(\max_i f_i\) and \(\sum_i f_i\) are proper exactly when \(D\neq\varnothing\); if \(D=\varnothing\), both equal \(+\infty\) everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properness boundary for finite maxima and sums of extended-real functions.

children.title: Affine Transformation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral structure under affine transformations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine precomposition and value-function images; properness is stated explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine pullback of \(g\) is \[(A,b)^*g(x):=g(Ax+b).\] It is polyhedral because \[\operatorname{epi}((A,b)^*g)=\{(x,t):(Ax+b,t)\in\operatorname{epi}g\}\] is an affine inverse image of a polyhedron. It is proper exactly when \((b+\operatorname{range}A)\cap\operatorname{dom}g\ne\varnothing\). The infimal image of \(f\) under \(A\) is \[(Af)(y):=\inf\{f(x):Ax=y\},\] with value \(+\infty\) when the fiber is empty. When this value function is proper, it is polyhedral, its finite infima are attained, and \[\operatorname{epi}(Af)=\{(Ax,t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine transformation calculus has two complementary operations. Pullback composes a polyhedral convex function with an affine map and corresponds to taking an inverse image of its epigraph. Infimal image minimizes a polyhedral convex function over each linear fiber and corresponds to taking a linear image of its epigraph. In finite dimensions both epigraph operations preserve polyhedrality; a finite infimum in the infimal image is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(A,b)^*g\text{ is polyhedral, and a proper }Af\text{ is polyhedral with attained finite fiber minima}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a polyhedral domain \(C\), the pullback of \(\delta_C\) is \(\delta_{\{x:Ax+b\in C\}}\).
The domain of the infimal image is \(\operatorname{dom}(Af)=A(\operatorname{dom}f)\), a polyhedron.
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, then \((Af)(y)=f(A^{-1}y)\).
Coordinate elimination and orthogonal projection are infimal-image operations.
Restriction to an affine subspace is expressible through affine pullback after parametrizing that subspace.
immediate_consequences_latex: Affine changes of variables preserve polyhedral convexity.
Projection of a polyhedral epigraph produces a finitely representable marginal function.
boundary_notes: The affine pullback can be improper if the affine range misses the domain.
For nonpolyhedral closed convex functions, a linear epigraph image need not be closed and finite infima need not be attained.
The infimal image may take value \(-\infty\); properness excludes that case.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Function under Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function of a proper affine pullback is obtained by applying the linear part of the affine map to the recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=f(Ax+b)\) be proper, where \(f\) is proper polyhedral convex. Then \[g^\infty(d)=f^\infty(Ad)\quad(d\in\mathbb R^n).\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}g)=\{(d,\tau):(Ad,\tau)\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g^\infty=f^\infty\circ A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession calculus for a proper polyhedral affine pullback.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precomposing a polyhedral convex function with any affine map preserves polyhedral convexity. Properness holds exactly when the affine map reaches the original domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(g(x)=f(Ax+b)\). Then \[\operatorname{epi}g=\{(x,t):(Ax+b,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\},\qquad \operatorname{dom}g=A^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f-b).\] Thus the epigraph of \(g\) is an affine inverse image of a polyhedron and is polyhedral. Convexity is preserved by affine precomposition. The function \(g\) is proper if and only if its displayed domain is nonempty; no injectivity or surjectivity assumption on \(A\) is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=f(Ax+b)\) is polyhedral convex and is proper exactly when \(\{x:Ax+b\in\operatorname{dom}f\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine precomposition, without any rank assumption on the linear part.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of an Affine Image Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of an infimal affine image is obtained by adjoint precomposition of the source conjugate, plus the translation pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(y)=\inf\{f(x):Ax+b=y\}\), with empty-fiber value \(+\infty\), and suppose \(h\) is proper. Then for every \(u\in\mathbb R^m\), \[h^*(u)=f^*(A^{\mathsf T}u)+\langle b,u\rangle.\]
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h^*(u)=f^*(A^{\mathsf T}u)+\langle b,u\rangle\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugate of a proper infimal affine image.

notation.meaning: Adjoint of the linear part of the affine map
Fenchel conjugate of the affine image function

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Image Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine image assigns each target the least source value over its fiber. Excluding unbounded-below fibers, it is proper polyhedral convex and has the affine image of the original domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine image function of \(f\) under \(T(x)=Ax+b\) is \[h(y)=\inf\{f(x):x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ Ax+b=y\},\] with the empty-fiber infimum defined as \(+\infty\). Its effective domain is \(A(\operatorname{dom}f)+b\). Because a finite-dimensional polyhedral optimization problem attains every finite infimum, its epigraph satisfies \[\operatorname{epi}h=\{(Ax+b,t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\] This linear-affine image is polyhedral. Since \(f\) has a nonempty domain and no fiber has value \(-\infty\), \(h\) is proper polyhedral convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(y)=\inf\{f(x):Ax+b=y\}\) is proper polyhedral convex with \(\operatorname{dom}h=A(\operatorname{dom}f)+b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infimal affine image, with exclusion of unbounded-below fibers.

notation.meaning: Infimal image of f under the affine map

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Epigraph Transport
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of an infimal affine image is exactly the affine image of the source epigraph. Polyhedrality makes this projected epigraph closed and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \((y,t)\), finite-dimensional polyhedral attainment gives \[(y,t)\in\operatorname{epi}h\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{there exists }x\text{ such that }Ax+b=y\text{ and }f(x)\leq t.\] Consequently, \[\operatorname{epi}h=\{(Ax+b,t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}=(T\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{R}})(\operatorname{epi}f).\] Linear images of finite-dimensional polyhedra are polyhedra, so the transported epigraph is closed and polyhedral. The exclusion of value \(-\infty\) ensures that this epigraph represents a proper extended-real convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}h=(T\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{R}})(\operatorname{epi}f)\), hence \(\operatorname{epi}h\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph transport for the finite-dimensional polyhedral infimal image.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient-Space Factorization of a Rank-Deficient Pullback
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-deficient affine pullback is constant on kernel cosets and factors uniquely through the quotient by the kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g(x)=f(Ax+b)\), then \(g(x+d)=g(x)\) for every \(d\in\ker A\). Hence there is a unique function \(\bar g\) on \(\mathbb R^n/\ker A\) such that \(g=\bar g\circ q\), where \(q\) is the quotient map. The map induced by \(A\) is an isomorphism from \(\mathbb R^n/\ker A\) onto \(\operatorname{range}A\); if \(g\) is proper polyhedral convex, then so is \(\bar g\) under any finite-dimensional identification of the quotient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=\bar g\circ q\), with \(\bar g\) proper polyhedral convex and \(\mathbb R^n/\ker A\cong\operatorname{range}A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural effect of a nontrivial kernel on affine precomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Mapping Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank deficiency is harmless for feasible precomposition, but an infimal image fails properness when a nullspace direction decreases the source function without bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For precomposition \(g(x)=f(Ax+b)\), rank deficiency causes constancy along \(\ker A\), but properness requires only \(A^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}f-b)\neq\varnothing\). For the infimal image \(h(y)=\inf_{Ax+b=y}f(x)\), feasible fibers have recession directions in \(\ker A\). A fiber is unbounded below exactly when there exists \(d\in\ker A\) with \(f^\infty(d)<0\). Hence \[h\text{ is proper}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^\infty(d)\geq0\text{ for every }d\in\ker A.\] Under this condition, finite fiber values are attained and \(h\) is polyhedral convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Affine precomposition needs only domain feasibility, whereas the infimal image is proper exactly when no \(d\in\ker A\) satisfies \(f^\infty(d)<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct feasibility and recession effects caused by a nontrivial nullspace.

children.title: Marginal-Value Function Calculus
children.top_down_role: Marginal functions inherited from polyhedral projection.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper polyhedral convex function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional partial minimization of a jointly polyhedral convex function; the resulting marginal is required to be proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The marginal-value function obtained by eliminating \(y\) is \[p(x):=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R^m}F(x,y).\] Its domain is the coordinate projection \[\operatorname{dom}p=\{x:\exists y\text{ with }(x,y)\in\operatorname{dom}F\}.\] If \(p\) is proper, then it is polyhedral convex and every finite value is attained: \[p(x)\in\mathbb R\implies \exists y_x\in\mathbb R^m\quad p(x)=F(x,y_x).\] Its epigraph is the projection \[\operatorname{epi}p=\{(x,t):\exists y\text{ such that }F(x,y)\le t\}\] of \(\operatorname{epi}F\) onto the \((x,t)\)-coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A marginal-value function records the optimal value after minimizing a jointly polyhedral convex function over an auxiliary variable. Its domain is the projection of the joint domain. When the marginal is proper, projecting the joint polyhedral epigraph gives another polyhedral epigraph, and every finite optimal value has an attaining auxiliary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y),\qquad \operatorname{epi}p=\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}(\operatorname{epi}F),\] and a proper \(p\) is polyhedral with attained finite minima.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Let \(A(x,y)=x\). Then \(p=AF\) is the infimal image of \(F\) under the coordinate projection \(A\).
If \(F(x,y)=\varphi(x,y)+\delta_Q(x,y)\) with \(Q\) polyhedral and \(\varphi\) max-affine, then \(p\) is the value function of a finitely constrained polyhedral optimization problem.
special_cases_latex: For \(F(x,y)=\delta_Q(x,y)\), \(p=\delta_{\operatorname{proj}_xQ}\).
A parametric linear-program value function is a marginal of a jointly polyhedral objective and feasible-set indicator.
Fixing no retained variable yields the scalar infimum of \(F\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The marginal domain is polyhedral.
A proper marginal has a finite max-affine-plus-indicator representation.
Nested elimination of finitely many blocks can be performed by repeated marginalization.
boundary_notes: The marginal can be improper if the objective is unbounded below along an eliminated fiber.
Without polyhedrality, an epigraph projection can fail to be closed, so closure qualifications may be required.
The argmin mapping may be set-valued or unbounded even though each finite value is attained.

notation.meaning: Coordinate projection onto the retained variable and epigraph height.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Minimization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a proper polyhedral convex function over selected variables yields a proper polyhedral convex marginal, provided no fiber is unbounded below. Its epigraph is a projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the marginal function \[v(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^p}F(x,y),\] using \(+\infty\) when no \(y\) gives a finite value. Polyhedral attainment of every finite infimum yields \[\operatorname{epi}v=\{(x,t):\text{there exists }y\text{ with }F(x,y)\leq t\}=\pi_{x,t}(\operatorname{epi}F).\] The projection of a finite-dimensional polyhedron is a polyhedron, so \(v\) is polyhedral convex. Since \(F\) is proper, some marginal value is finite; the exclusion of value \(-\infty\) therefore makes \(v\) proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^p}F(x,y)\) is proper polyhedral convex and \(\operatorname{epi}v\) is the projection of \(\operatorname{epi}F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional partial minimization of a proper polyhedral convex function.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness certify the value of each feasible parameter fiber.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(x\in D\), a primal-feasible \(y\) and \(\lambda\in\Lambda\) are optimal if and only if \[c^{\mathsf T}y=\lambda^{\mathsf T}(Hx-r).\] Equivalently, optimality is characterized by \[Gy+Hx\le r,\qquad \lambda\ge0,\qquad G^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-c,\qquad \lambda_i(Gy+Hx-r)_i=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,q).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\) and \(\lambda\) are optimal if and only if their objective values agree, equivalently if complementary slackness holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise certificate for a finite value of the seed's parametric linear program.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Max-Affine Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-program duality represents the value function as a finite maximum of affine dual-value functions on its feasible parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[D=\{x:\exists y,\ Gy+Hx\le r\},\qquad \Lambda=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^q:G^{\mathsf T}\lambda=-c\}.\] If some fiber is feasible and every feasible fiber has finite optimal value, then \(\Lambda\ne\varnothing\) and \[v(x)=\begin{cases}\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\lambda^{\mathsf T}(Hx-r),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}\] The maximum is attained on every feasible fiber and equals the maximum over the finitely many vertices of \(\Lambda\).
assumptions_latex: At least one parameter fiber is feasible, and no feasible fiber is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v=\max_{\lambda\in\operatorname{vert}\Lambda}\lambda^{\mathsf T}(H\,\cdot-r)+\iota_D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of the right-hand-side-parametric linear program in the seed.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Value Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parametric linear program’s optimal value is polyhedral convex in the parameter when some fiber is feasible and no feasible fiber is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \[v(x)=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}y:y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ Gy+Hx\leq r\}.\] Equivalently, \(v\) is the partial minimum of \(F(x,y)=c^{\mathsf T}y+
obreak\iota_P(x,y)\). Its epigraph has the projection representation \[\operatorname{epi}v=\{(x,t):\text{there exists }y\text{ such that }Gy+Hx\leq r,\ c^{\mathsf T}y\leq t\}.\] This is a projection of a polyhedron and hence is polyhedral. Feasibility at some parameter and absence of unbounded-below feasible fibers make \(v\) proper.
assumptions_latex: The parametric linear program is feasible for some parameter and is never unbounded below on a feasible fiber.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(x)=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}y:Gy+Hx\leq r\}\) is a proper polyhedral convex function of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal-value representation for a right-hand-side parametric linear program.

notation.meaning: Polyhedral feasible set in parameter-decision space

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Cone of a Projected Polyhedral Epigraph
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone of an exactly projected polyhedral epigraph is the corresponding projection of the lifted epigraph's recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{epi}F\) and \(L=\pi_{x,r}\). If the proper polyhedral marginal \(g(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{epi}g=L(P)\), then \[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}g)=L(\operatorname{rec}P)=\{(d,\tau):\exists e\text{ with }(d,e,\tau)\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}F)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}g)=\pi_{x,r}(\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}F))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession geometry accompanying exact polyhedral epigraph projection.

notation.meaning: Projection retaining x and epigraph height

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Projection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper polyhedral marginal has an epigraph equal to the projection of the original epigraph, so the marginal remains polyhedral and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(r\in\mathbb{R}\), polyhedral marginal attainment gives
\[(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m:\ (x,y,r)\in\operatorname{epi}F.\]
Consequently, \(\operatorname{epi}g\) is the linear projection \(\pi_{x,r}(\operatorname{epi}F)\). Since a linear image of a polyhedron is a polyhedron, \(g\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous polyhedral convex function.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}g=\pi_{x,r}(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper polyhedral marginal functions.

notation.meaning: Projection retaining the first and epigraph coordinates

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Test for Fiberwise Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a nonempty polyhedral fiber, absence of a negative vertical recession direction is equivalent to a finite attained minimum; zero-recession directions form the optimizer set's recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\) such that \(\phi_x(y)=F(x,y)\) is proper. Then \[\inf_yF(x,y)>-\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F^\infty(0,d)\geq0\quad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb R^m.\] In this case the infimum is finite and attained, the argmin is a nonempty polyhedron, and \[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname*{argmin}_yF(x,y))=\{d:F^\infty(0,d)=0\}.\] If some \(d\) satisfies \(F^\infty(0,d)<0\), then \(g(x)=-\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper lower-semicontinuous polyhedral convex.
The fiber function \(y\mapsto F(x,y)\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)\in\mathbb R\) and is attained iff \(F^\infty(0,d)\geq0\) for every \(d\); a negative value implies \(g(x)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp classification of a nonempty polyhedral fiber by its vertical recession directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Attainment Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral marginal attains every finite value. Nonattainment occurs only through infeasibility or unbounded decrease, producing an infinite marginal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), exactly three value regimes are possible. If \(g(x)=+\infty\), the fiber \(\{y:F(x,y)<+\infty\}\) is empty. If \(g(x)\in\mathbb{R}\), the polyhedral optimization problem attains its value and
\[\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}F(x,y)\ne\varnothing.\]
If \(g(x)=-\infty\), no finite minimizer exists. Thus failure of attainment occurs only at the improper-value boundary, not at a finite marginal value.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[g(x)\in\mathbb{R}\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname*{argmin}_{y}F(x,y)\ne\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes finite-value attainment from infeasibility and unboundedness.
