children.top_down_role: Infimal combination in the finitely represented convex regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Subgradient Decomposition Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible decomposition is optimal exactly when the two summands have a common subgradient at its components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f\square g\) is proper, \(u=x+z\), and \(f(x),g(z)\) are finite. Then \[f(x)+g(z)=(f\square g)(u)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \partial f(x)\cap\partial g(z)\ne\varnothing.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x,z\text{ solve the decomposition problem at }u\iff\partial f(x)\cap\partial g(z)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality certificate for an attained polyhedral infimal-convolution decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Criterion for Properness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral infimal convolution is proper exactly when no opposite pair of recession directions decreases the combined cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) and \(g\) be proper polyhedral convex functions. Then \[f\square g\text{ is proper}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^{\infty}(d)+g^{\infty}(-d)\ge0\quad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb R^n.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\square g\text{ is proper}\iff f^{\infty}(d)+g^{\infty}(-d)\ge0\ \forall d\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundedness boundary for convolution of two proper polyhedral convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Polyhedral Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two proper affine functions can have an infimal convolution equal to negative infinity everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \(f(x)=x\) and \(g(x)=0\). Both are proper polyhedral convex functions, but \[(f\square g)(u)=-\infty\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f\square g)(u)=-\infty\) for every \(u\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal example showing why properness of the convolution must be assumed.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Minkowski Sum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of a proper polyhedral infimal convolution is the Minkowski sum of the input domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) and \(g\) are proper polyhedral convex functions and \(f\square g\) is proper, then \[\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective-domain formula for proper binary polyhedral infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper infimal convolution of two polyhedral convex functions is polyhedral, has the displayed epigraph image, and attains every finite value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[(f\square g)(u)=\inf_{x+z=u}\bigl(f(x)+g(z)\bigr).\]
Its epigraph is the linear image
\[\operatorname{epi}(f\square g)=\{(x+z,r+s):(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f,\ (z,s)\in\operatorname{epi}g\}.\]
Hence \(f\square g\) is lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral. Moreover, for every \(u\in\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)\), the infimum is attained by some decomposition \(u=x+z\).
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}(f\square g)=\{(x+z,r+s):(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f,\ (z,s)\in\operatorname{epi}g\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional polyhedral infimal convolution.

source_witnesses.locator: 4.5 Infimal Convolution and Conjugacy p. 102

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infimal Convolution of Polyhedral Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional two-function infimal convolution, with a separate properness condition for the resulting value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal convolution of \(f\) and \(g\) is \[(f\square g)(x):=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^n}\{f(z)+g(x-z)\}.\] Its domain is the Minkowski sum \[\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g.\] Its epigraph satisfies \[\operatorname{epi}(f\square g)=\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g.\] Hence \(f\square g\) is polyhedral convex. If it is proper, then for every \(x\) with finite value there exist \(z,w\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(z+w=x\) and \[(f\square g)(x)=f(z)+g(w).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution minimizes the sum of two functions over all decompositions of the argument. For polyhedral convex inputs, the epigraph is the Minkowski sum of the two polyhedral epigraphs and is therefore polyhedral. Its effective domain is the sum of the input domains. When the convolution is proper, every finite infimum is attained by at least one decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(f\square g)(x)=\inf_{z+w=x}(f(z)+g(w)),\qquad \operatorname{epi}(f\square g)=\operatorname{epi}f+\operatorname{epi}g,\] with attainment of every finite value when \(f\square g\) is proper.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Define \(F(z,w)=f(z)+g(w)\) and \(A(z,w)=z+w\). Then \(f\square g=AF\) is an infimal image.
The operation is commutative and associative wherever the extended-real expressions are well-defined.
special_cases_latex: For indicators, \(\delta_C\square\delta_D=\delta_{C+D}\) for nonempty polyhedra \(C,D\).
If \(g=\delta_{\{0\}}\), then \(f\square g=f\).
If \(g=\delta_C\), then \((f\square g)(x)=\inf_{z\in x-C}f(z)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A proper finite infimal convolution of polyhedral functions is closed.
Optimal decompositions exist at every point of its effective domain.
Finite iterated infimal convolutions remain polyhedral when the resulting function is proper.
boundary_notes: Properness can fail through unbounded descent, producing the value \(-\infty\).
For general nonpolyhedral closed convex functions, the epigraph sum may require closure and the infimum may fail to be attained.
This definition uses exact, not approximate, infimal convolution.

notation.meaning: The Minkowski sum of the effective domains.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel Conjugacy in the Polyhedral Class
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper polyhedral convex function, with the Euclidean pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel conjugacy for proper polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Fenchel conjugate of \(f\) is \[f^*(y):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\}.\] Polyhedral conjugacy is the restriction of this operation to the polyhedral convex class: if \(f\) is proper polyhedral convex, then \(f^*\) is proper polyhedral convex. Since a proper polyhedral convex function is closed, biconjugacy gives \[f^{**}=f.\] Thus conjugation is an order-reversing involution on proper polyhedral convex functions: \[f\le g\implies f^*\ge g^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral conjugacy is Fenchel conjugation applied to proper polyhedral convex functions. The conjugate takes the supremum of the affine functions in the dual variable generated by primal points. Polyhedral structure is preserved, and because proper polyhedral functions are closed, applying conjugation twice returns the original function. Functional inequalities reverse under conjugation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ proper polyhedral}\implies f^*\text{ proper polyhedral and }f^{**}=f.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The epigraph of \(f^*\) is described by the family of inequalities \(s\ge\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\), which reduces to finite polyhedral data when \(f\) is finitely generated.
Fenchel equality \(f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\) is equivalent to \(y\in\partial f(x)\) and to \(x\in\partial f^*(y)\).
special_cases_latex: The conjugate of a polyhedral indicator is a polyhedral support function.
The conjugate of a finite max-affine function has polytope domain.
The conjugate of an affine function is an indicator of a singleton, up to an additive constant.
immediate_consequences_latex: Domains, affine pieces, and recession restrictions exchange roles under conjugacy.
Polyhedral subdifferentials can be read symmetrically from \(f\) and \(f^*\).
boundary_notes: The conjugate of a finite-valued function need not be finite-valued.
Improper functions require separate conventions and are excluded here.
Polyhedral preservation is a finite-dimensional result in this form.

source_refs.locator: §19, Theorem 19.2 and its displayed conjugate representation, p. 171; §12, Theorem 12.2 on biconjugacy, p. 102

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugates of Max-Affine Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a finite affine maximum is a linear-program value over convex coefficients reproducing the requested slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[f^*(y)=\min\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i b_i:\lambda\in\Delta_k,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i a_i=y\right\},\]
where the minimum over an empty feasible set is \(+\infty\). Thus \(\operatorname{dom}f^*=\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}\), and \(f^*\) is a polyhedral convex function obtained as the value function of a finite-dimensional linear program.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is defined by \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le k}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^*(y)=\min\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i b_i:\lambda\in\Delta_k,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i a_i=y\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite max-affine functions on Euclidean space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex Representation of the Conjugate of a Finite Affine Maximum
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_p\in\mathbb R^n\), \(b_1,\ldots,b_p\in\mathbb R\), and \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i)\). Let \(\Delta_p=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^p:\sum_i\lambda_i=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Globally finite max-affine convex functions and their exact finite-dimensional Fenchel conjugates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conjugate of \(f\) is the polyhedral value function \[f^*(y)=\min\left\{-\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i b_i:\lambda\in\Delta_p,\ \sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i a_i=y\right\},\] with the convention that the minimum over an empty feasible set is \(+\infty\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{dom}f^*=\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_p\}.\] For every \(y\) in this convex hull, the displayed minimum is attained; outside it, \(f^*(y)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a finite maximum of affine functions is obtained by expressing the dual argument as a convex combination of the affine slopes and minimizing the correspondingly weighted negative intercepts. Its effective domain is exactly the convex hull of the slopes, hence a polytope, and the finite-dimensional linear minimum is attained on that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^*(y)=\min_{\lambda\in\Delta_p}\left\{-\sum_i\lambda_i b_i:\sum_i\lambda_i a_i=y\right\},\qquad \operatorname{dom}f^*=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i\}_{i=1}^p.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The epigraph admits the lifted description \[\operatorname{epi}f^*=\left\{(y,t):\exists\lambda\in\Delta_p,\ y=\sum_i\lambda_i a_i,\ t\ge-\sum_i\lambda_i b_i\right\}.\]
The conjugate is the lower convex envelope of the finite point data \((a_i,-b_i)\), allowing repeated slopes.
special_cases_latex: If \(p=1\), then \(f^*(y)=-b_1\) at \(y=a_1\) and \(+\infty\) elsewhere.
If every \(b_i=0\), then \(f\) is a support function of \(\operatorname{conv}\{a_i\}\) and \(f^*=\delta_{\operatorname{conv}\{a_i\}}\).
Repeated slopes retain only the largest intercept in \(f\), equivalently the smallest negative intercept in the conjugate data.
immediate_consequences_latex: The conjugate is proper polyhedral and has bounded effective domain.
Optimal multipliers provide barycentric coordinates for the dual argument.
Faces of the slope polytope correspond to collections of affine pieces exposed by primal directions.
boundary_notes: The formula is specific to a globally finite maximum; a domain-restricted max-affine function contributes additional recession generators and dual inequalities.
The representing affine family need not be irredundant.
The conjugate is generally extended-valued even though \(f\) is finite everywhere.

notation.meaning: The standard probability simplex in \(\mathbb R^p\).
The convex hull of the affine slopes.

children.title: Indicator–Support Conjugacy
children.top_down_role: The set–function duality interface for polyhedral sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Domain of a Polyhedral Support Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron's support function is finite precisely on the negative polar of its recession cone, and it is finite everywhere precisely when the polyhedron is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(C^\infty=\operatorname{rec}C\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=(C^\infty)^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\langle y,d\rangle\leq0\ \text{for every }d\in C^\infty\}.\] Thus \(\sigma_C(y)<+\infty\) exactly when \(y\) is nonpositive on every recession direction of \(C\); in particular, \(\sigma_C\) is finite everywhere exactly when \(C\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=(C^\infty)^\circ\), and \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\mathbb R^n\) if and only if \(C\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued directions of the support function of a nonempty polyhedron.

notation.meaning: Negative polar of the recession cone

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator–Support Conjugacy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a closed convex set's indicator is its support function, and conjugating the support function recovers the indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, Fenchel conjugacy gives
\[\delta_C^*(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle=\sigma_C(y).\]
Because \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, biconjugacy yields
\[\sigma_C^*=(\delta_C^*)^*=\delta_C.\]
If \(C\) is polyhedral, both functions are polyhedral convex functions, although \(\sigma_C\) may take the value \(+\infty\) when \(C\) is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\delta_C^*=\sigma_C,\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_C.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy for closed convex, especially polyhedral, sets.

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Support Functions p. 135

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty closed convex set; in the polyhedral specialization, assume that \(C\) is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set–function duality for nonempty closed convex sets, specialized to the polyhedral class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The indicator and support functions of \(C\) are \[\delta_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\qquad \sigma_C(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle.\] They form a Fenchel-conjugate pair: \[\delta_C^*=\sigma_C,\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_C.\] If \(C\) is polyhedral, then both functions are polyhedral convex. The support function may take value \(+\infty\) when \(C\) is unbounded; its effective domain is the barrier cone \(\{y:\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle<+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex indicator encodes membership in a closed convex set, while the support function records the supremum of each linear functional over that set. Fenchel conjugation exchanges these two functions. For a polyhedron, both are polyhedral convex, although the support function can be extended-valued if the set is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\delta_C^*(y)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle=\sigma_C(y),\qquad \sigma_C^*=\delta_C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The set is recovered from its support function by \[C=\{x:\langle y,x\rangle\le\sigma_C(y)\ \forall y\}.\]
A closed convex set is polyhedral if and only if its support function is polyhedral.
Fenchel equality for this pair is \(x\in C\) and \(\langle y,x\rangle=\sigma_C(y)\), meaning that \(x\) maximizes the functional \(\langle y,\cdot\rangle\) over \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\{c\}\), then \(\sigma_C(y)=\langle y,c\rangle\).
If \(C\) is a polytope, \(\sigma_C\) is finite max-linear.
If \(C=K\) is a closed convex cone, \(\sigma_K=\delta_{K^\circ}\) under the polar convention \(K^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\le0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Set inclusion reverses support inequalities: \(C\subseteq D\implies\sigma_C\le\sigma_D\).
Minkowski addition becomes functional addition: \(\sigma_{C+D}=\sigma_C+\sigma_D\).
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed convex set, the biconjugate recovers its closure rather than the original set.
Nonemptiness is required for a proper indicator and support function.
The polar-cone sign convention must be fixed when using the cone special case.

notation.meaning: The nonpositive polar cone under the stated convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Face Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel equality pairs exposed epigraph faces of a polyhedral function and its conjugate through mutually inverse subgradient incidences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\), the set
\[E_y=\{(x,f(x)):f(x)-\langle y,x\rangle=-f^*(y)\}\]
is an exposed face of \(\operatorname{epi}f\). Dually, for \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\),
\[E_x^*=\{(y,f^*(y)):f^*(y)-\langle x,y\rangle=-f(x)\}\]
is an exposed face of \(\operatorname{epi}f^*\). Their incidences are characterized by
\[y\in\partial f(x)\Longleftrightarrow x\in\partial f^*(y)\Longleftrightarrow f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed epigraph faces induced by Fenchel equality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel Contact Faces of Conjugate Polyhedral Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex and let \(f^*\) be its conjugate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed lower faces and their primal–dual contact relation for a conjugate pair of finite-dimensional polyhedral functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\), define the Fenchel contact face of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) by \[E_f(y):=\{(x,f(x)):f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\}.\] It is the exposed lower face on which the affine minorant \(x\mapsto\langle y,x\rangle-f^*(y)\) equals \(f\). Its primal projection is \[X_f(y):=\{x:y\in\partial f(x)\}=\partial f^*(y).\] Symmetrically, for \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[E_{f^*}(x):=\{(y,f^*(y)):f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\},\] whose dual projection is \(\partial f(x)\). The defining incidence is symmetric: \[y\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\iff x\in\partial f^*(y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual vector exposes a lower face of the epigraph of a polyhedral function wherever its associated affine minorant is exact. The points projecting from that face are precisely those whose subdifferential contains the dual vector. The same equality exposes the corresponding face for the conjugate function, giving a symmetric primal–dual incidence relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[y\in\partial f(x)\iff (x,f(x))\in E_f(y)\iff (y,f^*(y))\in E_{f^*}(x)\iff x\in\partial f^*(y).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The face \(E_f(y)\) minimizes the linear functional \((x,t)\mapsto t-\langle y,x\rangle\) over \(\operatorname{epi}f\), with minimum \(-f^*(y)\).
The contact relation is the graph of the polyhedral subdifferential mapping \(\partial f\), inverted by \(\partial f^*\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), \(E_f(y)\) projects to the exposed face \(\operatorname{argmax}_{x\in C}\langle y,x\rangle\).
For a finite max-affine function, \(\partial f(x)\) is the convex hull of the slopes active at \(x\).
If \(f\) is affine, the primal contact face is its entire graph for the unique dual slope.
immediate_consequences_latex: All nonempty contact faces are polyhedral.
Larger primal contact sets correspond to dual vectors lying in lower-dimensional subdifferential strata, expressing the usual incidence reversal.
The subdifferential graph is symmetric under exchanging \((f,x)\) with \((f^*,y)\).
boundary_notes: The construction concerns exposed lower faces, not arbitrary faces of the full epigraph.
Empty contact faces occur when the chosen dual vector is outside \(\operatorname{dom}f^*\) or the supremum is not attained; polyhedrality gives attainment for finite relevant values.
This record defines the face correspondence and does not assert a dimension formula.

notation.meaning: The lower epigraph face exposed by \((y,-1)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Growth and Solution-Geometry Data of a Polyhedral Convex Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be a proper polyhedral convex function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional recession, sublevel, and minimizer geometry associated with a proper polyhedral convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The growth–solution geometry of \(f\) is encoded by the recession function \(f^\infty\), its recession cone, the sublevel polyhedra, and the minimizer set: \[\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=0^+(\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad R_f:=\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\},\] \[L_r(f):=\{x:f(x)\le r\},\qquad S_f:=\operatorname{argmin}f=\{x:f(x)=\inf f\}.\] Each nonempty \(L_r(f)\) is a polyhedron and has recession cone \(R_f\). If \(S_f\ne\varnothing\), then \(S_f=L_{\inf f}(f)\) is a polyhedron and \(0^+S_f=R_f\). Thus directions with \(f^\infty(d)\le0\) are precisely the directions along which every nonempty sublevel set, including the solution set when it exists, recedes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The growth–solution geometry of a polyhedral convex function consists of its recession function, the directions of nonpositive asymptotic growth, its sublevel polyhedra, and its minimizer set. All nonempty sublevel sets share the same recession cone. When the minimum is attained, the minimizer set is the lowest nonempty sublevel set and has that same recession cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0^+L_r(f)=R_f=\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}\] for every nonempty sublevel set, and \[0^+S_f=R_f\] whenever \(S_f\ne\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A vector \(d\) lies in \(R_f\) exactly when \(f(x+td)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(t\ge0\).
The constancy space is \(R_f\cap(-R_f)=\{d:f^\infty(d)\\le0,\ f^\infty(-d)\le0\}\), and it is the lineality space of every nonempty sublevel set.
special_cases_latex: If \(R_f=\{0\}\), every nonempty sublevel set is bounded.
If \(f=\delta_C\), then \(R_f=0^+C\), and every nonempty sublevel below \(+\infty\) equals \(C\).
If \(f\) is finite max-affine, \(f^\infty(d)=\max_i\langle a_i,d\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An attained minimizer is unique only if the polyhedral solution set is a singleton; boundedness alone does not imply uniqueness.
Any nonzero direction in \(R_f\) makes every nonempty sublevel set unbounded.
The recession function of a proper polyhedral convex function is itself polyhedral.
boundary_notes: The solution set can be empty when the infimum is not attained or equals \(-\infty\).
Directions with positive recession value can still belong to the recession cone of the domain, but not to the recession cone of a sublevel set.
This definition records global asymptotic geometry, not local error-bound constants.

notation.meaning: The recession cone of the function and of every nonempty sublevel set.

children.title: Polyhedral Recession Functions

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Recession Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral function's recession function is the maximum of its affine slopes on feasible recession directions and is infinite outside them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), define
\[f^\infty(d)=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}.\]
This value is independent of \(x_0\), and the polyhedral representation gives
\[f^\infty(d)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\langle a_i,d\rangle+\delta_{\operatorname{rec}P}(d).\]
Thus \(f^\infty\) is positively homogeneous and polyhedral, finite precisely on \(\operatorname{rec}P\), and records the maximal affine slope along each feasible recession direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f^\infty(d)=\max_{1\le i\le k}\langle a_i,d\rangle+\delta_{\operatorname{rec}P}(d).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional growth under a max-affine-plus-indicator representation.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex and choose any \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional asymptotic directional growth of a closed proper polyhedral convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The recession function of \(f\) is the positively homogeneous proper convex function \(f^\infty:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined epigraphically by \[\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=0^+(\operatorname{epi}f).\] Equivalently, for every direction \(d\), \[f^\infty(d)=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t},\] independently of the chosen \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). If \[f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C(x),\] then \[f^\infty(d)=\max_i\langle a_i,d\rangle+\delta_{0^+C}(d).\] In particular, \(f^\infty\) is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function measures the asymptotic slope of a polyhedral convex function in every direction. Its epigraph is the recession cone of the original epigraph, and its value is the limiting difference quotient from any point in the effective domain. In a max-affine representation restricted to a polyhedral domain, the intercepts disappear, the affine slopes remain, and directions outside the domain recession cone receive value plus infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=0^+(\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad f^\infty(d)=\max_i\langle a_i,d\rangle+\delta_{0^+C}(d).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(d\), \[f^\infty(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x+d)-f(x)\bigr).\]
A pair \((d,\nu)\) belongs to \(0^+(\operatorname{epi}f)\) exactly when \(f(x+td)\le f(x)+t\nu\) for every \(x\) and \(t\ge0\).
special_cases_latex: For finite max-affine \(f\), \(f^\infty(d)=\max_i\langle a_i,d\rangle\) everywhere.
For an indicator \(f=\delta_C\), \(f^\infty=\delta_{0^+C}\).
For an affine function \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+\alpha\), \(f^\infty(d)=\langle a,d\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The function recession cone is \(\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}\).
The constancy space is \(\{d:f^\infty(d)le0,\ f^\infty(-d)\le0\}\).
Every nonempty sublevel set has recession cone \(\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}\).
boundary_notes: The recession function can take value \(+\infty\) for directions outside \(0^+(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
The base-point limit formula uses closedness; proper polyhedral convex functions are closed.
The recession function records first-order asymptotic growth and discards all affine intercepts.

notation.meaning: The recession cone of a nonempty closed convex set \(C\).

children.title: Level-Set Coercivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Bounded and unbounded level-set behavior.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level-Bounded and Recessionary Regimes of a Polyhedral Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex, and set \(L_r(f)=\{x:f(x)\le r\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global finite-dimensional coercivity and sublevel boundedness, characterized through the polyhedral recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is level-bounded when every sublevel set \(L_r(f)\) is bounded. It is coercive when \[\|x_k\|\to\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x_k)\to+\infty\] for every sequence \((x_k)\). In finite dimensions these conditions are equivalent. For a proper closed convex function, and hence for a proper polyhedral convex function, they are also equivalent to \[\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}=\{0\}.\] Thus the bounded-level regime is characterized by strictly positive recession value in every nonzero direction where \(f^\infty\) is finite. The unbounded-level regime occurs precisely when some nonzero \(d\) satisfies \(f^\infty(d)\le0\); then every nonempty sublevel set is unbounded in direction \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral convex function is level-bounded when all of its sublevel sets are bounded, and coercive when its values tend to plus infinity along every sequence escaping to infinity. In finite-dimensional space these are equivalent. They hold exactly when the only direction of nonpositive recession growth is the zero direction. If a nonzero direction has nonpositive recession value, every nonempty sublevel set recedes along that direction and is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is coercive}\iff f\text{ is level-bounded}\iff\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}=\{0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because every nonempty sublevel set has recession cone \(R_f=\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}\), one nonempty sublevel set is bounded if and only if all nonempty sublevel sets are bounded.
For a max-affine-domain representation, level-boundedness is equivalent to \[\{d\in0^+C:\langle a_i,d\rangle\le0\ \forall i\}=\{0\}.\]
special_cases_latex: A finite max-affine function is coercive exactly when \(\max_i\langle a_i,d\rangle>0\) for every nonzero \(d\).
An indicator \(\delta_C\) is level-bounded exactly when the nonempty closed polyhedron \(C\) is bounded.
If \(f\) has a nonzero constancy direction, it cannot be level-bounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: A proper lower semicontinuous level-bounded function attains its minimum; hence a coercive proper polyhedral convex function has a nonempty compact polyhedral minimizer set.
In the unbounded-level regime, the same recession direction certifies unboundedness of every nonempty sublevel set.
If one nonempty sublevel set is bounded, all nonempty sublevel sets are bounded.
boundary_notes: Coercivity does not imply strict convexity or uniqueness of a minimizer.
An unbounded effective domain does not by itself prevent coercivity.
Empty sublevel sets are bounded by convention but do not determine the regime; at least one nonempty sublevel is needed for the recession test.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Recession
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty sublevel set has recession cone equal to the directions in which the function's recession value is nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[d\in\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^\infty(d)\le0.\]
Equivalently, a direction remains in the sublevel set from every point of \(L_\alpha\) exactly when the function has nonpositive recession growth in that direction. Hence all nonempty sublevel sets of \(f\) have the same recession cone. For polyhedral \(f\), this cone is polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:f^\infty(d)\le0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession cone of any nonempty convex sublevel set.

source_witnesses.locator: 9.1 Lower Semicontinuous Convex Functions p. 157

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Growth of Coercive Polyhedral Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed polyhedral convex function is coercive exactly when it has a global positive linear lower-growth bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper closed polyhedral convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), coercivity is equivalent to the existence of \(c>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \[f(x)\geq c\|x\|_2+\beta\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n.\] Thus coercive polyhedral functions have a uniform positive linear growth rate at infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, and polyhedral on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is coercive}\iff\exists c>0,\beta\in\mathbb R\;\forall x:\ f(x)\geq c\|x\|_2+\beta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative growth formulation specific to the coercive polyhedral regime.

notation.meaning: A positive uniform linear growth rate.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper polyhedral convex function is coercive exactly when every nonzero direction has strictly positive recession growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is coercive, meaning
\[\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x_k)\to+\infty,\]
if and only if
\[f^\infty(d)>0\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}.\]
Equivalently, \(\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}=\{0\}\). In the polyhedral case this is also equivalent to boundedness of every nonempty sublevel set, and the minimum of \(f\) is attained on a nonempty compact polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is coercive}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^\infty(d)>0\ \text{for every }d\ne0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coercivity criterion for proper polyhedral convex functions.

source_witnesses.locator: 9 Lower Semicontinuous Convex Functions p. 157

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Linear Growth of Coercive Polyhedral Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative growth form specific to the coercive polyhedral regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper closed polyhedral convex function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), coercivity is equivalent to the existence of constants \(c>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \[f(x)\ge c\|x\|_2+\beta\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n.\] Thus a coercive polyhedral function grows at least linearly at infinity; mere divergence without a positive linear rate cannot occur in this class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed polyhedral convex function is coercive exactly when it admits a global positive linear lower-growth bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, and polyhedral on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ coercive}\iff\exists c>0,\beta\in\mathbb R\;\forall x:\ f(x)\ge c\|x\|_2+\beta\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Linear Growth of Coercive Polyhedral Functions
Noncoercive Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noncoercivity occurs exactly when a nonzero direction has nonpositive recession growth, making every nonempty sublevel set unbounded along a ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is noncoercive exactly when there exists \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\) satisfying \(f^\infty(d)\le0\). For every nonempty sublevel set \(L_\alpha\), such a direction obeys
\[x+td\in L_\alpha\qquad(x\in L_\alpha,\ t\ge0),\]
so \(L_\alpha\) is unbounded. The cases \(f^\infty(d)<0\) and \(f^\infty(d)=0\) respectively represent strict recession descent and a nonascending escape direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is noncoercive}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists d\ne0:\ f^\infty(d)\le0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of coercivity through a nonpositive recession direction.

source_witnesses.locator: 9 Lower Semicontinuous Convex Functions p. 157

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Sublevel Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedral sublevel is bounded exactly when its nonpositive recession cone contains only the zero direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(L_\alpha\) is a nonempty polyhedron,
\[L_\alpha\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha=\{0\}.\]
Using level-set recession, this becomes
\[L_\alpha\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:f^\infty(d)\le0\}=\{0\}.\]
Thus the bounded-sublevel boundary is reached when the nonpositive recession cone first contains a nonzero direction; that direction generates an unbounded ray in every nonempty sublevel set.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L_\alpha\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary between bounded and unbounded polyhedral sublevels.

children.title: Polyhedral Attainment Geometry
children.top_down_role: Solution-set structure and finite-value attainment in the polyhedral regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Value Attainment Geometry of a Polyhedral Convex Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral, meaning that \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a polyhedron. Equivalently, \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C(x)\) for a nonempty polyhedron \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, closed proper polyhedral convex functions; the definition records the finite-infimum regime and its solution-set geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite-value attainment geometry of \(f\) is the pair \(\mathcal A(f)=(v_f,S_f)\), where \[v_f:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\in\mathbb{R},\qquad S_f:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:f(x)=v_f\}.\] In the polyhedral regime, the requirement \(v_f\in\mathbb{R}\) entails \(S_f\ne\varnothing\), and \(S_f\) is a polyhedron. Thus finite infimum, attainment, and a polyhedral solution set are the defining components of this geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed polyhedral convex function having a finite infimum, its attainment geometry is the ordered pair consisting of the optimal value and the set of minimizers. In this regime the minimizer set is nonempty and polyhedral.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A(f):=(v_f,S_f)\) with \(S_f=\{x:f(x)=v_f\}\ne\varnothing\), and \(S_f\) is polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(S_f=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:0\in\partial f(x)\}\).
For every \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), \(S_f=\{x:f(x)\le \beta\}\) when \(\beta=v_f\), so the solution set is the lowest nonempty level set.
special_cases_latex: If \(f(x)=c^Tx+\delta_C(x)\) for a polyhedron \(C\), then \(S_f\) is the optimal face of the associated linear program whenever the optimal value is finite.
immediate_consequences_latex: The finite-value regime excludes unattained finite infima for proper closed polyhedral convex functions.
\(S_f\) is closed and convex and has finitely many faces.
boundary_notes: The definition does not cover the case \(\inf f=-\infty\).
Finite attainment can fail for general closed convex functions lacking polyhedral or comparable coercivity assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Minimizer Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-below proper polyhedral function attains its minimum on a polyhedron characterized by zero subgradients and zero recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite infimum \(m\) is attained, and
\[\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{x:0\in\partial f(x)\}=\{x:f(x)\le m\}.\]
Consequently, \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\) is a nonempty closed polyhedron. Its recession cone satisfies
\[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname*{argmin}f)=\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\}=\{d:f^\infty(d)=0\},\]
where the final equality follows because finite boundedness below excludes directions with negative recession value. The minimizer set is bounded exactly when this cone is \(\{0\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{x:0\in\partial f(x)\}=\{x:f(x)\le m\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of minimizers for bounded-below polyhedral objectives.

source_witnesses.locator: 9 Lower Semicontinuous Convex Functions p. 157

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Value Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed polyhedral convex function attains its infimum whenever that infimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, convex, and polyhedral. If its optimal value \(\alpha:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\) is finite, then the level set \(\{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is nonempty. Equivalently, there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) such that \(f(\bar x)=\alpha\), so \(\operatorname{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed polyhedral version, obtained from linear-programming attainment.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Recession and Barrier Cones p. 128

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed polyhedral convex function fails to attain a minimum exactly when a recession direction drives its value to minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper closed polyhedral convex function \(f\), finite-valued nonattainment cannot occur. More precisely, \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing\) if and only if \(\inf f=-\infty\). This occurs if and only if there is a recession direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) satisfying \(f^\infty(d)<0\); along every ray \(x+td\) contained in the domain, \(f(x+td)=f(x)+t f^\infty(d)\) for all sufficiently large \(t\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing\iff\inf f=-\infty\iff(\exists d\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{dom}f))\ f^\infty(d)<0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the only nonattainment mechanism for proper closed polyhedral convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Controlled Solution Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone of a nonempty polyhedral minimizer set consists exactly of domain recession directions having zero recession cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:=\operatorname{argmin}f\) be nonempty. Then \(S\) is a polyhedron, and boundedness below implies \(f^\infty(d)\geq0\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Its recession cone is exactly \[\operatorname{rec}S=\{d\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{dom}f):f^\infty(d)=0\}.\] Consequently, \(S\) is bounded if and only if the displayed cone equals \(\{0\}\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}S=\{d\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{dom}f):f^\infty(d)=0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Geometry of a Set-Valued Mapping
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) be a set-valued mapping with graph \(\operatorname{gph}S:=\{(x,y):y\in S(x)\}\). Its domain, range, inverse, and fibers are defined from this graph by coordinate projection and exchange.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional multifunctions represented either by one convex polyhedron or by a finite union of polyhedral graph pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedral set-valued geometry of \(S\) is the graph-based system \[\mathfrak G(S):=\big(\operatorname{gph}S,\operatorname{dom}S,\operatorname{rge}S,S^{-1}\big),\] restricted to mappings for which \[\operatorname{gph}S=\bigcup_{k=1}^N G_k\] with \(N<\infty\) and each \(G_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) a polyhedron. Here \(\operatorname{dom}S=\{x:S(x)\ne\varnothing\}\), \(\operatorname{rge}S=\{y:S^{-1}(y)\ne\varnothing\}\), and \(S^{-1}(y)=\{x:y\in S(x)\}\). If \(N=1\) and \(G_1\) is convex, \(S\) has a convex polyhedral graph; otherwise the finite union defines piecewise-polyhedral geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping has polyhedral set-valued geometry when its complete graph is a finite union of polyhedra. Its domain, range, values, and inverse values are the corresponding sections or projections of that graph. A single convex polyhedral graph is the convex subclass.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many polyhedra \(G_1,\ldots,G_N\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) whose union is \(\operatorname{gph}S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathfrak G(S)=(\operatorname{gph}S,\operatorname{dom}S,\operatorname{rge}S,S^{-1})\) is the induced polyhedral graph geometry of \(S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y\in S(x)\iff (x,y)\in\bigcup_{k=1}^N G_k\).
\(x\in S^{-1}(y)\iff (y,x)\in\operatorname{gph}S^{-1}\), where \(\operatorname{gph}S^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}S\}\).
special_cases_latex: Subdifferentials of proper lower-semicontinuous convex piecewise linear-quadratic functions are piecewise polyhedral.
Normal-cone mappings of nonempty polyhedra are piecewise polyhedral.
immediate_consequences_latex: Each graph piece induces polyhedral sections and polyhedral coordinate projections.
Inversion preserves the finite-union-of-polyhedra property.
boundary_notes: The union need not itself be convex.
Closed values alone do not imply a polyhedral graph.

notation.meaning: Inverse multifunction obtained by exchanging graph coordinates.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active Affine Pieces and Domain Constraints
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Bx\le d\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}\ell_i(x)+\delta_C(x)\), where \(\ell_i(x)=\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper polyhedral convex functions in a fixed finite max-affine-plus-indicator representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), the active-piece geometry is the pair of finite index sets \[I_f(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\ell_i(x)=f(x)\},\qquad J_C(x):=\{j:(Bx)_j=d_j\}.\] The set \(I_f(x)\) records the affine pieces attaining the maximum, while \(J_C(x)\) records the domain inequalities active at \(x\). The local first-order data are the active slopes \(\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\) and the active domain normals \(\{B_j^T:j\in J_C(x)\}\). Points with the same pair \((I_f(x),J_C(x))\) have the same active-piece pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral convex function written as a finite maximum of affine functions on a polyhedral domain, the active-piece geometry at a domain point consists of the affine indices attaining the maximum and the domain inequalities holding with equality. Their slopes and constraint normals are the local first-order generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I(x):=(I_f(x),J_C(x))\) is the active-piece pattern at \(x\), with generators \(\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\cup\{B_j^T:j\in J_C(x)\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(i\in I_f(x)\iff (x,f(x))\) lies on the epigraph facet \(t=\ell_i(x)\).
\(j\in J_C(x)\iff x\) lies on the boundary hyperplane \(B_jx=d_j\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(J_C(x)=\varnothing\).
If \(|I_f(x)|=1\) and \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(f\) is locally affine at \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Only finitely many active patterns can occur.
Each exact active pattern is described by finitely many linear equalities and strict inequalities.
boundary_notes: Active index sets depend on the chosen finite representation; redundant pieces or constraints can enlarge them.
The induced subdifferential is representation-independent even when active labels are not.

knowledge_statements.title: Active Affine Pieces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a domain point, the active affine pieces are exactly those attaining the maximum in a fixed finite max-affine representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}(a_i^\top x+b_i)+\delta_D(x)\) and \(x\in D\), the active affine-piece index set is \[I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:a_i^\top x+b_i=f(x)\}.\] Thus an index is active precisely when its affine function attains the finite maximum defining \(f(x)\). The set \(I(x)\) is nonempty for every \(x\in D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Active Domain Faces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active domain inequalities determine the local face, and their outward normals generate the domain normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(D=\{x:Cx\leq d\}\) and \(x\in D\), define \(J_D(x):=\{j:C_jx=d_j\}\). The minimal face of \(D\) containing \(x\) in its relative interior is determined by these active equalities. Its normal geometry is \[N_D(x)=\operatorname{cone}\{C_j^\top:j\in J_D(x)\}.\] Hence the active domain face contributes precisely the conical combinations of outward normals of active defining inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_D(x)=\operatorname{cone}\{C_j^\top:j\in J_D(x)\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal Active Face of a Polyhedral Domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:Bz\le d\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron. For \(x\in C\), put \(J_C(x):=\{j:B_jx=d_j\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedral domains, including lower-dimensional domains; normal cones are taken in the ambient Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The active domain face at \(x\in C\) is the minimal face of \(C\) containing \(x\), namely \[F_C(x):=\{z\in C:B_jz=d_j\ \text{for every }j\in J_C(x)\}.\] It is characterized by \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F_C(x)\). Its boundary normal geometry is the polyhedral cone \[N_C(x):=\{u:\langle u,z-x\rangle\le0\ \forall z\in C\}=\operatorname{cone}\{B_j^T:j\in J_C(x)\}+\operatorname{lin}(C-C)^\perp.\] Thus the active face fixes both the local feasible directions and the domain-normal contribution to first-order convex geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a polyhedral domain, the active domain face is the smallest face containing that point. It is obtained by imposing equality on every inequality active at the point. The point lies in the relative interior of this face, and the corresponding active normals generate the domain normal cone, together with the orthogonal complement required for a lower-dimensional domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_C(x)=\{z\in C:B_jz=d_j\ \forall j\in J_C(x)\}\) is the unique face satisfying \(x\in\operatorname{ri}F_C(x)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F_C(x)=\bigcap\{F:F\text{ is a face of }C,\ x\in F\}\).
Two points \(x,z\in C\) lie in the relative interior of the same face exactly when their minimal active faces coincide.
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), then \(F_C(x)=C\).
If \(x\) is a vertex, then \(F_C(x)=\{x\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The tangent cone and normal cone are constant on \(\operatorname{ri}F\) for each face \(F\) of \(C\).
A polyhedron has only finitely many active domain faces.
boundary_notes: With redundant inequalities, \(J_C(x)\) is representation-dependent, but \(F_C(x)\) and \(N_C(x)\) are intrinsic.
For a full-dimensional domain, the orthogonal-complement term is \(\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Minimal face of the domain containing x.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Region Complexes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine-piece comparisons and domain faces partition the domain into finitely many polyhedral cells with constant active patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For index sets \(I\) and \(J\), let \(R_{I,J}:=\{x\in D:I(x)=I,\ J_D(x)=J\}\). Each nonempty \(R_{I,J}\) is a relatively open polyhedron described by affine equalities and strict affine inequalities. The closures of these regions, together with all their faces, form a finite polyhedral complex whose union is \(D\). On the relative interior of every cell, both active patterns are constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonempty cells \(R_{I,J}\) and their faces form a finite polyhedral complex covering \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common refinement induced by affine comparisons and domain faces.

notation.meaning: Region with a fixed active pattern.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C(x)\), where \(C=\{x:Bx\le d\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron. Let \(I_f(x)\) and \(J_C(x)\) denote the active affine and domain indices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For index sets \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,q\}\), define the exact active region \[R_{I,J}:=\{x\in C:I_f(x)=I,\ J_C(x)=J\}.\] The active-region complex is \[\mathcal K(f,C):=\{\overline{R_{I,J}}:R_{I,J}\ne\varnothing\},\] together with all faces of these closures. Each nonempty \(R_{I,J}\) is a relatively open polyhedral cell described by equality of the active affine values and strict domination over inactive pieces, along with equality or strict slackness of the domain inequalities. The cells partition \(C\), and activity is constant on each cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active-region complex is the finite collection of closures of all nonempty regions on which the active affine pieces and active domain inequalities are exactly constant, augmented by their faces. These relatively open polyhedral cells partition the polyhedral domain.
assumptions_latex: A finite max-affine representation of \(f\) and a finite inequality representation of \(C\) are fixed.
Only nonempty exact-activity regions are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\bigsqcup_{R_{I,J}\ne\varnothing}R_{I,J}\), and \(\mathcal K(f,C)\) is the induced finite polyhedral cell system.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(R_{I,J}=\{x\in C:\ell_i(x)=f(x)\ \forall i\in I,\ \ell_k(x)<f(x)\ \forall k\notin I,\ B_jx=d_j\ \forall j\in J,\ B_rx<d_r\ \forall r\notin J\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), the cells are determined solely by ties among the affine pieces.
For a single affine piece, the complex reduces to the face stratification of \(C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Subdifferential of a Polyhedral Convex Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex and write \(f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C(x)\) with \(C\) polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex subdifferentials at every point of the effective domain, including relative-interior and boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f=C\), the subdifferential polyhedron is \[\partial f(x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(z)\ge f(x)+\langle v,z-x\rangle\ \forall z\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\] If \(I_f(x)=\{i:\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i=f(x)\}\), then \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}+N_C(x).\] This set is nonempty, closed, convex, and polyhedral. For \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\), define \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential polyhedron at a domain point is the set of all vectors satisfying the global subgradient inequality. For a max-affine polyhedral function on a polyhedral domain, it equals the convex hull of active affine slopes plus the domain normal cone, and is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}+N_C(x)\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\).
\(f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)\) for every direction \(d\).
special_cases_latex: When \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), the normal term vanishes and \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\).
For \(f=\delta_C\), one has \(\partial f(x)=N_C(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at an interior point precisely when all active slopes coincide.
The recession cone of \(\partial f(x)\) is \(N_C(x)\) up to the lineality induced by the affine hull.
boundary_notes: The displayed generator formula assumes a max-affine-plus-indicator representation.
Subdifferentials of nonpolyhedral convex functions need not be polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside a full-dimensional polyhedral domain, the subdifferential is the convex hull of gradients of the active affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every \(x\in\operatorname{int}D\), the indicator term has normal cone \(N_D(x)=\{0\}\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I(x)\}\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex. For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the set \(\partial f(x)\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity is measured by affine dimension of the subdifferential; singleton values constitute the zero-dimensional stratum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the subgradient multiplicity index by \[\mu_f(x):=\dim\operatorname{aff}\partial f(x),\qquad x\in\operatorname{dom}f.\] For each \(r\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), the multiplicity stratum is \[\mathcal S_r(f):=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:\mu_f(x)=r\}.\] In a fixed active-region decomposition, \(\partial f(x)\) has constant polyhedral generator structure on the relative interior of every cell; refining those cells by the dimension of the resulting subdifferential yields a finite polyhedral stratification. The uniqueness stratum is \(\mathcal S_0(f)=\{x:\partial f(x)\text{ is a singleton}\}\); the union \(\bigcup_{r\ge1}\mathcal S_r(f)\) is the multiple-subgradient locus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subgradient-multiplicity index at a point is the affine dimension of its subdifferential polyhedron. Points with a common index form multiplicity strata. Dimension zero means a unique subgradient, while positive dimension means multiple subgradients. For a polyhedral convex function these sets admit a finite refinement by polyhedral active regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}f=\bigsqcup_{r=0}^n\mathcal S_r(f)\), with \(\mathcal S_0(f)=\{x:|\partial f(x)|=1\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in\mathcal S_0(f)\iff\partial f(x)=\{v\}\) for some \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
For an interior max-affine point, \(\mu_f(x)=\dim\operatorname{aff}\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_f(x)\}\).
special_cases_latex: At an interior point with one nonredundant active slope, \(x\in\mathcal S_0(f)\).
At a full-dimensional domain boundary, nontrivial normal-cone directions force \(\mu_f(x)\ge1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The multiple-subgradient locus is controlled by finitely many active-piece and active-face patterns.
On the interior of the effective domain, \(\mathcal S_0(f)\) is the differentiability locus.
boundary_notes: Cardinality is not used because every nonsingleton convex subdifferential is typically infinite.
For lower-dimensional domains, ambient singleton uniqueness differs from uniqueness of the intrinsic projected subgradient.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient-Uniqueness Cells
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior cell has unique subgradients exactly when its active-gradient hull is one point; the same gradient then applies throughout the cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\operatorname{int}D\) be a cell on which \(I(x)=I_R\) is constant. Then every point of \(R\) has a unique subgradient if and only if \(\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_R\}\) is a singleton. knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Subgradient Cells
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cell has multiple subgradients exactly when its active-gradient hull plus its domain normal cone has positive dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a cell with constant active-piece and active-face patterns. For every \(x\) in its relative interior, \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_R\}+N_D(R).\] The cell is a multi-subgradient cell exactly when this polyhedron has affine dimension at least one. Multiplicity may therefore arise from distinct active gradients, from a nontrivial boundary normal cone, or from both mechanisms.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq D\) is an active-region cell with constant active sets \(I_R\) and \(J_R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall x\in R)\ |\partial f(x)|>1\iff\dim(\operatorname{conv}\{a_i:i\in I_R\}+N_D(R))\geq1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Directional Derivatives
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible point, the directional derivative is the maximum slope among active affine pieces on tangent directions, and is infinite outside the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in P\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the one-sided directional derivative exists in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). Its finite part is the support function of the active slopes, restricted to feasible first-order directions: \[f'(x;d)=\begin{cases}\max_{i\in I(x)}a_i^\top d,&d\in T_P(x),\\+\infty,&d\notin T_P(x).\end{cases}\] Hence \(d\mapsto f'(x;d)\) is a polyhedral sublinear function.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^\top x+b_i)+\delta_P(x)\), where \(\delta_P\) is the convex indicator of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f'(x;d)=\begin{cases}\max_{i\in I(x)}a_i^\top d,&d\in T_P(x),\\+\infty,&d\notin T_P(x).\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional max-affine representation with a polyhedral effective domain.

notation.meaning: indices of affine pieces active at x
tangent cone to P at x

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_i(\langle a_i,x\rangle+\alpha_i)+\delta_C(x)\) be proper polyhedral convex, and fix \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided directional derivatives of extended-real-valued finite-dimensional polyhedral convex functions, including infeasible directions at domain boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedral directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) is \[f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}.\] It is the positively homogeneous polyhedral convex function \[f'(x;d)=\begin{cases}\max_{i\in I_f(x)}\langle a_i,d\rangle,&d\in T_C(x),\\+\infty,&d\notin T_C(x),\end{cases}\] and equivalently \[f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)=\sup_{v\in\partial f(x)}\langle v,d\rangle.\] Thus it is a local piecewise-linear first-order model on the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the one-sided rate along a direction. For a polyhedral convex function, it is finite exactly on the tangent cone of the domain and there equals the maximum of the active affine slopes applied to the direction. Equivalently, it is the support function of the subdifferential polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;\cdot)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}\) is a proper polyhedral convex, positively homogeneous function with domain \(T_C(x)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\delta_{T_C(x)}(d)+\max_{i\in I_f(x)}\langle a_i,d\rangle\).
\(v\in\partial f(x)\iff\langle v,d\rangle\le f'(x;d)\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(T_C(x)=\mathbb{R}^n\).
If one affine piece is active and \(x\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(f'(x;d)=\langle a_i,d\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Directional behavior is determined by finitely many active slopes and tangent-cone faces.
The derivative model is piecewise linear on a finite polyhedral conic subdivision.
boundary_notes: Directions outside \(T_C(x)\) have derivative \(+\infty\) under the extended-real convention.
The statement concerns the convex one-sided directional derivative, not a symmetric derivative.

notation.meaning: Tangent cone to the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph Geometry of a Polyhedral Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional primal-dual geometry of the convex subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subdifferential graph geometry of \(f\) is the subset \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f:=\{(x,v)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n:v\in\partial f(x)\}.\] Equivalently, \[(x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle.\] For polyhedral convex \(f\), this graph is a finite union of polyhedra. A finite active-region decomposition of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) gives graph pieces on which the active affine indices, active domain face, and polyhedral description of \(\partial f(x)\) are fixed. The first coordinate is primal and the second is dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential graph is the set of all primal points paired with their subgradients. The same pairs are exactly the equality cases of the Fenchel inequality. For a polyhedral convex function, this graph is a finite union of polyhedra indexed by finitely many active primal and dual patterns.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\{(x,v):f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle\}\) is piecewise polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\iff(v,x)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*\).
\(\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\{(x,v):x\in\partial f^*(v)\}\) after exchanging coordinates.
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), the graph is \(\operatorname{gph}N_C\).
For affine \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+\alpha\), the graph is \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{a\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal projection is \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f=\operatorname{dom}f\) in the polyhedral regime.
The dual projection is \(\operatorname{rge}\partial f=\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*\).
boundary_notes: The graph is generally nonconvex even though every value \(\partial f(x)\) is convex.
Piecewise polyhedral does not mean that the whole graph is one polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Polyhedral Subdifferential Graphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdifferential graph of a polyhedral convex function is a finite union of polyhedra indexed by compatible active faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist finitely many polyhedra \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_N\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\), indexed by compatible active faces of the epigraph, such that \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\bigcup_{k=1}^N Q_k.\] Consequently, \(\partial f\) is a piecewise-polyhedral multifunction, although its complete graph need not be convex.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\bigcup_{k=1}^N Q_k\] for finitely many polyhedra \(Q_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph decomposition induced by finitely many active epigraph faces.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subdifferential graphs of finite-dimensional polyhedral convex functions admit finite active-set decompositions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Polyhedral Decomposition of a Subdifferential Graph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition applies to subdifferential mappings whose graphs admit a finite polyhedral covering; polyhedral convex functions form an important special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subdifferential graph of \(f\) is piecewise polyhedral if there exist an integer \(N<\infty\) and polyhedra \(G_1,\ldots,G_N\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\bigcup_{k=1}^N G_k.\] The sets \(G_k\) are graph pieces and need not be disjoint or convex as a union. A representation may be refined so that each piece corresponds to a fixed primal active region and a fixed face of its subdifferential value. For proper lower-semicontinuous convex \(f\), this property is equivalent to \(f\) being piecewise linear-quadratic; hence every proper polyhedral convex function has a piecewise-polyhedral subdifferential graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subdifferential graph is piecewise polyhedral when it is the union of finitely many polyhedra in the product of primal and dual spaces. The pieces may overlap, and the whole graph need not be convex. For proper closed convex functions this is equivalent to piecewise linear-quadratic structure of the function.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\partial f\) is the convex subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\bigcup_{k=1}^NG_k\) for finitely many polyhedra \(G_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\partial f\) is a piecewise-polyhedral mapping.
For proper lsc convex \(f\), \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) is piecewise polyhedral if and only if \(f\) is piecewise linear-quadratic.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is polyhedral convex, it is piecewise linear-quadratic with zero quadratic terms.
If \(f=\delta_C\) for a polyhedron \(C\), then \(N_C\) has a piecewise-polyhedral graph.
immediate_consequences_latex: The inverse mapping \((\partial f)^{-1}\) is piecewise polyhedral.
Every graph point lies in at least one finite-dimensional polyhedral graph piece.
boundary_notes: A finite union of polyhedra is not necessarily a polyhedron.
The decomposition is not unique and can be refined without changing the mapping.

notation.meaning: A polyhedral subset of the primal-dual product space.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Graph Strata
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each subdifferential graph stratum couples a primal face of a polyhedral function with the dual face selected by Fenchel equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fenchel equality gives \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\}.\] On every relatively open polyhedral stratum, the primal points \(x\) lie in the relative interior of a fixed face of the polyhedral complex of \(f\), while the corresponding subgradients \(y\) lie in a fixed dual face determined by equality.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}\partial f=\{(x,y):f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle\},\] with each graph stratum coupling a primal face to a dual face.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-equality strata for finite-dimensional polyhedral convex functions.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Fenchel equality correctly represents the subdifferential graph, but the stronger claim about every relatively open polyhedral stratum coupling fixed primal and dual faces does not define the stratification or the relevant face complexes. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Strata of a Polyhedral Subgradient Graph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\) be proper polyhedral convex. Choose a finite relatively open polyhedral partition \(\mathscr R\) of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) such that \(Q_R:=\partial f(x)\) is constant for \(x\in R\), after refining by active graph patterns.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional graph stratification; strata are indexed by a primal activity cell and a relative-interior face of its dual subdifferential polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R\in\mathscr R\) and a nonempty face \(H\) of \(Q_R\), define the primal-dual graph stratum \[\Gamma_{R,H}:=R\times\operatorname{ri}H\subseteq\operatorname{gph}\partial f.\] Equivalently, every \((x,v)\in\Gamma_{R,H}\) satisfies \[v\in\partial f(x),\qquad x\in\partial f^*(v),\qquad f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle.\] The collection of all nonempty \(\Gamma_{R,H}\), with a common polyhedral refinement when necessary, partitions the subdifferential graph into finitely many relatively open polyhedral primal-dual cells.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual graph stratum pairs a relatively open primal activity cell with the relative interior of a face of its constant subdifferential polyhedron. Every pair in the stratum satisfies both reciprocal subgradient relations and Fenchel equality. A finite refinement yields a partition of the whole subdifferential graph.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathscr R\) is a finite active-pattern refinement on which the subdifferential value is constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma_{R,H}=R\times\operatorname{ri}H\) is a relatively open polyhedral subset of \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\), and finitely many such strata cover the graph.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((x,v)\in\Gamma_{R,H}\Rightarrow (v,x)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*\).
Each stratum lies in the Fenchel-equality set \(\{(x,v):f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle\}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), strata couple relative interiors of faces of \(C\) with relative interiors of faces of their normal cones.
If \(f\) is affine, there is one stratum \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{a\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Exchanging primal and dual coordinates sends the stratification to one for \(f^*\).
Primal and dual activity remain constant within each stratum.
boundary_notes: A preliminary refinement may be needed because a coarse primal active cell need not make every dual face label constant.
The strata are relatively open; their closures may overlap along lower-dimensional strata.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse Subdifferential Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugacy exchanges primal and dual subdifferentials: the inverse of the subdifferential of a convex function is the subdifferential of its conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[y\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(y)=\langle x,y\rangle.\] Therefore \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\), and \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*\) is obtained from \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) by exchanging the primal and dual coordinates. If \(f\) is polyhedral, then so is \(f^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*,\qquad \operatorname{gph}\partial f^*=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate inversion of convex subdifferentials; polyhedrality is preserved.
