knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(f^*(v):=\sup_x(\langle v,x\rangle-f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed proper finite-dimensional convex functions; polyhedrality is imposed for the finite graph-piece specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse subdifferential geometry of \(f\) is the inverse multifunction \[(\partial f)^{-1}(v):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:v\in\partial f(x)\}.\] Conjugacy identifies it exactly with the subdifferential of the conjugate: \[(\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*.\] Equivalently, for every \(x,v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[v\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\partial f^*(v)\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle.\] Consequently, \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*=\{(v,x):(x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\}\). If \(f\) is polyhedral convex, then \(f^*\) is polyhedral convex and both graphs are finite unions of polyhedra exchanged by the coordinate-swap map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse of the subdifferential sends a dual vector to all primal points having it as a subgradient. For a proper closed convex function this inverse is exactly the subdifferential of the convex conjugate. Their graphs are obtained from one another by swapping primal and dual coordinates; polyhedral graph structure is preserved.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
For the final specialization, \(f\) is additionally polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\) and \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f^*=\{(v,x):(x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\iff x\in\partial f^*(v)\).
\(v\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle x,v\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\delta_C\), \((N_C)^{-1}=\partial\sigma_C\).
If \(f\) is differentiable and strictly convex with an invertible gradient, then \(\nabla f^*=(\nabla f)^{-1}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Domain and range exchange: \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f^*=\operatorname{rge}\partial f\).
Piecewise-polyhedrality is preserved by inversion.
boundary_notes: The equality with \(\partial f^*\) requires proper closed convexity.
The inverse can be multivalued even when one of the subdifferentials is single-valued on part of its domain.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\operatorname{gph}S:=\{(x,y):y\in S(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional multifunctions classified by the geometry of their complete graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedral set-valued mapping family consists of two nested graph classes. The convex-polyhedral class is \[\mathcal P_{n,m}:=\{S:\operatorname{gph}S\text{ is a polyhedron in }\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\},\] and the piecewise-polyhedral class is \[\mathcal{PP}_{n,m}:=\left\{S:\operatorname{gph}S=\bigcup_{k=1}^NG_k,\ N<\infty,\ G_k\text{ polyhedral}\right\}.\] Thus \(\mathcal P_{n,m}\subseteq\mathcal{PP}_{n,m}\). Membership is a property of the complete graph, not merely of individual values. Coordinate exchange preserves both classes, so \(S\) and \(S^{-1}\) belong to corresponding classes simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-polyhedral multifunction has one polyhedral complete graph. A piecewise-polyhedral multifunction has a graph that is a finite union of polyhedra. The first class is contained in the second, and both are preserved by taking the inverse mapping.
assumptions_latex: All graph pieces are finite-dimensional polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\in\mathcal P_{n,m}\) iff \(\operatorname{gph}S\) is polyhedral, while \(S\in\mathcal{PP}_{n,m}\) iff its graph is a finite union of polyhedra.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(S\in\mathcal{PP}_{n,m}\iff\exists G_1,\ldots,G_N:\ y\in S(x)\iff(x,y)\in\bigcup_{k=1}^NG_k\).
\(S\in\mathcal P_{n,m}\iff S^{-1}\in\mathcal P_{m,n}\), and likewise for \(\mathcal{PP}\).
special_cases_latex: Polyhedral convex processes are positively homogeneous members of \(\mathcal P_{n,m}\).
Subdifferentials of convex piecewise linear-quadratic functions belong to \(\mathcal{PP}_{n,n}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Domains and ranges are finite unions of polyhedra, and are polyhedra in the convex-graph subclass.
Every value is a finite union of polyhedra; in the convex-graph subclass every nonempty value is a polyhedron.
boundary_notes: Having polyhedral values for every input does not by itself imply a polyhedral graph.
A finite union of polyhedra may be nonconvex and disconnected.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Polyhedral Graphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is convex polyhedral when its complete graph is one polyhedron in the product of its domain and range spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is a convex polyhedral multifunction if its complete graph \[\operatorname{gph}F:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m:y\in F(x)\}\] is a polyhedron, equivalently an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces. In particular, every value \(F(x)\) and the domain \(\operatorname{dom}F\) are convex polyhedra, allowing the empty set as a value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is convex polyhedral exactly when \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is a polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set-Valued Mapping with a Convex Polyhedral Graph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\). A polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) is an intersection of finitely many closed affine half-spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional set-valued mappings whose entire graph, rather than merely each value, is one convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(S\) has a convex polyhedral graph if \[\operatorname{gph}S:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m:y\in S(x)\}\] is a polyhedron. Equivalently, there exist a finite number of rows and matrices \(A\), \(B\), and a vector \(c\) such that \[y\in S(x)\iff Ax+By\le c.\] Consequently, \[S(x)=\{y:By\le c-Ax\},\quad \operatorname{dom}S=\{x:\exists y,\ Ax+By\le c\},\] and the inverse graph is obtained by exchanging \(x\) and \(y\). Empty values are permitted outside the projected domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping has a convex polyhedral graph when all input-output pairs satisfying the mapping form one polyhedron. Equivalently, membership can be expressed by finitely many joint linear inequalities in the input and output. Every value is then a polyhedron, and the domain is the polyhedral projection of the graph.
assumptions_latex: The complete graph is required to be one convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}S=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le c\}\) for some finite linear-inequality system.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(S(x)=\{y:By\le c-Ax\}\) for every \(x\).
\(\operatorname{gph}S^{-1}=\{(y,x):Ax+By\le c\}\) is also a polyhedron.
special_cases_latex: If the graph is a polyhedral cone, \(S\) is a polyhedral convex process.
A single-valued affine mapping on a polyhedral domain has a convex polyhedral graph.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty value \(S(x)\) is closed and convex polyhedral.
Both \(\operatorname{dom}S\) and \(\operatorname{rge}S\) are polyhedra because linear images of polyhedra are polyhedral.
boundary_notes: Polyhedral values at each point are insufficient without a joint finite graph representation.
A piecewise-polyhedral graph need not be a convex polyhedral graph.

notation.meaning: Data of a finite joint inequality representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is piecewise polyhedral when its graph is a finite union of polyhedra, without requiring the union to be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is piecewise polyhedral if there exist finitely many polyhedra \(P_1,\ldots,P_N\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[\operatorname{gph}F=\bigcup_{j=1}^N P_j.\] No convexity of the union is required. The convex-polyhedral class is the special case in which the complete graph itself is one polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}F=\bigcup_{j=1}^N P_j\] for finitely many polyhedra \(P_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite-union convention; the complete graph need not be convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-union definition of a piecewise-polyhedral multifunction

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The finite-union definition is precise and fits the piecewise-polyhedral graph leaf, but the record has no cited source. An authoritative reference with a specific definition, section, or page locator is required.

children.title: Polyhedral Convex Processes
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous polyhedral multifunctions and their dual geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Convex Processes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral convex process is a positively homogeneous multifunction whose complete graph is a convex polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(H\) is a polyhedral convex process if \(\operatorname{gph}H\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) is a convex polyhedral cone. Equivalently, \(0\in H(0)\), \(H(x_1)+H(x_2)\subseteq H(x_1+x_2)\), and \(H(\lambda x)=\lambda H(x)\) for every \(\lambda>0\), with a polyhedral graph. Its dual geometry is encoded by the polar cone \((\operatorname{gph}H)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\) is a polyhedral convex process exactly when \(\operatorname{gph}H\) is a convex polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous multifunctions represented by convex polyhedral cones.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard graph-cone definition of a polyhedral convex process

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The graph-cone definition fits the leaf and the definition content kind. The asserted equivalent multifunction formulation is convention-sensitive, especially at the zero scalar and for empty values, and no source is supplied. A specific source defining convex processes and their polyhedral specialization is required.

children.title: Polyhedral Multifunction Calculus
children.top_down_role: Structure-preserving operations on polyhedral multifunctions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), and let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be a set-valued mapping with graph \(\operatorname{gph}F:=\{(x,y):y\in F(x)\}\). A set is polyhedral when it is the intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex polyhedral multifunctions and graph operations representable by finite linear systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multifunction \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) is polyhedral when \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is a polyhedral convex set. Polyhedral multifunction calculus is the collection of graph operations obtained from finite Cartesian products, intersections, inverse images under linear maps, inverses, and compositions: \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\) and \(\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)=\{(x,z):\exists y,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F,\ (y,z)\in\operatorname{gph}G\}\). An operation belongs to this calculus when its output graph is obtained from finitely many polyhedral graphs by affine slicing, finite intersection, coordinate permutation, Cartesian product, and linear projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-valued mapping is polyhedral exactly when its graph is a convex polyhedron. Its calculus consists of operations whose output graphs are constructed from finitely many such graphs using affine slices, finite intersections, products, coordinate permutations, and projections. This includes inversion and composition, with the intermediate value in a composition eliminated by projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is polyhedral}\iff\operatorname{gph}F\text{ is polyhedral}\), and every graph produced by the specified finite affine-intersection-product-projection operations is polyhedral.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exist matrices \(A,B\) and a vector \(c\) such that \(\operatorname{gph}F=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le c\}\).
Equivalently, \(F(x)=\{y:By\le c-Ax\}\) after choosing a finite inequality representation of its graph.
special_cases_latex: For a polyhedral set \(P\subseteq X\), the constant mapping \(F(x)=P\) has graph \(X\times P\).
If \(F\) and \(G\) are polyhedral, then \(F^{-1}\) and \(G\circ F\) are polyhedral whenever the displayed finite-dimensional composition is used.
immediate_consequences_latex: Domains and ranges of polyhedral multifunctions are polyhedral because they are coordinate projections of the graph.
Fibers \(F(x)\) are polyhedral for every \(x\), including the empty fiber.
boundary_notes: This definition concerns convex polyhedral graphs; finite unions of polyhedra are piecewise-polyhedral rather than necessarily polyhedral.
Infinite-dimensional projections need not preserve the same finite linear representation.
review_flags: No inspected source locator was available for the exact graph-calculus definition and closure scope.
A verifier should confirm whether the node intends convex-polyhedral or piecewise-polyhedral multifunction calculus.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral multifunction calculus
Polyhedral Multifunction Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The image of a polyhedron under a multifunction with a polyhedral graph is polyhedral because it is a coordinate projection of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The restricted graph \(\operatorname{gph}F\cap(S\times\mathbb{R}^m)\) is a polyhedron. Its projection onto the range coordinates is therefore the polyhedron \[F(S)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^m:\exists x\in S\text{ such that }(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}.\] In particular, each value \(F(x)\) is polyhedral by taking \(S=\{x\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(S)=\{y:\exists x\in S,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\] is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Images of polyhedral sets under convex-polyhedral multifunctions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional linear projections preserve polyhedrality

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The image formula and finite-dimensional projection claim are mathematically standard and fit this property leaf, but the record has no source reference. The projection rationale alone is insufficient under the citation requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Multifunction Inverses
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse of a polyhedral multifunction is polyhedral because its graph is obtained by swapping the graph's coordinate blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F^{-1}:\mathbb{R}^m\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) by \(F^{-1}(y)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:y\in F(x)\}\). Then \[\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\{(y,x)\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n:(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}.\] Since exchanging coordinate blocks is an invertible linear map, \(F^{-1}\) also has a polyhedral graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\] is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph inversion by exchanging domain and range coordinates.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-graph coordinate swap is precise and fits this property leaf, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied. A source supporting preservation of polyhedrality under graph inversion is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Multifunction Compositions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The composition of two polyhedral multifunctions is polyhedral, since its graph is a projection of the joined graph constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph of the composition is \[\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F,\ (y,z)\in\operatorname{gph}G\}.\] This set is the projection of a polyhedron in \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^p\), so it is a polyhedron; no additional qualification is required in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{gph}(G\circ F)=\{(x,z):\exists y,\ (x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F,\ (y,z)\in\operatorname{gph}G\}\] is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional composition of convex-polyhedral multifunctions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: intersections and coordinate projections preserve finite-dimensional polyhedrality

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The joined-graph projection formula is correct in finite dimensions and the property kind fits the composition leaf, but the record lacks a cited source with a specific locator. Standard-field rationale is insufficient by itself.

children.title: Polyhedral Certificate-Stability System
children.top_down_role: Qualitative and quantitative consequences of finite linear representation.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_query: Schrijver, Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - 7.1 Cover Inequalities for the 0,1 Knapsack Problem p. 282

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P(b):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), let \(P(b)\) be nonempty at a reference parameter \(\bar b\), and write \((u)_+\) componentwise. Distances are taken with fixed norms on the relevant finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite linear inequality systems viewed simultaneously through infeasibility certificates, residual error bounds, and perturbation stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral certificate-stability system is a finite linear representation \(Ax\le b\), together with: (i) a dual certificate cone \(K:=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^m:A^{\mathsf T}y=0\}\), where \(y\in K\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) certify infeasibility; and (ii) a stability modulus \(\kappa\ge0\) for which \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P(b))\le\kappa\|(Ax-b)_+\|\) whenever \(P(b)\ne\varnothing\). A parameterized family has the certificate-stability property on \(B\) when the same certificate rule is valid for every \(b\in B\) and one finite \(\kappa\) applies throughout the stated region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral certificate-stability system packages a finite inequality system with two consequences of its linear representation. Nonnegative left-null multipliers having negative pairing with the right-hand side certify infeasibility. When the system is feasible, a finite constant bounds distance to its feasible set by the positive-part residual. Uniform certificate-stability on a parameter region requires the same rules and one finite residual-to-distance modulus throughout that region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining data satisfy \(K=\{y\ge0:A^{\mathsf T}y=0\}\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\Rightarrow P(b)=\varnothing\), and \(P(b)\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(x,P(b))\le\kappa\|(Ax-b)_+\|\) for all \(x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The error-bound component is metric subregularity of the residual mapping \(x\mapsto Ax-b+\mathbb R_-^m\).
The certificate component states that infeasibility is separated from the cone \(\{Ax+s:x\in\mathbb R^n,\ s\in\mathbb R_-^m\}\) by a nonnegative multiplier.
special_cases_latex: Equality constraints can be represented by paired inequalities, producing unrestricted multipliers as differences of nonnegative multipliers.
For a fixed matrix \(A\), a Hoffman constant can serve as \(\kappa\) for every feasible right-hand side under fixed norms.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero certificate is finitely checkable through linear equalities, inequalities, and one strict scalar inequality.
Small residual implies proximity to feasibility whenever the stability component applies.
boundary_notes: The title is an umbrella term rather than a universally standardized named object.
The displayed definition does not assert a uniform modulus when the coefficient matrix also varies.

notation.meaning: Feasible polyhedron for right-hand side b.
Cone of nonnegative left-null certificate multipliers.

review_flags: The node title appears synthetic and no inspected source establishes this exact packaged definition.
Separate sources are needed for the alternative certificate and the uniform Hoffman-type stability statement.

children.title: Polyhedral Theorems of the Alternative
children.top_down_role: Named certificate families for finite linear systems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a finite linear feasibility system be represented by a matrix-vector pair, and let its proposed certificate consist of finitely many multiplier equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear, affine, conic, strict, or mixed-strict feasibility systems admitting finite dual certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral theorem of the alternative is a pair of finite systems \(\mathcal P\) and \(\mathcal D\), called the primal feasibility system and dual certificate system, such that for every admissible data instance exactly one system is solvable: \[(\exists x\;\mathcal P(x))\ \mathbin{\dot\vee}\ (\exists y\;\mathcal D(y)).\] The certificate conditions must imply that every primal constraint combination selected by \(y\) yields an impossible scalar relation, so simultaneous solvability is excluded; exhaustiveness requires a certificate whenever the primal polyhedron is empty. Farkas, Gordan–Stiemke, and Motzkin alternatives are members distinguished by whether the primal constraints are affine, homogeneous, strict, or nonstrict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral theorem of the alternative pairs a finite primal feasibility system with a finite multiplier certificate system. For every data instance, exactly one has a solution. The certificate combines the primal constraints into an impossible scalar relation, and every infeasible primal instance must possess such a certificate. Different named alternatives correspond to affine, homogeneous, strict, and mixed-strict systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every admissible instance, \((\exists x\;\mathcal P(x))\mathbin{\dot\vee}(\exists y\;\mathcal D(y))\), where \(\dot\vee\) denotes exclusive disjunction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Primal feasibility is equivalent to nonexistence of a dual certificate: \(\exists x\,\mathcal P(x)\iff\neg\exists y\,\mathcal D(y)\).
Primal infeasibility is equivalent to dual-certifier feasibility: \(\neg\exists x\,\mathcal P(x)\iff\exists y\,\mathcal D(y)\).
special_cases_latex: Farkas alternatives cover affine equality or inequality systems.
Gordan–Stiemke alternatives cover homogeneous systems, while Motzkin transposition covers mixed strict and nonstrict inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: Infeasibility has a finite-dimensional multiplier witness.
Alternative systems provide separation certificates for disjoint polyhedral sets and cones.
boundary_notes: Exact certificate signs and normalizations depend on the chosen primal convention.
This schema does not itself specify a computational complexity bound or a numerical tolerance for approximate certificates.
review_flags: No inspected source locator supports the exact umbrella schema and named-family scope.
Each named alternative requires sign conventions to be checked against an authoritative statement.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral theorem-of-the-alternative schema

children.title: Farkas Certificate Family
children.top_down_role: Conic and affine certificate variants for linear feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization of Strict Farkas Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every strict equality-form Farkas certificate can be positively scaled so that its pairing with the target equals minus one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y\geq0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\), then \(\widehat y=y/(-b^{\mathsf T}y)\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\geq0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y=-1\). Conversely, every \(\widehat y\) satisfying the normalized system is a Farkas infeasibility certificate for \(Ax=b,\ x\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat y=y/(-b^{\mathsf T}y)\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\geq0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y=-1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization of equality-form Farkas infeasibility certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Farkas Certificate Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic equality form of Farkas' alternative and its infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \(Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\); or \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge 0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\). Thus a vector \(y\) satisfying the second system certifies infeasibility of the first by a finite matrix-vector calculation. Equivalently, either \(b\) belongs to the cone generated by the columns of \(A\), or a linear functional separates \(b\) strictly from that cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either a vector is a nonnegative combination of a matrix's columns, or a computable separating vector certifies that no such combination exists, but never both.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(\exists x\ge0:Ax=b\bigr)\mathbin{\dot\vee}\bigl(\exists y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\bigr).\)

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1. Polyhedral Cones and Farkas' Lemma p. 102

children.title: Gordan–Stiemke Alternative Family
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous strict and nonstrict alternative families.

knowledge_statements.title: Gordan–Stiemke Alternative Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gordan and Stiemke pair homogeneous strict or nonstrict systems with mutually exclusive nonnegative or positive null-vector certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Gordan's alternative states that exactly one of \[\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ Ax<0,\qquad \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m:\ y\ge0,\ y\ne0,\ A^\top y=0\] is feasible. Stiemke's alternative states that exactly one of \[\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ Ax\le0,\ Ax\ne0,\qquad \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m:\ y>0,\ A^\top y=0\] is feasible. All vector inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Gordan and Stiemke homogeneous alternatives each contain exactly one feasible system.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two standard homogeneous alternatives, with componentwise inequality conventions explicit.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Gordan and Stiemke homogeneous alternatives

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The displayed Gordan and Stiemke systems are plausible standard sign variants, but the record flags convention sensitivity and supplies no source. Their exact strict and nonstrict formulations require an authoritative theorem-level locator. These are theorems of the alternative, so `theorem`, rather than `duality`, is the appropriate content kind for this terminal container.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Vector inequalities are componentwise; \(u>0\) means every component is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous linear systems with strict and nonstrict orthant conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Gordan–Stiemke alternative family comprises the two homogeneous exclusive alternatives: Gordan's form states that exactly one of \[(\exists x\in\mathbb R_+^n\setminus\{0\}:Ax=0),\qquad(\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:A^{\mathsf T}y>0)\] holds. Stiemke's strict-kernel form states that exactly one of \[(\exists x\in\mathbb R^n:x>0,\ Ax=0),\qquad(\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ne0)\] holds. The family is homogeneous: every feasible nonzero witness may be multiplied by a positive scalar without changing its status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gordan's alternative pairs a nonzero nonnegative vector in the kernel of a matrix with a multiplier whose transposed image is strictly positive; exactly one exists. Stiemke's form exchanges strictness: either the kernel contains a strictly positive vector, or a multiplier has a nonzero nonnegative transposed image. Every witness is homogeneous and represents a positive ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one system in each displayed pair is feasible: \((\exists x\ge0,\ x\ne0,\ Ax=0)\mathbin{\dot\vee}(\exists y,\ A^{\mathsf T}y>0)\), and \((\exists x>0,\ Ax=0)\mathbin{\dot\vee}(\exists y,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ne0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Gordan's certificate asserts strict separation of the column dependence cone from a nonzero nonnegative kernel direction.
Stiemke's certificate may be written as a nonzero vector in \(\operatorname{range}(A^{\mathsf T})\cap\mathbb R_+^n\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A^{\mathsf T}y>0\), then no nonzero \(x\ge0\) can satisfy \(Ax=0\).
If \(A=0\) and \(n>0\), the primal member of both pairs is feasible and the certificate member is not.
immediate_consequences_latex: The existence of positive or nonnegative kernel vectors has a finite homogeneous dual certificate.
Strictness placement distinguishes the two named members of the family.
boundary_notes: The convention \(u>0\) means componentwise strict positivity, not merely \(u\ge0\) and \(u\ne0\).
Degenerate zero-dimensional spaces require separate conventions and are excluded.

notation.meaning: Every component of u is strictly positive.

review_flags: No inspected authoritative locator supports both named forms in the stated convention.
The verifier should check naming conventions because Gordan and Stiemke variants are interchanged in some texts.

children.title: Motzkin Transposition Family

knowledge_statements.title: Motzkin Transposition Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed strict and nonstrict linear system is infeasible exactly when it admits the stated nonnegative Motzkin multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems has a solution. The primal system is \[Ax<b,\qquad Cx\leq d.\] The alternative system is \[y\geq0,\quad z\geq0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y+C^{\mathsf T}z=0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y+d^{\mathsf T}z\leq0,\] together with \[y\neq0\quad\text{or}\quad b^{\mathsf T}y+d^{\mathsf T}z<0.\] Thus infeasibility of the mixed primal system is certified by nonnegative multipliers satisfying the alternative system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of the displayed primal and alternative systems is feasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional mixed strict–nonstrict linear alternative.

notation.meaning: Multipliers for strict and nonstrict constraints.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite-dimensional Motzkin transposition theorem

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^q\). All vector inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional mixed systems containing strict and nonstrict affine linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Motzkin transposition family associates the mixed primal system \(Ax<a,\ Bx\le b\) with the certificate system \[y\ge0,\quad z\ge0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y+B^{\mathsf T}z=0,\quad a^{\mathsf T}y+b^{\mathsf T}z\le0,\quad\bigl(y\ne0\ \text{or}\ a^{\mathsf T}y+b^{\mathsf T}z<0\bigr).\] The Motzkin alternative is the exclusive assertion that exactly one of the primal and certificate systems is feasible. The final disjunction prevents a zero or noncontradictory multiplier from being counted as a certificate when strict inequalities occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Motzkin transposition treats a system containing both strict and nonstrict inequalities. Its certificate uses nonnegative multipliers that cancel all variable coefficients, produce a nonpositive scalar combination of right-hand sides, and additionally either place positive weight on a strict inequality or make that scalar combination strictly negative. Exactly one of the mixed primal system and certificate system is solvable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\exists x:Ax<a,\ Bx\le b)\mathbin{\dot\vee}(\exists y,z\text{ satisfying the displayed certificate conditions})\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Primal infeasibility is equivalent to feasibility of the displayed multiplier system.
The last condition is equivalent to \((a^{\mathsf T}y+b^{\mathsf T}z<0)\lor(y\ne0)\) under the other certificate constraints.
special_cases_latex: When there are no strict inequalities, the family reduces to a Farkas-type certificate with a strict negative scalar condition.
When there are no nonstrict inequalities, it gives an alternative for \(Ax<a\) using \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), and the corresponding nontriviality condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: Infeasibility of a mixed strict-nonstrict linear system has a finite multiplier witness.
The theorem distinguishes failure caused by strict constraints from ordinary weak separation.
boundary_notes: Dropping the final nontriviality disjunction admits the zero multiplier and destroys the alternative.

children.title: Finite Infeasibility Structure
children.top_down_role: Dimension-sensitive and irreducible witnesses of infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite infeasibility structure of a convex constraint family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex sets, with linear inequalities represented by closed halfspaces. For \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), set \(C_I:=\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional finite convex feasibility, emphasizing small and inclusion-minimal infeasible subfamilies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The finite infeasibility structure of \(\{C_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is the collection \[\mathcal I:=\{I\subseteq[m]:C_I=\varnothing\},\qquad \mathcal M:=\{I\in\mathcal I:C_J\ne\varnothing\ \text{for every}\ J\subsetneq I\}.\] Members of \(\mathcal I\) are infeasible subsystems and members of \(\mathcal M\) are minimal infeasible subsystems. In \(\mathbb R^n\), the family has a dimension-sensitive witness when every infeasible full system contains some \(I\in\mathcal I\) with \(|I|\le n+1\). For linear inequalities, multiplier certificates provide a second finite structure through inclusion-minimal supports of nonnegative infeasibility multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite infeasibility structure records every index set whose associated constraints have empty intersection and, within it, every inclusion-minimal infeasible index set. A dimension-sensitive witness is an infeasible subfamily containing at most the ambient dimension plus one constraints. For linear inequalities, the supports of nonnegative alternative-theorem certificates give an algebraic representation of the same localized-witness idea.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I=\{I:C_I=\varnothing\}\) and \(\mathcal M=\{I\in\mathcal I:\forall J\subsetneq I,\ C_J\ne\varnothing\}\), with a Helly-size witness satisfying \(|I|\le n+1\) whenever the finite convex family is infeasible.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(I\in\mathcal M\) iff \(C_I=\varnothing\) and \(C_{I\setminus\{i\}}\ne\varnothing\) for every \(i\in I\).
For a linear system \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), a certificate support is \(\operatorname{supp}y:=\{i:y_i>0\}\) for a nonnegative Farkas multiplier \(y\).
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb R\), every infeasible finite convex family has an infeasible subfamily of at most two members.
For halfspace systems in \(\mathbb R^n\), minimal infeasible subsystems need not all have size \(n+1\), but at least one small witness exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every infeasible finite family contains an inclusion-minimal infeasible subsystem.
Finite infeasibility can be localized to a bounded-size subsystem in fixed dimension.
boundary_notes: Minimal means inclusion-minimal, not minimum cardinality.
The bound \(n+1\) concerns finite convex families in \(\mathbb R^n\), not arbitrary nonconvex constraints.

notation.meaning: Family of inclusion-minimal infeasible index sets.

review_flags: No inspected source supports the combined set-theoretic and multiplier-support formulation.
A source is needed for the precise Helly dimension bound in the intended constraint setting.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness of the Helly Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There are d+1 closed halfspaces whose full intersection is empty although every proper subfamily intersects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge1\), define \[C_i:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:x_i\ge0\}\quad(i=1,\ldots,d),\qquad C_{d+1}:=\left\{x:\sum_{i=1}^dx_i\le-1\right\}.\] Then \(\bigcap_{i=1}^{d+1}C_i=\varnothing\), while deleting any one member makes the intersection nonempty. Hence the \(d+1\) bound in Helly's theorem is sharp even for closed halfspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_{i=1}^{d+1}C_i=\varnothing,\qquad\bigcap_{i\ne j}C_i\ne\varnothing\ \text{for every }j.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A family of d+1 halfspaces showing that the ambient Helly number cannot be reduced.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C_1,ldots,C_m\) be a finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\), with \(m\ge n+1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families of convex sets in a fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \(\{C_i\}_{i=1}^m\) satisfies the Helly feasibility principle in dimension \(n\) when \[\left[\forall I\subseteq[m],\ |I|\le n+1:\ \bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\ne\varnothing\right]\Longrightarrow\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\ne\varnothing.\] Equivalently, if the entire family is infeasible, then some subfamily of at most \(n+1\) sets is already infeasible. For a finite linear inequality system in \(\mathbb R^n\), each \(C_i\) may be taken as a closed halfspace, so feasibility of every subsystem of at most \(n+1\) inequalities implies feasibility of the complete system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Helly feasibility principle says that a finite convex feasibility problem in n-dimensional space is feasible if every subsystem containing at most n plus one sets is feasible. In contrapositive form, every infeasible finite family has an infeasible witness of at most n plus one members. Linear inequalities are covered because each inequality defines a convex halfspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[\forall I\subseteq[m],\ |I|\le n+1,\ \bigcap_{i\in I}C_i\ne\varnothing\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i\ne\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i=\varnothing\Rightarrow\exists I\subseteq[m]\) with \(|I|\le n+1\) and \(\bigcap_{i\in I}C_i=\varnothing\).
It suffices to test subfamilies of exactly \(n+1\) members when \(m\ge n+1\), because any smaller subfamily can be extended.
special_cases_latex: In \(\mathbb R^1\), pairwise intersection of finitely many intervals implies common intersection.
For halfspaces in \(\mathbb R^n\), infeasibility has a witness involving no more than \(n+1\) inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: An inclusion-minimal infeasible finite convex family has cardinality at most \(n+1\).
Fixed dimension bounds the size of a localized infeasibility witness independently of the total number of constraints.
boundary_notes: Finiteness of the family is part of this formulation; infinite-family variants require additional compactness assumptions.
Convexity is essential, and the numerical bound may improve when all sets lie in a lower-dimensional affine subspace.

notation.meaning: Index set of a constraint subfamily.

The exact finite-family and ambient-dimension hypotheses require source confirmation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_iC_i=\varnothing\Rightarrow\exists I,\ |I|\le r+1,\ \bigcap_{i\in I}C_i=\varnothing.

children.title: Minimal Infeasible Subsystems
children.top_down_role: Irreducible constraint subsystems serving as localized certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Support Farkas Certificate for a Minimal Linear Subsystem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal infeasible linear subsystem has a Farkas certificate with strictly positive weight on every constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_Ix\le b_I\) be a minimal infeasible subsystem of finitely many non-strict linear inequalities. Then there exists \(y\in\mathbb R_{++}^{I}\) such that \[A_I^{\mathsf T}y=0,\qquad b_I^{\mathsf T}y<0.\] It may be normalized so that \(b_I^{\mathsf T}y=-1\). Moreover, every Farkas certificate supported within \(I\) has positive weight on every index of \(I\).
assumptions_latex: \(A_Ix\le b_I\) is finite and minimally infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y>0:\ A_I^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ b_I^{\mathsf T}y=-1.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier structure forced by irreducibility of a finite non-strict linear inequality system.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence and Helly Size of Minimal Infeasible Subsystems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite infeasible family has an irreducible infeasible subfamily, and convexity bounds each such subsystem by the applicable Helly number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every infeasible finite family \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) contains an inclusion-minimal infeasible subfamily. If the sets are convex subsets of an affine carrier of dimension \(r\), every minimal infeasible subsystem \(I\) satisfies \[|I|\le r+1.\] In particular, for subsets of \(\mathbb R^d\), \(|I|\le d+1\).
assumptions_latex: For the cardinality bound, the sets are convex in an affine carrier of dimension \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists I\text{ minimal infeasible},\qquad |I|\le r+1\text{ in the convex r-dimensional case}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction and dimension bound for irreducible witnesses in finite convex families.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let constraints \(g_i(x)\le0\), \(i\in[m]\), be given on a common domain \(X\). For \(I\subseteq[m]\), define \(S_I:=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\le0\ \forall i\in I\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite constraint systems; the polyhedral specialization uses affine functions on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An index set \(I\subseteq[m]\) is a minimal infeasible subsystem if \[S_I=\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad S_{I\setminus\{i\}}\ne\varnothing\ \text{for every }i\in I.\] Thus infeasibility is destroyed by deleting any one constraint. For an affine system \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), a multiplier-supported certificate is localized to \(I\) when \(y_i=0\) for \(i\notin I\), \(y\ge0\), \(\sum_i y_i a_i=0\), and \(\sum_i y_i b_i<0\). The minimal subsystem and a support-minimal multiplier certificate are related notions, but support minimality of a particular certificate is not included in the definition of a minimal infeasible subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal infeasible subsystem is an infeasible collection of constraints that becomes feasible whenever any single member is removed. In a linear inequality system, its infeasibility may be witnessed by a nonnegative multiplier supported on its indices. Inclusion-minimality of the constraints is distinct from support-minimality of an individual multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\text{ is minimally infeasible}\iff S_I=\varnothing\ \text{and}\ \forall i\in I,\ S_{I\setminus\{i\}}\ne\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(I\) is inclusion-minimal in \(\{J\subseteq[m]:S_J=\varnothing\}\).
Equivalently, \(S_I=\varnothing\) while \(S_J\ne\varnothing\) for every proper subset \(J\subsetneq I\).
special_cases_latex: For finite convex constraints in \(\mathbb R^n\), every minimal infeasible subsystem has at most \(n+1\) members under the Helly hypotheses.
A pair of inconsistent scalar bounds \(x\le a\) and \(x\ge b\) with \(a<b\) forms a two-constraint minimal infeasible subsystem.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every infeasible finite constraint system contains at least one minimal infeasible subsystem.
Each constraint in a minimal infeasible subsystem is indispensable to that subsystem's infeasibility.
boundary_notes: Minimal means inclusion-minimal, not a subsystem of smallest possible cardinality.
Redundant duplicates cannot both be indispensable members of the same minimal infeasible subsystem.

children.title: Polyhedral Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Residual, distance, and growth relationships specific to polyhedral systems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\ne\varnothing\). Fix norms and define \(r(x):=\bigl((Ax-b)_+,Cx-d\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global finite-dimensional error bounds for a fixed feasible linear equality-inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral error bound for \(P\) is an inequality \[\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H\,\|r(x)\|\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n,\] where \(H<\infty\) depends on the coefficient matrices and chosen norms but not on \(x\). The least admissible constant is the error-bound modulus \[H_*:=\sup_{x\notin P}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,P)}{\|r(x)\|}.\] A local polyhedral error bound replaces all \(x\) by points in a specified neighborhood. For a fixed finite linear system, the canonical Hoffman property is the existence of a finite global modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral error bound controls the distance from any point to a nonempty polyhedral feasible set by a norm of its violated inequalities and equality residuals. A global bound uses one finite constant for every point. The smallest such constant is the supremum of the distance-to-residual ratio outside the feasible set. A local bound restricts the points to a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_*:=\sup_{x\notin P}\operatorname{dist}(x,P)/\|r(x)\|<\infty\), and every \(H\ge H_*\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H\|r(x)\|\) for all \(x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The solution mapping \(S(u,v):=\{x:Ax\le b+u,\ Cx=d+v\}\) has a Lipschitz-type inverse estimate at the unperturbed right-hand side.
The residual mapping \(R(x):=(Ax-b,Cx-d)+(\mathbb R_-^m\times\{0\})\) is globally metrically subregular at \(0\).
special_cases_latex: For inequalities only, \(r(x)=(Ax-b)_+\).
For equalities only, the estimate reduces to distance from \(x\) to \(\{z:Cz=d\}\) controlled by \(\|Cx-d\|\), provided the affine set is nonempty.
immediate_consequences_latex: A sequence with residual converging to zero has distance to \(P\) converging to zero.
Residual tolerances translate directly into geometric feasibility tolerances through \(H\).
boundary_notes: The feasible-set nonemptiness assumption is essential because distance to the empty set is not finite.
The modulus depends on norms and representation; adding or rescaling constraints changes the residual and may change the constant.
review_flags: No inspected locator supports the exact equality-inequality Hoffman formulation.
The claimed global scope and dependence of the modulus require authoritative evidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral residual error bound

children.title: Hoffman Error-Bound Family

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Hoffman Modulus
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal Hoffman modulus is the least constant converting the constraint residual globally into distance to the feasible polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\ne\varnothing\), define \[H_*(A,C,b,d):=\inf\left\{H\ge0:\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H\left\|((Ax-b)_+,Cx-d)\right\|\ \forall x\in\mathbb R^n\right\}.\] The Hoffman theorem states that this modulus is finite.
assumptions_latex: The residual and distance norms are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_*(A,C,b,d)<+\infty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least global residual-to-distance constant for a fixed consistent mixed linear system and fixed norms.

notation.meaning: Least valid global Hoffman constant for the displayed system and norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Consistency Boundary for the Distance-to-Feasibility Form
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an empty feasible set, infinite point-to-set distance cannot be bounded by a finite linear-system residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\varnothing)=+\infty\), no finite \(H\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H\|((Ax-b)_+,Cx-d)\|\), because the residual is finite for every finite \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No finite Hoffman constant exists in the ordinary distance-to-feasibility formulation.}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the ordinary point-to-feasible-set formulation for an inconsistent system.

assumptions_latex: Fixed norms are used on all finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(H<\infty\) such that \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\leq H\|((Ax-b)_+,Cx-d)\|\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Distance induced by the chosen norm.
Hoffman constant depending on the matrices and norms.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global error bound for mixed linear equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a constant \(H\geq0\), depending only on \(A\), \(C\), and the selected norms, such that every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\leq H\left\|\big((Ax-b)_+,\,Cx-d\big)\right\|.\] Consequently, the distance to the nonempty polyhedron \(P\) is controlled globally by the magnitude of the violated inequalities and equality residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a consistent finite linear system, distance to feasibility is globally bounded by a constant times its constraint residual.

children.title: Weak Sharp Minima for Polyhedral Problems
children.top_down_role: Objective-growth geometry around polyhedral solution sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Growth Is Not Weak Sharpness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic objective is too flat near its minimizer to satisfy a positive linear weak-sharp bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^2\), the minimizer set is \(S=\{0\}\), but no \(\alpha>0\) satisfies \(x^2\ge\alpha|x|\) for all sufficiently small nonzero \(x\). Thus this convex nonpolyhedral objective does not have weak sharp minima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\alpha>0:\ f(x)-\min f\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\quad\forall x.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that convexity and attainment alone do not imply linear objective growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Sharp Minima for Polyhedral Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global weak-sharp growth for minimizing a polyhedral convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and polyhedral convex. Suppose \(g^*:=\inf g\) is finite and \(S:=\operatorname*{argmin}g\neq\varnothing\). Then there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that
\[
g(x)\ge g^*+\alpha\,\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\qquad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}g.
\]
Consequently, the objective residual globally bounds distance to the solution set: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le \alpha^{-1}(g(x)-g^*)\). This includes minimizing a polyhedral convex objective over a polyhedron by absorbing the feasible-set indicator into \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral convex problem with a nonempty solution set has linear objective growth away from that set, so objective residual globally bounds distance to optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and polyhedral convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\alpha>0\;\forall x\in\operatorname{dom}g:\ g(x)-g^*\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\).

notation.meaning: The set of global minimizers of g.
Euclidean distance from x to S.

knowledge_statements.source_title: Weak Sharp Minima for Polyhedral Problems
knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), let \(f^*:=\inf_{xi X}f(x)\), and let \(S:=\operatorname{argmin}_{xi X}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional optimization; the polyhedral regime takes both the feasible set and the objective epigraph to be polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The solution set \(S\) is a set of weak sharp minima of order one with modulus \(\alpha>0\) when \[f(x)-f^*\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\qquad\text{for every }xi X.\] The weak-sharpness modulus is \[\alpha_*:=\inf_{xi X\setminus S}\frac{f(x)-f^*}{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}.\] Thus global weak sharpness is equivalent to \(\alpha_*>0\). A local version requires the inequality only for \(x\) in a neighborhood of \(S\). For a polyhedral problem, this definition applies when \(X\) is polyhedral and \(f\) is a proper polyhedral convex function on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty solution set is weakly sharp when objective suboptimality grows at least linearly with distance from that set. The largest possible growth coefficient is the infimum of the objective-gap to distance ratio over nonsolutions. Positive modulus gives global weak sharpness; restricting the inequality to a neighborhood gives local weak sharpness. In a polyhedral problem, the feasible set and objective epigraph have finite polyhedral representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is globally weakly sharp}\iff\alpha_*:=\inf_{xi X\setminus S}(f(x)-f^*)/\operatorname{dist}(x,S)>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For any \(0<\alpha\le\alpha_*\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\alpha^{-1}(f(x)-f^*)\) for all \(xi X\).
The objective gap is a global error-bound residual for the solution set.
special_cases_latex: For a linear program, \(f(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x\) on a polyhedral feasible set.
For unconstrained polyhedral convex minimization, take \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and polyhedral \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An objective-gap tolerance \(f(x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) implies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\varepsilon/\alpha\).
Every point outside \(S\) has strictly positive objective gap when a positive global modulus exists.
boundary_notes: Weak sharpness does not require the minimizer to be unique.
This order-one definition differs from quadratic growth, which uses \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)^2\).
review_flags: No inspected source locator supports this exact weak-sharpness definition and polyhedral specialization.
The assertion that a given polyhedral problem has positive modulus is not made without evidence.

children.title: Piecewise-Polyhedral Regularity Principles
children.top_down_role: Local residual stability of piecewise-polyhedral mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedral Failure of Linear Residual Control
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smooth mapping x ↦ x² has no linear residual error bound at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\{x^2\}\) at \((0,0)\), one has \(F^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\), while metric subregularity would require \(|x|\le\kappa x^2\) near zero, which fails for every finite \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is not metrically subregular at }(0,0).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar example showing that smoothness alone does not imply metric subregularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Polyhedral Multifunction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is piecewise polyhedral when its graph is a finite union of convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multifunction \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) is piecewise polyhedral when \(\operatorname{gph}F=\bigcup_{i=1}^N Q_i\) for finitely many convex polyhedra \(Q_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{gph}F=\bigcup_{i=1}^N Q_i\quad\text{with each }Q_i\text{ a convex polyhedron}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional graph class used by the local regularity principle.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Calmness Form of Metric Subregularity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction's local residual error bound is equivalent to calmness of its inverse solution map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is equivalent to calmness of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x)\): there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\kappa\ge0\) such that \[F^{-1}(y)\cap U\subseteq F^{-1}(\bar y)+\kappa\|y-\bar y\|\mathbb B\qquad(y\in V).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is metrically subregular at }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff F^{-1}\text{ is calm at }(\bar y,\bar x).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent inverse-map formulation of the local residual estimate.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Polyhedral Regularity Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric subregularity of finite-dimensional piecewise-polyhedral multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) have a graph that is the union of finitely many convex polyhedra, and fix \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Then there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa\ge0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\le \kappa\,\operatorname{dist}(\bar y,F(x))\qquad(x\in U),
\]
with the right side interpreted as \(+\infty\) when \(F(x)=\varnothing\). Thus every piecewise-polyhedral multifunction is metrically subregular at each point of its graph; equivalently, its inverse is calm there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-dimensional piecewise-polyhedral multifunction has a local error bound: distance to a fixed inverse image is controlled by the corresponding residual.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is a finite union of convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: The graph of the multifunction F.
The inverse image of the fixed value y-bar.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local stability properties of polyhedral multifunctions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^nightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) have a polyhedral or finite-union-of-polyhedra graph, and let \((\bar x,\bar y)i\operatorname{gph}F\). Let \(\mathbb B\) denote the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local Lipschitzian stability, distinguishing calmness from the Aubin property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is calm at \((\bar x,\bar y) when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(Li[0,infty)\) such that \[F(x)
 V
i F(ar x)+L\|x-ar x\|\mathbb B\qquad(xi U).\] It has the Aubin property at \((\bar x,\bar y) when there are such \(U,V,L\) satisfying \[F(x_1)
 V
i F(x_2)+L\|x_1-x_2\|\mathbb Bi\qquad(x_1,x_2i U).\] Polyhedral mapping stability is the study of these finite-modulus properties as consequences of a polyhedral graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness bounds values near a reference output at a perturbed input by the reference fiber plus a linear displacement radius. The Aubin property is stronger: it compares nearby localized fibers at any two nearby inputs. Polyhedral mapping stability concerns when finite moduli for these properties follow from polyhedral or piecewise-polyhedral graph structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Calmness is defined by \(F(x)\cap V\subseteq F(\bar x)+L\|x-ar x\|\mathbb B\); the Aubin property is defined by \(F(x_1)\cap V\subseteq F(x_2)+L\|x_1-x_2\|\mathbb B\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Calmness of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y) is metric subregularity of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x) under the standard localized conventions.
The Aubin property of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y) is metric regularity of \(F^{-1}\) at \((\bar y,\bar x).
special_cases_latex: For a single-valued map, the Aubin inclusion reduces locally to ordinary Lipschitz continuity.
A constant polyhedral multifunction is calm and has the Aubin property with modulus \(0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The Aubin property implies calmness at the same graph point.
Finite stability moduli convert parameter perturbations into linear bounds on localized solution displacement.
boundary_notes: A polyhedral graph alone does not make every inverse or localization globally Lipschitz with one universal modulus.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Lipschitz Stability Does Not Imply Single-Valuedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral multifunction can be upper Lipschitz with modulus zero while having many values at every parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=C\), where \(C\) is a non-singleton convex polyhedron. Then \(\operatorname{gph}F=\mathbb R^n\times C\) is convex polyhedral and \(F(x)\subseteq F(\bar x)+0\|x-\bar x\|\mathbb B\) for all \(x\), although \(F\) is nowhere single-valued.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a non-singleton convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is upper Lipschitz with }L=0\text{ but is not single-valued}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarifies the exact strength of Robinson's set-valued inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Robinson Polyhedral Multifunction Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robinson's finite-dimensional upper-Lipschitz property, stated as calmness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) be a polyhedral multifunction, meaning that \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is a finite union of convex polyhedra. For every \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(L\ge0\), such that
\[
F(x)\cap V\subset F(\bar x)+L\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\mathbb{B}
\qquad(x\in U).
\]
Hence \(F\) is calm, also called upper Lipschitz continuous, at every graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional polyhedral multifunction is locally upper Lipschitz at every graph point: nearby localized values remain within a linear enlargement of the reference value set.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is a finite union of convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)\cap V\subset F(\bar x)+L\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\mathbb{B}\) locally around \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Solution Maps Need Not Be Single-Valued or Bounded
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral optimizer map can have an unbounded continuum of solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If there are no effective constraints and \(c=0\), the linear program minimizes zero over \(\mathbb R^n\), so \(S(b,0)=\mathbb R^n\). Piecewise-polyhedral graph structure alone therefore implies neither single-valuedness nor local boundedness of the solution map.
assumptions_latex: The objective is identically zero and there are no effective constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Values and Closed Graph
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each optimizer set is empty or a closed convex polyhedron, and the full parameter-solution graph is closed and piecewise polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S(b,c)=\operatorname*{argmin}\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b\}\) with fixed \(A\), every value \(S(b,c)\) is empty or a closed convex polyhedron. The finite active-set representation also makes \(\operatorname{gph}S\) a closed finite union of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(b,c)\text{ is empty or a closed convex polyhedron, and }\operatorname{gph}S\text{ is closed and piecewise polyhedral}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequences of the immutable seed's finite active-set graph representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Solution Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbed minimizers represented through a polyhedral subdifferential inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and polyhedral convex. Define the tilted solution map by
\[
S(p):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\varphi(x)-\langle p,x\rangle\}.
\]
For every \((p,x)\), Fermat's condition gives
\[
x\in S(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\in\partial\varphi(x),
\]
so \(S=(\partial\varphi)^{-1}\). The graph of \(\partial\varphi\), and therefore the graph of \(S\), is a finite union of convex polyhedra. Thus \(S\) is a piecewise-polyhedral multifunction of the perturbation \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimizer map for linear perturbations of a polyhedral convex function is the inverse subdifferential and has a graph formed from finitely many polyhedra.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and polyhedral convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=(\partial\varphi)^{-1}\) and \(\operatorname{gph}S\) is a finite union of convex polyhedra.

notation.meaning: The solution set under linear perturbation p.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical region of a parametric polyhedral problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(pi\mathcal P
i\mathbb R^k\) parameterize a finite-dimensional linear or polyhedral optimization problem. Let \(S(p) be its solution set and \(I(p,x) the active-constraint index set at a feasible pair \((p,x).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polyhedral parameter partitions on which an active face and associated solution formula remain invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A critical region is a maximal connected polyhedron \(R
i\mathcal P\) for which there exist a fixed active index set \(I\), a fixed optimal face type, and matrices \(K\), \(k\) such that, for every \(pi\operatorname{ri}R\), the designated solution selection satisfies \(x(p)=Kp+k\), remains feasible and optimal, and has active set \(I(p,x(p))=I\). Critical-region stability at \(\bar pi\operatorname{ri}R\) means that some neighborhood of \(\bar p\) relative to \(\mathcal P\) lies in \(R\), so the active structure and affine solution formula persist there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical region is a maximal connected polyhedral parameter cell on whose relative interior a chosen optimizer is affine and has one fixed active-constraint pattern and optimal face type. A reference parameter is critically stable when it lies in the relative interior of such a cell, ensuring that sufficiently small admissible perturbations preserve the same structural regime and affine formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(pi\operatorname{ri}R\), \(x(p)=Kp+k\), \(x(p) is feasible and optimal, and \(I(p,x(p))=I\); if \(\bar pi\operatorname{ri}R\), these properties persist on a relative neighborhood of \(\bar p\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A critical region can be described by the parameter inequalities obtained after substituting \(x(p)=Kp+k\) into primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and the fixed active-set conditions.
Critical-region stability is local constancy of the active regime together with affine dependence of the selected solution.
special_cases_latex: For a nondegenerate multiparametric linear program with a fixed optimal basis, the basic solution is affine in the parameter on its basis-feasibility region.
For a strictly convex multiparametric quadratic program with affine parameter dependence, the optimizer is unique and piecewise affine under standard regularity conditions.
immediate_consequences_latex: The selected solution is Lipschitz on each critical region with modulus bounded by the operator norm of \(K\).
Structural changes can occur only when the parameter crosses a region boundary or encounters degeneracy.
boundary_notes: At a region boundary, several active regimes may be valid and the active set need not be locally constant.
Without uniqueness or a prescribed selection, the entire solution set need not equal one affine graph on a region.

Finite Critical-Region Cover and Piecewise-Affine Optimizer
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finitely many polyhedral critical regions cover the feasible parameter set, with a continuous affine optimizer formula on each region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P=\{p:\exists x,\ Ax\le b+Ep\}\). Under \(Q\succ0\), every \(p\in\mathcal P\) has a unique optimizer. The finitely many nonempty regions obtained from linearly independent KKT active subsets cover \(\mathcal P\), and \(p\mapsto x^*(p)\) is continuous and piecewise affine on this finite polyhedral cover.
assumptions_latex: The objective and constraints depend affinely on the parameter as in the immutable seed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P=\bigcup_I\mathcal R_I,\qquad p\mapsto x^*(p)\text{ is continuous and piecewise affine on }\mathcal P.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global assembly of active-set regions for the strictly convex multiparametric quadratic program in the immutable seed.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Region Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral parameter regions for a strictly convex multiparametric quadratic program with a fixed linearly independent active set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,q,r\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric with \(Q\succ0\), and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(F\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^r\), and \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times q}\). For \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^q\), consider
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+(c+F\theta)^{\mathsf T}x
\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax\le b+E\theta.
\]
Fix \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(A_I\) has full row rank. The KKT system
\[
\begin{pmatrix}Q&A_I^{\mathsf T}\\A_I&0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x_I(\theta)\\\lambda_I(\theta)\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}-c-F\theta\\b_I+E_I\theta\end{pmatrix}
\]
has a unique solution affine in \(\theta\). Define
\[
\mathcal R_I:=\{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^q:A_{I^c}x_I(\theta)\le b_{I^c}+E_{I^c}\theta,\ \lambda_I(\theta)\ge0\}.
\]
Then \(\mathcal R_I\) is a polyhedron, and \(x_I(\theta)\) is the unique optimizer for every \(\theta\in\mathcal R_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly convex multiparametric quadratic program, a fixed linearly independent active set produces affine primal and multiplier formulas. The parameters for which these formulas satisfy primal and dual feasibility form a polyhedron, and the primal formula is the unique optimizer throughout that region.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric and positive definite.
All decision and parameter spaces are finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R_I\) is polyhedral and \(x^*(\theta)=x_I(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\in\mathcal R_I\).

notation.meaning: The critical region associated with the index set I.
The affine primal and active-multiplier solution of the fixed-active-set KKT system.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Persistence at a Zero Multiplier
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a zero active multiplier, arbitrarily small perturbations can make the constraint enter or leave the active set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x\tfrac12x^2-px\) subject to \(x\ge0\). Its unique solution is \(x(p)=\max\{p,0\}\). At \(p=0\), the constraint is active with zero multiplier; it is active for \(p<0\) and inactive for \(p>0\). The reference active set therefore persists on no neighborhood of zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: I(p)\text{ is not locally constant at }p=0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional parametric quadratic program exhibiting an active-set change when strict complementarity fails.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Persistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict primal and dual margins ensure local persistence of an active set in a strictly convex multiparametric quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric with \(Q\succ0\), and consider, for \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^q\),
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+(c+F\theta)^{\mathsf T}x
\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax\le b+E\theta,
\]
where all remaining matrices and vectors have compatible finite dimensions. Fix \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\) such that \(A_I\) has full row rank, and let \(x_I(\theta)\) and \(\lambda_I(\theta)\) be the affine solution of the corresponding equality-constrained KKT system. Suppose that, at \(\bar\theta\in\mathbb{R}^q\),
\[
A_jx_I(\bar\theta)<b_j+E_j\bar\theta\quad(j\notin I),
\qquad
\lambda_i(\bar\theta)>0\quad(i\in I).
\]
Then there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar\theta\) such that, for every \(\theta\in U\), the unique optimizer is \(x_I(\theta)\) and its active constraint set is exactly \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly convex multiparametric quadratic program, strict inactive-constraint slacks and strictly positive active multipliers at a reference parameter persist locally. Hence the same active set and affine optimizer formula remain valid nearby.
assumptions_latex: At \(\bar\theta\), every constraint outside \(I\) has strict slack and every multiplier indexed by \(I\) is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists U\ni\bar\theta\;\forall\theta\in U:\ \mathcal A(x^*(\theta),\theta)=I\) and \(x^*(\theta)=x_I(\theta)\).

notation.meaning: The active constraint set at x for parameter theta.

Degenerate Simultaneous Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At degenerate interfaces, multiple constraints may change simultaneously and neighboring active-set labels need not differ by one index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If several nonredundant slack or multiplier functions vanish at the same parameter, or if the active normals are dependent, crossing an interface can change several active indices, admit several valid active-set descriptions, or alter multipliers without changing the primal optimizer. knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Region Boundary Equations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical-region interface lies on a zero-slack or zero-multiplier hyperplane arising from a nonredundant region inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal R_I=\{p:s_j^I(p)\ge0\ (j\notin I),\ \lambda_i^I(p)\ge0\ (i\in I)\}\), every relative-boundary point at which a displayed inequality is locally nonredundant satisfies at least one equality \(s_j^I(p)=0\) or \(\lambda_i^I(p)=0\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal{R}_I\) and \(\mathcal{R}_J\) share a facet, then on that facet either an inactive slack reaches zero, \[s_k(p)=b_k+E_kp-A_kx_I(p)=0,\] or an active multiplier reaches zero, \[\lambda_k(p)=0.\] Under nondegeneracy and a transversal crossing, the first event adds \(k\) to the active set, while the second removes \(k\).
