children.title: Incremental Hull Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Progressive hull and facet construction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R^d\), and put \(P_k=\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}\). Assume an initial index \(k_0\) is chosen so that \(P_{k_0}\) has the intended affine dimension and its facets and incidences are available.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional point-set hull construction using facet visibility; lower-dimensional inputs require computation in their affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incremental hull method constructs \(P_{k+1}=\operatorname{conv}(P_k\cup\{a_{k+1}\})\) from a representation of \(P_k\). If \(a_{k+1}\in P_k\), the representation is unchanged. Otherwise, a facet \(F=\{x\in P_k:u_F^Tx=\beta_F\}\), with \(u_F^Tx\le\beta_F\) on \(P_k\), is visible when \(u_F^Ta_{k+1}>\beta_F\). The update deletes visible facets, retains nonvisible facets, and creates facets \(\operatorname{conv}(R\cup\{a_{k+1}\})\) over horizon ridges \(R\), namely ridges incident to both a visible and a nonvisible facet, subject to removal of redundant or coplanar descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incremental hull algorithm inserts points one at a time. At each insertion it either detects that the new point already lies in the current hull or identifies the current facets visible from that point. Visible facets are removed, nonvisible facets remain, and new facets are formed by joining the new point to the horizon ridges separating visible from nonvisible facets. Redundant or coplanar facet descriptions are normalized after the update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_{k+1}=\operatorname{conv}(P_k\cup\{a_{k+1}\}),\qquad \mathcal F_{k+1}=(\mathcal F_k\setminus\mathcal V_k)\cup\{\operatorname{conv}(R\cup\{a_{k+1}\}):R\in\mathcal H_k\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A facet is visible exactly when the new point lies strictly outside its supporting halfspace.
The horizon is the boundary, within the boundary complex of \(P_k\), of the union of visible facets.
special_cases_latex: For \(d=2\), visible edges form a boundary chain and the horizon consists of its two endpoint vertices.
When \(a_{k+1}\in P_k\), \(P_{k+1}=P_k\) and no combinatorial update is required.
immediate_consequences_latex: After all insertions, \(P_m=\operatorname{conv}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}\).
The insertion order changes intermediate hull sizes and work but not the final convex hull.
boundary_notes: Degenerate inputs may create nonsimplicial facets or multiple coplanar supporting facets, so a simplicial-only update rule is not part of this definition.
The definition specifies the update family, not a complexity guarantee for point location, visibility testing, or incidence maintenance.

notation.meaning: Facets of the current hull visible from the inserted point.
Horizon ridges between visible and nonvisible facets.
Facet set or normalized facet representation of the current hull.

review_flags: The supplied sources did not provide an inspectable locator for the incremental visible-facet and horizon-ridge update.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Convex-Hull Construction
Incremental Hull Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build a hull by inserting points, ignoring interior points and replacing the visible boundary by faces joining the new point to the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with an affinely independent subset and its simplex hull \(P_k\). For each remaining point \(x_{k+1}\), first test membership in \(P_k\). If \(x_{k+1}\in P_k\), leave the hull unchanged. Otherwise identify the faces visible from \(x_{k+1}\), remove the visible boundary portion, and join \(x_{k+1}\) to the exposed horizon faces to obtain \(P_{k+1}=\operatorname{conv}(P_k\cup\{x_{k+1}\})\). Stop after every input point has been processed.
assumptions_latex: A valid face representation of \(P_k=\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}\) is maintained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After the last insertion, the maintained representation describes \(\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional incremental convex-hull construction.

notation.meaning: partial convex hull after k insertions

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports incremental hull construction.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The record has the correct algorithmic role and matches incremental hull construction at a high level. The visible-boundary and horizon update, initialization outside the affine hull, and maintained face representation are not supported by a cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Beneath–Beyond Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete facets visible from the new point and cone the new point over each horizon ridge, retaining the nonvisible old facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Classify each facet of \(P\) as visible from \(x\) when \(x\) lies strictly beyond its supporting hyperplane. Let \(\mathcal H_x\) be the ridges incident to both a visible and a nonvisible facet. Delete all facets in \(\mathcal V_x\); for every ridge \(R\in\mathcal H_x\), create the candidate facet \(\operatorname{conv}(R\cup\{x\})\), orient its supporting inequality inward, and discard duplicates or nonfacets. Retain every nonvisible old facet and output the resulting facet set.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is a full-dimensional polytope represented by its facets.
\(x\notin P\) is the next point, and all visibility tests are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The updated facets bound \(\operatorname{conv}(P\cup\{x\})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondegenerate facet-update form of beneath–beyond.

notation.meaning: facets visible from the inserted point

knowledge_statements.title: Insertion-Order Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Point order does not change the final hull, but it can change partial hulls, intermediate face counts, and consequently the algorithm’s work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a permutation \(\pi\) of \(X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\), define \(P_k^{\pi}=\operatorname{conv}\{x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(k)}\}\). Although \(P_n^{\pi}=\operatorname{conv}(X)\) for every \(\pi\), the sequence \(\bigl(f(P_k^{\pi})\bigr)_{k=1}^n\), and hence the number of visibility, adjacency, and face-update operations, need not be permutation invariant. Therefore insertion order is an algorithmic parameter even though it does not affect correctness.
assumptions_latex: A deterministic incremental hull algorithm processes a finite point set \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^d\).
Its intermediate work is determined by the faces of the partial hulls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Different insertion orders can yield different intermediate face counts and running times while producing the same final hull.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of intermediate combinatorics, not of the final convex hull.

notation.meaning: number of faces of a polytope

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports insertion-order sensitivity.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Property is the appropriate content kind for insertion-order sensitivity, and the final hull is plainly permutation invariant. The asserted consequences for visibility, adjacency, face-update counts, and running time depend on the particular incremental algorithm and cost model, neither of which is specified or sourced.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Incremental Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coplanarity and boundary insertions make strict visibility tests ambiguous, so naive updates can lose incidences or duplicate faces unless degeneracy is handled explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x\in\partial P_k\), then \(x\) can lie on supporting hyperplanes of several incident faces without being strictly beyond any of them. Likewise, more than \(d\) input points may lie on one facet, so horizon ridges and candidate facets may be duplicated or non-simplicial. Consequently, an update based only on strict signs can omit incidences or retain duplicate faces. Correct implementations must use exact zero-sign handling together with symbolic perturbation, lexicographic rules, or explicit non-simplicial incidence maintenance.
assumptions_latex: An incremental hull method maintains faces using sidedness and incidence predicates.
The input may contain affine dependencies, coplanar points, or points on existing faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict visible–invisible classification alone is insufficient; degeneracy handling is required for a valid irredundant hull representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for naive incremental face updates under degeneracy.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports degenerate incremental regimes.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Failure_boundary is the correct role for this terminal container. The degeneracy phenomena are plausible, but the claim that strict-sign updates omit incidences or retain duplicates and the listed sufficient resolution strategies require a source specific to degenerate incremental hull algorithms.

children.title: Traversal-Reduction Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Traversal and reduction methods based on bases, orbits, or subproblems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal O\) be a finite set of polyhedral objects to be produced, \(S\) a finite state space, and \(\pi:S\to\mathcal O\) a surjection. Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(S\) identifying states representing the same object, symmetry orbit, basis class, or reduced subproblem.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A unifying exact-enumeration definition for basis traversal, orbit reduction, and decomposition into canonically represented subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A traversal-reduction method consists of a connected state graph \(G_S=(S,E_S)\), a reduction map \(\rho:S\to S\), and a traversal rule such that \(\rho(s)\sim s\), \(\rho(\rho(s))=\rho(s)\), and \(s\sim t\Rightarrow\rho(s)=\rho(t)\). Thus \(R=\rho(S)\) contains exactly one representative of each equivalence class. The algorithm traverses only reduced states, or reduces every generated neighbor before duplicate suppression, and reports \(\pi(r)\) according to a specified output-equivalence rule. Completeness requires that the reduced transition graph induced by \(r\to\rho(t)\) for \(\{r,t\}\in E_S\) reaches every required representative from its root set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A traversal-reduction algorithm explores a graph of bases, orbit representatives, or subproblems while applying an idempotent canonical reduction. Equivalent states must reduce to the same representative, and every representative must remain reachable in the reduced transition graph. Outputs are attached to representatives using an explicit rule so that symmetry or redundant state descriptions do not cause omissions or uncontrolled duplication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\rho(s)\sim s,\quad \rho^2=\rho,\quad s\sim t\Longrightarrow\rho(s)=\rho(t),\quad R=\rho(S)\cong S/{\sim}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The restriction of the quotient map \(S\to S/{\sim}\) to \(R\) is a bijection.
Canonicalization may occur before insertion into a traversal queue or after neighbor generation, provided transitions are interpreted in the reduced graph.
special_cases_latex: For basis traversal, states are feasible bases and \(\sim\) may identify bases defining the same degenerate vertex.
For symmetry reduction, \(\sim\) is membership in the same group orbit and \(\rho\) chooses one canonical orbit representative.
For decomposition, states are subproblems and reduction removes subproblems certified equivalent or dominated under the declared output rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: At most \(|R|\) canonical states need be retained for duplicate suppression.
Completeness is a reachability condition on the reduced graph, not merely on the unreduced state graph.
boundary_notes: A reduction that identifies states with different required outputs is invalid unless the output rule reconstructs the omitted outputs.
The definition supplies no polynomial bound for canonicalization, adjacency generation, or the number of reduced states.

notation.meaning: Map from traversal states to represented polyhedral objects.

review_flags: Traversal-Reduction Algorithm Family is an umbrella label; no inspected source stated this combined basis-orbit-subproblem definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Traversal with Canonical Reduction
Basis-Pivoting Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traverse feasible bases by simplex-style pivots, convert each basis to its basic feasible solution, and deduplicate bases representing the same vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial feasible basis \(B_0\). At a current feasible basis \(B\), enumerate admissible exchanges of one basic and one nonbasic index; solve the associated ratio test and retain exchanges producing feasible adjacent bases. Traverse the resulting basis graph using a visited-set or a canonical parent rule, outputting the basic feasible solution associated with each encountered basis. When degeneracy assigns several bases to the same vertex, identify equal solutions before output. Stop when no unexplored feasible pivot remains.
assumptions_latex: Feasible bases and their adjacent pivots can be enumerated exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pivot traversal enumerates all reachable basic feasible solutions; deduplication maps them to the vertices of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex enumeration through feasible-basis adjacency.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports basis-pivoting enumeration.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind fits Basis-Pivoting Methods. For the mixed equality-and-inequality representation, the record does not define the standard-form basis model, ratio test, or conditions ensuring that the traversed feasible-basis graph covers every vertex. These details cannot be validated without a specific source.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Reduction Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonicalize objects under a finite symmetry group and traverse only unseen orbit representatives, optionally reducing neighbor generation with stabilizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select a seed \(s_0\in S\) and store \(\operatorname{can}(s_0)\). For each stored representative \(s\), generate its adjacent objects, replace every neighbor \(t\) by \(\operatorname{can}(t)\), and enqueue only canonical representatives not previously stored. Stabilizers may be used to generate one neighbor from each stabilizer orbit. Terminate when the queue is empty and output the stored representatives, optionally with orbit sizes \(|\Gamma|/|\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(s)|\).
assumptions_latex: A finite group \(\Gamma\) acts on a finite polyhedral object set \(S\).
The action preserves the adjacency or incidence relation used for traversal.
Orbit equivalence and stabilizers can be computed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method outputs one canonical representative of each \(\Gamma\)-orbit in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit-representative traversal under finite polyhedral symmetry.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports symmetry-reduced enumeration.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and orbit-canonicalization theme fit Symmetry-Reduction Methods. Adjacency preservation alone does not ensure that traversal from one seed reaches every orbit unless the underlying object graph is connected or seeds cover all components. No source is supplied to resolve this missing coverage hypothesis or support the stabilizer reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Decomposition Methods
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve polyhedral tasks cell by cell, glue identical objects across common faces, and remove subdivision-only faces to recover global data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute the required faces, generators, or adjacency data separately on each cell \(P_i\). For every nonempty common face \(P_i\cap P_j\), identify local objects representing the same geometric face or generator and reconcile their incidences. Internal faces belonging only to the subdivision are removed when the desired output concerns \(P\) rather than the complex \(\mathcal C\). Completeness requires that every global object be represented in at least one cell and that all duplicate local representations be identified.
assumptions_latex: A polyhedron \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is expressed as a finite union \(P=\bigcup_{i=1}^m P_i\).
Each cell \(P_i\) is polyhedral and intersections \(P_i\cap P_j\) are common faces or empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Locally computed objects, identified consistently on shared faces, reconstruct the corresponding global objects of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local computation and gluing over a face-to-face polyhedral decomposition.
review_flags: The precise decomposition objective is ambiguous from the node path.
No supplied locator supports the gluing conditions.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Principle is a plausible content kind for the terminal container, but "required" and "global" objects are not fixed, and local faces or generators do not in general become global objects merely by identifying duplicates and removing subdivision-only faces. A task-specific reconstruction criterion and supporting source are needed before the mathematical statement can be determined reliably.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Traversal Architectures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combine decomposition, local adjacency traversals, deterministic boundary ownership, and global canonical keys to enumerate objects without omissions or cross-subproblem duplicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the search into \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\), select a seed for each nonempty subproblem, and run a local adjacency traversal within each \(S_i\). For every encountered object \(s\), compute a global key \(\kappa(s)\); output it only if that key has not appeared in another traversal. Boundary objects generate transfer tasks for adjacent subproblems according to a deterministic ownership rule. Terminate when all local queues and transfer queues are empty. Correctness requires coverage by the subproblems and connectivity of each locally traversed component from its seeds.
assumptions_latex: A finite polyhedral search space has computable local adjacency.
A partition into subproblems and a canonical global identity test are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The architecture enumerates the global objects without omission and suppresses duplicates across local traversals.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic decomposition-plus-traversal enumeration architecture.
review_flags: Hybrid architecture is underspecified by the node path.
No supplied locator supports this algorithmic formulation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits Hybrid Traversal Architectures, but the search objects, subproblem boundaries, transfer relation, ownership rule, and global key are only schematic. The stated coverage and local-connectivity conditions do not by themselves formalize termination or omission-free enumeration, and no source supports this architecture.

children.title: Polyhedral Query-Complexity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Structural diagnostics, encoding models, output sensitivity, and computational failure boundaries.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_query: Schrijver, Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an instance \(I\) encode one or more rational polyhedra in an explicitly declared representation. Let \(L(I)\) be its input encoding length, \(d(I)\) its ambient or affine dimension, and \(K(I)\) the encoding length of a requested output.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact deterministic complexity classification; arithmetic-operation and approximate numerical models must be declared separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral query-complexity specification is a tuple \((\mathcal I,\mathcal R,Q,\mathcal M,\mu)\), where \(\mathcal I\) is an instance class, \(\mathcal R\) its representation scheme, \(Q:\mathcal I\to\mathcal Y\) a decision, search, optimization, counting, enumeration, or conversion query, \(\mathcal M\) a computational model, and \(\mu(I)=(L(I),K(I),d(I),\ldots)\) the size parameters. A complexity classification is meaningful only relative to this tuple: decision and search time are measured against input length and certificate size, whereas enumeration and conversion additionally distinguish preprocessing, delay, total time, output size, and working space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral query-complexity taxonomy fixes the represented instance class, the precise query, the computational model, and all size parameters before assigning a complexity label. It separates decision, search, optimization, counting, enumeration, and representation conversion. For output-producing tasks it records preprocessing, delay, total time, output length, and space, rather than treating input size as the only parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Spec}(Q)=(\mathcal I,\mathcal R,Q,\mathcal M,\mu),\qquad \mu(I)=(L(I),K(I),d(I),\ldots).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Two complexity assertions concern the same formal problem only if their instance domains, accepted encodings, output semantics, and computational models agree.
An enumeration problem can be represented as a map \(Q(I)=(y_1,\ldots,y_{N(I)})\) together with an order-insensitive correctness relation and separate resource measures.
special_cases_latex: A feasibility query has Boolean output and may use a feasible point or infeasibility certificate.
An \(H\)-to-\(V\) conversion query has potentially exponential \(K(I)\), so input-polynomial and output-polynomial time are distinct notions.
immediate_consequences_latex: A polynomial arithmetic-operation count does not by itself imply polynomial bit complexity.
Complexity statements with fixed dimension are not interchangeable with statements in which dimension belongs to the input.
boundary_notes: The taxonomy does not assert that a particular polyhedral query belongs to any complexity class.
Numerical conditioning and tolerance-dependent approximate answers require parameters beyond rational encoding length.

notation.meaning: Bit length of the encoded input instance.
Bit length of the requested explicit output.

children.title: Representation Validation Query Family
children.top_down_role: Decision and simplification tasks for represented polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validation Queries for Explicit Polyhedral Representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P_H=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b,8=Cx=e\}\) be an \(H\)-representation and \(P_V=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L\) a generator representation, where \(L\) is a linear subspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validation and simplification of finite rational representations; approximate equality under floating-point tolerances is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The representation-validation query family consists of decision or search maps that test whether a finite description denotes the claimed polyhedron and whether its entries are necessary. For an inequality \(a_i^Tx\le b_i\), redundancy means \(\{x:A_{-i}x\le b_{-i},Cx=e\}\subseteq\{x:a_i^Tx\le b_i\}\). For a generator \(v\in V\), redundancy means \(\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L=\operatorname{conv}(V\setminus\{v\})+\operatorname{cone}(R)+L\). Cross-representation validation asks whether \(P_H=P_V\), equivalently whether both inclusions hold. A simplification query returns an equivalent description containing no entry redundant under the selected representation semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representation validation covers exact questions about finite inequality, equation, vertex, ray, and lineality descriptions. It tests redundancy by deleting one entry and asking whether the represented set changes, tests equality of two descriptions by mutual containment, and may return an equivalent irredundant description. The semantics must distinguish points, rays, and lineality generators because their deletion criteria differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[a_i^Tx\le b_i\text{ is redundant}\iff P_{H,-i}\subseteq\{x:a_i^Tx\le b_i\},\qquad P_H=P_V\iff(P_H\subseteq P_V\ \wedge\ P_V\subseteq P_H).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: An inequality is redundant exactly when removing it leaves the feasible set unchanged.
For nonempty \(P_{H,-i}\), redundancy of \(a_i^Tx\le b_i\) is equivalent to \(\sup\{a_i^Tx:x\in P_{H,-i}\}\le b_i\), with the extended-value convention.
special_cases_latex: Feasibility validation asks whether the represented polyhedron is empty.
Irredundancy validation returns true precisely when no tested inequality or generator can be removed without changing the represented set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Mutual containment reduces equality validation to two one-sided validation tasks.
A valid simplifier must preserve the represented set, not merely the optimum of one selected objective.
boundary_notes: Duplicate inequalities can both be individually redundant under some deletion conventions; the convention for simultaneous versus individual deletion must be fixed.
Minimal cardinality and irredundancy are different: an irredundant representation need not solve a globally minimal-description problem.

notation.meaning: The inequality system with row i deleted.
Point generators, recession-ray generators, and lineality subspace.

review_flags: No inspected source stated the combined inequality, generator, equality, and simplification query family at a precise locator.
knowledge_statements.title: Validation Queries for Explicit Polyhedral Representations
Polyhedral Membership Queries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check all inequalities in an H-representation, or solve for convex and conic generator coefficients in a V-representation; violations or feasible coefficients are certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\), membership holds exactly when every component of \(Ay-b\) is nonpositive; a row \(i\) with \(a_i^Ty>b_i\) certifies nonmembership. For \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\), membership holds exactly when there exist coefficients \(\lambda_v\geq0\) and \(\mu_r\geq0\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v=1\) and \(y=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vv+\sum_{r\in R}\mu_rr\). Such coefficients certify membership; infeasibility of this linear system certifies nonmembership through a linear-separation certificate.
assumptions_latex: Either an inequality or a generator representation of \(P\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The query returns whether \(y\in P\), with an explicit feasibility or violation certificate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership certificates for inequality and generator representations.
review_flags: Supplied convex-set locator is only indirectly relevant to computational membership certificates.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is an appropriate content kind for this membership-query leaf, and the H- and V-representation membership conditions are mathematically standard. However, the cited locator on outer descriptions of closed convex sets does not specifically support the generator representation or the claimed computational certificates, and "infeasibility ... through a linear-separation certificate" does not state the dual certificate. A source with a specific locator covering polyhedral generator membership and Farkas/separation certificates is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Containment Queries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One polyhedron lies in another exactly when every defining inequality of the latter has maximum value at most its right-hand side over the former.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each inequality \(c_j^{\mathsf T}x\le d_j\) defining \(Q\), solve the linear optimization problem \(\sup\{c_j^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\). Then \[P\subseteq Q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sup_{x\in P}c_j^{\mathsf T}x\le d_j\ \text{ for every }j.\] Thus containment reduces to one linear-programming query per inequality of \(Q\). If \(P=\varnothing\), every inequality passes under the stated convention; if an objective is unbounded above, containment fails.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) and \(Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Cx\le d\}\), with rational data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq Q\iff \sup_{x\in P}c_j^{\mathsf T}x\le d_j\) for every row \(c_j^{\mathsf T}\) of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Containment of two rational polyhedra given by inequality representations.

notation.meaning: The polyhedron whose containment is tested.
Row defining the j-th inequality of Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Redundancy Queries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is redundant exactly when its maximum left-hand side over the other constraints does not exceed its right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inequality \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) is redundant precisely when deleting it does not enlarge the represented set: \[P=P_{-i}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_{-i}\subseteq\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sup_{x\in P_{-i}}a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i.\] Hence redundancy is decided by a linear program over the remaining constraints. Under \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\), an inconsistent remaining system makes the deleted inequality redundant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) is redundant iff \(\sup_{x\in P_{-i}}a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy in a finite inequality representation of a polyhedron.

notation.meaning: System obtained after removing constraint i.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

knowledge_statements.title: Generator Redundancy Queries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point generator is redundant exactly when it is a convex combination of the remaining generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point generator \(v_i\) is redundant when its deletion leaves the convex hull unchanged. Equivalently, \[\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}=\operatorname{conv}\{v_j:j
e i\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v_i=\sum_{j
e i}\lambda_jv_j\] for some coefficients satisfying \(\lambda_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_{j
e i}\lambda_j=1\). Feasibility of these linear equalities and inequalities is therefore a generator-redundancy query.
assumptions_latex: At least one generator remains after deleting \(v_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_i\) is redundant iff \(v_i\in\operatorname{conv}\{v_j:j\ne i\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite point generators of a polytope; ray redundancy requires a separate conic criterion.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural Diagnostics of a Represented Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a rational polyhedron given by a finite \(H\)- or generator representation. Write \(\operatorname{aff}P\) for its affine hull and \(\operatorname{rec}P\) for its recession cone when \(P\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact structural queries used before representation conversion or face enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A geometric diagnostic query is a decision or search map returning one or more intrinsic invariants of \(P\): emptiness; \(\operatorname{aff}P\) and \(\dim P=\dim(\operatorname{aff}P)\); lineality \(\operatorname{lin}P=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P)\); pointedness, defined by \(\operatorname{lin}P=\{0\}\); and boundedness, defined for nonempty \(P\) by \(\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}\). A certificate-producing diagnostic returns data verifying the answer, such as a feasible point, an affine-hull system, a nonzero lineality vector, or a nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A geometric diagnostic query computes or decides structural invariants of a represented polyhedron before conversion or enumeration. The core diagnostics are emptiness, affine hull, affine dimension, recession cone, lineality, pointedness, and boundedness. Search variants return explicit witnesses, such as a feasible point or a nonzero recession or lineality direction, rather than only a Boolean answer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{lin}P=\operatorname{rec}P\cap(-\operatorname{rec}P),\qquad P\text{ pointed}\iff\operatorname{lin}P=\{0\},\qquad P\text{ bounded}\iff\operatorname{rec}P=\{0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For nonempty closed convex \(P\), \(d\in\operatorname{rec}P\) exactly when \(x+td\in P\) for every \(x\in P\) and \(t\ge0\).
A nonempty polyhedron is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^d\) precisely when \(\dim P=d\).
special_cases_latex: For \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), every recession direction satisfies \(Ad\le0\), and every lineality direction satisfies \(Ad=0\).
For a polytope, the recession cone and lineality space are both \(\{0\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A vertex can exist only when the polyhedron is pointed, although pointedness alone does not assert nonemptiness.
Dimension and lineality diagnostics determine whether subsequent computations should be performed in a lower-dimensional quotient or affine hull.
boundary_notes: The recession cone is conventionally diagnosed only after nonemptiness or with an explicitly stated convention for the empty set.
Facial enumeration, representation conversion, and optimization are downstream tasks rather than diagnostic invariants in this definition.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the nonempty polyhedron.
Largest linear subspace contained in the recession cone.

review_flags: Available sources separately support recession and normal-cone notions but not this complete diagnostic-query family at one exact locator.
knowledge_statements.title: Structural Diagnostics of a Represented Polyhedron
Affine-Dimension Queries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine dimension equals the dimension of the span of all differences between feasible points and any fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine hull and affine dimension of \(P\) satisfy \[\operatorname{aff}P=x_0+\operatorname{span}\{x-x_0:x\in P\},\qquad \dim(\operatorname{aff}P)=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-x_0).\] Consequently, an affine-dimension query asks for the rank of the direction space generated by feasible-point differences. Equivalently, the dimension is one less than the maximum number of affinely independent points contained in \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(\operatorname{aff}P)=\dim\operatorname{span}(P-x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine dimension of a nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rational computation from an inequality representation after feasibility has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each row \(a_i^Tx\le b_i\), solve \(\max\{b_i-a_i^Tx:x\in P\}\). The row belongs to \(I_=\) exactly when the optimal value is zero; a positive or unbounded value means it is not universally tight. After collecting \(I_=\), return \(n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{I_=})\). For rational input, polynomial-time linear programming and rational rank computation make this procedure polynomial in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Test each inequality for universal tightness by linear programming, then compute the rank of the universally tight rows.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\text{ has rational binary data}.
Linear-programming calls use exact rational decision criteria.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim P=n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{I_=})\text{ is computable in polynomial bit time}.

notation.meaning: Universally tight row indices found by the LP tests.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Dimension Algorithm for an H-Polyhedron

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided certificate for the claimed affine dimension of a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A claim \(\dim P=r\) is certified by feasible points \(x_0,\ldots,x_r\in P\) that are affinely independent together with valid affine equations \(Cx=d\) for all \(x\in P\) such that \(\operatorname{rank}C=n-r\). The points prove \(\dim P\ge r\), while the equations prove \(P\subseteq\{x:Cx=d\}\) and hence \(\dim P\le r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affinely independent feasible points give a lower bound on dimension, and enough independent valid equations give the matching upper bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim(\operatorname{aff}P)=r.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Affine-Dimension Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Hull from Universally Tight Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine dimension of a nonempty polyhedron supplied by an inequality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), with rows \(a_i^T\), and let \(I_=:=\{i:a_i^Tx=b_i\ \forall x\in P\}\). Then \[\operatorname{aff}P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_{I_=}x=b_{I_=}\},\qquad \dim P=n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{I_=}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull is cut out exactly by the input inequalities that are tight at every feasible point; affine dimension is ambient dimension minus their rank.
assumptions_latex: I_=\text{ indexes the inequalities tight throughout }P.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{aff}P=\{x:A_{I_=}x=b_{I_=}\},\quad \dim P=n-\operatorname{rank}(A_{I_=}).

Lineality-Space Queries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty inequality-defined polyhedron, the lineality space is exactly the null space of its constraint matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The recession cone of \(P\) is \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}\). Its lineality space is \[\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap\bigl(-\operatorname{rec}(P)\bigr)=\{d:Ad=0\}=\ker A.\] Therefore a lineality-space query for an inequality representation reduces to computing a basis of the null space of \(A\); its dimension is \(n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap(-\operatorname{rec}(P))=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lineality of a nonempty polyhedron in inequality form.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Boundedness Queries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty polyhedron is bounded exactly when its recession cone contains only the zero direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedron \(P\) is bounded exactly when it has no nonzero recession direction: \[P\ \text{is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad\le0\}=\{0\}.\] Thus boundedness is a homogeneous linear-feasibility question. For example, it can be tested by deciding whether \(Ad\le0\) admits a nonzero solution after imposing a normalization that excludes \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is bounded iff \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\), equivalently iff \(Ad\le0\) implies \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness of a nonempty polyhedron via its recession cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointedness Queries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty inequality-defined polyhedron is pointed exactly when its constraint matrix has trivial null space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The polyhedron \(P\) is pointed when it contains no affine line. For a nonempty inequality representation, \[P\ \text{is pointed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ker A=\{0\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{rank}(A)=n.\] Hence pointedness can be decided by a rank or null-space computation on the constraint matrix, independently of \(b\), once nonemptiness has been established.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is pointed iff \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\), equivalently iff \(\ker A=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointedness means absence of an affine line in a nonempty polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), let \(x\in P\), and define \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^Tx=b_i\}\). If \(\operatorname{rank}(A_{I(x)})=n\), then \(x\) is a vertex and \(P\) is pointed. Conversely, when \(P\) is pointed, it has a vertex \(x\), and every vertex satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(A_{I(x)})=n\). Thus a feasible point with full-rank active normals is a complete existential certificate of pointedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointedness is certified by a feasible point whose active constraint normals span the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is pointed}\iff \exists x\in P:\operatorname{rank}(A_{I(x)})=n.

children.title: Enumeration-Sensitive Complexity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Complexity viewpoints accounting for potentially large outputs.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an instance \(I\) of encoded length \(L=L(I)\) have a finite output set \(Y(I)=\{y_1,8,\ldots,y_N\}\). Let \(K=K(I)=\sum_{j=1}^N|y_j|\) be the total encoded output length, and let \(T_j\) be the time at which the \(j\)-th distinct output is produced.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite enumeration with explicitly encoded outputs; the chosen output order need not be canonical.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An enumeration algorithm is output-polynomial if its total time is bounded by a polynomial in \(L+K\). It is incremental-polynomial if the time to produce the first \(j\) outputs is bounded by a polynomial in \(L+\sum_{i=1}^j|y_i|\) for every \(1\le j\le N\). It has polynomial delay if preprocessing time, every gap \(T_{j+1}-T_j\), and termination time after the last output are bounded by a polynomial in \(L\). Polynomial-space enumeration additionally requires working storage polynomial in \(L\), excluding the write-only output stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumeration-sensitive complexity measures computation against both input and produced output. Output-polynomial time bounds the whole run by input plus total output length. Incremental-polynomial time bounds every prefix of the run by the input plus that prefix's encoded output. Polynomial delay bounds preprocessing, every inter-output pause, and final termination by an input polynomial. Space is measured separately and normally excludes the write-only output stream.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{\mathrm{total}}\le\operatorname{poly}(L+K),\qquad T_j\le\operatorname{poly}\!\left(L+\sum_{i=1}^j|y_i|\right),\qquad \max_j(T_{j+1}-T_j)\le\operatorname{poly}(L).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Polynomial delay is a uniform input-polynomial bound on the time between consecutive observable enumeration events, including start and termination.
Output-polynomiality permits long delays before an early output when the eventual output is large; polynomial delay does not.
special_cases_latex: If \(N\) and every \(|y_j|\) are polynomial in \(L\), an output-polynomial algorithm is an ordinary polynomial-total-time algorithm.
A reverse-search enumerator can have polynomial space even when \(N\) is exponential, provided local adjacency and parent operations use polynomial space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any explicit enumerator needs at least \(\Omega(K)\) total output-writing time in a bit model.
An exponential number of vertices or facets does not contradict output-polynomial complexity.
boundary_notes: Polynomial total time in \(L\) alone is impossible for explicitly written superpolynomial output.
Duplicate outputs, compressed output, and randomized expected delay require separate semantics not included here.

notation.meaning: Total encoded length of all distinct outputs.
Time at which the j-th distinct output is emitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Output-Sensitive Enumeration Complexity
Input-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Input-sensitive polynomial complexity bounds complete enumeration time only by input length, so it requires polynomially bounded total output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An enumeration algorithm has input-sensitive polynomial total complexity when there is a polynomial \(p\) such that, for every instance \(I\) of encoding length \(N\), it outputs the complete solution family and terminates within \[T(I)\le p(N).\] Because output must be written, this guarantee is possible only on instance classes whose total encoded output length is polynomially bounded in \(N\). The bound does not adapt to the realized number or size of outputs.
assumptions_latex: An enumeration instance has binary encoding length \(N\).
Writing one output object incurs at least its encoded length in time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Input-sensitive total time has the form \(T(I)=O(p(N))\), independently of the realized output size.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total enumeration time measured solely as a function of encoded input size.

notation.meaning: Bit length of the input encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Output-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Output-sensitive complexity measures total running time using both input length and the actual encoded output length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A total-time bound for an enumeration algorithm is output-sensitive when it is expressed in terms of both the input length \(N\) and the realized total output length \(M(I)\): \[T(I)\le f\bigl(N,M(I)\bigr).\] The dependence on \(M(I)\) permits instances with exponentially many or exponentially long outputs. The term output-sensitive alone does not require \(f\) to be polynomial; that stronger requirement is total-polynomial complexity.
assumptions_latex: An instance \(I\) has input length \(N\) and total encoded output length \(M(I)\).
Running time includes the cost of writing all outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An output-sensitive bound is an explicit estimate \(T(I)\le f(N,M(I))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive total running time for finite polyhedral enumeration.

notation.meaning: Total encoded length of the realized output.

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Sensitive Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total-sensitive complexity requires complete enumeration time to be polynomial in the combined input and actual output lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An enumeration algorithm has total-sensitive polynomial complexity if a polynomial \(p\), independent of the instance, satisfies \[T(I)\le p\bigl(N+M(I)\bigr)\] for every input \(I\), where \(T(I)\) includes complete output and termination. This is an output-sensitive polynomial guarantee on aggregate running time; it does not by itself bound preprocessing time or the delay between consecutive outputs.
assumptions_latex: An instance \(I\) has input length \(N\) and total encoded output length \(M(I)\).
The algorithm enumerates every output exactly once and terminates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total-polynomial complexity means \(T(I)\le p(N+M(I))\) for some polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total-polynomial, also called total-sensitive, enumeration complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Delay Enumeration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial delay uniformly bounds preprocessing, every gap between outputs, and final termination by a polynomial in input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An enumeration algorithm has polynomial delay if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that, on every input of length \(N\), the time before the first output, the time between consecutive outputs, and the time from the last output to termination are each at most \(p(N)\). Writing costs are included, so each emitted object must have polynomial encoding length. Polynomial delay does not, without an additional condition, imply polynomial space.
assumptions_latex: An instance has encoding length \(N\) and a finite ordered output sequence.
The cost of writing each output is charged to its adjacent delay interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial delay means every preprocessing, inter-output, and final termination interval is bounded by \(p(N)\) for one polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delay complexity for finite enumeration, including preprocessing and termination.

children.title: Dimension-Parameterized Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity distinctions controlled by whether dimension is fixed.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I\) be a rationally encoded polyhedral instance, let \(L=L(I)\) be its input length, and let \(d=d(I)\) denote an explicitly selected dimension parameter, such as ambient dimension, affine dimension, or codimension.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact parameterized resource bounds; the selected meaning of dimension is part of the problem specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dimension-parameterized complexity statement specifies the dependence of a resource \(T(I)\) on both \(L\) and \(d\). The problem is fixed-parameter tractable with parameter \(d\) when \(T(I)\le f(d)L^c\) for a computable \(f\) and a constant \(c\) independent of \(d\). It is in the slice-wise polynomial or \(\mathrm{XP}\) regime when \(T(I)\le L^{g(d)}\) for a computable \(g\). A fixed-dimension polynomial result means that for every constant \(d_0\), instances with \(d(I)=d_0\) admit a polynomial bound in \(L\), whose degree or coefficient may depend on \(d_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dimension-parameterized analysis records separately how running time depends on encoding length and a chosen notion of dimension. Fixed-parameter tractability permits arbitrary dependence on dimension only as a multiplicative factor, with an input exponent independent of dimension. XP permits the polynomial exponent to depend on dimension. Merely proving polynomial time for every fixed dimension does not by itself establish fixed-parameter tractability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathrm{FPT}:\ T(I)\le f(d(I))L(I)^c,\qquad \mathrm{XP}:\ T(I)\le L(I)^{g(d(I))}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: An \(L^{d+O(1)}\) algorithm is slice-wise polynomial but is not, from that bound alone, fixed-parameter tractable.
A fixed-dimension theorem is a family of input-polynomial bounds indexed by constants \(d_0\).
special_cases_latex: When \(d\) is globally bounded, both FPT and XP bounds reduce to polynomial bounds in \(L\).
Parameterizing by codimension may yield a different classification from parameterizing by ambient dimension.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any claim that suppresses dimension-dependent constants must state whether dimension is fixed or part of the input.
Output-sensitive parameterized enumeration may replace \(L\) by \(L+K\) while retaining the same distinction between \(f(d)(L+K)^c\) and \((L+K)^{g(d)}\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not claim that any particular conversion or enumeration problem is FPT or XP.
Arithmetic-operation bounds require a separate bit-length analysis when the input is rational.

notation.meaning: Declared dimension parameter of instance I.
Computable functions depending only on the parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Dimension and Parameterized Complexity Regimes
Fixed-Dimension Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With dimension fixed, running time is polynomial in input bit length, although constants and exponents may depend arbitrarily on dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral query or computation is polynomial-time in fixed dimension when, for every constant \(d\), there are constants \(C_d>0\) and \(c(d)\ge0\) such that every rational input of bit length \(N\) in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is processed within \[T_d(N)\le C_dN^{c(d)}.\] Both constants may depend arbitrarily on \(d\). Therefore this regime asserts polynomial dependence on \(N\) separately for each fixed dimension and does not by itself give fixed-parameter tractability in \(d\).
assumptions_latex: The ambient dimension \(d\) is fixed independently of the input.
Polyhedral data are rational and represented in binary with total length \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-dimension polynomial complexity has the form \(T_d(N)=O(N^{c(d)})\) for each fixed \(d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical polynomial-time regime with dimension treated as a constant.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Dimension Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When dimension is part of the input, polynomial time requires one polynomial in total input length whose degree does not depend on dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of rational polyhedral instances is polynomial-time solvable in the variable-dimension regime if there are an algorithm and a polynomial \(p\), independent of the dimension \(d\), such that every instance of total binary length \(L\) is solved using at most \(p(L)\) bit operations. A bound \(L^{g(d)}\) with unbounded \(g\) does not establish polynomial-time solvability in this regime, although each fixed-\(d\) restriction has a polynomial bound in \(L\).
assumptions_latex: The input is a rational polyhedral instance represented by a binary string of total length \(L\).
The ambient dimension \(d\) is part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial time in the variable-dimension regime requires a bound \(p(L)\) for one polynomial \(p\) whose degree is independent of \(d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity convention when dimension belongs to the input.

children.title: Rational Bit-Complexity Model
children.top_down_role: Finite-bit representations, exact arithmetic, and certificate size.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Rational Bit Model for Polyhedral Computation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Every rational scalar is stored in reduced form \(q=p/r\), where \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(r\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,r)=1\). Matrices, vectors, polyhedra, and certificates are encoded as finite strings of such integers plus structural metadata.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Turing-style bit complexity for finite rational input and output; unit-cost real arithmetic is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\ell(z)=1+\lceil\log_2(1+|z|)\rceil\) for \(z\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\ell(p/r)=\ell(p)+\ell(r)\) for a reduced rational. The encoding length \(L(I)\) is the sum of scalar lengths and dimension, sign, and incidence metadata. An exact algorithm's time is the number of bit operations on a Turing-equivalent machine, and its space is the maximum number of working bits. It is polynomial-bit-time when both the number of arithmetic operations and all intermediate operand lengths are bounded so that total bit operations are polynomial in \(L(I)+K(I)\). A certificate is polynomial-size when its encoded length is polynomial in \(L(I)\) and exact verification uses polynomially many bit operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rational bit-complexity model stores every rational as a reduced numerator-denominator pair and measures the entire binary encoding. Running time counts bit operations, so large intermediate numerators and denominators matter even if the arithmetic-operation count is small. Explicit output length is included for conversion and enumeration. Certificates must have polynomial binary length and be exactly verifiable in polynomial bit time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\ell(p/r)=\ell(p)+\ell(r),\qquad L(I)=\sum_{q\in I}\ell(q)+\ell(\text{structural data}),\qquad T_{\mathrm{bit}}=\#\text{ bit operations}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Clearing denominators gives an integer encoding only after the bit growth of the common multiplier is included.
A strongly polynomial arithmetic-operation bound and a polynomial bit bound are distinct properties.
special_cases_latex: For integral \(A,b\), the scalar contribution is \(\sum_{ij}\ell(A_{ij})+\sum_i\ell(b_i)\).
A rational feasibility witness has polynomial certificate size only when all numerator and denominator lengths are polynomially bounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: Unit-cost arithmetic on unbounded integers cannot establish polynomial bit complexity.
An output-polynomial conversion bound must count the binary lengths of output coordinates, not only the number of vertices, rays, or facets.
boundary_notes: Floating-point rounding, condition numbers, and approximate feasibility belong to a numerical model outside this definition.
The precise binary serialization may vary by polynomially equivalent conventions, but the convention must be fixed.

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of an integer or reduced rational.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Rational Bit Model for Polyhedral Computation
Rational Input Encoding
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary; total input length includes every coefficient, dimension, constraint count, and matrix structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write each rational coefficient uniquely as \(q=s a/b\), where \(s\in\{-1,1\}\), \(a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(a,b)=1\), with zero encoded separately. Define \(\ell(q)=O(1)+\lceil\log_2(a+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(b+1)\rceil\). For an explicit system \(Ax\le b\), its rational input length \(L\) is the sum of coefficient lengths together with binary encodings of \(m\), \(d\), and the matrix structure. Complexity polynomial in \(L\) is invariant under standard encodings up to polynomial factors.
assumptions_latex: The polyhedron is presented as \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:Ax\le b\}\) with rational data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The input size is the sum of the binary lengths of all encoded coefficients and structural indices.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Arithmetic Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact bit complexity charges rational operations according to operand lengths and requires polynomial control of both operation count and intermediate data size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact-arithmetic bit complexity of an algorithm is the number of Boolean operations required to execute it when integers are stored in binary and rationals are stored as reduced numerator-denominator pairs. Consequently, an arithmetic operation is not assigned unit cost independently of operand size: addition, comparison, multiplication, division, and greatest-common-divisor reduction are charged according to the bit lengths of their operands. A polynomial bit-complexity guarantee must bound both the number of arithmetic steps and the maximum intermediate length \(B\) by polynomials in the input length \(L\) and any explicitly declared output length.
assumptions_latex: Inputs and all required outputs are rational and represented in reduced binary form.
Arithmetic is performed exactly, without rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bit complexity counts Boolean work on operands of their actual, possibly changing, binary lengths.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model cost for exact rational polyhedral computation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Turing bit-complexity model for exact rational computation

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate Coefficient Growth
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Few exact arithmetic steps can still require exponential time and space when intermediate numerators or denominators grow exponentially.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an exact computation, let \(B\) be the maximum binary length of any numerator or denominator appearing in an intermediate value. An arithmetic-operation bound polynomial in \(L\) yields a polynomial bit bound only when the costs of operations on \(B\)-bit operands and the growth of \(B\) are also polynomially controlled. For example, the recurrence \(z_{k+1}=z_k^2\), initialized by \(z_0=2\), performs only \(k\) multiplications but produces an integer having \(2^k+1\) binary digits. Thus unit-cost arithmetic can conceal exponential coefficient growth.
assumptions_latex: An exact algorithm starts from rational input of binary length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomially many arithmetic operations do not imply polynomial bit complexity unless \(B\) is polynomially bounded in \(L\) and required output size.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient growth as the boundary between arithmetic and bit complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Encoding Size
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A usable polyhedral certificate must have polynomial binary length and admit polynomial-time exact verification, not merely exist as a real witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational certificate \(y\) for a polyhedral assertion is polynomially encoded when its canonical binary representation has length \(S\le p(L)\) for some polynomial \(p\), and a deterministic verifier can check the asserted rational equalities, inequalities, and index conditions in time polynomial in \(L+S\). Merely proving that a real-valued witness exists is insufficient: the certificate claim additionally requires a rational witness whose numerators, denominators, number of components, and auxiliary indices have polynomial total length. Certificate size is measured separately from the size of any representation that the certificate validates.
assumptions_latex: A certificate consists of finitely many rational vectors or indices checked by exact arithmetic.
The original instance has binary length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial certificate requires both polynomial verification time and encoding length \(S\le\operatorname{poly}(L)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding requirement for rational polyhedral certificates.

children.title: Representation-Conversion Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial and numerical obstacles to reliable representation conversion.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure Boundary for Explicit Polyhedral Conversion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) map an input representation \(R_{\mathrm{in}}(I)\) of a rational polyhedron to a required explicit output representation \(R_{\mathrm{out}}(I)\). Write \(L(I)\) and \(K(I)\) for their respective bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact explicit representation conversion; compressed, approximate, and oracle outputs define different problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An instance family \(\mathcal F\) lies beyond the input-polynomial representation-conversion boundary when \(K(I)\) is not bounded by any polynomial in \(L(I)\) on \(\mathcal F\); no algorithm writing the full output can then run in time polynomial only in \(L(I)\). A conversion is also outside a claimed exact bit model if its representation semantics omit required lineality or recession data, or if intermediate or output coefficient lengths are not controlled by the stated resource bound. Numerical failure is separately present when a tolerance-based procedure does not guarantee a representation of exactly the same set under the declared input semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conversion failure boundary separates failures caused by unavoidable output size from failures of representation semantics or arithmetic. If a short input can require a superpolynomial explicit output, input-polynomial conversion is impossible because writing the answer already takes too long. Exact conversion also fails when recession or lineality information is lost or when coefficient growth is ignored. Approximate numerical conversion is a different problem unless exact set equality is guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bigl(\forall p\in\mathbb R[t]\ \exists I\in\mathcal F:\ K(I)>p(L(I))\bigr)\Longrightarrow T_C(I)\not\le\operatorname{poly}(L(I))\text{ for every explicit writer }C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The combinatorial output barrier may be expressed using the number of required facets, vertices, or rays when every output item needs at least one encoded bit.
Output-polynomial solvability is not ruled out by a superpolynomial relation between \(K\) and \(L\).
special_cases_latex: An \(H\)-polytope with exponentially many vertices crosses the input-polynomial boundary for explicit \(H\)-to-\(V\) conversion.
For unbounded polyhedra, a point-only output is not a valid generator conversion unless rays and lineality are represented elsewhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: A lower bound from explicit output size does not establish computational hardness beyond output writing.
Exact and floating-point converters cannot be compared without aligning their correctness relations.
boundary_notes: This definition does not identify which concrete polyhedral families exhibit exponential representation gaps.
Degeneracy can increase algorithmic work without necessarily increasing minimal output size and is therefore a separate obstacle.

notation.meaning: Declared input and required output representation schemes.

review_flags: No inspected source provided a precise unified definition of combinatorial, semantic, coefficient-growth, and numerical conversion boundaries.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure Boundary for Explicit Polyhedral Conversion
Combinatorial Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is combinatorially degenerate when more constraints are active than the rank needed to describe its local face; redundant inequalities can create degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in P\), define the active set by \(I(x)=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\}\). The feasible point \(x\) is combinatorially degenerate when the active description contains more constraints than are needed to determine its local face; equivalently, \(|I(x)|>\operatorname{rank}A_{I(x)}\) after equations defining the affine hull are treated consistently. In particular, a full-dimensional polyhedron has a degenerate vertex when more than \(d\) inequalities are active there. Degeneracy is representation-dependent because redundant inequalities can create additional active constraints without changing \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy occurs when the active constraint normals contain redundant local incidence information.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal active-set degeneracy for inequality descriptions.

notation.meaning: active constraint set at a feasible point

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard active-set definition of primal polyhedral degeneracy
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The active-set formulation is representation-dependent and requires a source fixing how affine-hull equations and redundant inequalities are treated. Without that convention, the claimed equivalence is not reliable enough for candidate review.

knowledge_statements.title: Output-Size Explosion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cube has only twice as many inequalities as dimensions but exponentially many vertices, so complete inequality-to-vertex conversion cannot always run in time polynomial only in its input size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_d=[0,1]^d\). Its inequality description consists of the \(2d\) inequalities \(0\le x_i\le 1\) for \(i=1,\ldots,d\), whereas its complete vertex description contains exactly the \(2^d\) vectors in \(\{0,1\}^d\). Therefore, any algorithm required to write every output vertex performs at least \(\Omega(2^d)\) output operations on this family. An explicit inequality-to-vertex conversion cannot consequently have running time polynomial only in the input length for variable \(d\); its complexity guarantee must account for output size or impose an additional restriction such as fixed dimension.
assumptions_latex: The input is the explicit inequality description of the cube \(Q_d=[0,1]^d\).
The required output is a complete explicit list of its vertices, and the ambient dimension \(d\) varies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any conversion algorithm that explicitly emits every vertex requires at least \(\Omega(2^d)\) output operations on this family.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unavoidable output-sensitive boundary for explicit inequality-to-vertex conversion.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit cube family directly establishes exponential output size

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Reliability Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near-zero determinant and residual tests can be misclassified by rounding, corrupting the face lattice unless predicates are certified or sufficiently separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the two-dimensional row vectors \(a_1=(1,0)\) and \(a_2=(1,\varepsilon)\). The determinant deciding their independence equals \(\varepsilon\). If a floating-point evaluation incurs absolute error comparable to \(u\), then for \(|\varepsilon|\lesssim u\) the computed sign may be zero or incorrect. A representation-conversion algorithm using this predicate can consequently merge distinct facets, create spurious incidences, or omit vertices. Reliability therefore requires exact or certified predicates, adaptive precision, or an explicit lower separation bound keeping every decisive nonzero predicate safely above its error bound.
assumptions_latex: Geometric predicates are evaluated using finite-precision floating-point arithmetic.
The conversion procedure branches on signs of determinants or residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without separation bounds or certified arithmetic, sufficiently small perturbations can reverse combinatorial decisions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision failure of combinatorial predicate evaluation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-precision sign tests fail when predicate magnitude approaches rounding error
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The scaled two-dimensional determinant example supports the stated finite-precision failure mechanism, and failure_boundary fits the container. A source is required for the error model and the certified-predicate remedies.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Degenerate Input Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a fixed finite collection of continuous decisive predicates, a nondegenerate input is near-degenerate when its smallest absolute predicate value is positive but below a declared tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite family \(\mathcal{P}\) of continuous determinant, slack, or multiplier predicates whose signs determine the relevant combinatorial decisions. At a parameter value \(t\) for which every decisive predicate is nonzero, define \(\delta(t)=\min_{p\in\mathcal{P}}|p(A(t),b(t))|\). For a declared tolerance \(\tau>0\), the input is near-degenerate when \(0<\delta(t)\le\tau\). It is exactly degenerate relative to \(\mathcal{P}\) when \(p(A(t),b(t))=0\) for at least one decisive predicate \(p\). Along a sequence of nondegenerate inputs with \(\delta(t)\to0\), perturbations of vanishing magnitude can reach a predicate-zero boundary and may change the inferred combinatorial representation.
assumptions_latex: The input is a parameterized rational inequality system \(A(t)x\le b(t)\).
A finite family \(\mathcal{P}\) of real-valued decisive predicates is fixed, and every map \(t\mapsto p(A(t),b(t))\) for \(p\in\mathcal{P}\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nondegenerate input is near-degenerate at tolerance \(\tau>0\) when its minimum absolute decisive-predicate margin satisfies \(0<\delta(t)\le\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Procedure-relative predicate-margin condition for proximity to combinatorial degeneracy.

notation.meaning: fixed finite family of decisive predicates

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P(u)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron depending on data or a parameter \(u\), and let \(f_u:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be an objective whose polyhedral structure is explicitly represented.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A chapter-boundary object connecting polyhedral geometry to optimization models, solution maps, certificates, and sensitivity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedral optimization interface is the set-valued and extended-value map generated by the family \(\inf\{f_u(x):x\in P(u)\}\): \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in P(u)}f_u(x)\) and \(S(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P(u)}f_u(x)\). The interface includes declared geometric data sufficient to express feasibility, recession behavior, optimal faces or active pieces, and exact optimality certificates. Values use the conventions \(v(u)=+\infty\) when \(P(u)=\varnothing\) and \(S(u)=\varnothing\) when the infimum is not attained. The interface does not prescribe a particular optimization algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimization interface packages a polyhedral feasible-set family and a structured objective into its value function and solution mapping. It also specifies which geometric objects carry feasibility, recession, active-set, optimal-face, and certificate information. Empty feasible sets and unattained or unbounded problems use explicit extended-value conventions. The interface describes the mathematical boundary between geometry and optimization algorithms, not an algorithm itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[v(u)=\inf\{f_u(x):x\in P(u)\},\qquad S(u)=\{x\in P(u):f_u(x)=v(u)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the indicator \(\delta_{P(u)}\), the same interface is \(v(u)=\inf_x(f_u+\delta_{P(u)})(x)\) and \(S(u)=\operatorname*{argmin}_x(f_u+\delta_{P(u)})(x)\).
A certificate interface augments \((v,S)\) with a relation \(\mathcal C(u,x,z)\) whose satisfaction declares the status certified by \(z\).
special_cases_latex: Linear optimization uses \(f_u(x)=c(u)^Tx\).
Polyhedral nonsmooth optimization uses a max-affine objective plus a polyhedral indicator.
Parametric optimization permits the right-hand side, objective, or both to depend on \(u\).

Recession diagnostics are required to distinguish a finite optimum from an objective unbounded below.

Smooth nonpolyhedral objectives may be placed over a polyhedral feasible set, but their analytic theory is not supplied by this interface definition.

Set of minimizers at parameter u.
Indicator taking zero on P and positive infinity outside P.
