knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional obstruction to inferring closedness from a lifted conic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define \(P:\mathbb S^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by \(P\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{smallmatrix}\right)=(a,b)\). Then \(P(K)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\), which is not closed; for example, \((1/k,1)\in P(K)\) converges to \((0,1)\notin P(K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection of the two-by-two positive-semidefinite cone is nonclosed, so a closed lifted cone need not produce a closed represented set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ closed}\not\Rightarrow P(K)\text{ closed}.

Conic Form Equivalence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of exact reformulation and strong dual conclusions for conic forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Conic primal-dual algebra guarantees weak duality but not feasibility stability, attainment, or zero gap. A sharp obstruction occurs when the linear image \(A(K)\) is not closed: choosing \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\) makes \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), infeasible although feasible right-hand sides approach \(b\). More generally, conversion to conic form is value- and solution-equivalent only when auxiliary-variable projection exactly reproduces the original feasible set and objective. Without a constraint qualification such as Slater’s condition, strong duality and dual attainment require separate verification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak duality survives generally, but nonclosed cone images, inexact lifted projections, or failed constraint qualifications can destroy equivalence, attainment, or zero gap.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(A\) is linear.
For the exhibited boundary, \(A(K)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\), exact conic feasibility fails at \(b\); without constraint qualification, strong-duality conclusions are unavailable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invertible Conic Reformulations Preserve Primal-Dual Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive equivalence boundary separating coordinate changes from noninvertible lifts and projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:E\to E'\) be a linear isomorphism and \(K'=T(K)\). Replacing \(g(x)\in K\) by \(Tg(x)\in K'\) preserves feasibility, primal attainment, and relative strict feasibility. Multipliers correspond by \(y'^*=T^{-*}y^*\), with \(\langle y'^*,Tg(x)\rangle=\langle y^*,g(x)\rangle\); consequently the associated dual objectives, gaps, dual attainment, and complementarity are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible change of conic coordinates preserves primal and dual behavior; noninvertible lifting or projection need not.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y^*\longleftrightarrow T^{-*}y^*\text{ gives a pairing- and value-preserving primal-dual equivalence}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-Value Equivalence of an Exact Conic Lift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precisely separates primal equivalence from dual and topological equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Z,E\) be finite-dimensional spaces, \(K\subseteq E\) a closed convex cone, \(B:X\to E\) and \(C:Z\to E\) linear, and \(d\in E\). A lift \[L=\{(x,z)\in X\times Z:Bx+Cz-d\in K\}\] with objective \(\widetilde f(x,z)\) is primal-value equivalent to \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\) when \[S=\operatorname{proj}_X L\quad\text{and}\quad \inf\{\widetilde f(x,z):(x,z)\in L\}=\inf_{x\in S}f(x).\] The stronger fiberwise condition \(\widetilde f(x,z)=f(x)\) for every \((x,z)\in L\) guarantees the value identity. Neither condition alone guarantees closedness of \(S\), attainment, Slater regularity, or equivalence of the associated conic duals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact lift preserves projected feasible variables and the primal value, but those identities alone do not preserve closedness, attainment, constraint qualifications, or dual behavior.

\(B:X\to E\) and \(C:Z\to E\) are linear and \(d\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact projection plus objective-value preservation gives primal-value equivalence only; additional regularity is required for topological or dual equivalence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Specialization of the Generic Conic Dual Template
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the generic pair \(\inf\{c^Tx:Ax-b\in K\}\) and \(\sup\{b^Ty:A^Ty=c,\ y\in K^*\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface-level specialization to LP, second-order-cone, and semidefinite models; it does not develop the modeling theory of those classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conic-duality specialization is obtained by selecting a concrete cone and its pairing: \[K=\mathbb R_+^m,\qquad K=\prod_{i=1}^q\mathcal Q_{r_i},\qquad\text{or}\qquad K=\mathbb S_+^r,\] where \(\mathcal Q_r:=\{(u,t):\|u\|_2\leq t\}\) and matrices use \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\). These cones are self-dual, so the dual template retains the same cone type for its multipliers. The resulting pairs are, respectively, linear-programming, second-order-cone, and semidefinite primal–dual representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generic conic dual is specialized by substituting a standard cone and its natural inner product. The nonnegative orthant produces linear programming, a product of Lorentz cones produces second-order-cone programming, and the positive-semidefinite cone with trace pairing produces semidefinite programming. Each listed cone is self-dual, so its dual multipliers have the same structural cone constraint as the primal slacks.
assumptions_latex: The generic conic primal–dual template is expressed using a closed convex cone and its dual.
For the matrix specialization, the ambient space is \(\mathbb S^r\) with trace pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Substitution of \(\mathbb R_+^m\), \(\prod_i\mathcal Q_{r_i}\), or \(\mathbb S_+^r\) yields the LP, SOCP, or SDP dual pair, respectively.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The specialization map replaces the abstract memberships \(s\in K\), \(y\in K^*\) by coordinate inequalities, Lorentz inequalities, or positive-semidefinite inequalities.
special_cases_latex: Products containing different standard cones yield mixed conic formulations, with the dual cone equal to the corresponding product of dual cones.
immediate_consequences_latex: Weak duality has the same slack–multiplier pairing form in all three specializations.
Complementarity becomes coordinatewise products, Lorentz-cone orthogonality, or trace orthogonality.
boundary_notes: Exponential, power, and other nonsymmetric cones require their actual dual cones and are not included in the three-way interface stated here.
Strong-duality hypotheses are not part of this specialization definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Programming Feasibility and Unboundedness Alternatives
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an LP dual pair, feasibility of one side and infeasibility of the other forces the feasible side to be unbounded; both sides can instead be infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
(P)\quad\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},
\qquad
(D)\quad\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le c\}.
\]
If \((P)\) is feasible, then either \((D)\) is feasible and both programs attain a common finite optimum, or \((D)\) is infeasible and \((P)\) is unbounded below. Symmetrically, if \((D)\) is feasible, then either \((P)\) is feasible and both programs attain a common finite optimum, or \((P)\) is infeasible and \((D)\) is unbounded above. Both programs may be infeasible; for example, \(A=[0]\), \(b=1\), and \(c=-1\) give \(0x=1\) in \((P)\) and \(0y\le-1\) in \((D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One-sided feasibility with opposite-side infeasibility forces unboundedness of the feasible side, while simultaneous infeasibility is possible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status alternatives for the equality-form primal and inequality-form dual linear programs.

notation.meaning: The displayed primal and dual linear programs.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Programming Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear programming is conic programming over the self-dual nonnegative orthant; feasible primal and dual programs attain equal optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \((\mathbb R_+^n)^*=\mathbb R_+^n\), the conic pair specializes to
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},
\qquad
\max_{y\in\mathbb R^m}\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le c\}.
\]
For every feasible \(x,y\), weak duality gives \(b^Ty\le c^Tx\). If both programs are feasible, their optimal values are finite, each program has an optimal solution, and the values coincide. A feasible pair \((x,y)\) is optimal exactly when its slack \(s=c-A^Ty\ge0\) satisfies \(x^Ts=0\).
assumptions_latex: Both displayed linear programs are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}=\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le c\}\), and both optima are attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form linear programming as conic duality over the nonnegative orthant.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[

\qquad
(D)\quad\sup\{b^Ty:A^Ty\le c\},

if either problem is feasible with a finite optimal value, both problems attain optimal solutions and their values are equal. If \((P)\) is unbounded below, then \((D)\) is infeasible; if \((D)\) is unbounded above, then \((P)\) is infeasible. Hence, if one problem is feasible and the other infeasible, the feasible problem is unbounded in its optimization direction. Both problems can be infeasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Cone Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order cones are self-dual; two-sided strict feasibility yields equal attained primal and dual values, with complementary cone pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Each Lorentz cone \(Q_n=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n-1}:t\ge\|u\|_2\}\) is self-dual, so a second-order cone program and its dual use the same product cone \(K=\prod_{i=1}^r Q_{n_i}\). For the pair
\[
\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\},
\qquad
\max\{\langle b,y\rangle:c-A^*y\in K\},
\]
if there exist \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}K\) with \(Ax_0=b\) and \(y_0\in F\) with \(c-A^*y_0\in\operatorname{int}K\), then both optima are attained and \(p^*=d^*\). Every optimal feasible triple \((x,y,s)\), with \(s=c-A^*y\), satisfies \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\).
assumptions_latex: For integers \(r\ge1\) and \(n_i\ge1\), let \(E=\prod_{i=1}^r(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n_i-1})\) and \(K=\prod_{i=1}^r Q_{n_i}\), where \(Q_n=\{(t,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{n-1}:t\ge\|u\|_2\}\).
\(F\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(A:E\to F\) is linear, \(b\in F\), and \(c\in E\).
There exist \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}K\) with \(Ax_0=b\) and \(y_0\in F\) with \(c-A^*y_0\in\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=d^*\), both optima are attained, and every optimal feasible triple satisfies \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong duality for finite-dimensional second-order cone programs under two-sided strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise geometric form of complementary slackness for product second-order cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_i=(t_i,u_i)\in Q_{n_i}\) and \(s_i=(\tau_i,v_i)\in Q_{n_i}\). For \(x=(x_i)_i\) and \(s=(s_i)_i\),
\[
\langle x,s\rangle=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle x_i,s_i\rangle=0\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
For each block with \(x_i\ne0\) and \(s_i\ne0\), block complementarity is equivalent to
\[
t_i=\|u_i\|_2>0,
\qquad \tau_i=\|v_i\|_2>0,
\qquad v_i=-\frac{\tau_i}{t_i}u_i.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Product-cone complementarity is blockwise; two nonzero complementary Lorentz vectors are boundary vectors with oppositely directed spatial parts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\) holds exactly blockwise, with antiparallel boundary geometry on every nonzero complementary block.
knowledge_statements.title: Lorentz-Block Complementarity Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Slater Does Not Ensure Primal Attainment in SOCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of same-side attainment under only primal strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Q_3=\{(t,u,v):t\ge\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\}\), the second-order-cone program
\[
\inf\{t-u:(t,u,v)\in Q_3,\ v=1\}
\]

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-semidefinite cone is self-dual; two-sided strict feasibility gives attained strong duality and trace complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the trace inner product, \((\mathbb S_+^n)^*=\mathbb S_+^n\). Hence the semidefinite primal-dual pair is
\[
\min_{X\succeq0}\{\langle C,X\rangle:\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\},
\qquad
\max_{y\in\mathbb R^m}\left\{b^Ty:C-\sum_{i=1}^m y_iA_i\succeq0\right\}.
\]
If the stated primal and dual strictly feasible points exist, both programs attain their optima and \(p^*=d^*\). For every feasible \((X,y,S)\), where \(S=C-\sum_{i=1}^m y_iA_i\), the objective gap equals \(\langle X,S\rangle\ge0\); consequently, feasibility together with \(\langle X,S\rangle=0\) characterizes optimality.
assumptions_latex: There exist \(X_0\succ0\) satisfying \(\langle A_i,X_0\rangle=b_i\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(y_0\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \(C-\sum_{i=1}^m(y_0)_iA_i\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=d^*\), both optima are attained, and every optimal feasible triple satisfies \(\langle X,S\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong duality for equality-form semidefinite programs under two-sided strict feasibility.

notation.meaning: Real symmetric matrices with the trace inner product.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-geometric refinement of trace complementary slackness for positive-semidefinite primal and dual slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X,S\in\mathbb S_+^n\), the following conditions are equivalent:
\[
\operatorname{tr}(XS)=0,
\qquad X^{1/2}SX^{1/2}=0,
\qquad XS=SX=0,
\qquad \operatorname{range}(X)\perp\operatorname{range}(S).
\]
Consequently, a feasible SDP primal-dual pair has zero objective gap exactly when its primal matrix and dual slack have orthogonal ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For PSD matrices, trace complementarity is equivalent to a zero matrix product and orthogonality of their ranges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle X,S\rangle=0\iff XS=0\iff\operatorname{range}(X)\perp\operatorname{range}(S)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semidefinite Primal–Dual Pair under Trace Pairing
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathbb S^r\) be the real symmetric matrices with \(\langle X,Y\rangle:=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\), and let \(\mathbb S_+^r\) be the self-dual positive-semidefinite cone. Set \(\mathcal A x:=\sum_{j=1}^n x_jA_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional semidefinite programming in affine-matrix-inequality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A_1,\ldots,A_n,B\in\mathbb S^r\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), the semidefinite primal–dual pair is \[(P_{\rm sdp})\quad \inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{c^Tx:\mathcal A x-B\succeq0\},\] \[(D_{\rm sdp})\quad \sup_{Y\in\mathbb S^r}\{\operatorname{tr}(BY):\operatorname{tr}(A_jY)=c_j\ (j=1,\ldots,n),\ Y\succeq0\}.\] The adjoint satisfies \(\mathcal A^*Y=(\operatorname{tr}(A_1Y),\ldots,\operatorname{tr}(A_nY))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SDP minimizes a linear function subject to an affine symmetric matrix being positive semidefinite. Under the trace inner product, the positive-semidefinite cone is self-dual. Hence the dual variable is a positive-semidefinite matrix, its trace pairings with the coefficient matrices reproduce the primal objective coefficients, and its trace pairing with the constant matrix is maximized.
assumptions_latex: The matrix space uses the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical dual is \(\sup\{\operatorname{tr}(BY):\mathcal A^*Y=c,\ Y\succeq0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Dual feasibility is \(Y\succeq0\) together with \(\operatorname{tr}(A_jY)=c_j\) for every \(j\).
For feasible \((x,Y)\), the gap is \(\operatorname{tr}(Y(\mathcal A x-B))\).
special_cases_latex: Diagonal coefficient matrices reduce the semidefinite cone constraint to componentwise linear inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: The feasible-pair gap is nonnegative.
Complementarity is \(\operatorname{tr}(YS)=0\) for \(S=\mathcal A x-B\succeq0\); for positive-semidefinite \(S,Y\), this is equivalent to \(SY=YS=0\).
boundary_notes: Strict feasibility or another constraint qualification is needed for standard strong-duality conclusions.
Complex Hermitian SDP uses the Hermitian trace pairing and is outside this real-symmetric formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Value, Dual Value, Gap, and Attainment
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((P)\) be a minimization problem with feasible set \(X\) and objective \(f\), and let \((D)\) be an associated maximization dual with feasible set \(Y\) and objective \(g\). Values lie in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Min-primal/max-dual convention; value equality and attainment are treated as logically separate properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[p^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x),\qquad d^*:=\sup_{y\in Y}g(y).\] When both values are finite, the value duality gap is \(\Delta^*:=p^*-d^*\). The primal value is attained when \(\operatorname{Argmin}_X f:=\{x\in X:f(x)=p^*\}\neq\varnothing\); the dual value is attained when \(\operatorname{Argmax}_Y g:=\{y\in Y:g(y)=d^*\}\neq\varnothing\). Weak duality is \(d^*\leq p^*\), zero value gap is \(p^*=d^*\), and strong duality means zero value gap, with attainment stated separately whenever required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal value is the infimum of the primal objective over its feasible set, and the dual value is the supremum of the dual objective over its feasible set. For finite values, their difference is the value duality gap. Attainment means that a feasible point realizes the relevant infimum or supremum. Weak duality, equality of values, primal attainment, and dual attainment are distinct predicates.
assumptions_latex: \((P)\) is oriented as a minimization problem and \((D)\) as a maximization problem.
The numerical gap \(\Delta^*\) is used only when \(p^*,d^*\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value relation is classified by \(d^*\leq p^*\), the gap \(\Delta^*=p^*-d^*\), and the two independent attainment predicates.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite values, zero gap is \(\Delta^*=0\).
Primal attainment is equivalent to existence of \(x^*\in X\) with \(f(x^*)=p^*\), and dual attainment is analogous.
special_cases_latex: If feasible \(x^*,y^*\) satisfy \(f(x^*)=g(y^*)\) under weak duality, both values are attained and equal.
immediate_consequences_latex: Value equality alone does not imply that either optimal value is attained.
Attainment on one side does not by itself imply attainment on the other side.
boundary_notes: Expressions such as \(+\infty-+\infty\) or \(-\infty-(-\infty)\) are not numerical gaps.
Some literature includes one-sided or two-sided attainment in its definition of strong duality; this record keeps those predicates explicit.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((P)\) minimize \(f(x)\) over \(x\in X\), and let \((D)\) maximize \(g(y)\) over \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the weak-duality relation for a minimization primal and maximization dual; no regularity or attainment hypothesis is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((P),(D)\) satisfies weak duality when \[g(y)\leq f(x)\qquad\forall x\in X,\ \forall y\in Y.\] Consequently, in the extended-real order, \[d^*:=\sup_{y\in Y}g(y)\leq p^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x).\] For the conic pair \(f(x)=c^Tx\), \(g(y)=b^Ty\), \(Ax-b\in K\), \(A^Ty=c\), and \(y\in K^*\), the pointwise inequality is \[c^Tx-b^Ty=\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\geq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak duality means that every feasible dual objective is no larger than every feasible primal objective. Therefore the dual supremum is no larger than the primal infimum. In conic programming, the difference between the two feasible objective values is the pairing of the primal slack with the dual-cone multiplier, which is nonnegative by their cone memberships.
assumptions_latex: \((P)\) is a minimization problem and \((D)\) is a maximization problem.
For the conic formula, \(Ax-b\in K\), \(y\in K^*\), and \(A^Ty=c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(y)\leq f(x)\) for every feasible pair, and hence \(d^*\leq p^*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every dual-feasible point defines a valid lower bound on every primal-feasible objective value.
For finite values, weak duality is equivalent to \(p^*-d^*\geq0\).
special_cases_latex: In LP, the feasible-pair gap is \(y^T(Ax-b)\geq0\) with both vectors componentwise nonnegative.
In SDP, the gap is \(\operatorname{tr}(YS)\geq0\) for \(Y,S\succeq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A feasible pair with equal objective values is primal–dual optimal.
A dual-feasible objective value is an independently checkable lower bound for a primal minimization problem.
boundary_notes: Weak duality does not assert equality of values, feasibility, finiteness, or attainment.
For a maximization primal and minimization dual, the bound orientation is reversed.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Bound Orientations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For primal minimization, dual feasible values are lower bounds and primal feasible values are upper bounds; the directions reverse for primal maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a primal minimization problem and its Lagrange dual maximization problem, weak duality has the orientation
\[
g(y)\le d^*\le p^*\le f(x)
\]
for every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\). Thus each dual-feasible point supplies a lower bound on the primal infimum, while each primal-feasible point supplies an upper bound. If the primal is instead posed as a maximization problem with a dual minimization problem, the orientation reverses: primal-feasible values are lower bounds and dual-feasible values are upper bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(p^*=\inf_{x\in P}f(x)\) is a primal minimization value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(y)\le d^*\le p^*\le f(x)\) for all \(x\in P\) and \(y\in D\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a primal optimization problem have feasible set \(X\) and objective \(f\), and let a dual problem have feasible set \(Y\) and objective \(g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Both conventional orientations are covered explicitly; all comparisons are between feasible objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the min-primal/max-dual orientation, weak dual bounds satisfy \[g(y)\leq f(x)\quad\forall(x,y)\in X\times Y,\qquad \sup_{y\in Y}g(y)\leq\inf_{x\in X}f(x),\] so dual-feasible points give lower bounds. In the max-primal/min-dual orientation, weak dual bounds satisfy \[f(x)\leq g(y)\quad\forall(x,y)\in X\times Y,\qquad \sup_{x\in X}f(x)\leq\inf_{y\in Y}g(y),\] so dual-feasible points give upper bounds. A dual-bound orientation is the chosen one of these two paired order conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a minimization primal with a maximization dual, every dual-feasible value is a lower bound on every primal-feasible value. For a maximization primal with a minimization dual, every dual-feasible value is an upper bound. The term dual bound is therefore incomplete unless the primal and dual optimization orientations are stated.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual feasible sets and objective directions are specified.
The pointwise feasible-pair inequality holds in the selected orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Min/max duality produces certified lower bounds, whereas max/min duality produces certified upper bounds.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Negating both objectives transforms the min/max convention into the max/min convention.
The two conventions express the same order principle after exchanging infimum with negative supremum.
special_cases_latex: A lower-bound certificate \(L\) for \(\inf f\) becomes the upper-bound certificate \(-L\) for \(\sup(-f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The sign of a reported primal–dual gap must match the chosen orientation.
Feasible dual values can be compared with incumbent primal values to form one-sided optimality intervals.
boundary_notes: Mixing formulas from opposite orientations can reverse a valid bound.
Extended-real infeasibility conventions must be handled before interpreting a numerical bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Weak-Duality Gap Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly positive dual lower bound converts the absolute primal–dual gap into a relative primal-suboptimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in P\) and \(y\in D\) be feasible and suppose \(0<g(y)\le p^*\le f(x)\). Then
\[
0\le \frac{f(x)-p^*}{p^*}\le \frac{f(x)-g(y)}{g(y)}.
\]
Consequently, \(f(x)-g(y)\le\varepsilon g(y)\) implies \(f(x)\le(1+\varepsilon)p^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(x\in P\) and \(y\in D\) are primal and dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative primal-objective certification when the dual bound is strictly positive.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Duality Certification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible primal-dual pair with gap at most epsilon certifies that each objective value lies within epsilon of the primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given feasible \(x\in P\) and \(y\in D\), the computable gap \(G(x,y)=f(x)-g(y)\) is nonnegative and certifies
\[
0\le f(x)-p^*\le G(x,y),
\qquad
0\le p^*-g(y)\le G(x,y).
\]
Therefore \(G(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) is a verifiable certificate that \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal in objective value and that \(g(y)\) approximates \(p^*\) within \(\varepsilon\). The certificate uses only primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and evaluation of the two objectives.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in P\) is primal feasible and \(y\in D\) is dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le p^*-g(y)\le f(x)-g(y)\) and \(0\le f(x)-p^*\le f(x)-g(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A posteriori optimality and accuracy certificates from weak duality.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((P)\) minimize \(f\) over \(X\), let \((D)\) maximize \(g\) over \(Y\), and assume weak duality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic exact feasibility certificates and their finite-gap quality measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weak-duality certificate is a dual-feasible point \(\hat y\in Y\) together with its certified bound \(L:=g(\hat y)\), satisfying \[L\leq f(x)\qquad\forall x\in X.\] If a primal-feasible point \(\hat x\in X\) is also supplied, the certificate interval is \[g(\hat y)\leq p^*\leq f(\hat x),\] and its primal–dual certificate gap is \[G(\hat x,\hat y):=f(\hat x)-g(\hat y)\geq0.\] The pair is an \(\varepsilon\)-certificate when \(G(\hat x,\hat y)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible point certifies a global lower bound for a primal minimization problem. When a primal-feasible point is also available, the two objective values bracket the unknown optimum. Their nonnegative difference is the certificate gap. If that difference is at most a prescribed tolerance, the pair certifies that the primal point and dual bound are each within that tolerance of the common bracketed value.
assumptions_latex: Weak duality holds: \(g(y)\leq f(x)\) for all feasible \(x,y\).
For an \(\varepsilon\)-certificate, \(\hat x\in X\), \(\hat y\in Y\), and \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(\hat y)\leq p^*\leq f(\hat x)\), and \(G(\hat x,\hat y)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies an objective bracket of width at most \(\varepsilon\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f(\hat x)-p^*\leq G(\hat x,\hat y)\) and \(p^*-g(\hat y)\leq G(\hat x,\hat y)\).
A zero-gap feasible pair is an exact primal–dual optimality certificate.
special_cases_latex: For a conic pair, \(G(x,y)=\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Either endpoint of the certificate interval is a valid one-sided bound.
A sequence of feasible pairs with gaps converging to zero yields converging objective brackets, even if limit points are not asserted.

A certificate gap is attached to a feasible pair and differs from the optimal-value gap when the pair is suboptimal.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(d^*:=\sup_{y\in Y}g(y)\) be finite values satisfying \(d^*\leq p^*\). Let \(X^*:=\{x\in X:f(x)=p^*\}\) and \(Y^*:=\{y\in Y:g(y)=d^*\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued min-primal/max-dual pairs under weak duality; infeasibility and infinite values are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The duality-gap attainment regime is the tuple \[\mathcal R:=\bigl(\Delta^*,\mathbf 1_{X^*\neq\varnothing},\mathbf 1_{Y^*\neq\varnothing}\bigr),\qquad \Delta^*:=p^*-d^*\geq0.\] Its gap component is either zero or positive, while each attainment component records whether the corresponding extremum is realized. Thus zero gap and positive gap each admit four formal attainment patterns: both sides attain, only the primal attains, only the dual attains, or neither side attains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite primal and dual values under weak duality, a regime is specified by the numerical optimal-value gap and two independent indicators recording primal and dual attainment. Equality of values does not determine attainment, and attainment does not determine equality of values. The classification therefore retains all three pieces of information rather than collapsing them into a single strong-duality label.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite-valued pair belongs to exactly one tuple \((\Delta^*,a_P,a_D)\in[0,\infty)\times\{0,1\}^2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(a_P=1\iff X^*\neq\varnothing\), and \(a_D=1\iff Y^*\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Gap Without an Exact Pair
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible primal-dual gaps can approach zero arbitrarily closely, but no feasible pair realizes zero gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume weak duality, nonempty feasible sets \(P,D\), and \(p^*=d^*=v\in\mathbb R\), with at least one of \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in P}f(x)\) and \(\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in D}g(y)\) empty. Then \[\inf_{(x,y)\in P\times D}\bigl(f(x)-g(y)\bigr)=0,\] and for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there are \(x_\varepsilon\in P\) and \(y_\varepsilon\in D\) such that \[0<f(x_\varepsilon)-g(y_\varepsilon)<\varepsilon.\] No feasible pair has zero objective gap.
assumptions_latex: Weak duality holds: \(g(y)\le f(x)\) for all \((x,y)\in P\times D\).
At least one primal or dual optimizer set is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{P\times D}(f-g)=0,\qquad f(x)-g(y)>0\ \text{for every }(x,y)\in P\times D.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of finite zero gap when at least one optimum is not attained.

notation.meaning: Common finite primal and dual value.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Gap without Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal infimum equals the dual supremum finitely, but the common value is not attained on at least one side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A primal-dual pair is in the zero-gap-without-attainment regime when
\[
-\infty<d^*=p^*<+\infty
\]
but
\[
\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in P}f(x)=\varnothing
\quad\text{or}\quad
\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in D}g(y)=\varnothing.
\]
The equality concerns infimum and supremum values only; it does not assert the existence of a feasible pair whose objectives equal the common value. The regime includes one-sided nonattainment and simultaneous primal-dual nonattainment.
assumptions_latex: At least one of \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in P}f(x)\) and \(\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in D}g(y)\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=d^*\in\mathbb R\) while at least one optimal solution does not exist.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value equality distinguished from existence of primal or dual optimizers.

notation.meaning: Sets of attained primal and dual optimizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Feasible-Gap Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under weak duality, a feasible primal-dual pair with equal finite objectives is exactly a certificate of attained zero-gap optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume weak duality, \(g(y)\le f(x)\) for every \((x,y)\in P\times D\). If \(x\in P\) and \(y\in D\) satisfy \(f(x)=g(y)\in\mathbb R\), then \[f(x)=p^*=d^*=g(y),\] so \(x\) and \(y\) are primal and dual optimizers. Conversely, any attained zero-gap optimal pair has equal objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)=p^*=d^*=g(y),\quad x\in\operatorname{argmin}_{P}f,\quad y\in\operatorname{argmax}_{D}g.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality characterization of the attained zero-gap regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Gap with Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both sides attain finite optimal values, and the attained primal and dual objectives are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A primal-dual pair is in the zero-gap-with-attainment regime when there are \(x^*\in P\) and \(y^*\in D\) such that
\[
f(x^*)=p^*=d^*=g(y^*)\in\mathbb R.
\]
Equivalently, both optimal sets are nonempty and an attained primal-dual optimal pair has objective gap zero.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(D\) are the primal and dual feasible sets, with objectives \(f:P\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:D\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
There exist \(x^*\in P\) and \(y^*\in D\) attaining \(p^*\) and \(d^*\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite strong duality with optimizers on both sides.

notation.meaning: Primal-dual gap at an attained pair.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((P),(D)\) be a min-primal/max-dual pair with finite values \(p^*,d^*\in\mathbb R\) satisfying weak duality \(d^*\leq p^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite positive gaps only; infeasible sides and infinite or undefined gaps are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair is in a nonzero duality-gap regime when \[\Delta^*:=p^*-d^*>0.\] Its attainment subtype is determined independently by \[a_P:=\mathbf1_{\operatorname{Argmin}P\neq\varnothing},\qquad a_D:=\mathbf1_{\operatorname{Argmax}D\neq\varnothing}.\] Hence a finite nonzero-gap regime is recorded as \((\Delta^*,a_P,a_D)\in(0,\infty)\times\{0,1\}^2\). No primal-feasible and dual-feasible pair can have equal objectives in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero duality-gap regime occurs when both optimal values are finite and the primal infimum strictly exceeds the dual supremum. Whether either extremum is attained is separate, so positive-gap problems may be classified by primal and dual attainment indicators. Because every feasible primal objective is at least the primal value and every feasible dual objective is at most the dual value, equal feasible objective values are impossible when the optimal-value gap is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta^*\in(0,\infty)\), with attainment subtype \((a_P,a_D)\in\{0,1\}^2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(\eta>0\) such that \(g(y)\leq f(x)-\eta\) for every feasible pair, with the largest such uniform separation equal to \(\Delta^*\).
Strong duality fails in the value-equality sense.
special_cases_latex: For conic programs satisfying the strict-feasibility and boundedness hypotheses of the conic-duality theorem, this regime is excluded.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every feasible-pair certificate gap is at least \(\Delta^*\).
No zero-gap primal–dual certificate exists.
boundary_notes: A dual-infeasible or primal-unbounded problem is not assigned a finite positive gap by this definition.
Failure of attainment with \(p^*=d^*\) belongs to a zero-gap nonattainment regime, not here.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Finite Duality Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal and dual values are both finite but differ by a strictly positive finite amount, regardless of attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A primal-dual pair has a positive finite duality gap when both optimal values are finite and
\[
0<\Delta:=p^*-d^*<+\infty.
\]
Equivalently, weak duality is strict at the level of optimal values: every dual-feasible objective is bounded above by \(d^*\), every primal-feasible objective is bounded below by \(p^*\), and these best bounds remain separated by the finite amount \(\Delta\). This classification is independent of whether either optimal value is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(p^*=\inf_{x\in P}f(x)\) and \(d^*=\sup_{y\in D}g(y)\) follow the primal-minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite strict separation between primal and dual values under minimization orientation.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Duality Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite duality gap occurs when the defined extended-real difference between the primal and dual values is positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal minimization problem with extended-real value \(p^\star\) and a dual maximization problem with extended-real value \(d^\star\), define \(G=p^\star-d^\star\) whenever this difference is defined. The pair has an infinite duality gap when \(G=+\infty\). Under weak duality, this occurs exactly when either \(p^\star=+\infty\) and \(d^\star<+\infty\), or \(p^\star\in\mathbb R\) and \(d^\star=-\infty\).
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual extended-real optimal values satisfy weak duality: \(d^\star\le p^\star\).
The indeterminate differences \(+\infty-(+\infty)\) and \(-\infty-(-\infty)\) are excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real classification under weak duality.

notation.meaning: Primal and dual extended-real optimal values.
Extended duality gap when the difference is defined.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-to-Infinite Gap Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-to-infinite transition occurs when finite gaps approach a parameter boundary where one primal-dual value separates from the other without finite bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A parameterized primal-dual family undergoes a finite-to-infinite gap transition at \(t_0\) if \(G(t)\) is finite for parameters \(t<t_0\) arbitrarily close to \(t_0\), but \(G(t_0)=+\\infty\). Such a transition requires loss of extended-value boundedness at the boundary: along some sequence \(t_k\\to t_0\), either \(p(t_k)\) ceases to be bounded above while \(d(t_k)\) does not approach \(+\\infty\), or \(d(t_k)\) ceases to be bounded below while \(p(t_k)\) does not approach \(-\\infty\).
assumptions_latex: For every parameter \(t\), weak duality gives \(d(t)\le p(t)\).
The gap \(G(t)=p(t)-d(t)\) is defined in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(t)<+\\infty\) for \(t<t_0\), while \(G(t_0)=+\\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric boundary between finite and infinite gaps.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The asserted sequence condition is not necessary: both values can diverge in the same extended-real direction while their finite differences diverge, and boundary discontinuities provide further counterpatterns. The ordered parameter domain and one-sided approach are also unspecified. A source supporting a precise transition definition and characterization is required.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(d^*:=\sup_{y\in Y}g(y)\) be finite values for a min-primal/max-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued problems; nonattainment is distinguished from infeasibility and unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Primal nonattainment means \[X\neq\varnothing,\quad p^*\in\mathbb R,\quad \{x\in X:f(x)=p^*\}=\varnothing.\] Dual nonattainment means \[Y\neq\varnothing,\quad d^*\in\mathbb R,\quad \{y\in Y:g(y)=d^*\}=\varnothing.\] The primal–dual nonattainment regime is specified by which of these predicates holds: primal-only, dual-only, or two-sided nonattainment. Each may coexist with zero gap \(p^*=d^*\) or, when allowed by the problem class, with a finite positive gap \(p^*>d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite primal value is not attained when the primal feasible set is nonempty but no feasible point realizes its infimum. Dual nonattainment is defined analogously for a finite supremum. The combined regime records whether nonattainment occurs only on the primal side, only on the dual side, or on both. This classification is independent of whether the two finite values are equal.
assumptions_latex: The relevant feasible set is nonempty.
The relevant optimal value is finite.
No feasible point realizes the relevant infimum or supremum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonattainment is the emptiness of the optimizer set despite nonempty feasibility and a finite extremal value, classified separately on the primal and dual sides.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Primal nonattainment means every \(x\in X\) satisfies \(f(x)>p^*\), while a sequence \((x_k)\subseteq X\) exists with \(f(x_k)\to p^*\).
Dual nonattainment means every \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(g(y)<d^*\), while a sequence \((y_k)\subseteq Y\) exists with \(g(y_k)\to d^*\).
special_cases_latex: A strictly feasible, bounded conic primal can fail to attain its infimum even though its dual attains the same value; this is primal-only nonattainment with zero gap.
When both primal and dual strictly satisfy the hypotheses of the standard conic-duality corollary, two-sided attainment holds and all nonattainment regimes are excluded.
immediate_consequences_latex: A finite-valued nonattained problem has optimizing sequences but no optimizer.
Zero value gap does not by itself produce a feasible zero-gap pair if either side fails to attain.
boundary_notes: An empty feasible set is infeasibility, not nonattainment under this definition.
An objective diverging to \(-\infty\) in a minimization problem or \(+\infty\) in a maximization problem is unboundedness, not finite nonattainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal nonattainment means the primal has a finite infimum and feasible minimizing sequences, but no feasible point achieves that infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal problem exhibits primal nonattainment when its feasible set \(X_P\) is nonempty and its finite infimum \(p^\\star=\\inf_{x\\in X_P}f(x)\) is not achieved: \[\\{x\\in X_P:f(x)=p^\\star\\}=\\varnothing.\] Equivalently, every feasible point satisfies \(f(x)>p^\\star\), although there exists a minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subset X_P\) with \(f(x_k)\\to p^\\star\). This condition concerns attainment, independently of whether the dual value equals \(p^\\star\).
assumptions_latex: The primal feasible set \(X_P\) is nonempty.
The primal value \(p^\\star=\\inf_{x\\in X_P}f(x)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\\operatorname{argmin}_{x\\in X_P}f(x)=\\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued primal infimum without a minimizer.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Primal-Dual Optimality Characterizations p. 154

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual nonattainment means the dual has a finite supremum and feasible maximizing sequences, but no dual-feasible point achieves that supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual problem exhibits dual nonattainment when its feasible set \(X_D\) is nonempty and its finite supremum \(d^\\star=\\sup_{y\\in X_D}g(y)\) is not achieved: \[\\{y\\in X_D:g(y)=d^\\star\\}=\\varnothing.\] Equivalently, every dual-feasible point satisfies \(g(y)<d^\\star\), although there exists a maximizing sequence \((y_k)\subset X_D\) with \(g(y_k)\\to d^\\star\). This condition concerns attainment, independently of whether the primal value equals \(d^\\star\).
assumptions_latex: The dual feasible set \(X_D\) is nonempty.
The dual value \(d^\\star=\\sup_{y\\in X_D}g(y)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\\operatorname{argmax}_{y\\in X_D}g(y)=\\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued dual supremum without a maximizer.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Primal-Dual Optimality Characterizations p. 154

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous nonattainment means that both primal and dual optimal values are finite, yet neither problem has an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal-dual pair has simultaneous nonattainment when both finite optimal values exist but neither is achieved: \[p^\\star=\\inf_{x\\in X_P}f(x)\\in\\mathbb R,\\qquad d^\\star=\\sup_{y\\in X_D}g(y)\\in\\mathbb R,\] while \[\\{x\\in X_P:f(x)=p^\\star\\}=\\varnothing,\\qquad \\{y\\in X_D:g(y)=d^\\star\\}=\\varnothing.\] This regime may occur with zero, positive, or otherwise specified finite duality gap; simultaneous nonattainment alone imposes no equality between \(p^\\star\) and \(d^\\star\).
assumptions_latex: Both feasible sets \(X_P\) and \(X_D\) are nonempty.
Both optimal values \(p^\\star\) and \(d^\\star\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\\operatorname{argmin}_{x\\in X_P}f(x)=\\varnothing\) and \(\\operatorname{argmax}_{y\\in X_D}g(y)=\\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neither finite optimal value is attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Attainment Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymmetric regime has a finite optimizer on exactly one side; equality of primal and dual values does not rule this out.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal-dual pair lies in an asymmetric attainment regime when exactly one optimizer set is nonempty: \[(S_P\\ne\\varnothing\\ \\text{and}\\ S_D=\\varnothing)\\quad\\text{or}\\quad(S_P=\\varnothing\\ \\text{and}\\ S_D\\ne\\varnothing).\] Here \(S_P=\\{x\\in X_P:f(x)=p^\\star\\}\) and \(S_D=\\{y\\in X_D:g(y)=d^\\star\\}\), with both values finite. Value equality \(p^\\star=d^\\star\) does not by itself exclude asymmetry, because strong duality concerns optimal values rather than attainment on both sides.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual feasible sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of the primal and dual optimizer sets is empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactly one side attains its finite value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong duality for a primal–dual pair
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(P\) be a minimization problem with extended-real optimal value \(p^*=\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\), and let \(D\) be a maximization dual with value \(d^*=\sup_{y\in Y}G(y)\). The dual construction is assumed to satisfy weak duality: \(G(y)\leq F(x)\) for every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition concerns equality of optimal values. It does not by itself assert feasibility, finiteness, attainment, existence of multipliers, or validity of any particular constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\text{Strong duality holds for }(P,D)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p^*=d^*.\] A strong-duality theorem family is a collection of results giving explicit hypotheses under which this equality holds, possibly together with separately stated primal or dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong duality means that the primal infimum and dual supremum are equal. A strong-duality theorem additionally specifies hypotheses that guarantee this equality; attainment and finiteness are separate assertions unless explicitly included.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If both values are finite, strong duality is equivalent to vanishing optimal duality gap: \[p^*-d^*=0.\]
If the dual value is written as \(q^*=\sup_y q(y)\), the same definition is \[\inf_{x\in X}F(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}q(y).\]
special_cases_latex: For a Lagrangian dual, \(q(y)=\inf_x L(x,y)\), so strong duality is \[\inf_{x\text{ feasible}}F(x)=\sup_{y\text{ dual feasible}}\inf_x L(x,y).\]
Fenchel and conic duality are members of this family after their associated primal and dual value functions are specified.
immediate_consequences_latex: If feasible points \(\bar x,\bar y\) satisfy \(F(\bar x)=G(\bar y)\), weak duality makes both optimal and establishes strong duality.
Strong duality alone permits nonattainment on either side; equality of two unattained finite values still satisfies the definition.
boundary_notes: The equality is interpreted in the extended-real sense only when the adopted duality framework makes that comparison meaningful.
Some authors use “strong duality” for equality plus dual attainment. This record reserves attainment for an additional conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Strong Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this finite-dimensional convex program, a finite primal value and Slater's condition imply equality of the primal and Lagrange-dual values and attainment of the dual optimum, but not necessarily primal attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \[p^\star=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in\mathbb R^n,\ f_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax=b\}\] and its Lagrange dual \[d^\star=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m,\,
u\in\mathbb R^q}g(\lambda,
u),\qquad g(\lambda,
u)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,
u).\] Under the stated finite-dimensional convexity, finiteness, and Slater assumptions, \[p^\star=d^\star,\] and some \((\lambda^\star,
u^\star)\) attains the dual supremum. This theorem does not assert primal attainment.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f_0:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, and each \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), is convex.

The map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^q\), the primal value is finite, and there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\) satisfying \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for every \(i\) and \(A\bar x=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=d^\star\), and the dual supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Slater theorem with dual attainment.

notation.meaning: Lagrangian for multipliers \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\nu\in\mathbb R^q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Rockafellar Duality Does Not Imply Primal Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior qualification, finite value, zero gap, and dual attainment do not guarantee primal attainment; minimizing the exponential with a zero linear map is a counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=e^x\), \(g(z)=0\), and \(A=0\) on one-dimensional Euclidean spaces. Then \(f\) and \(g\) are proper closed convex functions and \(A(\operatorname{ri}\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}\operatorname{dom}g=\{0\}\ne\varnothing\). The primal value is \(\inf_x e^x=0\), but it is not attained. Since \(f^*(0)=0\) and \(g^*=\delta_{\{0\}}\), the Fenchel dual is attained at \(y=0\) with value \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Fenchel–Rockafellar hypotheses hold and the dual maximum is \(0\), while \(\operatorname*{argmin}_x e^x=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp primal-attainment boundary for the finite-dimensional theorem in the seed.

notation.meaning: Indicator of the singleton containing zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Rockafellar Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions in finite dimensions, the relative-interior qualification and a finite primal value imply equality of the Fenchel primal and dual values and attainment of the dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[p^\star=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(f(x)+g(Ax)\bigr)\] and \[d^\star=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^m}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\bigr),\] the stated relative-interior qualification and finiteness of \(p^\star\) imply \[p^\star=d^\star=\max_{y\in\mathbb R^m}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\bigr).\] Thus the Fenchel dual has an optimizer. If a primal minimizer \(x^\star\) exists, primal-dual optimality is equivalent to the existence of a dual optimizer \(y^\star\) satisfying \[-A^*y^\star\in\partial f(x^\star),\qquad y^\star\in\partial g(Ax^\star).\]
assumptions_latex: The functions \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, closed, and convex.

The map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(A(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f))\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\ne\varnothing\), and \(p^\star=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}(f(x)+g(Ax))\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel–Rockafellar theorem with relative-interior qualification and finite primal value.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) and \(\mathcal K\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal K)\), and let \(A:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K\) be bounded linear. Define \(f^*(u)=\sup_x(\langle u,x\rangle-f(x))\) and similarly for \(g^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This record defines the standard convex-composite Fenchel–Rockafellar pair and its strong-duality relation. It does not assert a qualification or attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[p^*=\inf_{x\in\mathcal H}\bigl(f(x)+g(Ax)\bigr),\qquad d^*=\sup_{y\in\mathcal K}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\bigr).\] \[\text{Fenchel--Rockafellar strong duality holds}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p^*=d^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel–Rockafellar primal minimizes a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function plus a convex function composed with a linear map. Its dual maximizes the negative sum of the corresponding conjugates, with the adjoint coupling. Strong duality means equality of these values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_x\bigl(f(x)+g(Ax)\bigr)=\sup_y\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: After replacing \(y\) by \(-y\), an equivalent sign convention is \[\sup_y\bigl(-f^*(A^*y)-g^*(-y)\bigr).\]
For \(A=\operatorname{Id}\), the pair becomes \(\inf_x(f(x)+g(x))\) and \(\sup_y(-f^*(-y)-g^*(y))\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(g=\iota_C\) produces minimization of \(f\) over a closed convex set \(C\).
Taking one function to be an indicator of an affine constraint recovers an equality-constrained Lagrangian dual.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under an appropriate domain qualification, the conjugate identity behind the dual is exact rather than merely lower-semicontinuously closed.
When primal and dual solutions exist, optimality can be expressed through the conjugate equality conditions associated with \(f\) and \(g\).
boundary_notes: The displayed signs are conventional; alternative but equivalent dual formulas arise by changing the dual variable's sign.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, replacing strong-relative-interior conditions by finite-dimensional relative-interior conditions can be invalid.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Slater Does Not Ensure Primal Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated-cone problem can be strictly primal feasible with a finite but unattained primal infimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K=\{(u,v,t)\in\mathbb R^3:u\geq0,\ v\geq0,\ 2uv\geq t^2\}
\]
and consider
\[
\inf\{v:(u,v,t)\in K,\ t=1\}.
\]
This problem is strictly primal feasible and has finite value \(p^\star=0\), but it has no primal optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the displayed closed rotated second-order cone.
The affine constraint is \(t=1\), and the objective is \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem satisfies primal conic Slater and has \(p^\star=0\), but the infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp same-side-attainment boundary for the primal-Slater conic strong-duality theorem.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Slater Conic Strong Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite dual value and relative strict dual feasibility imply zero conic duality gap and primal attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
p^\star=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:x\in K,\ Ax-b\in C\},
\qquad
d^\star=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:y\in C^*,\ c-A^*y\in K^*\},
\]
suppose \(d^\star\) is finite and there exists \(\bar y\in\operatorname{ri}C^*\) such that
\[
c-A^*\bar y\in\operatorname{ri}K^*.
\]
Then \(p^\star=d^\star\), and the primal infimum is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are nonempty closed convex cones.
The dual value is finite and the displayed dual relative-Slater point exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=d^\star\), and some primal-feasible \(x^\star\) attains \(p^\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric dual-relative-strict-feasibility form of finite-dimensional conic strong duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Strong Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this finite-dimensional conic pair under the nonnegative dual-cone convention, relative strict primal feasibility and a finite primal value imply zero gap and dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(K^*=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:\langle z,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}\) and \(C^*=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:\langle y,w\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }w\in C\}\). Consider \[p^\star=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:x\in K,\ Ax-b\in C\}\] and \[d^\star=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:y\in C^*,\ c-A^*y\in K^*\}.\] Under the stated relative strict-feasibility condition and finiteness of \(p^\star\), \[p^\star=d^\star,\] and some dual-feasible \(y^\star\) attains \(d^\star\).
assumptions_latex: The sets \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) are nonempty closed convex cones, \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
The primal value is finite, and there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}K\) such that \(A\bar x-b\in\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=d^\star\), and the dual optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic Slater theorem using the nonnegative dual-cone convention.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative dual cones, defined by \(K^*=\{z:\langle z,x\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }x\in K\}\) and analogously for \(C^*\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper closed convex. Set \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the conjugate conic pair obtained by minimizing a closed convex function over a cone. Linear conic programming is a specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[p^*=\inf_{x\in K}f(x),\qquad d^*=\sup_{y\in K^*}\bigl(-f^*(y)\bigr).\] \[\text{Conic strong duality holds}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p^*=d^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization of a closed proper convex function over a closed convex cone, the conjugate dual maximizes the negative conjugate over the dual cone. Conic strong duality means equality of those two optimal values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\inf_{y\in K^*}f^*(y).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the polar cone \(K^\circ=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\leq0\ \forall x\in K\}\), one may write the dual variable as \(-y\in K^\circ\).
The formulation follows from Fenchel duality by writing the primal objective as \(f+\iota_K\), since \(\iota_K^*\) is the support function of \(K\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=\langle c,x\rangle+\iota_{\{x:Ax=b\}}(x)\), the pair reduces to the usual linear conic primal and dual.
Choosing \(K\) as a nonnegative orthant, second-order cone, or positive-semidefinite cone gives linear, second-order-cone, or semidefinite duality.
immediate_consequences_latex: A relative-interior qualification can guarantee both zero duality gap and dual attainment when the primal value is finite.
The dual cone is closed and convex even if the original cone is not assumed self-dual.
boundary_notes: The sign of the dual cone depends on whether a source uses a polar or positive-dual convention.
Strong duality is distinct from strict feasibility and from complementary slackness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Slater Does Not Ensure Same-Side Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp attainment boundary for the primal-Slater form of conic strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K=\{(u,v,t)\in\mathbb R^3: u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge t^2\}
\]
be the rotated second-order cone, and consider
\[
\inf\{v:(u,v,t)\in K,\ t=1\}.
\]
The point \((1,1,1)\) is strictly feasible because \(2>1\). The infimum equals \(0\), since \((u,v,t)=(1/(2\varepsilon),\varepsilon,1)\) is feasible for every \(\varepsilon>0\), but no feasible point has \(v=0\). Thus primal conic Slater and a finite primal value do not imply primal attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotated-cone program can be strictly primal feasible with finite but unattained primal infimum, so primal Slater guarantees opposite-side attainment only.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the displayed closed convex rotated second-order cone.
The equality constraint is \(t=1\) and the objective is \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\star=0\) is finite but is not attained, despite primal strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(U\) be paired locally convex spaces and let \(F:X\times U\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex perturbation function. Define the value function \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in X}F(x,u)\). For \(u\in U\), the associated conjugate dual value is \(d(u)=v^{**}(u)\), whenever the dual pairing and conjugates are well defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This candidate fixes a perturbational meaning of “stable” and “total.” Terminology varies across duality frameworks, so exact source support is still required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\text{Stable strong duality at }\bar u\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v(\bar u)=v^{**}(\bar u)\in\mathbb R\ \text{ and }\ \partial v(\bar u)\neq\varnothing.\] \[\text{Total strong duality on }U_0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\forall u\in U_0)\;v(u)=v^{**}(u)\ \text{ and the prescribed dual optimum is attained}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable duality at a perturbation means exact primal–dual value equality there together with a supporting dual multiplier. Total duality means that the corresponding equality and stipulated dual attainment hold for every perturbation in a stated parameter set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[v(\bar u)=v^{**}(\bar u),\quad \partial v(\bar u)\neq\varnothing;\qquad (\forall u\in U_0)\ v(u)=v^{**}(u).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The condition \(y\in\partial v(\bar u)\) means \[v(u)\geq v(\bar u)+\langle y,u-\bar u\rangle\quad(\forall u\in U).\]
When the perturbation dual is represented explicitly, a subgradient at \(\bar u\) corresponds to an attained dual multiplier under the adopted sign convention.
special_cases_latex: At \(\bar u=0\), stable duality specializes to the unperturbed primal–dual pair.
If the property holds for every \(u\in U\), it is total on the full perturbation space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Stable duality includes more information than equality at a single value because it records a supporting multiplier.
Total duality implies pointwise zero duality gap throughout its declared parameter set.
boundary_notes: Lower semicontinuity of \(v\) at one point alone need not imply dual attainment.
The terms “stable,” “strongly stable,” and “total” are not uniform across sources; this formulation requires targeted verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable and total perturbational duality
Stable Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable duality means the perturbation value has a supporting hyperplane at the reference parameter, equivalently a subgradient that attains the zero-gap dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex perturbation model \(v(u)=\\inf_x F(x,u)\), stable duality at the unperturbed parameter means that a supporting affine minorant exists at \(u=0\): there is \(y^\\star\) such that \[v(u)\\ge v(0)+\\langle u,y^\\star\\rangle\\qquad\\text{for every }u\\in U.\] Equivalently, \(y^\\star\\in\\partial v(0)\). Fenchel conjugacy then yields \[v(0)=\\sup_{y\\in U^*}\\bigl(-v^*(y)\\bigr)=-v^*(y^\\star),\] so the associated perturbation dual has zero gap and attains its optimum.
assumptions_latex: The perturbation value function \(v:U\\to(-\\infty,+\\infty]\) is proper and convex on a finite-dimensional space.
The unperturbed primal value \(v(0)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stable duality at \(0\) is equivalent to \(\\partial v(0)\\ne\\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation-value formulation in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Total Duality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total duality combines a finite zero duality gap with existence of both a primal optimizer and a dual optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal-dual pair has total duality in the finite-valued attainment sense when \[p^\\star=d^\\star\\in\\mathbb R,\\qquad S_P=\\{x\\in X_P:f(x)=p^\\star\\}\\ne\\varnothing,\\qquad S_D=\\{y\\in X_D:g(y)=d^\\star\\}\\ne\\varnothing.\] Thus total duality combines strong duality with attainment of both optimal values. It is strictly stronger than value equality alone and stronger than one-sided attainment supplied by many constraint qualifications.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual feasible sets are nonempty.
Their optimal values \(p^\\star\) and \(d^\\star\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^\\star=d^\\star\), with nonempty primal and dual optimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero gap with attainment on both sides.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Finite zero gap with bilateral attainment is a precise condition, but “total duality” has multiple established meanings, including properties quantified over families of objectives or perturbations. The cited sections must be inspected or replaced with a source explicitly supporting this local definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-to-Total Duality Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable duality crosses into total duality when the unperturbed primal infimum is attained; without primal attainment, zero gap and a dual certificate are insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the perturbation framework, stable duality follows from \(\\partial v(0)\\ne\\varnothing\), which supplies a dual optimizer and zero gap. The boundary to total duality is primal attainment: \[S(0)=\\{x:F(x,0)=v(0)\\}\\ne\\varnothing.\] Hence stable duality becomes total duality when the unperturbed infimum is also attained. If \(S(0)=\\varnothing\), the pair may retain a supporting dual certificate and exact value equality while failing total duality solely through primal nonattainment.
assumptions_latex: A proper convex perturbation value function \(v\) has finite value \(v(0)\).
Stable duality holds through some \(y^\\star\\in\\partial v(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total duality additionally requires attainment of \(v(0)\) by a primal point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal attainment separates stable from total duality.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Fix a class \(\mathfrak P\) of convex primal–dual instances. For each instance \(\pi\in\mathfrak P\), let \(p^*(\pi)\) and \(d^*(\pi)\) denote its primal and dual values, and let \(Q(\pi)\) be a checkable condition involving domains, generalized interiors, continuity, closedness, or polyhedral structure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is a definition of a qualification route, not a claim that every listed regularity notion is equivalent or necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[Q\text{ is a regularity route to strong duality on }\mathfrak P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (\forall\pi\in\mathfrak P)\;Q(\pi)\Longrightarrow p^*(\pi)=d^*(\pi).\] If the route includes attainment, that additional conclusion must be stated separately as \[Q(\pi)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{Argmax}D_\pi\neq\varnothing\quad\text{or}\quad\operatorname{Argmin}P_\pi\neq\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularity route is a precisely quantified sufficient condition that guarantees equality of primal and dual values for every problem in a declared convex problem class. Any attainment guarantee is an additional part of the route, not implicit in the term regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\forall\pi\in\mathfrak P)\;Q(\pi)\Rightarrow p^*(\pi)=d^*(\pi).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a Fenchel sum, common routes ensure exactness of \((f+g)^*=f^*\square g^*\), which yields the associated value equality.
For perturbation duality, a route may instead guarantee closedness of the value function at the reference perturbation and existence of a supporting functional.
special_cases_latex: Slater strict feasibility is an inequality-constrained route.
Strong-relative-interior, core, continuity-at-a-domain-point, and finite-dimensional relative-interior conditions are alternative routes in suitable function-space settings.
Polyhedral structure can weaken the interiority required of the polyhedral part.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two routes may yield the same value equality while differing in attainment or multiplier boundedness.
Failure of a sufficient route does not establish failure of strong duality.
boundary_notes: A qualification must be tied to a precise problem class; transferring it unchanged between finite- and infinite-dimensional spaces is unsafe.
Necessity is not part of this definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Convex Slater Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary Slater requires a point in the interior of the common domain that satisfies all affine equalities and every convex inequality strictly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the convex program \(\inf\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ Ax=b\}\), the ordinary convex Slater regime is the qualification
\[
\exists\bar x\in\operatorname{int}D\quad\text{such that}\quad A\bar x=b\quad\text{and}\quad f_i(\bar x)<0\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Thus strict feasibility is required for every convex inequality, while affine equalities are imposed exactly.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordinary Slater condition holds precisely when such a strictly feasible \(\bar x\) exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inequality-constrained convex programs with affine equalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior Slater replaces ordinary interior by the relative interior of the common domain while retaining strict inequalities and exact affine equalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Conic Slater Condition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual conic Slater requires a dual multiplier whose slack lies in the interior of the dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic pair
\[
\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\},\qquad
\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:c-A^*y\in K^*\},
\]
the dual conic Slater condition is
\[
\exists\bar y\in\mathbb R^p\quad c-A^*\bar y\in\operatorname{int}K^*.
\]
Equivalently, \((c-\operatorname{range}A^*)\cap\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone and \(\operatorname{int}K^*\neq\varnothing\).
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear, with \(b\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\bar y\in\mathbb R^p\) such that \(c-A^*\bar y\in\operatorname{int}K^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Slater Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic Slater requires the affine feasible set to contain a point in the interior of the primal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the conic primal problem
\[
\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\},
\]
the primal conic Slater condition is
\[
\exists\bar x\in\operatorname{int}K\quad\text{with}\quad A\bar x=b.
\]
Equivalently, the affine feasible space \(\{x:Ax=b\}\) meets the interior of the ordering cone. This is the strict-feasibility qualification paired with the dual constraints \(c-A^*y\in K^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone with nonempty interior.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) is linear, with \(b\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conic Slater holds if and only if the affine constraint intersects \(\operatorname{int}K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Partially Polyhedral Slater Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The refined condition requires strict slack only for nonpolyhedral inequalities; polyhedral inequalities and affine equalities need merely be feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The partially polyhedral Slater condition for \(\inf\{f_0(x):f_i(x)\leq0,\ Ax=b\}\) is
\[
\exists\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D:\quad A\bar x=b,\qquad f_i(\bar x)\leq0\ \text{for }i\in P,\qquad f_i(\bar x)<0\ \text{for }i\in N.
\]
Thus polyhedral inequalities need only be feasible, whereas strict slack is imposed on every nonpolyhedral inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) indexes polyhedral convex inequalities, and \(N=\{1,\ldots,m\}\setminus P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partially polyhedral Slater predicate is feasibility on \(P\), strict feasibility on \(N\), and relative-domain feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Form of the Relative-Interior Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain-difference relative-interior condition is equivalent to the image of the first domain's relative interior meeting the second domain's relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. Then \[0\in\operatorname{ri}\bigl(\operatorname{dom}g-A(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr)\] if and only if \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\cap A\bigl(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\bigr)\ne\varnothing.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper convex functions on finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g-A(\operatorname{dom}f))\iff \operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\cap A(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f))\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional formulation using relative interiors of the two effective domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Qualification Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator-function Fenchel pair has attained zero gap even though zero lies on the relative boundary of its domain difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \(A=I\), \(f=\delta_{(-\infty,0]}\), and \(g=\delta_{\{0\}}\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}g-A(\operatorname{dom}f)=[0,+\infty),\qquad 0\notin\operatorname{ri}[0,+\infty).\] Nevertheless \[\inf_x\{f(x)+g(x)\}=0\] is attained at \(x=0\), while \[\sup_y\{-f^*(-y)-g^*(y)\}=0\] and every \(y\le0\) is dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\notin\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g-A(\operatorname{dom}f)),\quad p^*=d^*=0,\quad \operatorname*{argmax}d=(-\infty,0].
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel pair with attained zero gap although the domain-difference qualification fails.

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic-Core Qualifications

For the convex set \(C=\operatorname{dom}g-A(\operatorname{dom}f)\), the intrinsic-core qualification is

0\in\operatorname{icr}C.

For a convex set, \(x\in\operatorname{icr}C\) means that \(\operatorname{cone}(C-x)\) is a linear subspace of \(Y\). Hence the displayed qualification is equivalent to requiring \(0\in C\) and \(\operatorname{cone}C\) to be a linear subspace, not necessarily all of \(Y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quasirelative interior consists of points at which the closure of the generated feasible-direction cone is the closed linear span of the translated set. The associated qualification requires the origin to be such a point of the residual set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in\operatorname{qri}C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\overline{\operatorname{cone}C}=\overline{\operatorname{span}C}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a convex set in a locally convex space, a standard normal-cone characterization is that the normal cone at a quasirelative-interior point is a linear subspace, when the required separation hypotheses hold.
For a domain-difference set \(C=\operatorname{dom}f-A(\operatorname{dom}g)\), the qualification is applied to that exact set rather than separately to the two domains.
special_cases_latex: In finite-dimensional spaces, quasirelative interior agrees with relative interior for nonempty convex sets.
A convex set may have empty relative interior but nonempty quasirelative interior in infinite dimension.
immediate_consequences_latex: The inclusions \(\operatorname{ri}C\subseteq\operatorname{qri}C\subseteq C\) hold under the cited Hilbert-space definitions.
Using quasirelative interior can formulate qualifications when stronger generalized interiors are empty.
boundary_notes: The closure in the definition is essential.
A quasirelative-interior condition may need extra closedness or separation assumptions to imply exact duality or attainment.
