knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and continuity qualifications for exact conjugacy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f,g\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) with \(\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\). Define the infimal convolution \((f^*\square g^*)(u)=\inf_v(f^*(v)+g^*(u-v))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This family replaces direct strict feasibility by regularity of functions or epigraphical constructions. The displayed continuity route is one precise canonical member.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuity qualification is \[\operatorname{cont}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing,\] where \(\operatorname{cont}f\) is the set of points at which \(f\) is finite and continuous. A closedness qualification requires the relevant infimal convolution or perturbation epigraph to be closed and exact at the dual argument. Under the cited continuity condition, \[0\in\operatorname{sri}(\operatorname{dom}f-\operatorname{dom}g),\qquad (f+g)^*=f^*\square g^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuity qualification requires one convex function to be continuous at a point in the effective domain of the other. A closedness qualification directly requires the epigraphical or infimal-convolution object used by duality to be closed and exact at the relevant argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(f+g)^*=f^*\square g^*\quad\text{with the infimum attained at each finite argument under the cited exactness result}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The continuity condition may be stated as existence of \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}g\) at which \(f\) is finite and continuous.
Exact closed infimal convolution means \[(f^*\square g^*)(u)=\min_v\bigl(f^*(v)+g^*(u-v)\bigr)\] whenever the value is finite.
special_cases_latex: In finite dimension, a proper convex function is continuous on the relative interior of its effective domain relative to that domain's affine hull, subject to the appropriate ambient restriction.
Polyhedral convex functions supply closedness through structural routes that may require weaker domain intersection.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact conjugate calculus yields the associated Fenchel value equality.
Exactness records dual attainment for the decomposition variable, while mere equality after lower-semicontinuous closure need not.
boundary_notes: Continuity must be taken in the topology and affine setting used by the theorem.
Closedness of each function separately does not automatically make every projected epigraph or infimal convolution closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Criterion for Closedness at the Reference Parameter
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper finite-dimensional convex value function is closed at zero exactly when it is lower semicontinuous along every sequence converging to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex with \(v(0)<+\infty\). Then \[v(0)=v^{**}(0)\] if and only if every sequence \(y_k\to0\) satisfies \[v(0)\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}v(y_k).\] This pointwise condition need not imply global epigraphical closedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v(0)=v^{**}(0)\iff \bigl(\forall y_k\to0,\ v(0)\le\liminf_k v(y_k)\bigr).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pointwise lower-semicontinuity formulation of value-function closedness at zero.

notation.meaning: Fenchel biconjugate of the value function.

knowledge_statements.title: Value-Function Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value function is closed at zero when it equals its biconjugate there; this equality yields the perturbation dual value with no gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The value function is closed at the reference perturbation when
\[
v(0)=v^{**}(0).
\]
Since \(v^*(y^*)=\Phi^*(0,y^*)\), this condition gives
\[
\inf_x\Phi(x,0)=v(0)=\sup_{y^*\in\mathbb R^m}\{-\Phi^*(0,y^*)\}.
\]
Thus pointwise closedness of the perturbation value at zero is exactly the biconjugate equality needed to exclude a primal–dual value gap; it does not by itself assert attainment of either optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(v(y)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x,y)\) is proper and \(v(0)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closedness at zero is \(v(0)=v^{**}(0)\), and then \(v(0)=\sup_{y^*}\{-\Phi^*(0,y^*)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise closedness criterion for perturbation duality.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the perturbation function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness of a Perturbation Value Function at the Origin
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex function and define the perturbation value function \(p:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(p(u)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}F(u,x)\). The unperturbed problem has value \(p(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex perturbation theory; closedness is imposed at the distinguished parameter \(u=0\), not necessarily globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The value function is closed at the unperturbed parameter when \[p(0)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(0),\] where \(\operatorname{cl}p\) is the lower-semicontinuous hull of \(p\). If \(0\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}p)\), this is equivalent to \[p(0)\leq\liminf_{k\to\infty}p(u_k)\quad\text{for every sequence }u_k\to0.\] When \(p(0)\in\mathbb{R}\), the condition excludes arbitrarily small perturbations whose limiting optimal values lie strictly below the unperturbed value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the perturbation value function \(p(u)=\inf_x F(u,x)\), value-function closedness at the origin means that \(p(0)\) equals the value of the lower-semicontinuous hull of \(p\) at zero. Provided \(0\) lies in the closure of the effective domain, equivalently every sequence \(u_k\to0\) satisfies \(p(0)\leq\liminf_k p(u_k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p(0)=(\operatorname{cl}p)(0),\qquad 0\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}p)\Longrightarrow p(0)\leq\liminf_{u\to0}p(u).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite \(p(0)\), closedness at zero is equivalent to lower semicontinuity of \(p\) at zero.
Equivalently, \((0,p(0))\) belongs to the closed epigraph of \(p\) without a downward jump at \(u=0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(p\) is globally closed, then it is closed at \(0\).
If \(p\) is continuous at \(0\), then it is closed at \(0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For the standard convex perturbation dual, finite \(p(0)\) and lower semicontinuity at zero rule out a duality gap.
boundary_notes: Closedness at zero does not require continuity or upper semicontinuity there.
The definition alone does not assert attainment of the infimum defining \(p(0)\).

notation.meaning: Lower-semicontinuous closure of the extended-real-valued function \(p\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Sublevel Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value function is epigraphically closed exactly when all its real sublevel sets are closed; for a proper convex function this is closed convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the following are equivalent: \[\operatorname{epi}v\text{ is closed};\qquad v\text{ is lower semicontinuous};\qquad \{y:v(y)\le\alpha\}\text{ is closed for every }\alpha\in\mathbb R.\] When \(v\) is proper and convex, these conditions say precisely that \(v\) is a closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}v\text{ closed}\iff v\text{ lower semicontinuous}\iff (\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R)\,\{v\le\alpha\}\text{ closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent level-set formulation of epigraphical closedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphical closedness means the value function has a closed epigraph, equivalently is lower semicontinuous; consequently it equals its biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Epigraphical closedness of \(v\) is the condition
\[
\operatorname{epi}v=\{(y,r)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R:r\geq v(y)\}\quad\text{is closed}.
\]
For a proper extended-real-valued function in finite dimensions, this is equivalent to lower semicontinuity:
\[
v(y)\leq\liminf_{k\to\infty}v(y_k)\quad\text{whenever}\quad y_k\to y.
\]
In particular, epigraphical closedness implies \(v=v^{**}\), hence the biconjugate equality at every perturbation where \(v\) is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex perturbation value function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Epigraphical closedness means that \(\operatorname{epi}v\) is closed, equivalently that \(v\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global epigraph criterion for closed convex value functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraphical Closedness at a Perturbation Fiber
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x)\), and set \(E=\operatorname{epi}p=\{(u,r):p(u)\leq r\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local epigraphical property at the fiber over \(u=0\); this is distinct from requiring the entire epigraph to be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The value system is epigraphically closed over \(u=0\) if every convergent sequence \((u_k,r_k)\in E\) satisfying \(u_k\to0\) and \(r_k\to r\in\mathbb{R}\) has \((0,r)\in E\). Thus \[\bigl[(u_k,r_k)\in\operatorname{epi}p,\ (u_k,r_k)\to(0,r)\bigr]\Longrightarrow p(0)\leq r.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}p)\cap(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{epi}p\cap(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epigraphical closedness over the unperturbed parameter means that the epigraph of \(p\) contains every finite limit point whose parameter coordinate tends to zero. Equivalently, its closure introduces no new point on the vertical fiber \(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{epi}p)\cap(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R})=\operatorname{epi}p\cap(\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(u_k\to0\) and every convergent majorant sequence \(r_k\to r\) with \(p(u_k)\leq r_k\), one has \(p(0)\leq r\).
When \(p(0)\) is finite and \(0\in\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{dom}p)\), the condition is equivalent to lower semicontinuity of \(p\) at zero.
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{epi}p\) is globally closed, it is epigraphically closed over every parameter.
For a proper convex \(p\), global epigraphical closedness is the usual definition of a closed convex function.
immediate_consequences_latex: No finite epigraph sequence approaching the zero fiber can converge strictly below \(p(0)\).
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}F\) does not by itself guarantee closedness of its projection \(\operatorname{epi}p\).
The condition concerns finite height limits; behavior at \(+\infty\) is encoded through extended-real conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Domain Form of the Continuity Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper finite-dimensional convex value function, ambient continuity at zero is equivalent to zero lying in the interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Then \(v\) is finite and continuous at \(0\) in the ambient Euclidean topology if and only if \[0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}v).\] If \(\operatorname{dom}v\) has empty Euclidean interior, this ambient qualification cannot hold; relative continuity on the affine hull is a distinct formulation.
assumptions_latex: Continuity is taken in the ambient Euclidean topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ is finite and continuous at }0\iff 0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}v).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional ambient-topology characterization of continuity at the reference perturbation.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuity Qualification Is Not Necessary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singleton-domain value function is not ambiently continuous at zero, yet its perturbation dual has zero gap and is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge1\) and \(\Phi(x,y)=\delta_{\{0\}}(x)+\delta_{\{0\}}(y)\) on \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m\). Then \(v(y)=\delta_{\{0\}}(y)\), which is finite but not ambiently continuous at \(0\). Nevertheless \(\Phi^*(0,y^*)=0\) for every \(y^*\), so \[\inf_x\Phi(x,0)=0=\max_{y^*}\{-\Phi^*(0,y^*)\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(\delta_{\{0\}}\) is the convex indicator of the singleton zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ is not continuous at }0,\qquad \inf_x\Phi(x,0)=\max_{y^*}\{-\Phi^*(0,y^*)\}=0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation model showing that zero gap and dual attainment can hold without ambient continuity at the reference parameter.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator of the singleton zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuity-Point Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity of the perturbation value at the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex and let \(p(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\) be proper. If \(p\) is finite and continuous at \(0\), then \(\partial p(0)\ne\varnothing\). For every \(y\in\partial p(0)\), Fenchel equality gives \(p(0)+p^*(y)=0\), while \(p^*(y)=F^*(0,y)\). Consequently,
\[
\inf_xF(x,0)=\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\{-F^*(0,y)\}.
\]
Hence continuity at the reference point yields both zero duality gap and a dual optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity of a proper convex value function at the reference perturbation produces a supporting subgradient, which is a dual optimizer and establishes strong duality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial p(0)\ne\varnothing\) and \(p(0)=\max_y\{-F^*(0,y)\}\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the value function at zero
Fenchel conjugate of the perturbation function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity-Point Qualification for a Convex Value Function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex perturbation value function, with \(p(0)\in\mathbb{R}\). Continuity is understood relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}p)\) when the domain is lower-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex value functions; the qualification is local at the unperturbed parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The continuity-point qualification holds at \(0\) when \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}p)\) and \(p\) is finite and continuous there relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}p)\): \[u_k\in\operatorname{dom}p,\quad u_k\to0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p(u_k)\to p(0).\] For a proper convex function in finite dimensions, membership \(0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}p)\) supplies this relative continuity automatically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuity-point qualification declares the unperturbed parameter \(0\) to be a relative-interior point of the effective domain at which the finite convex value function \(p\) is continuous. Thus values along every domain sequence converging to zero converge to \(p(0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}p),\qquad \lim_{\substack{u\to0\\u\in\operatorname{dom}p}}p(u)=p(0)\in\mathbb{R}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Relative continuity means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(u\in\operatorname{dom}p\), \(\|u\|<\delta\) implies \(|p(u)-p(0)|<\varepsilon\).
special_cases_latex: If \(0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}p)\), ordinary ambient-space continuity applies.
If \(\operatorname{dom}p\) is an affine set, its relative interior equals the entire domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: Continuity at zero implies value-function closedness and epigraphical closedness at the zero fiber.
The qualification precludes both downward and upward finite jumps along feasible perturbations.
boundary_notes: Continuity relative to the effective domain does not control sequences outside that domain, where \(p\) may equal \(+\infty\).
Lower semicontinuity alone is weaker because it permits upward jumps.

notation.meaning: Relative interior of the effective domain in its affine hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure-Driven Regularity for a Convex Program
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider minimizing a proper convex \(f\) over \(X=P\cap C\), subject to convex inequalities \(g_i(x)\leq0\), affine inequalities \(h_j(x)\leq0\), and affine equalities \(s_k(x)=0\), where \(P\) is polyhedral and \(C\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programming with regularity supplied by polyhedral and affine structure together with strict feasibility only for genuinely nonlinear constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The program is structure-regular when there exist points \(\bar x,\hat x\) such that \[\bar x\in P\cap C,\quad g_i(\bar x)<0\ \forall i,\quad h_j(\bar x)\leq0\ \forall j,\quad s_k(\bar x)=0\ \forall k,\] and \[\hat x\in P\cap\operatorname{ri}C,\quad h_j(\hat x)\leq0\ \forall j,\quad s_k(\hat x)=0\ \forall k.\] The definition separates nonlinear strict feasibility from compatibility of the affine-polyhedral subsystem with the relative interior of the nonpolyhedral set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structure-driven regularity holds when all nonlinear convex inequalities admit a strictly feasible point, while the affine constraints admit a point in the polyhedral part and the relative interior of the remaining convex set. The two witnessing points may differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists\bar x\in P\cap C:\ g(\bar x)<0,\ h(\bar x)\leq0,\ s(\bar x)=0,\qquad \exists\hat x\in P\cap\operatorname{ri}C:\ h(\hat x)\leq0,\ s(\hat x)=0.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb{R}^{n}\), the second condition reduces to feasibility of the affine-polyhedral subsystem.
If there are no nonlinear inequalities, no strict inequality is required.
immediate_consequences_latex: With finite primal value, this qualification is a standard route to equality of primal and dual values and attainment of the Lagrange dual optimum.
boundary_notes: The definition does not require affine inequalities to hold strictly.
It is tailored to the displayed decomposition; changing which constraints are absorbed into \(P\) or \(C\) can change the stated qualification.

notation.meaning: Convex polyhedral component of the underlying set.
Possibly nonpolyhedral convex component of the underlying set.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Regularity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite polyhedral Fenchel problem has no duality gap, and its dual optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal problem \(p^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\), define the Fenchel dual value by \[d^*=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\{-f^*(-A^{\mathsf T}y)-g^*(y)\}.\] If both functions are proper closed polyhedral convex functions and \(p^*\) is finite, then polyhedral closedness of the associated perturbation epigraph gives \(p^*=d^*\). Moreover, some \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) attains the displayed supremum.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) are proper closed polyhedral convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=d^*\), and the dual supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel duality for fully polyhedral objectives.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a proper convex perturbation function and \(p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedral convex programs and their perturbation value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perturbation system is polyhedrally regular when \(F\) is polyhedral convex, meaning \[\operatorname{epi}F=\{(u,x,r):F(u,x)\leq r\}\] is a nonempty polyhedral convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{m+n+1}\), and the unperturbed value \(p(0)\) is finite. In this regime \(p\) is itself polyhedral convex; hence it is closed at every point of its effective domain, including zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polyhedral regularity means that the epigraph of the joint perturbation function \(F\) is a polyhedral convex set and that the unperturbed optimal value is finite. Partial minimization then produces a polyhedral convex value function \(p\), so its value is closed at zero without a separate interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}F\text{ is polyhedral},\quad p(0)\in\mathbb{R},\quad p(u)=\inf_xF(u,x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A proper convex function is polyhedral exactly when its epigraph is the intersection of finitely many closed halfspaces.
special_cases_latex: Linear programs and finite-dimensional convex programs with piecewise-affine objectives and polyhedral feasible systems fit this definition.
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal solution set and multiplier set, when described by the associated polyhedral program with finite value, are polyhedral convex sets and are nonempty.
The value function has no lower-semicontinuity defect at an effective-domain point.
boundary_notes: Conic programs over nonpolyhedral cones, such as semidefinite cones, are not polyhedral in this sense.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine constraint is regular when it meets the relative interior of the objective domain; finite problems then have strong duality and dual attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(p^*=\inf\{f(x):Ax=b\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Refined Slater Qualification with Affine Constraints
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider a convex program with domain \(D\), convex inequalities \(f_i(x)\leq0\), and affine equalities \(Ax=b\). Suppose \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\) are affine and \(f_{k+1},\ldots,f_m\) may be nonlinear convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programming; affine inequalities are exempted from strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine-constraint regularity condition holds when there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D\) such that \[A\bar x=b,\qquad f_i(\bar x)\leq0\quad(1\leq i\leq k),\qquad f_i(\bar x)<0\quad(k<i\leq m).\] Thus strict feasibility is demanded only for the nonaffine inequalities; affine inequalities and equalities need only be feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine-constraint regularity is the refined Slater condition: a relative-interior point of the common domain satisfies all equalities, satisfies affine inequalities non-strictly, and satisfies every nonaffine convex inequality strictly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}D:\ A\bar x=b,\ f_i(\bar x)\leq0\ (i\leq k),\ f_i(\bar x)<0\ (i>k).\]
special_cases_latex: If every inequality is affine, the qualification reduces to feasibility by a point in \(\operatorname{ri}D\).
If no inequality is affine, it reduces to the ordinary relative-interior Slater condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: For a convex problem with finite optimum, the refined condition is a standard sufficient qualification for strong duality and dual attainment.
boundary_notes: An affine inequality active at every feasible point does not violate the condition.
Relative interior, rather than ambient interior, is essential when \(D\) lies in a proper affine subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Polyhedrality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When one Fenchel term is polyhedral, ordinary domain membership suffices for that term, while the nonpolyhedral term retains a relative-interior condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p^*=\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\), suppose that the nonpolyhedral term satisfies the relative-interior requirement while the polyhedral term is merely finite at the image point: \[A(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f))\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing.\] If \(p^*\) is finite, then \[p^*=d^*=\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\{-f^*(-A^{\mathsf T}y)-g^*(y)\}.\] Thus relative-interior membership is required only for the nonpolyhedral component in this partially polyhedral setting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f))\cap\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\) implies Fenchel strong duality and dual attainment when the primal value is finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One polyhedral term weakens the usual relative-interior qualification.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a convex program be represented on \(X=P\cap C\), where \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is polyhedral and \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is convex, with affine constraints collected into the polyhedral part and remaining convex inequalities represented separately.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional programs whose data contain both polyhedral and genuinely nonpolyhedral components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The program is partially polyhedral when its feasible system admits a decomposition \[X=P\cap C,\qquad P=\{x:Bx\leq d,\ Ex=e\},\] with \(P\) polyhedral, while \(C\) and at least one remaining proper convex function need not be polyhedral. A compatible partial-polyhedral qualification requires strict feasibility only for the remaining nonaffine inequalities and requires the affine-polyhedral subsystem to intersect \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial polyhedrality means that a designated portion of the feasible geometry is representable by finitely many affine equalities and inequalities, while another convex set or function may remain nonpolyhedral. Regularity tests exploit the polyhedral block by imposing strict feasibility only on the genuinely nonlinear inequalities and relative-interior compatibility on the remaining convex block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[X=P\cap C,\qquad P=\{x:Bx\leq d,\ Ex=e\}\text{ polyhedral},\qquad C\text{ convex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The indicator of the underlying set decomposes as \(\delta_X=\delta_P+\delta_C\), with \(\delta_P\) polyhedral convex.
special_cases_latex: Full polyhedrality occurs when \(C=\mathbb{R}^{n}\) and all remaining objective and constraint functions are polyhedral.
A second-order or semidefinite cone intersected with linear side constraints is typically only partially polyhedral.
immediate_consequences_latex: Affine constraints contained in \(P\) need not be strictly satisfied in a structure-adapted constraint qualification.
boundary_notes: Partial polyhedrality alone does not guarantee strong duality; compatibility or strict-feasibility hypotheses may still be required for the nonpolyhedral block.
The decomposition must be specified because the same feasible set can admit several representations.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a minimization problem have primal value \(p^*\), Lagrange dual function \(q(y)\), dual value \(d^*=\sup_{y\in Y}q(y)\), primal solution set \(X^*\), and dual solution set \(Y^*=\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in Y}q(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-valued convex Lagrange duality; the definition records the standard consequences once equality and attainment are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strong-duality consequence package holds when \[p^*=d^*\in\mathbb{R},\qquad Y^*\neq\varnothing,\] and every primal-dual feasible pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X^*\times Y^*\) has zero gap. In a Lagrangian formulation this means \[q(y^*)=L(x^*,y^*)=f(x^*)=p^*,\] together with complementary slackness and Lagrangian minimality of \(x^*\) at \(y^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong-duality consequence package consists of equality of the finite primal and dual values, existence of a dual optimizer, and zero gap for primal and dual optimizers. In a Lagrangian model, an optimal pair also satisfies complementary slackness and minimizes the Lagrangian in the primal variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p^*=d^*\in\mathbb{R},\qquad Y^*\neq\varnothing,\qquad q(y^*)=L(x^*,y^*)=f(x^*)\ \text{for }(x^*,y^*)\in X^*\times Y^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a primal-feasible and dual-feasible pair, equality of the two objective values is a zero-duality-gap certificate of optimality.
special_cases_latex: Under Slater-type conditions for a convex program with finite optimum, the package includes attained optimal multipliers.
For conic programs under an appropriate strict-feasibility hypothesis, the package reduces to equal objective values plus cone complementarity.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any feasible equal-value primal-dual pair is optimal on both sides.
Optimal inequality multipliers satisfy complementary slackness.
boundary_notes: Equality \(p^*=d^*\) alone does not imply primal or dual attainment.
The definition concerns exact duality and does not cover asymptotic or approximate certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Subgradient Characterization of Zero-Gap Dual Solutions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Supporting subgradients at the reference parameter are exactly the dual optimizers whose objective value equals the finite primal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)\) be proper and convex with \(v(0)\in\mathbb R\). Since \(v^*(y)=F^*(0,y)\), a vector \(y^*\) satisfies \[v(0)=-F^*(0,y^*)=\sup_y\{-F^*(0,y)\}\] if and only if \(y^*\in\partial v(0)\). Thus the zero-gap dual solution set is exactly \(\partial v(0)\).
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a proper convex perturbation function on finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise characterization for a proper convex perturbation value in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the perturbation function.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Existence Does Not Imply Primal Existence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous perturbation value can have an attained zero-gap dual while the unperturbed primal infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F(x,u)=e^x+u^2\) on \(\mathbb R^2\). Then \(v(u)=\inf_xF(x,u)=u^2\) is finite and continuous everywhere, so \(\partial v(0)=\{0\}\) and the associated dual attains \(v(0)=0\). Nevertheless, \(F(x,0)=e^x>0\) for every \(x\), hence \(\operatorname*{argmin}_xF(x,0)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual solution set is nonempty, but \(\operatorname*{argmin}_xF(x,0)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of dual attainment from primal attainment in a continuous perturbation model.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Solution Existence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity of the convex perturbation value at zero produces a subgradient that attains the dual optimum and establishes zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(u)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}F(x,u)\) be the value function of a convex perturbation model. If \(v\) is proper and continuous at \(0\), then \(v\) is subdifferentiable there. For every \(y^*\in\partial v(0)\), Fenchel equality gives \[v(0)=-v^*(y^*)=-F^*(0,y^*)=\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\{-F^*(0,y)\}.\] Hence the dual problem has a solution and its value equals the unperturbed primal value.
assumptions_latex: \(v(u)=\inf_x F(x,u)\) is proper and continuous at \(u=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial v(0)\neq\varnothing\), and every \(y^*\in\partial v(0)\) attains \(\sup_y\{-F^*(0,y)\}=v(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual attainment derived from subdifferentiability of the perturbation value.

notation.meaning: Convex conjugate of the perturbation function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Dual Optimal Solution
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q:Y\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) be a concave dual objective on a nonempty dual-feasible set \(Y\), and let \(d^*=\sup_{y\in Y}q(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual attainment for a maximization-form dual problem; equality with a primal value is not built into the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dual optimal solution exists when the dual supremum is attained: \[Y^*:=\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in Y}q(y)=\{y\in Y:q(y)=d^*\}\neq\varnothing.\] Equivalently, there is \(y^*\in Y\) satisfying \(q(y)\leq q(y^*)\) for every \(y\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual-solution existence means that the supremum of the dual objective over the dual-feasible set is achieved by at least one feasible dual point. The set \(Y^*\) of such maximizers is therefore nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists y^*\in Y\quad\forall y\in Y:\ q(y)\leq q(y^*)=d^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{argmax}_{y\in Y}q(y)\neq\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: For a Lagrange dual, a dual solution is an optimal multiplier vector.
For a conic dual, a dual solution consists of a feasible equality multiplier and cone slack attaining the dual value.
immediate_consequences_latex: If strong duality also holds and a primal optimizer exists, pairing either optimizer with the other yields equal optimal objective values.
boundary_notes: A finite dual value does not by itself imply attainment.
Dual-solution existence does not by itself imply zero duality gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Existence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slater regularity guarantees nonnegative inequality multipliers and equality multipliers supporting every attained convex optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\leq0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,r\) and \(Ax=b\). Under Slater's condition, every primal minimizer \(x^*\) admits multipliers \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^r\) and \(
u^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that, for \[L(x,\lambda,
u)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i f_i(x)+\langle
u,Ax-bangle,\] one has \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x L(x,\lambda^*,
u^*)\) and \(\lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\) for every \(i\).
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex and \(A x=b\) is affine.
There exists \(\bar x\) with \(A\bar x=b\) and \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for every \(i\).
The primal minimum is finite and attained at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\lambda^*\geq0\) and \(\nu^*\) such that \(x^*\) minimizes the Lagrangian and \(\lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programs satisfying Slater's condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of Lagrange Multipliers at a Primal Optimum
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\leq0\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), \(h_j(x)=0\), \(j=1,\ldots,p\), and \(x\in X\). Let \(L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\sum_j\nu_jh_j(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional Lagrange multipliers associated with a specified primal optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Multipliers exist at a primal optimum \(x^*\) when there is \((\lambda^*,
u^*)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}	imes\mathbb{R}^{p}\) such that \[\lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\quad orall i,\qquad x^*\in\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda^*,
u^*).\] When strong duality holds, such a pair is dual optimal and satisfies \(q(\lambda^*,
u^*)=f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier existence at \(x^*\) means that nonnegative inequality multipliers and unrestricted equality multipliers can be chosen so that complementary slackness holds and \(x^*\) minimizes the resulting Lagrangian over the underlying set. Under strong duality these multipliers solve the dual problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists(\lambda^*,\nu^*)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{p}:\quad \lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\ \forall i,\quad x^*\in\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda^*,\nu^*).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under strong duality, multiplier existence at \(x^*\) is equivalent to the existence of a dual optimizer that forms a zero-gap pair with \(x^*\).
special_cases_latex: With only equality constraints, the multiplier vector \(\nu^*\) is unrestricted in sign.
With only inequality constraints, the multiplier vector lies in \(\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Complementary slackness forces \(\lambda_i^*=0\) whenever \(g_i(x^*)<0\).
boundary_notes: Multipliers depend on the chosen constraint representation.
Existence does not imply uniqueness; redundant or degenerate constraints may yield many multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Optimality Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under attained strong duality, primal and dual solutions correspond exactly to saddle points of the Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the primal value be \(p^*=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\) and the dual value be \(d^*=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)\). Assuming \(p^*=d^*\), a feasible pair \((x^*,y^*)\) attains the primal and dual values if and only if \[L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\quad\text{for all }x\in X,\ y\in Y.\] Thus primal-dual optimal pairs are exactly the saddle points of the Lagrangian.
assumptions_latex: \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}\) is convex in its primal argument and concave in its dual argument.
The primal and dual values are finite and equal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,y^*)\) is primal-dual optimal if and only if it is a saddle point of \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle-point characterization under attained strong duality.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a Lagrange primal-dual pair, let \(X_{\mathrm f}\) and \(Y_{\mathrm f}\) denote the primal- and dual-feasible sets, and let \(f\) and \(q\) be their objectives.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence under finite strong duality; no differentiability is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal-dual optimality correspondence is the relation \[\mathcal{O}:=\{(x,y)\in X_{\mathrm f}\times Y_{\mathrm f}:f(x)=q(y)\}.\] Under finite strong duality, \[\mathcal{O}=X^*\times Y^*.\] In the Lagrangian representation, membership in \(\mathcal{O}\) is equivalently characterized by primal feasibility, dual sign feasibility, complementary slackness, and \(x\in\operatorname{argmin}_{z\in X}L(z,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual optimality correspondence relates a primal-feasible point and a dual-feasible point when their objective values agree. Under finite strong duality, these equal-value feasible pairs are exactly all pairs formed from a primal optimizer and a dual optimizer. They can also be described through complementary slackness and Lagrangian minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal{O}=\{(x,y)\in X_{\mathrm f}\times Y_{\mathrm f}:f(x)=q(y)\}=X^*\times Y^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For inequality and equality constrained problems, \((x^*,(\lambda^*,\nu^*))\in\mathcal O\) exactly when \(x^*\) is feasible, \(\lambda^*\geq0\), \(\lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\), and \(x^*\) minimizes \(L(\cdot,\lambda^*,\nu^*)\).
special_cases_latex: For differentiable convex programs, Lagrangian minimization can be expressed by vanishing Lagrangian gradient.
For nonsmooth convex programs, it can be expressed by a subdifferential inclusion.
immediate_consequences_latex: Either member of an equal-value feasible pair certifies optimality of the other.
The correspondence is empty if either optimum is unattained.
boundary_notes: Without strong duality, an optimal primal-dual pair can have unequal objective values and therefore lie outside \(\mathcal O\).
The Cartesian-product identity presumes both optimal sets are nonempty.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the convex program \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\leq0\) and \(h_j(x)=0\), with Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\sum_j\nu_jh_j(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An exact KKT-dual certificate is a triple \((x,\lambda,\nu)\in X\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}\times\mathbb{R}^{p}\) satisfying \[g_i(x)\leq0,\quad h_j(x)=0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\quad\forall i,j,\qquad x\in\operatorname{argmin}_{z\in X}L(z,\lambda,
u).\] Equivalently, \((\lambda,
u)\) is dual feasible and \[q(\lambda,
u)=L(x,lambda,
u)=f(x),\] so the certificate exhibits a primal-feasible and dual-feasible pair with zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact KKT-dual certificate consists of a primal point and multiplier vectors satisfying primal feasibility, nonnegativity of inequality multipliers, complementary slackness, and global minimization of the Lagrangian in the primal variable. These conditions give equal primal and dual objective values and therefore certify both sides as optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[g(x)\leq0,\quad h(x)=0,\quad \lambda\geq0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0,\quad x\in\operatorname{argmin}_{z\in X}L(z,\lambda,
u).\]

The certificate is equivalently a primal-dual feasible triple satisfying \(f(x)=q(\lambda,
u)\).

When the relevant subdifferential sum rule applies, Lagrangian minimization is equivalent to \(0\in\partial_xL(x,\lambda,
u)+N_X(x)\).
special_cases_latex:
If \(X=\mathbb{R}^{n}\) and all functions are differentiable, stationarity becomes \(\nabla_xL(x,\lambda,
u)=0\).
For affine conic models, stationarity and complementarity reduce to the standard conic primal-dual equations.

Inactive inequality constraints have zero certified multipliers.

Approximate KKT conditions require explicit residual tolerances and are not included here.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) be proper convex functions, let \(h(x)=Ax-b\) be affine, and let \(X\) be a nonempty closed convex set. Define \(L(x,\lambda,
u)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\langle\nu,Ax-b\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programs; stationarity is stated using the convex subdifferential and normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A triple \((x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) satisfies the convex KKT conditions when \[x^*\in X,\quad g_i(x^*)\leq0,\quad Ax^*=b,\quad \lambda^*\geq0,\] \[\lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad 0\in\partial_xL(x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*)+N_X(x^*).\] The five components are primal feasibility, dual-sign feasibility, complementary slackness, and stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex KKT system requires a feasible primal point, nonnegative inequality multipliers, complementary slackness, and stationarity of the Lagrangian after including the normal cone of the underlying convex set. Equality multipliers are unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x^*\in X,\ g(x^*)\leq0,\ Ax^*=b,\ \lambda^*\geq0,\ \lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0,\ 0\in\partial_xL(x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*)+N_X(x^*).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Stationarity is equivalent to \(x^*\in\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) whenever the displayed subdifferential represents the subdifferential of the Lagrangian plus the indicator of \(X\).
special_cases_latex: For differentiable data and \(X=\mathbb{R}^{n}\), stationarity is a gradient equation.
For nonsmooth data, stationarity is a subgradient inclusion.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any convex KKT triple is primal-dual optimal with zero gap when the Lagrangian stationarity condition is sufficient for global minimization.
Under a suitable Slater qualification, every primal optimum admits KKT multipliers.
boundary_notes: Sufficiency follows from convexity; necessity generally requires a constraint qualification.
The normal cone term must not be omitted when \(X\neq\mathbb{R}^{n}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convex KKT conditions combine feasibility, nonnegative multipliers, complementary slackness, and vanishing Lagrangian gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\leq0\) and \(Ax=b\), a triple \((x^*,\lambda^*,
u^*)\) satisfies the smooth convex KKT system precisely when \[f_i(x^*)\leq0,\quad Ax^*=b,\quad \lambda_i^*\geq0,\quad \lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\] for every \(i\), together with \[
abla f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i^*
abla f_i(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}
u^*=0.\] These equations encode primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness, and stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The smooth convex KKT system consists of primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementarity, and gradient stationarity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional convex inequality programs with affine equalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smooth convex KKT system consists of primal feasibility, nonnegative inequality multipliers, complementary slackness, and vanishing gradient of the Lagrangian. Because the equality constraints are affine, their gradients are constant and their multipliers are unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x^*)\leq0,\ h(x^*)=0,\ \lambda^*\geq0,\ \lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0,\ \nabla_xL(x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*)=0.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Convex KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth KKT replaces gradient stationarity by inclusion of zero in the multiplier-weighted sum of convex subdifferentials and equality normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\leq0\) and \(Ax=b\), a triple \((x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) satisfies the nonsmooth convex KKT system when primal feasibility, \(\lambda^*\geq0\), and \(\lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\) hold, and \[0\in\partial f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i^*\partial f_i(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}\nu^*.\] Equivalently, compatible subgradients can be selected whose multiplier-weighted sum plus the equality normal is zero.
assumptions_latex: The equality constraint is \(Ax=b\), and all relevant subdifferentials at \(x^*\) are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nonsmooth KKT stationarity condition is \(0\in\partial f_0(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i^*\partial f_i(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}\nu^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential KKT system for finite-dimensional convex programs.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in X} f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\leq0\), where \(f,g_i\) are real-valued convex functions on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space and \(X\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth convex inequalities; stationarity uses convex subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((x^*,\lambda^*)\in X\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{m}\) satisfies the nonsmooth convex KKT system when \[g_i(x^*)\leq0,\qquad \lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\] and there exist \(v_0\in\partial f(x^*)\), \(v_i\in\partial g_i(x^*)\), and \(n\in N_X(x^*)\) such that \[v_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\lambda_i^*v_i+n=0.\] Equivalently, \(0\in\partial f(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i^*\partial g_i(x^*)+N_X(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonsmooth convex KKT system requires primal feasibility, nonnegative multipliers, complementary slackness, and a balance of one objective subgradient, weighted constraint subgradients, and a normal to the underlying set. This balance replaces the smooth Lagrangian gradient equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[g(x^*)\leq0,\quad \lambda^*\geq0,\quad \lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0,\quad 0\in\partial f(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i^*\partial g_i(x^*)+N_X(x^*).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If the standard subdifferential sum rule holds, stationarity is \(0\in\partial(f+\sum_i\lambda_i^*g_i+\delta_X)(x^*)\).
special_cases_latex: When \(X=\mathbb{R}^{n}\), the normal-cone term is \(\{0\}\).
When every function is differentiable at \(x^*\), the inclusion reduces to the smooth gradient equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any feasible triple satisfying this system is globally primal optimal by convexity.
Under Slater's condition, every primal optimizer has nonnegative multipliers satisfying the system.
boundary_notes: The displayed Minkowski-sum form presumes subgradients are nonempty at the candidate point.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, additional topological qualifications may be required.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Form of Conic Complementarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible cone slack and positive-dual multiplier are complementary exactly when the negative multiplier is normal to the cone at the slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a closed convex cone, \(s\in K\), and \(y\in K^*:=\{u:\langle u,k\rangle\ge0\ \forall k\in K\}\). Then
\[
\langle y,s\rangle=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -y\in N_K(s),
\]
where \(N_K(s)=\{u:\langle u,k-s\rangle\le0\ \forall k\in K\}\). Consequently, for \(s=b-Ax\), primal conic feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity are equivalently expressed by \(-y\in N_K(b-Ax)\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle y,s\rangle=0\iff -y\in N_K(s).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent normal-cone representation of complementarity in the affine conic KKT system under the positive dual-cone convention.

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to K at s

knowledge_statements.title: Conic KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic KKT combines primal and dual cone membership, orthogonal complementarity, and stationarity of the conic Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(b-Ax\in K\), a pair \((x^*,y^*)\) satisfies the conic KKT system exactly when \[b-Ax^*\in K,\qquad y^*\in K^*,\qquad \langle y^*,b-Ax^*\rangle=0,\] and \[0\in\partial f(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}y^*.\] The first two relations are primal and dual conic feasibility, the inner-product equality is conic complementarity, and the inclusion is stationarity for the Lagrangian \(f(x)-\langle y,b-Ax\rangle\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a closed convex cone with dual cone \(K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conic KKT requires \(b-Ax^*\in K\), \(y^*\in K^*\), \(\langle y^*,b-Ax^*\rangle=0\), and \(0\in\partial f(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}y^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Subdifferential KKT system for a single affine conic constraint.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be a nonempty closed convex cone with dual cone \(K^*=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\). Consider \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and \(\max\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\in K^*\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear conic optimization with the stated primal-dual sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A triple \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) satisfies the conic KKT system when \[Ax^*=b,\quad x^*\in K,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y^*+s^*=c,\quad s^*\in K^*,\] and \[\langle x^*,s^*\rangle=0.\] The first line is primal and dual feasibility; the last equality is cone complementary slackness. Together they imply \(\langle c,x^*\rangle=\langle b,y^*\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conic KKT system consists of primal feasibility in the cone, dual feasibility in the dual cone, the dual stationarity equation, and orthogonality of the primal cone variable and dual slack. This orthogonality is conic complementary slackness and yields equality of the primal and dual objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[Ax^*=b,\ x^*\in K,\ A^{\mathsf T}y^*+s^*=c,\ s^*\in K^*,\ \langle x^*,s^*\rangle=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a primal-dual feasible triple, \(\langle x^*,s^*\rangle=0\) is equivalent to the zero-gap identity \(\langle c,x^*\rangle=\langle b,y^*\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}\), complementarity becomes \(x_i^*s_i^*=0\) for every coordinate.
For the positive-semidefinite cone, complementarity is \(\langle X^*,S^*\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(X^*S^*)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every conic KKT triple is primal and dual optimal by weak duality.
Under suitable strict feasibility and boundedness, optimal primal-dual solutions satisfy this system.
boundary_notes: Strict feasibility is not part of the KKT system itself; it is a qualification used to guarantee existence of solutions satisfying it.
For non-self-dual cones, primal and dual cone memberships must not be interchanged.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficiency and necessity regimes for KKT systems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f,c_1,\ldots,c_p:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(C=\{x:Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0\ (j=1,\ldots,p)\}\). For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(\mu\in\mathbb R_+^p\), set \(L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,Ax-b\rangle+\sum_j\mu_jc_j(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programming with affine equalities, convex inequalities, and possibly nonsmooth data. Sufficiency and necessity are treated as logically distinct validity properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KKT system at a feasible point \(\bar x\in C\) is \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+A^*\lambda+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\partial c_j(\bar x),\qquad \mu\in\mathbb R_+^p,\qquad \mu_jc_j(\bar x)=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p).\] A class \(\mathcal P\) of such programs is a KKT-sufficiency regime if, for every program in \(\mathcal P\), \[\bar x\in C\ \text{and KKT holds at }\bar x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x).\] It is a KKT-necessity regime if, for every program in \(\mathcal P\), \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists(\lambda,\mu)\ \text{satisfying KKT at }\bar x.\] It is an exact KKT regime when both implications hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the convex program with feasible set \(C\), the KKT system consists of primal feasibility, nonnegative inequality multipliers, stationarity of the Lagrangian, and complementary slackness. A problem class is a sufficiency regime when every feasible KKT point is globally optimal. It is a necessity regime when every optimal point has at least one KKT multiplier. It is exact when both implications hold. Convexity supplies the usual sufficiency direction, whereas the necessity direction generally requires a constraint qualification such as the basic constraint qualification or an appropriate Slater condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{exact KKT validity}=\text{KKT sufficiency}+\text{KKT necessity}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When the data-generated normal cone \(N'(\bar x)\) equals the geometric normal cone \(N_C(\bar x)\), optimality at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to the KKT stationarity and complementarity system.
For differentiable finite-valued data, stationarity becomes \(\nabla f(\bar x)+A^*\lambda+\sum_j\mu_j\nabla c_j(\bar x)=0\).
special_cases_latex: Under weak Slater qualification, the KKT conditions are necessary and sufficient for minimizing a convex objective over \(C\).
For affine equality and inequality constraints, the basic constraint qualification holds at every feasible point.
immediate_consequences_latex: Failure of a necessity qualification may leave the sufficiency implication valid while allowing an optimizer with no KKT multiplier.
An exact regime permits optimality to be certified by a finite primal-dual system.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert KKT sufficiency for nonconvex objectives or constraints.
Constraint qualifications concern necessity and multiplier existence; they are not part of complementary slackness itself.

notation.meaning: Normal cone generated from the displayed constraint representation at \(\bar x\).
Convex-analytic normal cone to the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Sufficiency under Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex program, every feasible KKT triple certifies global primal and dual optimality with zero duality gap, without requiring a constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\leq 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,r\) and \(Ax=b\). If \(x^*\) is primal feasible, \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^r\), \(\lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\) for every \(i\), and \[0\in\partial f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i^*\partial f_i(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}\nu^*,\] then \(x^*\) is a global primal minimizer, \((\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) is dual optimal, and \(p^*=d^*=f_0(x^*)\). No constraint qualification is required for this sufficiency implication.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex, and \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear with \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
The triple \((x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}_+^r\times\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfies primal feasibility, complementary slackness, and convex KKT stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) is globally primal optimal, \((\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) is dual optimal, and \(p^*=d^*=f_0(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global sufficiency of KKT conditions for finite-dimensional convex programs; no constraint qualification is required for this direction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0\}\), where \(f\) and every \(c_j\) are proper convex functions and the equality constraints are affine. Let \(\bar x\in C\), \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(\mu\in\mathbb R_+^p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global sufficiency for finite-dimensional, possibly nonsmooth convex programs. No constraint qualification is imposed for this implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KKT-sufficiency property under convexity is the implication \[\left.\begin{array}{l}0\in\partial f(\bar x)+A^*\lambda+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\partial c_j(\bar x),\\ \mu_jc_j(\bar x)=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p),\\ A\bar x=b,\quad c_j(\bar x)\leq0,\quad\mu_j\geq0\end{array}\right\}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x).\] Equivalently, a feasible primal-dual triple \((\bar x,\lambda,\mu)\) satisfying KKT is a global optimality certificate for \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex program has KKT sufficiency when every feasible point \(\bar x\) admitting multipliers \((\lambda,\mu)\) with nonnegative \(\mu\), Lagrangian stationarity, and complementary slackness is a global minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\). This direction does not require Slater’s condition: it uses the convexity of the objective and inequality functions together with affine equalities. In the nonsmooth case, stationarity is expressed by a subdifferential inclusion rather than a gradient equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x\in C\ \text{and}\ (\bar x,\lambda,\mu)\ \text{satisfies KKT}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Stationarity is equivalent to \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\mu)\) for the convex Lagrangian.
Together with complementary slackness, \(L(\bar x,\lambda,\mu)=f(\bar x)\); hence the same triple realizes a zero primal-dual gap.
special_cases_latex: If all data are differentiable, replace the subdifferential inclusion by \(\nabla_xL(\bar x,\lambda,\mu)=0\).
With no inequalities, the condition reduces to feasible affine-equality stationarity \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)+A^*\lambda\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Any two feasible KKT points have the same optimal objective value.
A constraint qualification is needed only to ensure that optimizers admit multipliers, not to validate an already available convex KKT certificate.
boundary_notes: For nonconvex data, KKT conditions are generally only local first-order conditions and need not imply global optimality.
The inclusion assumes that the displayed subdifferential sum correctly describes the convex Lagrangian subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.title: KKT Necessity under Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard Slater condition, every attained optimum of a finite-dimensional convex program with affine equalities admits ordinary KKT multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\leq 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,r\) and \(Ax=b\). Suppose that a minimizer \(x^*\) exists and that there is \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(A\bar x=b\) and \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for every \(i\). Then there exist \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^r\) and \(\nu^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[0\in\partial f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i^*\partial f_i(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}\nu^*,\qquad \lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\quad\text{for every }i.\] Together with primal feasibility and \(\lambda^*\geq 0\), these are the KKT conditions at \(x^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex, and \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear with \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
There is \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(A\bar x=b\) and \(f_i(\bar x)<0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^r\) and \(\nu^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying KKT stationarity and complementary slackness at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT necessity under the standard Slater qualification for finite-dimensional real-valued convex inequality programs with affine equalities.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f,c_1,\ldots,c_p:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper convex functions and \(C=\{x:Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0\}\). At \(\bar x\in C\), let \(N_C(\bar x)\) be the normal cone and let \(N'(\bar x)=\operatorname{Im}A^*+\{\sum_{j\in J(\bar x)}\mu_js_j:\mu_j\geq0,\ s_j\in\partial c_j(\bar x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programs. Necessity is stated locally at an optimizer through BCQ and globally for the representation through weak Slater qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: KKT necessity under qualification at \(\bar x\) is the property \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x),\qquad N'(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R^m,\ \mu\in\mathbb R_+^p\] such that \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+A^*\lambda+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\partial c_j(\bar x),\qquad \mu_jc_j(\bar x)=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p).\] The equality \(N'(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\) is the basic constraint qualification. A representation is in a weak-Slater necessity regime when there exists \(x_0\in C\) satisfying every nonaffine inequality strictly; then the displayed KKT necessity holds at every optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal point satisfies qualified KKT necessity when the normal cone generated by the stated constraints equals the true normal cone of the feasible set at that point. Under this basic constraint qualification, the convex optimality inclusion can be represented by equality multipliers and nonnegative inequality multipliers, producing stationarity and complementary slackness. Weak Slater feasibility is a representation-level condition that guarantees this necessity property for every optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x\ \text{optimal and BCQ holds at }\bar x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad M(\bar x)\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: BCQ at \(\bar x\) is equivalent to requiring KKT multipliers for every real-valued convex objective minimized over \(C\) at \(\bar x\).
Weak Slater qualification requires \(Ax_0=b\), nonstrict satisfaction of affine inequalities, and strict satisfaction of all nonaffine inequalities.
special_cases_latex: For an inequality-only system, the ordinary Slater condition \(c_j(x_0)<0\) for all \(j\) implies necessity.
For a polyhedral feasible set given by affine equalities and inequalities, BCQ holds without strict feasibility.
immediate_consequences_latex: Under qualification, the KKT multiplier set at every optimizer is nonempty.
Without qualification, an optimizer may exist although the data-generated multiplier representation is empty.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal and Abnormal Fritz John Multipliers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fritz John multiplier is normal when its positive objective multiplier can be normalized to KKT form and abnormal when that multiplier is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible point \(x^*\), a nonzero Fritz John multiplier tuple \((\lambda_0,\lambda,\nu)\), with \(\lambda_0\ge0\) and \(\lambda\ge0\), is normal when \(\lambda_0>0\) and abnormal when \(\lambda_0=0\). A normal tuple can be scaled to \(\lambda_0=1\), giving an ordinary KKT multiplier system; an abnormal tuple cannot be so normalized.
assumptions_latex: \((\lambda_0,\lambda,\nu)\ne0\) satisfies the Fritz John stationarity, sign, and complementarity relations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_0>0\Rightarrow\text{normal and KKT-normalizable};\qquad \lambda_0=0\Rightarrow\text{abnormal}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of Fritz John multiplier systems by the objective multiplier.

knowledge_statements.title: Fritz John Necessity Without Constraint Qualification
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained differentiable convex optimum always has a nontrivial Fritz John system, but without qualification its objective multiplier may vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable and convex, and consider minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le0\) and \(Ax=b\). At every attained optimum \(x^*\), there exist \(\lambda_0\ge0\), \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^r\), and \(\nu\in\mathbb R^m\), not all zero, such that
\[
\lambda_0\nabla f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i\nabla f_i(x^*)+A^{\mathsf T}\nu=0,
\qquad
\lambda_i f_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,r).
\]
No constraint qualification is required. Without qualification, however, the available system may have \(\lambda_0=0\) and therefore may not be normalizable to ordinary KKT form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(\lambda_0,\lambda,\nu)\ne0\text{ satisfying Fritz John stationarity, signs, and complementarity}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable convex-program specialization of the qualification-free Fritz John necessary condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Abnormal-Multiplier Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This convex problem has a unique optimum but, without qualification, admits an abnormal Fritz John multiplier and no ordinary KKT multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the convex program \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}x\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad x^2\leq 0,\] the unique feasible and optimal point is \(x^*=0\), and Slater's condition fails. No \(\lambda_1\geq 0\) satisfies ordinary KKT stationarity \(1+2\lambda_1x^*=0\). The Fritz John system does admit the nonzero abnormal multiplier pair \((\lambda_0,[1m\lambda_1)=(0,1)\), which satisfies \(\lambda_0+2\lambda_1x^*=0\). Thus failure of qualification can leave only an abnormal multiplier while ordinary KKT multipliers do not exist.
assumptions_latex: The convex program is \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}}x\) subject to \(x^2\leq 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique minimizer \(x^*=0\) admits an abnormal Fritz John multiplier but no ordinary KKT multiplier.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete convex failure of ordinary KKT necessity when constraint qualification is absent.

notation.meaning: Objective multiplier in the Fritz John system

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider inequalities \(c_j(x)\leq0\) with a feasible point \(x\) and a dual-feasible multiplier \(\mu\in\mathbb R_+^p\). Define the nonnegative slack vector \(s=-c(x)\in\mathbb R_+^p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary finite families of scalar convex inequalities, viewed as the complementarity component of a primal-dual or KKT certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((x,\mu)\) satisfies complementary slackness when \[\mu_jc_j(x)=0\quad\text{for every }j=1,\ldots,p.\] Because \(\mu\geq0\) and \(c(x)\leq0\), this is equivalently \[\langle\mu,c(x)\rangle=0,\qquad\text{or}\qquad \langle\mu,s\rangle=0\quad(s=-c(x)\geq0).\] Componentwise, each constraint obeys the alternative \[c_j(x)<0\Longrightarrow\mu_j=0,\qquad \mu_j>0\Longrightarrow c_j(x)=0.\] Thus the inequality multiplier and the associated primal slack cannot both be strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary slackness requires each nonnegative inequality multiplier \(\mu_j\) to have zero product with its constraint residual \(c_j(x)\). Equivalently, the multiplier is orthogonal to the nonnegative slack \(s=-c(x)\). Every inactive inequality, meaning \(c_j(x)<0\), must therefore have zero multiplier; every positive multiplier can occur only on an active inequality. The converse implications need not hold, since an active constraint may have a zero multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\leq\mu\ \perp\ -c(x)\geq0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mu_jc_j(x)=0\) for all \(j\).
\(\mu^Tc(x)=0\) under \(\mu\geq0\) and \(c(x)\leq0\).
\(\operatorname{supp}(\mu)\subseteq J(x)\), where \(J(x)=\{j:c_j(x)=0\}\).
special_cases_latex: For one inequality, complementarity is \(\mu\geq0\), \(c(x)\leq0\), and \(\mu c(x)=0\).
For a linear program with slack \(s=b-Ax\geq0\), it is \(\mu_js_j=0\) for every row.
immediate_consequences_latex: Complementarity makes the Lagrangian correction vanish at the certified primal point: \(L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)\) when equality constraints are feasible.
Only active inequalities can contribute to KKT stationarity.
boundary_notes: Complementary slackness alone does not imply stationarity, primal optimality, or dual optimality.
Ordinary complementarity permits the degenerate case \(c_j(x)=0\) and \(\mu_j=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Inequality Complementarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every inequality, the nonnegative multiplier times the nonnegative slack is zero; equivalently, the multiplier is zero whenever the inequality is inactive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and suppose \(g_i(x)\le 0\) and \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Ordinary inequality complementarity is the condition
\[\lambda_i g_i(x)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]
Equivalently, for \(s=-g(x)\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), it is \(\langle\lambda,s\rangle=0\), or componentwise \(\lambda_i s_i=0\) for every \(i\).
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), \(X\) is a real vector space, \(x\in X\), and \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_i g_i(x)=0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar inequality form of complementary slackness at a primal–dual feasible point.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(s,\mu\in\mathbb R^p\), where \(s\) represents primal inequality slacks and \(\mu\) represents the corresponding dual multipliers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional componentwise complementarity for scalar inequalities; this is the orthant instance of conic complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An ordinary inequality-complementary pair is a pair \((s,\mu)\) satisfying \[s\in\mathbb R_+^p,\qquad \mu\in\mathbb R_+^p,\qquad \langle s,\mu\rangle=0.\] Since every term \(s_j\mu_j\) is nonnegative, the orthogonality condition is equivalent to \[s_j\mu_j=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p).\] For constraints \(c_j(x)\leq0\), taking \(s_j=-c_j(x)\) gives the mixed complementarity notation \[0\leq\mu_j\ \perp\ -c_j(x)\geq0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary inequality complementarity is complementarity in the nonnegative orthant. Both the slack vector \(s\) and multiplier vector \(\mu\) are componentwise nonnegative, and their inner product is zero. Nonnegativity makes this equivalent to the coordinate equations \(s_j\mu_j=0\). Hence each coordinate lies on one of the two axes of the two-dimensional nonnegative quadrant, with the origin allowed. For a constraint \(c_j(x)\leq0\), its slack is \(s_j=-c_j(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(s,\mu)\in\mathcal C_{\mathbb R_+^p}:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R_+^p\times\mathbb R_+^p:\langle u,v\rangle=0\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(s\geq0\), \(\mu\geq0\), and \(s\odot\mu=0\).
For every \(j\), either \(s_j=0\) or \(\mu_j=0\), with both allowed to vanish.
\(\operatorname{supp}(s)\cap\operatorname{supp}(\mu)=\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: For \(p=1\), the complementarity set is \((\mathbb R_+\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R_+)\).
For linear inequalities \(Ax\leq b\), use \(s=b-Ax\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strictly positive slack forces its multiplier to zero.
A strictly positive multiplier forces the associated inequality to be active.
boundary_notes: The condition does not require strict complementarity; the pair \((s_j,\mu_j)=(0,0)\) is admissible.
Signs must be adjusted if inequalities are written with the opposite convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity and Exposed-Face Membership
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each member of a complementary pair lies in the exposed face of its cone selected by the other member.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, \(s\in K\), and \(y\in K^*\). Then \(\langle y,s\rangle=0\) exactly when \[s\in K\cap y^\perp\qquad\text{and}\qquad y\in K^*\cap s^\perp.\] The sets \(K\cap y^\perp\) and \(K^*\cap s^\perp\) are exposed faces of \(K\) and \(K^*\), respectively.

\(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(s\in K\), and \(y\in K^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Complementarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slack in a closed convex cone and a multiplier in its positive dual cone are complementary exactly when their inner product is zero; for the nonnegative orthant this is componentwise complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, and define \(K^*=\{y\in E:\langle y,z\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }z\in K\}\). A pair \((s,y)\in K\times K^*\) is complementary precisely when
\[\langle y,s\rangle=0.\]
Equivalently, \(y\in K^*\cap s^\perp\) and \(s\in K\cap y^\perp\). For \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^m\), this becomes componentwise inequality complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(K^*=\{y\in E:\langle y,z\rangle\ge 0\text{ for every }z\in K\}\), \(s\in K\), and \(y\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle y,s\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic complementarity using the positive-dual convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementarity between a cone and its dual
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and define \(K^*=\{y\in E:\langle y,z\rangle\geq0\ \forall z\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed-cone complementarity. The cone need not be polyhedral or self-dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((s,y)\in E\times E\) is complementary with respect to \(K\) when \[s\in K,\qquad y\in K^*,\qquad\langle s,y\rangle=0.\] The associated complementarity set is \[\mathcal C_K:=\{(s,y)\in K\times K^*:\langle s,y\rangle=0\}.\] Equivalently, \(y\) belongs to the normal cone of \(K\) at \(s\) under the convention \(N_K(s)=\{v:\langle v,z-s\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in K\}\) precisely when \(-y\in N_K(s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic complementarity pairs a primal slack \(s\) in a closed convex cone \(K\) with a dual variable \(y\) in the dual cone \(K^*\), requiring their inner product to vanish. Dual feasibility makes the inner product nonnegative for every primal cone element, so equality identifies the boundary incidence underlying a conic KKT system. With the stated normal-cone sign convention, complementarity is equivalent to \(-y\in N_K(s)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\leq_K s\ \perp\ y\geq_{K^*}0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((s,y)\in\mathcal C_K\).
\(s\in K\) and \(-y\in N_K(s)\).
\(s\in K\cap y^\perp\) and \(y\in K^*\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^p\), conic complementarity is the componentwise system \(s_jy_j=0\).
For the positive-semidefinite cone, \(S,Y\succeq0\) and \(\langle S,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(SY)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal slack belongs to the exposed face \(K\cap y^\perp\).
If \(s\in\operatorname{int}K\), complementarity forces \(y=0\); if \(y\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), it forces \(s=0\).
boundary_notes: For non-self-dual cones, the two members lie in different cones \(K\) and \(K^*\).
The normal-cone equivalent changes sign under the opposite normal-cone convention.
