knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x\) satisfy inequalities \(c_j(x)\leq0\), let \(s_j=-c_j(x)\geq0\), and let \(\mu_j\geq0\) satisfy \(s_j\mu_j=0\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary finite inequality systems. Strict complementarity is defined coordinatewise and is stronger than complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complementary pair \((s,\mu)\in\mathbb R_+^p\times\mathbb R_+^p\) is strictly complementary when \[s_j+\mu_j>0\quad\text{for every }j=1,\ldots,p.\] Together with \(s_j\mu_j=0\), this means that exactly one of \(s_j\) and \(\mu_j\) is positive for each index. In constraint notation, \[c_j(x)=0\Longrightarrow\mu_j>0,\qquad c_j(x)<0\Longrightarrow\mu_j=0.\] Thus \(J(x)=\operatorname{supp}(\mu)\), where \(J(x)=\{j:c_j(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity excludes the degenerate coordinate where both an inequality slack and its multiplier vanish. For every inequality, either the constraint is inactive and has positive slack with zero multiplier, or it is active and has a positive multiplier. Equivalently, the active set equals the support of the multiplier vector. The definition presupposes ordinary complementary slackness and adds the strict inequality \(s_j+\mu_j>0\) at every coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s\geq0,\quad\mu\geq0,\quad s\odot\mu=0,\quad s+\mu\in\mathbb R_{++}^p.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(j\), exactly one of \(s_j>0\) and \(\mu_j>0\) holds.
\(s+\mu\) lies in the interior of \(\mathbb R_+^p\).
special_cases_latex: For one inequality, strict complementarity means either \(s>0,\mu=0\) or \(s=0,\mu>0\).
In a linear program, every primal inequality row is assigned exclusively to positive slack or positive dual multiplier.
immediate_consequences_latex: No active inequality has a zero multiplier.
The active set can be recovered from the multiplier support.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every solvable standard primal-dual LP pair has at least one strictly complementary optimal solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Strict Complementarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each scalar inequality, the complementary slack and multiplier satisfy strict complementarity when exactly one of them is positive.

Equivalently, exactly one member of every pair \((s_i,\lambda_i)\) is positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a polyhedral complementarity system represented by a subspace \(L\), strict complementarity consists of nonnegative orthogonal vectors \(z\in L\) and \(z^*\in L^\perp\) whose supports are complementary. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face-relative strict complementarity for general cones
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional inner-product space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and let \((s,y)\in K\times K^*\) satisfy \(\langle s,y\rangle=0\). For a face \(F\unlhd K\), define its conjugate face \(F^\triangle:=K^*\cap F^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General closed-cone formulation intended for nonpolyhedral cones. Relative interiors replace coordinatewise positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complementary pair \((s,y)\in K\times K^*\) is face-strictly complementary when there exists a face \(F\unlhd K\) such that \[s\in\operatorname{ri}F,\qquad y\in\operatorname{ri}F^\triangle,\qquad F^\triangle=K^*\cap F^\perp.\] Equivalently, if \(F_s\) is the unique minimal face of \(K\) containing \(s\), strict complementarity requires \[y\in\operatorname{ri}(K^*\cap F_s^\perp).\] This definition makes the primal and dual elements relatively interior to mutually complementary faces rather than merely orthogonal boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonpolyhedral cone, strict complementarity is naturally expressed through faces. The primal slack \(s\) must lie in the relative interior of a face \(F\) of \(K\), while the dual variable \(y\) lies in the relative interior of the conjugate face \(K^*\cap F^\perp\). Ordinary conic complementarity only requires membership and orthogonality; face-strict complementarity additionally requires maximal relative-interior placement within the corresponding complementary faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[s\in\operatorname{ri}F_s\quad\text{and}\quad y\in\operatorname{ri}(K^*\cap F_s^\perp).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^p\), the face-relative definition reduces to \(s_j+y_j>0\) together with \(s_jy_j=0\) for every \(j\).
special_cases_latex: For the positive-semidefinite cone, the condition corresponds to complementary ranges with \(\operatorname{rank}S+\operatorname{rank}Y\) equal to the matrix dimension.
For a self-dual cone, both members lie in \(K\), but generally in different complementary faces.
immediate_consequences_latex: The minimal face containing \(s\) is exposed by every \(y\) in the relative interior of its conjugate face.
The pair cannot lie in proper subfaces of the selected complementary faces.
boundary_notes: For nonexposed faces, conjugate-face operations may not give a one-to-one facial correspondence without additional regularity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrange multiplier set for a convex program
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0\}\), where \(f\) and \(c_j\) are proper convex functions. Fix an optimal point \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programming with nonsmooth stationarity expressed by convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Lagrange multiplier at \(\bar x\) is a pair \((\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R_+^p\) satisfying \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+A^*\lambda+\sum_{j=1}^p\mu_j\partial c_j(\bar x),\qquad \mu_jc_j(\bar x)=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p).\] The multiplier set is \[M(\bar x):=\{(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R_+^p:\text{the displayed conditions hold}\}.\] Equivalently, \((\lambda,\mu)\in M(\bar x)\) when \(\bar x\) globally minimizes the convex Lagrangian \(L(\cdot,\lambda,\mu)\) and the inequality correction vanishes at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplier is a dual vector that represents the normal needed to balance the objective subgradient at an optimal feasible point. Equality multipliers are unrestricted, inequality multipliers are nonnegative, stationarity holds, and complementary slackness removes inactive inequalities. The collection of all such pairs is the multiplier set \(M(\bar x)\). For a convex problem, membership is equivalently characterized by global minimization of the Lagrangian at \(\bar x\) plus feasibility and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[M(\bar x)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R_+^p\quad\text{is the set of all KKT dual representations at }\bar x.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(0\in\partial_xL(\bar x,\lambda,\mu)\) and \(\mu^Tc(\bar x)=0\).
\(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_xL(x,\lambda,\mu)\), \(\mu\geq0\), and complementary slackness holds.
special_cases_latex: For differentiable data, stationarity is \(\nabla f(\bar x)+A^*\lambda+\sum_j\mu_j\nabla c_j(\bar x)=0\).
For affine constraints, \(M(\bar x)\) is described by linear equalities and inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: For the convex model in the cited source, multiplier sets attached to any two primal optimal solutions coincide.
The multiplier set is convex; it may nevertheless be empty, a singleton, nonunique, or unbounded depending on qualification and redundancy.
boundary_notes: Existence of an optimizer does not automatically imply \(M(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\).
Redundant equality constraints can create affine directions of nonuniqueness in \(\lambda\).

notation.meaning: Set of all Lagrange multiplier pairs at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Existence for Polyhedral Constraints without Slater Strictness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every optimizer of a differentiable convex objective over a nonempty polyhedron admits KKT multipliers, even when no point satisfies all inequalities strictly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable, and let
\[P=\{x:Cx\le d,\ Ax=b\}\]
be a nonempty polyhedron. If \(x^*\in P\) minimizes \(f\) over \(P\), then there exist \(\lambda\ge0\) and \(\nu\) such that
\[\nabla f(x^*)+C^\top\lambda+A^\top\nu=0,\qquad \lambda_i(C_i x^*-d_i)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]
No strictly feasible point is required. Redundant equality rows may destroy uniqueness or boundedness of \(\nu\), but not existence.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable.
\(P=\{x:Cx\le d,\ Ax=b\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist sign-compatible inequality multipliers and equality multipliers satisfying stationarity and complementary slackness at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier existence from polyhedral normal-cone geometry rather than strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Existence Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slater feasibility and primal attainment ensure the existence of optimal inequality and equality multipliers satisfying the KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider minimizing \(f_0(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le 0\) and \(Ax=b\). Under the stated Slater condition, every optimizer \(x^*\) admits multipliers \(\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(\nu^*\) such that
\[0\in\partial_x L(x^*,\lambda^*,\nu^*),\qquad \lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]
Together with primal and dual feasibility, these are the KKT conditions. The multipliers attain the Lagrange dual optimum, so the primal and dual optimal values coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex and \(A x=b\) is affine.
There is \(\bar x\) with \(A\bar x=b\) and \(g_i(\bar x)<0\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(\lambda^*\ge 0\) and \(\nu^*\) satisfying stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex program under Slater’s condition.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a convex program \(\min\{f(x):Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0\}\) and an optimizer \(\bar x\), let \(M(\bar x)\) denote its KKT multiplier set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programs; existence is separated from boundedness and uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The program is in a pointwise multiplier-existence regime at \(\bar x\) when \[M(\bar x)\neq\varnothing.\] A constraint representation is in a uniform multiplier-existence regime when \[\forall f\ \forall\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x),\qquad M_f(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\] for the specified class of convex objectives. The basic constraint qualification \(N'(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\) gives pointwise existence. Weak Slater qualification gives uniform existence for the convex constraint representation: there is \(x_0\in C\) satisfying every nonaffine inequality strictly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier existence means that the KKT multiplier set at an optimizer is nonempty. A pointwise regime guarantees this for one optimizer and objective; a uniform regime guarantees it for every optimizer of every objective in the stated class. Basic constraint qualification is a pointwise condition equating the data-generated and geometric normal cones. Weak Slater qualification is a practical representation-level condition that supplies multiplier existence throughout the convex problem class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{BCQ at }\bar x\ \Longrightarrow\ M(\bar x)\neq\varnothing,\qquad \text{WSA}\ \Longrightarrow\ M(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\ \text{for every optimizer}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a solved convex program, multiplier existence is equivalent to existence of a saddle point of the Lagrangian with the optimizer as its primal component.
It is also equivalent to existence of a dual maximizer attaining the primal value when the cited Lagrangian dual framework applies.
special_cases_latex: For affine equality and inequality constraints, existence holds whenever an optimal solution exists.
For inequality-only convex programs, a strictly feasible point is the ordinary Slater existence condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: Existence permits an optimizer to be accompanied by a finite-dimensional dual certificate.
Existence alone does not control the size or cardinality of \(M(\bar x)\).
boundary_notes: Weak Slater allows affine inequalities to be nonstrict; strong Slater requires all inequalities strict and adds independence of equality normals.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, additional topological hypotheses are generally required.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M(\bar x)\subseteq\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R_+^p\) be the KKT multiplier set of a convex program at an optimal point \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional multiplier sets. Cardinality is classified independently of boundedness, although convexity sharply restricts the finite cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multiplier cardinality regime at \(\bar x\) is classified by \[M(\bar x)=\varnothing\quad\text{(nonexistence)},\] \[|M(\bar x)|=1\quad\text{(unique multiplier)},\] or \[|M(\bar x)|>1\quad\text{(nonunique multipliers)}.\] Since \(M(\bar x)\) is convex, the nonunique case contains a nontrivial line segment and hence is uncountable. Thus a nonempty finite multiplier set is necessarily a singleton. For the right-hand-side perturbation value function \(P(u,v)\), when the sensitivity identification \(\partial P(0,0)=-M(\bar x)\) holds, uniqueness is equivalent to differentiability of \(P\) at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier cardinality distinguishes no multiplier, exactly one multiplier, and multiple multipliers. Convexity rules out a multiplier set with two or any other finite number greater than one: two distinct multipliers generate an entire segment. Under the standard perturbation-value correspondence, the singleton regime is exactly the regime in which the value function is differentiable at the unperturbed right-hand side; a non-singleton set produces a set-valued first-order sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0<|M(\bar x)|<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |M(\bar x)|=1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Uniqueness means \(M(\bar x)=\{(\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\}\).
Under \(\partial P(0,0)=-M(\bar x)\), uniqueness is equivalent to \(P\) being differentiable at \((0,0)\).
special_cases_latex: Linear dependence among equality normals can force infinitely many equality multipliers.
A positive-definite primal objective may give a unique primal solution while multipliers remain nonunique.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonunique convex multiplier set has continuum cardinality.
Uniqueness supplies a single first-order price vector for admissible right-hand-side perturbations.
boundary_notes: Uniqueness of the primal optimizer does not imply uniqueness of multipliers.
Differentiability equivalence requires the stated sensitivity identification and local finiteness assumptions for the value function.

knowledge_statements.title: LICQ Is Sufficient but Not Necessary for a Unique Multiplier
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent active gradients can coexist with a unique KKT multiplier because multiplier sign restrictions may eliminate every nonzero feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^2}-x_1\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1\le0,\quad x_2\le0,\quad x_1+x_2\le0.\]
At \(x^*=(0,0)\), all three inequalities are active and their gradients \((1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\) are linearly dependent. Stationarity and nonnegativity require
\[-(1,0)+\lambda_1(1,0)+\lambda_2(0,1)+\lambda_3(1,1)=0,\qquad \lambda\ge0,\]
whose unique solution is \(\lambda=(1,0,0)\). Thus active-gradient linear independence is sufficient but not necessary for multiplier uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: The stated two-dimensional linear convex program is considered at the KKT point \(x^*=(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active gradients are dependent, but the KKT multiplier is uniquely \((1,0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness boundary for the active-gradient linear-independence uniqueness condition.

notation.meaning: Multiplier vector for the three inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique-Multiplier Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear independence of active constraint gradients makes the stationarity representation, and therefore the KKT multiplier, unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a KKT point, complementary slackness fixes \(\lambda_i^*=0\) for every inactive index. Stationarity is
\[
abla f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i\in I(x^*)}\lambda_i^*
abla g_i(x^*)+A^	op
u^*=0.\]
If the active inequality gradients and equality-constraint gradients are linearly independent, this linear representation of \(-
abla f_0(x^*)\) is unique. Hence any two KKT multiplier pairs coincide, including all inactive components fixed at zero.
assumptions_latex: The convex constraint functions are differentiable at a KKT point \(x^*\).
The vectors \(\{\nabla g_i(x^*):g_i(x^*)=0\}\) together with the columns represented by \(A^\top\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KKT multiplier pair \((\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) is unique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional KKT system under linear independence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\lambda,
u)\in M(x^*)\), and let \(I=\{i:g_i(x^*)=0\}\). The set \(M(x^*)\) contains a multiplier distinct from \((\lambda,
u)\) if and only if there exist \((d,\eta)
e(0,0)\) and \(t>0\) such that
\[d_{I^c}=0,\qquad \lambda_I+t d_I\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}d_i
abla g_i(x^*)+A^	op\eta=0.\]
In that event, \((\lambda+s d,
u+s\eta)\in M(x^*)\) for every \(s\in[0,t]\).
assumptions_latex: All functions are differentiable at the fixed KKT point \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(x^*)\) is non-singleton exactly when the stated nonzero sign-feasible null displacement exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Multiplier Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed differentiable solution, the multiplier set is closed and convex; two distinct multipliers generate an entire segment of multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The KKT multiplier set at \(x^*\) is
\[M(x^*)=\left\{(\lambda,
u):\lambda_I\ge0,\ \lambda_{I^c}=0,\ 
abla f_0(x^*)+\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i
abla g_i(x^*)+A^	op
u=0ight\}.\]
It is the intersection of an affine set with coordinate half-spaces, hence is closed and convex. A multiple-multiplier regime occurs exactly when \(M(x^*)\) contains distinct pairs; then every convex combination of those pairs is also a multiplier.
assumptions_latex: All objective and constraint functions are differentiable at a fixed feasible point \(x^*\).
At least one KKT multiplier exists at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiplier set is closed and convex; multiplicity means it contains two distinct points.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Stationarity Dependencies as Degeneracy Sources
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sign-compatible dependencies among active gradients or equality rows generate alternative multipliers; a null direction of the equality transpose generates a full affine line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\lambda,
u)\) be a KKT multiplier at \(x^*\), with active set \(I\). If \((d,\eta)
e(0,0)\) satisfies
\[d_{I^c}=0,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}d_i
abla g_i(x^*)+A^	op\eta=0,\]
and \(\lambda_I+t d_I\ge0\) for some \(t
e0\), then \((\lambda+t d,
u+t\eta)\) is another KKT multiplier. Thus redundant active inequalities, vanishing active gradients, and dependent equality rows create multiplicity whenever the corresponding direction is sign-compatible. In particular, every nonzero \(\eta\in\ker A^	op\) generates the line \((\lambda,
u+s\eta)\), \(s\in\mathbb R\).

At least one KKT multiplier \((\lambda,\nu)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every stated sign-compatible homogeneous dependency generates distinct KKT multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Degeneracy Sources
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing x subject to two identical constraints requiring x to be nonnegative has the unique optimizer zero but a whole line segment of nonnegative KKT multipliers whose components sum to one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the problem of minimizing \(f(x)=x\) over \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) subject to \(g_1(x)=g_2(x)=-x\le 0\), the unique optimizer is \(x^*=0\). Its KKT multiplier set is
\[M(x^*)=\{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb{R}_+^2:\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\}.\]
Thus duplicated active constraints can produce infinitely many multipliers despite a unique primal optimizer.
assumptions_latex: Minimize \(f(x)=x\) over \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) subject to the duplicated inequalities \(g_1(x)=g_2(x)=-x\le 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(x^*=0\), the multiplier set is \(\{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb{R}_+^2:\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A redundant active-constraint example producing multiplier degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness–Multiplicity Transitions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multiplier is unique on either side of zero, but when the parameter makes the two active constraints identical at zero, the multiplier set becomes a line segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), minimize \(x\) subject to \(-x\le 0\) and \(-x-t\le 0\). The optimizer is \(x^*(t)=\max\{0,-t\}\). If \(t>0\), the unique multiplier is \((\lambda_1,\lambda_2)=(1,0)\); if \(t<0\), it is \((\lambda_1,\lambda_2)=(0,1)\). At \(t=0\),
\[M(x^*(0))=\{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb{R}_+^2:\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\}.\]
Thus multiplier uniqueness changes to multiplicity when the two active constraints coincide.
assumptions_latex: For \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), minimize \(x\) over \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) subject to \(-x\le 0\) and \(-x-t\le 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KKT multiplier is unique for \(t\ne 0\), whereas at \(t=0\) the multiplier set is \(\{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\in\mathbb{R}_+^2:\lambda_1+\lambda_2=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric collision of active inequalities marking a uniqueness-to-multiplicity transition.

notation.meaning: Parameter controlling coincidence of the active constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Cone Criterion for Multiplier Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty smooth KKT multiplier set is bounded exactly when its homogeneous stationarity system has no nonzero sign-compatible recession direction; redundant equality rows force unbounded equality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I=\{i:g_i(x^*)=0\}\), and suppose \(M(x^*)\ne\varnothing\). Then
\[\operatorname{rec}M(x^*)=\left\{(d,\eta):d_I\ge0,\ d_{I^c}=0,\ \sum_{i\in I}d_i\nabla g_i(x^*)+A^\top\eta=0\right\}.\]
Consequently,
\[M(x^*)\text{ is bounded}\iff\operatorname{rec}M(x^*)=\{(0,0)\}.\]
In particular, if \(\ker A^\top\ne\{0\}\), every nonempty multiplier set is unbounded in its equality-multiplier component.

The KKT multiplier set \(M(x^*)\) is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed optimizer, a uniform strict-feasibility margin bounds all inequality multipliers, and full row rank of the equality system then bounds the equality multipliers, so the KKT multiplier set is nonempty and bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated assumptions, the KKT multiplier set at \(x^*\) is nonempty. Every multiplier pair \((\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) at \(x^*\) satisfies
\[\sigma\|\lambda^*\|_1\le f_0(\bar x)-p^*.\]
Moreover,
\[A^\top\nu^*=-\nabla f_0(x^*)-sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^*\nabla g_i(x^*).\]
Because \(A\) has full row rank, the set of such equality multipliers is also bounded. Hence the KKT multiplier set at \(x^*\) is nonempty and bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex and differentiable, \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\) has full row rank, and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\).
\(x^*\) is an optimizer of the problem with constraints \(g_i(x)\le 0\) and \(Ax=b\).
There are \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\sigma>0\) such that \(A\bar x=b\) and \(g_i(\bar x)\le-\sigma\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The KKT multiplier set at the fixed optimizer \(x^*\) is nonempty and bounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness of the multiplier set at a fixed optimizer of a finite-dimensional differentiable convex program under quantitative Slater feasibility.

notation.meaning: Inequality and equality KKT multipliers at the fixed optimizer.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M(\bar x)\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+p}\) be the KKT multiplier set at an optimizer \(\bar x\) of a finite-dimensional convex program with affine equalities and convex inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programs. Boundedness is a property of the whole multiplier set, not of a selected multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multiplier set is bounded when \[\sup\{\|(\lambda,\mu)\|:(\lambda,\mu)\in M(\bar x)\}<+\infty.\] It is in the nonempty compact multiplier regime when it is nonempty and bounded, since the KKT-defined set is closed in finite dimensions. In the cited formulation, the strong Slater assumption consists of linear independence of the equality normals together with existence of \(x_0\) such that \[Ax_0=b,\qquad c_j(x_0)<0\quad(j=1,\ldots,p).\] For an optimizer, this assumption characterizes the regime in which \(M(\bar x)\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplier boundedness means that one common finite norm bound applies to every admissible multiplier pair. Because the multiplier set is closed in finite dimensions, nonemptiness plus boundedness is equivalent to nonempty compactness. Strong Slater qualification eliminates both inequality recession directions and equality-multiplier directions caused by redundant equality constraints; in the cited convex formulation it is necessary and sufficient for the multiplier set to be nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{SSA}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M(\bar x)\ \text{is nonempty, compact, and convex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Boundedness is equivalent to the recession cone \(M(\bar x)^\infty\) being \(\{0\}\) for a nonempty closed convex multiplier set.
Nonempty compactness is equivalent to existence of \(R<\infty\) with \(M(\bar x)\subseteq R\mathbb B\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A^*\) has a nontrivial kernel, then any equality multiplier can be shifted along that kernel, so \(M(\bar x)\) is unbounded whenever nonempty.
For inequality-only problems, strong Slater reduces to existence of a point satisfying every inequality strictly.
immediate_consequences_latex: A continuous linear functional of the multipliers attains its maximum and minimum on a nonempty compact multiplier set.
Boundedness controls the range of first-order sensitivity prices.
boundary_notes: Weak Slater may guarantee nonemptiness without boundedness.
Compactness does not imply uniqueness; a compact multiplier set may contain many points.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Cone Characterization of Multiplier Boundedness
Joint Inequality and Equality Right-Hand-Side Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strong duality, the negative inequality and equality multipliers jointly form a subgradient of the value function with respect to both right-hand-side perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[v(u,w)=\inf\{f_0(x):g_i(x)\le u_i\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax=b+w\}.\]
If strong duality holds at \((u,w)=(0,0)\) and \((\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) is an optimal multiplier pair, then
\[v(u,w)\ge v(0,0)-\langle\lambda^*,u\rangle-\langle\nu^*,w\rangle\]
for every perturbation in the effective domain. Hence
\[(-\lambda^*,-\nu^*)\in\partial v(0,0).\]
If \(v\) is differentiable at the origin, its right-hand-side derivatives uniquely determine both multiplier components.
assumptions_latex: The jointly perturbed value function \(v(u,w)\) is defined as stated.
\((\lambda^*,\nu^*)\) is an optimal multiplier pair at \((0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((-\lambda^*,-\nu^*)\in\partial v(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-slope interpretation of both inequality and equality multipliers under joint right-hand-side perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Multipliers as Sensitivity Objects
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal multiplier is the negative of a supporting slope of the value function with respect to constraint relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every perturbation \(u\) for which \(v(u)\) is defined, the multiplier \(\lambda^*\) supplies the global affine estimate
\[v(u)\ge v(0)-\langle\lambda^*,u\rangle.\]
Therefore \(-\lambda^*\in\partial v(0)\). In particular, when \(v\) is differentiable at zero, the inequality multiplier is uniquely determined as \(\lambda^*=-\nabla v(0)\); without differentiability, optimal multipliers represent supporting slopes of the value function.
assumptions_latex: Let \(v(u)\) be the optimal value with constraints \(g_i(x)\le u_i\) and \(Ax=b\).
Strong duality holds at \(u=0\), with an optimal inequality multiplier \(\lambda^*\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-\lambda^*\in\partial v(0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Right-hand-side sensitivity of a convex inequality system.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^p\), define \(C(u,v)=\{x:Ax=b+u,\ c_j(x)\leq v_j\}\) and \(P(u,v)=\inf\{f(x):x\in C(u,v)\}\). Assume the unperturbed convex problem has a finite attained value \(P(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Right-hand-side sensitivity for finite-dimensional convex programs. The sign convention follows perturbations \(Ax=b+u\) and \(c(x)\leq v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiplier \((\lambda,\mu)\) is a sensitivity object for \(P\) when it supplies the global affine support inequality \[P(u,v)\geq P(0,0)-\langle\lambda,u\rangle-\langle\mu,v\rangle\qquad\forall(u,v).\] Equivalently, \[(-\lambda,-\mu)\in\partial P(0,0).\] For the convex perturbation model in the cited source, the multiplier set satisfies \[-M=\partial P(0,0).\] If strong Slater qualification holds, \(P\) is finite near the origin and \[P(u,v)=P(0,0)+\sigma_M(-u,-v)+o(\|(u,v)\|).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multipliers act as sensitivity objects by furnishing subgradients of the optimal-value function with respect to constraint right-hand sides. With the displayed perturbation convention, the negative multiplier vector is a subgradient of \(P\) at the origin. Hence every multiplier gives a global affine lower estimate for the perturbed value, while the full multiplier set gives all first-order slopes. Under strong Slater qualification, the support function of the multiplier set is the directional first-order term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[M= -\partial P(0,0),\qquad P'(0,0;u,v)=\sigma_M(-u,-v)\ \text{under the stated regularity}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \((\lambda,\mu)\in M\) if and only if the displayed affine support inequality holds for every perturbation.
If \(M=\{(\bar\lambda,\bar\mu)\}\), then \(\nabla P(0,0)=(-\bar\lambda,-\bar\mu)\).
special_cases_latex: For a perturbed equality \(Ax=b+u\), \(-\lambda_i\) is the corresponding value-function slope.
For a relaxed inequality bound \(v_j\), monotonicity gives the sensitivity component \(-\mu_j\leq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Multiplier uniqueness is equivalent to differentiability of \(P\) at the origin under the local finiteness regime.
A compact multiplier set gives finite directional first-order sensitivity in every perturbation direction.
boundary_notes: Changing the perturbation sign convention changes the sign relating multipliers and subgradients.
Without local finiteness or qualification, \(P\) may take infinite values nearby and ordinary first-order sensitivity may fail.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(p^*=\inf\{f(x):Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0\}\) with Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,Ax-b\rangle+\sum_j\mu_jc_j(x)\). Define \(\psi(\lambda,\mu)=\inf_xL(x,\lambda,\mu)\) for \(\mu\geq0\), and \(\psi=-\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian dual certificates for finite-dimensional minimization with affine equalities and inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual certificate family is \[\mathcal D:=\{(\lambda,\mu,\beta):\lambda\in\mathbb R^m,\ \mu\in\mathbb R_+^p,\ \beta\in\mathbb R,\ \beta\leq\psi(\lambda,\mu)\}.\] A member certifies the universal inequality \[\beta\leq L(x,\lambda,\mu)\quad\forall x,\] and therefore the primal lower bound \[\beta\leq f(x)\quad\forall x\in C,\qquad\beta\leq p^*.\] The tight certificate value associated with \((\lambda,\mu)\) is \(\beta=\psi(\lambda,\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual certificate consists of equality multipliers, nonnegative inequality multipliers, and a scalar lower bound dominated by the dual function. Since feasible primal points annihilate equality terms and make inequality terms nonpositive, every such certificate gives a valid lower bound on every feasible objective value. The family contains certificates of varying quality; maximizing the tight value \(\psi(\lambda,mu)\) is the Lagrangian dual problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\lambda,\mu,\beta)\in\mathcal D\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\beta\leq p^*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A tight certificate is a dual-feasible pair \((\lambda,\mu)\) together with its value \(\psi(\lambda,\mu)\).
\(\beta\leq\psi(\lambda,\mu)\) is equivalent to \(\beta\leq L(x,\lambda,\mu)\) for every \(x\).
special_cases_latex: For a linear program, finiteness of \(\psi\) imposes the usual dual linear equality, and \(\psi\) becomes the dual objective.
For a conic program, membership of the dual variable in the dual cone replaces componentwise nonnegativity.
immediate_consequences_latex: The best value furnished by this family is the dual optimum \(d^*=\sup_{\lambda,\mu\geq0}\psi(\lambda,\mu)\), with \(d^*\leq p^*\).
A certificate attaining \(p^*\) proves zero duality gap and primal optimality of any feasible point with objective \(p^*\).
boundary_notes: A dual-feasible certificate need not attain the best dual value.
Without strong duality, even the best certificate may be strictly below \(p^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Feasible Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative inequality multiplier together with any equality multiplier yields a dual lower bound on the primal optimum; pairing it with a feasible primal point gives a certified suboptimality bound, and a zero gap certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(\nu\in\mathbb{R}^p\), weak duality gives
\[d(\lambda,\nu)\le p^*.\]
If \(x\) is primal feasible, then
\[d(\lambda,\nu)\le p^*\le f_0(x).\]
Thus \(d(\lambda,nu)\) certifies a lower bound on the minimization optimum, and \(f_0(x)-d(\lambda,nu)\) certifies an upper bound on the suboptimality of \(x\). A zero gap certifies primal and dual optimality.
assumptions_latex: Minimize \(f_0(x)\) over \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le 0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(Ax=b\), and let the optimal value be \(p^*\).
The candidate dual variables satisfy \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) and \(\nu\in\mathbb{R}^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(\lambda,\nu)\le p^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificate for finite-dimensional minimization with inequality and equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p^*=\inf\{f(x):Ax=b,\ c_j(x)\leq0\}\), let \(L(x,\lambda,\mu)=f(x)+\langle\lambda,Ax-b\rangle+\sum_j\mu_jc_j(x)\), and let \(q(\lambda,\mu)=\inf_xL(x,\lambda,\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificates for primal minimization. The certificate remains valid without primal attainment or strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dual-feasible bound certificate is a pair \((\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R_+^p\) for which \(q(\lambda,\mu)>-\infty\). Its certified bound is \[B(\lambda,\mu):=q(\lambda,\mu).\] Certificate validity is the quantified relation \[B(\lambda,\mu)\leq f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\text{ satisfying }Ax=b\text{ and }c(x)\leq0,\] and hence \[B(\lambda,\mu)\leq p^*.\] Given a feasible candidate \(\hat x\), the computable primal-dual certificate gap is \[G(\hat x;\lambda,\mu):=f(\hat x)-B(\lambda,\mu)\geq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible bound certificate is any equality multiplier and nonnegative inequality multiplier for which the Lagrangian dual value is finite. That value is a rigorous lower bound on every feasible primal objective value and therefore on the primal optimum. If a feasible candidate \(\hat x\) is also available, subtracting the certified lower bound from \(f(\hat x)\) gives a nonnegative optimality gap. A zero gap certifies that both the candidate and the dual certificate are optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[q(\lambda,\mu)\leq p^*\leq f(\hat x),\qquad 0\leq f(\hat x)-p^*\leq G(\hat x;\lambda,\mu).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The scalar \(B\) is certified when \(B\leq L(x,\lambda,\mu)\) for every \(x\), with \(\mu\geq0\).
For the tight bound at fixed multipliers, \(B=\inf_xL(x,\lambda,\mu)\).
special_cases_latex: In linear programming, a dual-feasible vector directly supplies the usual dual objective lower bound.
If \(G(\hat x;\lambda,\mu)=0\), then \(\hat x\) is primal optimal, \((\lambda,\mu)\) is dual optimal, and there is no duality gap.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any positive gap gives an a posteriori upper bound on the suboptimality of \(\hat x\).
Maximizing \(B(\lambda,\mu)\) over dual-feasible multipliers improves the certified lower bound.
boundary_notes: If \(q(\lambda,\mu)=-\infty\), the pair gives no finite bound certificate.
Weak duality validates the bound but does not guarantee existence or attainment of an optimal dual certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-feasible point and dual-feasible multipliers satisfying stationarity and complementary slackness certify optimality and zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(x^\star\) is primal feasible, \(\lambda^\star\ge 0\), and \(q(\lambda^\star,
u^\star)>-\infty\). If \[0\in\partial_xL(x^\star,\lambda^\star,
u^\star),\qquad \lambda_i^\star g_i(x^\star)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\] then \(x^\star\) minimizes \(L(\cdot,\lambda^\star,
u^\star)\). Consequently, \[q(\lambda^\star,
u^\star)=L(x^\star,\lambda^\star,
u^\star)=f(x^\star)=p^\star.\] Thus primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity, and complementary slackness form a verifiable primal–dual optimality certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper closed convex functions.
The primal problem is \(p^\star=\inf\{f(x):g_i(x)\le 0,\ Ax=b\}\), with Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\langle\nu,Ax-b\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\) and \((\lambda^\star,\nu^\star)\) are primal and dual optimal, and \(f(x^\star)=q(\lambda^\star,\nu^\star)=p^\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient KKT certificate for a finite-dimensional convex program with inequalities and affine equalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Optimality Certificate for a Convex Program
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. Consider \(p^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\leq0\}\), the Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)\), and the dual function \(q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex inequality-constrained minimization; the certificate itself is sufficient without a constraint qualification, while necessity requires primal and dual attainment with zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\in X\times\mathbb{R}^m\) is a primal–dual optimality certificate when \[g(\bar x)\leq0,\qquad \bar\lambda\geq0,\qquad \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,\bar\lambda),\qquad \bar\lambda_i g_i(\bar x)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Equivalently, it certifies the equality chain \[q(\bar\lambda)=L(\bar x,\bar\lambda)=f(\bar x),\] so weak duality yields \(q(\bar\lambda)=p^*=f(\bar x)\). Thus \(\bar x\) is primal optimal, \(\bar\lambda\) is dual optimal, and the primal–dual gap is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual certificate consists of a primal-feasible point and a nonnegative multiplier vector such that the point globally minimizes the corresponding Lagrangian and every multiplier is complementary to its constraint slack. These conditions make the Lagrangian value, primal objective value, and dual value equal, thereby certifying optimality of both points and a zero duality gap. Conversely, an attained primal–dual optimum with zero gap satisfies these conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\) is certified exactly by primal feasibility, dual feasibility, Lagrangian minimization, and complementary slackness; these imply \(f(\bar x)=p^*=q(\bar\lambda)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Lagrangian minimization condition is equivalent to \(0\in\partial(f+\sum_i\bar\lambda_i g_i+I_X)(\bar x)\).
When all functions are differentiable and \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), stationarity becomes \(\nabla f(\bar x)+\sum_i\bar\lambda_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For a linear program, the conditions reduce to primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness.
immediate_consequences_latex: Either member of a certified pair supplies an attained bound equal to the other member's objective value.
No separate comparison with an unknown optimizer is required.
boundary_notes: Without zero-gap dual attainment, an optimal primal point need not admit such a multiplier certificate.
Approximate residual and gap certificates are separate notions and do not satisfy these equalities exactly.

notation.meaning: Indicator function of the set X, equal to zero on X and positive infinity outside X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constraint Qualification Is Not Needed for Certificate Sufficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between verifying a supplied KKT certificate and guaranteeing that such multipliers exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the stated convex program, primal feasibility, \(\lambda\ge0\), stationarity \(0\in\partial_xL(x,\lambda,\nu)\), and complementary slackness are sufficient for primal–dual optimality without any constraint qualification. A constraint qualification is needed only for converse assertions guaranteeing that an optimizer admits such multipliers; its failure does not invalidate a KKT tuple that has already been verified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint qualifications govern existence or necessity of KKT multipliers, not the sufficiency of a verified convex KKT certificate.
assumptions_latex: The objective and inequality functions are convex and equality constraints are affine.
A primal-feasible KKT tuple with sign-compatible multipliers is explicitly given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuple certifies global primal and dual optimality without Slater or another constraint qualification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tolerance-Indexed Family of Approximate Primal–Dual Certificates
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For the convex program and Lagrangian \(L\) defined locally, fix nonnegative tolerances \(\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_{\mathrm p},\varepsilon_{\mathrm d},\varepsilon_{\mathrm s},\varepsilon_{\mathrm c},\varepsilon_{\mathrm g})\). Let \([u]_+\) denote componentwise positive part and let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a fixed norm.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programming; this record defines a general tolerance-indexed family rather than asserting that every approximate algorithm produces one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The approximate-certificate family \(\{\mathcal C_\varepsilon\}_{\varepsilon\geq0}\) consists of pairs \((x,\lambda)\in X\times\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \[\|[g(x)]_+\|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm p},\qquad \|[-\lambda]_+\|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm d},\] \[L(x,\lambda)\leq\inf_{z\in X}L(z,\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm s},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m|\lambda_i g_i(x)|\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm c},\] and, whenever a computable dual lower bound \(q(\lambda)\) is finite, \[f(x)-q(\lambda)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm g}.\] Thus \(\mathcal C_0\) is the exact certificate set, while \(\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon'\) componentwise implies \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon\subseteq\mathcal C_{\varepsilon'}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate-certificate family is a collection indexed by tolerances. Membership records bounded primal infeasibility, bounded multiplier infeasibility, approximate minimization of the Lagrangian, bounded complementarity error, and—when available—a bounded primal–dual gap. The zero-tolerance member is the exact certificate set, and enlarging any tolerance can only enlarge the family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon\) is defined by the five displayed error bounds, with \(\mathcal C_0\) exact and \(\mathcal C_\varepsilon\subseteq\mathcal C_{\varepsilon'}\) for \(\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon'\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The approximate Lagrangian-minimization condition is equivalent to \(0\in\partial_{\varepsilon_{\mathrm s}}(L(\cdot,\lambda)+I_X)(x)\).
special_cases_latex: A residual-only family omits the gap requirement when evaluating \(q(\lambda)\) is impractical.
A gap-only family restricts to primal- and dual-feasible pairs and retains only \(f(x)-q(\lambda)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm g}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Each tolerance identifies which part of exact optimality is relaxed.
The nesting property supports stopping rules with decreasing tolerance schedules.
boundary_notes: Small residuals do not imply a small distance to the solution set without an error-bound or regularity assumption.

Strong-Monotonicity Residual Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strongly monotone residual operator, residual size divided by the modulus bounds distance to its unique zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(T\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone, \(0\in T(z^\star)\), and \(v\in T(z)\), then \[\|z-z^\star\|\le\frac{\|v\|}{\mu}.\] In particular, \(\|v\|\le\mu\varepsilon\) certifies \(\|z-z^\star\|\le\varepsilon\).
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is \(\mu\)-strongly monotone for some \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(v\in T(z)\) satisfies \(\|z-z^\star\|\le\|v\|/\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance certificate for a strongly monotone residual inclusion.

notation.meaning: Computable graph residual at the candidate.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Alone Gives No Linear Error Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small monotone-operator residual need not linearly control distance to the solution set; an error-bound property is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The map \(T(t)=t^3\) is monotone and has the unique zero \(0\), but \[\frac{\operatorname{dist}(t,T^{-1}(0))}{|T(t)|}=\frac1{t^2}\to+\infty\quad(t\to0,\ t\ne0).\] Thus monotonicity alone does not imply a local linear residual-to-distance bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite local constant \(C\) satisfies \(|t|\le C|T(t)|\) for all sufficiently small \(t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a linear residual-distance certificate under monotonicity alone.

notation.meaning: Zero set of the residual operator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directly checkable residual certificate for approximate KKT satisfaction.

For differentiable convex \(f,g_i\), define \(L(x,\lambda,

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity residuals certify approximate KKT satisfaction, but not automatically a numerical objective-error bound.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable convex functions. For \((x,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\), define primal, dual, stationarity, and complementarity residuals using fixed norms.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional convex inequality-constrained problems; nonsmooth stationarity requires a distance to a subdifferential and is outside this precise formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[r_{\mathrm p}(x)=\|[g(x)]_+\|,\qquad r_{\mathrm d}(\lambda)=\|[-\lambda]_+\|,\] \[r_{\mathrm s}(x,\lambda)=\left\|\nabla f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x)\right\|_*,\qquad r_{\mathrm c}(x,\lambda)=\|\lambda\odot g(x)\|.\] The aggregate KKT residual is \[R(x,\lambda)=\max\{r_{\mathrm p}(x),r_{\mathrm d}(\lambda),r_{\mathrm s}(x,\lambda),r_{\mathrm c}(x,\lambda)\}.\] A pair is an \(\varepsilon\)-residual certificate when \(R(x,\lambda)\leq\varepsilon\). It is exact precisely when \(R(x,\lambda)=0\), in which case primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity, and complementary slackness all hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual-based certificate attaches a nonnegative scalar to each KKT condition: constraint violation, negative multipliers, stationarity error, and complementarity error. Their maximum is the aggregate residual. A pair is certified to tolerance epsilon when this maximum is at most epsilon. A zero residual is exactly the KKT system in the stated smooth convex regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,\lambda)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-residual certificate if and only if \(R(x,\lambda)\leq\varepsilon\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using separate tolerances gives \(r_j\leq\varepsilon_j\) for \(j\in\{\mathrm p,\mathrm d,\mathrm s,\mathrm c\}\).
For a constrained set \(X\), stationarity may be replaced by \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\nabla f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i\nabla g_i(x)+N_X(x))\).
special_cases_latex: For equality constraints, the primal residual uses the norm of the equality defect and the corresponding multipliers are unrestricted.
immediate_consequences_latex: The residual provides a directly computable termination statistic when function values and derivatives are available.
Zero aggregate residual recovers an exact primal–dual certificate under the stated convex assumptions.
boundary_notes: Residual magnitude depends on scaling, the selected norm, and the representation of constraints.
A small residual alone gives no universal objective-gap or distance-to-solution bound.
review_flags: A source supporting this exact aggregate residual and its scaling conventions was not located.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Norm Requires an Error-Bound Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for converting a stationarity residual into distance to the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Monotonicity alone does not yield a uniform linear residual-to-distance certificate. For \(T(t)=t^3\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(T\) is monotone and has the unique zero \(t^\star=0\), but \[\frac{|t-t^\star|}{|T(t)|}=\frac1{t^2}\to+\infty\quad\text{as }t\to0,\ t\ne0.\] Thus no constant \(C<\infty\) satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(t,T^{-1}(0))\le C|T(t)|\) near zero; strong monotonicity, metric subregularity, or another error bound is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small monotone-operator residual need not linearly control solution distance; an error-bound property is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No finite local constant \(C\) satisfies \(|t|\le C|T(t)|\) for all sufficiently small \(t\).

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Norm Requires an Error-Bound Property
Gap-Based Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any feasible primal–dual pair, the computed gap bounds both objective errors; a gap at most ε therefore certifies ε-optimality of both reported objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every primal-feasible \(\hat x\in X\) and dual-feasible \(\hat y\in Y\), the gap \(G(\hat x,\hat y)=f(\hat x)-q(\hat y)\) satisfies \[0\le f(\hat x)-p^\star\le G(\hat x,\hat y),\qquad 0\le d^\star-q(\hat y)\le G(\hat x,\hat y).\] Hence \(G(\hat x,\hat y)\le\varepsilon\) is an absolute \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate for both reported objective values, without requiring strong duality or attainment of the optimal values.
assumptions_latex: \(p^\star=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(d^\star=\sup_{y\in Y}q(y)\), with weak duality \(q(y)\le f(x)\) for all feasible \(x,y\).
The reported points \(\hat x\in X\) and \(\hat y\in Y\) are respectively primal and dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(f(\hat x)-q(\hat y)\le\varepsilon\), then \(f(\hat x)-p^\star\le\varepsilon\) and \(d^\star-q(\hat y)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute primal–dual gap certificate under weak duality.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a minimization problem have primal feasible set \(P\), objective \(F:P\to\mathbb{R}\), dual feasible set \(D\), and dual objective \(Q:D\to\mathbb{R}\), with weak duality \(Q(y)\leq p^*\leq F(x)\) for all \((x,y)\in P\times D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Any weakly dual primal–dual pair with finite evaluated objectives; feasibility must be established independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal-feasible \(x\in P\) and dual-feasible \(y\in D\), define the primal–dual gap \[G(x,y)=F(x)-Q(y)\geq0.\] The pair \((x,y)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-gap certificate if \[0\leq G(x,y)\leq\varepsilon.\] It then certifies the two-sided enclosure \[Q(y)\leq p^*\leq F(x)\] and the individual errors \[0\leq F(x)-p^*\leq\varepsilon,\qquad 0\leq p^*-Q(y)\leq\varepsilon.\] A zero-gap certificate has \(F(x)=Q(y)=p^*\), hence both feasible points are optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gap certificate is a primal-feasible and dual-feasible pair whose objective values differ by at most epsilon. Weak duality places the unknown optimal value between those two values, so the same epsilon bounds both primal suboptimality and dual suboptimality. At zero gap, both members are optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y)\leq\varepsilon\) certifies \(Q(y)\leq p^*\leq F(x)\) and errors of at most \(\varepsilon\) on both sides.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The condition is equivalent to the certified interval \([Q(y),F(x)]\) having width at most \(\varepsilon\).
A relative gap may be defined by normalizing \(G(x,y)\) with a stated positive scale, but that is a distinct convention.
special_cases_latex: For linear programming, \(G(x,y)\) is the usual difference between primal and dual linear objectives.
For Lagrangian duality, one may take \(Q(y)=q(y)=\inf_z L(z,y)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate gives an objective-quality guarantee without knowing an optimizer.
Any feasible pair with finite gap supplies simultaneous upper and lower bounds.
boundary_notes: An objective gap does not control distance to the solution set without growth assumptions.
Infeasible approximate iterates do not qualify unless feasibility errors are incorporated separately.

knowledge_statements.title: Radius-Based Approximate-Subgradient Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient of norm delta certifies objective error at most epsilon plus R delta when a radius R to an optimizer is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\) and \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}F\), then \[F(x)-F(x^\star)\le\varepsilon+\langle g,x-x^\star\rangle\le\varepsilon+\|g\|\,\|x-x^\star\|.\] Consequently, a verified bound \(\|x-x^\star\|\le R\) certifies \(F(x)-\inf F\le\varepsilon+R\|g\|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)-\inf F\le\varepsilon+\|g\|\,\|x-x^\star\|\), hence \(F(x)-\inf F\le\varepsilon+R\|g\|\) whenever \(\|x-x^\star\|\le R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-optimality certificate from a nonzero epsilon-subgradient and a known distance radius.

notation.meaning: An epsilon-subgradient at the candidate point.
Verified upper bound on distance to an optimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: No Scale-Free Norm Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small nonzero subgradient alone does not bound objective error; geometric or growth information is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(t)=\delta t+\iota_{[0,R]}(t)\), one has \(\delta\in\partial F(R)\) and \[F(R)-\inf F=\delta R.\] Thus fixed \(\|g\|=\delta>0\) is compatible with arbitrarily large objective error as \(R\) grows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta\in\partial F(R)\) while \(F(R)-\inf F=\delta R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of scale-free value certification from a nonzero subgradient norm alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Subgradient Certificates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero belonging to the ε-subdifferential is equivalent to the point being globally ε-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\partial_\varepsilon F(x)=\{g\in\mathbb R^n:F(z)\ge F(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\}.\] Then \(0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\) exactly when \(F(z)\ge F(x)-\varepsilon\) for every \(z\). Equivalently, \[F(x)\le\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^n}F(z)+\varepsilon.\] Consequently, the explicitly checkable inclusion \(0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\) is a global \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\) if and only if \(F(x)\le\inf_zF(z)+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence between epsilon-stationarity with zero subgradient and global epsilon-optimality.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and set \(h=f+I_C\). Fix \(x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex minimization, including nonsmooth and extended-valued objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}h\), the \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential is \[\partial_\varepsilon h(x)=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:h(z)\geq h(x)+\langle s,z-x\rangle-\varepsilon\ \text{for every }z\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.\] The point \(x\) carries an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate-subgradient optimality certificate when \[0\in\partial_\varepsilon h(x).\] This condition is equivalent to \[h(x)\leq\inf_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}h(z)+\varepsilon,\] or, on the feasible set, \[f(x)\leq f(z)+\varepsilon\quad\text{for every }z\in C.\] More generally, \(s\in\partial_\varepsilon h(x)\) is equivalent to the Fenchel residual bound \[h(x)+h^*(s)-\langle s,x\rangle\leq\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate-subgradient certificate for constrained convex minimization is the inclusion of zero in the epsilon-subdifferential of the objective plus the feasible-set indicator. It is exactly equivalent to the point having objective value within epsilon of the global infimum. A nonzero approximate subgradient is equivalently certified by a Fenchel–Young residual no larger than epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial_\varepsilon(f+I_C)(x)\) if and only if \(f(x)\leq\inf_{z\in C}f(z)+\varepsilon\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(s\in\partial_\varepsilon h(x)\iff h(x)+h^*(s)-\langle s,x\rangle\leq\varepsilon\).
For \(\varepsilon=0\), the certificate becomes the exact Fermat condition \(0\in\partial h(x)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), the certificate is \(0\in\partial_\varepsilon f(x)\).
For differentiable unconstrained \(f\), exact certification reduces to \(\nabla f(x)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The certificate directly bounds global objective suboptimality by \(\varepsilon\).
The sets are monotone: \(\partial_\varepsilon h(x)\subseteq\partial_{\varepsilon'}h(x)\) whenever \(\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon'\).
boundary_notes: Approximate subgradient membership need not bound distance to an optimizer.
For nonconvex functions, the displayed global affine-minorant definition is generally too restrictive for local stationarity.

If \(g\in\partial_\varepsilon F(x)\), then \[F(x)-F(x^\star)\le \varepsilon+\langle g,x-x^\star\rangle\le\varepsilon+\|g\|\,\|x-x^\star\|.\] Consequently, any verified bound \(\|x-x^\star\|\le R\) makes \(F(x)-\inf F\le\varepsilon+R\|g\|\) a computable certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Small Subgradient Norm Alone Is Not a Scale-Free Value Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of geometric or growth information when converting a nonzero approximate subgradient into objective error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is no universal function of \(\|g\|\) alone that bounds \(F(x)-\inf F\) over all proper convex functions and points with \(g\in\partial F(x)\). Indeed, for \(F(t)=\delta t\) on \([0,R]\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise, at \(x=R\) one has \(g=\delta\in\partial F(R)\) and \(F(R)-\inf F=\delta R\), which is arbitrarily large for fixed \(\delta>0\) as \(R\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small nonzero subgradient does not by itself bound objective error; a radius, growth condition, or comparable scale is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta\in\partial F(R)\) while \(F(R)-\inf F=\delta R\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let data \(d\) determine two witness sets \(W_{\mathrm P}(d)\) and \(W_{\mathrm A}(d)\), representing a primary system and an alternative system.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasibility systems for which an exact theorem of the alternative has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An alternative-based status certificate system is a pair of predicates \[\mathsf P(d;u)\quad(u\in U),\qquad \mathsf A(d;v)\quad(v\in V)\] satisfying, for every admissible datum \(d\), \[\bigl(\exists u\in U:\mathsf P(d;u)\bigr)\ \dot\vee\ \bigl(\exists v\in V:\mathsf A(d;v)\bigr),\] where \(\dot\vee\) denotes exclusive disjunction. A primary-status certificate is a witness \(u\in W_{\mathrm P}(d)\); an alternative-status certificate is a witness \(v\in W_{\mathrm A}(d)\). Validity therefore requires both disjointness, \[W_{\mathrm P}(d)\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow W_{\mathrm A}(d)=\varnothing,\] and exhaustiveness, \[W_{\mathrm P}(d)=\varnothing\Rightarrow W_{\mathrm A}(d)\neq\varnothing.\] In optimization, the first witness commonly certifies feasibility or strict feasibility, while the alternative witness is a multiplier, separating hyperplane, or recession direction certifying the complementary status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternative-based status system consists of two explicitly checkable witness predicates. For every admissible instance exactly one witness set is nonempty. A witness from the primary set certifies one status, such as feasibility, while a witness from the alternative set certifies its mutually exclusive counterpart, such as infeasibility. Both mutual exclusion and exhaustiveness are part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(W_{\mathrm P}(d)\) and \(W_{\mathrm A}(d)\) is nonempty for every admissible datum \(d\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The defining relation is \((W_{\mathrm P}(d)\neq\varnothing)\iff(W_{\mathrm A}(d)=\varnothing)\).
special_cases_latex: Farkas, Gordan, Stiemke, and Motzkin systems instantiate the definition with linear equalities or inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: A returned witness has a status interpretation that can be checked directly from the instance data.
The absence of a primary witness is converted into the existence of an alternative witness.
boundary_notes: Mutual inconsistency alone is insufficient; an exhaustive alternative theorem is also required.
Weakly infeasible conic systems may defeat finite strong-separation certificates and therefore require a refined status system.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For each datum \(d\), let \(S_1(d)\) and \(S_2(d)\) be two explicitly specified systems of equations, inequalities, or cone-membership conditions with solution sets \(F_1(d)\) and \(F_2(d)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical and mathematical form common to finite-dimensional alternative theorems; the actual systems and regularity hypotheses must be supplied by a concrete member.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A theorem of the alternative is an assertion that, for every datum \(d\) satisfying stated hypotheses, exactly one of \[S_1(d):\quad u\in F_1(d)\] and \[S_2(d):\quad v\in F_2(d)\] is solvable. Formally, \[ orall d,\qquad  igl(F_1(d)
eq\varnothing igr)\ \dot\vee\  igl(F_2(d)
eq\varnothing igr).\] Equivalently, it combines weak exclusion \[F_1(d)
eq\varnothing\Rightarrow F_2(d)=\varnothing\] with the alternative existence implication \[F_1(d)=\varnothing\Rightarrow F_2(d)
eq\varnothing.\] In convex applications, \(S_1\) is generally a feasibility system and \(S_2\) is a separating or dual-multiplier system whose strict inequality makes simultaneous solvability impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A theorem of the alternative states that exactly one of two fully specified systems has a solution for every admissible instance. It contains two ingredients: a solution of one system excludes every solution of the other, and failure of the first guarantees a witness for the second. In convex optimization, the second system usually expresses separation through multipliers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1(d)\neq\varnothing\) holds exactly when \(F_2(d)=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The assertion may be written as \((\exists u:S_1(d,u))\iff\neg(\exists v:S_2(d,v))\).
special_cases_latex: Farkas alternatives use nonnegative multipliers.
Gordan and Stiemke alternatives exchange strict primal positivity with homogeneous dual conditions.
Motzkin alternatives combine strict and non-strict inequalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: An alternative witness is a finite certificate of failure of the primary system whenever the concrete theorem guarantees exhaustiveness.
boundary_notes: The hypotheses establishing exhaustiveness are part of each concrete theorem and cannot be omitted.
An ordinary duality statement is not automatically a theorem of the alternative unless the two solvability claims are exhaustive and exclusive.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be a convex cone generated by the feasible combinations of a system, and define its polar cone by \(C^\circ=\{y:\langle y,z\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear, conic, and constraint-qualified nonlinear convex alternatives represented through cone membership or global Lagrangian inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Farkas lemma family is the collection of alternatives having the canonical separation form \[b\in C\quad\dot\vee\quad \exists y\in C^\circ:\langle y,b\rangle>0,\] with sign-reversed polar conventions giving equivalent variants. Its members replace \(C\) by a cone or upper image determined by the problem data and express the separating functional through nonnegative multipliers. The linear member takes \(C=\{Ax:x\geq0\}\). A conic member takes \(C=A(K)\) for a convex cone \(K\), subject to closedness sufficient for strong separation. A nonlinear convex member replaces membership by the implication \(g(x)\leq0\Rightarrow f(x)\geq0\) and certifies it through \(f(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)\geq0\) for every \(x\), with \(\lambda\geq0\) under an appropriate constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Farkas family consists of alternatives between representability in a convex cone or upper image and a strict separating functional. Linear, conic, and nonlinear convex forms differ in the object being separated and in the regularity needed to guarantee a separator, but each turns failure of a feasibility or implication system into a multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A Farkas-type member has mutually exclusive primal membership and strict polar-separation alternatives, with hypotheses ensuring exhaustiveness.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the dual cone \(C^*=\{y:\langle y,z\rangle\geq0\ \forall z\in C\}\), the alternative is \(b\in C\) or \(\exists y\in C^*:\langle y,b\rangle<0\).
special_cases_latex: For finitely generated cones, closedness is automatic.
Nonlinear convex Farkas statements require a condition such as strict feasibility or affine constraints with a relative-interior feasible point.
immediate_consequences_latex: A separator is an independently checkable infeasibility or implication certificate.
boundary_notes: If the relevant conic image is not closed, a point in its closure but outside it need not admit a strict separator.
Different sign conventions change displayed inequalities but not the underlying alternative.

notation.meaning: Polar cone under the nonpositive inner-product convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Inequality-Form Linear Farkas Alternative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A system Ax≤b is feasible unless a nonnegative row combination cancels the variables and makes the combined right-hand side negative; exactly one alternative holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one of the systems \[Ax\le b\] and \[y\ge0,\qquad A^\top y=0,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0\] is solvable. In the second system the strict inequality can be normalized to \(\langle b,y\rangle=-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x:Ax\le b\) and \(\exists y\ge0:A^\top y=0,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional non-strict inequality form of the linear Farkas lemma.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Farkas Alternatives
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly one of the following holds: Ax=b has a nonnegative solution, or a vector y has nonnegative A-transpose image and a strictly negative inner product with b; the latter vector certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one of the following systems is solvable: \[\text{(P)}\quad Ax=b,\qquad x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\] \[\text{(D)}\quad A^\top y\in\mathbb R_+^n,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0,\qquad y\in\mathbb R^m.\] A solution of \(\text{(D)}\) is a finite certificate that \(\text{(P)}\) is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x\ge0:Ax=b\) and \(\exists y:A^\top y\ge0,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form finite-dimensional Farkas alternative.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Inequalities between vectors are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real linear systems; no constraint qualification is needed because the finitely generated cone \(A\mathbb{R}^n_+\) is polyhedral and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear Farkas alternative associated with \((A,b)\) consists of the systems \[\mathrm{(P)}\quad Ax=b,\qquad x\geq0,\] and \[\mathrm{(F)}\quad A^Ty\leq0,\qquad b^Ty>0.\] Exactly one of \(\mathrm{(P)}\) and \(\mathrm{(F)}\) is solvable. Equivalently, \[\exists x\geq0:\ Ax=b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(A^Ty\leq0\Rightarrow b^Ty\leq0\bigr)\ \text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}^m.\] A vector \(x\) is a feasibility certificate; a vector \(y\) satisfying \(\mathrm{(F)}\) is a Farkas infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a matrix A and vector b, exactly one of two systems is solvable: b is a nonnegative combination of the columns of A, or there is a vector y whose inner products with all columns are nonpositive while its inner product with b is strictly positive. The first witness certifies feasibility and the second certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\exists x\geq0:Ax=b)\ \dot\vee\ (\exists y:A^Ty\leq0,\ b^Ty>0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(b\in A\mathbb{R}^n_+\iff b^Ty\leq0\) for every \(y\) satisfying \(A^Ty\leq0\).
Changing \(y\) to \(-y\) yields the convention \(A^Ty\geq0\) and \(b^Ty<0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has columns \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), feasibility means \(b\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Any Farkas vector rules out every nonnegative solution of \(Ax=b\).
Linear infeasibility therefore has a finite, directly checkable certificate.
boundary_notes: Replacing the strict inequality \(b^Ty>0\) by a non-strict inequality destroys exclusivity.
Free primal variables or mixed inequalities require a transformed but equivalent Farkas form.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Conic Images Destroy the Strict Alternative
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed semidefinite image has infeasible right-hand sides that cannot be strictly separated, so the unqualified conic Farkas alternative fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define \(A:\mathbb S^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by \(A(X)=(X_{11},X_{12})\). Then \[A(K)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] which is not closed. For \(q=(0,1)\), \(q\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\). Consequently, \(A(X)=q,\ X\succeq0\) is infeasible, but no \(y\) satisfies \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle q,y\rangle<0\).
assumptions_latex: \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) with the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\in\operatorname{cl}(A(K))\setminus A(K)\), and infeasibility of \(A(X)=q,\ X\in K\) has no strict conic Farkas separator.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp closed-image boundary for the finite-dimensional conic Farkas alternative.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Farkas Alternatives
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed image cone, either b has a conic preimage or a dual-cone vector strictly separates it, but not both.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the closedness assumption on \(A(K)\), exactly one of the following systems is solvable: \[\text{(P)}\quad x\in K,\qquad Ax=b,\] \[\text{(D)}\quad A^\top y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0.\] A vector satisfying the second system strictly separates \(b\) from \(A(K)\) and certifies infeasibility of the first. The closed-image hypothesis is essential for this strict finite-dimensional alternative in general conic systems.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex cone and \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear.
The image cone \(A(K)\) is closed, and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\exists x\in K:Ax=b\) and \(\exists y:A^\top y\in K^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\) holds.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-image finite-dimensional conic Farkas alternative.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to F\) be linear, and let \(b\in F\). Define \(K^*=\{s\in E:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic feasibility under the explicit closed-image hypothesis \(A(K)\) closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that the conic image \(A(K)\) is closed. The conic Farkas alternative consists of \[\mathrm{(P)}\quad \exists x\in K:\ Ax=b,\] and \[\mathrm{(F)}\quad \exists y\in F:\ A^*y\in K^*,\quad \langle y,b\rangle<0.\] Exactly one system is solvable. Equivalently, \[b\in A(K)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle y,b\rangle\geq0\ \text{for every }y\text{ with }A^*y\in K^*.\] A vector \(y\) satisfying \(\mathrm{(F)}\) is a strict conic-separation certificate for infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the image of a closed convex cone under the constraint map is closed, either b has a representation Ax with x in the cone, or a dual vector y has nonnegative pairing with every representable vector but negative pairing with b. Exactly one alternative holds. The closed-image hypothesis excludes weak infeasibility at the boundary of the image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(A(K)\) is closed, then \((b\in A(K))\ \dot\vee\ (\exists y:A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle y,b\rangle<0)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The dual condition says \(y\in(A(K))^*\) and \(\langle y,b\rangle<0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb{R}^n_+\), the result reduces to a linear Farkas alternative.
For self-dual cones, such as the positive semidefinite cone under the trace inner product, \(K^*=K\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A strict dual separator certifies primal conic infeasibility.
Closedness makes every infeasible right-hand side strongly separable from the conic image.
boundary_notes: The image of a closed nonpolyhedral cone under a linear map need not be closed.
If \(b\in\operatorname{cl}A(K)\setminus A(K)\), neither primal feasibility nor a strict Farkas separator holds.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the nonnegative pairing convention.
