knowledge_statements.statement_title: Family of saddle objects induced by a coupling function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be nonempty sets and \(K:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). Define \(P(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}K(x,y)\) and \(D(y)=\inf_{x\in X}K(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract deterministic saddle objects, independent of convexity or attainment assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The saddle-object family generated by \((X,Y,K)\) is the tuple \(\mathcal S(K)=(P,D,p,d,G,\operatorname{Sad}K)\), where \(p=\inf_XP\), \(d=\sup_YD\), \(G(x,y)=P(x)-D(y)\), and \(\operatorname{Sad}K=\{(x^*,y^*):K(x^*,y)\le K(x^*,y^*)\le K(x,y^*)\ \forall(x,y)\in X\times Y\}\). The gap satisfies \(G(x,y)\ge p-d\ge0\). A pair is a saddle point precisely when it attains both envelope optima and has zero gap; equivalently, \(P(x^*)=K(x^*,y^*)=D(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single coupling function induces a primal envelope, a dual envelope, two optimal values, a primal-dual gap, and a saddle set. These are treated as one family because they encode the same minimax system from complementary viewpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal S(K)=(P,D,p,d,G,\operatorname{Sad}K),\qquad G(x,y)=P(x)-D(y)\ge p-d\ge0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x^*,y^*)\in\operatorname{Sad}K\Longleftrightarrow P(x^*)=K(x^*,y^*)=D(y^*).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(p=d\) and both envelope optima are attained, \(\operatorname{Sad}K=\operatorname{argmin}P\times\operatorname{argmax}D\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every saddle point has zero gap.
A strictly positive minimax gap forces the saddle set to be empty.
boundary_notes: Zero gap at an arbitrary pair requires the pair also to lie in the primal and dual domains under consideration.
Extended-real arithmetic must avoid undefined expressions such as \(+\infty-(+\infty)\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty convex sets, and let \(K:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic minimization in the first variable and maximization in the second; extended values may encode constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}K(x,y)\) is convex–concave when \(x\mapsto K(x,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\), and \(y\mapsto K(x,y)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Its dual orientation is \(\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}K(x,y)\). A solution is a pair \((x^*,y^*)\) satisfying \(K(x^*,y)\le K(x^*,y^*)\le K(x,y^*)\) for all \(x,y\). Convexity-concavity is structural; equality of the two values and attainment are additional properties, not part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex–concave saddle problem minimizes a function that is convex in the minimizing variable and maximizes it in a variable in which it is concave. Its solution is a mutual best-response pair satisfying the global saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K(\cdot,y)\ \text{convex}\ \forall y,\quad K(x,\cdot)\ \text{concave}\ \forall x,\quad \min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}K(x,y).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x^*,y^*)\ \text{is a solution}\Longleftrightarrow x^*\in\arg\min_{x\in X}K(x,y^*),\quad y^*\in\arg\max_{y\in Y}K(x^*,y).\]
special_cases_latex: Bilinear matrix games have \(K(x,y)=\langle Ax,y\rangle\) on convex strategy sets.
Lagrangian saddle problems use \(K(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,g(x)\rangle\) on an appropriate multiplier cone.
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal envelope \(x\mapsto\sup_YK(x,y)\) is convex.
The dual envelope \(y\mapsto\inf_XK(x,y)\) is concave.
boundary_notes: Convexity-concavity alone does not guarantee minimax equality on noncompact sets.
The opposite concave–convex convention is obtained by interchanging the two variables and optimization directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Value and Fenchel Dual of a Bilinear Saddle Model
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing the bilinear Fenchel saddle function over the primal variable produces the standard Fenchel dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, \(K:X\to Y\) linear, and \(f\in\Gamma_0(X)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(Y)\). For \[L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),\] one has \[\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=-f^*(-K^*y)-g^*(y).\] Thus the lower saddle value is \[\sup_{y\in Y}\{-f^*(-K^*y)-g^*(y)\},\] the Fenchel dual of \(\inf_x\{f(x)+g(Kx)\}\). Equality with the upper value requires a separate strong-duality qualification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual objective obtained by minimizing the Fenchel bilinear saddle function in its primal variable.

notation.meaning: adjoint of the linear coupling map

knowledge_statements.title: Bilinear Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional convex–concave model with bilinear coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper closed convex functions. A bilinear saddle model is
\[\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g(y).\]
On \(\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g\), the map \(x\mapsto\Phi(x,y)\) is convex for every fixed \(y\), while \(y\mapsto\Phi(x,y)\) is concave for every fixed \(x\). Its saddle problem is \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear saddle model adds a linear pairing between primal and dual variables to separate convex penalties, producing a function convex in the primal variable and concave in the dual variable.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g(y)\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\).

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Space Lifting of Finitely Many Composite Terms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finitely many composite terms can be stacked into one product-space operator with a separable conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_i:X\to Y_i\) be linear and \(g_i\in\Gamma_0(Y_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,r\). On \(Y=\prod_{i=1}^rY_i\), define \[Kx=(K_1x,\ldots,K_rx),\qquad G(u_1,\ldots,u_r)=\sum_{i=1}^rg_i(u_i).\] Then \(G^*(y_1,\ldots,y_r)=\sum_i g_i^*(y_i)\) and \[f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^rg_i(K_ix)=\sup_{y\in Y}\left[f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-G^*(y)\right].\]
assumptions_latex: Each \(Y_i\) is a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)+\sum_i g_i(K_ix)=\sup_y\{f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-G^*(y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregation of finitely many separately dualized terms into one product-space bilinear model.

notation.meaning: product of the component range spaces

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel saddle representation of a linearly composed convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K:X\to Y\) be linear, and let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(h:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper closed convex functions. Fenchel conjugacy gives
\[h(Kx)=\sup_{y\in Y}\{\langle Kx,y\rangle-h^*(y)\}.\]
Consequently, whenever the displayed supremum is interpreted in the extended-real sense,
\[\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+h(Kx)\}=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}\{f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-h^*(y)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex objective containing a linear composition becomes a saddle problem by replacing the outer function with its Fenchel conjugate representation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(h\) are proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)+h(Kx)=\sup_{y\in Y}\{f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-h^*(y)\}\).

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the outer function

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(h:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic composite saddle model with separable convex terms and bilinear coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A composite saddle model is generated by \(K(x,y)=g(x)+\langle Ax,y\rangle-h(y)\) and the problem \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}K(x,y)\). The function is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\). A saddle pair \((x^*,y^*)\) satisfies \(K(x^*,y)\le K(x^*,y^*)\le K(x,y^*)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\). Its primal objective is \(g(x)+(h+\delta_Y)^*(Ax)\); its dual objective is \(-h(y)-(g+\delta_X)^*(-A^*y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The composite model adds a convex primal term and a concave dual term to a bilinear interaction. Maximizing out the dual variable produces a conjugate composite primal objective, while minimizing out the primal variable produces its Fenchel dual envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\{g(x)+\langle Ax,y\rangle-h(y)\},\quad P(x)=g(x)+(h+\delta_Y)^*(Ax),\quad D(y)=-h(y)-(g+\delta_X)^*(-A^*y).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Absorbing the set constraints into the functions gives \(\widetilde g=g+\delta_X\), \(\widetilde h=h+\delta_Y\), and \(K(x,y)=\widetilde g(x)+\langle Ax,y\rangle-\widetilde h(y)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(h=\delta_Y\), the primal nonsmooth term is the support function \(\sigma_Y(Ax)\).
Equality-constrained convex optimization is obtained by taking an unrestricted dual variable and a linear Lagrangian coupling.
immediate_consequences_latex: The saddle conditions are equivalent to \(-A^*y^*\in\partial(g+\delta_X)(x^*)\) and \(Ax^*\in\partial(h+\delta_Y)(y^*)\).
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert existence of a saddle pair.
If nonconvex terms or nonlinear nonaffine coupling are introduced, this canonical convex–concave composite class no longer applies.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Lower Value of the Conic Saddle Model
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing the conic Lagrangian produces the conjugate dual objective over the positive dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) linear, \(K\subseteq Y\) a closed convex cone, and \[L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle,\qquad y\in K^*.\] Then \[\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y)=-f^*(-A^*y)-\langle b,y\rangle,\] so the lower saddle value is \[\sup_{y\in K^*}\{-f^*(-A^*y)-\langle b,y\rangle\}.\] Equality with the constrained primal value requires an independent conic strong-duality condition.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone and \(K^*=\{y:\langle y,k\rangle\ge0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_xL(x,y)=-f^*(-A^*y)-\langle b,y\rangle\) for \(y\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic dual objective obtained by minimizing the conic Lagrangian over the primal variable.

notation.meaning: adjoint of the conic constraint map

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian saddle model for an affine conic constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, let \(b\in Y\), and let \(C\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone with dual cone \(C^*=\{y\in Y:\langle y,c\rangle\geq0\ \text{for every }c\in C\}\). For a proper convex function \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), define
\[L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle,\qquad (x,y)\in X\times C^*.\]
Then \(L\) is convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\), and
\[\sup_{y\in C^*}L(x,y)=\begin{cases}f(x),&b-Ax\in C,\\+\infty,&b-Ax\notin C.\end{cases}\]
Consequently,
\[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in C^*}L(x,y)=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ b-Ax\in C\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic constraint is encoded by maximizing a bilinear Lagrangian over the dual cone: feasible points retain their objective value, whereas infeasible points receive infinite value.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in C^*}L(x,y)=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ b-Ax\in C\}\).

notation.meaning: dual cone of the constraint cone

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex sets and let \(K:C\times D\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar's extended-real saddle-function convention; both orientations are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(K\) is concave–convex when \(u\mapsto K(u,v)\) is concave on \(C\) for every \(v\in D\), and \(v\mapsto K(u,v)\) is convex on \(D\) for every \(u\in C\). It is convex–concave when the two curvature requirements are reversed. Either orientation is called a saddle function. For the concave–convex orientation, a saddle point with maximization in \(u\) and minimization in \(v\) satisfies \(K(u,v^*)\le K(u^*,v^*)\le K(u^*,v)\) for every \(u\in C,v\in D\). Extended values permit convex constraints in the minimizing variable and concave constraints in the maximizing variable to be incorporated into the function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle function is separately concave in the variable to be maximized and convex in the variable to be minimized, or the same structure with the roles reversed. Its saddle points are simultaneous global maximizers and minimizers in the respective sections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K(\cdot,v)\ \text{concave}\ \forall v\in D,\qquad K(u,\cdot)\ \text{convex}\ \forall u\in C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A convex–concave function \(L(x,y)\) becomes concave–convex after interchanging its arguments: \(K(y,x)=L(x,y)\).
special_cases_latex: Every bilinear form is both concave and convex in each variable and therefore is a saddle function in either orientation.
A finite continuous concave–convex function on a closed convex product admits canonical lower and upper simple extensions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Partial supremum over the concave variable produces a convex function of the convex variable.
Partial infimum over the convex variable produces a concave function of the concave variable.
boundary_notes: Separate convexity-concavity does not mean joint convexity.
Allowing both \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) requires orientation-sensitive domain conventions.

notation.meaning: product domain of the two saddle variables

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Saddle Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle function is closed when its proper convex sections are lower semicontinuous and its proper concave sections are upper semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A saddle function \(L\) is closed when, for every \(y\) for which \(L(\cdot,y)\) is proper, the convex function \(x\mapsto L(x,y)\) is lower semicontinuous, and, for every \(x\) for which \(L(x,\cdot)\) is proper, the concave function \(y\mapsto L(x,y)\) is upper semicontinuous. Equivalently, its proper convex sections have closed epigraphs and its proper concave sections have closed hypographs.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional spaces, and \(L:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) has convex \(x\)-sections and concave \(y\)-sections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\) is closed precisely when every proper convex section \(L(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous and every proper concave section \(L(x,\cdot)\) is upper semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sectionwise finite-dimensional definition; improper sections are excluded from the closure requirement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness of an extended-real saddle function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K:\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be concave–convex. Let \(\operatorname{cl}_1K\) denote sectionwise concave closure in the first variable and \(\operatorname{cl}_2K\) sectionwise convex closure in the second variable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar's finite-dimensional extended-real closed-saddle-function theory; closedness is weaker than being simultaneously sectionwise closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two concave–convex functions \(K,L\) are equivalent when \(\operatorname{cl}_1K=\operatorname{cl}_1L\) and \(\operatorname{cl}_2K=\operatorname{cl}_2L\). The saddle function \(K\) is closed when both \(\operatorname{cl}_1K\) and \(\operatorname{cl}_2K\) are equivalent to \(K\). Its lower closure is \(\operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\), and its upper closure is \(\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K\). It is lower closed if \(K=\operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\), upper closed if \(K=\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K\), and fully closed if \(K=\operatorname{cl}_1K=\operatorname{cl}_2K\). Every lower-closed, upper-closed, or fully closed saddle function is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness for a saddle function is defined through both sectionwise closure operations and their common equivalence class. Lower and upper closures can differ, so ordinary closedness does not require a single representative to equal both extremal closures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\ \text{closed}\Longleftrightarrow \operatorname{cl}_1K\sim K\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{cl}_2K\sim K,\quad K\ \text{lower closed}\Longleftrightarrow K=\operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Within a closed equivalence class, the lower-closed representative is the least member and the upper-closed representative is the greatest member.
special_cases_latex: A finite saddle function on all of \(\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\) is fully closed because its finite convex and concave sections are continuous.
immediate_consequences_latex: The only improper closed saddle functions are the constant functions \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\).
boundary_notes: In general \(\operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\neq\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K\).
For a convex–concave orientation, the order called lower or upper is reversed.

notation.meaning: concave closure in the first variable
convex closure in the second variable

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Saddle-Function Classes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two saddle functions are equivalent when their closed convex sections in the first variable and closed concave sections in the second variable coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Two proper saddle functions \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are equivalent, written \(K_1\sim K_2\), when
\[
\operatorname{cl}_x K_1=\operatorname{cl}_x K_2
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{cl}_y K_1=\operatorname{cl}_y K_2.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{cl}_x K\) is obtained by replacing every section \(K(\cdot,y)\) by its lower-semicontinuous convex closure, while \(\operatorname{cl}_y K\) replaces every section \(K(x,\cdot)\) by its upper-semicontinuous concave closure. Thus an equivalence class records the same closed convex and concave section data even when representatives differ at boundary points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(K_1,K_2:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper saddle functions, convex in the first variable and concave in the second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_1\sim K_2\) exactly when both sectionwise closures agree.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses sectionwise convex and concave closures in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: sectionwise lower-semicontinuous convex closure in the first variable
sectionwise upper-semicontinuous concave closure in the second variable

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence class of closed saddle functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K,L:\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be concave–convex, with sectionwise closures \(\operatorname{cl}_1\) and \(\operatorname{cl}_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed proper concave–convex saddle functions in Rockafellar's equivalence-class framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functions \(K\) and \(L\) are equivalent, written \(K\sim L\), when \(\operatorname{cl}_1K=\operatorname{cl}_1L\) and \(\operatorname{cl}_2K=\operatorname{cl}_2L\). For a closed convex bifunction \(F\), its saddle class \(\Omega(F)\) consists of all concave–convex functions between the lower representative \(\underline K(u,v)=\langle Fu,v\rangle\) and upper representative \(\overline K(u,v)=\langle u,F^*v\rangle\): \(\underline K\le K\le\overline K\). Every member is closed and equivalent; conversely, every equivalence class of closed concave–convex functions has this form for a unique closed convex bifunction. For proper closed functions, the class is also uniquely determined by the common kernel, the restriction to the relative interior of the effective product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent saddle functions have identical concave and convex sectionwise closures. Each closed class has a least lower-closed representative and a greatest upper-closed representative, and every intermediate concave–convex representative describes the same regularized saddle problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\sim L\Longleftrightarrow \operatorname{cl}_1K=\operatorname{cl}_1L\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{cl}_2K=\operatorname{cl}_2L,\qquad \Omega(F)=\{K:\underline K\le K\le\overline K\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Two closed proper concave–convex functions are equivalent if and only if they have the same kernel.
special_cases_latex: The lower and upper simple extensions of a finite saddle function on a nonempty convex product are equivalent.
immediate_consequences_latex: Equivalent saddle functions have the same saddle value and the same saddle points whenever these exist.
Equivalent closed saddle functions have the same subdifferential.
boundary_notes: Pointwise equality is stronger than equivalence and is not required on boundary points of the effective domain.
The class must not be treated as an arbitrary collection: its extremal representatives are fixed by the closure operations.

notation.meaning: closed saddle-function equivalence class associated with \(F\)
adjoint concave bifunction in Rockafellar's bifunction correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Saddle Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Saddle conjugacy combines an infimum over the convex variable with a supremum over the concave variable and is involutive up to sectionwise closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conjugate saddle function on \(Y^*\times X^*\) is
\[
K^*(y^*,x^*)=
\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}
\bigl\{\langle x^*,x\rangle+\langle y^*,y\rangle-K(x,y)\bigr\}.
\]
It is convex in \(y^*\) and concave in \(x^*\). With the same pairing and variable-order convention, applying saddle conjugacy twice yields the sectionwise closed representative of \(K\); equivalently, the saddle biconjugate belongs to the same closed saddle-function class as \(K\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional paired spaces with duals \(X^*\) and \(Y^*\).
\(K:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a proper closed saddle function, convex in \(x\) and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K^*\) is convex in \(y^*\), concave in \(x^*\), and saddle biconjugation recovers the closed equivalence class of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convex-first, concave-second conjugacy convention.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stated with the convex-first concave-second saddle-conjugacy convention

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The duality kind fits, but saddle conjugacy is convention-sensitive and the stated signs, variable order, optimization order, and biconjugation claim cannot be validated without an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower, upper, and class-valued saddle conjugates
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K:\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be concave–convex, and let \((u^*,v^*)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar's finite-dimensional conjugacy for concave–convex extended-real saddle functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the lower conjugate by \(\underline K^*(u^*,v^*)=\sup_v\inf_u\{\langle u,u^*\rangle+\langle v,v^*\rangle-K(u,v)\}\), and the upper conjugate by \(\overline K^*(u^*,v^*)=\inf_u\sup_v\{\langle u,u^*\rangle+\langle v,v^*\rangle-K(u,v)\}\). Always \(\underline K^*\le\overline K^*\). If \(K\) is closed, these two functions are respectively lower closed and upper closed and belong to one equivalence class. Any closed saddle function equivalent to both is called a conjugate saddle function of \(K\). Conjugacy is therefore single-valued at the level of equivalence classes, symmetric, and involutive up to equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Saddle conjugacy applies opposite minimax orders to the bilinear pairing minus the original saddle function. The two resulting representatives can differ pointwise, but for a closed saddle function they determine one conjugate equivalence class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\underline K^*(u^*,v^*)=\sup_v\inf_u\Phi(u,v;u^*,v^*),\qquad \overline K^*(u^*,v^*)=\inf_u\sup_v\Phi(u,v;u^*,v^*),\] where \(\Phi=\langle u,u^*\rangle+\langle v,v^*\rangle-K(u,v)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a closed class \(\Omega(F)\), the conjugate class is \(\Omega(F_*)\), where \(F_*\) is the inverse concave bifunction.
special_cases_latex: The constant closed saddle functions \(+\infty\) and \(-\infty\) are conjugate to one another.
immediate_consequences_latex: A conjugate of a closed proper saddle function is proper.
Conjugating a conjugate returns the original closed equivalence class.
boundary_notes: The lower and upper conjugates need not be identical as pointwise functions.
The order of \(\inf\) and \(\sup\) is essential and follows the concave–convex orientation.

notation.meaning: inverse bifunction associated with saddle conjugacy

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the convex program \(\min_{x\in C}f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le0\) for \(i\le r\) and \(f_i(x)=0\) for \(i>r\), where \(C\) is convex, the inequality data are convex, and the equality data are affine. Let \(E_r=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\lambda_i\ge0\ (i\le r)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programming with inequality and affine equality constraints, using the extended Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended Lagrangian is \(L(\lambda,x)=f_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i(x)\) for \(\lambda\in E_r,x\in C\), with the standard extended values outside these domains. A Lagrangian saddle certificate is a pair \((\lambda^*,x^*)\) such that \(L(\lambda,x^*)\le L(\lambda^*,x^*)\le L(\lambda^*,x)\) for every \(\lambda\in E_r,x\in C\). Such a pair consists exactly of a primal optimal solution and a Kuhn–Tucker multiplier vector. Equivalently, it satisfies primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness, and stationarity of the Lagrangian in \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangian saddle certificate is a feasible multiplier–primal pair that maximizes the Lagrangian over multipliers at the chosen primal point and minimizes it over primal points at the chosen multiplier. In convex programming this is precisely a primal optimum together with a Kuhn–Tucker multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L(\lambda,x^*)\le L(\lambda^*,x^*)\le L(\lambda^*,x)\quad\forall\lambda\in E_r,\ \forall x\in C.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f_i(x^*)\le0,\ \lambda_i^*\ge0,\ \lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\ (i\le r),\quad f_i(x^*)=0\ (i>r),\quad 0\in\partial_xL(\lambda^*,x^*).\]
special_cases_latex: For differentiable data and \(C=\mathbb R^n\), stationarity becomes \(\nabla f_0(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i^*\nabla f_i(x^*)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The saddle value equals both the primal optimum and the attained dual value.
The certificate implies zero Lagrangian duality gap.
boundary_notes: Existence of a saddle certificate generally requires an appropriate constraint qualification or an independently established multiplier.
For nonconvex programs, these conditions need not characterize global optimality.

notation.meaning: multiplier set with nonnegative inequality multipliers

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle–Optimality Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangian saddle point is equivalent to feasibility, complementary slackness, and global minimization of the Lagrangian at the stated multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The saddle inequalities
\[
L(x^*,\lambda)\le L(x^*,\lambda^*)\le L(x,\lambda^*)
\quad\text{for all }x\in X,\ \lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m
\]
hold if and only if
\[
g_i(x^*)\le0,\qquad \lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),
\qquad x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda^*).
\]
Whenever these conditions hold, \(x^*\) minimizes \(f\) over the feasible set: weak duality and the two saddle inequalities give \(f(x^*)\le f(x)\) for every feasible \(x\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex, \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are convex, and \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) is a saddle point exactly when primal feasibility, complementary slackness, and minimization of \(L(\cdot,\lambda^*)\) hold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inequality-constrained convex program.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical convex inequality-constrained Lagrangian saddle criterion

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically coherent and fits the saddle–optimality leaf, but it has no inspectable theorem or section citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle–Strong-Duality Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangian saddle point exists at a pair exactly when that pair attains both primal and dual optima with zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
p^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_i(x)\le0\},
\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda).
\]
Then \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) satisfies the Lagrangian saddle inequalities if and only if
\[
f(x^*)=p^*=d^*=q(\lambda^*).
\]
Thus a saddle point implies zero duality gap and attainment of both primal and dual values. Conversely, primal feasibility of \(x^*\), dual feasibility of \(\lambda^*\), their respective optimality, and equality \(f(x^*)=q(\lambda^*)\) imply
\(L(x^*,\lambda)\le L(x^*,\lambda^*)\le L(x,\lambda^*)\) for every admissible \(x\) and \(\lambda\).
assumptions_latex: \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)\) is the Lagrangian of a convex program over \(X\), with \(q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) is a saddle point if and only if both optima are attained there and \(f(x^*)=q(\lambda^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attained strong duality for convex inequality constraints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical attained strong-duality characterization by a Lagrangian saddle point

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The attained strong-duality correspondence is coherent and the duality kind fits, but no authoritative locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saddle points and attained strong duality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), with primal value \(p=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}K(x,y)\) and dual value \(d=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}K(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract deterministic minimax duality with explicit attainment requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strong minimax duality means \(p=d\) with a finite common value. Attained strong duality means additionally that there exist \(x^*\in X\) and \(y^*\in Y\) attaining the primal and dual envelope extrema. The saddle–strong-duality correspondence is \(\operatorname{Sad}K\neq\varnothing\) if and only if strong minimax duality is attained on both sides. More precisely, each saddle pair supplies primal attainment, dual attainment, and \(p=d=K(x^*,y^*)\); conversely, any pair of primal and dual optimizers under \(p=d\) is a saddle pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle point is the certificate form of attained strong duality. Value equality without attainment is weaker; once both extrema are attained, pairing their optimizers produces the saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\operatorname{Sad}K
eq\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow p=d\in\mathbb R,\quad \arg\min_x\sup_yK(x,y)
eq\varnothing,\quad \arg\max_y\inf_xK(x,y)
eq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x^*,y^*)\in\operatorname{Sad}K\Longleftrightarrow p=d=K(x^*,y^*),\ x^*\in\arg\min P,\ y^*\in\arg\max D.\]
special_cases_latex: For convex inequality-constrained optimization, an attained primal-dual pair with zero Lagrangian duality gap is a Lagrangian saddle point.
immediate_consequences_latex: A positive duality gap implies nonexistence of saddle points.
Under attained strong duality, the saddle set is the Cartesian product of the primal and dual optimizer sets.
boundary_notes: Strong duality stated only as \(p=d\) does not imply saddle existence without attainment.
Infinite common values are excluded from this finite-valued correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of the Exact Multiplier Set
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact multipliers associated with a fixed primal optimizer form a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a primal optimizer \(x^*\) and define
\[
M(x^*)=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m:(x^*,\lambda)\text{ is a Lagrangian saddle point}\}.
\]
Then \(M(x^*)\) is convex. In particular, if \(\lambda^1,\lambda^2\in M(x^*)\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), then \(t\lambda^1+(1-t)\lambda^2\in M(x^*)\).
assumptions_latex: The Lagrangian is affine in the multiplier vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(x^*)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex structure of the exact inequality multipliers associated with a fixed primal optimizer.

notation.meaning: Exact-multiplier set at the fixed optimizer.

Suppose \(x^*\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(g_i(x^*)\leq0\) for every \(i\), and \(Ax^*=b\). Define
\[L(x,\lambda,
u)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i g_i(x)+\langle
u,Ax-bangle.\]
For \((\lambda^*,
u^*)\in\mathbb R_+^m	imes Z\), the triple \((x^*,\lambda^*,
u^*)\) is a Lagrangian saddle point if and only if
\[0\in\partial f(x^*)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i^*
abla g_i(x^*)+A^*
u^*,\qquad \lambda_i^*g_i(x^*)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\]
Thus the saddle dual variables at \(x^*\) are exactly its KKT multipliers.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the convex program \(\min_{x\in C}f_0(x)\) subject to \(f_i(x)\le0\) for \(i\le r\) and affine equalities \(f_i(x)=0\) for \(i>r\). Let \(L(\lambda,x)=f_0(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(x)\) with \(\lambda_i\ge0\) for \(i\le r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex programming; multiplier existence is not asserted without a suitable regularity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal optimal solution \(x^*\), a vector \(\lambda^*\) is a Kuhn–Tucker multiplier precisely when \((\lambda^*,x^*)\) is a saddle point of the extended Lagrangian: \(L(\lambda,x^*)\le L(\lambda^*,x^*)\le L(\lambda^*,x)\) for all admissible \(\lambda\) and \(x\in C\). Equivalently, \(x^*\) is feasible, \(\lambda^*\) is dual feasible, \(\lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0\) for inequality constraints, and \(0\in\partial f_0(x^*)+\sum_i\lambda_i^*\partial f_i(x^*)+N_C(x^*)\). Thus the multiplier set at \(x^*\) is exactly the dual section \(\{\lambda:(\lambda,x^*)\in\operatorname{Sad}L\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The valid multiplier vectors associated with a primal optimum are exactly the dual components that complete it to a Lagrangian saddle point. The correspondence is expressed equivalently by feasibility, complementary slackness, and stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Lambda(x^*)=\{\lambda^*:(\lambda^*,x^*)\in\operatorname{Sad}L\}=\left\{\lambda^*:\begin{array}{l}\lambda_i^*\ge0,\ f_i(x^*)\le0,\ \lambda_i^*f_i(x^*)=0,\\0\in\partial_xL(\lambda^*,x^*)+N_C(x^*)\end{array}\right\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x^*\in\arg\min_{x\in C}L(\lambda^*,x),\qquad \lambda^*\in\arg\max_{\lambda\in E_r}L(\lambda,x^*).\]
special_cases_latex: For differentiable data, stationarity is the gradient equation plus the normal cone of \(C\).
For equality constraints only, the multipliers are unrestricted in sign.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every saddle multiplier attains the Lagrange dual optimum.
Complementary slackness follows from maximization over the nonnegative multiplier cone at a feasible primal point.
boundary_notes: A primal optimum may have no multiplier if constraint regularity fails.
Multipliers need not be unique, even when the primal optimum is unique.

normal cone to the convex set \(C\) at \(x^*\)

knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustive Saddle-Existence Obstructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite saddle point exists exactly when the minimax values agree and both outer optima are attained; failure of any one condition is an obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), let
\[
\overline v=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),\qquad
\underline v=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
A finite saddle point exists if and only if \(\underline v=\overline v=:v\) and there are \(x^*\in X\), \(y^*\in Y\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{y\in Y}L(x^*,y)=v,
\qquad
\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y^*)=v.
\]
Thus a strict minimax gap or nonattainment of either outer optimum precludes every finite saddle point.
assumptions_latex: The common value is finite whenever minimax equality is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite saddle existence is equivalent to finite minimax equality together with attainment of both outer extrema.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-gap and attainment obstructions for a finite-valued minimization–maximization saddle system.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle Nonexistence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment is indispensable even when primal and dual optimal values coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Equality of primal and dual optimal values does not by itself imply saddle-point existence. Consider
\[p^*=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}e^x=0\]
and regard \(L:\mathbb R\times\{0\}\to\mathbb R\), defined by \(L(x,0)=e^x\), as its Lagrangian. Its trivial dual value is
\[d^*=\sup_{y\in\{0\}}\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}L(x,y)=0.\]
Thus \(p^*=d^*=0\), but no \(x^*\in\mathbb R\) attains the primal value. Consequently no pair \((x^*,0)\) satisfies the saddle inequalities. Nonattainment on either side can therefore prevent saddle-point existence despite a zero duality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero duality gap is insufficient for a saddle point: minimizing the exponential has primal and trivial dual value zero, but no primal optimizer and hence no saddle pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p^*=d^*=0\), but the saddle-point set is empty.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty, and let \(\phi:X\times Z\to\mathbb R\). Define \(v_-:=\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\), \(v_+:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\), \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\), and \(Z^*:=\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, real-valued minimax problems under the convention that the first variable is minimized and the second is maximized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The problem is in a saddle-nonexistence regime precisely when its saddle set \(\mathcal S(\phi):=\{(x^*,z^*)\in X\times Z:\phi(x^*,z)\leq\phi(x^*,z^*)\leq\phi(x,z^*)\ \forall(x,z)\in X\times Z\}\) is empty. With finite minimax values, this occurs in either of two disjoint ways: the gap regime \(v_-<v_+\), or the nonattainment regime \(v_-=v_+\) with \(X^*=\varnothing\) or \(Z^*=\varnothing\). Equivalently, \(\mathcal S(\phi)\neq\varnothing\) exactly when \(v_-=v_+\) and both outer extrema are attained, in which case \(\mathcal S(\phi)=X^*\times Z^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle point fails to exist either because the max–min value is strictly below the min–max value, or because the two values agree but at least one outer optimum is not attained. When equality and both attainments hold, every pair in \(X^*\times Z^*\) is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal S(\phi)=\varnothing\iff \bigl(v_-<v_+\bigr)\ \lor\ \bigl(v_-=v_+\text{ and }(X^*=\varnothing\text{ or }Z^*=\varnothing)\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex:
\[\mathcal S(\phi)
eq\varnothing\iff v_-=v_+,\quad X^*
eq\varnothing,\quad Z^*
eq\varnothing.\]
Whenever the right-hand conditions hold, \(\mathcal S(\phi)=X^*\times Z^*\).
special_cases_latex: If \(X^*\) and \(Z^*\) are nonempty but \(v_-<v_+\), no pairing of their elements is a saddle point.
It is possible that \(v_-=v_+\) while \(Z^*=\varnothing\); the common saddle value then exists without a saddle point.
immediate_consequences_latex: A strict minimax gap is by itself a certificate of saddle nonexistence.
Equality of minimax values alone does not certify existence; attainment is independently necessary.
boundary_notes: The definition excludes pathologies involving indeterminate comparisons of infinite extended-real values.
Nonuniqueness of either optimizer set is not a failure regime: all cross-pairs remain saddle points when equality and attainment hold.

notation.meaning: Outer min–max minimizers and max–min maximizers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value and attainment obstructions for an arbitrary extended-real minimization–maximization saddle system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), define
\[
\overline v=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y),\qquad
\underline v=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
A finite saddle point exists if and only if \(\underline v=\overline v=:v\) and there are \(x^*\in X\), \(y^*\in Y\) such that
\[
\sup_{y\in Y}L(x^*,y)=v,
\qquad
\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y^*)=v.
\]
Hence a strict minimax gap, nonattainment of the upper value, or nonattainment of the lower value is sufficient to preclude every finite saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Saddle existence fails exactly when minimax equality or attainment of at least one outer optimum fails.
assumptions_latex: \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has finite lower and upper minimax values when equality is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite saddle exists exactly under minimax equality together with attainment of both outer extrema.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be nonempty strategy sets and \(\phi:X\times Z\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). Put \(p(x):=\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\) and \(d(z):=\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A structural definition covering minimax results with different compactness, semicontinuity, convexity, coercivity, and attainment hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A minimax theorem is an implication whose hypotheses on \((X,Z,\phi)\) ensure the interchange identity \(\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\). A minimax-theorem family is a collection of such implications organized by their sufficient hypotheses. An attainment-enhanced member additionally asserts nonemptiness of \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}p(x)\) and/or \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in Z}d(z)\); if both are nonempty, it also yields saddle points. The family therefore distinguishes value interchange from attainment rather than treating them as one condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimax theorem family consists of results that give sufficient conditions for interchanging \(\sup_z\inf_x\) and \(\inf_x\sup_z\). Individual members differ in their compactness, continuity, convexity, or level-boundedness assumptions and may or may not guarantee attainment and saddle points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{admissible hypotheses on }(X,Z,\phi)\Longrightarrow \sup_{z\in Z}d(z)=\inf_{x\in X}p(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The interchange identity is the zero-gap condition \(v_+-v_-=0\), where \(v_-:=\sup_Zd\) and \(v_+:=\inf_Xp\).
When both outer extrema are attained, the identity is equivalent to the existence of \((x^*,z^*)\) satisfying \(\phi(x^*,z)\leq\phi(x^*,z^*)\leq\phi(x,z^*)\) for all \(x,z\).
special_cases_latex: The bilinear simplex instance is the finite-game von Neumann family.
The continuous convex–concave instance on compact convex sets is the classical compact saddle-point theorem.
Noncompact members replace global compactness with compact level sets, coercivity, or recession conditions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every member strengthens the universal minimax inequality \(\sup_Z\inf_X\phi\leq\inf_X\sup_Z\phi\) to equality.
Attainment conclusions must be recorded separately from the value equality.
boundary_notes: The label denotes a family of formal implications, not a single hypothesis-minimal theorem.
Without suitable hypotheses, the minimax inequality can be strict.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Programming Form of Matrix Minimax
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite matrix minimax is an LP dual pair, and matching feasible payoff bounds certify equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the game value is the common value of \[\min_{p,v}\{v:p\ge0,\ \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}p=1,\ A^{\mathsf T}p\le v\mathbf1\}\] and \[\max_{q,w}\{w:q\ge0,\ \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}q=1,\ Aq\ge w\mathbf1\}.\] Feasible solutions with \(v=w\) certify optimal mixed strategies and the value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{v:A^{\mathsf T}p\le v\mathbf1,\ p\in\Delta_m\}=\max\{w:Aq\ge w\mathbf1,\ q\in\Delta_n\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: von Neumann Minimax Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite two-player zero-sum matrix-game form of von Neumann's theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and let \(\Delta_m\) and \(\Delta_n\) be the probability simplices. Then
\[
\min_{p\in\Delta_m}\max_{q\in\Delta_n}p^{\mathsf T}Aq
=
\max_{q\in\Delta_n}\min_{p\in\Delta_m}p^{\mathsf T}Aq.
\]
Moreover, there are \(p^*\in\Delta_m\) and \(q^*\in\Delta_n\) such that, for every \(p\in\Delta_m\) and \(q\in\Delta_n\),
\[
p^{*\mathsf T}Aq\le p^{*\mathsf T}Aq^*\le p^{\mathsf T}Aq^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite zero-sum matrix game has a value and optimal mixed strategies forming a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{p\in\Delta_m}\max_{q\in\Delta_n}p^{\mathsf T}Aq=\max_{q\in\Delta_n}\min_{p\in\Delta_m}p^{\mathsf T}Aq\), with an attained saddle pair.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), let \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\mathbf1^Tx=1\}\), \(\Delta_m:=\{z\in\mathbb R_+^m:\mathbf1^Tz=1\}\), and \(\phi_A(x,z):=x^TAz\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite two-player zero-sum matrix games with mixed strategies; both strategy sets are compact simplices and the payoff is bilinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The von Neumann minimax family is the class of triples \((\Delta_n,\Delta_m,\phi_A)\) indexed by finite real matrices \(A\). Its defining minimax relation is \(\max_{z\in\Delta_m}\min_{x\in\Delta_n}x^TAz=\min_{x\in\Delta_n}\max_{z\in\Delta_m}x^TAz=:v(A)\), with both outer extrema attained. A pair \((x^*,z^*)\) is an equilibrium precisely when \(x^{*T}Az\leq x^{*T}Az^*\leq x^TAz^*\) for every \(x\in\Delta_n\) and \(z\in\Delta_m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A von Neumann minimax problem is a finite zero-sum matrix game in mixed strategies. For every real payoff matrix \(A\), the maximizing player's guaranteed payoff equals the minimizing player's worst-case payoff, both optima are attained, and their optimal strategies form saddle pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{z\in\Delta_m}\min_{x\in\Delta_n}x^TAz=\min_{x\in\Delta_n}\max_{z\in\Delta_m}x^TAz=v(A).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x^{*T}Az\leq v(A)=x^{*T}Az^*\leq x^TAz^*\quad\forall x\in\Delta_n,\ z\in\Delta_m.\]
The equilibrium set equals the Cartesian product of the two players' optimal mixed-strategy sets.
special_cases_latex: For a pure-strategy saddle entry \(a_{ij}\), the unit vectors \((e_i,e_j)\) form an equilibrium.
If \(n=1\) or \(m=1\), the identity reduces to optimization of a linear function over one simplex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finite zero-sum game has a value and at least one mixed-strategy equilibrium.
The family is a bilinear specialization of compact convex–concave minimax.
boundary_notes: The statement does not assert existence of a pure-strategy equilibrium.
Infinite action sets require additional topological assumptions and are outside this finite matrix family.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness under Strict Convexity–Concavity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity in the minimizing variable and strict concavity in the maximizing variable make the compact minimax saddle pair unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the compact convex minimax assumptions, suppose additionally that \(f(\cdot,y)\) is strictly convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\) and \(f(x,\cdot)\) is strictly concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Then the saddle pair furnished by the minimax theorem is unique.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact convex sets.
\(f\) is continuous, strictly convex in \(x\), and strictly concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists exactly one saddle pair \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness refinement of compact convex minimax.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Compact Minimax
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous convex–concave minimax theorem with both feasible sets compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty compact convex sets. If \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous, \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex for every \(y\in Y\), and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave for every \(x\in X\), then
\[
\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)
=
\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}L(x,y).
\]
Both extrema are attained, and some \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) satisfies \(L(x^*,y)\le L(x^*,y^*)\le L(x,y^*)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous convex–concave payoff on compact convex sets has equal minimax values and an attained saddle point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) are nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_X\max_Y L=\max_Y\min_X L\), and a saddle point exists.

Let \(\phi:X\times Z\to\mathbb R\) be lower semicontinuous and convex in \(x\) for each fixed \(z\), and upper semicontinuous and concave in \(z\) for each fixed \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compact convex strategy sets with separately closed convex–concave payoff sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A compact convex minimax instance is a triple \((X,Z,\phi)\) satisfying the ambient conditions. Its defining relation is \(\max_{z\in Z}\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)=\min_{x\in X}\max_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\). Both extrema are attained, and the saddle set is nonempty and compact. Equivalently, if \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\max_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\) and \(Z^*:=\operatorname*{argmax}_{z\in Z}\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\), then \(X^*\) and \(Z^*\) are nonempty compact sets and the saddle set is \(X^*\times Z^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime consists of convex–concave minimax problems on two compact convex sets with the appropriate semicontinuity. The max–min and min–max values coincide, both are attained, and all pairs of outer optimizers are saddle points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\max_{z\in Z}\min_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)=\min_{x\in X}\max_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z),\qquad \mathcal S(\phi)=X^*\times Z^*\neq\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exist \(x^*\in X\) and \(z^*\in Z\) such that \(\phi(x^*,z)\leq\phi(x^*,z^*)\leq\phi(x,z^*)\) for all \(x,z\).
The two marginal functions attain a common finite value.

Finite zero-sum matrix games arise by taking \(X\) and \(Z\) to be probability simplices.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty compact convex subset of a Hausdorff topological vector space, let \(Z\) be a nonempty convex subset of a topological vector space, and let \(\phi:X\times Z\to\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Sion-family minimax instance satisfies: for every \(z\in Z\), the section \(x\mapsto\phi(x,z)\) is lower semicontinuous and quasiconvex on \(X\); and for every \(x\in X\), the section \(z\mapsto\phi(x,z)\) is upper semicontinuous and quasiconcave on \(Z\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sion's family permits one strategy set to be noncompact and replaces convexity and concavity by quasiconvexity and quasiconcavity. Under the stated semicontinuity conditions, max–min equals min–max, although a maximizing strategy need not exist.

Quasiconcavity of \(\phi(x,\cdot)\) means every superlevel set \(\{z\in Z:\phi(x,z)\geq\alpha\}\) is convex.

\[

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Noncompact Minimax Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coercivity of one primal slice and anticoercivity of one dual slice can replace compact domains and recover an attained minimax equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(f:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\). Suppose there are \(y_0\in Y\) and \(x_0\in X\) such that
\[
f(x,y_0)\to+\infty\quad\text{as }\|x\|\to\infty\text{ along }X,
\qquad
f(x_0,y)\to-\infty\quad\text{as }\|y\|\to\infty\text{ along }Y.
\]
Then
\[
\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}f(x,y)
=
\max_{y\in Y}\min_{x\in X}f(x,y),
\]
and the common finite value is attained by a saddle pair.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional spaces.
\(f\) is finite, continuous, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
One primal slice is coercive and one dual slice is anticoercive as displayed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite minimax values coincide and a saddle pair exists.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of attained minimax equality on finite-dimensional closed noncompact domains through two-sided level control.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact Minimax Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coercive convex–concave regime with neither strategy space compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous, convex in its first argument, and concave in its second. Suppose there exist \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y_0\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that
\[
L(x,y_0)\to +\infty\quad\text{as }\|x\|\to\infty,
\qquad
L(x_0,y)\to -\infty\quad\text{as }\|y\|\to\infty.
\]
Then a saddle point \((x^*,y^*)\) exists and
\[
\min_x\max_y L(x,y)=L(x^*,y^*)=
\max_y\min_x L(x,y).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposing coercivity conditions can replace compact strategy sets and yield an attained minimax equality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A saddle point exists and \(\min_x\max_yL(x,y)=\max_y\min_xL(x,y)\).

Define \(t(x):=\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)+\delta_X(x)\) and \(r(z):=-\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)+\delta_Z(z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional noncompact problems controlled by compact level sets rather than compact feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A level-compact noncompact minimax instance is one for which at least one of \(t,r\) is proper and, for every \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\), both level sets \(\{x:t(x)\leq\gamma\}\) and \(\{z:r(z)\leq\gamma\}\) are compact. The defining relation is the minimax equality together with nonempty compact outer optimizer sets. Consequently, the saddle set is nonempty and compact despite possible unboundedness of \(X\) or \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This noncompact regime replaces bounded strategy sets by level compactness of the two marginal objectives. Properness and compact level sets ensure minimax equality, attainment on both sides, and a compact saddle set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z),\qquad \mathcal S(\phi)\neq\varnothing\text{ and is compact}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A common sufficient form is the existence of \(\bar z\in Z\) and \(\bar\gamma\in\mathbb R\) with nonempty compact \(\{x\in X:\phi(x,\bar z)\leq\bar\gamma\}\), together with the symmetric condition for some \(\bar x\in X\).
Recession-based variants replace level compactness by equality of each marginal's recession cone and constancy space, but may yield existence without compactness.
special_cases_latex: If both \(X\) and \(Z\) are compact, level compactness is automatic.
One set may be compact while a single compact payoff level set controls the other set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Unbounded feasible sets do not by themselves cause minimax or saddle failure.
Coercive marginal behavior excludes escaping optimizing sequences.
boundary_notes: This record defines the level-compact branch, not every possible noncompact minimax theorem.
Compactness of only one marginal's level sets can establish equality and one-sided attainment but need not yield a saddle point.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper, convex in \(x\), and concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth convex–concave saddle systems, using convex subdifferentials of the two sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal–dual saddle system generated by \(L\) is the pair of inclusions \(0\in\partial_xL(x,y)+N_X(x)\) and \(0\in\partial_y[-L](x,y)+N_Y(y)\). Its solution set consists of pairs \((x^*,y^*)\in X\times Y\) satisfying both inclusions. Under the stated convexity–concavity assumptions, this is equivalent to \(L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\) for all \((x,y)\in X\times Y\). The first component is the primal stationarity condition; the second is dual stationarity with the sign appropriate to maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual saddle system combines the first-order convex optimality condition in the minimizing variable with the first-order concave optimality condition in the maximizing variable. Its solutions are exactly the saddle points of the convex–concave function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{Sol}(L):=\{(x,y):0\in\partial_xL(x,y)+N_X(x),\ 0\in\partial_y[-L](x,y)+N_Y(y)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x^*,y^*)\in\operatorname{Sol}(L)\iff L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\quad\forall(x,y)\in X\times Y.\]
Equivalently, \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}L(x,y^*)\) and \(y^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}L(x^*,y)\).
special_cases_latex: For differentiable \(L\), the inclusions become \(0\in\nabla_xL(x,y)+N_X(x)\) and \(0\in-\nabla_yL(x,y)+N_Y(y)\).
For unconstrained \(X,Y\), the normal-cone terms vanish.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every solution has zero primal–dual saddle gap.
If the saddle system has no solution, value equality may still hold when an outer optimum is unattained.
boundary_notes: For nonconvex–nonconcave functions, the inclusions need not characterize global saddle points.
The definition does not assert that the solution set is nonempty.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferentials of the corresponding sections.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Optimality Systems
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite Fenchel primal-dual solutions are exactly the pairs satisfying the coupled subgradient inclusions for the objective terms and linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The primal problem and its Fenchel dual are
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+g(Ax)\bigr),
\qquad
\sup_{y^*\in Y}\bigl(-f^*(-A^*y^*)-g^*(y^*)\bigr).
\]
Under strong-duality qualification, a pair \((x^*,y^*)\) is primal-dual optimal if and only if
\[
-A^*y^*\in\partial f(x^*),
\qquad
y^*\in\partial g(Ax^*).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
0\in\partial f(x^*)+A^*y^*,
\qquad
0\in\partial g^*(y^*)-Ax^*.
\]
These inclusions simultaneously encode primal stationarity and Fenchel equality for both conjugate pairs.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are real Hilbert spaces, \(A:X\to Y\) is bounded linear, and \(f\in\Gamma_0(X)\), \(g\in\Gamma_0(Y)\).
A qualification ensuring Fenchel strong duality holds for \(\min_x f(x)+g(Ax)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,y^*)\) is primal-dual optimal exactly when \(-A^*y^*\in\partial f(x^*)\) and \(y^*\in\partial g(Ax^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel primal-dual system for a composite convex objective.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and subgradient system fit the leaf, but 'a qualification ensuring Fenchel strong duality' is not an explicit hypothesis, and the cited section has not been confirmed to support this exact Hilbert-space formulation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, and let \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. Consider \((P)\ \inf_x\{f(x)+g(Ax)\}\) and \((D)\ \sup_y\{-f^*(-A^Ty)-g^*(y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fenchel composite duality; the system characterizes primal–dual optimal pairs when the displayed inclusions are solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal–dual optimality system is \(-A^Ty\in\partial f(x)\) and \(Ax\in\partial g^*(y)\). By subgradient conjugacy, the second inclusion is equivalent to \(y\in\partial g(Ax)\). A solution \((x^*,y^*)\) satisfies equality in both Fenchel–Young inequalities, hence \(x^*\) is primal optimal, \(y^*\) is dual optimal, and the primal and dual objective values coincide. Conversely, any primal–dual optimal pair with zero duality gap satisfies the system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the composite problem \(f(x)+g(Ax)\), the primal and dual variables are jointly optimal exactly when their subgradients are linked through \(A\) by \(-A^Ty\in\partial f(x)\) and \(y\in\partial g(Ax)\), assuming zero duality gap for the converse direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[0\in\partial f(x)+A^Ty,\qquad 0\in\partial g^*(y)-Ax.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[-A^Ty\in\partial f(x),\qquad y\in\partial g(Ax).\]
\[f(x)+f^*(-A^Ty)=\langle x,-A^Ty\rangle,\quad g(Ax)+g^*(y)=\langle Ax,y\rangle.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(g=\delta_C\), the second relation becomes \(y\in N_C(Ax)\).
If \(f\) and \(g^*\) are differentiable, the system becomes two coupled gradient equations.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every system solution has zero Fenchel primal–dual gap.
The system is the zero condition for a block monotone operator.
boundary_notes: Existence of a solution generally requires a qualification or other closedness condition.
Optimality without zero duality gap cannot produce a solution of this joint system.

knowledge_statements.title: The Sign in the Saddle Operator Is Essential
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating the concave-variable derivative is essential; the unsigned map can fail to be monotone even for a bilinear saddle function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L(x,y)=xy\) on \(\mathbb R^2\), the signed saddle operator is \(T(x,y)=(y,-x)\) and satisfies \(\langle Tz-Tz',z-z'\rangle=0\). The unsigned map \(S(x,y)=(y,x)\) is not monotone: for \(z=(1,-1)\) and \(z'=(0,0)\), \[\langle Sz-Sz',z-z'\rangle=-2<0.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(x,y)=(y,-x)\) is monotone, whereas \(S(x,y)=(y,x)\) is not.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bilinear example distinguishing the signed monotone operator from the unsigned partial-gradient map.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Monotonicity from Strong Convexity–Concavity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity and strong concavity make the signed saddle operator strongly monotone and its zero unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every \(L(\cdot,y)\) is \(\mu_x\)-strongly convex and every \(L(x,\cdot)\) is \(\mu_y\)-strongly concave, then for \((u_i,w_i)\in T(x_i,y_i)\), \[\langle u_1-u_2,x_1-x_2\rangle+\langle w_1-w_2,y_1-y_2\rangle\ge \mu_x\|x_1-x_2\|^2+\mu_y\|y_1-y_2\|^2.\] Hence \(T\) is \(\min\{\mu_x,\mu_y\}\)-strongly monotone when both moduli are positive and has at most one zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) satisfies the displayed quantitative monotonicity inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative monotonicity of the signed saddle operator.

notation.meaning: concave superdifferential in the second variable

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Monotonicity of a Closed Saddle Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed saddle subdifferential of a proper closed saddle function is maximal monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, and let \(L\) be a proper closed saddle function in Rockafellar's closed-saddle equivalence-class convention. Then \[T_L(x,y)=\{(u,-v):u\in\partial_xL(x,y),\ v\in\partial_y^+L(x,y)\}\] is maximal monotone on \(X\times Y\).
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a proper closed saddle function in Rockafellar's convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_L\text{ is maximal monotone on }X\times Y.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical maximality theorem under Rockafellar's proper closed-saddle-function convention.

notation.meaning: concave superdifferential in the second variable

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Saddle Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity and saddle optimality of the smooth operator induced by a convex–concave saddle function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and suppose \(L\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X\times Y\). Assume that \(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(X\) for every \(y\in Y\) and that \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave on \(Y\) for every \(x\in X\). Define
\[
F(x,y)=\bigl(\nabla_xL(x,y),-\nabla_yL(x,y)\bigr).
\]
Then \(F\) is monotone on \(X\times Y\): for all \(z,z'\in X\times Y\),
\[
\langle F(z)-F(z'),z-z'\rangle\ge 0.
\]
Moreover, \(z^*\in X\times Y\) is a saddle point of \(L\) on \(X\times Y\) if and only if
\[
0\in F(z^*)+N_{X\times Y}(z^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed gradient of a smooth convex–concave function is monotone, and its normal-cone inclusion characterizes constrained saddle points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) are nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(L\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X\times Y\).
\(L(\cdot,y)\) is convex on \(X\), and \(L(x,\cdot)\) is concave on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=(\nabla_xL,-\nabla_yL)\) is monotone, and \(z^*\) is a constrained saddle point if and only if \(0\in F(z^*)+N_{X\times Y}(z^*)\).

notation.meaning: Normal-cone operator of the feasible product set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone operator induced by a saddle function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets, and let \(L\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous convex in \(x\), and upper-semicontinuous concave in \(y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional set-valued operator formulation for possibly nonsmooth convex–concave saddle functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The monotone saddle operator associated with \(L\) is \(T_L(x,y):=(\partial_xL(x,y)+N_X(x))\times(\partial_y[-L](x,y)+N_Y(y))\). It is monotone when, for all \(u_i\in T_L(x_i,y_i)\), \(\langle u_1-u_2,(x_1-x_2,y_1-y_2)\rangle\geq0\). Its zero set is exactly the saddle set: \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point if and only if \((0,0)\in T_L(x^*,y^*)\). In the smooth case, the single-valued interior part is \((\nabla_xL,-\nabla_yL)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone saddle operator combines the subgradient in the minimizing variable with the negative subgradient in the maximizing variable and adds the two constraint normal cones. Solving the saddle problem is equivalent to finding a zero of this operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_L(x,y):=\begin{pmatrix}\partial_xL(x,y)+N_X(x)\\ \partial_y[-L](x,y)+N_Y(y)\end{pmatrix},\qquad \operatorname{zer}T_L=\mathcal S(L).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: In the smooth case, \(T_L(x,y)=(\nabla_xL(x,y)+N_X(x),-\nabla_yL(x,y)+N_Y(y))\).
The zero inclusion is the coupled primal–dual stationarity system.
special_cases_latex: When \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), only the sectional subdifferentials remain.
For a bilinear coupling plus separable convex terms, \(T_L\) has the standard skew-linear primal–dual block structure.
immediate_consequences_latex: The zero set of a maximal monotone saddle operator is closed and convex.
Strict monotonicity permits at most one zero.
boundary_notes: Maximal monotonicity may require closedness and regularity beyond bare monotonicity.
The sign in the dual component is essential; using \(\partial_yL\) would not encode maximization.

notation.meaning: Set of points mapped to a set containing zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Saddle Models
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional convex-concave saddle point is exactly a solution of the variational inequality generated by the primal partial subdifferential and the negative dual partial superdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=(x,y)\in X\times Y\), let \(\partial_y^+L(x,y)\) denote the concave superdifferential of \(L(x,\cdot)\) at \(y\), and define \(T(z)=\partial_xL(x,y)\times(-\partial_y^+L(x,y))\). A variational-inequality saddle model seeks \(z^\star\in X\times Y\) and \(g^\star\in T(z^\star)\) such that \[\langle g^\star,z-z^\star\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }z\in X\times Y.\] Equivalently, \(0\in T(z^\star)+N_{X\times Y}(z^\star)\). Under the stated hypotheses, this holds if and only if \[L(x^\star,y)\leq L(x^\star,y^\star)\leq L(x,y^\star)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X\text{ and }y\in Y.\]
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, and \(X\subseteq E\) and \(Y\subseteq F\) are nonempty closed convex sets.
\(L:E\times F\to\mathbb{R}\) is lower-semicontinuous and convex in its first argument and upper-semicontinuous and concave in its second argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is a saddle point if and only if \(0\in T(x^\star,y^\star)+N_{X\times Y}(x^\star,y^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth convex-concave saddle systems represented as variational inequalities.

notation.meaning: Saddle operator, with the concave superdifferential in the second component.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational-inequality model of a smooth saddle problem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be nonempty closed convex sets. Let \(L:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, convex in \(x\in X\), and concave in \(y\in Y\). Put \(C:=X\times Y\) and \(F(x,y):=(\nabla_xL(x,y),-\nabla_yL(x,y))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth convex–concave saddle problems represented as monotone variational inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variational-inequality saddle model is \(\operatorname{VI}(C,F)\): find \((x^*,y^*)\in C\) such that \(\langle F(x^*,y^*),(x-x^*,y-y^*)\rangle\geq0\) for every \((x,y)\in C\). Because \(L\) is convex–concave, this condition is equivalent to the saddle inequalities \(L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\). It is also equivalent to \((0,0)\in F(x^*,y^*)+N_C(x^*,y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth convex–concave saddle problem becomes a variational inequality on the product feasible set when the field is formed from the primal gradient and the negative dual gradient. Solutions of the variational inequality are exactly saddle points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\langle\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*),x-x^*\rangle-\langle\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*),y-y^*\rangle\geq0\quad\forall(x,y)\in X\times Y.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\quad\forall(x,y)\in X\times Y.\]
special_cases_latex: For unconstrained sets, the model reduces to \(\nabla_xL(x^*,y^*)=0\) and \(\nabla_yL(x^*,y^*)=0\).
A bilinear payoff produces an affine monotone field.
immediate_consequences_latex: The field \(F\) is monotone on \(C\).
If \(F\) is strictly monotone, the variational inequality has at most one solution.
boundary_notes: For nonsmooth \(L\), the appropriate model is a generalized variational inequality or monotone inclusion.
For nonconvex–nonconcave \(L\), the variational inequality expresses stationarity but not necessarily a global saddle point.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X,Z\) be nonempty and \(\phi:X\times Z\to\mathbb R\). Define \(v_-:=\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\), \(v_+:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)\), and \(\Gamma:=v_+-v_-\) whenever both values are finite.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global value-gap diagnosis for real-valued minimax problems; attainment failure is recorded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strict saddle-gap failure occurs when \(\Gamma>0\), equivalently \(v_-<v_+\). A zero-gap but uncertified-saddle regime occurs when \(\Gamma=0\) but one or both outer extrema are not attained. For a candidate pair \((x,z)\), its primal–dual saddle residual is \(G(x,z):=\sup_{z'\in Z}\phi(x,z')-\inf_{x'\in X}\phi(x',z)\geq0\). It vanishes exactly at saddle points. Thus \(\Gamma\) diagnoses failure of value interchange, whereas \(G\) diagnoses whether a particular pair is a saddle certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global saddle gap is the min–max value minus the max–min value. A positive gap means minimax interchange fails. The pairwise gap compares a candidate's worst dual response with its best primal response and equals zero exactly for saddle points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Gamma:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{z\in Z}\phi(x,z)-\sup_{z\in Z}\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x,z)\geq0,\qquad G(x,z)\geq0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[G(x,z)=0\iff \sup_{z'\in Z}\phi(x,z')=\phi(x,z)=\inf_{x'\in X}\phi(x',z).\]
\[\Gamma>0\iff \sup_Z\inf_X\phi<\inf_X\sup_Z\phi.\]
special_cases_latex: For convex–concave closed problems, lack of lower semicontinuity of an associated perturbation value at the origin can produce \(\Gamma>0\).
When \(\Gamma=0\) but the dual supremum is not attained, every pair has positive residual even though the values agree.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any pair with \(G(x,z)=0\) certifies \(\Gamma=0\) and attainment on both sides.
A positive \(\Gamma\) rules out every saddle point.
boundary_notes: The finite-value restriction avoids undefined expressions such as \(+\infty-(+\infty)\).
The global gap and pairwise residual are different objects and should not be conflated.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimum Pointwise Gap Equals the Minimax Value Gap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum of the pointwise gap is the upper-minus-lower minimax value gap; equality of values does not ensure attainment of a zero gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\underline v:=\sup_{y\in Y}\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y)\) and \(\overline v:=\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)\), and assume both values are finite. Then \[\inf_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}G(x,y)=\overline v-\underline v.\] Thus the pointwise gaps have infimum zero exactly when the minimax values agree, although no zero-gap pair need exist.
assumptions_latex: The pointwise gaps entering the infimum are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x,y}G(x,y)=\overline v-\underline v\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite lower and upper minimax values; the pointwise-gap infimum need not be attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap as Two Best-Response Residuals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The saddle gap splits into two nonnegative best-response residuals, both of which vanish exactly at zero gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x):=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)\) and \(d(y):=\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y)\). Whenever \(p(x)\), \(d(y)\), and \(L(x,y)\) are finite, \[G(x,y)=p(x)-d(y)=[p(x)-L(x,y)]+[L(x,y)-d(y)].\] Both residuals are nonnegative, so the gap vanishes exactly when both vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(p(x),d(y),L(x,y)\) are finite at the evaluated pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y)=[p(x)-L(x,y)]+[L(x,y)-d(y)]\), with both summands nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic decomposition of the unrestricted saddle gap when all terms are finite.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual gap is the worst dual improvement minus the best primal improvement. It is nonnegative, and a finite zero gap is equivalent to the saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal-dual gap of \((x,y)\in X\times Y\) is \[G(x,y):=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y),\] whenever the extended-real subtraction is defined. Since \(v=y\) and \(u=x\) are admissible, \(G(x,y)\geq0\). If both terms are finite, then \(G(x,y)=0\) if and only if \[L(x,v)\leq L(x,y)\leq L(u,y)\qquad(u\in X,\ v\in Y),\] so \((x,y)\) is a saddle point.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty sets, and \(L:X\times Y\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) has well-defined extended-real suprema and infima at the evaluated point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(x,y)\geq0\), and a finite pair has \(G(x,y)=0\) exactly when it is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrestricted gap for a minimization-maximization saddle convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal-dual gap of \((x,y)\in X\times Y\) is \[G(x,y):=\sup_{v\in Y}L(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}L(u,y),\] whenever the extended-real subtraction is defined. Since \(v=y\) and \(u=x\) are admissible, \(G(x,y)\geq0\). If both terms are finite, then \(G(x,y)=0\) if and only if \[L(x,v)\leq L(x,y)\leq L(u,y)\qquad(u\in X,\ v\in Y),\] so \((x,y)\) is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual gap is the worst dual improvement minus the best primal improvement. It is nonnegative, and a finite zero gap is equivalent to the saddle inequalities.
