knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For each \(i\), let \(F_i\) be a \(\nu_i\)-self-concordant barrier on an open convex domain \(D_i\) in a finite-dimensional space. Barrier parameters refer to the standard normalization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A definition of the standard construction calculus as a collection of parameter-tracked closure operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The barrier construction calculus consists of the following parameter-tracked operations: (i) affine pullback, \(F\mapsto F\circ(A\cdot+b)\), on \(\{x:Ax+b\in D\}\), preserving parameter \(
u\); (ii) addition on a common space, \(F_1+F_2\), producing a barrier on \(D_1\cap D_2\) with parameter \(
u_1+
u_2\); (iii) direct products, \((x_1,\ldots,x_m)\mapsto\sum_iF_i(x_i)\), with domain \(\prod_iD_i\) and parameter \(\sum_i
u_i\); and (iv) supported epigraph or compatible-composition lifts, with the parameter prescribed by the corresponding construction theorem. A valid construction must have nonempty open domain and must preserve boundary blow-up for the represented set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Barrier construction calculus means the closure rules that build new barriers from known ones while tracking domains and parameters. Affine inverse images preserve the parameter, sums construct barriers for intersections, separable sums construct barriers for Cartesian products, and specific epigraph or compatible nonlinear lifts have their own stated parameter updates. Domain nonemptiness and boundary behavior remain part of every construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The elementary affine, intersection, and product rules transform certified barriers into certified barriers with parameters \(
u\), \(
u_1+
u_2\), and \(\sum_i
u_i\), respectively.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The direct-product rule is the intersection rule after lifting each \(F_i\) to the product space by its coordinate projection.
special_cases_latex: Restricting a barrier to an affine slice is an affine pullback.
The logarithmic barrier for finitely many scalar inequalities is the sum of their scalar logarithmic barriers.
immediate_consequences_latex: Barrier parameters accumulate additively under independent constraint-family assembly.
Redundant represented constraints may enlarge the constructed parameter even when the underlying convex set is unchanged.
boundary_notes: Arbitrary nonlinear composition does not preserve self-concordance; compatibility hypotheses are essential.
Projection or partial minimization requires a separate implicit-barrier theorem and is not an automatic elementary rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Pullback and Restriction of a Barrier
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\to\mathbb R\) be a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier on an open convex set \(D\subset E_1\). Let \(\mathcal A:E_0\to E_1\) be affine, \(\mathcal A(x)=Ax+b\), and assume \(D_0=\mathcal A^{-1}(D)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine inverse images, including parametrized affine slices. The pullback Hessian may be degenerate if \(A\) is not injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine pullback barrier is \(\Phi:D_0\to\mathbb R\), \(\Phi(x)=F(Ax+b)\). It is a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier for the represented domain \(D_0=\{x:Ax+b\in D\}\), with \[D^k\Phi(x)[h_1,\ldots,h_k]=D^kF(Ax+b)[Ah_1,\ldots,Ah_k],\qquad k=1,2,3.\] If an affine slice \(D\cap(a+V)\) is parametrized by \(x=a+Bu\), its restricted barrier is \(u\mapsto F(a+Bu)\) on \(\{u:a+Bu\in D\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a self-concordant barrier with an affine map gives a barrier on the affine inverse image of its domain and preserves the barrier parameter. Restriction to an affine slice is the same operation after parametrizing the slice. Directional derivatives are obtained by applying the linear part of the affine map to every direction argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi=F\circ\mathcal A\) is a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier on \(\mathcal A^{-1}(D)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Affine restriction is pullback under the embedding \(u\mapsto a+Bu\).
For an invertible affine coordinate change, pullback and pushforward give equivalent barrier models with the same parameter.
special_cases_latex: For \(D=\mathbb R_{++}^m\) and \(\mathcal A(x)=b-Ax\), the pullback is \(-\sum_i\ln(b_i-a_i^Tx)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph Lift of a Self-Concordant Barrier
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier on an open convex domain \(D\subset E\). Define the closed epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R:t\geq f(x)\}\) and its open interior representation \(\mathcal E_f^\circ=\{(x,t):x\in D,\ t>f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph construction supported by the source. General perspective homogenization requires additional homogeneity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph barrier associated with \(f\) is \[F_{\mathrm{epi}}(x,t)=f(x)-\ln\bigl(t-f(x)\bigr),\qquad (x,t)\in\mathcal E_f^\circ.\] It is a \((\nu+1)\)-self-concordant barrier for \(\operatorname{epi}f\). The slack coordinate \(s=t-f(x)>0\) contributes one scalar logarithmic-barrier unit. When a positively homogeneous perspective \(p(y,\tau)=\tau f(y/\tau)\) is introduced for \(\tau>0\), its epigraph is the conic homogenization \(\{(y,\tau,t):\tau>0,\ t>\tau f(y/\tau)\}\); a barrier transfer to that cone requires a separately verified perspective or affine-composition theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-concordant barrier \(f\) yields a barrier for its epigraph by adding the logarithmic barrier of the positive epigraph slack \(t-f(x)\). The resulting parameter is \(\nu+1\). The usual perspective lift homogenizes the epigraph, but its barrier status is not automatic without the additional hypotheses of an applicable perspective construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{epi}}(x,t)=f(x)-\ln(t-f(x))\) is a \((\nu+1)\)-self-concordant barrier on \(\mathcal E_f^\circ\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using the slack variable \(s=t-f(x)\), the barrier is \(f(x)-\ln s\) subject to \(s>0\) and \(t=f(x)+s\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=-\ln x\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}\), the construction gives \(-\ln x-\ln(t+\ln x)\) on \(t>-\ln x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An objective epigraph can be incorporated into a barrier model with one additional certified parameter unit.
Affine transformations of \((x,t)\) can be combined with this construction by affine pullback.
boundary_notes: The construction requires that \(f\) itself be a self-concordant barrier, not merely an arbitrary convex function.
The source-supported epigraph formula should not be conflated with an unrestricted perspective closure rule.

knowledge_statements.title: Perspective Barrier Constructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the homogeneous inequality normals span the ambient space, the positive-scale logarithm plus the homogenized slack logarithms form an (m+1)-self-concordant barrier for the strict perspective epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K^{\circ}=\{(x,s,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+2}:s>0,\ t>a_i^{\mathsf T}x+b_is\text{ for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\}\), the function \(H:K^{\circ}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(H(x,s,t)=-\log s-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(t-a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_is)\) is an \((m+1)\)-self-concordant barrier.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph–Perspective Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective epigraph is the closed conic hull of the unit-scale epigraph, whose scale-one slice recovers the original epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closed perspective by \[\bar f(x,s)=\begin{cases}s f(x/s),&s>0,\\ f^{\infty}(x),&s=0,\\ +\infty,&s<0.\end{cases}\] Then \(\bar f\) is proper, closed, convex, and positively homogeneous, and its epigraph satisfies \[\operatorname{epi}\bar f=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}\bigl(\{(x,1,t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\bigr).\] Conversely, the unit-scale section recovers the original epigraph: \((x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) if and only if \((x,1,t)\in\operatorname{epi}\bar f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\bar f=\overline{\operatorname{cone}}\{(x,1,t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-perspective convention including the zero-scale recession face.

notation.meaning: Closed perspective of the convex function

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The representation is plausible and fits the correspondence leaf, but no citation is supplied. The exact closed-perspective convention, recession-face formula, and closed-conic-hull identity require an authoritative section, theorem, or proposition locator before review can determine reliability.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Domain Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At positive scale the lift evaluates the perspective; at zero scale it records recession behavior, and omitting that face can destroy closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the closed perspective, points with \(s>0\) satisfy \(\bar f(x,s)=sf(x/s)\), whereas the zero-scale face satisfies \(\bar f(x,0)=f^{\infty}(x)\). Thus finite points at \(s=0\) encode recession directions rather than ordinary evaluations of \(f\). A barrier constructed only on the positive-scale interior must diverge along finite interior sequences approaching \(s=0\) or any active lifted-domain boundary. If the recession face is omitted instead of closed by \(f^{\infty}\), the resulting perspective epigraph need not be closed.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex, with closed perspective \(\bar f\).
A lifted barrier is defined on the interior region with positive scale \(s>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The zero-scale face is governed by \(f^{\infty}\), while interior barrier blow-up occurs as scale or defining slack vanishes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary decomposition for closed perspective lifts and their positive-scale barriers.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the record has no source. The claims about the zero-scale recession face, barrier divergence at that face, and failure of closedness when it is omitted require an authoritative locator and convention check.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugating a logarithmically homogeneous barrier with the appropriate sign constructs a barrier having the same parameter on the polar dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K^*:=\{s\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle s,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in K\}\). Define
\[
F_{K^*}(s):=F^*(-s)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{int}K}\{-\langle s,x\rangle-F(x)\}.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{dom}F_{K^*}=\operatorname{int}K^*\), and \(F_{K^*}\) is a \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier there. An additive normalization constant in \(F\) changes only the additive constant in \(F_{K^*}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a cone is not full-dimensional, its own Euclidean interior is empty; if it is not pointed, its dual cone has empty Euclidean interior. Full-space primal-dual barriers therefore require full-dimensionality and pointedness.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Summing negative logarithms of positive linear slacks gives a self-concordant polyhedral barrier whose parameter equals the number of represented inequalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier Representations for Convex Quadratic and Lorentz Constraints
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(x)=\alpha+\langle a,x\rangle+\tfrac12\langle Ax,x\rangle\) with \(A\succeq0\), and let \(\beta\in\mathbb R\). Let \(A=B^*B\). The Lorentz cone is \(\mathcal L^{r+1}=\{(z,t):t\geq\|z\|_2\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex quadratic sublevel and second-order-cone representations with strictly positive slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strict quadratic sublevel domain is \(D_q=\{x:\beta-q(x)>0\}\). Its scalar logarithmic barrier is \[F_q(x)=-\ln(\beta-q(x)),\qquad x\in D_q,\] and is a \(1\)-self-concordant barrier for the corresponding second-order region. A norm inequality \(\|Bx+c\|_2<d^Tx+e\) is the affine inverse image of \(\operatorname{int}\mathcal L^{r+1}\) and therefore has barrier \[F_{\mathcal L}(x)=-\ln\bigl((d^Tx+e)^2-\|Bx+c\|_2^2\bigr),\] with parameter \(2\). Finite families are assembled by summing these barriers, so their certified parameters add.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic inequality with positive concave slack can use the negative logarithm of that slack as a one-parameter barrier. A second-order-cone inequality is represented by an affine Lorentz-cone map and uses the negative logarithm of the Lorentz quadratic form, with parameter two. Multiple quadratic or cone constraints are combined by summing their barriers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_q\) is a \(1\)-self-concordant barrier on \(D_q\), and \(F_{\mathcal L}\) is a \(2\)-self-concordant barrier on \(\{x:\|Bx+c\|_2<d^Tx+e\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Lorentz representation is \((Bx+c,d^Tx+e)\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal L^{r+1}\).
Completing the square or factoring \(A=B^*B\) converts many convex quadratic sublevel constraints into rotated or ordinary second-order-cone representations after introducing auxiliary variables.
special_cases_latex: For \(q(x)=\|x\|_2^2\) and \(\beta=1\), \(-\ln(1-\|x\|_2^2)\) is the unit-ball barrier.
For \(B=I\), \(c=0\), and scalar \(t\), the Lorentz barrier is \(-\ln(t^2-\|x\|_2^2)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Affine substitutions preserve the stated parameters.
A quadratically constrained convex program obtains an explicit barrier by summing one term per scalar quadratic slack or per chosen cone block.
boundary_notes: The scalar quadratic-slack formula requires the slack to be concave, equivalently the quadratic function in the sublevel constraint to be convex.
Different cone lifts of the same quadratic set can have different additive parameter certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Quadratic Barriers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex quadratic written as a Lorentz difference of squares has a negative-log barrier obtained by an injective affine pullback of the Lorentz-cone barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(x):=(c^Tx+d,Ax+b)\). For \(x\in D\), one has \(-q(x)=(c^Tx+d)^2-\|Ax+b\|_2^2>0\), and therefore \[F(x):=-\log(-q(x))=-\log\bigl((c^Tx+d)^2-\|Ax+b\|_2^2\bigr).\] Thus \(F\) is the affine pullback through \(T\) of the Lorentz-cone logarithmic barrier. The injectivity assumption on the linear part of \(T\) makes the pullback Hessian positive definite, and \(F\) is a self-concordant barrier on \(D\).
assumptions_latex: \(D:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:c^Tx+d>\|Ax+b\|_2\}\) is nonempty, and \(Ah=0\) together with \(c^Th=0\) implies \(h=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(F(x):=-\log(-q(x))\) is the injective affine pullback of the Lorentz-cone logarithmic barrier and is a self-concordant barrier on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex quadratic barriers obtained from an injective affine section of the Lorentz cone, with an explicit positive-sheet condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Cone Barriers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative logarithm of the Lorentz quadratic determinant is a parameter-two logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
F(t,u):=-\log\bigl(t^2-\|u\|_2^2\bigr),\qquad (t,u)\in L_{r+1}.
\]
Then \(F\) is a self-concordant barrier and satisfies
\[
F(\lambda t,\lambda u)=F(t,u)-2\log\lambda\qquad(\lambda>0).
\]
Thus \(F\) is \(2\)-logarithmically homogeneous and has barrier parameter \(2\). It diverges to \(+\infty\) as \(t^2-\|u\|_2^2\downarrow0\) within the cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(t,u)=-\log(t^2-\|u\|_2^2)\) is a \(2\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(L_{r+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Lorentz-cone barrier with parameter two, independent of cone dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-to-Cone Representations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A difference-of-squares quadratic inequality with its positive-sheet condition is exactly one affine Lorentz-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[q(x)\le0\ \text{ and }\ c^Tx+d\ge0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \|Ax+b\|_2\le c^Tx+d \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T(x)\in\mathcal{Q}_{r+1}.\] Likewise, \(q(x)<0\) and \(c^Tx+d>0\) are equivalent to \(T(x)\in\operatorname{int}\mathcal{Q}_{r+1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditions \(q(x)\le0\) and \(c^Tx+d\ge0\) are equivalent to one affine second-order-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact affine Lorentz-cone representation of a difference-of-squares quadratic together with its positive-sheet condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Quadratic Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic cone barrier requires a nonempty strict sheet, an explicit sheet choice, and removal of any directions on which the affine Lorentz representation is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D=\varnothing\), no ordinary barrier exists on the represented strict positive-sheet region. If \(q(x)<0\) is imposed without selecting the sign of \(c^Tx+d\), the positive and negative Lorentz sheets are combined; although each sheet is convex after the appropriate sign convention, their union is generally nonconvex. Finally, if a nonzero \(h\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(Ah=0\) and \(c^Th=0\), then \(T(x+\tau h)=T(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\tau\in\mathbb{R}\), so the pullback Hessian is singular along \(h\). A positive-definite local barrier metric then requires reduction by the flat directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Empty strict feasibility, omission of a sheet condition, or a noninjective affine Lorentz map prevents the intended full-dimensional quadratic-barrier interpretation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundaries caused by empty interior, an unselected quadratic sheet, or flat directions in the affine Lorentz representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Log-Determinant Barriers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative log-determinant is the canonical parameter-n self-concordant barrier on the positive-definite matrix cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\), define \(F(X):=-\log\det X\). Its first two derivatives are
\[
DF(X)[H]=-\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}H),\qquad D^2F(X)[H,H]=\operatorname{tr}(X^{-1}HX^{-1}H).
\]
The function \(F\) is self-concordant, tends to \(+\infty\) when a positive eigenvalue approaches zero, and satisfies
\[
F(\lambda X)=F(X)-n\log\lambda\qquad(\lambda>0).
\]
Hence it is an \(n\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\) denotes the cone of real symmetric positive-definite matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(X)=-\log\det X\) is an \(n\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\mathbb{S}_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric positive-definite cone with the trace inner product.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsymmetric Cone Barriers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential cone admits an explicit logarithmic self-concordant barrier, illustrating the cone-specific formulas needed for nonsymmetric cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On
\[
\operatorname{int}K_{\exp}=\{(x,y,z):y>0,\ z>0,\ r(x,y,z)>0\},
\]
define
\[
F_{\exp}(x,y,z):=-\log y-\log z-\log r(x,y,z),
\qquad r(x,y,z):=\log(z/y)-x/y.
\]
This function is a self-concordant barrier for the exponential cone and diverges when \(y\downarrow0\), \(z\downarrow0\), or \(r(x,y,z)\downarrow0\). Analogous cone-specific constructions, rather than symmetry-based determinant formulas, are required for power, entropy, and related nonsymmetric cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed logarithmic expression is a self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K_{\exp}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative nonsymmetric-cone construction using the exponential cone; not an exhaustive family classification.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonsymmetric cone barrier and the power-cone family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(K\subset E\) be a closed, pointed, full-dimensional convex cone. A cone barrier is defined on \(\operatorname{int}K\); symmetry, homogeneity of the cone, and self-duality are not assumed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth barriers on regular cones, emphasizing barrier constructions that remain valid without symmetric-cone geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonsymmetric-cone barrier is a self-concordant barrier \(F:\operatorname{int}K\to\mathbb R\) whose definition and validity do not require \(K\) to be a homogeneous self-dual cone. A canonical family is obtained for \(0<\alpha<1\) on the power cone
\[
K_\alpha=\{(x_1,x_2,z)\in\mathbb R_+^2\times\mathbb R:x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\ge |z|\}.
\]
On its interior,
\[
\Psi_{P,\alpha}(x_1,x_2,z)=-\log\!\left(x_1^{2\alpha}x_2^{2(1-\alpha)}-z^2\right)-\log x_1-\log x_2
\]
is a \(4\)-self-concordant barrier. Thus this family supplies explicit local metrics \(\nabla^2\Psi_{P,\alpha}\) and barrier parameters without invoking a self-scaled or symmetric-cone structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsymmetric-cone barrier is a self-concordant barrier on the interior of a regular cone whose construction does not assume that the cone is homogeneous and self-dual. For the power cone \(K_\alpha\), with \(0<\alpha<1\), the displayed logarithmic function is defined exactly where \(x_1>0\), \(x_2>0\), and \(x_1^{2\alpha}x_2^{2(1-\alpha)}>z^2\); it is a self-concordant barrier with parameter \(4\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Psi_{P,\alpha}\) is a \(4\)-self-concordant barrier for \(K_\alpha\), furnishing an explicit barrier family that does not depend on symmetric-cone scaling.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{int}K_\alpha=\{(x_1,x_2,z):x_1>0,\ x_2>0,\ x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}>|z|\}\).
special_cases_latex: For the one-sided power cone \(K_\alpha^+=\{(x_1,x_2,z):x_1,x_2\ge0,\ x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\ge z\}\), the source gives the \(3\)-self-concordant barrier \(-\log(x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}-z)-\log x_1-\log x_2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The barrier diverges when \(x_1\downarrow0\), \(x_2\downarrow0\), or \(x_1^\alpha x_2^{1-\alpha}\downarrow |z|\).
The parameter \(4\) controls the local-gradient inequality \(\|\nabla\Psi_{P,\alpha}(x)\|_{x,*}^2\le4\).
boundary_notes: The term “nonsymmetric” concerns the absence of a homogeneous self-dual cone structure; it does not mean that the Hessian is nonsymmetric.
Exponential- and entropy-cone barriers are nearby families but are not asserted by this record.

knowledge_statements.title: Hyperbolic-Polynomial Barriers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative logarithm of a degree-d hyperbolic polynomial is a parameter-d logarithmically homogeneous barrier on its hyperbolicity cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
F(x):=-\log p(x),\qquad x\in\Lambda_{++}(p,e).
\]
Then \(F\) is a self-concordant barrier for the open hyperbolicity cone. Homogeneity of \(p\) gives
\[
F(\lambda x)=F(x)-d\log\lambda\qquad(\lambda>0),
\]
so the barrier is \(d\)-logarithmically homogeneous and has parameter \(d\). Moreover, \(F(x_k)\to+\infty\) whenever \(x_k\) approaches a finite boundary point of the cone with \(p(x_k)\downarrow0\).
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(d\ge1\), hyperbolic with respect to \(e\).
\(\Lambda_{++}(p,e)\) is the connected component of \(\{x:p(x)>0\}\) containing \(e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=-\log p(x)\) is a \(d\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\Lambda_{++}(p,e)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guler-type barrier theorem for homogeneous hyperbolic polynomials.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier induced by a hyperbolic polynomial
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space. Let \(p:E\to\mathbb R\) be a nonzero homogeneous polynomial of degree \(d\), and fix \(e\in E\) with \(p(e)>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional homogeneous hyperbolic polynomials and the open hyperbolicity cone containing the distinguished direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polynomial \(p\) is hyperbolic with respect to \(e\) when, for every \(x\in E\), the univariate polynomial \(t\mapsto p(x-te)\) has only real roots. Its open hyperbolicity cone is
\[
\Lambda_{++}(p,e)=\text{the connected component of }\{x\in E:p(x)>0\}\text{ containing }e,
\]
and \(\Lambda_+(p,e)=\operatorname{cl}\Lambda_{++}(p,e)\). The hyperbolic-polynomial barrier is
\[
F_p(x)=-\log p(x),\qquad x\in\Lambda_{++}(p,e).
\]
It is logarithmically homogeneous of degree \(d\), since \(F_p(\tau x)=F_p(x)-d\log\tau\) for every \(\tau>0\). The canonical barrier theorem asserts that \(F_p\) is a \(d\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier for \(\Lambda_+(p,e)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous polynomial \(p\) is hyperbolic in direction \(e\) if every line parallel to \(e\) produces a real-rooted univariate polynomial. The component of \(p>0\) containing \(e\) is its open hyperbolicity cone. The associated barrier is \(-\log p\) on that component; homogeneity gives logarithmic degree \(d\), and the standard barrier result assigns parameter \(d\).
assumptions_latex: For every \(x\in E\), all roots of \(t\mapsto p(x-te)\) are real.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_p=-\log p\) is the canonical degree-\(d\) logarithmically homogeneous barrier on \(\Lambda_{++}(p,e)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\lambda_1(x),\ldots,\lambda_d(x)\) are defined by \(p(x-te)=p(e)\prod_{i=1}^d(\lambda_i(x)-t)\), then \(\Lambda_{++}(p,e)=\{x:\lambda_i(x)>0\ \forall i\}\).
special_cases_latex: For \(p(X)=\det X\) on symmetric matrices and \(e=I\), \(\Lambda_{++}(p,e)=\mathbb S_{++}^n\) and \(F_p(X)=-\log\det X\).
For \(p(x)=\prod_{i=1}^m a_i^Tx\), the barrier is \(-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(a_i^Tx)\) on the corresponding component.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(F_p(\tau x)=F_p(x)-d\log\tau\).
\(\langle\nabla F_p(x),x\rangle=-d\) wherever \(p(x)>0\).
boundary_notes: The real-rootedness condition is required in every direction \(x\), not merely near \(e\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex with nonempty interior and no affine line. For \(x\in\operatorname{int}Q\), form the polar of \(Q-x\) at level one.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional general convex domains without explicit algebraic structure; the construction is primarily existential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{int}Q\), define
\[
P_Q(x)=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:\langle s,z-x\rangle\le1\ \text{for every }z\in Q\},
\qquad V_Q(x)=\operatorname{vol}_n P_Q(x).
\]
The polar-volume universal barrier is
\[
U_Q(x)=c_1\log V_Q(x),\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}Q,
\]
where \(c_1>0\) is an absolute normalization constant. Universal-barrier theory states that absolute constants \(c_1,c_2>0\), independent of \(Q\) and \(n\), can be chosen so that \(U_Q\) is a \((c_2n)\)-self-concordant barrier for \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each interior point \(x\), translate the convex set by \(-x\), take its level-one polar, and measure the polar's \(n\)-dimensional volume. A fixed positive multiple of the logarithm of that volume is the universal barrier. Absolute constants make its self-concordance parameter proportional to the ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are absolute \(c_1,c_2>0\) for which \(U_Q(x)=c_1\log\operatorname{vol}_n P_Q(x)\) is a \((c_2n)\)-self-concordant barrier for \(Q\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_Q(x)=(Q-x)^\circ=\{s:\sigma_{Q-x}(s)\le1\}\), where \(\sigma\) is the support function.
special_cases_latex: When \(Q\) is bounded, every \(P_Q(x)\) contains the origin in its interior and has finite positive volume.
Affine changes of coordinates modify \(U_Q\) only by an additive constant determined by the determinant of the linear map.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every line-free finite-dimensional closed convex set with nonempty interior admits a dimension-controlled self-concordant barrier.
The resulting path-following iteration scale is governed by \(O(\sqrt n)\), apart from logarithmic accuracy factors.
boundary_notes: If \(Q\) contains a line, \(P_Q(x)\) is lower-dimensional and its \(n\)-volume vanishes, so this formulation is inapplicable.
The definition does not provide an efficient procedure for evaluating the volume or its derivatives.

notation.meaning: Polar set of \(Q\) relative to the interior point \(x\).

children.title: Universal Barrier Existence
children.top_down_role: Existence of dimension-controlled barriers for general finite-dimensional convex domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Barrier Existence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-dimensional line-free open convex domain has a self-concordant barrier whose parameter grows at most linearly with dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty open convex set containing no affine line. There exists a closed convex function \(F:D\to\mathbb{R}\) with \(F(x_k)\to+\infty\) whenever \(x_k\to\partial D\), satisfying \(\lvert D^3F(x)[h,h,h]\rvert\le 2(D^2F(x)[h,h])^{3/2}\) and \(\langle\nabla F(x),h\rangle^2\le cnD^2F(x)[h,h]\) for every \(x\in D\) and \(h\in\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(c>0\) is universal.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, open, convex, and contains no affine line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) admits a self-concordant barrier with parameter at most \(cn\) for a universal constant \(c>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, line-free convex domains; the claim records dimension-order existence rather than a sharp constant.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite-dimensional universal-barrier existence theorem

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the existence leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable source supports the precise hypotheses, barrier formulation, or dimension-order parameter.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal Q_n\) denote the class of closed convex sets \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\) with nonempty interior and no affine line. Let \(\mathcal B_\nu(Q)\) denote the class of \(\nu\)-self-concordant barriers for \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence statement for arbitrary finite-dimensional line-free convex domains; no efficient representation or evaluation oracle is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A class \(\mathcal Q_n\) has the dimension-controlled universal-barrier existence property if there is an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that
\[
\forall Q\in\mathcal Q_n\quad \mathcal B_{Cn}(Q)\ne\varnothing.
\]
The polar-volume construction realizes this property: for every \(Q\in\mathcal Q_n\), there are absolute constants \(c_1,c_2>0\) such that
\[
U_Q(x)=c_1\log\operatorname{vol}_n\{s:\langle s,z-x\rangle\le1\ \forall z\in Q\}
\]
belongs to \(\mathcal B_{c_2n}(Q)\). Thus barrier existence and parameter control depend only linearly on dimension, even when \(Q\) has no supplied algebraic description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal-barrier existence means that every closed, line-free convex domain in \(n\) dimensions has some self-concordant barrier with parameter at most a universal constant times \(n\). The polar-volume barrier establishes this property without requiring polyhedral, semidefinite, or other explicit structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C>0\) absolute such that \(\forall Q\in\mathcal Q_n\), a \((Cn)\)-self-concordant barrier for \(Q\) exists.

special_cases_latex: Bounded convex bodies satisfy the hypotheses automatically once they have nonempty interior.
A pointed full-dimensional closed cone satisfies the no-line hypothesis and therefore admits a dimension-controlled barrier, although a more structured barrier may be preferable.
immediate_consequences_latex: Lack of an explicit standard cone representation is not an obstruction to abstract barrier existence.
The existence parameter is independent of the number of inequalities in any particular description of \(Q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Volume Universal Barrier
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithm of the volume of the polar of the domain translated to the evaluation point gives a universal barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in D\), define the translated polar body \[D_x^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle y,z-x\rangle\le 1\ \text{for every }z\in D\}.\] Then \[F_D(x)=\log\operatorname{vol}(D_x^\circ)\] is finite on \(D\), tends to \(+\infty\) at \(\partial D\), and satisfies the self-concordance and gradient inequalities with parameter bounded by a universal constant times \(n\). Affine changes of coordinates alter \(F_D\) only by an additive constant.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, open, convex, and contains no affine line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_D(x)=\log\operatorname{vol}(D_x^\circ)\) is a dimension-controlled universal self-concordant barrier on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical polar-volume realization, stated up to an irrelevant additive normalization constant.

notation.meaning: polar of the translated domain about x

knowledge_statements.title: Entropic Universal Barrier
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel conjugate of a convex body's log-Laplace transform is a universal barrier, with dimension-order parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[A(\theta)=\log\int_K\exp(\langle\theta,z\rangle)\,dz\qquad(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^n).\] Its Fenchel conjugate \[F_K(x)=A^*(x)=\sup_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{\langle\theta,x\rangle-A(\theta)\}\] is finite precisely on \(\operatorname{int}K\), diverges as \(x\to\partial K\), and is a self-concordant barrier with parameter bounded by a universal constant times \(n\). At an attained supremum, \(x=\nabla A(\theta)\), so \(x\) is the mean of the corresponding exponentially tilted log-concave distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a convex body with nonempty interior.
The log-Laplace transform is formed using Lebesgue measure on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_K=A^*\) is the entropic barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\) and has dimension-order self-concordance parameter.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-body version of the entropic barrier; additive normalization of Lebesgue measure is immaterial.

notation.meaning: log-Laplace transform of uniform measure on K

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard entropic-barrier construction by convex conjugacy

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The conjugate log-Laplace representation fits the entropic-barrier leaf, but its boundary behavior and dimension-order self-concordance parameter lack a supporting source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Entropic barrier as a log-Laplace conjugate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a convex body with nonempty interior and positive finite Lebesgue volume. Pair \(\mathbb R^n\) with its dual by the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex bodies and the continuous uniform base measure; unbounded domains require a different base measure or conic formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the log-Laplace transform of Lebesgue measure restricted to \(K\) by
\[
A_K(\theta)=\log\int_K e^{\langle\theta,x\rangle}\,dx,\qquad \theta\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
Its Fenchel conjugate is
\[
A_K^*(x)=\sup_{\theta\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle\theta,x\rangle-A_K(\theta)\}.
\]
The entropic universal barrier of \(K\) is
\[
F_{\mathrm{ent},K}(x)=A_K^*(x),\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}K.
\]
Equivalently, when \(x=\nabla A_K(\theta)\), the maximizing parameter is \(\theta=\nabla A_K^*(x)\), and the Hessians satisfy \(\nabla^2A_K^*(x)=[\nabla^2A_K(\theta)]^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The entropic barrier is the convex conjugate of the logarithm of the moment-generating integral of the uniform measure on a convex body. Its natural domain is the body's interior. Primal points are means of exponentially tilted distributions, and the barrier Hessian is the inverse covariance matrix of the corresponding tilt.
assumptions_latex: Lebesgue measure is used as the reference measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{ent},K}=A_K^*\) on \(\operatorname{int}K\) is the entropic universal-barrier construction associated with \(K\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For density \(p_\theta(x)=\exp(\langle\theta,x\rangle-A_K(\theta))\mathbf1_K(x)\), \(\nabla A_K(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[X]\) and \(\nabla^2A_K(\theta)=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X)\).
\(A_K^*(x)=\langle\theta,x\rangle-A_K(\theta)\) whenever \(x=\nabla A_K(\theta)\).
special_cases_latex: Changing the reference measure by a positive constant adds a constant to \(A_K\) and subtracts the same constant from \(A_K^*\), leaving derivatives unchanged.
immediate_consequences_latex: The local metric of the entropic barrier is the inverse covariance metric of the exponential family.
Affine images of \(K\) induce the corresponding conjugate barrier up to an additive constant.
boundary_notes: This record does not assert an exact self-concordance parameter because the available local source corpus did not provide an inspectable statement of that theorem.
For unbounded \(K\), the Lebesgue log-Laplace integral need not be finite on all of the dual space.

notation.meaning: Log-Laplace transform of Lebesgue measure on \(K\).

review_flags: Needs an inspected authoritative source stating the entropic-barrier definition with its precise domain.
The available local references mention the entropic barrier bibliographically but do not support the complete formal definition.

children.title: Universal-Barrier Computability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Separation between barrier existence, parameter quality, and efficient oracle evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal-Barrier Computability Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A good universal barrier may exist geometrically while its value, gradient, and Hessian remain unavailable through an efficient oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A theorem asserting an \(O(n)\)-parameter self-concordant barrier \(F\) establishes neither an algorithm for computing \(F(x)\), \(\nabla F(x)\), and \(\nabla^2F(x)\), nor polynomial bounds for those computations. In particular, the polar-volume formula requires volume computation, while the entropic formula requires evaluating or optimizing a log-partition function. Consequently, a polynomial-time path-following claim additionally requires a specified input model and a polynomial-time exact or sufficiently accurate oracle for these quantities; barrier existence alone supplies no such oracle.
assumptions_latex: A convex domain is supplied only through an abstract membership or separation description.
No integration, sampling, or barrier-evaluation oracle is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of an \(O(n)\)-parameter barrier alone does not furnish a polynomial-time barrier oracle or path-following implementation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates geometric existence and parameter quality from algorithmic evaluation under an explicit input model.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: existential representation and oracle implementability are distinct complexity claims

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and local meaning are appropriate, but a formal input/oracle model and authoritative complexity source are required to support the computational separation claimed.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a convex set \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\) be supplied through an input representation \(\mathcal R(Q)\). Let \(F:\operatorname{int}Q\to\mathbb R\) be a self-concordant barrier.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational distinction between mathematical existence and usable second-order barrier access; the input representation and arithmetic model must be specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A barrier \(F\) is second-order oracle computable relative to \(\mathcal R(Q)\) if there is an algorithm which, for every rational interior query \(x\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), returns approximations to
\[
F(x),\qquad \nabla F(x),\qquad \nabla^2F(x)
\]
with prescribed error \(\varepsilon\), in time polynomial in the encoding length of \(\mathcal R(Q)\), \(x\), and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). A barrier model is Newton-tractable when it additionally permits the required linear systems in \(\nabla^2F(x)\) to be solved within polynomial resource bounds. The universal-barrier computability boundary is the logical separation
\[
\text{existence of a barrier with }\nu=O(n)\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad\text{second-order oracle computability}.
\]
For the polar-volume universal barrier, evaluating a volume and its derivatives is not generally supplied by the existence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A universal barrier can have an excellent dimension-dependent parameter yet still be unusable computationally. It crosses the practical boundary only when its value, gradient, Hessian, and Newton systems can be computed to requested accuracy in polynomial resources relative to the given representation of the convex set.
assumptions_latex: An explicit encoding \(\mathcal R(Q)\) and accuracy model are fixed.
Complexity includes derivative evaluation and Newton-system solution, not only evaluation of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The existence of a \(Cn\)-self-concordant barrier for every line-free \(Q\) does not by itself establish a polynomial-time barrier oracle for \(Q\).
special_cases_latex: For standard logarithmic barriers with explicitly listed affine inequalities, values, gradients, and Hessians are directly computable from the input.
For the polar-volume barrier, the defining volume may encode a substantially harder subproblem.
immediate_consequences_latex: Barrier parameter quality and per-iteration cost are separate complexity attributes.
An iteration bound expressed only through \(\nu\) is not an end-to-end running-time guarantee.
boundary_notes: The definition is relative to an input representation; a barrier can be tractable under one representation and intractable under another.
No unconditional hardness classification for a particular volume oracle is asserted here.

notation.meaning: Chosen finite representation of the convex set.
Cost of solving a barrier-Hessian Newton system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fenchel duality of nondegenerate self-concordant barriers
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional with dual \(E^*\). Let \(F:\operatorname{dom}F\to\mathbb R\) be closed, strictly convex, self-concordant, with open domain containing no affine line and with \(\nabla^2F(x)\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Legendre-type finite-dimensional self-concordant functions; conic sign conventions are deferred to the dual-cone construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Fenchel-dual barrier function is
\[
F_*(s)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}F}\{\langle s,x\rangle-F(x)\},
\qquad s\in\operatorname{dom}F_*.
\]
Barrier duality pairs \(x\) and \(s\) by
\[
s=\nabla F(x),\qquad x=\nabla F_*(s).
\]
At every such pair,
\[
\nabla^2F_*(s)=[\nabla^2F(x)]^{-1}.
\]
The dual function is self-concordant with the same self-concordance constant as \(F\). Hence the gradient map is a diffeomorphism from \(\operatorname{dom}F\) onto \(\operatorname{dom}F_*\), and primal and dual local metrics are inverse descriptions of the same pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Barrier duality is Fenchel conjugacy specialized to a nondegenerate self-concordant function. The primal gradient identifies the dual point, the dual gradient returns the primal point, and the two Hessians are inverses. Self-concordance is preserved under this operation.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is closed, strictly convex, and self-concordant on an open domain.
The domain contains no affine line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
For \(s=
abla F(x)\), \(
abla F_*(s)=x\), \(
abla^2F_*(s)=[
abla^2F(x)]^{-1}\), and \(F_*\) has the same self-concordance constant as \(F\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F(x)+F_*(s)=\langle s,x\rangle\) if and only if \(s=\nabla F(x)\).
\(\nabla F_*=(\nabla F)^{-1}\) on the respective open domains.
special_cases_latex: For \(F(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(\operatorname{dom}F_*=\mathbb R_{--}^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal local norm and dual local norm coincide under the Hessian identification.
Dikin ellipsoids in dual gradient coordinates are governed by the inverse primal Hessian.
boundary_notes: If the Hessian is singular, the inverse-Hessian formulation requires restriction to the effective affine hull or a generalized formulation.
For a barrier on a positive cone, the ordinary conjugate lives on the negative dual cone; a sign change produces a barrier on the positive dual cone.

notation.meaning: Dual point paired with \(x\) by \(s=\nabla F(x)\).
Algebraic dual of the finite-dimensional space \(E\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Barrier Construction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logarithmically homogeneous conic barrier yields a barrier with the same parameter on the positive dual cone by sign-adjusted conjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \[F_*(s)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{int}K}\{-\langle s,xangle-F(x)\}.\] Then \(F_*\) is a \(
u\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K^*\). For every \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\), the point \(s=-
abla F(x)\) lies in \(\operatorname{int}K^*\), attains the conjugate pairing, and satisfies \(-
abla F_*(s)=x\). Thus conjugation transfers the barrier without increasing its parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a regular cone and \(K^*=\{s:\langle s,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\).
\(F\) is a \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_*(s)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{int}K}\{-\langle s,x\rangle-F(x)\}\) is a \(\nu\)-barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the positive-dual-cone convention and the corresponding sign-adjusted Fenchel conjugate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign-adjusted conjugate barrier on the dual cone
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subset E\) be a closed, pointed, full-dimensional convex cone and \(K^*=\{y\in E^*:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\ \forall x\in K\}\). Let \(F\) be a nondegenerate \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional logarithmically homogeneous conic barriers and the positive-dual convention for \(K^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
F_*(s)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{int}K}\{\langle s,x\rangle-F(x)\},
\qquad s\in-\operatorname{int}K^*.
\]
The dual-cone barrier induced by \(F\) is the sign-adjusted conjugate
\[
F^\dagger(y)=F_*(-y)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{int}K}\{-\langle y,x\rangle-F(x)\},
\qquad y\in\operatorname{int}K^*.
\]
The primal-dual point associated with \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) is \(y=-\nabla F(x)\). At this pair,
\[
\nabla F^\dagger(y)=-x,
\qquad
\nabla^2F^\dagger(y)=[\nabla^2F(x)]^{-1}.
\]
Moreover, \(F^\dagger\) is logarithmically homogeneous of degree \(\nu\), up to the additive normalization inherited from conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary Fenchel conjugate of a logarithmically homogeneous barrier on \(K\) is naturally defined on the negative dual cone. Composing it with the sign map yields a barrier on the positive dual cone. The pairing is \(y=-\nabla F(x)\), and the dual Hessian is the inverse primal Hessian.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a nondegenerate \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
The dual cone uses the convention \(\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(F^\dagger(y)=F_*(-y)\) defines the conjugate barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K^*\), with \(
abla^2F^\dagger(-
abla F(x))=[
abla^2F(x)]^{-1}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(y=-\nabla F(x)\iff x=-\nabla F^\dagger(y)\).
\(F(x)+F^\dagger(y)=-\langle y,x\rangle\) at paired points.
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(F(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i\), the dual construction gives \(F^\dagger(y)=-\sum_i\log y_i\) up to an additive constant.
immediate_consequences_latex: The gradient map \(-\nabla F\) sends \(\operatorname{int}K\) onto \(\operatorname{int}K^*\).
Primal and dual barrier parameters agree under conjugacy.
boundary_notes: The sign in \(F^\dagger(y)=F_*(-y)\) is essential under the positive-dual convention.
The construction assumes Legendre nondegeneracy; degenerate cones require passage to their linear span.
review_flags: The positive-dual sign adjustment is an explicit convention combining the cited Fenchel and logarithmic-homogeneity statements.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Metric Pairing
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At gradient-paired points, the dual barrier Hessian is the inverse primal Hessian, and their local norms match through the Hessian map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H_x=
abla^2F(x)\) and let \(s=-
abla F(x)\). Differentiating the inverse gradient correspondence gives \[
abla^2F_*(s)=H_x^{-1}.\] Hence, for \(h\) in the primal space and \(u\) in its dual, \[\|h\|_x^2=\langle H_xh,hangle,\qquad \|u\|_{*,s}^2=\langle u,H_x^{-1}uangle.\] In particular, the Hessian map is an isometry in the sense that \(\|H_xh\|_{*,s}=\|h\|_x\).
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(F_*\) are the paired barriers of the dual-cone construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla^2F_*(s)=[\nabla^2F(x)]^{-1}\), so primal and dual local norms are paired isometrically.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric identity at gradient-paired primal and dual interior points.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Hessian inversion under smooth Legendre conjugacy

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The inverse-Hessian metric identity fits the property leaf, but a source must establish the needed smooth Legendre correspondence for the paired barriers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse-Hessian pairing of primal and dual local metrics
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F\) and \(F^\dagger\) be a nondegenerate conjugate pair of conic barriers on \(\operatorname{int}K\) and \(\operatorname{int}K^*\). Pair \(x\) and \(y\) by \(y=-\nabla F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Riemannian norms at exactly conjugate primal-dual points; arbitrary unpaired points are not covered.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set
\[
H_x=\nabla^2F(x),\qquad H_y^\dagger=\nabla^2F^\dagger(y).
\]
The primal-dual metric pairing at \(y=-\nabla F(x)\) is the inverse relation
\[
H_y^\dagger=H_x^{-1}.
\]
Consequently, for \(u\in E\) and \(v\in E^*\), define
\[
\|u\|_x^2=\langle H_xu,u\rangle,
\qquad
\|v\|_{y,\dagger}^2=\langle v,H_y^\dagger v\rangle.
\]
Then the Hessian identification is an isometry:
\[
\|H_xu\|_{y,\dagger}=\|u\|_x,

aqquad
\|H_y^\dagger v\|_x=\|v\|_{y,\dagger}.
\]
Thus the primal tangent metric and dual cotangent metric encode the same quadratic geometry at conjugate points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At points paired by the barrier gradient, the dual barrier Hessian is exactly the inverse of the primal barrier Hessian. Applying the primal Hessian to a primal direction preserves its norm when the result is measured in the dual metric, and conversely for the dual Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla^2F^\dagger(y)=[\nabla^2F(x)]^{-1}\), and the Hessian maps are mutual isometries between the paired local norms.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For all \(u\in E\), \(\langle H_xu,H_y^\dagger H_xu\rangle=\langle H_xu,u\rangle\).
For all \(v\in E^*\), \(\langle H_y^\dagger v,H_xH_y^\dagger v\rangle=\langle v,H_y^\dagger v\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For the orthant barrier, \(H_x=\operatorname{Diag}(x_i^{-2})\) and the paired point is \(y_i=x_i^{-1}\), so \(H_y^\dagger=\operatorname{Diag}(x_i^2)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The unit Dikin ellipsoid at \(x\) maps under \(H_x\) to the unit dual Dikin ellipsoid at \(y\).
Newton directions may be expressed equivalently in primal or paired dual coordinates.
boundary_notes: The identity is exact only at conjugate points; Hessians at independently chosen \(x\) and \(y\) need not be inverses.
This metric pairing does not assert the stronger existence of a self-scaled scaling point for every arbitrary pair.

notation.meaning: Dual barrier Hessian at the conjugate point \(y\).
Local norm induced by the dual barrier Hessian.

review_flags: The norm-isometry equations are the direct metric formulation of the cited inverse-Hessian identity.

children.title: Self-Scaled Metric Matching
children.top_down_role: Specialized symmetric-cone geometry underlying scaling points.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Scaled Metric Matching
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-scaled barrier supplies a unique point whose Hessian maps any chosen primal interior point to its paired dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every primal-dual pair \((x,s)\in\operatorname{int}K\times\operatorname{int}K^*\), there exists a unique \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) such that \[H_wx=s,\qquad H_w=\nabla^2F(w).\] The positive-definite map \(H_w\) sends \(K\) onto \(K^*\) and identifies the local primal and dual metrics. The point \(w\) is the scaling point of \((x,s)\); its existence for every interior pair is special to self-scaled barriers and the associated symmetric-cone geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique scaling point \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) satisfying \(\nabla^2F(w)x=s\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-scaled-barrier metric matching; this specialized property characterizes symmetric-cone scaling geometry.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: defining metric-matching property of self-scaled barriers on symmetric cones

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The statement fits self-scaled metric matching, but existence, uniqueness, and the cone-isomorphism assertion depend on the precise normalization and definition of a self-scaled barrier and require a theorem-level source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nesterov–Todd scaling point and matched metric
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subset E\) be a pointed convex cone with nonempty interior and let \(F\) be a self-scaled barrier for \(K\). Let \(K^*\subset E^*\) be the dual cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialized self-scaled geometry, available for symmetric-cone barrier structures rather than arbitrary self-concordant barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) and \(s\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), the self-scaled metric-matching point is the unique \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) satisfying
\[
\nabla^2F(w)x=s.
\]
The positive-definite operator
\[
T_w=[\nabla^2F(w)]^{1/2}
\]
is the associated scaling map. It matches the pair because
\[
T_wx=T_w^{-1}s,
\]
where the adjoint identification is understood between \(E\) and \(E^*\). Equivalently, the single Hessian metric at \(w\) transports the primal point \(x\) to the dual point \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-scaled barrier assigns every interior primal-dual pair a unique scaling point \(w\). The Hessian at \(w\) maps the primal point to the dual point. Its positive square root places both points at the same location in scaled coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique \(w\in\operatorname{int}K\) with \(\nabla^2F(w)x=s\); for \(T_w=[\nabla^2F(w)]^{1/2}\), \(T_wx=T_w^{-1}s\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(s=H_wx\) with \(H_w=\nabla^2F(w)\).
\(T_w^2x=s\) and hence \(T_wx=T_w^{-1}s\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(F(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i\), \(w_i=\sqrt{x_i/s_i}\).
For the positive-semidefinite cone, metric matching yields the matrix Nesterov–Todd scaling.
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal and dual variables have identical scaled representatives.
The scaling point supplies a symmetric local metric used by primal-dual search directions.
boundary_notes: General nonsymmetric cones need not admit a self-scaled barrier or such a scaling point for every pair.
The equation is stronger than inverse-Hessian pairing at conjugate points because \(x\) and \(s\) are arbitrary interior points.

notation.meaning: Positive square root of the barrier Hessian at \(w\).

children.title: Analytic Centers
children.top_down_role: Barrier-induced center concepts and their use in localization and initialization.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_query: Introductory Lectures on Convex Optimization: A Basic Course

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\subset E\) be a convex set with nonempty interior, and let \(F:\operatorname{int}Q\to\mathbb R\) be a closed, differentiable, strictly convex barrier.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier-relative centers in finite dimensions; the center depends on the chosen barrier and need not exist on an unnormalized unbounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An analytic center of \(Q\) generated by \(F\) is a point
\[
x_F^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{int}Q}F(x).
\]
When \(F\) is differentiable and strictly convex, existence implies uniqueness and the center is characterized by
\[
\nabla F(x_F^*)=0.
\]
If \(F\) is a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier and the center exists, its local Hessian metric defines the center Dikin ellipsoid and satisfies the global localization bound
\[
\|x-x_F^*\|_{x_F^*}\le \nu+2\sqrt\nu,
\qquad x\in Q,
\]
while \(\{x_F^*+h:\|h\|_{x_F^*}<1\}\subset\operatorname{int}Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The analytic center is the minimizer of a selected barrier over the feasible interior. Strict convexity makes it unique, and differentiability makes zero barrier gradient its stationarity certificate. For a self-concordant barrier, the Hessian at the center also provides an inner Dikin ellipsoid and a parameter-controlled outer localization.
assumptions_latex: For the metric bounds, \(F\) is a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier and \(x_F^*\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_F^*=\arg\min_{x\in\operatorname{int}Q}F(x)\) is the barrier-generated analytic center, with \(\nabla F(x_F^*)=0\) under differentiability.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For differentiable convex \(F\), \(x_F^*\) is an analytic center if and only if \(0=\nabla F(x_F^*)\), provided a minimizer exists.
\(x_F^*\) is the zero-penalty endpoint of the central path generated by \(F\).
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=\{x:a_i^Tx<b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(F(x)=-\sum_i\log(b_i-a_i^Tx)\), the center satisfies \(\sum_i a_i/(b_i-a_i^Tx_F^*)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The analytic center is barrier-dependent rather than an affine-free center of the set alone.
The center Hessian supplies a canonical local norm for localization and initialization.
boundary_notes: A logarithmically homogeneous barrier on an unsliced cone has no finite minimizer because scaling decreases the barrier without bound.
If the barrier is not strictly convex, the argmin can contain more than one point.

source_refs.locator: §5.3.3, Definition 5.3.3 and Theorem 5.3.9, pp. 376–377

children.title: Bounded-Domain Analytic Centers
children.top_down_role: Barrier centers on bounded feasible interiors.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Domain Analytic Centers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable, strictly convex barrier that diverges at the boundary of a bounded convex domain has a unique analytic center, characterized by a zero gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(F:D\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy the stated assumptions. Then \(F\) attains its minimum at a unique point \[x_c=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}F(x).\] This point is the analytic center of \(D\) relative to \(F\), and differentiability gives the first-order characterization \[\nabla F(x_c)=0.\] The center depends on the chosen barrier.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, bounded, open, and convex.
\(F:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable, strictly convex, continuous, and satisfies \(F(x_k)\to+\infty\) for every sequence \((x_k)\subset D\) converging to a point of \(\partial D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a unique analytic center \(x_c=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in D}F(x)\), and it satisfies \(\nabla F(x_c)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness of the barrier-relative analytic center on a bounded full-dimensional domain.

notation.meaning: analytic center of D relative to F

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.5 Finding the analytic center p. 203

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Analytic center on a bounded barrier domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\subset E\) be a bounded closed convex set with nonempty interior. Let \(F:\operatorname{int}Q\to\mathbb R\) be a closed, strictly convex barrier, such as a nondegenerate self-concordant barrier.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional bounded feasible interiors; relative-interior formulations require first restricting to the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The bounded-domain analytic center generated by \(F\) is
\[
x_F^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{int}Q}F(x).
\]
Because \(Q\) is bounded and \(F\) is closed with barrier growth at the boundary, the minimum is attained in \(\operatorname{int}Q\); strict convexity makes it unique. It is equivalently the unique solution of
\[
\nabla F(x)=0.
\]
If \(F\) is a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier, the point is also the initial point of the exact central path
\[
x^*(t)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{int}Q}\{t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x)\},
\qquad x^*(0)=x_F^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded closed convex domain, a closed strictly convex barrier attains a unique interior minimum. This minimum is the bounded-domain analytic center, is characterized by zero gradient, and is the zero-penalty starting point of the barrier central path.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is bounded, closed, and convex with \(\operatorname{int}Q\ne\varnothing\).
\(F\) is closed and tends to \(+\infty\) at the boundary of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique \(x_F^*\in\operatorname{int}Q\) minimizing \(F\), and \(\nabla F(x_F^*)=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x_F^*=x^*(0)\) for the central path generated by \(F\).
For a polyhedral logarithmic barrier, \(x_F^*\) maximizes the product of the positive slacks.
special_cases_latex: For \(F(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^m\log(b_i-a_i^Tx)\), minimizing \(F\) is equivalent to maximizing \(\prod_{i=1}^m(b_i-a_i^Tx)\) over the strict interior.
immediate_consequences_latex: No external normalization is needed when the barrier domain itself is bounded.
The center supplies a strictly feasible initialization whenever it can be computed.
boundary_notes: Boundedness is a sufficient domain condition; some unbounded domains may admit minima for nonhomogeneous barriers, but not under the full hypotheses used for the standard localization result.
A bounded set with empty ambient interior must be treated in its affine hull.

source_refs.locator: §5.3.3, Definition 5.3.3; §5.3.4, equations (5.3.20)–(5.3.21) and the statement that boundedness and closedness give a unique center, pp. 377–379

children.title: Normalized Conic Centers
children.top_down_role: Center notions obtained after slicing homogeneous domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Conic Centers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic center is defined after choosing a bounded affine slice and minimizing the logarithmically homogeneous barrier on that slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because logarithmic homogeneity prevents \(F\) from having an unconstrained minimizer on \(K\), fix \(e\in\operatorname{int}K^*\) and minimize over \[S_e=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:\langle e,x\rangle=1\}.\] A normalized conic center is \[x_e\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S_e}F(x).\] When the minimum exists and \(F\) is strictly convex on the slice, it is unique. Its first-order condition is \(\nabla F(x_e)+\lambda e=0\) for some \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a regular cone and \(F\) is a logarithmically homogeneous barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A normalized conic center is a minimizer of \(F\) over \(S_e\), satisfying \(\nabla F(x_e)+\lambda e=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Center obtained by intersecting a homogeneous cone with a bounded affine normalization.

notation.meaning: normalized affine slice of the cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conic centers require a bounded affine normalization because logarithmic homogeneity precludes an unconstrained minimum

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the normalized-conic-center leaf and its conditional optimality statement is coherent, but no source supports the normalization, attainment, or uniqueness conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Analytic center of a normalized cone slice
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subset E\) be a closed, pointed, full-dimensional convex cone, let \(e\in\operatorname{int}K^*\), and let \(F\) be a nondegenerate \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous conic domains after an interior dual functional fixes scale; the unsliced cone has no finite analytic center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The \(e\)-normalized cone slice is
\[
S_e=\{x\in\operatorname{int}K:\langle e,x\rangle=1\}.
\]
Its normalized conic center is
\[
x_{F,e}^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in S_e}F(x).
\]
When the slice is nonempty and the restricted barrier is strictly convex, this center is unique. Its first-order characterization is
\[
\nabla F(x_{F,e}^*)+\lambda e=0,
\qquad \langle e,x_{F,e}^*\rangle=1.
\]
Logarithmic homogeneity gives \(\langle\nabla F(x),x\rangle=-\nu\), so necessarily \(\lambda=\nu\). Hence the normalized center is equivalently characterized by
\[
-\nabla F(x_{F,e}^*)=\nu e,
\qquad \langle e,x_{F,e}^*\rangle=1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone has no preferred scale, so a center is defined after slicing it by an interior dual functional. The normalized conic center minimizes the logarithmically homogeneous barrier on the slice \(\langle e,x\rangle=1\). It is the unique point whose negative barrier gradient equals \(\nu e\).
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a strictly convex \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous barrier on \(\operatorname{int}K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{F,e}^*=\arg\min\{F(x):x\in\operatorname{int}K,\ \langle e,x\rangle=1\}\), equivalently \(-\nabla F(x_{F,e}^*)=\nu e\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(y=-\nabla F(x)\), the center is the point paired with the dual ray representative \(y=\nu e\).
Changing the slice to \(\langle e,x\rangle=\rho>0\) scales the center to \(\rho x_{F,e}^*\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^n\), \(F(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i\), and \(e=\mathbf1\), the normalized center is \(x_i=1/n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Normalization removes the radial direction along which a logarithmically homogeneous barrier decreases without bound.
The center is covariant under simultaneous primal and dual affine cone isomorphisms.
boundary_notes: If \(e\notin\operatorname{int}K^*\), the slice can be empty or unbounded and a finite center need not exist.
The normalization functional is part of the definition; different \(e\) generally produce different centers.

source_refs.locator: §5.4.3, Definition 5.4.1 and equations (5.4.4)–(5.4.7), pp. 391–392; §7.3, equation (7.3.2), constrained analytic center

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\operatorname{int}Q\to\mathbb R\) be a nondegenerate self-concordant barrier. At \(x\in\operatorname{int}Q\), use the local dual norm induced by \(\nabla^2F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local, computable centering certificate for finite-dimensional smooth barriers; it does not require prior knowledge of the exact center value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0\le\beta<1\), a point \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}Q\) is a \(\beta\)-approximate analytic center of \(F\) if
\[
\lambda_F(\bar x)=\|\nabla F(\bar x)\|_{\bar x,*}
=\sqrt{\left\langle\nabla F(\bar x),[\nabla^2F(\bar x)]^{-1}\nabla F(\bar x)\right\rangle}
\le\beta.
\]
This is a local neighborhood certificate: \(\beta=0\) is exact centering, while \(\beta<1\) places the point in the standard full-Newton neighborhood. For a path objective \(f_t(x)=t\langle c,x\rangle+F(x)\), the analogous approximate-centering condition is
\[
\|tc+\nabla F(x)\|_{x,*}\le\beta.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate analytic center is an interior point whose barrier gradient is small in the dual norm defined by its own Hessian. The resulting quantity is the Newton decrement. Zero decrement means an exact center, while a threshold below one gives the standard local certificate used for initialization and path following.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is twice differentiable and self-concordant on \(\operatorname{int}Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is \(\beta\)-approximately centered exactly when \(\|\nabla F(\bar x)\|_{\bar x,*}\le\beta\).
equivalent_formulations_latex:
\(
abla F( ar x)^T[
abla^2F( ar x)]^{-1}
abla F( ar x)\le eta^2\).
The Newton step \(d_N=-[\nabla^2F(\bar x)]^{-1}\nabla F(\bar x)\) satisfies \(\|d_N\|_{\bar x}\le\beta\).
special_cases_latex: \(\beta=0\) gives \(\nabla F(\bar x)=0\), hence the exact analytic center when it exists.
For a central-path point at parameter \(t\), replace \(\nabla F(x)\) by \(tc+\nabla F(x)\).

children.title: Center Existence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Unboundedness, recession directions, and normalization failures preventing a finite center.

knowledge_statements.title: Center Existence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unsliced logarithmically homogeneous cone has no analytic center because scaling to infinity drives its barrier value to minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{int}K\) and \(t>0\), logarithmic homogeneity gives \[F(tx)=F(x)-\nu\log t.\] Therefore \(F(tx)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to+\infty\), so \(F\) has no finite unconstrained minimizer on \(\operatorname{int}K\). More generally, an unbounded feasible domain cannot have a barrier-defined center whenever a recession ray keeps the iterates feasible and the barrier values fail to rise along that ray. A bounded normalization removes this scaling obstruction only if the resulting slice is nonempty and bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is a \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous barrier on the interior of a regular cone \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unconstrained conic problem \(\inf_{x\in\operatorname{int}K}F(x)\) has value \(-\infty\) and no analytic center.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scaling obstruction for unsliced homogeneous cones; more general unbounded domains may fail by analogous recession behavior.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The exact scaling obstruction is mathematically standard and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but the cited recession-cone section does not inspectably support the logarithmically homogeneous barrier identity. The broader phrase 'fail to rise' is also too imprecise to serve as a general nonexistence criterion.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\operatorname{dom}F\to\mathbb R\) be a closed nondegenerate self-concordant barrier on an open convex domain containing no affine line.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact analytic centers; distinguishes bounded domains, recession behavior, and homogeneous conic scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the center-existence status of \(F\) by
\[
\mathsf{Center}(F)=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\operatorname{dom}F}F(x),&\text{if the minimum is attained},\\
\varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
For a self-concordant function on a line-free domain, boundedness below is the decisive finite-center boundary: if \(\inf F> -\infty\), the minimum is attained uniquely; if \(F\) is unbounded below, no analytic center exists. In particular, a \(\nu\)-logarithmically homogeneous cone barrier satisfies
\[
F(\tau x)=F(x)-\nu\log\tau,
\]
so \(F(\tau x)\to-\infty\) as \(\tau\to\infty\) and the unsliced cone has no finite center. A bounded barrier domain, by contrast, yields a unique center under closedness and strict convexity. Conic centers therefore require a bounded or otherwise coercive normalization slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite analytic center exists precisely when the barrier attains a lower bound. For the standard nondegenerate self-concordant setting, being bounded below guarantees a unique minimizer. Logarithmically homogeneous cone barriers violate this condition along every positive ray, so a cone must be sliced or otherwise normalized before a finite center can be defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathsf{Center}(F)\ne\varnothing\) when \(F\) is bounded below; an unsliced logarithmically homogeneous cone barrier has \(\mathsf{Center}(F)=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under the stated hypotheses, \(\mathsf{Center}(F)\ne\varnothing\iff\inf_{x\in\operatorname{dom}F}F(x)>-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Q\subset E\) be a finite-dimensional convex domain and let \(F:\operatorname{int}Q\to\mathbb R\) be a standard self-concordant barrier. The Hessian may be assumed positive definite for the inverse-Hessian formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional self-concordant barriers; distinguishes the parameter of a chosen barrier from the best attainable parameter for the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The barrier parameter of \(F\) is the least \(\nu\ge0\) such that, for every \(x\in\operatorname{int}Q\) and \(u\in E\),

\langle\nabla F(x),u\rangle^2

\nu_*(Q)=\inf\{\nu(F):F\text{ is a self-concordant barrier for }Q\}.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\to\mathbb R\) be a standard self-concordant function on an open convex set \(D\) in a finite-dimensional real vector space \(E\). For \(x\in D\), put \(H_x=\nabla^2F(x)\) and \(\|h\|_x^2=\langle H_xh,h\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition permits a singular Hessian through a directional inequality. The inverse-Hessian formula is asserted only when the Hessian is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The intrinsic gradient size of \(F\) at \(x\) is the least extended-real number \[g_F(x)^2:=\inf\{\eta\ge0:\ \langle
abla F(x),hangle^2\le\eta\langle H_xh,hangle\ 	ext{for every }h\in E\}.\] The global intrinsic gradient parameter is \[

u\)-self-concordant barrier exactly when \(

u\). If \(H_x\succ0\), then \(g_F(x)=\|
abla F(x)\|_{x,*}\), so the condition reads \(\|
abla F(x)\|_{x,*}\le\sqrt
u\) at every point. This quantity is intrinsic to the Hessian geometry generated by \(F\): both the covector \(
abla F(x)\) and its measuring norm are determined by the same barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point x, the intrinsic gradient size is the smallest constant whose square times the Hessian quadratic form dominates the squared directional derivative in every direction. A barrier has admissible parameter ν precisely when this global quantity is at most ν.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

u_{\mathrm{sc}}(K):=\inf\{\mu>0:K	ext{ admits a }\mu	ext{-self-concordant barrier}\}.\] A particular \(
u\)-self-concordant barrier therefore supplies the upper bound \(
u_{\mathrm{sc}}(K)\leq
u\). The certified value \(
u\) measures the complexity exposed by that barrier and its representation; it need not be invariant under redundant constraints, lifting, or a different choice of barrier for the same set.

\(F:K\to\mathbb{R}\) is a standard self-concordant barrier satisfying \(\|\nabla F(x)\|_{x,*}^2\leq \nu\) for every \(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(
u_{\mathrm{sc}}(K)\leq 
u\), while the parameter attached to a particular representation may exceed \(
u_{\mathrm{sc}}(K)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Complexity Interpretation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a linear objective with finite optimal value, the square root of the barrier parameter controls short-step central-path complexity, and a path parameter of at least ν/ε gives objective gap at most ε.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x(t):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}\{t\langle c,xangle+F(x)\}\), a short-step path-following method can increase \(t\) by a factor \(1+\Theta(
u^{-1/2})\) using a bounded number of Newton corrections. Thus increasing \(t\) from \(t_0\) to \(t_1\) requires \(O(\sqrt{
u}\log(t_1/t_0))\) corrections. Moreover, \(\langle c,x(t)angle-p^*\leq
u/t\), so \(t_1\geq
u/\varepsilon\) gives accuracy \(\varepsilon\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty open convex set and \(F:K\to\mathbb{R}\) is a \(\nu\)-self-concordant barrier.
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(p^*:=\inf_{x\in K}\langle c,x\rangle\) is finite, and the central points \(x(t)\) exist for the path parameters considered.
\(0<t_0<t_1\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and a short-step method maintains a fixed local central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of Newton corrections needed to increase the path parameter from \(t_0\) to \(t_1\) is \(O(\sqrt{\nu}\log(t_1/t_0))\), and \(t_1\geq\nu/\varepsilon\) ensures \(\langle c,x(t_1)\rangle-p^*\leq\varepsilon\).
